1. Digital Interview - HireVue

This was the first round of the placement process, it was a 15-minute interview on Hire Vue, with 6 basic HR
questions about my background. Those not familiar with HIreVue, it's basically a virtual interview, the
question will be displayed on screen and you will be given 40 seconds to prepare and then 3 mins to record
your answer. The 6 questions were same for everyone:

1. Why did you choose your current degree program?

2. What do you aim to gain from this internship?

3. Tell us about a challenging project experience.

4. How did you manage multiple priorities and time?

5. Tell us about a time when you realized you have a weakness and how did you try to overcome that?

6. What'd you like us to know more about you?

Don't use chat gpt, make your own answers and speak, do not read off any material, look at the camera and
speak. The max limit is 3 minutes per question doesn't mean you have to answer for that long you can stop
the recording whenever you feel like.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Technical Test - Online (120 Candidates)

Platform: Microsoft forms (No proctoring)
Time: 30 minutes
Format: 25 MCQs
Topics Covered: DSA, OS, SQL, Aptitude, Java and Python
The test was mcq based so not that hard, do java/python guess-output questions beforehand as they are
asked, don't get stuck on a question, time management is key.

3. Group Discussion - Online (80 Candidates)

The group discussion was held online on Microsoft Teams, we had 2 choices either give the GD from home
and reach college in-case of selection or go to college early and sit there and give the GD (depends how far
you stay from the college), choose accordingly, The Actual GD for me was a bit scuffed, time is less overall
only 30 mins, of which 2 mins are given after topic reveal to prepare a bit. Remember basic guidelines for
GD - pay attention when others talk, its not a debate so dont fight, introduction should be done only if 100%
confident in the topic. Conclusion should be as inclusive as possible in short amount of time.
Some topics:

1. Challenges/Opportunities for India in the Indian Subcontinent (Political)

2. Digital Twins (Technical)

3. Gen AI / Chatgpt (Technical)

4. Future of EVs (Hardware, Economical)

Tips: while in 2-min prep time, do not use chat gpt write down what you can think of, they will come to

know if you have searched online. A night before sit down and go throught current affairs in all the most
common domains.

4. Technical Interview (30 Candidates)

The Technical Interview is taken by a panel of 2 interviewers, they will grill you on your resume projects, so
make sure you are 100% confident about your projects, what tech you used, why you used it, how you used
it, etc. They will ask you in greater detail, remember in such interviews the flow of conversation is with you,
the way you explain will dictate what further questions the interviewer will ask you, for example while
explaining something you mention some jargon, they might take that and grill you on that further so speak
carefully.
My interviews were very chill, they first introduced themselves, then asked me to carry it further. Also they
offered me to eat a sandwich piece given to them, (Threw me off lol) but yea be chill / relaxed, don't ever
stop speaking there should not be any silence in between of your answers, if you dont know the answer ask
them some doubts or try suggesting some ideas, if the interviewer feels you don't know it he himself will
move further. They will also ask detailed questions on DSA in java, SQL and OOPS.
--- PAGE 3 ---

5. Leadership Interview - Techno HR (15 Candidates)

This is the final round, it's a bit different than the normal HR interview. It is like a techno-hr round where
the interviewer will ask you some things about your resume, where your interests are, basic questions not
too hard. Be calm and answer, in this interview, your body language, your facial expressions, your speaking
skills all will be observed. Lastly i was asked some basic HR questions like what are your strengths and
weaknesses how you overcame them, tell me about a time when your team had a conflict how you helped
resolved.
Finally after a Long and Vigorous Process, 7 people were selected.

Eligibility criteria include a minimum CGPA of 8.0 (reduced from an initial cutoff of 8.5), applicable to all
BTech branches and MCA, with no backlogs.
There were 3 rounds: Online Assessment, Technical Interview and HR Interview

1.  Online Assessment [155 students appeared for the test]

It was a 90-minute assessment conducted on Google Forms. It consisted of 70 MCQ questions, and
there were four sections - Java (18 questions), Python (17 questions), SQL (5 questions) and aptitude (30
questions). The correct answer would give you 1 mark, -0.25 for incorrect answer and 0 for not attempting.

2. Technical Interview [50 students were shortlisted]

The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, and I mentioned that Java is my primary language for
competitive programming. He then asked me what 'immutable' means in Java. I explained the concept of
immutability and used the String class in Java as an example. I mentioned that when two variables are
initialized with the same value, such as String name1 = "Hina"; and String name2 = "Hina"; they both point
to the same location in the String pool because the String object is shared. If the value of a ny String variable
is changed, it app ears as if the value is edited, but in reality, a new instance is created, and the reference is
updated to point to this new instance.
Then he asked me how I would create a custom class that behaves similarly. I initially said by using a
constructor, but he was not satisfied with that answer. He explained the question again by writing a scenario
on the paper. In this scenario, there was a class A with a variable declared and a constructor, and he specified
that each time a new object should be created and the value cannot be edited. When he mentioned that the
value cannot be edited, the final keyword came to my mind, but I was confused because String allows us to
reassign the value, though a new object is created. He gave me a hint by asking what happens when a class is
final. I said that we cannot inherit from it, and then he asked how we assign values I said using a setter method.
Class A will be final so that other classes cannot extend it and change its value, and the setter method will be
removed to ensure immutability. This approach follows standard industry practices, where each class typically
includes a constructor along with getter and setter methods.
He then asked me how to assign a value to a variable in class B from an object of class B within cl ass A,
ensuring that the value is assigned only once. I initially suggested making the variable in class B final.
However, he pointed out that changes to class B were not allowed. I then suggested using the constructor of
class A to initialize class B's va riable by passing the value through class A's constructor, which in turn calls
the constructor of class B. I asked him if this approach was correct, and he said it was only partially correct I
then requested him to explain the correct approach.

The interview lasted for 10 minutes. The panel interviewed each candidate for 10 to 15 minutes.

3. HR Round [ 17 students were shortlisted]

The HR and Technical Head were present who took our PPT.
HR asked me to tell me about my education and family background.  If I was comfortable with the hybrid
model and the location? What are your other interests?

The Technical Head asked if I had appeared for the CET and what my percentile was. Since I scored lower on
the company's aptitude test, he asked if I wasn't prepared  and what the reason was.  He also asked whether I
preferred backend development or full stack. I said full stack, so he requested that I explain one of my projects
where I used full stack technology. I explained it in detail, mentioning why I chose a particular tech stack and
what I learned from it.

They also asked what else I had studied on my own, apart from what was taught in college.
The final question was, "Do you have any questions for us?"

12 students were offered the job

journey.prep:
1. Always believe in yourself. Even if you get nervous before the interviews begin; do not

overthink and over-prepare at the last minute.
Believe me, experiencing anxiety is normal and a part of the process. Be calm before the
rounds (trust me you will still feel anxious, but keeping it simple is the way to go).

2. Always answer questions honestly and confidently. If you know the logic behind a

problem; but don't know how to proceed with it; explain your thought process in a point-
wise manner to the interviewers. This will show your clarity. Keep a smile on your face
during the interviews in general (don't fake it though - it will make you seem nervous).
Maintain eye contact with the interviewers (don't stare at them; but periodically w hile
answering questions do so)
However, if you have no clue or have just heard about the problem; honestly tell the
interviewers that you don't know the answer (or that you are not familiar with the domain

- if it's a question out of your area of strength). Partially explaining a potent ially wrong

approach is detrimental.

3. Don't entirely focus on DSA. Yes, it is important and you will be asked about it in the

interviews (especially in Tech Round 2).
However, there's a high probability that you will be purely asked about your projects; and
more importantly SQL and DBMS questions in general (read the interview commonly
asked DBMS questions). I was not asked about any OS questions; but only if you get
additional time for preparation; you should prepare it as well (since they may ask it).
Also, if you have listed a NoSQL database as a skill in your resume; like MongoDB in my
case, prepare the basic queries (CRUD operations) and read about it briefly (MongoDB
ATLAS, clusters and so on…). I was asked about it in my Tech Round 2. Do this after you
have prepared DSA and DBMS.

4. Regarding the OA (Online Assessment); try attempting as many questions as possible. We

had 60 questions (20 Math, 20 Verbal, 20 Analytical). Try to attempt at least 40 questions
in 40-45 mins. It's not necessary to attempt every question correctly. I properly attempted
about 40-45 in 50 mins.
If and only if; there is no negative marking (which will most likely be the case) try to take
an estimated guess for the remaining questions (narrow down the options & then guess); if
you believe estimation is taking time, blindly guess the answers (you still have a 1/4 chance
of getting it right).

5. Be extremely thorough with the projects listed in your resume. It's not necessary to list 4 -

5 projects. Even listing 2 -3 of your best projects can create a great impression on the
interviewers. In my case; the 3 projects that I had listed were mainly ML/DL  based with
data analytics incorporated (Tableau); with a single project being that of web development
(backend - Django).
Limit the projects mainly to your strongest domain. But have at least 1 project from a
different domain (since they will look for variety as well). Mention your contribution to
each project. It's better to mention it in the resume itself (in 2 -3 lines). Be genuine with
your answers. Elaborate upon the skills that you applied in the project. Only mention those
skills which you genuinely have (above 50 % of the knowledge). If you don't have any real
experience in the skill that you have mentioned; better to leave it out of the resume.

6. Lastly, during any round (be it technical/HR/GD) be the driving force of the interview. It's

not necessary to completely take over and start explaining everything in one go. Be
proactive and show that you are passionate about what you are doing; and that you really
would like to make a positive impact on the company.
Answer every question confidently and concisely. But do not deliberately give short
incomplete answers and wait for follow -up questions. This will show the interviewer that
you do not like to lead from the front and wait for other people to push you around . Give
answers; which you believe will properly be able to explain the interviewer's question.

Resources:

1. Do DSA from Striver (TakeUForward). Simply the best and clearest DSA course that I

have come across. (Instead of subscribing to TUF+; you can watch his YouTube playlists).
Practice the DSA questions on leetcode (mainly the top interview 150); & if time permits
do some problems from - codingNinjas/GFG and so on … (Practice his SDE sheet; or
whatever sheet you feel comfortable with.)

2. Prepare theory questions for DBMS (and if time permits OS - not necessary in general)

from InterviewBit (top 75 most commonly asked questions). You may use any other
website to do so; I found InterviewBit to be well-organized.  You can read from GFG as
well (although I find it relatively more time-consuming).

3. For quick SQL revision; read the entire syntax overview on W3Schools (I prefer keeping

it simple and just doing it for MySQL). Do as many problems of the Leetcode SQL 50 as
possible for practice.

4. Practice puzzles from GFG (mainly) and coding ninjas (as an additional resource; if time

permits). You will almost certainly be asked to solve at least one puzzle during your
interview rounds.
.

5. If time permits, watch Gaurav Sen's system design playlist on YouTube. Chances of

questions related to designing apps are very slim; but you may get some conceptual
questions (like vertical/horizontal scaling and so on…)

If you have any questions for me, you can connect with me & ask; on LinkedIn or by Mail.
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jay-nadkarni-232714172/
Mail: jayvnadkarni@gmail.com

That's it from my side.
ALL THE BEST FOR YOUR PLACEMENTS!!!

1st August, 2024 - Pre-Placement Talk (PPT)
2nd August, 2024 - Online Assessment (OA)
6th August, 2024 - Interview Rounds
Pre-Placement Talk for Nomura was held online on 1/8/2024. Pay attention during the PPT and
take note of the roles and responsibilities that are offered. After this, your resumes will be
collected; and your shortlisting for the OA will happen based on your  resume (Use FlowCV or
LaTex to make your resume).

1. Online Assessment (OA) [155 students]

After my resume was shortlisted; I gave the OA. This was a pure aptitude test (no coding questions
were asked). I had 60 mins to answer 60 questions. There were 3 sections: quantitative (math),
verbal and analytical (logic), each with 20 questions.

You can prepare for these questions from IndiaBix aptitude questions  or even solve basic GRE
questions (even if you don't intend to take the exam) since the format is very similar. In my case;
I did the latter.

I aimed to attempt as many questions as possible correctly in 45 minutes. It's practically impossible
to attempt all 60 properly (let alone get all correct) within this time.

I completed 40 -45 questions within 45 mins; after which I spent the remaining time making
estimated guesses for the remaining questions. Finally, I attempted 59 questions out of 60 (time
ran out while I was attempting the 60th). But you should try to attempt all the questions (if and
only if there is no negative marking).

My advice would be: solve the easiest questions first (those which have formulaic/direct answers);
then go to the medium ones (which click for you; but might take some time to solve) & approach
the hard questions (questions in which you have to think about the approach of solving or
extremely lengthy questions in general). You can take guesses for the hard ones at the end (if you
couldn't solve them) but try to crack the easy and medium ones.

Do not go section-wise; since you may leave out easy & medium questions of the other sections
while attempting the hard questions of your current section.

32 candidates were selected for the interview round for the ITD role and I was happy to be
one of them.

- I was shortlisted for both the ITD role (based on my OA results); and the GM role

as well (based on my resume). [Go directly to 'For ITD Role' if you just want to
know about it]

For GM (global markets) Role-

2. Group Discussion Round [40 Students]

5 groups of 10 students were formed. Our topic was Cryptocurrency - whether it was good or bad.
We were given 5 mins to prepare (I jotted down important points on a piece of paper).
At the start, everyone had to introduce themselves and the topic. I explained the topic at hand; &
what we might discuss today.
Then the full-fledged discussion started. I made  5-6 valid points. Referenced recent events
regarding the topic as well. Countered the arguments of my peers; which I thought were a bit
superfluous. Encouraged participation by encouraging my peers to continue from where I left off.
Spoke about both the pros and cons of Blockchain as a whole (mentioning Ethereum and Bitcoin-
specific points as well) - but not in the same entry (basically speaking about the pros & cons; but
during different entries with valid p oints). Maintained eye contact with my peers and had a
confident body posture.
Finally, everyone had to conclude. Summarized the discussion; told what issues we might have
missed during the discussion ( NFTs, Metaverse…). I concluded by saying; that overall, it was a
great discussion.
The total duration was 15 -20 minutes. 4 students from my group (including me) were
shortlisted for the next round.

3. Technical Round 1 [16 students]

There was a single interviewer; who greeted me. He asked me to introduce myself and what my
interests were. I properly introduced myself and told him about my passion for data analysis and
machine learning.

He then asked me questions regarding my projects (I explained to him about all 3 of my listed
projects; and my contributions in them).

My projects (for those who wish to know)-

- Anomaly Detection System (DetectX) - Made during Aeravat ML Hackathon

- Self-Driving Car in a Simulated Environment (using neural networks):  ongoing project (at

the time) for the college major project

- Food Delivery Website made using React and Django (Team Project). [Personally worked

on creating the admin dashboard and models -> as part of the backend]

He asked me about the difficulties that I faced in these projects and how I overcame them. Later,
he asked me some general questions like:

- Tell me about a time when you experienced failure. How did you cope with it? (told them about

my JEE results and my motivation to do better and learn from them)

- What mistake would you like to avoid that you might have made during a project of yours? Why?

(I explained it honestly. This depends from person to person)

Finally, he asked me some language-specific questions (after I told him that Python is my primary
prog. language):

- Difference between / and // in python (wrt division).

- What is monkey patching in Python?

(I was unable to answer this; basically, it means re-assigning the method inside a class as
another function outside it; so that the next time the class method is called; the modified
function gets called.)

- What is the init method in Python (in classes)? (Constructor. Explain the self keyword as

well here)

- How will you remove duplicates from an array and preserve the order?

(This was a DSA question. Since order needs to be preserved; we cannot directly use set
OR sort the array and then use it for loops… So I told him that I would use a dictionary/hash
map and explained my code properly, given below)

def remove_duplicates(arr):
seen = {}
result = []
for elem in arr:
if elem not in seen:
seen[elem] = True
result.append(elem)
return result

Later he asked me whether I had any questions for him.
(I asked him about the career growth opportunities at Nomura for a data-oriented person like me).

The total duration was 30-35 minutes. 6 students were selected for the next round, and I
was happy to be one of them).

4. Technical Round 2 [6 students]

There was a panel of 2 interviewers this time. Again, I was asked to introduce myself and elaborate
upon my projects. After doing so they started with the DSA and SQL questions:

- There is a key 'x' in a nested hash -map/dictionary at some unknown depth. Return the

value associated with that key. I gave the following solution (used yield => since there
might be multiple x keys (in different dicts))

def gen_dict_extract(var, key):
if isinstance(var, dict):
for k, v in var. items():
if k == key:
yield v
if isinstance(v, (dict, list)):
yield from gen_dict_extract(v, key)
elif isinstance(var, list):
for d in var:
yield from gen_dict_extract(d, key)

- What happens when the root of a BST is deleted?

(replace the root with either its inorder successor (smallest/leftmost node of the right
subtree)
or in order predecessor (largest/rightmost node of the left subtree))

- Finally, I was given a puzzle - Find the 3 fastest Horses. I was able to solve it properly.

Refer to solution: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/puzzle-9-find-the-fastest-3-horses/

Then they asked me if I had any questions. I asked them what exactly was expected from interns
at the GM role; and how is the work environment at Nomura.

The total duration was 30-40 minutes. The final selection for the GM role was going to
occur after TR2 and HR rounds were over (at once).

5. HR Round [6 students]

The HR interviewer was very friendly and relaxed. She told me to calm down and asked me
standard HR questions:

-  Introduction + Family Background

- What are my strengths and weaknesses?

- Where do I see myself in 5 years?

- How would I fit in at Nomura?

- How flexible and adaptable am I at learning new things?

- Tell me about when you experienced failure and how you overcame it.

Then she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked her about the overall work experience and
culture at Nomura. Additionally, I asked her about the variety of different people (from different
states/countries) that I would get to meet at Nomura.

The total duration was 15-20 minutes. My HR interview went very well. However, there
were only 2 vacancies for the GM role; and I was more suited for development; so in the
end I was selected for the ITD role.

2 students were finally selected for the GM roles.

For ITD (info tech div) Role- (for which I was shortlisted)

2.   Technical Round 1 [32 students]

There was a panel of 2 interviewers. They told me to introduce myself and got acquainted with my
areas of strength - Machine Learning, Data Science and Analytics in general. They asked me
questions regarding my projects thoroughly, like-

- What is your best project? Why is it so?

- What did you learn from this project? How did you work within a team (for the team

projects) and what you could have done better?

- Why was this model (for ML) preferable to you? Why not the others? …

Do thorough research and reading on your projects , and you will be able to answer the above
questions with ease.

Then I was asked language-specific questions in depth. I had told them that Python was my main
programming language in general - for DSA, ML, and backend (Django).

- They asked me about an iterator in Python and how to define it. He then asked me to explain

how it works; and how it is different from using loops. I explained it properly while giving
examples having the correct syntax. (iter -> keyword for iterator; next -> used to iterate
through the iterator)

- They asked me about what decorators (@decorator_name basically in Python) are and how

to define them. Upon explaining what they were; they asked me to manually write a
decorator function to be applied to another function. I was able to do so (since my Python
skills were very good).

- I was asked about generators and how to define them. (Basically , use the yield keyword

instead of return). They asked me about its advantages - we can use multiple yield
statements at the same level (not true for return); and that such functionality can enable
returning multiple things (useful for sequences) which is n ot possible with the return
keyword.

He then asked me to rate myself in Python proficiency: I rated myself 9/10.

Some more questions included-

- Defining normalization and explaining the different normal forms (I told them from 1NF

to 5NF but practically speaking telling till BCNF is fine)

- I was asked to explain NoSQL databases - and which one I used (MongoDB). They asked

me why I preferred it (good extensive documentation; MongoDB ATLAS enables cross -
connecting clusters with ease across the internet; most mainstream and in-demand NoSQL
db with good community support).
I was asked to write/explain the basic CRUD operations for MongoDB (insertOne,
insertMany, find, findbyID, updateOne, updateMany, deleteOne, deleteMany and so on…)

- Finally they asked me a basic SQL query (write a SQL query to find the employees who

have a salary greater than the average salary in their department.) I wrote it in MySQL
syntax.

SELECT e1.*
FROM employees e1
JOIN (
SELECT department, AVG(salary) as avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
) e2 ON e1.department = e2.department
WHERE e1.salary > e2.avg_salary

(Basically, a combination of self-join and group by)

Then they asked me if I had any questions for them. I asked 2 (one for each panellist)-

- What is the overall work culture at Nomura? How good is the team bonding?

process and that I was going in the right direction.

Solution: 8 ÷ (1 - 1 ÷ 5) = 10
Refer this: https://mindyourdecisions.com/blog/2015/09/20/viral-math-problem-from-
google-can-you-make-10-from-the-numbers-1-1-5-and-8/

questions. However, here they gave me slightly negative feedback; that I elaborated excessively

told them that I would be more concise from here on.

Then they moved on to the technical questions (mainly DSA)-

- How to check if a string is a palindrome or not without using any loops or inbuilt functions?

A combination of 2 pointer and recursion.

def is_palindrome(s, i=0, j=None):
if j is None:
j = len(s) - 1 - i
if i >= j:
return True
if s[i] != s[j]:
return False
return is_palindrome(s, i + 1, j - 1)

- They asked me what was Dijkstra's algorithm; and then told me to write the basic code for

finding the minimum distance using it (even pseudocode is fine).

# Graph is the form of adjacency linked list; also use priority queue (using heap)
Dijkstra(Graph, Start):
Dist = infinity for all nodes
Dist[Start] = 0
Queue = all nodes
while Queue is not empty:
Node = extract min from Queue
for Neighbor of Node:
if Dist[Node] + Weight(Node, Neighbor) < Dist[Neighbor]:
Dist[Neighbor] = Dist[Node] + Weight(Node, Neighbor)
Previous[Neighbor] = Node
return Dist

- I was asked about a challenging problem that I solved and how did I approach it?

(I told them about cherry pickup-II (and explained the problem properly). I deliberately chose
a very hard 3D DP problem since I wanted to showcase my problem-solving ability. I gave
them the memoization solution (after explaining the recursion first); but told them that further
slight space optimizations such as tabulation; and then space optimized tabulation are possible.
)

def cherryPickup(grid):
# Define a helper function to perform dynamic programming recursion
def _cherryPickup(row, col1, col2):
# Out of bounds check
if col1 < 0 or col1 >= n or col2 < 0 or col2 >= n:
return float("-inf")

# Memoization check
if dp[row][col1][col2] != -1:
return dp[row][col1][col2]

# Base case: last row
if row == m - 1:
if col1 == col2:
# Collect one cherry
return grid[row][col1]
else:
# Collect two cherries
return grid[row][col1] + grid[row][col2]

# Recursive case
max_s = 0
for d1 in range(-1, 2):
for d2 in range(-1, 2):
# Calculate the maximum number of cherries that can be collected
if col1 == col2:
max_s = max(max_s, grid[row][col1]
+ _cherryPickup(row + 1, col1 + d1, col2 + d2))
else:
max_s = max(max_s, grid[row][col1] + grid[row][col2] +
_cherryPickup(row + 1, col1 + d1, col2 + d2))

# Memoize the result
dp[row][col1][col2] = max_s
return max_s

SELECT window_function(column) OVER (

Frame_specification # is not necessary to mention this...

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Always believe in yourself. Even if you get nervous before the interviews begin; do not

overthink and over-prepare at the last minute.
Believe me, experiencing anxiety is normal and a part of the process. Be calm before the
rounds (trust me you will still feel anxious, but keeping it simple is the way to go).

2. Always answer questions honestly and confidently. If you know the logic behind a

problem; but don't know how to proceed with it; explain your thought process in a point-
wise manner to the interviewers. This will show your clarity. Keep a smile on your face
during the interviews in general (don't fake it though - it will make you seem nervous).
Maintain eye contact with the interviewers (don't stare at them; but periodically w hile
answering questions do so)
However, if you have no clue or have just heard about the problem; honestly tell the
interviewers that you don't know the answer (or that you are not familiar with the domain

- if it's a question out of your area of strength). Partially explaining a potent ially wrong

approach is detrimental.

3. Don't entirely focus on DSA. Yes, it is important and you will be asked about it in the

interviews (especially in Tech Round 2).
However, there's a high probability that you will be purely asked about your projects; and
more importantly SQL and DBMS questions in general (read the interview commonly
asked DBMS questions). I was not asked about any OS questions; but only if you get
additional time for preparation; you should prepare it as well (since they may ask it).
Also, if you have listed a NoSQL database as a skill in your resume; like MongoDB in my
case, prepare the basic queries (CRUD operations) and read about it briefly (MongoDB
ATLAS, clusters and so on…). I was asked about it in my Tech Round 2. Do this after you
have prepared DSA and DBMS.

4. Regarding the OA (Online Assessment); try attempting as many questions as possible. We

had 60 questions (20 Math, 20 Verbal, 20 Analytical). Try to attempt at least 40 questions
in 40-45 mins. It's not necessary to attempt every question correctly. I properly attempted
about 40-45 in 50 mins.
If and only if; there is no negative marking (which will most likely be the case) try to take
an estimated guess for the remaining questions (narrow down the options & then guess); if
you believe estimation is taking time, blindly guess the answers (you still have a 1/4 chance
of getting it right).

5. Be extremely thorough with the projects listed in your resume. It's not necessary to list 4 -

5 projects. Even listing 2 -3 of your best projects can create a great impression on the
interviewers. In my case; the 3 projects that I had listed were mainly ML/DL  based with
data analytics incorporated (Tableau); with a single project being that of web development
(backend - Django).
Limit the projects mainly to your strongest domain. But have at least 1 project from a
different domain (since they will look for variety as well). Mention your contribution to
each project. It's better to mention it in the resume itself (in 2 -3 lines). Be genuine with
your answers. Elaborate upon the skills that you applied in the project. Only mention those
skills which you genuinely have (above 50 % of the knowledge). If you don't have any real
experience in the skill that you have mentioned; better to leave it out of the resume.

References for Non-Tech (Finance or Consulting):
CFI for financial courses
IndiaBix and GeeksForGeeks to practice your aptitude
Daily News to be updated about the recent events (questions are asked about this)
For these roles, your soft skills need to be polished. To practice this, you can participate in case study competitions.
While you are focused on non-tech, you should not lose your technical touch. Many roles have special preferences for candidates with technical knowledge/background.
Maintain a diary/notebook for your interviews. Jot down what you did right and where you can improve. This self-reflection is very important to keep you grounded and focused. Make sure you correct yourself in the next interview.
Research the company principles/ pillars and tie your answers to them. I believe this is the most important tip.
The placement season is very hectic. Your friends will get placed before you and you might feel left out and dejected. However, it is important to understand that rejections do not deplete your value. Be confident and stay grounded. Practice meditation and focus on one thing at a time. You got this!
All the best!

Aptitude Round (55 mins)
Group Discussion (20 mins (can end before) + conclusion)
Technical Round (depends on the panel)
HR (5 - 10 mins)
Director (depends on the panel)
The process goes on throughout the day, so be prepared accordingly.

1. Aptitude Round [ 100+ candidates appeared for this round ]

Basic quant/arithmetic questions
If you're preparing for CAT, this will be very easy for you
You might not be able to complete all the questions. That's alright. Just make sure the ones you've done are correct
Tip: Work with assumptions to make your calculations easy
Practice: IndiaBix, GeeksForGeeks

2.     Group Discussion [ 48 candidates appeared for this round ]

The topic is given on the spot. You'll have 2 mins to gather your thoughts. Carry a notebook to jot down your points.
We were assigned For and Against roles for the particular statement. In the middle of the discussion, we were asked to speak for the other side without taking any time to think about the points.

Tips:

Jot down the points for both sides so you can have the advantage of speaking first when the sides are switched.
If someone else discusses a point that you had jotted down earlier, grab that opportunity to say that you agree with their point and provide some additional information for the same.
It's okay not to be the first one to speak; what is important is the you deliver without fumbling and back your points with valid facts.
Practice: TPO GD sessions and communication skills lectures in your first-year

3.    Technical Round [ 18 candidates appeared for this round (6 panels - 3 from each panel) ]

For my panel, this was a thoroughly resume-based round
If you are unaware of the answer to a question, calmly say so. Although this does not always work, what is important is to not panic. The moment you panic, it's game over.
Make sure you are putting all the projects you are confident of. They can be the easiest projects but if you can answer any question that is thrown at you, you will certainly earn some extra points. Besides, these projects will boost your confidence.
I had won a case study competition and I put that up in my projects list. I was asked a lot of questions about that and even asked to show the presentation I made.
There were some situational questions in addition to the resume-based ones.

Tips:

It is very important to be aware of your body language and present yourself confidently. For example, I have a habit of fiddling with my thumbs even when I am not anxious. It leaves a negative impression on the interviewer. Instead, I learned to keep my hands on my lap which helped me hide this habit.
This day will be very long, so try your best to be fresh mentally.
Listen to interviews and ask your friends (who you think are better at giving interviews than you) to take some mocks for you.

3. HR Round [ 12 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was a normal HR round. You can refer to videos and look up frequently asked HR questions and prepare their answers beforehand.
One tip is to pay special attention to the PPT. You will find something to ask the HR representative at the end of this round. It is important to show that you are interested in joining the company; asking questions subtly shows your interest.

3. Director Round [ 12 candidates appeared for this round (no rejects from HR) ]

This was the most difficult round. From the moment you enter, the directors are out for your blood. They want to see if you will crack under pressure. The questions can be about literally anything and they will grill you irrespective of your answer. They want to test your promptness and composure.
The only tip I can give you for this round is to be calm.
This round can be really unnerving but if you give this interview as if you are playing a game, this round can be really fun.

4 students were offered the job.

Eligibility criteria was above 70% in both 10th and 12th boards, CGPA: 7+

1. PPT

2. Online assessment (OA)

3. Technical Round

4. HR Round

1. Online Assessment: (209 students appeared, the test was held at the college)

This round was held in college just after the ppt. It was a 85 minute test held on hackerrank.
There were 30 MCQ's and one Coding Problem. 15 MCQ were based on Java, SQL, DBMS,
code snippets and expected output. And the other 15 questions were based on Aptitude.
Coding Question:
There is a ring with each node labeled from 1 to m. Starting from node 1. We were also given an
array of nodes to travel of size n and a time time array which tells the required time to go to any
adj node of size m. We can travel clockwise as well as anti-clockwise. We need to find the
minimum time required to visit all nodes.
Eg.
N=4
NextNodeTo Visit = [2, 3, 1, 3]
M =3
TimeToMove = |1, 4, 2]
Initially we are standing at 1
1
--- PAGE 2 ---
From 1 → 2
We can directly go from 1 → 2 cost = 1
We can choose path 1 → 3 → 2 cost= 1 + 2 = 3
From 2 → 3
We can directly go from 2 → 3 cost = 4
We can choose path 2 → 1 → 3 cost = 6
From 3 → 1
We can directly go from 3 → 1 cost = 2
We can choose path 3 → 2 → 1 cost = 6
From 1 → 3
We can directly go from 1 → 3 cost = 1
We can choose path 1 → 2 → 3 cost = 5
Min Sum = 1 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 8

2. Offline Technical Round [36 candidates appeared for this round]

The interviewers (2 interviewers) introduced themselves, then they analyzed my resume. The
interview started by asking why I chose Computer engineering as my career choice. Asked about
my favorite data structure and their real life applications. He told me to evaluate an infix
expression. I explained my approach to solve it using stack. Then he asked me to write a code to
count the frequency of every element from an array. He asked me about my weakness. He asked
if I preferred frontend or backend development. I shared that I have a preference for backend
development, but I also enjoy creating intuitive user interfaces on the frontend. Then we
discussed the tech stack I used in my internship and what all things I implemented there. He also
asked about the tech stack of projects, the database associated with it and difficulties faced. He
asked me if I wanted to go for masters. How did you work in group projects and what was your
role? Also we discussed the whole flow of the project. Then he asked me about ui/ux designing.
I mentioned all the HMI principles I knew (I had taken HMI in my OE) Which software used to
design wireframe. I answered figma. He questioned me how would you understand what ui
customer requires? Code reusability advantages in projects. How would you work so that if any
other developer works on the same project it would be easier for him. He also asked me how did
you implement theoretical knowledge in real life. We discussed more about SDLC.

3. Offline HR Round [ 16 candidates appeared for this round]

It was a 10-15 minute round.

• She asked me about my family background.

• If I wanted to do masters.

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Where do you stay.

• Also asked what I would do with my first paycheck.

• How was my previous interview

• She also asked me if i had any questions

• I Inquired about the company's ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) policy

o Asked about current clients
Finally results were announced, 12 students got selected, and I was one of them!

1. Round 1- Online Assessment

This was a pretty basic OA round which comprised of 60 question on:
a. Logical Reasoning
b. Quantitative aptitude

Verbal section had some long paragraph based question which was followed by 5 questions on

Quants had some interesting questions and were a bit trick you may watch a complete playlist

--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Round 2- Tech Interview 1(32 candidates applied for this round)

This was a purely technical and resume based round. As usual a brief introduction was asked
and post that we dived deep into the projects mentioned on my resume. (Make sure you are
thorough with all aspects of your project and what you want to mention and what not.) The
interviewer is more interested in what your role was and what you have done in the project
rather than the complete project and its details so make sure you are well versed with it.
The interview then steered towards OOPS and I was asked about Encapsulation and
Polymorphism quite deeply.

1. What is Encapsulation and Polymorphism

2. Types of Polymorphism

3. Difference between the two

4. Use of polymorphism in Inheritance. (Creating the object of child class while calling the

function of Parent class).
Make sure all your concepts on your primary coding language are crisp and clear and again the
interviewer will ask followup questions on what you answer so be smart on what and how you
answer each question. Also be prepared with 2-3 good UNCOMMON questions about the
company you are interviewing for. (As it may seem as the last bit of the interview though it helps
to leave a good impression on the interviewer)
This round for me went on for about 40-45 mins

3. Round 3- Tech Interview 2

This was the toughest and the biggest round for me literally, went on for more than 1.5hrs for
me. There were 2 Senior Associates as panelists for the interview. This interview did not revolve
around any specific topic rather it spanned over all the topics like:

1. Java Environment(As Java was my primary language)

2. OOPS

3. DSA

4. SQL

5. Puzzles

6. Guesstimates

7. Projects

8. Some HR Questions

This was hell of a round for me. They started off light with question about what is JDK,JVM etc
and Core JAVA concepts. Then jumped on to DSA.
Find Peak Element
Permutations
I was not asked to code rather they just wanted to know my approach towards these questions
and only Pseudo code was required. The interviewers are always helpful incases where you get
stuck with some edge cases, so please ALWAYS KEEP DISCUSSING YOUR
--- PAGE 3 ---
THOUGHT PROCESS with the interviewer. Then I was given a puzzle to solve which was
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/puzzle-4-pay-an-employee-using-a-gold-rod-of-7-units/. had
previously been through this puzzle thus was familiar with it. But make sure you dont allow the
interviewer to know this, always take your time and come down to the solution step by step.
Always remember the interviewer is MORE INTERESTED IN YOUR THOUGHT
PROCESS rather than you getting to the solution in a step or two. You could practice puzzles
at GFG and also watch youtube to understand the process. Moving on I was grilled through my
projects again. (Tip: Make sure you finalize the projects that you will be mentioning on your
resume ASAP and practice all sorts of questions on it using ChatGPT or any other resource. All
the interviewers will more or less ask the same questions on your projects and make sure you
don't lose the chance to IMPRESS them as you know what questions may be asked over what
you have mentioned on your resume.). Finally the interview ended with some Guesstimates like

1. How many tickets may be scanned at a metro Station in Mumbai

2. What would be the revenue generated by Wankhede Stadium through a season of IPL

A good playlist to get hang of Guesstimates:
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-q2MNxDekiSFUNcwCI-Q4-QqHWe5K42p&si=JhUmX-Dgf7i
MK5ko
Followed on with some HR questions like How would you manage a team with conflicting
interests? One of your lowest points at SPIT? Would you consider opting for masters of MBA in
the near future(Make sure you have a valid response to this question as it may be decisive on
your selection as it is very important to any company investing in you).

4. HR ROUND

Short 15-20 mins round. The interviewer was really sweet and didn't have any intentions to grill.
Simply asked me about how my day was and what my experience was and asked if I had given
interviews for any other companies. We went on to discuss just 1 question for almost 15 mins
which was Why you want to be a part of Nomura. Here I had prepared and went a bit off the
track to answer where I mentioned that obviously how the CTC attracts us and then mentioned
a few points about the Work Culture, Growth Opportunities and my interest in what I had to work
upon if I would Join Nomura. I think she was impressed upon how I was being honest and
mentioned the CTC part as we went on to discuss how she gets annoyed when people usually
butter up the Company's name in response to this question.
Tip: Make sure to practice a good amount of HR Questions as you don't want to be too frank or
too sophisticated while you're answering as the HR is always judging you by how and what you
are answering. They may try to calm you down as they want to see your actual personality and
not what you have prepared or what you are trying to be in front of them.

journey.prep:
1. While reading all the interview experiences and after your peer's interviewers don't build a mindset

about how your interview is going to be. Your interview will mostly be based on your past
--- PAGE 3 ---
experiences and your college journey. So it's okay if you feel you don't know the answer to a
question that was asked to someone else.

2. Prepare well for the aptitude tests. Start at least a month before your placements start.

3. Understand that some companies really focus on DSA while some companies don't, so prepare

accordingly. (I focused on DSA so much that I did not prepare for aptitude well personally.)

4. I had solved 600+ questions on leetcode with a contest rating of 1750+ but still I couldn't even clear

a single OA before UBS; so know it's not always your fault. It might just so happen that sometimes
mentally you won't be in the right position to solve questions. So don't beat yourself up and keep
preparing well for the up-coming opportunities. All you need is one good day where you clear the
OA and the interviews.

5. Believe in yourself and try not to think about the package/etc a lot because all that will do is distract

you from the main goal. During that time, ask the people around you what was asked and how did
their interviews go.

6. Always smile when you enter the interview and maintain that smile. ( This is very important, so even

if you say something wrong in the interview, accepting that mistake with a smile would give a much
better impression than pointlessly being fixated on that point and interviewer grilling you on that).
If you have any doubts you can reach me out on linkedn

Criteria: Class 10th & Class 12th: 70% and above B. Tech : 7 and above CGPA

1. Pre Placement talk (31st July)

2. OA (31st July)

3. Interviews(1st August)

1. Online Assessment Around 200 candidates appeared

Platform: Hackerrank
Time: 85 mins
Questions
15 Technical questions (mostly Java related)
15 Aptitude Questions
1 Coding question
Coding Question
There is a string which can have 3 possible letters a,b,c. Number of ways to make a pattern "abcabcabc..."
only by insertion
For example:
Given String "abacbc"
Output = 3
Explanation 'abcabcabc"
Solution:
Run a for loop from start to end and in that loop check for each character with the next character and how
many characters need to be inserted, ie:
if first character is a and second character is b you need to add 0 characters (none needs to be added)
if first character is a and second character is c you need to add 1 character (b)
if first character is a and second character is a again you need to add 2 characters (bc)
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Technical Interview Around 40 candidates were shortlisted

We were told to arrive at college by 9:30 a.m., with interviews starting around 11:00 a.m. Since my name
was second to last, I was worried that I might not get enough time to present myself well. But by the
time it was my turn, I was well-prepared and just focused on getting my points across to them clearly.
The interview started off with a "tell me about yourself question, so I told the panel about my college
journey from the first to the final year. Then they started asking me detailed questions about the things I
had mentioned in my resume. I was asked in-depth questions about my internship and my work there.
Then they asked me 2 coding questions:
In the first one they gave me a matrix and asked me to sort it
column-wise and row-wise simultaneously. I interpreted it wrong so they asked me to sort it row-wise first
and then column-wise. I was able to solve that quickly.
My next question was to count the number of occurrences of the word "test" in a sentence. I could easily
code this and solve the problem.
Later, they asked me a few questions based on Docker like :
How do you find the list of images on your machine?
How to find the active containers in the machine?
How to find all containers (active + not active) on your machine?
Some other questions that I was asked were:

1. Difference between abstraction and inheritance.

2. How to make a class immutable?

3. If I have a plan for higher studies?

4. What do I want to do in life? (This was in technical context so I told them I want to explore

various fields. (Preferrably say something from their JD))

5. Are you okay doing Selenium testing? (I said no humbly and backed that up with a proper

reasoning).
Also prepare beforehand what questions you are going to ask them and try to have a discussion over that
question (If it's purely a technical question).

3. HR Interview Around 20 candidates were shortlisted

This round was more like a background check. They asked me questions like- where do I stay, where my
parents work etc. To me, this didn't feel like a formal interview round. It seemed more like a discussion
to get to know me personally and assess my fit for the job.
Finally 12 students were selected!

journey.prep:
●  The  CGPA  criteria  may  or  may  not  be  mentioned  but  understanding  that  having  a  good  pointer  above

8 always helps. If you don't have one, try. But don't lose heart.

●  Prepare a lot for the GD, don't take it lightly ( Some others were much more prepared than me)

●  Focus on profile building from the get go.

●  Participate  in  case  studies  when  you  get  time,  and  good  ones.  So  that  you  end  up  learning  things  in

the process.

●  Work  to  get  summer  internships  if  you're  in  your  4th  sem  (I  started  looking  too  late  so  there  wasn't

enough time)

●  If  you  don't  have  an  internship  on  your  resume,  back  it  up  with  a  good  project  (I  had  a  3  statement

model with a common size statement, dcf model and ratio analysis in it)

●  Be  clear  in  your  finance  basics.  They  don't  expect  you  to  be  perfect  at  finance,  but  the  basics  are  a

necessity.

●  Be polite and well mannered at all times, it creates an impression.

●  Dress  well.  Light  shirt  (preferably  white),  dark  trousers.  If  you  have  a  suit  or  a  tie,  wear  it.  It  isn't

over-dressed.

●  Part time internships are a thing, so if you can handle one of them then why not try.

●  Interact with other people aiming for the same company, you'll grow together with them.

●  Don't get too over-confident ever about your selection, just keep working and praying.

●  Read  newspapers  and  follow  the  news  regularly!  Not  just  10  days  before  the  interview,  but  for  the

months to come.

●  Feel free to reach out to me in case of further queries.

*ALL THE VERY BEST*

1. Pre - Placement Talk: 2nd July

2.  Resume Screening: 4th July

3.  Online Aptitude Test: 6th July

Further Rounds took place offline on the 10th of July -

4.  Group Discussion

5.  Interview Round 1

6.  Interview Round 2

7.  HR Round

1.  Pre - Placement Talk

This  seemingly  unnecessary  round  is  actually  very  important.  This  is  the  first  impression  the  candidates  get
to  make  on  their  recruiters  so  make  the  most  of  it.  In  our  case  they  wanted  to  keep  the  talk  interactive  so
kept  asking  us  questions,  in  which  case  as  aspiring  employees  you  ought  to  try  and  interact  with  them.  But
try not to repeat points made by anyone else before you as it might not leave as good an impression.
Also,  keep  all  your  doubts  tailored  to  the  role  and  ask  good  questions.  One  more  thing,  in  case  they  do  not
ask  you  any  questions  or  don't  try  to  keep  it  interactive,  it  might  be  best  to  save  the  questions  towards  the
end as they might actually go for a common Q&A session.
The  pre-placement  talk  is  being  mentioned  as  the  first  round  as  it  is  a  very  crucial  opportunity  to  get  noticed
by the hiring managers so make the impression you would want them to remember you by.
Key points summarized -

●  Follow the decorum of the interaction, whether online or offline.

●  Ask good questions and try to answer any questions asked by the recruiters.

●  First impressions last.

2. Resume Screening

Your  resume  is  as  crucial  a  part  of  the  entire  selection  process  as  any  other.  Building  your  resumes  is  a
process  that  starts  not  from  the  day  application  deadline  is  released  but  from  the  1st/2nd/3rd  years  itself.  So
start ASAP. Try to tailor your resume to the role you are applying for.
All  the  resumes  have  to  pass  through  an  ATS  so  you  can  check  your  score  on  a  website  called
"ResumeWorded". My resume had a score of 60.
Key points regarding resumes -

●  They should be 1 page resumes as that's what is expected from freshers.

●  Make single column resumes in Latex format.

●  Try to keep all of the relevant coursework / competition / projects / internships in your resume.

●  Having 1-2 good finance projects on your resume helps.

●  If possible try to get a relevant internship so you have something more to talk about.

●  Participate in case study competitions.

●  Do some finance certifications and add them onto your resume.

All  these  points  are  just  suggestions  and  not  necessities  in  order  to  qualify  for  further  rounds.  I  will
elaborate  more  on  a  few  points  in  later  sections  of  the  document.  Results  were  declared  1  day  prior  to  the
OA Test i.e. on 5th July.

3. Online Aptitude test  (  97  candidates qualified for this round)

The  online  test  was  conducted  on  CoCubes  platform  for  us.  With  a  total  of  45  marks,  it  consisted  of  4
sections -

●  Finance  &  Accounting  (10)  :  This  section  contains  mostly  accounting  and  corporate  finance

questions. I think it had 1 question about puttable bonds.

●  Market Awareness (10)  : This section contained quite a few economy questions and current affairs.

●  Quantitative  Aptitude  (15)  :  This  was  a  quant  section  in  which  there  were  mostly  permutation,

probability and algebra questions. So this one is out and out mathematics.

●  Verbal Reasoning (10)  : This is an English section, pretty simple if you try to stick with the basics.

The  time  given  was  45  mins,  so  there  is  a  time  crunch  as  the  quant  section  is  tough.  So  try  to  segregate  the
sections  into  time  slots  so  you  don't  miss  out  on  any  section  in  the  end.  The  results  for  this  round  were
announced a day before the final day i.e. 9th July. So don't lose heart in the process and be prepared.

4. Group Discussion  (  72  candidates qualified for this round)

The  topic  for  the  group  discussion  was  revealed  on  9th  July  around  5pm  and  the  next  day  we  had  to  report
around  8:30  am  so  make  sure  to  do  your  research  prior  to  the  d-day.  Our  topic  was  "India:  the  5th  largest
economy".
Key points -

●  25-30 mins.

●  6 panels of 12 each.

●  You  can  carry  a  sheet  of  paper  with  you  as  reference  (but  avoid  looking  into  it  and  speaking  as  it

doesn't send the best message to the panelists).

●  We had 2 panelists and our group discussion was a moderated discussion.

●  Note  down  points  that  the  others  are  making  as  it  shows  your  sincerity  and  also  comes  in  handy  if

you're asked to conclude.

●  Try  to  have  at  least  3-4  entries  in  the  entire  discussion  and  at  max  1-2  entries  per  subtopic  (we  had

7-8  subtopics)  in  a  moderated  group  discussion.  Any  less  and  you  seem  underprepared;  any  more  and
you run the risk of coming off as too aggressive.

●  A  group  discussion  is  about  coming  to  a  conclusion  as  a  collective  unit,  so  try  not  to  refute  and  rebut

other candidates' points.

●  Be polite and extremely relevant.

●  Quality and relevance of points  matters a lot more than how many times you spoke in the GD.

●  Lastly, prepare well and from multiple viewpoints.

5. Interview Round 1  (  31  candidates qualified for this round)

Here  starts  the  real  interesting  part.  This  is  mostly  a  basic  finance  round  +  puzzles  +  mental  math.  The
interviewer  wants  to  check  your  basics  in  finance  and  how  quick  you  can  think.  At  times  guesstimates  are
asked  as  well,  but  I  don't  think  in  our  batch  a  lot  of  people  were  asked  those.  There  were  5  interview  panels,
mostly consisting of 1 panelist each, mine had 2 panelists though.
My Round 1 -

●  I wasn't asked any puzzles or mental math questions. Mine was an out and out finance round.

●  I  was  asked  about  bonds  (price  yield  relations,  yield  curves  &  inverted  yield  curves,  macaulay  &

modified durations)

●  Leading, Lagging indicators and their examples and relation with economic distress situations.

●  Next  was  the  accounting  section,  in  which  I  was  asked  the  relationship  between  the  3  basic

statements and how we make them.

●  I  was  asked  the  reason  for  positioning  the  3  statements  the  way  they  are  positioned  in  a  financial

model.

●  Lastly  in  the  accounting  section,  I  was  asked  what  impact  a  change  in  depreciation  would  have  on  all

3 statements with and without taxes and how it would affect the interest expenses.
Rounds  like  mine  would  be  one  of  the  rarer  occurrences  as  mostly  others  were  asked  puzzles  and  mental
math  questions  too.  So  be  prepared  with  them  as  well.  I  wasn't  given  any  sheet  of  paper  to  carry  out  the
rough work, for the accounting scenarios.
Some suggestions -

●  Have a good accounting background.

●  Be aware of financial markets.

●  Corporate finance is a key topic along with accounting and equities.

●  Do not worry about bonds much, as very few people were asked about them.

●  Go through and solve puzzles on your own.

●  Try to solve mathematical problems without actually writing them down, it'll help in the interviews.

6. Interview  Round  2  (Can't  say  how  many  qualified  for  this  round  as  the  interviews  were  conducted

parallelly)
I  got  the  longer  end  of  the  stick  in  round  1,  as  after  that  round  ,  my  round  2  was  mostly  relaxed.  Round  2  is
generally the Pro-Fit round. In that I was asked questions on my resume. My internship and my projects.
I  was  first  asked  to  introduce  myself  and  then  I  was  asked  which  are  the  top  3  stocks  in  India  by  market  cap.
When  I  answered  that  the  question  was  broadened  to  top  5  which  I  couldn't  get  right.  But  it's  fine  as  long  as
you try your best and are somewhat close.
The  questions  in  round  2  were  more  on  the  practical  side  of  things  and  I  was  asked  to  create  a  dummy
corporation  and  explain  what  it  does  and  what  its  costs  are  and  where  each  specific  item  is  put  in  the  cash
flow statement.
The  second  practical  question  was  about  mutual  funds  as  my  internship  was  regarding  those.  I  was  asked  to
act  as  a  financial  advisor  to  the  recruiter  and  ensure  a  suitable  investment  allocation  for  him  depending  on
his investment horizon and risk tolerance.

7. HR Round  (  15-17  candidates qualified for this round)

Lastly, the HR round. Here all of us were asked mostly the same questions. Namely -

●  Introduce yourself

●  Talk about your family

●  Higher education

●  Have you been in a situation where things were ethically not right, if yes how did you deal with it

●  What is your understanding of the role

●  Do you have any questions for me

It  is  important  to  understand  here  that  in  the  HR  round  it  doesn't  matter  what  you  say,  but  rather  how  you
say it. So practice how you're going to answer these as well.
(  11  candidates were finally shortlisted for CIB &  2  for fintech)

customSections.content:
●  The  CGPA  criteria  may  or  may  not  be  mentioned  but  understanding  that  having  a  good  pointer  above

8 always helps. If you don't have one, try. But don't lose heart.

●  Prepare a lot for the GD, don't take it lightly ( Some others were much more prepared than me)

●  Focus on profile building from the get go.

●  Participate  in  case  studies  when  you  get  time,  and  good  ones.  So  that  you  end  up  learning  things  in

the process.

●  Work  to  get  summer  internships  if  you're  in  your  4th  sem  (I  started  looking  too  late  so  there  wasn't

enough time)

●  If  you  don't  have  an  internship  on  your  resume,  back  it  up  with  a  good  project  (I  had  a  3  statement

model with a common size statement, dcf model and ratio analysis in it)

●  Be  clear  in  your  finance  basics.  They  don't  expect  you  to  be  perfect  at  finance,  but  the  basics  are  a

necessity.

●  Be polite and well mannered at all times, it creates an impression.

●  Dress  well.  Light  shirt  (preferably  white),  dark  trousers.  If  you  have  a  suit  or  a  tie,  wear  it.  It  isn't

over-dressed.

●  Part time internships are a thing, so if you can handle one of them then why not try.

●  Interact with other people aiming for the same company, you'll grow together with them.

●  Don't get too over-confident ever about your selection, just keep working and praying.

●  Read  newspapers  and  follow  the  news  regularly!  Not  just  10  days  before  the  interview,  but  for  the

resumes. The criteria focused on academic performance, relevant projects, internships, and
extracurricular activities. Out of these, 123 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

• a) Basic Aptitude (25 mins) (26 July 2pm)

quantitative questions. Resources like IndiaBix were helpful for preparation. Out of the 123, 57
candidates were shortlisted for the next Online test that happened around 1 hr later.
b) CS Fundamentals (35 mins)
This section included:

• 4 questions on input-output and basic data structures and algorithms (DSA), focusing on

Java-specific concepts.

• 6 questions on SQL, mostly at an easy level.

After this round, 38 candidates were further shortlisted.
--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Round 1 Interview [38 candidates appeared]

The first interview round was comprehensive, covering various aspects:

• Introduction and Projects:

• The interview started with the common question, "Tell me about yourself."

• A brief discussion followed on my data analytics project using Python, where I

explained the basic concept and what I did.

• Technical Questions:

• DSA Question 1: Given a sentence as a string, reverse each word and capitalize

the first letter. I proposed two approaches: one using a trimming function and loop
for reversing, and another using the split function in Java.

• DSA Question 2: Input a binary array and count the maximum number of swaps

of Os to make the final array have no consecutive ones. I suggested a brute force
O(n) solution using a simple for loop and checking neighboring values.

• SQL Queries:

• Print details of the student with the highest marks (using subqueries and aggregate

functions).

• Print the top 3 students based on marks (using ORDER BY with LIMIT or

correlated subqueries).

• Print the top 3 students based on marks in each division (using the

DENSE_RANKO window function with PARTITION BY).
They shortlisted 4 students from this round, skipping the second technical round, which was
unusual compared to previous years.

• What do you know about EDS?

• Why do you want to be a part of us?

o How is the process going?
o How many other companies have you applied to before this?
o Are you aware of the role and responsibilities?

• Describe a situation where nobody praised you, and you were on your own.

• Describe a situation where you manage time well.

• Where do you live? (I live in Bhandup, and the company is in Malad with timings

2-11 pm)

• How will you travel? (I said by bike, but she suggested it might be better if I shift

closer, which I said I would consider)

journey.howSecured:
Barclays organized an industrial-academia hackathon called Hack-O-Hire, which I had the opportunity to
participate in and win. The details of this experience are also mentioned in my LinkedIn post. Initially, there
were around 1,200 teams participating, and out of these, 28 teams were selected (5 from our college) for the
final hackathon, which was conducted at the Barclays Pune campus. Some of the candidates from these
shortlisted teams were given the opportunity to proceed directly to the interview stage, skipping the online
assessment round.

1. Technical Round [ 9 Candidates participated in this round - 3 Hackathon / 6 Cybershala]

My first round of interviews at Barclays was conducted online via Microsoft Teams by the Assistant
Director, and it lasted for about 45 minutes. The interview began with a brief introduction, during which I
highlighted my experience winning a hackathon on a cybersecurity problem statement. This led the
interviewer to ask some cybersecurity-related questions, such as What does a hacker typically do after
gaining access to a victim's system? and What are trojans, backdoors, and worms? He also followed up with
a specific question about how backdoors work.
Next, he asked me to open Notepad and discuss the components of the backend. He then instructed me to:

• Write code for a login page for both frontend and backend.

• Connect the login page to a database.

• Write JavaScript for the password field.

Following that, I was asked several questions on APIs:

• What is REST?

• Perform an API call using Postman.

• Explain the body, headers, and keys of a URL.

• Write API routing code.

• What is regex? He then asked me to write a regex expression for the password field.

He also inquired about the design aspects of an application, asking If you were creating an application, what
would your component roadmap look like? Later to write code to connect a database (any) to your web
application.
--- PAGE 2 ---
The interview concluded with some DSA-related questions:

• Write optimal code to calculate factorial.

• Given an unsorted array with 100 elements, add the 101st element in the correct position. This was

for a dynamic array, where the array has no fixed size, and each new number needs to be inserted in
the appropriate position.

2. Techno-HR Round [7 Candidates participated in this round - 3 Hackathon / 4 Cybershala]

My second round interview at Barclays began about 1-2 hours after the first round and lasted for about 1.15
hours. The interviewer was quite relaxed and even encouraged me to not be nervous before we started. He
opened the interview by asking me for a brief introduction, and then transitioned into several situational
questions.
One of the key questions was: You're working on a project with a deadline tomorrow, and you discover that
your selected model is showing a 25% risk. What approach would you take?
The majority of the interview involved situational questions like this. Afterward, he moved on to some
technical topics and basics of OOPS, DBMS such as:

• What is method overriding and function overloading?

• Why do we use OOP, what are the advantages of OOP, and can you provide real-life examples of

OOP?

• What is better between an array and a list?

The conversation then shifted to typical HR questions, such as:

• Provide an example where you did something extraordinary.

• Give an example where you and your colleagues had different opinions, and explain how you

handled the situation.

• Can you share an example where you realized you had made a mistake, and how did you deal with

it?

• Tell me something in your academic journey that you're really proud of.

• What are your plans regarding a master's degree?

• Do you have a dream company?

7 students were offered the role and I was one of them !!!.

Placement process consisted of 3 rounds. Online test (Test was to be taken from college only)  and  2 Interview
Rounds .

1. Online Test  :  [ No of candidates who appeared for this round  were 138 ]

The Online test was of 1hr 30 minutes .  It consisted of cs fundamentals mcq (variable marks), a 10 marks
sql query and a 50 marks coding question .The coding question was about string generation similar to this:
https://leetcode.com/discuss/interview-question/4006812/String-Generation-OA-Question
SQL was basic group by and order by  query where we had to group by according to a month . Make sure to
practice SQL of date and months questions.
I was able to solve 10 / 10 test cases ,  SQL and MCQS.

2. [Round 2 : Tech ] [ 34 students got shortlisted ]

Before the interview rounds, a Pre-Placement Talk was conducted .
The average duration of round 2 was 40-45 minutes.
My interviewer was Assistant Vice President ( Java Developer ) .
My interview started with a fun question: "Tell me something cool about yourself." After that, the interviewer
asked about my core strengths. Following this, they inquired about my Computer Science minor course, the
subjects it covered .
( All this are Trick questions so answer honestly and give proper reasoning for your answer  . )
Next, he asked me to explain my first two projects in depth and my specific role in them, especially if they
were group projects. I had worked on projects using both the MERN stack and Spring Boot, so he asked why
I chose two different tech stacks and which one I would prefer if given a choice, along with my reasoning.
We then shifted to Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA). First, he asked me about pointers and gave me a
task to write a code that adds two numbers using pointers. He also inquired why Java doesn't support pointers.
Afterward, he asked which data structure I like the most, and I answered "stacks and queues." He then asked
me to explain both data structures and give real -life examples where they are used. Finally, he asked if there
was any data structure or algorithm I didn't particularly like. I replied that while I don't dislike any, if I had to
prioritize, sorting algorithms would rank the lowest  . Following this, he asked me to write the code for the
Insertion Sort algorithm, explain it with a test case, and discuss its time and space complexity. We then moved
on to discussing other algorithms, their respective time and space complexities, and the scenarios where each
algorithm is most appropriate to use .
Later, he posed a thought-provoking question: " With AI/ML advancements today, why is there still a need for
software development engineers like us?" I answered  , and he seemed impressed with my response, even
appreciating how I presented it .
He then asked why I chose Electronics and Telecommunications (EXTC) as my major when I was clearly
interested in Computer Science. He further asked why I didn't opt for Computer Science (CS) directly.
He then asked me about my extracurricular activities, such as hackathons, case study competitions, and my
hobbies.
Towards the end , he asked the common interview question: "Why should I hire you over others?" Afterward,
he gave me the chance to ask him any questions. I made sure to ask questions that would genuinely interest
him and avoid questions like one my friend had asked about the Barclays logo and what it signifies, to which
they had no answer. So, I would advise avoiding such questions.

3. [Round 3 : HR] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round were 21 ]

Round 3 lasted for 20 minutes.
The interview began with the usual "Introduce yourself" question. After that, she presented me with a
situational question: "Let's say you are part of a team, and your manager consistently makes wrong
decisions for the team. What would you do?" I responded with multiple approaches, but she kept adding
new aspects to the scenario, testing whether I aligned with their company's values (RISES).
The second question was about smart work versus hard work. She asked, "If given the choice between
doing smart work and hard work, which would you choose and why?" I explained my reasoning for both.
The third question was a bit more personal--she asked me to convince her that I hadn't chosen Computer
Science for the high-paying jobs, but rather out of genuine interest and passion for the field.
With that, my interview concluded.
(Some of my friends were also asked technical questions, so it really depends on your panel and your
performance in previous rounds.)

4. Round 3 (PRANK round)

We all interns + grads were told to sit in the conference room except few. Then we were told that now
they will be calling out a few names who will not be selected for further process and have to leave the
conference room immediately. Everyone was very tensed. Then they told this was a PRANK and all of
you have been selected !!!!!

A total of 19 grads were selected!!

1. Online Assessment (61 students shortlisted for the OA)

This was an online assessment consisting of 4 sections conducted on Mettl Tests platform. The duration of the
entire assessment was 45 minutes.

1. SQL based MCQs (10 questions): Some general questions on SQL basics, queries, syntax etc.

2. Computer Fundamentals (10 questions): Mainly OOPs questions of easy difficulty

3. Simple Coding Problem: kth Maximum number in an array

4. Advanced Coding Problem: Longest Common Subsequence

The SQL MCQs were mostly easy/medium although some of the SQL problems were a bit tricky. OOPs
questions were pretty standard ones. Practicing MCQs on online platforms such as GFG was sufficient. I was
able to solve both the Coding problems while having spared time for the MCQs as well. The entire test was
only of 45 minutes however, so speed was key.

2. Tech Interview 1 (19 students appeared for the Interviews)

The interview is mainly about your resume and listed projects/internships. Expect question s based on
programming languages, SQL, questions on core computer subjects DBMS, OOPs, CCN and OS. I was also
asked questions on Python and Python libraries. List vs Arrays vs Tuples, explain the Pandas data frame,
NumPy arrays etc.  These questions are also dependent on the skills mentioned on the resume which is useful
to keep in mind. The round lasted for about 30-35 minutes.

3. Tech Interview 2

The interview started off with 'Tell me about yourself'. Following which I was told to write some SQL queries.
One of the problems were about a transaction table with used_id, date, security_id and the goal was to write a
query to retrieve the security_id and date which had the maximum transactions for that particular security_id.
After providing a solution to the above problem in SQL, I was asked to code for the same problem in any
preferred language and I was able to do the same. This duration of this round was about 40-45 minutes.
