1. API/ Frontend Development Round

2. Technical Round 1 (DSA)

3. Technical Round 2 (Relational database schema design and queries)

4. Culture Fit Round

1.     API / Frontend Round + Explanation [ 92 candidates shortlisted for this round based on resume]

First round was an API / Frontend Development R ound. You ca n choose to w ork on either the API
development (3 hours) or the frontend  (2 hours). I had chosen API development. A detailed document
describing all use cases, endpoints and sample inputs and outputs will be shared through mail  on the day
of interview. Some problem statements I have come across are: Library management system (admin can
post a boo k, users can borrow a book if it is not already borrow ed, browse different books using title
search), InShorts-like platform (admin can post shorts, users can search and filter shorts, view all shorts in
a sorted order).
Common requirements are of the form: allowing user to signup, login (auth using JWTs), allowing admin
to create a resource using an API key, allowing all users (unauthenticated as well) to browse all resources,
allowing authenticated users to book/borrow a resource or use advanced search and filters.  5-6 endpoints
had to b e developed. We were allowed to use any language and backend framework of our ch oice like
Node/Express, Python/Django or Java /Spring Boot, but the database must be compulsorily MySQL or
PostgreSQL.
After the development is done, there will be an evaluation o f your solution. I was asked to walk through
the database schema (tables and attributes) and then the entire code for the API, explaining in brief what
each file does and implementation of each endpoint. This was followed by demo o f the API, where the
panelists tested quite a few possible edge cases (invalid request body, un authorized acc ess, different
search, and filter queries). I had used ThunderClient extension for VSCode as REST API client.
Few things to remember for API round and some tips:

• Even if an error pops up during the demo or some edge cases do not pass, do not panic. Panelists will

ask you to fix the error there and will ask you to explain your approach/mistake. Even if your API fails

multiple edge cases, if you can fix those during the demo, there is a high chance you might get selected
for the next round.

• They might ask you to explain any line of your code during the walkthrough . So do not copy code

blindly without understanding what it does and have a basic understanding of all the libraries you have
used. I had mistakenly included cookie-parser middleware of Express in my code, and I was a sked
about it because there was no need of cookies in this project. Be honest in your answers.

• Make sure to push your final code on GitHub before the deadline . They might disqualify you if

your final push is after the deadline.

• Practice authentication, authorization using JWTS, CRUD operations, search, and filters beforehand

in the framework of your choice. Implementing the solution in 3 hours can be quite challenging if you
are out of practice or unfamiliar with these concepts. Keep a template ready for your project.

• Use enough dummy data to test all use cases of the API. I used Mockaroo to generate dummy data.

• Keep the API and schema as simple as possible. Make sure all the requirements in the document are

covered (including basic implicit ones such as password encryption and basic input validation), but do
not waste time adding extra features or implementing extremely complex use cases before completing
the requirements given in the document.

2. Technical Round 1 [18 candidates appeared]

This was a primarily DSA round. The round began with my introduction. Most students were only asked
DSA questions, but my pa nelists also asked a few other questions. A Google doc was shared and I was
asked to write pseudo code and any thoughts or answers on the doc. Following questions were asked:

1. Given a natural number n, find a natural number x (< n) such that sum of natural numbers before x is

equal to the s um of numbers after x up to n : I first showed the brute force solution with linear time
complexity, then optimized it to use constant time using the sum of first n natural numbers formula
(sum of first x - 1 numbers = sum of x + 1 to n → sum of first n numbers - x - sum of first x - 1
numbers).

2. House Robber and then House Robber II :  I started with the recursive solution, explained its time and

space complexity, then optimized it using dynamic programming . Then I was asked the variation of
the problem in which first and last houses are connected.

3. Square root of an integer : Gave both brute force and binary search solutions

4. You have a table in a database which contains data about app i nstalls (date of install, location, OS,

etc.). This table contains 10 mi llion records. You need to visualize this data ( number of installs in
different periods) but since it has a huge number of records and no index on date of install column , a
simple query cannot be used. How will you proceed?
I started by writing a simple COUNT(*)....GROUP BY query to get the number of monthly installs,
but was interrupted by interviewer saying that running this query will take a lot of time and resources
because of the huge volume of data. I answered that one way could be to break down the data into
chunks of rows,  run this query o n the chunks in parallel and aggregate t he results. Interviewer then
asked the term for this concept, which I could not answer. He later said that my idea was correct, and
the term he was looking for was database partitioning. I then spoke a bit about Hadoop and HDFS,
since I felt that these concepts were a bit similar

5. There is a backend application which has a POST endpoint which accepts a phone number in its request

body, and sends an O TP to the phone number through SMS. An attacker is hitting the endpoints
repeatedly which is causing a large financial loss t o the company. How can the com pany solve th is
without removing the endpoint?

Frankly I did not know the exact answer to this question. I talked about a similar problem I had solved
in a project of mine u sing cookies  to avoid mischievous use of a feature , but that was a different
scenario. I talked about IP blacklisting and rate limiting, but interviewers did not seem satisfied with
my answers. I do not know what the expected answer was.
Some of my peers were asked easy  and medium questions on sliding window (longest substring without
repeating characters, sliding window maximum), implementation of a hash map , a question on finding
missing number and duplicates using cyclic sort (similar to these questions)

3.    Technical Round 2 [10 candidates appeared]

I was asked to design a database schema for an e-commerce platform. I had to consider schema for users,
products, orders and reviews, relationships between these entities and different attributes involved.
Major focus was on the relationships, and the interviewer was asking about types of relationships between
different entities, various scenarios in which the schema might not work, and how I can modify the schema
to incorporate new requirements given by the interviewer (e.g. different products in a single order, different
variants of a single product, reviews being related to variant or product? etc.). I was also asked to normalize
the schema.
I was then asked a query on the schema I had created (top 10 products sold by volume in Mumbai). Since
the schema was highly normalized, it required a lot of joins.

4. Culture Fit round [7 candidates appeared]

This was a HR round. I was asked about my experience of the entire process, any feedbacks for the process,
my ambitions, my lowest point and how was I able to overcome, latest trends in technology I am interested
in, etc. I answered very honestly in this round as I had not prepared much for it.
3 STUDENTS WERE SELECTED FOR THE SDE ROLE

key before being returned

to answer within just one hour.

submitted it anyway and might have cleared some test cases. I'm confident that the second DSA
question was entirely correct. You couldn't see the number of test cases that had passed. Due to
time constraints, I wasn't able to finish the stats question as well. I attempted all the
multiple-choice questions, I don't believe there was any negative marking.

enthusiasm for Al, prompting the interviewer to inquire about my experience in the field. I
discussed my hackathon wins and the projects I had worked on.
The second interviewer then presented a Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) question: Group
Anagrams. I was asked to explain my approach and write pseudocode in a notepad. Following
this, I was given a puzzle similar to the Monty Hall problem. I correctly answered the puzzle and
explained the reasoning by discussing the probability involved. I made a small mistake in my
reasoning for the puzzle, and the interviewer asked me how I arrived at the answer. I explained
that I had seen a similar puzzle in a YouTube video, so I was familiar with it. While my
reasoning was close, it wasn't entirely correct.

interest in their ongoing work

4. Round 4 - Tech-2

The selection process was unclear, but those who advanced received emails. This round was also
30 minutes long and involved two interviewers one from HR and one technical.
The HR interviewer started with the usual "Tell me about yourself," and asked more questions
about my internship. We discussed my interests, and I was asked how I use Al in my daily life. I
mentioned using ChatGPT for assignments, understanding others' code, and various other tasks. I
also talked about experimenting with Stable Diffusion to learn how it works.
The technical interviewer then asked about a project where I created a neural network from
scratch. I explained that I did this to grasp the fundamentals and to be prepared to build custom
models if existing ones couldn't solve a problem. I also discussed the importance of
understanding backpropagation. He asked me about cross-entropy loss and the cost function,
which I had implemented, and I explained how these are used to calculate loss and adjust
parameters during backpropagation.
Finally, the HR interviewer asked me a guesstimate question. Getting the exact answer isn't
necessary; what matters is your approach to solving it. After this, I was asked if I had any
--- PAGE 5 ---
questions, I asked them how they would have approached the guesstimate, which led to a brief
discussion.
Pro Tip [For both tech rounds]

• Stay calm and be honest on your resume.

• Be thorough with your resume

• In your introduction, focus on the topics you are confident in, as the interview questions

will likely stem from those areas.

• Focus on clearly explaining your approach and keep engaging with the interviewer

throughout the process. This demonstrates your thought process and how you tackle
problems.

• If you're not fully prepared on a particular subject, either leave it off your resume or

avoid bringing it up during your introduction.

5. Round 4 - Chat with MD

The final round was a casual meeting with the Managing Director, where he informed us that we
would be receiving an offer. There wasn't much else discussed, and it was more of a relaxed,
informal conversation. We chatted about my family, with him asking about how many members
there are and what they do. He also asked how I was feeling about everything. It was a
lighthearted round. Before we wrapped up, he mentioned that the details of my work

location-whether Mumbai or Bangalore would be shared with me later.

Finally 3 students were selected and I was one of them.

3 rounds were conducted.

1. Online Assessment  - (Aptitude + CS Fundamentals + 1 DSA question)

2. Technical Round

3. HR Round

1.     Online Assessment  [Around 200 students appeared for this round ]

This was a 90-minute HackerRank Test that was to be given from college. It had three sections.

1. 15 questions on CS Fundamentals majorly focusing on OOPS, SQL and Java/C.

The questions were conceptual, testing fundamental knowledge of these subjects.

2. 15 Aptitude questions - Probability, Speed of Trains, Boats and Streams, Ratio and Proportion etc

Refer to IndiaBix for practicing such questions.

3. 1 DSA question:

severLoad = [3,4,5]
serverCapacity = [6,2,7]

Return a combination of the serverLoad array where sumOf(serverLoad[i]*serverCapacity[i]) is
minimum. If multiple combinations are possible, then return the lexicographically smallest array.

Base Idea:  Assign the smallest available serverLoad element to the largest available
serverCapacity element to get the minimum value for sumOf(serverLoad[i]*serverCapacity[i])

My Approach:

1. Create a min heap for storing serverLoad elements and maxheap to store serverCapacity

elements.

2. Create a hashmap to store the key->value as elementOfServerCapacity->indexOfServerCapacity

from the serverCapacity array.

3. As there can be same valued elements at multiple different indices, you can make the hashmap

of type (Integer,List) so that if the key is repeated, you can add the indices in the list.

4. Create a new answer array.

5. Remove minheap element, this is the element you want to place at a particular index in the

answer array.

6. Remove maxheap element, and search in the map for the key and you will get the list of indices

where you can add the minheap element

7. From this list of indices choose the last index in the list because you want the lexicographically

smallest possible combination.

8. Add the minheap element to that index, remove the last element from the list and add the list

back to the hashmap.

9. Do this until all elements of the heap are removed.

10. Return the answer array.

2. Technical Interview Round [ 36 students were selected ]

This was a 50-minute interview round consisting of 2 interviewers per panel.

The interviewer asked  me to introduce myself . After a brief 2 -minute introduction, ranging from my
academic projects to extra-curriculars, the interview pivoted to the projects I mentioned and their
explanations. Many of the candidate's interviews revolved around their projects/experience.

They asked me questions related to the scope of the project, the changes to be made in the future and how
I would make them. They were curious to know about how I contributed to the project and collaboratively
built and managed the work on my projects. Some basic questions were asked about the tech stacks used.

Moving on to the fundamental CS subjects such as DBMS, OOPS, Java, API etc. They presented a scenario
and asked me which type of database would be more useful and why. Difference between SQL and NoSQL
and its advantages over another. Different HTTP requests and their use cases. Questions on polymorphism,
its types and some cross questioning. They asked me about File Handling in Java . As I was unaware of
the concept, I said that I have used file handling in one of my projects using Java Script but I have yet to
explore the concept in Java. Difference between ArrayList and HashMap in Java and how can they be used
interchangeably. Can HashMap have objects as keys and other similar questions were asked.

Two Problem Solving questions.

1. Water Jug Problem

2. If 7 balls of the same weight and 1 heavier ball were present in a basket, just by using a weighing scale,

how would you find the weight of the heavier ball in minimum operations? O(1)

Lastly, the interview ended with me asking a question about the use of cloud computing at UBS.
The interviewers were friendly and quite interactive during the entire process.

3. HR Round [ Around 20 candidates appeared for this round ]

Program by UBS and that concluded the HR round.

1) Practice dsa by giving leetcode contests consistently and upsolve post contests.

2) See the execution time, constraints etc carefully for each problem. Sometimes, brute force

solutions get accepted. If you don't get an optimal solution, submit brute force and then move on.

3) DSA > JAVA > OOPS (practical implementation) > SQL > DBMS > OS > CIN

4) Take non-tech questions seriously, start preparing and mirror practicing before.

5) Remember the names of the interviewers and keep a note of it.

6) Takes notes or atleast screenshots during ppt of a company.

7) Give mock interviews to seniors, connect with alumni on linkedin and get mocks done.

8) Don't skip any company. Because campus placements are 50% skill + 50% luck, your selection

depends on the panel taking your interview.

9) Focus on optimizations in striver sheet problems, these optimizations might not help in online

assessment but would help in interviews.

10) Please make your resume using overleaf latex and not google docs.

11) Keep three types of explanations for projects

a) Short description
b) Explanation with technical jargons and project flow for a tech interview
c) Simple and easy to understand explanation for a non-tech person.

12) Maintain notes for revision, I recommend google docs, make a folder for placement prep and

separate google docs for each subject/technology/topics etc. Keep adding relevant screenshots.

13) Practice TOP 50 sql questions on leetcode.

14) Be well versed with schema and api responses for 3rd party apis / your own projects that you have

used.

15) Be ready for questions like why 'ABC technology and not 'XYZ' technology. Give metrics while

explaining

16) I recommend you to memorize solutions to standard and non-intuitive questions like josephus

problem, celebrity problem, tower of hanoi etc

17) Useful links:

a) Post contest leetcode: https://www.youtube.com/@ARYANMITTAL
b) Web dev: https://www.youtube.com/(@,WebDevSimplified
c) ML: https://www.youtube.com/@campusx-official
d) Projects: https://www.youtube.com/@piyushgargdev
e) Devops: https://www.youtube.com/@TechWorldwithNana
--- PAGE 4 ---
Tips if you have months left for placements:

1. For project, either of two types would help

a. Project with normal implementation but great cause, eg- My friend had developed a full
stack project for something related to police officers and stations. Was appreciated by senior
officer for the same
b. Project with complex implementation but normal cause, eg- I had a project which
compiles code and executes to give output (like leetcode). This problem statement sounds
normal and doesn't have much real world use case. But, I developed a good architecture for it
with modern tech like docker, rabbitmą, redis etc. I also had numbers to talk about, like 100
concurrent executions in 10-12 sec etc.
c. Plz don't waste time in generic problem statements and don't try to make projects in every
domain like BCT, ML, WEB. Learn the basics of each, but eventually master one thing. No
one cares in which domain you are making projects until the problem statement is cool

2. Try to get an internship (at least one). Don't go for html/css based internships, try to get in modern

techstack or atleast in vanilla js or jquery roles. If work is good and you are contributing, unpaid
internships are also fine (but remote).

3. Java or c++ or python is the most stupid question, Any language works

4. Dev vs CP vs DSA is also a stupid question. Try to identify in which domain you will be able to

get achievements. For eg- Eventually, I realized that I won't be able to win hackathons or do
something in open source, so I focused on leetcode (DSA) and had a Guardian rating when I applied.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) Practice dsa by giving leetcode contests consistently and upsolve post contests.

2) See the execution time, constraints etc carefully for each problem. Sometimes, brute force

solutions get accepted. If you don't get an optimal solution, submit brute force and then move on.

3) DSA > JAVA > OOPS (practical implementation) > SQL > DBMS > OS > CIN

4) Take non-tech questions seriously, start preparing and mirror practicing before.

5) Remember the names of the interviewers and keep a note of it.

6) Takes notes or atleast screenshots during ppt of a company.

7) Give mock interviews to seniors, connect with alumni on linkedin and get mocks done.

8) Don't skip any company. Because campus placements are 50% skill + 50% luck, your selection

depends on the panel taking your interview.

9) Focus on optimizations in striver sheet problems, these optimizations might not help in online

assessment but would help in interviews.

10) Please make your resume using overleaf latex and not google docs.

11) Keep three types of explanations for projects

a) Short description
b) Explanation with technical jargons and project flow for a tech interview
c) Simple and easy to understand explanation for a non-tech person.

12) Maintain notes for revision, I recommend google docs, make a folder for placement prep and

separate google docs for each subject/technology/topics etc. Keep adding relevant screenshots.

13) Practice TOP 50 sql questions on leetcode.

14) Be well versed with schema and api responses for 3rd party apis / your own projects that you have

used.

15) Be ready for questions like why 'ABC technology and not 'XYZ' technology. Give metrics while

explaining

16) I recommend you to memorize solutions to standard and non-intuitive questions like josephus

problem, celebrity problem, tower of hanoi etc

17) Useful links:

a) Post contest leetcode: https://www.youtube.com/@ARYANMITTAL
b) Web dev: https://www.youtube.com/(@,WebDevSimplified
c) ML: https://www.youtube.com/@campusx-official

1. For project, either of two types would help

a. Project with normal implementation but great cause, eg- My friend had developed a full
stack project for something related to police officers and stations. Was appreciated by senior
officer for the same
b. Project with complex implementation but normal cause, eg- I had a project which
compiles code and executes to give output (like leetcode). This problem statement sounds
normal and doesn't have much real world use case. But, I developed a good architecture for it
with modern tech like docker, rabbitmą, redis etc. I also had numbers to talk about, like 100
concurrent executions in 10-12 sec etc.

The interview started around 9:30 in the morning. It started with the introduction: Tell me about

interviewer went through my resume and asked me to give a detailed overview of an event I
attended at NIT Trichy. He asked me about the various activities conducted there, what all
things I learned, and my overall experience.
Next, he asked me to explain the projects listed on my resume. There were few
counter-questions regarding how I implemented specific functionalities, and he asked why I
chose Flutter, in one of my project. After a brief discussion, he asked me which programming
language I was comfortable with, to which I responded, Java (Oracle focuses on Java).
He then asked me some technical questions related to polymorphism, early binding, late
binding, encapsulation and the main pillars of OOPs (Try to answer every question with an
example). What is Multithreading? He also asked if I was familiar with file operations in Java
and whether I had used them in any of my projects.
Next, I was asked to write a program on paper to find duplicate values in an array of string
values, such as I'"aa", "bc", "cd"
', "aa", " de" ], without using HashMap. I was also
asked to find the minimum and maximum values in a linked list, and to check if the given string
is palindrome or not (I gave a recursive solution), reverse a string without using any built-in
method. I was able to write all the programs.
Then, a few situation-based questions like - Suppose you're working on a project with a
colleague from the mechanical department who lacks technical expertise. How would you
effectively collaborate with him to ensure the project's success, while addressing any technical
challenges that arise?
Suppose you are managing both your tech team and a client, explain the key steps involved
from project initiation to delivery. How will you handle both of them? As I answered, to which he
said you are missing out on something, after a hint i said feasibility study which was correct.

situation properly and make sure your answer reflects key skills like teamwork, time

very well, and I was able to answer all the questions confidently.

3. Technical Round 2 + HR [ Around students students were shortlisted for this round]

The second round started around 2:30 pm after the lunch break. It started with the panelist
introducing himself, he was a Senior Lead with expertise in software development and product
implementation at Oracle. He then reviewed my resume and asked me to introduce myself.
Following this, he asked me to explain one of the project listed on my resume. (Only include
those projects you're 100% confident about, as they may ask in-depth questions).
Then he asked me about MVC architecture and whether I used it in my project to which I
replied Yes! and I explained it, then the following question was how does mvc works in your
project. I explained the complete flow of the project. Then next was where do we write Business
logic? So I explained that the Model handles the application's data and business logic, while the
controller manages how user input from the View interacts with the Model. He then asked me to
explain client-server architecture, what is REST API?, and why is an API considered
RESTful? I was able to answer these questions confidently.
Next question was If I was familiar with microservices, to which I said I'm not much aware of
the concept, he responded, "Okay, no problem." He then asked me about multithreading and
told me to write a query to find the highest salary for each department. I did that part.
Then I was asked to write on paper how to hash a string by replacing each character with a
letter which is 5 letters ahead alphabetically.
Since I had mentioned various sports achievements, he asked situation-based questions about
my strategy and planning, particularly focusing on how I would manage my team. One of the
situation based question was: Suppose you are leading a team on a critical project with a
short deadline, but one team member is underperforming. How would you help them
improve, keep the project on track, and keep the team motivated?
He also asked me about the certifications listed on my resume. At times even if you don't know
the exact answer it's okay, try to explain your approach. They want to see your ability to tackle
problems, how confident you are,and how eager you are to learn. They don't expect you to
know every answer so be calm and answer wisely.
Finally, he asked if I had any questions. I asked a few questions, including: What is the work
culture of Oracle?, What specific skills and attributes are essential for success in this role at
Oracle?. Overall, it was a really long interview, but I had a great experience.

The entire selection process took place in their office, creating an atmosphere of anticipation and focus. We
were asked to report by 11 AM, and the day's events concluded by 6 PM. It was a long, eventful day, broken
down into multiple stages, each testing different skills.

1) Aptitude Test:

The first challenge was an aptitude test--24 questions to be solved in just 30 minutes. The difficulty level
ranged from easy to medium, but there were a few tricky ones that kept us on our toes. The questions were a
blend of mathematical concepts, including probability, logical problems, and a few coding-related ones that
touched on data structures. There were also SQL queries to interpret and questions on OOP fundamentals.
While most questions could be managed with a clear head, a couple demanded extra thought and were likely
designed to test deeper problem-solving abilities.

2) Coding Test:

Next came the coding test. We were tasked with solving five questions within 35 minutes. For each, we had to
write pseudo-code, except for one that required a direct answer--an interesting problem about doors and
multiples (100 doors, each opened or closed based on multiples of numbers from 1 to 100, and we had to
figure out how many would remain open). One problem was a variation of the classic LeetCode "Stock Buy
and Sell - 1", while another dealt with finding anagrams from a set of strings. Then, there was a question on
matching parentheses--definitely a logic-based brain teaser. There was one more problem, but I can't recall
the specifics at the moment. The challenge here was heightened by the fact that everything had to be done on
pen and paper, which meant no quick fixes or auto-corrections--just raw thinking and careful planning.

3) Interview Round 1:

For some, the first interview was in-person; for others, it was conducted online. This round primarily focused
on projects and SQL knowledge--indexes, queries, and the like. The interviewer dove deep into every project
or skill mentioned in my resume, dissecting each one to understand my level of expertise. It wasn't a nerve-
wracking experience, though. The interviewer was genuinely curious and very patient, creating a friendly
environment that allowed me to explain my work in detail. I could tell they were looking for depth and clarity
rather than just surface-level understanding.

4) Interview Round 2:

The second interview was a bit more technical. It started with logical reasoning and basic data structures and
algorithms. I was asked to insert values into a binary search tree and predict what the final tree would look
like. Another question asked if binary search could work on an unsorted array, which led to a discussion about
sorting and search algorithms. There were also two puzzles thrown in for good measure, designed to test my
problem-solving agility. SQL came up again, with questions about different types of indexes and how they
function. Inorder tree traversal was another key topic, and I had to demonstrate my knowledge in a way that
showed both theoretical understanding and practical application. And at the end, space and time complexity of
various sorting algorithms. When should one prefer a particular sorting algo.

5) Interview Round 3:

The final interview was a brief, informal chat, lasting less than 10 minutes. It was more about assessing my
thought process and less about grilling me on technical concepts. One interesting question that came up was:
"You are organizing a football tournament, how would you create a database schema for efficient
management?". There were also questions about the workings of DFS (Depth First Search) and BFS (Breadth
First Search), but they were presented in a very relaxed manner.

By the end of the day, I had learned a lot, both from the questions posed and the experience itself. One crucial
tip for anyone going through a similar process: always have a few questions prepared for the interviewer.
Whether you ask the same questions in every round doesn't matter; it shows genuine interest in the role and
the company.

3 students were selected.

Process had 4 rounds (OA + 3 Interview Rounds (2 Tech + 1 HR))
1.
Online Assessment [ 156 students appeared]
The online assessment consisted of 73 questions with a total duration of 90 minutes, conducted on Unstop.
The assessment was divided into three sections, each allocated 30 minutes:

1. Aptitude Section: 40 questions covering Basic Maths, Logical Reasoning, and Probability.

2. Core Subjects Section: 30 questions focused on subjects like DBMS, Python, Computer Networks,

and Operating Systems.

3. Coding Section: 3 coding questions:

o (a) A String subsequence problem. Link
o (b) A sliding window problem (medium-level LeetCode question).

• (c) A Graph traversal problem. (level Order)

I managed to fully solve the String subsequence question and partially solve the Graph traversal question,
where only three test cases were not passing. Due to the limited time, I couldn't attempt the sliding window
question.
Key Takeaway: Time management is crucial in this round. Try to attempt as many MCQS as possible, and
for the coding section, focus on completely solving 1-2 questions to maximize your score.

2. Tech Interview-1 [ 40 students shortlisted]

In this round, the interviewer first asked me to introduce myself and then discuss one of the projects from
my resume. Following this, I was asked to write an SQL query to find the 10th highest salary of an
employee. I was also given another SQL query involving group by and a subquery, and I was asked to
predict its output. As I have used pandas in one of my projects he asked me the basic syntax question to
define a dataframe and save as a csv file.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Next, the interviewer asked for the easiest way to swap two variables in Python. We then moved on to a
discussion about various cloud platforms, where I mentioned that I have basic knowledge of AWS and plan
to learn more in my current semester, as I have chosen Cloud Computing as one of my electives. The
interviewer also asked about SaaS and laaS, which I wasn't familiar with, so I explained that I haven't
studied them yet but am eager to learn.
The discussion then shifted back to SQL, focusing on advanced concepts such as dimension tables, fact
tables, and factless tables. I was able to explain only the basics, as I wasn't deeply familiar with these topics.
The interviewer was very friendly and took the time to explain the concepts I didn't fully understand.
Towards the end of the interview, I was asked about my hobbies. I also asked the interviewer two questions
before the interview concluded.
Tip: Take your time to fully understand the questions before answering. If you don't know the answer to a
question, honestly admit it and express your willingness to learn.

3. Tech Interview 2 [ 18 students shortlisted(12 for FE role + 6 for ML role) ]

This round was focused on my resume. The interviewer started by asking me to introduce myself and then
requested that I explain the K-means algorithm, which I had used in one of my projects. I provided an
explanation using a numerical example. Following this, I was asked about my MERN stack project.
The interviewer then asked me to write a Node.js code snippet to fetch data from an API. Afterward, we
discussed JWT and cookies, including how I implemented them in my project. I was also asked to explain
the difference between encryption and hashing.
Next, the interviewer asked about Socket.io and WebSockets, which I had used in my project, and asked me
to write code to enable socket communication between two users. We then discussed the chat schema I used
in the project.
Finally, I was given a simple DSA question to reverse a string without using any extra space. I wrote the
code on paper using the two-pointer swap technique and thoroughly explained my approach. The interview
concluded after I asked the interviewer a question.

3. HR Round | 6 students shortlisted (4 for FE role + 2 ML role) ]

At the start of the round, the interviewer introduced himself and explained that this wasn't a formal
interview but rather a discussion. He then gave a brief overview of Quantiphi. After that, he asked me to
introduce myself, focusing on my interests, hobbies, family background, and aspirations to join Quantiphi,
while excluding any technical skills and project details.
The interviewer then proceeded with some basic HR questions, such as:

• Why are you interested in this role?

What motivates you?

• Do you want to pursue higher studies?

--- PAGE 3 ---
It was a casual discussion overall.
Tip: Be very transparent about who you are. Don't hesitate or fabricate answers. Be curious and answer with
confidence.
Total 5 students were selected and I was one of them for the FE (Data Engineer) Role.
Backstory:
The placement process can be quite hectic, so it's essential to be well-prepared. Starting in July, I began
applying to every company that I could. Overall, I completed 12 online assessments and went through 5 tech
interviews and 2 HR interviews. After facing consecutive rejections, I started feeling a bit demotivated.
However, each interview taught me valuable lessons and helped me improve for the next one, building my
confidence and sharpening my skills.
Then, I had an opportunity to apply for a Consultant role at Oracle, which is a mixture of tech+nontech,
whereas I was more interested in core tech roles. However, I felt I had no choice but to go for it. After
clearing Oracle's online assessment, I found out that the interview would be scheduled a week later for
oracle. Just before the interview day, I had another online assessment for Quantiphi. I took the assessment
and cleared it. The next day, I had two interviews scheduled one for Oracle and one for Quantiphi.
The Quantiphi interview was scheduled first on that day. Since I had been preparing for Oracle all week, I
didn't expect to clear the Quantiphi interview. But fate had other plans. I managed to clear all the interview
rounds for Quantiphi and, as a result, didn't need to attend the Oracle interview. This was fortunate since I
was more interested in the tech role at Quantiphi.

help of DOM he said somehow correct but what exactly performs so I tried to remember what that single
entity can be so I answered him babel coz I read it in React that for browser to understand JS it uses babel as
React uses JSX. But he was like you're close but not exactly. (I googled it afterwards may be the answer was
engine.) Then he said it's ok and moved to next section.

Then he started questions based on my resume. He asked me, Let's say from the projects you've mentioned
in your resume you have to design one project from scratch how will you do ?? and what extra features you
will add? I chose my E -commerce project, I will first find out the critical and non -critical tasks. Then I will
design the database and then I will decide which database to use (SQL/NOSQL). Then I will decide the
TechStack. After that I'll start coding and then I will think of optimizing as my priority will be achieving the
required functionality.

Then he asked me to explain the project of one of my Internships (I had done 2 internships). Then he asked
me questions like why did you chose this TechStack? What improvements you can do ? How can you scale
and optimize it?

Then he asked me If I am familiar with Machine Learning?
I told that my Major project is in the field of NLP and in previous semester I had Machine Learning subject
so I've idea about it. Then he told me to explain my Major Project and asked questions on that.

After this he gave me one DSA based question. [question link attaching below].
I was able to answer this question but my approach was taking o(n) time. He asked me to optimize it to O(n/2).
I asked him if he can give any hint and he gave me one hint I told him another approach based on hint but then
again it was not covering all test cases and I got stressed and confuse at that time(please don't to this as this
can affect your performance and thinking ability) and was not able to give optimize answer. Interviewer was
so polite he said it's ok I am not expecting you to code it right now as we were discussing all on Notepad.

At this point he was done asking questions and asked If I've any questions for him (Please ask 1-2 question)
i)I asked what does exactly Edra Labs do ? ( As there was no much information about them online because
they started just 8 months back)
ii)I asked if he can brief me on the projects he worked ? (Here I got to know that they're also working on the
NLP projects and that's why he got interested when I mentioned about my major Project in NLP domain I feel
it helped me.)

After interview was done I was on phone call with my friend who was also in the process and had interview
around scheduled explaining about my interview and I remember telling him yaar mera selection nhi hoga as
I was not able to optimize the answer to O(n/2). During the call I got to know someone is calling but I thought
it could be one of my friend but then second time when I looked who is calling it was call from the Edra Labs
so I picked it up and then hopefully I was selected for next round which was scheduled around 6:15.

So don't loose hope !!
This is the list of questions I got one day before my interview from previous experiences that were available
online and most of the questions were same so please refer this and the DSA question I mentioned above is
also in this list ( integer range ke related hai).
Second Round Questions

4.  Technical Interview [Around 3-4 candidates were shortlisted]

Interview started with interviewer introducing himself. He was senior Data engineer at Edra Labs.  Then he
asked me to introduce myself.
Then he asked me about the project that I did in my recent internship. After this he asked me to open the code
that I written for the machine coding round. And he told me to explain the code line by line and he caught one
of the mistake in my code it was not mistake in logic but it actually happened from my end while commenting
the code during optimizing it during machine coding round. By mistake I commented the important line of
code which was to ensure thread safety. Then he asked me what will happened If  parallel requests come to
that API endpoint. I told him theoretically but then he asked me to code it. Honestly I had no idea about
sending parallel requests, at first I literally opened my application in two browsers and I myself got to know
that this is completely wrong. Then I told him that I can write one script and I'll create two threads to send
request to that API endpoint. He told me to write it as I was not sure I asked him if I can take help from internet
he gave the permission. I found 1-2 solutions and I tried copying it as most of the time our approach  is let's
copy first and then see what errors we're facing and then resolve. Then he asked me in between do you know
what this code is exactly doing? I said not exactly but I feel it might be the solution. Then he said if you don't
know anything exactly why are you just blindly copy pasting it and at this point I just lost all my hope thinking
I've made very bad impression. Then he said it's ok I was not expecting you to write working code can you
tell me about what and how much do you know about threads in general. And then I explained everything
about threads like why threads? what is multithreading? What is deadlock? What is mutual exclusion? What
is thread safety? etc,etc. And he was satisfied with all my answers.
Then he asked me about my Major project and interview was done he asked If I have any questions for him.
I asked  same questions about Edra Labs ,their vision and ongoing projects.

After this round I though the process is done as we were told that there are going to be 3 rounds only. But
around 7:10 I again got call that I've my HR round scheduled at 7:15 which was unexpected !!

5. HR Round[2 candidates were shortlisted]

This was like any of the typical HR round and the questions were

1) Tell me about yourself.

2) Tell me about your family members and their background.

3) Explain one of the project of your internships.

4) Experience from your internship.

5) Why did you choose engineering?

6) Are you comfortable with work from office?

7) What is your Dream company?

8) Have you applied in any other company?

9) Are you planning for higher studies?

10) Why Edra Labs?

Then I asked 1-2 questions about company's goals and work culture.

Both the candidates were put on hold by company and the result was going to be declared next day via TPO.

On next day around 4.00 pm I got call from TPO saying I got selected. I was the only candidate that got
selected.

Process Date: Online Assessment on 10th July and Interview Rounds on 15th July.

1. Screening Test Round: (90 minutes, Online Mode)

This was an online assessment consisting of three questions: 2 DSA based and 1 SQL, on Hackerrank.

• DSA Q1: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/maximum-people-a-person-can-see-while-

standing-in-a-line-in-both-direction/
First implemented using Brute Force and passed some testcases. Then optimized it using
Stack to pass all.

• DSA Q2: https://leetcode.com/problems/odd-string-difference/description/

Solved this question using two HashMaps, one for storing the patterns with their
corresponding count and another to store the patterns to their corresponding string.

• SQL: https://www.chegg.com/homework-help/questions-and-answers/7-sql-game-

streaming-service-user-engagement-analysis-popular-game-streaming-service-wants-
q131717774
This problem statement involved three tables as input and required multiple joins and
subqueries. I wasn't able to solve this one.

Candidates who were able to solve at least two questions were considered. Although there might
have been a time criteria (earliest submission) as not everyone who solved two questions were
selected.
Around 48 candidates were selected for the next round.

2. Offline Technical Round 1: (50 minutes)

Note: The panel I was allotted to was the toughest, with similar questions asked to other candidates
in the same panel. The interviewer focused more on core Java concepts and workings rather than
DSA or resume-based questions. This situation is rare, so don't feel demotivated. Focus on OOPs,
core subjects, DSA, and have a good understanding of your preferred language.
The interview began with the question, "Tell me about yourself." When I mentioned my preferred
language is Java, he asked what I have used from the Collections framework. Then, he inquired about
the implementation of HashMaps in Java and how a String object gets hashed and stored in the map.
I wasn't sure about the exact implementation, so I tried explaining my understanding, but he wasn't
satisfied. I admitted that I didn't know.
Next, he asked: given two lists containing characters (where the frequency and order of characters
don't matter), compare the two lists for equality. I suggested using a Set to store characters from one
list and then check the other list against this Set. He said I couldn't traverse the list. I considered
using the .equals() method, but it also iterates internally. I asked for a hint, and then he asked me
whether we can add the whole list of characters into a Set. I explained that although we can add the
whole list, this wouldn't work since both list objects would be seen as different, even with the same
unique characters.
He then moved to Multithreading. The scenario involved multiple threads accessing a method,
where each new thread must be allocated a unique successive ID, starting from 100. I suggested
using semaphores for mutual exclusion and was asked to implement it, but I didn't know how. He
also asked me another question to which he only said that it was company-level Java (I don't recall
the exact question).
Next, he asked me to create a custom comparator for an employee class to first sort by name
lexicographically, and if names are the same, then by age in ascending order. He then asked how to
create an immutable class. Initially, I said encapsulation, but he pointed out it wouldn't work. I then
mentioned using the `final` keyword, but he wasn't satisfied. He later explained that creating a clone
of the original object and returning the clone instead of the main object is the solution.
At last, he asked a SQL question: https://www.w3resource.com/mysql-exercises/join-exercises/write-
a-query-to-get-the-department-name-and-number-of-employees-in-the-department.php which i was
able to solve.
Overall, I felt really underconfident after this round as I was asked about Java in depth (not just basic
OOPs and DSA level that I had done). But still I tried explaining my thought process to him before,
rather than just saying that I didn't know. At the end, I asked him some questions such as his role in
MSCI and how the MSCI India Index competes with NIFTY etc.

Around 30 candidates were selected for the next round.

3. Offline Technical Round 2: (35 minutes)

The interviewer was friendly. He scanned through my resume and asked me about the Amazon ML
summer school program that I had mentioned I was selected in. Then he moved on to my internship
asking about the project I worked on and the tech stack I used. I had used an LLM in one of my
projects so he asked me further questions on that like how I implemented it, how I optimized it etc. I
had mentioned Java and Python in my resume so he asked me which language I prefer/use for what,
he asked why I preferred to do DSA in Java and not Python and also asked which one is faster.
Then he asked me a situational question that since my interest was in ML and DS, and if in the
company I was assigned a project not in a different field. At the end, I asked him some questions like
what exactly is ESG and what does it mean to invest 'sustainably', his role and some of the projects
he is working on. He explained well and gave a detailed answer.

Around 16 candidates were selected for the next round.

4. Offline HR Round: (30 minutes)

The interviewer was friendly. She introduced herself first and then asked me 'Tell me about yourself'.
Then she proceeded with asking a brief overview of all my projects, to which I explained the project
outline and the tech stack used. She asked whether I had any financial background since MSCI is a
financial firm. Then she mentioned that she was pulling out my previous round feedback and asked
me about my first round specifically. To which I answered simply that I felt underconfident during
that round as most of the questions that were asked were high-level java concepts, which I wasn't
able to implement as I hadn't encountered it before but I still tried to explain it theoretically and also
explain my thought process. She then asked me about my family background, and whether I would
be open to working on a project in different domain than ML or DS. At the end, I asked her some
questions such as what her work experience in MSCI was and how was it different from the previous
firms she worked in.

Finally, around 7 candidates got the offer.

Tips:

• Practice DSA and cover all standard questions, you can follow Striver's SDE sheet.

• Prepare all the most asked interview questions of core subjects like DBMS, OS and SQL from

GFG and Leetcode.

• Prepare and structure your 'Introduce yourself' well, include some background about

yourself rather than just technical aspects. This can give some talking points to the
interviewer and it will set the tone for the interview.

• Clarify the question with the interviewer to see if you understand it correctly.

• Ask for hints if you are not able to solve/answer the question, show the interviewer that you

are at least trying to solve and explain your approach.

• Have an explanation ready for every point that is mentioned in your resume.

• Read about the company beforehand and also note the names of your interviewers as it may

be asked in the next round.

All the best!!!

1. [Online Assessment] [291 candidates had applied]

4 Ques to be solved within a time limit of 1hr 30 min.
Ist 2 easy questions were related to XOR, 3rd ques was based on strings, and the last question was a
medium problem on dfs.
(Tip: Don't skip any questions just because they involve bitwise operations. Many students left these
questions solely due to the presence of XOR operation.)
Question 1: We need to determine the number of subarrays whose elements' XOR result has an even number
of divisors. The optimal solution involves excluding all subarrays whose XOR results are perfect squares.
However, in this case, a brute force approach also worked.
Question 2:Output the lexicographically smallest array, where you can perform array swapping operation
(any number of times) on index i, j (i<j) where arr[i]^arrli] < 4. Any basic sorting algorithm, along with the
specified XOR condition, would work.
Question 3: Given a binary string of length 'n', and 'q' queries having ranges 1 to r. For every query, you
have to sort the elements in the range 1 to r on the original string to obtain a new string. Output the number
of unique strings that would be obtained after all q queries.
Ques 4: Given a directed graph and q queries related to it. The queries could be of 3 types. Add a
dependency, remove a dependency, query for checking a transitive dependency. Just apply dfs
I was able to solve the first 2 questions completely and passed 8/10 test cases for the 3rd question. The top
30 students irrespective of the score were selected (mostly everyone who got selected had solved more or
less 2 ques).

2. Technical round 1[30 candidates were shortlisted]

--- PAGE 2 ---
Question 1: Number of Flowers in Full Bloom (was asked across all panels)
Question 2: https://algo.monster/liteproblems/1643 (was asked only in a few panels)
For the first question, I initially provided a brute force solution and then suggested an improved approach
using a priority queue. However, the interviewer was looking for the most optimal solution. He gave me a
hint, and with that, I was able to solve the problem using binary search
This question was one of the toughest questions asked overall. I was able to give the intuition but could not
arrive at a proper solution.

3. Technical round 2 [13 candidates shortlisted]

Question 1: Given a grid of NxM size, initially all the boxes would be filled with 0, and another
array of pair of integers which mention that on i-th day, (x,y) box would be flooded with water (can be
represented with 1, and 0 would mean that the grid isn't flooded). Find the maximum day for which I can
travel from 1st to the last row (meaning from the next day there will be no path from where i can start in the
first row and reach the last row because of the obstacles.)
Question 2: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable
For the 1st question I initially gave multiple complex approaches but then my interviewer asked me to think
of a solution which is a bit less complex. I gave a brute force approach and then we worked towards
optimizing the solution by using dfs+binary search.
As soon as the interviewer explained the second question, I realized that it required the use of the disjoint set
union data structure, as I had solved similar questions before. I explained my approach without any help
from the interviewer and then coded up the entire solution on paper, which increased my chances of moving
to the next round.

4. Hiring Manager round [9 candidates shortlisted]

This was the final round which went on for about an hour or so and my interviewer asked me questions on
my resume. Since I had done an internship he started off by asking me questions on that (what was my role,
how many team members was I working with and what were my key learnings). Next he moved on to my
committee experiences. He basically wanted to assess my leadership and team member skills. Since I hadn't
mentioned about one of my experiences as an executive head in the oculus events I gave him that example.
He asked me questions like how did I form the team, how did I resolve conflicts, and whether the events'
ideation was solely mine or not. Then he asked me what was the app that I used the most. He directly asked
me about the system design for this one. Since this question has been repetitively asked for multiple years I
had prepared this one and answered youtube since it has a simpler architecture as compared to other apps.
The next question he asked was that if I had unlimited resources what was one one world problem that I
would solve. After answering this question he asked me to suggest any new feature that I would want in the
Phonee app. He asked me a few questions after this which I can not recall and we ended the round.
--- PAGE 3 ---

journey.howSecured:
1. Coding Test:

This was conducted on the HirePro platform. It consisted of 15 aptitude questions, 20 technical questions
(SQL, MS Excel, Programming Basics, and Basic Statistics) and 2 coding questions (Both Easy) -

- Question 1: Given an array of numbers and a value k, we first had to find the corresponding AND

array by getting arr[i]&k for every element in the array and then

- Question 2: Given an array of stocks, each stock was represented by a number and the person will

buy the stock if that stock is palindrome and non negative so print yes else print no.
Eg:- stock = [121, -11, 23], output = Yes, No, No
I was able to solve both the coding questions but my aptitude didn't go as well but the technical questions
went well.

2. Technical Round 1: [38 students appeared]

This round lasted around 50 minutes to an hour. My interview was online, and it began with a short
introduction and from there the interviewer asked me some situational questions on React.js as that was my
primary skill. After this he asked me to explain the OOP concept and the 4 pillars along with the question on
why multiple inheritance is not possible in java using classes and how we will implement it using interfaces.
Then he asked me about try catch and why we use it. After this he asked me to explain authentication and
authorization. I explained with the example of a login page and then for authorization I explained JWT
tokens and how we use middleware for auth. Then he said what if we have dynamic user roles and we want
authentication for each role (Eg user1 should not be able to use user2 apis and user2 should not be able to
use user3 apis and so on) I answered by saying that since we have their roles in the Database we can include
user role in the token and for every api we will check in the middleware if the appropriate user is accessing
that api. After this he moved on to DSA, only my panelist was asking DSA questions. They were the
following -

- Given a linked list and two variables m and n, you have to delete n nodes after every m nodes. I

explained using two pointers and keep in mind the edge cases as well when m and n can be null.

- The second question - Valid Parentheses

At the end he asked me a simple aptitude question where I had to find the angle between the hour and
minute hand when the time is 1:30 (135 degree).
--- PAGE 2 ---
Tip: Remember to stay calm and answer the question with examples like when explaining abstraction you
can give an example of abstract class car and an abstract method engine (since every car will have its own
implementation of engine). Also whenever you want some time just ask the interviewer that you need some
time to think it's completely fine and while solving DSA questions keep talking about what you are trying to
do and while writing the code explain the interviewer as you write the code.

3. Technical Round 2: [ 12 students appeared ]

This round was offline and lasted around 30 - 35 minutes. The interviewer began by asking for an
introduction and then he asked me questions about my freelance project which I was working on and asked
why that particular tech stack. I was using MySQL there so he started asking questions about that, like how
are you using Node.js to run SQL queries, how many connections can you keep, are you re creating the
connections for every query or you have established one connection and keep it as it is. He grilled me quite a
bit here but I was able to answer decently. Then he asked about my second work experience and then some
questions about it as well like what was my contribution there etc. Then he said that he was satisfied and got
everything so the interview was done. This scared me a bit since the person before me was interviewed for
more than an hour. So I asked if he had any feedback for me. He said they give the feedback to HR and
based on feedback of every interview they decide if they want to proceed with the candidate but he told me
not to worry as he was happy with the interview. Another question I asked was about the crowdstrike issue
and if that affected the bank.
Tip: Keep a smile on your face throughout the interview. The interviewers are very friendly and you just
need to show them that you know everything that is on your resume.

4. HR Round: [ 8 students appeared ]

This round was online and lasted for 30 - 40 minutes. There were two HR's and they started by asking how
my day has been up till now. Then they asked me to introduce myself followed by questions like what is my
family background, what are my hobbies, what I do for fun, which was the last book I read and what lesson I
learnt from it (since I said reading books as one of my hobbies). Then they asked me in what way do I think
technology will affect the banking sector in the coming years. My initial answer was the offline processes
getting automated and making use of Al to improve customer services but they were not satisfied with my
answer so I asked for some time to think and then said that we still manually add cash to ATMs when they
run out of cash so making Smart ATMs which print appropriate amount cash if they run out and the Offline
KYC being done online with document verification done online as well and they said they liked this answer.
Then they asked me why I want to join IDFC and strengths and weaknesses and then asked me if I had any
questions for them. I asked for some information about the role and again the crowdstrike question.
Tip: Keep smiling and think before answering. Also when saying weakness say something and that you are
working on it and pay attention in PPT because you might get the answer of why you want to join the
company from there.
--- PAGE 3 ---

5. Techno HR Round: [8 students appeared]

So this round took place one day after the HR round took place (on 1st August). The interviewer was a
senior manager. He began by asking for my introduction. Since I mentioned that I had won a hackathon in
my introduction he asked me about that hackathon and what we created and what was my contribution. He
then asked me about React.js and why use it instead of vanilla JS. Then he asked about state management in
React and what is redux. After this he asked me to explain any one DSA algorithm. I explained Binary
Search. He then asked me about the Time and Space Complexity. I don't remember the other questions but
he asked some more questions about CS fundamentals. Then he asked why I wanted to join IDFC and if I
had any questions. I again asked the crowdstrike question and asked that due to that issue have you
reconsidered using third party services because of it. He really liked my question and answered it and the
interview was done.

6. Technical Round 3: [8 students appeared]

So just when we thought (and were told) that everyone was selected, we got a call again and got told that we
have another interview with the senior MD. But when I joined the call, there were two senior engineers who
were going to take the interview and the senior MD was just present in the call (audio and video off just
listening ig). This round also began with an introduction after which just like the previous round they asked
me about the hackathon and what was the project, what was my contribution, what were the issues we faced
while creating the project. They then asked which language I use, I said for DSA I code in python to which
they asked me the difference between cpp java and python and why python. I said that it was interpreted and
why because I was doing a DA course and the youtuber who I followed for DSA coded in python as well
and it was easy to code and better to understand. Then he asked about javascript whether it was a compiled
language or interpreted to which he asked then what is the difference between js and python. I answered that
python was more readable and in python we don't declare the data type whereas in js we have to use var, let
and const. Then they asked which data structure can be used for the forward and backward button in the
browser. I said we can use stack. Two stacks, one for the backward and another for the forward and then I
took some time to check it and then explained to them my approach of using them. They then asked what
other data structure we can use, I took some time and said doubly linked list or even a graph and they were
satisfied with the answer. They then asked if I had any questions and I asked the same questions as the
previous round and they liked the question too and answered it and the interview was done.

journey.prep:
1. The placement process can indeed be a challenging experience, but with each failure comes the

opportunity to learn and grow. This was my fourth interview, and while I wasn't initially a very patient
person, the process taught me the value of patience and the understanding that what is meant for you will
eventually come your way. It's important not to lose hope and to keep trying until the very end. The first
round, typically the online assessment, can feel unpredictable for most companies, as many candidate s
solve all the questions but only a few are shortlisted. If you don't clear the first round, keep practicing and
don't be discouraged. Over time, you will get shortlisted. In the meantime, ensure you are well -prepared
by covering all relevant topics and acquiring essential skills.

2. I prioritized overall development and avoided focusing on one specific area. Through my projects and

DSA problem-solving, I developed both the necessary technical skills and aptitude. In my first year, I
participated in various committees and NGOs, and in my third year, I took on the role of Girls' Class
Representative (CR), which further enhanced my profile. Many candidates tend to have similar
backgrounds, so it's important to offer something unique. Firms like KPMG, in particular, value
candidates with a distinct, forward-thinking mindset.

3. Placements often mostly an element of luck, but your hard work is equally important. Trust the process

and consistently put forth your best effort.

You can feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/rupali-sawale-00b169261/

1. Aptitude Round

2. Group Discussion

3. Technical Round 1 (Interview with Technical Head)

4. HR Round (Interview with HR manager)

5. Technical Round 2 (Interview with KPMG's Director and Partner)

1.     Aptitude Round

The online assessment test was aptitude based a nd consisted of 45 questions on hire pro platform there were
three sections Analytical Reasoning, Quantitative Aptitude, and Verbal Ability, with 15 questions
in each section . All the questions were of medium level  and there was no specific time constraint for sections.
29 candidates were shortlisted .
For the aptitude I would suggest solving questions on IndiaBix platform and careerride youtube playlist
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tnc9ojITRg4&list=PLpyc33gOcbVA4qXMoQ5vmhefTruk5t9lt .

2. Group Discussion [21 candidates appeared for this round ]

This round was a Group Discussion (GD) with 9-10 participants in each panel. The topic given to us was
"Electric Vehicles in India: Why are they used, and what is their impact?" We were provided two minutes
to think, during which I began noting down key points. Initially, I focused on pollution caused by vehicles.
As the discussion progressed, other candidates talked about pollution and the affordability of electric
vehicles in rural areas. I chose to highlight the depletion of fuel as a more pressing conce rn than the
financial aspect. At the end of the discussion, each participant was given the opportunity to conclude with
a single statement. It's important to note that if you're unfamiliar with the topic or don't have many points
to contribute, it's perfectly acceptable to observe others and respond accordingly. My advice is to maintain
confidence, speak only relevant points, maintain fluency,  and ensure proper body posture throughout the
GD.

3. Technical Round 1 (30-35 mins approx)

My interview was primarily focused on my resume. The interviewer was approachable and supportive
throughout the process. He started with the usual question, "Introduce yourself," and then asked for a brief
overview of one of my full stack projects, which w as a group project. Then asked about my role in the
project. After providing a detailed explanation, he shifted to security -related questions about the project,
asking how I would secure the website and the steps I would take to ensure its safety.
Since my resume was technical based, the discussion moved toward data science. He asked me to define
data analytics and inquired about the subjects covered in my data science coursework. He also noticed my
interest in both data science and web development and asked why I was pursuing a role  in cybersecurity.
I responded thoroughly, taking about 2-3 minutes to explain my reasoning.
Later, he asked some basic questions about computer networks. Although I hadn't specifically studied
cybersecurity or revised topics from computer networks  but still , I was able to answer his questions  on
computer networks , and he also offered guidance when needed.
One piece of advice: Avoid attempting to answer questions you're unsure of. Interviewers are experienced
and knowledgeable, and they prefer concise, relevant responses rather than unnecessarily drawn -out
answers.

4. HR Round  (15-20 mins approx)

The HR round was quite relaxed as well. She began by asking about my previous rounds and the name of
the interviewer who conducted my technical interview. Since she had been part of my panel during the Group
Discussion (GD), she inquired why I hadn't spoken earlier and only contributed later. I explained that the
initial discussion was centered around fin ancial topics, so I took a moment to consider more significant
concerns. I also mentioned a few points I had planned to discuss but couldn't due to time constraints.
Following this, she asked about my family background and why I wanted to join KPMG.
She concluded the interview by asking if I had any questions for her. I inquired about the work culture at
KPMG, and we had a discussion on this topic for about five minutes

4.   Technical Round 2 (Interview with KPMG's Director and Partner) (2 5-30 mins approx) [6

candidates got offer]
This round was a mix of both HR and resume-based questions. The interviewers were quite approachable
and began with the typical "Introduce yourself" question . They then asked about the three project I had
submitted and proceeded to ask basic-level questions related to computer networks.
Given that one of my projects involved machine learning, they inquired about the difference between
machine learning and artificial intelligence. They also asked me about the Convolutional Neural Network

(CNN) algorithm, which was mentioned in the same project.

The interview then shifted to HR-related questions, such as my family background, why I was interested
in the role, and where I see myself in the next five years.
The results were announced on October 3rd, 2024, and I was one of the six candidates who received an
offer.

journey.prep:
• For ppt

Make sure to attend every pre-placement talk (PPT) attentively, whether it's online or offline. Actively
engage with the company representatives and ask thoughtful questions about the company, job
description, and recruitment process. It's important to leave a positive impression on the HR team, so
ask meaningful questions that show your interest and understanding of the role.

• For Online Assessment

For aptitude preparation, practice regularly on platforms like IndiaBix. You can also refer to
YouTube channels such as Carrer rides, campus Monk, or any other channel, but it's best to
stick to one consistently instead of switching between multiple sources --most of them cover
the same topics, just with different teaching styles. Also, avoid getting stuck on aptitude
preparation for too long.
For DBMS and OS, I recommend following Love Babbar's playlist and supplementing it with
theory from GeeksforGeeks (GFG). For Computer Networks (CCN), you can find good

resources on YouTube, but I personally relied on Karia Sir's notes. If you attend CCN lectures
regularly, that should also be sufficient.
For DSA, there are numerous resources available online. Start by mastering the basics and
practicing on platforms like LeetCode, Codeforces, or Coding Ninjas. If you have enough time,
I highly recommend following Striver's A to Z DSA playlist and solving the prob lems
thoroughly. A to Z
If you're short on time, focus on Striver's SDE sheet or LeetCode's Top 75 questions for
efficient preparation.
For Java, you can refer to Kunal Kushwaha's playlist or JavaTpoint for comprehensive learning
resources. I recommend covering all the theory, especially Java and OOP concepts, from
JavaTpoint. https://www.javatpoint.com/java-tutorial

• For Interviews

For interviews, it's crucial to participate in as many mock interviews as possible, as they are very
helpful for the actual interviews. Perfect your self -introduction and ensure you know your resume
inside and out, word for word. Prepare for standard HR qu estions by researching them online, and be
honest about your experiences--never lie on your resume. Give it your best shot, and also make sure
to practice puzzles; aim to solve at least the top 100 puzzles from GeeksforGeeks. Puzzles
It's helpful to practice guesstimates with friends or solo and review situational questions in advance.
This will build your confidence and improve your approach during interviews. Always start by
explaining your approach before diving into the solution, and keep interacting with the interviewer as
you code. If you get stuck, don't hesitate to ask for hints --it shows you're open to guidance and
collaborative problem-solving!

"Confidence in your abilities is key to making a positive impression."

• General tips

The placement process can be truly challenging --Deloitte is my 30th application! Throughout this
journey, holding on to faith and patience is essential. Never give up, and always put forth your best
effort. It can feel discouraging when friends get placed b efore you, but keep believing in yourself.
Your opportunity will come too. Remember, everything happens for a reason, and while luck can play
a role, it's ultimately your hard work and smart work that can truly change your path. Keep pushing
forward, stay consistent, and trust the journey--you're closer than you think!
Remember this: in Mumbai, if you miss one local train, another one is always on the way. Just like
that, if one company doesn't work out at S.P.I.T., another will come along. So, don't feel disheartened
if one opportunity doesn't go your way--stay resilient!

Whenever it feels like you've reached your limit, remember: you're closer to your goal than you think.
Take that next step with courage and confidence--you're on the brink of something great. Believe in
yourself; you can do it!!

For any doubts you can connect with me on LinkedIn
sahil tayde

1. [Online Assessment] [100+ candidate] Aptitude + Coding

The test consisted of five sections, each with a time limit. In the aptitude section, each question required
a minimum of 45 seconds to complete. For the coding section, we were given 35 minutes to solve two
coding problems. The coding questions were relatively easy, but time management was crucial.

2. Interview [34 candidates]

After the online assessment, 34 students were shortlisted for the interview round, which was conducted online.
Though we could attend the interview from anywhere, I would suggest giving it from the TPO office for a
better setup.
My interview started at 10 AM. It began with a request to introduce myself, followed by some basic questions
on probability, such as the probability of getting heads and the probability of getting two consecutive heads.
Next, we moved on to the coding section. I was asked to solve two problems using a code editor:

1. Finding the factors of a number

2. Calculating the sum up to a given number

After coding, the interviewer shifted to Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts. They asked about the
importance of OOP, had me write pseudocode to implement inheritance, and discussed the significance of
inheritance. I was then asked to write a code to find the second-highest number in an array. Initially, I provided
a solution using array sorting, but the interviewer wasn't satisfied and asked for optimization. I then offered a
solution using a set, which they accepted. They also advised me to ask clarifying questions before jumping to
a solution.
Toward the end, the interviewer asked if I had any questions, and I inquired about the job description and
current projects. The technical section was mixed with a few soft skills questions as well, such as how I would
handle a team member not contributing in a group project or how I would manage conflict within a team.
It's worth noting that the interview structure varied based on the panel. Some panels focused only on technical
questions, others on soft skills and management, while my panel asked a blend of both.
After this round, a few candidates were called for a second interview, but I wasn't. I thought I might not make
it and was already gearing up for the next opportunity. However, after a long wait of around six hours, the
final results were announced. Fifteen students were selected, and I was one of them.
