There were a total of 3 rounds in the process. Before this there was a resume-shortlisting round.

1. SQL Round

2. Problem Solving Round

3. Culture Fit Round

1.

Round 1: SOL Round [ 46 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

The round was conducted in offline mode but on Gmeet with 1 interviewer in the panel. However some
panels had 2 interviewers. This round was entirely based on SQL for me and went on for about 20-25 mins.
Firstly, the interviewer asked me to introduce myself. Keep the introduction short, upto 40 sec. The
schemas for the questions were shared to me on the Gmeet chat along with the required questions one by
one. I was asked to copy these on the Notepad and write queries for the same. I was asked to solve 6 queries
ranging from leetcode easy to medium. The queries included topics like JOINS, AGGREGATE
FUNCTIONS, WILDCARDS, SUBQUERIES. Make sure you discuss the details about the schema with
the interviewer like the datatypes of the column, Primary Keys, etc. During my interview, even the columns
which consisted of numbers entirely were in the string format so pay attention to such details. Also, discuss
your approach with the interviewer and make sure to explain why you are using the necessary functions
while writing the query. I was also asked the difference between WHERE and HAVING and their use
cases. For a few of the queries the interviewer had asked me to give multiple approaches so be prepared for
that and if you are not able to give any just say so to the interviewer, they don't expect you to know
everything.
Some of us faced some connectivity issues during the start of the interview, so keep your laptops connected
to the WiFi and do not panic even if things like this happen just let the interviewer know about the same.
I was told that in some of the panels along with the SQL queries, the interviewer had also asked questions
about their projects based on the resume, so be prepared for that as well.
--- PAGE 2 ---

Round 2: Problem Solving Round [24 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

This round had a panel of two interviewers. The round started with a brief introduction of myself. This
round could be divided into two parts:

1) Guesstimates 2)Puzzles

I had a web- development project on my resume so the interviewer asked me "Why didn't I apply for the
SDE roleại Try to answer this question in a way that will support your decision of applying for the Data
Analytics role. Then I was asked to give a brief overview of the same project. The interviewer followed this
up with a guesstimate "What are the number of daily active visits on your website". I asked some
preliminary questions to clear the details about what I had to find. While solving the guesstimates and
taking approximations, always explain the reasons to the interviewer for the same. Next, I had mentioned
basketball on my resume which interested the interviewer. He asked me about my favorite team and then
asked a guesstimate to calculate the number of tickets sold by the team. However, after some initial
calculations he changed the question to calculate the total seating revenue generated by the team in a
single season. Again this was a guesstimate question so I asked some preliminary questions and confirmed
my approximations with the interviewer.
The next part of the interview was based on Puzzles and SQL. Firstly I was asked to write a SQL query. I
was unable to write the query but I explained my approach to the interviewer which was partially correct
and she seemed satisfied with it. Next she gave me the "3 ANTS AND TRIANGLE" puzzle which I was
able to solve with a hint from the interviewer. Make sure to explain your thought process to the
interviewer while thinking about the solution. The chances are that your approach is correct and just
missing a small point.
After this the interviewer asked me if I had any questions. I asked them a question related to my
web-development project which was somewhat similar to WorkIndia.
Overall, this round lasted for about 1 hr.

Round 3: Culture Fit Round [9 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

My interview was at 10pm since I was the last candidate to be interviewed. This was a complete offline
round with a face to face interview. The interview began with my introduction and asked me how I
developed interest in Data Analytics. Then he went through my resume and asked about a case study
competition that I had participated in. I gave a brief overview of the case study that we did after which he
enquired about my team. One of my team members had been interviewed just a couple of interviews ago so
he asked a couple of questions about the case study(The interviewer was probably verifying what I was
saying and if that matched with what he had said about the case study). Then he asked me whether I read
books or not. Try to be honest while giving answers to such questions like in my case I said I am more
interested in visual media rather than books.
Next, he asked me whether I was interested in the product or the business side. We then discussed my
hobbies and whether I was still pursuing them. He inquired about where I live, my family and what is their
opinion about me moving to Bangalore. He also asked me why I was not interested in going for higher
studies.
Finally he asked me why I did web-development when I wanted to work in the Data Analytics field and
then we discussed my projects. Overall, this was not a typical HR interview but more of a discussion to
--- PAGE 3 ---
understand my personality and if my values align with theirs. Answer the questions with a mix of your
own ideas and keeping the job profile in mind. The interview lasted for about 30-35 minutes.
A total of 5 students were finally offered the job including me.

1. CGPA: I recommend maintaining a high CGPA if possible but please ensure you don't have any

backlogs. But skills are really of a really high essence. Some startups that visit the campus perform
an internal shortlisting and set a criterion of 8.5 or higher. However, if your CGPA is low, don't
worry--most companies don't have strict requirements.

2. The harsh and sometimes really brutal reality of placements is that most of it is based on sheer

luck. Its possible that your interviewer has a possible bias towards a particular skill maybe, or he
already has made up his mind on your resume or maybe you'r e the last in the panel in case it might
be difficult but certainly not impossible. Or there were a negligible amount of people chosen from
your panel. It may also happen that during online assessment you got a more difficult DSA ques
because in OA what matters is how many test cases you passed, they don't care whether your ques
was easy, medium or difficult. But remember at the end you need to be lucky just once. Rejections
are bound to happen, learn from it, you get maturity, knowledge and a reality check through
rejections as well which might help you down the line surely

3. One thing which you need to convince is you're keen to learn, you're a fast learner, you're

curious and you are a good fit . Once you've done this you're going to be a keen prospect for the
interviewer. For resources, most of my batchmates have already posted material do refer that I'll
send a few as well

4. For CPP programmers: There are some companies that require Java or atleast some basics of

Java as a knowledge base, so my recommendation would be to go through some MCQ's and some
notes which I have mentioned or whichever you feel comfortable with as this might help you out in
OA as well as in the interview process, as the company would be happy you're fine with working
with the language and don't have any self bias about it.

journey.howSecured:
Barclays came on campus (7 CGPA and above) after hiring candidates from Hackathon and Cyber -
Shaala on 11th September, for the Online Assessment.
The process was : Online Assessment, Technical Round, Technical + HR round, PRANK Round
NOTE: PPT was held for the OA shortlists, the interviewers introduced themselves before the
interviews. If anything like this happens do note the interviewer's names and any crucial info as this
proved to be a massive help for me in round 2!
NOTE 2: Barclays and its RISES principles, these both go really hand in hand, try to relate your
work, your projects, your values to HR questions in a way that shows that you have integrated the
RISES principles without being way too obvious

1. [Online Assessment] [ 138 candidates appeared for this round ] - 11th September

This is a very crucial round as the majority of the elimination happened in this round. But the
questions were relatively doable. The section consisted of 12 MCQ's (40 -60 mks), 1 SQL EASY

(20mks) question and a Leetcode medium - Hard difficulty coding question (50 mks). The MCQ's

were allotted a GOOD chunk of marks some were, so be wary of that as well. They consisted of
mainly
6-7 output based questions (Pseudocode, Java code, CPP codes)
2-3 DBMS based questions (joins, DML, DDL operation types and SQL query related) Couple of
DSA based MCQ's
You need to have a strong hold on Java (basic knowledge of syntax and some concepts will also do),
DBMS, SQL and DSA to clear this round
The SQL query question was where we were supposed to simply use where clause and basic logic
used in EASY questions to get the required output
The coding question was on String Generation where
Given a string St of length L1 consisting of Latin uppercase alphabets only and a string 52 of length
12 consisting of characters 7 and F's only.
Generate a lexicographically smallest string S of length (L1+L2-1) such that a substring of length
L1 in string S starting Index (0 <i< L2) is equal to ST if and only if i element of 52 is 'T (without
quotes) else not.
Find the lexicographically smallest string S which satisfies the given condition.
I passed all the testcases of this question. What helped in my case is I completed my MCQ's in very
less time so I could give more time on coding, keep note of this. Also as mentioned the MCQ's
weighed a lot, so take care of that as well as many people were able to clear this round by just passing
5-8 cases as well by performing good with the MCQ's

2. [Technical Round 1] [ 34 candidates who appeared for this round ] - 12th September

(After round 1, I was hopeful for round 2 as the coding q was not completely passed by many people
so I got a head start for preparing for my interviews, many people who got shortlisted in the end didn't
think they would be, so don't do that mistake, any preparation you do will be useful somewhere or the
other.)
This Interview spanned about 40-45 minutes.
Don't be nervous as that could be your downfall. Students were divided into 9 panels and the interview
process started at 11:30. My interview was 3rd in my panel so I made sure to keep myself mentally
prepared and focused as well as talking to my classmate s which made me much less anxious. I got to
know my interviewer's name quite a while before my interview so I was prepared for the same.
Interview started with some slow paced Yes/No questions on my resume which was done to test my
patience and to control the pace of the interview (at such times just keep your cool and try to be
elaborative with your answers irrespective of them being Yes/No).
Then came intership's experience based questions in which basic things like overview of the work and
accomplishments were being asked.
Then the interviewer asked about my branch and why I still want to pursue a field in IT/SDE and why
not core (You need to prepare this answer beforehand or at least be mentally prepared as to how to
tackle this question. You can use real life examples or situations which swayed you in this field. Don't
give a really generic answer to this question as they have been interviewing for quite awhile and your
impression would really sink in this case).
Next he came to projects, he liked the premise of one of my projects so jumped into the details of it,
he asked about the projects in a little unconventional way which threw me off a bit, so beware of such
stuff. Then he inquired about my hackathons and some more skills mentioned in my resume. Then he
jumped to code-languages. He asked have I used C++ in any project and not just as a programming
language as I had mentioned it was the language I was proficient at. Then he asked if I was experienced
with Java along with C++ and Python (Most MNC's prefer Java so even if you're a CPP coder like me
or Python, try to learn Core Java concepts through Youtube -I referred to Kunal Kushwaha and
InterviewBit). I mentioned I know some concepts and am keen to learn more (They mainly want people
who are keen to learn and fast learners, so keep note of that). He seemed satisfied with my answer and
moved on to the next question as a follow up on previous ones. Asked me about my knowledge of
pointers in CPP and told me to impl ement a Linked List using pointers and then asked some more
questions about my work in hackathon and 1 basic HR question and that was it.
Then he asked if I had any questions to ask him. I asked a couple of them and the interview ended.
Few really good questions we must ask which will sway the interviewer's interest in our way but more
importantly, the interviewer could remember you by the questions you asked as well.

3. [Technical + HR round] [ Around 22 candidates who appeared for this round ]

During the interview process, I found it helpful to take note of the interviewers' names, as they were
introduced during the PPT. This knowledge proved advantageous in the second round, particularly
when many candidates struggled to recall their interviewers' names, I had insight into my interviewer's
area of expertise, which aided my responses.
The interview lasted approximately 25 to 30 minutes. While most candidates experienced a
combination of technical and HR questions, some faced additional technical inquiries, especially
related to testing. It's essential to remain adaptable and open-minded throughout the process.
My interview commenced with the classic "Tell me about yourself" question. This is a crucial aspect
of the interview, as it sets the tone and allows you to steer the conversation. I provided a clear and
concise response regarding my academic background, wh ich seemed to resonate positively with the
interviewer.
The discussion then shifted to my internships and projects. I took the opportunity to explain my projects
while subtly integrating the RISES principles where applicable.
Following this, the interviewer posed an SQL query question that was straightforward but included
certain restrictions. I was able to answer it effectively and move on to the next question.
Next came an HR scenario: "If you were assigned a job that you truly disliked, how would you approach
this situation?" I crafted a detailed and thoughtful response, anticipating potential follow-up questions,
which ultimately led the interviewer to refrain from asking any further inquiries.
The interview concluded with a few questions from me directed at the interviewer, allowing for a well-
rounded exchange.
[ 19 students were offered the job ]

4. Prank Round

I was done with both my interviews at around 4:50 pm and was anxiously waiting for the results. There were
rumors that they are going to conduct one more round. At around 6.15 pm all except 2 or 3 of the candidates
shortlisted for the second round were called inside room 105. They first announced that they were keeping 1
more interview round and asked everyone if there was any problem. Then they said that they will be calling
out a few names who will not be selected for further process and have to leave the room immediately. Then
they revealed that this was a PRANK and all of you have been selected!

0. [Coding Round (OA)] [291 shortlisted (*Everyone who applied)]

Platform: DoSelect || Questions: 4 || Time: 1hr 30mins

Tips:

1. You don't need to solve all questions to get shortlisted (it's points-based with each question having

100 points, with partial marking based on the number of questions)

2. Read all questions properly and then focus on the ones which you are sure you can do.

3. Try your brute force approach (or whatever approach that comes to your mind first), there's a high

chance that most test cases or all will be accepted.

4. You should be aware of how to take i/p in your specific language, especially for space-separated lists

as input.
Questions:

1. Subarray XOR question with divisibility check

Given: An array of length n, find the (sum of lengths/count [not sure which]) of subarrays whose
XOR (^) has an even number of divisors
Approach: Bruteforce passed all test cases → O(n')

• Using 2 loops get all subarrays → O(n?)

• Perform xor of each of those arrays → O(n)

Find the number of divisors for the XOR'ed value and if the number number of
divisors is even, then add it to the ans (it was either to return the number of such
subarrays or to add up the lengths of such subarrays) → O(sqrt(x)) [here x is the max
value of xor operation that might be possible i.e. INT_MAX]

2. XOR-based Sorting

Given: An array of length n, make it as sorted as possible (and print it) i.e. lexicographically ordered
with a constraint that you can swap any two values only if their XOR is less than 4
Approach: Bruteforce passed 9/10 test cases → O(n?)
--- PAGE 2 ---

• Using two nested loops i and j, check if arr[i] > arr[j] and (arr[i])XOR(arr[j]) < 4 then

perform a swap

3. Unique String with sub-string sort queries

Given: A binary string of length n consisting of O's and 1's and k queries consisting of a pair (Ir),
sort the substring(between 1 and r) in the original string and return the number of unique strings after
performing the operations k times.
Approach: Bruteforce passed 2/8 test cases → O(k*nlogn)

• For each operation, create a new string with the sorted substring from index 1 to r, 1 and r

were one indexed

• Add the new string to a set and after all queries return the length of the set

• Optimization, instead of sorting, we can perform a counting sort. This is because of the nature

of the string containing only O's and 1's, so instead of the Onlogn) due to sorting we can
reduce that part to O(n) making the overall time complexity as O(k*n)

4. Dependency question

Given: N number of initial edges (transitive dependencies) of a directed Graph, Perform three types
of operations given k operations
Approach: 9/9 test cases passed
Create an initial graph (adj list or instead of a list in the hashmap, you can have a set making
the delete operation more efficient),
Types of operations, Given k operations,
Type 1: Insert a new dependency i.e. add a new edge u,v to the pre-existing graph → O(1)
Type 2: Delete a dependency i.e. edge u,v (not necessary that it already exists) → O(1)
Type 3: Given u,v check if a path exists between them (apply DFS), the exact wording wasn't
to check if a path exists but after giving it some thought and dry running the example test
case it was easy to understand → O(V + E)
[Technical Round 11[30 Shortlisted]
This interview happened the very next day of the OA so there was little to no time for any last-minute prep.
The interview began with my introduction followed by my interviewer's introduction. It is important to be
attentive to their intro. Asking questions at the end of the interview aligning to their role makes a difference.
In my case, the interviewer was a backend developer managing customer experiences (such as the chatbot in
the app). I was curious about the fact that they had 100+ microservices, something that was highlighted
during the PPT. Also, I was curious about their reliance on cloud providers (if any, SPOILER alert, they
don't use any cloud providers, everything is on-premise). I asked these 2 questions at the end of the
interview and we had quite a discussion on them. Also, my interviewer was quite impressed with my
introduction as he found it to be quite relevant, especially my work experience and the cloud part that I had
worked on.
I was asked 2 DSA questions, the second one was common for all panels occurring concurrently.

1. Given an array of messaging queues, each element in the array houses the number of messages in

each queue. At time H minutes, all the messages in the queues get cleared out. You have a
single-threaded process that can consume K messages/minute. Find the minimum k value such that
you can consume all messages present in each queue before the reset operation happens after H
minutes. The consuming process can't move to the next queue until all messages have been
--- PAGE 3 ---
consumed. Also if you have say 30 messages in queue 0 and your K is say 32, that means you'd have
cleared 30 messages and you could still clear 2 more messages of the next queue but that isn't
allowed, you have to wait and then move to the next queue.
Before proceeding with the question I was asked whether I knew what async messaging queues were
and I had previously used Apache Kafka for my final year major project which left a good
impression at the very beginning of the interview.
Approach:

• Over the top of my head, I said that the max value of the array should be the K value, but that

was wrong because there is also the I value that you need to consider. Also at this point, I
clarified with the interviewer that the value of H should necessarily be greater than or equal
to the length of the Queue to which the interviewer agreed.

• The interviewer then gave me the correct answer for the initial test case which made me

realise that it could be any value between the minimum and maximum value of the array.
After which it dawned on me that this is pretty much a binary search with a check function
that verifies whether or not the selected value (mid) works within the H value constraint

• To solidify my approach, I asked for another test case and performed a dry run explaining

each step to the interviewer. He agreed that this was the correct and optimal approach.

2. Given an array of pairs of start and end time (s,e) indicating when a flower is visible in a garden

where s and e are inclusive. Find the number of flowers that are visible to the i person given we
have the time at which the person visits the garden:
Approach:

1. (Brute force) Simply go through the people, with a nested loop and go through the pairs of

start and end time and you can find the number of visible flowers. This approach but the TC
would be ON*M), where N is the number of people and M is the number of flowers.

2. I was asked to optimise and after talking about the complexity of the previous solution, All I

could think of was binary search. I just straight up asked the interviewer what the expected
TC would be of the optimal solution and they said if they told me that I would know exactly
what to do. So I asked for one more test case and tried my binary search approach by sorting
the pairs based on start time. It was correct for person[0] but not for person[1]. When I did
this dry run, the interviewer told me that I was on the right path and asked me to maybe think
of using two binary searches as my approach was failing for a specific edge case.

3. I then made a sorted copy of the pairs, sorted based on the end times and tried my same

approach, I performed 2 binary searches, the first one returned the index up to which all
flowers had been sown using the check that the start_time <= target (ith persons visit time).
This consisted of flowers that died as they no longer were visible.

4. This is where the second Binary search comes into play, you find the number of flowers that

have died (i.e not visible) before the target time i.e check if end time < target.

5. The number of flowers visible is the absolute difference between the two indexes returned

from each of the Binary Searches
I was asked my preferred language to code and then I was asked to write the code for both problems and a
brief description of the Time and Space complexity of the solutions.

Tips:

--- PAGE 4 ---

1. A wrong approach won't reduce your chances of getting selected, the interviewer will immediately

correct you. All you have to do is understand why your approach is wrong and then patch your
approach or move to a new approach.

2. Ask for test cases and do dry runs on them whilst explaining your approach. You can ask for hints

but don't ask for optimal time complexity hints.

3. Time and Space complexity is a must.

After asking my questions, I was sent for my 3i round immediately, instead of the 2"d round
2.
[Technical Round 21[14 Shortlisted]
In my case, this round happened after round 3. I had 2 interviewers in my panel and was again asked 2 DSA
questions. Similar to the previous round I was first asked my introduction but I purposefully cut short on it,
because I was informed that this Round would have 2 questions that had to be solved within 50 minutes
with the last 5 minutes for Questions from my end.

1. Given a N*M matrix initially set to O's, where 0 indicates land and 1 indicates water. Each day at

some i, j the land will turn into water, this is the provided input, with the number of rows and cols.
We have to find the max day on which we could still reach the last row from the top row.
Approach:

1. Started with explaining the brute force approach, performing dfs from each element of the top

row (if it is O) and if we reach the bottom then we return true. Followed by which we will fill
the grid based on the input one by one and trying the dfs operation again. This approach was
agreed to be correct but an optimization was needed.

2. I struggled a bit here for a few mins, I did optimize it slightly but that would reduce the

amortized complexity rather than the asymptomatic complexity and is much more reliant on
the Test case.

3. I asked for a hint on what exactly from my approach should I optimise because I was clear

that there is no other way better way than DFS to know if I can reach the bottom. The
interviewer agreed and said that I needed to reduce the number of DFS calls that I was
making. That's when it struck me that I have to perform a binary search on the input array
(indicating positions) fill up to the mid of each iteration of the binary search and then perform
DFS. This approach was accepted by both interviewers followed by being asked to write and
explain the code and a time complexity discussion.

2. LC 1579. Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable

This question was quite tricky, I knew this question and the name of the algorithm (Union-Find) that
is required to solve this question as it was part of this year's LC Daily questions. I had forgotten how
the algorithm worked, so I proceeded to solve it with a completely open mind.
I gave them a backtracking approach but at the same time I acknowledged that the Time Complexity
of such a solution would be exponential. After this the interviewer gave me a hint regarding how I
should treat Alice and Bob as 2 different graph components. This is exactly what I had done while
solving this question on LC but without knowing how the algo worked completely, I was again stuck
I took a few test cases to try and get to the answer of that test case. Using the previous hint, I created
the two components and then told the interviewer that the superimposition of both graphs would
result in the graph consisting of the minimum edges. They agreed but by that time I had run out of
time. I was quite nervous that maybe I had flunked this round but the interviewer told me that I
--- PAGE 5 ---
should look up the Union-Find Algorithm and also that I was pretty close to the solution which gave
me some hope.
I asked a few questions based on their role, they both were in the same team working as Sr. Backend
Developers in the Billings team (the section of recharges, bill payments, etc in the app)

3. [Tech+HR Round (Hiring Manager Round)| [9 Shortlisted]

I was interviewed by the App Dev Manager at PhonePe who led around 20 teams at PhonePe. This was not
exactly an HR round because the people interviewing had technical knowledge. Now that I'm writing about
this experience, one thing that I feel helped seal the deal with my manager was that I was quite considerate
about my behaviour, For example: I had to take the stairs to reach the lab where my interview would take
place and as soon as I got in along with the interviewer, he asked me about the 1s work exp on my resume.
As soon as I started my breath got heavy because I came in a hurry and took the stairs, the interviewer told
me that at one point he was also on the other side and that it was alright if I needed a break for a few
minutes. I asked whether I could have some water and also asked him If he wanted some water.
After I was back in a minute or two, the interviewer asked a few questions such as where I live and a bit
about my family members, their background, etc. These are standard questions that are asked to calm a
candidate down.
Tip: You can always ask for a few minutes before the interview especially if you need water or something
specific.
After these standard questions, we came back to the initial questions, about my work exp. There was a
detailed discussion on how I was able to get that opportunity (it was a freelance gig). A bit about how it
works, the system design, etc. The reason for the opportunity was because of my contribution in building
TechRace which then made the interviewer a bit more interested in it. We then discussed in length about
TechRace. This also got my interviewer curious about how and why I had learned Flutter.
After that, we moved to another project which was built at a hackathon. After I told him that I used to
actively participate in a hackathon before the placement season, He asked me a few situational questions
such as what would you do if your team member wasn't delivering things on time, how would you tell a
person that they are not fit for the task, have you ever had a conflict with any team member or teacher.
After this, I was asked about a feature that I'm impressed with; in any app or website and also a feature that
I'd like to see in some app. I was also asked my favourite app in context to these questions. I spoke about
Spotify and how they put the lyrics feature behind a hard paywall i.e. you need premium to view them. He
then asked me what would I do differently in this case as also the company needs to earn money as well. So
I gave him an example of a soft paywall, similar to the analyze complexity button on leetcode as it allows
2-3 free tries each day and Spotify could do the same. The interviewer liked this approach.
For the feature that I found impressive, I spoke about the Tap to Pay feature, present in apps like Gpay,
Paytm and PhonePe(I said I was not sure it is present in PhonePe). After that, I explained how I tried a
hacky way of trying to get it to work with the Mumbai Metro Card using an NFC reader app that can clone
and read data from an NFC card i.e. tap to pay cards. I told him that on inspection I found an encrypted
string. But when I tried to use it on the Metro terminal that didn't work. After this, the interviewer asked me
how the entire process works in reality. I spoke about tokenization and how some data is added as a payload
--- PAGE 6 ---
such as user_id and encrypted using some asymmetric hashing algorithm with the metro servers having the
public key that can decrypt the payload and then check in the DB if I have enough money to travel and
based on that the metro gate is opened.
I was asked about what domain I would build my startup in, given I was provided with the required capital. I
told him about an Idea that I had which I had implemented as my Semester long Mini Project.
I was also asked if I'd like to join the App team or Backend team at PhonePe and also questions such as
whether I would choose Cross-platform (Flutter, React native) or Native (Kotlin, Swift) for building a
production app. I chose Native and explained why as well.
I was asked a few basic HR questions like strengths that make me different from other candidates my
weaknesses and how I've grown away from them.
At the end, I asked them about why they were not relying on any cloud providers (as stated in the previous
round but I forgot to ask the reason at that time). I asked a few more questions which led to a deep
discussion on how PhonePe used React Native to integrate components from their Partners like Ixigo for
flight booking within the App (built with Kotlin for Androd and Swif for iOS). Also when we left, I opened
the door for him and I thought that he had left while I was turning off all the lights and fans, but he waited
whilst holding the door for me and may have noted that down as well. These basic etiquette also play some
role so be on your A-game.
6 candidates received the offer. This year all of us received I+FTE offers.

While filling out form we were asked to fill any two preferences. My 1st preference was Software
Engineer and 2nd was SQL Developer.
l.
Online Assessment [ 155 students appeared for this round]
It was an offline Google Forms test that consisted of a total of 70 questions, covering Java, Python,
MySQL, and Quantitative Aptitude. The test was conducted for 90 minutes with a marking scheme of
(+1/-0.25).

• Java (18 questions)

The majority of the Java questions focused on predicting the output of given code snippets.
The topics covered included Java streams, filtering, lambda expressions, Comparators,
multithreading, etc. There were 3-5 questions on OOPS theory.

• Python (17 questions)

The Python section primarily involved predicting the output of code. The topics focused on
OOPS, lists, and some general Python questions.

• MySQL (5 questions)

--- PAGE 2 ---
2.
In this section, we had to predict the query. The topics included joins, aggregate functions,
and others. The difficulty level of these questions was comparable to the medium level
questions in the database section of LeetCode.

• Quantitative Aptitude (30 questions)

This section was quite challenging. The questions were based on topics such as mixture or
alligation, probability, permutation and combination, problems on trains, speed and distance,
etc.
Technical Interview [ 49 students appeared for this round]
There were a total of 8 panels, with distribution based on role preference. My panel included 4
candidates, and I was the last one to be interviewed. There were two interviewers in my panel. The
interview lasted approximately 55-70 minutes.

1) How was your test?

2) What is your primary language?

3) Why did you choose JAVA? [ Try to use few benefits of JAVA and then include what motivated you

to use JAVA (I said about how the 2nd sem course on OOPS with C++ motivated me)]

4) Why JAVA is called as Object Oriented Language? (4 pillars of OOPS)

5) Define all 4 pillar of OOPS

6) Use three classes Shape, Rectangle, Square to explain all those concepts (Write code on paper).

Many follow up questions were asked on this.
Few of them are:

• Initially i didn't mentioned whether my Shape class is abstract or Interface.

So they asked me when do you use Shape class in this scenario? Then i introduced interface
in my code.
Following with what is Abstract class and Interface in JAVA. Differences between them.
While giving answer I introduced Diamond problem in JAVA. ( Issue with Multiple
Inheritance in JAVA). Then they asked me can you define methods in abstract class and in
interface.

• Then one of the interviewer gave me 4 codes of creating an object of the class (Considering

shape is not an interface) then told me to tell how they would run or behave. While answering
one of the code i introduced super keyword. And there were follow ups on this as well.

7) Then they gave me a simple question to write a code to print 1 to n numbers without using for loop.

8) Then they move forward with SQL query. They just asked one sql query to me but i was expecting

more follow ups on the basis of tables they gave me.
Employee Table
Department Table
emp_id
name
salary
city
dept_id
dept_id name
Find the max salary on the basis of each city and the name of person getting that salary.

9) At last they asked me a well known puzzle: Puzzle Mislabeled Jars - GeeksforGeeks

10) Finally they asked me if I have any questions for them.

I asked them two questions:
Q1) I asked them that they had mentioned in their ppt that ESG's was introduced in 2021 in ISS, so
what were the changes you would have been observed in ISS growth wrt to ESG during these 3
years? (My interviewer was working in ESG from last 3 years)
Q2) What if government releases a new policy that has to be implemented by the next day itself? As
clients would be expecting the changes by the next day. So what do ISS would do if they got into
--- PAGE 3 ---
some situation like this? [This was a random question I thought (I personally think it was not a good
question but luckily interviewers were appreciating the above questions)]

3. HR Round [ 17 students appeared for this round]

In the final round, there were two interviewers: the HR representative and the Director of ISS. The
interview lasted approximately 25 minutes.

1. They asked me about my day.

2. Then asked me about my Introduction including my family background, what i do in my free time

and where do I live?

3. Then told me to take one project which you like most or enjoyed most and give me a brief

introduction about it. [I mentioned my Major project as it was the one which i have been working on
for 4 months and gave them a brief introduction]

4. Then asked me about challenges faced in this project [I discussed how I was working on Texas

instruments microcontroller and how I was able to gather information from the documentation of diff
microcontrollers of the same family to sort the issues which i was facing]

5. As i had mentioned about playing/watching cricket as my hobby in my introduction, HR asked about

the recent series between India and Sri Lanka [ I told her that after T20 world cup 2024 I have not
watched any live match. I do know about this series but i am unaware of the results ]

6. She asked me if I had sat for any other companies that visited the campus?

7. Are you comfortable with travelling?

8. Then she told me that would you be open for the different role as well because they are hiring in

general and not for a specific role?

9. At last they asked Do you have any questions?

I asked few question:

• What would be the differences be between my collaboration with teams at ISS and the

collaboration which I did in one of my project discussed? Then I asked a follow up: Can you
elaborate more on global collaboration at ISS which you mentioned?

• After that I elaborated more that how i documented my Major project (as it was govt funded

project and would be active for more 2-3 years and the requirements from sponsors do
change. So we have documented it in a way that if anyone had to work on that project can
continue it easily with help of our documented work). So at ISS the documentation is
completed after the project or while working on that project like I did?
Finally 12 students got the offer!!!

journey.prep:
1. CGPA: I recommend maintaining a high CGPA if possible. Some startups that visit the campus

perform an internal shortlisting and set a criterion of 8.5 or higher. However, if your CGPA is low,
don't worry-most companies don't have strict requirements.

2. The harsh reality of placements is that most of it is based on sheer luck. From my experience, I can

tell that it may happen that your interview went very well and you were not selected or your panel
was extremely strict and was asking very difficult questions. It may also happen that during online
assessment you got a more difficult DSA ques because in OA what matters is how many test cases
you passed, they don't care whether your ques was easy, medium or difficult.
But remember at the end you need to be lucky just once.

3. Learn to handle rejections, as they are part of the process. Personally, I gave interviews in 11

companies and in 3 of them I got rejected in the last(HR) round. Getting rejected at the last stage can
be really disheartening, and it takes a lot of resilience to pick yourself up and start preparing for the
next company from scratch.

4. Do show the interviewers that you are eager to learn new technologies and adapt to different

challenges. Highlight your curiosity and openness to growth, as many companies value candidates
who are proactive about upskilling and staying updated with industry trends. Demonstrating this
mindset can set you apart from others.

5. Even if Java is not your primary language, it's beneficial to learn the basic concepts and practice a

few programs on the online GDB. Many companies visiting campus tend to prefer Java, so having a
solid grasp of it can significantly improve your chances during interviews.
I am not attaching any links for DSA, OOPS, Java etc. Most of my peers have done that so do refer to their
docs.
Feel free to contact me for any doubts -: linkedin
Finally all the best and remember "What is meant for you will find its way to you." So don't give up.

Initially, the CGPA requirement for applying was set at 7, but it was later communicated by the TPO that
candidates with a CGPA above 6.5 are eligible to apply.

1. Online Test [138 students appeared for this round]

The online test took place on campus on 11/9/24. We were asked to report to the college at 7.45 am and the
test was scheduled at 8 am.
The test was 1 hr 30 mins long. It consisted of CS fundamentals MCQS (variable marks), a 10 marks SQL
query and a 50 marks coding question.
There were 12 MCQS in total that were mostly related to OOPS, SQL and general output of the given code
snippets.
The coding ques was similar to
https://leetcode.com/discuss/interview-question/4006812/String-Generation-OA-Question
The SQL query was really simple, I don't remember it exactly but I could solve it easily with a simple
'WHERE' clause.
--- PAGE 2 ---
I was able to solve most of the MCQS, SQL and passed 8/10 test cases of the DSA ques.
Try to solve DSA ques first as it has the most marks and can solely decide whether you get selected for the
next round or not. First, try to pass as many test cases as possible using a brute force approach, and then
focus on optimizing the solution.
After this, the shortlist was announced on the same day at 5pm. 34 students were shortlisted for the PPT and
interview rounds which were scheduled the next day.
PPT
The pre-placement talk (PPT) was scheduled for 12/9/24. The shortlisted candidates were asked to report
to Room 105 at 9:00 AM, but the PPT actually began at 10:40 AM. Make sure to pay attention during
the PPT, as they covered important details about Barclays' history, locations, roles, and values. The
interviewer may ask questions like, "What do you know about Barclays?" or "What was your favorite
part of the PPT?"

3. Technical Interview [ 34 students appeared for this round]

Duration -: 1 hr 15 mins
Immediately after the PPT the interviews were scheduled. There were a total of 9 panels taking
interviews simultaneously. I was last in my panel. When I was called for the interview it was announced
that it was lunch time and my interview will be conducted after lunch. But until then they released a
preliminary shortlist for the second round for those who were done with their interviews.
So my round actually happened at 3pm. I was first asked to introduce myself and explain my projects.
Make sure to have a good introduction and when discussing your projects, start by explaining the
problem statement, followed by the team size, your role and contributions, the technology stack used,
and finally, the use cases of the project. If the project was a part of a hackathon do mention that.
The project discussion lasted approximately 25-30 minutes. Since my projects were primarily focused on
machine learning and deep learning, I was asked to explain some of the algorithms I used, how I collect
and ensure the quality of the data, and how my projects would function in real-time scenarios.
After that, the interviewer asked if I was familiar with OOPS and requested explanations of inheritance
and polymorphism. I was then asked to write code demonstrating method overriding and method
overloading. Since I mentioned that my preferred language was Java, I was asked about multiple
inheritance and the diamond problem in Java and how to resolve it. I explained that it can be solved
using interfaces, leading to further questions on that topic. The interviewer also asked about the
@override keyword in Java and what would happen if it was not used. I was grilled a lot on method
overriding and was given multiple scenarios to determine the outcomes.
Then he moved on to DSA. The interviewer first asked me about the data structures I knew. I answered
Stacks, Queues, Linked-List, Hashset and Hashmap. I did not mention trees and graphs because I had not
revised them recently. Then he asked me to write a code to implement Linked List, Stack and Queue
--- PAGE 3 ---
from scratch on a piece of paper. After that he gave me a scenario where in a class is given and an array
is given inside the class and I was supposed to write 2 functions one for stack and another for queue such
that whenever the respective function is called the array would behave according to the stack or queue
operations.
The questions were not very difficult but the interviewer grilled me a lot on every point of the interview.
However, they were very considerate and guided me if I made any mistakes or went off track.
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I inquired about what a typical day would
look like if I were working at Barclays and how the technology team collaborates with other teams, such
as risk management.
It may happen that you are still not done with your first interview and you have some people who are
already done with their HR rounds. Try to stay calm in these situations.

4. Techno - HR interview [ 21 students appeared for this round]

Duration -: 30 mins
Different people had different experiences in this round. For some, it was a direct HR interview, while
for others, it was a combined tech and HR interview. In my case, it was entirely resume-based.
After 2 mins of completing my first interview, I was called for the second round. The interviewer started
by saying you have had a long wait for the first round and now immediately you have been called for the
second round so I won't be asking you much. So again the interviewer asked me to introduce myself.
In the HR round, do mention hobbies in your introduction. I mentioned traveling and exploring different
places as one of my hobbies. So the interviewer asked about the places I visited recently.
After this the interviewer gave their formal introduction and explained to me the values of Barclays.
I mentioned in my introduction that my CGPA was above 9. The interviewer then asked how I managed
to maintain such a high CGPA, especially given my background in EXTC while studying predominantly
computer science subjects. They then asked me whether I would prefer a job in core or software. For
people belonging to EXTC background this question will be always asked directly or indirectly in the
interviews.
Then they moved on to my resume and asked me about my projects which I had worked on. Again as
most of my projects were related to ML they asked me to explain the model building process right from
collection of data to deploying the model. Then they asked if I had any knowledge of DevOps. I shared
my understanding of the concept.
Finally they asked whether I would be willing to work on a tech stack I have never used before. This is a
very common question. Do answer this question with utmost positivity and give examples for the same.
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I asked about the training program at
Barclays.
For this round particularly do read about the values of Barclays 'RISES" from their website.
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Prank Round

I was done with both my interviews at around 5 pm and was anxiously waiting for the results. There
were rumors that they are going to conduct one more round. At around 6.15 pm all except 2 or 3 of the
candidates shortlisted for the second round were called inside room 105. They first announced that they
were keeping 1 more interview round and asked everyone if there was any problem. Then they said that
they will be calling out a few names who will not be selected for further process and have to leave the
room immediately. Then they revealed that this was a PRANK and all of you have been selected!
A total of 19 students received the FTE offer.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. CGPA: I recommend maintaining a high CGPA if possible. Some startups that visit the campus

perform an internal shortlisting and set a criterion of 8.5 or higher. However, if your CGPA is low,
don't worry-most companies don't have strict requirements.

2. The harsh reality of placements is that most of it is based on sheer luck. From my experience, I can

tell that it may happen that your interview went very well and you were not selected or your panel
was extremely strict and was asking very difficult questions. It may also happen that during online
assessment you got a more difficult DSA ques because in OA what matters is how many test cases
you passed, they don't care whether your ques was easy, medium or difficult.
But remember at the end you need to be lucky just once.

3. Learn to handle rejections, as they are part of the process. Personally, I gave interviews in 11

companies and in 3 of them I got rejected in the last(HR) round. Getting rejected at the last stage can
be really disheartening, and it takes a lot of resilience to pick yourself up and start preparing for the
next company from scratch.

4. Do show the interviewers that you are eager to learn new technologies and adapt to different

challenges. Highlight your curiosity and openness to growth, as many companies value candidates
who are proactive about upskilling and staying updated with industry trends. Demonstrating this
mindset can set you apart from others.

5. Even if Java is not your primary language, it's beneficial to learn the basic concepts and practice a

few programs on the online GDB. Many companies visiting campus tend to prefer Java, so having a
solid grasp of it can significantly improve your chances during interviews.
I am not attaching any links for DSA, OOPS, Java etc. Most of my peers have done that so do refer to their
docs.
Feel free to contact me for any doubts -: linkedin
Finally all the best and remember "What is meant for you will find its way to you." So don't give up.

1. Online Assessment (36 questions in 2 hours)

1.     Online Assessment Test  (All those who applied for OFSS were allowed to give the test)

The test was conducted on Hackerrank platform and there were 36 questions divided into 3 sections
(1 coding+20 core subjects MCQ+15 Aptitude MCQ) which were to be solved in 2 hours time. You
were allowed to switch between sections.

a. Coding Section:
Only one coding was asked and everybody had received different coding questions.

Question: Determine whether a triangle formed by three points (x1,y1),(x2,y2) and (x3,y3) is non-
degenerate. Also two more points A(ax,ay) and B(bx,by) were given and we had to tell whether
the lie inside or outside the triangle together or individually. We had to return a number based on
the various possible which could happen (A inside triangle and B outside, both inside triangle
inside and A outside triangle or both outside the triangle).

Reference to what I did in the question:
i. Check whether triangle is valid or not if three points are given:
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/check-whether-triangle-is-valid-or-not-if-three-points-
are-given/
ii. Check whether a given point lies inside a triangle or not
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/check-whether-a-given-point-lies-inside-a-triangle-
or-not/

b. Aptitude questions:
There were  15 M.C.Qs which were easy and majorly comprised of basic verbal and quants
questions
I used IndiaBix to practice aptitude questions : https://www.indiabix.com/

c. MCQS on Core Subjects: This section had 20 M.C.Qs on core subjects and JAVA.

I gave mcq mock tests for various core subjects in the website below:
https://www.codehelp.in/mock-tests

After this round 40 people were shortlisted.

2. Technical Interview (40 people were shortlisted for this round)

Before this round there was a Pre Placement Talk in which they explained about the company. This ppt
was in online mode.
So the round started with the interviewer asking me to "Introduce yourself" question. Then he asked me
about my hobbies and how was my day until now. He then also asked me how many interviews I have
given till now and how was that experience. I told him that this is my second interview and also about the
experience of the previous interview.
Then he came to my resume. He asked me to explain the first project mentioned in my resume which was
my major project. I explained it to him in detail. He was convinced.
Then he asked me whether I was comfortable in JAVA or not to which I replied that all the oops concept
was taught to me in JAVA and apart from that the Dsa problems were solved by me in python.  Then he
asked me what are all the things I knew in oops. I replied to him by telling the 4 pillars and then he asked
to explain all the pillars. Then he told me to write a code on a paper showcasing inheritance concept. I
was able to do that easily.  Then he told me to modify the same code to showcase the overloading and
overriding concepts.
Then he asked me about JVM. I explained it to him and drew the entire JVM architecture on sheet and
explained each component properly (fyi he did not ask me draw the architecture but since I was aware
about it, I drew and explained it to him properly). He was quite satisfied with my answer.
Then he asked me what if the heap is running out of memory then what you will do? So I told him that I
would use the concept of garbage collection. I elaborated on garbage collection and also wrote a code
explaining garbage collection concept on paper (again fyi he did not asked me to do so but since I knew I
did it anyways). The interviewer was quite impressed with the answer.
He also asked me about threads in JAVA which I explained him by talking about the 2 ways you can
implement threads and also wrote a code for both ways. The interviewer asked me a tricky question on
try catch blocks in the code written which I was able to solve  (What if multiple catch blacks are there in
code, then which catch and how many block/blocks will run).
Then he asked me what are design patterns in JAVA. Luckily one of my friends who had the same panel
as mine went before me and told me about this question asked. So in the meantime I prepped for this
question if asked which the interviewer did eventually. I explained him about one of the design pattern out
of five which is the singleton pattern which is a design patterns type  and wrote the code implementing
singleton class. I told the interviewer that I am not aware of any other pattern.
Then he asked questions on SQL like triggers which I said to him that I am not aware of it .Then he asked
me about views which I explained to him. Then he asked me about left outer join  and all other joins

which I explained to him by drawing a Venn diagram for each of them. He also gave me a basic SQL
query on left join and inner join.
Then he asked me about the git commands  I have used till now. I told him about command like
push,clone,commit and explained them.
Then he asked me about SDLC(Software Development Life Cycle)  where I named a few models like
agile,waterfall and devops but was able to explain only two of them(waterfall and devops) .
He also asked me I have worked on react or not(it was mentioned in my resume),to which I replied that I
have worked on few solo projects on react but since the re were some  better presentable projects that's
why I haven't  showcased them in my resume.
After that the interview concluded and I asked him one question.
The question was regarding what was expected from us in the associate consultant role. What would we
work on?

Advice: If there's any concept which you are 100% confident of, go beyond what's expected by the

interviewer and elaborate much more on it. You can do it by drawing/writing on a sheet to showcase
your deep understanding of the concept to impress the interviewer.

Advice: If there is any concept which you are not aware of, don't get nervous. Always have a smile

on your face.

After a few minutes I was told that I have been selected for the next round and was told to have lunch and be
ready for next round by exactly 2 pm.

3. Techno-HR interview

I was the first one to be called after the break. The interviewer went through my  resume first. Then
asked me to introduce myself. He then asked me whether I had lunch or not to which I replied honestly
that I did not because I was very nervous and didn't feel like eating. He chuckled a bit.
Then he asked me about my hackathon project which was a chrome extension for visually disabled
people. I explained him what it exactly did and what's the purpose of it and how it can benefit people
with vision disabilities.
He then came to the other projects mentioned in my resume and asked me about them one by one.
I explained him my first project without going too deep into it. Then he asked about the second project
which was lab inventory web application project. He asked me to explain about it and gave me a piece
of paper and told me to write a piece of code describing an html file and something related to loading
a csv file in JAVA or c. Here I was unable to understand what he actually expected from me and I
became a bit nervous. However what I did was I diverted his question by asking him whether he wants
to know what I have done in inventory project(about which I knew A-Z). The interviewer paused for a
second and said to me to proceed with writing the code about the project. The project was based on

flask so I wrote one of the GET methods in my project and explained it to him. Then he told me to
write the same code in JAVA or c to which I took some time to think about and eventually said that I
don't know. Then he told me to parse a csv file having 100 records and 10 columns in JAVA or C.
I again told him that I am not sure how to do it in these languages but I can do it in python to which
he agreed and I wrote the entire code. He then asked me to read a file in JAVA or C. I knew how to
read a file in JAVA as I had done it in one of my projects. Then he went inquired a bit more about it
to which I had no answers.
He then asked me the difference between c and JAVA to which I was not able to tell much about.
Then I asked him with a smile whether he could asked me between any language other than C. He too
chuckled with me and asked me difference between JAVA and C++.I gave him minimum 5 points
of difference. He was satisfied with the answer.
Till now I understood that the interviewer was looking for some JAVA or c skilled guy so I went on a
5-minute talk explaining the chain of events leading to why I don't code more frequently in JAVA and
c anymore and prefer to code in python.

Advice: Read the room. Try to understand the demands of the interviewer. If you are somehow

not able to answer a chain of question related to a particular concept/language/subject. Try to
come up with a genuine answer explaining how and why you feel you are not confident in it and
also suggest the alternatives to the particular concept/language/subject  on which you are
confident about.
My aim was to assure him that I can answer his questions but the language expectation is problem
here. He heard me out my problem here and nodded with a smile on his face.
He then asked me "Where do u see yourself in 5 years" followed by "What was the lowest point in
your life".
He then told me that we are done with the interviews and I asked him for how long has he been with
oracle, his experience in oracle and what has he been currently working on. He talked about it briefly
and shook my hand as I was stood up and was about to leave the room.
In the end 19 students were selected and I was one of them.

journey.prep:
o DSA is crucial as most companies include at least one coding question in their online
assessments. Interviews involve a bit of luck and depend significantly on the panel you get.
Therefore, focus on clearing the online assessments (OA), as your chances of getting selected
increase once you clear them.
Solve LeetCode daily questions and participate in weekly/biweekly contests. For additional
practice, take part in virtual contests. Follow resources like the Striver A2Z sheet and Aryan
Mittal's daily questions and post-contest upsolving strategies.
Try to have a  group with 2-3 friends to discuss solutions post-contest. This will expose you
to various approaches and ultimately increase your knowledge. Consistent practice and
collaborative learning will improve your DSA skills and enhance your chances of performing
well in technical interviews.
o Computer fundamentals are also important. Focus on OOPs >= DBMS > OS > CN.
o Keep patience. Placement is one of the most hectic schedules. Don't be upset if you get
rejected sometimes; you might be hard on your luck. UBS was my 4th interview. I got
rejected at PhonePe, Work India, and IDFC. God is very kind; He may have different plans
for us. So just trust  God and keep working hard.
o If possible, try to build unique projects and deploy them.
o Practice SQL and aptitude; don't take them lightly
o Try to give mock interviews by connecting with seniors trust me it helps a lot

1. Pre Placement Talk (31-07-2024)

2. Online Assessment (31-07-2024, right after PPT)

3. Interview Rounds (01-08-2024)

1. Online assessment [209 students appeared for the test]

The test was conducted on 31/7/2024 on the Hackerrank platform in college offline. There were 30 MCQs:
15 Technical - Java, SQL, DBMS, and 15 Aptitude. There was also one coding question. My question was
given a string s consisting of characters a, b, and c. In one operation, you can add any one character at any
position. The task is to convert the string into the format abcabc… We have to return the minimum number
of operations to perform this task.
Test Case:
Input: string = bb
Output: 4
Explanation:
abb -> abcb -> abcab -> abcabc (Total 4 insertions)
I solved the coding question completely and most of the mcq's and got shortlisted for the next round

Tips:

Generally, I recommend starting with the coding question. If you solve the coding question, you will likely
get shortlisted. Even if you don't find the optimal approach, try to solve it using brute force and aim to pass as
many test cases as possible. Some students did not pass all the test cases but were still shortlisted based on
MCQs and aptitude. The MCQs and aptitude questions were relatively easier, so having a basic understanding
of the fundamentals will help you.

2. [Technical Interview] [36 students appeared for this round]

a. The interview lasted for 40-45 minutes. My panel consisted of 2 members.
b. It started with "Tell me about yourself."
c. They then asked about my projects. One of my projects was based on SQL, so they told me to draw the
schema and write all the mapping relation tables. They also gave me 2 -3 SQL queries. I was not able to
solve one query, but I answered the remaining ones, which satisfied the interviewer.
d. They asked me to explain all my projects listed on my resume.
e. They asked a few basic DSA questions:

• What is an array?

• In which cases is a linked list better than an array?

• What is a stack?

• What is a queue?

f. They asked what a singleton class is, but I was not aware of it. I told them so. Later, they asked if
multiple inheritance is allowed in Java, why it is not allowed, and how to implement multiple inheritance
in Java.
g. Later he asked me "Which sport do you play ?" I answered as cricket so he asked "tell a game which
you play on board" so I mentioned chess . So he told me to implement chess game using OOP'S in java
h. We had a discussion about my ML project mentioned in my resume. Questions were like:

• Why Random Forest?

• Explain the full process of how to implement the model.

• And some basic ML questions

i.  He asked me where I see myself in 5 years.
j. Also atlast they asked if I had any questions for them (Always ask some question)

Tips:

• Know your resume very well. If you are unable to answer a question, accept that you don't know. Even

I was not able to answer some questions.

• The technical interview can be DSA-based or project-based, depending on the panelists, so be prepared

for both situations.

• If you have mentioned any projects, make sure you know everything about what you have done in that

project. Ask yourself what questions can be asked and be prepared for them.

• Search for top interview questions for Java/full stack/ML on InterviewBit/GFG and go through the

most frequently asked questions depending on your tech stack.

• Be ready for some HR questions as well; they can be asked.

3.[HR round] [Around 20 students appeared for this round]
The HR round was a bit relaxed and lasted for just 5-7 minutes.

1. It started with the question, "Tell me about yourself?"

2. Then, they asked about my family background. I mentioned that my father is a police officer.

3. She asked why I am not aiming for a government job, and we had a discussion about the private sector

versus the government sector.

4. Next, she asked what I do other than coding. I replied that I play cricket and also mentioned other

extracurricular activities I participated in during college.

5. Lastly, she asked if I had any questions for her. (Always ask some questions during this part.)

At the end, 12 students got the offer.

[ 4 Rounds ]

1.     [Aptitude Test]

This test consisted of 3 sections :
a) English Proficiency
b) Logical Reasoning
c) Quants
It was an online test.
When preparing for an aptitude test like the one you're about to take, it's crucial to understand the test
structure and strategize accordingly. The test consists of 60 questions to be completed within 60 minutes,
giving you only one minute per question on average.
  Quantitative Aptitude and Logical Reasoning: The questions in these sections range from easy to
medium difficulty. While they may not be overly challenging, they can be tricky and time-consuming,
especially if you get bogged down in calculations or overthink the logic puzzles. The key here is to
practice extensively (GFG & IndiaBix) so that you can quickly recognize the types of problems and
solve them efficiently.
  English Proficiency: This section includes lengthy paragraph-based questions, which typically test
your reading comprehension, vocabulary, and ability to interpret and analyze text. These questions can
be particularly time-consuming, so it's important to read the passage swiftly but carefully. Look for key
information that will help you answer the questions without needing to re-read the entire passage.

2. [Technical Round 1]

I was interviewed by the Assistant Vice President of ITD at Nomura. The round began with the most
common question: "Walk me through your resume." It's important to note that while answering this
question, you are not expected to explain every line of your resume in detail. The interviewer is
primarily interested in a brief overview of your skills, projects, and professional experience (if any).
The interviewer was quite friendly and conducted the interview more like a conversation rather than a
Q&A session. Regarding the technical aspects, I, along with other candidates, was mainly asked
fundamental questions on operating systems, OOPs, Python, and one DSA question (primarily focused
on sorting algorithms and their time complexity). You can also expect a guesstimate question.
Additionally, I was asked two puzzle questions:

1. Three bulbs and three switches.

2. Nine marbles, out of which eight marbles weigh the same. How do you find the odd one out with

the minimum number of comparisons?
There were also questions on RAM and ROM (SSD, HDD), as well as a few fundamental questions
about the roles of an investment bank and the basics of finance. It's beneficial to have some knowledge
in these areas.
The interview lasted around 45 minutes. At the end, we were given the opportunity to ask the
interviewer a question. Since I knew who was going to interview me, I had already researched his role
on LinkedIn. He specialized in testing and CI/CD, so I asked him questions related to these concepts.
I was shortlisted after this round, along with 15 other candidates, making a total of 16 candidates who
were shortlisted.

3. [Technical Round 2]

I was interviewed by two senior associates from Nomura. The first question they asked was about my
industrial internship. When answering this question, it's important to use the WHY, WHEN, & WHAT
format. This round was quite grilling, and the interviewers were somewhat intimidating. However, their
main objective was to assess my confidence and body language while responding to their questions.
They might interrupt you with another question while you're answering the previous one, but don't worry
if this happens--it's just a test of your temperament and domain knowledge.
Regarding the technical questions, I was asked a couple of DSA problems:

1. A 2-D matrix question where I had to find the largest number that can be constructed by

traversing from the first row to the bottom row, which can be solved using the graph concept of
DFS traversal.

2. A string anagram question.

Both of these questions are available on LeetCode. I initially provided a brute-force approach, explained
the time complexity, and validated my solution with the test cases they provided. I was also asked to
optimize the time complexity, which I successfully did for both questions, and the interviewers were
quite satisfied with my solutions and their efficiencies.
Since I had mentioned machine learning and visualization on my resume, they asked me about
Statistical Analysis. Specifically, they asked me to explain the difference between mean and average.
They also questioned me about AP (Arithmetic Progression) and GP (Geometric Progression) and
presented me with a puzzle based on these two series. Additionally, they tested my knowledge of core
Java, particularly threads and OOPs concepts.

This round lasted around 50 minutes, and I was shortlisted for the HR round.

4. [HR]

You can expect this round to be more of a Techno-HR interview rather than just typical HR questions. I
was primarily asked about my projects, particularly the difficult situations I encountered and how I
resolved those challenges. Situational-based questions were also a key part of the interview (you can
refer to IndiaBix for HR questions).
During this round, it's essential to be completely yourself. While it's good to have a structured approach
to answering HR questions, make sure your responses don't sound too rehearsed or idealistic. Keep your
answers specific and to the point--avoid over-elaboration.
Finally, after this round, 8 people, including myself, were selected.

3. [Technical Round 21 [ 13 candidates were shortlisted]

The interview started at around 2pm. Again this round was solely DSA based.
Initially the interviewer asked me for my introduction and then a jist about my resume and then the DSA
question started.
The 1 st question was:
https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-max-number-of-edges-to-keep-graph-fully-traversable/descriptio
This question was quite tricky, I knew this question and the name of the algorithm (Union-Find) that
is required to solve this question as it was part of this year's LC Daily questions.
So I was easily able to provide the solution to this question. The interviewer then asked me about the time
complexity and told me to write the pseudo code of the solution.
The 2nd Question:
Given N*M grid initially with all 1's in it. We can start from 1st row and can move in any direction. The
goal is to reach the last Column. Each day a coordinate will be provided, and a blocker will be added to
the given coordinate. The question was to find the day from which we no longer will be able to reach the
last column.
I started with the brute force approach of using dfs for each case and then finding the answer. Later i tried to
optimize it but the interviewer was looking for a much better solution. After thinking a lot i was still not
able to reach a solution.
The interviewer then told me that we could binary solution for this question.
Hater understood the reason and then the interviewer asked me to write the pseudo code for it. Which i did.
The 3rd Question:
This question was a medium leetcode question: https://leetcode.com/problems/decode-ways/description/
I quickly gave the recursion solution for it and then optimized it by giving the memoization solution and
then the tabulation solution for it.
Then I wrote the pseudo code and explained the time complexity for the same.
The interviewer then asked if i had any questions for him, I asked about the technical challenges the
company was facing. We had a discussion about it and the round ended.
