journey.howSecured:
The entire Barclays drive had three rounds: starting with the Online Assessment (OA) round, followed by a Technical Interview, and then a Techno-HR round. There was no GPA cutoff this year; however, I would still recommend maintaining a GPA above 8.5 to always be on the safer side. The pre-placement talk took place just before the technical round, unlike the usual PPTs that occur for all candidates before the OA. Barclays conducts its PPT for candidates shortlisted only from the OA. Please be attentive and make sure to note down the points they mention during the PPT, as it helps you prepare well about the company. A company will always prefer a candidate who is well-aware of its mission, values, and objectives.

1. Online Assessment [ 133 students appeared for this round ]

It was conducted on 26th July 2025 at 11am. The OA round lasted 90 minutes and included 15 questions: 13 MCQs on CS fundamentals (specifically OOPS and DBMS), 1 moderate DSA question, and 1 easy SQL question.

In the CS fundamentals part, they particularly focused on Java output-based questions, some of which involved recursion and inheritance. Some MCQs were weighted differently (2, 4, 5, or 6 marks), so it was crucial to get the 6-marker ones correct. One question I remember involved several abstract classes and functions. The main function attempted to instantiate these abstract classes, which would lead to a compilation error, as an abstract class can never be instantiated. This question was lengthy, but if you looked carefully, the answer was obvious at a glance. It was important not to get such questions wrong, especially since they were 6-markers. Another question asked for the default values of instance variables of type boolean and int, the answers being false and 0 respectively. There was also a question on try catch blocks where I had to determine the output. One Java function involved finding the maximum value and its correct output. Additionally, there was a question that provided options for SQL queries, and I had to select the correct one based on a given table schema. It's really important to read each question properly and carefully, without missing any details.

For the SQL question, I was given a single table and had to find customer IDs and calculate a final amount that was 50% more than customer's salary who had a major accident, had a savings account, and an active salary and insurance account . It was an easy question where we were just required to apply multiple AND conditions based on the listed criteria.

The DSA question was similar to : Lexicographical String

Approach: I used a brute-force approach and managed to pass all the test cases. First, I constructed a result string with a length equal to len1+len2-1 (where len1 is the size of str1 and len2 is the size of str2). For every index i in str1 where the value was 'T', I ensured that the substring starting at i in the result exactly matched str2. If any conflict occurred during this placement, I returned an empty string. After placing all 'T'-based substrings, I filled the remaining uninitialized positions with 'a'. Next, for each 'F' position in str1, I checked if the corresponding substring in the result matched str2. If it did (which it shouldn't), I tried to change at least one unfixed character in that range by incrementing it, as long as it wasn't already locked from a 'T' placement. If fixing wasn't possible, I returned an empty string. Finally, the result string was returned after satisfying all 'T' and 'F' constraints.

Most of the students had completed the DSA and SQL questions, so everything boiled down to the MCQ round, which decided who would proceed to the further rounds.

2. Technical Interview Round [ 37 candidates appeared for this round ]

Stay calm, be composed, and trust in what you've studied. The interviewer will ask questions that are important and showcase your problem-solving abilities, not random, vague ones.

My interview began with the interviewer asking for my introduction. It's crucial to prepare your introduction in a way that clearly highlights your strong topics; with a bit of luck, you might only get questions on those areas, but be prepared for everything. The interviewer then asked me to rate my development, DSA, SQL, and database skills. After that, he started by asking me to write a few SQL queries: first, to find the Nth record from a table, and then to find the 7th highest salary from a given set of records. Following this, he asked about the order of execution for any given SQL query. For better clarity, refer to following article Execution Order of SQL Query

Next, he asked several questions about databases, specifically the reasons for choosing a particular database and under what circumstances. Essentially, he wanted to test my capability to implement the appropriate database for a given problem and the reasoning behind that choice. Ensure you provide proper reasons and clarity for your database selection. He also asked how I would optimize a given query search.

After this, he shifted to my resume and asked me to explain my internship project and exactly what I did in it and what were the various challenges I faced in it, which was the most critical bug/error I faced and how did I eliminate it. Always be prepared for questions about your project's goals, objectives, architecture, challenges faced, advantages, disadvantages, the reason for choosing your tech stack, the various alternatives to your tech stacks, possible scalable solutions, and what you learned from it. For every question you're asked, ensure you explain the concept first, followed by an example, and then a real-life application, along with its advantages, disadvantages, and any possible concerns. For one of my projects, I was asked to explain how JWT Tokens works at a core level, followed by a detailed explanation of RBAC . Make sure to explain using a pen and paper, as this demonstrates the clarity of your understanding.

From another project, they asked for the reason behind choosing the IPFS system over Docker, how I would ensure the confidentiality of a user uploading a file to my application, and how I would check if a file had been tampered with. For this, I tried to explain the working of IPFS in detail. As my resume showcased more of my machine learning capabilities, they asked for the reasons behind choosing various algorithms, what would have happened if I had chosen a different algorithm, and how I decide which algorithm is best for a model. What are the various steps involved in deciding which algorithm is best for a given problem. They also asked for the reason behind choosing ROC over accuracy and sensitivity. Always be honest with your answers; if you don't know something, try to relate it to the most relevant concept. They want to

test how you react in such situations, so explain your thought process and how you would tackle the issue. To my surprise, I wasn't asked a single OOPS question throughout my interview. Communicate with your interviewer and ask for hints if you get stuck on a question. The more vocal you are with your thoughts, the better idea the interviewer will get about how confident you are with your answers. There's no need to worry even if you're wrong; just stay calm.

He then asked me, being "more of an ML guy," how I would work on a leader's project with different requirements. In such a situation, you need to showcase your fast learning ability and how well you can adapt to new technologies. I tried to answer by saying that even though I am an ML guy, I have built a few MERN stack-based projects along with projects that use Python with Django, so shifting to a different tech stack would actually help me learn even more new things. I also mentioned that ML is something I am quite familiar with, more inclined towards, and have always loved developing projects around.

At the end, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. I had thoroughly reviewed their PPT, which mentioned that GenAI and ML domains are areas they are currently exploring. So, I asked them about the current stage of Barclays' use of GenAI at a production level and how a new intern could get into such teams and collaborate with everyone.

3. Techno HR round [ 21 appeared for this round ]

The way the first round went for me, I didn't expect to be shortlisted for the next one. I was actually heading home when I found out I was selected for the Techno-HR round and that my interview was in the next 10 minutes. I came running back, calmed myself down, and got ready for it. This round, which was the penultimate one, lasted about 50 minutes. It started with a brief introduction of myself, where I was asked to mention who I am in real life, what qualities set me apart from others, things I like and dislike, the projects I've built with their detailed descriptions, and their social impact. I was asked the following questions:

● Tell me about a situation where you were ashamed of yourself.

● What was a time in your project when your teammates had to suffer because of you?

● Suppose one of your teammates is not willing to work with you; how would you react in that situation?

● Describe a situation in life where you had to make a decision for your team that wasn't welcomed and what was its impact?

● What was that one moment in life when you earned the respect of others?

● Mention a situation where you had to form a cross-dynamic team (people of different ethnicities and age groups), and how did you coordinate with them?

● Suppose you have a conflicting idea that doesn't really work well with your project, but you've worked quite hard on it and want it to be incorporated. However, other teammates aren't willing to accept it; what would you do?

● Describe a moment when you were a liability for the team--basically, you were present but couldn't contribute anything.

● While working in the internship, was there a time when you faced a situation where you got a sudden, revised deadline that was very difficult for you to manage?

● What were some of the major challenges you faced while developing your projects?

● You were given very less time to develop a project by your manager; what would you do in that situation?

Barclays strongly believes in its RISES values: Respect, Integrity, Service, Excellence, and Stewardship.

At the very end, they called 16 people to the Conference Room, where they dramatically announced that these were the individuals who had cheated in the Barclays placement and were therefore "invited to come and join Barclays :) " It turned out to be a small prank on their part, a way to try and scare us. I was honestly filled with so many emotions; tears started rolling down as, after so many rejections and moments of self-doubt, I was finally able to crack Barclays. It really hammered home the idea that fortune favors the brave. People often say that luck contributes a bit to placements, and I do agree with that, but ultimately, you need to put in so much hard work that your efforts clearly shine through, helping you clear each and every round. It's that consistent dedication that truly makes the difference in the end.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) It's never too late to start, but the moment you do, ensure you give your 100%.

2) Never compare yourself to others. Always remember, if someone is good at a particular thing, you'll be good at another.

3) Have your fundamentals and basics cleared and spend as much as time you can on improving those skills

4) DSA is a mandatory thing to learn, without saying.

5) You won't be able to survive just on your tech skills; you need your communication skills so you can portray yourself effectively.

6) Learn development properly, no need to gpt hamesha. There were instances where few of my friends were asked to write a part of their code that they implemented in their projects

7) In an interview, always be true to yourself. Don't fake anything you don't know. Know your resume in and out.

8) Companies prefer candidates who have interned before because it tends to give you an idea of how exactly you'll work in a larger organisation.

9) Trust the process. There will be times when you will be upset , you will self-doubt your skills, knowledge, and everything you've learned. During this time, stay motivated, have good friends around you, and talk to your family. No need to worry about things that haven't happened.

10) During your interviews, be confident in your answers. Your interviewer will try to trick you.

11) Overall you need to be good in Oops , DBMS , SQL , OS, CN and all those concepts and techstack you have mentioned in your resume. System Designing is a hot topic.

12) Don't neglect the Aptitude section. IndiaBIX is a good platform where you can practice it. Also, refer to GeeksforGeeks for puzzles; they might get asked sometimes.

13) Placement kaafi lamba process hai, and you will realise you are in a good college. Companies aayengi, guys, so eventually you will get placed.

Study material I referred to during my prep:

1) System Design : If you have good amount of time to study system design in depth

2) System Design : If you are short on time

3) DSA Striver's Sheet

4) One of the finest DSA based yt channels for concept clarity

5) CP Sheet by TLE Eliminators

6) Oops in CPP

7) Oops in Java

8) DBMS : Codehelp - Lecture Notes + Slides

9) Google Drive for necessary pdfs

10) Practise SQL questions

11) CPP secret

12) GFG and InterviewBits are the best platforms for referring any interview based questions on any topic and do give it a glance before you go for your interviews

You are your own warrior, and you are here to claim that one seat

There were 3 rounds, one online assessment and two interview rounds. The people who were shortlisted for the UBS Campus Hackathon were directly eligible for the interviews.

1. [PPT and Online Assessment] [ 173 candidates appeared for this round ]

There was an eligibility criteria of 7+ CGPA.

There was an online PPT, after which a test was conducted on campus. There were 30 MCQs and 1 DSA question. 30 MCQs were split into 15 Aptitude + 15 Technical questions on topics like OOPS, Programming, DBMS, etc.

As I was a UBS campus hackathon participant, I was directly eligible for the interviews and didn't need to appear for this test. The hackathon was conducted in March (4 months before the hiring process), where you needed to give an online assessment of a similar pattern. I was able to solve the DSA question fully There were 10 candidates shortlisted for this (2 from second year and the rest of 3rd year). We had to go to the hack which was conducted in the UBS Airoli/Pune office. There were multiple colleges participating, teams were formed of 6 ppl who may/may not be from the same college. The students from Mumbai colleges had to be in the Airoli office. There were 3 problem statements which were pretty doable, and it's a nice experience so make sure you go for it. My problem statement was a Learning Management System for rural schools to connect volunteers and school students. You get to see the work culture, connect with mentors and gain valuable exposure. There were a total of 20-odd teams, and even if you didn't win the hackathon you're still eligible for a direct interview, your performance is what matters.

There were a total of 20 candidates selected after this round (14 through OA + 6 Hackathon participants)

2. [Technical Interview] [ 20 candidates appeared for this round ]

There were 6 panels for the candidates, and the interviews for Summer interns and placements were held together. Some panels had 1 interviewer while some had 2. They asked me for my introduction, interests beside coding, my goals/aspirations at the start to get me comfortable, then asked about the projects I had done, especially a project in which I had used AI. I had told them about my GenAI experience, which I had also shown in the UBS Hackathon, so they asked me about that as well. They focussed mainly on AI, considerations in AI, how to make sure AI is safe and efficient for banks, how would you handle different responses of AI for the same request/prompt. I was comfortable with both Python and Java so they asked me which I prefer. I said I do DSA in python and development in Java, which they were satisfied with. I was then asked about DevOps, which I just had a basic idea about, but they were very considerate and explained it to me as well. They asked me a few logical puzzles and as I had practiced such questions on GeeksForGeeks I was able to solve them. They then asked if I had any questions for them and I asked them about their experience in UBS and the work they got to do/kind of projects they built. 10 students were selected after this

Tips:

● Know your resume perfectly, and use your introduction as well as other answers to guide the interview in the direction you want.

● Make sure your answers align with the job description and try to read up more on recent technologies and their impacts on your project/the company.

● Your introduction should be detailed but not too long, cover all main points and topics like DSA, projects, hackathons, work experience, etc. Give a brief overview of the work you did, the fields you're interested in and how you've used those in your projects.

● Know your projects thoroughly, not code but the core concept, the flow. You should be able to tell the interviewer why you built a project and what problem it solves or what you learnt from it

3. [HR Round] [ 10 students appeared for this round ]

In this round, the HR already knew me because of the hackathon so she didn't ask me many questions about UBS/why I wanted to join. She asked me about the hackathons I had participated in and how my experience was. I was then asked about my family, where I live and some general questions.

[ 6 students were offered the job ]

journey.prep:
1. The most important advice for any interview I could give you is to always smile. Be graceful about your mistakes.

2. Do not claim to know something you do not know. That is a massive red flag.

3. The interviewers are human. Appeal to their human nature. They're tired and bored after long days of continuous interviews too.

Resources (For the lazy folk):

1. SQL: DataQuest for LMR, SQLZoo for a one sitting full syllabus study. Practice Leetcode SQL if the syntax tends to slip from your mind and if application of certain functions tends to slip from your mind.

2. DSA: The usual resources are great. Follow those diligently. If you have the time and you love coding, give the CSES Problemset a shot. I'm at the Mathematics section and it's really fun!

3. OS: Any YT course will do if you're studying it for the first time. If you're reading this the night before the interview, just read up on Processes and Threads, Process Scheduling, Synchronization, Memory Management, Filesystems and I/O. If you have more time, this Overview by InterviewBit is pretty swell!

4. CCN: Same as OS. LMR. Very, very LMR (Ye toh karke hi jao pls).

Mistakes that I made that I feel you can learn from:

1. I thought Aptitude was silly. It still is, but trust me, it's better to be able to do it faster than to have to walk yourself through every problem every time. That is tiring and gets old fast, and you often end up running out of time. Practice Aptitude. It never hurts.

2. Keep your primary language your primary language. That means that if you do DSA in C++, please know the ins-and-outs of the language. Do not go about mastering all languages. If you're just starting out, it may be simpler for you to do your DSA practice in Java, just to cover your bases with technical MCQs (Russell didn't care about language, they cared much more about the depth of your technical understanding, but not all companies are like this)

3. Write. Code. Feels dumb? Trust me, it isn't. That notebook is the OG IDE.

PS: Read all the interview experiences in the folder. Everyone has covered what they remember of the process, so everyone may have missed something or the other.

Placements need skill and practice. But they're also, to an extent, very much a game of LUCK. Do not be demotivated by rejections. Be confident in yourself.

OFF-CAMPUS IS VERY MUCH A THING, AND YOU MUST WORK FOR THAT TOO. All career migrations post-college will be off-campus! So prep for off-campus!

I'm always available on LinkedIn! You can also reach out to me on +91 8779410757 (Whatsapp)

Best wishes for your placements!
journey.howSecured:
The process had a resume shortlisting round, after which we had 3 rounds at their office in Goregaon.

Round 1: Written Test (MCQs, and some Coding Questions)

Round 2: Technical Interview I

Round 3: Interview With the Director (Techno HR, with a focus on Tech)

1. Resume Shortlisting [Not really sure about the number for App Dev specifically, but across about 5-6 intern roles they had 9k applicants]

The application and shortlisting were entirely run by Russell Investments on Workday. SPIT's placement office circulated a short form so they could see who had applied, but the company did the actual screening, communication and interviews. HR communicated with students directly.

I remember receiving a call from HR around 5 o'clock somewhere around the end of February. Keep in mind to be polite and courteous during all such calls. That means, you must:

- Wait for the person speaking to complete what they've said.

- Slowly and carefully articulate any questions (and I mean, ANY) you may have. Be diplomatic in their framing.

For your reference, things that may have influenced their shortlisting:

a. My LinkedIn b. My GitHub

Not linking my Leet/CF because it wasn't there in the resume I shared with Russell.

2. Written Test (40 mins) [ 87 candidates were shortlisted for this round ] [NON ELIMINATORY]

We were invited to Russell's office at Oberoi for this round. It was a pen paper test, with 10 Technical MCQs on CS Fundamentals (DBMS, CCN, OS, OOPS, Data Structures), 10 Aptitude MCQs, and 3 DSA problems out of which we were expected to solve 2. The first problem expected the implementation of the Bubble Sort Algorithm. The second was to Find the duplicate in an array in O(n) and by using O(1) extra space, and the third was to check if a given string is valid, given certain heuristics (Valid Parentheses problem) [Use a stack]. These were not very complex problems. (I'm not sure how much it really mattered, but a lot of us (including me) attempted all three coding problems. Make of that what you will)

For this round, I encourage you to keep a calm and collected mind, and to practice writing code by hand. Do not, and I repeat, do not use ChatGPT while writing code in your primary language as much as you can avoid it.

3. Technical Interview 1 [ All candidates who wrote the test ]

We were slowly called for an interview with a panel of 2 extremely experienced professionals. My interview was actually pretty late, but it extended so long I remember some of my friends scolding me for taking so long.

My interviewers were of varied domains. One was a highly experienced app developer, and the other was a DevOps engineer. This is important context to understand the rest of the interview

I walked in (asked their permission before entering), smiled, and extended my hand to them to shake. Start with the person closest to you, it's more natural. This gesture automatically familiarises you to them (especially since in tech, handshakes aren't all that common, so it helps break the ice).

We moved onto the interview.

They asked me to introduce myself. By then, we'd already had a short laugh over the water glass. This made the interview start with all of us smiling. I had a 3-min elevator pitch (fancy term for your answer to 'tell me about yourself') (I've memorized this and timed myself to stick to 3 minutes)

Then, we had the technical knowledge part of the interview first.

DSA:

1. Have you studied DSA? Yes, I have. What data structures comfortable with? I am comfortable with Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues. While I do know and have studied Graphs and Trees, I cannot claim mastery.

2. How would you reverse this array in-place?

3. They had my sheet. They asked me to walk them through my implementations for all 3 codes.

4. Suppose you're building a news aggregation app. A user searches for "climate policy India". Your backend search engine finds matching articles. But instead of just showing the title + link, you want to show a snippet of the article text that contains all three search terms, so the user immediately sees the context. To do that, you need to find the smallest window in the article text that contains all the query words. This is a classic sliding window + hash map/frequency counter problem. [Note: this is not the exact question, I have forgotten the exact one. But I remember the implementation, so I have done my best to create a similar problem statement so you can relate to the scenario]

DBMS:

1. A JOIN Query (joining 3 tables)

2. Do you know what a view is?

3. What's an index?

4. Find the Top-N Highest Salary

CCN:

1. TCP vs UDP

2. What happens when you click a URL?

3. What's a REST API?

Now, here's a place where my resume got me into a spot of trouble.

I have mentioned I know 'RESTful APIs' in my skills. I do know REST APIs. Thing is, I didn't know what the '-ful' part meant. (Arre REST, RESTful, same hi laga tha) So my interviewer asks me, this is a REST API. You've mentioned a RESTful API. What's that?

I didn't know at all. So, I smiled and said, I know how REST APIs work and I've built them, but I'm not fully sure what the '-ful' part means. I assume it has something to do with the principle of REST → statelessness, resource-based URIs, use of HTTP verbs, etc. [PS: I made this up. I didn't know at the time either. By sheer luck, this is the right answer. So, the moral of the story, say something]

Resume:

1. I had an Embedded systems experience on my resume. Interviewers are usually more than happy to hear about your experience. Talk about it with as much passion as you can muster. You must be able to explain what the company does, how you contributed, so on and so forth. If you were at a startup, highlight how you wore multiple hats, learned quickly, and adapted to a fast-moving environment. If it was a larger company, talk about working within established systems, collaborating across teams, and how your work contributed to the bigger picture. Personally, I talked to them about the product of the startup, how my work was on the product itself, and how I fixed a critical bug in the firmware code.

2. One of my interviewers was an experienced App Developer. He was extremely interested in the BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) work I'd done at my internship. Here's what he asked me: -> How does BLE connection establishment normally work? -> Why did you need a custom three-way handshake instead of relying on BLE's built-in connection mechanisms? -> How did you measure the "74% reduction" in sync issues?

None of this may apply to you. But the questions were pretty in-depth (BLE is just one line on my resume) so be prepared for this kind of deep-dive

3. The other interviewer, a DevOps engineer, was very interested in my project Percy, an AI-driven system optimizing CI/CD pipelines, automating testing, enhancing the developer experience. She asked me for the system design, which I drew on a sheet with simple boxes and arrows. She had many questions about my design choices (Why are you maintaining the data in a JSON, why are you using Celery here, how would you integrate this into an existing CI system) She asked me what an AST was, and how it helped in documentation generation. She also interspersed some technical knowledge questions, like what's the difference

between on-prem and cloud servers, what you'd have to take care of in an on-prem server which cloud providers cover for you (I probably didn't answer this as well as I could have)

Once they were done with their questions, they asked me if I had any questions for them. Honestly, I did (like have actual questions. Not just 'ask for the sake of asking, ask something')

1. What does the work of an App Developer look like at Russell?

2. Do you attend client meetings?

3. How are teams structured?

4. What are your office timings like?

5. How does your CI/CD pipeline work, could you please give me a very very quick overview?

4. [Round 3 Name] [ 14 candidates appeared for this round ]

My round 2 was with a senior director who sits in London. He'd come to India for some other work. He was in charge of their data (very important in any financial firm) and had a very intimidating presence. I will admit, I was very terrified. It had been a long wait (this interview happened at 4:30, when my previous interview had ended at 1ish) so the tension had had time to build up as well.

He was very polite. I shook his hand with a smile. He asked me to work him through my resume (the same 3 min elevator pitch)

He was very, very interested in my experience. He wanted to know all about the product, the use, and the clinical trials associated with the product. He asked me about how a day working at a startup as a firmware intern was, how I debugged the cause of the lag in transmission, how the fix was approved, and how we tested it. He wanted to know about my knowledge of Alpha/Beta testing, SDLC.

Then, he asked me to write a simple SQL query to find all entries for October 2024, sorted by day, given that each entry was in DATE format in SQL. Now, this is an easy question, but I blanked. I cannot explain why. I could not remember LIKE in SQL, probably because I was so intimidated. In this situation, drink water. If you know something, but you're unable to answer, drink water. It provides a separate stimulus to your mind and helps clear stress.

Then, I said - the exact term is slipping my mind, but this is how the query would be structured. And as I wrote that down, I remembered LIKE and wrote that down as well.

He seemed happy with the answer. He moved onto some technical questions:

1. On-prem versus cloud (here, I ended up cross-questioning him a bit too. Keep it conversational! He seemed to want to talk)

2. How data is stored in a financial firm

Then, he shifted to cultural fit questions.

1. Tell me a situation where you were frustrated with a team mate. How did you work past the frustration?

2. What, according to you, is the most challenging part of working with a team?

The rest has slipped my mind, but it was somewhat around this.

Once he was done, he asked if I have any questions for him. I asked questions based on the talks we'd had in the morning with the Director of Application Development-

1. Could you tell me why you've opted for Snowflake as your Cloud Vendor?

2. How do firms like Russell deal with damages to on-prem servers?

3. What would you expect from an intern like me?

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. The most important advice for any interview I could give you is to always smile. Be graceful about your mistakes.

2. Do not claim to know something you do not know. That is a massive red flag.

3. The interviewers are human. Appeal to their human nature. They're tired and bored after long days of continuous interviews too.

Resources (For the lazy folk):

1. SQL: DataQuest for LMR, SQLZoo for a one sitting full syllabus study. Practice Leetcode SQL if the syntax tends to slip from your mind and if application of certain functions tends to slip from your mind.

2. DSA: The usual resources are great. Follow those diligently. If you have the time and you love coding, give the CSES Problemset a shot. I'm at the Mathematics section and it's really fun!

3. OS: Any YT course will do if you're studying it for the first time. If you're reading this the night before the interview, just read up on Processes and Threads, Process Scheduling, Synchronization, Memory Management, Filesystems and I/O. If you have more time, this Overview by InterviewBit is pretty swell!

4. CCN: Same as OS. LMR. Very, very LMR (Ye toh karke hi jao pls).

Mistakes that I made that I feel you can learn from:

1. I thought Aptitude was silly. It still is, but trust me, it's better to be able to do it faster than to have to walk yourself through every problem every time. That is tiring and gets old fast, and you often end up running out of time. Practice Aptitude. It never hurts.

2. Keep your primary language your primary language. That means that if you do DSA in C++, please know the ins-and-outs of the language. Do not go about mastering all languages. If you're just starting out, it may be simpler for you to do your DSA practice in Java, just to cover your bases with technical MCQs (Russell didn't care about language, they cared much more about the depth of your technical understanding, but not all companies are like this)

3. Write. Code. Feels dumb? Trust me, it isn't. That notebook is the OG IDE.

PS: Read all the interview experiences in the folder. Everyone has covered what they remember of the process, so everyone may have missed something or the other.

Placements need skill and practice. But they're also, to an extent, very much a game of LUCK. Do not be demotivated by rejections. Be confident in yourself.

OFF-CAMPUS IS VERY MUCH A THING, AND YOU MUST WORK FOR THAT TOO. All career migrations post-college will be off-campus! So prep for off-campus!

journey.prep:
Why I Got Selected & What Helped Me

One of the key things that helped me was consistent LeetCode practice over a long period. I didn't just aim to solve problems--I made sure I understood why certain solutions worked and why others failed. For particularly tough problems, I sometimes spent 2-3 hours just breaking them down, revisiting them until I gained full clarity.

After exams, I specifically revised graph algorithms, solving the entire graph section on CSES Problem Set and also picked some hard problems on trees and graphs to stretch my thinking. That gave me a strong base for several questions that came up during the tech interviews.

Another factor that I believe played a big role was my calm and composed attitude during the Tech Round 2 and the Hiring Manager Round. I didn't panic, even when I didn't know a solution completely--I asked clarifying questions, discussed trade-offs, and tried to reason through the problem.

Areas I Could Have Improved

Despite the positives, there were definitely areas where I could've done better:

● I didn't prepare enough for system design. While I had some basic understanding, I could have been more confident if I had practiced it more through mock interviews or small-scale design exercises.

● I should have invested more time in revisiting my own projects. Especially the ones I had mentioned on my resume--some schema-level or implementation-specific details were fuzzy, which could have been avoided with better preparation.

General Tips for Candidates

● THINK OUT LOUD during the interview.

● Solve a lot of DSA . For DSA, start with neetcode.io , then move on to Striver's A2Z sheet. I first completed about 15 problems from each topic on neetcode.io [Around 2.5 months] . After that, I focused on DP, Arrays, and Binary Search from Striver's sheet [Around 3 months]. For graphs, I followed the YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/@codestorywithMIK , which has many solved questions across topics--definitely check it out. I also solved the CSES graph section and used ChatGPT to get questions combining multiple topics like DP on graphs and graph + bitmasking.

● And as I said, don't just run behind getting the correct solution--explore the wrong solutions also. Wrong answers teach 10x more than the correct ones. Spend good time around each question. Don't be in a race to finish off questions; it's about understanding deeply, not just ticking boxes.

● A correct code/approach in the interview does not guarantee your selection, nor does a wrong one deny you. It's all about how well you are able to explain and articulate your thoughts.

● Revise your resume and projects thoroughly: Be ready to discuss your contributions, system design choices, and technical decisions. Know the why behind each decision, not just the what.

● Stay calm and composed during interviews: Your attitude matters as much as your answers. If you get stuck, ask clarifying questions, explain your thought process, and don't panic.

● Avoid comparing yourself to others: On the interview day, many people will be talking about how their rounds went, what questions they got, or how confident they feel. Don't let it overwhelm you. Stay focused on your own preparation and performance.

● Be humble and helpful: Everyone around you is equally nervous and aiming for the same goal. Be kind, share a smile and help others if they need it. You're not competing against each other--you're just trying to show your best.

● Take notes during the Pre-Placement Talk: Interviewers often refer to company-specific terms, metrics, or philosophies. Jotting them down can give you an edge during interviews.

● Be mindful of your grooming and energy: Wear something you're confident in (formals preferred), get a good haircut , get enough sleep, and arrive on time. First impressions do matter.

● Don't take failure personally: Not every round or result defines your intelligence or hard work. Learn from it and move forward. You only need one opportunity to click.

● Believe. If you're someone who places faith in God, then trust that everything happens in its own time--God has a plan for you.

You can contact me on WhatsApp. +91 9152752492.

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [ 200+ Candidates , 7th July]

The Online Assessment was conducted on 7th July 2025 via the DOSelect platform. It was a 90-minute test originally scheduled to begin at 4:00 PM but was delayed due to technical issues, and my test eventually started around 4:40 PM. Despite the delay, I stayed calm and maintained a composed attitude. I proactively communicated with the DOSelect support team to resolve the issue. Interestingly, the same individual who assisted me during the technical glitch later appeared in my HRM interview, and I believe my calm response left a positive impression.

Before the OA began, a pre-placement talk was held from 2:30 PM to 3:30 PM. I made it a point to take notes during the session, especially on important points such as the company's vision, founding inspiration, growth metrics, and their underlying technologies and architecture like microservices and scalability. These notes proved useful in later interview rounds, particularly when I had to refer to PhonePe's infrastructure, scalability, and database systems.

All students who applied were allowed to take the OA, and there was no shortlisting prior to the test. Shortlisting after the assessment was based on problem-solving accuracy, the efficiency of code, the number of passed test cases, and behavioral logs captured by DOSelect's secure browser, which monitors for tab switches, fullscreen exits, and suspicious activity.

Test Structure & Questions

● 1. Friendship Clusters Problem: Given a list of integer pairs representing friendships, determine the minimum number of additional friendships required to make all people directly or indirectly friends with each other. If person A is friends with person B, then all their friends are also friends. Approach:

○ Modeled it as a graph.

○ Used DFS to find the number of connected components (disjoint sets).

○ Final answer = number of disjoint sets - 1.

○ Issue: Got a stack overflow on one large test case due to recursion depth but chose to move on since I had to manage time.

○ Could have used DSU

● 2. Array Assignment with Max Difference Constraint Problem: Given an array with some pre-assigned elements and a constraint k, find the number of valid ways to assign the remaining elements such that the difference between adjacent elements is at most k. Each element must be between 1 and 100. Approach:

○ Used recursive backtracking with memoization.

○ Solved 7 out of 12 test cases.

● 3. Pair with Bit Position Sum Constraint Problem: From an array, pick two numbers (a pair) whose sum is exactly s such that the total of positions of set bits in both numbers is less than or equal to k. Count the number of such pairs. For example, consider the number 12. Its binary representation is 1100, and the set bits are at positions 2 and 3 (starting from position 0 on the right). So, the sum of bit positions is 2 + 3 = 5. Approach:

○ Brute-forced through all pairs.

○ Calculated set bit positions using bit manipulation.

○ All test cases passed except one.

● 4. House Assignment with Friend Constraints Problem: Given friend pairs and their house preferences (4 houses with limits), assign each student a house such that:

○ Friends don't get the same house

○ House limits are respected Input Challenge: Input was provided as a complex nested list (e.g., [[h1, h2], [h2, h3]]) with no clear count of friend pairs.

● Approach:

○ Due to lack of time and complexity of parsing, printed "possible" as a fallback solution.

○ Managed to pass approximately 60% of the test cases.

During the test, I faced a Wi-Fi issue and had to switch networks. Since DOSelect tracks activities like fullscreen exits and network changes, I immediately called the representative to inform them and ensure they witnessed the switch. I also followed up with the POC to document the situation properly. Transparency during such incidents is crucial, as it helps protect against being falsely flagged for violations.

The test results were released around 9:30 PM, leaving me with very little time to revise or prepare. We were asked to report the next morning by 8:00 AM, so I had to make the most of the limited time. While traveling in the local train and metro, I made sure to quickly go through some previously asked problems and revise key topics like graphs.

Additionally, it's important to groom yourself well before the interview. Dress professionally--wear formal attire--as it helps create a good first impression and shows that you're taking the process seriously.

Round 2 - Technical Interview (First Tech Round) [30 students]

I reached campus at 7:30 AM. At 8:30 AM, interview batches were announced; I was in the second batch. The first batch started at 9:00 AM, so I had an hour to calm down and prepare. At 10:00 AM, my turn came. I knocked, entered, shook hands with the interviewer, who introduced himself as an App Developer at PhonePe. I gave a brief self-introduction, then the interview started.

Question 1: Minimum Number of Operations to Sort a Binary Tree by Level

He opened with a medium-level tree problem and asked me to explain the logic before jumping into code.

I explained that I would do a BFS traversal of the tree, level by level. For each level, I'd collect all the node values into a list. Then, I'd make a sorted copy of that list. Using a map of value → index from the original list, I would compare the original and sorted arrays index by index. If the values at index i didn't match, I'd swap them in the original array and increment a counter. I would also update the map after every swap. This technique is similar to solving the minimum swaps to sort an array problem.

He listened carefully and seemed satisfied. After a few clarifying questions, he asked me to write the code and then discuss the time complexity. I did both. Although he mentioned he was expecting a graph-based approach, he acknowledged that my solution was valid and handled the problem efficiently. We had a brief back-and-forth on potential optimizations and edge cases.

Question 2: Find the K-th Smallest Sum of a Matrix With Sorted Rows

This was a tough one. I started with a brute-force approach: generate all possible sums by combining one element from each row and storing the results in a max-heap of size k. He immediately asked why I was using a max-heap instead of a min-heap.

I explained my reasoning -- that the max-heap would help keep track of the k smallest sums by discarding the largest as new smaller ones come in. He looked a bit surprised but agreed with my logic once I did a dry run of the approach.

Then he asked me to optimize the solution. I took a pause to think but couldn't come up with an efficient algorithm on the spot. I admitted that I was stuck and asked for a hint. He kindly walked me through a more optimized method.

He then asked whether duplicates could occur in the sums. I answered yes. He asked why, and I gave a correct explanation. When he asked how to avoid duplicates, I suggested using a HashSet to track visited combinations. He nodded and seemed happy with that answer.

Post-Interview Conversation

After the technical questions, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about a couple of app features and their color palette choices--he smiled and admitted those weren't part of his responsibilities but still gave me general answers. Then I asked him about their tech stack, and he shared that they had recently started using React Native. Before I could ask why, he explained the reasoning behind the shift in detail, which I found really insightful.

Post-Interview Reflection

The interview ended around 11:00 AM. Although I was relieved it was over, I didn't feel too confident, especially about the second question. I overheard a few other candidates saying they had solved it, which made me a bit anxious.

The results were expected soon, but they didn't come until 3:00 PM. During this waiting period, some candidates were called for Technical Round 2, while others moved on to HR interviews.

To keep my nerves in check, I spent the time revising System Design concepts, casually discussing things with friends, and grabbing some refreshments. Those small breaks helped me ease the pressure and clear my head for whatever was coming next.

3. Round 3 - Technical Interview (Final Tech Round) [ Around 11 students]

Time: Around 3:00 PM onward Duration: Approx. 1 hour

By 3:00 PM, I had gotten quite relaxed after the long wait. I made sure to stay composed and walked into the interview room calmly. I knocked, asked for permission, and entered. The interviewer greeted me with a handshake and introduced himself. He mentioned that he works on KYC, user verification, and database systems at PhonePe.

I introduced myself in a similar way, giving a brief about my background, skills, and a short description of one of my projects. Without wasting any time, he jumped straight into the first question.

Question 1: Lava Brick Heat Loss in Matrix

Problem Description: Given a matrix where each element represents the heat removed from a lava brick when it passes through that cell. Starting at position (0, 0), you must reach (n-1, m-1) with minimum total heat loss.

● At any point, you must move exactly 3 steps in one direction (up, down, left, right).

● After completing those 3 steps, you must immediately change direction (no continuing in the same direction).

● You cannot reverse direction.

My Approach: I immediately recognized that the problem could be treated as a graph traversal problem.

● I considered each cell as a node, and the edges as moves with the weight equal to heat loss.

● I suggested Dijkstra's Algorithm and explained in detail about the characteristics of Dijkstra and why it was suitable for this weighted graph problem.

● I also highlighted the need for a modified state: i, j, direction, steps_remaining, total_weight.

He asked me to explain it visually, so I first drew a standard Dijkstra graph, showed how it processes nodes, and then extended it to demonstrate why additional state parameters (like direction and steps) were necessary in this case. I justified this as expanding the graph to a more detailed representation of possible paths.

Code Implementation: He then asked me to write the code. While implementing:

● I paused to ask him a few clarifying questions regarding direction changes and boundaries, and he was supportive in answering.

● I realized I had missed the relaxation condition, so I asked if I could write a generalized version elsewhere in the code. He agreed.

● Some directional code blocks were repetitive, so I asked if I could omit them with comments for clarity. He agreed again.

I then completed the code with detailed comments and added placeholders for repeated blocks and the generalized relaxation. After that, he asked me to explain the code again and discuss the time and space complexity, which I did thoroughly. He verified the logic and moved to the second question.

Question 2: Painting the Walls - Leetcode

Problem Setup: He presented the problem in an incomplete form (as I understood it), giving only a partial description and asking me to proceed with a solution based on it. I kept asking for clarification, but he insisted that this was all the information I would get.

My First Attempt: I assumed a possible setup and gave him a brute-force-style solution. For the sample test case, it passed. However, he then gave me another test case where my approach failed. I revised my logic and proposed another solution. He pointed out that it would also fail and asked me to come up with a counter-example that would break my logic.

I took a moment to think and asked if I could get a glass of water. He nodded. I joked, "Will this disproving of my own solution count?" He smiled and said, "Yes, yes," while laughing. Eventually, I did manage to find a test case where my solution would break.

At this point, he provided the full problem statement, mentioning that it involved dynamic programming. I initially struggled to grasp the direction of the solution, so I asked for the constraints. Once I had them, I was able to identify the DP approach.

My Final Solution: I explained a recursive + memoized solution, wrote the code, and discussed both time and space complexity. I also explained how the solution could be converted into a bottom-up (tabular) DP formulation.

Post-Interview Interaction

Once the technical questions were done, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about:

● The challenges faced in KYC and verification systems

● What is that random message which gets sent when someone links their UPI/Bank?

● His most impactful contribution to the PhonePe ecosystem

He answered each of them in detail, sharing both technical and team-level insights.

Before I left, he smiled, shook my hand again, and said:

"You're the most calm and relaxed person I've spoken to today."

With that, the interview ended on a positive and memorable note.

Round 4 - Hiring Manager Interview

Time: Just 10 minutes after Round 3 Interviewer: Same person who handled my technical issue during the Online Assessment (OA)

I wasn't sure if he remembered me from our earlier interaction during the OA when I had technical issues, but he greeted me with a smile and a handshake. Without much small talk, he asked me to introduce myself.

Self-Introduction and Resume

I gave the same structured introduction I'd prepared--covering my name, background, skills, and a quick summary of my project. He asked me if I was tired to which I replied yes but equally excited.

He scanned my resume for about a minute and then asked me to pick the most exciting and challenging project and walk him through it.

I began by explaining:

● What the project was about

● The goal and motivation behind it

● The tech stack used

● My specific role in the team

When I mentioned that my role involved designing model schemas, he immediately asked me to list down the tables and their schemas. I admitted I couldn't recall all of them in full detail but shared the key tables and schema structure from memory.

He then asked me to walk through the user flow in the project. Since the project involved GenAI, he had several follow-up questions on how I integrated it. I explained the RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) architecture and how I approached prompt tuning. I also admitted that my tuning approach wasn't based on any specific methodology--it was entirely experimental and observation-driven.

He asked what hallucinations in GenAI meant, and I explained that too.

API Design & Project Ownership

He then asked about a few specific APIs used in the project. I clarified that I didn't personally implement those but had a rough understanding. I even drew a high-level diagram of how I thought the flow might look.

To show stronger ownership, I brought up another project I worked on using MERN stack, where I had built the APIs myself. I explained:

● API structure

● How user authentication worked

● Use of JWT tokens and hash functions

He then asked, "Where is the hash code stored?" I answered "in the virtual environment," but he pointed out that this would be a security issue, which I acknowledged, adding that I hadn't deeply explored that side yet.

System Design: YouTube

Next, he asked about my most used app. I said YouTube, and he asked me to explain how its APIs might work. I confirmed whether he wanted a project-level view or a system design-level view, and he chose the latter.

I started explaining:

● DNS lookup

● API gateway

● Load balancing

● Service-based architecture

● Horizontal scaling

He then asked how I would handle video feeds. I explained that:

● Videos would be delivered in chunks

● Additional content would load only when the user finishes scrolling the current chunk

Then came the key question: "How would you decide which videos to send?"

I said that would be handled by a recommendation system. He challenged me further: "Assume you're just launching YouTube--how would you build a basic recommender without ML?"

I proposed a rule-based scoring system, explaining that:

● We'd gather user data like subscriptions, likes/dislikes, history, location, etc.

● Each video would have associated tags

● Based on parameter weights, we'd assign a score to each video

● The highest scoring videos would be sent as feed chunks

He seemed satisfied with the logic and the non-ML approach.

Behavioral and Personal Questions

He shifted toward more personal questions:

Q: "How has choosing CSE in SPIT changed your personality?" I responded:

● I've moved beyond solving only textbook problems to asking what, why, and how behind everything

● I now approach problems by fixing first, identifying root causes, then redesigning

● My curiosity has grown, and I challenge myself often

● I introspect and verify facts before raising questions

Q: "What would you do in case of a conflict with a manager or teammate?" I gave a real example where we had to choose between Django and MERN for a project. Although we had used Django in a previous winning hackathon, I convinced the team logically to go with MERN this time based on:

● Current requirements

● Ease of debugging

● Flexibility of tech

I emphasized that I prefer direct communication, avoid miscommunication, and back my arguments with facts and logic.

Q: "How have the past 6 months been for you?" I highlighted:

● The value of courses like Machine Learning, Distributed Computing, Blockchain, Business Analytics

● How they improved my clarity of concepts and curiosity

● Every course had a mini project, which taught me about deadlines, collaboration, debugging, quick learning, handling people and team-building

Questions I Asked the Interviewer

He then gave me the chance to ask questions. I asked:

1. " I referred to points from the pre-placement talk. PhonePe was launched in 2016, what was its founding inspiration?"

2. "Why hasn't PhonePe moved to AWS, Azure, or GCP? How do you handle so many transactions on your own infra?"

3. "How has PhonePe managed to capture such a huge customer base in rural India, despite strong competitors like GPay?"

He gave thoughtful answers and mentioned:

● Hiring the right people

● Emphasis on financial discipline

● Focus on long-term survivability and execution

As the conversation wrapped up, I smiled and said:

"So that saying about pressure turning coal into diamonds is true?"

He smiled back, and then I asked him if he had any feedback for me.

The results came at 7:45 PM. 7 people got selected.

journey.prep:
1. Placements are one of the most trying yet important phases of life and you will definitely come out on the other side, a stronger and more confident person. This was my 6th process (OAs excluded!), so learn to take setbacks in a positive way and just keep preparing for your destined company.

2. ATS score checker : http://resumeworded.com/ (try to get >80)

3. Python essentials : Neetcode YT playlist , Blind 75 , Python for Everybody by University of Michigan (Coursera certification). Keep revising CS fundamentals (OS, CCN, DBMS, OOPs) as they are asked in a lot of tests and interviews both.

4. Aptitude : IndiaBix Start aptitude practice early on! Do not underestimate it or think "yeh toh easy hai ho hi jayega". Speed and accuracy only comes through consistent practice and you can't go from 0-100 in aptitude just in one night before your test.

5. For GDs, build your communication skills and quick thinking as they look for people who add value to the discussion by stating relevant points in a concise and articulate manner. The frequency honestly does not matter much, if you speak only 2 times but in a confident and agreeable manner then that would be better than hijacking the whole discussion and arguing with people.

6. On your interview day, remain calm and composed and meditate/listen to songs/think of God (whatever works for you). Try to focus more on the process rather than the outcome to stop overthinking and believe in yourself!!! Stop worrying about the result and just give your best and if it still does not turn out the way you wanted, there is something better in store for you.

journey.howSecured:
1. Pre-placement Talk

If you're seriously interested in a company, it's really important to attend the PPT and moreover, really pay attention to what exactly they are looking for, information about the role (location, CTC, I+P or not, etc.), company values and what they do. In this case, the role is that of Corporate Trainee and it has further categories like Developer and Data Scientist that they would decide based on our profiles.

- You can take note of things you find important and want to remember for interview rounds.

- In case of virtual PPTs, keep screenshots of slides with company values, their achievements, skills required etc.

2. Resume Shortlisting

This is a very crucial step and many deserving people sometimes fail to get their resume shortlisted (happened with me in certain initial companies) due to ignoring these basic points:-

● CGPA! Even though it cannot compensate for your lack of skills, maintaining a decent CGPA can definitely save you from being eliminated if the company has internal criteria for filtering out candidates. As far as I have seen, having a CGPA of >7.5 is good enough and will make you eligible for all companies. However if you want to guarantee that they don't eliminate you from their side, stay above 8 just in case. (Mine bordered around 7 which was a mistake on my part but I kinda made up for it through my resume and other areas, so luck is a big factor and if you don't have a good CGPA don't get demotivated because many companies look at your overall profile as well).

● ATS! Since it is unclear what the resume shortlisting criteria is for each company, do not think ATS score does not play a role. There may be times when HRs do not want to look through the resumes of 200-300 candidates so they simply filter on the basis of ATS score. So focus on increasing your resume's ATS score as much as you can (>80 on Resume Worded is great), and there are many techniques to do that by including stats, action words, at least 1 work experience and 2-3 good projects that actually add value, leadership roles, etc.)

● JD! Tailoring your resume according to the role and company you are applying for is really important, so please have a good look at the JD provided (things like skills required, role of intern, what the company does) and strategically include things that will give you an advantage when you talk about them during your interview. In my case, the role wasn't very specific like an SDE or DA or a non-tech role so what worked for me was showing versatility through projects and courses/certifications by adding 2 ML/Data Science related projects and 1 deployed fullstack project. Also, I researched a bit about what the company's main business is and accordingly included an AI-based loan underwriting agent project for brownie points.

You can get a better idea through my resume that I used for Mahindra Finance: Akshata_Mahindra_Resume.pdf

3. Aptitude Test [~150 candidates got resume shortlisted and attempted this round]

This round was conducted on the YUGMA platform and consisted of 100 questions (covering quants, aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal aptitude and behavioral/situation based questions) to be solved in 1 hour. The challenge here was not in the difficulty of the questions but rather effective time management, and also the fact that each question had negative marking as well. I started from the beginning and had solved about 15-20 questions when I realised that there were so many questions to be done in a limited time. I then started solving the behavioral and verbal questions first as they were pretty easy and obvious to answer so they would secure marks, and after covering all those I moved on to the remaining quant questions which revolved around topics like speed distance and time, percentage, profit loss, discounts, etc. which were very doable. Practicing from IndiaBix is more than enough to prepare for aptitude based questions and I also think quick strategising and presence of mind really played a role here. Keeping in mind the negative marking, I left out 10 questions which I was very unsure of. They had purposely included some very indecipherable questions where it wasn't clear what exactly needed to be done. All I can say is just trust your gut and if you really don't know what to do in a question, simply leave it (ofc only in OAs with negative marking). I think ppl who got >70 questions correct were selected after this round.

4. Coding Test [70 candidates shortlisted from previous round]

This was conducted on Assesshub and had 2 sections :-

- The first section had around 20 MCQs on basic python input/output questions which are very doable if you know Python basics like loops, variables, conditional operators, etc.

- The second section had 3 DSA questions (Leetcode easy level) to be solved in Python only. I was able to do these quickly, having been coding in Python since 1st year, but if you are a beginner you can practice with Blind 75 sheet on Neetcode as they have really good solution tutorials in Python. It was a relatively easy coding round as compared to other OAs I had given before, but attention to detail was really important here since for output questions some options were very similar to each other so we

needed to read the code and each option properly. Also, the IDE for DSA questions was quite different to usual ones so we had to adapt our code according to the given main function. I was able to solve all 3 DSA questions and almost all MCQs correctly, and I submitted way before the test ended so maybe both speed and accuracy could have been a factor behind shortlisting for next round.

5. Group Discussion (GD) [29 candidates shortlisted from previous round]

We were divided into panels of 6 and I was in the first one. Before starting the GD, we were briefed about general rules to be followed and time guidelines (9 mins for discussion + 1 min for concluding). The topic given to us was "Technology : Boon or Bane" and we were strictly told to be either for or against but not both. After getting the topic, we had a minute to gather and jot down our thoughts. Here, I prepared my points according to technology being a great boon since that is what I believe. However once the GD started, I was the 3rd person to speak up and everyone before me had spoken for the motion so I spontaneously decided to speak about technology being a bane and wrote down 2-3 points that came to my mind while others were speaking. While this could have been a mistake, I thought in the moment that if everyone speaks for the motion then it would be a very dull discussion with all of just saying "I agree with you…" , and I trusted in myself to speak on the spot without a lot of preparation so my communication skills helped me here. I presented a different viewpoint and was the only one who spoke against the motion (that possibly caught the interviewers' attention).

6. Personal Interview (PI) [11 candidates shortlisted from previous round]

After getting shortlisted from GD, all of us had 2 interviews : technical and HR, neither being eliminatory. They said they would take into account all our scores (aptitude, coding, GD, PI) and accordingly come up with a result in the end. Both the interviews were in no particular order and I had my HR round first:

a) HR : This was a 45-minute long, rigorous HR interview where the Head of HR basically wanted to assess our inner personalities and culture fit rather than technical prowess. She started with my family background, upbringing, what all places I have been to, etc. and also asked about which project taught me the most valuable life lessons and which one made me encounter the most challenges and self-doubts, with simultaneous follow-up questions for each. One important thing here was that I remembered their DE&I (Diversity, Equity & Inclusion) framework from the PPT and subtly included these values in my answers. She asked me a lot of questions about my life experiences and lessons I had learnt along the way to know what kind of a person I am. Towards the end I was also asked if I had come across any unethical practices around me and how I had reacted to them. As far as I could make out from her response to my answers, they look for people who know how and when to speak against something so it's always good to have some answer for these questions. Even if you haven't experienced something, have a presence of mind and think of the most suitable response rather than just saying "No" or "I don't know". Towards the end, she asked me if I had anything to ask her and since I had not really prepared for an HR-specific question I just asked "What are the company's expectations from me in terms of beliefs and values if I get selected?" Again I reiterate, it is always better to have some decent response rather than saying "Nothing".

b) Technical : This interview also lasted around 40 minutes and revolved around technical and resume based questions in depth. The interviewer was friendly and polite, starting with asking me for a brief introduction and then moving on to my projects and work experience. He focused more on

my 'Smart Returns' project and wanted to know how we decided on the problem statement and how exactly we were solving the problem at hand, what the end results are, detailed explanation of the project workflow and how different technologies are integrated together. He then went on to ask me about a case study along similar lines, it was regarding a demand-based shipping feature for orders on Amazon. I explained about a solution through data driven demand forecasting models to predict order volumes for a particular location depending on various factors like age group, economic capacity, geography, etc. He seemed satisfied with my response and asked me how accurate an ML model would be in such a case. I estimated a >80% accuracy since Amazon is a big company operating since long ago so they would have a large customer database hence we would get good accuracy through data analytics. He then asked me how we would handle the 20% inaccurate demand forecasting done by the ML model, and for this I suggested another feature so that the company's customer satisfaction rating and profitability do not get largely affected. He constantly tried to check if I was confident in my responses and finally seemed satisfied with my answer.

5 students got the final offer, and I was extremely grateful to be one of them.

A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round &

Finally, 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day,5/08/25. The CGPA Criteria for SDE

was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was further reduced to 7.5. It may not be the case for next year

if they don't want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting: [ Approx 150-160 students]

Tailor your resume according to the JD of the company and your strong skills. Once your resume is finalised, evaluate its compatibility with ATS. Tools like Resume Worded can help and aim for a score of 65 or above. The shortlist of candidates selected for the Online Assessment and Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was released on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM.

2. Pre-Placement Talk:

The Pre-Placement Talk was conducted online on 4th August 2025 at 5:00 PM. The information shared during Pre-Placement Talks is extremely valuable, so it's important to be attentive -- not just to the content of the presentation, but also to the names and roles of the presenters. I made it a point to take SS and jot down the specific examples used while the speaker explained some of the company's financial services. You can make use of all these points in the HR round and also while asking questions at the end of your interviews.

3. Online Assessment: (Approx. 160 students appeared, invigilated by the company)

The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. +1 was given for each correct answer and -0.25 for incorrect ones. You were allowed to use the system calculator.

The assessment covered four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude. The Java and Python part was mostly output-based MCQs, with a prime focus on OOPS concepts, errors, exceptions, stack, queue and all types of sets in Java. The SQL part was relatively easy with just queries as an answer. The aptitude had a total of 30 questions, and it had all types of questions you could find on Indiabix. So I would suggest solving questions whose concepts are known to you.

4. Technical Round 1: [44 students appeared] 1 interviewer in my panel

I was the 2nd last person in my panel, and the panellist was the same who invigilated my classroom during

the test. In the panel distribution list, the name of the panellist was given, so I had looked her up on LinkedIn (it helps to ask questions at the end of the interview). My panellist was very careful and also cheerful while taking the interviews, as I gave my interview at 6:30 in the evening when many students had already given their HR round and had gone home. So do not panic and get stressed the whole time ur sitting outside TPO. The interview started by asking my name and how my test was. I explained that I solved most of the Java and Python part, but the aptitude was a little lengthy. No introduction was asked to me. Then she asked me what I had prepared for the interview, and I said that I had prepared DBMS, OS, SQL, OOPS, JAVA. Be careful what you say in this part, as they will ask in depth about these topics. She asked me briefly about my first project and then started asking SQL queries. The first question was about giving the maximum salary in each dept, and then followed by a query for the top 2 salaries in each dept. I had to write the query on paper. Then she added a gender and city column to the same table and told me to give names of female employees who have the max salary in that dept.

Then she asked me two puzzles:

1: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzle-mislabeled-jars/

2: There is a lotus in a pond that grows double its size each day. On the nth day, it covers the entire pond. On which day will it cover 1/8 th the pond?

I knew the 1st puzzle as I had prepared the top 100 puzzles from GFG. But the 2nd one was new, but I tried to solve it on paper while explaining my approach. Then, when I could not explain, I asked for hint and then was able to solve it.

Then I was asked OOPs in JAVA. Where I was given the shapes, rectangle, square and rhombus, and to use oops concepts to depict their classes. So Shape was interface, rectangle and rhombus were abstract classes and square extended both rhombus and rectangle. Which led to the discussion on interfaces, abstract classes and the diamond problem in Java. The keyword super was also asked.

Then at last I was asked the DSA question of replacing a certain value from a linked list via in-place no using another linked list. I was told to write the code on paper.

Remember to be honest and think out your solutions loudly. If you do not know the answer, ask for hints; the interviewer is there to guide you.

5. HR Round: [15 students appeared] 2 panellists

Started with my family background, why CSE-AIML as a branch, where do you live, would travelling be easy? I was asked only about my academic scores -- SSC, HSC, CET percentile, and CGPA.

Then came a question to explain my favourite project, to which I described my major project. Then they went deep by asking me in detail about this project. How I came up with the problem statement, the whole design of how it works, my role in it, as I did the Ml part, they asked me about the data used, models used and the whole pipeline. Problems I faced while working on the project. They also asked the same questions about my other project. As my resume was inclined more towards ML and genai, they were concerned about my role in ISS, as they don't use much AI and ML in their projects. But I convinced them that to use mML models we need proper backed knowledge too, which I had in Flask and my basics were clear in the languages of Java and Python, so coding would not be a problem. They also asked how I keep myself updated with the latest technologies to which I answered I read news on the inshorts app. The interview ended when I asked the interviewers a question about my day as an intern at ISS

This round was a little more inclined towards my projects and my understanding of it. Very few Hr questions were asked.

journey.prep:
1) It's very very important to not lose hope or give up. Right till the start of my 3rd year, I was planning to do Non Tech and not even sit for tech companies. But my internship changed my perspective. I started DSA, more dev, and things started falling into place. So even if you haven't started yet, it's never too late. Just work hard and give it your all.

2) Luck is a major major factor in placements. Do not underestimate it, but also do not let it affect you as well.

3) Resume building is very crucial. Know the format well, ONLY INCLUDE WHAT YOU ARE CONFIDENT ABOUT, learn the concepts if you have lied on your resume.

My Resume - Aman_Kanojia_Resume.pdf

4) Pick a programming language to master. I chose Python. Companies prefer Java a lot, almost all of them. So maybe go for that or C++, and practice Python every now and then.

5) Giving contests on Leetcode or Codeforces (again, Competitive Programming can help a lot, it's not required though). This will help you learn to code under time constraints.

6) Build your communication skills, very important for interviews. Maybe help each other by taking each other's interviews. I had been good at it, so I didn't prepare much. But one can rehearse, get some tips from youtube and participate in competitions for it.

It is very important to know how to answer your interviewers be it Tech or HR. Always greet when you enter, wait for their offer to take a seat, greet when leaving. These minor things leave an impact. Know how to build stories around your answers from past experiences, or maybe even lie a little, elaborate on your answers, give some extra information to what you're asked to show how you stand out. These things specifically help in HR rounds a lot.

Prepare a good introduction about yourself. It should include the following points:

● First greet and thank for the opportunity

● Name, degree, college and year. Where you've been born and brought up (cover this in like 2 short sentences max)

● A brief about your skills (like good fundamentals in Full Stack Development or Machine Learning, built scalable projects)

● Mention your internship experience if you have any in 2-3 lines, what you did there and how it was for you

● Give an overview of 1 or 2 of your projects, what they are and what they solve. Unless asked for, don't explain more projects.

● Then cover any extracurricular activities apart from Tech, like I was the Head of Marketing for Oculus. Your experience in it and what you did.

● Move on to any achievements, competitions, hobbies (all of this in one line)

● And lastly, but most importantly, briefly explain why you are a good fit for the role by matching with JD and covering your skills.

Any introduction anywhere between 30 seconds to 1.5 minutes is good enough.

7) DSA is not only going to get you better at Data Structures and Algorithms, but also build your logical thinking and fluency with the language you code in.

Resource - https://takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course/strivers-a2z-dsa-course-sheet-2/

This right here is your Bible for DSA, and I'd personally recommend Striver's videos. You can also take a look at Neetcode 150. Striver's SDE sheet is when you're well versed with DSA.

8) Prepare for OOPS, preferably in Java, and the language you are confident about.

Resource- OOP 1 | Introduction & Concepts - Classes, Objects, Constructors, Keywords

CheatSheet- https://whimsical.com/object-oriented-programming-cheatsheet-by-love-babbar-YbSgLatbWQ4R5paV7Egq Fw

For Java - https://www.tpointtech.com/java-tutorial

9) Prepare for DBMS and SQL from Love Babbar's videos.

DBMS - Introduction to DBMS Placements Course 2022

SQL - Leetcode SQL 50 is more than enough https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

10) Prepare for Puzzles and Guestimmates as well.

Puzzles - https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/top-100-puzzles-asked-in-interviews/

Guesstimates - Videos on youtube Cheatsheet - https://180dcsrcc.in/guesstimate-cheat-sheet-2024/

11) You can prepare for System Design as well, which I have done. Even if it's not asked directly, it improves your understanding of concepts very well. Although you can easily skip this.

12) GFG is great for questions on Core Concepts (OS, CCN, Language specific)

13) Prepare Aptitude questions from IndiaBix - http://indiabix.com/aptitude/questions-and-answers/

14) Have at least 3 projects ready. They shouldn't be too simple, having some impact is always appreciated. Projects on Development or Machine Learning are the most common.

15) Actively participate in Hackathons, maybe even Case Study Competitions (it will give you more confidence)
