The company came with 3 roles - GM, ITD and CDO. We were required to fill in 2 of our preferences. The ITD role had an aptitude test and shortlisting for GM and CDO roles were done on the basis of our resumes. I had applied for ITD and GM.

1. Pre-placement Talk - 28th July

2. Aptitude Test (for ITD, not GM, but the year prior, there was an aptitude test for GM as well) - 31st July

3. Group Discussion Round - 1st August (up to the HR round)

4. Technical Round-1

5. Technical Round-2

6. HR Round

Now the further rounds were conducted for just me and another student after we cleared HR (no clear reason was given as to why)

7. Virtual Techno HR Round 1 - 4th August

8. Virtual Techno HR Round 2 - 4th August

I'll cover details of the OA (Aptitude Test) very briefly. Around 180+ students applied for the OA. It was a 60 minute exam with 20 questions on Analytical, Verbal and Quantitative Sections each (thus total 60 questions), conducted on MeritTrac's Platform - Pariksha. The questions were easy to medium. What mattered most was speed. I was able to complete around 55 questions by the end, and tried smart guesses for the rest, as there were no negative marking. So solve the easier questions first, as you can switch between questions and sections.

The OA results came at around 7 in the evening. Shortly after the shortlists for GM and CDO also came out. I was shortlisted for ITD and GM roles. Generally all shortlists come a day prior to the interviews. So if one is selected for interviews, for that day they should go through their Resume very well first and foremost. BE VERY THOROUGH ON WHAT YOU ADD ON YOUR RESUMES, otherwise it's better to skip that skill. Then quickly try revising basic concepts, DSA notes if you have any, and skim through the interview experiences of that particular company, as it gives you a fair idea of the process. These are the things that I did.

The below part is only going to be focused for the GM role. For ITD, there are other interview experiences in the drive which you can check out.

GM Role JD — [GM SPIT Tech focused Intern role_JD - 2025.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KUDTxqKGzFo4TAcIPeuM3FuueHTeXrsT/view?usp=sharing)

Some people have misconceptions that the role is Non Tech, but it's not the case. It's a Tech Role which you can see in the JD.

1. Group Discussion [ 19 students appeared for this round ]

The 19 students were split into two panels. There were around 9 students in my panel. The topic was given to us directly during the GD (no prior indication), and no phones allowed, pure brainstorming. The topic was relatively easy to prepare on - 'Is AI making us Smarter or Dependent'. I had gathered my panel members prior to the round and advised them that we should do the GD collaboratively, allowing everyone to keep their points, and avoid opposing and conflicts as much as possible, which would give everyone a fair chance. This worked, and the GD went very smooth, and lasted for around 30 minutes. I made around 3-4 valid points. Make sure to actively participate in the discussion, but not dominate it as well. The key is to be confident, be active and try to maintain fluency. The motive of the GD is just to see how well and actively a student participates, contributes and presents their ideas in a discussion. Take a pen and paper to jot down points. Examples of GDs on youtube, are more than enough to prepare.

2. Technical Round-1 [ 10 students appeared for this round ]

The round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself.. I introduced myself, told him about my internship and my contribution to it. Then I talked about my projects, giving him some overview about them, to which he would ask some questions in between regarding them. Then he began asking some basic questions, such as defining data structures like Hashmap, Stack, Queue, LinkedList, etc. This was pretty easy, so I even explained some extra info for each, such as what is collision in hashmap, struct of LinkedList,etc and gave examples for each. Then he proceeded to ask two easy level DSA questions:

1) Implement Queue using Stack - Simple implementation using 2 stacks

2) Remove duplicates from an array (order should be maintained) - Using a Hashmap to maintain order and remove duplicates. I solved both of them very quickly, and the interviewer only needed the logic, no code or pseudocode. Then he asked me briefly about my experience with Flask, React, etc (they were mentioned in the JD), but didn't ask any questions about them. He then asked me if I knew Python, to which I replied that it was my primary language. Then he proceeded with asking multiple questions on Python. Some of them were:

1) Simple questions like the difference between List and Tuple. Which of them can be used as a key in a dictionary, which cannot, and why not.

2) What is List Comprehension and what's the syntax

3) How dictionaries work in Python, how to sort them by keys and by values.

4) OOPs questions in python and how is it implemented in Python, what are abstract methods, and access modifiers in python.

5) What are Decorator Functions in Python (he asked me to write a decorator function)

6) What is args and kwargs

7) Write a function to convert a Flattened Dictionary into an Unflattened Dictionary. E.g) Flattened Dictionary : table= {'a.b.c':1, 'd.e':2, 'f':3} as input should give Output: table={a:{b:{c:1}}, d:{e:2},f:3} I wrote a recursive function explaining each step while writing the function, and was able to solve it in some time. He wanted to check how efficiently I write codes in python.

I was able to answer all questions except the syntax of the decorator wrapper function. I asked him a question about the role and his experience at the end. The interview lasted for around 35 minutes.

3. Technical Round-2 [ 6 students appeared for this round ]

The interviewer looked through my resume and asked me a question on what Apache Kafka is and how it works (it was mentioned on my resume). I explained all the concepts related to Kafka, how they work, gave examples of their use-case and real life scenarios, and how I implemented it into my project. Then he gave me two tables, and asked me to first tell him what I can infer from it, and then write the SQL query for it.

The question was as follows: Given a table, lets say Table, for every Note, print the entire row with the max Tranche Transactions Note Pipeline Tranche

T1 N1 P2 2

T2 N1 P1 1

T4 N2 P1 2

T1 N2 P1 1

T2 N3 P2 1

Output: Transactions Note Pipeline Max_Tranche

T1 N1 P2 2

T4 N2 P1 2

T2 N3 P2 1

I had messed up a bit initially, to which the interviewer gave me a hint, after which I was able to solve the query. The query included Sub Query, Aggregation, Grouping and Join concepts. It was as follows:-

SELECT t2. Transactions, t2. Note, t2. Pipeline, t2. Max_Tranche FROM ( SELECT MAX(Tranche), Note AS Max_Tranche FROM Table GROUP BY Note) AS t1 JOIN Table AS t2 ON t1. Note=t2. Note

After this he began asking me questions on core DBMS. Some of the questions were:

1) What is RDBMS? Why is it used?

2) What is Normalisation and what is its purpose? What are the pros and cons of an overly normalized table and a completely unnormalised table

3) What is Indexing, how does it work? Why is it beneficial? Which data structure is used for it, and how does it work? When is it a good option and when is it not?

4) What is Partitioning and Sharding. What's the difference?

5) What is Data Replication? Why is it important?

6) What is a Composite Key? How is it different from the Primary Key

7) What is a Foreign Key and what happens when you delete a row with a primary key as the foreign key to another table. How do you resolve the error? There were a few more basic questions, I don't remember clearly. I was able to answer all the questions asked to me, and I tried to always give some extra info related to the solution. The interviewer seemed content with all my answers. After this he was about to ask me a DSA question, but asked to just explain Collision in hashmaps, that's it. At the end I asked him how the transition from college to corporate is, and what was his experience. The interview lasted for around 25-30 minutes.

4. HR Round [ 4 students appeared for this round ]

The interview began with the interviewer asking me a brief intro about myself, what I've done and what are my skills, and my experience as the Head of Marketing at Oculus. He then asked me about my understanding of the JD. I replied according to what I had researched about it. Then he asked me for the top 3 qualities about myself, and a little about my internship. He then asked me what drives me to do more. Looking at my CGPA, he asked me if I was in the top 30% of my class, and why I was not higher. Then he asked me a tricky question, which was "When should one do MBA" (he wanted to check if i had any plans for it). I turned it around by stating that the correct question should be "Why MBA", and started building around it. He proceeded to ask me questions about my family background and where I live. He also mentioned that my travel from Colaba to Powai won't be so joyous, to which I said I'm accustomed to it, and might consider shifting. He asked me to rate myself in coding, what would be my actions if someone is better at it, at work, and what ratio would I draw between tech and finance market during my work. Lastly, I made comments on how I'm a good fit for the role, as the role serves both verticals of Tech and Finance, and I have the appropriate technical, communication skills and the business acumen required.

So the key to clearing HR is being honest, confident and not lying. You do need to build stories around your answer, give examples from your experiences and never give single statement answers. Apart from that they want to see how you present yourself, your expressions, and how you handle pressure. They don't want robots who just know how to work.

Note - After this round, only one student was immediately selected, and me and another candidate were scheduled for more Virtual Interviews on 4th August (1st was a Friday, and offices are closed on weekends, hence Monday). However we did figure out that we were being considered for different roles, as

the other candidate had a completely Non Technical and Financial Background, and his process was different as well.

No clear reason was given as to why this was being done. But I need to admit, I was a bit confused and slightly disappointed. The next 2 days were very stressful, somewhat torturous, as no information was given regarding what will be the next rounds, how they will go about and why they were scheduled.

But it's very important to keep your composure, not lose hope. I kept talking to two of my friends who really supported me during the process, to keep my mind off these things. I didn't exactly prepare anything extra in those 2 days, as I believe there's no point to it, and it's just gonna add more pressure. I did prepare for some common HR questions though.

On Sunday night, the TPC instructed me to keep my phone on the entire time the next day, as even they didn't know when the interviews would be scheduled. So I was ready in formals and my laptop from 8 in the morning. Later I was informed that my interview is at 2:30 pm.

5. Virtual Techno HR Round-1

It began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself and talk a bit about my internship and projects, and how I did them. She then said she'll be asking me questions on Python, to which I thought it would be like the last round, but it wasn't the case. She began by asking me what's the difference between loc and iloc. I thought she meant about the 'Lock' in threading in python, to which i explained everything. She then told me she means loc and iloc in Pandas. I was taken aback at that time as i had never done pandas specifically, which i told her as well. Regardless, she went to ask me questions on Pandas, like:

1) loc and iloc

2) How to drop null values

3) How to fill in rows with null values

4) How to merge two dataframes

5) What's the difference between Left merge and Right merge

I explained approaches for all of them, but did not know the syntax for them, which I honestly told the interviewer.

She then asked me some behavioral questions. She asked me how I would proceed if I had worked on something, which was later discarded because the manager feels there's a more optimal approach. I replied honestly that I would try to understand the situation and adapt to the better solution, as we always go through that in DSA. Then she asked me what I do if I'm stuck somewhere and not able to solve a certain problem or write some code. I explained that I tend to read documentations first, then try sites like StackOverflow, maybe ask my peers or seniors, and then lastly try some AI tools like ChatGPT or Claude. She asked me in what ratio, which approach I would use. Then she asked me what I would do if a member in my team is slacking in terms of work or not performing. I gave an appropriate answer, saying I would discuss with that member first, try to understand the problem, if it still doesn't solve it, i'd probably escalate to the manager. I gave example scenarios or past experiences for each answer as well.

At the end, I made a statement that although the interview started on the wrong note, as I wasn't able to give the syntax for Pandas, I'm a quick learner and can adapt well to new technologies, instances of which I have proved earlier. To this she said it's alright.

The interview lasted for around 45 minutes.

In all honesty I had almost given up hopes as I was not able to give good responses to the technical questions. Also the other candidate had given a good interview, and another round was already scheduled for him at 6:30 (not for me till then). Just as I gave up, I received a call from the TPC that we both have been called to the office the next day at Powai. However, I had been shortlisted for the OA of another company for the next day, so he asked me to make a decision, to which I said I want to proceed with Nomura (obviously). Later the people at Nomura themselves said that they don't want me to miss my OA for another company, and that they're ready to immediately take the next round at 7:30 PM. So I rushed back to my laptop in formals.

6. Virtual Techno HR Round-2

The interviewer (she was taking the interview from her home as well, as it was too late) began by asking me to give an introduction about myself, my projects, my experiences and so on. Then asked me to explain in detail about one of my mentioned projects, and what state it is in now. I gave a complete explanation of the architecture, high level design, working, flow, use of the project, and how it was used in a real competition. She then asked me what challenges I faced during that project, and how I solved them. She asked if I had ever worked with something that was new to me in a short period of time. She then asked me about my internship experience and what was my most important learning there. She also asked me what I did as the Head of Marketing at Oculus.

She then asked a few python questions. She told me that there's a lot of electronic data coming in continuously, and we only have limited memory resources. So how would I process the data? I told her that I would use Pagination to split the incoming data into chunks, then use multithreading to parallelly process the data, with each thread responsible for some chunk of data, and finally use the garbage collector to discard threads not in use. She was satisfied with the answer. She then asked me what are lambda functions and asked me multiple implementations of it. The other questions were very easy.

Then she asked me about my hobbies and if I had any questions. By the end the interview almost became a bit casual, we were almost just conversing at that point. The interview lasted for around 35 minutes.

Later I was told the results will be announced the next morning. At that point I completely stopped thinking about what could happen. I reached college for the next OA, at my desk in the designated classroom, and with just a few minutes to the OA, Sparsh Ma'am from the TPO came and informed me that I have been selected, and I do not need to give the OA. I reconfirmed it with her, as I was not expecting the results to come so randomly. Alas, I took a sigh of relief.

At the end I was selected from the 2 candidates giving the extra interviews, and one was initially selected on the first day itself. So 2 people for the GM role.

A Small Overview of my Placement Process Experience:

So the entire placement process was a complete rollercoaster ride in itself, and there were a lot of ups and downs. About some other companies I applied for, I reached the JPMC interviews but couldn't appear for them due to a family emergency. This taught me that there are some things which are beyond our control. I reached the HR round for Work India but was one of the 2 students out of 4 who weren't selected. So you never know what requirements the companies have, and you may get rejected even at the last minute.

Other times either I couldn't clear the OA, and for one of the companies I couldn't sit for the OA because the CG criteria for it was 8, and I had a CG of 7.9. (Try to keep your CG above 8)

So yeah, there's a lot going on, and a lot of luck (trust me, a lot !!) involved in the process. But I think overall, if you've worked hard, and if you have the skill sets, you'll end up in one of the good companies regardless. Just remember to not give up, have faith in yourself and keep trying. Everything happens for a reason.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) It's very very important to not lose hope or give up. Right till the start of my 3rd year, I was planning to do Non Tech and not even sit for tech companies. But my internship changed my perspective. I started DSA, more dev, and things started falling into place. So even if you haven't started yet, it's never too late. Just work hard and give it your all.

2) Luck is a major major factor in placements. Do not underestimate it, but also do not let it affect you as well.

3) Resume building is very crucial. Know the format well, ONLY INCLUDE WHAT YOU ARE CONFIDENT ABOUT, learn the concepts if you have lied on your resume.

My Resume - Aman_Kanojia_Resume.pdf

4) Pick a programming language to master. I chose Python. Companies prefer Java a lot, almost all of them. So maybe go for that or C++, and practice Python every now and then.

5) Giving contests on Leetcode or Codeforces (again, Competitive Programming can help a lot, it's not required though). This will help you learn to code under time constraints.

6) Build your communication skills, very important for interviews. Maybe help each other by taking each other's interviews. I had been good at it, so I didn't prepare much. But one can rehearse, get some tips from youtube and participate in competitions for it.

It is very important to know how to answer your interviewers be it Tech or HR. Always greet when you enter, wait for their offer to take a seat, greet when leaving. These minor things leave an impact. Know how to build stories around your answers from past experiences, or maybe even lie a little, elaborate on your answers, give some extra information to what you're asked to show how you stand out. These things specifically help in HR rounds a lot.

Prepare a good introduction about yourself. It should include the following points:

● First greet and thank for the opportunity

● Name, degree, college and year. Where you've been born and brought up (cover this in like 2 short sentences max)

● A brief about your skills (like good fundamentals in Full Stack Development or Machine Learning, built scalable projects)

● Mention your internship experience if you have any in 2-3 lines, what you did there and how it was for you

● Give an overview of 1 or 2 of your projects, what they are and what they solve. Unless asked for, don't explain more projects.

● Then cover any extracurricular activities apart from Tech, like I was the Head of Marketing for Oculus. Your experience in it and what you did.

journey.howSecured:
Initially it was announced the process would be an OA test, Group discussion, 2 Technical rounds and 1 HR round. But the group discussion was cancelled and they directly moved to technical rounds after PPT.

1. [OA test] [ About 20 candidates for second role only ]

It was a simple aptitude test of 45 minutes which had 55 questions with 3 sections being Aptitude, Quantitative analysis and verbal ability. Test was fairly easy and mutual discussion among other candidates made it evident the cutoff was a bit low. Though questions were easy, what mattered here was solving speed.

It was conveyed that those who applied for the first role and cleared the test of the first role were allowed to sit for the second round directly if applied.

2. [Technical round 1] [ 14 candidates ]

They proceeded to take technical rounds and skipped the GD round after a brief online PPT which was conducted along with SPCE students. 14 candidates were divided into 2 panels of 7 candidates in each. Interviews were conducted online form on microsoft teams and were spaced in 20 minutes per interview.

As soon as my interview started, I was asked to introduce myself. I started by talking about my current branch and hobbies and how I am interested in software engineering. But I fumbled hard. I was stammering. But during this first 1 min of introduction the interviewer interrupted me and asked me to take a pause because he needed to attend a call. After he was done with the call in a minute he asked me to speak further. I asked him if it was okay to start over to which he said yes. From here on it went smoothly. I was able to smoothly speak and introduce myself, my hobbies and interests. In my resume I had mentioned my recently completed remote internship and 3 projects. He proceeded to ask me about my internship, my designation, what I did in the internship and the project I got to work on. I described everything in detail for quite a while. He then asked me about my projects, first one being ML based. So he started asking me what I used, and asked some small questions on the concepts I mentioned in the bullet points and also on the technologies used. He moved on to the second project, which was a small AI based project I built in a hackathon. I described the entire pipeline of the project and how I built it from

scratch in detail. He was impressed with this. He then asked me about my skills I mentioned, one of which was google cloud platform which I hadn't touched in a while and feared I might fumble this. He also added another question on genAI with it which I answered first and managed to somehow dodge the question on GCP.

He then ended the interview. Interview was a total of 30 minutes so he didn't get to ask much on my other skills. He did ask about my hobbies one of which was Linux and Linux distro hopping which he was surprised to hear about. Other candidates were asked some other basic CS fundamental questions and basic DSA. Basic DSA was mostly just either sorting algorithms or questions on time complexity of given operations.

3. [Technical round 2] [ 6 candidates ]

6 candidates were divided into 2 panels again.

This time, the interviewer in my panel was a partner. He asked me to introduce myself, which I gave very similar to my first interview. He proceeded to ask about my internship more in this round. But as I was describing the project in the internship, I was interrupted. Interviewer suddenly asked me about location preference which I felt was strange for a technical round. He then ended the interview, which made it not even hit the 10 minute mark.

4. [HR round] [ 4 candidates ]

4 candidates were moved further in the process.

HR round was mostly chill, HR asked basic behavioural questions (ex. How would you deal with conflict between two team members, etc.). And ended the interview by asking location preference and if we were mentally ready. It was about 10 minutes in duration.

Out of these 4 candidates from HR round, 3 were sent a Letter of Intent and 1 candidate from the technical round 2 was also sent a letter of intent.

● Master your OOPs concepts -- a majority of the questions came from this area.

● If you know the right answer, be confident. Sometimes interviewers may challenge you on purpose just to test your conviction.

● Know your resume inside out. Don't include anything just to fill space -- if it's on there, be ready to discuss it.

● For coding problems, always start with the brute force approach. Then discuss how you can optimize it.

● Keep talking through your thoughts during the coding part. Don't go silent. The interaction matters as much as the solution.

3. Techno-HR round [19 candidates appeared]

The Techno-HR round began with the usual "Introduce Yourself" question, which helped set a comfortable tone. The interviewer then asked an interesting question: why do you think Java was designed using OOPs? That opened up a deeper conversation about OOP concepts, and he followed up with questions around interfaces, inheritance, and the use of extends and implement keywords.

He then asked me about my internship--what kind of work I did there--and specifically wanted to hear about an incident where I got stuck and how I handled it. It was a good opportunity to share real experience and reflect on problem-solving skills in a work environment. After this, we had a friendly chat about how the software development landscape is evolving. The interviewer casually mentioned how coding nowadays is becoming more about configuring libraries and tools (like in Python) rather than writing every line from scratch. I agreed, and we discussed how that shift is changing the way developers work.

The conversation was very calm and natural. The interviewer was chill and approachable, which made me feel at ease. At one point, he asked me if I preferred being a full-time developer who just codes, or if I'd enjoy a hybrid role like a business analyst--someone who handles tech but also communicates and collaborates with other teams. I appreciated this question because it showed that they were interested in how I see myself professionally, beyond just my tech skills.

After this, he moved to the HR-style situational questions. One of them was quite interesting: he gave me a scenario where I had a deadline the next day, but a teammate was stuck on something. Helping them might mean I'd have to work overnight to finish my own tasks. What would I do? I gave a fairly standard answer--saying that I'd help because it's about the team's success, not just mine. But he challenged me, saying that if I helped, I might lose my own flow and have to restart everything later, which would waste time.

While he was talking, someone served him coffee. He took a sip while reviewing my resume, and I quickly made a connection. I said, "Just like you took a sip of coffee to refresh yourself before continuing, I'd do the same if I were stuck--I'd take a short mental break, help my teammate, and come back even more focused." That spontaneous answer really clicked with him, and I could see he was impressed.

Then came the question: "Why Barclays?" I had already prepared a response that included their core values--RISES--and wove it into a story that reflected my interest in both tech and impact. He seemed satisfied with the answer.

He also asked me if I preferred working in silence or in a collaborative, discussion-heavy environment. After that, there were a few more classic HR questions--strengths and weaknesses, whether I know anything about finance or investment banking, and if I'd be open to learning a completely new tech stack. He specifically asked if I'd be okay moving away from Java and diving fully into Python or something else if the role required it. I assured him I'm open to learning whatever is needed to grow and contribute effectively.

As the interview was coming to an end, he said he was done and asked if I had any questions for him. I said I wasn't aware of his position and would love to know more about his role. We ended up having a nice chat about his responsibilities and how teams work at Barclays. It gave me a deeper insight into the company's structure and culture.

The round lasted for around 40 to 45 minutes, and overall, it felt more like a thoughtful conversation than a strict interview.

I'd say it's really important to be aware of Barclays' RISES values and try to include them naturally in your responses to situation-based questions. Preparing some standard HR questions in advance helps a lot, especially if you can back up your answers with real stories. In my case, I used internship experiences and examples from project collaborations. It's also important to interact with the interviewer--don't just turn it into a Q&A session. Try to make it a discussion. Stay attentive, because small things happening around you can give you the spark for a clever or memorable answer--but make sure you don't get distracted. And lastly, whatever your strengths are, try to reflect them--directly or indirectly--throughout the interview. One more thing that really helped me was paying attention during the PPT (Pre-Placement Talk). Some of the things discussed there--especially around the company's work culture, Barclays' values, and the tech stack they use--came in handy during the HR and project discussion parts. So I'd strongly suggest taking notes during the PPT, because it can give you useful context and even points to connect during the actual interview.

There was one coding question, which was exactly the same as one asked in a previous Barclays placement drive (here's the link). The SQL part was relatively easy--just a basic query where we had to use a WHERE clause along with an AND condition.

Placement Preparation Tips

1. Start Early with Core Subjects

Begin your placement preparation as early as possible. Focus on fundamental computer science subjects such as DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs). Make concise, revision-friendly notes for these subjects to help during the last-minute prep. Also, research frequently asked interview questions to become familiar with recurring patterns and concepts.

2. Resume

Your resume should reflect your actual knowledge and experience. Avoid adding skills or technologies that you cannot explain if asked in the interview it may come off as dishonest and create a negative impression. At the very least, ensure you understand the basic concepts of everything mentioned. Tailor your resume slightly depending on the specific role you're applying for.

3. Pay Attention to the Company Presentation

The first step in most placement processes is usually a company presentation. Be attentive and note important details about the company's history, products, services, and culture. If you have doubts about the roles and responsibilities, clarify them early. This will help you make an informed decision and also position yourself as someone who is genuinely interested in the company.

4. Practice is Key for Online Assessments

For Online Assessments (OAs), consistent practice can make a big difference. Participate in coding contests and take timed tests to improve your problem solving speed and accuracy. This will also help you identify your weak areas and improve over time.

5. Approach Interviews Calmly and Confidently

In interviews, focus on explaining your approach clearly rather than jumping to give the right answer immediately. Interviewers are more interested in your thought process and problem- solving skills. Staying calm and confident shows that you can perform under pressure, which is an essential trait for any role.

6. Stay Positive and Keep Improving

Finally, don't lose hope if things don't go as planned. Focus on how you can improve your chances of getting selected. Understand your strengths and weaknesses, and keep refining them throughout the placement season. Persistence and continuous improvement are key.

1. Online Assessment

The OA had 3 sections

Coding questions were super direct and easy:

Q1: Find numbers between X and Y whose sum of digits is equal to the highest digit of the number. (E.g., 100: 1+0+0 = 1, and highest digit is also 1) Q2: Return the count of elements whose position changed after sorting and whose position remained same. (E.g., 2 1 3 4 → 1 2 3 4 → Count = 2, 2)

2. Technical Interview 1 [ 41 candidates were selected ]

Started with a quick intro exchange. The interviewer was chill and said he'll go through my resume while I solve a DSA question.

Before starting, he asked what data structures I'm familiar with. I mentioned stacks, queues, linked lists, graphs, hashmaps, and priority queues. I didn't mention trees on purpose, since I wasn't confident and didn't want a question from that topic.

Q1: LRU Cache (just the logic was enough) Q2: Reverse Linked List (this had to be coded live)

I clarified doubts and kept explaining my thought process. If you're stuck, talk it out, they guide you. (For the LRU question, I initially started with a solution that was quite far from the correct approach. The interviewer noticed this and helped guide me a bit. He then asked me to take some time to think it through. After that, I was able to figure out the correct and optimal solution.)

Then we moved on to resume and project discussions.

He gave me a solid tip:

"If you're giving results (Eg. reduced response time by 80%) in your projects, make sure they're real and not simulated."

Next came:

● Straightforward OOPs pillars

● REST API basics (since it was in my resume)

● Asked what is idempotency -- I blanked out and said so. He was chill about it.

● PUT vs PATCH -- discussed that too.

Wrapped up with me asking about automation in banking.

Tip: Stay calm even if you miss something. Don't panic. Just be honest and smile through it.

3. Technical Interview 2 [ 22 candidates were selected ]

Again, a friendly start. This time two interviewers were there.

I was asked about my strongest skills. I said DBMS, SQL, and Java.

He first asked the port numbers of MySQL and PostgreSQL, which I didn't know. Then:

● Sharding, partitioning, and database optimization.

● Write an SQL to count students with the same name grouped by year.

● A Java function to put(key, value) and get(key), twist was that value can be any type (int, string, etc. in the same map). You are allowed to use HashMap.

I tried many ways but couldn't crack that multi-type value part.

They were cross-questioning a lot -- not to grill, but to test confidence. Stick to your answer unless you're really wrong.

They also asked:

● About my projects

● How form data is stored in a DB the process flows.

● Something on database indexes and B-tree (I didn't know and said so)

● Asked about JWT tokens in depth.

The interview ended with me asking a question:

"How do you decide which new tech or feature to adopt?"

This round was more of a stress test not to check if you know everything, but to see how you stay calm under pressure, explain your thoughts clearly, and stick to your answers with confidence. They also wanted to see if you communicate clearly and can admit honestly when you don't know something, without losing confidence.

● "How was your day?"

● "Where do you stay?"

● "Tell me something not in your resume."

● "Apart from salary, what do you look for in a company?"

Then came some situational questions, like:

● "What would you do if ICICI gave you a job offer with the same pay?"

● "What if your teammate is not cooperating on a project?"

● "What would you do if your manager calls you out during a team meeting?"

● "What quality in a person irritates you the most?"

● "What if your manager has those traits that irritate you?"

● "How do you handle conflict or disagreement in a team?"

● My projects

● Some basic questions on what I worked on

SHORTLISTING FOR CDO WAS BASED ON OA AND RESUME

2. [Tech Interview] [8-CDO, 28-ITD, 19-GM ]

I was interviewed for the Chief Data Officer (CDO) role, and there were two interviewers taking the interview simultaneously. The conversation began with a simple "Introduce yourself" question.

As they went through my resume, they noticed that I had done a lot of hackathons and development-focused projects. Since the role was related more to data analysis, they asked me about my interest in the role and whether I'd be comfortable switching gears from development.

I answered honestly. I mentioned that while my journey started from the development side and I naturally feel inclined toward it, I've also worked on projects that align with data roles and would be comfortable and interested in this direction as well.

Project Discussion

They asked me to explain two ML-related projects:

1. Rapid Compliance Checker (RAG-based)

I explained the RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) architecture used in this project. They asked a follow-up: "RAG gives k results. What if only 1 is relevant and the rest are not?"

I answered by talking about an optimized approach using Graph RAG, which helps improve contextual relevance and filter better responses using semantic relationships.

2. Voice Automation Platform

This project included a smart suggestion engine which detects tasks and offers to perform them. The suggestions were based on Gemini. They grilled me a bit here -- especially about how Gemini handles sensitive or inappropriate language.

For example, they asked what would happen if someone asked Gemini to send a bad word/abusive message. I replied that Gemini won't acknowledge such prompts, but in case it does, we can fine-tune the model or even build a custom LLM to avoid that. They mentioned the cost of fine-tuning, so I proposed a lighter solution -- prompt-level checks to prevent such actions rather than acknowledge them.

DSA Question

They asked me if I was comfortable with Python, to which I said yes.

Question:

Group the anagrams from the list: ["abc", "cba", "tea", "eat", "pig", "gpi", "pay"]

I was able to solve it immediately -- and instead of using a dictionary (map), I used a 26-sized array for each word. When asked why, I explained that it avoids extra space overhead, while maintaining the same time complexity.

System Design: ATS Scanner

Next, I was asked to design an ATS (Applicant Tracking System) Scanner that could fetch the 5 most relevant resumes for an SDE role.

I drew the RAG-based architecture again, explaining each step:

● Document Retrieval

● Chunking resumes

● Vector embedding and storing

● Extracting keywords from the job description (like expected technologies and tools)

They asked how I would extract these keywords. I gave an example using Nomura's JD, which had a "Technologies we expect" section. I mentioned we can automate the extraction using LLMs.

SQL Questions

They gave me a complex SQL query involving DENSE_RANK. I was able to understand and write the query within 2 minutes. They seemed quite impressed and also appreciated that I clarified the question properly before answering.

Closing Conversation

A Twist After the HR Round

After the round ended, the HR simply told me, "Your process for today is over, you can go home now."

I was shocked and confused. Usually, candidates are asked to wait or are given further instructions. So, I went to the placement coordinator and asked what this meant.

Turns out, it was a bit of a prank or a surprise moment -- and I was actually selected.

There were 3 rounds for this process all within the span of 4-5 days. Schedule:

1. Pre Placement Talk (Microsoft Teams): 10-07-2025 from 11.30am - 12.30pm

2. Online Assessment(Hackerrank): 10-07-2025 from 4.30pm- 6.30pm .

3. Interview Rounds (SPIT Campus): 14-07-2025 Make sure you are prepared beforehand as you will be notified a day prior to the OA Test and the Interviews of shortlisted candidates.

1. Round 1: Online Assessment [ 197 students appeared and it was conducted in college]

Platform: Hackerrank Time: 85 mins Questions

● 15 Technical Questions: These questions were based on CS Fundamentals majorly focusing on DBMS, OOPS, SQL and Java.

● 15 Aptitude Questions: The questions were easy to moderate. They were based on probability, profit/loss, sets, finding missing elements in series, mirror images, and answering the question on the basis of a given graph and statistics.

● 1 Coding question: Given an array of integers representing the latencies of different servers, your task is to find all pairs of latencies with the minimum absolute difference. Each pair should be returned in ascending order (i.e., [a, b] where a < b), and the final list of pairs should be sorted in lexicographical order. Return the result as a 2D array of these latency pairs. For example, if the input is [4, 2, 1, 3], the sorted latencies are [1, 2, 3, 4]. The minimum absolute difference is 1, and the valid pairs with this difference are [1, 2], [2, 3], and [3, 4]. So, the output would be [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]].

Python approach i used: To find all pairs of latencies with the minimum absolute difference, first sort the array. Then, loop through the sorted array to calculate differences between consecutive elements. Track the smallest difference. If a new smaller difference is found, reset the result list with that pair. If the difference equals, add the pair to the result. Finally, convert the flat result list into a 2D array of pairs and return it. This ensures all closest latency pairs are captured and sorted correctly.

2. Round 2: Technical Interview[ 16 students were shortlisted for this round]

We were asked to report to college by 9:00 a.m., with the interviews beginning around 10:30 a.m. We had been informed a day prior to carry a fully charged laptop, an updated resume with a passport-size photograph affixed, and to be dressed in complete formals.

My interview began with a "Tell me about yourself" question, but the interviewer specifically asked me to walk through my journey like a story from childhood till now and talk about everything I had done or achieved. Then he asked me why I chose diploma. Since the interviewer wasn't familiar with the diploma system, I also explained the entire process and its structure.

The conversation then shifted to my projects. He asked why I chose to build them, what problems they solved, what challenges I faced, and how I overcame them. Most of my interview revolved around my major projects. I focused on explaining the logic, technologies used, and real-world relevance.

He then asked me about my favorite programming language and why?., and he gave me a to write a code on paper. The task was to print all missing numbers between a given list, like [1, 3, 4, 99]. After that he told me to walk through the code. I explained my approach: first sort the list, then use a loop to identify gaps and print missing numbers.

Next, the interviewer shifted to puzzles. He asked three logical/aptitude problems. The first was the classic Water Jug problem: how to measure 4 liters using 3L and 5L jugs. The second was the Torch and River puzzle involving four people with different crossing speeds (1, 2, 5, 10 minutes) and a single torch. I explained the optimal 17-minute solution. The third puzzle involved burning two uneven candles to measure 45 minutes which I solved using the trick of burning one from both ends. I answered all three correctly, which seemed to make a positive impression.

Toward the end, he asked me about my family background, including where I'm from and what my parents do. Finally, he gave me the chance to ask a question. I asked him what skills I should start learning if I got selected for this role.

Overall, the interview was a balanced mix of resume discussion, problem-solving, and personal insight and felt more like a two-way conversation than a strict Q&A.

3. Round 3: HR Interview[ Around 8 students were shortlisted for this round]

This round felt more like a personal interaction than a formal interview. The questions were mostly background-oriented they asked where I stay, what my parents do for a living, and about my general family environment. It seemed like they were trying to get to know me better on a personal level and assess whether I would be a good cultural fit for the organization.

They also asked me how my technical interview went and followed up with questions like why I didn't continue my engineering at the same college where I completed my diploma. The entire round was quite short, lasting around 10-15 minutes.

Even though it was a light discussion, I would still recommend preparing well for generic HR questions including your strengths, passions, future plans, family background, and work preferences. Also, make sure to attend the Pre-Placement Talk and take notes many HR questions indirectly relate to the company culture and role expectations discussed during the session.

Finally results were announced, 3 students got selected, and I was one of them.

1. OA: (75 minutes) (~240 Candidates appeared)

This was an online assessment consisting of three questions: 2 DSA based and 1 SQL, on Hackerrank. The DSA questions were randomly selected from a pool of questions.

● DSAQ1: (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/python-program-to-find-uncommon-words-from- two-strings/ ) The first question was to find uncommon words from two strings, given the full sentence string separately. This was an easy question using split() and a two-pointer approach.

● DSA Q2: (https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-or/description/) The second question involved maximizing the OR value (OR of all elements) in an array, given you can multiply any element by 2, at most k number of times. I did manage to pass all test cases for this one, although not with an optimal solution.

● SQL Q3: This was a SQL question involving two tables related to voter information.

The goal was to return a summary of each state, showing the names of voters who voted in that state along

with the number of times each voter voted.

Given Tables:

Voters: Votes:

voter_id | name voter_id | state

---------|-------- ---------|-------

1 | Tanvi 1 | California

2 | Gaurang 2 | California

3 | Drishya 2 | California

4 | Rahul 1 | California

4 | Texas

Expected Output :

state | voters_summary

--------------|---------------------------

California | Tanvi x 2, Gaurang x 2

Texas | Rahul x 1

I wasnt able to solve this question, as it involved use of CTEs and Group_Concat, etc..

Solving 2 DSA questions fully was enough to qualify for the next round, which I did. Around 41 students were shortlisted for Tech Round 1.

2. Offline Technical Round 1: (30-45 minutes)

I was firstly asked to introduce myself. Then, the interviewer delved into my resume, particularly focusing on a GenAI project, which I described to him in detail. He further questioned me about how vector databases work in LangChain, and what cosine similarity is. I was well aware of these topics and answered them appropriately.

He also asked me about static and dynamic components in React. Since I'm not primarily a frontend person, I mentioned the single basic React project I made in my first year, how I used components as reusable entities, and what I could make out by the name dynamic components, while clearly mentioning that it had been a while for me working with React and frontend in general.

He also asked me what I knew about MSCI - I had researched the website beforehand and gave the appropriate answer.

Then, I was asked a simple question of reversing a string, using OOP. I just created a class with a string as an attribute, and a method for string reversal. And the interviewer was satisfied with that.

A SQL query was presented, based on INNER, LEFT, and RIGHT JOIN where tables contained equal entries (These were two different tables with only 'id' as the attribute). This was more of a trick question as all these joins would result in the same table with 6 rows where a.id = 1 and b.id = 1. I too found it tricky first and described the theory about these joins, stating that, according to my knowledge, all the tables should be the same, as mentioned above. To which the interviewer replied that yes, this is the right answer.

Another SQL problem involved: Given a table Products (pid , ..) and Orders (pid, oid), find the products that are unsold. The key here was to consider that orders are only logged for products that are sold (as there is no 'status' column). This could then be solved by simply LEFT JOINING Products and Orders and selecting where oid = NULL.

A puzzle was given: 6 balls of different weights and a weighing machine. Find the heaviest ball while using the weighing machine the minimum number of times. Here I was unable to arrive at a number less than 6 with various combinations. So he gave me a hint that we can also put multiple balls on the scale at once. Then I realized we can split the balls into groups of 3 and pick the heavier group and repeat a similar process with the heavy group.

Then he opened for questions. First, I asked him about himself. Then I asked a question about MSCI particularly, that given they manage such huge amounts of indexes, there must be a large amount of data to be processed, and that too in real time, so how is all this managed. His answers to both the questions were very detailed and he seemed happy.

A proper shortlist wasn't announced in this round, as after the first round itself, people who were selected were called for the second, while those who were rejected were informed so. Around 20-22 students may have been selected in total.

3. Offline Technical Round 2: (45-60 minutes)

"How does your typical day go?" - This was a question that I wasn't expecting or prepared for as the first question. I answered covering my college routine, assignments, LeetCode practice, and working on projects/hacks.

"What have you done in your college life overall?" - I answered this honestly, explaining that I explored React in my first year but realized it wasn't my cup of tea, then started with Django and also learning ML since last one year, also mentioning my elective "build LLM from scratch" which I had taken last sem as a PE.

"What are your hobbies?" - I play chess as a hobby, my rating is 1000 rapid on chess.com and around 700 in blitz and bullet. Apart from that I also play keyboard as a hobby, again not professionally, but as a hobby.

"Write down an algorithm to teach someone new to the keyboard." - The question was ambiguous, so I asked for clarification. To which he said, "just describe how you would teach keyboard to a beginner." So I explained the entire process from basic keys, chords, and once they reach a certain level (which can be determined by tests), teaching them basic songs, and advanced songs once they advance tests.

"Design an ER diagram based on whatever I explained" - .I started with a users table, a courses table, a courseTaken table (with FK to user_id and course_id) which can be joined, then a table for lessons (FK to course_id), and tests (FK to lessons). The key here is not to describe each and every table or attribute, but to describe the core tables and keep them normalized, avoiding any redundant tables, etc. Since I have designed SQL schemas for a lot of my Django projects, I was fairly confident in designing and explaining this and also ready to explain further.

Then I was asked about my projects which I started to describe. The interviewer interrupted and asked about a particular project, which was the Alumni-Connect App I made during the SIH finals. I described all the features correctly. He then asked how the alumni would benefit from this, to which I replied we also had a job portal where alumni can list referrals they have, which would then also benefit them. Also, our college has a business incubation system where student-startups can be incubated and they can also hire students from the college through this portal. Then he asked about the role of AI in this project as my resume and intro pointed towards that. I said that in this project there was a very small role of AI, in the FAISS based recommendation system to recommend alumni/student profiles based on a user's own profile/resume. I explained the working in detail.

Then he asked about my profile, being focused towards AI and Python, what I would do If I knew there was remotely no use of AI and Python in my role. I answered that, given enough time, I would learn whatever technology is offered, while also making suggestions from my side that maybe AI can make this particular part of the application better, and maybe we can integrate an AI part externally through APIs, while not moving away from the main tech stack of the applications, may it not be Python.

Puzzle: "Split or Steal" - Two people play a game, each time: if they both split, they get equal reward; if one splits and one steals, the stealer gets all of the reward; if both steal, no one gets the reward. This is repeated for n turns (n=20,100). What strategy would you use to maximize your reward? This is more to check the thought process rather than a right answer. I too started with the simpler strategy to always steal, so we at least win the game, even with minimal reward, but then the interviewer told me, "why do you think the other will also always steal?" To which I gave the better solution: to start by splitting, and if the other person steals repeatedly, we too start to steal a couple of times, to indicate that "We're not giving steals for free" and the other person would also not earn anything if they kept stealing.

He then asked me about GROUP BY and HAVING in SQL. I did answer that it is used to filter after the use of GROUP BY ,within the groups, but I think I could have maintained more clarity in that answer. He then asked me the difference between data warehouses and

relational databases. I didn't have much idea of warehouses other than the fact that they're used to store large amounts of structured data, while relational databases are used in order to describe relations and whenever there are joins. He did grill me that joins can also be done in warehouses, to which I agreed that I didn't have much idea about warehouses. I told that relational databases are particularly useful to show relations like foreign keys, example: posts, comments, etc.

Then he opened for questions, and I asked him about himself (because MSCI interviewers generally don't introduce themselves at the start and the HR may ask who you interviewed with to check you). He was an SPIT alum himself, and worked at MSCI on the data engineering side. Then I asked about what he expected from freshers at MSCI to which he replied smilingly that "I don't expect much from freshers except basic logical and problem-solving skills and decent projects, and once they join in they can be groomed according to the role if the basic requirements are considered."

Around 10 students were selected for this round.

The HR Round was very chill and I was asked very basic questions:

"Introduce yourself professionally," based on my projects and as a person, and where I live. My branch is Data Science, but my projects were ML-based, so I was asked about the difference between ML and Data Science and what I was actually interested in, to which I replied that ML and Data Science are dependent upon each other, and that I'm trying to explore the entire pipeline, and ML is just a part which helps overall.

She asked about my family background. She too asked, "Do you know about MSCI?" and "How do you know about it?" - I told her whatever I researched and that I knew about MSCI since it has been coming to college for placements for the last few years. She asked if I invest or plan to invest - I don't invest currently, as I am less into the finance side, but I plan to invest.

But still, I find many courses from top institutions online itself, which makes me question whether doing a masters is worth it. Hence, I want to first work in the industry and while focusing on upskilling myself through such online courses and then take a call on it. She also asked whether I would be able to relocate / which location I would prefer.

replied that I was moving my chair throughout, which showcases my nervousness, but that she understood that this may happen during an interview and advised not to do it generally.

journey.howSecured:
A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round & Finally 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day 5/08/25. The CGPA Criteria for SDE was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was further reduced to 7.5. May not be the case for n ext year if they don 't want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above.

(I have included CGPA)

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting: (In this case it was CGPA shortlisting , but still I have provided guidance for Resume shortlisting )

Always tailor your resume to align with the specific job description of the role you're applying for. These adjustments don't need to be major -- simply swapping a project, updating certifications, or modifying the skills section can make a significant diff erence.

Ensure that your resume maintains visual and structural consistency. Avoid mixing date formats, bullet styles, or using bold/italic formatting inconsistently across sections. A clean, well-organized resume gives a strong first impression.

Once your resume is finalized, evaluate its compatibility with Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS). Tools like Resume Worded can help -- aim for a score of 65 or above.

Initially, the CGPA eligibility criteria for th is role was set at 8.5, but it was later relaxed to 7.5. The shortlist of candidates selected for the Online Assessment and Pre -Placement Talk (PPT) was released on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM.

2. Pre-Placement Talk:

The Pre-Placement Talk was conducted online on 4th August 2025 at 5:00 PM.

The information shared during Pre-Placement Talks is extremely valuable, so it's important to be attentive -- not just to the content of the presentation, but also to the names and roles of the presenters. I made it a point to take multiple screenshots and jot down the specific examples used while the speaker explained some of the company's financial services. These details often come in handy during interviews.

While it's a good idea to ask thoughtful questions at the end of the session, it's even smarter to hold back a few insightful ones. Save them for your interview -- this gives you an opportunity to show continued curiosity and engagement with the company during later stages.

3. Online Assessment: (Approx. 160 students appeared, invigilated by the company) The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. The marking scheme awarded +1 for each correct answer and imposed a -0.25 penalty for incorrect ones. The assessment covered four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude.

Java (18 Questions): This section focused heavily on fundamental OOP concepts in Java. Topics included the Collection Framework (TreeMap, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, ConcurrentHashMap, ArrayList), access modifiers, threads and multithreading, keywords like synchronized and volatile, compile-time and runtime polymorphism, interfaces, abstract classes, exception handling, enums, and functional methods like map, filter, and reduce. Most questions were of the "guess the output" type. Although my primary DSA language is C++, I had thoroughly studied and revised Java concepts beforehand. A great resource for MCQ practice: Java Practice - Sanfoundry

Python (17 Questions): Similar to Java, the Python section included "guess the output" questions involving OOP concepts, inheritance and MRO (Method Resolution Order), shallow vs deep copies, list comprehensions, slicing, dictionaries, sets, stacks, and queues. Many questions required careful dry runs and a strong grasp of Python's internal behavior and edge cases. A good practice resource: Python Practice - Sanfoundry SQL (5 Questions): This section tested practical SQL query-writing skills. The difficulty level was moderate, with questions based on GROUP BY, JOIN, ORDER BY, UPDATE, DELETE, and various date functions. Some tricky questions involved updating joined or aggregated tables. Attempt only if

confident. Highly recommended: Top 50 SQL Questions - LeetCode

Aptitude (30 Questions): This was arguably the most challenging section. It covered clock problems, speed and distance, trigonometry, upstream-downstream problems, probability, combinatorics, statistics, geometry, family relationships, and financial mathematics (including stocks and investments). Some questions were quite verbose and difficult to interpret, and I couldn't solve a few. Two great resources for aptitude practice are:

 YouTube Aptitude Series by CareerRide

 IndiaBix Aptitude Practice

I performed well in the Java, Python, and SQL sections but found the Aptitude section challenging. In total, I attempted around 50-55 out of 70 questions. Fortunately, I was among the 44 students shortlisted out of 160.

Final Tips: Keep your technical concepts in Java and Python fresh, practice aptitude regularly to build speed, and remain calm under pressure. Time constraints will challenge everyone equally -- focus on accuracy, avoid panic, and read questions carefully.

4. Technical Round 1: [44 student appeared] 2 interviewers in my panel

As I mentioned earlier, I was unsure of whether I 'd be selected for interviews or not. So, I was keeping my cool and doing last minute revisions for Java. Around 12:15 pm we received the shortlists and I was delighted to see my name at the 17 th position. I quickly had a small snack before the interviews start so that I am not empty stomach (make sure to eat at least a little and not be completely empty stomach due to stress/tension). I was very lucky with my interview slot and timings, I was scheduled for 2nd interview in my panel. My interview lasted about 30-40 minutes. And there were 2 interviewers in my panel. Even if your interview gets scheduled late, don't worry and do your best.

I will keep my experience as detailed as possible.

I entered the cabin and greeted both the panelists, they asked me about my name and branch (Didn't ask me to introduce myself). They asked me why did I choose Data Science branch. I was honest and said that during that time I was naïve and wanted to pursue a career in data science without much understanding of it, I basically explained how I understood and explored other options and found my interest in software development. They asked me what backend technol ogies I had explored, I had done Node.js + Express framework and Django in python. He disappointedly asked whether I had not tried Java for backend. I answered this question very carefully and told him that I had studied Java for my

2nd Sem and then I had developed games like Snake and minesweeper using Java, and like justified that I know Java. Whereas for backend development my fundamentals are clear enough that switching the language won 't be an issue for me. He was happy with my response. Then he shifted the interview towards Java OOPs, He showed me one of the question from Java section in OA.

He started asking whether do I see something wrong in Class Person or a way we can make it better. I suggested making string private and having getter and sette r method to ensure that the name string is not directly accessible from outside of class and only via getter and setter method. He asked me which concept was OOPs is this, I answered Encapsulation and explained what it meant in this scenario .

He then asked me about the output of the code, I answered "2 100". Later they asked me how can I make the output to be 1 100. So, I suggested overriding equals and hashcode methods provided my HashMap class in Person class to behave such that if the name is equal, It will treat it as same object otherwise as different object. He also asked to improve the declaration of HashMap object. At first, I couldn't understand what exactly was needed to be done, I suggested having Person class object be immutable as there is a risk of key getting corrupted due to change in data within a Person object. Then they asked a follow up on what is a immutable class, I explained how to make a class immutable and also mentioned about enums. For the earlier question, Later they give me hints and I understood and explained that having a ref of parent and object of child class is a better practice in Java, as you can change the object to any other child of the parent without having to change the ref.

Map<Person, Integer> mp = new HashMap<>();

was the answer they were looking for. I needed hints but I caught on to it at the very end. They asked me to write a very simple program to remove all the white spaces from a string and return the string. I requested whether I could use C++, and I wrote it on piece of paper, I started by writing #include<stdio.h> but they said it's fine and write the logic, so I made a function with proper name like removeWhiteSpaces and passed in the string and simply iterated over it and checked whether if the character is non space then append it to ans string and return ans. The interviewer commented that he liked how I made a function instead of writing in Main.

Then they asked me about a simple S QL query involving a join and order by and limit to get the first row. I also said that it's possible to use max(date) to get the row with latest date.

The interview questions ended on a brighter note.

Questions I asked to interviewers:

1. I asked them to introduce themselves and their role.

2. How is AI being integrated within I SS and what's its impact has been for ISS. (I tried to enter the convo when they jokingly said that people in the company sometimes don't understand their own code as they use AI and that is why they do code reviews. Here I tried to showcase how I personally use AI as more of a tutor for learning and deep diving into concepts)

3. I don't remember exactly how but they were talking about data scrapping , and I took the opportunity and I replied that I have experience with data scrapping as well and how I made a s cript to scrape linkedIn profile data from their user urls using selenium and beautiful soup.

By the end of this, they asked me where do I stay and whether commute will be a problem.

And just after 10 minutes of leaving the cabin at 2 pm, I was notified that I have been shortlisted for next round. Why I Think I Got Selected:

 Timing & Luck: I got an early interview slot, which helped.

 Confidence & Communication: I stayed composed and articulated my thoughts clearly.

 Honesty: I was transparent about what I knew and didn't.

 Engagement: I asked meaningful questions and engaged in a two-way conversation. Even if you don't know something don't stay completely silent and keep processing your thoughts out and don't panic. Your personality and confidence also matters, try to work on soft skills and effective communication. Give as much mock interviews as you can to better prepare yourself.

In total 15 students were shortlisted for HR round including me.

Tips:

 Do not lie on your Resume but you can smartly change phrases so that your resume looks good.  Do not throw the sheets/papers in which you did your OA questions. They can be asked in an interview.  Make sure if you are adding any links then they are clickable in your resume  Prepare well around your resume projects & its tech stack. You can ask your friend to keep on cross questioning you on them  Prepare a couple of scenarios (even if fake) about disagreement in the team, or any times that you have shown leadership/ team spirit. These questions are very common too.  If you don't know the answer or you are not able to recall it, try to put it across politely instead of saying something wrong  Think out loud when solving a DSA problem/ SQL query but when saying a theory answer try to sort of structure it in your mind first. Make use of technical terms & examples where possible

5. HR Round: [15 students Appeared] 2 panelists

My HR round started at around 3:50 pm, I had prepared in advance for all the common HR questions which could be asked. Even if you get caught off guard do not panic and be calm and collected, answer it genuinely. My HR round lasted for about 30 minutes.

I entered the room and greeted the interviewers, their first question was do you know us. I had paid attention to PPT so I knew their names and I h ad mentioned that their cameras were not working properly so I didn 't realize it instantly but by listening to their voice. They first asked me about my education from 10 th, 12th and College CGPA and Cet score. I answered the question by making a narrative about how I wasn't very studious and how I got serious about studies and answered each question. They asked me about my family background, make sure to answer only what is needed and not more than that. I showcased how being a single child, my parents have been supportive and available for me. She also asked whether I knew the office location and visited the NESCO IT park, I replied with correct answer and was honest that I hadn't been there.

She asked me about why did I pursue CSE DS, I again answered gen uinely and told her the truth. She asked me about my 1st coding project, I mentioned I had gotten into game development using Unity and later using Java built snake and minesweeper games. She also asked me about masters and would I want to pursue it. I answered no (I genuinely hadn't planned for masters) mentioned that how skills, experience and practical knowledge in industry is required to stay relevant and masters is more theoretical and academia focussed. So, I would rather up skill myself while working in a job. She pressed on even more about the fact that aren't my parents insisting for me to do masters since I am a single child. Again, I thought carefully and answered that it was different during my father's time where a degree was required to grow in pharmaceutical companies. Whereas in tech I don't need as much

education, having experience and skills are the most important thing. (Try to justify the trade off between masters and job)

How do I stay relevant about the tech news. I said Youtube, Reddit, Twitter and justified my perspective. She started asking me about my perspective about AI, I made sure to answer everything positively. I said AI is a tool and won't completely replace a human, at least not until there is a very fundamental change in how AI works. I made sure to cover the positive aspects of AI, she said would it have any impact on jobs? And I said that due to this for example 10 people doing some work would be reduced to 5 -6, but there could be other jobs for managing agentic AI systems. She asked me how would I make sure I don 't get replaced with AI. I again answered that not staying in the comfort zon e for a long time is the key and always having continuous growth and learning is essential.

She also asked me about my hobbies, I answe red reading, table tennis, badminton, swimming. I made sure to elaborate on how reading was not my strong point and how I developed that skill effectively. Sir had only asked me a single question about what is my preference regarding application developer and AIML. I made sure to answer diplomatically, I said my primary focus is on developing software either for clients or for some internal company usage, and within software development I want to keep my options broader and so that I am able to figure out my interests, etc. And how I could maybe help others get a new perspective in software development processes using my ML and Gen AI knowledge, so no knowledge ever goes waste. She lastly asked where do I stay and whether commute would be a problem for me. I live in thane so I said it won't be a big issue for me as I have been travelling for SPIT for the past 3 years. And if I do find it difficult, I would simply shift closer towards the company and ensure it doesn't hamper my work.

I made sure to ask decent questions:

1. How is data staleness managed as old data cannot be served to clients

2. Since ISS is multi -national company serving over 15+ countries , how do they manage and maintain regulatory compliance for each country.

3. How does team and project allotment work for interns and freshers in ISS

HR Interview Tips:

1. Maintain Eye Contact Ensure steady, natural eye contact with the interviewer. It shows confidence and helps build a connection, but avoid staring as it may come across as forced.

2. Be Mindful of What You Share Avoid oversharing personal experiences that don 't directly address the question. Focus on relevant, concise answers that highlight your suitability for the role.

3. Use the STAR Method Structure your answers to behavioral questions using the STAR me thod (Situation, Task, Action, Result). It provides clarity and demonstrates a problem -solving mindset.

4. Show Respect in All Responses Be polite and professional. Even casual or off -topic comments should be delivered respectfully to avoid unintentionally off ending the interviewer.

5. Frame Strengths and Weaknesses as Narratives Share your strengths and weaknesses with context. Use short stories or examples (real or carefully crafted) that showcase growth and self -awareness.

6. Avoid Monologues Don't treat your ans wers like speeches. Keep the conversation balanced, concise, and interactive. Know when to stop and where to elaborate.

7. Display Confidence and Personality Strong communication and soft skills often outweigh technical skills in HR rounds. Let your personality come through --be confident, composed, and clear.

8. Always be Positive Always answer all questions in a positi ve manner and I 'll suggest don't ask for feedback in an HR interview, you can in a technical round if you feel that you 've done great.

9. Always Deny plans for Higher Studies

Never show interest or accidently hint your passion for academia and research . Prepare solid reasons to justify why you're choosing industry over academia, or it may become your reason for rejection.

Lastly, 12 students were selected out of 15, including myself. 2 for Data quality, 2 for software testing, 8 for Software Engineering.
