1. Pre - Placement Talk: 24th June

2. Resume Screening: 27th June

3. Online Aptitude Test: 28th June Further rounds took place offline on 2nd July

4. Group Discussion

5. Interview Round 1

6. Interview Round 2

7. HR Round Resume Screening Your resume is as very crucial a part of the entire selection process as any other. Building your resume is a time consuming process, so allot enough time for it. Try to tailor your resume to the role you are applying for. All resumes are screened by an ATS (Applicant Tracking System), so you can check your score on websites like "ResumeWorded". My resume had a score of 72. Key points regarding resumes - They should be 1 page resumes as that's what is expected from freshers. Make single column resumes in Latex format. Try to include all relevant coursework / competition / projects / internships in your resume. Having 1-2 good finance projects on your resume helps. Participate in case study competitions. Do some finance certifications and add them onto your resume. You can make minor changes to your resume that you are taking for your interviews. Results were announced 1 day prior OA Test around 9. Online Assesment (67 Students were shortlisted) The online test was conducted on campus. With a total of 45 marks, it consisted of 4 sections - Finance & Accounting (10): This section contains mostly accounting and corporate finance questions. I think it had 1 question about puttable bonds. Market Awareness (10): This section contained quite a few economy questions and market sentiment questions, I had something related to " what is the exemption on taxes for investing in government pension schemes", so focus on market situations and terms, be aware of

current affairs just to be safe Quantitative Aptitude (15): This section focused on permutations, probability, and algebra questions. So this one is out and out mathematics. Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension (10): This is an English section, pretty simple if you try to stick with the basics. The time given was 45 mins, so there is a time crunch as the quant section is tough, the VARC section is easy but time consuming. So try to segregate the sections into time slots so you can attempt as much as possible. The results for this round were announced a day before the final day i.e. 1st July. So don't lose heart in the process and be prepared. Group Discussion (37 students were shortlisted) Group discussion Topic - "Central Banks' Diverging Paths Amid Geopolitical Stress - The Bank of England maintains rates at 4.25% due to global uncertainty, while Norway and Switzerland have opted for rate cuts. Explore how central banks should balance inflation control with growth risks, particularly in the context of conflicts or trade wars." The moderators also introduced subtopics during the discussion. As far as I remember, these included "Views on Forex reserves", "What are the impacts of having different views and policy of central banks" Ensure you contribute at least 3-4 meaningful qualitative points. Try to work as a team, acknowledge others points and add on to it. Make sure you speak for 45 sec - 60 sec per point so the moderator takes note of you. The discussion time was 20 mins and last 10 min were for summary We had 3 panels for GD Interview Round 1 (22 students were shortlisted) The round consisted of accounting questions, Corporate Finance, puzzles, mental maths, market awareness. The following are the questions that were asked to me. The change in depreciation and taxes and what are its effect on the financial statements. Latest IPO and M&A What is capital restructuring and why is it done. I had made a DCF valuation project, so I was asked questions about it. I was asked to calculate 57 × 63. Be sure to explain your approach. Other people were also asked the values of roots i.e 2,3,10 etc. I had done the forage investment banking simulation course, so a few questions on them. The round lasted for 30-40 mins. I was last in panel but was called early which took me by shock. If you are not able to answer anything don't panic makes sure you tell the thought process and approach for it. If you make a mistake or there is some misunderstanding in what you were supposed to answer DO NOT PANIC, --your interview isn't over. One or two mistakes are acceptable so keep your head down and focus on answering the rest of the questions properly. Once the GD is done you might receive the order of interview, but always be ready there can be changes in last minute and you can be called anytime

Interview Round 2 (12-15 students were shortlisted) This round was taken by the manager for CIB, the duration of this round was only 7-8 minutes. The round consisted of 30-35 rapid fire questions. I was asked to explain the DCF valuation model I had made. I was also asked questions on WACC, Beta, Financial Ratios, Talk about any stock for 30 seconds--its market capitalisation, stock value any and everything you know about it. I was asked if I invested in stock, to which I answered no. I was able to answer all the questions correctly. Make sure you are thorough with all the formulas. My round 2 was scheduled a minute after my round 1 so be ready. Everything happens simultaneously and can be chaotic, so be relaxed, focused and calm. HR Interview (10 students were shortlisted) This round was informal and relaxed, lasted for 10-15 mins. I was asked to briefly talk about my resume and explain one of my leadership roles. I was asked about my family background. I was asked did I know what exactly my job role is and how my past work and leadership experience can help me to better in the internship. 10 students were selected for CIB banking role Important Tips 1. The core essence of the process is not about how much you know but whatever you do, how well-versed you are in it. So focus on learning things deeply rather than trying to do a lot of things. 2. Resources CFI courses - Accounting Fundamentals, Corporate Finance, Reading Financial Statements Udemy - The complete investment banking 2025 Forage - Jp Morgan Investment banking job simulation YouTube - DCF valuation, How are 3 financial statements linked, 2008 financial crisis, SVB bank collapse, what is SENSEX AND NIFTY, how is GDP calculated, Adani-Hindenburg saga, Puzzles - GFG 100 puzzles Quants- IndiaBix.com

3. During interviews, always maintain proper posture, have a smile on your face, do not panic even if you are unable to answer and at least let the interviewer know what approach you're thinking about.

4. The entire placement cycle is very hectic and stressful but it is important to stay in the present and study without worrying about external factors like market situation, recession, etc. Believe me, it never goes to waste. If you have prepared honestly, you will get opportunities.

5. If you have any questions,, I'll be more than happy to help. You can reach out to me directly on WhatsApp or Linkedin. All the best My Resume for reference: Link

journey.prep:
For preparing for placements and internships, be prepared with:

DSA: It is asked by most companies in Online Assessments and Interviews. Without DSA, you won't be able to clear OA and appear for interviews. Apart from doing DSA sheets also give contests to practice solving questions randomly with a time limit. If possible, do CP. It is not necessary but being good at CP gives an edge in OA.

Aptitude: Some companies ask aptitude questions in OA. I did not explicitly practise as I was confident about it but do practise if you are not sure.

CS Fundamentals: These are very important for interviews and OA.

OOPS in Java (and your preferred language as well), SQL, DBMS are most important. OS, CCN and system design are also important.

Resume: You should know your resume well. Have 2 good projects in your resume. It's good to have internships but not necessary.

Communication is very important in interviews and be prepared for HR Type questions as well. Companies might have other requirements like Machine Coding Rounds, Puzzles, Group Discussion, guesstimates, etc.

CGPA is important. Try to keep your CGPA above 8 (ideally 8.5). Many companies had their shortlisting criteria for OA as 8 and for some it was 7.5 and so on. The higher your CGPA, the more companies you get to appear. Initially, only CGPA till 5th semester was being considered for placements. From 2nd week of august, CGPA till 6th semester was considered. Also make sure you don't have any active backlogs

Russell Investments conducted their first internship drive in India for our batch which included many roles. TPO informed us about 3 roles: Technology Intern, Business Process Automation Intern, Investment Research Intern. The rest of the interview process was done completely at their office or through online interviews. The HRs informed us directly about rounds through mail or calls.

1. Written Test (40 minutes)[30 on day 1 and approx. ~25 on day 2]

● 10 Aptitude MCQ

● 10 CS Fundamental MCQ

● 3 coding questions (Attempt any 2) - Valid Parenthesis, Binary Search Pseudo code, Find Second Max Element in array.

This test was very easy. Also, this was not an elimination round.

2. Technical Interview 1 [30 on day 1 and approx. ~25 on day 2]

This interview was conducted by a Frontend Developer and Devops Engineer.

The interview focused mainly on my resume. The discussion was regarding my internship and my projects. Apart from this I was asked 1 leetcode easy question - find common elements in 2 strings. A few database related questions were asked as well.

3. Technical Round 2 [ No of candidates who appeared for this round ]

This round was conducted by the Director of Application Development.

The interviewer focused on my resume. He asked me questions about my projects from a business perspective. Like why would organizations choose my applications above other companies or build it in house. I was questioned about SDLC and Testing. Apart from that, I was asked about my interests. The interview ended with me asking him questions.

Till here, the entire process was conducted in 1 day at their office. The selected candidates(6 total - 4 from day 1 and 2 from day 2) were allotted the role Intern, Application Development.

The process was over and I assumed that I had been rejected. But a week later, I received a call from the HR that they wished to conduct additional rounds in my case. At that time, I asked HR clearly if the rounds were for the same role to which she said yes. Later on, I got to know that the additional interviews were for the Automation team.

Technical Interview 3

This round was conducted by Application Development Manager in the Automation Team on Microsoft Teams.

I was asked a leetcode easy question on arrays and a question on joins in SQL. I was asked 4 principles of OOP which I explained with examples. I was asked to write an efficient sorting algorithm that sorts the array till a particular index only. I chose to write the Merge Sort Algorithm. I was asked some CCN questions related to HTTP and Rest APIs which I don't remember now.

Managerial Round

This round was taken by the Head of Automation online a week after the previous interview.

She asked me to introduce myself and share my resume. She asked me the language I was most comfortable in and asked me to rate myself in it. I rated myself 7/10 in C++ and said it was the language I used for DSA and CP. She googled C++ and asked me a very random question related to pointers. I was not able to answer the question. I did not know that keyword but explained pointers in C++ and why they are important. This discussion went on for 15 minutes where we discussed the difference between C++ and Java, use of C++ for building games, etc. As the allotted time was over, I was unable to ask any questions.

A few hours later, I received the mail that I have been selected for the technology intern role.

When I received my offer letter it said 'Intern, Data Automation'. That is when I realised I was interviewing for a different team in my last 2 interviews. So, finally 8 technology interns(of which 5 were from SPIT) were selected with 6 in App Dev and 2 in Automation. There is not much difference in the roles, I guess, as we worked on the same projects and technologies.

I am writing this interview experience 5 months after my interviews. So, I am not able to recall all the questions. But from a preparation perspective for Russell, you need to have a strong hold over CS Fundamentals and know your resume well. Also, practice aptitude if necessary.

Process Date: 11th Sept 2025 (OA), 12th Sept 2025 (Interviews)

1. Resume Shortlisting (~100 students appeared)

So the process started with resume shortlisting. I'm not entirely sure about the exact numbers, but I think around 100 people applied for this role. The company shortlisted around 50 students based on our resumes.

My advice to you guys would be to align your resume with the job description. If they're asking for ML skills, show ML projects. Don't just randomly put projects that don't relate to the role.

Results: 50 students moved forward to the Online Assessment.

2. Online Assessment (~50 students appeared)

The OA lasted 60 minutes. There were 20 MCQs and 4 coding questions. The catch was once you submit a question, you can't revisit it -- this put some pressure on me.

Coding Questions:

Q1. Check if the previous element is smaller than the current element; if yes return true, else false. (This one was straightforward)

Q2. Previous Greater Element problem (Standard stack question)

Q3. Some DSA question related to gradient descent - honestly, I couldn't understand this one properly. It was confusing.

Q4. Rotate array by 2, then you get a string, and if you find any element from that string in your array, replace it with the given element. (Took me some time to understand what they were asking)

I solved 2 coding questions completely. The MCQs were easy to medium, but because I spent time on coding, I couldn't solve all MCQs. Java wasn't available as a language, but since I usually code in C++, it wasn't a problem for me.

When the results came out, only 10 students were shortlisted, and I was one of them.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (10 students appeared)

I started by introducing myself. They immediately dived deep into my projects, which I had prepared for. Then they gave me the Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II problem. I already knew it from Striver's DP sheet, so I explained the DP approach confidently. They then asked for the O(n) linear approach -- I explained but made a small mistake. They kindly corrected me and said, "You're on the right track." That encouragement boosted my confidence mid-interview.

They also asked me about the difference between React and normal HTML/CSS and some questions related to my resume .

Then came a rapid-fire round: factorial (loop & recursion), recursion issues (I said TLE), which DS recursion uses (Stack), why use DP, assigning priority to objects (I said priority queue). I liked this part because it felt like a fun quiz rather than grilling.

Some other candidates were asked to open Google Colab do some visualizations/operations on dataset; I wasn't asked that.

Overall, my interview went well.

Shortlist: 5 students.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (5 students appeared)

We started again with a quick intro and discussion of one of my hackathon projects. Then they gave me a case study:

"You're a Senior Data Analyst at AuxoAI. Microsoft needs 1000 applicants for a job. You have job seeker data from your client. How would you select 1000 candidates for that job role?"

I gave some thought then I said I'd parse resumes using pyresparser and extract features like skills, education, location, and experience, and a few more features that I don't clearly remember now.. My output would be "Eligible/Not Eligible." I initially said Naive Bayes for the model.

Then they asked how I'd handle candidates backing out at the last moment. At first, I overcomplicated it -- I said I would check factors like college tier (if someone is from a top college, they might get better offers), location preferences, salary expectations, and experience level. I thought of approaching it with regression, reasoning that more experienced candidates usually want better opportunities.

But they immediately pointed out that this is actually a classification problem. At that moment, I realized my mistake, smiled, and corrected myself: "In that case, I will use Logistic Regression to classify whether a candidate is likely to back out or not."

I felt like I redeemed myself here by being honest and flexible.

Other candidates were asked guesstimates -- so be ready for that too.

Shortlist: 3 students.

5. HR Round (3 students appeared)

This was just a casual chat. They asked about my family, where I stay, etc. It lasted 5-10 minutes. After such heavy technical rounds, this felt like a breather.

Selected as AI Engineer Intern at AuxoAI with PPO opportunity.

Useful Tips

● For aptitude, use Indiabix and Career Ride YouTube channel.

● For coding, Striver's sheet (especially DP) + LeetCode.

● For SQL, do 50 questions on LeetCode and 50 general SQL problems.

● For ML, Krish Naik's channel is excellent.

● Be ready for case studies -- think aloud, they like your approach even if it's not perfect.

● Don't panic if your language isn't available -- have C++ or Python as backup.

● Be honest if you make mistakes -- it's better than faking an answer.

All the very best! Feel free to reach out if you have any questions. Always happy to help!

● MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor, as most students were able to fully solve the DSA and SQL questions. Focus on practicing MCQs extensively, especially during the final phase of your placement preparation. I personally used GeeksforGeeks and Sanfoundry for preparing Java/C++ MCQs.

● Always make sure to go through the types of questions a company has asked in previous years. This proved to be very helpful for students who had done so for this OA :)

● If you're unable to think of an optimized solution right away, start with a brute-force approach or use the hit-and-trial method. The goal is to pass as many test cases as possible within the limited time, even if the logic isn't the most efficient initially.

● Make sure you have ample sleep before the day of the interview as it is going to be a very long day ahead.

2. Tech Round 1 [37 candidates appeared, 19 Shortlisted] (Lasted around 45 Minutes)

The round began with the typical "Introduce Yourself" question. It is important to plan this thoroughly, as it often sets the tone for the rest of the interview. A well-structured introduction can guide the flow of the conversation toward your strengths and areas you are most comfortable discussing. While introducing yourself, try to subtly highlight any project/internship/competition that might catch the interviewer's interest.

In my case it was a website which I had made for my father's company which automated a lot of repetitive tasks. The interviewer was curious about the same and we went on to discuss it for a couple of minutes.

Next, I was asked to code the classic string permutations problem. Always make sure to explain your thought process and dry run for the same first then start coding. Even while coding, explain each line as you are typing.

Then we had a discussion about some of my other projects in my resume and the interviewer questioned me for my choice of the tech stack for each of them.

The interview concluded with me asking two non-technical company related questions.

Tips:

● In case you are asked a question which you have seen/solved previously, do not make the mistake of directly jumping onto the optimized solution. Start off with the brute force, then go on to explain how you would improve your code to get the most optimal

solution possible. You do not want the interviewer to know that you are already aware about the problem.

● If you are stuck on a question, first explain your approach to the interviewer and ask for hints afterwards. Most of the time, they are interested in your thought process and how well you are able to communicate and understand the problem.

● Have 2-3 unique projects which you can talk hours about. Have the what, why and how prepared for each project ready. It is always a plus if you've worked on a project with real world impact.

● Try to use SQL databases as many times, you might be asked to discuss the schema designs.

3. Techno-HR round [19 candidates appeared] (lasted around 45 minutes)

It was a technical + HR for most of the candidates, but in my case it was completely HR based. The round started again with the introduce yourself question. This time, I made sure to give more emphasis towards my position of responsibilities and the competitions I had taken part in. Following are the questions asked:

● How did I deal with team conflicts that might have occurred during the span of my tenure

● Another question focused on whether I had ever faced a situation where I had to make an unethical decision, and how I dealt with it

● My strengths and weaknesses. (Ensure that you mention the steps you are taking to overcome your weaknesses)

● Where do I see myself in 5 years

● How would I go on to work on a piece of tech that I have little to no idea about

Tips:

● Research about the company values beforehand and try to answer the questions organically in a way which aligns with them, for Barclays, these included RISES principles

● Thoroughly explain your thought process for decision-making questions, including how you weighed the pros and cons in each scenario.

● Try to ask good questions at the end of the interview. This is to ensure that the interviewer remembers you throughout the process

A quick backstory about my placement journey -

I began my DSA preparation after the 5th semester but had shifted focus entirely to investment banking for the three months leading up to placement season. Unfortunately, I couldn't clear the Group Discussion round of the J.P.M.C interview, which was a major setback. It was disheartening, as I hadn't ever expected to be eliminated in the very first round.

It was hard for me to switch back to DSA after the long break. But after a lot of practice, I was able to get back on track. After facing 6 rejections, I was able to crack this offer.

Things to keep in mind:

● Your communication skills matter a lot during the interview. Practice thinking out loud while solving DSA problems

● A well crafted resume can help you right from shortlisting to the final HR round. Aim for an ATS score of 70+ on platforms like Resume Worded

● Gear up for a potential emotional roller coaster, bound by anxiety, fear, hope(lessness), and joy at last. This phase of life will teach you a lot, make sure to learn from every rejection. All you need is one good day. Sooner or later, if you've prepared sincerely, that day will come.

● Make sure to participate in Hackathons (and Case Study Competitions if you are preparing for PM/IB/DA roles). They are a great way of developing good projects and learning new things.

● If you're preparing for a non-tech role, evaluate whether you can also do at least basic DSA preparation in parallel. It proved to be one of the best decisions in my case.

● If you don't get selected, don't be disheartened there's always another company and another chance. Stay focused, stay hopeful, and keep moving forward.

ALL THE BEST FOR YOUR PLACEMENT !!

journey.howSecured:
1) OA

2) Technical Interview 1

3) Technical Interview 2

4) HR Interview

1. OA [ 120+ Appeared ]

All students who applied sat for the OA But then came the first twist: only shortlisted students were allowed to appear for the test, and several of us found out last minute that we weren't eligible. There were no clear guidelines on the basis of rejection -- it could have been 12th-grade marks, CGPA, or something else entirely. From this, I realized maintaining a strong academic record,

Coming to the OA itself -- the aptitude section had a heavy focus on seating arrangement problems. I'd say around 5-6 questions were based on circular and linear seating. My aptitude went very nice

The real challenge came in the coding section. We had 3 questions to solve in just 30 minutes. One was the classic House Robber problem, which I tried to approach using binary search. My logic and functions worked fine when I tested them with static input, but I struggled a lot with handling input and array initialization in the given environment. Even the enhanced for-each loop wasn't working as expected. I ended up trying 3 different variations, but none passed due to these input issues. Because of that, I couldn't solve any coding problem, which was very disappointing since the logic part was actually clear to me.

On the aptitude prep side, I realized that platforms like IndiaBix are no longer enough. Even after solving everything on IndiaBix, I got rejected in many companies , because their aptitude level was higher. For serious prep, I would strongly recommend going through R.S. Aggarwal's aptitude book, because companies are raising the bar year by year.

2. Group Discussion [ 60 students ]

After the OA results were out, I found myself shortlisted for the Business Analyst (BA) role. Honestly, I wasn't very interested in BA and had only planned to attend to avoid any demerits.

The next morning, I got to know that candidates could apply for a role change, but it required HR approval and would be considered purely on the basis of the resume. The catch was: before applying for any other role (like Framework Engineer or MLE), all BA-shortlisted candidates first had to clear the Group Discussion (GD) round. If you failed the BA GD, you were out of all roles.

There were about 60 students shortlisted for BA, divided into 6 groups of 10 each. For the GD, we were given 1.5 minutes to jot down points and structure our thoughts. My group's topic was: "9-to-5 Job vs Startup."

The discussion went really well for me. I didn't start or conclude, yet I still made it to the next round. This made me realize an important point: it's not always mandatory to be the first or last speaker to get noticed. What really matters is how meaningful and relevant your contributions are during the discussion.

3. BA Round 1

The interview started with the classic "Introduce yourself," where I briefly covered my projects, achievements, and interests. The interviewer immediately pointed out, with a smile, that my resume didn't have a single mention of the word "business" -- and we both laughed at that.

He then picked up on my Profit View project (Virtual Trading System) since he himself was very interested in the stock market. He asked me to explain it in detail, which I did confidently. The follow-up questions were challenging:

● "Suppose you have 8 billion customers next day -- how would you handle scaling, and what would be your revenue model?"

● "What is the highest stock in the Indian stock market?"

● "Why did you integrate AI into this project?"

● "Which is better: AI or human intelligence?"

I answered these from a market perspective, staying practical and confident. He also tested me on current market knowledge: "The market is bad right now, which sectors would you invest in?" Another situational question was: "If you're in a 3-member team (1 stock market expert, 2 developers), and the industry stakeholder wants a new feature X that clashes with your ideas -- whom will you listen to?"

Then, he switched to my Legal AI project. He grilled me on technical details -- models like BERT, PEFT, Microsoft Phi-2, and why I chose them. He also asked: "How many cases are filed daily in the Mumbai High Court?" (a guesstimate question linked to my project domain).

Towards the end, he challenged me on role alignment: "Why join Quantiphi as a BA when your resume shows you're a developer?" I explained my reasoning, and he also asked me about Quantiphi's competitors. Finally, he pressed me multiple times on my preference -- BA or FE. I stayed consistent and confidently said Framework Engineer every time, despite the follow-up trick questions.

The interview lasted around 40-50 minutes, and it was intense but engaging. Before wrapping up, I asked him if he was personally interested in stock markets. He smiled and said yes -- he actively invests too. That made for a nice ending to the discussion.

4. FE Round 1

After being promoted to the Framework Engineer role (based on my resume), my interview started with the usual introduction. The interviewer then moved into some basic technical questions, like the difference between C++ and Java.

From there, the focus shifted to my projects.

● On Profit View, he asked me about the working of the system, why I chose specific technologies, and the role of message queues and Redis caching.

● Next, we moved to Mark Me. I explained for 2-3 minutes straight, covering why I chose the project, the problems we faced, and how we solved them.

● Chronologically, he then asked about Legal AI. Specifically, he wanted me to explain what RAG is. I gave a detailed 2-3 minute explanation of my pipeline -- including saving data in Astra DB and the flow of the retrieval process. He seemed quite impressed with this project. ●

Since my primary language is Java, I expected some heavy DSA questions, but surprisingly, he only asked very basic ones. For example:

● "Given the area of a circle, find its radius."

● A couple of easy SQL questions -- one on filtering (like names ending with "YADAV") and one on simple joins.

The entire interview lasted 40-45 minutes.

Key Takeaways:

1. The interviewer was more interested in my projects because they had practical use cases and impact.

2. For one of my friends, the interviewer asked a much tougher question: "Write code to fetch live coordinates of the user without using any reference docs " So the difficulty can vary a lot.

4. FE Round 2

My second interview was quite short and casual, lasting only about 15-20 minutes. It began with a simple "Introduce yourself," and I kept my introduction brief and to the point.

The interviewer mainly focused on my projects:

● He first asked about Profit View (Stock Market Project).

● Then he moved to Mark Me. Since I mentioned that I am a follower of ISKCON, he lightly questioned me on how I manage to work on stock market projects, considering it's not typically encouraged. This part felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

After that, he asked about the databases I knew and a couple of very basic questions on the difference between SQL and NoSQL. He also asked about the backend technologies I'm familiar with, but only at an informational level -- there was no deep cross-questioning.

Towards the end, he asked the standard "Why Quantiphi? Who are Quantiphi's competitors?" and reminded me that the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) is very important, as it helps us understand the company better before interviews.

Overall, it was a light and comfortable interview -- more of a discussion than a grilling session -- and the interviewer seemed satisfied with my answers.

5. HR Round

Unlike a typical HR round, this one focused on management and stakeholder questions. The panel began by asking me to introduce myself -- but specifically told me not to mention any projects. They then asked several situational questions like:

● "If your team members are not working, how would you tackle them?"

● "How would you convince stakeholders to buy your product?"

At one point they said: "You are linking each question to your project -- what possible flaws can you detect in the project? If you knew them, what actions did you take to overcome them, and how would you still manage to retain consumers even after those problems?" I explained everything properly: how we identified flaws, the corrective steps we implemented, and the communication/mitigation strategies we used to keep users engaged despite issues.

Since I was leading a team of four on my ongoing project, I used those experiences to answer the management scenarios -- showing concrete examples of problem detection

After nearly 3 hours of waiting, results were announced around 9:30-10 PM: 8 students were selected (3 FE, 2 MLE, 3 BA).

journey.prep:
Here are some resources I used for interview preparation:

Using all of these for preparation as early as possible is important. Start at most 6 months before the placement period begins. Ensure you know every single programming language and framework on your resume as much as possible. Also, add good projects to your resumes. Ones that solve real-world problems, and are innovative and unique. Ensure they are uploaded to your Github account or, even better, deployed on a public URL. Doing an internship before the placement period is also recommended.

For DSA: Use Striver's A2Z DSA course https://takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course/strivers-a2z-dsa-course-sheet-2/

For OOPS, DBMS, OS: Use https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/

For Git/Github and Computer Networks: Watch Kunal Kushwaha's videos. https://www.youtube.com/@KunalKushwaha

For Aptitude: Solve questions from https://www.indiabix.com/

For SQL questions: Use SQL 50 from Leetcode and keep solving from the SQL section. SQLBolt is a good resource for beginners.

For System Design: Watch Gaurav Sen's videos: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SqcXvc3ZmRU&list=PLMCXHnjXnTnvo6alSjVkgxV-VH6EPyvoX&a b_channel=GauravSen

⚠ A Final Note:

Placements are heavily dependent on luck, 80-90% of the process is. Luck decides which questions you get in the test, what sort of interviewer you get, what mood they are in, etc. Many people better than me were unplaced at the time of me typing this sheet out. The only thing you can do is work as hard as you can to maximize your luck at any point. I had applied for 16 companies on campus, getting rejected in 4 interviews, and unable to clear 12 OAs. All it needs is one breakthrough.

If not now, then some company will take you up later. If you see your friends get placed before yourself, it's completely natural to feel dejected. The important thing is to remember that you aren't any worse than those around you for not getting selected yet. Just remain calm, do not underestimate yourself, do not keep any excessive expectations (since they can cause pressure) and keep yourself disciplined throughout this hectic period. Take frequent breaks, meditate, and get outdoor time. It is important.

Some online tests are not proctored. No matter how tempting it may seem, DO NOT CHEAT, you will end up paying for it sooner or later (not my own experience FYI). Work hard and get placed on the basis of your merits.

Alright, that's my experience! I hope it gave some valuable insights and was of help to you. Feel free to contact me on my LinkedIn.

☆ Remember to trust the process! ☆
journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process had 3 stages; Online Assessment, Technical Interview and HR Interview. The Pre-Placement talk was carried out at SPIT, in-person by the TransUnion team, prior to the Online Assessment.

1. [Online Assessment] [ 87 students appeared for this round ]

On the basis of their resumes, 87 candidates were shortlisted for the test out of those who applied for TransUnion. The test was conducted on 4th September. It lasted for 1 h 30 min, from 14 00 to 15 30. The test was conducted on SHL and calculators were allowed. There were 4 sections in the test:

Mathematical Aptitude. Puzzle and Pattern based Aptitude. Coding section. English Vocabulary and Grammar section.

A. Mathematical Aptitude involved questions like ratios, proportion, simple interest, time, etc. Example:

● If a train travels 120 km in 2 hours, how long will it take to travel 300 km at the same speed?

● Divide ₹720 among A, B, and C in the ratio 2:3:4.

B. Puzzle and Pattern-based Aptitude involved questions like finding the odd one out, guessing the next number, etc. Example:

● Find the odd one out: 121, 144, 169, 196, 225, 242

● What comes next in the series: 2, 4, 8, 16, ?

C. The English vocabulary consisted of questions like finding the correct sentence or understanding the conveyed message from a passage. Example:

● Choose the grammatically correct sentence: A) He don't like playing cricket.

B) He doesn't likes playing cricket. C) He doesn't like playing cricket.

● From the given passage, what is the main idea the author is trying to convey?

D. Coding questions consisted of 2 questions of varying difficulty. I received 2 fairly easy questions.

Q1: You are given an array of orders. Find the Order ID of every order in the array. (There was a lot more to the question, I forgot the rest, sorry about that guys :P) Solution: The order ID is calculated by summing all the digits of each element in the array. (The question was framed in a confusing manner, making it seem more difficult than it actually was. I got the solution by analysing the results which followed that format.) Example: Input: [123, 56, 89] Output: [6 (1+2+3), 11 (5+6), 17 (8+9)]

Q2: You are given a 1-indexed array of people with labels 1 to n. For the next m turns, you have to swap the people with specified labels (e.g., '1, 5' means swap 1 and 5's place). After m swaps, return the person at kth index. Example:

● Initial array: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

● Swaps: [(1, 5), (2, 4)] After swaps: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

● If k = 1, return 5.

Tip: For the Online Assessments, I would suggest doing timed practice of aptitude questions and coding questions too. Be sure to practice CodeForces questions as their style (the way they accept inputs and return outputs) can be quite different from LeetCode questions.

2. [Technical Interview] [ 32 students appeared for this round ]

The interviews began the very next day, on 5th September, 10 00 onwards. There were 3 panels, with each containing 2 people who would interview you at the same time. I entered and greeted the panelists. The 2 panelists asked me to introduce myself. I stated my name, where I was studying, and I gave them a brief, yet comprehensive overview of my projects. They asked which programming language I am most comfortable with, which framework I use the most, which frameworks I have used that contain my main programming language, and 'who was the last person you argued with?'

About my projects, they asked me what ML model I used in one, what is the full-form of OCR (since one of my projects had it) and some other surface-level questions.

Then came a DSA question. It was 'You have an array containing elements. Find all of the duplicate elements. Eg: Input: [1,2,3,6,1,1,4,2,2,2,9], Output: [1,2]'. I stated that we can use a hashmap, traverse the entire array, and implement a frequency counter for each element. After that, we use another for loop on the hashmap to select any element which has a frequency over 1. They asked me the time complexity and whether it could be optimised.

They asked me about Object-Oriented Programming. I stated that I was more comfortable with OOP in Java than in Python. Then they asked me to state what pointers are and the difference between Byte and byte in Java.

Finally, an SQL question. We have a table, and we want to delete records containing email of a certain value. We had to write the SQL query on paper. I was also asked how SQL tables reduce query runtimes in case of extremely large tables, to which I replied 'indexing'. They also asked for the explanation of indexing, which I gave along with a real-life analogy.

Lastly, they asked me whether I had any questions for them. I asked them what goes on behind-the-scenes before TransUnion decides to venture or expand into a new area or sector, how they decide whether it is worth venturing into or not. They liked the question and gave a rough idea since they didn't have the answer to this, being software developers, they weren't in charge of these decisions.

Finally, I shook hands firmly with them as I got up, thanking them for their time and closing the door behind me as I left.

The interview lasted only 15-20 minutes. (Every other applicant was surprised, too, since interviews last for 30-45 minutes on average.)

Tips:

Be confident and explain everything clearly. To explain your projects in detail without going on for too long, preferably use an established method like the STAR method.

If you don't know something, DO NOT go on a long-winded, vague explanation in hopes that it will be correct. Just say you don't know it, or you have done it, but forgotten, and the interviewers will move on to the next question. (I did so with the Byte vs byte question and the optimization technique for the DSA question).

The above point also applies to answers you are unsure about. Be confident and stick with some answer. Interviewers test your conviction and willpower, they don't expect you to know everything they ask anyway.

Know your resume in and out. Explain your projects properly and clearly, without sounding too vague. Do not fake anything in it.

When explaining your DSA question's solution, state and explain your thought process as if it were a tutorial of some sort, rather than going silent completely. Start with the brute force-approach and then provide an optimised solution if prompted.

3. [HR Round] [ Approximately 12 students appeared for this round ]

I was asked basic HR questions. I introduced myself, and explained my projects along too, hence they asked questions about the projects on my resume. These questions weren't about the tech and more about what I considered before implementing features in them. They asked me about general limitations that could arise in my project and how I would deal with them.

They moved on to ask me about my family, about their occupations, where I stay, which location I would like, and whether I was open to relocation. Then, they proceeded to ask me why I wanted to work at TransUnion, what my greatest strength is, and how I became good at it. I was also asked why I chose AIML in engineering.

The interview ended with me asking the interviewers the same question I asked in the first interview round (since I got only a rough answer). They answered it in greater detail and I shook hands firmly with them as I got up, thanking them for their time and closing the door behind me as I left.

The interview lasted 15-20 minutes.

Important Tip: Be attentive during the pre-placement talk. Take notes if need be. You MUST remain familiar with what the company does, their values, and what they expect from the average applicant, be it technical skills or soft skills. Work on your communication skills. Even if you have good knowledge, how you convey it might make the difference. Take part in mock interviews and mock speeches to reduce nervousness.

4. [Final Round] [ 8 students appeared for this round ]

Everyone was called outside the TPO and made to sit in room 105, including the TPCs. The TransUnion team entered and stated that only 2 students were selected. The remaining 6 had to go home.

Just kidding. This was a prank round.

All 8 people who cleared the HR round were selected for TransUnion.

[ 8 students were offered the job ]

Here are some resources I used for interview preparation:

Using all of these for preparation as early as possible is important. Start at most 6 months before the placement period begins. Ensure you know every single programming language and framework on your resume as much as possible. Also, add good projects to your resumes. Ones that solve real-world problems, and are innovative and unique. Ensure they are uploaded to your Github account or, even better, deployed on a public URL. Doing an internship before the placement period is also recommended.

For DSA: Use Striver's A2Z DSA course https://takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course/strivers-a2z-dsa-course-sheet-2/

For OOPS, DBMS, OS: Use https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/

For Git/Github and Computer Networks: Watch Kunal Kushwaha's videos. https://www.youtube.com/@KunalKushwaha

For Aptitude: Solve questions from https://www.indiabix.com/

For SQL questions: Use SQL 50 from Leetcode and keep solving from the SQL section. SQLBolt is a good resource for beginners.

For System Design: Watch Gaurav Sen's videos: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SqcXvc3ZmRU&list=PLMCXHnjXnTnvo6alSjVkgxV-VH6EPyvoX&a b_channel=GauravSen

⚠ A Final Note:

Placements are heavily dependent on luck, 80-90% of the process is. Luck decides which questions you get in the test, what sort of interviewer you get, what mood they are in, etc. Many people better than me were unplaced at the time of me typing this sheet out. The only thing you can do is work as hard as you can to maximize your luck at any point. I had applied for 16 companies on campus, getting rejected in 4 interviews, and unable to clear 12 OAs. All it needs is one breakthrough.

If not now, then some company will take you up later. If you see your friends get placed before yourself, it's completely natural to feel dejected. The important thing is to remember that you aren't any worse than those around you for not getting selected yet. Just remain calm, do not underestimate yourself, do not keep any excessive expectations (since they can cause pressure) and keep yourself disciplined throughout this hectic period. Take frequent breaks, meditate, and get outdoor time. It is important.

Some online tests are not proctored. No matter how tempting it may seem, DO NOT CHEAT, you will end up paying for it sooner or later (not my own experience FYI). Work hard and get placed on the basis of your merits.

Alright, that's my experience! I hope it gave some valuable insights and was

journey.prep:
1. Try to have C++ or Python as your primary language and then study OOPS in Java for a well- rounded knowledge base. Even though I knew to solve the coding questions and would have solved all of them collectively in less than 10 minutes(but in Java), my rigidity with Java would have resulted in a costly fumble. 2. The aptitude section for AuxoAI was of a moderate to high difficulty level .I personally used my strong intuition of mathematics to solve the questions. While I had all the time in the world to solve the questions , it won't always be the same .I solved 18-19 questions .

Resources: This video is a goldmine for probability. PROBABILITY in 1 Shot | From Zero to Hero | JEE Main & Advanced

Overall 10 students were selected for the interviews and I was glad to be among them.

3. [Technical Round 1]: ( 10 Students appeared for this round)

The results for the OA were declared around 12 in the night and the interviews were scheduled from 11 in the morning. There were 2 interviewers in each panel. I introduced myself to the panel and then they asked me to select a project on which a deep dive could be possible . I chose the first project on my resume(It was a LSTM+ XGBOOST hybrid model ) , where I explained in detail the methodology of the project .They proceeded by asking the information about the columns used and why only those were selected, the source of the data , the number of rows present , and related questions. They then asked me to tell the metrics of the model (R2_SCORE and the MSE error) and inquired about the mathematical formulas of the metrics

and the intuition behind them.(Some questions such as "explain R2_score to a layman" were also asked. Then I was asked in detail (bohot depth me gaye) about XGBOOST and LSTM and the mathematical intuition behind them .I answered almost all the questions correctly and they were pleased with my fundamentals. They asked me about the gradient descent algorithm and how it works and its mathematical intricacies(fundamental understanding of coordinate geometry and curves is needed). Finally I was asked a bit about GEN-AI . To wrap up the interview , I was asked a simple DSA question. ( Sieve of Eratosthenes) . The expectation was to write a working code . I explained the brute force solution and then explained in detail the optimal approach . I coded the solution (easy tha) and they were pleased by it(it seemed) .Next I was asked about the TC and the SC of the solution ,and I correctly answered it. The interview concluded with me asking a question to the panel . The round lasted around 40 minutes.

Tips: 1. Have strong fundamentals of machine learning and mathematics.

2. Be calm.

4. Technical Round 2 : (5 students appeared for this round) The interview started with my introduction to the panel and another discussion on my projects ensued. They asked many questions on the projects , the technical difficulties and the non technical difficulties which I faced (This was a group project). I was asked about gradient descent and was able to answer almost all the follow up questions on it . Following this, I was asked to design a chatbot for some application (I think this was to check the understanding of the software development cycle ). While I initially stumbled , I was able to rectify and refine my approach iteratively . Finally I was asked a guesstimate on the number of pizzas eaten on a Saturday night in India. The round lasted around 30 minutes.

Tips: 1. In the guesstimate, I did all the calculations mentally , rather than on paper. This can help you . Also it is important to break the problem statement into smaller parts and then find the solution. 2. Be calm.

Round 5: HR ROUND (3 students appeared for this round): This was an informal round conducted by the MD of the company. It lasted around 10 minutes for me .It was just an informal chat wherein he asked me about my day , how do I feel about the situation and just some information on the company .

Tips:

1. A calm mind is the need of the hour .You might be put in unknown and extreme high pressure situations throughout the whole placement process and it is important to not lose your sense of reasoning .

2. Prepare answers for standard HR questions beforehand (jot down the main points) and then try to relate all these points to weave a story .

The interviews concluded by 7 pm on 12/09/25. After that, I departed for my home .But the results were not announced that night and also the following night .It was a really long wait and finally the results were announced on 15/09/25. I was selected finally.

Resources: 1. For Machine Learning and Deep Learning ,CampusX has the best playlist on YT.

1. Playlist name: 100 Days of Machine Learning

2. Playlist name:100 Days of Deep Learning 3. He is making some new playlists on advanced topics as well , do check it out .

2. 3BLUE1BROWN (YT channel ) has some playlists on mathematics. Do check it out . 3. For Puzzles: Since this is a machine learning role , puzzles would be asked mostly on probability(like coins and cards), also you can refer to GFG for top 100 puzzles. 4. DSA: Follow Striver's sheet and then specifically pick some questions from a topic which can help you revise the entire topic. Just do those questions before the OA.(just a suggestion).

General Tips and a small peek into my journey:

1. My placement journey would not have been possible without the constant support of my parents and friends. Have a strong group of people around you who genuinely wish for your success. I feel blessed and lucky to have so many good people in my life. Also , be genuinely happy about others' achievements.

2. Believe in God's plan.

3. My placement journey lasted 78 days. I cleared the online assessments of General Mills (summer intern ) , PhonePE , ZETA , IDFC , BrowserStack , BlackRock , Mahindra and then finally AuxoAI. I was rejected in the initial rounds in General Mills ( was asked a NP hard problem) , PhonePE( I was not confident enough and thus underperformed ), IDFC (was asked about cloud, Springboot ( topics which I did not study) ), Browserstack. I reached the last round in ZETA but was rejected. In BlackRock , I was not given a chance to give an interview even after clearing the OA (was waitlisted ). Throughout this process , I was not asked about any of the projects in even 1 of the interviews and then in AuxoAI , I was asked in detail about my projects(I honestly built the projects) . So , it was a bad streak of luck(for about 2 months) .The thing to note here is that it is fine to take a break of 1- 2 days after a rejection and then have a fresh start leaving everything behind .

4. Patience is something which is quite underrated in this journey. While people around you might be in a hurry to get placed, it is important to keep calm, think rationally, and then take any decision.

5. Luck and the importance of timing cannot be understated in this journey. While consistently getting the toughest questions in OAs (randomized questions in OA) broke me , I was really lucky that AuxoAI came for hiring. Luck evens out in the end (law of averages) but for luck to be on your side, you should be ready to work really hard even in adversity.

I sincerely hope that each one of you achieves more than what you dream of, finds great success, and be satisfied. May your batch perform even better than our batch.

All the very best !!

journey.prep:
● Communication skills and confidence are key and be you, be honest.

● Always take a pause and understand if the interviewer is keeping pace with you.

● Try hard, think out loud, ask for hints if you're stuck.

● If you need a minute to think or frame an answer, ask the interviewer for the same.

● Stay confident, a partially correct answer with 100% confidence is better than a fully correct answer with 50% confidence.

● Always give examples while explaining stuff wherever possible, preferably something relatable.

● Keep questions ready for the interviewer, they always ask if you have any questions for them, never say no here.

● Be attentive during the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) as you'll get enough content to ask relevant questions.

● Your introduction should be short and to the point, and mention things you are good at as the interviewer may lead the discussion based on them.

● Be well versed with your resume from top to bottom.

● Don't just focus on DSA completely, make projects (do them yourself and try to participate in hackathons as winning is not important, the learning is) and have internship experience too.

● Always have a smile on your face and be interactive with your interviewer, even while solving something share your thought process.

● Interviewers are not just assessing your technical skills, they are also assessing your mindset and your approach.

● Don't follow previous interview experiences blindly, as those are from people who got selected but those who didn't may have had completely different experiences, so be confident in your strong points.

My few previous experiences :

I was also selected for the JPMC CFG hackathon (a hiring hackathon), and since my hackathon experience went great, I was quite hopeful of converting it into an offer. Unfortunately, it didn't work out. I even skipped some companies because I was confident about CFG, but sometimes things don't go as planned.

Throughout the placement season, I cleared almost all the OAs for which I applied, but I was not able to convert them into a final selection. This placement phase really tested my patience to the extreme. Even after doing well in interviews, selections didn't happen. I gave interviews for JPMC Fintech, PhonePe, MSCI, IDFC, Nomura (GM role), BlackRock, EDS, and finally got selected at Oracle.

Every interview taught me something new. I don't consider these as failures, but rather as a learning process that helped me finally get selected.

● MSCI interview: I was asked to implement a max heap from scratch (which I managed to do), system design of WhatsApp/messaging system (with focus on group messaging), syntax of sharding in MongoDB (which I didn't know), and to write a Node.js server connection code. The lesson here: always expect the unexpected.

● IDFC interview: I was grilled deeply on Java, Spring Boot, and core implementations of data structures like Map and Set. I was also asked the detailed system design of a URL shortener (my mistake was not preparing system design properly even after being asked about it in MSCI). On top of this, I had to code on their compiler. I explained my code perfectly, but the compiler wasn't running it. The interviewer thought it was my mistake, and that shattered my confidence, leading me to make further errors. Later, I found out their compiler had an issue, and my code was correct all along. The learning: be confident in what you know, and don't let external factors shake your confidence.

● EDS interviews: Both rounds went pretty well. But in the last round, it came down to me and one other candidate. The other candidate was selected due to CGPA and their primary language being Python. Sometimes, despite a good performance, external factors can decide the outcome.

Through all these interviews, I lost my patience many times and even thought of giving up. Giving 100% each time and still not getting through was extremely stressful. But looking back, every rejection just made me stronger. I now believe that some things fall apart to make way for better ones. This was just the start of my career journey, and it has made me tougher for the future.

Placements are honestly based on luck to some extent, but if you don't give your 100%, even failures won't teach you anything. You need to be patient, learn from your failures, and put in more effort the next time. Not every day will be your day, but one day will surely be yours -- and no one can take that from you. So always keep a smile, keep working hard, and stay strong.

If you have doubts do not hesitate to contact me : LinkedIn

Contact no. : +91 9028361188

1 OA (Online) 1 Tech Interview (Offline)

1 Tech + HR (Offline)

1 HR(Offline)

1] OA [ No of candidates who appeared for this round : around 120 , shortlisting criteria : 7 CGPA and 70% in 10th and 12th]

So, our OA was actually supposed to be offline in college, but thanks to the rain it got shifted online at the last moment. The test was for 95 minutes.

It started off with 32 MCQs covering stuff like LLMs, Cloud, basic aptitude, api knowledge and some core tech subjects. There were also a few graph-related ones like articulation points and DFS traversal.

After that, there were 2 coding questions (everyone had different sets). Mine were:

1. We were given a list of requests, each having a user ID and a timestamp. The task was to decide whether each request should be allowed or not. A request could only be allowed if the user had made fewer than k requests in the last 1-minute window. Example: n = 3, user = [1, 1, 1], timestamp = [6, 10, 65], k = 2 Output → [1, 1, 0]

2. Two interns had to complete n tasks. Out of these, the first intern had to do exactly k tasks and the second intern would do the rest. Each intern had rewards for every task, and we had to maximize the total reward. Example: n = 5, reward_1 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], reward_2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 3 Output → 21

Tip from me: Since you could navigate between questions, it's better to attempt the coding ones first (they weren't too hard) and then move on to MCQs. Completing both coding questions was super important to get shortlisted for interviews.

Only 25 students were shortlisted for interviews after OA.

They had the PPT (pre-placement talk) only for the shortlisted candidates. It lasted for about 45 minutes and started at 10:15 AM. The company gave a brief introduction about what they do. My advice would be to pay close attention during the PPT, because it really helps when you want to ask relevant questions later.

After that, the interview rounds started at 11 AM.

It turned out to be a pretty tiring day for me because there was no fixed order for interviews. First, they collected our resumes, and then the interviewers just picked any resume randomly. Whoever's resume they picked was called in. I was eagerly waiting for my turn, but no luck. By that time, many students were already done with their 2nd round, and a few had even completed their 3rd and final interviews--while I hadn't even started my 1st round yet.

Still, I stayed calm, because I had faced a similar situation during my BlackRock interview. Back then, I was also one of the last ones to be interviewed, and even though I did well, I wasn't shortlisted for the next round. This time, I just kept my patience. Finally, I was the very last candidate called in for the 1st round, and my interview began around 3:45 PM.

2] 1st Technical Interview [25 students appeared for this round] There were 4 panels for Round 1. For me it was a cakewalk -- mine lasted only about 10-15 minutes (I think being the last one actually helped). I heard other people's interviews went on for 30 minutes to an hour.

They started by asking me for a short intro and then jumped straight into four basic DSA questions: find the second-maximum element in an array, remove duplicates, check if a string is a palindrome, and write any recursive function (I wrote factorial and explained how recursion works). These were easy, but the interviewer was clearly testing how fast and clearly you think -- they asked me to write pseudocode for each one. I finished the pseudocode in about 5-6 minutes.

After that they asked what my primary coding language was and whether I'd done development in Java. I was honest and said I hadn't. Then we moved on to REST APIs -- I had to write a basic fetch request, explain query parameters and how they work, and discuss alternatives to query params. Finally they asked a basic SQL join syntax and that wrapped up my first interview.

I freaked out a little after because it was so short and I was last -- many people were already on their 2nd or even 3rd rounds while I hadn't finished Round 1. But within 5 minutes they called me for Round 2, so I relaxed a bit.

Tip: Some students were grilled pretty hard on Java -- things like file handling, inline functions, REST APIs, and Postman. A Postman question was "How would you test two APIs where the output of one is the input of the other?" -- so make sure you can explain chaining API calls clearly. Also, those who had knowledge of Spring / Spring Boot were questioned in much more detail, so be thorough if you mention it on your resume. Some candidates were asked about MongoDb and were asked to write basic fetch and how to save on db queries and connections queries.

3] 2nd Tech+ HR [15-16 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was the techno-HR round. Five minutes after I finished Round 1, I was called for Round 2 -- this one was taken by one of the directors of OFSS (the same person who did the PPT), so paying attention during the talk actually helped. This round was totally resume-driven -- no DSA, SQL, or puzzles.

The interviewer went through my resume and then we started with a short intro. He was super friendly and asked about my JEE journey, why I chose SPIT instead of an IIT/NIT, and why I went into engineering -- those are open-ended, so be honest. He asked about my primary coding language and what made me pick it, then asked me to explain a recent project and drilled a few follow-ups. He also asked about my positions of responsibility -- what my role was and how I balanced it with academics.

Since I'd been the marketing head, he gave me a Shark-Tank style task: imagine he was Jack Ma with 200 million to invest -- pitch one of your crowdfunding projects and convince him to invest. At first I started explaining the project, then realized I needed to market it -- so I switched to a pitch mode and that worked out well; the interviewer seemed happy.

He then asked some Java basics: what the import statement does, the difference between interfaces and abstraction (I gave examples), packages in Java, and to explain the static and final keywords. At the end he asked if I had any questions. From the PPT I remembered they mentioned AI models, so I asked whether Oracle (or the company) was building in-house AI models and how those models are affecting the company -- I also asked his view on whether AI is a boon or a curse for people in tech. We wrapped up, shook hands, and I left. It lasted for around 35- 40 mins.

In my opinion this round was mainly to assess mindset, attitude toward tech, and confidence. My tip: be yourself, be confident, and know your resume inside out.

Only 9 students were shortlisted further.

4] HR [ 9 candidates appeared for this round ]

As soon as my 2nd round ended, I was called in for the 3rd and final round.

This one was more of a formality -- the HR even mentioned it wasn't really an "interview," just a basic conversation. She asked me how my day had been so far, then a few simple things like my nationality and whether I was open to relocation. After that, she gave me a small situation-based question: "Imagine you're a team lead and a conflict breaks out between two high-temper teammates -- how would you handle it?" I answered confidently about keeping calm, listening to both sides, and resolving it fairly. She seemed satisfied with my response and told me to wait for the results once everyone else was done.

After some time, when all the interviews wrapped up, they finally announced the results. Out of everyone, 9 students were offered the job -- and I was one of them.

Useful Resources I Followed :

● DSA: Regular practice on LeetCode and giving contests on Codeforces and LeetCode. This really helps with clearing the OA. I also referred to Strivers A2Z DSA Course/Sheet for structured prep.

● Aptitude: It's just as important as DSA, so don't ignore it. I prepared closer to the placement season using Indiabix and CodeHelp Mock Test.

● SQL (Super Important): Practice in-depth because it's asked both in OA and interviews. I used Leetcode SQL problems. Make sure you cover:

○ Last Minute Revision (articles, cheat sheets, Interview Questions)

○ DBMS + SQL In depth

○ Advanced SQL topics like window functions, triggers, procedures

● OOPS (VVIMP): Don't leave this for the last minute. Learn in detail

● OS (Can keep for last-minute but practice properly): inDetail Important topics → Paging, Threading, Semaphores. Notes are handy here too.

● CCN (Computer Networks, can also keep for last-minute): CCN Revise important concepts, practice a bit in detail.

● System Design: A few companies do ask for it. Practice some examples to be safe -- YouTube System Design channels are helpful.

● Most important resource for me was GFG (GEEKSFORGEEKS ) -- for last-minute preparation it helped me a lot.

● If your primary language is Java, then practice advanced topics in detail such as synchronization, multithreading, exception handling, file handling, memory leaks, and implementation of various data structures in the Collection Framework.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
● Communication skills and confidence are key and be you, be honest.

● Always take a pause and understand if the interviewer is keeping pace with you.

● Try hard, think out loud, ask for hints if you're stuck.

● If you need a minute to think or frame an answer, ask the interviewer for the same.

● Stay confident, a partially correct answer with 100% confidence is better than a fully correct answer with 50% confidence.

● Always give examples while explaining stuff wherever possible, preferably something relatable.

● Keep questions ready for the interviewer, they always ask if you have any questions for them, never say no here.

● Be attentive during the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) as you'll get enough content to ask relevant questions.

● Your introduction should be short and to the point, and mention things you are good at as the interviewer may lead the discussion based on them.

● Be well versed with your resume from top to bottom.

● Don't just focus on DSA completely, make projects (do them yourself and try to participate in hackathons as winning is not important, the learning is) and have internship experience too.

● Always have a smile on your face and be interactive with your interviewer, even while solving something share your thought process.

● Interviewers are not just assessing your technical skills, they are also assessing your mindset and your approach.

● Don't follow previous interview experiences blindly, as those are from people who got selected but those who didn't may have had completely different experiences, so be confident in your strong points.

My few previous experiences :

I was also selected for the JPMC CFG hackathon (a hiring hackathon), and since my hackathon experience went great, I was quite hopeful of converting it into an offer. Unfortunately, it didn't work out. I even skipped some companies because I was confident about CFG, but sometimes things don't go as planned.

Throughout the placement season, I cleared almost all the OAs for which I applied, but I was not able to convert them into a final selection. This placement phase really tested my patience to the extreme. Even after doing well in interviews, selections didn't happen. I gave interviews for JPMC Fintech, PhonePe, MSCI, IDFC, Nomura (GM role), BlackRock, EDS, and finally got selected at Oracle.

Every interview taught me something new. I don't consider these as failures, but rather as a learning process that helped me finally get selected.

● MSCI interview

chart.

decisions.

ﬁll by understanding the ﬂow chart and by options given in the

mcq.

specially very in-depth topics which no one teaches.

2. Technical Round 1 [ 35 candidates appeared for this round]

So my technical round was scheduled at 9.30 am and it was an online interview on Webex Platform Interview began with my introduction , keep it short and crisp , REMEMBER your entire interview will go around your introduction so make sure to say things you know , dont fake it As well as dont even think or try to cheat on online interviews as many of them were caught by TPO and strict actions were taken Then the very first question was asked to me about What was my most recent project I have worked on ? Explaining the entire project , I started explaining The architecture of the project and the purpose of the project. There will be a lot of cross questioning on your projects so have thorough understanding on them After some more chit chatting on projects and resume , panelist jumped on DSA I was asked a famous question of Linked List (How to detect a Cycle in a Linked List) As soon as i started with the optimal approach of Slow and Fast Pointers , the interviewer said me not to use this method and think of an optimal approach other that this KEY Point - Never jump directly on optimal approaches , walk through brute better and optimal in a structured manner Then after some time the next questions was on my primary language , I answered C++ Follow up question immediately - WHY C++ and not JAVA , what are the primary differences between them and some more questions around it were asked Then the interviewer started asking about OOPS concepts About Four Pillars and differences between them , I answered it very confidently using examples to demonstrate better understanding ,

Q) Applications with examples on all four pillars with understanding on each one of them and what are the differences between between some concepts of OOPS in java and c++ like in c++ we can inherit from multiple parents and in java we cant , then whats the solution for java he asked and follow up on what i was saying REMEMBER - he will ask follow ups on what you say and grill till a point he knows that you know the concepts well , so dont fake it answer it honestly. Q) Difference between interfaces and abstraction , static , can we instantiate objects or not Q)I am creating my own language in which we can instantiate static , What will be the core difficulties and challenges and how would you resolve them. KEY - Deep Understanding of OOPS was very essential as half of my interview revolved around it In between some Managerial HR type questions were also asked , just communicate well here nothing much for these questions,

Dont let any awkward silence to be created at any time , You can take some time from the interviewer to think and then answer , So just be confident and you are good to go

At the end of the interview he asked me about how good knowledge do you have about finance and like some common questions on do you manage your portfolio , what type of investments do you do and We discussed on that for about 5-10 minutes , Here you can show how eager you are to learn and break into finance The discussion went so well that the interview started becoming a talking session . Then he asked me about current affairs and what latest news I had read on BlackRock

I had read some news so I could answer these questions very well . Then I was asked, "Do I have any questions for them ? Never say no , always prepare some good questions to be asked at the end of the interview which gives them the feeling of eagerness to learn

TIP- However good your technical skills might be , but if you can't communicate and convey and make them understand about your thought process then its no use So yes work on your soft skills as well

3. Technical Round 2

Dont know how many got call for 2nd interview Round 2 was a bit more formal and short than the previous round , as usual started with my introduction and then on projects and resume as i mentioned in round 1

Then on a specific project he started grilling me Q)Screen was shared and i was asked to open Notepad and write down schema of my project , how i passed that data on backend and questions related to storing them on databases Q)I was asked to write a few SQL queries regarding the schema i made Have a good knowledge of JOINS , GROUP BY , WINDOW FN , DATE FN and you are good to go

After this schema design and querying again we moved to OOPS Started with fundamental questions and gradually complexity was increasing , so even if you dont know the exact answer , try to gather some points and convey the thought process in between Q)I was asked on how i used concepts of OOPS in each project and how i utilized the four pillars Here explain the architecture and gist of project and then go on with the answer to how OOPS played a major role in each projects in some or the other way

I wasnt asked many development questions , but my friends were asked questions on React and Backend , so read the JD for the role you are applying for and have ideas in some way or the other.

PRANK ROUND (THERE WAS NO HR ) During the BlackRock process, after finishing my two technical rounds, our TPC told us about the prank round that had been taken earlier by our TPO head, Mr. Vinod Sikka. On the same day, I also had an EDS interview scheduled at their office, so I was really stressed trying to manage both. While waiting for the BlackRock result, the tension kept building, but finally, my name was announced for the SDE role. That moment was such a big relief and honestly one of the happiest feelings--I realized how important it is to stay calm under pressure and I felt super excited to join BlackRock.

Read some more interview experiences on GFG as well of students from VIT

1. Online Assessment [ 191 applied on unstop and 133 shortlisted for test ]

The test was held on campus on unstop with rigorous proctoring. It contained 3 sections - Aptitude, Technical MCQ, and coding. Each section had a sectional timer.

Aptitude(40 questions in 35 mins) - questions were very easy and you need to only score good in this setion for further calls for business analyst role. I was able to solve 30+ questions correctly but cutoff was too low because 60 students were called for business analyst gd.

Technical MCQ (33 questions in 25 mins) - questions were from various topics like html, css , javascript, java , oop, dbms and os. This section was of a moderate level and I was able to score decent enough questions correctly.

Coding( 3 questions in 30 mins) - There were 3 coding questions I don't remember all 3 but 1 was on graph traversal . Remember it was not like leetcode question solving where you are already given driver code and you just have to write the function and return the expected value. You have to write input and output coding statements also.

2. Group Discussion (Only for business Analyst role) [ 60 students appeared ]

There were 6 groups of 10 each . Topic was given on the spot and every group got a different topic. Our topic was - The role of social media in shaping consumer trends. 3 students were selected out of 10 from my panel and I was one of them. Here are some of the tips from my side -

1. Always start the gd - I started the gd addressing the group clearly channelised the whole flow and told the topics that would be discussed. I spoke 4-5 times clearly and loudly and explained my point with many real life examples and experiences Out of the 6 groups , around 24 candidates were shortlisted for interview round 1.

2. Technical Interview - Round 1 [ 24 candidates appeared ]

My interview started with a basic introduction and he got very interested in asking about my startup that I worked on during my 2 nd and 3 rd year. He asked many follow-up questions and I was able to answer all of them clearly. Then he asked about my ml project that I have worked on in one of the hackathons. I explained it well and he asked related questions and kept asking levelling up the difficulty. He gave me many situation based questions that the deadline of a project is 2 weeks but tech team is not working efficiently what will you do?? Then he moved to a guesstimate question to tell the number of users you can get of your turf booking app (my startup) in the first quarter in kolkata. I explained him my approach and he was very convinced. He asked me why Quantiphi. When I expressed my interest he dropped the bomb by asking tell me 3 projects quantiphi is working on right now. It was really awkward because I didn't knew about it but he said its okay that's for your time. After a longggggg wait of 3 hours I got mail from unstop that my 2 nd round is scheduled at 6pm.

3. Technical Interview - Round 2 [ 12 candidates appeared ] This round was online and it was to be held at 6 but further delayed to 7pm. It was pretty chill he started by asking my introduction and he was also interested in my startup work ( that impressed everyone ngl ). Then he asked tell me what does quantiphi do and 3 projects ( same questwion again haha but this time I prepared it well). Then he asked many questions related to python . He also gave 2-3 situational based questions ans waas happy after my answers. He gave feedback that he liked my communication skills and I can really handle client side of sales and analysis well. Finally at 9.50pm results were announced and out 6, 3 people were selected for business analyst role and I was one of them. Total 8 students were selected- 3 for ba , 2 for ml, 3 for fe
