1. Online Assessment [ Students with >=7 CGPA ]

The first stage was an online assessment consisting of a single DSA question + 4 logic/Aptitude questions. The DSA question was mainly based on mathematical reasoning rather than complex data structures.

After this round, 24 students were shortlisted .

2. Predictive Index Assessment [ 24 students ]

The shortlisted candidates were asked to complete a Predictive Index assessment the following day. This assessment was focused more on behavioural and personality evaluation rather than technical skills.

After this stage, 13 candidates were shortlisted for the interview process .

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (Online) [ 13 students ]

The first technical round was conducted online on a coding platform called Meetl.

The interview focused on:

• Core Java fundamentals

• Java Collections Framework

• Object-Oriented Programming concepts

• DBMS basics

• Data Structures and Algorithms I was given two DSA problems:

• One was Leetcode easy level.

• The second problem was of medium difficulty (roughly LeetCode medium level) .

I had to write the code for both problems and explain the logic clearly . After this round, 3 out of the 13 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (Onsite) [3 students]

This round was conducted onsite at the company office and was a pen-and-paper coding round.

This interview again focused heavily on OOP concepts and Java fundamentals.

Some of the questions included:

• Explanation of Parent p = new Child() and Child c = new Parent() along with reasoning.

• Typecasting in objects.

• Lambda functions in Java.

• Streams in Java.

• Serializable interface.

• Questions about my hackathon experiences and projects.

After this , the interviewer asked 4 DSA questions

1. Linked List

Delete a node in a singly linked list in constant time.

2. Array Problem

Find the second maximum element in an array using one pass and constant space.

3. Integer Stream Problem

The interviewer described a scenario where a large stream of integers flows into a queue throughout the day, with the constraint that the difference between consecutive numbers is always 1.

At the end of the day, we need to answer q queries asking whether a specific number x appeared in the stream, and the requirement was to answer queries in constant time and constant space.

4. Array Partition

Given an array, divide the elements into two arrays such that the difference between their sums is minimum . ( time complexity of order 1 )

The problems themselves were not difficult but were slightly tricky and required reasoning/proof .

I wrote code for all four problems and explained the logic clearly. The interviewer seemed satisfied with both my OOP explanations and DSA solutions.

The next day I received a call from HR saying that the feedback was positive, and I was invited for the next round.

5. Technical Interview Round 3 (Senior Engineering Manager) [ 2 students ]

This round was again conducted onsite and a pen-and-paper round .

The interviewer was an Engineering Manager who had been with the company for around 11 years.

The round began with questions on the Java Collections Framework, after which the discussion went deep into HashMap internals.

I had to explain:

• How key-value pairs are stored

• Load factor

• Rehashing

• Collision handling

• How collision handling worked before Java 8 and after Java 8

After this discussion, I was asked to write a Student class with attributes:

• name

• id

• marks

I wrote the class and implemented the constructor.

Then the interviewer asked whether we could directly use this class as a key in a HashMap.

This question was meant to check my understanding of equals() and hashCode().

I explained:

• The default implementations provided by the Object class

• How they compare memory references

• Why overriding them is necessary for logical equality

I then implemented:

• equals() using student id

• hashCode() accordingly

I also explained what would happen if we did not override these methods.

Next we discussed:

• Comparable vs Comparator

• Writing a Comparable implementation

• Writing a Comparator for a different custom sorting strategy

• What the return values -1, 0, and 1 represent

The interviewer then moved to JDBC, which I had not worked with before, so I honestly mentioned that I had not used JDBC.

We then discussed SQL concepts, including:

• Different types of joins

• Database indexing

• Data structures used in indexing (B-Trees)

Finally, the interviewer asked two logical puzzles:

Puzzle 1: 25 Horses and 5 Tracks

Find the top three fastest horses.

Puzzle 2: 2 Eggs and 100 Floors

Determine the highest floor from which an egg can be dropped without breaking.

The interviewer was mainly evaluating how I approached the problems and broke them down logically, rather than expecting an immediate answer.

I struggled a bit with the horses puzzle, but with some hints I eventually arrived at the solution.

I had mixed feelings after this round because the puzzle part did not go perfectly.

6. Technical Interview Round 4 ( Online ) [ 2 students ]

After about a week, HR informed us that there would be one final technical round.

This round was conducted virtually and had two interviewers:

• One senior engineering leader from the US

• One engineer from the Mumbai office ( if selected , he/she will be your manager )

This round was more conversational compared to previous rounds.

We started with a discussion about my projects and hackathon experiences. I was asked about the most challenging aspects of my projects and how I approached solving them.

One interesting question was about a product in the market that I admire or would like to work on , and I spoke about a technology product I had seen on Shark Tank India.

The discussion then moved into database concepts, including:

• Relational vs Non-relational databases

• MongoDB

• Redis ( Since I had used in my project )

• Why Redis, despite being very fast, is usually not used as a primary database for large systems

I was also given a probability puzzle involving 50 black balls and 50 white balls distributed across two bags , where the goal was to maximize the probability of drawing a black ball.

I initially took some time to reason about the problem, and with a hint from the interviewer I arrived at the correct solution. Towards the end of the interview, the discussion became more open -ended. I asked about a concept the interviewer mentioned called the S2 geometry data structure , which is used for geospatial indexing in systems like Google Maps.

I also asked what areas a new engineer should focus on during the first few months after joining .

Overall I was able to answer all questions in this round , but again felt dumb because I took a lot more time than required on that simple probability puzzle , brain felt saturated at that moment and stopped thinking, but with one hint from interviewer , arrived at the ans .

After this round, there was a long silence from the company for around 14-17 days. During this time, another candidate who was interviewing along with me received a call from HR for the HR discussion round, while I did not receive any update.

Naturally, I felt that my process might have ended there. However, after around two weeks, I unexpectedly received a call from HR informing me that my profile had been moved to a different team internally, and because of that, I would have to go through two additional technical &/ team rounds which were scheduled immediately on the next day .

7. Technical Interview Round 5 ( Online )

The fifth round was conducted by a manager from the Mumbai office with around 7 years of experience. The interview was relatively short and focused mainly on Java fundamentals and problem solving.

He first asked me about the internal working of HashMap, where I explained buckets, key-value storage, hashCode(), equals() , collisions, collision handling, etc.

Then he moved to a DSA problem similar to the "Search Suggestions System" problem on LeetCode.

Similar to : Leetcode Search Suggestions

I came up with a sorting + string prefix matching based solution. O(n^2) and coded the approach and output was correct.

Although the problem had a more optimized binary search based approach possible, he did not ask me to optimize further once the logic and output were correct . The round ended after he asked whether I had any questions for him.

8. Technical Interview Round 6 ( Online )

The sixth and final technical round was with a senior engineer from the US team who had around 15 years of experience. This round was very different from the previous ones.

It was not focused on coding or rapid-fire technical questions. Instead, it was more of a deep two-way discussion about the team, their domains, systems, and the type of work they do. He spent a significant amount of time explaining the team structure and the backend systems they work on.

I asked a few thoughtful questions regarding the domain and one specific question that he appreciated a lot during the discussion. I also asked him what I should focus on learning before joining so that I could reduce the amount of training effort required from the team side once I joined. He seemed to like that question as well, and the overall interaction was very positive and engaging. The conversation lasted for around one hour.

After these rounds, I received a call from HR stating that all interviewer feedback was positive and that the final HR discussion round was scheduled.

The HR round mainly covered resume overview, family background, relocation, future plans, joining timeline, and compensation discussion.

Toward the end of the HR round, I was also introduced to the manager(same person who took my second last interview) of the team I would potentially join, and we discussed the team goals and what I should focus on before joining.

After the HR round, there was another waiting period because the profile had to go through final approval from the US side. Around a month later, I finally received the official confirmation and offer from the company for the role of Junior Software Engineer.

journey.howSecured:
The process had 4 rounds.

1) OA

2) Technical Interview 1

3) Technical Interview 2

4) HR Interview

Quantiphi offered 3 roles, FE (Framework Engineer), MLE (Machine Learning Engineer) and BA (Business Analyst). We were supposed to order our preference in the Superset Application.

(To read the ML Interview Experience skip over to page 3)

1. OA [ 133 Appeared ]

We had 3 sections

1) Aptitude, Logical & Verbal Reasoning: 40 Questions - 30 Minutes

2) CS Fundamentals: 33 Questions - 25 Minutes

3) Coding Problems 3 Questions - 30 Minutes The amount of time was limited, so speed was the key to getting through in this round.

The first section was mostly as expected, but there were quite a few difficult problems on permutations and a few other topics. There were also a lot of problems on Area and Volume calculations (What is the profit if you sell the material extracted from a pyramid (and a cone) for 10 Rs/cm^3 and you bought the pyramid for 200). But I had to skip most of these because the time was limited and we didn't have calcis allowed. My advice would be to attempt this section in multiple iterations, solving the easiest questions in the first one, then the next and so on. Can't stress this enough, but time is a huge constraint here so manage it well. The second section was CS fundamentals (and little dev too). We had general theory based questions from OOPs, DBMS and OS. This was pretty standard. There were unexpected questions though that were the you know it or you don't type. The final Section had 3 coding problems. An easy one, an easy-medium and a difficult one.

● A thief wants to rob all the houses in a village. There is an array of the number of houses in each neighbourhood and the maximum amount of time(hours) he can take. At what minimum speed in houses per hour does he need to rob to clean the entire village ? You just need to take the sum of the houses and divide this number by the total time to get the rate of robbing. Round it off to the higher number and return the integer answer.

● A question very similar to the House Robber Problem from Leetcode. It was a basic include-exclude DP problem with one if condition. I didn't even need to apply DP as the first Recursive code that I ran passed all testcases. Link

● You are given an undirected graph of n islands, each with a loot value, and edges representing travel paths between islands with their travel times. A pirate may start from any island, traveling along available paths, and can visit each island at most once. The total loot is the sum of the visited islands' values, while the total time is the sum of the travel times along the chosen path. Find the maximum loot the pirate can collect. I was able to solve the first 2 problems but ran out of time attempting the 3rd one.

2. FE Interview 1 [ 17(FE) + 17(MLE) + 58(BA - GD followed by interviews)] [ 4:30 PM]

I had mistakenly selected FE as my first preference so I informed my FE Interviewer that I wanted MLE. We had been notified of this inward mobility for Roles in the Presentation. I was asked to complete this interview after which my request would go on to be processed.

We started with this round with me introducing myself and the interviewer going through my resume. We discussed all my projects (2 ML, 2 Dev) one after another and he asked plenty of questions as I was explaining. Be thoroughly prepared with your projects and don't fake anything. You should be prepared to answer questions like "Why did you use this service and not the other (Postgres vs Mongo, AWS vs Azure, etc) ?", "Are there any live applications that provide this service, how does your project compare to theirs ?", "What changes would you make if you wanted to serve 10k users with your project (Scalability is a very popular question) and other questions that question the inner mechanics of your project like "What purpose does this feature resolve ?", "Couldn't you have simplified things this way, your approach is very inefficient." and so on. Not every interviewer goes in this deep but there are ones that do.. (Baker 😭)

After the resume we started with his questions. He didn't ask any really difficult questions on DSA or SQL that needed time, this was more of an itinerary of easy to medium theory and coding problems. Here are a few of those:

● Do you know about normalization ? What is the difference between 1NF and 3NF normalization ?

● What is polymorphism ? How do we implement it ?

● Can you tell me about Indexing ? What are the drawbacks of Indexing ?

● Write an SQL query to remove duplicate entries from a database. (I used row_number() and partitioned by PK, after which I removed all entries with a row_num higher than 1)

● Can you do this problem without using windowing functions ?

There were quite a few questions around this difficulty level and I was able to answer most of them. After this round I was asked to appear for Interview 2 where I was informed that I will now be taken to their ML Engineer to appear for MLE Interview 1.

3. MLE Interview 1 & 2 [ 6:30 PM & 7:30 PM]

I would like to start this section with an overview of what I think of ML Interviews. These are just the views of a guy that has given 2 ML interviews so read them with a grain of salt. There is no defined structure to gauge a candidate's ability for an ML position at the graduate level. So Interviewers are going to ask you a very wide variety of questions and your selection depends on how much you can impress them across the duration of the exchange. Here is my personal order of importance for the subjects of your interview:

1) Your Projects: Can't stress this enough, but your projects are your best shot at showcasing your skills to the interviewer and showing how deep of an understanding you have in the concepts you've used in these projects. The interviewer can't just ask you to explain the architecture of a GNN Model to test you because that isn't something you can expect the average candidate to know. You need to dominate this discussion and tell the interviewer of every sellable skill you've utilized. Tell him about the nature of the dataset you used, about the challenges you faced in feature engineering, about the tools you used to clean/filter the data and augment samples. Tell him about why you chose your Model over the alternatives (for me it was why I chose BiLSTM over LSTM and GRU) and about the architecture of your model and what understandings you derived while working on the model and so on.

2) Fundamentals: The interviewer will then start asking questions to test your fundamentals such as

● What is regression ? How do you differentiate between it and classification ?

● What do you mean by clustering ?

● What will you do if your dataset has a lot of missing values ?

● Why do some models with good training accuracy have bad test accuracy ?

● What is bias vs variance tradeoff ?

● What are false positives and negatives ?

● What are precision and recall and when do they become useful ?

● What metrics did you use to judge your model and explain the significance of each metric ? (I answered the confusion matrix, classification report containing accuracy, precision, recall, f1- score, and the Learning curve comparing training and validation sets) There will be plenty of questions like this and they can be prepared for in advance.

3) Your Knowledge of ML Models: In the midst of the questions focusing on fundamentals, the interviewer also kept asking me questions on popular models. These included

● What is Linear Regression ? Is it related to Logistic regression ?

● Please explain how a Decision Tree works ? Can you draw an example for us ?

● Why do we need Unsupervised Learning ? Can you talk about any popular models Unsupervised Learning holds ?

● What is an ensemble model ?

● What will you do when faced with an Image based dataset. Having a basic understanding of these models is sufficient, you don't need to be an expert in everything.

I think this discussion includes most of the questions asked to me during the interviews. I'll list the few remaining questions here:

● The interviewer asked me if I had deployed any models ?

● He asked me if I had worked with NLP ? (I started talking about the need to process words and the Bag-of-Words Model. I had very surface level knowledge on this matter..)

● He then started to ask more detailed questions related to NLP but I was unable to answer them, from his body language it seemed like he expected a little more. In popular ML culture we see everyone talking about Deep Learning but NLP spans a whole lot of projects too and is not as much talked about. Can read a few things up.

● He presented to me a situation where I had a dataset of sentences that were classified as good and bad and we needed a model that could predict sentences in this manner.

This concludes almost all of what I was asked in MLE Interviews 1 and 2. I haven't separated the interviews into two sections because the flow of the interviews was very similar and it didn't make sense to separate them. The only difference was that the second interview didn't involve as many fundamental questions as the first one and was a little more intense. There was a bit of grilling involved in both the interviews and the first one went on for over an hour. The second one was a bit short at 30 minutes. This was followed by the HR interview. The selection from FE/MLE/BA Interview 1 to Interview 2 was very brutal. The rate of progression from Interview 1 to Interview 2 at Quantiphi was far lower than the average company.

4. HR Interview [ 13 shortlisted, 3 MLE and 10 FE+BA] [ 8:30 PM]

This was a typical "HR Interview". There weren't any tough questions, just enquiring things about you. Questions included. It lasted a relaxed 15-20 minutes. After the HR interview we had to wait for almost an hour as all the Interviewers and Execs discussed amongst themselves. Finally the shortlist was released around 10 PM and 8 candidates were selected. The selectees were 2 from MLE, 3 from FE and 3 from BA.

I am attaching this drive link with the resume I applied with, along with other pdfs that might be relevant to your preparation.

I am also attaching this link where I have discussed my entire placement process, and what is the best way to prepare for Non-tech jobs, including how I made my resume, how to answer the questions - etc.

I have mentioned most of the relevant details above, but some general tips:

1. THE most important thing to remember is that there is always a luck factor involved in these processes - you might have done everything right but sometimes it just is not your day. You can either sulk and waste your time or try to learn from your mistakes, get an outside perspective and keep on learning.

2. Be prepared for the worst, the whole 'placement season' might be just 2 weeks but it might also be 6 months. Do not be anxious about the whole thing - just stay calm and hope for the best.

3. Practice your Interview skills a lot, even if you have excellent communication skills. I probably gave 10 interviews to my brother/ seniors/ roommates. I also probably took 30 odd interviews of friends and roommates. This is the only way to practice giving answers in a professional capacity.

4. The shortlist names are usually revealed just 15/16 hours before the interview or test, so you need to prepare without worrying about the results.

5. Practice generic HR questions - What are your short term and long term plans, plans for further studies (always SAY NO), etc - I will try to give an ideal response and in detailed answer in the doc attached above.

6. People either smile too much or don't smile at all, or avoid eye contact. All of these can negatively affect your chances.

7. Be humble and show curiosity and eagerness to learn. Don't let the interviewer think you are arrogant or a know-it-all.

8. Make a lot of projects - it is the BEST way to learn new concepts and it will allow you to pick and choose appropriate projects for each company to ensure you can put your best foot forward.

9. DO NOT TRY to do everything all at once. Almost all sources of studies/ projects are good enough if you complete them - but if you keep hopping from one source to another, you will end up with nothing done. Set strict deadlines to motivate yourself to finish your work.

10. Talk to your seniors in your target company, talk to people already working in your target industry, and talk to your TPCs, all of them can give you great insights and guidance not just for your placements but for your future career.

11. In case you wish to connect with me, drop me a text on LinkedIn.

Skills and relevant links :

1. Data Analytics: Alex the Analyst - A complete Data Analyst Bootcamp(Python, SQL, Tableau, Power BI, Excel, AWS, etc ), enough to prepare you for most analyst roles. Completely free with a certificate as well!

2. SQL: SQL50 to practice questions

3. Python: For last minute Syntax revision: All Python Syntax in 25 Minutes - Tutorial

4. If you are interested in Finance: The Valuation School is the BEST channel I can recommend, you can also make financial models to add in your portfolio. Other than this, read about terms from Investopedia - Will elaborate more on the doc shared above.

5. Quantitative Aptitude: Read R.S. Agarwal (Shared in the Drive), practice from IndiaBix. For companies like JPMC - you should do CAT level questions.

6. Case Studies: The best way to learn Case studies is by participating in actual competitions, in the last year I participated in a LOT of competitions, all from Unstop. I think I made over 50 PPTs which directly or indirectly prepared me for a lot of questions, even guesstimates. I have also shared a book which helped me make better PPTs for my competitions. You can get other books as well if you just Google - Case study books IIM

7. Guesstimates: I never prepared for guesstimates from any fixed source - but I maintained a book with a lot of information that might help - India's population, Tier wise cities and population, gender ratio, population split by age, unemployment rate, inflation rate, etc. You should read/listen to a few case studies to understand how to approach the problem and how to talk about them. I will also share a very detailed approach to this in the doc.

8. Puzzles: I have been watching riddles/puzzles since my first year from TED-Ed. - There are more riddles other than this playlist, you will find them all in the channel itself. TedEd will help you visualise your problems and help you understand how to approach such problems. Also practice the puzzles in GeeksForGeeks - It is the best website to study anything related to coding or for Job prep.

9. I also did some questions from CodeForces - it will help you develop logical reasoning - not necessary though.

BEST OF LUCK.

DON'T WORRY - IT WILL ALL WORK OUT IN THE END!
journey.howSecured:
The information you gather from the pre-placement talk is extremely crucial as it can make the difference between your selection and rejection. I tailored my resume, answered the interview questions and asked my own questions entirely based on what was said during the pre placement talk.

So take screenshots of the PPT, note down what points they talk about, and then try to think of questions to ask or topics to talk about based on your experience and their requirements.

1. Resume Shortlisting

We were asked to submit our resume on 22nd July, so I made changes based on what my seniors had done and what I felt were appropriate.

Make sure that you tailor your resume every time you apply for a different role. I had applied for 4 companies ( 2 on-campus and 2 off-campus) and I had a different resume for each. They do not have to be big changes, you might just change a project, or add different certifications or change your skills. Make sure that your resume is consistent throughout (Avoid using different date formats, using different bullet types or using Bold or Italics randomly).

After your resume is ready, check your ATS score from 'Resume Worded' : https://resumeworded.com/), anything above 65 is good enough.

The results came out on 23rd July at around 6 pm, so instead of worrying about the results you need to prepare for OA and interviews.

2. Online Assessment (OA) [ 107 students appeared (approx) ]

This was a 60 minute exam with two sections: Quant and Coding. It was a pen and paper test with 8 questions of Quant which had a +3, -1 scheme; 2 questions of Python/pseudo code and 4 questions of SQL.

I felt the quant round was easier as compared to other companies. I have shared all the relevant links in the end to help you prepare. In general the questions are: Find the age, work done and time taken, relative speed, probability and PnC.

The Python part was really just to see your pattern recognition skills. We had to find the sum of n terms of the series given. The first one was easier and of 1 mark : 0, 2, 6, 12, 20, 30……. The second one was of 3 marks with the logic : [ x3 - (x+1)] : -1,-1, 5, 23, 59, 119........... People were either unable to think of the logic or they forgot to find the sum and just wrote the logic. To avoid such mistakes, make sure you read the questions at least twice, once before solving the question and once in between.

The SQL round was of medium difficulty with four questions of 2 marks each. There were questions based on Select, Join (Inner and Right), aggregate functions and Window functions. I practiced SQL using Leetcode's SQL50 and watched a Youtube playlist.

Each section had an individual cutoff so you need to make sure you perform well in each section. I think 18/24 in Quant and 12/24 in Coding was the cutoff but this is just my estimate.

3. Interview Round 1 [ 24 candidates were shortlisted ]

This round lasted 15-20 minutes per candidate with 3 panels of 2 people each: one HR and one technical expert. The questions asked were based completely on the resume, they enquired about each section, projects done, position of responsibilities, certifications and co-curricular activities. They asked a lot of questions on my major project which used Python for data analysis, where they also asked me to write down the formula for single linear regression and multiple linear regression. They also asked me why I chose to do each project and what could be their applications.

They also asked me some concepts based on statistics which I was not sure about - if such a situation arises, be very clear with them that you are not sure of the concept and take a short guess about what it could be. Do not waste their time by pretending to think or give an incorrect answer confidently.

Then they asked me why I was interested in this role, to which I answered by talking about different points throughout my resume. In their pre-placement talk, they mentioned that a Business Analyst needs to know all aspects of a business in order to derive insights for different projects. So, I tried to show them how I have covered all bases due to my committee experience, my projects and my certifications. I also talked about how I liked the JD (Job description) of Incred specifically since it will be high impact work with high ownership. They asked follow up questions on how I know about this and I mentioned that it is one of their values available on the website. In the end, I asked them some questions about their upcoming IPO and how it will impact the day to day working of my job - this was done mostly to show that I had done my study on the company and am aware of their future plans.

The best way to approach such resume based rounds is by taking charge or "breadcrumming", where you end your introduction with a point that they would like to hear more about. For example, at the end of my intro, I told them how I believe I am an ideal candidate for this position because of my Minors in Management from SPJIMR and asked them, "May I elaborate on it?". After each

answer, I tried to add a point in the end that will lead them to ask me a question about something I know the answer to.

Some people were asked questions on writing a simple code for Pandas or Numpy since they mentioned it in their resume, so make sure that you know each and every word of your resume, why it is important and if there are any alternatives.

4. Interview Round 2 [ 11 candidates were shortlisted ]

I was first asked to go through my resume in detail, where I mentioned my Minors in Management from SPJIMR, my projects (the objective, tools I used, industrial application, relevance to the role applied), my committee experience ( along with my learnings and relevance) and my case study competitions ( the problem statement in short and my solution). There were a couple of follow-up questions on the Minors and about the case studies.

This was a guesstimate based round. I was asked how many units of electricity are consumed in India in one year. I was asked to assume that each electrical appliance consumes one unit of electricity in one hour. I started by asking whether I should just consider houses or industries as well. They told me to just consider houses. I then divided the whole problem into smaller parts, India into 4 tiers of cities and the year into three seasons. I also divided the population by 5 assuming that some families have 3 people but some have 6 or more so 5 is a fair guess. Then I made assumptions on how many appliances must be used in each household based on the tier of the city. I also made changes based on the season, for eg, there will be more lightbulbs used during winters since the nights are longer.

I was asked some questions in between, unrelated to the case study, like "Name 10 Tier 1 cities in India". After this they asked me follow-up questions on what could be the potential factors for less electricity in tier 4 cities ( Poor connectivity, cost, and poor infra maintenance), and how I will provide electricity to these cities and what factors I will consider (Coal power plants, nuclear power plants and alternate sources of energy), (Factors : long term environmental impact, cost per unit electricity, set-up cost of each plant, units of electricity required).

After this, I asked a couple of questions on how the use of AI can cause data security concerns and I finished the interview by asking, "If I am selected for this role, what should my roadmap look like to help me be better prepared for when I join?" - This last question shows your excitement for the job and commitment to the company.

A lot of other candidates were asked to take different approaches for their guesstimates, so you must know several common ways to approach any problem. The people who messed up their guesstimates were asked a case study question - for eg. what features would you add in GPay to make it better?

Interviewers care about how you approach any problem and not the exact answer - Just keep talking about why you are making any assumptions and what do you hope to achieve from it. Keep asking questions regarding the things you are not sure about and make sure that you are confident in the approach you are taking. Sometimes they may cross question you to judge your confidence, just justify your approach and make revisions if you think they made a good point.

In the end, 3 candidates were offered a job.

journey.prep:
I will highly Recommend doing CP as alot of Codeforces and Algorithmic Questions were there. If you are someone who has not done CP than as of now Try to do CP 31 sheet from TLE Eliminators atleast till 1500 Rating starting from 1100 that will boost your confidence.

Have Practice of explaining solutions that is more Important than actually Solving the Problem. I used to Practice it at home that how I will show Interviewer about my Intution and how I exactly came up with this Particular Approach.

Try to do time bound Practice for OA. You can try Virtual Contests on Codeforces and Leetcode. They are very nice for Practice. If you have CF fear then also it's fine You can practice Leetcode. Leetcode is more than enough.

Make sure to revise standard DSA questions (Striver's SDE sheet Highly Recommended). As there are some questions for which a Particular Optimization is not possible until you have studied it from Somewhere. Also do make sure to star mark the ones which you felt alot tougher and do make the notes that what particular point about that Problem made you star mark that Problem it will help alot at the end moment I just revised my marked notes on striver tuf website in metro (20 minutes) that's it.

Try to learn some Advanced concept as well as Topics which were never asked are getting asked nowadays. Some Important ones which I feel you should do Binary Lifting (was asked this year to Panel 1), Tries (was asked in 2 different rounds to many People), DP (digit DP and DP with Bitmasking Watch kartik arora YT videos for both)

Also, have some good projects on Resume on which you are strong enough to talk on even for hours If someone wants you to. Try to solve some real world problem. Problem doesn't need to be too big even If a small issue is there and you have figured it you that will make a lot of sense than someone who is having complete GIT cloned project.

Specifically for PhonePe make sure to learn System Design of Any app as this is for sure guaranteed question in HR Round. If you don't have time then let me tell you Youtube had the easiest architecture of all the Apps out there (That one Neetcode video is more than enough if you have done Basics of System Design)

At the End Remember It is not the last opportunity You will be having a lot of better options further as well. Just make sure to give your 100% Best so that you don't have Anything to Regret.

Resources (Which I followed) :

1. DSA :

During My Time (2022) Codehelp DSA series was the most popular one but

Nowadays, many of people also follow striver that's completely your choice.

Codehelp DSA Playlist (All the Topics Except for Graph, DP)

Striver For Graph and DP

I personally have followed alot of Playlists for Dp for CP mainly : Priyansh Aggrawal Vivek Gupta

Binary Search , Two Pointers and DSU : Codeforces EDU Section (Atleast 2 Practice sets)

2. Web Development :

HTML CSS JavaScript : Apna College

React : Traversy Media Codevolution

NodeJs ExpressJS : Any One Shot Video which You can understand

First learn this fast to get the basics clear

Then Pick Some Random Projects from JS mastery and try to follow end to end and then go for your own Project and make sure you include Github link and Demo video link from Yt that makes really good Impression.

3. Core CS :

For Core CS just have a look at GFG top 100 Questions for each of these subjects

OOPS : Rohit Negi

DBMS : Code Help

Operating System : Gate Smashers

Computer Networks : Gate Smashers

4. System Design :

High Level Design : Concept and Coding

Low Level Design : Coder Army (Not Important for PhonePe)

For any further help feel free to Reach out to me - LinkedIn

1. Online Assessment [ All the students who had Applied appeared for it Nearly 200+]

We were Asked to report at 1 : 40 PM for PPT (Pre Placement Talk) followed by OA.OA was initially scheduled at 3 : 30 PM however it started nearly at 4 : 00 PM.

Total 4 Questions were there in this Round and duration was 90 Minutes (1 and Half Hour)

Question 1 :

Reference Question : Connected Components in an Undirected Graph

It was mostly Like this same question we have to figure out the Number of Connected Components and we were asked to finally print the final cost where cost was 1 for connecting 2 different components.

I instantly came up with approach of DSU and coded it in nearly 8 to 10 Minutes as DSU is my favourite Data Structure. I got all the Test cases Passed and got AC on it.

However, few people also solved it by using BFS / DFS. But One common mistake which I noticed was alot of people even after realizing that it was a DSU question were not able to code DSU. So, I would suggest stop using Templates at least one month before Placement. It was an easy one If you have command on DSU. I would strongly recommend to learn DSU as it is favourite Topic of every PBC.

Question 2 :

Reference Question : Array Description

It was Almost same as this question from CSES. A slight change was there that At max Difference can be till k instead of 1 where k was an Integer Provided in the Input. I had solved this problem alot of times before still was not confident to code it that fast so decided to go for 3rd one and then came to it and coded it. I was able to solve all the test cases apart from 5 test cases which I was not able to figure out initially but later on realized that I was not doing Modulo 1e9 + 7 and the moment I did that all the test cases got Passed.

Question 3 :

You were provided with an Array of length n and a variable s and a Variable k. Your task was to print the number of pairs where sum of two elements was equal to s and sum of bit positions of 1 of those numbers should be less than or equal to k.

Ex.: n = 5 arr = [1 2 7 3 5] This is the Array and say s = 10 and k = 5

So, Answer will be 1 in this case as 3,7 is the Only Pair satisfying the conditions. Here 3 + 7 = 10 and In binary 3 = 011 and 7 = 111. For 3 There is a 1 at 0th position and another one at 1st position so sum of bit positions = 1 and for 7 there is 1 at 0th,1st and 2nd Position so sum of bit positions = 3. So, total sum of bit Positions = 1 + 3 = 4 which is less than k in this case.

The trick in this question was the constraint as n was at max equal to 1000 so O (n*n) can be easily passed. So, without even a single thought I applied Brute Force I got all the Test Cases Pass. One thing I noticed was though I read the question completely but while Implementing I forgot to check the bit positions condition and just checked the condition of pairs sum equal to s but still I got and all the test cases got passed. But after realising that later on I again came back to it even after getting AC I improved the code as we were Informed that code will be seen and on the basis of that shortlisting will be done. This was an easy Problem mostly was there for speed solving.

Question 4 :

Reference Question : M-Coloring Problem

It was mostly like this same Problem with Proper story Plot but the Main trick in this Problem was to take the Input as they didn't mentioned that what number of edges were to be taken as an Input. I didn't met a Single Person who had solved it completely. I was nearly having more than half an hour. I tried Applying all the different techniques which I knew mainly I tried using getline as I code in C++ but that didn't worked. One thing which alot people did was they directly Printed possible as answer can either be Possible or Impossible. On printing Possible nearly 7 of 11 test cases were getting Passed. I knew this trick but didn't used it as it was Mentioned in PPT that code will be reviewed by Phone Pe Team. I also knew that last year with 2 complete and half Partial submissions candidates have received call.. So, I was almost sure that I will be getting the OA shortlisting.

30 Candidates were Shortlisted after OA Round. List came nearly around 10 : 00 PM and we were asked to report at 8 : 00 AM the next day.

2. Technical Round 1 [ All 30 shortlisted Candidates gave this Round ]

There were 3 Panels. I was in 2nd Panel. So, have to wait for 1 hour from 9 to 10. Then some of my friend from panel 1 after first Round told me that they were asked questions on Binary Search and Binary Lifting. I was quite confident afterwards as these are My most strong topics in CP. Then Finally I went for Round 1. Interviewer Didn't at all looked at my resume and not even asked for My Introduction. He tried to make me comfortable and then directly started with the Problem. He was very helpful in entire Round. Question 1 : I had never seen exact same question Previously.

Problem Statement : You are given a Binary Tree and for each level you have to find minimum number of swaps to sort nodes of that Particular level and at the end you have to return the total Number of swaps required for all the levels of tree.

I started with explaining that how we'll take all the nodes of each level using queue and store it in vector. So, question boils down to finding minimum number of swaps required for sorting the elements of a vector and likewise we can do for all the Levels. Now, thing was How can we solve it for a particular vector. I directly gave him the Merge Sort approach which seemed appropriate to me at that time. However he didn't looked satisfied with merge sort. So, I decided to go for another approach through I was not having any other approach but with nearly 3 minutes of strong thinking I cam up with Approach of DSU (As I mentioned earlier it is my most favourite data structure so I almost try it in every question)

I explained him that we can find Number of cycles using DSU and total number of swaps will be equal to size of a Particular component - 1 and likewise we can add it for all the components. But then He asked me how will I code DSU as Numbers can be 1000,200 or any big number then I told him about Coordinate Compression and with that it becomes a standard DSU Problem. He just looked too satisfied with approach. Then He asked me to code it. He asked me to write complete code along with syntax with Proper Assumptions on Paper. I was completely Comfortable in it and coded it Properly.

Question 2 :

Reference Question : Maximum Sum Combination

It was exactly this same Problem but the change here was that there can be n arrays not necessarily 2 Arrays. I had solved the above mentioned Problem. So, directly came up with Priority Queue but was not able to figure out for n arrays. I tried alot of Approaches but was not able to come up with a complete correct solution. At once even Interviewer stopped looking at me and was doing his own work. But I was still explaining him My approach without stopping which I have learned from Striver's Media.net Experience that you should never sit Blank in Interview even if you know that your Approach is complete wrong. As in real life Industry work not necessarily you will be having solution of every Problem but one thing which should be there in you to continuously try for finding the solution.

3. Hiring Manager Round [ Around 16 students]

After hearing everyone's experience I was not quite confident that whether I will be getting call or not. But all of sudden I received a call from my TPC and all of sudden I ran for taking my resume from My Bag and went for HM Round. He was Managing Head at PhonePe and was just too good and helpful. This round was highly focused on my Resume.

Even He didn't looked at hard copy of my resume and instead he was having my resume open on his Laptop. Even he didn't asked me the Standard Introduce Yourself Question and rather directly started with my Projects and asked about my One project on which I was confident enough. I explained him my Test My Case Project which is a Chrome Extension I made for Codeforces for validating Test Cases. He looked interested to know how it exactly worked I explained him it's complete working and then he asked why I made this to which I replied I made it for myself as I was facing that issue on Codeforces which I think made a Good Impression on him. Then he grinded me on my resume with questions like My leadership qualities, My role as Executive in IETE and a lot of such questions. Then he asked me

My most frequent used App to which I replied Youtube as I knew he will be asking me the System Design / Architecture of Youtube. I had read a lot of Past Year Experience of PhonePe due to which I knew this is sure shot question for PhonePe HM round. Later on he asked me to tell how Youtube Recommendation system works to which I took him to complete Core CS, ML and DSA which is My strong zone. (I wanted to show that I had good command on Core CS) Then He asked me a lot of Behavioral questions on which I was almost prepared. He also asked me my weakness to which I replied that I over optimize things as I come from CP background and then told him that I am continuously trying to Improve it. Then at the end, He asked me Tell me a Reason why we should not hire you to which I replied that I don't think so I have any such qualities and I do possess all the main qualities required for SDE 1 at PhonePe and even If I don't have I will learn them faster. He then asked me to ask any questions I had then I asked him few questions which I prepared during the PPT (Pre Placement Talk) which made him feel that I was highly focused during PPT. He looked Impressed and I almost knew that I am getting the call for final Round.

4. Technical Round 2 [ Around 11 students]

I received the Message that I have been shortlisted for 3rd and Final Round of the Day which is Technical Round 2. At the very beginning of this I was told that I have been strongly recommended by Manager Sir. The Interviewer was very helpful and talked with me for a while to make me comfortable. Then He started with DSA questions

Question 1 :

Reference Question : Drunken Maze

Don't worry It was not the same Problem but it was very easy as compared to the above Problem with just Direction condition. As I had solved this Problem just recently I directly told him the Approach to which he was satisfied and directly told me to do the code. I asked him what is the Expectations with Quality of code to which he replied he has to show My code to the Team. So, I maintained High Quality of Code which I had practiced a lot for Interviews. He looked satisfied with the code and then fast forward he asked me the follow ups to which I replied very faster. (Graphs have always been my strongest Part in my Complete Coding Journey thanks to Striver for that)

Question 2 :

Reference Question : Painting the Walls

Interviewer directly Showed me on Leetcode Itself and asked me for the Approach after looking directly at constraints I directly replied with DP without a Second thought to which he agreed. I gave him 4 different recursive functions on the spot all of which were correct. But he wanted me to tell the approach using only those dp states which he want. I was not able to figure out exactly the states he wanted but eventually with certain talk with him I gave him the approach he wanted. I asked him that should I go for code to which he said Time's Up. But then He said that don't worry You are good guy for PhonePe to which I replied "Ok, So let's meet in the Office" This was something I had never thought I will say to my Interviewer. He replied with yess for sure. With that I came out from Interview Room.

I was the first one to Complete all the 3 Rounds and So, I knew that I have to wait for nearly 2 hours and eventually all of us ended up waiting for nearly 3 to 3 and half hours and finally Shortlisting Came. 7 of Us were hired with (Internship + FTE offer). Later on I got to know that I was the first one ever from EXTC department to get into Phone Pe. To someone like who always wanted a PBC to work on it felt like dream come true and that everyday grinding just seemed worth it.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
I will highly Recommend doing CP as alot of Codeforces and Algorithmic Questions were there. If you are someone who has not done CP than as of now Try to do CP 31 sheet from TLE Eliminators atleast till 1500 Rating starting from 1100 that will boost your confidence.

Have Practice of explaining solutions that is more Important than actually Solving the Problem. I used to Practice it at home that how I will show Interviewer about my Intution and how I exactly came up with this Particular Approach.

Try to do time bound Practice for OA. You can try Virtual Contests on Codeforces and Leetcode. They are very nice for Practice. If you have CF fear then also it's fine You can practice Leetcode. Leetcode is more than enough.

Make sure to revise standard DSA questions (Striver's SDE sheet Highly Recommended). As there are some questions for which a Particular Optimization is not possible until you have studied it from Somewhere. Also do make sure to star mark the ones which you felt alot tougher and do make the notes that what particular point about that Problem made you star mark that Problem it will help alot at the end moment I just revised my marked notes on striver tuf website in metro (20 minutes) that's it.

Try to learn some Advanced concept as well as Topics which were never asked are getting asked nowadays. Some Important ones which I feel you should do Binary Lifting (was asked this year to Panel 1), Tries (was asked in 2 different rounds to many People), DP (digit DP and DP with Bitmasking Watch kartik arora YT videos for both)

Also, have some good projects on Resume on which you are strong enough to talk on even for hours If someone wants you to. Try to solve some real world problem. Problem doesn't need to be too big even If a small issue is there and you have figured it you that will make a lot of sense than someone who is having complete GIT cloned project.

Specifically for PhonePe make sure to learn System Design of Any app as this is for sure guaranteed question in HR Round. If you don't have time then let me tell you Youtube had the easiest architecture of all the Apps out there (That one Neetcode video is more than enough if you have done Basics of System Design)

At the End Remember It is not the last opportunity You will be having a lot of better options further as well. Just make sure to give your 100% Best so that you don't have Anything to Regret.

journey.prep:
● Strengthen Your Core Subjects: Ensure you have a strong understanding of Computer Science fundamentals like OOPS, DBMS, OS, and CN. Many of the MCQs in the OA round and questions in technical interviews are directly based on these concepts.

● DSA is Crucial: Practice coding questions regularly. Completing Striver's A-Z DSA sheet is highly recommended. It will help not only for the OA but also for the technical interviews.

● Java Concepts: Since Java is a preferred language in many companies (including Barclays), you should know about its internal workings. Learn about JVM, JDK, JRE, memory model, autoboxing, generics, garbage collection, lambda expressions, comparators, TreeMaps, etc.

● Aptitude Practice: Don't ignore aptitude. Practice questions from IndiaBix and PrepInsta. They're helpful for logical reasoning and quick decision-making.

● Competitive Programming: While not mandatory, doing CP improves your problem-solving speed and ability to think under pressure. Start with the CP-31 sheet by TLE Eliminators. Try solving questions on platforms like CodeChef, CodeForces, and LeetCode regularly.

● SQL & DBMS: Basic SQL questions can be game-changers. Make sure you know how to use SELECT, WHERE, AND, and basic joins. Also, revise normalization, indexing, ACID properties, and ER diagrams.

● Behavioral Round Prep: Be honest. Your attitude and ability to work in teams matter just as much as your technical skills. Interviewers can detect fake responses.

● Watch & Read: For DBMS, OS, and other core topics, Love Babbar's playlists are very beginner-friendly. His notes are also helpful before interviews.

● Stay Consistent & Positive: Placement season is stressful. Not clearing a test or getting rejected after interviews is normal. Don't compare your journey with others.

Luck plays a role too, from the question you get in OA to which interviewer panel you face. Focus on continuous improvement.

● Stay Connected: Build a peer group that supports and motivates each other. Help your friends and ask for help too.

● Final Word: Never lose hope. Everyone gets placed at their own time. What matters is persistence and faith in your own abilities.

If you have any doubts or need help during your placement journey, feel free to reach out to me. I'm happy to help in any way I can. Connect with me on LinkedIn
journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [Number of candidates: 135]

The Online Assessment was a 90-minute test consisting of 15 questions:

● 13 questions were based on core CS subjects like Java, OOPS, DBMS, CN, and OS.

● 1 SQL question which was very simple, requiring the use of basic WHERE and AND conditions.

● 1 DSA coding question which was repeated from last year: Lexicographically Smallest String After Applying Operations (JobOverflow link).

Tips:

● Make sure to go through previous years' OA questions; the coding question may be repeated.

● Brush up on Java theory and basic DBMS/OOPS concepts.

● SQL basics (especially filtering rows using WHERE and logical operators) should be known.

● Practice DSA regularly using Striver's A-Z sheet to improve speed and accuracy.

2. Technical Interview Round 1 [Number of candidates: 37]

The round began with the interviewer looking at my resume. He asked me to explain any one of my projects. I picked one and walked him through it. He then asked if I had faced any challenges during the project. I mentioned encountering the CORS error, which I had seen in almost every project I built.

He asked how I resolved it. I explained that I used the cors library in the backend to allow the frontend domain to access backend resources. He seemed somewhat satisfied but pointed out that since CORS is a browser-based issue, I should reflect more on why the backend is used to resolve it.

He then asked whether I had used AI/ML in any of my projects. I mentioned that I had completed two college courses : Generative AI and LLMs, but had not integrated them into my projects.

Coding Questions:

He then gave two pattern-printing questions with the condition that I could use only two for loops in total.

Question 1 (n = 5):

*

**

***

**

*

I asked a few clarifying questions (like whether n is always odd) and wrote an example to confirm. I ended up using a while loop externally and nested for loops internally. The interviewer said this was partially correct, as the ideal solution required only two for loops total.

Question 2:

X*X*X

X*X*

X*X

X*

X

This one was easier. I solved it using two for loops and printed X for odd indices and * for even indices using the modulo operator. He was satisfied with my approach.

Java Concepts:

He asked whether Java was my primary language, and I confirmed it. Then he asked multiple Java-related questions:

● HashMaps: How are they implemented? I spoke about hashing techniques like linear probing and explained how linear probing works.

● Time Complexities: I said HashMap provides O(1) average-case and O(N) worst-case complexities. He asked whether search operations can also take O(N), to which I answered yes, due to the linear scan in probing.

● Hashing Properties: I mentioned hashing should be low-cost and reduce collisions. He was looking for additional properties that I couldn't recall.

● Primitive Data Types in HashMap: I said Java does not allow primitive types, only wrapper classes. He asked how primitives are converted into objects, and I correctly answered "autoboxing."

● List vs HashMap Search: I said HashMap has better search performance (O(1) avg) than a List (O(N) worst).

● TreeMap with Objects as Keys: I said it is possible and explained by giving an example of a Person class, which contains name and age as attributed, and using a TreeMap<Person, Integer> with a lambda comparator, e.g., sorting by name using a.name.compareTo(b.name). I also mentioned the need to override hashCode() and equals() methods in such classes.

The interviewer seemed moderately satisfied and selected me for the next round.

3. HR Interview [Number of candidates: 21]

This round was purely HR for me, while many others had a techno-HR round.

● The interviewer started by asking me to introduce myself. I included my internship experience at Triblet SportsTech, where I worked on UI/UX design using Figma.

● He asked what I would do if I didn't have access to Figma, Canva, or any other design tool. I said I would collaborate with my team and sketch designs manually, referring to existing designs from the internet.

● He asked if I had worked in a team. I replied yes and explained that I worked with two other teammates to design desktop and mobile layouts based on the company's theme.

● He inquired if there were any disagreements in the team. I shared a scenario where we had conflicting ideas about a design. I suggested we consult the founder/co-founder and some users to make an informed decision.

● He asked whether I ever took credit for someone else's work during my internship. I said no and gave an example of when I was helped by teammates and gave them full credit during a meeting with the founder.

● He presented a hypothetical: What would I do if I had to deliver a project in a week using C#, which neither I nor my team knew, and my teammates were busy? I responded that I'd learn the basics of C#, implement 2-3 core functionalities, and communicate with the project manager to request a 2-3 week extension while possibly offering extra features to make up for delays.

● Finally, he asked if I had taken undue credit during college. I honestly admitted that I once overstated my contribution to a major project presentation, but I later felt guilty and learned from the experience.

In total, 16 students were selected.

journey.prep:
1. Know your Resume INSIDE OUT: Make sure you have at least some idea about each and every word written on your resume. Please don't write anything that you have no idea about, it will create a very bad impression

2. DSA is Important: Though I was not asked about complex DSA, it is always good to be prepared about anything and everything. I started my DSA (leetcode) prep after my 2nd year ended, and I followed Striver's A2Z DSA course for it. Though it prepared me for all sorts of patterns and topics, I still lacked the intuition. I can solve questions when they are related to some patterns, but it takes a fairly large amount of time to decode the problem when it is something completely new. Therefore, I feel you should have both Intuition and Pattern recognition. I will suggest starting with Leetcode daily questions to build your intuition starting from your 3rd sem. Gradually from there, transition into topics and their questions and then start with the sheet. This will make sure you have both the Intuition and Pattern Recognition.

3. Internship experience adds value: My interview had good questions about my internship. It's important to clearly explain what you worked on, what you learnt and what impact you had.

4. Build Projects that have some value: Do not build generic projects, try to see what real-world problems can you solve and try to solve that in your projects. It may not be perfect, but is still way better than something too generic.

5. Communication is super important: See I have some friends who have a great technical profile but are rejected because of their soft skills. You may be a genius, but if you can't make the world aware about it, then what's the point? Hence try to focus on being vocal about your thought process, maintain good eye contact, a sincere smile, practice articulating your thoughts well, don't speak too fast or too slow or too vague. Take pauses wherever required, try to structure your answers.

THAT'S IT, there's no Rocket Science in it! If possible and time permits, try to do a couple of mock Interviews, it will greatly help.

6. Consistency and Discipline over EVERYTHING: Whatever you do, stay consistent with it. I remember, when starting out, I used to get anxious when I couldn't solve a problem, but with time and effort, I did manage to solve those.

7. Sometimes, it's not your fault: See, you are about to have a completely new experience in your life. There will be times when things will just not work out, no matter how much effort you put in, something undesirable will happen. It is 60% skills and 40% LUCK according to me!

I lost opportunities in MSCI, UBS because the test platform had some issues. I lost Barclays. I lost IDFC First Bank because I was asked something that was not in my knowledge and I got anxious answering that (that's a different story altogether haha)

Then I had prepared for Hyperverge so well, I spent almost 2-2.5 days, still was not shortlisted.

It is what it is!

These are the times you should stay calm, trust your efforts, spend time with your loved ones, trust whichever god you believe in. Don't take too much stress, don't let it take a toll on your health.

Trust me on this,

Jab nahi hona hota toh kuch bhi karlo nahi hota

BUT JAB HONA HOTA HAIN TOH KUCH BHI KARLO, HOKAR HI REHTA HAIN.

Because sometimes, all your plans fail, because of GOD's PLAN!

THERE'S AN OFFER WAITING FOR EACH AND EVERY ONE OF YOU!

If there's anything you would like to ask me in particular, aaram se reach out to me on my LinkedIn

All the best for your Placements 🤞🤞

P. S.

Some Resources:

1. DSA: Follow Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet - it's structured, beginner-friendly, and covers all essential

topics and patterns. Do some daily questions before starting this (as mentioned above)

2. SQL: Practice from LeetCode's Top 50 SQL Questions - great for query writing and real interview

problems.

3. DBMS: Watch this DBMS video - it covers everything you need for interviews.

4. Core Subjects (OS, CN, OOPs): Refer to GeeksforGeeks - it's sufficient for brushing up on the

most asked concepts in interviews.

You may also refer:

Kunal Kushwaha for Java OOPs if you have time.

Networks Cheatsheet by Love Babbar (covers almost everything in CN plus mostly asked questions)

OS in one video by Anuj Bhaiya

5. System Design: Go through System Design Article.

Tip: You can skim through it and skip advanced topics like Kafka.

6. Tech Cheatsheet: View the Cheatsheet here, I got this from my senior -- it includes useful resources

across key topics. Feel free to use and share!
journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [ 187 candidates appeared for this round ]

Platform: Microsoft Forms (Proctored) Questions: 20 (MCQs) Time: 30 mins Note: There was no auto submit, so make sure to click the submit button before the time ends. Only then your submission will be recorded.

The questions were very basic but it spanned almost all the subjects and topics, from DBMS, CCN, OS, OOPS (guess the output), Programming (Java and C++ and I think 1 question was from C too). Questions were also from Quantitative Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, English (basic grammar, synonyms, antonyms).

Some tips for this round:

1. Keep your basics for these subjects crystal clear. Start preparing for core subjects and aptitude 3-4 months before the season starts. I started late and made some mistakes with earlier companies. So start as early as possible.

2. Revision is the key here. Due to Hyperverge's case study I did not study much for this OA, but my preparation and revision helped. I had made notes in my 2nd year about those subjects. Also I had made formula sheets about Aptitude which helped. So I just revised these things and went for the OA.

3. One important thing I noticed is that the questions were not section-wise so be prepared to see an aptitude question just after an oops question.

My test went pretty well and I was shortlisted for the next round.

2. Digital Interview [ 45 candidates appeared for this round ]

Platform: HireVue Type of Questions: Typical HR and behavioural questions. Time per question: Max 3 mins per question. You can stop the recording once done. Preparation time: 30 seconds before the 3 mins start. Note: There is no button to pause/retry the recording, you have 3 mins to record the answer and a single attempt. You go to the next question after one is done.

Questions that were asked:

1. Why did you choose your current degree program?

2. What do you aim to gain from this internship?

3. Tell us about a challenging project experience.

4. How did you manage multiple priorities and time?

5. Tell us about a time when you realized you have a weakness and how did you try to overcome that?

6. What'd you like us to know more about you?

These questions were the same for everyone.

Some tips for this round:

1. Please focus on speaking and articulating your thoughts well. Try to think how you will structure your answer in the given 30 seconds.

2. Do not make any scripts, or use GPT in any form for making these answers, because that will completely look unnatural.

3. I think they did observe the body language and eye contact with the camera. So try to maintain a good posture, hand movements and good eye contact with the camera. Keep a decent smile (don't overdo) on your face while speaking the answers. Visualize as if you are speaking to a real person, it helps.

3. [Oncampus F2F Interview: Technical Round] [ 34 candidates appeared for this round ]

There were 2 panelists. One of them was fully Technical and the other was both Technical and HR (I think).

We were called at 9:30 am in the morning. The TPCs collected all our resumes before the Interviews began. I was called in, the interview started with an excited greeting and warm welcome from their side. The Panelists were super friendly and since I was a little bit nervous, they fully made me feel comfortable. They first glanced over my resume for 10-20 seconds and then asked me to introduce myself. I had prepared two different kinds of introductions, one for technical and one for HR. I gave the technical one here. I had mentioned Java OOPs in my introduction and resume, so they started with that. They asked to explain in detail, what is OOPs, what the pillars are, and give me examples for each with code. Trick to remember the pillars is: A PIE

Challenge 1: Here I got my first challenge of the Interview. I started with A i.e. Abstraction. I gave an example of a car and its engine and that each engine might have a different implementation, but the programmer need not care about the implementation, he just has to use the defineEngine() method. I then gave the code for it. After this, the Interviewer said take this Car example only and all the remaining pillars! This was the first SHOCK. We usually prepare different examples for each pillar but I think he knew this so he kind of restricted it to a single example to test my understanding. I did not have such examples, but my understanding was very good so I took a couple of mins but made the examples and their code. They were impressed by my understanding and that I on my own insisted on writing the code. Though I do DSA in C++ which is why my Java syntax had a couple of errors. He pointed out that but then I explained to him and he said it is completely fine.

Then they came to my Internship. I had done an internship in GenAI and the project was very unique. They asked me what I did, what was my project (high level explanation followed by technical details), how was the experience, what learnings I got from it etc. They were impressed with the project idea and asked me what is the current status and how are they going to proceed with it (as I had completed my tenure there).

Challenge 2: A DSA question. They then gave me a DSA question. It was: Given a string, delete the minimum number of characters, such that the string becomes a Palindrome. Return this minimum number. You need not return the palindrome string, just the number is enough.

I suggested a two-pointer approach first, where I would just do counter+= 2 when there is a mismatch of characters. I explained it well and wrote the code for it followed by the TC and SC. They were not very satisfied with the approach and gave me an edge case where this solution might fail. It was like: a b a b d a. Here if we compare b and d, then the solution just fails badly. I acknowledged my mistake and asked for a couple of minutes to think of a different solution. After some time, I explained that two pointers might work, we just need to handle such cases. So maybe we can try all ways → that's recursion. I developed an approach quickly with the TC and SC.

I then drew a recursion tree and did a dry run. He seemed satisfied with the response. I was about to write the code but he said, it's okay no problem, we understand the approach, let's move forward.

I was somewhat disappointed in the back of my mind about the question but I tried to focus on what's coming. Next they asked me about my projects. They went really in-depth about every project both from a technical and a business perspective. They also asked about the challenges that I faced in these projects and how I overcame them. So please be ready to answer everything, the how, why, what, when EVERYTHING!

I had links to the Github Repos of all the projects, and they were quite happy to see that. They also asked me whether any of these projects are deployed. One of them was and they opened it. I had deployed my best project and it was also the 1st one in my resume. They opened it, and they were quite satisfied with the UI and initial appearance of the application. Then, bhaai, they tested almost all the features of the application. I prayed to god, please make everything work (haha). They were happy to see that everything was working (though slightly buggy) but they were quite impressed with the project. See make sure if you have deployed something, test everything before your interviews begin. This was a rare case that they checked everything, so be prepared for this too.

At this point, the Interview was going very well and I was very happy.

After this, the female panelist started asking some HR questions like, have you worked in a team? How was the experience? What will you do where there is a conflict in the team? What if you don't like your seniors' approach and you think you have a better way? Some scenarios were also given to me. She was quite impressed with the way I answered the questions with a decent structure and my overall way of speaking and body language.

Some more questions on my projects were asked. The Interview then concluded with the Interviewers asking me if I have any questions for them. I had prepared some questions so I asked them.

1. How is Baker Hughes as an Energy Tech Company using AI? How is AI helping? Any specific projects on which AI is being used?

2. How has Baker Hughes contributed to your personal and professional growth?

We had a healthy discussion on both the questions for some time. Overall the Interview lasted about 50 mins I think.

3. [Oncampus F2F Interview: Techno HR Round] [15 candidates appeared for this round]

As my round 1 ended, within 10-15 mins I was immediately called for round 2. I WAS SO HAPPY !

I entered the room, and to my surprise, there was only 1 panelist and she was the HR I think. Again it started warm greeting and a welcome from her side. She asked me how am I doing, how my day was going and all. The Interview started with the introduction of course. Here I gave the HR introduction. For the HR introduction, make it less technical overall. Like:

1. Your background before SPIT

2. Technical skills but highlight them on a higher level

3. Add your internship learnings than the technical details

4. Finally, blend in your hobbies at the end. Like I did: "when I am not coding or working on my tech projects, you can find me ….."

She complimented me on my introduction! She started asking if I have worked in a team, how was the team, were there any conflicts, how did I resolve them, what was my role in the team etc. Then she gave me a situation: 'Imagine you are working in a team and you are the lead. Now one of your teammates is intentionally not working at the speed which was required, you have to deliver the project to the client tomorrow morning. So you have 1 night, what will you do? How will you handle your team, the client and that one teammate?' Make sure that you have at least some prep to answer such questions. Like I started by highlighting the fact that project is the most important thing here, so I will start by communicating with the team-mate and understand his position and why he is not working. Is there any way I can help him? etc.

Just ensure that you think of some different answers or ways than the most obvious ones. We had a good discussion on this question.

Then since my Internship and projects had a lot of AI, she asked me: 'According to your knowledge about AI from your Internship and projects and your knowledge about Baker Hughes, where do you think Baker Hughes might be using AI?' I asked the exact question in the previous round, so I smartly blended their answer and added some points of my own. She was quite satisfied with my response.

She then asked me why I want to join Baker Hughes, and I prepared an answer for this too so I gave that.

The Interview ended with me asking her the same question I asked in the previous interview.

Overall, I would say my experience in this interview was very positive. I was very happy when I came out and honestly relieved too.

Interview lasted for a good 30 mins I think!

Out of the 15 candidates, 9 were selected and I was one of them!!

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Know your Resume INSIDE OUT: Make sure you have at least some idea about each and every word written on your resume. Please don't write anything that you have no idea about, it will create a very bad impression

2. DSA is Important: Though I was not asked about complex DSA, it is always good to be prepared about anything and everything. I started my DSA (leetcode) prep after my 2nd year ended, and I followed Striver's A2Z DSA course for it. Though it prepared me for all sorts of patterns and topics, I still lacked the intuition. I can solve questions when they are related to some patterns, but it takes a fairly large amount of time to decode the problem when it is something completely new. Therefore, I feel you should have both Intuition and Pattern recognition. I will suggest starting with Leetcode daily questions to build your intuition starting from your 3rd sem. Gradually from there, transition into topics and their questions and then start with the sheet. This will make sure you have both the Intuition and Pattern Recognition.

3. Internship experience adds value: My interview had good questions about my internship. It's important to clearly explain what you worked on, what you learnt and what impact you had.

4. Build Projects that have some value: Do not build generic projects, try to see what real-world problems can you solve and try to solve that in your projects. It may not be perfect, but is still way better than something too generic.

5. Communication is super important: See I have some friends who have a great technical profile but are rejected because of their soft skills. You may be a genius, but if you can't make the world aware about it, then what's the point? Hence try to focus on being vocal about your thought process, maintain good eye contact, a sincere smile, practice articulating your thoughts well, don't speak too fast or too slow or too vague. Take pauses wherever required, try to structure your answers.

THAT'S IT, there's no Rocket Science in it! If possible and time permits, try to do a couple of mock Interviews, it will greatly help.

6. Consistency and Discipline over EVERYTHING: Whatever you do, stay consistent with it. I remember, when starting out, I used to get anxious when I couldn't solve a problem, but with time and effort, I did manage to solve those.
