My Experience and Key Lessons:

Placements are honestly all about luck, timing, and having faith in yourself. My experience was nothing less than a rollercoaster ride. I got shortlisted for almost every company in resume screening, cleared several online assessments, and reached multiple interviews -- but I also made silly mistakes that cost me offers early on.

Then came 14th August -- the day everything changed. This morning, I was giving interviews for Baker Hughes. My technical round went really well, and within 10 minutes, I was called for the HR round which also surprisingly went smooth. By noon, I was told my chances of getting selected were very high.

In the middle, I got the message: I was the only student shortlisted for the final round with Hyperverge from their entire Mumbai drive. I was happy, but also very confused -- which one to choose?

Around 3.30 pm I had been selected by Baker Hughes ,but with great support from TPO, especially Zeeshan Sir, the company agreed to let me decide after the results.

So, while everyone else was celebrating after Baker Hughes, I was baffled and busy preparing for my Hyperverge interview.

By evening, I had offers from both companies. It was a tough choice -- one was a core tech role, the other was an APM role that aligned with my passion. I listened to my heart and finally chose Hyperverge.

● Believe in timing. Even after multiple rejections, the right role will come at the right time.

● Keep your LinkedIn profile updated -- companies really do check it.

● Be thoroughly familiar with your resume -- every point should be something you can explain confidently.

● For puzzles and brainteasers, practicing from GeeksforGeeks puzzles is more than enough Top 100 Puzzles Asked In Interviews - GeeksforGeeks

● During the interview, stay calm and confident -- don't overthink or try to be someone you're not.

● Be yourself -- authenticity leaves a lasting impression.

● For Guestimates I used this: Guesstimate Framework

● I used this to go through specific topics and tools related to product management,don't read the entire doc (it's way too long and bloated) just take a glance and see those only those topics which you need to study: Complete APM Tools Study Guide

● You can contact me any time for any help and guidance: https://www.linkedin.com/in/heenal-patel-447772283/ | 8657094834

It's a very tough phase, but remember this too shall pass. Wishing you all the best for your placements!
journey.howSecured:
1. Case Study Round [86 candidates appeared from SPIT. The process was conducted simultaneously at both SPIT and KJ Somaiya, the total number of candidates was approx 200+]

We were provided with a Notion file containing two problem statements. The final deliverables for both were:

● A presentation deck (PDF format)

● A short video presentation (max 5 mins) that shows both you and the deck. In the video explain your approach to problem framing and how you developed the solution

We had to choose one among the following two problem statements:

Problem Statement 1:

Design a Lightweight KYC App for Bharat

Context:

You are the Associate Product Manager at a tech startup building digital onboarding solutions. Your company is launching a mobile app targeting rural and semi-urban India, where smartphone specs are low-end, bandwidth is limited and users may not be digitally literate.

The app must support:

● Digilocker-based KYC

● Document-based KYC (Aadhaar, PAN, DL, VoterID)

● Face authentication (liveness, facematch checks)

● Integration with other client apps (SDK integration, web-redirection, etc.)

● Offline & retry-friendly mode

Your Task: Design the KYC solution end-to-end, keeping in mind the following:

1. Product Design & UX:

● How will the app work for users with low digital literacy?

● What will the user flow look like (screens, guidance, fail-safes)? Create wireframes.

● What offline/low-network support will you offer?

2. Features:

● Suggest and implement 2-3 innovative features to improve trust or ease of use using LLMs.

● How will you prioritise which features to build? Create a Prioritisation Matrix

3. Technical Architecture:

● How will you optimize SDK size?

● What trade-offs will you make between on-device vs server-side processing (e.g., facematch, liveness)?

● How will you handle low bandwidth and retry/resume flows?

4. Miscellaneous:

● How would you measure the success of the app?

● Any security concerns and how you'll solve them?

Problem Statement 2:

AI‑Enabled Loan Underwriting Agent for Rural and Semi‑Urban India

Context:

You are an Associate Product Manager at a tech startup developing lending solutions. Your company is launching a mobile app designed for rural and semi‑urban India. The app must work reliably on low‑spec smartphones, work with limited bandwidth, and be user‑friendly for individuals with low digital literacy.

The app must support:

● Instant Personal Loans

● AI enabled underwriting and lending

● Low customer default rates

Your Task: Design an end‑to‑end Loan Underwriting solution taking into account the following key areas:

● Features:

● What specific problems will your solution address? How will you prioritise the most important problems?

● Create two to three innovative features powered by LLMs( Eg: AI agents, Dynamic orchestrators) that can improve underwriting accuracy or ease of use

● How will you decide which features should be built first? Provide a clear prioritisation matrix

● Product Design and User Experience:

● How will the app accommodate users with low digital literacy?

● Describe the user flow for every step of the journey (To be created for every feature)

● Create Wireframes showcasing this solution (To be created for every feature)

● Technical Architecture:

○ Present a high level system design architecture that supports your AI enabled underwriting feature

○ Explain how you will handle low bandwidth environments, especially retry and resume logic to ensure a seamless experience

● Additional Considerations:

○ How will you define and measure success for the app (including key performance indicators)?

○ What security concerns must you address, and how will you mitigate them?

NOTE: For both of the ps, we were allowed to use LLMs or AI tools such as Lovable for ideation. But the final submission must be fully original.

My approach for this round:

● Selecting the problem statement:

○ During the presentation, it was evident that the company emphasized KYC, since that aligns with their core use case.

○ Based on this, I chose Problem Statement 1 - Design a Lightweight KYC App for Bharat.

● Initial research and documentation:

○ Before jumping into deck preparation, I conducted thorough research.

○ Explored articles, government research reports, and examined existing government KYC apps in detail.

○ Captured all useful insights and points in a structured document.

● Preparing the deck:

○ Once the research and documentation were complete, I began working on the presentation deck.

○ There was no page limit specified, so I created a comprehensive 15-page deck.

○ I structured the flow using the CUPS-PDM framework for clarity and coherence.

Deck structure using CUPS-PDM:

○ Context: Included all research findings, statistics, and key numbers to set the stage.

○ User Personas: Defined different user types, highlighting their characteristics and specific problems.

○ Problems: Listed all issues, clearly showing their cause and effect relationships.

○ Solution: ■ Designed solutions feature-wise, ensuring each one addressed previously identified problems as well as the pain points in the problem statement. ■ Included LLM-powered features to demonstrate how these can make the KYC process more efficient and convenient.

○ Wireframes: ■ Since AI tools were allowed, I used v0 by Vercel to create wireframes. ■ Prepared a detailed document specifying app design guidelines - from colors, buttons, and icons to text and overall flow to give it as a prompt. ■ Added all generated screens into the deck to visualize the user journey.

○ Technical Architecture: ■ Built a very detailed architecture slide, focusing on what, why, and how each approach would solve the problem. ■ Covered all pain points mentioned in the problem statement.

○ Metrics: Concluded with success metrics to measure the impact of the solution.

● Key principle followed:

○ I ensured every single detail in the deck had a clear justification.

○ Avoided adding features blindly -- everything was backed by reasoning, research, and alignment with user needs.

Key Takeaways for Preparing the PPT:

● Avoid long paragraphs; use bullet points for clarity.

● Choose neat, professional fonts that are easy to read.

● Use icons and images wherever possible to make slides lively and colorful.

● Add light-colored background boxes behind text to differentiate sections on a page.

● Maintain a consistent heading style on every slide.

● Stick to a uniform color palette throughout to give a cohesive look.

● Start with a minimalist Canva template to save time.

● Avoid wasting time on animations -- since the final submission is PDF, animations won't be visible and take extra effort to set up.

● Use varied slide layouts for different sections to keep it engaging.

● Include as many icons as possible for better visibility and quick understanding.

5-Minute Presentation Video : My Advice and Experience

● Record in a proper environment:

○ Wear a formal shirt and present in a quiet place with no disturbance.

○ Do not leave this task for the last minute - it looks short but can take multiple takes to get right.

● Be prepared for technical issues:

○ You may face network problems, mic glitches, or recording errors, so keep buffer time.

○ In my early attempts, I froze on camera and lost track of what to say -- this is normal, but plan for it.

● Keep your delivery natural:

○ Don't write or read a script - it's obvious and makes you sound robotic.

○ If needed, keep a small note of points to maintain flow instead of memorizing word-for-word.

○ Speak calmly, explain your thought process, and pitch the product naturally.

● Focus on the flow of content:

○ In 5 minutes, highlight why you chose this approach and how it impacts the problem statement.

○ Do not just read from the PPT - explain rather than narrate slides.

○ Keep it conversational but structured so it feels confident and authentic.

● Watch your timing carefully:

○ In my initial recordings, I overshot to 12-15 minutes, which forced multiple retakes.

○ Practice summarizing to stay within 5 minutes.

● Tools I used:

○ I used Zoom to record, presenting the PPT side-by-side with me visible.

2. Domain Knowledge Interviews (Online) [ 5 candidates appeared for this round ]

Preparation:

○ Having justification for every word in my case study.

○ Anticipating all types of questions related to my case study.

○ Revisiting core product management concepts (since this round was domain-focused).

○ Practicing redesigns and new feature ideas for commonly used apps (WhatsApp, Instagram, food delivery apps, Google Drive).

○ Learning how to answer trade-off questions in a structured manner.

○ Reviewing every project and internship on my resume.

○ Preparing approaches for puzzle questions and guesstimates.

Interview Experience:

● Duration: 1 Hour

● Mode: Online (Google Meet)

The interviewer began by introducing himself and then asked me to introduce myself. One of the first questions was:

Being a computer science student with so many hackathon experiences, why product management?

I had prepared for this. I explained that I was always more interested in user-centric thinking, fascinated by how apps are designed and tailored for different users, and that I enjoy working on Figma designs. In hackathons, my approach was always to present solutions not just as projects, but as complete products with thorough research, wireframes, and business models, which gave my teams an edge.

Case Study Discussion:

The interviewer shared his screen with my PPT and asked me to present it. I followed the same calm, natural approach I used in my video presentation but went deeper into the reasoning behind each decision.

● He asked how I gathered the information and why I chose this approach.

● I realized that every word I used could become a question, so I spoke very carefully.

He asked: What is an SDK, and why would a company use it instead of building one themselves?

● I first explained what an SDK is.

● Then I justified with examples: E-commerce apps use PhonePe or Razorpay SDKs because payments aren't their primary focus. Similarly, apps integrate Google Sign-In to save time and resources.

● This reasoning with examples impressed him.

Prioritization and Metrics Question:

He then asked: If you had to choose between two features : photo verification vs offline-first, which would you prioritize as a PM, and on what basis?

I explained using the impact vs effort framework:

1. First discuss feasibility and required resources with the tech team.

2. Conduct user research to gauge impact and need.

3. Align the decision with company goals.

4. Choose the feature that balances user needs and business objectives.

Business & Market Thinking:

Next, he asked: If you had to take a ride, would you choose Ola or Uber? State three metrics.

I answered:

● Ratings/reviews

● Time to reach

● Pricing (including coupons/deals)

Puzzle Question:

The puzzle: 101 coins, one counterfeit, identify in two weighings if it's lighter or heavier.

● I began by noting down key points and clarifying constraints.

● I divided the coins into three groups of 33, with 2 coins left aside, and explained different cases step by step.

● He was satisfied with my systematic approach.

Guesstimate Question:

The guesstimate: How many fine dining restaurants are there in Mumbai?

● I first asked clarifying questions (big restaurants only or small ones too?).

● He said only fine dining restaurants, so I based my estimate on Mumbai's 600 sq km area.

● I used my local knowledge: In a 1 km area near my home, there are about 12 restaurants. In some areas, maybe 4-5, and in upscale areas like Powai, around 15.

● I took an average of 10 per sq km → ~6000 restaurants.

● Initially, I wrongly assumed distance as the unit (thinking from my house as center), then corrected it to area-based reasoning, which I explained clearly.

● He appreciated how I self-corrected and justified the change in approach.

Closing the Interview:

At the end, I was asked if I had any questions. Always prepare 2-3 thoughtful questions beforehand , never say "no," as it shows lack of interest.

I asked:

Product managers are often called the CEO of a product, but what do they actually own? What are their responsibilities?

The interviewer gave a detailed explanation in response.

3. Culture Fit Round [ 1 candidate appeared for this round ]

I was the only candidate selected for this final round.

The interview was online on Google Meet, lasting around 45 minutes. Compared to the earlier rounds, this was much more chill and relaxed. The interviewer emphasized that he wanted honest answers, so don't take much time and say whatever comes to you naturally.

The interviewer asked me to describe my journey from the start.

● I began with my passion for design, and how tough it was initially to adjust in an environment where I felt lost.

● Over time, my interest grew towards UI/UX, leading me to take freelance projects, internships, and hackathon experiences.

● I also spoke about being Head of Events at WIE-IEEE, which involved strategic thinking, event planning, budgeting, and making events engaging to attract people.

● I shared how pitching to stalls for the Women's Week event helped me better understand stakeholder needs.

● Taking hackathon projects beyond just code and bugs, and presenting them as complete products with design and business aspects, deepened my passion for product management.

Key Questions and My Responses:

● You've done 5 internships in 6 months , why so many? Wasn't one enough? How did you prioritize tasks? Wasn't it overburdening? I explained that I never treated internships as just tasks to meet deadlines. Design is something I love, so it never felt like a burden. I can spend hours on Figma, presentations, and product design and that enthusiasm drives me. The interviewer appreciated this perspective. I clarified that my focus was on learning and impact rather than just ticking off tasks, which kept me motivated and balanced.

● Tell me about your best friend in college, what would they say about your strengths and weaknesses? I gave an honest answer about how my friends perceive me, highlighting collaboration, creativity, and persistence as strengths, and mentioning areas I actively work to improve.

● As a product manager, what would you like to spend most of your time doing? I explained that I would love to focus on user research, product strategy, and translating insights into design decisions, because that's where I feel I add the most value.

● If you had abundant money, would you still want to work? If yes, what would you do? I said I'm a creative person who can't sit idle.

○ I would probably teach Figma or create a product management roadmap on YouTube.

○ I would take a world tour to explore ideas and experiences.

○ If I had significant resources, I would start my own startup, which the interviewer liked.

● Looking at our website, what would you improve in its UI? I suggested keeping the color palette and tone as it is but adding a subtle AI-inspired design touch such as a glowing element in the logo or subtle interactive visuals to make it look distinctly AI-driven. The interviewer appreciated this as a unique idea.

● With so many skills and achievements, why is your CGPA 8 and not higher? I explained that I believe real learning happens outside the classroom. I chose to invest my time and prioritized building practical skills, taking internships, participating in hackathons, and gaining real experience over chasing high marks in subjects that were less relevant to my career path.

● Which is your least and most favorite subject? I answered honestly: Computer Communication Networks (CCN) as my least favorite and Design Thinking as my most favorite because of its user-centric problem-solving approach.

At the end, he asked if I had any questions. I prepared in advance and asked:

1. What would my typical day look like as a product manager?

2. What are the top three skills required to contribute effectively as a product manager? This wrapped up the interview on a positive note.

Finally, I was the only one getting the offer (including both SPIT and Somaiya).

journey.howSecured:
Placement Process:

1. Online Assessment (OA)

2. Technical Interview Round

3. HR Interview Round

1. Round 1: Online Assessment [ 197 students ] ( 11/07/2025 )

Eligibility: Minimum CGPA of 7.0+

UBS had come to campus in the month of march for selection of students for campus hackathon. For the hackathon they had conducted an online assessment. The shortlisted candidates for campus hackathon were directly eligible for interviews. I was one of them.

The assessment was largely the same for both hackathon and placement selections. It included technical MCQs focused on Computer Science fundamentals such as Data Structures & Algorithms, DBMS, and OOPs. There were also questions on error identification, output prediction, and one coding question based on DSA. The coding problem was of moderate difficulty, and I successfully passed all the test cases.

A total of 10 were shortlisted. 2 from Second year and 8 from Third year. The hackathon was a really great opportunity for getting to know the work culture at UBS and also connecting with the mentors.

For such rounds I recommend to

● Practice aptitude and DSA problems regularly.

● Be comfortable with Java syntax and core concepts of OOP.

● Brush up on CS fundamentals like DBMS, OS, and basic algorithms.

● Focus on accuracy and efficiency during coding questions.

2. [Technical Interview] [ 16 students ] ( 14-07-2025 )

There were a total of 16 candidates selected for this round. ( 15 through OA and 1 hackathon participant ).

We were asked to report to campus at 9 am. The interviews started at around 10 am. There were 6 panels for the candidates, and the interviews for Summer interns and placements were held together. They began with placement candidates. They first asked me to introduce myself and to mention all the core subjects that i had till now. I mentioned the Minor course in Banking technology and they seemed interested in it. And he asked me to explain what the course contained and a discussion for 3-5 minutes. Next they moved on to core subjects, asking some questions on OS and some questions on DSA. Then he asked me about my work in the internships and this conversation lasted for 7 - 10 minutes. He asked what exactly the work was about and he asked some in-depth questions regarding different specific implementations. They asked me about my interest in Computer Engineering and why this specific field. I was asked a question about implementation of a monopoly board game in abstract terms, the classes and data structures used. There were few questions on my implementation, I was able to answer all, except one. I was not sure about the question but I mentioned my answer and said that I would be able to append to my answer if I could actually get into implementing it or drafting it.

Tips:

● You should know your resume completely, why and where a particular tool, framework or language was used. What was your role in the projects, What is it about and the concepts used in the project.

● For OOPS : java docs and any book about OOP language that covers from the fundamentals (eg. Java programming from the ground up )

● For Data Structures : college syllabus is sufficient but Being well versed with implementations may be helpful.

The good part was that we got to attempt the test online from home since it was raining heavily that day, which definitely reduced some stress. Overall, the OA was moderately difficult. The key was to maintain speed while balancing accuracy across both the technical and reasoning sections.

The first question was the usual: "Tell me about yourself." I gave a brief overview of my education background, technical skills, and the projects I had worked on. From there, the interviewer moved straight into my project section.

I mentioned my CI/CD project, so most of her questions revolved around Kubernetes, kubectl, Jenkins, Minikube, replicas, and how Kubernetes detects high traffic. I was able to answer most of them confidently, though I struggled with a couple of deeper ones. She appreciated my overall understanding and moved on.

Next, she asked me to write a simple REST API using the @GetMapping annotation, and then to draw the architecture showing frontend-to-backend connectivity. After that, we shifted to Java -- she asked

about the differences between Java and C++, their advantages, data types in Java, and the types of for loops.

Then came a quick DSA question: reverse a string. It was straightforward, and I solved it easily. She followed it up with two basic SQL queries, one using WHERE and ORDER BY, and another involving an INNER JOIN.

After the technical part, she asked a few situational questions like "How would you disclose bad news if you were a manager?", "How do you handle stressful situations?", and "What did you learn from such experiences?"

We ended up having a really good discussion around these. At the end, she asked if I had any questions. I asked her two things "What advice would you give to freshers joining Oracle?" and "How is Oracle adapting to AI?" That sparked another nice conversation, and overall, the interview felt very friendly and conversational rather than intense. This round lasted for about 40-45minutes.

3. TECHNICAL ROUND 2 [ around 20 students appeared for it ]

The second round started almost immediately after the first barely a five-minute break. I greeted the interviewer, and we shook hands. He began by asking how my first interview went. Since it had ended on a friendly note, I felt quite confident and shared my experience with him.

He then asked me to introduce myself and followed it up with an interesting question, "What mistakes did you make in your previous interview?" I mentioned one of my small mistakes and explained how I had already learned from it and corrected it. He seemed to appreciate that honest answer.

Next, he started asking questions about my AI project mainly what it does, why it's needed, and how it works in practice. He even asked me to show the deployed version of the project. After that, we moved to SQL, where he asked about different types of joins and cursors, which I was able to answer confidently.

Toward the end, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him the same ones as before "What advice would you give to freshers?" and "Will the duties of an Associate Consultant be completely technical, or will they also involve functional responsibilities?" That led to another engaging conversation. I also mentioned that my previous interviewer had told me about Oracle's AI initiatives, so I asked him a bit more about that too.

Overall, it was a short and smooth round, around 15 minutes long. The discussion felt more like a conversation than an interrogation. I was lucky with my panel some other panels went on for over an hour and a half.

4. HR ROUND [ Around 12 students appeared for it]

The HR round was short, lasting about 5 minutes. The HR started with some basic questions about my nationality, and whether I was aware of the role Oracle was offering. She then asked if I would be comfortable with relocation.

I lightened the mood with a joke, saying I definitely wouldn't reject Oracle.

1. Round 1 Online Assessment [All who registered]

The First round (60 Questions) was the online assessment having 3 sections (No Negative Marking): Section 1: 15 Minutes, 15 Questions About: Logical based thinking. Questions were asked on patterns and reasoning. Useful Tip: Questions might appear tricky. Since this will be the first section you will be attempting - the key part here is to balance your time as 15 minutes is less for this section. Go through all the questions and solve according to easiest to difficult strategy. Section 2: 15 Minutes, 15 Questions About: English Language based. Questions were asked on grammar, arranging the sentences in the chronological order , comprehension etc. Useful Tip: Section is straight forward with the basic level of English you will be able to crack this easily. Time is not an issue here, just have to think calmy. Section 3: 40 Minutes, 30 Questions About: Technical Based. Questions were ranging from the topics of Object Oriented Programming, Database Management Systems, Computer Communication Networks, Data Structures and Algorithms etc. Useful Tip: Questions here were of easy to moderate level. A key part here is to take the smart guess when not sure. Some of them are objective based theory while some will be solving according to a data structure or so.

2. Round 2: Technical Interview Round [18 Candidates appeared for this round]

This round will last for about 45 minutes to 1 hour. The best tip would be to remain calm and smile in this situation. The interviewer is judging you on the depth of your knowledge and the way you explain which highlights your communication.

As any interview would start, the first question asked was - Introduce yourself. The key part here is to spend a bit more time and highlight the aspects that you want the interviewer to ask you. This is

going to form the base of your interview. I talked about my internship experience and current projects in web development and also the brownie points that I had won multiple hackathons and worked at NGO. Consequently, the first half shifted on my projects and work experience where I was asked to explain about it in depth and then further was asked situational based questions - Were these collaborative projects? If yes and a conflict arose then how would you manage it? (Another question) If some of your team mates were not on the same page then what would you do? (Another one) How would you approach people when you had to build a project on a tech stack th at you don't know? The way I answered these questions was that I took examples of the projects and explained each one of them highlighting that I have been in these situat ions and have leadership qualities.

Then the next part of the interview was on the aspects they had mentioned in their job description - Data Analytics and Cloud Computing. (Questions like - What is cloud computing?) They don't expect me to have in depth knowledge on them but I gave an overview on them and they were happy about it.

The third phase of this interview spanned on the DBMS. I was asked about SQL and what I knew about it. Then I was asked to design a schem a for a School. I used the "Thinking Out Loud" method

- which is essentially whatever I wrote I spoke about why I wrote it and then added the constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY). I did this so that the interviewer know the process in which I am thinking. After this I was asked to explain the Schema. The interview then asked me SQL Queries on the same. The queries were related to the Schema I made, and one of the questions on which the interviewer emphasized was the difference between the HAVING and the WHERE clause.

Since I had an interesting resume, they again came back to my work experience and then ended the interview by asking - Why choose General Mills? Researching about the company helps here. 1. Online Aptitude Test [ 180+ students appeared]

This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine - PARIKSHA, The test consisted of 60 questions, divided equally into Analytical, Quantitative, and Verbal sections, with no negative marking. The total time was 60 minutes, so time management was crucial.

The level of difficulty was easy to medium, but the Analytical section had around 8-9 Data Interpretation

(DI) questions which were quite lengthy. A key point -- check in advance if a calculator is allowed. In my case, it was allowed, but we were not informed clearly, which made solving DI questions more time-consuming. If calculators aren't allowed, I suggest using the round-off method to reach the closest answer faster.

Tip: Start with the Verbal section -- passages and sentence-based questions were straightforward. Quants was easy too, but DI can eat up time if you don't plan ahead.

Resources I used:

● IndiaBix: Pick a topic, then practice multiple pages, not just the first set -- the site has commonly asked questions with clear solutions.

● YouTube: CareerRide Aptitude is a good channel for learning tricks of aptitude. https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpyc33gOcbVA4qXMoQ5vmhefTruk5t9lt&si=GM_wTZqebs-y0 zAF

Insider tip: If Nomura is visiting other colleges a day or two before, try to connect with students from those campuses -- the topics and question patterns are often similar. 😉

2. Technical Interview I [ 28 candidates were selected ]

The list of selected candidates from the aptitude test was declared on 31st July at 7 PM, and my Technical Interview Round 1 was scheduled the very next morning , so there were hardly a few hours to prepare!

How I prepared: I quickly revised my Java OOPs concepts, core SQL queries including window functions, self joins and cross joins. I also went through my projects thoroughly -- focusing on questions like "Why did I choose this tech stack?" and "What could have been an alternative approach?"

The interview: I entered the room, greeted the interviewer and asked permission to sit. He was very polite and friendly. The very first question he asked was, "What's the meaning of your name?" Then he asked me to introduce myself , he specifically suggested covering my bachelor's degree, any internships, and the tech stack I worked on.

Tip: While introducing yourself, explain a basic overview of your best-known project -- this helps you lead the interview in a direction you're comfortable with.

After the introduction, he asked me to explain all my projects briefly, and my specific role if it was a group project. Next, he asked about my subjects during Bachelors and Masters , which ones I liked and disliked. He moved on to, "Why should we select you? What skills do you have?" here I highlighted my strong academic background, and connected it to my previous answers for example, mentioning that although I didn't like a particular subject, I still managed a good CGPA.

Then came the practical task: He asked me to convert my e-commerce project (originally in MERN) to Java -- and gave me some time to think and explain.

Tip: Always think aloud -- even if the interviewer pretends to be busy, they are paying attention to how you approach a problem, not just the final solution.

Unexpected twist: Midway through, the interview was paused and all candidates were called to give the aptitude test again the panel suspected some unfair practices in the earlier round.

This surprise test had 3 questions:

1. Aptitude: A tap can fill a tank in 10 hrs, B in 8 hrs, and C can empty it in 12 hrs. If all three are open, how long will it take to fill the tank?

2. DSA: Maximum Subarray Sum , I wrote the brute force approach, but explained the optimized Kadane's Algorithm logic too.

3. SQL: Find the employee(s) with the highest salary under each manager. I didn't remember the exact syntax but mentioned how it could be solved using GROUP BY and window functions (PARTITION BY).

Tip: They don't expect perfect answers they value your approach, logic and thought process more. Write down whatever valid, strong ideas you have.

In any round, explain your thoughts well , clarity and confidence matters!

After the retest, the results were declared out of 28 students, only 7 were selected, out of which 2 were directly promoted to Round 2 , I was one of them. The exact criteria were not disclosed.

3. Technical Interview II [ 7 candidates were selected out of 28 ]

This round was much more technical and intense , they really grilled me for almost an hour. There were two panelists in the room. I handed over my resumes and the interview began.

Again, I was asked to introduce myself , Tip: Always use words you're confident about, and never fake your resume ,they read every single line carefully.

The first panelist asked which project I was most comfortable with. I chose my AI Interviewer System and explained that I had actually deployed it. She asked me to explain the entire architecture, what tech stacks were used, and why I chose them.

Since the project included session analytics, she gave me a situation: "How would you get the analytics for how many people answered a particular question and analyze it based on their scores?" I suggested storing each question separately instead of an entire session and comparing strings but she wasn't convinced. I then proposed a DB design change using foreign keys. I asked for hints but realized they were more interested in seeing how I think, so I kept explaining my thoughts in all directions.

Then the second panelist shifted the focus to Data Structures. I honestly said I only had a basic idea. He asked about HashMaps, for example: "Can a key in a HashMap be a class?" I answered yes, but with constraints, although I couldn't recall all the details. He also asked me about Stack and Heap memory, Object and reference , where are they stored etc. He asked about sorting algorithms how Quick Sort, Merge Sort work, their time complexities, best & worst cases, Bubble Sort, BST etc. He also asked me to write short code snippets showing different time complexities as well as the sorting algorithms. I initially mixed up Bubble Sort with Insertion Sort, but when he cross-questioned, I immediately spotted my mistake and corrected it.

They switched back to another project of mine and asked deep questions about it. One tricky yet simple question was: "What happens if you keep pressing the submit button repeatedly but the data hasn't been stored yet?" I gave multiple approaches but she wasn't satisfied and kept grilling me, which led to a chain of questions about REST APIs the difference between GET, POST, PUT methods, when to use which, how to handle listing all products vs. a single product, and whether parameters can be accessed from the URL in a GET request. I could answer some parts confidently. She then asked me to explain the entire e-commerce

application workflow, cart, wishlist, order, everything as well as authentication and authorization techniques I implemented.

The other panelist asked about my comfort level in Java. I said I knew the basics. He mentioned some advanced concepts I didn't know, and I honestly admitted it. So he switched to OOPs concepts. I explained encapsulation, inheritance, and also mentioned that multiple inheritance is possible through interfaces. However, since I had just revised Java a day before, I wasn't fully clear on how interfaces enable multiple inheritance internally, so they grilled me on this too. I still shared what I thought could be the reason, showing my thought process.

He then asked, "How would you design any project?" I said I'd start with gathering requirements, spend good time finalizing the database design (and I admitted that in my past project, I had picked MongoDB mostly because it's easy to use and scalable, but this interview made me realize there are many more factors to consider).

Suddenly, they shifted to HR questions:

● "What if your project partner is not working?" I said I'd first try the approach-discuss method, but she wasn't fully convinced, so I added that I'd take necessary steps to inform the reporting manager if required.

● "What would you do if you want to prove your point and reject another idea?" -- she grilled me here too, testing my approach to conflict resolution.

At the end, I asked for feedback -- she said I should expand my thought process more!

Tips:

● Be confident about whatever you say -- but also make sure it's logically sound.

● Don't bluff -- honesty stands out more than pretending to know everything.

● They test how you think, not just how much you know.

4. HR Round [ 3 candidates were selected out of 7 ]

The HR round was quite relaxed and straightforward. The HR asked me about where I live, and why I chose SPIT despite being rank 1 in the entrance. We spoke about my hobbies, my strong academic background, and why I wanted to work at Nomura. He also asked about my plans for further studies just to understand my long-term goals.

Overall, it was a friendly conversation and a positive way to wrap up the entire process!

All 3 candidates were selected for the ITD role.

1. Maintain a Good CGPA: Keep your CGPA above 7.5-8, as it helps meet eligibility criteria and creates a strong first impression.

2. Resume Preparation: o Use a standard, professional template (e.g., Overleaf Resume Template). o Make it ATS-friendly; check your score on Resumeworded (aim for 60+). o Be truthful--only include skills, projects, and achievements you can confidently discuss. Prepare 4-5 points for each.

3. Company and Role Research: o Understand the company's work, culture, and role requirements. o Prepare relevant questions to ask the interviewer --it shows interest and preparation. o Read the job description carefully and incorporate keywords into your answers.

4. HR Preparation: o Prepare for standard HR questions in advance to stay confident. o Keep answers authentic and personal; avoid over -reliance on AI for this.

5. DSA and Problem Solving: o Focus on understanding questions thoroughly rather than just solving many. o Solve standard problems first; daily practice on platforms like LeetCode or GeeksforGeeks helps. o Participate in contests to improve time management, an essential skill for coding rounds. o Always check constraints; write brute -force solutions first if optimal solutions are not obvious.

6. Core Subjects: o Prioritize important subjects like DBMS and CCN--often asked in technical interviews. o Choose open electives wisely (e.g., DBMS) to strengthen placement -related knowledge.

7. Programming Skills: o Master your primary language's basics. o Be confident discussing syntax, concepts, and memory management. o Practice explaining your approach during coding rounds; interviewers often guide you if stuck.

8. Team Motivation: o Collaborate with peers with similar goals. o Motivate each other, take progress follow-ups, and push to stay on track.

9. Handling Rejections: o Treat rejections as learning opportunities. Focus on areas you can improve. o Placement success also involves timing and luck, stay confident and persistent.

10. Additional Skills: o Develop puzzle-solving and critical thinking through platforms like GeeksforGeeks. o Practice guesstimates to improve analytical reasoning. o Participate in mock interviews to enhance confidence, communication, and interview stamina

The placement process can be very hectic, and facing failures along the way is normal. Don't give up-- keep giving your 100% and continue preparing consistently. In the end, all your hard work and perseverance will be worth it..

Process Date: 4th -5th September 2025

Ensure your resume is ATS-friendly with standard formatting and clear headings, and maintain a CGPA of 7.5 or above, as most companies require this. TransUnion criteria: 7 CGPA

The selection process consisted of the following rounds:

1. Pre-Placement Talk (PPT)

2. Online Assessment

3. Technical Interview

4. Techno HR Interview

1. Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) The PPT was conducted offline and began a little late as all the company team members had not yet arrived. During this time, the HR ma'am interacted with us informally and invited five volunteers to perform a short skit. I was one of the participants in this activity. I advise actively participating in such activities, as they showcase confidence, help during the HR rounds, and leave a positive impression on the recruiters.

Afterward, the company representatives delivered their presentation, providing a detailed introduction about the organization, its work culture, and the career opportunities available. I would also suggest asking relevant doubts and clarifying queries during the PPT, as it demonstrates genuine interest in the company and further strengthens your impression.

2. Online Assessment [87 students appeared for this round]

The Test was conducted on 4th September from 14:00 to 15:30 (1 hour 30 minutes). The test was hosted on SHL, and calculators were allowed. It consisted of four sections:

1. Logical Aptitude: Easy to medium-level questions, including puzzles and pattern-based problems such as finding the odd one out or guessing the next number. Example questions included: o Find the odd one out: 121, 144, 169, 196, 225, 242 o What comes next in the series: 2, 4, 8, 16, ? 14 questions were to be solved in 14 minutes.

2. Quantitative Aptitude: Questions on topics like ratios, proportions, simple interest, and time & work. Example questions: o If a train travels 120 km in 2 hours, how long will it take to travel 300 km at the same speed? o Divide ₹720 among A, B, and C in the ratio 2:3:4 12 questions were to be solved in 12 minutes.

3. Coding Section: Two coding questions were provided, with difficulty varying randomly among candidates. o My questions were:

1. Count the frequency of special characters in a string.

2. Count the frequency of numbers in a given number. 50 minutes were allotted for this section.

4. Verbal/English Section: Questions focused on grammar, vocabulary, and comprehension. Example: o Choose the grammatically correct sentence: ▪ He don't like playing cricket. ▪ He doesn't likes playing cricket. ▪ He doesn't like playing cricket. o Understand the main idea conveyed in a passage. 12 questions were to be solved in 14 minutes.

Note: The coding section difficulty varied significantly for different students. Some received easy questions involving HashSets or HashMaps, while others got challenging Dynamic Programming problems. My experience was comparatively easier, as my questions focused on counting frequencies, which I could solve efficiently within the time limit.

Tip: Start practicing aptitude questions well before placements, as most companies include them in their selection process. Additionally, regularly practice Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) to handle coding sections efficiently.

3. Technical Round [32 students appeared for this round] [30-35 mins]

I. Introduction and Projects

• The interview began with a general introduction, followed by a discussion of my projects.

• Projects and Challenges: I was asked to explain all my projects in detail and describe the challenges I faced during implementation.

• Language Preference: The interviewer inquired about my preferred programming languages and which ones I was most proficient in.

II. Java and C++ Deep Dive The main technical discussion focused on my Java project.

• Core Java Questions: o Why I chose Java for the project. o Key differences between Java and C++. o How Java achieves platform independence. o Which file is generated upon Java code execution. o The role of JVM and JRE in making Java platform-independent.

• Memory Management in Java (Interview Q&A): The interviewer asked about types of memory in Java. I explained that the primary memory areas relevant for program execution are Heap and Stack: o Heap: Stores all objects and class instances created at runtime. o Stack: Stores local variables, method call frames, and references to objects in the heap.

o Example: In public static void main(String[] args), local variables like integers or references are stored on the stack, while objects created using new inside main are stored on the heap.

III. Data Structures (Scenario-Based) The interviewer presented real-life scenarios and asked which data structure I would use.

Scenario 1: Stock Market Prices

• Scenario: You are developing an application to track stock market prices throughout the day. You need to quickly retrieve the price of a stock at specific integer times, such as 9, 10, 11… 3.

• Question: Which data structure would you use to efficiently store and retrieve these prices, and why?

Scenario 2: Digital Signature (Undo/Redo)

• Scenario: You have developed an application where, at the final step, the user needs to provide a digital signature. If the user creates a signature but is not satisfied, they can clear it and create a new one. Later, they realize that the previous signature was better.

• Question: How would you retrieve the previous signature? Which data structure would you use and why?

IV. Coding and Problem Solving (Palindrome)

• Problem: Check if a given string is a palindrome. My Approach ➔

• Initial Solution: Brute-force approach using extra space--reverse the string and compare with the original.

• Optimization: Explained time and space complexity of the initial approach, then provided an optimized two-pointer solution.

• Execution: Wrote the optimized code, explained it, and performed a dry run with a test case.

V. SQL Query

• Problem: Two tables of sales data were provided.

• Approach: Asked clarifying questions, explained the thought process, and decided to use Joins and GROUP BY to handle multiple entries per customer.

• Solution: Wrote a correct SQL query incorporating both Joins and aggregation functions.

VI. Closing

• The interview concluded with questions about my extracurricular activities.

• I also asked 1-2 questions regarding the company's work culture and upcoming projects.

4. Techno HR Round [10 students appeared for this round] [15-20mins]

The interview began with my introduction, during which I introduced myself and briefly summarized my background. They then asked me about my projects, and I provided a concise overview of each. Following this, they inquired about my achievements and participation in hackathons.

They also asked which interview I was currently giving and why I was not selected in previous attempts. The discussion then shifted to TransUnion, where I was asked why I chose the company, what kind of work TransUnion does, and why I wanted to join. They also asked about my position and responsibilities in various committees, including how I mentored juniors and managed my tasks.

Next, the conversation moved to my certifications, including where I completed them and my basic technical knowledge. They also asked why I am switching from Electronics to Tech, my weaknesses, my residence, family, and how I managed extracurricular activities alongside traveling. I was also asked about my career aspirations and where I see myself in the next five years. Towards the end, the interviewers gave me the opportunity to ask questions and clarify any doubts regarding the company or the role.

After the process completion 8 students got an offer and I was one of them.

Useful Tips:

1. Maintain a Good CGPA: Keep your CGPA above 7.5-8, as it helps meet eligibility criteria and creates a strong first impression.

2. Resume Preparation: o Use a standard, professional template (e.g., Overleaf Resume Template). o Make it ATS-friendly; check your score on Resumeworded (aim for 60+). o Be truthful--only include skills, projects, and achievements you can confidently discuss. Prepare 4-5 points for each.

3. Company and Role Research: o Understand the company's work, culture, and role requirements. o Prepare relevant questions to ask the interviewer --it shows interest and preparation. o Read the job description carefully and incorporate keywords into your answers.

4. HR Preparation: o Prepare for standard HR questions in advance to stay confident. o Keep answers authentic and personal; avoid over -reliance on AI for this.

5. DSA and Problem Solving: o Focus on understanding questions thoroughly rather than just solving many. o Solve standard problems first; daily practice on platforms like LeetCode or GeeksforGeeks helps. o Participate in contests to improve time management, an essential skill for coding rounds. o Always check constraints; write brute -force solutions first if optimal solutions are not obvious.

6. Core Subjects: o Prioritize important subjects like DBMS and CCN--often asked in technical interviews. o Choose open electives wisely (e.g., DBMS) to strengthen placement -related knowledge.

7. Programming Skills: o Master your primary language's basics. o Be confident discussing syntax, concepts, and memory management. o Practice explaining your approach during coding rounds; interviewers often guide you if stuck.

8. Team Motivation: o Collaborate with peers with similar goals. o Motivate each other, take progress follow-ups, and push to stay on track.

9. Handling Rejections: o Treat rejections as learning opportunities. Focus on areas you can improve. o Placement success also involves timing and luck, stay confident and persistent.

10. Additional Skills: o Develop puzzle-solving and critical thinking through platforms like GeeksforGeeks. o Practice guesstimates to improve analytical reasoning. o Participate in mock interviews to enhance confidence, communication, and interview stamina

The placement process can be very hectic, and facing failures along the way is normal. Don't give up-- keep giving your 100% and continue preparing consistently. In the end, all your hard work and perseverance will be worth it..

Recommended Resources

• DSA: Striver A2Z DSA

• DBMS: YouTube DBMS Playlist, InterviewBit DBMS Qs, GeeksforGeeks DBMS Qs

• OS: YouTube OS Playlist

• C++ & OOPS: C++ OOPS, Java OOPS, GeeksforGeeks OOPS

• Aptitude: Aptitude Playlist, IndiaBix

• SQL: practice problems on HackerRank and LeetCode, Do SQL top 50 from leetcode.

If you have any questions or need guidance, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn. My LinkedIn- LinkedIn ALL THE BEST!!!

So here's a short gist of my college years. Honestly, I didn't have a great start--my PTR was 7.35(currently it's 8.25, keep it above 8), and it's not like I was busy with DSA or projects. In fact, the first two years I was pretty lost and didn't do much prep at all. Later, I finally buckled down and started DSA.I tried covering as much as I could before placements, but still couldn't clear the OAs. I sat for around 15 to 20 companies and got rejected in all of them. By the end, I was the only one in my group still unplaced.

I'm telling you this because the process can get really tough. Maybe everyone around you will get placed before you, maybe your PTR won't meet the cutoffs, and yeah--there'll be a lot of tough days. But don't give up. Enjoy the whole ride--the rejections and the successes--because that's what makes it easier to handle.

And the most important thing: have fun! It's college--you won't get this time again. And also everyone has a different approach to studying , if u have a different one dont think its wrong .

DOCUMENTS I REFEREED :

Java in OOPs is important as much as dsa is so cover that . And as much as DSA is hyped, focus on java & sql too .

JAVA : Kunal Khushwaha

SQL : leetcode top 50

journey.howSecured:
There were 4 rounds : OA , TR1 , TR2 and HR round . The OA was conducted on 15th sept which had 2 dsa qts and 32 mcqs - 20 computer fundamentals + 12 apti qts. Before the technical round 1 we had a ppt where I asked 2 questions . It didn't play a very important role for me but it might help you , so ask if you have even a small doubt in your head don't hesitate to ask but if you don't it's okay, no pressure .

1. Tech Round 1 [ No of candidates who appeared for this round : 25] [30-40 mins]

The PPT was supposed to start at 8:45 but actually began around 10, and the interviews started at about 11:30. I know the waiting can be really nerve-wracking, but try to stay calm if possible.

During my interview, I went in and greeted the interviewer with a handshake. She started by asking me for my introduction, and then the very first question was: Why Oracle? (I was asked this in all rounds). I answered by mentioning something I remembered from the PPT--that Oracle has a presence in almost 125 countries--so she could see that I had paid attention.

Next, she gave me a very simple coding question: adding two numbers. She wanted to understand how I wrote the code. As a follow-up, she asked about function declaration vs. function expression. After that, she asked me to write an SQL query to select all names starting with my name using the like operator. Then, we moved on to HR-style questions. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses, and then asked: If you had all the resources you needed, what product would you build using your skills?

I also got some puzzles. For example: If I had 1 cm³ cubes, how many would I need to fill a 9 cm³ cube?

She asked me CSS questions too. One was whether I had used a CSS framework (I said I had worked with Tailwind CSS). Then she asked about the main box styles in CSS. At first, I misunderstood and said flex, grid, etc., but what she was looking for was padding, borders, margins, etc. She also asked: What is absolute positioning? (and wanted me to show it by drawing) and What is the default positioning?

Another puzzle was the classic jug problem: You have a 5L jug and a 3L jug. How will you measure exactly 4L without any measuring device?

She also touched on OOP and C++ concepts, like polymorphism (and asked me to write it down), what I would call an overloaded constructor in the parent class, the difference between agentic AI and generative AI, and what inline functions in C++ are. At the end, she asked if I had any questions, and I asked her two.

Now, here's the important part: I did not know the answers to all the questions, and I wasn't able to solve both the puzzles. But I made sure to walk her through my thought process and explain the solutions I was considering. I also asked for hints when I needed them. It's not about always having the correct answer--it's about how you approach the problem and how you carry yourself throughout the process. Don't be scared. You'll feel very nervous outside, but once you're inside, just sit and talk as if you're chatting with a friend. And remember: it's okay if you don't know something. Nobody knows everything. What matters most is keeping an open mind and thinking freely.

2. Technical Round 2 [Duration : 30 mins ]

For Tech Round 2, I was called in within 20 minutes. The interviewer was very chill and said he wouldn't start with technical questions. Instead, he began by asking me where I live and Why Oracle. While I was answering, he noticed I mentioned AI and became very interested. Since I had completed an internship in generative AI, he asked me to explain it and draw the flow. This was a project I knew well, so I explained everything in detail. While I was drawing, he mentioned that he used to live where I do, and we had a short discussion about that.

After that, he asked a simple DSA question: detect duplicates and print their count. Then he asked me to write an SQL query to find the third-highest rank in a given dataset, and later to implement the same logic in C++.

He asked me Why Oracle once again, and I repeated the point I had mentioned earlier from the PPT. At the end, he asked if I had any questions, so I asked a few, and we discussed them.

3. HR round[10mins and 9 ppl]

This was NOT an elimination round,just a formality round .I was asked about my nationality, willingness to relocate, plans for a master's degree, who I live with, and my hobbies. She also mentioned that the final results would be based on Round 1 and Round 2. Finally, she asked if I had any questions.

Stages: Resume Shortlist → Pen & Paper Test → Technical Interview → Final Interview

Resume Tips:

The shortlisting was relaxed with a 6.0+ CGPA cutoff. I submitted a tech-heavy resume, but in hindsight, adding one or two business case studies or cross-functional experiences would help. Focus on data-driven and machine learning projects.

1. Pen Paper Test :- Candidates Appeared: 102 | Test Duration: 1 hour

● Section 1: Aptitude (8 Questions, +3/-1) Topics included:

○ Coordinate geometry (line/curve equations)

○ Speed-distance

○ Work-time

○ Number systems Time management is key -- solve this in 15-20 mins max.

● Section 2: No Negative Marking (12 Marks Total)

○ Python Pseudo-code (4 Marks):

■ Predict the sum of the series: 0, 2, 6, 12, 20, 30... (1 mark)

→ Pattern: n2+nn^2 + nn2+n

■ Another sequence (3 marks): -1, -1, 5, 19... - slightly tricky and I couldn't fully crack it → Don't panic if one question goes wrong

○ SQL (8 Marks): Tables: Student, House, Test Sample queries:

■ Avg/Max/Min marks per student

■ Second-highest marks

■ Rank houses based on top performer

■ List test types and students who didn't attempt them

Prep Advice:

● SQL: Leetcode Top 50 is enough

● Apti: Practice from IndiaBIX

● Python: Brush up number series logic & patterns

● Tip: Don't freeze. Presence of mind > perfection

Do the SQL top 50 on leetcode that would be enough.

● Resume deep-dive (Types of ML Algorithms/Technologies used, and Why)

● ML algorithm intuition: R², RMSE, classification metrics. (Because It was on my resume)

● Career goals and why shift from tech to analyst role Others were asked SQL joins, Pandas basics, API logic -- nothing too difficult if you built your projects yourself.

○ Ask clarifying questions

○ Segment the problem

○ I wasn't exact, but spoke aloud my approach and kept calm

journey.prep:
Focus on your CGPA. During our time, many compa nies had a minimum CGPA criteria of 7.5, which led to a large number of students being filtered out even before getting the opportunity to sit for the company. It really hurts when you don't even get the chance to appear despite having the skills.

Placements are a tiring yet humbling process. I had reached the HR rounds of InCred and Quantiphi before this opportunity, and both interviews went really well, but I couldn't make it to the final shortlist. That's when I truly realised how important factors like CGPA and luck can be in the placement journey. Sometimes, even after giving your best, things don't work out --but they prepare you for the opportunity that's meant for you.

My personal suggestion would be during your 6th semester, shut out the noise around you and just believe in your hard work . When your day finally comes, everything will start to make sense ,you'll realise why you weren't selected earlier and how it was all just a testing phase before something bigger. Having your family and supportive friends around you trule encourag es you to not get carried away by rejections and prepare for upcoming companies.

Study everything that's commonly asked in interviews. In placements, being a jack of all trades often works better than excelling in just one domain. Practicing DSA is important, of course, but relying only on it won't help much--only 4-5 companies are heavily DSA-focused and I realized it much much later. The rest mostly have doable coding questions in their online assessments and give high importance to aptitude, which most students tend to ignore.

For interviews, know your resume inside out--every project, every line. SQL is the underdog in placements, so make sure to practice it thoroughly beforehand.

When it comes to projects, having a simple project that you understand deeply is far better than having an overly complex one that you can't explain properly. Lastly, know your OS, CN, and DBMS concepts really well--many companies ask questions from these subjects. End-moment preparation won't help much here, so start early. I'd recommend watching CodeHelp's OS playlist, which is around 30 hours long--it's a time investment that's truly worth it.

All the very best for your placements! Give your best, trust the process, and have faith in your hard work. Everything will fall into place when it's meant to. God does have a plan for all

For any queries or doubts:

https://www.linkedin.com/in/kanishka-amritkar/
journey.howSecured:
The eligibility criteria required a minimum of 6.0 CGPA in college and 60% marks in both 10th and 12th

1. [Aptitude Round] [All students from Comps,AIML,DS and having minor in computers from EXTC were eligible for the process]

The Aptitude Round consisted of 100 questions covering Quantitative Aptitude, Geometry, Verbal Ability, and Logical Reasoning to be solved in 1 hour. The quantitative section in cluded problems on percentages, ratios, time and work, and geometry -based questions. The verbal section tested grammar, reading comprehension, and vocabulary, while the reasoning section focused on analytical thinking. In addition to these, there were a few behavioral and situational questions such as "If your team member isn't contributing effectively, what would you do?" to assess decision-making and teamwork skills. Overall, the round focused on both technical and behavorial assessment.

This round followed a +4 -1 marking scheme so make sure to attempt the questions you are fully sure about, I managed to solve 94 questions. Since navigation was allowed,I quickly solved logical verbal and behavorial questions in the first 20 minutes and then proceeded to do the aptitude questions.

I practiced Quantitative, Logical, and Verbal Aptitude questions from IndiaBix, and most importantly taking their timed tests greatly helped me improve my speed and time management skills, which play a crucial role in performing well in aptitude exams.

2. [Coding Round] [ 72 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

Round 2 consisted of two sections - the first focused on basic Python MCQs, while the second included easy-level coding questions similar to those found on LeetCode. The only programming language allowed was Python. I was able to solve all the coding questions and pa ss all the test cases, along with answering almost all the MCQs correctly. This round was quite doable, and the key differentiator turned out to be time . Candidates who managed to solve almost all questions accurately and submitted their test about 15 minutes early were the ones who proceeded to the next round .

but since only allowed programming language was python and my primary language was Java,I practiced some basic questions from this youtube channel. https://youtu.be/78FsbjYSWIU?si=ehBIXHc3uNnGOLEF This has around 100 coding questions which will give you a strong grasp of the basics For other DSA rounds,Practice Striver's sheet being well versed with it will help you clear DSA coding rounds of almost all the companies. I practiced python mcqs from Sanfoundry(It has 1000 mcqs but to be able to be quick with mcqs that much of practice will really be worth it as you would have seen or solved all the questions in the past).

3. [Group Discussion Roud] [25 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

The topic given to us was "Technology: Boon or Bane." Candidates who expressed their points in a clear, concise, and professional manner, speaking confidently and with good articulation, were the ones selected for the next round.

4. [Technical Interveiw] [11 students were selected for this round]

The interview was primarily focused on Python and Machine Lea rning. The interviewer was very particular about the answers and often went into detailed discussions. He began by asking me to introduce myself. Since I had researched Mahindra Finance beforehand, I knew that one of its key sectors deals with loan approva l, which aligned well with my credit risk modelling project. I mentioned this connection during my introduction, which led him to ask several project -related questions.

He asked which algorithm I had used, and since I had applied SMOTE during preprocessing , he asked me to explain SMOTE along with its advantages and disadvantages. He then asked me to draw and explain the working of Random Forest and justify why it performed better than XGBoost in my case.

Next, he moved on to questions about my dataset. My p roject involved two datasets that I had merged, so he asked me to write the pandas query for merging them using the ID column as the key. He further asked detailed questions about the types of columns in my dataset and their relevance.

The discussion then shifted to model evaluation metrics, where he asked me to explain precision, recall, and accuracy, and to justify which metric mattered the most in my project context.

After that, he presented a case study scenario: "If Uber ride prices suddenly increase f rom ₹400 to ₹800 within 10 minutes in the same location, how would you identify and fix the bug in your ML model?" He asked me to describe the parameters and features I would use in such a model. He then gave another scenario: "If all drivers in a certain area stop accepting Uber rides and instead take private trips, how would your model detect such behavior?" I explained my approach, mentioning that one of the parameters would be peak -hour timings. He further asked how I would determine peak hours without having an existing dataset.

The interview concluded with me asking him three questions about Mahindra Finance's advancements in Machine Learning and how the company is integrating AI into its operations. Overall, it was a highly engaging and technical discussion that tested both conceptual understanding and practical problem -solving.

5.[HR Round] The HR round surprisingly lasted for around 45 minutes, during which the HR was noting down my answers carefully. The discussion mainly revolved around situational and behavioral questions. I was given several case-based scenarios such as how I would handle a situation where a team member is not contributing effectively, or how I would respond if I witnessed something wrong happening around me. The HR wanted to understand my thought process, decision-making, and ability to handle real-life workplace challenges. Overall, it was a situational round focused on assessing attitude, ethics, and teamwork rather than technical knowledge.

Finally 5 students were selected :)

journey.howSecured:
1. Round 1 Online Assessment [All who registered]

The online assessment round consisted of 60 questions and had a duration of 1 hour and 10 minutes. There were three sections: logical reasoning, language proficiency and technical questions.

Logical reasoning: This section was of 15 minutes(15 questions) and itcontained basic questions related to math, patterns, sequences. The 15 minutes time was less for thissection.

Language proficiency: This section was of 15 minutes(15 questions) and itcontained questions related to basic English. The time was sufficient for solving this section.

Technical questions: This section was of 40 minutes(30 questions). It contained questions ranging from topics of Database Management System, Computer Communication and Networks,Object Oriented Programming,Operating Systems and Data Structures and Algorithms.

2. Technical Round [ 18 students were shortlisted for this round]

This round lasted for 45 mins to 1 hour . The interviewer began by asking which subject excites me the most and I chose App development. I was given a case study to design an app. The task began with me asking relevant questions to understand the requirements thoroughly. I had to consider factors like the app's functionality, user experience, and the overall system architecture. Once Ihad enough information, I proposed a design that detailed both the frontend and backend components, explaining how they would interact. A key focus was on scaling the app from 3,000 to 30,000 users, and I discussed strategies like efficient data storage, user management, and backend optimization to handle the increased load. The interviewer tested my ability to break down the problem, gather requirements, and present a robust, scalable solution.

Following this, I was asked about storing large amounts of data using Firebase, which had been a core part of my previous app development experience. The interviewer wanted to understand if I knew how to handle scalability issues in Firebase, especially with large databases. I explained Firebase's strengths in handling real-time data but also discussed its limitations when itcomes to scaling beyond certain thresholds. This led to a deeper conversation about database management, where I was quizzed on concepts like BCNF and normalization. I answered these questions, elaborating on whether normalization is needed for small databases. While I wasn't very familiar with microservices, the interviewer was helpful in explaining key concepts, and Ipicked up the basics quickly, which allowed me to respond to further questions.

Toward the end of the interview, the case study was revealed to be based on an app the interviewer had already developed, providing a real-world context to the task. I asked how they had solved the scalability problem in their app and was curious about their experience at General Mills. The interview tested my ability to think critically,learn on the go and apply theoretical knowledge to practical challenges. It wasn't just about technical expertise but also about showing my problem-solving skills and willingness to engage with new concepts and feedback. Overall, it was an insightful experience that showcased my strengths and highlighted areas where I could continue to grow.

3. HR- Based Round [ 10 students were shortlisted for this round]

In my HR interview, the panel consisted of two interviewers who started by asking me to introduce myself and share a bit about my family background. After that, they posed an interesting question--if I hadn't chosen to pursue engineering, what other career path would I have taken. They then moved on to ask where I see myself in the next five years and how my friends would describe me, giving me a chance to reflect on both my professional goals and my personal traits.

The interview then touched on some of the major decisions I've made, as they asked me about the easiest and most difficult decisions I've taken so far in life. Iwas also asked to explain about one of my projects in brief. Finally, I was asked why I wanted to join General Mills, which allowed me to express my interest in the company. At the end of the interview, I had the opportunity to ask them questions.

The key is to stay calm and maintain a friendly smile throughout the process. Answer the questions confidently and ensure that your responses reflect genuine interest while aligning with the company's values and goals.

4 students were offered internships after this round.
