1. OA Round [ 135 candidates appeared, 37 shortlisted]

Eligibility criteria required a CGPA of 7+. There was also some kind of shortlisting based on resumes. The OA round comprised of 3 sections:

Section 1: MCQs mainly covering concepts of OOPs, SQL queries, output based questions based on Java/C++. This was randomized, some people got java based output questions, while others got C++. Most of the questions were OOPs/output related, with a couple of SQL questions.

Section 2: DSA question : String Generation OA question. This question had been repeated by Barclays in previous couple of years, so it was advantageous for students who had practiced the PYQ. Furthermore, test cases were weak, so it was possible to pass all test cases with some simple logic, without a very complex algorithm.

Section 3: SQL query, easy level. Was solvable with some where clauses. Some students got an SQL query that involved extracting the month from a date along with basic logic.

#Tip1: Ensure that you are really clear conceptually with OOPs, as different MCQs had differing weightages attached to them. MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor as most students could solve the DSA question and SQL query fully.

#Tip2: Apart from SQL50 on LeetCode, ensure to familiarize yourself with basic String and Date functions and their syntax in SQL.

2. Tech Round [ 35 candidates appeared, 19 Shortlisted]

We weren't told at what time exactly our individual interviews would be, instead every person was being called and sent to their respective panel. This was a long and drawn out process, and intern and grad interviews were ongoing at the same time. The interviews started at 10am after the PPT, and my interview was finally conducted at 3:30pm. It went on for around 30 mins.

The interviewer started off by testing me on my knowledge of Java & OOPs.

Q. What is inheritance? -> (standard explanation with info about what is inherited from the base class.) Q. In the eg below, how can i call x function in class A in the following cases:

● Inside class B

● By creating an object of B Class A{ void x(){ System.out.println("A"); } } Class B extends A{ void x(){ System.err.println("B"); } }

-> Case 1: Using the super keyword. I then clarified what the super keyword is used for - all parent constructors, variables and functions, except for those which are private and static.

Case 2: Here, I first clarified with the interviewer what the reference type of the object was. This allowed him to further interrogate me about reference type, and what would happen in both cases, where reference type was of A and B. He also asked me if reference type A was even allowed. This in turn allowed me to further elaborate on the difference between references and objects and what each of them are used for. Finally, I answered that we can either make another function in B that calls on the original function in A by using super keyword, or we can make the function in A and B static, and then define the reference type to be A. Since static functions are not inherited, this would call the class in A. This also allowed me to state what run-time polymorphism is, and how the static keyword works.

Q. What is garbage collection in Java? -> Basic answer about cleaning up null objects.

Q. What is memory management in Java? -> I expanded upon what each of heap and stack memory stores.

Q. Which version of Java do you use? -> I stated that I use Java versions 8 and above, highlighting how version 8 onwards, Java introduced flexibility in interfaces and expanded upon how default and static were allowed, and what their use cases were.

#Tip1: At first glance, the questions seem really basic and straightforward. However, how you decide to answer the question and how in depth you go with the explanation lets the interviewer know about your critical thinking skills, how you analyze a problem and how much of the topic depth you are aware of.

#Tip2: Interview rounds really are a test of your mental strength. Try not to worry too much if your interview is happening late, my interview was last on my panel and only lasted 30 mins compared to other interviews which went for an hour and above. I had mentally given up hope since it had been 7 hours of just sitting and waiting, and some students had started with their round 2 while I hadn't even given my round 1. Such situations might be inevitable, so try not to focus on areas that are out of your control. But try not to let it affect your mindset in the interview, just focus on giving your best performance.

The interviewer then moved on to 2 easy level DSA questions.

Q. Sum of digits of a number, till you reach a single digit. Eg. 54312 = (5+4+3+1+2) = 15 = (1 + 5) = 6

Q.Given an array of positive and negative numbers, sort the array into alternating positive and negative elements.

Then we moved on to the projects on my resume, and he asked me questions off of the points I had mentioned in bullets - implementation, why I used a certain thing, etc.

He also asked me if I've worked with cloud deployment, to which I replied honestly with no - but I have deployed my application on render, and explained deployment steps and what CORS is.

I wasn't asked anything regarding SQL, but some other panels did - some things purely depend on your panel and your luck.

#Tip3: Ensure that you really know your projects inside out. It's not necessary to be able to reproduce the code, but you must be aware of the logic and be prepared to justify your design choices. You may ask any LLM to generate relevant questions based on your projects to gain a better understanding of scalability and differing implementation methods.

#Tip4: It's always better to say I don't know over giving a wrong answer.

3. Techno HR round[ 19 candidates appeared]

After 2 hours of anxiously wondering if my name would be called or not, I was called in for the next round. The interview started off with him asking me to introduce myself. I introduced my name, branch, 2 main projects and included a line about the reason I want this job - because I like the satisfaction of debugging something and solving a problem. This led to him starting off with a scenario based problem where he introduced a bug in my project. Thankfully, I had considered all possible edge cases when I was designing my project, so I was able to convince him that my project would not encounter the bug he had explained.

#Tip1: Your introduction really sets the tone for the interview, and allows you to navigate through the topics you want the interviewer to probe you on. I hadn't even planned on including the last line, it was just

something that spontaneously came up in my head and I just said it. I would advise against this - as the interviewer may ask you questions you are unprepared for.

#Tip2: Even if your project is relatively simple, think of making it a complete product. This includes handling edge cases, how your system is designed to scale, and a secure user experience. My main project scope was really simple, but there were enough technical details to discuss with the interviewer because of the extensive tech stack and how I designed the system.

He asked me to design the schema of the project. He then basically gave a scenario where referential integrity of a foreign key was being violated, and asked me if it was possible and why or why not. He then gave a scenario based question based on the project, where a junior disagreed with a certain part of the implementation, and how i would handle it. We then had a discussion on polling vs queuing which was relevant to the logic in my project.

#Tip3: An obvious tip but do keep RISES in mind whenever you're answering any situational questions. Also, prepare scenarios where you demonstrated RISES just in case you're asked about it.

He then asked me if I knew what Binary Search was, its time complexity, and showed me a simple function with a double for loop and asked me for its time complexity (O(n2)).

He then asked me if I was comfortable with python since I had an ML project on my resume. I replied that I wasn't too confident with the language and syntax, as I had mainly used it for its libraries. He then asked what language he could ask questions on, to which I replied with Java.

He then gave me the example:

A one = new A("xx", 1) A two = new A("xx", 1)

Q. Can we do one == two? -> We can, but it will be false as it compares two different objects.

Q. How will you check if the values are equal then? -> By overriding the .equals() method.

He also asked me about PostGreSQL vs MySQL, which I was unable to answer.

Lastly, I was asked another situational question where an important presentation is in my laptop, and if I would give my credentials in such a situation to my friend. I answered no as that would be a security risk.

Some people had this round as a purely HR round, others Techno-HR round.

16 candidates were offered the job.

journey.prep:
1. Maintain a Balance between DSA and Development Skills- It's important to have a balance between (DSA) and development skills. As Companies like UBS can ask questions from either area--or both--depending on the interviewer's background. So, ensure that you're prepared with core CS concepts, practical development knowledge, and also practice solving logical puzzles, as these are frequently asked to assess your analytical thinking.

2. Know Your Resume--But Also Know the Why- Don't just memorize what's on your resume--be prepared to reason every line. Have solid, well-thought-out reasons for every project, internship, or achievement listed. Be ready to explain your decision-making process and choices (e.g., why you chose a particular tech stack, what your contribution was in a team project, etc.).

Tip: Tailor your prep based on the company's JD and recent trends. For example, during our time, everything somehow looped back to AI--so having at least one AI-anchored use case or understanding really helped. Keep an eye on what's hot in the industry and align your resume or project examples accordingly.

3. Ask Smart, Genuine Questions- Interviews are a two-way street. Asking insightful questions (e.g., about the interviewer's role, company innovation, or tech culture) shows that you're truly interested and not just trying to land a job.

4. Participate in Hackathons--Especially Company-Specific Ones General hackathons help you get comfortable with ideation, teamwork, and presenting under pressure. This will prepare you well for company-specific hackathons, which are more than just coding competitions--they're also a chance to understand the company culture, network with employees, and demonstrate your compatibility.

Tip: Don't be disheartened by rejections. There's always a factor of timing and luck involved, so keep showing up and learning from each experience.

5. Last but Not the Least -- Communication is the Salt- Like salt in food -- unnoticed but essential. You may know everything, but if you can't express it well, it won't land. So practice speaking about your work, projects, and decisions. Give mock interviews. Talk to friends, mentors, and seniors. Record yourself explaining concepts( i personally did this very much to know how i should express). The more you speak, the more confident and structured you'll become. Force yourself to get comfortable with being uncomfortable. That's how you grow.

1. DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet , neetcode

2. SQL: SQL 50 3. OOPS, DBMS, CCN, OS: refer quick one shot and GeeksforGeeks

4. Puzzels: InterviewBit, interviewKickStart , GeeksforGeeks

1. Online Assessment + UBS Campus Hackathon

I had taken part in the UBS Campus Hackathon in April 2025, So as a finalist, I got a direct exemption from the online assessment for campus placements at UBS -- straight to the interview round To get into the hackathon, the first step was clearing an online assessment which in March. It was a 50-minute test with MCQs on Java and core CS subjects like DSA, OOP, DBMS, and OS, along with one coding question. The coding part was varied for each student, like there was a set of 4-5 questions, and anyone could get any one of them. Mine was manageable, and I was able to solve it completely.

From our college, 11 students got shortlisted for the main hackathon round. UBS had made really good arrangements -- from food and logistics to event flow. Teams were randomly formed with 6 members each, and although all of my teammates were from SPIT, we were all complete strangers. It felt a bit awkward at first, but it turned out to be a great experience -- collaborating with new people helped break the ice quickly.

Each team had 3-4 mentors assigned, and they rotated throughout the day. All of them were approachable and gave useful feedback from time to time. One of the mentors took a special

interest in our project , just asking us to explain our part, our thought process, and what our plan was and all.

Our problem statement was about solving the teacher shortage in some rural schools by building a smart platform that connects volunteers with schools and students. It was exciting to work on something with real-world impact and see how tech can be used for social good. The feedback from mentors and UBS professionals helped us refine our ideas and presentation.

If you get the chance to participate, go for it. And if participating, make the most of those interactions, ask questions, share your progress, and take their suggestions seriously. Be open, interact with your team, make the most of mentor sessions, and enjoy the whole experience -- not just the coding part. It's a great mix of learning, networking, and fun. :)

2. Technical Interview [ 20 candidates were shortlisted ]

The technical interview process started around 10 AM, and each interview lasted approximately 45 minutes to 1 hour. My interview went on for about 50 minutes and was conducted by a panel of 2 interviewers. It began with a basic introduction, followed by a resume walkthrough. They went through my achievements and then moved on to my projects. I was asked to explain one of my main projects in detail. The questions that followed included:

● Is it an individual or group project?

● What was your role and contribution?

● How did you come up with the idea?

● Business-oriented questions like:

○ How would you scale the project?

○ Would a subscription model work for your application?

○ Why would a user choose your app?

○ How would you handle randomness in the generated results?

● Tech-specific questions like:

○ Why did you choose this tech stack?

After project-related questions, they gave me a few real-world scenarios. For example:

● "If you're building a loan allocation model, how would you prevent it from being biased based on gender, age, caste, etc.?" This led to a few follow-up questions based on the approach I explained.

● Another scenario: "If you're building an e-commerce platform, what modules would you include? What all aspects would you focus on? And how would you divide the work among a team of three?"

Next, I was asked some technical/conceptual questions:

● Minimum 5 key differences between C, C++, and Java

● Some DevOps-related questions

● Questions on frontend frameworks -- which ones I've worked with, and whether I've used Angular

They also asked a couple of classic puzzle questions to assess logical thinking:

● The 8-ball puzzle (find the heavier ball using minimum weighings)

● A father-child age puzzle (when will the father be thrice the child's age)

At the end, make sure to ask them a few questions as well. It's a good way to show interest and curiosity:

● I asked about their roles at UBS and how their journeys had evolved in the company.

● I also asked about UBS's innovation initiatives, specifically in the areas of blockchain and AI.

3. Technical Interview

I had another round of interview which was more of a techno-behavioral (tech + HR) round. It lasted about 40-45 minutes and this time there was just one interviewer. The round started with a basic introduction, followed by a detailed walkthrough of my resume. Interestingly, the interviewer asked me to narrate my journey as a story -- starting from school up to getting into SPIT. While I shared my story, he interrupted occasionally with questions about the decisions I had made along the way, just to understand my approach and reasoning behind them. He asked me weather I wasfine with relocation or not. Then we discussed one of my notable hackathon wins -- the Smart India Hackathon. He asked:

● What did you build?

● What was the overall journey like?

● What challenges did you faced?

● How many team members were involved?

● What was your specific contribution?

After that, the round became more analytical with a set of 4 puzzle questions:

1. Two candles , each take 1 hour to burn -- how would you use them to measure 45 minutes?- link

2. Bridge puzzle -- 4 people with different speeds, 1 torch, 2-person limit: how to cross with minimum total time?- link

3. Poisoned bottle puzzle -- 1000 bottles, 1 is poisoned, you have 10 test strips: how to find the poisoned one in minimum time? -link

4. 2 eggs, 100-floor building -- from which floor will the egg not break? - link

At the end of the interview, I asked him about his journey to UBS and his current role at the company and How does UBS support internal mobility -- switching teams, locations, or

roles?... it went like a normal discussion where the interviewer shared his complete journey with me.

3. HR Interview [ 10-11 candidates where shortlisted]

My HR round was conducted just five minutes after my second technical interview and was quite simple and fast unlike other HR interview rounds. It was a pleasant surprise when the HR greeted me with a smile, mentioning I was a "known face" , likely because of the interaction during the UBS hackathon. That instantly made the interaction feel more relaxed.

The questions were more of a background check than a deep HR evaluation. She asked:

● Where I stay

● How my technical rounds went and what kind of questions I was asked

● Details about my internships -- what I did, whether they were paid or unpaid

We also spoke briefly about my hackathon experience and how I contributed to the team.

While it may have felt informal, I understand the importance of playing this round carefully. HR rounds often assess not just communication skills, but also culture fit, clarity, and honesty. Keeping a genuine smile, staying confident, and being authentic helped maintain a positive impression throughout.

6 students were offered the role and I was one of them : ).

1. Online Assessment (MCQ Round)

2. Machine Coding Round (Don't be afraid after reading "Machine Coding Round"; see below for what I've written)

3. Interview

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Online Assessment (MCQ Round) [ 92 candidates appeared for this round ]

Platform : HackerEarth Eligibility: CE and CSE (For the 2025 passout batch, EXTC was also eligible, so for 2027, anything could happen.) There was a 7.5+ CGPA criteria to apply. (Just telling in case you don't know -- the college considers CGPA of only 5 semesters till the 6th sem result is out. In our case, from August 8th, they began considering the 6th semester CGPA as well)

There were 21 technical MCQs and 50 mins were given, but 15-20 mins were more than enough to complete everything. Since there was a lot of time, I noted down a few points and some less-known theory questions:

1. In VB-style, -1 is true and 0 is false

2. Output-based question on recursion

3. What is Anonymous FTP

4. What is CORS

5. What is lazy loading

6. How to select an HTML tag using ID

7. Questions based on HTTP status codes - so study all status codes

8. DHCP is an application-level protocol

9. One question was on operator precedence - had to evaluate an expression

10. There was a question asking for the order from bottom to top for elements (terms like relative, absolute, z-index were mentioned)

11. Again, a question on order of console.log() means asking for output which involved Promises and setTimeout - basically question on event loop (Study the event loop in JS - one of the favorite interview questions when it comes to JS)

12. Ping does not use port

13. Valid ping command - remember all octets must be numbers between 0 to 255, other options had URLs so were invalid

14. One SQL question on joins - options had actual SQL queries

A key point: They evaluate not just your MCQ score but also shortlist based on your resume, so ensure it highlights solid development skills.

11 candidates were shortlisted for the next round, but out of those, 2 got oﬀers from Barclays and 2 from IDFC. So ﬁnally only 7 candidates appeared for the next round.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Machine Coding Round [ 7 candidates appeared for this round ] [Oﬄine] [ 2hrs ]

As I mentioned, don't be afraid after reading "Machine Coding Round." It's just a problem statement, and you need to provide a solution. BrowserStack has been using the same problem statement for the last 3-4 years. The problem involves implementing Socket. IO for real-time updates, so make sure you're comfortable with it.

We were called to BrowserStack's oﬃce in Goregaon for the machine coding round and interview.

HR called every selected candidate 2 days before the interview to invite us to their Goregaon oﬃce. On the call, she mentioned there would be 2 rounds: machine coding and then an interview. She also said the machine coding problem statement requires knowledge of Socket. IO and suggested practicing for the machine coding round.

Candidates were divided into batches, with 5 candidates per batch and one mentor per batch. On the same day, there were candidates from other colleges too. I think there were about 12 batches in total. I was in Batch 1 with 5 candidates, all from our college. The other 2 candidates from our college were in Batch 2 with 3 candidates from a diﬀer ent college.

Instructions Provided to Us:

What to bring:

● Personal laptop

● Hard copy of resume

● Government-issued photo ID

Ensure the following setup on your laptop before the interview:

● Compiler/interpreter of your preferred programming language

● IDE/code editor of your choice

● Root/admin access to the system

● Latest version of Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge

We were allowed to use our personal laptops, and Google and GPT were permitted.

Problem Statement:

(You'll ﬁnd it in a GitHub repo too - my solution is linked at the end of this section.)

This problem requires you to implement a log-watching solution (similar to the tail -f command in UNIX). However, the log ﬁle is hosted on a remote machine (same machine as your server code). The log ﬁle is in append-only mode.

You need to implement the following:

● A server-side program to monitor the given log ﬁle and stream updates as they happen using Socket. IO for real-time communication. This will run on the same machine as the log ﬁle. You can use any programming language for the server.

● A web-based client (accessible via a URL like http://localhost/log) that displays updates in the ﬁle in real-time, without requiring a page refresh. The page should load once and keep updating. On initial load, the user should see the last 10 lines of the ﬁle.

Problem Constraints:

● The server must push updates to clients in real-time using Socket. IO.

● The log ﬁle could be several GBs. How do you optimize retrieving the last 10 lines?

● The server should not retransmit the entire ﬁle every time; it should only send updates.

● The server must handle multiple clients simultaneously.

● The web page should not stay in a loading state after the ﬁrst load and should not reload thereafter.

● You may not use oﬀ-the-shelf external libraries or tools to read the ﬁle or provide tail-like functionalities (except Socket. IO for real-time updates).

You'll be evaluated on code quality, testability, modularity, and handling of corner cases.

In this round, you can ask the mentor any doubts. At the end, the mentor will review your solution and test it thoroughly. For me, the mentor asked me to open the URL in two browsers, perform a hard refresh, and test edge cases. He also used a bash script to simulate automatic updates in the text ﬁle, adding \n, \t, and \r characters to check if everything worked correctly.

Tip: Know every single line of your code and why you wrote it, as the mentor will ask about your logic and the reasoning behind speciﬁc lines, especially how you implemented Socket. IO for real-time updates.

After this round, we had lunch at their oﬃce through their catering service. Then, after lunch, they announced the results, and only 3 candidates were selected for the next round.

Sometimes they also ask this PS:

Browser automation without using automation frameworks.pdf

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. Interview Round [ 3 candidates appeared for this round ] [ 50-55 min in my case]

The interviewer was the Director of Engineering. He kicked things off by introducing himself and then asked about my CET, SSC, and HSC scores, and why I chose SPIT. After that, he asked me to give a quick introduction about myself. Then, he asked about my internship experience, specifically what I did during it and what kind of work I handled. I shared details about my role, the tasks I contributed to, and the impact I made, like leading development or solving specific challenges. Once I was done, he explained the interview flow: first, we'd dive into my projects, and then he'd test my problem-solving skills.

He started with, "Tell me about a project where you faced a lot of difficulties and challenges." So, I began explaining one of my projects, and while I was talking, he jumped in with questions. He asked about specific situations where I hit technical roadblocks, how I resolved them, and how I tackled things overall.

Then came the "why" questions:

● Why did I pick Next.js over React.js for my project? (I used Next.js, so I explained my reasoning--stuff like server-side rendering and better SEO.)

● Why SQL over NoSQL? Then, in SQL, why PostgreSQL over MySQL? What was the reason behind these choices?

● What if I had used a NoSQL database for the same project? How would it have impacted things?

After the "why" questions, he dug deeper into scaling and deployment:

● How would I scale up my existing project?

● What factors did I consider when deploying my project?

● How was I monitoring things post-deployment, and why did I choose Vercel for deployment?

● Since I used NeonDB (PostgreSQL), what features did NeonDB provide that helped throughout my project?

After the project discussion, we moved to a DSA question: Daily Temperatures. It's a classic Monotonic Stack problem. He asked me to write proper code on paper and do a dry run with the example he gave. I walked through the solution, explaining the stack logic and how it tracks indices to compute the result.

All three of us landed the offer! 🏆🏎

journey.howSecured:
There were a total of 3 rounds: OA, TECHNICAL-1, HR/TECHNO-HR

1. OA Round [135 Candidates Appeared]

The eligibility criteria mentioned was 7+ CGPA, but in reality, only those with 7.5+ were shortlisted.

The OA round [106 marks] had 3 sections:

Section 1: MCQs [46 Marks]

The MCQs were of medium to hard level, and covered topics like Java, OOP, SQL, a few pseudocodes, and C++/C snippets too. Make sure you know OOP, SQL, and Java inside out if you want to crack Barclays. Try to strengthen your core subjects in the 2nd year itself, and practice MCQs in your 6th sem.

Section 2: Coding Question

The coding question was the same as last year, so there's a good chance they'll repeat it next year too.

Link to the question: Leetcode Discuss - String Generation OA Question

The solution on Leetcode is very lengthy and not intuitive (uses DP + KMP).

Here's the greedy solution I used (passes all test cases):

class Solution {

public String generateString(String str1, String str2) { int n = str1.length(), m = str2.length(); int sz = n + m - 1; char[] ans = new char[sz]; boolean[] mod = new boolean[sz]; java.util. Arrays.fill(mod, true);

// 1. Satisfy all 'T' positions for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { if (str1.charAt(i) == 'T') { for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) { int pos = i + j; if (ans[pos] != 0 && ans[pos] != str2.charAt(j)) return ""; ans[pos] = str2.charAt(j); mod[pos] = false; } } }

// 2. Fill unassigned positions with 'a' for (int i = 0; i < sz; ++i) { if (ans[i] == 0) ans[i] = 'a'; }

// 3. Enforce 'F' positions for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { if (str1.charAt(i) == 'F') { if (matches(ans, i, str2)) { int change = -1; for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) { int pos = i + j; if (pos < sz && mod[pos]) change = pos; } if (change < 0) return ""; ans[change] = 'b'; mod[change] = false; } }

}

return new String(ans); }

private boolean matches(char[] ans, int i, String s2) { if (i + s2.length() > ans.length) return false; for (int j = 0; j < s2.length(); ++j) { if (ans[i + j] != s2.charAt(j)) return false; } return true; } }

If you want to practice or run your own approach, you can try it here: Lexicographically Smallest Generated String - Leetcode

Section 3: SQL Query

I got a very easy SQL query based on basic filtering using WHERE and AND. Some people got slightly trickier ones - for example, extracting a month from a date.

2. Technical Round [37 Candidates Appeared]

This round varied for everyone - some were asked core subject questions, some were asked about their resumes (VERY IMPORTANT: know your resume inside-out), and others were asked system design basics. Barclays focuses more on "WHY" than just "HOW."

For me, I was asked a DSA question, a puzzle, a system design question, and a SQL query.

● Introduction: I introduced myself and mentioned that I enjoy solving DSA on Leetcode and building projects that solve real-world problems. (He wrote this down - probably why he asked me DSA and Design questions).

● DSA Question: He asked me to help sort an array using Merge Sort. I explained the recursion tree, merging logic, why Merge Sort is better than other algorithms, and its time complexity. Then I wrote the code, explained it line by line, and did a dry run with 2-3 examples.

● IDE & Debugging: He asked if I'd used IntelliJ. I said I used to but switched to VSCode since it's better for Dev too. Then he asked how I debug code - I explained all my approaches: using the VSCode debugger, adding print statements, and dry-running edge cases.

● Puzzle Question: Q: Cut a cake into 8 equal parts with 3 cuts. Ans: Two vertical cuts through the center → 4 slices. One horizontal cut across all → 8 slices. (Think 3D!)

● Design Question: Design a Railway Management System. At first, I misunderstood and started with schema design. Then I asked for a hint - he asked questions like: "How to assign platforms?", "How to prevent collisions?", etc. I gave solutions for each.

● SQL Query: Q: Return departments with more than 15 employees. Ans: Simple LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, and HAVING COUNT(*) > 15.

Tip from this round: Try to think in your head first, structure your answer, and then speak. (I asked for feedback and this is what he told me LOL). But never stay quiet for too long. If you need time, ask for a moment, and speak out your thoughts. Start with what you know and go step-by-step toward optimization.

3. HR / Techno-HR Round [21 Candidates Appeared]

Some had a Techno-HR round, others had just HR. For me, it was purely HR.

● Basic HR questions: Tell me about yourself, why Barclays, etc.

● A lot of behavioral questions - try to align your answers with RISES values of Barclays.

16 Students were offered the job, and 3 were waitlisted.

journey.prep:
1. Craft a solid self-introduction -- it's your first impression, so make it count.

2. Take notes during the pre-placement talk -- they can help you frame personalized questions during the interviews.

3. Practice a backend framework like Django or Express -- learn to set up a server, design schemas, and build basic APIs beforehand. I had done a Django course on Udemy - Django Masterclass : Build 9 Real World Django Projects

4. I personally did Neetcode 150, then practiced LeetCode daily and previous contest questions. Focus on mastering fundamentals and recognizing patterns, not chasing streaks or ratings. You can also do Striver's A2Z DSA sheet.

5. Use Indiabix and GFG to revise fundamentals of DBMS, OS, OOPs and CCN. DBMS is the main priority, as the interviews revolved around being able to apply the concepts you learned in DBMS. Just some basic knowledge of OS, OOPS and CCN was required for the rapid fire round.

6. LeetCode's Top 50 SQL Questions are more than enough to get a strong grip on SQL basics and variations.

7. Don't panic in interviews -- it's okay to ask for help; interviewers are usually very supportive. Think aloud throughout each interview -- it helps the interviewer follow your approach and gives them a chance to guide you if needed.

Feel free to contact me on LinkedIN - https://www.linkedin.com/in/manankher/
journey.howSecured:
There were 5 rounds in total, all conducted in a single day. Try to prepare yourself on API development, either Django or NodeJS/ExpressJS. Also practice SQL queries from SQL 50, and learn the basics of designing schemas. Also, all the interviews were conducted online, and we had to sit in the panel room allocated to us, and join the interview meet link on our laptop.

Resume Shortlisting: Shortlisting was done based on the resumes that we had submitted on Superset when we applied to WorkIndia. Also, while applying, in the form they had asked whether I had plans to go for Masters later on. To this, I said NO. For the resume, follow the format of Jake's resume, and try to keep it 1 page. Properly include your experience, projects and skills, and make sure you can speak about anything that you put in your resume.

Jake's Resume Format

MananKher__Resume.pdf

1. Rapid Fire Round [ 72 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was the first round, and we were all asked to arrive by 8:25 am, and were asked to assemble in 103 by 8:50 am. We thought that we would first receive instructions on how the rapid fire round would be like. But at 9 am sharp, we all receive an email, containing a google form link, and one of the WorkIndia coordinators comes into the room, and tells us to start the test immediately, and that the form will stop taking submissions after 9:15 am. So make sure you have your wifi and laptop battery charging setup. Luckily I was already connected to the wifi and had my laptop charged, so I was able to start the test immediately.

It was an MCQ test which contained basic technical questions on Java, Python and C++, like answering the time complexity, space complexity and output of code snippets. Some questions on basic OS and CCN like deadlocks and DNS, some github commands like listing all branches, stash and pop. Some questions on prefix and postfix increment operators, and some basic data structure questions like which data structure is LIFO, FIFO. The objective is to answer as many questions as you can within 15 min. It contained around 40 to 50 questions. I was able to answer all of them, some with a little uncertainty, and submit.

2. Debugging Round [ 46 candidates appeared for this round ]

For this round, we had to join the meet link on our laptop. The interviewer then asked whether I prefer Django or NodeJs. I chose Django. Then he sent a link to a small existing django codebase containing an Attendance Tracker project, with a README file containing instructions on what was to be performed. Initially, while starting the server, there were 2 bugs that were required to be fixed.

One bug was in the models.py, a syntax error in the choices parameter passed to a models. CharField.

Expected syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices=[('active', 'Status active'), ('inactive', 'Status inactive')]) Given syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices=['active', 'inactive'])

The second bug was in the views.py, another syntax error in which the key of a python dictionary was being accessed incorrectly.

Expected syntax: [s["name"] for s in students] Given syntax: [s.name for s in students]

After fixing the errors, I started the server. The server was running now. After this, I was asked to implement an API endpoint to mark a student's attendance. For this, I was initially adding an attendance field in the existing Student table. But the interviewer asked me for a better way. So I made a separate table, Attendance, which can contain the student_id as foreign key and a date field, to store when the attendance was marked. Then, there was another constraint that a student cannot mark attendance again on the same date. For this, I used the unique_together model option within a Meta class to make the composite field (student_id, date) unique. The interviewer was happy with this. Then I started implementing the API endpoint, and wrote the url and the handler function. But time was running short, so the interviewer just asked to write a comment inside the handler function on how I would implement the endpoint.

Throughout the round (around 45 min), I kept telling the interviewer my thoughts and the steps I am taking. Also, googling and using stack overflow was allowed, but no LLMs. The interviewer will judge you based on your knowledge of the programming language, the backend framework, and most importantly your ability to ask the right questions and google them, and find out the answers. I had googled the syntax for using choices parameter, the syntax for implementing the unique together and also the date field.

3. DSA Round [ 15 candidates appeared for this round ]

The DSA Round was also conducted in online interview form, and we had to write code on google docs. The questions were of leetcode easy and medium difficulty. The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself. Make sure you have a proper introduction ready, which briefly covers your education, your internship experience and high impact projects. Also, create an introduction which aligns with the company's principles.

First question: You are given a positive integer N. Find X such that the sum from 1 to X-1 equals the sum from X+1 to N. For this, I first suggested the brute force algorithm of iterating through all elements from 1 to N, then for each element, running 2 for loops to calculate the 1-X-1 and X+1-N sum, giving a O(n^2) TC. I then optimized it by suggesting a prefix sum approach. First, we calc the total sum using the sum of n natural numbers formula, and then iterate from 1 to N, calc prefix sum, and subtract from total sum. So whenever left and right sum become equal, we return that element X. I wrote this code, then the interviewer then told me to optimize it further. So I suggested a binary search approach, and conditions would be if leftSum>rightSum, e=mid-1 and if leftSum<rightSum, s=mid+1, else return mid. Also, I was asked to optimize space complexity as well, so I used the same formula to calculate leftSum (1 to X-1 sum), instead of prefix array. I wrote this code, then the interviewer asked to optimize it even further. I took some time, but thought that if I want to optimize from O(logn), there must be a direct formula. Thats when it clicked me, that I can write an equation, and solve it for X.

leftSum = rightSum (x-1)x/2 = totalSum - leftSum - x (x-1)x/2 = n(n+1)/2 - (x-1)x/2 - x (x-1)x = n(n+1)/2 - x x^2 - x = n(n+1)/2 - x x^2 = n(n+1)/2 X = sqrt(n(n+1)/2)

The interviewer then asked, what does this signify. I said that X will be the sqrt of sum of the n natural numbers. He was happy with this, and explained me that for a solution to exist, the sum of the n natural numbers must be a perfect square.

Second Question: https://leetcode.com/problems/majority-element/description/ I first suggested a brute force approach by creating a hashmap (dictionary in python) and storing the frequency of all elements. Then iterating through the hashmap, and returning the element whose frequency is greater than n/2.

The optimal approach with constant space complexity is Moore's Voting Algorithm. Majority Element - Leetcode 169 - Python

During the DSA round, I was asked why I preferred using Python. I explained that I initially used C++ and had solved around 150 questions on LeetCode in it. But later, I switched to Python because its simpler syntax allowed me to focus more on understanding the logic behind each problem, rather than the boilerplate code. This helped me improve my problem-solving skills more effectively.

Tip: If you switch languages for DSA, be clear about your reason, it's not about which language is "better", but what helps you learn and think better.

Third Question: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/find-a-repeating-and-a-missing-number/ For this, I was only able to suggest the approach with the frequency array / hashmap. The interviewer wanted me to optimize the space complexity. I started thinking in terms of slow and fast pointer, but on dry running, that approach didn't work. Then the interviewer gave me a hint that I can modify the array in-place. I started thinking along those lines, maybe swapping the numbers. But time was up, and I

wasn't able to optimize it. The interviewer then asked me if I had any questions. I asked them about the various microservices they have built, and what different architectures they have used, along with the methodology they take while deciding the appropriate architecture for these services.

Finally, after receiving the answer, I thanked every person on the call, by their first name.

At this point, I felt I might not get selected for the next round, since I couldn't come up with the most optimal solution for the third question. Still, I kept my hopes up and didn't give up. I began preparing for the next round anyway, asking ChatGPT to help me build schemas for applications like a job recruitment platform.

After quite some time, I finally received the link for the next round! The waiting period can be really nerve-wracking, but it's important to stay calm and think positively. Don't be disheartened if your interview doesn't go as expected, it's never truly over until the list of shortlisted candidates for the next round is out.

Bonus Question (asked to one of my friends): https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-size-subarray-sum/description/ A further variation of this was asked, by allowing negative integers to exist in the array.

4. Schema Design Round [ 7 candidates appeared for this round ]

In this round, I was given a problem statement of an Ecommerce Platform on google docs, along with its various requirements. Also, 2 bonus requirements were given of implementing coupons for orders, and a referral system. Initially, I focused on the main requirements, and identified the main entities from them. I wrote down the table names. Then I started building the relations between these tables, with the help of foreign keys, along with the necessary attributes for each of them. While building the schema, I made sure to obey the normal forms like 1NF and mentioned these terms while making the schema. Make sure that you keep properly explaining the interviewer your thought process behind each and every step, and also make sure to ask doubts on things that might not be clear in the problem statement. I had asked some questions, like should I also focus on the merchant's side, or only on the customer's side, and difference between inventory and warehouse, as it was not very clear from the problem statement. Explain the cardinality of each relationship you are creating (one-one, one-many, many-many).

After creating a rough schema, the interviewer then identified certain areas that could be improved, normalized further. I listened thoroughly and made these changes, and explained how this approach would be more effective in preventing data redundancy. I was then asked to write 2 SQL queries on the schema I had built. This included finding the delivery times of the recent orders, along with their delivery locations. I used JOIN, ORDER BY, LIMIT, DATEDIFF function for subtracting the placed_at from the delivered_at. Then I was asked to find the average delivery time, for which I used the aggregate function.

As I had time remaining, I also went ahead and implemented the bonus requirements. The referral table would be a unary, many-many relationship, and contains referred_by and referred_to (both foreign keys to User table)

Finally, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. I asked him what his first six months at WorkIndia were like. He mentioned that he had joined recently, and that while the initial weeks can be hectic, things become smoother as you get familiar with the processes.

I shared my own experience from an internship at a startup, where the first couple of weeks were also hectic for me, since I was learning a new tech stack while working on live features. But once I got used to the codebase, I was able to contribute meaningfully and build exciting features. That sense of solving real-world problems was deeply satisfying. The interviewer appreciated this and mentioned that I would be a good fit for a startup like WorkIndia.

I would advise learning CTEs while solving SQL 50, because they are a powerful way of dividing your SQL query into manageable and easy-to-understand sequential steps.

5. Culture Round [ 4 candidates appeared for this round ]

The culture round felt more like a meaningful conversation than an interview. The interviewer was very friendly, and there's truly no need to be nervous. We spoke about my journey, passions, values, and experiences. It was a heart-to-heart.

The questions covered:

● What got you into this field? Why engineering and not any other role?

● Tell me about your journey so far, your internship, and what you learned from your peers.

● Lowest point in your life and academics.

● Your family, your interests, your short- and long-term goals.

● What do you consider as "good work"?

I answered honestly, sharing how I got into tech through PC gaming and modding, inspired by my grandfather's tech-savviness. I spoke about learning QBasic in school, then Java, and how my love for coding naturally led me to engineering, where I could solve real-world problems and innovate.

I reflected on my regret of not joining any committee in first year, which limited my exposure, but after second year, I made it a point to step out of my comfort zone: applying for internships, connecting with people on LinkedIn, and seeking out opportunities.

I also shared my internship experience, the meaningful features I built, and how much I learned from my mentors and colleagues. I opened up about my family's support, and my goal to help them by becoming financially independent and making them proud.

When asked about what "good work" means to me, I shared how participating in hackathons changed my perspective. Earlier, good work meant building something cool solo using a new tech. But through hackathons, I realized that true good work is about team collaboration, communication, and building something together that no one could have done alone. It's about leveraging each person's strengths, validating each step as a team, and delivering something meaningful as one unit.

Finally, I asked the interviewer:

● How did WorkIndia start, and what impact were you hoping to create?

● How do you deal with scam jobs on the platform?

● From the core values in the WorkIndia PPT, which one do you consider most important?

It was a genuine and fulfilling conversation where I could truly be myself.

Tip: Don't prepare scripted answers. Reflect on your journey, speak from the heart, and be honest. This round isn't about checking boxes, it's about understanding who you are and what drives you. Also, have a good idea about the companies that you have interned at. The interviewer might ask certain questions like when was the company founded, or how old was your mentor in the company, not to grill you, but to verify authenticity and see how well you know your own experiences. Be honest, and don't try to bluff. It's totally okay to say "I'm not sure" rather than guess.

2 students were offered the role. It was a long day, and the results weren't announced immediately. They got announced after we went back home.

This was the second time Lombard visited the campus.

There were 4 rounds for this process. It was announced that the recruitment process would include:

1. Online Assessment (OA).

2. 2 Technical Interviews.

3. HR Interview

1. Aptitude and Technical Test [90 mins]:

The first round was a comprehensive test that included aptitude, technical multiple-choice questions (MCQs), and coding. It was divided into 7 sections, and the total duration was 90 minutes. The first section was a coding question (DP) which was to be completed in 30 minutes. The other 6 sections were MCQ questions. The aptitude section was timed and non-navigable, meaning you can navigate between questions but once you exited this section, you couldn't return to it.

The remaining 6 sections covered topics like Database Management Systems (DBMS), Data Structures (DS), Computer Networks (CN), Object Oriented Programming (OOPS), Operating System (OS) and Aptitude.

2. Technical Interview 1 [50-60 mins]:

This round was one of the main rounds of the interview process, lasting approximately 40-45 minutes. It primarily focused on my resume, core technical knowledge, and problem-solving approach.

a. Introduction & Resume Discussion

The interview began with a brief self-introduction, followed by an in-depth discussion of my resume. The interviewers focused on a project where I had implemented multi AI-agents. I was asked questions related to:

● What AI agents are

● Their implementation

● Their working mechanism

● The overall architecture and design decisions

b. System Architecture, AWS, Docker & Kafka

Since AWS, Kafka, and Docker were mentioned in one of my projects, the interviewers explored these topics in detail.

● I was asked to explain the complete architecture of the project.

● One of the interviewers then asked me to list and explain the AWS S3 and Docker commands I was familiar with.

● I was asked about the working of AWS Glue and AWS Athena, including how they are used for data crawling and querying.

● I was asked whether MongoDB can be set up using Docker, to which I answered yes.

● Following this, I was asked to explain all the commands required to set up MongoDB from scratch inside a Docker container, including container creation and configuration.

c. Authentication & Security (JWT)

The discussion then moved to authentication concepts, specifically:

● What is JWT?

● Access Tokens and Refresh Token

● Edge cases related to access and refresh token handling

● Differences between JWT-based authentication and session-based authentication

d. Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS)

Next, I was asked questions related to OOPS fundamentals, including:

● The four pillars of OOPS

● SOLID principles

● Inheritance and its different types

e. SQL & Database Concepts

The interviewers then covered basic SQL concepts, which included:

● Types of joins in SQL

● ACID properties

● Order of execution in SQL queries

● Writing a SQL query to filter duplicate rows from a table

f. Overall Experience

Overall, this was a relatively easy and well-structured round. The key takeaway is to:

● Be confident while explaining your projects and technical concepts

● Stay calm during problem-solving

● Clearly communicate your thought process, as the interviewers were more interested in understanding how I approach problems rather than just the final answer

3. Technical Round 2 [15-20 mins]:

a. Project Discussion

This was the easiest interview. The interviewer asked me to choose any one project that would impress him with my skills and explain it thoroughly. Then he asked follow-up questions on that, which also included a few questions on the tech stack mentioned for each project.

b. Internship & Achievements

He then moved on to the Internship section and Achievements. He asked about hackathons, including which project I made in which hackathon, what problems I faced, and how I tackled them.

For this round, you must have to know each and every feature of the project that you have mentioned, along with the tech stack you have mentioned.

4. HR Round [10-15 mins]:

The final round was a 10-15 minute interview. Make sure you are well prepared for generic HR questions.

The interviewer started with questions such as:

● Where do I belong from

● Where do I currently stay

● How many family members I have and what they do

● Why I am interested in an insurance firm

He then picked one of my projects and asked me to consider a scenario where users are ghosting the platform and how I would expand the business across geographies.

It was more of a conversation-based round aimed at assessing my mindset, thought process, and long-term goals.

5 students were offered the role and I was one of them !!!

1. Resume Shortlisting

1. Resume Shortlisting [ Everybody above 6 CGPA applied ]

Applications opened on Superset on 1st September with a minimum eligibility criteria of 6 CGPA. However, during the shortlisting stage, only students with 7.5 CGPA and above were considered. Resume shortlisting was done based on keywords in the resume, required skills, or possibly relevant internships and projects. After this round, 13 students were shortlisted, and the list was announced on 8th September.

Pre-Placement Talk -

The PPT was conducted just before the interviews on 10th September by TransBnk's CTO and HR. They explained about the company--how they started, what motivated them, their current situation, and the type of candidates they were looking for. They also gave us an overview of the company's complete workflow.

I am specifically mentioning this round because attending PPTs and interacting with the presenters can really help during interviews. This worked for me too--I asked a few questions during the PPT based on the homework I had done about the company beforehand. This showed my genuine interest, and they answered my questions in detail. Then we were introduced to the two panelists who would conduct the technical interviews--both were senior developers at the company.

2. Technical Interview [ 13 students appeared ]

The first panelist started the interview by asking me for my introduction. He then went into detail about my internships and asked me to explain my projects. I explained all my projects thoroughly. After that, he went through the skills section of my resume and asked whether I had learned those skills through my college curriculum. I clarified that I had self-studied most of them.

He then noticed the extracurricular skills mentioned in my resume and seemed curious, so we had a short discussion about them for about a minute. After this, he began asking technical questions based on my resume and projects. He asked me about JWT, its working, and format, which I explained in detail. He also asked the difference between JWT and Session, along with some follow-up questions. Later, he moved on to questions about Java, including multithreading, its types, and working. Since one of my projects involved AWS, he asked me to explain AWS, its services, use cases, and overall working. Finally, he said, "That's all from my side," and handed it over to the second panelist.

The second panelist gave me a problem on paper: Missing and Repeating Number I directly explained my optimal approach based on equations and then wrote pseudo code on paper. He was satisfied with my explanation.

Next, he gave me a slightly tricky problem: "How would you sort a file containing numbers of size 8GB when you only have 6GB RAM?" He asked me to sit in another cabin and solve it while he interviewed the next candidate. I wrote down multiple approaches (not code, just logic) and then went back to explain them. My approaches included swap memory, virtual memory, and an external merge sort-based approach. They seemed satisfied with my answers.

This round lasted for about 25-30 minutes.

3. HR Interview [ 6 students appeared ]

After almost 2 hours of waiting and the lunch break, I was called for the HR interview. There was one panelist, the same person who had presented the PPT and was the HR representative of the company.

The interview began with my introduction, followed by an overview of my projects and internships. He then asked about my internships in detail. The discussion moved on to my interests, future goals, 5-year and 10-year plans, and whether I had any plans for pursuing a master's degree. I explained my reasons clearly.

He then grilled me for a while on one question: "Would you start your own venture if you had the right resources and people?" After that, he asked why I chose engineering and why I pursued a diploma instead of HSC. He also asked me to share something that wasn't mentioned on my resume.

Towards the end, he said, "That's all from my side," and asked if I had any questions. I asked him a couple of questions about the company, which he answered in detail. I also gave some inputs in between, showing that I had done my homework about the company. He even recalled the question I had asked during the PPT. The interview concluded after about 20 minutes.

The results were announced after all interviews were completed. They played a small prank on us by calling four of us into a cabin and saying they had only three vacancies, asking who would back off. After a tense moment, they revealed they were just kidding and offered jobs to all four of us. 🎊

Round 1: Online Aptitude Test

Approximately 150-160 students participated in this on-campus round. The test was divided into four sections with a marking scheme of +1 for a correct answer and a penalty of -0.25 for an incorrect one.

● Java (18 Questions): This section focused on fundamental concepts, including output-based questions, threads, Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs), and the Stream API.

● Python (17 Questions): Similar to the Java section, it covered basic Python principles like slicing and OOPs concepts.

● SQL (5 Questions): This part involved basic SQL queries where I had to select the correct query for given table structures from multiple-choice options.

● Quantitative Aptitude (30 Questions): This section featured a wide range of topics, including questions on stocks, simple and compound interest, speed of a boat, probability, and permutation and combination.

Round 2: Technical Interview

Forty-five candidates were shortlisted for the technical round. My interview, which lasted about 15-20 minutes , began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself. Following my introduction, I was asked to explain one of my projects in detail.

Key discussion points included:

● Java Collections Framework: I was asked, "What do you know about the Collection framework?". I confidently answered that the framework consists of interfaces like List, Map, Set, and Queue, and classes such as ArrayList and LinkedList. When asked about the hierarchy of the framework, I replied that I didn't remember it completely.

● Code Explanation: The interviewer presented a code snippet from the aptitude test related to encapsulation and asked me to explain its functionality and output. I explained how the code worked and what the result would be.

● Object-Oriented Concepts: As a follow-up, I was asked how I would initialize a variable without using a setter method. I answered that I would use a constructor. I was then asked how to make the class immutable. I explained that I would make all variables private and final, remove the setter methods, initialize variables only through the constructor, and make the class final so it could not be extended. The interviewer questioned if I was sure about making the class final, and I confidently confirmed that it is necessary for immutability.

● Data Structures: I was then asked to explain the output of a code snippet from the aptitude test that used a Map and a List. I had to describe what the output would be if I used a HashMap, HashSet, TreeSet, and LinkedHashSet for a specific input.

It was noted that the interviewer for my panel conducted interviews quite swiftly, with some lasting only 10 minutes.

Round 3: HR Interview

Fifteen candidates advanced to the final HR round. The panel consisted of the company's HR representative and the Managing Director of the Mumbai office. My interview lasted for about 30 minutes and covered the following areas:

● Introductions and Background: The HR representative asked if I knew who they were, and I replied that I unfortunately did not. They mentioned they had presented at the pre-placement talk, and I explained that I had to attend the session while traveling due to lectures, which they understood. They then introduced themselves. I was then asked to introduce myself and detail my educational journey starting from my 10th-grade school.

● Personal Details: I was asked where I reside, how many members are in my family, and if I was aware that the company was located in Goregaon and how I would travel to the office.

● Project Discussion: The HR representative asked about my project, what I liked about it, and what parts were difficult to implement. Later, the MD asked me in detail about all the technologies I was comfortable with and went through my projects in fine detail.

● Career Aspirations: The HR representative asked me what kind of role I was looking for, specifying backend, frontend, or something else. I replied that I was flexible, eager to learn new technologies, and didn't mind working in any role.

Following the interview, I was told that I could leave and that the results would be shared with the TPO at the end of the day.

Useful Tips:

*Practice DSA properly ,Even Though I was not Asked to code anything I was well prepared for DSA questions.

*Be Thorough with the Basics of the Courses you have mentioned in your resume.

*Be Thorough with your projects.

All the best for Placements !!

He then asked me to explain each project listed on my resume and the motivation behind them. I explained why I chose each project. I gave an overview of the features, frameworks/languages used, and the event flow for each project.

He also asked in-depth questions about the keywords in my project section, like APIs and machine learning models. He asked, "What are APIs?", "What are API response codes?", "What is an API token and why is it important?", and "Have you built an API?" For the college recommendation app I worked on, I explained the ML model, even though it was handled by another team member, emphasizing the need to fully understand all aspects of a project.

The interviewer pointed out flaws in my projects, and I explained my approach to fix them and why the issues occurred. For example, in a 24-hour hackathon, time constraints prevented full implementation. He also asked how Iwould implement security layers in each project.

We discussed the Flutter framework and Firebase. He asked if I had experience with NoSQL databases, to which I responded that Firebase Realtime Database is a NoSQL database. When asked about AWS and Kafka, I admitted I had read about them but didn't have in-depth knowledge.

Lastly, he presented a scenario: if a transaction occurred in Mumbai at 11:20, followed by another in Pune 20 minutes later, how would I detect fraud? I acknowledged that Iwasn't sure of the exact technology to use, but my approach would involve calculating the time difference and distance between the two locations to determine ifthe transaction was possible.

Questions in Logical reasoning were easy, although some were lengthy. As the question paper has no negative marking, I would suggest applicants to blind attempt the unattempted at the last minute for any additional stroke of luck. Logical reasoning had questions like blood relations, ordering between people, solving a set of instructions to get output, pattern detection etc. English was fairly easy, mainly with sentence ordering, and grammar correction type questions. Vocabulary was easy as well. For computer, CCN and OS, algorithm types questions were asked. Half were easy to recall, some were more difficult. A standard algo question would ask which mcq fits the missing part of algo, etc. DSA questions were easy, basically a dry run of how the mentioned data structure would look like at the end if a given set of inputs were fed into it. One important topic that had 5+ questions was the different topologies and technologies in computer networks (router, hub, switch, mesh topology, etc.) Students are recommended to learn their individual functions and advantages. 2. Technical Interview [ 18 candidates were shortlisted for this round ] --- PAGE 2 --- My tech interview went for 45 minutes-1 hour, and every aspect of my resume was asked, and they also put some HR questions in between. I was asked really basic questions like reversing a number or finding if the string was a palindrome. I was asked about the theory of individual data structures and their real life applications. In DBMS, they asked to explain ACID properties, especially atomicity, and the difference between SQL and NoSQL. They drew a table and asked me 2 queries for such. I remembered the logic but not the syntax, so they allowed me to explain the logic to them. I was also given another table and asked how it could be simplified (basically normalization). From my projects listed, I was asked the flow, the planning and asked to explain about the project and technologies in depth. Based on my committee and project experience, I was asked about conflict resolution, how I mediated issues, leadership examples, etc. Some panels would ask my peers on the sections (DSA, dev, etc) they were most comfortable with, while mine asked for everything.
