The process was as follows:

Online Assessment Based on Python, C++, Easy/Medium DSA

Technical Round C++/Python in depth, Medium DSA, Probability Stats

HR Round Standard HR questions

This is going to be a long one.

1. [Round 1 - Online Assessment] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round: 60-70 ]

The OA consisted of 5 sections and was conducted on Imocha safe assessment browser:

● C++ MCQs

● Python MCQs (mainly NumPy and statistics-based)

● Aptitude MCQs (standard, mostly easy)

● Python coding

● C++ coding

The coding questions were DSA/implementation based. Some candidates received harder problems, but mine were very straightforward.

Python coding question: You are given transaction data with categories and amounts. The task was to compute the total amount spent per category and print it as a float. Essentially, maintain a dictionary with category -> total amount.

C++ coding question: Given an integer k and an array, compute the running average over the last k elements. Example:

arr = [100, 200, 300, 400], k = 3 i = 0: 100 / 1 = 100 i = 1: (100+200) / 2 = 150 i = 2: (100+200+300) / 3 = 200 i = 3: (200+300+400) / 3 = 300

I don't remember the mcq questions well, but knowing intermediate c++ and python helped me. Also python mcqs were mostly around statistics and numpy functions like cumulative sum, median, etc.

The OA was in a very unexpected format and since the languages to use were so limited, many people gave up halfway in the test. (Also quite a few for being flagged as cheating)

My OA round, unlike everyone, was very eventful. Initially, I did not have access to a Windows laptop, which was required for the test, so I had given up hopes of even trying for the OA, but fortunately, my friend Asim helped me at the last moment. The OA program crashed midway (saying that I'm sus) and I had to wait till I got a fresh new link. The HR and support team were really very nice that they helped me and also arranged the new test (I was able to prove my innocence). I gave the OA after everyone finished and they stayed with me for invigilation as well. I hurriedly finished the OA and in the hurry, I wasn't able to think logically and thus, I couldn't solve the c++ dsa question. Again I had no expectations that I would even make it into the interviews.

2. [Round 2 - Technical] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round: 9 ]

My panel was conducting 1-1.2 hrs of interviews, mostly focused around c++ (in depth), medium/hard dsa, and probability statistics. My interview was by far the longest i.e. 2 hrs. It started with my introduction, surprisingly they weren't as interested in my projects and internship and only inquired basic information on it while also asking whether they are in c++ or not.

They then asked me if I am confident in c++ or python, choosing c++ he asked me what's the difference between struct and a class. He also asked me what's the difference between c and c++, I answered having objects, to which he responded that we can make objects in c too (he's right about it technically speaking). Then they asked me what I know about oops in c++. I answered with 4 pillars of oops. Then he asked me which one I know the best, I answered polymorphism and explained runtime and compile time polymorphism, with code examples and also how compiler evaluates them (the compile stage and how runtime is evaluated with vptrs and vtable, I didn't go much deep in this to the function pointers but he was satisfied with my explanation). After that he asked me about the second best oops pillar that I know of, I answered with encapsulation and explained intuitively with real life examples and had to write code for the same.

Then he asked me about my favourite topic in c++, to which I answered templates and then I explained how the compiler evaluates templates (in the compile time itself). Then we discussed about how and when std::vector resizes, how can we check when the vector resizes. I answered that we can check resizing by seeing the operation time consumed. He said that it may be possible that the CPU is too fast and we can't even measure the difference. Then he answered it for me, saying that the address of the vector changes. Hearing this, it clicked to me so I explained it further that

resizing is done by creating a new vector of double the "capacity" and then the elements are copied into the new vector. He then also asked me about size vs capacity in this context and asked whether I can implement it. After which he asked me the difference between std::array and std::vector.

The conversation then moved on to memory management, starting with the difference between "malloc" and "new" keywords in c++ (new just calls the destructor of the class automatically). Then I was told to write some code about runtime polymorphism using the malloc keyword, it was basically creating class pointers and showing runtime polymorphism with it. (I was used to using new instead but the interviewer kindly gave me a hint that it needs typecasting when used with malloc). Then I also explained about upcasting and downcasting using Class pointers.

After which he asked me why even bother using heap memory? I answered that we can use it for storing large objects, to which he replied that if I have lots of memory it won't be a problem. Then I said that we can use it for dynamically allocating memory at runtime, when we don't know the size of the object at compile time. To which he confirmed that I am correct and added that heap memory is much faster (I think he meant it is faster for larger objects). I also explained about the need for destructors citing examples of sockets and files.

He asked me if I knew anything else in c++, so I answered with smart pointers, after which he asked me about why they are used. Then he asked me whether I know about mutexes and locks, after hearing a yes, he asked me what is a spin lock? I couldn't answer it. Next, he also had a question which I found tricky because I didn't understand the question well enough. He asked me whether some memory allocated in the constructor for a non member of the class, then when do we release it.. I was assuming he is talking about a stack memory variable, but he meant heap one. The answer was to deallocate it in the constructor itself.

Then he moved on to asking if I know about any other core subjects. Judging from the first part of the interview, I felt that saying any topic which I don't know absolutely 100% would be a disaster. So I answered with OS CPU scheduling and deadlocks. After explaining that, he asked me whether I knew about TCP/UDP (which was written in the JD requirements btw) and which core subject it belonged to. He asked me difference in TCP, UDP and an example where to use them.

Then they came to dsa questions which I honestly didn't do well, first they started with standard min stack question, given a stack, create a getMin with O(1) complexity. I initially forgot the two stack approach code so I gave them a single stack of pair<int, int> where pair.first is the element and pair.second is the minimum till now. He acknowledged the solution was correct but he specified that I cant change the data type of the stack. then I told him about the two stacks approach, to which he replied that it is taking too much space complexity, finally after 15 mins of me struggling he told me the answer that we can instead store pseudo elements in the stack (I saw this approach at neetcode.io/solutions/min-stack but I forgot it during the interview).

Then he gave me a detect cycle in linkedlist, which as well I forgot the iteration condition, and then figured out after some time, communicating entire thoughts continuously is a must. Then he asked me to also find the node starting the cycle while pointing out possible segmentation fault in my code in three places. The last dsa question I was asked was find the missing element. After listening to this I felt very relaxed because it's an easy question. I answered with xor of array method, to which he nodded. Then he asked me about another approach, he said let's say if it's sorted, what

now? I was a bit stumbled so I answered binary search without thinking. He clarified I was wrong. He then said me that it needs to be faster. I assumed he meant faster than O(n), and I went ahead scratching my head for another 5 minutes. I answered that all I can think of is Sum of natural numbers formula. He said it's in the right direction. But I kept on thinking that he wanted O(logn) or O(1) solution. He clarified this miscommunication and then I wrote the code for it using std::accumulate method, to which he asked what's the complexity of that method.

Later the second panelist started by asking if I had done probability and statistics during my course. He started with linear regression, asked me about it, and then gave me some data to perform it and evaluate it.. I said I dont recall the formula. He then asked me about uniform distribution, to which I answered slightly correctly. I explained my thinking with examples. I also explained about PMF and PDFs (in general what they are). After which he looked over my projects, one with ML catched his attention which was "DsaBuddy", he asked for explanation on what I did in it. It was a Random Forst model predicting next dsa problem to give to a person to learn, I told him about features used. He asked me about Random forst and decision trees, I explained them in detail. He asked me how can I get which feature is most important, which I forgot at the time. He also asked me to give an example decision tree based on my project and then he asked me why use random forest over decision tree. Then he also asked me about some Classifier in tensorflow which I couldnt answer. Later, he asked me about Lasso and Ridge and what's difference between them.

He then asked me about a logical puzzle, given a revolver gun which has 6 slots and two bullets placed consecutively. Which is higher probability that next shot will fire the bullet? There were two cases here that in the first fire, the bullet was not in the slot, and second case that bullet was present and it had a malfunction. I plotted down the cases and in each case calculated probability of shuffling and not shuffling. He later informed me of a mistake that after the first misfire, the revolver moves one section ahead automatically which I didnt account.

Then he asked me about gaussian distribution, to which I could explain what it is and the standard deviation and mean in it. he asked me about expectation of x general formula which I couldn't recall. Then he asked me about the gaussian distribution's PDF which I could remember only some parts, and writing just some parts of it he was satisfied with it.

3. [Round 3 - HR] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round: 9 ]

Fortunately, every candidate was given the chance to appear for the HR round as soon as their Technical round was done. This meant all 9 candidates appeared for both the interview rounds without any shortlisting.

The HR interview was short, also luckily I met the same HR who stayed with me in the OA. I started with my introduction, then I was asked about my parents' professions and whether I have siblings. I was also asked about 3 positives and 3 negatives about myself (classic strengths and weaknesses. I made a slight mistake that after recognizing this question I kept on saying "strength" and "weakness" instead of positive/negative as they said). Then they asked me why I'm pursuing this degree, whether I have plans for higher studies, how I would rate myself in c++ and python and finally if I have any questions for them. I answered all the questions citing story-type examples from my work experience and school and college life.

After this round, two students, including myself, were selected, while two others were asked to appear for a confirmation round. Since no one was selected in the confirmation round, the company decided to conduct another hiring process, similar to the earlier one, for students who had not attempted the Online Assessment. In this process, one student was selected.

[ In total 3 students were offered the job ]

Lessons learned:

Maintain your composure at all times. I can't remember how many opportunities I lost due to this. My ability to perform in stressful situations was almost non-existent because for practicing dsa I was always in a learning attitude. In an interview this was never the case since it can determine your future. I would recommend doing codeforces and leetcode contests as much as you can. For this particular interview, I never really had any hopes because I thought my dsa skills are not worthy of a quant position. So I was again in the same learning attitude.

Be 110% confident in yourself, chances are that then they will perceive you at 70%. (But please justify it too) I never made my introduction good to catch attention, I was only speaking about what I did. No one is interested in what you did. You need to communicate what you can do that can benefit them. I learned this from my friend Asim. So in this interview, I played entirely on my strengths, i.e. understanding the language at a very deep implementation level. I had web development projects and experience, but in my intro I told them that I also made a small mini project in rust by parsing my linux configuration file. I use Arch Linux and I use vim btw. (I actually said this in the interview too)

Don't let any incorrect answer derail your confidence. I initially had a very good interview in the first half and mid was very bad, but I didn't mind it much so I caught up in the last parts.

Be humble. Placements are a humbling experience. The earlier you accept it, the easier it gets for you.

Communicate your thoughts well, and remember it is a two way street. My entire DSA answers were very bad, but since my interviewer was very nice, he gave me feedback on whether I am going in the right direction or not. In most of the common cases, you will have to judge this by yourself by observing the interviewer very attentively. I think I never realised this since I was always focused on the right answer and speaking it as fast as I can.

Have a good resume such that it looks filled completely, leaving any empty whitespaces signals that you haven't done anything and memorize your resume on your fingertips so that any keyword or any related keyword is known to you and you can talk about it for a good 2 minutes at minimum. For example, I mentioned "BERT" model in my projects section, then the interviewer asked me about Transformer architecture along with BERT. Also single keyword also has variations to ask on, like on WebSockets I was asked about the http upgrade packet to ws:// protocol and another time I was asked about how sockets communicate (classic socket bind/accept diagram). If you are short on time, I recommend you to look out on at least 25 common interview questions on each tech keyword you mention on your resume.

Practice speaking a lot. I was a dead silent introvert (my literal speaking capacity is 2-3 hrs after which I have a sore throat). I followed Vinh Gang youtube and Matt Huang youtube to learn how to communicate better. It does not matter how good you are if the person in front of you doesn't understand what you say.

Fomo is only as long as you let your emotions control you. In my friend group I was one of the last people to get placed, and most of the higher paying companies already came and went. It is easy to say but hard when it's on you. I did feel panicked but I was confident due to having a solid internship experience.

Saying that Placement is luck based is an understatement. It is Swiss cheese luck, there are lots of factors, many of which you can't even think of, which are needed to have good luck in order to succeed. I hope my case is evident for this point. But you do need to do the needful so that when the opportunity strikes you are ready to go in.

Research the company very well before giving any interview. I have been asked if I know the company's business even in technical rounds. I used perplexity deep research for this and it helped me understand their businesses as well as the HR stuff. Highly recommended. Also have a look at the Companies Expert youtube for prepping on all those HR questions. HR questions sound stupid at first, but they are very psychological in nature. Understanding what questions mean to ask what is very very important.

The last lesson I would say is to keep persevering. I was not able to accept the rejections at first, but then I heard my Uncle's story:

He graduated from a Tier-3 college and remained unemployed for 1.5 years in poverty. Eventually, he approached placement agencies that provide training and subsequent job opportunities in exchange for 50% of the candidate's salary after securing employment and also an upfront non refundable fee in lacks. While most candidates did not receive opportunities through this route, he succeeded and even outperformed a candidate from NIT Trichy in the interview. Today, he is working at Intel in Silicon Valley.

He also struggled for admission into college, it was raining heavily in Mumbai the day he went for admissions, and almost the entire college was empty because of the immense rains, he got the admission because he reached there when only 3 students came that day.

There are many such stories that we don't know the struggle behind. I am lucky that my employment was not critical for my family's survival. If that's not you, then I hope God bless you.

Resources I used (ordered in importance I gave them, YMMV):

DSA:

● I initially did some CP on codeforces and Atcoder, solving around 30 Leetcode problems, so before placements I did 90% of Neetcode 150.

● Overall I would say my strategy was bad, I was ok at Graphs, Dp but I wasnt as good at problem solving so I couldn't clear elite company OAs. Not knowing standard leetcode problems also put me at risk of bad interviews.

● I would suggest doing CP for at least 6 months, regardless of your interest in it and memorizing NC 150, in the sense that you can recognize the type of problem from NC 150 list. This would give the best of both worlds but I was a bit late in doing so.

● I wanted to do the striver sheet earlier but since it had 179 problems I couldn't have spared time for it.

● So for learning, I watch Striver A-Z course YouTube playlists on each topic like dp, graph, stacks and queues, etc. And for practicing I used Neetcode. (highly recommended)

● I was particularly bad at managing stress during OA and interviews, many times I went blank only to come out and solve the entire solution. Solving CF or LC contests can help with this.

● I had started CF with CP 31 sheet: https://www.tle-eliminators.com/cp-sheet

● I also solved a searching and sorting, dp, sliding window from CSES problemset to learn some patterns/ways to do things: https://cses.fi/problemset/

Aptitude:

● Since I was a DSE, I lacked good math skills, so I used this youtube playlist to gain basic understanding: Aptitude Preparation for Campus Placement - YouTube

● Then I went on this playlist but only for very important topics like speed-dist, trains, mixtures, etc: Quantitative Aptitude Tutorials - YouTube

● Then after that I felt I lacked speed so I kept on watching random trick videos on "imran sir maths" yt channel. By far this helped me most. I would suggest his videos as a must watch for "Time & work" and "Coding Decoding" topics. I was able to solve those questions in 30-45 seconds after some practice.

● The standard indiabix is also good, I personally never did it for all topics because many questions were too repetitive, and it takes a bit longer.

SQL:

● Since I had good fundamentals understanding, this wasn't even an issue. I was able to solve many Hard SQL problems just by intuition, but sadly those didnt accept any partial answer like Dsa questions.

● If you have no idea on sql syntax, start with this video and go in depth on joins, etc. I can vouch for this since I learned mysql from here about 4 years ago in my diploma: SQL Tutorial - Full Database Course for Beginners

● After knowing this, if you have time, please do solve Leetcode Sql 50 sheet. And try to go from naive to optimal query by learning as many new functions as you can.

● Once done with this, go onto understanding case statements and window functions in sql. I will suggest only 5 most common window functions are more than enough. I learned these from chatgpt. Learning case statements is best ROI on your time vs frequency of being asked.

● Learn about unions, I personally never used them but it is a good to know for your tech interview.

● After this, you can learn about Date and String functions. Understand how to use them and also memorize all the formats like %y, %B, etc. Learn about 20 most commonly used functions in both categories.

● SQL OA questions 90% of the time revolved around manipulating the type, extraction in string and dates like using instr(), left(), trim(), date_format(), etc. Know well about this.

● Finally boss of all topics, recursive CTE. I never learned this topic, but I forgot the count of how many OAs I couldn't solve just because I didn't know this.

HR questions:

● I only ever gave one HR interview, so I am not the best person for advice on this. I read just this one article with 50 hr questions: https://www.interviewbit.com/hr-interview-questions/

● I also had memorized 5 incidents, like 5 positive ones and 5 negative ones. Negative ones need to show your learning and how you overcame it, not that u still have it.

● I used one of these incidents in my "strengths" answer, where I said I have high versatality, citing example of my work at navy. I won't tell that to you here :)

● Also have at least 60-70% understanding on what company does and what they are. I used perplexity pro a lot to research about companies in one go.

Tech mcq stuff:

● I never really had to prepare for it because I was a core dev profile. I would say know about these topics well:

● Git: it was asked in workindia oa in detail, about commands.

● Java/Oops: many OAs asked java code for oops and their output.

● Python: 2-3 OAs also asked about python, won't say super necessary, but knowing more has always been helpful for me.

● System design: I heard many places asking about nosql, horizontal scaling and all, I will say Gaurav Sen's youtube playlist on this is more than enough.

● General languages: I recommend roadmap.sh for understanding depth on tech topics, it is an overkill though, so for short and sweet u can see: https://learnxinyminutes.com/

● Also keep a deep understanding on every tech keyword you mention on your resume. I was asked about WebSockets, the flow of info, the starting http upgrade msg etc.

OOPS:

● I had a solid understanding on oops because of my diploma. I will say these topics are important:

● 4 Pillars of OOPS all with a real world example.

● Java inner classes, static inners and stuff. (vvimp)

● Constructors logic, when which one gets called on which object.

● Know about the final keyword on all classes, methods and variables.

● Know all ways to use super and this keyword.

● Know access modifiers.

● Know about Object class methods like hashCode(), toString(), etc.

● Know about deep and shallow copying (in all languages preferably, Python, Java and C++)

● instanceof operator

● Why and how string is immutable in java

● Composition vs Inheritance (vimp for interviews)

● I won't say this list is exhaustive, so please refer JavaTpoint for OOPs in Java. best resource for it, but takes time.

Schema Design:

● I won't say this is important but may get asked sometimes. This is just writing down relations and/or making ER diagrams.

● Important to know about:

● ER diagrams, EER constructs.

● Plot out entities and just keep on joining them with relations.

● Be alert when making relationships and entity structure, you may get told to write a query for the same.

Finally, if you wish to connect or ask any questions, feel free to reach out to me on my Linkedin.

Wish you the best of luck.

1. Online Assessment [135 students appeared for this round]

• The online assessment was conducted on HackerEarth and had a 90-minute time limit.

• It consisted of 12 technical MCQs, 1 SQL query, and 1 coding question.

The MCQs were based on CS fundamentals, OOPs, SQL, and code snippet output prediction.

The SQL question was simple and could be solved using a basic WHERE clause with some AND conditions. It required interpreting a table to calculate compensation.

The coding question was string-based, required generating a lexicographically smallest string based on mapping rules from two input strings S1 and S2 (containing only 'T' and 'F').

You had to construct an answer string such that:

o For index i, if S2[i] is 'T', the answer substring starting from i should match S1. o If S2[i] is 'F', then at least one character in that range must differ from S1.

The solution required both brute-force thinking and careful handling of edge cases to ensure the final string was valid and lexicographically smallest.

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/ https://www.thejoboverflow.com/p/p1926/

Note: The test was exactly the same as the one conducted for the Barclays Summer Internship last year, including the coding and SQL questions. In fact, Barclays has been repeating the same test pattern and questions for the past two years, so going through previ ous year test experiences can give you a strong edge.

2. Technical Round [37 students shortlisted]

The interviews began around 10:30 AM, but I was called only after the lunch break at 3:00 PM. So, if your slot is later in the day, there's no need to worry, delays are normal.

My interview began with a brief introduction round. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, followed by questions about my family background, CGPA, and whether I was satisfied with my college and academic performance so far.

Next, he asked me about my primary programming language, to which I responded Java. He then asked a simple DSA question on finding duplicates in an array. He handed over his laptop and asked me to code the solution in as many ways as I could.

• I first implemented the solution using a HashSet.

• After that, he asked me to make a few variations in the code, which I successfully implemented.

Following that, the discussion moved to Java concepts and Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs). The interviewer then focused deeply on Exception Handling in Java. He:

• Asked several questions, ranging from basic to advanced level.

• Requested me to code examples using try-catch-finally blocks directly on his laptop.

• Asked about different types of exceptions, their behavior, and expected outputs.

• Also made me predict the output of the code I had written, then verify it by running the program.

While coding and answering, I made a few minor mistakes, but nothing major. The interviewer seemed okay with them, so don't stress too much over small slips.

Lastly, we discussed one of my projects, where I gave an overview and explained the problem statement, tech stack used, and key features.

At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him about his role at Barclays and the technologies he works with.

That concluded my first technical round.

3. HR Round [21 students shortlisted]

Just 10 minutes after my technical round, I was called in for the HR interview.

The HR round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself, followed by questions about the hackathons I had participated in and won.

He then asked me about the company values that were shared during the pre-placement talk (PPT session). He wanted to know:

• What those values meant to me personally

• And how I had implemented any of those values in my daily life

We then had a detailed conversation about the committees I was a part of, and this part of the discussion went on for quite some time.

Towards the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I took the opportunity to ask about:

• The team he leads at Barclays

• And what kind of work his team is involved in

This brought the HR round to a close.

In total, 16 students, were selected.

journey.prep:
1. Let's start with the preparation phase before the placement season. The most important part is DSA this will help you clear a lot of Online Assessments for all the major companies. Start as early as possible, the earlier the better. Also what is more important than starting early is maintaining consistency. I was one of the first people to start DSA during the start of 3rd year but then left it

midway for almost the entire Sem 5. Do not make this mistake, once you start make it a habit to do DSA everyday even if it is just one question.

2. You can follow a sheet like Striver's A2Z Sheet or NeetCode or do a combination of both like I did. Start with Striver's SDE Sheet or NeetCode 150 whichever you are comfortable with if you feel confident about Data Structures or go for A2Z Sheet or NeetCode 250 if your basics aren't clear. For Recursion, DP and Graphs make sure to strictly follow Striver and his respective playlists on the topics as it is the best resource on the internet for these topics. The rest you can do from either.

3. Another aspect of DSA is explaining your approach. You may be amazing at DSA but if you cannot explain your approach none of it is any use. When practicing LeetCode, although this might take additional time, but try explaining your approach in your head while you are solving the question

4. Try to do LeetCode contests if you have the time or you complete DSA early enough to practice time management and make sure to practice company style story based questions for OA practice using ChatGPT. You can also experiment with CP if you enjoy doing LeetCode and DSA although I wouldn't recommend it for those of y'all who are doing it for the sake of placements like I was.

5. Next comes SQL, this may seem like an easy topic but this is very crucial as it is asked in almost all interviews. Start with a basic crash course of SQL like Apna College or some other channel to learn basic topics like GROUP BY, ORDER BY, SELECT, JOINS and other basics. Once you have a basic understanding of these jump directly to SQL 50 from LeetCode as the more you practice the better you will be. For each question in SQL 50 if you don't get the solution, go through the solutions of other people or the editorial by LeetCode if given. Do not directly move to ChatGPT that won't help you understand and explore.

6. For OOPS follow Kunal Kuswaha's playlist for OOPs that is the best there is. There is nothing additional required. If you are also working with some other language like C++ or Python refer to OOPs in those languages through ChatGPT and Google. Do preparation for OOPs toward the end of the preparation phase with 2-3 weeks left for the placement season so as to remember the concepts better. After all of this try doing some OS and CCN if time permits.

7. I would recommend doing an internship or two and if you have already done one, make sure to present it well in your resume as this carries a lot of weight. It basically shows the interviewer that other companies also decided to work with you and you have already worked in a professional environment. Even if you do not have an internship, add 3-4 good and diverse projects in your resume so that you can stand out from the crowd. Keep in mind that everyone is going to do normal web dev projects, so to stand you must do different projects that integrate multiple things and try to do a project that includes an AI workflow.

8. Make sure that you know each of your resume projects inside out and you can talk about them for hours with the interviewer. Try to only add projects that you have actually worked on and even if you do add a project right from the internet which I wouldn't recommend but in extreme cases if you do make sure that you put it into ChatGPT or CoPilot and know every aspect of it.

9. Now for the interview part, once you clear the OA try to get a good night's sleep before the interview day but in case it is your first interview and you have a habit and can manage with less sleep, I would recommend that you prepare well the night before if there is something you haven't. Again I would only recommend this if you have done it a lot of times over the years during exams. I did this exact thing and I was a bit sleepy on the D-Day but it was worth it otherwise I wouldn't have been well prepared, so manage your risk accordingly.

10. On the day of the interview, there can be a possibility that your interview might be scheduled later in the day so during this time keep talking to people around you or do some last minute revision but do not overthink and get tensed about your interview. Even if your friends aren't with you, talk to other people so that you get engaged and it takes the edge off.

11. Lastly remember that no matter how much you prepare there will always be situations that work against you like curveball questions you hadn't expected or a stubborn interviewer or any other situation that you did not expect so always be ready for such things. Also be mentally prepared to face ample rejections before you even get an interview or get placed. I got my first interview after facing more than 6-7 OAs and faced 3 interviews before I got placed and for each of these I managed to reach the final round and then got rejected. Keep in mind that this is a part of the placement proces and always be ready to get up and move on.

Resources:

Category Resource/Platform Key Strategy/Notes

OA & Aptitude IndiaBix Good for topics including (percentages, ratios, time-distance).

DSA Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet Understanding patterns is crucial. Always spend 30-45 mins before looking at the solution. I had solved around 75% of the SDE sheet.

Java OOPs Kunal Kushwaha Playlist & If you have time, go through the entire playlist as it is very GFG Notes extensive

DBMS GFG, Code-Help Babbar Supplement lecture notes with these for fast review.

CN GFG CN Notes Supplement lecture notes with these for fast review.

OS GFG OS Notes Supplement lecture notes with these for fast review.

SQL Leetcode 50 questions This should be enough for most of the on campus roles.

Interview ChatGPT Quick and reliable tool to research company background, tech Prep stack, and everything related to your resume or interview answers.

HR Indiabix+ChatGPT Use them to prepare for general HR questions. Use LLMs to tailor your answers according to company values.
journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment Round [137 students appeared for this round ]

This was the initial screening phase which consisted of three sections:

a. Aptitude Section (15 questions) b. CS Fundamentals (20-30 questions) c. Coding Section (2 questions)

The aptitude section consisted of pattern recognition, profit and loss, ratios, statistics. In the CS Fundamentals section questions were based on Core CS, DBMS, OS, SQL and questions based on output prediction using flowcharts/ code snippets. The coding section had two questions as follows:

I. Given an array of integers, find out which numbers would be at the same place and which numbers would have changed positions after sorting the array. (I was able to pass all but one test cases i.e. 9/10)

II. Given a range of numbers X, Y you had to find the sum of all golden numbers. A golden number would be defined such that the sum of its digits - maximum digit out of all digits is equal to the maximum digit. (eg: 3003: sum = 6, max_digit = 3, sum - max_digit = 3). (I was able pass 9/12 test cases)

Important Tips for OA:

1. Time management is the most important aspect of an OA. You must attempt easy and especially short questions first and then go to longer ones. Understand what the question is asking before jumping to the answer and sometimes just try option elimination if nothing works.

2. Keep 30-45 seconds at the end reserved for unattempted questions. This time is basically for those questions that you have absolutely no idea how to answer. You quickly select random options for these and since there are no -ve marks make sure to attempt each question.

3. For aptitude questions refer to IndiaBix and make sure to study up on statistics formulas as they are usually asked in IDFC OAs.

4. For the coding section, the questions for any company are never straightforward; they will give some kind of a pointless story which will take you a minute or two to read and some more minutes to comprehend. These won't be your typical LeetCode questions. I would suggest that toward the end of your preparation phase practice a few of these questions by asking ChatGPT to generate such lengthy story based company OA style questions.

2. Technical Round 1 [40-45 students were selected for this round]

The round started with the interviewer asking me to take him through my resume. Keep this about 60-90 secs max. Then from my introduction he picked up my experience in python and started asking me questions on the language. These basic to in depth questions about the language and its working. He asked me about break, continue & pass, list vs tuple, lambdas, docstring, memory management, garbage collection in python etc. I managed to answer almost all them. The main reason was that I had studied the "Python interview questions" from GeeksforGeeks and most of the questions were exactly the same or similar to it so make sure to study those. Then he asked me some questions on C++ like virtual functions, friend keyword, multiple inheritance and the diamond problem etc. Then he asked me if I knew anything about Operating Systems to which I said I had basic understanding of multithreading and processes which was taught to us in our academics and in theory. He asked me how to run a python program on a UNIX server which I did not. Then he asked about thrashing in an OS which I again wasn't aware of. Next he moved on to DBMS and Schema design. He gave me a situation where I had to design the schema for a hotel which took bookings from customers on their own website and aggregators like MakeMyTrip, TripAdvisor etc. I designed the schema and at each stage communicated with the interviewer on my choice and he would give me hints and direct me if I was drifting in the wrong direction. After a lot of cancellations and reiterations I arrived at the final schema. Keep in mind to keep explaining why you were adding certain tables or columns in your schema. Next he asked to write an SQL query to find the number of room bookings in each quarter which I wrote very easily. He then asked me to update this to find the percentage occupancy in each quarter. He then connected this database scenario to techno-hr questions. He put me in a situation where if I got a call from a customer saying that they had booked a room and made the payment but did not receive a confirmation what would I do. Then he changed it to the booking type being a third party aggregator and the booking of the customer was the next day. I connected this with a situation which I had actually faced during the Coldplay concert in Ahmedabad where our hotel denied us the online booking we had done after reaching there. After he was satisfied with all my answers and a few follow ups, he was finally done and asked me if I had any questions. Make sure to prepare 2-3 good questions based on the company for this beforehand as this creates a great impression and shows that you are serious about the company. I asked him about the GenAI and ML projects that the company had been working on and would be undertaking for internal tools as well as consumer facing tools.

PRO Tips for Technical Rounds:

1. Make ChatGPT your friend as there is no better tool for interview preparations.

2. Know your resume forwards and backwards without missing a single piece of information. Also prepare for in-depth questions for each part of the resume. Sometimes an interview might take a point in your resume and ask very in-depth questions to test your understanding. Use ChatGPT for this and ask it to give curveball questions too.

3. Make sure to keep the points in your resume as honest as possible and don't mention something you lack understanding in. If extremely necessary to include a part you might not know about, make sure to understand it in-depth one day before the interview. Keep in mind that the interviewer is sitting with a laptop and you're not.

4. I would advise that you learn OOPs concepts in Java as a lot of companies have Java as a requirement or at least have some projects of Java in their systems. Then learn those same concepts in your preferred language.

5. For each language you mention in your resume, go through its interview questions from GFG because a lot of times they cover almost everything about the language.

6. Technical Interviews are as much a psychological game as they are about your technical skills. The interviewers will ask you questions on what you have mentioned in your resume and based on what you answer. Make sure to drop hints of where you want to lead them. A lot of the time they might end up asking exactly that.

7. Be confident and honest in your answers and if you are asked something you don't know or to write a code whose syntax you do not recall, try explaining the concept and approach and related concepts you know. Most of the time that is what interviewers are looking for. If there comes a point where you have absolutely no clue of what you are asked, just be straight with them and say that you haven't learnt or worked with this particular concept instead of making up a useless explanation.

8. This is to be followed for all interviews and this is one of the most important aspects of an interview, keep a good eye contact with the interviewer. This might not seem like anything but it conveys that you are confident in your abilities and your answers, otherwise you come across as underconfident especially during HR interviews.

3. Technical Round 2 [ 22 students were shortlisted for this round ]

The round again began with a typical "Introduce yourself". Then they gave me scenarios and told me to identify what data structures would be used in those scenarios. The first scenario was that there were usernames and each had details which would have to be accessed so what DS would be used to which I answered HashMap for O(1) lookups. Then he updated the scenario such that the details of the user would need to be updated constantly. I was still adamant on using a HashMap since lookups would be O(1) but that was not what they wanted. After the interview I realized that they were expecting me to consider this as a normal database and looking for the answer to be B-Trees which are used for data storage in SQL and NoSQL Databases. Next they moved on to OOPs where they asked me to write one or two codes in Java. Next they jumped to Exception Handling and asked me what it was in Java. I told them about checked and unchecked exceptions and try catch. They asked me if it was possible to create custom exceptions in Java and then asked me to write code for a custom exception. I did not remember the exact syntax but I still wrote what I remembered and then explained it to them. Then I was asked about the difference between Exception and RuntimeException and why I inherited the RuntimeException class in my custom exception class. Next came questions on Object class of Java and what equals method is in Java. I knew about Object class being

the topmost class of Java which all classes inherited from but was not aware of equals so told them it was a method of the String class then they said it was of Object class. Now they moved on to 1-2 questions from my resume. I was asked why I used the Llama2 Model in my internship to which I explained about the company's requirements of privacy and budget constraints. Then they saw Git and GitHub and asked the main difference between them. Then they gave a situation where there are two branches one is the main branch and another is the dev branch where a feature was being developed. Say a developer was working on a feature in the dev branch and a constraint was to be created that they could push the code automatically once there were no merge conflicts. I suggested using admin approval before the code was pushed but they wanted it to be done automatically to which I did not know the answer.

Additional Tips for Technical Round:

1. Prepare a clear introduction of yourself well before the interviews. Don't ever think that you can wing it, but at the same time do not rote the intro, prepare points that you want to convey and define a clear flow.

2. Keep your introduction short but make it a story where each point connects to the next and relate it to the role. Also set clear boundaries about what you do and don't know in the intro itself. For example I had used Python for ML and data projects, C++ for DSA and recently learnt Java only for OOPs so I made this very clear in the introduction. This ensures that the interviewer doesn't ask you anything out of scope. The more generalized your introduction is, the more curveballs you could potentially face.

3. HR Round [ 9 students were shortlisted for this round ]

This was your typical HR interview where the interviewer was trying to get to know you and understand if your values aligned with that of the company's. The interview started with her asking me the purpose of this HR interview. Next she asked me to tell her about my resume and something that wasn't in it. Then she asked me about the challenges I have overcome. I was asked what my ideal company would look like where I would enjoy working at. Then I was asked about my ideal manager who I would love to work with to which I connected to my experience where I had talked to a senior of mine who was working at IDFC currently and the way he helped me, worked like a charm. Then I was asked what I knew about IDFC and why I wanted to work there. Next came the Work from home vs Work from office question. I was asked what my thoughts were about both of them and which of them I believed in, be sure to support your answer with adequate reasoning. Then she gave me a situation where I was the team lead for a project for a very important stakeholder who had given us a hard deadline but I found out that it would be impossible to deliver at that date. What would be my approach to this, providing a buggy software which would work for a few days and the client would be happy for now and then it would break down at a later date or do you delay the launch and take the heat but deliver the complete software. Now comes another situation where my manager does not assign me to any important projects or any meaningful work for that matter so what would be my approach to this. I told her about being direct in this situation and confronting my manager and politely explaining the situation. She said what if he/she doesn't give me the time of day to confront them. After she was satisfied with my answer she asked me about my experience at Oculus as a Marketing head and what challenges I faced while leading such a large team. Finally she told me there was one last question or at least that's what she told me. She asked me about my weakness and then based on that created situations. She asked me what if my manager was someone who micromanaged me constantly and check in every 10 minutes what I would do. She reiterated various aspects of this scenario and told me she was done

with the interview after she was satisfied with all my answers. Finally she told me if I had any questions and I asked a couple of questions and I was done.

PRO Tips for HR Round:

1. Think of HR round as a chess match where you have to constantly think, react and plan ahead for every move you make, with the addition that your moves are being constantly judged. My interviewer was someone who was in the HR industry for 15 years and yours would also probably be someone with the same experience so they know people very well, so always be on your guard and say things that actually do align with what you believe in.

2. Be honest but not too honest. This might seem confusing but HR representatives can usually identify when you're lying very easily. Now for the not too honest part, whatever you answer though the actual reason might be something else, mention that, but additionally connect it to the company's values and requirements. For example, for the work from home question some of you might prefer that but the company has work from office policy so align your answer such that you believe in work from home but are open to work from office.

3. Align your answers with the company values and your own experiences. Why this is important is because when you just state facts as an answer but you connect it with an actual experience, it becomes a story which always has great value in interviews not just HR but technical ones too.

4. Another important tip which will help you navigate HR easily is not to keep it one way where they ask and you answer. Try keeping it two-way where you ask them questions based on their questions and your answers and if you are confident enough try adding in a funny remark or two to make the atmosphere less tense.

5. Remember the names of your previous interviewers as it might be asked during HR and it is also a good practice to know it if you do get selected. Usually each interviewer introduces themselves at the start itself but in case someone does not, make it a practice to ask their names at the end of the interview.

3. Final Screening Round [ 9 students were shortlisted for this round ]

This interview was taken by the senior management of IDFC and it was more of a formality but still do not take this lightly as one student was eliminated in this round. The interview was online where the interviewer asked me to take him through my resume. I had a project where I had used Selenium so he asked what Selenium was, what it was used for and what was its use case in my project. Then he asked how I usually approached any problem I was given. Then he came to time complexity analysis and asked what it was. He then asked me the purpose of the big O notation and then asked me if I had to find the time complexity of an algorithm how I would approach that. He then asked a couple of questions which I do not remember and then he asked if I had any questions and that was it.

8 students were offered the job at the end

Initially there was a Resume Shortlisting and a list was shared of candidates applicable to attend the interview process. The entire process was scheduled on 9th July itself from morning to evening and all interviews were conducted in an online mode.

1. Rapid Fire Round [ 72 students were present for this round ]

As the name suggests, we had to attempt 40-50 questions in a 15 minute window so both accuracy and speed were essential. The questions were like : time/space complexity of code snippets, calculating the expected output of a given code and fundamental questions like if a = 10 then what will a++ + ++a equal to - answer is 22. The snippets were a mix of Python,CPP and Java codes so cannot isolate one language to focus on. There were also CS fundamental questions like OS,CCN and Git commands.

2. Debugging Round [ 46 students appeared for this round ]

We were sent a GMeet link where the interviewer asked for a choice between JS or Python. As I did DSA in Python and was aware of both Flask and FastAPI, I chose Python. I was a bit scared as the codebase shared was in Django so i told the interviewer honestly that I was aware of Flask and FastAPI so he asked if I wanted to switch to Express and JS or would I like to try Django as Google/StackOverflow/Documentation (everything except AI) was allowed so I stuck with Django and was able to debug the errors. Specific questions were

asked related to the errors so it is important to understand the error and explain your intuition as to why the error may have occurred and then solve it. General questions related to Git or the MVC folder structure in a codebase were also asked.

3. DSA Round [ 15 students appeared for this round ]

This was the ﬁrst time I was told to introduce myself, I was not prepared for this so always be prepared for this question else it sets an impression that you are not even prepared for the basic most obvious questions. I was lucky enough that this did not affect me. Overall the panelists asked candidates to only write pseudocode on Google Doc but i was expected to code and run it on GDB probably bcuz i code in Python so they wanted to see the output. There were 2 interviewers in the GMeet and I was asked this question :

In a gaming tournament unique ids are to be assigned from 1 to N to N participants, there might be some invalid ids already assigned in between and we need to assign them values acc to the next smallest valid number from 1 to N. So if the given array is 1,0,2 then 0 is invalid then answer should be 1,3,2. Another example test case :

Input : 2,0,4,-6,9,6 Output : 2,1,4,3,5,6

So my initial approach was to iterate over the array and put numbers already valid in a Set in Python which translates to a unordered_set in CPP. Now start a loop from i = 1 to N and check if it exists in the set , if not then replace the ﬁrst invalid number in the array with the current i. This is O(N) time and space. I was asked to reduce the space after this. I asked if the order matters while assigning values, so the interviewer cleared that the only expectation is 1 to N, nothing else matters. So my next approach was to sort the array and check if 1 to N exists in it with Binary Search( lower_bound ), if not replace the ﬁrst invalid position with the current missing number. This is NlogN time and constant space. I was asked to bring time back to O(N). I took a lot of time here and asked for hints where the interviewer told me try to establish some relation between indexes and validity of a number which eventually led me to a Cycle Sort solution where there is a special case that if the input is strictly between a given range like 1 to N then sorting can be done in O(N). Pls read about this on GPT/Google, the solution goes as : We will try to place the already valid numbers on their correct indexes which will leave only invalid numbers on indexes where there should have been something else, now in another iteration from left to right we change the invalid numbers to valid because based on indexing we know the next valid number. I was able to code my initial 2 solutions but messed up something in the last one but the interviewer said that was ok.

I should've read about UNIX/OS fundamentals thoroughly as I was unable to answer those questions. Secondly I should've already thought about the loopholes my projects have.

Process Date: 26th July, 2024

Placement Process Overview

The placement process at Barclays involved three rounds, starting with an online assessment and progressing to two interview stages. On July 26th there was an online assessment, followed by interviews on July 29th. Out of 133 participants who appeared for the online assessment, 37 were shortlisted for the first technical interview. Subsequently, 21 individuals advanced to the final Tech + HR round,

Round 1: Online Assessment (90 minutes)

The Barclays online assessment was a three-part test consisting of MCQs, a SQL query, and a coding problem. The MCQs were the key differentiator for shortlisting.

1. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

These questions tested foundational knowledge across various programming languages and concepts.

● Core Language Concepts: Questions involved predicting the output of short code snippets in languages like C++ and Java. Topics included pointers, bitwise operators, control flow (continue), and variable scope.

● Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): This section focused on OOP principles, such as the difference between abstract classes vs. interfaces and method overriding vs. overloading. It also covered topics like the impossibility of overriding private and static methods and the order of class initialization.

● Exception Handling (Java): Questions evaluated an understanding of try-catch-finally blocks. A key point was knowing that a return statement in a finally block overrides any return from try or catch, and that System.exit() prevents the finally block from executing.

2. SQL Questions

This section included both a query and theoretical MCQs.

● Queries: The questions required you to apply your SQL knowledge to real-world scenarios. This involved using multi-table joins to combine data, filtering data by date using functions like EXTRACT(MONTH FROM date), and translating complex business rules into a single SELECT query.

● SQL Theory: MCQs tested your knowledge of commands like DROP vs. TRUNCATE vs. DELETE. A crucial distinction was the difference between an equi join (which uses only =) and an inner join (a broader category of joins).

3. Coding Problem

The coding problem was a single, complex challenge that required careful logical thinking.

● "String Generation": The task was to create the lexicographically smallest string S based on a pattern string (S1) and a rule string (S2) of 'T' (true) and 'F' (false) constraints.

● Solution Logic: The recommended approach was to first satisfy all 'T' constraints. Then, fill the remaining positions with the smallest possible character, 'A'. Finally, iterate through all 'F' constraints and minimally modify the string (e.g., change the rightmost 'A' to a 'B') to break any invalid matches while preserving the lexicographical order. This problem went beyond a simple build-and-check method, demanding a more nuanced strategy to correct violations.

Round 2: Technical Round 1

Following the online assessment, 37 participants were shortlisted for the interview rounds. There were five interview panels, and I happened to be assigned to one of the more challenging ones. My interviewer was highly experienced and went into very detailed questions on every topic. This round lasted for approximately an hour.

The interview began with a standard introduction, after which I was asked to brief him about my projects. He then inquired about the programming languages I was comfortable with. Following this, he asked me to explain the concept of method overloading and to write a Java program demonstrating a real-world example, encouraging me to think beyond common examples like 'Area' or 'Vehicle'. He then moved on to an in-depth discussion about my projects. Noticing my significant frontend projects, he transitioned into detailed questions about React and HTML. He gave a scenario about creating a dropdown within another dropdown using React and asked about the distinction between a textbox and a textarea. Further questions included how to limit the number of words in an input field and how to display the count of letters already entered. While I couldn't recall every specific detail, I explained my approach clearly.

He then asked detailed HTML questions, presenting a scenario where he needed to input seven addresses in a form. He asked how I would extract the second address, impose a limit on the number of addresses, and manage IDs if they were assigned sequentially (e.g., 1 for the first address, 2 for the second). Specifically, he asked what would happen to ID 1 if the first address was deleted--would it be reassigned, or would a new one be created? He also wanted to know how I would track the total number of addresses.

After assessing my Java knowledge, he shifted to SQL. He asked if I knew about Procedures and Triggers, to which I confirmed. He then asked for an explanation and relevant queries. At this point, I honestly confessed that I hadn't practiced writing queries for procedures and triggers, but I explained the underlying concepts. I remained calm and continued to answer all his questions. He then inquired about the partitioning concept in DBMS and what partitioned tables are, asking me to write a query for it. Finally, he asked about different types of indexes in DBMS. The interview concluded with a question about the risks a bank might face and potential solutions.

I left this round feeling devastated and demotivated, convinced it had gone terribly wrong and almost on the verge of tears.

Round 3: Tech + HR Round

To my surprise, I was called for this final round, which shortlisted 21 candidates. This round lasted for about half an hour. The interviewer started by sharing the positive feedback he had received from my first interviewer, which was a huge relief and a pleasant surprise given how I felt after the first technical round.

He then asked me to describe my internship experience and elaborate on my projects, cross-questioning me further to see my understanding and contributions. Following this, he moved on to the HR-specific questions. He asked classic questions like "Why do you want to join Barclays?" and a challenging scenario: "If another company offered you double the salary, would you switch?" He also presented situations involving workplace ethics and problem-solving, such as: "If your manager gives you a task with an unrealistic deadline, how would you approach it?" and "You've completed your work for a strict weekend deadline and left for vacation, but midway, you realize you forgot to push an important update to GitHub. How would you resolve this?" Another thought-provoking question was: "If you were stuck on a project you built from scratch, and a friend helped you resolve a small error that had a big impact, and then you were nominated for an award for that project, would you accept the award or tell your team members about your friend's contribution? Discuss the pros and cons of each decision." He asked many more similar situational questions.

I ensured to be confident and true to myself in my responses, which seemed to satisfy the interviewer. At the end, I took the opportunity to ask him about his role and what Barclays expects from interns, specifically if prior knowledge of finance is required. With these questions, the interview concluded.

Areas for Improvement, Preparation, and General Tips

My selection was largely due to my ability to stay calm under pressure, even when faced with questions I couldn't fully answer. My honesty about my limitations, coupled with explaining my approach or conceptual understanding, showed integrity. My detailed preparation in OOPS, Java, HTML, React, SQL, and DBMS fundamentals was crucial, especially since MCQs were a deciding factor in the initial round. In the HR round, being confident, truthful, and demonstrating problem-solving skills with practical reasoning helped immensely. Engaging the interviewer and asking relevant questions also showed genuine interest and initiative.

It's crucial to not only know what a concept is but also how to implement it with code or queries.

By keeping these points in mind, and remembering to stay confident and true to yourself, you can significantly improve your chances during the placement process.

2. Technical Interview (Out of 27 students who appeared, 15 were selected for next round)

This round lasted for about 25-30 minutes. The process began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself, followed by a few questions related to my resume. Since I'm from Jammu and currently studying in Mumbai, they asked why I chose to come so far for my education. They also inquired about my interest in the IT sector and whether I genuinely wanted to pursue a career in this field. This was a brief conversation before the technical questions started.

Next, I was asked to explain one of the projects I had listed on my resume. I selected a project and went into detail about it. The interviewer asked why I chose specific technologies for the project (e.g., "Why did you use Next.js instead of React?"). They also wanted to understand the relevance of the project: whether it had any real-life application and if it was solving a real-world problem.

After that, we moved on to questions related to computer science fundamentals. I was given real-life scenarios and asked how I would solve certain problems. One question I remember was about withdrawing money from an ATM. The question was: If money is debited from your account but not dispensed by the ATM, what could be the issue and how would you resolve it?

Another technical question involved synchronizing two APIs: If the result of the first API is used as input for the second, how would you avoid any errors or overlaps during this process?. Then, the interviewer asked few questions on OOPS and DBMS.

To clear this round, it's important to be thoroughly prepared with your resume and solid in your understanding of computer science fundamentals.

2. HR [Out of 15 students who appeared, 13 were selected]

The interview started with the typical question: "Introduce yourself." After that, I was asked a series of behavioral and personal questions, including:

• When did you take a position of responsibility? What challenges did you face, and how did you overcome them?

• How many members are there in your family? Do you often have conflicts with your siblings?

• Can you share an experience where you worked in a team, and there were differences in opinions? How did you resolve the conflict or handle clashes between your views and those of your team members?

The interviewer also wanted to assess my general awareness and asked for my opinion on the current situation in Gaza and the Israel conflict. This round lasted around 20-25 minutes.

I wasn't fully prepared for this type of questioning, but I stayed honest and answered each question based on the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) approach. It's crucial to stay calm and composed. Even if you don't have an immediate answer, take a moment to think it through and respond confidently.

That said, it's always a good idea to practice these types of questions beforehand with friends or family through mock interviews. This helps you prepare and handle such rounds more smoothly.

A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round & Finally 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day. The CGPA Criteria for SDE was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was further reduced to 7.5. It may not be the case for next year if they don't want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above.

1. Resume / CGPA Shortlisting:

Curate your resume to align closely with the company's job description, emphasising your key strengths. After finalising it, evaluate its ATS compatibility using platforms such as Resume Worded, targeting a score of 65 or higher. The shortlisted candidates for the Online Assessment and Pre -Placement Talk (PPT) were declared on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM.

Pre-Placement Talk

While the process was originally planned to take place offline, it was later shifted to an online format and conducted at 5 PM on 4th August. During the PPT session, make it a point to listen attentively and note down the names and roles of the presenters -- this small detail can prove valuable in later interactions.

Preparing in advance is equally important; gather basic information about the company such as its founding year, current CEO, and tagline. These details are not only potential question topics but also help you make a positive impression by showing genuine interest. Toward the end of the PPT, consider asking well-thought- out questions to demonstrate engagement, though it's not mandatory.

If you prefer, you can reserve your questions for the post-interview phase, where they may carry even greater impact.

2. Online Assessment: [ Approx. 160 students appeared ]

The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. +1 was given for each correct answer and -0.25 for incorrect ones. We were allowed to use the system calculator. It was invigilated by the company executives.

The assessment covered four major sections: Java (18), Python (17), SQL (5), and Aptitude (30) - Total 70 questions.

The Java and Python sections were largely output-based MCQs, with a strong emphasis on OOPS concepts, errors, exceptions, stacks, queues, and all types of sets in Java. Some questions, such as "Determine the total number of swaps in the given array using bubble sort" (with an array provided), were a bit time-consuming. It's advisable to tackle such questions later and prioritize quicker ones first. Make sure you are thoroughly familiar with Java and Python syntax. Since Python was my secondary programming language, I struggled with 2-3 questions due to not knowing the exact syntax.

For SQL Section, queries were asked for the given table and the required output. The queries covered topics like aggregate functions, date functions, subqueries. The questions were on easy to medium level but all the options looked similar at first sight - but had slight differences, making it a bit time-consuming and needing a double check.

I was able to complete the first three sections in 40 minutes, leaving the remaining 50 minutes for the aptitude section.

The Aptitude round consisted of the normal Quantitative Aptitude questions such as Percentages, Ratios, Time-Distance, Boat Upstream-Downstream, Probability, Data Interpretation etc. The questions were on an easy level with few medium ones. The key was to identify and solve questions you are most confident and are well versed with required formulae or logic.

3. Technical Round: [ 44 students appeared ]

I was the last candidate in my panel, and my panelist was the Associate Director at ISS-STOXX. My interview lasted for about an hour -- the only panel to conduct interviews for that long. It began at 7:30 PM, by which time many students had already completed their HR rounds and left. So, if you find yourself waiting outside the TPO for hours, don't panic or stress yourself out.

The interview began with her asking my name. She then went through my resume and asked about my internship, which I had completed during my diploma. She asked me what skills I had acquired during the internship and my overall experience.

Next, she asked what I had prepared for the interview. I mentioned DBMS, OS, SQL, OOPS and also added that I had studied software testing. Be careful whatever you mention will be explored in depth. She then asked for a brief explanation of one of my projects, followed by a few questions on its implementation.

Since I had stated Java as my primary programming language, she asked me a few questions about JDK, JRE, and JVM, and then about how and why Java is considered platform -independent. Make sure you are clear on these basic Java architecture concepts.

The discussion then moved to SQL queries. The first was to find the maximum salary in each department, followed by the query to find the top two salaries in each department. I had to write the queries on paper. She then added gender and city columns to the same table and asked for the names of female employees with the maximum salary in their respective departments.

Next, the discussion moved to OOP concepts in Java. I was asked to briefly explain the four pillars of OOP. Then, the interviewer presented a few classes -- Shape, Rectangle, Square, and Circle -- and asked me to apply inheritance to them. Initially, I designed Shape as an interface and implemented hierarchical inheritance, where Rectangle, Square, and Circle each implemented the Shape interface. She then encouraged me to think of a more convenient approach. That's when I realized she was expecting multilevel inheritance, such as Shape → Rectangle → Square, since every Square is a Rectangle . Following that, she introduced a Rhombus class and asked me to integrate it into the inheritance tree. Initially unsure, I asked about its properties and understood that, just like every Square is a Rectangle, every Square is also a Rhombus. I then attempted to inherit Square from both Rectangle and Rhombus, which led to a discussion on the diamond problem in Java, its solutions, and the use of the super keyword.

Then came the DSA questions, the first question was to remove all occurrences of a given key from a linked list. I explained my approach in detail before writing the source code. I fumbled slightly while handling the pointers but kept thinking aloud and explaining my reasoning. I la ter wrote the correct code and dry -ran it on both the given list and an additional test case to check for edge cases. The second DSA question was straightforward -- return true if there are three consecutive odd numbers, else return false.

Finally, I was asked a commonly known puzzle: Mislabelled Jars

The interview concluded with me asking the panelist about her own experience at ISS -STOXX -- current role in the company, and experience in the tech industry.

4. HR Round: [ 15 students appeared ]

There were two interviewers in this round -- the same ones who had conducted the pre-placement talk. I would advise remembering their names, as interviewers sometimes ask if you know them. I was again the last candidate for the HR round, which lasted about 30-35 minutes and ended around 10 PM.

The conversation began with an introduction about myself and my family background, followed by questions about my 10th-grade percentage, diploma percentage, and current CGPA. My diploma caught their attention, and they asked why I chose to pursue a diploma instead of completing 12th grade and attempting JEE/CET. I'd advise all DSE students to prepare well for this question, as it is frequently asked in interviews.

Next, they asked about my interest in technology. I shared that I had been passionate about full stack development since my diploma days. This led to a question about my favourite project, for which I described one of my ML projects. They probed deeper into it -- asking how I came up with the problem statement, the overall design, the reason behind my choice of technology, possible alternative technologies, and potential edge cases. They also asked about the challenges I faced during development.

Since my resume listed two ML projects and only one fully dedicated full stack project -- and I had chosen an ML project as my favourite -- they expressed concern about my fit at ISS-STOXX, as the company doesn't work extensively with AI/ML. I clarified that although the projects were ML-based, their core still relied on full stack development fundamentals -- including a robust backend, scalable database, and interactive frontend. When given a hypothetical choice between working on a completely full stack project or a purely ML project at ISS, I confidently said I would choose the full stack one, as it has always been my forte and I am excited to explore the technologies ISS uses.

The interviewer knew that the last company which came before ISS-STOXX was Nomura, and asked why I couldn't clear its process. This led to questions about how many interviews I had given before, and why I thought I couldn't clear them. My suggestion to others would be to answer such questions honestly, showing self-awareness about areas of improvement and demonstrating that you have worked on them.

The interview concluded with me asking if the company organizes internal hackathons or other competitive events for employees. They replied that, at present, they do not, but expressed strong interest and agreed that it was indeed a great idea that I gave them. I added that hosting such events could enhance interaction among employees, encourage exploration of new technologies, and ultimately benefit the company.

The final results came at around 11 PM.

Finally, 12 students got the offer !!
