Before the OA, only students belonging to CE or CSE branch and having CGPA 7.5 and above were shortlisted for the OA, so a significant number of students were in-eligible to apply.

SO PLEASE MAKE SURE TO MAINTAIN GOOD CGPA. (AT LEAST 8)

Pay attention in PPT and interact with the company employees so that they remember you.

1. Online Assessment

Around 66 students appeared for the test, since IDfy had come for two roles ( SE and ML ) ,there were two different tests, one for SE and other for ML ( students had to choose a role before giving the OA).

The test for SE was conducted on Hackerrank for 90 minutes, and everything was proctored. The test consisted of 3 sections having 1 DSA, 2 SQL , 2 REST API questions respectively.

Every candidate did not get the same DSA question, I had got an easy one. The question was to check whether a password was strong or weak, for the password to be weak there were certain conditions that had to be satisfied like "contains only lowercase or uppercase letters" or "contains only numericals" or "contains a substring which is present in banned_words list". The constraints were also not very big so brute force worked here, just remember to put the words present in banned_words list in a set for fast lookup otherwise certain test cases won't pass due to TLE. Since this question was easy, I finished solving this question in 10 minutes.

Next was the SQL section, this section was tough and this is the game changing section because very few people know SQL very well so solving this section completely will definitely give you an edge over others. Both SQL questions had multiple tables, so I don't remember the exact questions, the first question could be solved by join and using group by and aggregate function. The second question was a notch above the first one, this question involved multiple joins and we had to use subquerier to further process the table before joining with other tables ( eg : adding a new column of data ) . The inner queries further contained aggregate and group by clauses, so this can become overwhelming to understand the exact flow, the trick here was to use WITH clause to separate out the inner query logic to make the query more readable and understandable. This section took most time because of the complexity involved. Since I had quickly solved the DSA question, I could devote more time to this section.

PLEASE TAKE SQL SERIOUSLY, IT SEEMS EASY UNTIL IT ISN'T, SO PRACTISING SQL IS VERY IMPORTANT.

Leetcode SQL 50, CodeChef, Hackerrank, are some of the good resources to start with. A day prior to the OA I practised from this site to brush up my SQL knowledge.

Next was the REST API section, each question instructed us to create a get method using any language like C, C++, Java, JavaScript (Node JS) , Python etc and hit a URL to get data and apply the given filter and return the filtered data. But the catch was, we had to do it from scratch, no framework, no code autocomplete, no external help, so knowing the exact syntax was the key here. I knew how to make a REST API in Java using Spring Boot Framework but I had no idea how to create the Get method from scratch in Java and since most of time had gone in SQL section, I did not have time to think about the syntax in JavaScript, so I could not solve both REST API question.

Since I had solved the DSA and SQL section completely I got shortlisted for the interview but some of the other shortlisted candidates had solved some sections partially. But to remain on the safe side, try to solve all questions, even partial is enough SOMETIMES, not every time.

I feel clearing the OA is the toughest task because of the competition and time pressure. I was fortunate enough to have only 66 students for the OA, other times I had to compete with 100+ students, so focus on getting proficient in DSA, SQL , Computer Fundamentals and Aptitude. I had given the OA of 5-6 companies before IDfy and cleared the OA of only 3-4 of them because I couldn't solve a DSA question fully or due to aptitude, so please focus on them early on.

2. Technical Round

Only 8 out of 66 candidates were shortlisted for the interview round. The shortlist came at 7:30 pm a day before the interview and we also had Baker Hughes PPT and test a day before the interview, so I did not have much time to prepare for the interview. Since I had read previous year interview experience, I focused on the projects listed on my resume, like tech stack, features, architecture diagrams etc.

We had to arrive by 9 am. There were three panels. I was first in my panel, my interview started around 10:30 am. So my interview started with the interviewer downloading the results of OA. He saw my results and said that I had the highest score so he was impressed by it. Then he introduced himself and his role at IDfy ( he also asked some points from the PPT, so remember to pay attention in the PPT ), then he read my resume, each and every point, then he told me to introduce myself. I mentioned my education background, a short description about my projects, and my interests ( prepare a good 1-2 min introduction beforehand, use chatgpt or other AI tools to refine it ). I had mentioned Formula 1 as one of my favourite sports to watch, fortunately my interviewer was also a formula 1 fan so we had a good brief conversation about the sport. Then the interviewer said that he would focus on three sections of my resume, technical skills, projects and internships. He started with a question, in which programming language was I most comfortable in and how would I rate myself in that language. I mentioned Java. He then started with Oops in Java, he asked me about polymorphism, diamond problem, how interfaces solve the diamond problem, static keyword, how static variables and static methods are different from each other. I answered all these questions correctly and gave examples where ever needed to explain the concept. Then he asked me to write the code for Destructor in Java. I was unsure whether Destructor existed in Java, so I mentioned this at the start but since I was unsure, I thought for a while and said that, to implement a Destructor we have to make the object null so that Garbage Collector will destroy the object. The interviewer said that my initial answer was correct that Destructor did not in Java, so he told me to have more confidence in my answer ( honestly I did panic a little after this so I drank water to calm myself ), after this he gave me a DSA question to solve, the question was there are a list of transactions given , the format was same as the ones given in a passbook , so there was a transaction description, credit amount, debit amount and current balance. Initial balance was given and we had to flag any transactions which are erroneous, the transaction was erroneous when current balance was not correct. For example, if the initial balance was 100 , credit was 10 , so the current balance should be 110 , if it was otherwise then we will flag this transaction as wrong. This was an easy question, simple math was required, only thing required were string functions like split, parseInt to get data from string. First, I verbally explained my approach then proceeded to write the code on paper ( remember to write clean and readable code ). Once this was done the interviewer proceeded with SQL queries, he gave me two schemas, Employee and Department. He asked three queries, I don't remember exact questions but I had used joins,

group by and aggregate functions to solve them ( remember to think clearly, ask for time to think and break down the problem, then join the solutions)

Next, the interviewer asked which was my favourite project, he read the project description. I had mentioned JWT, so he started by asking what is JWT and describe its structure, how did I implement it in my project, then he asked about REST APIs, difference between get, put , and post, whether we can create a new entry in db using get request (we can by sending the data as path variable or query parameter, but its not a good practise).

Then he said he was done with the interview and asked whether I had any questions. I asked two questions and the interview ended, my interview lasted for around 50-60 minutes.

After finishing my interview, I was instructed by our TPO to wait for the results till 1 pm. We initially thought that we would have to wait for another round at least, but then the company official said that no more rounds will be taken and final results will be announced on the basis of the first interview round. Two of the candidates had a second interview round but I did not.

Around 3:30pm, the results were announced, a total of 5 candidates were selected and fortunately I was one of them.

Additional Tips and Resources:

● Placements are tough, remember to stay calm, and patient. I was so disappointed with myself when I could not even crack the first round of many companies that I started to self-doubt myself. Keep your head down, and keep grinding.

● Luck definitely plays a part in placements, so focus on what you can control which is skills. Remember consistency is key, whether it's DSA or academics. I had a good CGPA, but since I was not consistent enough in DSA so I could not crack other high paying companies.

● Have good projects, and remember to justify specific things about the project, like tech stack, architecture etc.

● If you are familiar with Java, then master it, if not, at least know the basics like OOP concepts.

● I did not give a single HR Round, so I don't have any experience in that, but prepare for HR Round because it can happen that you clear all technical rounds but fail to clear the HR Round.

● Practice giving answers in front of a mirror or give mock interviews to your friends, this improves your communication skills.

● Follow Striver's sheet for DSA, give contests on leetcode, codechef, codeforces, this helps because you get a habit of solving questions with time pressure.

● Aptitude is very important, a lot of companies ask in OA, use this. Practise timed tests to really mimic the test environment. I started aptitude late, don't make this mistake.

● Puzzles are a common way to test critical thinking in interviews so practise from GeeksForGeeks.

● System design is a common question in interviews even for freshers so practise from GeeksForGeeks. Use chatgpt to understand the specific terminologies, and practise questions like how to scale a specific system ( for example your projects ).

● Guesstimates can also be asked, so prepare them if required ( this should be done only when you have ample amount of time ).

● During interviews, maintain eye contact while answering, be calm and ask for help if required, interviewers don't mind giving hints, they want to know your thought process.

● Remember to fill all the required application forms while applying, companies are strict and don't accept any excuses for any delay or missing application details. I missed filling one registration form while applying for IDFC First Bank, so I could not even give its' OA. Don't make this mistake.

● A lot of companies also hire through hackathons like Nomura, JPMC, Morgan Stanley, Adobe etc so keep an eye on them and practise development side by side.

Feel free to contact me for any queries Phone: +91 8600143101 LinkedIn

ALL THE BEST GUYS

1. OA round [ 92 appeared ]

Platform : HackerEarth Eligibility: CE and CSE, 7.5 CGPA cutoff . 21 MCQ questions were asked in 50 min, primary HTML CSS JS SQL CCN questions were asked. The test was proctored and offline. The questions were easy to medium level. If you have built projects using JS it would be a piece of cake and the entire test could be completed in 30 mins max. Accuracy matters over here for clearing the cutoff.

2. Machine Coding Round [ 11 shortlisted 7 appeared ]

It was conducted in Batches offline in the BrowserStack office in Oberoi Commerz 2. Due to the limited number of students they had confined a single batch for SPIT. The PS for the machine coding round is shared below:

This problem requires you to implement a log-watching solution (similar to the tail -f command in UNIX). However, the log file is hosted on a remote machine (same machine as your server code). The log file is in append-only mode. You need to implement the following:

● A server-side program to monitor the given log file and stream updates as they happen using Socket. IO for real-time communication. This will run on the same machine as the log file. You can use any programming language for the server.

● A web-based client (accessible via a URL like http://localhost/log) that displays updates in the file in real-time, without requiring a page refresh. The page should load once and keep updating. On initial load, the user should see the last 10 lines of the file. Problem Constraints:

● The server must push updates to clients in real-time using Socket. IO.

● The log file could be several GBs. How do you optimize retrieving the last 10 lines?

● The server should not retransmit the entire file every time; it should only send updates.

● The server must handle multiple clients simultaneously.

● The web page should not stay in a loading state after the first load and should not reload thereafter.

● You may not use off-the-shelf external libraries or tools to read the file or provide tail-like functionalities (except Socket. IO for real-time updates). You'll be evaluated on code quality, testability, modularity, and handling of corner cases.

The Machine coding round began at 10:30 AM and we were given roughly 2 hrs to build the backend server. You may find the solutions online, but an optimal solution that caters to the edge cases of the invigilator is preferred. You are not allowed to use any AI agents or LLMs or medium articles during this round, our invigilator was right beside us. You may refer to the documentation for development. You can interact with the invigilator during the round. Primary goal is to develop the solution using Socket. IO , I preferred NODE for the backend and socket implementation to display logs realtime with a confined Buffer to prevent parsing the logs. The invigilator would test it on multiple edge cases, like real time parsing, multiple browser compatibility with realtime logs and order in which they appear or cases where '\n' appears while parsing logs. If it passes all the cases and you are able to explain your code really well then you would be moved forward to the next round.

3. Director Of Engineering Round [ 3 shortlisted ]

For preparation you may go through medium or GFG articles. Mine was an interesting one, I was the only one who had an online interview with the Senior Director in the office for 30 mins. He read my resume and given that I had worked with a corporation with exposure to multiple hacks and techstacks, was exempted from basic questions. I was asked about one of my favourite projects and what role did I play in that project. Then moved on to internship experiences, what tasks did I perform in Russell Investments as Summer Intern, what project did I work on. He asked if I had exposure to Prod and deployment which I explained pretty well. I was quickly moved to behavioral questions like how will I tackle Deadlines, How will I deal with my teammate who differs in an opinion. It was the most fun director round.

All the 3 received the offer.

journey.prep:
1. Prepare for Quantitative Analysis and Aptitude: For companies like KPMG, aptitude and quantitative analysis play an important role. Practice regularly on platforms like GeeksforGeeks, IndiaBix, or other competitive aptitude sites. Time management is crucial, so focus on both accuracy and speed.

2. Resume: o Use a clean and professional format, such as a LaTeX template. o Keep your resume ATS-friendly to increase the chances of being shortlisted. o Be precise and impactful: describe your projects in 2-3 points each, and quantify your achievements wherever possible. Numbers and results stand out. o Prepare your resume thoroughly from start to finish: Make sure you are familiar with every detail, description, and word mentioned in it, so you can confidently discuss any aspect during the interview. Being well-versed with your own resume shows professionalism and

helps you answer questions accurately and convincingly. Parnika Das Resume

3. Internship and Work Experience: From my observation, candidates with some form of internship experience tend to have an advantage, especially in technical rounds. Even part-time internships or summer projects provide real-world exposure and talking points for interviews. This is not a strict rule, but it definitely helps strengthen your profile. (It helped me a lot to stand out)

4. Strengthen CS Fundamentals and DSA: Prepare both the theory and coding aspects of computer science. This includes: o Data Structures & Algorithms (DSA) o Computer Science fundamentals like Operating Systems, DBMS, Networking, etc. o Solve as many coding questions as you can. Do the questions on your own, and if you are not able to do it, learn it from any explanation video and do it by yourself. Follow the Strivers' sheet or Leetcode Top Interview 150. And for SQL, you can solve LeetCode SQL 50. o Practising coding problems regularly will build confidence for technical interviews.

5. Communication is Key: Your ability to communicate effectively is often the first impression you make. Clear and confident communication can give you a significant edge over other candidates. Practice introducing yourself, explaining your projects, and discussing your experiences concisely and engagingly.

6. Maintain Confidence and Positivity: o Keep a smile on your face during interviews. o Show confidence without arrogance. (Most Important) o Put in the effort to make a strong impression on the interviewer.

7. Academic Performance Helps: A good academic record (preferably 7.5 GPA or above) adds weight to your profile. However, academics alone are not enough - balance it with projects, internships, and skills.

8. Early and Consistent Preparation: o Start placement preparation as early as possible. o Maintain a healthy balance between studies, skill-building, and personal life. o Consistent effort beats last-minute cramming. o

9. Resilience and Patience: Placement journeys are rarely smooth: o At first, you may struggle with clearing online assessments. o Even after clearing OA rounds, you might get rejected in interviews. o Sometimes, rejection happens even after the HR round, which can be heartbreaking. Key: Don't lose hope. Hard days are part of the journey, and persistence is what separates success from failure. Give your 100% in every attempt, but also accept that luck plays a great role.

10. Believe in Yourself: o Put in your best effort. o Keep improving, learning, and refining your skills. o Stay motivated, even when facing setbacks.

My Overall Placement Experience

I started my journey by attempting several Online Assessments (OA), which were initially challenging. Gradually, as I improved my speed and accuracy, I began clearing OAs after 5 tests or something, but then faced rejections in interview rounds. In one process, I was even rejected after the HR round, which was very disheartening. During my interviews, I focused on presenting my projects, internships, and experiences clearly, highlighting the technologies I worked with, challenges I faced, and how I resolved them. I made sure to stay confident, smile, and communicate effectively, which helped me leave a positive impression. I practised quantitative aptitude, DSA, and CS fundamentals rigorously and maintained a decent academic record alongside internships and projects. I also asked thoughtful questions about the role and career growth, which left a strong impression on the interviewers. Despite the ups and downs, I learned to stay persistent, balance preparation with personal life, and give my best in every attempt . Receiving the Letter of Intent from KPMG was the culmination of all the hard work, and the experience was truly unique compared to my peers. I believe the key takeaways were patience , consistency, preparation, and belief in oneself.

All the Best!!!

The selection process for the Analyst - Tech Enablement Role (KPMG 2nd Role) was officially announced on 3rd September 2025. Initially, it was mentioned that the process would include an Online Assessment (OA), followed by a Group Discussion, two Technical Rounds, and one HR Round. However, the Group Discussion round was later cancelled, and the process moved directly to the Technical Interviews after the Pre-Placement Talk. Our process took place online from college.

1. [Online Assessment Test] [ About 20 candidates for second role only]

The Online Assessment (OA) was held on 8th September 2025 and was of easy to medium difficulty. It mainly focused on Quantitative Analysis, along with other aptitude -based questions. It consisted of 55 questions with 3 sections being Aptitude, Quantitative Analysis and Verbal Ability. The test was for 40 minutes only. It was proctored with camera access and full -screen mode enabled, ensuring a monitored and fair evaluation environment. Each question required proper calculations, logical thinking, and step -by-step solving; there were no simple one-word or direct MCQ-type questions. It required quick problem -solving skills as the time limit was quite tight. Both speed and accuracy played a crucial role in performing well in the assessment. It was conveyed that those who applied for the first role and cleared the test of the first role were allowed to sit for the second round directly if they applied.

2. [Technical round 1] [ 14 candidates]

After the announcement, the process began with a brief online Pre -Placement Talk (PPT) conducted jointly with SPCE students (their offer and role were different). The session was quite informative, covering details about KPMG as an organisation, what the firm does, its service lines, work culture, and the type of work we would be involved in. They also explained that the role would include client interactions, analytical work,

and frequent travelling as part of on-site engagements. Following the PPT, the Group Discussion round was skipped, and the process moved directly to the Technical Interviews. A total of 14 candidates were shortlisted and divided into two panels, with 7 candidates in each. The interviews were conducted online through Microsoft Teams, with each slot spaced approximately 20 minutes apart. The overall process was well-organised and smooth, giving candidates ample time to prepare between rounds. I was the first candidate to be interviewed in my panel. The interviewer began the conversation in a friendly manner by asking how I was doing, which helped ease the initial nervousness. He then asked me to introduce myself, following which he requested me to give a brief overview of my work experiences. Since I had three prior work experiences, including one at Amazon India, he showed particular interest in understanding the kind of projects I had worked on. He went in-depth about my responsibilities, the technologies I was introduced to, and how I managed and contributed to each project. We discussed the challenges I faced, the problem-solving approaches I used, and the overall learning outcomes from each role. My interview didn't follow the typical question-answer format; instead, it felt more like an engaging discussion about my experiences and professional journey. The interviewer seemed genuinely interested in understanding how I applied my knowledge in real-world scenarios, which made the interaction quite comfortable.

After discussing my work experiences, the interviewer moved on to ask about my academic background. He asked me what subjects I had learned during my computer engineering course and what I was currently exploring. I mentioned that I was learning about emerging technologies like Cloud Computing and Blockchain, which naturally led to a deeper conversation about new advancements in technology. He seemed interested and asked me which of the latest technologies fascinated me the most and why, along with a few related follow-up questions. After that, he shifted the focus toward Computer Science fundamentals. He asked me about the different sorting algorithms I had explored and specifically questioned me on the difference between Bubble Sort and Merge Sort, discussing their time complexities and use cases. He also asked me to tell him the pseudo-code of the merge sort algorithm briefly. He then moved to Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) , asking me to explain the fundamentals , such as stacks and queues, along with their real-life applications. For instance, he gave examples like the undo-redo functionality in applications and how it relates to stack operations. He also asked me some OOPs fundamentals as well but not so much in depth. The discussion was quite interactive, as he appreciated the logical reasoning behind my answers and encouraged me to explain concepts in my own words.

Towards the end of the interview, he asked me if I had any questions for him. I took the opportunity to ask about the key responsibilities I would have as an Analyst at KPMG and also inquired about the career growth opportunities within the organization. He seemed particularly impressed by the second question, appreciating my curiosity about long-term development. He then explained both aspects in great detail , describing the nature of the work, the kind of projects analysts are involved in, and the structured growth path within KPMG. It was an insightful conclusion to the interview and gave me a clearer understanding of the role and the organization's work culture. He then ended the interview. The interview was around 45 minutes, so he didn't get to ask much about my other skills. He didn't ask about my projects and all. Other candidates were asked some other basic CS fundamental questions, hobbies, projects and basic DSA.

3. [Technical round 2] [ 6 candidates]

6 candidates were divided into 2 panels again.

In the second round, the interviewer in my panel focused primarily on my projects rather than my internship experiences. He began by asking me to introduce myself, and then I briefly mentioned my internships. After that, he delved deeper into my latest projects, asking me about how I implemented them, the tech stacks I used, the challenges I faced, and how I resolved them. I had four projects in total, and he specifically asked about my final year project as well as my first two projects -- one based on Kubernetes and the other on Machine Learning. He was keen to understand which projects were group projects and which were individual, and for the group projects, he wanted to know my specific contributions and how I coordinated with my team. The interview was relatively brief, lasting around 25 minutes, but it went well. Towards the end, he again asked if I had any questions. I asked about the kind of work an Analyst does and the typical career progression from Analyst to Associate Consultant, which he explained in detail. Unlike some other candidates, I was not asked about location preferences. Everything was going smoothly, and the interaction felt positive and engaging. Unfortunately, despite a good technical discussion, I did not get selected for the HR round.

4. [HR round]

The HR round was a brief 10-minute online meet that mainly covered basic HR questions. I was asked about my hobbies, strengths and weaknesses, and why they should hire me. The conversation felt largely formal in nature, serving more as a procedural step rather than a detailed interview. Shortly after this call, I received my Letter of Intent from KPMG. Overall, this experience was quite different from what my peers and friends went through, making it a unique and memorable process.

Out of these 4 candidates from the HR round, 3 were sent a Letter of Intent and 1 candidate from the technical round 2 (that was me) was also sent a letter of intent.

1. Pre Placement Talk (Microsoft Teams): 10-07-2025 from 11.30am - 12.30pm

2. Online Assessment(Hackerrank): 10-07-2025 from 1.30pm- 3.30pm .

3. Interview Rounds (SPIT Campus): 14-07-2025

1. Online Assessment [Everyone who applied]

There was an OA round ofc, but for the finalists of the UBS India Campus Hackathon, they were directly exempted from the UBS campus placement online assessment and advanced straight to the interview round. I was also exempted from the OA round due to this. Participating in the hackathon not only helped us connect with amazing peers and mentors but also gave me valuable insights into real-world problem-solving and what companies like UBS look for in candidates. If you ever get such opportunities, DO NOT MISS IT, being a winner of this hackathon gave me an edge in every interview I faced afterward.

For those who had to take the OA, it consisted of aptitude questions, MCQs on core CS fundamentals (like predicting code outputs), and one key coding problem. The coding questions varied--some received complex ones like greedy or 3D DP, while others got easier two-pointer problems. We had an OA round of exactly similar format during the hackathon selection process which shortlisted 11 people from the college for the hackathon at UBS offices. Clearing most of the test cases was critical, most shortlisted candidates passed nearly all, though a few made it with partial success too, via their good aptitude scores. So, performance mattered, but luck had its part as well.

2. Technical Round -1 [20 candidates were shortlisted]

We were asked to report to college by 9:00 a.m., with the interviews beginning around 10:30 a.m. My panel had 2 interviewers, one of them started with asking me about the problem statement i was given during the hackathon, and about the solution, I explained to him in detail about everything about the hackathon right from the start to end of the 24 hrs. Then since our solution consisted of an LLM, he asked me more about how would you ensure that the LLM gives correct answers? And asked why Gemini over other LLMs? He also inquired about OpenAI's Whisper model in depth since that was also being used in a lot of projects of mine. He then asked me how would you reduce the latency of Whisper for a large audio file to which I replied of an idea of dividing the audio file into various chunks and performing parallel processing (multithreading) on them to get the transcriptions in faster time. He was convinced about my solution.

Then the other panelist gave me a coding question on finding the longest palindromic substring -> https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-palindromic-substring/description/, this was a LC medium. I started with the brute force approach of recursively moving the 2 pointers and then memoizing it. She was satisfied with the approach and didn't ask for the most optimal one. After this I was asked some basic questions like why DSA in python and not other languages? To which my answer was clear that I had done everything from backend frameworks like Django, FastAPI to AI/ML, and had around 3+ YOE of using python. Lastly they also gave me a situation about how I would maintain data integrity in one of my projects.

After this the panelists asked if I had any questions. I asked them about how Agentic AI is being used and in what domains are UBS planning to do so. I also asked about reasons behind why their merger faced so many issues and how UBS plans to avoid those issues.

Note: For some candidates they took multiple technical interviews, while for some they took a technical & just an HR interview only

3. HR Round [10-11 candidates were shortlisted]

This was quite simple and straightforward unlike other HR interviews. She remembered my face during the hackathon as I was involved in the final pitch as well, so she didn't ask much about HR questions, rather a simple background check about my family and whether I am fine with relocation or not.

Tip: See, HR interviews may seem simple but you need to understand and play safe here, as this is also the round where you have a lot to lose. So don't take it lightly and be well prepared with your answers. Stick with a genuine smile throughout the interviews, so even if you make a

mistake, accepting that mistake with a smile would give a much better impression than pointlessly being fixated on that point.

6 students were offered the role and I was one of them.

1) Online Assessment Round:

The online assessment was conducted on the HackerRank platform, consisting of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes. The test covered a mix of topics including Computer Networks, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two coding problems based on Tree and Dynamic Programming (DP).

There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested basic to intermediate understanding of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical sections focused on logical reasoning and quantitative aptitude, including probability-based word problems and short analytical puzzles.

The good part was that we got to attempt the test online from home since it was raining heavily that day, which definitely reduced some stress. Overall, the OA was moderately difficult. The key was to maintain speed while balancing accuracy across both the technical and reasoning sections.

IMPORTANT NOTE: We had given OA for the Associate Application Developer, and we weren't told that the selection for Associate Consultant would be taken according to this OA result. So if you are giving the test for Associate Application Developer then give it 100%.

2) Technical Round I : [27 students were selected for the technical interview]

The interview started after a PPT presentation from Oracle at around 12:00 PM.

We had 6 panelists and I was in the 1st 6 group. So I was taken to the room where my panelist was sitting. As soon as I entered the room, The interviewer stood and walked towards me to

greet me with a FIRM handshake (i have emphasized firm because it is important as it shows how confident you are). After all the greetings, he asked me about how my day was, and frankly speaking that day we had our MSE and we had just given our test and came for the interview. So I told the interview about it, and he talked about it for almost 5-10 mins about my day.

After this casual conversation, he asked me which programming language I was comfortable with. I told him I was comfortable with c++. So he firstly asked me the difference between for and while loop, is there any difference. I answered the way he wanted and then he asked me to print numbers between 5 and 10 using a while loop. I wrote the code directly and explained it to him. Then he gave me two strings, one with all capital letters and another string with the same letter but a mixture of small and capital letters, and asked me to return true if the string matched or return false if it didn't. There was no restriction in using the in-built function of the language. So I simply used the direct string comparison. Then he modified the question that he wanted two equal strings even though they have different ascii values to return true while comparing. Here I used the in-built function of string to capitalize the whole letter in both the string and then compared it. While coding he wanted me to include a try-catch function for any error handling, but I hadn't revised that topic so I honestly told him that I hadn't revised the error handling section but I explained how error handling would work if included. He was satisfied with my answer.

My interviewer then shifted to the DBMS topic and gave me 2 questions to solve.

1. Two table i.e. The Train and Destination table was given to me and he had asked me to find the cost of all the trains that stop and start from Mumbai. So this question was easy, we just had to join two tables and use the where clause to find the answer.

2. Same two tables and was asked the train with the highest travel time.

Later he asked me about all the projects I had done. He asked me whether the projects done were individual projects or not. All the projects I had mentioned were all group projects. As it was all a group project, he asked me what exactly my role was in each project and what was the purpose of our group choosing those topics for our project. And with these questions my interviewer concluded with the interview and asked me whether I had any question for him. I had asked him about his role in OFSS and asked him what role we would play in the company as a fresher.

So I was interviewed for almost 40 min and the interview ended on a good note.

NOTE: Don't throw things randomly on the resume and even while answering the question asked by the interviewer as it would lead to many follow up questions related to it and if you couldn't answer those questions it would affect your result. So be HONEST and give the interview with confidence, it's ok if you are unable to answer the question, you can tell the interviewer that you are unable to recall the concept, but would be able to tell it once revised. HONESTY and CONFIDENCE is the key for any successful interview.

2) Technical Round 2: [ around 20 students appeared for it]

After my round 1 interview, nearly 15 min later i was asked to be ready for round 2 interview. I was taken to the room for round 2 and the interviewer greeted me and immediately started with the interview.

The Interviewer asked me to explain one of my AIML projects in detail. He wanted me to explain the whole project in such a way that i am explaining it to a non tech background person. So I started with a brief description about my project and then dived deeper into the explanation about the models that I had used. I systematically explained to him how the system architecture looks like and works. He was satisfied with the explanation, then he moved on to my Web project. He asked me about the purpose of choosing a book reading website and what new features were added in comparison to the inspired website. So I explained to him about the project and the purpose of the project along with what new features we had added.

Then he started to ask me about the techstack that i had worked on and why those techstack were used. He later grinded me upon the programming language that I had written on the resume. He first asked me to write a code to open a file and read the file in python language. Before i started with writing the code i asked him a follow up question of what type of file does he want me to read, he gave me the benefit of doubt to use any file type. So I used a CSV file as the input file to be read, and I wrote the code in python. I used pandas to read the file and show the content of the file. After this he started with OOPS questions, he asked me to explain encapsulation, overloading and overriding.

My interviewer then shifted to DBMS and asked me a question where I had to use JOIN and GROUP BY to solve the question. So basically most of the round people are being asked questions related to JOIN and Clauses. So focus on these topics and practice it.

After this i was asked a guesstimate question where i want to find the fastest route and mode of transport from my house to my college. He gave me the benefit of doubt to choose any method or electronic device to find out the optimal route and transportation. I answered the question using google maps, so hi follow up question how would you choose the transportation. My answer for guesstimate could have been wrong or not, but I explained what I know and concluded with the interview.

NOTE: As you can see in this round it was mostly about my resume, so it would be best for you to know what you are writing on your resume, whether you actually know it or not, before interview LEARN EVERYTHING IN YOUR RESUME so that whatever you are asked from your resume you able to answer it properly.

This round also took around 45-50 min to conclude.

Round 3 : HR round : [ Around 12 students appeared for it]

The HR round was more of a formality. The HR asked a few basic questions such as my nationality, hobbies, and whether I was satisfied with the compensation offered. She also asked if I had any questions for her, to which I responded with two simple queries related to the company culture and growth opportunities.

After this round, there was a short waiting period of around 45 minutes while the panel discussed the results. Finally, the results were announced -- 12 students were selected for the role, including 6 from MCA and 6 from B.Tech.

Everything you mention should highlight how effective and valuable you can be for the company. After introducing myself, the interviewer asked me which programming language I was most proficient in. I said Java, as it's my favorite language and I usually solve coding problems in it.

She then asked me a few OOPs questions -- what is Abstraction, Polymorphism, why one should learn Java, and why Java is platform-independent. Since we had prepared well for topics like Collections Framework and Multithreading (as Oracle often asks these), I was confident. Next, she asked why I had chosen MongoDB for my projects. I had mentioned both MongoDB and MySQL in my resume, so I explained my choice based on schema flexibility and scalability, describing how MongoDB scales both horizontally and vertically. I also added that relational databases are equally important because they follow ACID properties, ensuring data integrity and security. She seemed very happy with this answer.

She then asked about the machine learning algorithms I had used in my projects. One of the questions was to explain Naïve Bayes, which I had used during the initial phase of my project. I didn't give a detailed example but explained how it works and why it's effective.

Tip: If you've implemented any functionality, make sure you understand the high-level flow, how you implemented it, and how it actually works in the backend.

Later, she asked a few questions on Authorization and Authentication, including how JWT (JSON Web Token) works.

After that, she moved on to two basic DSA questions:

Swap two numbers without using a third variable.

Reverse a string.

For on-campus interviews, string-related questions are very common, so make sure to prepare linear data structures thoroughly.

Finally, she asked some basic SQL questions -- definitions and the differences between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP commands. Some questions about View how does data in view table get updated even it does not support DML

After that, my interview concluded.

2) Technical Round 2: [ around 20 students appeared for it]

Round 2 began with a quick greeting, and the interviewer immediately moved to a DSA question, asking for the solution in Java. The problem was: given an array of strings, convert all elements into camel case and then sort them based on the first character of each element. I wrote the complete solution, explained my approach, and he seemed satisfied with my explanation. After that, he asked two simple SQL questions -- one on LEFT JOIN and another on a basic aggregate function. I solved both queries and also mentioned that if a similar question appeared, I could handle it using the GROUP BY clause.

Afterward, he reviewed my resume and asked me to elaborate on any one of my projects that I could explain well. I confidently replied that I could explain any of the three projects mentioned in my resume, so he asked me to choose one. I described the project in detail, and he didn't interrupt or cross-question, indicating that my explanation was clear.

He then asked a few personal questions -- where I was from and about my role as the Point of Contact for the Alumni and Mentorship Program at SPIT. My advice is to answer such non-technical questions smartly. You can add a touch of personality or humor to make the conversation more engaging and reduce nervousness. Interviewers usually appreciate candidates who are not only technically strong but also have good communication and interpersonal skills.

For me, this approach worked really well -- the interviewer became more comfortable, and our interaction felt natural. We both enjoyed the conversation, and overall, the second round went very smoothly for me.

Round 3 : HR round : [ Around 12 students appeared for it]

The HR round was more of a formality. The HR asked a few basic questions such as my nationality, hobbies, and whether I was satisfied with the compensation offered. She also asked if I had any questions for her, to which I responded with two simple queries related to the company culture and growth opportunities.

After this round, there was a short waiting period of around 45 minutes while the panel discussed the results. Finally, the results were announced -- 11 students were selected for the role, including 6 from MCA and 5 from B.Tech.

journey.howSecured:
The process consisted of 3 rounds 1 Test and 2 technical rounds. The Entire process including interviews was online.

1. Technical and Aptitude Test

The round had a mix of technical and aptitude questions, with a total duration of about 90 minutes. It was a proctored test and divided into three sections: Aptitude, DSA, and SQL. All the questions were MCQ-based, so no actual coding was required.

For the aptitude part, the questions were pretty standard--quant, reasoning, and problem-solving type. Practicing from Indiabix is more than enough. I'd suggest taking timed mock tests, because I personally lost a few easy marks just due to time running out :(

The DSA section had MCQs on topics like BSTs, AVL Trees, Merge Sort, time complexities, and guess-the-output questions. Nothing too unexpected, but you need your basics really clear. GeeksforGeeks (GFG) is the best prep source here.

Finally, the SQL section was entirely Oracle SQL based. Lots of questions on joins, subqueries, aggregate functions, etc. If you're comfortable with writing and analyzing queries, you'll be fine

Overall, it was a balanced test--no coding, just solid concepts and quick thinking.

2. Technical Interview I [ 40 - 50 mins]

here were two interviewers, and the interview began with a quick introduction where I had to talk about myself and my general hobbies. After that, they asked me about the programming languages I was comfortable with, and I said Python. From there, the discussion moved to OOPs concepts in Python. They asked me to share my screen and write a simple Car class with a few objects. Then they followed it up with questions on types of constructors and some magic methods I had used. They specifically asked about the use of __new__ and __call__ methods.

Next, I got a string parsing question where I had to convert data into a list of dictionaries. The problem was straightforward, and I felt communication skills played a big role in explaining my thought process clearly.

They also gave me a SQL question where I had to calculate the average ratings for a movie using two tables with joins. After that, there was a question on data warehousing concepts, which I wasn't familiar with and I straight away said I dont know it.

The interview wrapped up with a few questions about BlackRock as a company and why I was interested in working there.

3. Technical Interview II [16 Students ][30-40 mins]

This round had one senior interviewer who handled all the questions. He began with a quick introduction and even asked me to recall who had taken my Round 1, which I honestly couldn't remember .

Next, he went through all the projects from my resume and asked about the tech stack used. Since the role was for Data Engineering and most of my projects were in ML/Data Science, he wanted to know why I still felt I was a good fit.

After that, he asked me how to store a polynomial and gave around 5-6 SQL queries verbally. I requested to share my screen and solve them on notepad, and he was fine with that.

He then moved on to questions about RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) and asked if I was comfortable with it. Towards the end, the questions shifted to my daily use of AI, and he wrapped up by asking a thought-provoking one: "Why hire people when AI can already generate code?"

journey.prep:
This was the 7th company I interviewed for, so from all my rejection experiences here's what not to do:

1. You don't need to shoehorn technologies that you're barely familiar with into your resume. It's not even about honesty--most of the time it just does more harm than good. I've seen people with HTML/CSS projects in their resume get into elite companies. A lot of interviews only test your computer fundamentals and whether you know the things you're claiming to know. So keep your resume simple and limited to things you are sure about, because you'll only make things harder for you by putting in things you don't know.

2. It's not a viva, so don't just answer--explain. For example, if they ask you about foreign keys, don't just give them the definition. Tell them what it is, why you use it, how you use it, and maybe throw in an example if you can. The more you talk, the fewer questions they'll ask.

3. In Interviews only you know what your project is so if they ask u to explain it dont start throwing technical jargon immediately. Tell them what your project does and its features first and only get technical if they specifically ask you to.

4. It took me an embarrassing number of interviews to realize sometimes I speak really fast, so the person I'm talking to doesn't even understand what I'm saying. In interviews, don't rush. Speak slowly and clearly, and give mock interviews to your friends so they can help you fix simple mistakes like these.

As for what to do, GFG is good for all the core subjects and check out top 20 puzzles on GFG, a lot of companies ask questions from that. Remember examples for OOPs and DBMS concepts.

Placements are a tough time for everyone. Don't start panicking or get demotivated after rejections just keep applying and trying your best.
journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [ Around 90 Students Appeared ]

The Round Consisted of 4 Sections Logical Aptitude, Quantitative Aptitude, Coding and Verbal Section Everyone had 2 different coding questions and the difficulty was pretty random. Some got really easy hashset or hashmap questions and some got hard dp questions. I got a simple array question where i had to add the elements from alternate indexes and this leetcode.com/problems/maximum-number-of-weeks-for-which-you-can-work/

2. Technical Round 1 [Around 30 students appeared in this round ]

There were two interviewers for every panel. In my interview I was asked to introduce myself and then the panel first asked me about my projects, focusing mainly on the idea and what it does rather than the technical details. Since one of them was a blockchain project, they asked how I verified users in it and that was the only technical question I was asked related to my projects.

Then the discussion moved to OOPs. They asked me what is oops and then asked about encapsulation, polymorphism and to write code for method overriding. They asked me the difference between final, finally and finalize in Java. After that, I was asked to write code to print prime numbers from 1 to 100. I gave the brute-force solution, and was prepared to give the optimal answer if they asked but they didn't ask me to optimize further.

One interviewer then asked about AI, ML, and DL, and how I would approach building a chatbot for student queries. I tried explaining, but wasn't doing a good job so they told me it was fine if I didn't know. They actually first asked me if I knew AI and I thought they meant like in general so i said yes. I didn't have any AIML projects on my resume. If they ask you if you know smth that is not on your resume, try to clarify what they mean and it's okay to accept that it's not your strong suit. But only if it's not on your resume.

Then I was asked to rate myself in SQL, explain normalization, and give an example. I created a table and applied 1NF, and they said that was enough. I was asked about joins and they also asked me to write a query to find the top 10 students with the highest marks.

They gave me the Lion, Goat, and Grass puzzle, which I already knew, but I clarified the rules before explaining the solution.

Towards the end, I was asked about a challenge I faced in my project, so I shared how I resolved a feature issue in my major project. Finally, I asked the interviewers about their roles and whether there was anything I should start learning that would help me if I joined TransUnion. They suggested a few technologies they use at TransUnion.

3. HR round [ 10 Students appeared in this round ]

There were two interviewers in this round too. The round started with my introduction and then they asked me to explain my projects, again, focusing only on the idea and features, and then asked what was unique about one of them. I was also asked about the technologies I'm familiar with and whether I had any cloud experience. I honestly told them I know the basics but don't have practical experience. They then asked what I knew about TransUnion and if I recognized them from the PPT. I remembered their names from the session but not their roles. Other questions included my family background, willingness to relocate, challenges I faced in college, and whether I had worked on team projects and dealt with conflicts.

At the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked the same thing, if there was anything I could start learning now that would help me at TransUnion, and they gave me some useful advice. Since the PPT had mentioned a budget for learning and certifications, I asked about that and that concluded the round.

8 students got the offer in the end.

journey.prep:
OA's: Brute force almost always works. And every minute is valuable. Code up the brute force, see if it runs. Probably will. And don't get intimidated by how many leet problems other people have done. On-campus OA's are easy. Don't need to be a specialist on cf to solve them. But if you have:

- A year before placements: do give as many cf contests as you can. They teach you how to think. I;m not saying rank push. But get yourself to a spot where you can solve div 2 A and B always, and C at least half the time.

- Or if you have very few months before placements and you don't have a single leet problem. Do top interview 150, then some 10-20 random medium/hards, and you're good to go tbh. But do all of them like they haven't been solved yet. Think till you either come up with the solution or are weeping profusely. I could clear 2 out of 3 OA's with that prep level, but your batch could be stronger than ours so work relative to that.

Some life advice no one asked for:

- If I could go back in time I'd be more consistent for longer durations in my DSA journey, and wouldn't stop giving CF contests for hackathons. I didn't evaluate my strengths correctly and let peer pressure guide me to a path that wasn't made for me. Don't make that mistake. You won't get a chance to try everything, so only let your judgement guide you. Whether you wanna win hacks, or contribute to open source, or do internships, or build creative projects, or be a competitive coder. Give your all at whatever you pick. Don't do what your friends are doing. Pick friends that are doing what you want to do. Oh and don't be a phoney. Only pick the CS journey if you're passionate about it. If you're not and you still have to pick it, then convince yourself that you're passionate about it. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Technical Interviews: Doesn't happen often but being a jack of all trades actually helped me in this round. I was able to answer any questions that came up, in terms of tech stack. I was asked a lot of questions about the various technologies I'd used, from common ones like React, Springboot, Node to relatively eccentric ones like Vue and Go. If they aren't in your resume, you won't be asked about them. But if they are, and you can answer the questions, that leaves an impression because it shows your passion.

For interviews my advice will always be to stop preparing answers. Ad lib. Improvise. Read books, watch shows, interact more, touch grass, IDK whatever you need to do. But hey, what do I know? Whatever suits you in your opinion is probably better for you than what I can tell :) Also sorry for making this IE this long goddamn. And also for the shite formatting lol.

Lastly, don't be stressed about placements. It's better to feel less happy when you're finally placed, than to feel more sad every time you're rejected. So walk into your first test assuming it'll take 50 more of these before you're finally placed. Make these tests/interviews feel like a chore, not a burden. Also get CTC out of your mind. You young as hell. Think about the work you'll get to do, that's way more important.

All the best y'all!

Feel free to connect and ask questions; Linkedin haters, hmu on whatsapp: 7718965798

Or let's play a game of chess!

Misc. (for EXTC peeps): This company does not have any implicit or explicit bias against us. I'm not saying others do, but I can say for sure that this one doesn't. It's a good opportunity. Just make sure they get to know you're truly passionate about CS. Reach out and connect with me any time, and I will help you out to the best of my capabilities. Some companies don't allow EXTC, some don't allow pointers less than 8. But just know that it's all the same when you finally get a shot. Good luck guys.
journey.howSecured:
1. OA [No CGPA criteria AFAIK so everyone was eligible to sit for the OA]

The OA was a coding test, 75 minutes in duration. There were 2 coding/DSA problems and an SQL problem. The coding problems were both pretty basic and brute force would usually pass for all. I used Python. And I'd recommend using it if you haven't started with any language yet, because I think it's faster to type out :)

○ Problem 1: There's a keypad. Each key takes a certain amount of time to press every time you press it. Input is a list of integer pairs like [[0,2], [1,6], [3,8], [2, 4], …]. Here, [0,2] means 'a' took 2 seconds to be pressed and so on. So all letters (keys) are 0 indexed starting from 'a'. The output should be the letter of the key that had the maximum pressing time. I just created a pair ret = [-inf, -inf], and traversed the input, let's call the current pair cur, and whenever cur[1] > ret[1], set ret = cur. In the end just return the character associated with ret[0].

○ Problem 2: Input is a string. This string's various substrings contain multiple permutations of the word "programmer" as subsequences. The task is to find the number of letters between the first and last such substring. For example:

"rgtscmpxmrreoqwiqwrgmttpmrreoa"

Here, the highlights are the first and last such substrings in the given string and answer is 6. (oqwiqw).

Many ways to solve this.

- Brute Force: Create a frequency map of the string "programmer". Now traverse the input string, and starting from each index, traverse ahead while building a temporary frequency map of this traversal. The first time this temp map becomes equal to our og freq map, store the final index of the current traversal. The last time that happens, store the first index of the final traversal. Then subtract both and add 1 and return.

- That's O(n^2) but coding it up took like 10 minutes. Rather I could have just done the above starting from the first index first, then reverse the input string and do it from the

first index again, and store the final index of both, fix the reversed index, subtract, add 1.

○ Problem 3: Given 2 tables, States, and Votes. The Votes table has the votername, state voted for. Return, for each state, a comma separated concatenated string of name of voter, and number of votes given, in the same cell. Example output:

state votes

Texas John Doe x 2, Jane Doe x 8, …

California Tyler Durden x 6, Jack x 9, …

Simple problem, but you have to remember the aggregate function's name that concatenates strings over the table. Logically it should be called something like agg_str() or str_agg() as it is in Postgres, but it is GROUP_CONCAT() in MySQL. This was given in the previous experiences but I guess I'd missed it. Don't make that mistake. Go through each and every single previous year experience from '24, '25 and this year's. They're the most efficient revision you'll get.

41 people were shortlisted. All solved at least the 2 coding problems. I'm guessing there was a time cut-off of 40-50 minutes max.

2. Technical Interview L1 [ 41 people ]

This round, for me, was just DSA questions with a few introductory questions about my projects and internships. As I entered, the first thing I was asked was the full form of MSCI. I got the last word wrong. He said "It's International! You should at least know this much bro!" and we laughed about it. Then he asked me what problems were there in the OA. I briefed him on shorter versions of the questions and explained how I solved them. He then apologized for jumping directly to questions and we introduced ourselves to each other. He was excited for the process and ended up taking a good 5 minutes introducing himself. I'd recommend developing the skill of ad libbing answers to these questions. Preparing "scripts" for intros, personal questions, even project questions kills your flow and the interview's vibe. It's meant to be a fun conversation. Don't make it boring or dull for the interviewer or yourself. I took my time, introduced myself, my internships and projects in depth for about 5-10 minutes.

He started asking DSA questions. The first one was how to check if there are cycles in an undirected graph. I know. Simple af. I didn't understand at first and misunderstood that it was directed and started explaining a topo sort approach (Kahn). He then said "it could be directed or undirected". And then my brain froze up. I got really confused and just could not think at all anymore. If that happens, drink some water or something to give your brain time to get back to normal. He saw me being confused af and he was like aight let's move on. He then asked how to get the top view of a binary tree (horizontal difference). Then right/left view (bfs). Then a matrix problem, a spin on the "number of ways to get from top left to bottom right cell of a matrix" problem (simple 2d dp). So all the dsa problems were very basic. When you get something wrong, be graceful about it. I was very surprised that I got selected for the next round.

He then asked me a little about my projects, and how I handled authentication in them, and how to do it without using a third party service. I replied "using JWT" and that building a middleware that verifies the JWT header was a viable solution. He inquired a bit about my knowledge of JWT. I told him whatever I knew about it.

He asked me whether I know what flexbox is. I described its usecase, and compared it to css grids which came later but are much cleaner for 2d layouts. I added that flex animates while grid doesn't. But I now think that wasn't completely true. He asked me whether I've ever written pure CSS. I said even while using bootstrap (which I did in an internship), we have to write pure CSS to style low level bootstrap components, so yes I have.

He then asked me why I want to pursue a career in software when I am from the EXTC branch. I just explained to him how I'd found the EXTC syllabus more interesting and why, before I took admission. But actually studying something and building projects based on that knowledge is very different from what its syllabus looks like on a table of contents. I frequently built IOT projects in my first year and worked with various microcontrollers like the ESP and STM32; Over time, I found myself more drawn to the coding side -- not just programming the microcontrollers, but also building client-facing software for those systems. That naturally pulled me deeper into core CS subjects, which I studied alongside my coursework. It wasn't an easy switch but I'm glad I made it, and now I have knowledge on both ends of the technology spectrum.

My interview went like a very interesting conversation you have with a friend. A lot of it was just him talking about his work at MSCI and me asking questions, or me talking about my internships and projects, both of which he found interesting. I'd frozen up on one question and still I was called for the next interview. Some people had answered all of theirs right and still weren't. It's a combination of the panel and your conversation skills. To be safe, get every question right. But if you don't, be graceful about your wrong answers. Make a joke about it. Keep the interview light and always keep a classy, genuine smile up throughout.

People were being called for the next round one by one as their reviews were coming in. I don't know the exact figure but I don't think more than 30 people got through.

3. Technical Interview L2 [ I think around 25-30 people probably got through]

Always walk in with a bright smile and a "how are you". Don't be a drag and just walk in and sit. Shake their hand. Lighten up the environment. Ask them about their day. The first thing I was asked this time was again the full form of MSCI. I said Morgan Stanley Capital International and was promptly shut down. "We don't have a full form". "Always the trick questions", I lamented jokingly and we laughed about it. He asked about my day and who my previous interviewer was. Then he opened his laptop and on it, my resume. (By the way, this round's interviews were taken by the Executive Directors of MSCI.)

He began by asking me to introduce myself. Then he asked me which project I would like to start with. I went with the first real-world project I'd ever built: Techrace. He opened the github repo. I'd drafted a nice ReadMe which he read through while I described it. I told him how I'd been part of the backend team of 2, and that Techrace is a location based treasure hunt, where clues are provided to players and they've to reach the locations, and there are powercards yada yada (I'm sure y'all know what it is). He

asked me what db we used. We used Firebase RTDB for real time streaming, and Firestore for static data. He asked me to describe the schema and the whole architecture. I took my time, about 5 minutes. He asked me why RTDB. I explained that team state, powercard timestamps, and location data are better stored in the RTDB. He asked me why. That data requires real time sync and it's a real time game, it needs lower latency; also rtdb has some offline support so I plugged that in. "So the client side application would read directly from the rtdb for some features?". Yep. "Isn't that unsafe?". It seems like there would be data inconsistencies, but the client was not allowed to write to the db, only read from it; and the reads would only be on non-critical data.

"Suppose I apply the freeze on a team, and at the approximately same time someone else applies the freeze on the same team. What happens?". I covered a piece of paper in the JSON schema of the application, the model of the powercard states, and the controller for powercard usage. I explained that using the async-mutex npm module, we create mutex states of each team stored in a js object in-memory. When the request to freeze team 007 comes from team 069, and it reaches the controller, Mutex.acquire() is called on the state of that team. When the request to freeze 007 then comes from team 420, if the lock is not released yet, the respective error object is thrown for the later request. He asked me to write the full code and I obliged. He asked which other tech on my resume has the mutex functionality. After a bit of thought, and mentioning Java for its semaphore functionality, I realized he was talking about golang.

"Very good. Now, what happens if there is a loading error and I click a powercard twice? How much of my balance will be deducted?". I explained that we couldn't handle concurrent requests in-game because of our lack of knowledge back then. "How would you do it?". I said I could create a similar object of lock states for the requestor. He found that to be smart but asked me to think further for a better solution. I said I could apply high precision rate limiting, or enforce time gaps between requests. "Gaps for erroneous requests can also vary". DB-level transaction control is offered by firebase. He questioned its thoroughness. I conceded I didn't know any more solutions. He revealed assigning UUIDs for each request from each user is the best way. Requests with the same UUID are erroneous.

He asked a few questions about the stack and what exactly my part was in the backend. I said I was doing the C of the MVC, aside from the error handling and frontend interfacing. We moved on to my next project, which was a pure Java based low latency stock exchange engine core, with a spring boot wrapper for the communication layer.

I explained to him the full architecture of the entire system. He asked me to jot down the db schema. I did. He asked me some questions about the schema. I answered them, but while I did I realized he was going deep into the database side of this project which was not the purpose of the project at all. I explained to him the purpose of the project was to replicate the structure and architecture of a real stock market engine core and use an object oriented approach for the prototype while also keeping it as low latency as possible. He then started asking me questions about the business logic once he realized the persistence layer mustn't be as well thought out whereby.

So no persistence? How do you process this very important data? In-memory. Using relevant data structures. So all the DSA knowledge doesn't go to waste. What data structures did you use?

So there will be 2 order books for each company, buy and sell. For price-time priority, each limit price will be stored in a sorted hashmap, specifically a TreeMap. And the orders at each price will be stored in a doubly linked list. Why TreeMap? What's a TreeMap? And he asked about its abstracted implementation. I explained the whole Map, Hashmap, SortedMap, TreeMap hierarchy, and it's built on Red-Black trees.

Why a doubly linked list for orders? Couldn't you use a- Yes I initially used a queue for it, but when I benchmarked the engine, order cancellation was a bottleneck. DLLs have faster removal. Sketch the OOP model I wrote down a summarizing code of how the whole system worked. While answering all of the above questions too, I'd been sketching detailed figures while explaining everything so he is on the same page the whole time.

Then, based on the rough ER diagram I'd drawn prior, he asked me a few questions. To simplify the only sorta challenging one: Tables: User (uId, uname, balance, holdings), Trades (tradeId, sellerId, buyerId, volume, price). Return the number of times I have sold and bought a set of stocks. I first misunderstood it such that I have to return that for every user. So I wrote a subquery that left joins User with Trades on uid = sellerid, and returns uname, count(tradeid) as sells. And I explained that a parent query can return the name, sells and buys. He explained he only wanted it for one user, which I said would just be a join and where clause for both buy and sell and he agreed. He said there's a much easier way to do this and that there's no time now but I should think about it. I said every time I've ever used a subquery, there's turned out to be much easier ways to do that task that made me facepalm. That made him laugh.

He then asked me about my internships, and asked me why I've only done ones in front-end roles. I said I got them based on the level of skills and knowledge I already had at the time, and I was much better at frontend technologies at the time of beginning them. He asked what the biggest obstacles had been for me on the technical and the professional side of my projects or internships, and how I'd overcome them.

He asked me if I had any questions for him. I asked him how long he's been with the company and how his experience has been. He didn't seem very interested in answering questions like these so I switched it up and asked him what type of work could I expect to be assigned if I were in his team. He said he has no idea what type of work is even assigned to immediate interns and we laughed a bit about that. The whole interview went perfectly. I think it could be the longest L2 interview of the day - it lasted for about 1.5 hours.

Around 9 candidates were selected for the HR round. I was probably the 4th. I was called in as soon as I came out of the interview.

3. HR Interview [9 candidates]

I was asked about my day till then, and how the rest of my interviews had been. I'll just list all the questions then a bit about my approach for answering them.

- About yourself and your family. Your hobbies.

- About yourself professionally.

- So many technologies in your project, why not stick to one.

- Have you worked in a team?

- Prefer working in a team or solo.

- Why xyz internship

- Extra curricular activities in college life?

- Our work hours can be off putting to some. Can you handle them?

- Prefer Mumbai or Pune?

- You trade, so will you be ok with the company telling you to stop because of our rules?

- What have been your biggest strengths and weaknesses throughout your professional life.

Be genuine, and explain with thorough examples. Your aim is to convince them of your answer's sincerity, not just tell them your answer.

Again, I can't stress this enough, smile.

5 people were offered the internship in the end.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
OA's: Brute force almost always works. And every minute is valuable. Code up the brute force, see if it runs. Probably will. And don't get intimidated by how many leet problems other people have done. On-campus OA's are easy. Don't need to be a specialist on cf to solve them. But if you have:

- A year before placements: do give as many cf contests as you can. They teach you how to think. I;m not saying rank push. But get yourself to a spot where you can solve div 2 A and B always, and C at least half the time.

- Or if you have very few months before placements and you don't have a single leet problem. Do top interview 150, then some 10-20 random medium/hards, and you're good to go tbh. But do all of them like they haven't been solved yet. Think till you either come up with the solution or are weeping profusely. I could clear 2 out of 3 OA's with that prep level, but your batch could be stronger than ours so work relative to that.

Some life advice no one asked for:

- If I could go back in time I'd be more consistent for longer durations in my DSA journey, and wouldn't stop giving CF contests for hackathons. I didn't evaluate my strengths correctly and let peer pressure guide me to a path that wasn't made for me. Don't make that mistake. You won't get a chance to try everything, so only let your judgement guide you. Whether you wanna win hacks, or contribute to open source, or do internships, or build creative projects, or be a competitive coder. Give your all at whatever you pick. Don't do what your friends are doing. Pick friends that are doing what you want to do. Oh and don't be a phoney. Only pick the CS journey if you're passionate about it. If you're not and you still have to pick it, then convince yourself that you're passionate about it. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Technical Interviews: Doesn't happen often but being a jack of all trades actually helped me in this round. I was able to answer any questions that came up, in terms of tech stack. I was asked a lot of questions about the various technologies I'd used, from common ones like React, Springboot, Node to relatively eccentric ones like Vue and Go. If they aren't in your resume, you won't be asked about them. But if they are, and you can answer the questions, that leaves an impression because it shows your passion.

For interviews my advice will always be to stop preparing answers. Ad lib. Improvise. Read books, watch shows, interact more, touch grass, IDK whatever you need to do. But hey, what do I know? W

1. Online Assesment Round: (36 questions, 120 minutes)

2. Technical Interview I

3. Technical Interview II
