1. Online Assesment Round:

The online assessment round was conducted on the HackerRank platform. It consisted of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes, covering topics from Computer Networking, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two DSA questions based on sliding windows and trees. The sliding window problem was easy, while the tree problem was of medium difficulty.

There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested the basics of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical questions focused on aptitude and logical reasoning, which included probability-based problems and short analytical puzzles.

We had to take the test from home due to heavy rainfall, which made it impossible to conduct the online assessment on campus that day. The overall difficulty level of the test was slightly higher. I was able to solve the sliding window question completely and the tree problem partially, along with most of the aptitude and core subject MCQs.

Note: This test was conducted for the OFSS Associate Application Developer role. Although I was not selected for the interviews for that position, OFSS returned a few days later to hire for the Consultant role. They shortlisted candidates based on the performance in the same test conducted

for the Developer role, and by God's grace, I was shortlisted. So, make sure to give your 100% in this test!

2. Technical Interview I:[ 27 students got selected for this round]

The interviews began soon after the pre-placement talk ended at around 12:00 p.m.

I was allotted to Panel 1, and I was the second candidate from my panel to be interviewed. As soon as I entered the room, the interviewer greeted me, offered me a seat, and asked me to introduce myself. After my introduction, he went through my resume and asked about the first project mentioned in it. He then questioned some of my technical choices, such as why I used JavaScript for the project, why I didn't use Next.js, and how I would convince him to use React instead of Next.js.

Since I had used a Sentence Transformer model in my project, he asked me whether I was familiar with NLP. I told him that NLP is one of my core subjects this semester. His focus then shifted to NLP-related questions -- he asked me about vectorization, tokenization, sentiment analysis, stopwords, and the difference between RAG and LLM. As I had my NLP mid-semester exam just two days earlier, I was confident and able to answer most of his questions well.

Then his focus shifted to DSA, and he gave me a question on valid anagrams to solve. I wrote the pseudocode for it on paper, and the interviewer seemed quietly satisfied with my approach. After that, he asked me to write code to sort a string, which I implemented using bubble sort.

Next, the discussion moved to DBMS and SQL. He asked me to write a query to find the second-highest salary, which I solved using subqueries. Then he asked for the average salary department-wise, which can be done using either GROUP BY or window functions--I chose to solve it using window functions. He further asked about the difference between SQL and NoSQL, how to optimize a database, and the difference between partitioning and sharding, as well as between vertical and horizontal partitioning.

He also questioned me about candidate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys. Since I had mentioned MongoDB in my technical section, he asked me how to fetch the second-highest salary using MongoDB.

After that, he moved to OOPs concepts and asked me to elaborate on the four pillars of OOPs with real-life examples. As my primary programming language is C++, he still asked whether multiple inheritance is supported in Java, along with some basic questions on memory management in Java.

He then shifted to React, asking about Hooks, followed by some basic questions on Postman, Thunder Client, Git, and GitHub.

At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions for him. I inquired about the type of work involved in the role and the training process. The entire round lasted for about 40-45 minutes.

Note: It is not necessary to give the correct answer to every question the interviewer asks. The key is to stay confident throughout. If you don't know the answer to a question, avoid directly saying "I don't know." Instead, try to relate the question to some relevant concepts and explain your thought process. If the interviewer is still not satisfied, you can politely say, "I'm not completely sure about this, but I'll definitely look into it."

3. Technical-Interview II [ Around 20 students got shortlisted for this]

For this round, I was the second candidate in my panel to be interviewed. This round was purely focused on databases and lasted for around 50-55 minutes. All the questions were based on SQL, MongoDB, and Database Management Systems (DBMS).

The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself, and then, similar to the first round, he asked me to explain my first project. He also asked me to design the schema of my project on paper. While designing, I explained my approach, discussed how I chose the primary keys, the cardinalities, and the relationships between tables.

After that, he asked me to write several SQL queries--around 7 to 8 in total--and I was able to solve all of them. There were also some output prediction questions. He asked me the difference between DROP, TRUNCATE, and DELETE commands, and in which scenarios DELETE is used. I explained that DELETE is used with the WHERE condition. Then he gave me the query DELETE FROM table; and asked whether it would work without a WHERE condition. I answered that it would work, but it would be slower than DROP since it deletes the rows one by one.

Next, he asked about ACID properties, deadlocks, and the types of SQL commands. I mentioned DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL. He then asked me to elaborate on TCL commands, and I explained COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT. He also asked a scenario-based question related to SAVEPOINT, which I was not completely sure about, so I politely told him that I was not very familiar with that concept.

Then he moved on to ask the difference between functions and procedures, gave me a query to write a trigger, and followed up with multiple questions on views, joins, aggregate functions, procedures, UNION, and UNION ALL. He also asked about cursors in databases--which I honestly didn't know--and several questions on indexing, including the difference between

clustered and non-clustered indexes, and whether indexing would be effective for a table with millions of rows, along with a few scenario-based questions.

I was able to answer most of the questions in this round, except for one or two. Overall, I was quite confident about my performance, and I was shortlisted for the HR round.

4. HR Round[ Around 12 students got shortlisted for this]

This round was more of a casual discussion and confirmation round, but I was quite nervous before it began. When I entered the room, the HR interviewer noticed my nervousness and kindly asked me to take a few deep breaths to relax.

He then asked me about my nationality, strengths and weaknesses, and my extracurricular activities. I mentioned that I enjoy playing and watching cricket. He asked me who my favorite cricket player was, and I said Virat Kohli. We spent the next 2-3 minutes discussing Virat Kohli's mindset and attitude, which made the conversation more engaging and comfortable.

This round lasted for about 7-8 minutes.

After the HR round, 12 candidates received job offers, and I was one of them.

There were a total of 3 rounds : OA Tech Interview Round HR round

They were all conducted on the same day - 5/08/25. Initially the criteria was 8.5 cgpa but then it was reduced to 7.5 cgpa. Preplacement talk was conducted on 4/08/25 at 5:00 pm. Make sure you pay attention to the PPT as it will help you to ask good questions to the interviewers. If you can't think of any good questions, take screenshots during the PPT if it is online and then you ask chatgpt to give some good and unique questions.

1. Online Assessment [ Around 150]

The OA consisted of four sections and it was taken on Google Form and there were a total of 70 Mcq questions to be done in 90 minutes. 1 mark was awarded for every correct question and 0.25 marks were deducted for every wrong answer.

Java (18 questions) The questions were mostly based on guess the output on topics which included multithreading, OOPS, enum, access modifiers, collection frameworks, interfaces, streams. Though my primary language was C++ and I knew the basics of Java, I thoroughly prepared for OOPs and a few advanced topics of Java . I tried to guess the output questions based on java from multiple sources on the internet.

Python(17 questions) The questions were based on topics like lists comprehension, stacks, OOPs, shallow and deep copies and on basic concepts. I prepared for python in a day and tried to solve as many questions as I could from the internet.

SQL(5 questions) There were queries based on Group by, Where, Joins, Order by and Delete. The options were very close to each other so read it carefully.

Aptitude (30 questions) The questions were based on topics like stocks, profit-loss, train problems, probability, permutation-combination, boat-stream problems, speed-distance.

Tips So for Aptitude I was left with only 32-35 mins as I spent much time in java and python and also started 10 mins late so I tried to solve only those questions that were easy in the first go and skipped the ones which I thought might be time consuming. So I would advise you to first just solve those questions which are easy and not waste your time solving the difficult ones as there might be questions ahead which can be solved in seconds and due to time constraints you might miss them.

For Java, prepare in depth and have a good understanding of java and do practice as many guess the output questions as possible.

2. [Techincal Round] [ 45 students (8 students in Testing)]

My interview began with the interviewer asking if my primary programming languages were Java and Python. I clarified that my strengths lie in Java and C++, and that I am not very well-versed in Python. This led to the follow-up question, "Then how did you clear the Python test in the morning?"

I answered honestly, explaining that I had researched the company's past interview patterns on Google and found that Python was frequently used in their tests. So, I prepared for it in advance--just enough to clear the assessment--while still having only a basic understanding of the language. I also mentioned that certain programming concepts, such as object-oriented programming (OOP), are similar across Java, C++, and Python.

He then asked me to elaborate on these similarities. I spoke about OOP concepts like encapsulation, polymorphism, overloading, and overriding. The conversation shifted to access modifiers, where I initially forgot to mention "default" but quickly remembered and explained all four in detail.

Next, he asked questions about my projects. Since two of my projects were built using Flutter with Firebase, he wanted to know why I chose Flutter as my tech stack and why Firebase was my database of choice. He also asked why I didn't use React Native, given its similarities to Flutter. I realized the importance of being ready to justify tech stack decisions, so I explained my reasoning clearly.

He then moved to my third project, which was based on the MERN stack. Here, he asked why I used MongoDB, what specific problem my project was solving, and why I chose React. He also asked me to explain JWT authentication. So I explained its three parts in detail and he asked me scenarios like handling invalid tokens.

From there, the questions expanded to cookies--what they are, how they work, and how I implemented them in my project. Since my project also used WebSocket, he asked a few technical questions on that as well. I noticed a pattern: most of his questions were based on what I had mentioned in my answers, which made me realize the importance of only bringing up topics I could discuss confidently.

The technical section also included a DSA question based on strings. The problem was to count the number of words that are the same in a given substring. Initially, I was a little confused because of the word "substring," so I asked for an example to clarify. Once I understood, I confirmed my approach with him, then provided a HashMap-based solution, which he approved. I wrote the solution in C++ on paper, and he later asked me to traverse the map in a different way, which I did successfully.

He then tested my database knowledge by asking which databases I was familiar with. I mentioned SQL, MongoDB, and Firebase. This led to an SQL query question involving two tables with a common attribute id. He wanted me to update the category column in table1 with values xyz only for rows where the id was present in both tables. My first query was a bit complex, so he asked me to simplify it, which I managed to do.

He also asked HTTP status codes and basic API concepts--first the full form of API, then how it works.

At one point, he paused the technical discussion and invited me to ask questions. I asked about the merger between ISS and STOXX and how it affected the company. He explained and then he mentioned that now they are shifting from Angular to React. I followed up by asking why that shift was made. I also asked a question related to the testing role, which he answered in detail.

After the short break, he asked about my favorite subject in 12th grade. I said Chemistry, so he asked basic questions like the symbol for water, what happens when hydrogen is added to water, and symbols for nitrogen and nitrogen oxide.

The topic then moved to testing. I explained the two types--manual and automation--and further broke them down into functional and non-functional testing. When asked if I had ever done testing, I shared an example: during my curriculum, I cloned a banking website from GitHub and ran various test cases, including edge cases. He then asked about the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), which I couldn't answer so he gave me a brief explanation.

Since testing was my second preference, he asked if I was genuinely interested in it. I reassured him that I was, stating that I am equally interested in testing and development, though I am not looking to work in machine learning or data roles at this point.

Before wrapping up, he also asked where I live and about my family background.

Tips One key takeaway was that the interviewer often picked questions based on what I said, so it's important to speak about things you can confidently explain in depth and you should be knowing your resume really well. Mention only those things in the resume which you know in detail and if you are adding any project from github you should know it in and out. If you have chosen Testing as your second preference make sure you prepare a proper justification for that and also make sure you have some basic understanding of Testing.

3. [HR Round] [15 students]

My interview started with me greeting them and they began to ask me where I live and then how much I scored in CET, JEE, SSC and my current CGPA. Then they asked me what is testing and what are different types of testing. I explained whatever I knew in detail. They were still not convinced since Testing was my second preference and questioned me that you have no project related to testing so is it that you are sure you want to do the role of Testing Engineer. I said Yes and gave them an explanation of whatever I could think of at that point of time. Then they asked how I decided to choose the Testing role but I told them that I don't know anyone who has knowledge about Testing so I googled about testing role and then I decided to take it. But this was not the correct way of saying because it seems that an uninformed decision was taken so make sure you show them that you take decisions wisely and be prepared for giving such kind of explanation. Then they asked me to go out and talk to my senior or professors about the testing role and what it is exactly and what a Testing Engineer exactly does. At this point I thought they would reject but I went out and Thanks to TPO that helped a lot to connect to me seniors of ISS Stoxx and they

explained me clearly and then I went to interviewer again after they were done taking others interviews and I explained them in detail whatever I understood and they also asked me who did I talk to and then I thanked them and left the room.

[12 students were offered the role including me ]

journey.prep:
● Start early with DSA and development. It gives you a very strong edge over others. You may think that you have a lot of time, indeed it is true, but do not underestimate the power of consistency and long time efforts. Most people do not start preparation until they have completed their 5th semester. I started in the 3rd semester with DSA and development in the 4th semester.

● Do not be stuck in the "Dev or DSA" hell. YOU MUST HAVE BOTH OF THEM AT A PRETTY GOOD LEVEL. Nowadays everybody knows the MERN stack and it has become the new normal, do not limit yourself to only one technology. Explore other technologies as well like Java Development, Spring boot, etc. Make some projects which actually solve real world problems, not just a CRUD application with some eye-catching UI which is made by vercel v0 or claude.

● Participate in hackathons and solve their problem statements, even if you cannot win the hackathon do not stop building the application for the problem. You will anyways have a solid project with you if you keep on working with the statement.

● Do not ignore system design. It is now becoming common to ask system design to freshers and may happen that it will become a part of your process like DSA. At least know the basics of HLD, LLD and have a knowledge about the famous questions of system design. Use Aryan Mittal for system design.

● Give leetcode/codeforces/codechef/atcoder contests, they help you keep your mind in the correct momentum which is needed during the placement season. You cannot stop your mind midway through the season. Having internships with proper firms gives you an edge, because nowadays everybody has some kind of internship experience. If you do not have an internship, then you have to work a little more to compete with the ones having internships. Do not get inferiority complex with the people who have summer internships or any other. Hard work and consistency makes a lot of difference.

● DO NOT EXPECT THE PLACEMENT SEASON TO BE VERY SMOOTH. You have to be mentally strong for this and rejections are a part of it. I messed up my PhonePe interview because I did not know a specific advanced DSA concept (Binary Lifting) which led to my rejection. Do not think that advanced topics are not required for freshers. You never know what is waiting for you.

● Do not follow just one DSA sheet. One sheet may have concepts which the other may not. Go with striver, babbar for DSA. For CS fundamentals use Babbar, Kunal Kushwaha for OOPS. Do competitive programming, use TLE eliminators for that. Use TLE post contest discussion, they usually have solutions of up to 4-5 problems. Even if you have a low rating, watch and solve the later problems as they involve some good concepts which can sometimes pop up in front of you, and your mind gets trained to handle tougher problems.

● Keep your CGPA good enough, at least try to keep it above 8, it will help you to sit for all the companies. Sometimes the outcome is not in your hands, you may not pass the OA even after completely solving all the questions (happened to me with Zeta). Just make peace with it and look for the next company. Don't give a second thought to what is in the past. Don't let it bother you.

● Keep working and you will make it where you deserve. Hard work can never go in vain. Do not fall into that hardwork vs smartwork and all that superficial stuff. Keep it simple and drag yourself through it. Do not jumble yourself in tutorial hell, how to give interviews, how to smartly approach a problem, bla bla bla. Just be you and practice hard.

You may contact me here: Linkedin Resume: Link

All the best.
journey.howSecured:
● The Placement process started with the announcement of the PPT (pre-placement talk) which was in the second last week of July. The dates of OA (online assessment) were announced shortly and were scheduled for the next week.

● A total of 4 interview rounds were conducted, excluding the online assessment. There were 2 technical rounds, 1 HR discussion round and the last Business round which turned out to be a technical and curriculum discussion round for me.

● The placement process for IDFC is too hectic because of so many rounds and the rigorous nature of interviews. I would advise not to go lightly and do not hope for any chill interview rounds, the selection is also too strict and depends entirely on the first 2 technical rounds. The people who passed the technical interviews and appeared for the HR round were all selected except a few people which was really disheartening.

1. Online Assessment [ 135 candidates appeared for this round ]

● This round was conducted on the campus, it was around 1hr 15 minutes test. The criteria for this round was on the basis of branches. EXTC was not allowed to sit for the process and were informed almost 10-15 minutes prior to the OA.

● The test consisted of 3 sections, General aptitude, CS fundamentals, DSA

● In the aptitude section, normal aptitude questions like probability, profit loss, worker problem, speed and time were asked. There were around 15 questions and we were given 25 minutes to solve them. The aptitude test I felt was easy and was solvable (I hate aptitude and do not practice for it and just tend to skip them in the test if I could not get the idea by seeing the question (absolutely not recommended ❌❌❌)). For aptitude refer indiabix website, and practice quantitative and pattern recognition questions.

● The next section was on CS fundamentals. It included questions from DBMS, OS, CCN, OOPS. Basic questions were asked in this section, such that if you have a good knowledge of your syllabus from the 2nd year then you would be able to tackle this section fairly. You can refer to Babbar's youtube channel for DBMS, OS and Kunal Kushwaha for OOPS.

● The third section was DSA. The questions asked in this section were fairly straightforward and were solvable by any brute force idea. The problem with this section was with the different programming languages (ideally should not happen, but happened with Java and Python people). I did not have to think on this section as I directly implemented the solutions.

1. The first problem was that we needed to find the sum of good numbers from a range [l, r], a good number is a number in which the difference between the sum of all the digits in the number and the largest digit is exactly equal to the largest digit. Eg 3003 ((3+0+0+3)-3 == 3). The brute force idea worked but gave TLE in most languages like C++, Java. I implemented it in C and was able to pass all the test cases.

2. The second problem was to find out that after sorting an array how many elements did not change their position. Again a fairly simple problem and just using the inbuilt sort function worked, I did it in C++ and passed all the test cases. Again, it was a problem with Java and Python people with the input and test cases. For passing the online assessment, I recommend practicing aptitude and do not skip it like I did because solving aptitude along with DSA will help you get an edge over others. Do leetcode, codeforces, codechef or any other platform that you like, DO NOT skip over any advanced DSA topic however difficult it may seem (cost me my phonepe interview had I known lifting beforehand). Solving advanced DSA problems helps you build the instinct where you do not have to put efforts into coming up with a solution.

After this round around 45 candidates were selected. The mistakes in the DSA section were taken into account by the company and the students who wrote a correct solution were selected.

2. Technical Round 1 [ 45 candidates appeared for this round ]

● This round was conducted on campus on 30th July in the morning. There were 9 panels and each panel had 2 interviewers. This round mainly focused on the core CS knowledge of the candidates like basic data structures, OOPS, Schema Design, etc. The round lasted around 45-50 minutes.

● When I entered the room, they shook hands with me and told me to sit. They did not ask for my introduction (I was not asked to introduce myself in any interviews I gave (don't know the reason behind that)). They took a copy of my resume, took a look at it and then asked whether I am ready to start with the interview.

● They started with very very basic questions on data structures like what are the types of data structures (linear, non-linear), when to use which, what is stacks and queues, how will you implement stack using queues and vice-versa, what are linked lists and their types. They were very basic questions and if you have even the lowest level of knowledge then you should be able to answer their questions without hesitation. (I would suggest when you are definitely clear with the answer, make some stories and tell, do not tell directly, this allows you to cover time and list down some extra points in front of the interviewer which many candidates would not have mentioned had they been in a hurry.)

● Then he asked me about my primary programming language. I said I use C++ for problem solving, Javascript and Nodejs for I/O intensive developmental tasks and Java Springboot for CPU heavy developmental tasks. So they went ahead to ask about OOPS of C++ and Java. I

was told to explain every concept with respect to both of the languages and highlight the differences between them.

● He asked me about polymorphism, inheritance, the diamond problem of multiple inheritance and how it is handled in Java and C++, friend functions and classes with their counterparts in Java. When to use Java, when to use C++. He basically asked me the whole of OOPS, in about 25 minutes and I was able to answer all of the questions.

● Next he gave me a situation of an online shopping platform which will sell products of all the types like electronics, clothes, food and everything, basically Amazon. He asked me how I would design the schema of this platform and handle the categories of products. He asked me how I will make the foreign key relations, what kind of attributes I store and how many tables would I require.

● Then on this schema he asked me to find products of a particular category, a particular brand, and above a particular rating. He told me to write a query on that and I was able to write the query (it was a simple query of inner join with some where clauses).

● Next he asked me how I track the trends of the customers who visited the platform. To this I answered by keeping the search history, keywords, order details and similar preferences of the user in a vectorized form inside the database and using it to predict the preferences of the users. I went a bit into machine learning for this question and was able to tell them the flow on how we will gather the data of user behaviour and use it to suggest similar products to the customer to boost the business.

For the technical round, I would suggest having a strong knowledge of the CS fundamentals and programming languages on your finger tips. It is not an exaggeration, this is what makes a difference while giving the feedback. Be calm in the interview and answer every question to the point, by making some stories to sugarcoat your answer. If you absolutely know the answer to a question, cook the response as much as you can, do not give straightforward answers like some AI or a robot. Keep your theory knowledge crisp with reasons for every fact, you need to know what is happening and why something is made in a certain way.

After this round around 22 candidates were shortlisted for the next round

3. Technical Round 2 [ 22 candidates appeared for this round ]

● This round was conducted on campus on 30th July. There were 6 panels and each panel had 2 interviewers. This round focused on core development knowledge, system design and problem solving. This round lasted around 45 minutes and was fast paced. We were expected to answer quickly like a rapid fire round, the interviewer did not show any kind of expression from which students could make out whether they were satisfied with the answer or not.

● They started by asking me about my day, I told them it was going fine uptill now. Then they proceeded to test my developmental knowledge by asking deep questions like what is actually nodejs and why it was developed. Then they proceeded to ask some system design questions like how would you scale a system if a lot of users came to your application. They did not even listen to the full answer, interrupted between every question and changed to the

next question abruptly. This would have been a tactic to test the candidate in difficult situations and how they would react under pressure.

● I heard from other candidates that they were taunting the students like "you fumbled here how would you handle in IDFC" or "you have mentioned so and so technology on your resume then you should be aware of it".

● They then proceeded to ask me a DSA question, only my panel was asking DSA. The problem required me to find the longest palindromic substring in a given string. The problem could be found on leetcode (5th problem on leetcode). They told me I have 15 minutes to code for the solution. The panelist handed me their macbook and told me to write the code on an online compiler. I had to write in codeforces style i.e. taking the input and then printing the longest palindromic substring. They did not care about the most optimal approach or the time and space complexity. They just wanted a working code and also did not provide any details about the question like constraints and all. After coding they asked me to explain the approach I took. It was a fairly simple problem and I was able to solve it in about 10 minutes. Thinking out loud, or explaining while coding was not at all required, their sole purpose was to get a working code.

● After this they tried to run the code but the online compiler was not working due to some internet issues. In spite of this they told me that my code is incorrect and has errors that is why it was not working. I argued with them that the code I wrote could not be incorrect and made them try running the code meanwhile the other interviewer went on to ask further questions.

● He asked me a puzzle. I have coins of denominations {1,2,5} and had to make a sum by taking at least one coin from every denomination. There was no logic involved in this puzzle and I just had to mod the sum by every denomination. While I was answering this the other interviewer finally ran the code by installing a GCC compiler on his macbook and accepted that the code was working perfectly. This gave me an edge as the other candidates in my panel faced a similar issue of the online compiler not working. Be prepared to face tougher situations as the purpose of further rounds is to test how mentally strong you are. DO NOT MELT IN FRONT OF THE INTERVIEWER HOWEVER RUDE OR UNINTERESTED THEY MAY SEEM. If the interviewer interrupts you in between, take it as a positive point because you were already on the right track and they got it, that is why they change the questions. Have confidence in yourself and do not underestimate yourself, if you are sure of something then do argue with the interviewer, sometimes they are also at fault.

After this 9 candidates were selected for the HR round.

4. HR Round [ 9 candidates appeared for this round ]

● The HR round was pretty chill. She was taking around 45 minute interviews of the candidates but due to time constraints (it was past 6 in the evening), she took the remaining candidates' interviews for about 15-20 minutes each.

● She started by asking how my day was, when I came to college for the interviews and how was the interview process in general. She asked where I stay and asked what my parents do.

● She asked me pretty straightforward behavioral and situational questions. She started by asking what if the manager is out of reach and does not reply, what will you do. Then she asked what if the manager micro-manages you, what will you do in this scenario.

● She also asked what would be my melting point (the point where you feel you will leave the company). All the questions were pretty standard, and I used pretty standard answers that chatGPT gives when we ask it to prepare for the HR round.

● The candidates who got shortlisted for the HR round were most probably guaranteed of the job, so the HR round was not very serious. The HR lady on the outside told us not to worry, they will try their best not to reject anyone after this. Prepare for the HR round by chatGPT. They ask pretty standard questions and you are expected to give their standard answers as well, like a viva. Try to stay calm and smile in front of the HR

All 9 candidates appeared for the next round.

5. Business Round [ 9 candidates appeared for this round ]

● This round was like a mere formality in the beginning as we have come a long way in clearing three intense interviews throughout the day. The interview was about 30 minutes and this was conducted in online mode because it was too late in the evening. Initially it was planned to take this round for half of the candidates on the next day, but we insisted to the HR lady (she was very friendly) to take it and complete it today itself, and they did so.

● Initially we were completely unaware as to what will be asked in this round as the HR also did not have any idea about the business round. She told us it may be related to the college curriculum that we have studied till now or something like that.

● The round for me turned out to be another technical round. The interviewer first asked me about my favorite subjects in college to which I answered DBMS, OS, Distributed Computing. So he began asking about DC. He asked me about system scalability, design patterns and concurrency in the case of distributed systems. I was well versed with DC in my sem 6 so I was able to answer all the questions pretty easily.

● He then asked me the difference between frontend and backend (I don't know why such a question), so based on my answer he started cross questioning me about the difference between UI/UX and some other jargon. I was able to answer all the questions but felt that the interview didn't go as intended. Be ready for surprises as this round was not initially planned. IDFC is known to have many interview rounds before selecting the candidates. Also do not assume that if you have come this far then it is absolutely guaranteed that you will get selected, as one candidate was not selected after these 4 rigorous interview rounds. I don't know the reason for that but it was pretty unfortunate.

Finally 8 candidates were finally selected for IDFC.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
● Start early with DSA and development. It gives you a very strong edge over others. You may think that you have a lot of time, indeed it is true, but do not underestimate the power of consistency and long time efforts. Most people do not start preparation until they have completed their 5th semester. I started in the 3rd semester with DSA and development in the 4th semester.

● Do not be stuck in the "Dev or DSA" hell. YOU MUST HAVE BOTH OF THEM AT A PRETTY GOOD LEVEL. Nowadays everybody knows the MERN stack and it has become the new normal, do not limit yourself to only one technology. Explore other technologies as well like Java Development, Spring boot, etc. Make some projects which actually solve real world problems, not just a CRUD application with some eye-catching UI which is made by vercel v0 or claude.

● Participate in hackathons and solve their problem statements, even if you cannot win the hackathon do not stop building the application for the problem. You will anyways have a solid project with you if you keep on working with the statement.

● Do not ignore system design. It is now becoming common to ask system design to freshers and may happen that it will become a part of your process like DSA. At least know the basics of HLD, LLD and have a knowledge about the famous questions of system design. Use Aryan Mittal for system design.

● Give leetcode/codeforces/codechef/atcoder contests, they help you keep your mind in the correct momentum which is needed during the placement season. You cannot stop your mind midway through the season. Having internships with proper firms gives you an edge, because nowadays everybody has some kind of internship experience. If you do not have an internship, then you have to work a little more to compete with the ones having internships. Do not get inferiority complex with the people who have summer internships or any other. Hard work and consistency makes a lot of difference.

● DO NOT EXPECT THE PLACEMENT SEASON TO BE VERY SMOOTH. You have to be mentally strong for this and rejections are a part of it. I messed up my PhonePe interview because I did not know a specific advanced DSA concept (Binary Lifting) which led to my rejection. Do not think that advanced topics are not required for freshers. You never know what is waiting for you.

● Do not follow just one DSA sheet. One sheet may have concepts which the other may not. Go with striver, babbar for DSA. For CS fundamentals use Babbar, Kunal Kushwaha for OOPS.

1. Online Assessment

2. Technical Round

3. HR Round

1. Online Assessment + UBS Campus Hackathon

In March 2025, I participated in the UBS Campus Hackathon selection process, which began with an online assessment consisting of 50 minutes of multiple-choice questions and a coding problem. The MCQs focused on Java and core computer science fundamentals such as data structures, OOP, operating systems, and databases. The DSA problem varied for each candidate mine was on the easier side, and I was able to solve it successfully, passing all test cases and completing the assessment early.

Following the results, 11 students from our college were shortlisted to participate in the hackathon. Teams were randomly allocated, and I was initially nervous since all my teammates were complete strangers. But it turned out to be a great way to connect, collaborate, and step out of my comfort zone. Our problem statement was about addressing the shortage of teachers in Zilla Parishad schools by creating a smart platform to connect them with volunteer educators, a solution that helped our team win 2nd runners-up at the hackathon.

One of the best parts of the hackathon was how supportive and involved the mentors and UBS professionals were. They were really friendly, easy to talk to, and genuinely wanted us to do well. We had regular check-ins with them, and they gave us helpful feedback on everything from our idea to how we presented it. If you're participating, make the most of those interactions, ask questions, share your progress, and take their suggestions seriously. It's not just about improving your project, but also about learning how things work in the real world and understanding what companies like UBS look for.

As a finalist, I also received a direct exemption from the UBS campus placement online assessment, which allowed me to proceed straight to the interview round.

2. Technical Interview [ 20 candidates were shortlisted ]

So, my UBS technical interview began on a pretty comfortable note. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, and then we dove straight into my internship experience and projects. He seemed genuinely interested not just in what I had done, but also in the problems I was trying to solve, the features I had built, and my overall thought process. One of my projects was based on workflow automation, which led to an interesting discussion about the human-in-the-loop concept and where automation should be balanced with human oversight.

He also asked me about the UBS hackathon project, which I had mentioned on my resume. We discussed the problem statement and what I personally contributed to the project. Then he asked if I had used AI in any of my projects, and we had a short conversation about that as well.

After that, he moved on to ask about my 10th and 12th qualifications, which I hadn't included on my resume. It was a bit unexpected, but the flow was smooth and conversational, so I didn't feel nervous.

I had about 4 days to prepare for the interview, and based on seniors' experiences, I expected questions mostly around internships, projects, and CS fundamentals. So I focused my prep on those areas. But right in the middle of the interview, the interviewer surprised me by saying, "I'll be asking you 3 puzzles now." That definitely caught me off guard, because I hadn't focused much on puzzles during my prep -- apart from just reading the ones mentioned in previous interview experiences.

Puzzle 1: The Candle Puzzle (link)

He asked: "You have 2 candles and a matchbox. Each candle takes exactly 1 hour to burn. How can you measure 45 minutes?" My first thought was to break one candle in half, but he pointed out that wouldn't give an accurate 30 minutes. After asking for a hint, he told me, "The middle of the candle is the key." That's when I realized I could burn the first candle from both ends, making it burn out in exactly 30 minutes. At the same time, I'd light the second candle from one end. When the first one finishes, I'd then light the other end of the second candle, making it burn in 15 minutes, totaling 45 minutes. He appreciated the logic and said I had cracked the tough part well.

Puzzle 2: The Poisoned Bottle Problem (link)

This one was trickier. He said: "You have 1000 bottles, one is poisoned. You have 10 test strips, and results take 24 hours. How can you identify the poisoned one?" I wasn't sure of the exact approach but suggested dipping strips in multiples (2, 3, etc.). He said I was thinking about grouping but wouldn't be able to narrow it down precisely. He then gave a hint "Label the bottles" and asked me about bits. I realized he was referring to binary encoding, and I mentioned that I could assign a unique binary number to each bottle. But even with that, I couldn't fully figure out the logic. Before moving on, I asked if he could explain it. At first, he said no, but eventually, he shared the solution which was based on checking the bit pattern of the test strip results after 24 hours to pinpoint the poisoned bottle.

Puzzle 3: The Bridge Crossing Problem (link)

Before this one, he told me "You'll be able to crack this," which somehow made me feel more pressured. The problem: "Four people need to cross a bridge. They take 1, 2, 5, and 10 minutes. Only two can cross at a time, and they need a torch to cross. What's the minimum time to get all across?" I tried pairing the slowest with the fastest, with the fastest returning which gave me a total of 20 minutes. But he said the optimal answer was 17 minutes. I explained that my idea was to always have the fastest person return with the torch. He said I was thinking in the right direction, but I still couldn't land on the right sequence. He eventually explained it, and honestly, looking back, it seems so simple now. But in the moment, when you're under pressure, even the simplest things feel difficult if you're not calm.

At the end of the interview, I asked him two questions: one about what sets UBS apart technologically compared to other banks, and another about his own experience having spent 24 years in the investment banking sector, what made him join UBS and stay. He answered both very thoughtfully, sharing insights into UBS's strong tech-first mindset and what stood out to him compared to other firms he had worked at. It felt less like a formal Q&A and more like a genuine, engaging conversation and with that, the interview wrapped up.

Tips:

● Stay calm. Interviews can be nerve-wracking, but your ability to think clearly under pressure is just as important as your technical skills.

● Know your projects well. Be ready to explain why you made certain decisions, not just what you did. You should be able to defend your choices confidently.

● Think out loud. Don't go completely silent while solving problems. Share your thought process; it helps keep the conversation going and shows how you approach challenges.

● Be honest if you're stuck. It's okay to ask for a hint or say you're not sure, what matters is how you handle the situation.

Note: For some candidates they took multiple technical interviews, while for some they took a technical & just an HR interview only

3. HR Interview [ 10-11 candidates where shortlisted]

The HR interview was quite short and honestly felt more like a friendly conversation than a formal interview. The interviewer was from the Mumbai branch, and since I had already interacted with her during the UBS Hackathon, she remembered me, which immediately made things more relaxed and comfortable.

She started by asking whether I had participated in any other hackathons after the UBS one. I shared that I had, and she asked me to talk about the differences I noticed between those experiences and the UBS hackathon. After that, she briefly revisited my hackathon experience at UBS, asking how I found it overall. We then moved on to a basic background check. She asked about my family and whether I was planning to pursue higher studies like a master's degree (I said no). And that was it we wrapped up in under 10 minutes.

6 students were offered the role and I was one of them (5/6 were hackathon finalists).

Stay Positive and Believe in Yourself : The placement process can be long and stressful. Losing hope or feeling demotivated is absolutely normal, but always believe in yourself and keep putting in consistent effort. Better things are on the way. Talking to your friends and family during tough times really helps keep your mind calm and motivated.

Prepare Based on Company Patterns : Go through previous interview experiences for the company you're targeting. Some companies grill your resume thoroughly, some focus on Java or DSA, while others might focus on computer fundamentals. Knowing the pattern helps you prioritize topics effectively.

Know Your Resume Inside Out : Be prepared for questions like "Why did you build this project?" or "How would you improve it further?". Small bluffs are fine, but avoid putting anything on your resume that you can't confidently explain.

Cover Both DSA and Fundamentals : Don't limit yourself to DSA alone. Computer fundamentals like OS, DBMS, OOPS, and Networks are equally important. For DSA, go through Striver's Sheet and give contests on CodeForces and LeetCode. For computer fundamentals, practice from Sanfoundry or GFG. These will help you in Online Assessments as well as interviews.

Stay Calm During Interviews: Interviews can be nerve-wracking. I once felt nervous in an interview and ended up answering wrongly, which got me frustrated and affected my confidence

for the remaining questions. To avoid this, practice mock interviews with friends or seniors. They help you get comfortable under pressure.

Trust the Process and Don't Compare :Trust God's plan and your own journey. Failures are an unavoidable part of growth. Don't compare yourself with others--it only adds unnecessary stress. 1. Online Assessment [ 191 applied on unstop and 133 shortlisted for test ]

The test was held on campus via Unstop with rigorous proctoring. It contained three sections - Aptitude, Technical MCQs, and Coding. Each section had a sectional timer.

● Aptitude (40 questions in 35 mins) - The questions in this section were easy, but the main challenge was time management. Don't spend too much time on a single question; try to solve as many as possible within the time limit.

● Technical MCQs (33 questions in 25 mins) - This section included Web Development (HTML, JavaScript-based) questions, as well as questions on OS, DBMS, and OOPS. The questions were mostly standard, but some were tricky and required careful attention.

● Coding (3 questions in 30 mins) - There were three coding questions:

1. Minimum Robbing Speed - A thief wants to rob all the houses in a village. Given an array representing the number of houses in each neighborhood and the

maximum amount of time (in hours) available, find the minimum speed (houses per hour) required to rob the entire village.

2. House Robber Problem - This was the classic House Robber problem from LeetCode, solvable using a standard Dynamic Programming approach.

3. Maximum Loot on Islands - Given an undirected graph of n islands, each with a loot value, and edges representing travel paths with travel times, a pirate can start from any island and visit each island at most once. The total loot is the sum of the visited islands' values, while the total time is the sum of the travel times along the chosen path. The task was to find the maximum loot which can be solved by direct Dijkstra's Algorithm.

I was able to solve the first two questions but couldn't attempt the third one due to time constraints.

2. Technical Interview - Round 1

The interviews were conducted the next day and FE was my first preference . I was shortlisted for FE role . Although there was an option for students to switch roles as well. Some students had their interviews in online mode, while others had them offline. Mine was in offline mode.

The interview started with my introduction. Then the interviewer asked me about my Major Project focusing mainly on its real-world application .Next he asked me about my Internship project at TCS and asked me to explain it in detail which I have implemented using Google Cloud Platform. Then he asked me simple programming question of Checking whether a number is pallindrome or not. I have started with brute force approach and then explained the optimal one .He also asked me questions about the other projects mentioned in my resume, focusing mainly on how I implemented specific features and the reasoning behind them .Finally I asked the interviewer a question and the interview was concluded.

I was able to answer almost every question in this round and felt confident that I would advance to the next round. This interview lasted for around 45 mins.

3. Technical Interview - Round 2

After about 30 minutes, I was informed that I had been selected for the second round and was called in for the interview.

This interview started with a self-introduction. Then, the interviewer asked me about my internship project. He further asked about the difference between SQL and NoSQL in DBMS, followed by a discussion on normalization. After that, he asked me to design a database schema for a company with users as students, employees, teachers, and staff. His main objective was to assess my understanding of storing data in a normalized form. Next, he asked me to write a SQL query on the schema I had designed, having GROUP BY and ORDER BY operations. After this, he asked about the difference between JWT and Cookies. He then moved on to Sockets and Polling concepts. Further, he asked some basic Python questions such as the difference between lists and tuples and how multiple inheritance works in Python. Finally, he asked me about my Major Project.

In this round, the interviewer cross-questioned frequently to test my depth of knowledge . I was able to answer almost every question except for the one on Sockets, where the interviewer gave me a hint, after which I was able to respond correctly.

Tip: Try to answer theoretical questions with real-life use cases or examples to demonstrate a deeper understanding of the topic

4. HR Round

After about an hour, I was informed that I had been selected for the HR round.

The HR round began with my self-introduction, followed by questions about my family background and where I live. Then, the interviewer asked me to pitch one of my projects of my choice in one minute as if I were pitching it to an investor. He also asked about the challenges I faced while working on that project. Next, he moved on to behavioral questions such as:

If I assign you a project about which you have no prior knowledge, how would you approach it?

If you are assigned three tasks with tight deadlines, how would you prioritize and work on them?

He also asked a guesstimate question to estimate the number of daily users on YouTube. Lastly, he asked me why I want to join Quantiphi and where I see myself in the next five years.

Around 9 PM, all interviews were concluded, and the team went inside the conference room to discuss the results. Everyone waiting outside was very tense, and I was silently praying to God. Finally, around 9:45 PM, the results were announced--8 candidates were selected, including me (for the FE role). Among the selectees, 2 were for MLE, 3 for FE, and 3 for BA roles.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Stay Positive and Believe in Yourself : The placement process can be long and stressful. Losing hope or feeling demotivated is absolutely normal, but always believe in yourself and keep putting in consistent effort. Better things are on the way. Talking to your friends and family during tough times really helps keep your mind calm and motivated.

Prepare Based on Company Patterns : Go through previous interview experiences for the company you're targeting. Some companies grill your resume thoroughly, some focus on Java or DSA, while others might focus on computer fundamentals. Knowing the pattern helps you prioritize topics effectively.

Know Your Resume Inside Out : Be prepared for questions like "Why did you build this project?" or "How would you improve it further?". Small bluffs are fine, but avoid putting anything on your resume that you can't confidently explain.

Cover Both DSA and Fundamentals : Don't limit yourself to DSA alone. Computer fundamentals like OS, DBMS, OOPS, and Networks are equally important. For DSA, go through Striver's Sheet and give contests on CodeForces and LeetCode. For computer fundamentals, practice from Sanfoundry or GFG. These will help you in Online Assessments as well as interviews.

Stay Calm During Interviews: Interviews can be nerve-wracking. I once felt nervous in an interview and ended up answering wrongly, which got me frustrated and affected my confidence

for the remaining questions. To avoid this, practice mock interviews with friends or seniors. They help you get comfortable under pressure.

Trust the Process and Don't Compare :Trust God's plan and your own journey. Failures are an unavoidable part of growth. Don't compare yourself with others--it only adds unnecessary stress. Virat Kohli waited 18 years to win his first IPL trophy, while Rohit Sharma lifted his first one just a year after the league began . Everyone has their own timeline; enjoy your journey without rushing through it.

JUST TRUST THE PROCESS. ALL THE BEST !!!

1. Technical Test (240 students appeared, 27 selected)

During my technical test, which lasted 1.5 hours, I encountered questions across SQL, Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), and Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts. The test was a mix of multiple-choice questions (MCQs), which asked for the output of given programs, and theory-based questions. There were also some specific questions about inheritance, exploring the fundamentals of OOP.

One of the SQL tasks required me to write a query that extracted the month from a date column and filtered the results to show only those where the month was October. This combination of theoretical and practical questions tested both my conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in real-time.

Additionally, the technical test featured a high-weightage DSA question where points were awarded based on the number of test cases passed. The problem was quite challenging, with 8 hidden test cases and 2 visible ones. The task required constructing the lexicographically smallest string of length m+n−1, given two input strings of length m and n. The second string contained only 'T' and 'F', and wherever there was a 'T', I had to copy the entire first string from the start. For positions marked by 'F', the substring starting from that character in the result needed to be unequal to the first string. The solution had to return -1 if it was impossible to construct such a string. This problem tested my understanding of string manipulation and logic-based problem-solving.

2. Technical Interview Round (27 students appeared, 15 selected)

I was first asked to introduce myself, after which the focus shifted to DBMS JOINS. I had to draw Venn diagrams representing the different types of joins and write queries for each. The interviewer provided two tables, "employee" and "department," and asked me to explain the different joins--inner, left, right, and full--and how they differ.

We also discussed my projects, and I was asked to write basic for and while loops. The interviewer then posed an interesting question about the while loop: whether incrementing the loop variable before or after the statements inside the loop would make a difference.

3. HR Round (15 appeared, 13 selected)

In my HR round, the interviewer started by asking me to introduce myself and talk about my projects. Then, I was presented with a few scenarios.

In one scenario, I was part of a team of six, and both I and another person were assigned the same task by the line manager, who was supposed to distribute different tasks to everyone. The other person completed the task first and received appreciation. I responded that I would review their work and aim to improve it from my perspective.

Another scenario involved working in a team of two, where my teammate had no knowledge of the required tech stack, and we had a deadline. I explained that I would provide resources, help them learn the necessary concepts, and work together to meet the deadline.

Finally, I was asked to explain and differentiate between machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, data analytics, and supervised learning.

[ 13 students were offered the job ]

1. Online assessment (280+ candidates)

The first round was an online assessment held in the college lab. Despite being an online test, itwas monitored closely toensure fairness. The test consisted of:

● 12 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) on topics such as data structures, algorithms, and aptitude.

● 1 coding question, which required solving a problem using programming logic.

● 1 SQL question, where candidates had to write a query based on agiven dataset.

The time duration for this round was 1 hour. Out of 280+ candidates, 35 were shortlisted for the next round based on their performance.

Preparation Tips:

● For the MCQs, focus on core subjects like data structures, algorithms, and basic aptitude. Websites like GeeksforGeeks, LeetCode, and HackerRank are excellent for practicing these.

● The coding question required a solid understanding of programming. Practice coding problems from competitive platforms and make sure to brush up on common algorithms.

● Prepare SQL queries and database management concepts, as SQL questions often focus on real-world applications.

On the day of the test,ensure you manage time efficiently between the MCQs and the coding questions. Double-check your SQL query for syntax and logic errors.

Resume Pointers:

● Highlight projects involving coding, data structures, and databases.

● Include any relevant certifications in programming or SQL that demonstrate your skills.

2. Technical Interview (35 candidates)

After the online assessment, 35 candidates were shortlisted for the technical interview, which was conducted offline the next day. This round involved in-depth questions about:

● Your technical knowledge of programming languages, data structures, and algorithms.

● Problem-solving skills,where you might be asked to solve problems on a whiteboard or explain your thought process.

● Questions about projects listed on your resume, with particular emphasis on your role,challenges faced, and how you overcame them.

The interview lasted for around 30-40 minutes per candidate, and 15 people were shortlisted for the next round.

Preparation Tips:

● Review your resume thoroughly, especially the projects and technologies you mentioned.

● Practice explaining complex technical concepts in simple terms. Mock interviews can help with this.

● Prepare for questions on problem-solving using DSA (Data Structures and Algorithms) by solving problems from LeetCode and InterviewBit.

On the day of the interview, stay calm, maintain clarity in your answers, and don't hesitate to ask for clarification ifneeded. Always explain your thought process when solving problems.

3. HR Interview (15 candidates)

The final round was an HR interview, conducted offline in the evening of the same day. In this round, the HR panel focused on:

● Behavioral questions to assess your personality, teamwork skills,and how you handle pressure.

● Questions about your career goals, strengths, weaknesses, and why you're interested in the company.

● Situational questions, where you may be asked how you would handle a particular scenario in the workplace.

This round was relatively short, around 15-20 minutes per candidate. After this round, 13 candidates were finally selected for the role.

Preparation Tips:

● Practice answering common HR questions like "Tell me about yourself", "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?", and "Why should we hire you?".

● Be honest about your strengths and weaknesses, and give examples that show how you've worked on improving your weaknesses.

● Ensure you are well-versed with the company's background, culture, and the role you're applying for.

On the day of the HR interview, be confident, maintain good body language, and ensure your answers reflect apositive attitude and willingness to learn.

journey.prep:
1. Nervous? Don't worry, just go and give the interview, everything will be fine after the first round. That day I realized my communication skills were much better than I expected them to be (Well they are worse for some personal reasons). Your words should reflect wisdom.

2. I didn't win any hackathons but had attended some and had experience. I was asked about hackathons in each round so try to go for as many as you can and try to work in a team. Don't just make PPT but also develop something as a team.

3. I didn't have any internship, I had projects but having an internship would definitely help.

4. I always tried to make fun and useful projects.

5. I used Go as my main language for development (Try it if you have time it is way more fun than Javascript).

6. The core subjects, the system design for your projects and follow-up questions are must.

7. Attending coding contests or virtual contests on Leetcode/Codeforces will help to solve problems under pressure.

8. Of course know your resume inside out. DO NOT add anything that you don't know properly.

9. If you don't know something don't tell them beforehand unless asked.

10. If your answer is NO just say it loud and clear as if you don't regret it just like an army personnel or just without any hesitation but humbly. Don't say it softly like you are scared.

11. I talked to a senior and my friends and fine tuned my resume accordingly.

12. Many candidates were multiple time hackathon winners and had internships but were still rejected, so always get your fundamentals right no matter what you have achieved.

13. One final thing is whenever you contact any senior, don't just ask about how they did it, also ask about what mistakes they made and why they were rejected. I wasn't able to clear PhonePe OA and then went on to clear UBS and MSCI OA's and was selected for UBS.

4. Operating Systems: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces

All candidates who had applied were to give a UBS culture test (not timed) and Aptitude test (2 rounds 6 minutes speed based pattern recognition + 6 minutes 18 questions paragraph based). This test was to be given from home by applying on UBS website.

Some failed to give this test and were not shortlisted for OA.

1. Online Assessment [ 173 candidates appeared ]

Platform: HackerRank (Oncampus) Time Limit: 90 minutes

Format: 15 Aptitude + 15 OOPS/Java/SQL/DSA + 1 Coding Question

Section 1: 15 Aptitude questions were pretty much doable based on sets, probability, statistics, and some could be just answered by looking at the given graph (It was initially not very visible, just pull the image then it'll be clearly visible).

Section 2: 15 OOPS/Java/SQL/DSA were very basic if you have fundamental knowledge. The OOPS questions were in Java but even if you are from C++/Python background then knowledge of OOPS would help you clear it. SQL was simple syntactical as well. Some questions were also MCQ based on DSA like inorder of a given tree.

Section 3: The coding question was a bit tricky to understand. I can't clearly remember it but it was to be done by using TreeSet / PriorityQueue in Java.

I tried the coding question first for about 20 minutes but was able to pass just 1 test case then my platform was stuck for about 10 minutes so I quickly informed the invigilator. After the problem was solved (I didn't get my time back) I proceeded to section 2 and did that quickly and then completed section 1. Then I went on to the coding question which then I tried using PriorityQueue till the end of the time it passed 9 test cases and the assessment was finally over.

6 of the candidates were part of UBS Hackathon who had appeared for an OA in March 2025 so they were directly shortlisted for interviews, so 14 candidates (including me) were shortlisted from July 2025 OA (A rather low number of candidates).

2. Technical Round [ 20 candidates appeared ]

The round started by the interviewer going through my resume in the meantime asking me to introduce myself. Then he asked me to tell me my favorite project among the projects in my resume. I was told to draw the architecture of that entire project on a paper and explain each and every component. 3/4 of my projects were in Go (Rare to find such people). Then I was asked some system design based questions.

1. Your setup is in Andheri (Mumbai) and a person accessing from USA is observing latency, what will you do?

2. How will you handle millions of users?

3. How will you handle large file responses?

Then I was asked to differentiate between SQL and NoSQL databases (Now keep in mind NoSQL doesn't just mean MongoDB there are many other than that like Cassandra, Redis etc. so answer accordingly). Then he asked me which one is better: SQL or NoSQL? I had also mentioned horizontal scaling so I was also asked about that.

Then I was given a SQL query to solve which included JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING + COUNT. My approach was using LEFT JOIN but interviewers approach was using INNER JOIN. Both worked. I had mistakenly switched the table names (Do not panic, shrug it off like it never happened).

I was asked about my most favorite (Operating Systems) and least favorite (FOSIP) subject. I was asked how many threads does a core have? Do they run in parallel? How did I manage to clear my least favorite subject?

A very very simple programming question was also asked. Then he asked me about the internal working of HashMap, time complexity of each type of working then about sorting algorithms and their time complexity and how do the ones having logarithmic time complexity work.

I was asked about Hackathons and the role of each member. I mentioned I had gone to some but didn't win any so he said winning isn't important, the experience gained is much more important.

I was then given the bridge puzzle Link. My answer was higher so he told me to improve it. I wasn't able to do it (Do not panic, shrug it off like it never happened).

Then came some HR questions:

1. Strength and weakness?

2. How are you improving your weakness?

3. One mistake you never repeated?

4. What do you know about UBS?

5. Why do you want to work for UBS?

6. What is the latest news you have heard about UBS?

7. Family background?

Then he asked whether I had any questions for him. I asked:

1. First of all I asked his name since he didn't mention it.

2. How is your typical day at UBS?

3. What is your favorite part of the work at UBS?

It was such a long round that I don't even remember the time.

3. HR Round 1

This round was entirely based on behaviour. I answered it loud and clearly like an army personnel without flinching.

1. Tell me about your entire life journey from place of birth, 10th school and percentage, 12th college and percentage, CET score, how I landed in SPIT?

2. What was my first preference, SPIT or VJTI?

3. Favorite thing about SPIT?

4. Do you have any internship experience?

5. Have you been to hackathons?

6. What was the problem statement? (We had a long discussion on this)

Then he asked whether I had any questions for him. I asked:

1. What learning opportunities and certifications does UBS provide?

2. Are those certifications just relevant within UBS or even for outside companies?

3. How is the role switching process in UBS?

The round lasted about 10-15 minutes. I was so much in army mode that after the interview when the TPC asked me something I mistakenly said YES SIRRR!! loudly.

4. HR Round 2

This round was just a background check and behavioural of about 5 minutes.

1. Why Computer Science Engineering?

2. Hackathon experience?

3. Open for relocation?

4. Are parents open for relocation?

Finally after a long wait 6 students (including me) were offered the role.
