● 18 Mar 2025: Results declared. Resume: at the time of applying:- Russell_Resume.pdf

How applications & shortlisting worked:

● The application and shortlisting were entirely run by Russell Investments on Workday. SPIT's placement office circulated a short form so they could see who had applied, but the company did the actual screening, communication and interviews. HR communicated with students directly.

● The opening received applications from many colleges (VJTI, IIT Bombay, Thakur, Somaiya, VESIT, DJ Sanghavi, etc.) -- so this was effectively a campus-pool + off-campus hybrid. It wasn't restricted to a single campus TPO.

● Russell had over 9,000 applications across approximately 5-6 internship roles. They selected a very small number of candidates out of that pool (23 across all roles and 6 for app dev).

● Make sure to have a refined resume, a good cgpa (I'd recommend having 8+, but try to keep at least 7.5+ otherwise you'll miss out on a few), some achievements to get shortlisted (there were people with very good resumes but were kept on waitlisted).

● Along with a good resume also try to keep linkedin and github maintained. (My github & linkedin).

Interview Day schedule:

1. Arrival & welcome (9:30 AM): We were asked to come to their Goregaon office by 9:30 AM. The day began with HR welcoming everyone and explaining the schedule.

2. Orientation sessions: The HR Head gave a brief intro followed by sessions from senior leadership -- the Managing Director and various Directors. Each speaker explained what Russell does, company culture, client focus, and what the tech teams build. These talks were delivered in a training room (like a PPT walkthrough) and were surprisingly detailed.

3. Written Assessment (~11:00 AM): After the intro sessions we took a pen-and-paper assessment (details below).

4. Panel interviews (L1 - about 5-6 panels): Post-assessment we moved into technical rounds -- there were multiple panels running in parallel across the day. My technical panel was mid-morning/early-afternoon and lasted roughly 50-60 minutes. Several other panels ran alongside it.

5. Refreshments and waiting: Between rounds we were given refreshments and asked to wait in a common area. There were several short breaks.

6. Final rounds (L2 - 2/3 panels): After the technical panels, a small batch of candidates (about 10 for app dev) were shortlisted for final Director-level/ hiring-manager conversations. Those rounds lasted about 25-30 minutes each. After finishing, we were sent home around 6:00 pm and informed that the results would be shared via HR in a few days.

7. Result: On 18 March 2025 Russell announced the results; six technology interns were selected for the Application Developer role (four of us were from SPIT).

1. Written assessment [around 30-35 candidates on day 1 had given for app dev role]

● Format: Pen-and-paper, 40 minutes total, weightage 5 marks. Note: the test was explicitly not eliminatory -- it contributed to evaluation but was not a strict knockout.

● Sections & content:

○ 10 aptitude questions -- pattern recognition, sequences, next-word / next-number style problems (IndiaBix-style).

○ 10 CS fundamentals MCQs -- typical core topics (DBMS, SQL, OS, networking basics, OOP/OO design).

○ 3 very easy coding problems -- solve any 2 (but I personally solved all three):

1. Valid parentheses (stack application).

2. Missing number in an array of size n−1 containing numbers 1..n (classic sum/XOR trick).

3. Binary-search style problem.

● My experience: The test was easier than I expected -- I finished all sections comfortably and had time to attempt the third coding question as well. The coding questions tested basic logic, nothing too difficult.

● Preparation tips for this round: Regular aptitude practice (IndiaBix, common OA Questions) and brushing up on core CS topics (DBMS, OS basics, OOP) is sufficient. For the coding questions, having a command of stacks, arrays, binary search and basic bit tricks helps, you can extrapolate to covering linear structures and basic sorting algorithms.

2. Technical interview 1 [All candidates who had given round 1]

Duration & setting: About 50-60 minutes, weightage 10 marks, in a room with a senior technical panel. There were 5-6 panels running -- mine was led by a very experienced interviewer (16 years of experience). The panelists were senior, technically-minded people who actually head teams.

Flow of the round (how it started):

● We began with a firm handshake and a short personal introduction. I handed over my resume and gave a structured 1-2 minute elevator pitch touching on my background, projects, and what I enjoy building. The interviewer asked me to go tell something that was not on my resume, followed by a deep dive into overall technical discussion.

Project deep-dive:

● I had listed a mobile app project that used Firebase as the backend. The panel headed into why I chose Firebase, how I implemented authentication, how I structured the database, how I handled sync/real-time aspects, and where I would change things for scale. They liked concrete answers (why a NoSQL approach was chosen for an app prototype, when SQL would be preferable in industry scenarios, etc.).

● Be ready to explain the what, how, and why for each project -- not just what you implemented but design tradeoffs and alternate approaches.

System design & architecture discussion:

● They asked higher-level architecture questions: how to design an auth flow, how to approach scalability, where to put the session store, and how to handle concurrent users. They deliberately pushed to see whether I understood tradeoffs.

● They asked "cloud feels slow -- how would you improve performance?" -- this opened a discussion on caching, caching DB queries, denormalization vs normalization tradeoffs, and batching or asynchronous processing for heavy tasks.

● They explored my approach to problem statements and use cases, focusing on how I solve problems, the technical considerations I account for, and how I tackle challenges while building a project from scratch.

● My hackathon experience, particularly winning at SIH, impressed them due to the scale of the hackathon and demonstrated my ability to design and plan projects effectively, both technically and strategically.

Data structures & algorithms:

● Two easy to med DSA problems were asked (Linked Lists and Stacks were explicitly covered). For each, the panel expected: clarifying questions, a brute-force approach, and then progressive optimization to a satisfying solution with complexity analysis. I emphasise thinking out loud -- walking through examples and edge cases, and then writing pseudo-code. They also expected short runtime/space tradeoff discussions.

● Important behavioural tip from this round: do not pretend to know an optimized solution even if you do -- state the brute-force first, then show how you would improve it. They frequently picked words I said and asked follow-ups, sometimes on tangential points I mentioned casually.

● A brief discussion about the assessment questions was held; the questions were relatively easy, and the interviewer was very relaxed. There was a lighthearted moment when I mentioned solving all three questions, after which they asked me to explain the approach for just one of them.

● In some panels, if a candidate solved only two questions, the third question (from the assessment) would be asked in the interview. The assessment questions were generally easier than the interview questions, so solving and explaining one clearly in the interview left a positive impression. So if you know all 3, you could just solve 2 and take a chance that you might get asked the 3rd one in the interview.

SQL & fundamentals:

● A simple SQL query was asked (a simple JOIN query with some conditions). Beyond writing the query, they asked how to optimize it (indexes), and what a stored procedure and trigger is.

Cloud & deployment:

● We discussed on-premise vs cloud: I explained that cloud simplifies scaling and managed services but can have latency trade-offs; for performance-critical pieces, edge or hybrid approaches might be appropriate. They asked about packaging and deploying an app, so mention containers, CI/CD pipelines and dockers but I was not much aware of it so just stated my limited knowledge of those terms and didn't elaborate much.

● ! DO NOT SAY ANY THINGS THAT YOU ARE NOT AWARE OF !

○ It is always good to say that you don't know rather than saying something wrong or the interviewer sensing that you are not much aware of the topic.

Behavioral & communication expectations in the round (key):

● Think out loud, ask for constraints, write the brute force approach and then optimize, and write pseudo-code once the approach is agreed upon. Test your solution with 1 example.

● If stuck, say "I need a minute to think" (they prefer structured thinking). Interviewers will often ask to justify your step; do not be defensive if they probe -- it's expected.

My personal takeaways from Round 1:

● Be crisp about your projects. When you mention an implementation detail casually, the panel will latch on to it and probe deeper -- so be deliberate with your words.

● Explain tradeoffs instead of one-line answers. For example, saying "I used Firebase" should be followed by why (speed of development, managed auth, real-time DB) and when you'd not use it (complex relational joins, transaction-heavy systems).

● It was a varied experience from panel to panel, some panels had hard DSA Q solving, some evolved around resume, some went in depth with SQL, some were in detail about sorting algos, so you can't exactly predict what can be asked but it is good to cover basics and know your resume well.

3. Hiring Manager Round [On day 1, about 8-10 students had been shortlisted ]

● On paper, this round was worth around 10 marks, but the final decision largely rested with the directors and hiring managers. Although marks were assigned, I don't think the selection was purely based on scores.

● After the technical panels, Russell conducted further shortlisting: they called a small set of candidates (about 10) for the director/hiring-manager-level conversation. Some candidates were taken aside and told they would not be moving forward. There were moments of waiting and refreshment breaks while panels and shortlists completed.

● My final round was with the Director at app dev (about 23 years of experience) -- this round was intentionally more conversational and lasted around 25-30 minutes. The Director started with a friendly tone (asked about my day, understood nerves, and deliberately relaxed the conversation). He dived on my ability to:

○ Break down end-to-end use cases and how I would approach them from design to deployment.

○ Explain the SDLC and the phases where I'd focus depending on a product's maturity.

○ Discuss DevOps basics -- pipelines, infrastructure, monitoring, and release strategies.

○ Handle behavioral scenarios: working under deadlines, facing ambiguity, collaborating with non-tech stakeholders.

● This round evaluated structured thinking, cultural fit, communication and ownership more than raw coding skill.

Result & offer:

● Results were declared on 18 March 2025. For the Technology Intern (Application Developer) role, 6 interns were selected; 4 of those were from SPIT.

● The entire hiring process felt based on merit: there were students from many colleges in the applicant pool, and Russell reviewed candidates from across campuses.

My internship (brief reflection on the actual internship work):

● Now that I have completed the internship and am writing this, I can say it was very valuable. I worked on two substantive problem statements that had real ownership and impact. Weekly cross-team sessions introduced us to internal flows -- not just tech teams but business and product -- which helped me understand financial domain flows. Mentors were supportive and assigned meaningful responsibilities; interns even presented to Heads across offices and the MD at times. The exposure to the financial-services ecosystem, real production constraints, and presentation experience was invaluable.

What I did well (strengths that helped):

● Clear, confident resume projects articulated with "what/how/why" rather than surface-level bullets.

● Practiced think-out-loud approach during DSA -- started with brute force and improved the solution.

● Paid attention to system-design tradeoffs (Firebase vs SQL, on-prem vs cloud) and explained reasoning.

● Maintained composure in the final director round (honest about nervousness, but confident on substance).

● Prepared practical examples and could tie academic knowledge to project reality.

What I could have done better (honest learnings):

● I could have prepared a more concise elevator pitch specifically tailored to the role.

● I could have rehearsed a few more behavioral stories with specific metrics (S-T-A-R with numbers).

● I could have been even more deliberate when using throwaway words (they sometimes pick up on casual mentions).

● Improve clarity on when to choose SQL over NoSQL in enterprise scenarios -- have ready examples of data models to explain the choice (this is one thing I learnt really well during my internship).

What all to focus on (not just for Russell but for overall on campus tech placements):

i. Core CS fundamentals (must-do):

● Refresh DBMS basics: normalization, indexing, JOINs, transactions.

● Review Operating Systems basics.

● Networking fundamentals.

● OOPs: basic patterns and why you'd use them. (for other on campus companies, focus on doing OOPs in Java, Russell evaluated me on my overall knowledge, not a particular language)

ii. Coding & DSA (practical):

● Do arrays, linked lists, stacks/queues, trees, hashing, binary search.

● Practice medium problems on NeetCode or Striver; quality > quantity.

● When solving: ask clarifying Qs, present brute-force, optimize, write pseudo-code, test with examples, always dry run.

iii. System design / architecture:

● Practice small designs: auth flow, notifications system, basic microservice breakdown.

● Read about caching strategies (LRU caches, Redis, Hive), CDNs, load balancers, queues, and patterns for scaling. Head First Design Patterns helps for design patterns; for system design, learn common building blocks and tradeoffs.

iv. Cloud & DevOps basics:

● Know the basics of Cloud, how to deploy and its performance metrics.

● Be familiar with the basic terminologies of DevOps.

v. SQL practice:

● Do focused practice: LC SQL 50 and W3Schools/TutorialsPoint for syntax and edge cases. Learn and read the basics of indexing.

vi. Aptitude & fit:

● Warm up with IndiaBix style aptitude practice; be fast and accurate for the OAs.

vii. Project preparation:

● Know your resume projects inside-out. For each project, be ready to answer: architecture diagram, deployment steps, bottlenecks encountered, alternate designs, and "if I had more time, I would…".

viii. Soft skills & behavioral:

● Prepare 6-8 STAR stories: leadership, failure & learning, conflict, impact, ownership. Use metrics where possible.

● Prepare a few smart questions tailored to the interviewer's role (not generic company questions).

ix. General longer-term preparation (CGPA, internships, hackathons):

● CGPA: Maintain at least 7.5+; higher CGPA helps in shortlisting. Beyond ~8 it doesn't add much (except for firms like ISS & JPMC which prefer 8.5+).

● Internships: Even a small/unpaid internship adds credibility -- shows real-world exposure, teamwork, and practical application beyond coursework.

● Hackathons: Actively participate in hackathons; they build problem-solving under deadlines, give concrete projects to showcase, and often impress interviewers more than certificates.

x. Always tailor your resume according to the role and JD provided but never lie on it.

Interview day strategy:

Before the interview:

● Sleep well (8+ hours), eat a light breakfast, arrive 15 minutes early.

● Review bullet points of your projects, resume, and a short list of behavioral stories.

● Carry multiple printed copies of your resume (ensure it's set to A4 size in Overleaf for proper length and accurate print layout).

During the interview:

● Start strong with a calm introduction -- firm handshake, clear voice, concise 1-2 minute summary.

● Think out loud. Interviewers care about the process. Say constraints aloud; ask clarifying Qs..

● Brute force → optimize. If you can't find the optimal immediately, start with a simple solution and refine.

● Write pseudo-code and test it with sample input (edge cases included).

● If stuck, request a minute to organize thoughts -- better than blundering through.

● Ask intelligent, role-specific questions at the end. Tailor them to the interviewer's background.

After the interview:

● Be polite and composed. Hope for the best and prepare for the worst.

Questions to ask the interviewer (tailor them):

● Have some questions prepared beforehand but there's no need to just stick to those, listen to when the interviewer introduces themselves and ask questions that would be relevant to them and their team, not just company related questions that you had looked up earlier.

● For a technical interviewer: "What are the core problems the team is solving this quarter?" / "What does success look like for an intern in just 8-12 weeks?"

● For a manager/director: "How does the team measure impact?" / "Which areas should new joiners focus on to be productive quickly?"

● Avoid generic questions like "Tell me about the company"; tie your question to the person (e.g., "You mentioned X in your talk -- could you elaborate on how the team handles Y?").

Final tips & mindset:

Confidence + Humility: Be confident about what you know; be humble and honest about gaps. It's far better to say "I don't know that detail, but here's how I'd find/approach it" than to bluff.

Clarity of thought: Structured answers beat long-winded ones. Use short steps and call out assumptions.

Consistency over cramming: Daily steady practice (2-3 hours) is more effective than a single marathon.

Focus on learning concepts, reasoning, and fundamentals: Don't just chase numbers and get behind solving X number of Qs, achieving Y rank or winning Z hackathons, always keep learning as your core, pay importance to understanding from basics, success will follow.

Build projects that teach you tradeoffs: Real projects (even simple ones) let you answer "why" questions convincingly.

Health & mental prep: Sleep, minimal caffeine, and small relaxation techniques (deep breaths) before a round help dramatically.

Common pitfalls (avoid these):

● Jumping straight into code without confirming problem constraints.

● Not testing solutions with examples and edge cases.

● Overpromising or fabricating experience from your resume.

● Being too generic in behavioral answers -- always add specific outcomes and numbers.

● Not asking any questions at the end or asking questions that show lack of preparation.

Useful Resources:

● Aptitude: IndiaBix practice problems.

● DSA: NeetCode / Striver.

● SQL: W3Schools, practice LC SQL 50 problems.

● Design patterns & architecture: Head First Design Patterns (intro).

● CS Fundamentals: Make use of GPT to generate a list of topics, and Claude to make elaborate notes, use GFG, InterviewBit for core subjects as well.

● General interview prep: Do refer to interview exps, look up ambition box as well.

● Practice & exposure: Participate in hackathons -- the learning is often more valuable than winning (projects + deadlines teach you a lot).

Remember, placements can be a tough journey. It's important to realistically assess your chances, see which companies visit your college, and understand what opportunities align with your capabilities.

The main thing in on campus placements are LUCK, LUCK and LUCK!

So, if you get an opportunity for a good summer internship, it's wise to take your best shot at it and secure a strong backup. Then, you can focus on preparing for off-campus opportunities if you feel you can achieve even more. On-campus, apart from 1-2 exceptions, most companies fall within a similar range of CTC, and nothing is guaranteed. Even after solving thousands of questions, unexpected issues like technical errors can occur on d-day.

In short: aim for a good summer internship, keep a solid backup plan, and prepare for off-campus placements at a steady pace.

ALL THE BEST! You can contact me any time for any help and guidance: (+91 8169617362) / https://www.linkedin.com/in/sanjeev-ratnani/

journey.prep:
● Balance DSA & Development: Don't get stuck in the DSA vs. Development debate. Strive to maintain a healthy balance between both. While DSA and CP build problem-solving skills, in interviews your projects and CS fundamentals often take center stage.

● Maintain a CGPA of 8+: Aim for a CGPA of at least 8.0 to ensure eligibility for most on-campus companies. No matter how skilled you are, missing eligibility criteria due to CGPA can be disheartening.

● Revise CS Fundamentals: Core subjects like OOPs, DBMS, OS, CN, and SQL are crucial. These are frequently asked in interviews and can make or break your performance.

● Basic System Design Knowledge: Get familiar with basic system design concepts. I was asked about this in my PhonePe HM round, so don't ignore it.

● Master One Language: Be fluent in at least one programming language--C++ in my case, but Java or Python are equally good. Depth matters more than breadth here.

● Build Strong Projects: Have at least two solid and unique projects in your resume that you can explain thoroughly and confidently. Your ability to discuss them can drive the interview forward.

● Participate in Coding Contests: Regular participation in CP contests sharpens your thinking under pressure and builds speed--both essential in coding rounds.

● Stay Consistent and Positive: Do your best, be consistent, and give every opportunity your 100%. Remember, luck also plays a role on interview day. Don't get disheartened by rejections--keep going. Opportunities will come; just stay calm, hopeful, and focused.

journey.howSecured:
Hello guys,

The entire placement journey was both challenging and tested my perseverance. Before Barclays, I had cleared all the rounds at PhonePe but was unfortunately rejected in the Hiring Manager round. That experience was disheartening, especially because I had dedicated a lot of time and energy preparing for that opportunity -- consistently practicing on platforms like Codeforces, CodeChef, LeetCode, Atcoder, and CSES, etc

That setback impacted my confidence and performance in the subsequent companies. However, when Barclays visited our campus, I saw it as a fresh opportunity--and I'm happy to share that I cleared all the rounds successfully.

My key message to all future candidates is: have faith in yourself and in your efforts. If you've worked hard, it will pay off sooner or later. Rejections are part of the process, and luck does play a role. What matters most is giving your best every single time, regardless of the outcome.

1. Online Assessment Round [ 135 students appeared for this round and 37 students shortlisted]

The Online Assessment (OA) round was conducted on 26th July 2025 at 11:00 AM in offline mode at the college campus. The test was hosted on the HackerEarth platform. It consisted of a total of 15 questions, and the duration was 90 minutes.

The 15 questions were divided into the following three sections:

Section 1: MCQs (13 Questions) This section included multiple-choice questions from topics such as OOPs (Java), DBMS (SQL), code

snippet output-based questions, Operating Systems (OS), and Computer Networks (CCN). The MCQs were largely focused on Java OOPs concepts and were conceptual and slightly tricky. It is important to be well-prepared in core CS fundamentals. In my opinion, the MCQ section was the key shortlisting factor, as most students were able to solve the DSA and SQL questions.

Section 2: SQL Question (1 Question) This was a basic SQL query-based question involving date and time functions. The task was to find the names of employees who were working only in the month of October. I solved this using the WHERE clause along with the LIKE operator. Although this question was easy, I have encountered much more difficult SQL questions in assessments for other companies such as MSCI. Therefore, it is important to be well-prepared. I highly recommend practicing the SQL 50 questions sheet available on LeetCode, which I had completed prior to this test.

Section 3: DSA Coding Question (1 Question) Interestingly, this was the exact same question that was asked in the previous year's Barclays placement and summer internship OA. Since I was already aware of it, I was well-prepared.

Question link:

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/description/

Solution Link:

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/solutions/7042670/simple-greedy -constructive-approach-c-by-s03n

My Approach: I started with the DSA question and completed it first. Then, I moved on to the SQL question. Both were completed in about 15 to 20 minutes. After that, I carefully attempted the MCQ section, as I knew it would be critical for shortlisting.

Preparation Tips:

#Tip 1: Start preparing for core CS fundamentals and OOPs concepts 2 to 3 months in advance. Even though I code in C++, I prepared OOPs in Java specifically for such assessments.

#Tip 2: Practice the SQL 50 sheet on LeetCode thoroughly. Also, review window functions, as they are commonly asked in interviews.

#Tip 3: Begin DSA preparation at least 6 months before placements. I am more inclined toward DSA and competitive programming, so I maintained a daily streak on LeetCode and participated in contests. It's not mandatory to do competitive programming on platforms like Codeforces, but it definitely helps. You can refer to Striver's SDE Sheet for structured practice. I personally followed Love Babbar's DSA Playlist in C++ during my preparation.

2. Technical Round [ 37 Students Appeared and 21 Students Shortlisted ]

I cleared the OA round, and the interview process was scheduled on 29th July 2025. We were asked to report by 8:30 in the morning. However, since I stay in Kalyan, more precisely in Shahad, and it takes around 1.5 to 2 hours to reach college, unfortunately, I missed my train and reached college a little late. The Barclays Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) had already started, but in a hurry, I submitted one copy of my resume to the TPC and rushed to attend the PPT. Please make sure to come early and be on time. During the PPT, they discussed Barclays' RISES principles. While attending, make sure to note important points like their values, culture, company's Tech Stack, RISES principles, etc.

The first technical interview round began shortly after. I was called to panel number 4. I went there, knocked on the door, and asked for permission to enter. I greeted the interviewer, Mr. Rahul Sir, who was himself an alumnus of SPIT.

He started by asking how my day was and where I stayed. I shared that I commute daily via local trains and the metro, and how I manage my time effectively--solving problems, studying, and listening to music while traveling.

The discussion then moved toward my project section. I have a total of three projects listed on my resume, all of which are Full Stack MERN projects. He began with my third project, Zerodha. He asked me to explain the project. Then he asked how I take user info--does it include personal information like bank details? I answered yes, we take such details and perform encryption and hashing to secure them.

He then asked how the data gets stored in the database and which database I used. I explained that I used MongoDB, a NoSQL database, and also justified why I chose MongoDB.

Next, he moved on to my second project, Job Portal, which is a job application platform. He asked how job seekers' data and their experiences are stored in the database, how I collect the data, and how it gets reflected on the UI. When the recruiter clicks on the user details, how does the page render the information? What are the schemas for the candidates and recruiters?

I explained all of this on pen and paper. I also demonstrated how I implemented the .map() function in JavaScript and React to render user info dynamically. I described how I implemented dynamic search filters in the project.

After this, he came to my first project, StudyNotion, an EdTech platform. He asked why I created this project--what was the inspiration? I told him about my mentoring and teaching experience at Wegyan Institute, and how I wanted to build a platform where students could watch lectures if they missed offline classes. I also discussed features like assignments, DPPs, and other functionalities I implemented.

Later, he asked me some basic Java concepts. Although I am primarily a C++ programmer, I had also learned Java. So if you know Java, it will definitely help in the interview.

Make sure you know your resume thoroughly because they can ask anything and everything from it.

At the end of the interview, he said he was done with his questions and asked if I had any questions for him.

It's always a good idea to ask company-relevant questions to show your interest. I asked:

● What roles and responsibilities would I have if selected, and how can I improve in those areas?

● Can you share your role in the company and the department you work in?

● What is the most fun thing you love about working at Barclays?

He answered all these questions very well, and the interview finally concluded.

This round lasted for around 40 to 45 minutes.

3. Techno + HR Round [ 21 Students Appeared for this round ]

After the first round, I was a little bit confident that I had given my best in the interview and might be called for Round 2. So, I started preparing for standard HR questions using ChatGPT and also revised some questions I had written down in my notes. Meanwhile, I was called in for the second round.

The second round began, and the interviewer asked me how my first interview was. I replied that it went well and was taken by Mr. Rahul Sir, who is our alumnus, and that he shared how he got into Barclays, etc.

For some candidates, this round was a pure HR round, but for me, it was a mix--I was asked both technical and HR-based questions. The interviewer went through my resume and asked about JWT authentication, which I had mentioned in my project. He asked, "What exactly is JWT?" I explained how it contains three sections: payload, header, and signature. He then asked follow-up questions like what does "expiry" mean in JWT, is it set by default or manually, what is the main purpose of JWT, and whether it is stored on the client side or server side. I answered all these questions properly, and we had a discussion around cookies as well.

Later on, he asked how I learned multiple programming languages.

Then he asked, "Have you ever misunderstood anything? If yes, what action did you take, and what was the conclusion?" This was a good question, so I asked him if I could take a minute to think. He said yes. Then I told him about one incident from a past semester: I had misunderstood the exam schedule. I thought the next day was the OS paper, but it was actually the DAA paper. I had prepared for OS, but just 2 hours before the exam, I got to know it was DAA. However, since DAA was my favorite subject and I had solved thousands of problems related to Data Structures and Algorithms, I quickly revised my notes and gave the exam. I ended up scoring well. He seemed impressed with this response.

After that, he asked what contributions I had made in my group projects and about my hackathon experience. I answered everything in detail.

Then he asked, "Have you done anything in your life whose fruits are still being enjoyed by someone?" Since I had already mentioned that I mentored and taught more than 100+ students in offline batches, I told him that some of my students cracked the NEET examination with good marks. He then asked how I got into teaching just after giving my JEE Advanced exam, and also asked what my percentile was.

After all these questions, he said, "Good to know all these things from you," and then told me he was done with his questions. He asked if I had any questions for him.

I asked, "While working at Barclays, if I want to learn new technologies and frameworks, how can I do that and what is the process?"

This round lasted around 30 to 45 minutes.

Finally, 16 students were selected--and I was one of them.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
● Balance DSA & Development: Don't get stuck in the DSA vs. Development debate. Strive to maintain a healthy balance between both. While DSA and CP build problem-solving skills, in interviews your projects and CS fundamentals often take center stage.

● Maintain a CGPA of 8+: Aim for a CGPA of at least 8.0 to ensure eligibility for most on-campus companies. No matter how skilled you are, missing eligibility criteria due to CGPA can be disheartening.

● Revise CS Fundamentals: Core subjects like OOPs, DBMS, OS, CN, and SQL are crucial. These are frequently asked in interviews and can make or break your performance.

● Basic System Design Knowledge: Get familiar with basic system design concepts. I was asked about this in my PhonePe HM round, so don't ignore it.

● Master One Language: Be fluent in at least one programming language--C++ in my case, but Java or Python are equally good. Depth matters more than breadth here.

● Build Strong Projects: Have at least two solid and unique projects in your resume that you can explain thoroughly and confidently. Your ability to discuss them can drive the interview forward.

● Participate in Coding Contests: Regular participation in CP contests sharpens your thinking under pressure and builds speed--both essential in coding rounds.

● Stay Consistent and Positive: Do your best, be consistent, and give every opportunity your 100%. Remember, luck also plays a role on interview day. Don't get disheartened by rejections--keep going. Opportunities will come; just stay calm, hopeful, and focused.

Process involved:

1. Pre-placement talk

2. Aptitude test

3. Technical Interview 1

4. Technical Interview 2

5. HR Round

1. Preplacement Talk:

This was an online round. We were briefed about the company, its values and the roles they offered. There were 3 roles available for us in 3 different divisions, ITD, GM and CDO. It is recommended to have your webcam on and ask questions during the pre-placement talk.

2. Online Aptitude Test [181 Students appeared for the test] This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine - PARIKSHA. The test consisted of 60 questions, with 20 questions each in the verbal, analytical,

and quantitative sections, with no negative marking. The time limit was 60 minutes so timing is the key here. The questions were of easy-medium difficulty. Mostly, people use IndiaBix which is sufficient for practicing. I'd recommend solving the verbal and analytical questions first and then moving on to the quants as this section is time consuming. Some questions are purely in the test to waste your time. Try and identify these types of questions and keep them for the end. I split the test into 10 minutes for verbal, 15-20 for logical and 30-35 minutes for the quantitative section.

Somebody had mailed the TPO about a cheating scandal in the OA test which prompted the TPO to inform the company about the same. Things like these tarnish the reputation of the college and further discouraged the company from hiring more students.

Due to the allegations, Nomura decided to take another written OA which consisted of 1 DSA question, 1 quant and 1 sql query within 20 minutes.

The dsa question was pretty easy where we basically had to return the largest sum of a contiguous part of an array. Since the entire array was given to be positive you can just sum up all numbers and return the total sum. In case the array contains negative numbers, Kadane's Algorithm can be used to solve this problem. I had written both approaches in my solution describing the cases.

Again the quant and query were pretty easy.

They used this test to eliminate 20 of the 27 students from interviews directly.

I had given my 1st Technical Interview before this test.

2. Technical Interview - 1 [ Remaining 7 students from the written OA were shortlisted for this]

This round started at around 10 am. I was asked to introduce myself. It happened before the written OA test. Most of the early questions were based on my resume. I had mentioned a Spring Boot project and told him that Java is my primary programming language. So the next 80% of our discussion revolved around Spring Framework, Java and OOPS (I was very happy that he went towards this :) . He asked me about inheritance and polymorphism and gave me different scenarios. Also I was asked about binary search tree, quick sort algo and time complexity in general. Then I was asked about the actual implementation of HashMap in Java and how the internal methods are implemented (also asked about hashing function, collisions and how they are handled). Next I was given a simple SQL query and asked some HR type questions. Then we just talked casually about the entire placement process and asked me about my experience throughout the journey. At this point we were having just a normal conversation about stuff and he asked if I had any questions for him to which I asked a couple and the interview ended. This was a pretty chill experience for me since all the topics we discussed we my favs.

3. Technical Interview - 2 [6 students were shortlisted for this round]

This round started at around 2:30 pm post lunch. There were 2 interviewers in each panel for this round. He asked me to give my introduction but nothing from my resume lol. We started by discussing Spring Framework (yet again yess) and how it differs from MERN, its benefits and widespread use cases. We talked about JUnit testing and how unit testing works further delving into different types of testing methodologies. They went through my resume and asked me detailed questions about the technical skills that I had mentioned in the resume. I was asked questions about MERN stack and databases used in my projects. We had a discussion about JWT and how it works. I was also asked about Hadoop and how it works (I had mentioned hadoop on my resume). We also talked about how Spring Security works and how it is different from some other ways to secure web applications.

We discussed about Stripe (used in a project) payment gateway which is similar to razorpay and how it works. This was a relatively shorter round than the first one (1st was 75 minutes long ) which lasted around 40 minutes.

4. HR Round [ Total 3 candidates appeared for this round ] This was a pretty chill round as the HR and I were just having a fun conversation about my hobbies, Music, movies & series recommendations for him to which I recommended Chernobyl and The Green Book. Then he asked me how my usual day looks compared to the one we were having and I told him it had been unexpectedly smooth. I had mentioned a CFI course and he asked me about and I said it was purely out of curiosity about accounting. We talked about some things I had not mentioned on my resume and he wrapped things up from his side.

All 3 students (2 B.Tech + 1 MCA) were finally offered the role :)

Have 4-5 good projects covering important domains and use them appropriately for the JD you're applying for. Interviewers often ask 2-3 niche questions to try and shake your confidence. In such times, try and steer the discussion to the nearest relatable topic/case you can think of instead of saying idk.

For vague questions or scenarios be upfront and ask them the details before assuming especially for puzzles and dsa questions.

I had done 90% of the Striver's A2Z DSA course and solved LeetCode Daily problems, maintained a streak of 300+ which covered most of the DSA areas. This was certainly a bit overkill but I enjoyed solving it. Solving even about 150 varied and good quality problems are enough.

For SQL, leetcode-sql-50 will suffice (I personally did the first 30 only lol).

I didn't really practice for OAs specifically but Indiabix and Interviewbit are helpful.

I had made sure to do some web development in Spring Framework, since Java was my primary programming language.

Make sure every single thing mentioned on your resume is relevant and you have sufficient knowledge about the topics and projects mentioned.

Questions related to tech stack used, not used, why, how, are litmus tests for interviewers to test your technical knowledge and skills so be prepared for them.

The first few interviews might feel a bit overwhelming, but once you get the hang of it things get pretty easy. Keep a smile and just be yourself.

Some backstory up until this interview: Sometimes interview rounds are quite tough. I was asked 5 DSA questions in the MSCI process, one of which was to implement heapify process and I couldn't recall and that was the only thing which I couldn't answer which got me out. So sometimes even though you try your best, destiny wants you somewhere else :) I got shortlisted for interview rounds for JPMC, UBS, MSCI, IDFC before Nomura. IDFC was just a day before the Nomura OA and I had reached the final 4th round which was online which was taken by their IT Lead and welp I couldn't make it. I was pretty devastated with the result and my mental health took a hit since I was pretty confident on getting a positive result. I gathered all the courage for the Nomura OA the very next day and my friends & family helped immensely getting through that. The 15-20 days of placement season were no doubt some of the most tense days of my life. The uncertainty, series of negative results plays tricks on your psyche. There's a very good quote by Rick and Morty that sums up the process 'Everything will be fine in the end, Morty ; And if it isn't, it's not the end yet' eventually everything will fall into place that's for sure. It's ok to be anxious, there's no way not to be. Try and compose yourself and use the experience from negative results to iteratively work on weaknesses and better yourself.

Just know that some time in the future you will look back at this time and have a chuckle :)

Things might feel out of control or unlucky at times but have trust in your abilities and Keep giving your best cuz you only need luck to be on your side just once.

To everyone reading this, Best of Luck for your future escapades and know that you deserve the best!!

For any questions, you can find me here : LinkedIn : Shardul

journey.prep:
1. Aptitude Preparation:

○ Don't take aptitude lightly. I initially thought only a few companies would ask for it, but almost every company includes aptitude in their selection process.

○ In some of the companies, I was able to solve the coding questions, but I couldn't solve the aptitude questions correctly, so I wasn't shortlisted for the next round.

○ Start preparing at least one month before placements to build confidence and speed.

○ Resources for Aptitude: IndiaBix & FreshCareers

○ Tricks and Shortcuts for Aptitude: Imran Sir Maths & Last Moment Tuitions

2. DSA Preparation:

● Follow Resources:

○ Striver DSA Sheet (A to Z) - Covers all important DSA topics systematically. Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet

○ Aditya Verma's YouTube Channel: Offers detailed explanations and tutorials on various DSA concepts. Aditya Verma

● Daily Practice:

○ Solve problems on LeetCode daily. Starting just one month before placements is usually not enough. Regular practice builds speed, accuracy, and problem-solving intuition.

● Contests and Challenges:

○ Participate in daily/weekly coding contests. This helps improve problem-solving under time pressure and exposes you to a variety of question types.

3. SQL / Database Preparation:

○ Practice Queries: Solve at least 50 SQL problems on LeetCode covering different concepts like SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, subqueries, and aggregation functions.

○ Understand Concepts: Be clear about SQL vs NoSQL, normalization, relationships, and indexing.

○ Practical Application: Try to write queries on sample databases to understand how tables relate and how data can be extracted efficiently.

○ Understand ER Diagram to SQL Conversion.

○ Resources: GeeksforGeeks: Mapping from ER Model to Relational Model & CodeChef: ER Diagrams to Tables Practice Problems

○ DBMS One shot: DBMS Concept (For Concept Revision)

4. Javascript: Javascript

5. Java: Complete Java Programming Course

6. Output Guess Questions: Geeks for Geeks

7. Communication Skills / Soft Skills

Clarity and Confidence: Speak clearly and confidently during interviews. Avoid filler words and maintain a steady pace.

Think Aloud:

○ While solving coding or technical problems, explain your thought process aloud.

○ This helps the interviewer understand your approach, reasoning, and problem-solving skills, even if the final answer isn't correct.

Active Listening: Pay attention to the interviewer's questions and respond accordingly. Don't interrupt; it shows respect and good listening skills.

8. Believe in God's Plan / Stay Positive:

○ Trust that everything happens for a reason. Stay calm and positive throughout the preparation and interview process.

○ A strong mindset and faith can help you stay motivated even during challenges or setbacks.

BEST OF LUCKKK!!

If you need any help or want to know more feel free to reach out .

1. Resume Shortlisting

2. Pre Placement Talk

3. Technical Interview

4. HR Interview

1. Resume Shortlisting [Everyone above 6 CGPA applied ]

Applications opened on Superset on 1st September with a minimum eligibility criterion of 6 CGPA. However, during shortlisting, only students with 7.5 CGPA and above were considered. Shortlisting was done based on keywords in the resume, required skills, and relevant internships or projects. A total of 18 students were shortlisted, and the list was announced on 8th September.

Pre-Placement Talk -

The PPT was conducted just before the interviews on 10th September by TransBnk's CTO and HR. They explained about the company--how they started, what motivated them, their current status, and the kind of candidates they were looking for. I carefully noted down key points from the presentation that later came up in my technical interview. I made sure to connect what the presenters shared with the homework I had done about the company. This gave me clarity and confidence when interacting with the interviewers.

2. Technical Interview [ 18 candidates appeared for this round ]

The first round was taken by a panel consisting of two interviewers and lasted around 45 minutes to 1 hour. It began with a simple "Introduce yourself," after which they focused on my projects. They asked me to explain the workflow of my projects in detail. After discussing the projects, the interviewers shifted their attention to my technical skills and asked questions on RabbitMQ, OOP concepts, whether Java is single-threaded or multi-threaded, the difference between method overloading and method overriding, and the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases. They also asked about the internship I had done and

what work I had completed during it. At one point, they asked why I chose the SDE profile when my course is AIML.

They also asked questions on Spring Boot and React hooks. On the DSA side, I was given a coding problem to solve live on their laptop, which was the LeetCode problem Set Matrix Zeroes.

Tips & Takeaways:

For project-related discussions, it's really helpful to use the STAR method--first explain the situation your project was solving, then your role or task, the actions you took (technologies, code, concepts used), and finally the result or outcome. Make sure to be thorough with your resume and the skills you have mentioned, because interviewers often dive deep into whatever is listed. When discussing projects, including details about the code and how it works can make your explanation more clear and convincing.

3. HR Interview [ 6 candidates appeared for this round ]

The HR round began with a simple "Introduce yourself" question. After that, he asked me to explain my projects, but not in too much detail--just enough to understand my role and the technologies I worked with. He also asked about my strengths and weaknesses to get a sense of my personal and professional qualities. One of the key questions was why I chose to start my career at TransBnk instead of joining a bigger MNC. Towards the end of the round, he asked if I had any questions, and I asked, "How does TransBnk support fresh graduates in their career growth and learning?" This showed my interest in learning and developing within the company. The HR round lasted around 15 to 20 minutes and mainly focused on understanding my personality, motivation, and alignment with the company culture.

Tips & Takeaways:

● Be well-prepared with common HR questions, as most companies ask similar questions.

● Always ask a question at the end of the interview--it shows that you are genuinely interested in learning more about the company and its culture.

● Be confident while answering; do not appear hesitant or unsure.

● Maintain a positive attitude and always have a smile on your face throughout the interview.

4. Prank Round [ 4 candidates appeared for this round ]

After the HR round, there was a funny prank round. They called four people and said that only three seats were available, so someone would have to back out. Naturally, it created a little tension, but then they revealed that it was a prank and that all of us were actually selected for TransBnk. It was a light-hearted way to end the process and made the announcement memorable.

4 students were offered the job and I am one of them.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

2. Technical Interview Round

3. HR Interview Round

1. Online Assessment Round ( 197 Students ) ( 11/07/2025 )

UBS had a criteria of 7+ gpa till 3rd semester( I was in Summer breaks of 4th Sem to 5th Sem when the company came for internships). So 226 Applicants Filled the google form but along with filling the google forms you also need to register on their website. Only 197 registered on their website and hence the rest were not eligible for OA round. Before OA round there were 2 assessments on their website

UBS culture matching test

Aptitude

You can prepare for this just by searching about those on google/youtube ,etc.

Next there was the OA round.

It was a 90min Online Test on HackerRank.

There were 15 java/dbms/data structure questions + 15 Aptitude questions + 1 DSA question

Aptitude Questions included :

Sets questions ( just revise the sets from 12th standard or DSGT)

Probability ( just revise class 12th probability)

Basic graph interpretation ( class 10th graph knowledge would work)

Passage based questions

For the passage based questions just remember to extract the relevant information only. Remember this is important. It will have a lot of irrelevant information and take a lot of time if you read it entirely.

DSA Question:

They asked pretty easy questions. Just based on Arrays, HashMap, basic techniques like sliding window,prefix-suffix,etc. So just preparing for basics would also work, no need to go through DP on trees,etc.

My question was:

You will be given an array of size n. You need to divide the array in 2 parts such that the sum of the number of distinct elements from the left part and right part is maximum. You need to return that maximum sum.

constraints : 1<n<10e5

Example : 3 1 4 1 5

So here , if i partition them like 3 1 and 4 1 5 then no. of distinct elements of 3 1 is 2 and for 4 1 5 is 3 so sum is 5 , where as if i partition them like 3 and 1 4 1 5 then the no. of distinct elements would be 1 and for the 1 4 1 5 it would be 3 so sum is 4. But by partitioning 3 1 and 4 1 5 we got the sum as 5. So that is the maximum that we need to return.

My Approach:

So obviously brute force won't work as constraints are 10e5, So what i want ?

I want the left distinct + right distinct as max. So , let's think that i will try at every index that by partitioning at that index , what can be the sum and i will find the maximum among that.

Ok , so it will take O(n) , now I need to find the no. of distinct elements from left and right in either O(1) or in O(n). So brute force is just finding the no. of distinct elements every time. What if we just precompute those. Yes, we will use the prefix and suffix approach and that's it. We are good to go.

You can check out the code at : https://pastebin.com/G7g3Pm2n

So I advise that you focus on java and aptitude , dsa questions were pretty much doable.

Just be chill, you can do it, don't get too stressed, that's the advice.

2. [Technical Interview ] [16 Students] 14/07/2025

It was an offline face to face interview.

So the first question they asked me was what's your CGPA. I answered it, I guess I was the only one of

whom they wrote the GPA on the Resume. ( Maybe because it was high(9.79)). Next they asked me about

the Barclays minor as I was part of that. Next they asked me to introduce myself.

Then the next question was what's my strongest subject, what's the subject that I don't like.

Although I did say oops as my strongest subject they still asked only 3-4 theory questions and 1 written question.

Next they moved on to the Data Structures, they asked me a lot of questions on this. And asked very basic algorithm questions.

Then next they asked me 2 quizzes. One was on probability and other I avoided answering it.

Then next they asked me some DBMS questions. Then they asked me about github, leetcode,codechef profiles. Then they moved on to some HR questions. Although it was technical round but still they asked me

HR questions.(I don't know whether other's faced the same or not). Just make sure you attend the preplacement talk with them. That's enough for the knowledge regarding the company.

They also asked about my strengths, weaknesses, hobbies, extra-circular activities, where I live,what my parents do, etc all. Being a part of any committee and leading any position would work for extra circular activities.

For OOPS : java docs, Kunal Kushwaha, Durga Software Solutions and MOST IMP IS BY JUST RANDOMLY TRYING RANDOM CODES. I mean just write the random codes, what if i add static here , what if I add final here.

For Data Structures : As i said java they asked how internally java Collections implement these Data Structures, So make sure you see the actual implementation. Next, preparing well for even Semester exams was ok(not sufficient) for this. Just have a curiosity while preparing for semester exams you will learn some

Relevant things around the syllabus and that's sufficient.

For Algorithms : It was basic. Following any sheet might work. To be honest I didn't even refer to one. I just solved Random Questions. One of the key mentors is Sujal Das . Doing CP for this is extremely more than enough.

For DBMS : Pretty Basic Questions on this. But College Syllabus is not enough for this, You have to prepare

Well other than college syllabus.

3. [HR Round] [9 Students ] 14/07/2025

To be honest, for other people it was around 15-20 minutes grind. For me it was just 2 minutes of casual talk. They asked me where I live, what my parents do, from where I completed my 12th, why I didn't choose Walchand Sangli (I am from Solapur, I did my 12th from Walchand Solapur, They mis understood it as Sangli and hence asked). Also they asked what is Barclays Minor in my Resume. And that's it, I have literally listed entire HR round questions. They just asked me these questions and for others it was literal grind. So if you do well in the technical round, HR will be just a formality.

Finally 3 people got selected for Internships.

Eligibility Criteria was 6.5+ CGPA, No Backlogs and Resume shortlisting. All branches were eligible (not sure about MCA).

1. OA Round [167 candidates appeared, 46 shortlisted] (Invigilation was done by the company)

Platform: Microsoft forms

Duration: 30 mins

No. of questions: 25

The test consisted of topics covering SQL, output based questions (python/Java), Aptitude, OS, CCN, DSA, Cloud Computing. If you have a strong grip on CS core subjects, this test would be comparatively easier for you. Time management is key so attempt confident questions first, then move to elimination or educated guesses. I hadn't prepared for Cloud Computing and CCN well, which had cost me several marks, so make sure to cover these areas as well. (My story: After discussing with friends after the test, I was convinced I wouldn't be shortlisted. My dukh-daard-peedha continued, and with a heavy heart I went off to Taco Bell for lunch. To my surprise, while eating, I got an email from Baker Hughes saying I was shortlisted for the digital interview round. That instantly lifted my mood and I left for home and started preparing for it. So guys, don't lose hope until results are declared ;) )

2. Digital Interview [46 candidates appeared, 35 shortlisted]

This was conducted on the Hire Vue platform same as JMPC CFG. Below were the questions asked, these people are asking the same questions from the past two years so chances are they might repeat. Those who aren't familiar with this platform, it is basically an AI who would be taking your interview. The question will be displayed on the screen and you will be given 30 secs to prepare for it, then you need to record your answer for 3 mins but you can stop anytime you complete giving your answer. They are basic HR questions. The company's people will be evaluating later as well. The questions were:

1. Why did you choose your current degree program?

2. What do you aim to gain from this internship?

3. Tell us about a challenging project experience.

4. How did you manage multiple priorities and time?

5. Tell us about a time when you realized you have a weakness and how did you try to overcome that?

6. What'd you like us to know more about you?

Tip: Try to include as many keywords of the company's values as possible. And give answers from personal experiences. Don't try to read it from script, speak naturally.

( My Story: We had a deadline at 3 PM, so I sat for my interview around 2 PM. Just as I began answering the first question, the doorbell rang. Since I stay in a PG, I assumed someone else would open it. But it rang again, and that broke my flow and I ended up fumbling through the next two questions. Lesson: if you live in a PG, inform your roommates beforehand and handle distractions like the doorbell early on. Also, choose the quietest spot possible and keep your phone on silent. After this shaky start, I honestly had no hopes of being shortlisted for further rounds. They sent the shortlist by 13th of August, and as expected my name was not included in the list. Devastated, demotivated and feeling lost, I started evaluating my next company's options. In the next hour, they sent an additional shortlist with 3 students' names included and my prayers were answered, my name was in that. It turned out 3 people in the original list were already placed so they removed them and included the next 3 :D. I spent the entire night going through my resume and revising CS fundamentals. )

3. Technical Round [ 35 students appeared, 16 shortlisted ]

The offline interview was scheduled on 14th August, divided into 6 panels around 9:30 in the morning. And I was the first one to get interviewed in my panel. My panel consisted of two people, one sir was from AIML domain and there was another ma'am who was specializing in DevOps. It started on a light note with them asking, how I was feeling and how was the process till now for me. Then they asked for my introduction. Remember guys your introduction decides the flow for the rest of the interview, it should include your name, branch, proficiency in which languages, and your interest. I also included my projects and extracurricular activities, as well as my hackathon wins. Since Baker Hughes focused on sustainability and leadership, I had two projects related to it and my committee work to showcase those values. Then he asked to explain my first project, EcoVerse and focused on one particular feature which included giving ecofriendly alternatives of everyday products. I explained how we had scraped the data from another website and were using keyword based retrieval to display in the frontend. Then he asked me what if product category was not included in the dataset, then how would you classify the items, considering the same product can have different names with different brands, and also told me it was a large dataset which would simultaneously add new products on the fly. First, I came about the semantic similarity approach, which would retrieve on the basis of semantic meaning behind the product name so that even if the product has different names if their meaning is same they would still be considered equal, but they didn't seem satisfied with it. So, I thought about it for a minute and told them I would use KNN algorithm which would group similar products in one cluster and if a new datapoint were to arrive it would give recommendations with the nearest clusters. He later assured me that I was going in the right direction and asked me to come up with an approach that doesn't include a labelled dataset, so I said I would use K-means in that case and then asked me to explain the entire algorithm. The interviewers seemed satisfied with it. Later, he noticed I had a project that included OCR, so he inquired about what it does, and what challenges I will face if I worked on a real world dataset. I gave some problems, but he expected more, so I genuinely confessed as we had worked on a very structured dataset, these are the only problems we faced in our project. This seemed to convince him a bit. Later, he jumped

on some HR questions and asked what would I do if I were to get assigned to a monotonous task in the project? Then seeing how I had included React in almost all of my projects, inquired about why React and not Angular? I explained how I wanted to learn how to build end to end projects so after learning React, I shifted my focus on getting hands on backend development. Then ma'am asked me about my role as Carnival Executive head, why did I approach influencers as judges because in this generation anyone can be an influencer. To this I answered we onboarded only those influencers who have won some beauty pageant to have some relevance. She also asked if I had ever come across a situation where there was dispute in a group project and how did I handle it, what was my mindset? Then sir asked why I used MongoDB in my project and what was the need for it and its schema. Later the interview shifted to SQL, as I had mentioned in my introduction that I am proficient in it. He started off with basic questions, the difference between drop and truncate. Then asked which is faster delete or truncate. I answered truncate would be faster because delete includes a where condition, then he questioned me what if delete didn't have any condition then which would be faster, to this I again answered truncate but he looked at me doubtfully, so I confessed I was not sure. (Although later I found out I was right, he wanted an explanation but I was just giving an educated guess :P). Then I was asked how I would retrieve a unique row to which I first answered using the primary key of the table and select query, she later changed the question to unique values to which I answered using distinct keyword. Then I was asked the difference between rank and dense rank. It ended with them asking if I had any questions for them. I inquired how many years they have been working for Baker Hughes and what motivated them to join the company. (Bit of a bold move on my part xD, but they seemed to laugh it off and answered me.) This round lasted for about an hour for me.

I was not asked any questions related to DSA, OS, CCN some of the other students were asked in other panels. Including unique projects on your resume helps divert their attention there more, so try building such projects. And know the in and out about everything mentioned in your resume, even though it's a group project, it's important to know the entire flow of the project.

4. Leadership Round [16 candidates appeared, 9 were selected]

Within an hour of finishing my first round, I was called in for the second. Many candidates were still waiting to give their first, but that's the advantage of being among the earliest in your panel, make a good impression and you are set for the next round. The interview started off with her asking how my initial rounds of interviews went. I frankly answered that I wasn't expecting it to turn out this way and me coming to the final round. She was curious as to why I had this mindset. To which I told her about my previous experiences and how I used to get really nervous answering questions and was not able to clear other companies first rounds. So she asked what changed now. I answered I decided to just trust myself and god and go with the flow. I was asked to explain my favourite project, then asked me how many people were a part of it, I answered two. She asked what I would do if my teammate was not cooperating. Also asked situational questions if I were the product manager and the tech team has informed me that they won't be able to deliver the product in the given deadline, how would I handle this situation? Remember transparency and reliable product delivery are the core company values so answer these questions in that regard. Also, asked follow up questions like if the client was not ready to extend the deadline what would you do? To this I answered, I would first negotiate with the client if it were possible to drop certain functionalities so the tech team can speed up the process, because giving a non functioning and untested product is not a viable option. Then she noticed that I had used Power BI in one of my data analysis projects and asked me to explain it and later inquired if I knew any other power apps to which I honestly replied no. Later, questions about which upi app I used and why, if I could add

one more feature on it, what would it be were asked. She also put forth a technical question related to frauds happening on such apps and how would I handle them. The interview ended on a high note with me getting a chance to ask about her experience working for Baker Hughes, and she seemed very interested in answering my questions.

I was done with my interview and was waiting for the results. The process ended around 6 pm in the evening with 9 candidates receiving the offer. I was just glad to be one of them 😀

journey.howSecured:
There was an Online Assessment followed by 2 Technical Interview Rounds.

Since it was Pool Campus Placement various other colleges also participated in it.

1. [Online Assessment Test] (After PPT)

The online assessment round was fully MCQ-based with a total duration of two hours. The test was divided into three main sections: Aptitude, Technical, and Flowchart-based Coding. Each section had 3-4 subsections with individual timers ranging between 10 to 20 minutes, which made time management a very crucial factor. Students with cgpa>7.5 were allowed, and only a smaller percentage were shortlisted based on sectional performance and overall accuracy.

The Aptitude section consisted of questions from quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, and verbal ability. Topics like speed, time and distance, profit and loss, probability, puzzles, and data interpretation were commonly asked. The verbal subsection included paragraph-based comprehension questions that were strictly timed, requiring quick reading and precise answering. My approach here was to eliminate wrong options quickly and focus on accuracy instead of random guessing.

The Technical section tested core programming concepts, primarily object-oriented programming (OOPs) in Java, C++, and Python. Questions asked us to identify differences between abstraction and encapsulation, select the correct definition of method overloading versus overriding, or point out the role of garbage collection in Python versus destructors in C++. SQL-based MCQs included queries for finding the second highest salary, identifying invalid JOINs, and error-checking. There were also input-output questions where code snippets were given and we had to predict the exact output or the type of error (runtime or compile-time). I prepared for this by revising OOPs fundamentals and practicing SQL queries in advance, which helped me trace the logic accurately during the test.

The flowchart-based coding section was slightly different from standard coding rounds, as it involved tracing algorithms presented in flowchart form. Questions asked us to trace a given flowchart and select the correct output from the options. I managed this by simulating the flow on rough paper step by step, which reduced mistakes and saved time.

To prepare for this round, I practiced aptitude questions regularly on IndiaBix and GeeksforGeeks Aptitude. For technical sections, I revised OOPs concepts in depth and solved SQL MCQs from GeeksforGeeks SQL MCQs. I also focused on understanding common compile-time and runtime errors in different languages, as error-based MCQs were common. For flowcharts, I brushed up on the basics of loops, conditionals, and algorithm tracing.

On the day of the test, I made sure to keep rough paper ready for quick calculations and flowchart tracing. Since the subsections were auto-submitted after the timer,

I was careful not to spend too much time on any one question. Overall, the key points you need to learn is to manage time effectively, stay calm during timed reading comprehensions, and have strong fundamentals in OOPs and SQL.

2. [Technical Interview Round 1] [ 27 appeared (excluding 8 waiting not allowed)] .

The first interview round began with a polite greeting and a brief self-introduction, where I highlighted my academic background, project work, and any relevant experiences. The interviewer then asked me to explain my projects in detail, focusing on the technologies used, the challenges faced, and the outcomes. I was also asked about my work experience, hobbies, and the skills I had gained from practical exposure. From there, the discussion moved to technical fundamentals, where I was asked about the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming and to name the programming languages I was most comfortable with.

The interviewer also touched on role-fit and motivation questions, such as why I wanted to join BlackRock. I answered honestly, focusing on my interest in working with a global firm known for innovation and technology in finance.

When asked about my knowledge of finance, I admitted that I did not have sufficient background but emphasized my willingness and eagerness to learn, which the interviewer seemed to appreciate. Toward the end, I was given the opportunity to ask a question, and I inquired about his routine and experience at BlackRock, which led to a more casual and insightful exchange.

Throughout the interview, I made sure to remain confident and articulate in my responses, even though I knew it was challenging to stay composed in such situations. The interviewer maintained a friendly and supportive approach, which made the conversation more comfortable. My key takeaway from this round was that confidence, clarity in explaining one's projects, and openness to learning new domains like finance are crucial.

Links:

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/object-oriented-programming-oops-concept-in-java/

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzles/

3. [Technical Interview Round 2] (16 students appeared)

The second interview round was more project-focused and technical in nature. The interviewer began by asking me to choose one project that I would like to deep dive into. Once I selected the project, she asked detailed questions about its architecture, schema design, and the reasoning behind my technical choices. A key discussion point was on database design, where she asked me to compare SQL vs. NoSQL and explain which one I preferred in different scenarios. I elaborated on aspects like structured vs. unstructured data, scalability, and consistency, while also discussing how collections, documents, and sub-collections work in NoSQL databases.

The interviewer then shifted the conversation toward financial awareness, asking how I keep myself updated with current financial situations. I responded by mentioning sources like financial news portals, online articles, and business publications, while also admitting I was still in the process of building deeper financial knowledge. Moving further, I was asked data analysis-oriented questions such as how I handled datasets in my projects, what tools I used, and importantly, whether I had deployed my work or kept it at an experimental stage. I clarified the scope of deployment in my projects and described my exposure to end-to-end development.

Overall, this round tested my ability to defend my project choices, my database knowledge, my awareness of financial trends, and my practical experience in implementation. The interviewer maintained an analytical approach, probing deeper into technical and real-world application aspects, which made it important to stay structured in my responses and connect technical knowledge with practical use cases.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/introduction-to-nosql/

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/reactjs/react/

Prank Round

During the BlackRock process, after finishing my two technical rounds, our TPC told us about the prank round that had been taken earlier by our TPO head, Mr. Vinod Sikka. On the same day, I also had an EDS interview scheduled at their office, so I was really stressed trying to manage both. While waiting for the BlackRock result, the tension kept building, but finally, my name was announced for the SDE role. That moment was such a big relief and honestly one of the happiest feelings--I realized how important it is to stay calm under pressure and I felt super excited to join BlackRock.

The process had 3 rounds. First round OA,then the shortlisted candidates from the OA round had to attend the PPT ,followed by 2 interview rounds and one prank round 3 days after the OA round. Clearing OA is very tough as major filtering happens in this round. So being well versed with various aptitude, CS fundamentals' mcqs and coding questions is really important. Hence start practising for the same from the beginning.

1. Online Assessment Round [133 candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted in college on the Hackerearth platform. It had multiple mcqs based on java fundamentals mostly OOPS and some code snippets from which we had to guess the output. The mcqs were quite tricky. There was 1 coding question exactly same as this:

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/description/?envType=problem- list-v2&envId=string

And there one an easy SQL query,where we were to find the name of candidates who had made purchases in the month of October. I used MONTH() to solve it.

2. Technical Round [ 37 candidates appeared for this round]

Before this round there was PPT where we were told about company's values(RISES) and its work culture. It is very important to be attentive during the PPT as it helps a lot while answering in the interview rounds. So my Technical round was mostly theoretical ,testing my understanding of each and every concept. It lasted for about 45 minutes. Firstly I was asked to give my introduction, which should be given very thoughtfully as everything from there is based on what you have said. After that I was asked about the projects so I gave a brief about all the 4 projects I had mentioned and then he specifically asked me to explain the 4th project which was the major project. Know your projects inside out. After that he gave me an SQL query to write which was something like there are 2 tables department and employee and I had to find the names of departments where number of employees were more than 10. From this i said multiple words like joins, group by and all so he started asking what did each of them do and how will i use what kind of join in various cases. Satisfied from my answers he asked me the next question,which was based on OOPS design. Given a colony of ants,some ants were soldiers,some were workers and there was one quee n ant. Workers could act as soldiers during dangerous times. I had to represent this in class diagrams. It is very important that you keep talking to the

interviewer while solving such things as they want to know how you are thinking. Then he asked me where would certain functions lie ,in which class so like walk is general so it will lie in the main ant class then i was asked, how will you make sure that there is only 1 queen ant to which i answered using singleton class. Then I was asked how to empty an input field in react, where does js gets loaded browser side or server side and then I was asked the difference between C++ and Java then he gave me a scenario where i had to design windows 12 how would i do it with these 2 languages. Then I was asked basics about mongoDB and MySQLI wasn't asked any DSA question but many of my friends were asked DSA so be prepared for it. The interview ended with me asking him a few questions. Do learn LLD concepts as they were very important this year.

3. HR Round [ 21 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was a pure HR round for me but some others had a mix of technical + HR. So the Round started with where do I live ,then since the interviewer was an alumni of SPIT he told me how he used to travel to college. Then I was asked about my Minors degree fro m SPJIMR,what did i learn there and why i chose it. After that he told me to explain situations where I had used the RISES. This went well for about 15 -20 minutes and then it was some general talk ,me asking him a few questions and telling him why i chose c omputer science as a career, telling my weaknesses. It is very important to speak confidently in this round as you are mostly judged on your speaking skills and what type of answers you give.

After this there was a prank round where 16 candidates were called and finally we were told that we have been selected for the program.

It became clear that having a thorough understanding of my projects and past experiences was crucial for thisround.

In addition, I was presented with a case study that lacked many details, and I was expected to ask relevant questions to gather more information. This part of the interview aimed to assess my critical thinking, problem-solving skills,and how I approach complex, vague scenarios, especially from a machine learning perspective. I had toexplain my thought process and steps I would take to tackle the problem.

Having a strong grasp of my fundamentals, being well-versed in everything on my resume, and being able to clearly articulate my thought process helped me navigate the questions confidently.

Out of the 18 that appeared, 10 were shortlisted for the next round.
