In my HR round, I was primarily asked personal questions, with a focus on my interests and experiences outside of academics. One of the more unique questions was when they asked me to "sell" General Mills to them, which tested my knowledge of the company and the research I had done beforehand. There was also considerable attention on the committees and extracurricular activities I had been part of over the past two years, and they asked me to discuss both the positive and negative aspects of these experiences.

They were curious about my interests beyond my degree, and I was asked what I enjoy doing that isn't related to academics. They also inquired about my future aspirations, asking where I see myself when I'm 35 or 40. Another question focused on my reading habits, asking about the most recent book I had read and to discuss it. Additionally, I was asked how my friends perceive me, both in terms of strengths and weaknesses. Overall, it was a smooth and comfortable round where the main focus was on being authentic and honest in my responses.

Out of the 10 that appeared in the last round, 4 candidates were selected.

Online Assessment: this was the first round which consisted of 3 sections

1. general aptitude / reasoning - 20 min

2. Core cs fundamentals - 30 min

3. Coding Section - 40 min

Core cs fundamentals involved mcqs based on code snippets/flowcharts, DBMS, OS, SQL. It was completely language independent and basic level questions were asked.

Coding section involved two easy questions-

1. Given an array of integers, return the count of correctly placed and incorrectly placed integers if the array was sorted. It was quite easy and the attached problem is almost similar to it. (link)

2. Given 2 integers that represent a range from x to y, find the sum of all the golden numbers where a golden number is defined as a number whose sum of digits - maximum digit is equal to maximum digit (eg- 352: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10, max digit = 5, so 10-5 = 5 ie sum-maxd = maxd). I was not able to pass all the test cases idk if there was some issue with setting the testcase (did 7/10). This was the crux but the question was in a story format like we encounter over codeforces(so better if you are already familiar with that type)

TIPS:

● Time management is very important in the first 2 sections. Questions are doable but the decision to attempt or skip a particular question based upon time is more important.

● Many python users faced issues in this round and this was seen in PhonePe as well, so if you've enough time consider shifting to cpp/java

1. Technical Round 1 [ 37 candidates appeared for this round ]

This round was entirely about the basics of OOP and core subjects (OS and CCN) and schema design. It started with a short introduction followed by OOP fundamentals in your first language, mine was cpp so in depth questions related to friend functions/virtual keyword/multiple inheritance/destructors were asked followed by some questions related to OS and CCN. I was also asked about the basics of Cloud computing even though I didn't have any project related to it. So in this case answer honestly whatever you know and try to relate concepts.

Later the interviewer asked me to design a schema for an e-commerce platform, followed by how would you design a recommendation system over this and how would you store overhead data specifically in which tables. I was then asked to write a basic SQL query over these tables using 2 joins. This was extended into a discussion related to system design: how would you scale this, what databases will you use(sql/nosql/both with reasoning) and how would you prevent bruteforce attacks(IP blacklisting using Redis). This round went on for about 35-40 mins.

TIPS:

● Make sure you are clear with the basics of your first language and have some idea of OOP in Java too if java isn't your first language. Also never ignore OOP in your first language, even though you've mastered it in Java, have a basic understanding of how that works in your preferred language.

● Also from what I got to know, candidates who had their first language as Java, were also asked about development in Java (Springboot related) so be prepared to handle such situations.

● Design problems are to check how you approach a problem so take your time and think in 360 degree just to not miss out on any part. Make sure you ask genuine questions related to company tech at the end.

2. Technical Round 2 [ 22 candidates appeared for this round ]

This round was focused more towards resume and Low Level Design(LLD). After introduction I was drilled down on a single project where they even asked me how do you write config files, how do you build docker images and configure kubernetes and everything, so make sure you do projects yourself as they also check github in some cases. They also asked what all types of databases you've worked on apart from mongoDB and Mysql and what are their use cases(vector db and key value pair db like redis)

In the later part I was asked to give a low level design of a cab booking system (Ola/Uber). So in LLD, they expect you to use OOP and data structures and algorithms and I was asked to write code structure in cpp (classes, functions they will have, what each func will do and which data structure and algo it will use). Keep discussing with the interviewer what all things you are considering, like at the first step I asked if I had to design for both drivers and passengers so he said no continue only with passengers.

So I went on to do it that way and told them that Dijkstra's would be required but I won't simply apply it over all the drivers. I will set a radius range r initially small(lets say 500m) and if I found drivers within that range they would be sent to client side(passenger) and if not found the radius wound be increased to say 1km and the process would go on until a driver is encountered or we exceed the max radius which can be set to 5km. Along with this, I would also use a priority queue to keep track of "k" nearest drives in case the first one rejects or something(they see how you handle edge cases). I also mentioned that we would need to

implement a lock in a way so that 2 passengers don't book the same cab for diff destinations and explained how that part would be implemented in the driver part of the design. Then they asked follow up questions like what if multiple passengers are requesting the same driver then which passenger would be allocated to the driver (which actually happens in the real world). We kept discussing and enhancing the system and this round went on for 30 min or so.

TIPS:

● Yes surprisingly most of us were never asked about DSA problems.

● For all your projects make a google doc with all the important points/features, their implementation and tech stack as it becomes really easy to revise the entire project cause at the last moment we feel we need to revise everything.

● Also add to it what problems did you faced and how did you resolve them as it is a check question if you've done the project yourself or not

● Whenever you feel confused, communicate with the interviewer, they'll surely help you out. It's okay even if you ask them if you're doing right or not so they can guide you well to produce a solution.

3. HR Round [ 9 candidates who appeared for this round ]

It was a classic HR round, more of a conversation type where I was asked some basic questions like why do you want to join IDFC and all. I was given situations and was asked how would you resolve this. Here mainly they check if the candidate is culturally fit and would be able to coordinate with the team so just keep a good smile and try to connect answers to your own experiences. Mention about the ppt/research that you do which adds more weightage to your answer.

I was asked the following questions-

1. What one thing could piss you off at work?

2. How would you deal with a team mate who is not coordinating/communicating?

3. If you're a manager and supposed to give a best team member award, what criteria would you consider before deciding the winner apart from tech/development?

TIPS:

● Try to connect answers with company values. Read about their vision/mission, tagline, history, this really helps in HR based rounds.

● There might be some trick questions which play on our psychology so it is always safer to answer honestly.

● Be friendly with the interviewer and reflect your true personality.

4. Online Screening Round [ 9 candidates who appeared for this round ]

It was an extra round conducted online which started at 8:30pm. It was just a fitment round where I was asked to explain my projects to a very senior positioned interviewer which lasted for just 15 mins. There

I was directly asked to send the repo link of my project and explain it. Keep in mind don't take such a round lightly as elimination does take place here which unfortunately did happen for one of my peers. Some candidates were asked about the subjects in previous semester or the course work, so make sure you have an idea of that as well, they don't expect details but just the list of subjects and topics that you've learned.

The results were declared the next day and 8 students received the offer.

OA: (75 minutes) (~240 Candidates appeared)

This was an on-campus online assessment conducted on HackerRank, consisting of three questions: two DSA-based and one SQL. The questions were randomly selected from a pool, with most being LeetCode easy to medium level.

● DSA Q1: Slowest Key - LeetCode

Given a list of keypress logs as pairs (key, time), where key is an integer from 1 to 26 representing lowercase letters (1 → 'a', 2 → 'b', ..., 26 → 'z') and time is the cumulative time (in seconds) when the key was released, determine which key took the longest to press. The time taken for the first key is time[0], and for each subsequent key is time[i] - time[i-1]. Return the character that took the maximum time. It is guaranteed that this key is unique.

It's an easy single loop question, give it a try !

● DSA Q2: Distance Between "programmer" Substrings

Given a string containing exactly two non-overlapping occurrences of the word "programmer", possibly separated by arbitrary characters (e.g., "programxxxmerxxxxprogramxxmer"), determine the number of characters strictly between the first full "programmer" from the left and the last full "programmer" from the right.

Characters between may include any letters or symbols.

Example shown below -

I did using unordered_map and two pointers, give it a try !

● SQL Q3: Time and Amount Aggregation with Joins The question involved 2-3 tables and tested a strong understanding of JOINs, GROUP BY, and aggregations. It required summing durations in seconds and converting them to HH:MM:SS format using functions like SEC_TO_TIME, as well as converting cumulative amounts into billions. I chose to skip this question as I wasn't aware of the SEC_TO_TIME function at the time. However, such functions can often be discovered if you forget using IntelliSense by exploring related keywords.

My strategy was to solve DSA quickly, assess the SQL difficulty, and submit if it seemed too complex -- since submission time mattered and very few were able to solve SQL. This approach only works if you're well-prepared; don't skip doable questions.

Offline Technical Round 1: (30 minutes) (~40 Candidates appeared)

The round started with my introduction. I had prepared it well, covering languages I know, brief overviews of my three projects, extracurriculars, and leadership experience.

Tip: A strong intro is important--it sets the tone and flow of the interview. Practice it in front of someone beforehand, to make it smooth and confident.

She then asked about my DDPM ( Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models ) project. Since she wasn't very familiar with it, I explained it clearly using simple terms and a diagram, which she appreciated. Next, we discussed my first project which was an AI-assisted learning platform. I explained the idea, how I identified the problem, and the tech stack I used.

After that, she gave me two SQL questions.

Q.1 Find user IDs of users who have ordered products from more than one category.

I then explained that by grouping the results by user_id, I could use a HAVING clause with a COUNT(DISTINCT category) to filter for users who have ordered from more than one category. After I wrote the complete SQL query based on this approach, the interviewer was satisfied

Q.2 For each category, find the product that was sold the most (by total quantity ordered).

I shared my intuition to first group the orders by product to get the total quantity sold. Then, to use a window function to rank the products within each category based on their total sales. Finally, filter to get the top-ranked product per category. She was satisfied with the approach, and didn't expect to write the entire query.

After the SQL round, she asked two easy DSA questions:

Q1. First Non-Repeating Character - Leetcode I first explained the brute-force approach using two loops, then optimized it using a frequency vector to count frequencies and a second pass to find the first non-repeating character.

Q2. Climbing Stairs - Leetcode I related it to the Fibonacci series. Explained the recursive and DP approaches, but implemented the space-optimized (Thanks to striver) solution using two variables.

She also asked a few theory questions like encapsulation in OOP and indexing in databases, which I answered confidently with examples. At the end, I asked a prepared question related to the Barra product and RiskMetrics, she was working on it so she explained it well, and the interview concluded.

Offline Technical Round 2: (45 minutes) (~15 Candidates appeared)

The second round focused on evaluating my ability to think practically as a developer--beyond just coding skills.

We began with a short introduction, followed by a question about my future plans--whether I intended to pursue a master's degree or launch a startup. Since I had been part of the Entrepreneurship Cell at SPIT for two years. I responded honestly, stating that while I admire both academia and entrepreneurship, my goal is to grow in an industry setting.

Given my background in generative AI, he asked : With AI advancing rapidly, what is the role of a developer today? I highlighted that while AI has made remarkable progress, it still has significant limitations. It lacks genuine reasoning and primarily functions as a predictive model trained on past data. More importantly, AI cannot take accountability. Developers remain crucial for testing, debugging, refining logic, and owning the final product.

We then dove deep into my projects. I presented a generative AI-based application, clearly outlining the problem it solved, the tech stack used, and design decisions. A major discussion point was my use of MongoDB instead of a traditional SQL database. I explained that since LLMs can output structured JSON, it was easier and more efficient to store and manage data in MongoDB. The project didn't require complex joins or strict ACID compliance, and MongoDB's horizontal scalability and high performance made it a practical choice.

He also asked about the vector database I had used--Qdrant. I elaborated on why I chose it, highlighting its ability to perform advanced filtering during semantic search. I gave concrete examples from my project to justify the choice, and the conversation naturally progressed into the architecture, challenges faced, and how I overcame them.

Throughout the discussion, the focus remained on why I made certain technical decisions. We also covered theoretical questions--like the difference between a database and a data warehouse, and what an alternate key is. Rather than just naming types of keys, I walked him through the concept of alternate keys within a hierarchy of super, primary, candidate, and foreign keys.

Toward the end, he asked me about time complexity. Instead of giving definition, I explained it through real-world examples--demonstrating how analyzing time complexity helps identify performance bottlenecks across different hardware and programming languages.

One of the final questions was : Would you choose expensive infrastructure to reduce server load time, or stick to a budget and accept slower performance? I treated it as a real-life scenario. I said that in a perfect world with unlimited resources, we'd all want the best infrastructure--but in reality, we have to balance performance and cost. For instance, if I'm building an app like YouTube, users won't wait 20 seconds for a video to load. In such cases, performance becomes a priority. So I'd first identify the bottlenecks and then decide where to optimize for speed and where to save on budget--always keeping both business constraints and user experience in mind. He seemed satisfied with this practical outlook.

As the interview wrapped up, he asked if I had any questions. I asked about their adoption of generative AI. We had an engaging discussion on how they're exploring AI integration--whether through external APIs or on-premise LLMs. I also raised concerns around data security when relying on third-party APIs, especially for data-sensitive businesses. He acknowledged that the domain is still evolving, and while they're already using AI tools for tasks like code assistance, larger implementation plans are in the works.

Tip: In college or hackathon projects, we often neglect the feasibility and scalability aspects. It's still important to have a basic theoretical understanding of these, even if you don't have practical experience

Online HR Round : (15 minutes) (~8 Candidates appeared)

This was a relaxed and conversational round, primarily focused on understanding my personality and cultural fit. The interviewer began by asking about my family background and hobbies. I had prepared a brief HR-friendly introduction that covered my academic journey, family background, and my passion for playing musical instruments. He then asked what I knew about MSCI, to which I gave a detailed response--covering the company's role in global finance, its significance in investment decision-making, and how MSCI indices provide a global snapshot to help investors make informed choices. I also touched on the technical side of index construction. He expressed curiosity about my specialization in Data Science, and asked whether I'd be open to working in a different domain or department. I explained how my foundation in data science and my keen interest in generative AI have equipped me with strong analytical and adaptable skills. I assured him that I'm quick to learn and flexible enough to contribute effectively, regardless of

the specific domain. Towards the end, I asked a couple of questions--particularly about the scope of learning before the internship begins, since we had a semester gap, and inquired about growth opportunities within the company.

Overall, it was a smooth and engaging conversation that allowed me to present both my technical background and willingness to learn and grow.

Tip: Don't overlook the HR round. Be well-prepared with common HR questions and think through different scenarios in advance. You won't have much time to recollect answers during the conversation, as this round often tests your spontaneity and presence of mind

At the end, 5 students were selected.

journey.howSecured:
1. Technical Round

• For this round, I would recommend refreshing all the CS core subjects you have studied in earlier sems. Most common questions were regarding OOPs, DBMS, DS, CCN, etc. Regarding the interview itself, first the interviewer will ask you to introduce yourself. Its crucial to prepare a good introduction for yourself and to present it confidently. Ideally, it would include your academic background, achievements, and something personal like your hobbies. They might ask a few questions about your hobbies, so be prepared to answer the same.

• Next, they might ask you about the CS fundamentals in different subjects. You need to answer these confidently, and seek no validation from the interviewer. My interviewer gave no reaction at all beyond a 'yes' or an 'okay' to all my answers, which slightly threw me off. I later found out that this is just something they do to test the confidence of the candidates, so do not panic if your interviewer does the same.

• You might also be asked some questions pertaining to your particular skill set. Since I had mentioned my Competitive Programming profiles on my resume, my interviewer asked me about my favourite problem that I had solved.

• Next, I was asked to explain some of the projects on my resume. Make sure to review all your projects before going, as they do ask some very intricate questions regarding those. Try to convey as much information as possible in your answers, and for the umpteenth time, be confident. Depending on how specialized your project is, the interviewer may not know about the technologies in detail, so you can get away with making some statements that are not entirely true, if you are confident enough.

2. Techno-HR Round (15 candidates appeared for this round)

• This round was purely HR for some, and was a mix of techno-HR for others. The technical questions were not too different from what were asked in the first round, but some of the HR questions were very tricky.

• In my case, no matter how I answered, the interviewer seemed to dislike my answer, and would try to debate with me about it. You don't have to agree with the interviewer on every single point they raise, but be polite if you want to express that you disagree.

• If you did well on the technical questions in the round, you should mostly be fine even if the HR section was not that great.

journey.prep:
1. Be honest - don't fake your resume. They do read every line and can grill you on it. Only mention skills and projects you truly know. If at all you've added something extra, be as thorough with it as your other projects.

2. Be fundamentally strong - all your concepts regarding OOPs and DBMS need to be clear, as direct and indirect questions are asked on these topics.

7. Maintain a positive approach and greet them with a smile.

journey.howSecured:
1. Pre-placement Talk (Online)

2. Aptitude Test

3. Technical Interview 1

4. Technical Interview 2

5. HR Round

1. Online Aptitude Test [ 180+ students appeared] This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine - PARIKSHA, The test consisted of 60 questions, divided equally into Analytical, Quantitative, and Verbal sections, with no negative marking. The total time was 60 minutes, so time management was crucial. The level of difficulty was easy to medium, questions focused on topics like:

• Verbal - antonyms, prepositions, comprehensions, etc.

• Analytical - Statement & Implications, Graphs and Histograms followed by 4-5 Qs.

• Quants - Basic work & time, speeds, averages, profit & discounts, I started with the verbal section quickly completing it in almost 10-12 minutes. For passages, go through the questions first then look for those keywords. Quants & Analytical was easy to medium level. I felt like I had answered most of the questions correctly, except 2/3 which i couldn't come back to. Time management is the key here, practice giving timed tests on indiabix/ some other platform. We got the shortlist at around 7:00 p.m., and the interviews were scheduled at 9:00 a.m. on 1st August, so we hardly had any time to prepare. --- PAGE 2 --- I started by reviewing past interview experiences for potential questions and answers. I noticed that the concepts of OOPs and SQL were the most important, so I gave them the most weightage during my preparation. I revised all of my projects on the resume, the technologies implemented, and any possible questions on them. Apart from that, I revised all the essential concepts of Object-Oriented Programming, DSA, and DBMS. I ensured I was confident enough to answer all the questions and get at least 3 to 4 hours of sleep. On the interview day, I reached college at around 8:30 a.m. The interview started at 9:15 a.m. At around 11:50 a.m., there was a strange incident - we were informed about some possible malpractice in the assessment test that had taken place the previous day. As a result, we were told that there would be another screening test for the shortlisted candidates. This test was a pen-paper test and consisted of three questions - one each from DSA, aptitude, and SQL:

1. Aptitude: A tap can fill a tank in 10 hrs, B in 8 hrs, and C can empty it in 12 hrs. If all three are open, how long will it take to fill the tank?

2. DSA: Maximum Subarray Sum

3. SQL: Find the employee(s) with the highest salary under each manager. I tried writing optimal answers, and wherever I was unsure, I explained my thinking behind the answer. After this test, 7 candidates were shortlisted from the 28, and the interviews restarted.

2. Technical Interview I | 28 candidates were shortlisted, later reduced to 7] The interview: After the test, we had gone to eat something, but I was immediately called for my first interview. It started around 1:10 p.m. As I walked in, the interviewer asked me a few questions to make me feel comfortable. Then I started with my introduction, where I also mentioned two of my notable projects, achievements, and the tech stack. This led the questions to go straight to my projects first, which I was well-prepared for. I briefly explained the projects and the reason for using the specific tech stacks as well. Next, I was asked about the pen-paper test - my approach to solving it, and the time and space complexities involved. Then, the topic moved on to sorting algorithms and their complexities. When I mentioned On log n) for merge sort, I was asked in which cases the log n complexity is achieved. There was also some discussion about HashMaps vs Sets. I was asked about the toughest and easiest Leetcode problems l've come across. Next, discussion shifted to one of my projects, where there was some hardware implementation too. I was asked follow-up questions about the stack used (FastAPI and MySQL) - which HTTP verbs were used where, etc. I was also tested on OOPs concepts - overriding vs overloading, garbage collection (which I couldn't really answer in depth), and C++ vs Java since I've used C++. --- PAGE 3 --- A basic puzzle was also asked: Given 5, 5, 5, 5, 5 - get the answer = 125. DBMS concepts were also asked - like indexing and why insertion and updation become slower in an indexed database. We also discussed SQL vs NoSQL. No HR questions were asked. The interview went on for around 35-40 minutes.

3. Technical Interview II | 7 candidates were selected out of 28 ] I was called for Round 2 about 35-40 minutes after Round 1. There were 2 interviewers this time. Overall, Round 2 was a bit more challenging, as there were many follow-ups on every answer, leading to in-depth discussions. The interview started with my introduction again. The interviewers were very rigorous about my resume -- every project was discussed in detail, including follow-ups regarding the technologies used and how they were implemented. My contribution to each project was asked. After the resume discussion, I was asked several questions related to DBMS. I was given a sample table and asked to perform operations - it was a joins question. I began explaining my approach but was asked to just write the query directly. I was asked about normalization and denormalization, and had to explain all the forms with an example DB / real-life example. This included related topics like partial dependencies, etc. OOPs was also asked - I was asked to name the four pillars, explain each with a real-life example, followed by a code explanation. Then I was asked about the use of the super keyword, and questions regarding abstract classes vs interfaces, when to use which, etc. This interview went on for more than 40 minutes since there was a lot of explanation involved, followed by writing code/queries. At the end, I was asked what I do apart from studying, and why I am switching from EXTC to an IT-related role. My question to them was about their first experience in a corporate setup and how they adapted to the changes. One of the interviewers was very senior and couldn't recall his first experience, so I switched the question to his first experience at Nomura. The overall experience was very good - I never felt grilled or intimidated.

4. HR Round | 3 candidates were selected out of 7] The HR round was just a short formality since it was already around 4:30 p.m. The HR mentioned she too had a long day and wanted to wrap it up quickly. I was asked about where I stay, travel time, family background, and future plans. My follow-up question was about the employee volunteering programs she mentioned during the PPT. --- PAGE 4 --- 3 students were selected for the ITD role.

The entire placement process is a very long and stressful period. Before Nomura I had given 4 interviews, even reached the last round in 1 and got rejected. But the important thing in this process is that you have to keep patience and keep on pushing. Keep talking with your friends and your parents. Luck is a very important factor in this placement process but that too will only work if you keep working hard.

About GM Role :

On 31st July, at around 8p.m. I found out that my resume had been shortlisted for the GM role. I did not know anything about the role and called up a senior to find out about the role. Even though the JD says Global Markets Analyst(which sounds non-tech) the role is completely a tech based role which closely works with the Global Markets division of Nomura. The title of the JD even said tech focused intern. The senior told me that all the work he was doing there was tech related along with exposure to finance(something that I was looking for). He also guided me how to approach the interviews and how to prepare for GD which was going to be the first round.

GM JD - https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZnsTaifPX5qplLdzshR0_k1uR72aqFyr/view?usp=sharing

1. Group Discussion [18 Students appeared for this round]

The first round for GM is a Group Discussion round. This round lasted for around 30 minutes. We had a group of 8 students. The topic was pretty easy on is AI making us smarter or dependent. Before the GD we as a group had decided that we would not cut each other mid sentence(can disagree though). This ensured that our GD went smoothly without screaming or any fighting. The key in this round is to be confident in what you are speaking. Take a paper or a small notebook and note what your peers are saying as well so you can add to their points or disagree with them. Any youtube video showing how to act in a GD should suffice.

2. Technical Round-1 [ 10 students were shortlisted ]

After 10 minutes of finishing the GD, I was called for my interview.(So if you are the first one called up you might not get time to prepare so be ready beforehand). This round lasted for around 40 minutes. Firstly he asked me to introduce myself and walk through my resume. Simple DSA questions were asked like sort the array(I gave 4 approaches). I offered to write pseudocode for merge sort as well but the interviewer was

happy with my explanation. I was also asked to implement a linked list using a stack(simple 2 stack approach(a FIFO data structure using LIFO)). I was asked a few questions on linked list as well such as finding the middle of the linked list and checking if the linked list has a cycle or not(easy, slow and fast pointer approaches). He asked if I knew python but I told him I only used python for api calls to Gemini. He said it's fine and moved on. Then he asked on my projects and told me to draw the architecture of one of my projects.(a simple drawing of frontend, backend, load balancer and how the request is serviced). Middle of Linked List Linked list has a cycle or not Merge Sort

A few tips for this round:

1. Prepare a solid Introduction covering everything in your resume and focusing on stuff you are confident at.

2. Whenever given a question, walk through the entire solution from start to finish with the interviewer. They are more interested in how you are approaching the problem. If you don't know something, ask for a hint but don't go silent.

3. Practice DSA so that even if a simple question is asked you are able to confidently answer it.

3. Technical Round 2 [ 6 students were shortlisted]

I read the interview experience of my senior before this round and they said that Nomura asks puzzles. So I went through the first 10-15 puzzles of GFG top 100 puzzles. To my luck, I was asked one puzzle from there itself and I went through the solution of the puzzle in detail with the interviewer. After this I was given a medium level SQL query to solve. Given a table lets say Data, for every Note, print the entire row with the max transactions

Notes Pipeline Transactions

N1 P1 400

N1 P2 500

N1 P3 200

N2 P1 400

N2 P2 300

N3 P1 100

Output

Notes Pipeline Transactions

N1 P2 500

N2 P1 400

N3 P1 100

Normal GROUP BY notes would not work as then you wouldn't be able to print pipeline or else you would have to include pipeline in your GROUP BY as well but that would not give correct output.

ANSWER

Select d.notes, d.pipeline, d.transactions From Data as d INNER JOIN ( SELECT Notes, max(transactions) as maxtrn From data GROUP BY Notes) as t ON d.notes = t.notes AND d.transactions = t.maxtrn

Another way is to use WHERE (notes, transactions) IN and the same subquery as above

After this I was asked a DSA questions Merge Intervals. Again pretty standard. After this I was asked to walk through my resume projects and was asked some React questions related to Virtual DOM, hooks and callback questions. I was not very confident in all my answers but tried to answer as much as I knew. After this he also told me to explain the system of one of my projects and the use of RabbitMQ(which I had used). I was able to answer it. In the end I asked him a few questions about Nomura and if there was anything he would like me to explain again.

Puzzles

A few tips for this round:

1. Prepare all your Projects in your resume thoroughly. From tech stack to why did you use that tech stack. Whatever you use in your projects, lets say MERN, read top interview questions for it.

2. The JD mentioned python and React. I didn't know Python in detail so I honestly said I don't know and they were fine with it. Dont try to force something that u dont know because if they ask questions and you are not able to answer it leaves a bad impression.

3. Practice SQL top 50 on leetcode.

4. HR Round [ 4 students were shortlisted]

This was actually my longest round. The interviewer asked me a lot of questions. It started with my understanding of the role. Then he told me what I would have to learn for this role and I answered honestly that I didn't know half of the stuff mentioned in the JD. Then I was asked 3 words to describe myself. Then he asked me about my hobbies. He told me how my friends would describe me and 3 of my bad qualities as well. Then he asked me what gets me motivated and how to motivate me as well. He asked me about my family background. The key point for HR is to answer everything honestly. Don't prepare a lot before this round. Read a bit about the company and JD . They don't want someone who is mechanical.

2 students were offered the job for this role. I was one of them :)

1. [Online Assessment] [ 219 candidates appeared]

The assessment was conducted around 1hr after the ppt presentation (~4.30pm - 5pm). It was conducted on the DoSelect platform. The test contained 4 questions to be solved in 1hr 30 mins.

The webcam was on for the entire duration. There were also constraints on usb devices, so external keyboard and mouse may malperform. Do ensure a proper laptop with a webcam, keyboard and trackpad. The college wifi was not working properly so some of us had to use our own mobile hotspot to give the test, so ensure you have adequate internet connection.

I personally faced lag during the contest where the text input was delayed 3-5s, I was writing entire 2-3 lines and the UI would update it seconds later. Also there was no VIM or EMACS mode for editing, so keep that in mind.

A. You are given 'n' people, labeled from 1 to n. There are 'm' existing friendships represented by 2 arrays 'A' and 'B', each of size 'm'. The i-th friendship is between person A[i] and person B[i].

Two people belong to the same friend group if they are direct friends or have some indirect friendship.

Find the minimum number of friendships to be added such that every person belongs to the same friend group.

Input: The first line of each test case contains two integers n and m (1 <= n, m < 2*10^5) The second line of each test case contains m integers, a1, a2, … , an (1 <= ai <= n) The second line of each test case contains m integers, b1, b2, … , bn (1 <= bi <= n) Output: A single integer - the minimum number of friendships to be added.

Example input 4 2 1 3 2 4 Output 1

This can easily be solved by counting the number of connected components and returning the number of connected components - 1. I used DSU here and passed all test cases.

B. You have 'n' employees and have been given an array 'A' of size 'n', where A[i] indicates the number of ladoos the i-th employee receives. If A[i] = 0, it means the ladoos are not yet assigned. You are also given 2 integers 'm' and 'k'. Where 'm' is the maximum number of ladoos a single employee can get. And 'k' is the maximum allowed difference between adjacent employees.

Find the number of valid ways to assign ladoos to the unassigned positions such that. Each unassigned position gets a ladoo between 1 to m and the absolute difference between adjacent employees is at most k.

Input: The first line of each test case contains two integers n,m and k (1 <= n <= 10^4) (1 <= m <= 100) (1 <= k <= 30) The second line of each test case contains m integers, a1, a2, … , an (0 <= ai <= m) Output: A single integer - the total number of valid ways to assign the ladoos mod 1e9 + 7

Example: Input:

5 5 2 0 3 0 0 4

This was a simple 2D DP problem on counting, i just kept an array 'dp' of length 'm + 1', where dp[i] represents the number of ways to i ladoos currently. Calculated the dp by iterating over the n elements in array 'a'.

I passed most of the test cases except 2, where I didn't account for the first element being 0.

C. You have been given an array 'a' of length 'n' and an integer 'k'. For each element the value of a[i] is defined as the sum of (bit * position) where bit is the bit at the position starting from 1 from LSB in the binary representation of a[i]. E.g. for a[i] = 13; Binary representation of 13 = 1101 1 1 0 1 Position 4 3 2 1 Value = 4*1+3*1+2*0+1*1;

Find number of pairs(i ,j) such that value(a[i]) + value(a[j]) <= k

Input: The first line of each test case contains two integers n and k (1 <= n <= 10^5)(1 <= k <= 10^5) The second line of each test case contains m integers, a1, a2, … , an (0 <= ai <= 10^5) Output: A single integer - the total number pairs(i ,j) such that value(a[i]) + value(a[j]) <= k

Input: 4 20 5 6 7 8 Output: 1

The expected solution for this problem was to make the value array first, and then using sorting + 2 pointers to find the number of pairs in ( O(n.logn)). But I was running low on time so I wrote a brute force solution ( O(n^2)) in 5 minutes and it passed all test cases.

D. I don't remember this question, it was related to harry potter or something. The input format for this question was also not clear, so instead of wasting my time on it, I checked how the output was. We were supposed to print possible or impossible.

1. [Online Assessment] [219 candidates had applied]

4 Questions were to be solved in 1 hour 30 mins

a. You are given n people, labeled from 1 to n. There are m existing friendships represented by two arrays A and B, each of size m, where the i-th friendship is between person A[i] and person B[i].

Two people are considered friends if there is a direct or indirect connection between them (i.e., if they belong to the same connected group of friends).

Your task is to determine the minimum number of new friendships that must be formed so that every person is connected directly or indirectly--in other words, so that everyone belongs to a single connected group.

Input: N = 4, M = 2, A = [1, 3], B = [2, 4] Output: 1

This is essentially a connected components problem, where each group of friends forms a component, and the minimum number of new friendships required is simply:

Answer = Number of connected components − 1

This is because each new friendship can merge two components, and to connect k components into one, you need exactly k−1 connections.

b. You have N employees and are given an array P of size N, where P[i] indicates the number of ladoos the i-th employee receives. If P[i] = 0, it means the ladoos for that employee are yet to be assigned. You are also given two integers M and K:

● M is the maximum number of ladoos any employee can get.

● K is the maximum allowed difference in ladoos between adjacent employees.

Your task is to determine the number of valid ways to assign ladoos to the unassigned positions such that:

● Each unassigned position gets a value between 1 and M.

● The absolute difference between the ladoos of adjacent employees is at most K.

Input: N = 5, M = 5, K = 2 , P = [0, 3, 0, 0, 4] Output: 80

Initially, I approached this problem using backtracking. For each position with value 0, I tried assigning all values from 1 to M and recursively explored the possibilities while maintaining the K difference constraint between adjacent employees. I maintained a counter to track the number of valid configurations.

This approach worked for a few test cases and passed 4 of them. However, it was too slow for larger inputs due to recomputing overlapping subproblems, and I quickly realized that this was a Dynamic Programming problem.

Although I identified that memoization was required, I struggled to define the exact DP state due to time constraints.

Dp State: Let dp[i][prev] represent the number of ways to fill the array from index i onward given that the previous value was prev. Try all possible values from 1 to M at unassigned positions and memoize results to avoid recomputation.

c. You are given an integer n, an integer k, and an array arr of size n consisting of integers. For each element arr[i], convert it to its binary representation and define its value as:

Sum of (bit × position) where position is 1-based from right in the binary representation.

You need to find the number of pairs (i, j) such that:

value(arr[i]) + value(arr[j]) == k

Input: n = 4, k = 20, arr = [5, 6, 7, 8] Output: 1

● I looped from the least significant bit to the most significant bit, checking if each bit was set using (num >> bitPos) & 1.

● While doing this, I maintained a position counter (1-based from MSB) and added bit * position to the score.

After calculating the custom value, I stored it in an array and this transformed the question to check if the array has a pair for which the value is equal to k, I solved this using hashmap storing the frequencies and incrementing the count of the final answer.

This approach passed all regular test cases. However, one test case had a missing array input despite providing n. To handle this edge case, I wrapped the input parsing in a try-catch block, and in such a case, I returned 0.

Thanks to the optimized bitwise handling and proper input validation, I was able to solve all test cases correctly.

d. You are given:

● Four houses from Harry Potter: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, and Slytherin

● Two integers: n: number of students m: maximum number of students allowed in each house

● A list of friendships: pairs of integers (a, b) where student a and student b are friends and must be placed in different houses

● A strings, where the i-th string contains the allowed houses for the i-th student (e.g., "[["pref1, pref2"], [pref2]]" you had to parse the string and split them accordingly and store their preferences)

Your task is to determine if it is possible to assign every student to exactly one of their preferred houses such that:

1. No pair of friends is placed in the same house

2. No house has more than m students

3. Each student is assigned to one of their preferred houses

Print "possible" if such an assignment exists, otherwise "impossible".

This was the final and most complex question, especially due to the tricky input format:

● I had to read n and m

● Then an unknown number of friend pairs

● Followed by a single line of strings indicating preferences for each student

Because I was short on time and the input parsing itself was time-consuming, I chose not to attempt this question.

2. [Technical Round 1] [30 candidates were shortlisted]

In this round, we were divided into three panels of 10 students each, with each session lasting approximately an hour. I was a part of the third panel. Some candidates were asked to introduce themselves, while others were immediately given DSA problems. The interview followed a similar pattern to the previous years, although the difficulty level had noticeably increased this time, with topics like Trie and Binary Lifting also making an appearance.

I was first asked to introduce myself, after which I was presented with a DSA problem:

Problem: Given an array of integers (which may include both positive and negative numbers), find the maximum sum of a subarray that starts and ends with the same value. If no such subarray exists, return the Integer. MIN_VALUE.

I initially explained the brute force approach -- iterating through every possible subarray and checking if the first and last elements matched. Then, I discussed an optimized solution using a hashmap to store indices of elements and computing prefix sums to calculate the subarray sum in constant time. However, the interviewer pointed out that in cases where all elements are the same, this method could degrade to brute force in terms of time complexity.

To solve the problem efficiently, I used a prefix sum array to compute the sum between any two indices in constant time and maintained a hash map to track the first occurrence of each number. While iterating through the array, if a number had been seen before, I calculated the sum of the subarray between its first occurrence and the current index. If this sum was greater than the current maximum, I updated the answer. In cases where the computed sum was negative, I reset the first occurrence of that number to the current index to allow for potentially better subarrays in the future. For numbers appearing for the first time, I simply stored their index in the map.

This logic struck a good balance between efficiency and edge case handling. The interviewer seemed satisfied with the clarity and completeness of my explanation and asked me to write down the code for it.

The second question I was asked involved a binary tree and multiple queries, where each query was a pair (node, value)--and the same node could appear multiple times with different values. For each query, the task was to find the maximum XOR between the given value and any of the node values along the path from the root to the specified node. I initially proposed a brute force approach where, for each query, I would traverse the path from the root to the node and compute the XOR on the go. However, the interviewer asked me to optimize it. Recalling a previous problem I had solved involving maximum XOR using a Trie, I adapted that idea here. At first, I was constructing a new Trie for each query, but after a few hints from the interviewer, I realized that I needed to build the Trie dynamically as I traversed the tree, inserting values on the path and using a counter mechanism to keep track of the presence of values. While backtracking, I would decrement the counter or remove the value to reflect that the node was no longer in the current path. This allowed me to efficiently query for the maximum XOR at any point without rebuilding the Trie for every query.

After explaining the optimized approach using a Trie with dynamic insertion and backtracking, I was asked to code out the solution. I implemented the logic by building the Trie on-the-fly during a DFS traversal of the binary tree, maintaining a counter to manage insertions and removals as nodes entered and exited the current path. The interviewer seemed satisfied with both my thought process and implementation. The interview wrapped up with me asking him a couple of questions.

3. [Hiring Managerial Round] [14 candidates were shortlisted for round 2 (a mix of both HM and Tech Round 2]

After each panel finished, the students who showed strong technical skills were directly sent for the Hiring Manager (HM) round. I think this was done to check their communication and soft skills. In this round, many students were rejected even though they were very good at coding, so it was clear that this round tested more than just technical knowledge. My HM interview was taken by the Engineering Head at PhonePe. He started by asking how I was feeling and then asked me to introduce myself. He looked at my resume and began asking questions based on it. Since I had mentioned my internship, he started with that. I also told him about the freelance work I had done. He then asked in detail about the things I had built during my internship. After that, he moved on to my projects. All of my projects were from hackathons, so I was confident while explaining them. Then he asked me to choose one of my favorite apps and design its system. I explained my choices clearly and walked him through my thought process. At some points, he said my design might not handle large traffic, so I broke those parts down further and improved the design. In the end, he was happy with my final solution. The second half of the interview was mostly HR questions. I tried to answer honestly and gave real examples, even mentioning times when I was wrong and how my friends helped me understand things better. Showing a balanced and honest mindset helped. I ended the interview by asking him a few questions.

4. [Technical Round 2] [ 11 students were shortlisted for the final round]

This round was quite similar to the first technical round, where we were asked two DSA questions. The first question was: given a list of strings, return true if concatenating any two of them forms a palindrome. I started with the brute force approach, but the interviewer asked me to optimize it. I then explained a Trie-based approach where, before inserting a string into the Trie, I would reverse it and check if it already exists. I also maintained a pointer i to check if the remaining part of the string formed a palindrome. After some back and forth and dry runs, the interviewer was satisfied with my logic, asked about the time complexity, and then told me to write the code.

The second question was an array problem that was mostly greedy/observational. Despite several hints from the interviewer, I wasn't able to come up with the correct solution during the interview. He later shared the solution and asked me to prove why the approach worked mathematically. I tried to reason it out but couldn't come up with a complete proof. However, I did manage to explain a valid DP-based approach and correctly identified the DP state. Since time was up, we had to wrap the round, and I asked him a few questions before ending. I also requested him to walk me through the proof of the solution I couldn't solve. I checked the second question was rated 2700 on Codeforces (Problem Link), which explained its difficulty level.

Out of the 11 candidates, 7 were selected in the end and I was one of them.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Strong DSA skills are essential - PhonePe places heavy emphasis on problem-solving, with this year's difficulty being higher than usual. Topics like Tries, Binary Lifting were commonly asked.

2. CP is a bonus, not a requirement - Being comfortable with CP is a big plus as it improves your problem solving skills. I didn't do any competitive programming, but regularly attempting Leetcode contests and upsolving problems (sometimes trying to understand the 4th question) helped me grasp advanced topics and perform in a time bounded environment.

3. Internship experience adds value - My interview started with questions about my internship. It's important to clearly explain what you worked on and the impact you had.

4. Know your resume inside out - Be fully prepared to talk about everything on your resume, including freelance work, projects, and technical contributions.

5. Hackathon projects stand out - Projects from hackathons show real-world problem-solving and help you pitch confidently in interviews.

6. Good communication is crucial - Stay vocal, explain your thought process clearly, and engage with the interviewer. Many technically strong candidates were rejected due to weak soft skills.

7. Be consistent, not rushed - I couldn't even clear Barclays OA for the summer internship, but consistent DSA practice with concept clarity (not rote learning) made a big difference. I would say even 6-8 months of sincere dedication toward DSA can help you clear any OA.

Resources:

1. DSA: Follow Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet - it's structured, beginner-friendly, and covers all essential topics and patterns.

2. SQL: Practice from LeetCode's Top 50 SQL Questions - great for query writing and real interview problems.

3. DBMS: Watch this DBMS video - it covers everything you need for interviews.

4. Core Subjects (OS, CN, OOPs): Refer to GeeksforGeeks - it's sufficient for brushing up on the most asked concepts in interviews.

5. System Design: Go through System Design Article. Tip: You can skim through it and skip advanced topics like Kafka.

6. Tech Cheatsheet: View the Cheatsheet here, I got this from my senior -- it includes useful resources across key topics. Feel free to use and share!

All the best for your placements!

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [219 candidates had applied] Platform: DoSelect || Questions: 4 || Time: 1hr 30mins

I would advise you to skim through all the questions first and start with the one which seems familiar/ easy. I started with Q3, which I solved in 7-8 minutes. Then I moved to Q1, got stuck on an edge case due to limited debugging options, but managed to solve it in 20 minutes. I spent the rest of the time on Q2, implemented a recursive solution, and passed a few test cases.

1) You were given n people and 2 array A and B of size m, where each pair (A[i], B[i]) means that A[i] is a friend of B[i]. Also, friendships are transitive, so if x is a friend of y and y is friend of z, x is also friend of z. You were told to find the minimum no of new friendship such that everyone is friend is each other. Approach: The question can be easily solved by counting the no of components . I used DSU to find the no of connected components and return it -1, A DFS or BFS approach would have worked too.

2) You were given an array A which represented the laddoos given to n employees. Each person must receive atleast 1 and atmost m laddoos. You had to assign laddoos to employed who had received 0 laddoos such that the absolute difference between two employees is not more than k. And finally, you had to print the no of valid ways distributions. Approach: I thought of writing a recursive solution first and then optimizing it using memoization, but was only able to solve 5 test case. Thought of debugging it but the platform didn't allow to see print statements (tho after the test I got to know that you can see print statements via custom inputs). Gave approx. 45 mins to this problem but was not able to solve it completely

3) You had to find the count of unordered pair such that their sum is s and the total of set bits in both the number is <=k

Approach: As the constraint was small enough for O(N2) to work but I solved it in O(N) as it was quite similar to the famous 2 sum problem. So used a map to store numbers and if the complement (s-a[i]) is present in the map checked for the set bit condition.

4) The question didn't specify the no of edges so didn't even look at this question as I had no practice on how to take input of this kind. However, as the question only needed to print possible or not possible and each test case having only one result so just printing possible was enough to get 6/8 testcase right. And further as one of the wrong testcase was the sample one so hard coded it and got 7/8 right. Well, they did mention that code quality was being considered but taking into consideration that no one was able to solve this optimally and almost everyone printed possible, this question may as well have not been considered for the selection.

I solved 2 problems completely and 2 partially which was enough for being selected for the next round.

2. [Technical Round 1] [ 30 students appeared] All the 30 students were divided into 3 panels of 10 each. I was part of the 1st panel.

The interviewer introduced himself and ask for mine as well. I kept my into short as I wanted more time for the 2 problems.

Question 1: Find the peak element in a 2d matrix. Where peak element is defined as the element which is greater than its 4 adjacent neighbors.

Before starting the question, I made to fully understand the problem by clarified the constraints, is it 4-directional or 8-directional adjacency. I started with the brute force solution which was to iterate and see if the condition is met.

Then I showed him how monotonicity is maintained in a 1d array for finding the peak element and how we can use binary search to implement it. Thought of flattening the 2d array and applying binary search on it. However soon found out that it does not work. With the help of some hints from the interviewer, found the optimal solution which involved binary search with the search space as the range of rows/cols. He then asked me to code the solution of paper.

Question 2: You were given a tree and q queries. Each query had a start node, an end node and a destination. The task was to find the node which is at a minimum distance from destination while also being on the path from start to end node.

Ex: Consider the n-ary tree And the query [2,5,7].

The path from 2 to 5 would be 2->1->3->5 and out of all the node the node 3 is at minimum distance from 7 so the answer is 3.

It started by saying that we can precompute the distance between all pair of nodes (MSSP algorithm) by using Floyd-Warshall algorithm and then for each query find the path using dfs/bfs while also maintaining a parent array to track the path. And using the parent array to trace the path we see which node has the minimum distance from destination.

However, as the distance matrix takes O(N3) time to compute, it wasn't optimal so the interviewer asked me look the answer in terms of LCA (Lowest common ancestor). I tried to find some observations from the testcase and found that the answer can be one of the LCA (start, end), LCA (start, destination) and LCA (end, destination). Once these 3 nodes are found we can calculate the minimum distance from the destination. However, it was not optimal and time was up so left it there.

The interviewer then asked for any questions for him . I had researched about it and asked him .

I was not able to solve both the question however don't let it demotivate you. The interviewer is more interested on how you approach the question so be open to him and read out your thoughts out loud and ask him for any hints if needed.

To save some time, from each panel 3 were fast-tracked to give the HR round before 2nd tech round.

3. [Technical Round 2] [ 14 students appeared] My 2nd tech round happened after my HR round. And similar to 1st tech round we were asked to solve 2 questions. I was not asked for my intro this time.

Problem 1: Given a matrix of size m*n, each element had a heat value which I gained if I landed on it, I had to return the minimum heat with which I could reach bottom right corner from top left corner under the following constraints:

1. I could move left, right, bottom or top.

2. I could not retrace my path at any point.

3. I couldn't move the same direction more than 3 times.

I initially approached the problem using BFS, but since we're trying to minimize a cumulative cost (heat), I pointed out that Dijkstra's algorithm would be more suitable here.

I took 5 states in my heap as heat, x, y, prevDirection, countOfPrevDirection and implemented the standard Dijkstra with the constraint on the paper while considering the code quality as well. I was asked a follow up that what if I had to move k steps before changing direction. I handled that as well

Problem 2: The exact problem from leetcode I started with a greedy solution which as expected didn't work on a few cases. Then I thought about dp to which the interviewer said I was on the right track. I was able to find the state which is quite similar to 0/1 Knapsack but the interviewer was not satisfied. I then dry runed the test cases given by him and my solution worked. He was satisfied by my answer till the end of interview I then asked him what would the optimal solution be. He opened the leetcode question itself and showed the editorial. The editorial had the same solution as mine. He then shook hands with me and said "Well Done".

4. [Hiring Manager Round] [ 11 students appeared]

PhonePe's HR round isn't a typical HR round; it revolves more around the resume so be have good projects on it and (internship if any).

The interviewer was the engineer manager at PhonePe. He started by asking me to walkthrough my projects. Since two of them were hackathon-winning projects, I had a clear strategy on how to present them: I first explained the problem or need , then walked him through how I approached and solved it, which helped build curiosity around the tech stack I had used. He asked me about jwt and RSA algorithm. I was not sure about the e xact implementation of it but gave a rough idea to him. In one of the projects, I had worked on the entire software development lifecycle , and I made sure to highlight that experience specifically.

I also made sure to explain him about a dev Ops experiment that I had done which wasn't mentioned on my resume. He was quite impressed by this.

He then asked me about my favorite app and its most used feature and I answered with reddit. He went forward to ask me to implement the post feature from the DB selection to the schema and optimizations (Pagination, caching, etc.).

He then followed with typical HR question. I gave honest and diplomatic answers to him using real life examples.

I was one of the first to have concluded with all the rounds so had to wait 4 hours for the results to be announced

7 students received the offer.

journey.prep:
I wanted to share some of my thoughts after going through the interview process with companies like Baker Hughes, Dolat Capital, Quantiphy, and BlackRock. My main interest has always been in mathematical coding, and mathematical problems solving (which was thoroughly asked in dolat capital) rather than traditional DSA, so it was a surprise when my journey led me to a global marketing role.

What really struck me across all the interviews was that confidence is a huge part of the game. The interviewers valued direct and clear answers, and how you present your thought process seems just as important as the final solution. They almost always threw in a couple of really tricky questions that felt designed to see how you handle pressure. Honestly, getting through one of those tough problems gives you a major boost and makes the rest of the interview feel much more manageable.

A major wake-up call for me was in the Dolat Capital interview when they started asking deep questions about C++, which was definitely not my strong part. It taught me what I now call the "30% rule": even for your weakest subjects, try to have at least a basic, 30% level of understanding. It's far better than being caught completely off guard. Similarly, the BlackRock interview was an eye-opener. They did a deep dive into my project's architecture, asking about the data preprocessing pipeline and my storage choices. It made me realize that interviewers want to see that you can think about the entire system, not just the code you wrote.

In these 4 interviews, the common question was on my project. They told me to go through my projects and ask deeply on that one.

First, only list projects you are 100% confident you can defend, because they will ask tough, detailed questions. Second, be careful about listing an outlier tech stack. If one project uses a technology that doesn't fit the rest of your story, interviewers will zoom in on it.. Your projects should highlight your strengths, not create traps.

So, while my path took an unexpected turn, the technical interview process itself was an incredible learning experience. The biggest lesson was the importance of a balanced strategy: know your strengths, strategically cover your weaknesses, and always be ready to explain your thinking with confidence.

There were 3 rounds in this process. (For GM role)

1. Online assessment

2. Technical interview

3. HR round

1. Online Assessment[ 100 students appeared for this round]

This round was conducted on E-litmus platform and was proctored.

It consisted on mainly 3 sections and all were of objective type(mcqs):

1. Logical reasoning,verbal reasoning,aptitude

2. Coding / algorithms

3. DBMS and SQL

This was of 90 minutes, but each section and subsection had its own time limit set.

There were 4 subsections in 1st section, like verbal reasoning, logical reasoning, quantitative aptitude, and assertion reasoning type. All these subsections were easy to solve but lengthy, especially the quantitative aptitude one. Each sub section had its own time limit and navigation in subsection was not allowed, so had to carefully answer or leave the question. The questions were of cat-type basic aptitude and english questions, like speed and time, height and distance, work and efficiency, upstream and downstream, profit and loss, missing number or wrong number in the sequence.

The 2nd section had flowchart type questions based on an algorithm or a scenario like lottery system, shopping mart. It had 4-5 questions based on each scenario, so had 4-5 such scenarios and each flowchart had a missing box to fill for that algorithm. There were some loops based mathematical coding questions as well, like to test the divisibility by 17 , what should be the main line :- first n-1 digits - 5* last digit should be divisible by 17. Then there were lengthy loop questions to calculate some mathematical sequences, like agp, gp, sum of squares.

The 3rd section was of dbms and sql and had queries and database concepts like normalization, acid properties. Major questions were output type questions to the queries, like sysdate from dual, to_char function, and many more based on dual .

In the OA, try not to spend more time on just 1 question, as it was very much time bound, especially the flowchart questions and quantitative aptitude.

I was selected for the Global Marketing role which had 7 shortlists (3 waitlists). This round started with my introduction and the interviewer asked me to go through my projects. I mentioned about my film recommendation project, on which the 2 panelists asked me to explain its architecture, how will I expand the project to industrial level, which tech stack I used, and why so. 4. What are your weakness and what plan do you have to improve those aspects?

5. Few questions about BlackRock as a company and what does it do?

Total of 10 students were selected overall. 2 for Global marketing role.

journey.prep:
1. DSA Preparation Start DSA preparation early on. Try to consistently practice at least 1-2 questions every day. I personally followed Striver's SDE Sheet, which is very well-structured and covers most interview-relevant topics.

https://takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course/strivers-a2z-dsa-course-sheet-2

Always try to solve questions yourself first. If you're stuck, watch the video explanation but make sure to code it yourself afterwards. Keep revising important questions and try to identify and remember common problem patterns across topics.

2. Core Subjects - Java and OOPs I started with the basics of Java. Here's a link I referred to: https://youtu.be/eIrMbAQSU34?si=_Vq7MalRpZaXJsO9

For OOPs concepts, I followed Kunal Kushwaha's playlist, which explains everything in a beginner-friendly manner. Additionally, I read articles on GeeksforGeeks, which helped reinforce key concepts like encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction.

https://youtu.be/BSVKUk58K6U?si=NQVHOYRXLAgVkir6

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/object-oriented-programming-oops-concept-in-java/

3. DBMS (RDBMS) For RDBMS, I watched CodeHelp by Love Babbar's one-shot video. It covers almost all the concepts required for interviews.

https://youtu.be/dl00fOOYLOM?si=IE8ak_4YztXdYTOf

4. SQL I learned the basics from W3Schools and practiced extensively on LeetCode. I completed all 50 questions from the SQL 50 list and also solved 10-15 additional medium/hard-level questions to get more comfortable

https://www.w3schools.com/sql/default.asp

https://youtu.be/OT1RErkfLNQ?si=1Ctjw2Ud6hQRm-X-

https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

5. Operating Systems & CN For OS and Computer Networks, basic articles from GeeksforGeeks are more than enough. Focus on understanding concepts like process/thread, scheduling, memory management, TCP/IP, and HTTP. I wasn't asked this in interviews but some of my friends were asked about these subjects.

6. System Design in OOPs In some interviews, you're asked to design systems like a Library Management System, Parking Lot, or ATM Machine using OOPs concepts. So, be prepared to design small-scale systems applying classes, objects, inheritance, and design principles. Practice dry-running a few systems beforehand.

7. Final Interview Tips Before every interview, research the company, their culture, products, and latest updates. This not only helps you frame better answers but also helps you ask relevant questions at the end of the interview, which leaves a strong impression. Prepare an introduction which basically summarizes your resume. Know your projects and your resume very thoroughly.

If you have any questions, I'll be more than happy to help. You can reach out to me directly on WhatsApp or Linkedin.

All the best
