Online Assessment(75 mins, 2 Coding Qs, 1 SQL Qs)

Interviews:

1. Technical Round 1

2. Technical Round 2

3. HR Round

1. Online Assessment [Around 240 candidates appeared for this round]

There were 2 DSA questions and 1 SQL question in the online assessment and the time duration was 75 mins.

Q1 : Given an array of integers, find the sum of elements of all possible subarrays of the array. For example, if the input array is [1, 2, 3], then the sum of all possible subarrays is 20. The subarrays are: [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3] Sum = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 20 Here, I followed a brute-force approach by calculating all possible subarrays and maintaining the sum of all the subarrays. I was able to pass 14 out of 15 test cases.

Q2 : Given an array of integers, the task was to reach the end of the array while maximizing the score based on allowed jumps. There were two jump conditions:

1. I could take one step to the immediate right, i.e., i → i+1

2. I could take a jump of length p such that p is a prime number ending with 3 (e.g., 3, 13, 23, etc.).

The goal was to reach the end of the array while collecting the maximum possible score (i.e., sum of visited elements). I followed a dynamic programming (DP) approach and used memoization to avoid recomputation. At each index, I considered both the one-step jump and all valid p jumps. I recursively computed the maximum score possible from that point onward, and memoised the results.

Q3: This was a SQL question involving two tables related to voter information. The goal was to return a summary of each state, showing the names of voters who voted in that state along with the number of times each voter voted. Given Tables: Voters: Votes: voter_id | name voter_id | state ---------|-------- ---------|------- 1 | Tanvi 1 | California 2 | Gaurang 2 | California 3 | Drishya 2 | California 4 | Rahul 1 | California 4 | Texas

Expected Output : state | voters_summary --------------|--------------------------- California | Tanvi x 2, Gaurang x 2 Texas | Rahul x 1

The question was supposed to be solved using GROUP_CONCAT() I couldn't fully solve the question during the interview due to time constraints. Try to solve the DSA questions fully first as they have the most weightage to get selected for interviews.

2. Technical Interview 1 [ 39 candidates were shortlisted for this round. ]

The round lasted for approximately 50 minutes. The interviewer began by introducing himself, and then asked me to give a brief introduction. After that, I was asked two DSA questions.

Q1: Vertical Sum of a Binary Tree : The question was based on binary trees. I was asked to compute the sum of all elements in the tree that lie along the same vertical line, and return an array of sums for each vertical line.

For example, the output was expected to look something like: [4, 2, 12, 3, 7].

I suggested using a hash map to store the sum of nodes at each horizontal distance (HD). I used HD = 0 for the root, HD - 1 for the left child, and HD + 1 for the right child. As we traverse the tree, we keep adding values to the same horizontal distance key in the hash map. I mentioned that since Python dictionaries are unordered, we'd need to sort the keys before generating the final output array and coded up the entire solution on paper. I was asked to perform a dry run and the interviewer was satisfied with my solution and moved on to the next question.

Q2 : The second question was a standard problem on detecting a cycle in a directed graph. I approached the problem using a Depth First Search (DFS) technique. To handle the detection, I used two boolean arrays: one to keep track of all the nodes that had been visited globally, and another to track the nodes in the current DFS recursion path. I explained this logic clearly and proceeded to code the solution during the interview. I was asked to perform a dry run and the interviewer was satisfied with my approach.

After the DSA questions, the interviewer shifted the focus to my projects and began going through my resume. He asked me to briefly explain the projects I had worked on and the technologies I used. Following that, he delved deeper into the topic of authentication, asking both conceptual and implementation-related questions. He wanted to understand how I had implemented authentication in my projects and how the flow works in a typical web application. Specifically, he asked about JWT (JSON Web Tokens) and its structure. The questions included:

Q1 : What is present in the JWT header structure?

Q2 : What is the complete authentication flow, how the token is generated, returned to the client, stored, sent in subsequent requests, and how token expiry (token window) is handled?

Q3 : How can we implement role-based access control? Here I answered that we can use wrappers or decorators to restrict access to api endpoints and maintain security and role based access. Then there were several questions on databases.

The interview concluded with the interviewer asking me if I had any questions for him. I took this opportunity to ask about the advancements in AI and how they are being leveraged in the finance domain, where both high volumes of data and data integrity are critically important. The interviewer answered the question briefly and the interview ended.

3. Technical Interview 2 [ Around 20 candidates were shortlisted for this round. ]

The second interview lasted for about an hour. The interviewer began by introducing himself and then asked me to introduce myself. I gave a brief overview of my background, skills, and projects. He then asked me which topics in DSA I was most comfortable with. I mentioned that I enjoy working with graphs and heaps. Following that, he asked me to explain real-life applications of graphs, which I answered with relevant examples like in maps for determining shortest paths.

He proceeded to ask a DSA question, which was a variation of Dijkstra's algorithm. I was asked to code the solution on paper. I wrote the code and explained the entire logic. During the explanation, he asked several detailed questions about each part of my code--why I used heaps, how I handled initialization, and the overall structure of the solution.

He then asked me to think through potential edge cases and confirm whether my code handled them. After that, he asked me to do a dry run of the code. I walked him through the step-by-step execution, and he was satisfied with my explanation and approach. After the DSA question, the interviewer briefly moved on to my resume. He asked about my participation in hackathons and what I had implemented in one of them. He then asked about the projects listed in my resume, including their purpose and technical implementation.

Since I had mentioned LangChain in my resume, he asked several questions related to it. These included: what is LangChain, why is it used, what is LangGraph, why not build directly without LangChain, and what advantages it offers. I answered these questions based on my project experience. Next, he asked me to explain another project I had worked on, including the technologies I used. He then shifted focus to OOP concepts and asked questions about the static keyword, implementation of singleton classes, encapsulation, and interfaces.

After that, he asked me two SQL questions. He initially provided two tables: student and subject, and asked a medium-level SQL query involving joins, which I solved successfully. Then he added a third table called department and asked a follow-up query. I was able to solve all three queries completely, and the interviewer seemed satisfied.

Then he asked a few questions related to React like to explain the component structure, then explain the two hooks usestate and useffect. Then he asked about Virtual DOM and working of virtual DOM and how it improved efficiency. Then he asked some general topics like MongoDB and databases. He asked me to explain the differences between SQL and NoSQL databases, and in what scenarios I would choose one over the other. He also asked me to give two real-world examples where I would use both types, which I was able to answer.

Finally, he asked me about different types of NoSQL databases beyond key-value stores. I admitted I wasn't aware of all the types. He then asked about indexing in DBMS and whether indexing can be done in NoSQL databases as well.

The interview concluded after this discussion and I asked about how AI is leveraged in finance. He answered briefly and the interview concluded.

4. HR Round [ 8 candidates were shortlisted for this round. ]

The HR round was very relaxed and conversational. The interviewer was warm and made me feel comfortable from the beginning. It felt more like a discussion than a formal interview and lasted around 15 minutes.

1. Introduce yourself

2. Mention something interesting that is not in your resume

3. What do you like to do besides tech?

4. Explain two of your projects

5. Describe a time you worked in a team

6. Do you prefer working individually or in a team?

7. Where do you see yourself in 5 years?

8. Are you planning for higher studies?

For the question about higher studies, I responded that I'm not planning to pursue them. I shared that I believe gaining hands-on industry experience is the right path for me.

At the end of the interview, she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked about MSCI's commitment to ESG and climate initiatives, and how those values are integrated into the company's work culture. She appreciated the question and gave a thoughtful response before concluding the interview.

[ 5 students were offered the job ]

journey.prep:
Hard work is important, but preparing smart for an interview is also really important,reading through interview experiences and prepping accordingly is important .

1. There is a high possibility that even though you are the smartest , you might not end up having a good offer, and that's alright because placement has a huge chunk of your luck being on your side on that day. The day before I had a massive setback after being in college for 12 hours and facing a rejection from Barclays, I never thought I could crack 4 rounds the next day, but just believe in god's plans and in the hard work you have put.

2. Be true to yourself, copying other's projects, or lying in the interview won't land you up anywhere, you cannot always prepare everything for an interview just before it, so the other answers you give is by how much knowledge you have, which doesn't come in a day or two, you need to be consistent from the day you read this.

3. Keep your mind open during interviews, then only you can think of new examples, and answers also the point when the interviewer comes to your strongest point is when you should drag the interview and tell everything you know about it(in minute details, mine were my projects so I explained all of them in deep details.)

4. You need to consistently do DSA,so, in the last 1-2 months you can prepare for the other stuff( I started around 2nd year end and did consistently.)

5. Make your projects with a purpose, and if not at least keep an answer ready which is a real world scenario so u can mention how and why u did the project.

6. Losing hope and feeling demotivated in this period is absolutely normal , but just believe in yourself, keep doing that's the only way, this is just the beginning. Keeping yourself fit in that period is really important that's how you can keep your mind the most active so eat good and sleep well during that period.

1. DSA- Striver A to Z ( giving contests on codechef , codeforces also helped a lot to think quickly, though not compulsory.)

3. Aptitude-Indiabix & Aptitude Preparation for Placements #1 Introduction | Why Aptitude Is Important F…

[ List down the rounds that were conducted and any specific information related to it ]

1. [Online Assessment] [ Around 140 candidates ][28th July]

The OA consisted of 3 Sections,Logical reasoning(20 minutes),Aptitude(20 minutes) and DSA Questions (40 mins-2 questions). Each question was shut after that allotted time so make sure to read all instructions carefully, so you can attempt all questions. The MCQ's weren't from a specific section , you had to have knowledge about various sections like OOPS,SQL,Basics of development etc, aptitude solving, so there is no separate thing you could do for this section, its striking in the moment and some basic knowledge that you gathered over the years. No amount of mcq study could guarantee marks in this section, just answer the ones you are sure about and do a guess on others as there was not any negative marking.

Coming to the DSA section- there were 2 DSA questions, both were quite easy, the first was about sorting , the other one I don't remember the exact question but if you are able to solve Leetcode easy-medium section, this will be a cakewalk. I was able to pass all test cases for the first question, but left 3 test cases for the second one which was a case for almost every student , so relatively it was all the same , hardly anyone solved the entire question. So it's about you trying every solution, even brute force, that comes to your mind because you never know that's what everyone did.

2. [Technical Interview 1] [ 45 candidates shortlisted][30th July,2025]

There were 2 interviewers on the panel, so don't get intimidated. The interview began with "Tell me about yourself", you actually don't need immense prep for this one, just give them a basic overview of what all you did in college years(like DSA,dev,internship(if any),extracurricular activities) , I feel that's enough. Now this interview wasn't in any flow, they asked questions from all domains.

1. Basic Questions- Difference between Authentication and Authorization- I answered that followed by which they gave a scenario, there is a case wherein you have three sections , principle's cabin, teacher's cabin and the tpo office, everyone has an admin for that room, and a normal student who doesn't belong to any section needs access to one of these rooms(To clarify the instructions and problem definition wasn't as clear as I have mentioned here but over the discussion you kinda figure out the problem, so you need to DISCUSS with the panel about what you are thinking and if it matches with what they want an answer for, then proceed further, this tells them that you have a good habit of understanding problem statement clearly then moving to solution rather than just jumping without clear understanding). Initially I thought it was about jwt authorization but later I came to the conclusion that it had api keys involved and you had to give a token to everyone who requested it with an expiry time.-There is no certain prep you can do for these types of questions your dev concepts need to be clear which just comes by making projects.

2. OOPS- I was asked about multiple inheritance, the diamond problem I explained along with it, then about Private constructors(Singleton classes) and how they are called(getInstance method),abstraction,C++ vs Java(multiple inheritance,pointers,virtual inheritance).

3. Projects- Asked about how I implemented user authentication using Firebase(to which I gave a detailed explanation), why mongodb(explain abt sql vs no sql) db , why react(virtual dom etc),about use of api in projects.

4. I was asked for the system design of a URL shortener, to which I gave a rough answer(data structure to be used and flow of it).

3. [Technical Round 2] [22 candidates][30th July]

In this round with 2 interviewers again,it began with intro, then i was asked about

1. New vs malloc(keyword in java and c++), which is faster, which is better to which i wasn't really correct in all answers,to which the interviewer also said, "its visible , you aren't aware".

2. Then he asked about destructors and copy constructors, though I had read about them , due to his statement I just forgot about it.

At such points it's really important to keep your calm and look forward to points where you can show him your strengths.

3. Later I was asked a question to check if 4181 belongs to the fibonacci series(not normal fibonacci series printing) to which after some hints i was able to solve. For such non-traditional questions just keep thinking about different approaches and keep telling the interviewer, till he doesn't tell you to stop.

4. Later it came to some OOPS concepts again which were easy only, they did tell me to write pseudo code so even if your first language isnt java have a basic understanding of how to write classes and instantiate objects, and various keywords,they do tell you to write code.

5. Then came to my projects, and asked about various keywords, like JWT Auth,API's, DB storage, at such points its really important,that you explain them the motive behind each of your project and explain them key parts in detail, they just want to know that it's your original work that you created and with a purpose(is what the interviewer told me as a feedback.)

6. I was given a scenario about a project scaling and was given different scenarios and had to design schema for all of them and also write sql queries.

4. [HR Round] [9 candidates][28th July]

Initially it was for an hour, but later, due to time constraints it was for 20-25 minutes. Just be yourself in this interview they want to see the real you and align yourself with the company policies and motives. Also explain how you fit in the company giving real life examples. To be honest I didn't prepare anything for this round, just knew the policy(Always You First) and some motives(like ethics,etc). Take a few minutes to think,it gives you a lot many examples to speak about.

5. [Fitment/Tech round] [9 candidates ][28th July]

This one started at around 9:30 p.m. , we were at college from 8 a.m , be ready for such long days, and keep your mind prepared to answer equally well in such scenarios. I just left the hr round seconds within i was called for the next round, which was really quick.

This was about my favourite subjects I studied in the curriculum, then I made a mess here by saying soft computing(neural networks) which I had not revised after 4th sem. Then he ended up asking the difference between neural networks and machine learning, which set me a slight back, but took a pause of relief and thought , in basic

terms so i started with ml then recalled some of neural networks and finished the answers. Later he asked for an overview of all projects and this interview ended.

Results were declared next day and

[ 8 students were offered the job ]...

It's really important to study as per the interview experience , that guides you which topics are the most important for that company. Know your resume in and out and everything mentioned on it in detail, because that's the only piece of information they have about you, its ok to have less skills on resume but know everything in detail rather than having more and not knowing some.

1. [Online Assessment] [ 135+ Students were shortlisted ]

The OA had a few sections: Logical Aptitude, Technical Questions, and a final DSA section. Each section had its own timer. It's all about being choosy and smart enough to identify which questions are the low-hanging fruit for you.

Aptitude Section:---> Following is just the tentative vague description and not the exact question (I really can't remember the exact questions , but this description will really help you get a clear idea)

1)Coding-Decoding Analogy: If "FADE" is "GBWR" then follow the same pattern for some "xyzw" type of string 2)Number Theory: how many pairs(a,b) are there wherein division of a/b is not an integer {1,2,3,4…16} something like this. 3)Logical Reasoning Passage:A big 3-4 questions passage (Some 6 people , given word-equations(ratio etc) of relations of their savings and salaries) and then follow up questions (easy but time consuming) 4)Statistics: Mean , Variance , Standard deviation , Coefficient of Variation type of questions.(Mean of 10 students is 3 , but then some student has mark correction and then find new mean) 5)Basic Probability types question (12 box , 3 has trap , so P(no trap)) 6)Question like how many pair of letters are there for "HERITAGE" having as many letters as there in english alphabet series (something like this) 7)Profit % types question 8)Pipe-work time types question

Technical Section:---> 1)Proper Loops (do-while etc) as a figure , and then interpret the figure and tell how many times is the code running.

2) Some oops (basic) questions

3) Standard OS,CCN,DBMS,SQL questions 4)Port , Ping , Router , Queues , Quick sort , static keyword numerical , pointers numerical int arr[]= {10,20,30,40,50,60,70} then something like int *r=arr…. *r1=arr+2 …. *r2= arr+5… and then cout<< something related with r1, r2 etc

5) Binary search tree array ={4,1,2,16,8,33,62,76} something like this , what is left child of root. 6)Queue <int> of size 4, some position of front , rear pointers , removing 3 elements , and then MCQ based on the state of the queue. 7)2D matrix figure based manipulation question (flowchart based) 8)Mysql type question (easy)

9) OOPS (conceptual easy question) of inheritance , output based , etc 10)One crazy question about OS of CISCO organization for switches 11)Basic data structure type question (medium gate level question) : output based 12)How many times the flowchart's loop is running.

Coding question:--->

1) How many elements are there which are in the correct place and not in the correct place. Correct place means Rightly indexed when seen from a Sorted perspective. (easy isn't it?) ex: 1 3 2 4 sorted is 1 2 3 4 1 and 4 are in the correct place , whereas 3 and 2 are not in the correct place.

2) Given int x, int y and then count special numbers from x and y. Special number means SUM(DIGITS) == 2*(highest digit). Easy??

Points to ponder:--->

1) Be calm

2) Manage time smartly

3) Attack on low-hanging fruits first

4) Attempt questions which you are familiar first

5) Learn to leave lengthy questions

6) Don't get zoned out , every 1 minute has the same value :)

2. [Technical Round 1] [41 candidates ] (70-90 mins++) {Taken by 2 interviewers}

1) Introduce yourself

2) Was asked question on my projects

3) Specify about Skills , Tech Stack that you have practiced

4) DSA Question (Revolving around Bellman-ford algorithm)

5) What is a cloud? Proxy Server?

6) SQL vs Mongodb , which I have used in the project ? Why? Why not?

7) Real word Application for Abstraction , Stack , Queue and Tree and Graph

8) Port number of Mysql

9) Heavy discussion on my projects (AIML based) (Maths behind Random Forest , Logistic Regression) . Focus on Pipelines and Flow of building an ML Model (decide , Train , test , tune etc etc)

10) It is impressive if you have published some research paper (or it is in under progress)

11) Indexing in Databases

12) Varchar in SQL , why varchar ? How to change the Varchar (LENGTH) once the table is already created.

13) Triggers in SQL

14) Library in Python which I have used (numpy , nltk , pandas , sci-kit ,openCV)

15) Docker ? Kubernetes (I didn't know Kubernetes Technicality)

16) Was Asked about my approach to the latest DSA problem which I had solved (it was about Trie with Bits and finding the Maximum XOR )

17) Final question for the interviewer? : I asked : how was my interviewer and where am i lacking , they said it is important that as a developer , we must have some knowledge about cloud , how to deploy , some advanced real life usage of networking(ccn) , code to be written not just for localhost , but a scalable code for development+deployment etc.

Mind it:--->

1) Never give up while giving interview

2) Even if you don't know, try to struggle with the question , tell the interviewers about your perspective, they are really interested more on how you think about approaching a problem , if you succeed in this way then this is really impressive

3) Sometimes you may even get a question that "hey AIML project is all about templates etc ", that's where you must say that while making a project it is also about proper lifecycle of development and building model , which task? Which model? Why this? Why not that etc ?

4) Never say anything negative , it may backfire you during the interview.

5) Don't break down,if your interviewer is an expert in a field like (cloud computing) and you have zero idea on that field , just be real-self.

3. [Technical Round 2] [22 candidates ] (90-100 mins++) {Taken by 2 interviewers}

1) Introduce yourself

2) One DSA code to be written on an online compiler. Mine was an easy question: Find peak element in an (increasing and then decreasing type) of array (Binary search) , just ask a clarifying question , what if n==1?==2? and then what if len(decreasing part)==0?

3) Indexing in Database (but advanced level)

4) SQL query optimization, I was asked to first tell Select * from table with name like "T%" and then to optimize this query. (even if you don't know , just try to deliver a valid logic)

5) Again Applicability for all projects, WHY this ? WHY not that?

6) OOPS: Compile-time and run-time polymorphism (overloading , overriding ,constructor , public , private , inheritance , Abstraction , encapsulation ) All these in real-life

7) LLD design for Bank system , make classes , interfaces , controller(if you don't know , then study it beforehand) , methods , etc , clean code for RBI class (parent class) and then subclasses like IDFC bank , SBI bank etc , and each having some rules, compliance rules, seniorcitizen_Age etc , revolving around inheritance etc.

8) What happens when you type a message in whatsapp to your friend? what happens when you click on "send message" button.

9) How do you think messages travel from your phone to your friends phone? Protocols, headers , packets , trivial CCN stuff.

10) What are keys , why keys , normalization , MongoDB familiarity?

11) Code for Trigger (After Insert) , just insert the curTime in logs

12) Was asked about familiarity with Stored Procedures

13) Asked about HSS-Psychology course

14) Was asked about Data analytics and my QGIS findings of land cover change

15) Was asked about my (Airavat,Flipkart grid) Hackathon experience , projects etc

16) Final question for interviewers? I asked : Is there any way to do "Online transactions on mobile for metro between Ghatkopar and Azad Nagar without Internet" , then we had a healthy discussion for about 5+ minutes on this topic.

4. [HR Round] [9 Candidates] (20 mins++)

This was a fairly relaxed round, and the HR representative was very friendly and made me feel comfortable. The conversation included the following questions:

1) Something cool about me which I have not written on resume (I told about my love for chess)

2) Why do you want to join IDFC bank ? (Reality: Along with coding , I could know about ITR, finance , economics , equity , IPO , banking sector etc.)

3) Dream company apart from IDFC bank? (I told about my love for space , stars and ISRO)

4) How do you deal with rejections (on-campus 8 times )?

5) What if I wasn't selected today also? (Grind for the best opportunity)

6) Any creative Application ideas for HR? (I first bulleted the answer but she told me to think again and come up with a brilliant idea, so i presented my idea for emotion-detection-AI powered priority wise scheduler chatbot / employee-HR relation management site with color coding feature ). She was really impressed by this idea thought in a shorter timespan. Like she told me such an application is being used by her and that this idea was amazing.

7) Where do I live ? What do I do in my travel time to college?

8) Some behavioral question and that's it

9) Any final question for her :- I asked her about the Location for internship and then placement, She told that bootcamp may be in Banglore and then Joining for placement maybe in Mumbai.(most likely)

5. [Business Round] [9 Candidates ] (20-30 mins++){Taken by 1 interviewer}

Okay so I was pretty sure that yes I had made it to the end , and then we got to know that there is one more Technical Round with the senior engineers or VP or architects of the company.

It was an online round on Teams. I would recommend you to give it from college only , because there you will have support from college , TPO office , supportive TPCs (yes they really work hard for our placement for that entire day+night) ,Wifi , HRs etc. So even if there is some wifi problem or technical issue , they are there to handle it (SO GIVE IT FROM COLLEGE ONLY !!!)

1) Hey Tushar , Introduce yourself

2) Seen my resume (Screen shared)

3) Talked about my skills

4) Discussed about my projects (the one with the most impact driven cause to be discussed along with full flow , architecture , why this and why not that , the mathematics behind this-that , the impact it is having)

5) My interviewer was a senior architect. He was really very chill and made me feel comfortable even after facing some technical issues (wifi problem at 8:05 pm).

6) Final questions for him? :- I told him that I had presented my views(Technical round 2) on "online transactions on mobile without internet" and what his opinion was on this point. He praised this idea and said some work is going on by RBI and all banks and that there is a good scope in this field.

After appearing for almost 9 companies, cracking OAs , failing in some Round 1, sometimes Round 2 , Sometimes even after HR round :( , but that day I was confident that yes , I think I have cracked it. It was around 9pm when we left for our home.

Next Day , at 11:11 AM :) We got to know that 8 students have been selected for this role ,And finally the hectic game has finally reached its final Destination .

The company first conducted a pre-placement talk, which was followed by an online assessment few days later. After that 4 interview rounds were conducted on 30th July.

1. Online Assesment [ 135 students appeared for it]

This was conducted on the HirePro platform & duration was for 75mins. The test consisted of 3 sections, each with a time limit. The first section had 15 questions and was aptitude based wherein general questions on logical reasoning were asked. The second section had 25 technical questions based on Excel, CCN, OS, OOPs and Basic Statistics. The third section had 2 coding questions which were quite easy.

- Q1) How many elements are correctly sorted. Correct place means Rightly indexed when seen from a Sorted perspective. Ex: 1 3 2 4 5 sorted is 1 2 3 4 5 1 and 4 are in the correct place , whereas 3 and 2 are not in the correct place. So the result would be 2, 3 Since 2 are incorrect and 3 are correct

- Q2) Had to find the number of golden number in a given range where the golden number meant the sum of the digits of a number - max number = max number Ex: 325 is a golden number (3+2+5) - 5 = 5

2. Technical Round 1 [ 41 students appeared ]

Initially 47 to 50 students were there but then many got selected in barclays so finally 41 students had appeared for this round. This round lasted for me around 45 mins to 1hr. I was the 1st person that was to be interviewed in my panel. It started with my introduction and then he directly jumped into a DSA problem it was related to cache so we had a buffer size of N and whenever we pushed an element it had a certain TTL (time_to_live) so

suppose an element entered the buffer at 10:20 and its TTL was 2mins then at 10:23 it was supposed to be popped out of the cache and make room for other elements to enter. Initially i started with a hashmap solution but as soon as i started explaining i got the Priority Queue solution using heap here since my primary language was python he was checking my syntax or the function that i was mentioning with GFG and since in GFG the priority queue implementation was not the one using heap he started asking what is heap, heapify and balanced binary tree which i was able to explain it all.

Then he started grilling me on GenAI and bit of ML since my entire resume was based on that Q1) Difference between GenAI and unsupervised learning (Generates new content and solely revolves around the input to find structure) Q2) What is the output of unsupervised learning models (Clusters, Dimensionality Reduction) Q3) Architecture of GenAI (Input layer + Tokenization + Embedding + Transformer + Attention Mechanism+ Decoder/output generator) Here i gave a brief overview of each layer and was trying to keep it as detailed as possible since i didnt want him to ask any more question in depth over here since i hadnt done transformers architecture in detail. Q4) How does its matches the user context and generates an appropriate content (Semantic Similarity) Q4) What is RAG Q5) In a glimpse explain what is prompt engineering Q6) Since i had explained RAG with the example of a medical chatbot he asked if a user prompts and says he cant concentrate in his work but the bot doesn't have any idea, as concentrate is not there in its DB then what will i do to give a proper response, initially i had said if at any point the bot cannot give a proper advice then i would have a default response wherein it will provide a general physician and he can take his concern forward with him but this wasn't what he had expected he said that the chatbot should ask few more questions on what he i feeling so that he can reach a conclusion and then provide a solution

He did ask few more questions based on AIML which i am not able to recollect but then it ended with me asking a question based on AIs usage in IDFC and one common question

3. Technical Round 2 [ 22 students]

This round lasted for around 40 mins for me

Here i didnt even feel i would get selected as the people who had went previous to me were all coming out demotivated since they were asked questions based on system design, AWS, CCN and i hadnt prepared in that terms at all but i was lucky since i was not asked such Qs

DSA : Valid Parenthesis Resume Based:

1. Asked me to explain one of my data analytics project it was dashboard based then asked few questions based on that

2. Since I had SQL in my resume they asked me what kind of projects I have done. I explained one, then they asked few simple queries based on the project explained, they were based on aggregate, group by and one subquery related cant remember the exact questions but all of them was very easy.

3. What is Jupyter Notebook and why use it when you have PyCharm or other IDEs

4. Then they asked which OS did i use since OS was mentioned in my resume (I had said windows on my personal laptop and it was ubuntu on college PC) so they started asking some linux commands and more related to that

5. Since my primary language was python they asked few questions based on that like types of exception handling in python and revolved around that more

6. Then they gave me a usecase kinda question like suppose there would be finger scanner for storing many peoples data what all would be your approaches. This was kind of an open ended question they wanted to see my how i would approach it (Here i would say ask whatever question you can possibly ask, coz more than the answer they want to see what you think so i asked what kind of data will be stored they said 0s and 1s i instantly started thinking in terms of FOSIP though i couldnt think much but mentioned few of the things that i could remember like grayscaling image optimization, thresholding and RLE and as i kept answering i even asked do we need to even process on the storage part for that they said you may so i mentioned a bit about the server and load balancing since they had said millions of data will be there and so on to retrieve as and when needed so but this a gist there was a detailed conversation on this) There were few more questions but were based on fundamentals and were answerable and in the ending asked the same question as before.

4. HR [ 9 students]

This round for me was only for around 20 mins since it was getting really late they had to finish it and take another round online but for starting 3 or 2 people they took it for almost 1 hr.

Unlike other rounds this wasnt that restrictive it was pretty much chill and the HR was also kind and friendly She started by asking me to introduce myself without any tech aspect and anything which is not there in my resume (So here i would say try speaking something which would be cool and might impress them so i spoke about my part in my schools kho kho team and about my bharatnatyam career) Then asked Various questions like

1. Being a women if your idea didnt reach the higher management what would you do

2. Have you ever reached a meltingPoint, if yes then how did you deal with it

3. Why did you take CSE-AIML

4. A policy that you would want to be made compulsory by the company for all the women working

5. In 5 or 10 years where do you see yourself There were few more women based situationship based question (try being as diplomatic as you can)

4. Technical [ 9 students]

So they decided to take another round online and this was again pretty much chill Questions included are:

1. Introduce yourself

2. Why havent you done an internship

3. Was asked to explain one of my PowerBI project

4. Then asked where was each of the techs mentioned was used in the 3 of the projects that was there in my resume

5. Was all the mentioned fundamentals a part of your curriculum and if not which all

6. Timeline of my mentioned projects Again it ended with me asking a question but since mine was AI related i had no idea if it would be appropriate to ask since it happened so fast like right after my HR it was suddenly said there would be an online interview and i would be the 1st one to be interviewed, i forgot to ask what kind of interview this was gonna be or was the interviewer HR or what , so here i first asked what exactly was his role and then after understanding he was also from a tech background i put my question forward

One thing i would advice is before asking your question first think properly if it is a proper question for your interviewer it would be kind of weird moment for you if he/she wont be able to answer.

8 students got accepted and this result was announced next day

journey.prep:
1. My first interview was for an SDE role at WorkIndia. I cleared all rounds and interviews, making no mistakes from my side, answering all questions, and solving all the given DSA questions in an optimized way, yet I was still not selected for the HR round. The thing I learned is that placement remains a game of luck given that you have all the skills.

2. Tailor your resume according to the job description of the company, and make sure to include all the skills and projects relevant to the role you're applying for. Check for grammatical errors, as they can instantly create a bad impression. Also, check your ATS score online (websites like Enhancv and Resume Worded can help). Most importantly, never fake information in your resume, if you're caught, it leaves a lasting negative impression. Be true and genuine.

3. Always attend the PPT, as information such as the company's values or history shared during it is often asked in the HR round.

4. If you have consistently worked hard for your placements from the start, then even with some hard luck, you will eventually end up with a good placement. Just don't give up, keep trying and believe in the work you've put in so far.

5. I have always loved participating in hackathons, and I would highly recommend you take part in such coding competitions to continuously learn and grow your skills. You can read my post about my hackathon experiences here - link.

6. Focus on basic concepts, practice DSA regularly, as it requires consistency. Revise DBMS theory and SQL questions (especially the Top 50 SQL questions from LeetCode), review OS and CN, and try to learn Java, as it is required by many companies.

7. Whenever you learn new skills, make sure to first understand the basics and build a strong foundation. For example, if you're interested in machine learning, start with linear algebra and statistics, and try to understand each algorithm mathematically, you'll enjoy it even more.

8. Try to make open-source contributions and participate in events like Hacktoberfest, GSoC, etc. For that, your skills are your weapon, build strong foundations in whatever you are learning, and then collaborate with other developers online to expand your connections.

Feel free to reach out in case of any queries : GitHub, LinkedIn

A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round 1 Tech Interview Round 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day 5th Aug. The CGPA Criteria was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was further reduced to 7.5. The Pre-Placement Talk was conducted online on 4th Aug.

1. Online Assessment Round:

The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. The marking scheme awarded +1 for each correct answer and imposed a -0.25 penalty for incorrect ones. The test was divided into four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude. Personally, I found the Aptitude section to be the most time-consuming. Unfortunately, I had less time left for it since I spent most of my time working through the first three sections.

2. Technical Round 1: [44 student appeared]

I was the first candidate to be interviewed in my panel, and my interview took place from 1:15 - 2:05 PM.

It began with my introduction, followed by an in-depth discussion about my resume. The questions covered my education, professional experience (internship), projects, and my interest in hackathons. The interviewer was polite and seemed genuinely interested in my projects and my Data Science degree from IIT Madras. This part lasted about 15-20 minutes.

Next came the coding round. I was given a database schema and asked three SQL questions based on it. The first two questions were easy, similar to this question: Average Selling Price, while the third was of medium difficulty similar to this question: Monthly Transactions 1. The topics included aggregate functions, joins, and subqueries. I'd recommend practicing the "Top 50 SQL Questions" from LeetCode for such rounds.

After that, the Data Science/Python coding round began. The interviewer provided a CSV file and asked me to use any notebook platform (Google Colab, Kaggle, or Jupyter Notebook). The questions were based on Pandas and NumPy, and I was asked to:

1. Comment on the data quality (e.g., detecting anomalies like invalid syntax in the email column or negative salaries).

2. Suggest how to remove or replace such data.

Go through this link to practice such questions: link

Towards the end, the interviewer asked how I would travel if I got the opportunity and also inquired about my family background.

I was able to answer all the questions confidently, explaining each concept in detail. Since I hadn't faked anything in my resume, discussing my projects and experiences in depth felt natural and rewarding.

3. HR Round: [15 students appeared]

Since I was the first to be interviewed in my panel, I had to wait quite a while for the results. My HR round selection was announced only around 6:00 PM, which meant there were about four long, uneventful hours in between. That wait honestly felt like the most boring part of the day.

In both my technical and HR rounds, the interviewers showed a lot of interest in my Data Science degree from IIT Madras. The HR round itself was a classic one, focused more on understanding me as a person, my aspirations, and how I saw my future with the company. Some of the questions included:

● What are your future growth plans?

● Do you plan to pursue higher studies?

● Where do you see yourself in the next few years?

The tone was conversational, and the interviewer seemed genuinely curious about my career direction and motivations. It was less about testing technical knowledge and more about seeing whether I would be a good cultural and long-term fit for the organization.

------- Lastly, 12 students were selected out of 15, including me. 2 for Data quality, 2 for software testing, 8 for Software Engineering.

Most importantly, never fake information in your resume, if you're caught, it leaves a lasting negative impression. Be true and genuine.

3. Always attend the PPT, as information such as the company's values or history shared during it is often asked in the HR round.

4. If you have consistently worked hard for your placements from the start, then even with some hard luck, you will eventually end up with a good placement. Just don't give up, keep trying and believe in the work you've put in so far.

5. I have always loved participating in hackathons, and I would highly recommend you take part in such coding competitions to continuously learn and grow your skills. You can read my post about my hackathon experiences here - link.

6. Focus on basic concepts, practice DSA regularly, as it requires consistency. Revise DBMS theory and SQL questions (especially the Top 50 SQL questions from LeetCode), review OS and CN, and try to learn Java, as it is required by many companies.

7. Whenever you learn new skills, make sure to first understand the basics and build a strong foundation. For example, if you're interested in machine learning, start with linear algebra and statistics, and try to understand each algorithm mathematically, you'll enjoy it even more.

8. Try to make open-source contributions and participate in events like Hacktoberfest, GSoC, etc. For that, your skills are your weapon, build strong foundations in whatever you are learning, and then collaborate with other developers online to expand your connections.

1. Online Assessment [219 candidates appeared for this round]

4 coding questions were to be solved in 90 minutes.

Problem 1 You are given n people, labeled from 1 to n (<=1e5). There are m existing friendships represented by two arrays A and B, each of size m, where the i-th friendship is between person A[i] and person B[i]. Two people are considered friends if there is a direct or indirect connection between them (i.e., if they belong to the same connected group of friends). Your task is to determine the minimum number of new friendships that must be formed so that every person is connected directly or indirectly--in other words, so that everyone belongs to a single connected group. Approach: I figured it is a connected components problem, I had 3 options - dsu, dfs and bfs. I went with dfs as it was quicker to implement, the answer was the number of connected components - 1. I passed all test cases.

Problem 2 You are given n (<=1e4) employees, some already have been assigned ladoos and some aren't, you need to assign ladoos to the second type of employees such that the difference between ladoos assigned to adjacent employees doesn't exceed k (<=30 i believe) and the maximum number of ladoos any employee has is m (<=200). You need to return the number of valid ways to assign ladoos. Approach: I initially thought this was a greedy/math problem but the ambiguous case of adjacent employees with 0 ladoos led me to think it is a dp problem, also n*m being close to 1e6 assured me that it was. I applied backtracking and memoized it. My state was memo[i][prev] which is the amount of ways I can assign ladoos to employees from [i,n-1] with the value of the last employee's assignment being prev. The tricky part was to decide the lower and upper limit of how many ladoos to assign to the ith employee. I took it from max(1,prev-k) to min(m,prev+k). I could solve 11/13 test cases with this approach with a few hidden cases not budging even after optimizations.

Problem 3 You are given an integer n (<=1e3), an integer k, and an array arr of size n consisting of integers. For each element arr[i], you can find its value using the following operation: convert it to its binary representation and define its value as: Sum of (bit × position) where position is 1-based from right in the binary representation. You need to find the number of pairs (i, j) such that: value(arr[i]) + value(arr[j]) == k.

Approach: Due to the low constraints I didn't think much and applied 2 nested loops. I checked each pair using a lambda function for the condition mentioned by iterating bitwise over the numbers and incremented the response. I passed all test cases.

Problem 4 You are given:

- Four houses from Harry Potter: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, and Slytherin

- Two integers: n: number of students m: maximum number of students allowed in each house

- A list of friendships: pairs of integers (a, b) where student a and student b are friends and must be placed in different houses

- A list of strings, where the i-th string contains the allowed houses for the i-th student (e.g., "[["pref1, pref2"], [pref2]]" you had to parse the string and split them accordingly and store their preferences)

Your task is to determine if it is possible to assign every student to exactly one of their preferred houses such that:

1. No pair of friends is placed in the same house

2. No house has more than m students

3. Each student is assigned to one of their preferred houses

Print "possible" if such an assignment exists, otherwise "impossible" Approach: The question did not specify the number of friendships and the size of the list of strings, we were supposed to take the input as a stream. Since I didn't practice this type of input parsing, I couldn't solve this question. But since the input was small it could've been solved using backtracking i suppose.

Round 1 Summary: I could solve almost 3/4 questions and it was good enough to get me to the next round. My advice would be to not waste time on a question if it doesn't click, solve others and come back later. I solved 1->3->2 and due to increased confidence after solving 3, I could think of 2 without any pressure.

2. Technical Round - 1 [30 candidates appeared for this round] This round consisted of 2 coding questions which we were supposed to explain and code on pen paper. The interviewer asked for a brief introduction and then introduced himself before moving to the coding problems

Problem 1 Given an array of n (<=1e5) integers lying in the range [-1e9,1e9], return the maximum sum of a subarray that starts and ends with the same number. I could immediately think of hashing the minimum prefix sum of each unique number in that array to that number, when I encounter another instance of that number I could subtract the current prefix sum with the minimum prefix sum hashed to that number to get the max total sum of the subarray. Then I updated the map using the current prefix and continued. Finally I coded the solution for my approach. The interviewer was satisfied with my answer and asked the time complexity which was O(n).

Problem 2 Given a parents array of size n (<=1e6) which represents a binary tree and q (<=1e6) queries where queries[i]={node,value}, For each query, the task was to find the maximum XOR between the given value and any of the node values along the path from the root to the specified node, I initially gave a brute force dfs solution which ran in n*q, the interviewer asked me to optimize it and since values differed from query to query memoization wouldn't work. I thought for some time and then the interviewer hinted at using a trie data structure for storing nodes, I mentioned it had been a long time since I used it for solving problems and still attempted it, with a few more hints I could reach the solution. I needed to dynamically

create the trie and for each leaf node(in the trie) I could solve the queries that comprised of the tree node it represents. Since the query value is at max 1e6, its bitwise representation comprises 17-18 bits, making that the height of my trie. The interviewer then asked for the time complexity, which was O(17*17*n).

At the end he asked me whether I had any doubts and I asked about the async nature of PhonePe's systems and how a payment inconsistency is resolved which he explained stating that they constantly poll the NPCI servers for a response after a payment request has been initiated.

3. Technical Round - 2 [14 candidates appeared for this round]

This round had the same format as technical-1.

Problem 1 Given a matrix of size m*n (m*n<=1e6), each element had a heat value which I gained if I landed on it, I had to return the minimum heat with which I could reach {m-1,n-1} from {0,0} under the following constraints:

1. I could move left, right, bottom or top.

2. I could not retrace my path at any point.

3. I couldn't move the same direction more than 3 times. I mentioned that this seemed like a dijkstra problem to which the interviewer agreed, I considered the state of my heap as: {heat,x,y,prev,count} where {x,y} are the coordinates of the point that I landed on, heat is the accumulated heat, prev is the last move and count is a counter for move repetition. I maintained a matrix h[][] for storing minimum heat of each position and coded the solution. I mentioned that I could reduce my coordinates from 2 to 1 and compress the matrix h, but I went with this for simplicity. The interviewer agreed with my solution and asked a follow up question. He stated that if there was a minimum limit for moving in one direction before changing direction(say k) how would I adapt my solution. I stated that I could move k distance to the right and bottom of {0,0} and push those as the starting points to neglect minimum criteria to which he agreed.

Problem 2 Given 2 arrays cost and time each of size n where cost[i] and time[i] represent the cost of the ith painting and time required to paint it respectively by a paid painter. There was also a magic painter who could paint for free and painted 1 painting per unit time. But the magic painter could only work when the paid painter was busy. I had to return the minimum cost to paint all n paintings. I mentioned that there was a tradeoff between 1)choosing the cheapest painting c for the paid painter and for time t[c] the magic painter could paint t[c] expensive ones, and 2)choosing the most time consuming painting for the paid painter so that magic painter could paint more. I stated that in such a problem I had to consider all paths and hence it is a dp problem to which he agreed. I asked for a minute to think and came up with a state dp[i][rem] which is the minimum cost to paint [i,n-1] paintings where rem is the remaining paintings from [0,i-1]. There are essentially two options, use the paid painter and move to dp[i+1][max(0,rem-t[i])] or don't and move to dp[i+1][rem+1], at the base case check if rem is 0. He agreed and I coded out the solution.

In both of these rounds I made sure to communicate my thought process with the interviewer which is essential for them to understand how you approach a problem.

4. HM - Round [11 candidates appeared for this round] My HM interview was taken by the Engineering Manager at PhonePe. He started off by asking for my introduction and then started questioning me based on my resume. He asked about my internship experience

and what I learnt from it. I answered with an emphasis on the exposure I received to a real world codebase and system, and the design/devops concepts I could implement during it. He asked about the most difficult project, what made it difficult and how would I reapproach it if i could start over. He went on to ask similar behavioural questions regarding my projects and experiences. He then asked me about how I would design instagram stories to which I responded with a rank based algorithm where I'd assign points to each story according to the interaction with that user and give them a rank, I mentioned I'll use a map data structure to hash a pair of {rank,userId} to the array of urls of the photo/video content in the story and then cache stories using redis, or use a cdn. He then asked me about my most recent project and how much help did I take from llms in it to which I honestly replied stating that I used it for the ui of screens which I had a hard time figuring out, and also for debugging code. At the end he asked me if I had questions, I mentioned that in the PPT it was stated that there's a flat hierarchy structure at PhonePe, and I asked what it meant. He explained the hierarchy structure in depth. I also asked about the sports culture at PhonePe which he happily explained. The round went well overall and he wished me luck at the end. The key is to brush up your system design knowledge, both in general and PhonePe in specific, and be honest and expressive with your answers.

BlackRock shortlisted candidates for four different roles based on the online assessment and the preferences we had selected. The roles were: Aladdin Data (5 shortlisted + 1 waitlisted), Global Marketing (3 shortlisted + 3 waitlisted), Software Engineer (15 shortlisted + 3 waitlisted), and Software Engineer AWT (3 shortlisted + 1 waitlisted), making a total of 34 candidates including waitlists. I was shortlisted for the Software Engineer role, and I will be explaining my experience for this role further.

2. Technical Round 1 [18 candidates shortlisted]

My first technical round was conducted on the Webex platform and was scheduled at 12:00 PM. Since it had to be attended from the TPO office (on campus), I reached beforehand to ensure everything was set. Interestingly, my panel was moving faster than expected, and I was called in at around 11:30 AM, slightly ahead of time. When I joined, there were already two panelists present in the session.

The interview began with the usual greetings and the request to switch on my camera. Soon after, the panel directly moved into DSA-based questions.

The first problem given to me was:

Sort n elements (assume 100) in O(n) time complexity.

At first, I was taken aback because the sorting techniques I was confident with, such as Merge Sort and Quick Sort, typically work in O(n log n) time. I mentioned this to the panel, but they clarified that they were looking specifically for an O(n) solution. After taking a few minutes to think, I demonstrated the sorting of three elements in O(n) time using simple swapping. The interviewers seemed satisfied with my attempt, and they later explained that this problem could be efficiently solved using Cyclic Sort. I pointed out that this might increase the space complexity, but they assured me that it was acceptable. This exchange highlighted an important takeaway:

If you don't know the exact answer, keep communicating and explaining your thought process. Interviewers value your problem-solving approach as much as, or even more than, the final solution.

The next question was a classic 3-Sum Problem. I began with the brute-force approach, then optimized it by explaining the two-pointer technique. While presenting, I carefully analyzed and conveyed the time complexity of each approach. The panel seemed pleased with my structured explanation and progression from brute force to optimal.

After this, I was asked about my preferred programming language. I responded that I primarily use Java for problem-solving and Python for development. One of the interviewers, who was an expert in Java, proceeded to ask me several Java-related questions. These covered concepts from OOPs, threads, and exception handling. Since I had prepared well in these areas, I was able to answer confidently, and the panel appeared satisfied with my responses.

Finally, the round concluded with a puzzle question -- the famous 4 Litres Bucket Problem (reference link). I asked for some time to think and gradually explained my thought process while attempting different possibilities. Although I got stuck briefly, I managed to work through the problem and eventually reached the solution. The interviewers appreciated my persistence and logical reasoning throughout.

Towards the end, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I asked a couple of role- and company- related questions, which I believe is always a good practice as it demonstrates genuine interest in the company and the position.

3. Technical Round 2 [8 candidates shortlisted]

My second technical round lasted for about 40-50 minutes. It began with a polite exchange of greetings and a brief introduction from both sides, which helped create a comfortable environment. Unlike the first round, this interview was entirely based on my resume (resume_link) and my past experiences.

The interviewer first asked about the SCOPE program at JPMC that I had mentioned in my resume. I explained what the program was about, my role in it, and the key learnings I gained from the experience. She then shifted the focus to my internship, asking in-depth questions to understand my contributions and learnings better. During this discussion, she also asked whether I was comfortable working with Git and GitHub, which I confidently confirmed.

Next, she moved on to the projects listed in my resume. I described two of my projects in detail, focusing on their features, the technologies used, and the real-world problems they aimed to solve. Since one of my projects was from Smart India Hackathon (SIH), where I had emerged as a winner, it particularly caught her attention. She found it inspiring and appreciated how the project had a practical impact on real-world challenges. Her feedback was very encouraging, as she praised my problem-solving mindset and the relevance of my work.

Towards the end, she asked if I had any questions for her. I took the opportunity to ask two:

1. How BlackRock has contributed to her personal and professional growth.

2. How BlackRock is adapting to GenAI and AI/ML modules in its work environment.

She responded warmly, providing detailed and insightful answers to both questions, which gave me a deeper understanding of BlackRock's culture and vision. The interview concluded on a positive note with final greetings.

A small but important takeaway from this round is to always carry a smile and maintain a confident, positive demeanor throughout the interaction -- it goes a long way in leaving a lasting impression.

4. HR Round (Prank Round) [9 candidates shortlisted]

The next stage was supposed to be the HR round, but due to some unfortunate circumstances, BlackRock decided to terminate the process midway. However, our TPO was in constant discussion with them, trying to request and resolve the situation. As a result, instead of a formal HR interview, we had a small, unofficial one-on-one interaction with Sikka Sir, who offered valuable guidance and reassurance.

Later, the final results were announced by Sir himself in the conference room, where he also shared some inspiring words with us. In the end, 6 students were shortlisted for the Software Engineer role, and 3 were placed on the waitlist.

1. Online Assessment Round [100 + candidates appeared]

During the placement process, one of the key eligibility criteria was maintaining a CGPA of 7.5 or above. This benchmark served as the initial shortlisting factor and emphasized the importance of consistent academic performance. Apart from academics, the resume played a vital role in getting shortlisted. Having a properly formatted resume -- preferably in Jake's template style -- added a professional touch. What mattered more, however, was the project section of the resume. A strong resume required at least one major project with unique features that stood out from the rest, supported by a couple of smaller personal projects that showcased fundamental skills and hands-on experience. The project descriptions had to be written in bullet points, focusing on the specific features, outcomes, and technologies used. I also realized the importance of arranging projects in an order where the most impactful or "sellable" project was listed first, as it immediately captured the recruiter's attention.

The online assessment test was conducted on the eLitmus platform and was fully proctored. Since this was BlackRock's first visit to our campus, there were no prior student experiences to rely on. To prepare effectively, I searched extensively on the web for insights into the test pattern and previous questions. Fortunately, the test format I came across online turned out to be largely consistent with the one that was actually conducted. The test duration was 1.5 hours, and it was divided into three major sections: Aptitude, Programming, and SQL.

1. Aptitude Section The aptitude section was divided into three subsections -- Quantitative Aptitude, Data Checking/Data Accuracy, and Logical Reasoning.

o The Quantitative Aptitude questions revolved around standard topics such as arithmetic, percentages, ratios, and number systems, requiring both accuracy and speed.

o The Data Checking/Data Accuracy part was relatively straightforward and easy to solve. It primarily tested one's ability to identify inconsistencies or errors within datasets quickly.

o The Logical Reasoning subsection was interesting, involving questions on pattern recognition, sequences, and puzzles. The key here was to attempt as many questions as possible without spending too much time on a single problem. Proper time management was crucial in maximizing the score in this section.

Imp Links (Aptitude): IndiaBix, CodeHelp

2. Programming Section The programming part was unique compared to typical coding assessments, as it was split into two subsections: Flowcharts and Pseudocodes.

o In the Flowchart subsection, two flowcharts based on basic programming problems were provided. Each flowchart contained around 5-6 blanks that we had to fill in. The questions were objective (MCQ-based), where the correct option had to be chosen for each blank. One of the flowcharts was related to a string-matching algorithm, while the other was relatively simple and could be solved with a clear understanding of flow control.

o The Pseudocode subsection contained three MCQs based on different algorithms and data structures. Two of them were focused on Binary Trees/BSTs (covering fundamental operations like insertion, deletion, traversal, and calculating depth). The third question was based on AVL trees, specifically testing knowledge of rotateLeft and rotateRight operations (LL, LR, RL, RR). Since I had prepared these topics in advance, I was able to approach this section with confidence and accuracy.

3. SQL Section The final section of the test comprised 20 MCQs on Oracle SQL, which were mostly theoretical in nature. Compared to the earlier sections, this one was less time-consuming, as the time allotted was more than sufficient to go through all the questions. My preparation strategy for SQL involved practicing extensively on LeetCode's SQL50 problems, which helped me gain familiarity with various query patterns and functions. Although I had prepared using MySQL, I noticed that Oracle SQL had slight syntactical differences. In cases where I was unsure, I relied on logical reasoning and intuition to select the best possible answer.

Imp Links (Technical + SQL) : Topic wise, one-shot mcqs on GFG, Leetcode50 (Sql)

Overall, the test was balanced and well-structured, checking a candidate's aptitude, algorithmic thinking, and database knowledge. My preparation strategy -- focusing on aptitude basics, binary/AVL trees, flowcharts, and SQL practice -- played a significant role in boosting my confidence and helping me attempt the test effectively.

Tip : When attempting the test, it is advisable to start with the section you are most confident in. Prioritizing technical MCQs and SQL questions can be beneficial, as securing accuracy in these areas helps maximize your score. If aptitude is not your strong suit, it is better to attempt that section at the end. This approach ensures that you focus first on questions where you are more likely to score, while managing time effectively across all sections.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Don't lose confidence even if you face multiple rejections. I interviewed in 8 companies before BlackRock, and though I often felt demotivated, I eventually realized that things fall into place at the right time.

• Even if you feel others less deserving are getting placed, remember that your journey is unique. I had won multiple hackathons but wasn't placed initially -- yet I ended up in a top MNC like BlackRock, which I never even dreamed of.

• Stay confident and keep a smile throughout your interview. It creates a positive impression and shows your enthusiasm.

• Always interact with the interviewers. Don't stay quiet -- even if you don't know the exact answer, explain your thought process. Many times, they are more interested in how you approach the problem rather than just the final solution.

• Practice explaining your projects clearly in bullet points (features, technologies, and real -world impact). This not only shows clarity but also highlights your problem -solving ability.

• Know your resume inside out. HR and technical rounds can both heavily focus on what you've mentioned, so be prepared to discuss every detail confidently.

• Prepare both technical and behavioral aspects. While DSA and technical knowledge are crucial, soft skills, communication, and genuine interest in the company matter equally.

• Ask questions at the end. Always have 2-3 role- or company-related questions ready. This shows curiosity and genuine interest in the company.

• Be consistent in preparation. Whether it's aptitude, SQL, or programming, practicing regularly (LeetCode, mock tests, etc.) makes a big difference.

• Network smartly. Connect with seniors, peers, or professionals on LinkedIn to get insights into the process. Sometimes even small tips can give you an edge.

• And most importantly, trust the process. If one door closes, another one will open with an even better opportunity.

If you have any further doubts, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn :)
