1. Open Assessment (Sept 15, 2025)

2. Technical Interview - 1 (Oct 8, 2025)

3. Technical Interview - 2 (Oct 8, 2025)

4. HR Interview (Oct 8, 2025)

Note: The OA was common for both the Associate Consultant and Application Developer roles. Although I was not shortlisted for the Application Dev role after the assessment, I was later shortlisted for the Associate Consultant role based on the same OA performance.

1. Open Assessment [Eligibility criteria: 7 CGPA, with no current backlogs]

The OA was conducted on HackerRank, consisted of questions from the following:

● Data Structures & Algorithms (2 questions, everyone had different questions):

1. Based on Arrays - Easy difficulty

2. Based on Trees - Moderate difficulty

● Computer Science Fundamentals:

1. Computer Networks

2. Operating Systems

3. SQL (Joins, Aggregate functions, constraints)

● Aptitude & Reasoning:

1. Logical reasoning and probability based quantitative aptitude

2. Analytical puzzles

2. Technical Interview - 1 [27 students were shortlisted for this round]

The interview began with a brief self-introduction. I kept my response concise, summarizing what I have learned over the course of my studies, and highlighting my interest in Machine Learning. I also mentioned that Python is my primary programming language, while I'm comfortable with Java and SQL as well. I concluded with a short note on my long-term goals and hobbies.

The interviewer then moved on to discuss my projects. She began with my major project. I explained the idea behind it and what my specific contributions were. Next, she asked me about another project, which was an open-access platform for managing and exploring research papers. I described its main features and briefly outlined my role in developing its core functionalities.

After that, she reviewed the technical skills listed on my resume and asked several follow-up questions. When asked about my preferred programming language, I mentioned Python. She then asked why not Java, to which I explained that Python's simplicity, extensive libraries, and faster prototyping capabilities make it ideal for research or machine learning related tasks, which align more closely with my interests. When asked why many companies still prefer Java, I replied that Java offers better performance in large-scale enterprise systems, strong type safety, and a good support for multithreading and scalability.

She later asked some questions related to database design, including schemas and access controls along with some SQL functions. She then asked about the use of JavaScript - I explained that it is primarily used for adding interactivity to web pages and is essential for front-end development, especially when working with frameworks like React

She noticed I had mentioned Android SDK in my resume and asked whether I had built any Android apps. I mentioned that I had developed one as a mini-project during my second year in Java (though not listed in my resume) and asked me several related questions.

We also discussed the scalability differences between SQL and NoSQL databases, after which she moved on to Git and version control systems. I explained concepts like repositories, commits, branching, merging, and pull requests, and described how multiple developers collaborate using Git. I also shared a basic diagram to illustrate the workflow and mentioned common Git commands used for these operations.

The interviewer then moved to Data Structures, asking how linked lists work and their real-life applications. I answered honestly when I could not recall specific applications. I was then asked to write a function to calculate the first n Fibonacci numbers, which I implemented.

Next, she asked a few Linux command questions, which were fairly straightforward. She then asked about Tableau since I had listed it under my skills. When asked why Tableau and not Power BI, I responded that Tableau provides a more intuitive interface, faster data blending, and better integration with Python for analytics, making it a preferred choice for exploratory data analysis.

Finally, she asked a few questions about my certifications, which I had completed. When I was asked why I didn't have any formal internship experience, I explained that I didn't find opportunities that aligned with my interests at the time. Instead, I focused on personal and academic projects, which helped me apply my learning effectively.

3. Technical Interview - 2 [~20 students were shortlisted for this round]

This interview skipped the introductory "Tell me about yourself" and started directly with my projects. He began with my major project, asking me to explain it in detail again, and then moved on to some other project. He probed further into how I managed certain functionalities, how I implemented specific features, and posed hypothetical scenarios such as "If you were to implement X, how would you do it?". He also inquired whether the project was hosted, to which I replied, it was not, and asked a few other technical details. Overall, the focus was on being thorough and precise about my projects.

The discussion then shifted to SQL, where I was asked to write a query involving aggregate functions and GROUP BY. He also asked several Python-related questions, including the use of inbuilt functions, and explored my understanding of the language in detail.

He further revisited my technical skills listed on the resume, asking clarifying and in-depth questions. While he maintained a serious and formal demeanor, I remained calm and answered to the best of my ability.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Note: Both of these interviews lasted for around 45-50 minutes and were manageable as long as you remain calm, honest, and well-versed with every little detail mentioned in your resume, as the interviewer may ask in-depth questions based on your listed skills, projects, and certifications. I have attempted to include all the questions I was asked, although I may have missed a few, this experience reflects the overall structure and focus of the interviews.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

4. HR Interview [12 students were shortlisted for this round]

The HR interview was short, lasting around 5 minutes. It started with some basic questions, first confirming my nationality, followed by queries about the role being offered and the compensation details. She then asked if I would be comfortable relocating to any of the mentioned work locations, to which I replied yes.

Next, she inquired if I was planning to pursue higher studies, to which I replied no. When asked why, I mentioned that I didn't have any such plans in the near future, but might consider it a few years down the line if I ever decide to. The conversation then moved to whether I had any current offers or PPOs from other companies; I said no, and when asked if I had appeared for other interviews, I told her this was my first interview ever.

Overall, the round was relaxed and conversational, and all candidates who reached this stage were offered the position.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Personal Insights:

I was rejected in most of my earlier open assessments, and even when I cleared some, I was eliminated during group discussion rounds. I had been studying on and off for placements since they began in the month of July and by the end of September, I was honestly burnt out, mainly because I wasn't seeing any results despite putting in consistent effort and not getting shortlisted for interviews. Still, I kept reminding myself to stay patient and keep improving, and finally received this offer in the second week of October,

after nearly three months. I also started my placement preparation quite late compared to many peers (which in hindsight was a bad idea), but this made me realize that placement success isn't just about hard work, there's also a fair bit of timing and luck involved. What matters is staying consistent, realistic, and open to learning. Even if things don't work out right away, every attempt adds experience and clarity, and eventually, your effort finds its result.

Lastly, I had a CGPA of 7.66, which made me eligible for almost all companies, except maybe one (Zeta which had a requirement of 8+). Based on my experience, it's recommended to maintain at least a 7.5 CGPA, as that tends to be the minimum eligibility criterion for most companies during campus placements.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Areas of Improvement:

Looking back at the entire placement process, there are a few areas I believe I could have improved on:

1. Early and consistent preparation: I started my placement preparation quite late, which added unnecessary pressure toward the end

2. Confidence and composure: Showing structured thinking and confidence in your answers makes a big difference in how the interviewer perceives you, even if you don't get every answer right. It's important to remember that interviewers generally want you to succeed and are looking for how you approach problems, not just whether you know the exact answer.

Overall, this experience helped me identify where I stood technically and learned a lot about what to focus on moving forward.

journey.prep:
● Get used to rejections. Don't give up. During the entire placement season, I was very sick (even hospitalized before it began), had severe side effects that caused excruciating joint pains, and still had to travel 1 hour daily for online assessments and interviews. I faced rejections in interviews from PhonePe, Barclays, Nomura, and in the HR round of MSCI. Even during the ISS process I was not well. But I kept pushing myself -- just a little more every time.

● Stay connected to your friends. They help more than you can imagine -- conduct mock interviews, build projects together, prepare in groups. It really helps in keeping the momentum and staying motivated.

● Know all your projects well. I've often heard people say, "It was a group project, and I didn't work on that part." Personally, I'd strongly recommend not saying that. You usually have 3-4 projects on your resume, and you're expected to know all of them thoroughly.

● Some common resume/project questions:

○ Why this project?

○ Why this tech stack? (know as much as you can about that technology)

○ Alternatives to the technologies used?

○ Your exact role?

○ What did you learn?

○ What are the drawbacks?

○ What can be improved?

○ Can it scale? How is the architecture?

● While answering, never talk negatively about alternatives. Instead, explain why your chosen approach suits your project best.

● Avoid saying I don't know unless you have zero idea about the question.

● Don't restrict your thoughts completely, convey them to the interviewer and clarify doubts. During some interviews out of nervousness I didn't say a few things which potentially could have been answers which I regretted; avoid it.

● Don't be fooled by simplicity. After reading such experiences, you might feel that questions are easy/basic. That's a myth. Many people get easy panels or familiar questions. But rejections happen due to several other reasons -- timing, panel, tricky questions, or just not being the right fit. It's not always about luck or coincidence either -- some part of it is, but you should try to be as prepared as possible. Sometimes, when the panel has too many shortlisted candidates, they go tough. And if you answer those tough questions, you automatically stand out. The questions aren't impossible -- they're just a little tricky and layered.

● Never lose your calm. Always smile. Communication plays a huge role. Your presence, gestures, tone -- all matter. Highlight key words during your answers to guide the interviewer and keep the flow in your control.

● Read the Job Description. Align your strengths and weaknesses with the company's values and goals.

● Avoid last-minute prep. Don't rely on learning or reading something right before the interview.

● Have basic knowledge of System design not all companies ask them but phonepe, MSCI, Zeta, etc does.

● Prepare for a few HR questions beforehand.

Resources:

● Java and OOPs (refer at least the oops part): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL9gnSGHSqcnr_DxHsP7AW9ftq0AtAyYqJ

● Dbms: Complete DBMS in 1 Video (With Notes) || For Placement Interviews

● OS (Multithreading should be enough): Complete Operating Systems in 1 Shot (With Notes) || For Placement Interviews

● Indiabix for aptitude

● Sql top 50

● Striver Sheet for dsa is more than enough (unless you are appearing for phonepe).

Feel free to connect on LinkedIn.

All the very best!!! 😀
journey.howSecured:
A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round & Finally 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day 5th Aug. The CGPA Criteria for SDE was 8.5, later reduced to

8. It was further reduced to 7.5. May not be the case for next year if they don't want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above. We were supposed to enter 2 preferences and mostly all of them were selected for their 1st preference. Some were asked personally whether they would like to sit for their interviews for the 2nd preference. So choose your preferences wisely.

1. Resume based shortlisting

My resume The first round was a resume-based shortlisting. While the exact criteria were not disclosed, CGPA likely played a role. Here are some key points based on my experience:

● Mention only those skills in your resume that you are genuinely confident and comfortable with. Including too many skills can lead to complex and unexpected questions during the interview if not fully prepared.

● Try to have at least one solid project. If the project is unique it's awesome but irrespective of if it is or not, focus on scalability and optimizations techniques.

● Ensure that all links in your resume are valid and clickable. Interviewers do check them. Also, make sure your projects have a proper README to give a quick overview of the project.

● Making your resume quantifiable using metrics or measurable impact is a good practice, though it is not strictly necessary.

● Try to align your resume with the job description or your selected preference. In our case, we were asked to choose two preferences (i chose SDE and Data Quality). Fortunately I was selected for the SDE role otherwise my resume didn't have any data science projects.. But that might not always be the case so make your resume smartly.

● Even if a company lists many technologies in the JD, you don't need to include all of them in your resume--focus on those that match your strengths and the role you're aiming for.

2. Preplacement talk

Although the process was initially planned to be offline, it was later conducted online at 5 PM on 4th August.

Pay close attention to the PPT. Note down the names and roles of the presenters--it helps during interactions. It's also a good idea to do some basic research on the company beforehand, like the founding year, CEO, and tagline, as such questions can be asked and showing awareness leaves a good impression.

You may ask thoughtful questions at the end of the PPT session to show engagement, though it's not mandatory. Alternatively, you can save your questions for the post-interview phase if that feels more comfortable.

3. Online Assessment [Around 160 candidates]

This round was held around 9:30 AM. It consisted of 70 questions in 90 minutes, conducted via Google Forms at the college premises under the supervision of company professionals. The marking scheme was +1 for correct answers and -0.25 for incorrect ones. Only desktop calculators were allowed.

The test was divided into four sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude.

The Java section had easy to medium-level questions, mainly covering OOPs, collections, multithreading exception handling, enums, etc. Most questions involved code snippets where we had to predict the output. Although my primary language was C++, I had to prepare the Java Collections Framework separately. Previous years, topics like streams, generics, concurrenthashmap were also included, so it's advisable to prepare Java thoroughly. I remember I had solved 15/18 questions in this section. One or two were flukes.

The Python section included questions on OOPs, MRO (Method Resolution Order), list comprehensions, Counter, stacks, sets, slicing, and similar topics. Understanding the internal workings of Python is important--such as knowing when a copy is created, how mutability affects original data structures, and what happens when using mutable default arguments in functions. These concepts are frequently tested and can be tricky if not well understood.

The SQL section was straightforward. An input and a problem statement were given, and we had to choose the correct option--no actual coding was required. Questions were based on basic concepts like JOINs, WHERE and BETWEEN clauses, and GROUP BY. Preparing fundamental SQL queries is sufficient for this part.

I spent around 30-40 minutes on the Aptitude section after quickly completing the others. It was the toughest part of the assessment, with long and time-consuming questions, mostly based on IndiaBix. I avoided guessing and managed to attempt a fair number confidently. Topics included core areas like profit and loss, interest, speed and distance, permutations, and data interpretation, along with less common ones like banker's discount and stocks.

4. Technical Round 1 [45 students]

I wasn't very confident about my OA performance, but I still began revising key concepts like Java Collections and reviewed my resume. The shortlist was announced at 12:15 PM, and I was delighted to see my name on the list. There were two interviewers in my panel, and they started asking questions simultaneously. The first question was a self-introduction, where I briefly mentioned my name, branch, projects, internship, committee role, and achievements--keeping it concise.

Next, I was asked to explain the four pillars of OOPs. I gave clear explanations with relevant examples. They followed up with questions on common interview topics like the difference between encapsulation and abstraction, and abstract classes vs. interfaces. I was specifically asked about constructors, instantiation, and whether these classes can have methods with their own implementation. Up to this point, I answered confidently. However, I got confused when asked if abstract classes and interfaces can have variables. I recalled that abstract classes can, but wasn't sure about interfaces due to less hands on practice with OOPs. I answered that it's possible but not commonly practiced--something I feel I shouldn't have said, as it didn't make much sense. These small gaps in lesser-practiced topics can create confusion, but the interview moved on smoothly after that.

They then asked if I was comfortable with Java Collections, and the same question was repeated for Python. Saying no directly could have been a red flag, so I answered honestly yet strategically. I mentioned that C++ is my primary language and that I'm very comfortable with DSA in C++ and OOPs in Java. I also said that while I may not have in-depth hands-on experience, I have a good understanding of Java Collections and know the basic concepts well. This seemed to satisfy them.

The interviewers continued with OOPs-related questions and asked about the different types of inheritance. When I mentioned multiple inheritance, they asked whether it's allowed in Java. I explained that it's not supported in the same way as in C++, but it can be achieved through interfaces. That led to a follow-up: why it is designed that way, what the diamond problem is, and how Java solves it.

Next, they asked whether an object can be used as a key in a HashMap. I recognized this question from the online assessment and replied that yes, it's possible. They then asked me to code it. Instead of creating a new example, I intentionally used the same one from the OA. I had been advised to try and control the flow of the interview, and since I had already explored this problem further (including using GPT), I was confident about the follow-up questions.

I used the following structure:

This naturally led to the expected question: what is the size of the map?(because the value is same) I answered correctly--it's 2. The next question was how to make the size 1, even after inserting two objects. My first response was that using String keys with the same value would result in one entry due to string interning, but they asked me to solve it using the Person class itself. I took a moment and recalled that the .equals() method is used to compare keys. I explained that we need to override .equals() to ensure objects with the same attributes are treated as equal. The interviewer seemed happy with this answer. Though the answer should also have included the hashcode() function which I realised after the interview.

After that, the discussion moved to SQL. The questions were mostly basic, such as types of joins and the difference between left and right join. I explained that they are technically the same, and the only thing that changes is the order of the tables. I backed it up with an example, and the interviewer nodded in agreement. I was then asked how to filter results after using GROUP BY, to which I responded with the use of the HAVING clause. They also asked about the order of execution of SQL statements and whether it's possible to update a table using joins. I paused to think and said that while I haven't performed such operations directly, I believe it's possible if the update depends on the output of a join. I added that joins return a new table, so it might be a bit tricky. The interviewer pointed out that updates could depend on another table involved in the join, and that's when I realized the gap in my understanding.

I was also asked the difference between the PUT and POST methods. I gave the correct explanation, but since I hadn't actually used PUT in my projects, I became a bit unsure when asked if I was confident. I stuck to my answer but on questioning I accepted that I hadn't implemented it in any of the projects listed on my resume. In hindsight, if you're confident in your explanation, it's better to respond with certainty.

After this, I was asked to write a program to find the frequency of words in a sentence. I asked for permission to write it in C++, which they allowed. I used maps for storing frequencies and implemented the logic using stringstream. However, after writing the code, I realized I wasn't very clear about how stringstream works, though I still gave a rough explanation of its functionality. One part of the code included the operation map[word]++. The interviewer asked how I was incrementing the value if the word was not already present in the map. I explained that in C++, the default value for an int is 0 when a key is accessed for the first time, so the increment works. Then he asked about the default value for a string, and although I wasn't sure, I responded that I hadn't checked it specifically but assumed it would be null.

He then asked how to store the frequency using words like "one" or "two" instead of numbers. This caught me off guard. I said that it couldn't be done unless we predefined the mapping of numbers to words using another map. He still encouraged me to try, but I got confused. A few seconds later, he told me to leave it and moved on. I think the operation he asked for wasn't actually possible without an additional mapping.

He then asked about exception handling and this part went very smoothly. He gave a scenario with two catch blocks, one handling Exception and the next one IOException, along with a finally block. He asked how the code would behave if there was an exception during file reading. I replied that the code would not compile because the more specific exception, IOException, should come before the more general Exception. He then switched their order and asked again, and I answered correctly. After that, he asked what would happen if

there was a return statement in the try block. I said that the finally block would still execute. He further asked whether the return statement would still return a value, to which I responded yes.

The interview ended with me asking them a question. After coming out, I noticed that my interview had gone on for quite a long time--more than 45 minutes--while others were mostly done within 30 minutes, and some even in just 15-20 minutes. This made me nervous because it could mean many things. I also kept thinking about the few silly mistakes I made during the interview, like being unsure about a few answers as mentioned earlier and I had answered slightly wrong on the sql execution statements. Thankfully, friends came to the rescue again and helped calm me down. I then shifted my focus toward preparing for the HR round by going through common HR questions and the job description.

Tips:

As you might have noticed, my confidence was tested multiple times during the interview, and there were situations where the questions had logical answers, but I wasn't able to respond properly. Be prepared for this kind of pressure. According to a friend, one of my biggest weaknesses is being too honest in interviews--I tend to openly admit when I haven't done something, and I did that multiple times. It's better to avoid this.

Always try to relate your answer to something you know, even if you're not fully sure. Simply saying "I don't know" or "I haven't done this" isn't the best approach. Instead, respond strategically to keep the conversation in your control. Also, to understand your weak points and improve your delivery, I highly recommend doing mock interviews with friends--it really helps.

While explaining concepts, using examples is always the best approach as it makes your understanding clearer and more practical. While coding, speak out your thought process and approach unless you're specifically asked not to. This helps the interviewer understand how you think.

Also, keep a smile during the interview. Sometimes interviewers intentionally don't react to test your confidence. The way you enter the room, sit, and use gestures--all these non-verbal cues matter to some extent. While speaking, emphasize keywords intentionally. This can guide the interviewer to ask questions in areas you're comfortable with--for example, mentioning the diamond problem can lead the conversation in that direction.

5. HR Round [15 students]

The HR round took place around 6 PM and lasted approximately 30 minutes. The interviewers included the HR representative and the Managing Director of ISS.The first question was whether I recognized them, as they had presented the pre-placement presentation earlier. I answered correctly and acknowledged the importance of paying attention to such details.

Tip: Be prepared with another version of a non-technical introduction. In my case, I was asked only about my academic scores -- SSC, HSC, CET percentile, and CGPA -- and I gave a brief, to-the-point summary.

Next, I was asked why I chose computer science. I backed this up with a personal anecdote from my childhood and explained how my interest developed over time. I emphasized the genuine joy I feel when building real-life, working projects. I repeated this mindset throughout the interview to reflect my authenticity and passion for the field.

I was then asked about my family background. When they learned that my sisters had stable careers, they questioned why I wasn't pursuing a master's degree. I responded by again expressing my love for building applications and explained how I wanted to take the next step -- to move beyond smaller-scale projects and work on larger systems that could help me grow and contribute more meaningfully. This response seemed to resonate with them.

They also asked how I planned to commute to work.

Then came a question to explain my favorite project, to which I described my internship project. However, this part brought back an old memory -- in a previous HR round at MSCI, I was asked technical questions and didn't respond well, which may have contributed to my rejection. Similarly, here too, I was asked a technical question about the scalability of my internship project. My response wasn't very good. However, the Managing Director reassured me that he was more interested in my thought process, which helped a bit, but it still bugged me afterwards and reminded me of the earlier rejection.

They followed up by asking how I got the internship, what I liked most about it, and what differences I observed between working with college teammates versus an industry team.

Another important question came up -- they asked how I'd feel if I had to work with a completely new tech stack or domain, and whether that would make all my prior learning go to waste. I confidently said no, explaining that no matter the stack, core concepts like APIs, databases, and clean code remain relevant. Every tech stack has its own strengths, and if the use case or project demands change, I'm ready to adapt.

The interview ended with me asking them some basic questions.

Everyone was asked to go home and results would be announced late evening. Finally a list of 12 shortlisted individuals came out which had 8 SDEs.

journey.prep:
1. Start preparing beforehand, like start making your projects before the end of 6th semester, though it's never too late.

2. Hackathon projects are good but you should have one unique project as well.

3. Try using technologies which are used in big techs.

4. For DSA, I did leetcode and codeforces. Gave contests regularly for getting used to the time pressure.

5. CS core is important as well, DBMS and OOPS are the most important ones ( some people were asked about OS as well, so be ready)

5.1. For DBMS you can watch Love-Babbar's playlist.

5.2. For OOPS and JAVA, Kunal Khushwaha's playlist is best.

6. To practice SQL, you can use leetcode top-50 sql, it's enough I guess.

7. System design, I did not do specifically but atleast know a bit about this as well (specially about your projects).

8. Participate in such hackathons, Companies like UBS, HERE, Nomura and Barclays conduct such hackathons, it increases your chances of getting the opportunity significantly.

Also these hackathons are a good learning experience as you get mentored by industry experts and get networking opportunities.

9. Give mock interviews for both tech and HR rounds.

[ My resume ]

Feel free to contact me for any help on my LinkedIn profile.

All the best for the placement process !!
journey.howSecured:
● UBS Hackathon was conducted in April, Students participating in the hackathon were directly shortlisted for the Tech interviews.

● OA offline at college was the shortlisting criteria for the rest of the students.

● PPT was conducted a day before the OA.

● 14 people were shortlisted from the OA + 6 from the UBS hack.

● 1 tech interview was conducted for some people, whereas for some, there were 2 tech interviews.

● Eligibility criteria was above 70% in both 10th and 12th boards, CGPA : 7+.

1. Online Assessment [173 people appeared]

There were 2 tests focusing on aptitude (verbal and visual reasoning) and UBS cultural assessment, which everyone had to take (from home).

Then a hackerank test was conducted focusing on DSA and CS core which was skipped for hack participants.

2. Tech Interview [ 20 people] (25-30 minutes)

( 6 panels with 2 interviewers in some and 1 in some, Summer intern process was going on alongside as well )

It started with my introduction, then they asked me about one of my projects. I explained it in detail, including the tech stack used (what and why) and system design.

Then they asked me what changes I would make in the project.

Then some HR questions like :

1. If your friend is suggesting some other technology and you want to use something else, then what will you do?

2. If one of your team member is not giving his best, which is causing delays in deliverables, what will you do?

3. If a client has requested for some feature which does not align with the objectives of your project, what will you do?

4. What are the business opportunities of your hackathon project (which was made at UBS hack) ?

Then 2 puzzles:

1. A variation of this ( Hats puzzle ),The conditions were not specified properly or I did not understand them properly. ( I wasn't able to solve it, I thought this might cost me the opportunity)

2. Simple jug problem

Then about Inner,Left,Right and Outer join.

Then they asked me about any questions I had for them. ( Ask something relevant, either about their tech-stack, you can do some research beforehand.) I asked about their DevCloud project which was mentioned on GitLab.

[

Tips: Maintain eye contact with the interviewer, a smile would be helpful. Ask for hints if required. Be well versed with your resume (projects and internship if any). If you're explaining your project try doing it with a use case, it would show that it actually solves some problem.

Think before answering any questions as there will be follow up questions as well. Be ready for some HR questions as well; they can be asked in tech interviews as well. Answer HR questions carefully keeping the company's interests in mind.

]

3. HR Round [9-10 people appeared]

This round was just for 5 minutes, HR knew me from the hackathon so it helped. This round was chill, Questions:

1. Family background

2. Relocation

3. Other companies which conduct hackathons (Barclays specifically) and their procedure.

[ 6 students got the offer including me ]

All the best for the placement process !!

1. Resume Shortlisting

Out of all the applications received, 67 students were shortlisted for the next round, the Online
Assessment (OA). This stage is often underestimated, so it is highly recommended to prepare your
resume well in advance.
A good ATS score alone does not guarantee a resume shortlist. Although the minimum CGPA criterion
specified by the company was 7.0, maintaining a CGPA of 8.0 or above is recommended. Also, while not
explicitly mentioned in the eligibility criteria, a Class 12 score above 80% appears to be an unofficial
benchmark based on previous trends.
Do include one or two finance-related projects, relevant internship experience, participation in case
competitions (especially finalist or winning positions), and any relevant certification courses you have
completed.
Once the company shares the registration link after the PPT, make sure to submit your application as
early as possible.

2. Online Test

Our OA was held online from home. It consisted of 45 MCQS, with 1 mark for each question. The total
duration was 45 minutes, so speed and accuracy are very important.
Corporate Finance & Accounting (10 Questions):
This section had basic finance and accounting questions. Topics included inflation, repo rate, financial
statements, financial ratios, bonds (callable and put bonds), GDP, and other fundamental concepts. If
your basics are clear, this section is quite manageable.
Market Awareness (10 Questions):
This section was very random and mostly based on current affairs related to finance and business.
Reading financial news regularly and staying updated with recent developments can help, but many
questions are from the if you know it, you know it category.
Quantitative Aptitude (15 Questions):
The questions were similar to those on IndiaBix. AP & GP, Permutations & Combinations, Probability,
Ratios, Profit & Loss, Time & Work, Speed, Time & Distance, Mixtures, SI-CI.
English (10 Questions):
This section included 2 reading comprehension questions, several sentence correction and
--- PAGE 2 ---
grammar-based questions, along with vocabulary and basic English usage. There were around 2
questions based on bar graphs or pie charts. It was pretty straightforward.
For me, English and Quant were the easiest sections. Finance can also be a good scoring section if your
basics are clear. However, Market Awareness was the toughest, as it is largely based on current affairs
and can feel very random. My suggestion would be to maximize your score in the remaining 35
questions, where you have more control over your performance. Also, make sure to practice Quant
under time pressure, as managing speed is just as important as solving the questions correctly. For
OA-finance questions, focus more on accounting and other basics, rather than valuations.
Out of the 67 shortlisted candidates, 55 were selected for the next round (Group Discussion).

3. Group Discussion

Shortlists were announced late at around 8 PM, so it's important to continue your preparation until the
very end.
The GD topic was shared along with the shortlist.
GD Topic: "Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful
share of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are
approximately 2x longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial
metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
We were divided into 6 panels, with each pane; consisting of around 9 students. Around 20 minutes
were allocated, but this wasn't a typical GD. We were asked specific questions and were expected to
express our views only on those questions. Hence, it is important to understand the GD topic in depth,
research it thoroughly, and also think about the possible subtopics or follow-up questions that could be
asked based on the main topic.
Try to speak at least 2 to 3 times during the discussion, and make sure your points stay relevant to the
topic. Be clear and confident, and support your arguments with statistics or insights from reputed firms
such as BCG or Mckinsey wherever possible. Be civil throughout the discussion, listen to others, and
avoid trying to dominate the conversation.
Out of 55, 29 students were selected for the next round (Interview).

1. Interviews

There are 2 interviews, mainly focussing on your finance knowledge. Know your resume
inside out, and be thorough with your basics in accounting.
Round 1 (Around 45-50 minutes):

1. Tell me about yourself

2. Do you know about the 3 financial statements?

3. What is depreciation? Impact on income statement. He then gave several scenarios and asked about

impacts on income statement/cash flow. Many were trick questions, with the answer being no impact.

4. Any recent activities going on in the market? (IPO: its share price, market cap, ratios)

--- PAGE 3 ---
Here I also told him about Anthropic filing for an IPO draft recently, and discussed this in length. He
seemed impressed with the same, so find some unique topic to talk about, which highlights your in-depth
research and awareness of the market.

5. What is repo rate? How is it related to inflation? What is the current repo and reverse repo rate?

6. What does an Investment Banker do?

7. What is India's GDP? (Answer in crores)

8. What is Sensex and Nifty? How to calculate them.

9. What is PE ratio? Should it be high or low? Explain

10. What is Enterprise value? Formula. Why do we add debt and subtract cash to find EV.

11. Mental Math Qns: (do without pen paper)

• Square root of 0.1

• 78*83

• Average speed question (formula is 2xy/x+y)

12. Any questions? (Prepare 3-4 questions beforehand, and frame it in an interesting

way, shouldn't be a forced question)
My Round 2 was a cultural fit interview with the Vice President for the CRG role (25
minutes)

1. Introduce, why investment banking?

2. Walk through your DCF project. Explain WACC, beta

3. For which sector do we find beta values greater than 1?

4. When to not use DCF?

5. Other ways to perform valuation of a company? (Precedent transaction, Comparable Multiples, LBO)

6. EV/EBITDA, EV/SALES, PE. When do we use which ratio with an example?

7. A few tricky questions on EV/EBITDA, market capitalization and PE ratio

8. Why do Merger and Acquisitions take place, types of MnAs, recent MnAs you're aware about

9. One MnA which failed recently, and what were the possible reasons that led to its failure

Finally, 10 students were selected for the HR round. Few students did not have a round-two interview,
so do not lose hope.
HR Round was very chill, and just seemed like a casual conversation. Just stay confident, speak clearly
and emphasize on JPMC's core values.

1. Intro, why do you want to enter finance?

2. Do you know what will be your role as an Investment Banker?

3. Questions on my Minor subject

4. Best learning experience from a case study competition

5. Did you speak to a senior, who is involved with JPMC?

6. Any questions

All 10 students were selected for the Banking Role.

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [230 students]

The TPO informed us only a night before that Quantiphi was coming to campus, so everyone had
to apply overnight. Because of the shortage of time, I believe there was no resume shortlisting in
this drive. Keep in mind, though, that resume shortlisting is usually a major stage, since it alone
decides whether you even get to appear in the process. Try to keep your ATS score above 80
given the current level of competition, and include projects that are relevant to the kind of firm
you are applying to, whether tech or non-tech.
Coming to the Online Assessment, I went in feeling fairly hopeless. I had not cleared a single OA
in the previous one to two months, and I had even skipped the pre-placement talk. Do attend the
PPTs, because you never know which company's final HR round you might reach, and the HR
may ask you something taken straight out of the presentation. The OA was conducted on campus,
on Unstop, in a heavily proctored mode; the Unstop SmartHire + On-campus setup ensures
fairness.
The OA was divided into three sections: Aptitude and English (45 questions), CS Fundamentals
(30 questions), and 3 DSA questions, with a total time of 1 hour 30 minutes. The special feature
of this OA was that you were shortlisted for a role based on the section you excelled in. I did the
Aptitude and English sections quite well, while CS Fundamentals and DSA went average. I
managed to pass only a few test cases of one DSA question because there was no time left at all.
So plan your sections accordingly: if you think you can do well in Aptitude and English, focus on
that, and attempt DSA and CS Fundamentals seriously only if you are confident in them and
genuinely want to pursue the FE or MLE role. Many fairly smart students juggled between the
aptitude and DSA sections and could not get through the OA. Honestly, I had zero expectations of
clearing it until I learned that section-wise selection was in place.
The cutoff for the BA role was, I believe, quite achievable if you approached the paper wisely.
Around 60 students were shortlisted for the BA role and moved on to the Group Discussion
round. For English, read the questions carefully and pick the appropriate option; in many

questions the correct option was fairly obvious. For Aptitude, practise IndiaBIX thoroughly.

2. Group Discussion [around 60 students]

We were called in at 9 a.m. for our GDs. I was fairly confident about clearing the Group
Discussion, as this has always been my strong suit. There may be situations where your group
decides in advance who will start and who will conclude; try to make sure that does not happen,
and ask the group to let the discussion flow naturally. That said, everyone must remain respectful
of each other at all times.
Our topic was "Should 75% attendance be mandatory?". In our group we had already assigned
one person to start, although I made sure no further sequence was fixed. The person we assigned
began the introduction, then fumbled and stopped midway. That is exactly the moment you have
to seize, and carry the discussion forward.
In a GD you have to be loud enough to be heard by everyone, and especially by the panellist. At
the same time, if someone else is speaking, wait for them to finish before putting forward your
point. If you are unable to generate points of your own, take someone else's point, agree with it,
and rephrase it in a better way. If someone fumbles or cannot recall a point, help them out; that
shows you are actually taking part in a group discussion rather than delivering a one-way speech.
Ultimately it comes down to individual ability, but practice definitely helps.

3. Technical Round 1 [19-20 students]

This was the most dramatic turn of the entire day. Despite performing exceptionally well in the
GD, I was told that I had not been shortlisted for the next round. I went back home flabbergasted,
and just as I was about to open my front door, more than an hour later, I received a call from the
TPC saying there had been a mistake: another student's name had been shortlisted instead of
mine, and I had to attend the interview within 40 minutes. I rushed back downstairs in despair,
took a rickshaw from Kandivali, and was literally preparing for the interview in traffic. I had no
hopes left and simply wanted to get the experience and be done with it.
Then the technical interview began. The interviewer was quite friendly, and it was a one-to-one,
in-person interaction. She first asked me how the process had been so far. I replied that this was
the most unique process I had seen any company conduct, as it recognised candidates according
to their skill set instead of applying a blanket cutoff, and she agreed. Then came the usual "tell me
about yourself", followed by an explanation of my projects from scratch. After that she asked a
few questions: the difference between Gen AI and Agentic AI, the difference between AI and
ML, and what Big Data is. She then asked me to write a simple SQL query using LIMIT and
ORDER BY, followed by a few case study questions, such as how I would acquire new customers
for a retail store that operates both online and offline using data analytics.
One thing I would recommend is that, along with knowledge, you should be able to communicate
it well. Most of the time, interviewers for roles like this one are not looking for a completely
accurate answer; they focus on how clearly you can explain your thinking, how well you

communicate, and how confident you are. There was also a situational question: if you do not
know a technical term and are asked about it in a meeting, what would you do? The ideal answer
is that you would not try to deceive the client by making something up, but would instead take it
as a follow-up and get back to them later. When I answered this, the interviewer seemed quite
convinced and said that was more or less what she was looking for. The interview went on for 40
to 50 minutes and felt more like a conversation than a grilling, but the next interview was tougher.
10-12 students were shortlisted for Round 2.

4. Technical Round 2 [10-12 students]

After waiting for two to two and a half hours, I was called in for the second round of interviews.
The interviewer seemed friendly and initially asked me about my hobbies and similar things, then
moved on to a general introduction. After that, he asked me to explain two of my projects from
scratch in layman's terms. I was able to explain the entire pipeline clearly. You need end-to-end
clarity on your own projects, and you need to be able to explain them to someone who has no idea
what they are about. For this role, explaining technical projects in simple language to a
non-technical person was the main requirement, and that is why I kept getting questioned on my
projects.
After the projects, he moved on to some maths questions. One of them was: if 5 people build 5
houses in 10 days, how many days would 10 people take to build 10 houses? I answered
incorrectly at first, but he asked me to recheck, and then I stuck confidently to my final answer.
From previous Round 2 experiences, I knew that fumbling over your answer, whether it is right or
wrong, leads to immediate rejection.
After that, he asked which role I would be interested in. Make sure you study the JD properly and
answer accordingly. The interview went well, but I had low hopes, as most of my peers were
eliminated at this stage.

5. HR Round [7 students]

The HR round took place late at night, at 9:15 p.m., and everyone was clearly exhausted. The HR
came in, started with a general introduction and a few other questions, and mentioned that there
would be no technical questions at all in this round. He then asked me to tell him something
interesting about myself, and honestly, I could not recall a single interesting thing. I tried hard but
could not come up with anything, so he moved on to the next question.
He asked why, having had such a tech-oriented education and so many technical projects, I would
want to switch to the Business Analyst path. I answered clearly, without letting the previous
question affect me: even though I have worked on highly technical projects, I have also held
various positions of responsibility throughout my studies that required both technical and
communication skills.
He then asked me to name one skill I could count on for a lifetime. I thought of saying SQL, but
that would have been too narrow, so I answered public speaking, which is something I can truly

rely on.
After that came some basic questions, such as naming five specific things about Quantiphi and
describing my background. He then mentioned that I might have to work overtime and that the
work culture could be debatable, to which I replied that we had worked overtime throughout
engineering, so it is nothing new for me. There was a lot more that I had to respond to, but
including all of it would make this account far too long. The HR interview ended with me asking
two or three questions and listening carefully throughout. By the end it had become quite
conversational, and we both finished on a positive note.
THE KEY TAKEAWAY IS THIS: EVEN IF ONE QUESTION GOES WRONG OR
YOU ARE UNABLE TO ANSWER IT, DO NOT LET IT AFFECT YOUR OTHER
ANSWERS. THAT ONE GLITCH DOES NOT DEFINE THE OVERALL
INTERVIEW.
6 students were offered the BA role, 2 the FE role, and 1 the MLE role.

journey.prep:
1) Try to maintain a high CGPA. A lot of people say that CGPA is not important and anything above

8 works, but from what I have seen, that is not the case. A lot of companies mention a criteria of 7.5
or 8 in their application, but then while shortlisting, they end up only shortlisting students having a
CGPA above 8.5 or even close to 9. I would say a CGPA of 8+ is a must to participate in the
processes of a lot of good companies, but try to keep it above 8.5 if possible.

2) Learn and practice Java during your placement preparation. I cannot stress the importance of

this enough, as I personally used C++ throughout my coding practice and only knew the basics of
Java and OOP. A lot of banks/finance-related companies hire on campus, and most of those
companies require Java. I would suggest C++ only if you are doing competitive programming very
--- PAGE 9 ---
seriously, but otherwise, for DSA and on-campus preparation, just go with Java as your primary
language. It will be very helpful while giving OAs for companies and also during interviews.

3) Do not focus only on DSA. This is a mistake that I, along with many others, made during our

placements. The majority of our time was spent on DSA preparation, as we thought that was the
most important thing for clearing OAs. That is not true. Be consistent with your DSA practice and,
yes, cover all the concepts, but also focus on SQL (it is equally important as DSA, as almost every
single company asks it either in the form of MCQs or by asking you to write a query in the OA),
along with development and AI/ML concepts.

4) If you are from EXTC, try and cover core CS concepts early during your preparation, as these

concepts will require revision to make sure you are comfortable with them. Comps and CSE students
have these as part of their coursework, so it is relatively easier and less time-consuming for them, but
for EXTC, study these early and then keep revising them in between to make sure you do not forget.
Focus more on DBMS and OOPS, as these are the most frequently asked topics in all companies.
Also, try and give some time to OS and CCN concepts.

5) Prepare everything on your resume early. Do not be like me and wait for the interview call to

finally prepare my resume in depth and regret it later. The resume is something that will mostly be
the same throughout the placement season (except for some tweaks according to roles and
requirements), so prepare it well in advance and be prepared for every single word that you have
mentioned in it in detail. Only mention things you are confident about, and do not fake anything.

6) Try to give some mock interviews to your friends or family members if possible, as it will boost

your confidence. I did not do this, and I had also given no interviews before BlackRock, due to
which I had O confidence going into the interview. Speaking out about points on your resume or
certain concepts helps in boosting your confidence and will be beneficial during the interview.

7) Stay calm during the interview. Even if the interviewer asks a question that you do not know the

answer to, stay calm and try to answer it in some way, and be clear in explaining your thought
process and try to bring the interviewer back to a concept that you are comfortable in. Most of the
time, instead of testing your technical skills, interviewers are testing your ability to handle pressure,
and they are more interested in your approach.
My overall experience with placements:
From my experience, placements are a very luck based process. I would say they are 80% luck and maybe
20% of your skill. If luck is not with you, no matter how skilled you are there are chances that you will
remain unplaced for a while and you will see other people all around you getting placed and celebrating.
If luck is not with you, your resume itself might not get shortlisted-which is a very random process and
nobody knows how companies actually shortlist candidates. A lot of deserving candidates get left out despite
having a high ATS score and a decent cgpa and this might happen to you as well. You will feel very
frustrated at the time the shortlist comes out but try to stay calm and focus on the next opportunity you have
as placements go on for a long time and being frustrated and angry early will not help.
If you are in EXTC, be mentally prepared for a lot of frustration. Apart from all the luck being involved in
resume shortlisting and OAs having varied difficulties of questions for everybody in some companies, being
from extc will lead to you being ineligible for a lot of top high paying companies. Sometimes, you might be
eligible for application but when the shortlist comes out, you will find out only comps and cse students have
been shortlisted for the OA. During our placement season, a lot of top companies such as JPMC(for fintech
role), IDFC, UBS, Nomura, WorkIndia, Dolat Capital and a few others did not even allow extc students to
--- PAGE 10 ---
sit for the OA. This was all highly frustrating as we did not get the opportunity just because we are not in cse
or comps but nothing could be done other than waiting for whatever opportunity comes our way next.
Overall, I would say that stay patient and wait for that one lucky day where everything goes your way!

1) Pre Placement Talk

2) Resume Shortlisting
