5) HR Interview

1. Pre Placement Talk and Resume Shortlisting:

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was scheduled virtually on 6th August on Webex, as it was a pooled-campus
opportunity. I could not attend the PPT completely because I had an MDM lecture going on at the same
time. However, I would strongly advise attending the PPT and listening carefully to the points discussed, as
it can help you gain a better understanding of the company. It can also be helpful during the interview, as
you can refer to a point mentioned during the PPT, which might leave a good impression on the interviewer.
The eligibility criteria was simply having a CGPA above 7.5, and students from all branches were eligible to
apply. They had mentioned that there would be resume shortlisting, but in the end, I believe everyone who
applied got a chance to appear for the OA.
BlackRock did not conduct resume shortlisting, but many other companies do. Therefore, it is preferable to
maintain a resume with a high ATS score (try to keep it above 75) and tailor your resume according to the
JD and the role. However, while trying to maximize your ATS score or make yourself a better fit for the role,
do not add skills or technologies that you have absolutely no knowledge of, as they can come back to bite
you during the interview.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [285 candidates appeared ]

The test was conducted online from home on HackerRank. The total duration was 1.5 hours, and there were
7 sections, each of which was timed individually. Also the test was section locked so once a section was
submitted or if we ran out of time for a particular section, we cannot go back.
The first section was a coding question, for which we had 40 minutes. The question was different for
everyone, but in general, the difficulty level was quite high for most of us. In my case, I had to implement a
Fork/Join algorithm in Java for an airport luggage management system. The solution had to be implemented
using objects and classes. Since my primary language for problem-solving was C++, and this question could
only be solved in Java, I was unable to solve it.
An Al assistant was also available with the question, which could be used to ask queries related to the
problem, such as requesting an explanation or getting help with Java syntax.
The second section was also a coding question, and we had 15 minutes to solve it. Once again, the questions
differed for everyone. I got a codebase question based on Selenium. Honestly, 15 minutes was nowhere near
enough to solve it, as it was a very complex question that would easily take 10-12 minutes just to
understand. I was unable to solve this question either, so I moved on to the MCQ sections feeling quite
disappointed that I had not been able to solve either of the coding questions.
There were 5 MCQ-based sections after this:

1. Design Patterns (Advanced) - 15 questions, 6 minutes

2. Design Patterns (Basic) - 15 questions, 4 minutes

3. Fundamental AI Know-How, Cloud Services Exposure - 25 questions, 10 minutes

4. DB Concepts - ACID Properties, Transactions, DB Fundamentals - 25 questions, 10 minutes

5. Aptitude - 15 questions, 10 minutes

The questions in these sections ranged from easy to medium difficulty. The Design Patterns sections
involved questions based on LLD, SOLID principles, and related concepts. Most of the questions were
manageable even with a basic understanding of these topics. I had prepared these concepts for 1-2 hours the
day before the OA using ChatGPT, and I found that level of preparation sufficient to answer most of the
questions.
The AI Know-How section also involved basic questions on Al and machine learning, along with cloud
services such as AWS. Most of these questions were answerable with basic knowledge. Additionally, many
questions could be solved through option elimination, as there was often only one obvious option that could
be correct.
The DB Concepts section was also quite easy, as DBMS is asked by almost every company, and I had
prepared it well. The Aptitude section was not particularly difficult, but it was lengthy, and I found 10
minutes insufficient to answer all the questions.
After the test, I was quite disappointed because I had not been able to solve either of the coding questions. I
was very sure that I would not be shortlisted for the next round, even though my performance in the MCQ
sections had gone well.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After the OA, there was a 5-day gap before the results were announced. During this time, being very sure
that I would not be shortlisted after my OA performance, I was not focusing on interview preparation but
rather preparing in general for the OAs of other companies that were visiting the campus in the coming days.
However, the shortlist was released on 18th August at around 6 PM (interviews were to begin on 19th from
9 AM), and I was shocked to see my name on the list. My best guess after looking at the shortlist was that
BlackRock did not consider the OA results for whatever reason and rather shortlisted students based on their
CGPA. I am not sure why they did this, but I did not have time to think about all this when I saw my name
on the shortlist, as I was not at all prepared for an interview.
This was also the first interview that I would be giving during the placement season, so that was another
reason for me to stress about because I did not know how these interviews actually worked, except for
whatever I had read in previous interview experiences and what I had heard from friends.
After seeing my name on the shortlist, I started preparing everything that was on my resume in as much
detail as I could. The main focus was on preparing my projects, the tech stacks used, the architecture of the
projects, etc. Along with this, I also tried to prepare some of the design concepts that they had asked in the
OA and brushed up on some concepts of object-oriented programming.
I tried to cover whatever I could in the limited time I had and went to sleep, hoping for the best the next day.

2. Round 2 - Technical Interview [ 28 shortlisted and 10 waitlisted for SDE role ]

I received a call from the HR regarding the interview on the 18th, and I was informed that my interview
would start at 9 AM the next day. The interviews were scheduled virtually on the Webex platform, and we
were asked to report to the TPO at 8:30 AM and be ready by 8:50 AM for the interview. I was ready by
around 8:50, and at 8:55, I received a call from the HR asking me to join the link.
Introduction & Initial Questions
The interview initially started with one panelist. I greeted her, and she asked me to begin with an
introduction. I had prepared an introduction based on my resume using Claude, which covered all the
important points and ended with me mentioning my strongest project so that I could steer the interview in
that direction.
The interviewer heard my introduction and asked me some basic questions, such as:

• What languages I use for coding

• What tech stack I know

• What I am comfortable with

I answered by mentioning C++ as my primary language, so she immediately interrupted and asked me,
"What about Java and Python?" I mentioned that I had used Python in a few of my projects and had studied
object-oriented concepts in Java, so I had experience with both languages, but for problem-solving, I
primarily use C++.
For my tech stack, I mentioned most of what was written on my resume, and she seemed satisfied with it and
said, "Okay."
--- PAGE 4 ---
Next, she asked me how I make use of Al for coding, making projects, or learning purposes. I answered by
saying that for any problem I come across, I first try to come up with a solution or an approach in my mind.
I try to put it on paper, test it out with some examples myself, and then code it up. However, if I get stuck at
some point in my solution, or if I have a solution ready but am struggling with the implementation, I make
use of Al to help me and make my task easier. I also mentioned that I use Al to prepare certain concepts and
test myself on them by solving MCQ-based tests using ChatGPT or Claude.
Next, she asked me how the online assessment was and whether I found the questions challenging. I
answered honestly by stating that since the advanced coding question could only be solved in Java, and I
don't use Java for problem-solving, I could not solve it even though I could think of an approach. For the
second question, I was short on time and could not solve that one either. However, I stated that I was able to
solve most of the MCQs correctly within the allotted time.
She didn't really react to anything I was saying here, so I was not sure whether my answer was satisfactory
or not. This happened throughout the interview.
DSA Question - Valid Anagram
After this, she said something along the lines of, "Since you weren't able to solve the coding question in the
OA, let's solve one now," and asked me whether I knew what an anagram was. I said yes, and then she asked
me how I would code a solution to check whether two strings are anagrams or not.
Question on LeetCode: Valid Anagram
This was a very easy problem, and I started with a sorting-based approach and explained the approach in
detail. She did not ask me to open Notepad and write the pseudocode or anything, so I had to go through the
approach verbally.
After this approach, I stated the optimal approach of using a hashmap, but mentioned that we are
compromising on space complexity to improve the time complexity. When I said this, she asked me what the
time and space complexities were for both approaches, which I answered for every step of the code. She
said, "Okay," and seemed satisfied.
Chatbot / RAG Question
After this, she gave me a problem saying that suppose I want to build a chatbot in which we can feed a
document. The chatbot goes through the document, and later it is expected to answer any questions that we
have regarding the document or help us find any particular text in the document. She asked me how I would
build this chatbot and what the process would be.
I answered step-by-step, mentioning the use of vector embeddings and a RAG-based approach. Once again,
she just listened to whatever I said with an expressionless face, so I had no idea whether what I was saying
was what she was expecting or whether she expected something else. However, at the end of my
explanation, she said, "Okay," and moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Project discussion
The discussion then moved on to one of my projects. It was an Al-powered stock analytics platform. She
asked me to explain briefly what the project was about. I had prepared a short, one-minute introduction for
this project that covered everything the project does.
She asked about the tech stack and a point on my resume that stated that the project had 10+ REST API
endpoints. She asked me what these different endpoints were and what the user could see. I answered all of
this, and then she asked me how we were getting any of the stock-related data.
Here, I mentioned that this part took us a lot of time since we were unable to get proper data regarding stock
prices, historical data, etc. I told her that we tried to perform web scraping, but that was not working because
the NSE, BSE, and SEBI websites were strict and rate-limited us. Even AI tools were not helping us with
proper libraries that could be used. After a lot of research, we found some Python libraries that could help us
with the task without having to pay.
She said, "Okay," and asked how we were fetching news feeds as well and how we were scoring any
particular stock.
While she was asking this question, a second interviewer also joined the call.
Regarding the scoring, I answered honestly and told her that we lacked in-depth knowledge of finance, so
we relied on whatever was available online and made use of AI tools to help us create a proper scoring
system for any particular stock.
She then came back to the chatbot question and asked me what if she wanted to train that chatbot, or any
chatbot, continuously based on the output it was providing.
I answered by saying that I would store whatever output I get in some kind of data structure, such as a
vector, and feed it back to the chatbot to retrain it in a kind of feedback loop. I was not sure about this
answer, but the interviewer said, "Okay."
Up to this point, the interview was mostly going smoothly, except for maybe the last chatbot question.
However, now the second interviewer started asking questions.
FastAPI Discussion
My project used FastAPI, so she started by asking what FastAPI is, what REST APIs are, and why I used
FastAPI instead of Flask. I answered this and told her about the advantages of FastAPI and why it was a
proper fit for our project since the project was backend-heavy.
She said, "Okay," but like the other interviewer, she did not give away anything, so I still didn't know
whether my answers were satisfactory or not.
The discussion continued on FastAPI, and she asked me, "What if we want to write a GET method in your
project to fetch some data? How would you write it in FastAPI?"
I knew about the GET method and routing, but I was not very sure how I would write it or what the exact
syntax was for FastAPI, as I had mostly done full-stack development using MERN. I still explained it
--- PAGE 6 ---
verbally by giving her an example of a stock having a particular ID and how we could fetch data using GET
for that particular route.
She did not expect me to write the exact syntax on Notepad but was instead looking for the logic, so I guess
she was satisfied with this answer.
She then asked me if I knew what dependency injection was in FastAPI. Throughout this discussion, I
regretted not having studied FastAPI separately, as the entire discussion revolved around concepts that I did
not know fully because I had only used FastAPI in the project and knew some basics.
I answered based on whatever I understood from the term "dependency injection," and she said that
conceptually it was fine, but asked how I would implement it and why it is used in FastAPI. I did not know
the answer, so I told her that I was unable to recall the concept exactly, even though I had heard of it before.
She said, "No worries," and then moved on to the next question.
DBMS Discussion
The discussion then moved to DBMS. I was not very confident at this point, as I believed that the FastAPI
discussion had not gone very well.
The DBMS discussion started with her asking me the difference between SQL and NoSQL, which I
answered by giving examples. I ended my answer by mentioning ACID properties since I was confident in
them and wanted her to ask me that question. So naturally, she asked me to explain what the ACID
properties are, which I explained and also gave examples for.
After this, she asked me about the CAP theorem, which I explained. Then she asked me an interesting
question. She asked that since only two out of the three properties Consistency, Availability, and Partition
Tolerance are possible, which one would I compromise on in MySQL and which one would I compromise
on in MongoDB.
I was a little surprised by this since I only knew about the theorem and what it means and had never studied
its practical applications. So, I initially answered by saying that it depends on the situation and what the
application of the database is for.
She then asked me to take an example of my choice and explain. I started with MySQL and took the
example of a banking system, stating that I would compromise on availability in this case, as consistency is
important. Even if the server is unavailable for a short period of time, it wouldn't be as much of a problem
compared to the data being inconsistent.
She said, "Okay," and asked me about MongoDB. I was not sure about this, so I answered whatever came to
mind and told her that since MongoDB stores data in the form of documents and there are no joins in
MongoDB, it would be intolerant to partitions because the entire data is together. If we partition the database
and separate the data, it would be impossible to make sense of the separated data.
This most likely was not the answer they were expecting, but I explained whatever thought process I had,
and with that, they were done with the questions.
--- PAGE 7 ---
They asked me if I had any questions for them, and I asked them about their experience at BlackRock and
what kind of work I could expect if I joined as an intern. They answered this question and that concluded the
interview.
My interview lasted around 45 minutes. Most of the interviews across panels lasted around 30-45 minutes.
After the interview, I thought there was maybe a 50% probability that I would be called for Round 2, as
there were one or two questions that I was not able to answer very well.
However, some people got a call for their Round 2 interview within 5-10 minutes of their Round 1
interview, and this made me disappointed since I did not get the call.
We were all asked to wait until all the Round 1 interviews were done. During this time, I was talking to other
people and just passing time since I thought that I would not get a Round 2 call after seeing other people get
theirs immediately.
We had lunch and were waiting outside the TPO office without any hope when, suddenly, at around 2:30
PM, I got a call asking me to join immediately for Round 2.

3. Round 3 - Techno HR [ 16 candidates for SDE ]

This round was a techno-HR round for me but varied for everybody (I am guessing it depended on the
Round 1 performance). Some people had a techno-HR mix, while some had a purely technical round as their
Round 2.
There was only one panelist for this interview, and it began with me greeting him, following which he asked
about my day and my Round 1 interview. I answered honestly, saying it went well except for maybe one or
two questions, so he asked me what the questions were that I was not able to answer, to which I replied that
they were some DBMS and FastAPI questions. Up to this point, I was not sure whether this was a purely
technical round or an HR round.
The discussion started with him asking about my internship. He said that since I had worked in a corporate
environment before, how was the experience, what was different from attending college, and also asked me
to mention three positives about the company I worked at. I stated my experience, told him about the work,
how it was my first experience in an office, and how different it was from school or college. I also stated the
positives about the company, following which he asked me to state some negatives as well.
After this, he asked me what I understood by the term "client-side requirements" while working, to which I
answered regarding one of the clients of the company I worked at and what their expectations and
requirements were from the company. While I was answering this, he interrupted and rephrased his question
by saying that what he meant was, as a software developer, what all the company is expecting from my
software/application. So I answered along the lines of website/application availability, the ability to handle
traffic, scalability, etc., and explained everything in detail.
The discussion then moved to my stock analytics project, and he asked me to explain the project and what it
does. He asked me whether it was an individual or a group project, to which I answered that we were a team
of four. So he asked that since it was a team, we would have had some conflicts while building this project,
so how did we all resolve the disagreement/conflict? I answered this by giving an example of an actual
disagreement that took place and how we resolved it, and he seemed satisfied with the answer.
--- PAGE 8 ---
He followed it up by asking that suppose I work in a corporate environment and come up with an excellent
idea that I am 100% sure will work well for the company and will be beneficial, and I have conducted
complete research on it, but none of my other team members are listening and are disregarding the idea. In
this situation, how will I react and convince others?
I answered by saying that I will talk to everybody with an open mind, as I could be wrong, and explain all
the work and research that I have done and how it will be beneficial to the company. Even if, after
everything, they are not convinced, we cannot implement the idea, but I would at least request everybody to
listen to what I have to say first.
Next, he asked me that I would know what BlackRock does and that I would have researched the company,
so how would I integrate this stock analytics platform into BlackRock's tech, and how can this be beneficial
for the company? This turned out to be in my favour since BlackRock is an asset management company, so
the stock analytics project can fit perfectly, and I was able to answer this question very well, mentioning all
the advantages and the problems the project solves.
He then asked me that if I had to learn another programming language, which one would I learn? I answered
this by saying that instead of learning a new language, I would work on improving my Java and Python
skills, as they are heavily used in the industry, and adding a new language would not mean much if I am not
comfortable with it.
He then asked me a few questions on DBMS:

• What is DBMS?

• Why do we need DBMS?

• Difference between DBMS and RDBMS and two examples of SQL and NoSQL databases.

I was able to answer all these fairly easily since they were basics, and he seemed satisfied with the answers.
He then asked me if I had any questions for him, and I asked him the same question that I asked in Round 1
regarding his experience at BlackRock and what the expectations from me would be if I joined as an intern
in January. He answered this question positively, and that concluded my Round 2 interview, which lasted
around 25 minutes.
All students who were done with Round 2 were then asked to leave, and the results were announced the next
day at around 12 PM.
8 students were selected-7 for SDE and 1 for Aladdin Data.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) Try to maintain a high CGPA. A lot of people say that CGPA is not important and anything above

8 works, but from what I have seen, that is not the case. A lot of companies mention a criteria of 7.5
or 8 in their application, but then while shortlisting, they end up only shortlisting students having a
CGPA above 8.5 or even close to 9. I would say a CGPA of 8+ is a must to participate in the
processes of a lot of good companies, but try to keep it above 8.5 if possible.

2) Learn and practice Java during your placement preparation. I cannot stress the importance of

this enough, as I personally used C++ throughout my coding practice and only knew the basics of
Java and OOP. A lot of banks/finance-related companies hire on campus, and most of those
companies require Java. I would suggest C++ only if you are doing competitive programming very
--- PAGE 9 ---
seriously, but otherwise, for DSA and on-campus preparation, just go with Java as your primary
language. It will be very helpful while giving OAs for companies and also during interviews.

3) Do not focus only on DSA. This is a mistake that I, along with many others, made during our

placements. The majority of our time was spent on DSA preparation, as we thought that was the
most important thing for clearing OAs. That is not true. Be consistent with your DSA practice and,
yes, cover all the concepts, but also focus on SQL (it is equally important as DSA, as almost every
single company asks it either in the form of MCQs or by asking you to write a query in the OA),
along with development and AI/ML concepts.

4) If you are from EXTC, try and cover core CS concepts early during your preparation, as these

concepts will require revision to make sure you are comfortable with them. Comps and CSE students
have these as part of their coursework, so it is relatively easier and less time-consuming for them, but
for EXTC, study these early and then keep revising them in between to make sure you do not forget.
Focus more on DBMS and OOPS, as these are the most frequently asked topics in all companies.
Also, try and give some time to OS and CCN concepts.

5) Prepare everything on your resume early. Do not be like me and wait for the interview call to

finally prepare my resume in depth and regret it later. The resume is something that will mostly be
the same throughout the placement season (except for some tweaks according to roles and
requirements), so prepare it well in advance and be prepared for every single word that you have
mentioned in it in detail. Only mention things you are confident about, and do not fake anything.

6) Try to give some mock interviews to your friends or family members if possible, as it will boost

your confidence. I did not do this, and I had also given no interviews before BlackRock, due to
which I had O confidence going into the interview. Speaking out about points on your resume or
certain concepts helps in boosting your confidence and will be beneficial during the interview.

7) Stay calm during the interview. Even if the interviewer asks a question that you do not know the

answer to, stay calm and try to answer it in some way, and be clear in explaining your thought
process and try to bring the interviewer back to a concept that you are comfortable in. Most of the
time, instead of testing your technical skills, interviewers are testing your ability to handle pressure,
and they are more interested in your approach.

1) Pre Placement Talk - 24 June.

2) Resume Screening - 26 June.

3) OA - 27 June.

4) Interviews - 2 July.

1. Pre Placement Talk] [300 + students attended]

The pre placement talk for JPMC was conducted online via a zoom meeting on 24th June in the afternoon.
The hiring team consisted of HR, people from Corporate Risk, and also from the CIB department. All of
them briefed us in depth on the work JPMC does. It was a very informative session.
I would recommend paying utmost attention to what each and every person is saying in the PPT, and make
notes if possible. At the end of the PPT, we were allowed to ask questions if any. Please refrain from asking
questions related to the hiring process. Ask questions related to the job role, and only if you genuinely have
questions. Do not ask random and obvious questions. As many students were raising their hands in the zoom
meeting, only a few students were allowed to ask questions due to time constraints.

2. Resume Screening] [ Approx 150 - 200 students applied for Banking Role. ]

On 24th June itself, we had to apply on the JPMC website with our details and fill a google form. The
process of resume screening is a huge bottleneck so make sure your resume is tailored as per the role and
relevant. Allot enough time to prepare your resume. Do not blindly apply with your Tech resume. As seniors
have told, check your resume score on the Resume Worded website, and try to take it above 60. Mine was
somewhere between 65 and 70.
Note - I will recommend really giving enough time to prepare the resume for this role, make sure there are
no special characters in your resume, no mistakes and errors. I will suggest if you are keen on applying for
--- PAGE 2 ---
JPMC, prepare a non tech profile resume well beforehand, because the application process might take long
and has to be completed within 1 day.

3. [OA] [66-67 students were shortlisted to give the OA. ]

The shortlist for OA was given at 5:30 pm on the day before the OA was scheduled. The pattern for the
OA was given to us.
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounting. 10 Qns
Section 2: Market Awareness 10 Qns
Section 3 : Quantitative Aptitude 15 Qns
Section 4 : English Usage.
Our OA was scheduled at 10:30 am, in the morning. It was online from home, on a third party platform
fully proctored. Section 1 was medium difficulty overall, u need to prepare Financial Statements, basic
accounting and ratios well. Section 2 was tough, you need to prepare current affairs, currently ongoing
financial events well. Section 3 was easy to medium, simple aptitude questions. You need to prepare from
IndiaBix website. Section 4 was simple English, so it was a scoring and easy one.

4. [Group Discussion] [55 students were shortlisted for this round.]

The shortlist for GD was shared with us at around 8:30 pm on 1st July. Hence, it is important to keep
preparing for interviews even if you have no guarantee that you will be shortlisted. Due to heavy rains,
the JPMC hiring team decided to conduct an online selection process this year. However, all students
were supposed to be present on campus. 55 students were divided into 6 groups of approx 9 people in
each group. The GD was conducted on a zoom meeting. The topic for GD was given to us along with the
shortlist. The topic for GD was - suppose you are the CEO of a company and due to certain situations,
the lead time and cost of your shipping has gone up, how will you approach this problem. It wasn't word
to word like this, I am just giving you a basic idea of what it was about.
My group had 9 people and our GD started at 9:45 am on 2nd July. Since it was an online GD, everything
was structured, we had to raise our hands in order to speak and put forth our points. The panel consisted
of 2 people sitting in the JPMC office and was mainly moderated by the VP. The following 3 questions
were introduced to facilitate the GD:

1) How to approach the on paper losses that the company will bear

in this situation 2) Suppose a supplier needs your help in this situation, will you help them.

3) Once the

situation is eased, how will you approach to get back on track.
In my panel, most of us spoke a lot on each and every question being introduced by the panelists, the
moderator praised all of us at the end of the GD. I will suggest that you take 3-4 good entries in the GD
to get noticed. I took around 4-5 entries in the GD. Due to anxiety, I fumbled a lot while speaking,
however I was able to put forth my points strongly. Your points should not just repeat what has already
been said by someone else, instead it should add on to it or give a different angle to the situation being
discussed.
--- PAGE 3 ---

5. Interview Round, [29 students were shortlisted for interviews.]

My interview was scheduled at 12 p.m, however I got a call at around 11:30 from the interviewer, asking if I
could join the zoom meeting immediately. I immediately said yes and asked the TPO coordinators who
arranged a cabin for me.
The interviewer asked me to introduce myself. As soon as I was done introducing, he asked me apart from
M&A advisory what else Investment Banks do. I answered - Trading and Brokerage, Asset Management and
Capital Market stuff (ECM and DCM). He immediately asked to explain what Asset Management does. I
explained to him in simple terms about Asset Management. At this point he suddenly asked me the
difference between Asset Management and Private Equity. Now this was the point where I had to be super
careful, I wasn't aware much about Private Equity, and he really found it out fast enough. He suddenly
started asking me "Are you sure ?", "Is that really True?" to confuse me. Finally he explained to me briefly
about the exact difference.
The next question was "If you are a manager in asset management, what metrics will you use to determine
performanceằ
ẠạI replied with IRR and elaborated on two types of IRRS. He gave me a scenario related to that
and asked me to solve for both the types of IRRs. I was able to correctly calculate around 50-60% of the
sum, to which he seemed to be satisfied
Later he asked me to explain the happenings in the stock market in the last 6 months. This was a general
question so if you keep track of markets and basic news, you should be able to answer it correctly.
Lastly he gave me a simple sum: a person goes from A to B at 5 km/hr and returns from B to A at 10km/hr,
calculate the Avg speed. It took me 2 - 3 attempts to finally solve this question, however in each attempt my
thought process was correct, so he guided me through the question when necessary. I was able to solve the
question correctly in the end.
The interview ended with him asking me to drop off from the call without asking any questions.
Note - This interview was completely different from typical round 1 interviews being conducted for JPMC
banking roles, as you may read in other students' documents. The key to cracking interviews in such
scenarios is to talk out your thought process because that tells the interviewer if you are at least thinking in
the right direction, even though you are not able to reach the final answer.
Do not lose hope even if your interview goes tough. For many students, 2-3 technical rounds were taken
before advancing to the HR round. In my case, I was directly shortlisted for the HR round without any more
technical rounds. Do not lose hope or leave for home without having full confirmation that you are out of the
process. Always be ready and keep a positive mindset.
One more thing I will suggest during interviews - if the interviewer is correcting you and explaining
something to you, always listen to them positively and acknowledge them for the knowledge that they have
given to you.
--- PAGE 4 ---

6. HR Round] [10 students appeared for this round.]

It was around 3:45 pm and I finally decided to sit and apply for other tech companies that were coming to
the campus. Suddenly a list of students was declared and my name was in it. The HR round was again
conducted online via zoom meeting.
The round started with greetings. The HR Madam introduced herself and then asked me to introduce
myself. Later she asked me to explain any one of my projects. No further questions were asked regarding
my project. Then she asked me "If you are hiring for analysts / interns, what 3 qualities will you look for
in themại This is a standard HR question and there is no right / wrong answer. I answered the questions
and she seemed happy with it, because she extended more on the qualities that I mentioned. Later I was
given the chance to ask questions if any, so I asked 2 questions: one about the culture at JPMC, and
another about the attitude of interns which gets them hired for a full time role.
Note - In HR rounds, always be expressive and positive when you speak. Try not to talk about any
negative stuff, as it could give a bad impression about you. HR Rounds are generally very chill, you just
need to be yourself and be polite. Always greet the other person at the start and end of the interview.
The results were declared after about 45 minutes and all 10 students were selected.

I will just list down some things that are MUST DO before you interview for this role:
i) 3 financial statements - you should know them in and out, and how they are linked. ii) Accounting basics
and treatments for various scenarios. iii) Latest IPOs, M&As and some historic IPOs and M&As. iv)
Current affairs especially with respect to finance and economics like repo rate, inflation etc, gold prices etc.
v) Basic Financial Modeling - especially the DCF model since it is widely asked in IB interviews. vi)
Corporate finance and Ratios for analysis.
Luck plays a vital role in your selection, however I would say its 60% skill and 40% luck.
JPMC always declares shortlists barely 12-18 hours before the interviews and OAs, so keep preparing
without worrying about the outcome. If you don't get shortlisted, your knowledge will not go waste and will
come in handy at some point in your life.
Courses I would recommend: Complete Investment Banking Course on Udemy by Careers 365 - it helps to
conceptually understand everything about IB. If you have time you can even do the Forage IB job
simulation. Accounting Stuff - Yt channel for financial statements and ratios.
Lastly.. If you have any questions or need guidance wrt Tech /Non Tech, feel free to reach out to me on

journey.howSecured:
This year's drive was very PhonePe level. The OA was definitely more difficult than last year's OA. But I'll
say that in my opinion, the DSA asked in the technical rounds did become slightly easier than the ones
asked last year. (Still, the technical rounds were difficult, as, at the end of the day, its PhonePe :p)

1. Online Assessment [ Around 310 candidates appeared for this round]

Everyone with >6.5 CGPA was sent the link. I never checked the ATS score for my resume, although it's advisable
to do so.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points) We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers (capability),
plus an integer K denoting the maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A worker can only do a
task if their capability is greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to find the minimum value of k
(1 <= k<= K) such that all tasks are assigned and no worker does more than k tasks.
I used two pointers to efficiently allocate the tasks first and maintained a counter. I knew the optimal solution
required binary search on the answer, but I was confident my two-pointer approach would pass most test cases.
I coded it quickly to save time and planned to come back to it later. My approach passed 9/14 test cases. The
optimal approach is indeed doing a binary search on the value of k. This question was fairly easy and a lot of
people solved it.
Problem 2: Network Routers and Regions (70 Points) You are given a tree of N nodes and N-1 edges. The
network has exactly one central server, several routers, and multiple regions. The server connects only to
routers, routers connect to the server and one or more regions, and regions connect to exactly one router. We
had to determine the number of routers and regions.
This was again a fairly simple problem. The standard method most people used was creating an adjacency list:
the number of regions equals the nodes with degree 1, and the routers equal N - regions - 1.
I actually solved it using an entirely different method. I ran a BFS from each node to check if it was the central
hub, based on the observation that the maximum depth from the hub can only be 3. Once I tound the central hub,
the number of routers became adj[hub].size() and regions became adj[adj[hub][0]]. size(). Ikind of
overcomplicated this, but if it works, it works. Passed all test cases.
Problem 3: Codeforces 1665C (110 Points) The ideal approach can be found in the Codeforces editorial. I was
pretty much out of time from trying the 4th problem (which was a trap), so I just printed N. This passed 4/22 test
cases. We had to take the number of test cases as input first and run the solve function T times, making it very
--- PAGE 2 ---
Codeforces-like. I think they did this to avoid people brute-forcing or just returning standard values like -1 for
easy points.
Problem 4: Codeforces 8C (120 Points) This was a 2000-rated Codeforces bitmask DP problem. I don't even
know how to talk about this problem. I tried DP with bitmasking, which was the right approach, but coding it
would have taken 1.5 hours alone. I wasted a lot of time on this and eventually gave up.
In total, I solved 1 completely, got 9/14 on the first, and 4/22 on the third. Thanks to those 4/22 test cases on Q3, I
received an extra 15 points since that question had a high weightage. No one was able to solve 3 completely; the
maximum was around 2.5.
Keep in mind, your aim in these OAsis not to solve the questions completely, but to extract as many points
as you can. Build a habit of leaving questions if they feel like they are taking too much time, and always
solve the ones you feel confident in first. In my case, I solved the 50-point question first because it was the
easiest.
The shortlisting criteria ended up being around 1.5 questions. We received the shortlist around 10:00 PM, and
roughly 26 people were selected for the technical rounds.

2. Technical Round 1[26 people appeared]

We were asked to come at around 9:00 AM the next day. They called us in the order of how we finished in the
OA. I was in the second batch of students.
(For context, Batch 1 was osked "Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column" and something similar to
"LeetCode 992: Subarrays with K Different Integers". Batch 3 had "LeetCode 632: Smallest Range Covering Elements
from K Lists" and another question of graphs.)
Here is what I was asked in Batch 2:
Problem 1: LeetCode 827 - Making A Large Island (Pretty standard)
I started with a brute-force approach: doing a DFS for every 1 encountered. I then suggested optimizing it using
DSU pre-computation. He asked me not to use a DSU, so I proposed storing the parent for each component in a
separate auxiliary matrix.
He agreed both solutions would work, but he wanted me to try another method: assigning an ID for each
component directly inside the given matrix. I agreed it would work, but I pointed out that I generally avoid
modifying the given data in a problem as a standard engineering practice. He was satisfied with that reasoning,
had me write the pseudo-code, and we moved on.
Problem 2: LeetCode 3203 - Find Minimum Diameter After Merging Two Trees
I wasn't explicitly told this was a tree. I was only told it was a "cluster of N nodes and N-1 edges, and M nodes and
M-1 edgesi I asked him if it contained any cycles, and he told me to prove it myself. I proved it by observation,
since the clusters cannot be disconnected based on the problem constraints. I then asked, "Can I assume it's a
tree?" He asked me to prove that too, which I did using a tree's formal definition.
Note: Even though I knew it was a tree immediately, directly jumping to tree algorithms can get skeptical looks from
an interviewer. It's best to lead them to agree with you first.
I started with the brute force of trying every possible vertex pair from the two trees to find the maximum
distance. When asked to optimize, I said I would use the diameter of a tree to find the radius by doing d/2. He
asked how I would find the diameter, which led me to proving why the 2-DFS solution works. I proved my
--- PAGE 3 ---
algorithm by contradiction, constantly saying things like, "I claim that XYZ." We had a lot of to and fro, which is
very common.
He said, "It looks fair to me, you can assume this is right and continue." I handled the edge cases (like taking the
ceiling of d/2 if the diameter is odd, taking max (d1, d2, r1+r2+1)) and quickly fixed my logic when prompted. In the
meantime, he actually checked online about the 2-DFS solution and told me, "It's correct, don't worry. I checked it
online." I wrote the pseudo-code quickly. (Shoutout to Competitive Programming Handbook ")
Wrap Up & Takeaways
The round ended on a fun note, and I asked him about how PhonePe uses distributed services. He indirectly told
me to get ready for the next rounds.

• Communication is everything: My interviewer didn't know the standard 2-DFS diameter algorithm, so I

had to prove it to him. I kept asking if we were on the same page or if he wanted me to go more in-depth
just to show I was communicating properly.

• CP helps a lot: About 6-7 people in my batch of 10 solved both problems because 5 of us did CP

regularly, making this round relatively easy for us.

• Don't panic about HM routing: A few people were called directly for the HM round after this. Don't worry

if this happens or doesn't happen to you-they often call people for HM out of order just to run interviews
in parallel and save time.
Technical Round 2[16 people appeared] [Duration: ~1 hr]
This round was a rollercoaster. It started with my introduction and an unexpected question about why I built an
Al agent during my Russell Investments internship. I answered it well, but it definitely took me by surprise to get
a resume question in a technical round.
Problem 1: M - Candies (AtCoder DP contest - just look it up and go to the M problem)
I immediately recognized it as a DP problem. I explained the overlapping subproblems and defined my state as
dp[I][k] = dp[i+1][k-j] (where | can be a[i] at max).
I wrote the code, but then he asked me to dry run my O(nk^2) DP. I never dry run DP in Codeforces; I just trust my
transitions. I struggled to do it manually, and when I took too much time, he assumed my approach was incorrect
and wanted to move on. I almost lost hope, but I realized he had the wrong idea of my DP state. I calmly walked
him through my transition, and he agreed it worked. He wanted a prefix-sum optimization (which almost no one
got), but since time was running out, we moved to the next question. (So, make sure your interviewer is extremely
clear with your approach). Honestly, this was the question where I felt that I might be cooked, so I made it clear
to give my best shot. Even though I wasn't able to fill my DP table, I made sure to not stop thinking out loud while
Tilling my DP table up.
Problem 2: Maximum Strong Pair XOR II (LeetCode)
The question asked for the maximum XOR between two numbers with the condition abs(x-y) <= min(x,y).
Assuming x is less than y, I simplified this to y <= 2x. I talked through my thoughts out loud and suggested
running a binary search on the largest y such that y <= 2x, combined with a Trie. The tricky part was checking if
an active bit existed within that specific subarray. I'll be really honest here, I went completely blank after the 2nd
condition was put forth. I made sure to speak my mind out, saying things like "I've solved a similar problem with
BIT trie, "We should take the MSB complement first greedily, so I need a way to check if there exists complement
BIT", so yeah, I was struggling a lot, even then I received no help, so I figured I'm pretty much going to have to
derive from scratch. Seeing I have to do something with complement and I also need to have the valid indexes, I
--- PAGE 4 ---
got the intuition to store the indices directly in the Trie nodes. When checking for a complement bit, I'd just verify
if a valid index existed down that path. He was highly skeptical and did a lot of dry runs with me, but my logic held
up against every single test case. He finally let me treat the Trie as a black box and write the pseudocode. He was
impressed because he hadn't thought of that approach, and I was the only candidate across panels to use it.
Wrap Up
We had 5 minutes left, so we briefly revisited the DP question, and he reassured me my logic was fine. Yet, I could
only fill up half my DP table. At the end of the interview, I asked him how PhonePe handles deadlock
management in transactions.
The interview was way more difficult than round 1, where I had to talk a lot, although it was mostly me talking to
myselt.
Throughout the interview, I got zero hints and felt intimidated a few times, but I managed to convince him on both
approaches. When I asked for feedback, he smiled and told me, "In the HM round, make sure the projects on
your resume are actually built by you and not git cloned. HM Round bacha hai na?"
I knew right then I was moving forward. A lot of candidates got eliminated here because they couldn't solve the
Trie question.

3. HM Round [Around 9 people appeared for this round] [Around 2 hr ]

The HM round started late in the evening with an Engineering Manager at PhonePe. He opened by asking how the
OA was, and I told him I thought it was well-balanced but definitely more difficult than last year's. When he asked
how my day was, I went with, "Tiring but equally exciting" (copied from a senior's past PhonePe interview
experience
This was by far the most exhausting round for me, lasting a solid two hours. I was asked about every single thing
on my resume. He went all the way back to my position in the TPO and my experience at SPTBI from a year ago,
even though I had my recent internship at Russell Investments there. I honestly didn't think a recruiter would go
that far back, so be ready for anything.
To my surprise, he specifically targeted a project that was not my flagship project. I think he did this to check if I
actually knew the details of all my work, or if I had only prepared for the most impressive one. He spent about an
hour just scraping every little detail off my resume, to the point that I can probably recall it word-for-word now.
Guys, please prepare your resume extensively and most importantly, do not bluff.
He also threw in some generic behavioral questions:

• "How did you handle conflicts between teammates in the TPO/committee?"

• "Why did you choose statistics in TPO?"

• "How did you handle a conflict between you and your professor?"

• "What were your key takeaways from Russell Investments?"

Then, he asked if I had any startup ideas. I honestly pitched him an idea I had thought of, and he asked me to
explain the data flow of the startup. (So I guess keep a well-thought-out startup idea handy as a backup plan).
From there, he very smartly turned that conversation into a system design round for an Autopay system. We
discussed my designs, where they would fail, and what the improvements could be. He was discussing
everything in depth, going into things I didn't even know. But again, very smartly, he guided the conversation so
that he made me derive the solution that I thought I built on my own.
--- PAGE 5 ---
The interview ended on a positive note. When he asked if I had any questions, I asked him how PhonePe handles
the tradeoff between consistency and availability, since network partitions are a given. He very calmly and
intelligently explained the answer to me.
Final Results
The day ended with only 9 HM rounds being conducted (3 people had been rejected after Round 1 itself). After
10-15 minutes of internal discussion, they came out and announced the results.
A total of 6 offers were given out:

• 2 Internship + Placement (I+P)

• 4 Internship only (Performance-based PPO)

A small tip that genuinely helped me:
I fed ChatGPT previous PhonePe interview experiences, gave it a detailed prompt to act as an interviewer, and
used Voice Mode to simulate real interviews.
I honestly didn't have much time to prepare before the placement process because I was simultaneously
interning at Russell. Being at a disadvantage compared to many candidates who had more preparation time, I had
to make every hour count. Most of my time went into revising core subjects. I skipped DSA practice during the
final few days and relied almost entirely on GPT mock interviews because they gave me the highest return on my
limited time.
The biggest lesson I learned is that when placements are around the corner, optimizing your time matters more
than trying to do everything.
If you're someone who believes in God, trust His plan, especially during moments of fear, anxiety, or imposter
syndrome. Things have a way of working out if you keep putting in the effort.
Some tips that helped me:

• Do a lot of CP, especially CSES and AtCoder. With online assessments and interviews becoming

increasingly difficult, competitive programming gives you a huge advantage. Participate in contests
regularly. Striver's A2Z Sheet is almost a must. I had completed around 99% of it and marked selected
problems for revision, which made revising much easier.

• Always ask for the constraints first. They often reveal the expected time complexity and help you

converge on the optimal approach much faster.

• Don't stop at DSA. Have a solid understanding of distributed systems, system design, and software

engineering concepts. Show interviewers that you're more than just another CRUD developer. Having at
least one well-built distributed systems project on your resume goes a long way. My engineering
manager was impressed with one of my projects.

• Build projects with a purpose. Whether they solve a real problem or exist purely for learning, there

should be a clear motivation behind why you built them.

• There will be moments when you feel like you've already lost the interview. That's completely normal.

What matters is how you recover and continue thinking clearly instead of giving up mentally.

• Treat the interview as a conversation, not an exam. Keep checking whether you and your interviewer

are on the same page. Ask if they'd like you to go deeper into a particular idea or move on. The best
interviews feel like collaborative problem-solving sessions.
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Give as many mock interviews as you can. ChatGPT works surprisingly well, but if you have access to a

senior or mentor whose level you aspire to reach, that's even better. I was almost certainly not the best
DSA candidate in the process, but I was confident in one thing, that very few people could articulate their
thought process as clearly as I could. That's a skill I'd unknowingly been practicing for months by
discussing problems with friends, letting them solve them first, and then walking them through my
approach. Once everyone reaches a similar level of problem solving, communication is often what
decides who gets the offer.

• Articulation matters just as much as problem-solving, if not more. It doesn't matter how elegant your

solution is if your interviewer can't follow your thought process. Once you reach a certain level, many
candidates have similar DSA ability. What differentiates them is how effectively they communicate their
reasoning.

• For PhonePe specifically, don't over-prioritize core subjects. In my experience, they focused almost

entirely on problem-solving and projects rather than DBMS, OS, CN, or OOP.

• Know every inch of your resume. I was grilled extensively to verify whether I genuinely understood

everything I'd listed. Fortunately, I'd built every project from scratch rather than relying on vibe coding, so
I could confidently answer every question.

• Get enough sleep. It sounds simple, but being mentally fresh has a huge impact on how clearly you think

and communicate during interviews.

• Stop comparing yourself to everyone else. There will always be people who know more than you. At

the end of the day, your preparation, your mindset, and your performance are the only things you can
control. Give it your best, trust the process, and leave the rest to God.
Lastly, please please have trust in god. On my first day at Russell, I was already indirectly given a hint that I
won't be getting a PPO. Even though I was sad initially, I believed god had a plan for me, so yeah it worked
out for me.
In case of any queries / help, feel free to reach out to me.
Phone: 9619143930
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/aaryan-mantri/
Resume at the time of application:

• Aaryan_Mantri Tech_Resume (2).pdf (access using SPIT account)

In case of any further doubts, you can refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.

journey.prep:
1. CP isn't necessary, but it's definitely worth it.

2. Please work on your resume, including formatting. They've seen thousands of resumes, and they

must see a reason why you stand out. Resume can carry you way way ahead in interviews. (speaking
from experience)

3. Try to have some work experience under your belt, even better if you have done something

impressive (in my case for eg, my code was being used by 50+ startups on a daily basis).

4. DSA is a must. Follow striver/neetcode, and solve recent contest questions.

5. InterviewBit for Core prep, and IndiaBix for aptitude is good enough. Please don't make a mistake

like I did. Try to have one project dedicated to OOPS / Java, as interviewers like it. And don't ignore
core subjects, especially OOPS and DBMS. OS, CCN can be done 2-3 days before the interview. I
didn't even touch core subjects, so had my resume and DSA not been good enough, I probably
wouldn't have made it to even round 2.

6. Practise STAR method, most of the candidates lacked communication skills.

7. And lastly, please trust the process and trust God. There will be phases where you'll feel like

you're not improving and that's normal. What matters most is that you don't give up.
In case of any queries, please feel free to connect with me.

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Resume + Behavioural Interview)

1. OA (Probably more than 100 students appeared)

Honestly, I had decided I'll simply mark B for all aptitude questions and try to solve DSA thoroughly. I did
so, but in the DSA questions, I choked a lot. And I passed partial test cases in both ( 1-2 were left in first,
and only 2-3 passed in 2nd). However, I was able to solve them both after the test :p. I did not even expect
that I'll be shortlisted, so I went home and slept for 2.5 hours, and woke up to me being shortlisted (LOL).
Yeah so it was pretty much luck based for me, however, there were a handful of people who were able to
solve both the questions.
Aptitude had probability, combinatorics, ratio and proportion, profit/loss statements. Really really high
weightage of probability and ratio and proportion.
The first question in the DSA part was something like this :
Given an array, you can modify one number in the array such that the overall GCD of the array is as great as
possible.
Sol: Maintain a prefix and suffix GCD, and then at every index, take take ged(prefix[i-1],suffix[i+1]), and select
the maximum among them.
This was the most similar question I could find : Queries for GCD of all numbers of an array except
elements in a given range - GeeksforGeeks
The second question was :
CSES - Ferris Wheel
--- PAGE 2 ---
For OA, try solving 1400-1500s on codeforces, I think that's pretty much all you need. And please solve
aptitude questions, a lot. Aptitude alone could've shortlisted people.
Try maintaining a CGPA > 8 or 8.5, as it will make you eligible for any campus placements very very
comfortably.

2. Round 1 (Tech) [Around 40-50]

I was called in late (after all the other final shortlisted candidates were done with their round 2, I was about
to give my round 1 •°). The interviewer had two panelists, a male senior SWE, and a female app dev.
Both of them immediately recognized one of my projects, because the teammate that I had worked with
had already presented that during this round 1. So they kind of skipped over it. Then they asked me to
introduce myself. Keep it like a brief of your resume, something like this :
Hello, I'm Aaryan Mantri. I'm a third-year Computer Engineering student at Sardar Patel Institute of
Technology, expecting to graduate in May 2027. I'm maintaining a X CGPA (say only if it's high > 8.8) and
I'm deeply passionate about full-stack development and building efficient systems.
[work experience, if any, doesn't really matter as they don't expect much for a summer internship, but it does
help in interviews as you have something to talk about.]
On the project side, I'm particularly proud of [Project]', (explain project, why you made it, what effects it
had, your motivation behind it, and something unique that you did in that project, because look, they've seen
hundreds and thousands of projects, why does your project stand out?].
[Explain some achievements]
Finally, I've taken on several leadership roles. [Explain PORS (1-3 lines per POR)]. These roles have really
helped me develop my communication and leadership skills alongside my technical abilities.
I'm eager to bring this combination of hands-on development experience and leadership to a challenging
new role
Then since my resume was tilted towards a bit of system design, they asked me a question, "If I had to send
an excel with thousands of rows, how do I do iti And I wasn't even aware of such a situation, so I casually
said we can send it in batches/distribute it in a cache. And then we moved towards some DSA.

1. In an array of size N - 1, containing 1-n numbers, one of them is missing, find that number - > classic

XOR trick, but in my case I gave them two approaches, using the XOR trick, and sum of n natural
numbers formula.

2. Given a goal string and an input string, find if we can obtain the goal string by rotating the input

string.
Eg : Goal string = "HELLO"', input string = "LLOHE", output = true.
My approach: assign indexes to the goal string, like H = 1, E=2, ... O = 5, then plot it back to the
input string, so LLOHE becomes 3 4 5 1 2. Then there will only exist an utmost one or such index
where arr[i] > arr[i+1], in this case, only 5 > 1, elsewhere arr[i]<arr[i+1]. But it had a really easy
--- PAGE 3 ---
solution, that is to just concatenate the string and search for substring. They coined my solution as
"Sometimes we tend to over engineer questions" in a joking manner.
After that we moved on to Java, where I was asked some Java questions about constructors, abstract classes
(I failed both of them) and a pass by value vs pass by reference. I was also asked about virtual tables in C++,
which I wasn't aware of.
Then they asked me some puzzle questions
Frog in the Well, Math Puzzles
Tricky Logical Interview Problem | Genius Puzzles
They concluded by asking me if I had any questions for them. NEVER SAY NO HERE. Ask questions that
show your curiosity about the firm/Software Engineering in general.
Some questions :
I asked about

1. Why legacy codebases are not re written into clean and modular code, but are reused again and again

(they said that it's going to be financially expensive)

2. What does a daily scrum look like at Russell (I don't remember their answer)

2. Why is Russell Investments' logo blue in color i ("You'll have to ask that to the digital marketing

team)

3. [Techno HR [ 10-15 people appeared for this round]

Unlike many others, my 2nd round was very comfortable. The interviewer directly started with a DSA
question.
Given a singly LL, re-arrange the LL such that all even nodes come after the odd nodes. Additionally,
odd nodes should be sorted and even nodes must maintain their original order.
Eg: 187342
Sol :137842
Approach: I asked them if there were any additional constraints that I have to follow, to which he
answered that you can't use arrays, you have to use LL. To which I asked if I can use extra LL to store
some nodes, to which he agreed. ALWAYS ASK CLARIFYING QUESTIONS, IT WILL WORK IN
YOUR FAVOUR. Think out loud. I jotted down some steps, and kept asking him for discussions.
Always make the interviewer feel like you're discussing it with him, that's the entire key to cracking
interviews.
I explained my approach to him, which included splitting and storing odd and even valued linked lists
(1 7 3 and 8 4 2). Sort the LL using any sorting algorithm (merge sort + floyd's hare and tortoise
algorithm in my case), and then merge them back. So my question was a leetcode medium DSA
(modification of sort LL and separate LL). It was fairly quick. I explained the pseudo code to him and he
was satisfied with it.
Next, he asked me about lambda functions. I used an example of a DSA question and how I use lambda
--- PAGE 4 ---
functions in competitive programming, and how it has helped me.
He was done asking me questions, and then asked me if I had any questions, I asked him the same
questions I asked in round 1. Additionally, I also asked him if I can get to learn from different teams and
domains like Finance, Legal, Operations, as I may interact with them at Russell, which was a question he
really liked. NEVER ASK AN INTERVIEWER IF HE HAD EVER MESSED UP IN CODE 9.
I had my personal reasons to ask that, but if you want that role, please don't :p. Always ask questions
that make it seem like you're really interested and looking forward to joining the company, while
upholding learning ethics.
6 students were selected for the tech role, and 1 for the research role. I got in for the tech role.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. CP isn't necessary, but it's definitely worth it.

2. Please work on your resume, including formatting. They've seen thousands of resumes, and they

must see a reason why you stand out. Resume can carry you way way ahead in interviews. (speaking
from experience)

3. Try to have some work experience under your belt, even better if you have done something

impressive (in my case for eg, my code was being used by 50+ startups on a daily basis).

4. DSA is a must. Follow striver/neetcode, and solve recent contest questions.

5. InterviewBit for Core prep, and IndiaBix for aptitude is good enough. Please don't make a mistake

like I did. Try to have one project dedicated to OOPS / Java, as interviewers like it. And don't ignore
core subjects, especially OOPS and DBMS. OS, CCN can be done 2-3 days before the interview. I
didn't even touch core subjects, so had my resume and DSA not been good enough, I probably
wouldn't have made it to even round 2.

6. Practise STAR method, most of the candidates lacked communication skills.

7. And lastly, please trust the process and trust God. There will be phases where you'll feel like

you're not improving and that's normal. What matters most is that you don't give up.

Some brief useful tips:

• Maintain a CGPA of 8+ (for Russell Investments) and 8.5+ if possible (might help with other

companies apart from Russell Investments).

• Have at least one project on your resume which stems from an original idea and you have

implemented that original project idea completely by yourself. This will boost your chances to
clear almost all Resume Interviews provided you can explain your original idea and pitch its use
cases nicely to the interviewers). Having hackathon projects or youtube clones on your resume
is good but I believe self-implemented original and authentic ideas/projects shall help you stand
out the most.

• You don't need to be an expert but still try to have intermediate knowledge in OOPS, OS, syntax

etc.

• Lastly, and probably the most important insight, do CP, do CP, do CP. The problem-solving skills

you shall learn here will take you a long way ahead. Had I not done CP, I wouldn't have cleared
all test cases in both the programming questions during the OA. Very very few people < 5 I
believe) cleared both the programming questions during the OA and all of them were consistent
competitive programmers.
Thank you and all the best for your placements.
~ Aaryan Urunkar (+91 7977884919)

1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Resume + Behavioural Interview)

1. Online Assessment [ 100+ candidates appeared for this round]

The online assessment was a 1 hr MCQ + Programming test conducted on the Hackerearth platform.
There were 22 questions in total. 20 MCQs based on maths/logical reasoning and 2 programming
questions. The marks were distributed as follows: 4.00 for an MCQ and 20.00 for a programming
question. The only criteria here to be shortlisted to attend the OA was to have a CGPA >= 8.
The programming questions were of varying difficulty, the first one being a leetcode medium-easy
(Codeforces 1100 level) and the second one being a leetcode medium-hard (Codeforces 1400 level). The
first question required concepts such as sorting, greedy and two pointers. The second question was based
on number theory, prefix and suffix GCD's, and implementation. Very very few people managed to do
both of these questions during the OA.
The MCQs were majorly based on counting and combinatorics + probability. Hence 12th standard
combinatorics knowledge helped a lot here but it would have helped more if I would have brushed up the
concepts.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Interview Round 1[30+ candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted within 2 hours after the OA (approx 20 minutes after the OA results came
out). Since this was my second time giving interviews on campus, I didn't feel very nervous here.
Also, the interviewers were pretty welcoming so that helped me stay calm.
This interview was mainly a tech interview, with the interviewers diving majorly into topics such as
Data Structures, Operating Systems and various programming languages. I was asked a question
about Linked Lists which I couldn't solve. I asked if we could treat the question as a doubly linked
list, and the interviewers agreed. When I explained my approach they seemed satisfied and moved on
to the next question. The interview included a lot of syntax based questions, such as "What is a
struct?", "Difference between structs and objects?", "What does malloc) do?", "What does the
'new' keyword do?", "Write the code for a linked list".
Lastly, my final question included the interviewer testing me on topics like pass by value and pass by
reference. The total interview duration lasted around 20-25 minutes.

3. Interview Round 2[10+ candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted at varying times. For me I had it within 30 minutes after Interview Round
1 but some people had to wait 3-4 hours after Interview Round 1 to give their Interview Round 2.
This was a one-to-one round with the senior Director and felt more of a discussion rather than an
interview.
Initially the Director went through my resume and asked me to describe my best project. I described
my best project and he cross-questioned wherever clarification was needed, and suggested some
potential features and asked how I would implement them. Some extra questions included: "Why
did you decide to choose this particular project idea?", "I understand why this is your best project,
but can you please explain further why this is your most favourite projectiại
The project discussion lasted for 10-15 minutes. Post that the Director moved on to questions on the
more individual-level such as "What are your expectations from your career?"
", "What kind of work
would you like to do?", "How do you deal with frustration?" and a lot more. Honestly speaking, the
only right answer to these questions is to stay humble and answer originally rather than smartly.
In the end, when the Director asked if I had any questions, I asked the Director a few questions
regarding the JD of the role, "why do Russell Investments use the NET technology?" and even
asked the Director about himself, "Why did you decide to stick to the finance industry throughout
your career?". He seemed pretty welcoming and answered all questions in a very lucid and
professional manner.
In the end, 6 students were offered the Tech Intern Role by Russell Investments from among the total 7
shortlisted candidates (1 candidate was offered the Investment Research role).

1. Round 1 - Online Assessment [ 149 candidates appeared for this round]

This was a 45-minute online assessment carrying 100 marks. It consisted of 20 MCQS (worth 50 marks) and
5 SQL queries (worth 10 marks cach). The MCQs focused heavily on object-oriented programming concepts
and included language-specific programming logic questions in C, C++, and Java. It is important to revise
OOP concepts thoroughly and be familiar with the syntax and logic of all three languages. I primarily use
C++, so I was already comfortable with that section. For Java and OOPS, I referred to the PSOOP notes and
PPTs to brush up. The SQL section had one basic query using the WHERE clause, while the others were of
moderate to high difficulty. Knowledge of SQL date functions (like MONTHNAME) and string functions
(like CONCAT) was essential to solve these. Understanding core SQL concepts such as GROUP BY,
HAVING, LIKE, and JOINS is also important. Personally, I found the MCQS manageable and aimed to
solve them quickly and accurately to save time for the SQL queries. Since I hadn't revised string functions
well, I was able to solve only 3 out of the 5 SQL queries. For SQL preparation, I would highly recommend
using
resources
W3Schools
and
Apna
College's
SQL video
YouTube:
https://www.w3schools.com/sql/ and https://youtu.be/hlGoQC332VM?si=tfQubtGhr0SQMkSQ. Overall,
accuracy, speed, and solid revision of both programming concepts and SOL fundamentals are key to
performing well in this round

2. Round 2 -Technical Interview [38 candidates appeared for this round]

Based on the online assessment, 38 students were shortlisted for the interview round. Before the interviews
began, the Barclays team gave us a brief session introducing their culture, core values, and the overall
selection process. Coming to my interview, it started with a basic self-introduction. The interviewer then
asked me about my comfort level with SQL, following which he gave me a schema and asked a few queries
which I solved using SELF JOIN and GROUP BY with the HAVING clause. He then inquired about my
preferred programming language, which was C++. Based on that, I was asked to write a snippet involving
querying data from two nested maps (a map within a map). After this, he asked me conceptual and coding
questions related to Binary Search Trees (BSTs), including writing basic code snippets. The discussion then
moved to the projects section of my resume, where I was asked to briefly explain one of my projects.
Follow-up questions included how I handled security in the project, what the most challenging part was, and
how I approached solving it. The interviewer also gave a few scenario-based questions such as: how I would
ensure effective communication and equal contribution within a team, what I would do if asked to work with
a tech stack I was unfamiliar with, and how I would handle situations where my point of view differed from
--- PAGE 2 ---
my team members'-including whom I would listen to. There were also some questions related to Git,
especially about handling merge conflicts. Finally, the interviewer asked if I had any questions for him. My
interview lasted for about an hour, while some of my peers had interviews that concluded in 30 minutes-

- SO

don't panic whether your interview feels longer or shorter; each panel takes its own time to evaluate. In
summary, this round tested my SQL skills, coding/DSA fundamentals, understanding of my projects, and my
communication and problem-solving approach in team-based scenarios. I would suggest being well-prepared
with a strong self-introduction and at least a couple of meaningful questions to ask the interviewer. Also, it's
crucial to think out loud during problem-solving, even if your answer isn't perfect the interviewer is more
interested in your thought process than just the final solution. One very important thing to keep in mind is
that if you do not know the answer to a particular question, it is absolutely okay to politely say that you
don't know, rather than trying to make up something. Honesty is something Barclays values a lot, and being
transparent reflects positively on you. Confidence, clarity in communication, and showcasing your reasoning
are key to doing well in this round.

3. Round 3 -Technical Interview [19 candidates appeared for this round]

Based on the previous interview round, 19 of us were shortlisted for the second technical interview. This
round was quite similar in nature to the first technical round, again focusing on projects, backend skills,
database knowledge, and DSA. The interview began with the usual "Introduce yourself" question, after
which the interviewer moved straight to the projects section. He asked me which parts of the project I had
implemented personally and requested that I write a function related to the portion I had worked on. Since I
was comfortable with backend development, I wrote a function accordingly. Next, we discussed
databases he asked whether I was comfortable with SQL and NoSQL databases, to which I responded that
I had knowledge of both. He presented three schema diagrams and asked fundamental questions such as
identifying the primary and foreign keys, and which columns could potentially serve as keys. He also asked
a question related to data anomalies, specifically what would happen if an entry with a null foreign key were
inserted into a table. Following this, he gave me a few SQL queries involving JOINS and GROUP BY. The
interview then moved to object-oriented programming he asked how two objects could be compared, and
later inquired about my preferred programming language (which was C++). Based on that, he asked me to
explain the concept of a Doubly Linked List and write a couple of code snippets related to it. Finally, the
interview ended with him asking if I had any questions for him. Overall, this round tested similar skill areas
as the previous technical interview-SQL, programming fundamentals, object-oriented concepts, and depth
of involvement in projects. It was important to demonstrate clarity in thought, accurate understanding of
concepts, and hands-on experience in coding and database handling.
After all the interview rounds, 16 of us were finally selected and got the opportunity to intern at Barclays.

journey.prep:
Firstly this process is very very very tiring and exhausting and was a long one for me. It becomes very hard
to keep studying till the end as sometimes you are unable to get shortlisted even after meeting all the
requirements, clearing the online assessments becomes literally impossible and even after giving your
bestest interviews you don't get selected.
In this process I learnt in 3 months after getting rejected from JPMC twice, Wissen Technologies HR round
and Future First Game Round that your skills don't matter if you don't have luck by your side.
You may feel the interview was great but after realising you weren't shortlisted you will doubt yourself and
that is very much normal and will happen but keeping your composure during this time is important.
If you are from EXTC there are many companies that didn't allow EXTC to sit for placements. Some
companies might allow EXTC students to participate during your placement season, but it's good to be
prepared and start DSA (leetcode and codeforces contests more), Core CS, ML, System Design, etc from the
very beginning as it helps a lot.
Also a tech OA is not necessarily in leetcode format and the questions will also be in story telling so doing
codeforces is a must if you want to clear a proper tech OA. It is extremely important to practice DSA
everyday with different platforms such as HackerEarth (https://www.hackerearth.com/practice/interviews/),
HackerRank, etc. Also practice SQL 50 as it is very important for getting the plus points and making a
difference in the OA

1. Job Opening - 23/09/2026
