1.
Resume Shortlisting [~200 students had applied ]
por [abeersane_colgate.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1TDEOffpqW7fe-CR4uI0baEI9Fz7ofTpu/view?usp=sharing)
The criteria for applying on superset was 6.0 CGPA and class XII & class X was 60%.
Since this was a technical IT role at Colgate-Palmolive, I included a Power BI analytics project and two
Al/ML projects to highlight my analytical, programming, and problem-solving skills. I also emphasized
SQL, Python, databases, and AI tools to align my resume with the JD. I kept it to one page and tailored it for
an ATS score of 80+. Many times the ats doesn't matter as the company selects candidates based on their jd.
Your 12th-grade percentage and CGPA can play a significant role in shortlisting, as many companies have
eligibility criteria such as 80%+ in 12th and an 8+ CGPA but the further shortlisting sometimes might boil
down to 8.5+ CGPA in companies like EDRA Labs, BlackRock, Versor, (added major advantage in JPMC
CIB role too), etc. If you meet these requirements, that can be an advantage. However, at the end of the day,
shortlisting also depends on several factors, and luck plays a huge role in whether your resume gets selected
and it gets random too, but keep going.

2. Online Assessment [~almost everyone]

The OA was in MCQ format having 30 questions, also the test was from home on the AON platform which
is completely proctored
The OA covered DSA (binary trees, sorting algorithms, and Minimum Spanning Tree using Prim's
algorithm), Operating Systems (disk scheduling, CPU scheduling using SJF, and inode structures), and
DBMS (functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, and normalization forms such as 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and
--- PAGE 2 ---
BCNF). It also included Computer Networks, focusing on the OSI model and the Presentation Layer, along
with C++ programming concepts such as destructors, global and local variables, object creation, and output
tracing.

3. Group Discussion [30 students]

3 groups of around 10 candidates were formed, each with a different GD topic. My panel discussed "Does
Al reduce the importance of learning core technical skillsạtopic given on spot) and after a discussion of 15
mins another topic as a surprise was given spot :ồiIs the rise of 10 minute delivery a sustainable thing? Is
the model sustainable?". The GD was offline for around 20 minutes, with one minute to think and note
down points. I started the GD which gave me a very big advantage or the second option could be to
conclude the GD nicely. Starting or concluding the GD is a plus as you catch the panelist's attention quickly.
I got 4-5 opportunities to put forward my points, either continuing the discussion or presenting a positive
counter-argument. We had to find our own opportunities to speak. Be mindful of when to interrupt and when
to let others finish, ensuring your points are relevant and constructive. Being unique is mandatory as you
have to stand out in front of others.

3. Technical Interview [15 students]

From my experiences, one of the most important aspect here is when you are giving the interview, if your
interview is at the end your chances of qualifying are less honestly as they find better candidates towards the
start or the mid but don't lose hope as anything can happen as I was the last person to give the interview.
There were 2 panelists and the interview started with a brief introduction of myself and then they asked me
"how many interviews have I given in the past?, always answer honestly as they get to know if you are
lying. Then they told me to elaborate about a few interviews and what went wrong in the past. After this
there were several questions about my work experience like "what exactly did you do ?", "what was the tech
stack used?", "explain any one of the tech stack in depth(like how you implemented it and some theory
regarding the same)", "what was your contribution in the team?", etc.
They told me to explain the projects in some depth and also how are these projects relevant to the role, why
this tech stack, etc and then they asked me about my main programming language to which I answered Java,
then they told me if your main language is java then why doesn't any of your projects have java ?Here I told
them that I have a project in Java which I used for a hackathon after which they told me elaborate on the
project and asked in depth questions related to the project about the ps, why this database, etc.
Then they asked me some basic tech questions too such asẠỗạtell me the difference between the databases
mentioned in your resume(which were mongodb, postgres sql and mysql) with a example and which project
has which database (also they told me to mention the schema)", "why did you use fastapi in your 2
projects(also some knowledge on pydantic validation and features of fastapi) and why not any other
frameworkẠỊạ etc.
Towards the end of the interview they asked me some HR questions like "where did you implement your
finance and data analysis skills which you have mentioned in the resumeại some questions on
achievements," your strengths and weaknesses", "are you open to learn new tech stacks and are you open
to new roles apart from tech if you were to be selected for a full time roleạẠetc.
We were under the impression that a HR round was going to happen but it did not happen and they left.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I tried to keep the conversation playful, friendly, and positive throughout the interview.
In the end asked them 2 questions:

1. "As you mentioned in the pre placement talk that you have an experience of 14 years and roles keep

changing after 2-3 years, so how hard is it to switch from a X role to a Y role with different tech stacks?ại

2. "How does a candidate excel as an intern being different from others ?"

At around 3.00 pm the results were announced, 8 out of 15 students were offered the internship.

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA) - The first round was an online assessment. There was no

resume-based shortlisting before the OA, so eligible students could directly appear for the test.

Round 2: Interview - Candidates who cleared the OA were shortlisted for the interview round.

Result - After the interview, the final selection results were announced.

1. Online Assessment (OA) - 250 Candidates

The test had a duration of 3 hours and consisted of 4 questions. The questions were designed to test
problem-solving and coding ability, and candidates had to manage their time carefully across all four
questions.
Question 1 - Maximum Number of Balanced Substrings [EASY]
One of the relatively easier questions was based on a binary string consisting only of 0 and 1.
We had to divide the entire string into a maximum number of contiguous substrings such that:

1. Every substring must be balanced, i.e., it must contain an equal number of Os and 1s.

2. The substrings must follow an alternating boundary condition. If one substring ends with 0, the next

substring must start with 1, and vice versa.

3. The complete string has to be divided into such substrings. We cannot leave any characters unused.

4. If it is not possible to divide the complete string according to these conditions, we return - 1.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/problems/split-the-binary-string-into-substrings-with-equal-number-of-0s-an
d-1s/1
[not completely same in oa there was one more extra condition as i have mentioned]
--- PAGE 2 ---
Question 2 - Minimum Cost Path With At Most K Turns [MEDIUM]
https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-cost-path-with-at-most-k-turns/description/
Question 3 - DP: Making an Array Non-Decreasing [HARD]
Given an array, modify its elements to make it non-decreasing with minimum cost. Changing a value × to y
costs | ×-Y|. The problem requires finding the minimum total modification cost using DP.
https://leetcode.com/problems/make-array-non-decreasing-or-non-increasing/description/
[similar with the variation using only increasing version]
Question 4 - Complex DP Problem [Complex]
I don't remember the exact problem statement now. It was a complex Dynamic Programming problem and
was quite lengthy to read and understand. Considering there were already three other questions to work
through within the given time, I felt that spending too much time on this question would not be the best use
of the remaining time.
MY Personal Story of OA:
This OA was a little personal for me because I had already appeared for HackWithInfy earlier, and during
that OA I was quite nervous. There were questions where I could recognize the pattern and even knew the
possible approach, but I wasn't able to execute them completely under pressure. I ended up solving only
around 1.5 questions.
This time, when I sat for the Infosys campus OA, I decided to forget about that experience and just focus on
the test in front of me. I went in with a simple mindset: solve what I can, don't panic, and keep moving.
The first question looked fairly easy. I immediately thought of a greedy approach and started building the
logic. I spent around 20-25 minutes on it, but although my code passed some test cases, it wasn't
completely correct. Instead of getting stuck there, I decided to move on.
The second question was a DP problem, and initially it felt quite natural. I identified the states, thought
about the recursion and memoization, and implemented my approach. The sample test cases were passing,
but the hidden test cases failed. I spent around 30 minutes trying to figure out what I was missing. At this
point, around 1 hour and 15 minutes had already passed, and I started feeling a little panicked.
I took a moment, composed myself, and moved to the third question.
The third question was the hardest one, but somehow it clicked for me. I recognized that it could be solved
using recursion with a loop over possible choices, followed by memoization. I did a small dry run to
understand the states, wrote the recurrence, memoized it, and submitted.
And it passed all the test cases.
I remember feeling genuinely confident at that moment. The question that looked harder than the first two
had actually worked out for me in around 15 minutes. That gave me the confidence to continue rather than
worry about the questions I had struggled with earlier.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I then looked at the fourth question, but it was quite lengthy and complex. With the time available, I felt that
going after it from scratch would not be the best decision. Instead, I went back to the first question and tried
to identify the issue in my earlier approach. I was able to solve it in around 20 minutes.
With roughly 40 minutes remaining, I returned to the second question. I tried to fix my DP solution, but
unfortunately, I could only get some of the test cases to pass before the time ran out.
I finally submitted the OA with:

• 1 Easy question - completely solved

• 1 Hard question - completely solved

• 1 Medium question - partially solved

• 1 Complex DP question - not attempted

So overall, I managed to solve around 2.5 questions in terms of completion.
What I learned from the OA
For me, the biggest takeaway wasn't really about the number of questions I solved. It was about not letting
an earlier bad experience decide how I would perform this time.
In my previous OA, nervousness affected my ability to execute approaches that I actually knew. This time, I
still got stuck, I still had wrong submissions, and I still couldn't solve everything but I didn't let that stop
me. I moved between questions, came back to them when appropriate, and eventually cracked the question I
initially found the hardest.
Don't judge your performance in the first hour of an OA. One question clicking at the right time can
completely change your confidence.
PS: I had solved around 1,000 LeetCode problems by this point, but this OA still humbled me. I knew the
concepts, yet I made mistakes, got stuck, and had to make decisions under pressure. It reminded me that
DSA preparation is not just about the number of problems you solve. It is also about staying calm enough
to use what you already know when the clock is running.
Shortlisting for the Interview Round
After the OA, candidates were shortlisted for different interview processes based on their
performance in the assessment.
Students who solved around 1.5 questions were shortlisted for the Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE)
interview process, while students who solved 2 or more questions were shortlisted for the Specialist
Programmer (SP) interview process.
The exact level of the Specialist Programmer role (L1, L2, or L3) was not communicated to us during
the shortlisting or interview process.
--- PAGE 4 ---

2. [Offline INTERVIEWI [4 for SP/ 10 for DSE]

The interview was probably the most interesting part of the entire process for me. The interviewer had two
DSA questions ready on his laptop, and I was given around 45 minutes to solve any one of them.
I entered the room expecting a fairly serious start, but the interviewer first had a casual conversation with
me. He asked me about the best colleges in Mumbai and how I would rank colleges across Maharashtra. He
was from Bangalore and we ended up having a genuinely fun conversation. Looking back, I think this
helped me become comfortable before the actual technical discussion began.
Then, without even a formal introduction, he handed me the laptop and said to choose one of the two
questions and solve it.
DSA
Both questions were based on Dynamic Programming. I chose one which was similar in pattern to Matrix
Chain Multiplication.
I spent some time understanding the problem, writing down an example, and doing a dry run of my
approach. After around 15 minutes, the interviewer asked me about my progress. I hadn't written any code
yetI had only worked out the approach.
He then asked me to explain the problem and my approach. I explained the recurrence and my reasoning,
and he seemed satisfied with it. He then asked me:
"It will take you another 10-20 minutes to code it, right?"
I said yes and asked if I could continue coding.
He replied:
"Okay, let it be. We will continue with the technical interview."
And I remember thinking, "Ummmm... okay."
That was a good reminder that an interview isn't necessarily about completing every problem. The
interviewer had already understood that I knew how to approach the problem, so he decided to move on and
evaluate other areas.
Data Structures & Problem Solving
He then started asking me practical questions involving data structures.
For example:

• If you had to find the top K trending videos on You Tube, what would you use?

• If you wanted to add and remove songs from both the beginning and end of a Spotify playlist, what

data structure would you use?

• Questions involving priority-queue, deque, map, stack, etc.

--- PAGE 5 ---

• How would you find a particular number as quickly as possible if you were given 1 million

numbers?

• Standard time complexities of commonly used data structures and operations.

For the million-number question, I initially explained that if the numbers were sorted, I could use binary
search in O(log n), while searching an unsorted array would take O(n). He then clarified that he hadn't
asked me to store the numbers in a vector.
I then considered alternatives such as a map / binary search tree-based structure, depending on the
requirements.
The interviewer kept changing the conditions and asking follow-up questions rather than simply asking
textbook questions. This made the discussion much more conversational.
DBMS - The Deep Dive
After that, he asked me which CS fundamentals I had studied and told me to give them in my preferred
order.
I said:
DBMS → OOP → OS → CN
He started with DBMS, and this became the longest technical discussion of the interview. It went on for
almost 30 minutes, starting from basic concepts and gradually becoming much more advanced.
Some of the questions/topics he covered were:

• Normalization and denormalization

• Types of relationships in DBMS

• DELETE vs TRUNCATE

• Database indexes

• SQL joins

• ACID properties

• UNION vs UNION ALL

• Shared and exclusive locks

• Different types of database locks

• B-Tree and B+ Tree

• Hashing in databases

• Data partitioning

• Partitioning vs sharding

• CAP theorem

• Partition tolerance and real-world examples

• Database replication

• Dense vs sparse indexes

• SQL vs NoSQL

• Hashing vs encryption

--- PAGE 6 ---
The interviewer particularly deep-dived into hashing and CAP theorem, asking several follow-up
questions and real-world scenarios.
This was probably the part of the interview where I felt the most confident. I was able to answer every
question he asked, and at no point did I feel completely blank. He kept going deeper until I reached
something I genuinely didn't know.
What made the discussion interesting was that it wasn't just:
"Define this."
It was more like:
"Okay, but why?"
"Where would you use it?"
"What happens in this situation?"
"Give me a real-world example."
So understanding concepts was much more useful than simply memorizing definitions.
Electronics & Communication Background
Since my branch is Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering, he also asked me about the core
subjects I had studied.
I mentioned:

• Control Systems

• Digital Signal Processing

• Mathematics

He asked me some general questions around Laplace and Fourier transforms, including their equations
and basic applications.
This wasn't really a separate interrogation- it felt more like a conversation around the subjects I had studied,
and he expected me to remember the fundamentals despite moving towards software.
Computer Networks
We then moved to Computer Networks. Some of the topics discussed were:

• TCP vs UDP

• Authentication vs Authorization

• JWT

• Access tokens

• Refresh tokens

• DNS

• Proxy servers

• How an API request works end-to-end

--- PAGE 7 ---
Again, the questions were connected to practical implementations rather than just definitions.
Projects
Towards the end, we discussed my projects.
He asked me to explain one of my projects and draw its architecture. We then spent around 15-20
minutes discussing the project, including why I had designed it that way and questions around the
individual components.
I was able to explain the project and answer his questions, and he seemed satisfied with the discussion.
Finally, he asked if I had any questions for him.
I asked him about the kind of engineering problems and work engineers get to work on at Infosys. We had a
short discussion about that, after which I thanked him, shook his hand, and left the room.
A Few Honest Points About the Interview
I also want to mention a few things where I didn't perform perfectly, because I think these are equally
important for someone reading this experience.
In the Data Structure implementing questions, I was able to reach the correct approach, but I did need
hints and direction from the interviewer at certain points. I was able to build on those hints and explain
my reasoning, but I don't want to give the impression that I independently solved everything from scratch.
The important thing for me was that once I received a hint, I was able to understand it, incorporate it into my
approach, and move forward.
I also wasn't equally strong in Computer Networks. There were a few questions where I couldn't give
satisfactory answers or wasn't completely confident about the concepts. This was probably the area where I
felt I could have prepared better.
Apart from that, the rest of the interview went quite smoothly. The DBMS discussion in particular was long
and challenging, but I was comfortable with the concepts and was able to answer the questions and
follow-up questions. The project discussion also went well because I was able to explain the architecture and
the decisions behind it.
The Result
After the interview, there was obviously a lot of uncertainty. Even though I felt the interview had gone well
overall, I knew there were places where I had needed hints and places where I hadn't been able to answer,
especially in Computer Networks. So I didn't want to assume anything.
When the results were finally announced, I found out that I had been selected for the Specialist
Programmer L1 role.
There were two final selections from our SP/DSE interview group-I was selected for the SP L1 role,
and another student was selected for the DSE role.
Getting that result felt really special, especially considering how the process had started for me.
--- PAGE 8 ---
I had already experienced an OA through HackWithInfy where nervousness got the better of me. I had
walked into this OA with that memory in the back of my mind, but this time I consciously tried not to let it
affect me. Even during the OA, I had failed test cases on questions I thought I could solve, got stuck, and
had to change my strategy. But I kept going and eventually managed to solve the hard DP question
completely.
Then, in the interview, I couldn't finish the coding problem either. I needed hints in DSA, couldn't answer
some Computer Networks questions, and definitely wasn't perfect.
And yet, the overall process worked out.
That was probably the biggest lesson I took from the entire experience: you don't need to have a perfect
performance to get through a placement process. You need to keep yourself composed, be honest when
you don't know something, make the most of the things you do know, and keep thinking when the situation
doesn't go exactly as planned.
I feel grateful for the opportunity and, more importantly, for everything the process taught me. Looking
back, there are definitely things I would prepare differently especially Computer Networks and handling
DSA problems more independently during interviews. But I wouldn't change the fact that I went into the
process despite my previous nervous experience and simply gave it my best.
For anyone reading this who is preparing for placements: don't wait until you feel completely ready.
Prepare seriously, yes-but when the opportunity comes, go for it. Even if you make mistakes along
the way, you might surprise yourself with how far you can go.

journey.howSecured:
Important Dates

• Round 1 (Executive Summary): 4th - 11th June

• Round 2 (In-Person Presentation): 22nd June

• Round 3 (Hackathon): 3rd - 4th July

ROUND 1- Executive Summary

This is the preliminary round. You are given the problem statement and then expected to prepare a summary
document that explains what you understood about the problem and a brief explanation of your proposed
solution. The summary had to include sections such as:

• About Us

• Brief Understanding of the Problem Statement

• Proposed Solution

• Dependencies and Tech Stack

Our problem statement was about improving financial access for underprivileged people. Since everyone has
access to LLMs today, most teams end up proposing very similar solutions - websites, apps, chatbots. We
stood out by building on WhatsApp instead, since it's an app already used by millions across India and needs
no separate download or onboarding. That single decision became our biggest differentiator through every
round. Keep the summary crisp and well-structured. We also included a rough architecture diagram and a UI
mockup of the WhatsApp conversation flow, which I think helped the panel visualize the solution instead of
just reading about it.
Try and include architecture diagrams, UI mockups or any other visual references as they won't spend much
time on each document so you need to leave an impression in their minds and better present/convey your
solution.
--- PAGE 2 ---

ROUND 2: Presentation Pitch

26 teams were selected from our college for this round. We were required to prepare a presentation and pitch
it to the Nomura panel at our college. The format consisted of a 10-minute presentation followed by a
5-minute Q&A session. (The timings are quite strict so adhere to the time limit)
I would say this is actually the most important round out of all(even the final hackathon included) as this
round will set the entire tone for the final hackathon.
Keep the ppt around 10 slides and try to use as minimal text as possible. Judges won't spend time reading
your slides. Keep descriptive images in the slides if possible for eg we kept user journeys of various
intended users that showed not only the different users the solution was meant for but also highlighted the
different features that were there instead of making a text heavy slide for features.
Make sure to keep highlighting your key Point Of Difference, you should have no more than 1-2 POD that
would stick in the minds of not only the judges that are there on the panel of presentation but also the
buddies and mentors that would be present on the day of the hackathon. For us we were the "WhatsApp
Team" of the hack and every buddy present on the hack knew about our idea, they might not have
remembered our team name but knew what we were doing and came and interacted with us on the final day.
Lastly, don't try to pressure yourself to give a perfect pitch as things are bound to go wrong, be flexible,
know your idea thoroughly and don't wing the answer to a question with anything that you can't back.

ROUND 3: Final Hackathon

7 teams were shortlisted from our college and around 31 teams participated in the hackathon overall
This was probably the most memorable and exciting round.
The hackathon was held on 3rd and 4th July. We were asked to visit the Nomura office on 2nd July for tech
setup. Pick-up and Drop-off for all three days are provided by Nomura.
You'd be working on a remote desktop setup by nomura and would be asked to install all the requirements
on the setup day. But for us due to some errors we were allowed to install dependencies even during the
coding sprints. For this I'd recommend implementing 80-90% of your idea in the time you'd have before the
hackathon days. This would give you a better idea as to how to structure your workflow, what dependencies
are needed and most importantly what all errors you might face. Try and not use socket programing if
possible and if doing try and do it with free tier ngrok as that was the only thing that was working.
Each team will be assigned a buddy and a mentor, the buddy might be exclusive or common between teams
and the mentor had 4-5 teams under him. The buddy will be with you at all times and help you with anything
you need from refreshments to technical error, they won't help you solve code errors though. You will see
the mentor at only 3 instances, 1st would be at your 1st evaluation which would be around dinner time(make
sure to check the event planner that would be there to see exact times or ask the buddy). Here most teams
might be ahead of you which was the case with us too and we were panicking a bit, but make sure to explain
your idea properly to the mentor, the mentor may or may not be technically inclined so make sure to see to
that and answer accordingly and again don't make promises that you can't keep. Then the 2nd time would be
after the coding sprints are over again an evaluation would be done before the final presentations, and if you
are able to achieve everything that you told your mentor it would leave a great impression.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After the 2nd evaluation final presentation would start. The no. of panelists varies; it can be 5-8. There were
8 people in our panel,3 buddies, our mentor, 3 judges and even the CIO of Nomura Services India. If there are
more people in your panel don't panic, this actually means more people are interested in your idea, be calm,
present properly and answer the questions. If asked about a feature that you haven't implemented, address it
dont try to fake it, give an explanation as to how you could incorporate it in the project in the future. The
judges are not only accessing what you have built but also what your idea could become and how much of it
can be done by you.
In the end, be confident in your idea, don't try to show more than what you can actually implement and
enjoy the event as much as you can. Our team was arguably the most relaxed team there and we finished our
prototype 6-7 hrs before the coding time actually ended and still managed to win the hackathon, so don't
think that you need to make something complex and code for 24 hrs to win, your idea matters and the way
you plan and execute it matters.

journey.prep:
1. Prioritize Java preparation. Java is the most important subject throughout the

recruitment process. Focus on OOP, Strings, Collections, Exception Handling,
Multithreading, Streams, and commonly asked output-based questions.

2. Practice Java and Python MCQs from Sanfoundry. The Java MCQs are very similar

in style to the OA, and the Python section is excellent for revising concepts like MRO,
classes, dictionaries, sets, and tuples.

3. Create a quick revision quiz. If you're short on time, use Claude or another LLM to

generate an HTML quiz covering Java and Python concepts. This was one of the most
effective revision methods for me.

4. Revise SQL and Aptitude. Go through aggregate functions, basic SQL queries, joins,

and practice quantitative aptitude from platforms like IndiaBIX, especially topics such as
Time & Distance, Profit & Loss, Mixtures, Boats & Streams, and logical puzzles.

5. Practice Java coding syntax. Knowing the concepts alone is not enough-practice

writing Java code without an IDE. I occasionally mixed C++ syntax with Java, and
improving this would have made my interview smoother.

6. Know your resume thoroughly. Be prepared to explain every project, internship, and

technology mentioned on your resume. Interviewers often focus on your design decisions
and the reasoning behind your choices rather than just implementation details.

7. Stay calm and communicate your thought process. Your interview slot does not affect

your chances of selection-I was among the last candidates interviewed. Don't panic if
the interviewer has a neutral expression; explain your reasoning clearly, be honest if you
don't know something. Communication is the key...
journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of an initial resume shortlisting stage, followed by three
evaluation rounds: an Online Assessment (OA), a Technical Interview, and a combined
Techno-HR Interview. Throughout the interview process, the company placed a strong emphasis
on Java, and candidates were expected to demonstrate a solid understanding of Java
fundamentals, object-oriented programming, collections, multithreading, and related concepts.
So u need a strong hold over Java to clear this company
1.
[Online Assessment] [214 students were shortlisted]
The Online Assessment was the first elimination round after resume shortlisting. The company
was fairly lenient during the resume screening stage, and almost everyone who applied through
the campus recruitment process was shortlisted for the OA.
The assessment consisted of five sections and had negative marking:

• Java: 15 multiple-choice questions

• Python: 15 multiple-choice questions

• SQL: 3 multiple-choice questions

• AI: 10 multiple-choice questions

• Quantitative Aptitude & Logical Reasoning: 25 questions

There was sufficient time to complete the assessment, and time management was generally not
an issue.
Java Section (15 Questions)
--- PAGE 2 ---
Most questions were output-based and some of them were conceptually related to Java heap
memory. Some of the major topics covered included:

• String immutability

• Heap memory and object creation

• Object-Oriented Programming (inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, encapsulation)

• Java Collections Framework

• Java Streams API

• Exception handling

There were also conceptual questions on the Collections Framework, such as: What does
Collectors.groupingByO return? Map<K, List<T>
Python Section (15 Questions)
The questions primarily covered: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming, Method
Resolution Order (MRO), Multiple inheritance, Tuples, Sets, Dictionaries, List operations, Basic
Python built-in functions Many questions tested conceptual understanding rather than requiring
code writing. To prepare, I generated a large HTML-based quiz using Claude covering all these
Python concepts and repeatedly practiced those questions. If you're short on time, creating or
using such topic-wise quizzes is a very efficient revision strategy.
SQL Section (3 Questions)
The SQL section was straightforward. Questions covered: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM,
AVG, MAX, MIN), Basic SELECT queries, GROUP BY and Simple filtering conditions Since
all questions were multiple-choice, option elimination made this section quite manageable.
AI Section (10 Questions)
This was a relatively new section introduced in the assessment. The questions were not about AI
algorithms or machine learning theory. Instead, they presented Al-generated responses involving
Java, Python, or SQL and asked candidates to determine whether the generated answer was
correct or identify the correct alternative. The primary challenge in this section was not the
difficulty but the length of the questions. Reading each scenario carefully took a significant
amount of time.
Aptitude (25 Questions)
I personally found this to be the easiest section. Every standard questions were asked in this
section and few gfg puzzles were asked.... The only puzzles that I found particularly challenging
were: The 100 Prisoners Puzzle and The Nim Game Puzzle Apart from those, I was able to
solve nearly all the questions. I attempted 23 out of the 25 questions in this section.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Candidates with a decent aptitude background should be able to score well here.
[Technical Round] [ 44 candidates appeared]
Candidates who cleared the Online Assessment were shortlisted for the first interview round,
which was a dedicated Technical Interview. By the time my turn came, I was the last candidate
waiting outside the interview room. Nearly four to five candidates had already completed not
only their Technical Interview but had also finished their subsequent Techno-HR round.
One thing I would like to emphasize is that the order in which you are interviewed does not
affect your chances of selection. Even if you are among the last candidates, stay calm and
remain confident. My interview panel was progressing slowly, and despite being the last
candidate, I had a very positive interview experience. The interviewer maintained a completely
expressionless face throughout the interview, which initially felt intimidating. However, I later
realized that this was simply his interviewing style. Do not try to judge your performance based
on the interviewer's facial expressions they often deliberately avoid giving any hints about
whether your answers are correct.
The interview immediately began with Java and remained heavily focused on it. Although Java
is not my primary programming language (I am more comfortable with C++), I had revised the
fundamentals beforehand. From my discussions with other candidates, I found that if someone
was uncomfortable with Java, the interviewer was sometimes willing to switch to Python.
However, if you mention Java on your resume or claim familiarity with it, be prepared for
detailed questioning.
It started with What is an immutable class? Is String an immutable class? Why? The interviewer
System. out.println(s); I explained that the output would still be: Hello because String objects are
immutable and replace returns a new String rather than modifying the original object. He then
asked how I would make it print "World". I answered that the returned string should be
reassigned: s = s.replace("Hello", "World");
The discussion then moved to object comparison. The interviewer asked me to explain the
difference between: = and equals He provided a scenario involving a Student class containing
fields such as id and name and asked how I would override the equals method so that two
student objects could be compared logically rather than by reference. As a follow-up, he also
asked me to list some commonly used methods present in Java's Object class, such as equals,
hashCode, toStringO, getClass and what each method does..
Then we discussed about exception handling. What is difference between error and exception He
wrote a snippet of code where IO exception was caught after normal exception and asked to find
mistake in the snippet. Then we asked abt why general exceptions are caught later than specific
--- PAGE 4 ---
ones. He asked about the purpose of the finally block and when it executes. Additionally also
asked me to write a custom error class
I was asked to explain ArrayList and then solve a problem involving removing elements while
iterating through the list. I initially mentioned removing elements directly, but then discussed
why doing so causes a ConcurrentModificationException. I wrote the solution using an Iterator,
which safely removes elements during iteration. Although I occasionally made syntax mistakes
because Java is not my strongest language, I clearly explained the underlying concepts, which
the interviewer appreciated.
Then we moved onto SQL vs Nosql discussion CAP theorem and ACID properties..The
interviewer next asked me to write a Java thread using the Runnable interface. This naturally led
to several operating system questions, including Thread vs Process, Deadlocks and conditions
I was then given a simple coding problem: Find the frequency of every word in a given sentence.
I solved it by using a HashMap<String, Integer> to count the occurrences of each word. The
interviewer was more interested in my approach than in the exact syntax Surprisingly I wasn't
asked much on my resume..Some of my friends were asked about Rest APIs and basic Spring
questions as well..
[Techno -HR Round! [22 candidates appeared]
The final round was a Techno-HR interview, but don't mistake it for a purely HR round. Along
with behavioral questions, the interviewer also discussed my resume and one of my projects in
detail. The interview started with a brief self-introduction, followed by questions about where I
stay and whether I would be comfortable travelling from Mulund to the Goregaon office five
days a week. I was prepared for this and explained that I had been travelling a similar distance to
college almost every day for the past three years, so commuting would not be an issue.
I was then asked why I wanted to join ISS. I connected my answer to my interest in the fintech
domain and mentioned that, along with my engineering degree, I was also pursuing a Minor in
Management from SPJIMR, making the role a good fit for my long-term career goals. The
interviewer also asked which other companies I had applied to and why I wasn't selected. I
mentioned companies like UBS, Nomura, IDFC FIRST Bank, and J.P. Morgan, and explained
that every rejection helped me identify areas for improvement and motivated me to upskill
further. Another question was whether I would still join the company if I did not initially get my
preferred role, to which I replied that learning and growth within a good organization were more
important than the initial role.
The interviewer also asked about my hobbies. Since I mentioned football, there were a few
follow-up questions about recent matches and tournament results. I was then asked to describe an
--- PAGE 5 ---
incident that demonstrated accountability, where I shared an example of taking ownership of a
project task and ensuring it was completed successfully.
Towards the end, the interviewer randomly picked one of my projects from my resume instead of
letting me choose. The discussion focused much more on the design decisions than on technical
implementation. I was asked why I chose a particular architecture, why I selected certain
technologies, and what alternatives I had considered. One thing that worked well for me was
highlighting the initiative I had taken during the project rather than simply explaining what I had
built. Overall, my advice would be to prepare a good introduction, have a convincing answer for
"Why ISS?", revise every project on your resume thoroughly, and be ready with examples that
demonstrate accountability, ownership, and initiative.
[12 students were offered the job However later on 3 more students were added to the list...]

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Prioritize Java preparation. Java is the most important subject throughout the

recruitment process. Focus on OOP, Strings, Collections, Exception Handling,
Multithreading, Streams, and commonly asked output-based questions.

2. Practice Java and Python MCQs from Sanfoundry. The Java MCQs are very similar

in style to the OA, and the Python section is excellent for revising concepts like MRO,
classes, dictionaries, sets, and tuples.

3. Create a quick revision quiz. If you're short on time, use Claude or another LLM to

generate an HTML quiz covering Java and Python concepts. This was one of the most
effective revision methods for me.

4. Revise SQL and Aptitude. Go through aggregate functions, basic SQL queries, joins,

and practice quantitative aptitude from platforms like IndiaBIX, especially topics such as
Time & Distance, Profit & Loss, Mixtures, Boats & Streams, and logical puzzles.

5. Practice Java coding syntax. Knowing the concepts alone is not enough-practice

writing Java code without an IDE. I occasionally mixed C++ syntax with Java, and
improving this would have made my interview smoother.

6. Know your resume thoroughly. Be prepared to explain every project, internship, and

technology mentioned on your resume. Interviewers often focus on your design decisions
and the reasoning behind your choices rather than just implementation details.

7. Stay calm and communicate your thought process. Your interview slot does not affect

your chances of selection-I was among the last candidates interviewed. Don't panic if
the interviewer has a neutral expression; explain your reasoning clearly, be honest if you
don't know something. Communication is the key...

The placement process began with a Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), where the company introduced InCred
Finance, its business, the role being offered, and the kind of work expected from candidates. I would
strongly recommend paying close attention during this session, as it gives a clear idea of what the company
values and the type of problems they solve. Make note of any interesting points or initiatives that stand out,
as these can be useful during the interviews.
After the PPT, I went through InCred's website to understand their products, services, and business model in
more detail. It is helpful to know what the company does, how it operates, and how technology and analytics
are used within the organisation. If possible, also explore any blogs, articles, or technical resources related to
the company, as they provide additional context and can help you answer company-specific questions
confidently

1. Resume Shortlisting [ No of candidates -> ~250]

The next stage was the resume shortlisting process, which took place on 21st July. I personally did not make
any changes to my resume specifically for this role, as it already reflected my interests in Al and Machine
Learning. However, looking back, I believe there are a few things that can significantly strengthen a resume
for this role.
I would recommend having at least one strong project based on classical machine learning, such as
classification or regression models. Along with that, having projects in deep learning and Generative Al
application creates a well-rounded profile. In my case, my projects covered classical machine learning,
deep learning, and Generative Al, which demonstrated exposure to different areas of Al.
Another important aspect is having at least one meaningful internship experience. It does not necessarily
have to be in the exact same domain, but it should clearly demonstrate problem-solving skills and practical
industry experience.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Before submitting your resume, I also suggest checking it on Resume Worded and aiming for an ATS score
of 80 or above. While this is not a guarantee of selection, it helps ensure that the resume follows good
formatting and includes relevant keywords.
Finally, the most important point is that every project listed on your resume should be something you can
explain in depth. Be prepared to discuss your approach, the technologies used, the challenges you faced, and
the reasoning behind your decisions, as interviewers may ask detailed questions about any project you
mention.
Shortlisted Resume:
= [AnuraagBagal_data.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CRfgQ71mKfqX2-fW-wbfHCiMmA9qpdHH/view?usp=sharing)
2.
Pen-Paper Test [No of candidates -> 116] {75 mins}
Section 1: Aptitude (8 Questions, +3/-1)
Topics Included:

• Coordinate Geometry (Line & Curve Equations)

• Speed, Time & Distance

• Time & Work

• Number Systems

• General IndiaBIX-style aptitude questions

Difficulty: Easy to Moderate
My Attempt: Attempted 6 out of 8 questions to maintain good accuracy because of the negative marking.
Preparation Advice:

• Practice aptitude questions from IndiaBIX regularly.

• Accuracy is more important than attempting every question.

• Coordinate Geometry, Speed-Time-Distance, Work-Time and Number Systems were the major topics

asked

• If you finish the IndiaBIX questions, generate similar aptitude questions using ChatGPT or practice

from GeeksforGeeks.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Section 2: Technical (12 Marks, No Negative Marking)
Python Pseudo-code (4 Marks)
The Python section mainly tested logical reasoning through pseudocode and number pattern recognition.
Questions:
Predict the sum of a series (1 Mark)
Example:
3, 6, 15, 24, ...
Pattern:
n' + 2n
Predict the sum of the sequence (3 Marks)
Example:
2, 9, 28, 65, 126,...
Pattern:
n3 + 1
Preparation Advice:

• Be comfortable reading Python pseudocode.

• Revise loops, conditions and basic functions.

• Practice common quadratic and cubic number patterns.

SQL (8 Marks)
The SQL section consisted of multiple related tables followed by four SQL queries.
Tables: Salesperson, Regions, Quadrants
Questions Asked:

• Find Avg/Max/Min sales for each salesperson.

• Find the second-highest sale in every region.

• Rank regions based on average sales.

• Find salespersons who did not make a sale in their assigned region/quadrant.

--- PAGE 4 ---
Preparation Advice:

• Complete LeetCode SQL 50 thoroughly.

• Focus on JOINs, GROUP BY, HAVING, Window Functions, Aggregate Functions and Subqueries.

• If you find yourself weak in any SQL topic, generate similar tables and SQL questions using

ChatGPT and practice until you become comfortable with that concept.
Overall Preparation Advice

• SQL is the most important part of the written test, so prepare it thoroughly.

• Practice IndiaBIX aptitude questions to improve both speed and accuracy.

• For Python, focus on understanding pseudocode and number patterns rather than advanced

programming.

• Don't get stuck on one question. Move ahead and return later if time permits.

• From my experience, the test appeared to have a section-wise cutoff, so try to perform consistently in

both sections instead of relying on just one.

3. Interview Round 1 [No of candidates -> 29] {40 mins}

The first interview was a mix of technical and business-oriented questions. Based on previous interview
experiences, I was expecting the discussion to be largely technical, so I had primarily prepared my resume,
projects, and machine learning concepts. However, the interview turned out to be quite different from what I
had anticipated.
The interview began with my introduction. During my introduction, I mentioned my hackathon project,
which naturally led the interviewer to ask about it in detail. She asked several questions related to the
project, including:

• Why I chose the particular machine learning model.

• The features that were engineered.

• The evaluation metrics used.

• The meaning of AUC-ROC and F1-score.

• Why LightGBM was selected and how it was implemented.

This technical discussion lasted for less than 10 minutes. After that, the interviewer kept my resume aside
and shifted entirely towards business case studies and guesstimates.
The first case study involved a D-Mart store, where the ground floor generated 80% of the revenue while
the first floor generated 20%. I was asked how I would increase the first floor's contribution to 30%. I
--- PAGE 5 ---
started by structuring the problem and proposing one possible solution. The interviewer then asked me to
come up with another completely different approach. Since I had not practised many case studies
beforehand, I struggled to think of an alternative framework and was unable to expand beyond my initial
idea.
The second case study was about deciding where to open a new Starbucks outlet in Mumbai. My initial
approach was customer-centric, where I segmented the population based on purchasing power, footfall, and
the target demographic. The interviewer again asked me for another approach. After thinking for some time,
I requested a hint, following which she suggested considering geography. I then divided Mumbai into
different regions and discussed factors such as commercial areas, workplaces, accessibility, and customer
concentration while deciding the ideal location.
The next question was a guesstimate: Estimate the number of toasters sold in Mumbai every month.
I approached it using a structured estimation framework by making reasonable assumptions and calculating
the final estimate. The interviewer then asked me to solve the same problem using another approach, which I
attempted by changing the segmentation and assumptions.
Towards the end of the interview, I was given a short quantitative problem involving revenue percentages
based on the earlier D-Mart case. Although I understood the problem and was close to the solution, I could
not arrive at the correct final answer within the given time.
The interview concluded with the interviewer asking if I had any questions. I asked about the internship, the
technologies used by the team, and her role within the company. This led to a brief discussion about the
work culture and the nature of projects at InCred.
Preparation Tips
Although this round began with technical questions, the majority of the interview focused on case studies,
guesstimates, and structured business thinking. I would recommend preparing both technical concepts
and business problem-solving instead of focusing only on your resume.
Some topics that I found useful are:

• Basics of Machine Learning concepts related to your projects.

• Evaluation metrics such as Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.

• Be able to justify your model selection and explain your feature engineering process.

• Practise business case studies (market entry, revenue growth, profitability, location strategy, etc.).

• Practise guesstimates using multiple approaches, as interviewers may specifically ask for alternative

solutions.
Things to Remember

• Do not panic if the interviewer suddenly changes the direction of the interview.

• Think aloud while solving case studies so the interviewer can understand your reasoning.

• It is perfectly acceptable to ask for a hint if you are genuinely stuck.

• Confidence and a calm approach matter just as much as arriving at the perfect answer.

• Even if you feel the interview did not go perfectly, continue giving your best in the subsequent

rounds. I personally felt this round did not go very well, but I was still shortlisted for the next stage
--- PAGE 6 ---

4. Interview Round 2 [No of candidates > 11]

The final interview consisted of a panel of three members. Two of them were from the technical/business
team, while the third panelist mainly observed the interview and did not ask any questions.
The interview began with a brief introduction about myself. I spoke about my academic background, what
motivated me towards the FinTech domain, my participation in hackathons, and my internship experiences.
Based on my introduction, I was asked to rate myself in Python and SQL, for which I rated myself 8/10 in
both.
One of the interviewers jokingly asked whether I relied on ChatGPT while programming in Python. This
gave me the opportunity to explain one of my projects where I had implemented a Transformer model from
scratch using Python, NumPy, and PyTorch. We briefly discussed the implementation, after which the
interview moved away from technical questions. Compared to the first round, the technical discussion was
very brief.
The majority of the interview revolved around a single business case study.
Business Case:
I was asked to assume the role of the Head of Collections for a lending company.
The interviewer explained the following scenario:

• Around 90% of customers repay their loans on time.

• Out of the remaining 10%, around 5% are eventually recovered through the field agent team.

• The remaining 5% become unrecovered loans.

I was asked how I would improve this collection process.
Before answering, I first clarified what information and resources were available to me. I asked whether I
had access to customer information, field agents, and tele-calling teams. Initially, I approached the problem
from a business perspective by discussing customer features, credit scores, transaction history, underwriting,
and how analytics or machine learning could help identify customers who were likely to default.
The interviewer immediately pointed out that my solution was more suitable for the Head of Business,
whereas I was expected to think like the Head of Collections, where the loans had already been disbursed.
Instead of defending my answer, I acknowledged the feedback, took a minute to rethink the problem, and
completely changed my approach.
This time, I focused on improving the existing collection process itself. I discussed:

• Evaluating whether the tele-calling team was successfully reaching customers.

• Ensuring reminders and notifications were being delivered effectively.

--- PAGE 7 ---

• Identifying communication gaps between the company and borrowers.

• Using the field agent team not only for collections but also for educating customers about repayment

schedules, reminders, and app usage.

• Collecting insights from these interactions and passing them on to the business team so that future

lending strategies could be improved
The interviewer appreciated this revised approach and continued asking follow-up questions based on
different scenarios. One such question involved customers who deliberately refused to repay despite having
the capacity to do so. I discussed possible actions such as reducing future loan eligibility, increasing scrutiny
for repeat borrowers, limiting credit exposure, and initiating legal proceedings wherever appropriate.
The discussion continued for nearly 20 minutes, with the interviewers frequently asking me to justify every
statement I made. Rather than looking for one correct answer, they were more interested in understanding
my thought process and the reasoning behind my decisions.
Towards the end of the interview, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I enquired about the
technologies used during the internship, the type of machine learning models used within the company, and
whether interns would get opportunities to work closely with those models.
Overall, I felt this interview went significantly better than my first round. Although I come from a technical
background and had limited exposure to business case studies, I realised that clear communication,
structured thinking, and the ability to adapt after receiving feedback were equally important. Remaining
calm and articulating my reasoning clearly helped me throughout the discussion.
Preparation Advice:

• Prepare business case studies even if the role appears to be technical.

• Listen carefully to the interviewer's feedback and be willing to modify your approach.

• Think aloud while solving case studies so that the interviewer understands your reasoning.

• Communication skills play a major role in business-oriented interviews.

• If you receive feedback that your approach is incorrect, don't panic. Pause, rethink the problem, and

continue with a more suitable solution.
After the interview, we waited for around 2-3 hours before the final shortlist was announced.
A total of 5 candidates were selected for the role, and I was fortunate to be one of them.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Final Thoughts:
Going into the interviews, I expected them to be mostly technical. Instead, both rounds focused much more
on business case studies and practical problem-solving. One possible reason (though this is only my
assumption) is that my resume may have already demonstrated the technical skills they were looking for, so
they wanted to evaluate my communication and problem-solving abilities instead. However, many of my
peers had completely different interview experiences, so don't expect a fixed pattern, be prepared for both
technical and non-technical questions.
The biggest lesson I learnt was to stay calm. Even when I got stuck, I took my time, asked questions, and
explained my thought process clearly instead of panicking. Communication matters just as much as
technical knowledge.
For preparation, build a strong foundation in SQL, be comfortable with at least one programming language
(python), practice basic DSA, and start aptitude preparation a few weeks before placements.
Lastly, don't judge your interview performance too quickly. I walked out of my first interview convinced I
wouldn't be shortlisted, yet I made it to the next round. Placements are unpredictable, so stay confident, keep
preparing, and give every interview your best.

journey.prep:
• Resume (This is where placements actually begin)

Before worrying about OAs or interviews, ask yourself one question:
"Will my resume even get shortlisted?"

• Maintain an ATS score of 70+.

• Keep your CGPA above 8.0. If possible, 8.5+ is the safest zone and makes you eligible for almost

every company.

• Tailor your resume according to the Job Description (JD) instead of sending the same resume

everywhere.

• Keep different versions of your resume (SDE, ML, etc.) ready beforehand

• Every point on your resume should be something you can explain confidently for 10-15 minutes if

needed.

• Numbers always make your resume stronger. Quantify your work wherever possible.

• Keep your resume clean, one-page, and ATS friendly.

Personally, maintaining a good CGPA and tailoring my resume helped me get shortlisted for companies like
JPMC, AUXO AI, WorkIndia, as these were all the companies that sent out the applications by then.
Though I was not allowed to sit for JPMC.

• DSA & Competitive Programming

This is probably the single most important part of placement preparation. I never stopped doing DSA, even
while working on internships, hackathons, or personal projects.

• Be consistent rather than solving hundreds of questions in one week.

• Solve LeetCode Daily and GFG POTD whenever possible.

• Follow a structured sheet like Striver A2Z.

• Give as many LeetCode Weekly/Biweekly, CodeChef Starters, and Codeforces contests as

possible.
One regret I have is that I wasn't as consistent with Competitive Programming as I was with LeetCode and
GFG. Looking back, I definitely feel doing more contests would've improved my problem-solving speed.
Remember, Interviews test your thinking process. OAs test your speed. Practice both.

• Core Subjects

Never underestimate Computer Science fundamentals. Most interviewers are more interested in how well
you understand the basics than how many frameworks you've used.
Resources I Used :

• DSA: Striver A2Z Sheet (You can also go for CSES problem set)

• OOP (Java): Kunal Kushwaha

• DBMS: Love Babbar (One Shot)

• Operating Systems: College Notes + Online PDFS

--- PAGE 10 ---

• Computer Networks: College Notes + Online PDFs

• SQL: LeetCode SQL50

For SQL, completing SQL50 is more than enough for most companies. But you can definitely find some
other resources as well online.

• Development & System Design

Projects help you get shortlisted. Fundamentals help you clear interviews. Both are equally important.

• Build projects where you actually understand every design decision. Don't build basic projects, build

something that shows your understanding of the concepts and also that you can think at scale.

• Don't just integrate an API know why you chose it over alternatives.

• Learn System Design concepts like APIs, databases, authentication, caching, scalability, queues, and

deployment.

• Al can generate code today, but companies still need engineers who can design systems, justify

trade-offs, and solve real business problems.
One thing that really helped me during KakushIN was that I had already worked on similar projects and
spent time understanding System Design instead of only focusing on implementation.
Finally..., Placements are unpredictable. Sometimes you clear every round and still don't get selected.
Sometimes you don't even expect an opportunity, and it completely changes your journey. I got rejected in
the final rounds of summer internships I really wanted. I couldn't even sit for a few companies because my
hackathon dates overlapped with their placement process. I didn't win the hackathon either.
Yet somehow, that's where I received my first placement offer.
That's why I truly believe this: Hard work gives you the ability. Preparation gives you confidence. Luck
gives you the opportunity. None of them work well alone.
Keep learning.
Keep building.
Keep applying.
Your breakthrough might come from the place you least expect.

• Kakushin 10.0 Resources: • [Kakushin_10.0_Exceptions_Anurag](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1xrwWo5M7dpVgJd4o2OUDlKy2DvZXziHl?usp=sharing)

• LinkedIn: Anurag Singh

Background :
Before you start reading my experience, here's one thing I genuinely believe after going through this
journey: don't measure your preparation by your rejections. I used to think success was simply the sum
of hard work, skill, and luck. But after these last few years, I see it differently-it's multiplicative. You can
work incredibly hard and become technically strong, but if luck doesn't knock at least once, you'll keep
wondering when your turn will come. At the same time, luck alone won't help if you haven't prepared for the
opportunity. You need both.
--- PAGE 11 ---
I solved DSA problems, practiced CP, built projects, completed internships, explored System Design,
strengthened my CS fundamentals, participated in hackathons, and maintained a good 9+ CGPA. I was
preparing for the usual placement process-OAs, technical interviews, and HR rounds. But things didn't
always go my way. I couldn't make it through JPMC Code for Good, and after reaching the final round of
the Barclays Summer Internship, I was rejected there as well. Every rejection made me question myself,
but I refused to let one bad result define years of preparation.
When Nomura KakushIN 10.0 was announced, getting placed through a hackathon wasn't even on my
checklist. My team registered with a simple mindset: "Let's give it everything we've got and see where it
takes us." I never imagined that while preparing for traditional placements, my very first offer would come
through a hackathon. That was the biggest blessing-I got placed before the placement season had even
started. The flip side was that the hackathon overlapped with companies like IDFC and JPMC, and after
getting selected, I couldn't sit for any other companies. We also didn't win the hackathon, which honestly
hurt because we had poured everything into it. The next morning was the PhonePe OA; after an almost
sleepless 24 hours, I wasn't in the right state to prepare or perform. Looking back, I wouldn't change a thing.
If this journey taught me anything, it's this: prepare as if luck doesn't exist, but stay humble enough to
know that when your moment arrives, luck is simply rewarding the effort you've already put in.
All the very best! I hope to see you writing your own interview experience here next year.
