Overview of Nomura Kakushin 10.0 :
KakushIN 10.0 is Nomura's flagship innovation competition organized by the Information Technology
Division (ITD). Unlike traditional campus placements, KakushIN evaluates participants on innovation,
technical expertise, teamwork, and problem-solving through real-world business challenges.
Competition Overview :

• Team Size: 2 members

• Participants: 1000+ teams (National Hackathon)

• Grand Finalists: 31 teams

• Venue: Nomura Office, Powai

• Final Round: 24-hour on-site hackathon

Selection Process :

1. Executive Summary Submission

• Submit an innovative solution for the given problem statement.

2. Executive Summary Presentation

• Present the proposed solution before Nomura leaders and domain experts.

• Evaluation based on innovation, technical feasibility, scalability, and business impact.

3. Grand Finale

• Top 31 teams were invited to Nomura's Powai office.

• Build a working prototype within 24 hours.

--- PAGE 2 ---

• Final presentation and live demonstration before the judging panel.

Hackathon Logistics

• All finalists were called to the Nomura office one day before the hackathon for onboarding and

environment setup.

• Development was carried out on Nomura-provisioned AWS EC2 instances, accessed from our own

laptops.

• Participants were provided limited access to Agentic Al tools to assist with development.

• Mentors and judges regularly interacted with teams, reviewed progress, and provided guidance

throughout the event.

• Meals and refreshments were provided throughout the three-day event.

• Pickup and drop transportation was arranged by Nomura for all three days (setup day, hackathon day,

and wrap-up day), ensuring participants could focus entirely on the competition.
My Experience
It was a unique opportunity to experience how engineers solve problems in an enterprise environment,
collaborate under pressure, and build production-oriented solutions using industry-grade infrastructure.

1. Executive Summary Submission: [ Open to Everyone - Actual count was not disclosed ]

The first round required teams to submit an Executive Summary based on the given Problem Statement.
The objective was to propose an innovative, scalable, and technically feasible solution while clearly
explaining its business impact. Since our problem statement revolved around Agentic Al, we ensured that
the document focused not only on the final solution but also on how the agents interacted, communicated,
and made decisions through a well-defined workflow.
Key Components Included :

• Understanding of the Problem Statement

• Proposed Solution & USP

• Agentic AI Workflow

• High-Level Architecture Diagram

• Core Features & Business Impact

• Technology Stack & Deployment Plan

• Dependencies, Package Versions & Environment Details

Tips :

• Understand the Problem Statement first. Every feature should directly solve a problem mentioned

in the PS.

• Have a clear USP. Don't build generic features; give judges a reason to remember your solution.

• Document your architecture and Agentic AI workflow from Day 1-it becomes extremely useful

in later rounds.

• Lock your dependency versions early and verify compatibility. Fixing version conflicts during the

hackathon wastes valuable time.

• Understand every line of your solution. The judges can quickly identify whether something was

genuinely designed by your team or simply copied.
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Think from a business perspective first. Ask yourself,ạiIf I were the client, would this feature

genuinely solve the problem?" A technically brilliant feature that doesn't solve the business objective
adds little value.
Appendix Suggestion: Since the Executive Summary has a page limit, move detailed
architecture diagrams, complete Agentic Al workflow, API flow, database schema, dependency
list, version matrix, and implementation details to the Appendix. This keeps the main document
concise while providing supporting technical details if required.
I think the last tip is probably the biggest differentiator. Many teams spend time adding more features,
while very few spend time making sure everything works together without dependency issues. Having
a stable environment, fixed package versions, and a clear architecture saved us a significant amount of time
during the Grand Finale.

2. Executive Summary Presentation [26 teams were selected for this round]

After the Executive Summary evaluation, 26 teams from SPIT were shortlisted for the offline presentation
round. Nomura conducted the presentations on our campus, where HR representatives, Senior VPs, and
technical leaders visited SPIT to evaluate the shortlisted teams. There were 4 parallel panels, each
assessing teams independently as per the presentation guidelines. Our slot was scheduled after the lunch
break. Initially, the waiting made us anxious, but as time passed, we became more relaxed and used the
extra time to mentally rehearse our presentation one last time.
Presentation Structure

• 15 minutes - Presentation

• 5 minutes - Q&A

What We Focused On

• Clear understanding of the Problem Statement.

• High-level architecture and Agentic Al workflow.

• Business impact backed by research papers, news articles, and real-world statistics.

• UI mockups and implementation roadmap.

• Clear division of work between both team members.

• Practical implementation plan for the hackathon.

My Tips

• Follow the presentation guidelines strictly. Don't skip any section mentioned by Nomura.

• Manage your time well. Several teams couldn't finish within the allotted 15 minutes. We completed

our presentation almost exactly on time while covering everything we had planned.

• Keep the audience engaged. A presentation shouldn't feel like someone reading slides. We kept it

conversational, added light humour wherever appropriate, and made sure the panel remained
interested throughout.

• Have a USP. Give the judges something they'll remember after seeing 20+ presentations.

• Support your claims. Back important ideas with research papers, news articles, market data, or

statistics instead of making generic statements.
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Know your solution inside out. If you've mentioned a technology, architecture, or AI workflow, be

prepared to justify every design decision.
Q&A
Most of our allotted Q&A time was surprisingly spent discussing and appreciating different aspects of our
solution. Towards the end, the panel asked practical implementation questions such as:

• If you're shortlisted for the hackathon, how much of this solution can you realistically build in 24

hours?

• What happens if Al services are unavailable during the hackathon?

Fortunately, we had already discussed these scenarios while designing our architecture. Instead of
overpromising, we honestly explained what could be completed within the given timeline and how our
system would continue functioning with fallback mechanisms leading to graceful degradation if certain AI
components were unavailable. Since both of us had previously worked on similar Al-based projects,
answering these questions felt natural.
Overall, we walked out of the room feeling satisfied. We believed we had communicated our ideas well and
answered every question confidently. The results were announced 4-5 days later, and while waiting, I was
busy shifting to a new house, so I didn't have much time to overthink the outcome. Finally, during the IDFC
FIRST Bank PPT on 25th June, the TPC informed us that we had been shortlisted for the Grand Finale.
Orientation & Environment Setup: [7 Teams ]
The finalists were called to the Nomura Powai office one day before the hackathon. Think of it as a
Pre-Placement Talk, but much more hands-on. The entire day was dedicated to understanding the problem,
setting up our development environment, and making sure everyone was ready before the actual 24-hour
hackathon began.
What Happened?

• HR welcomed all the finalist teams and explained the schedule, rules, code of conduct, and

expectations inside the Nomura premises.

• The CSR team explained the business side of the problem statement and how our solution could

create a real impact for the NGO we were building it for. This helped us think beyond just writing
code.

• The Tech Team conducted a short masterclass on the tools we would be using during the hackathon,

including:

• Claude Code

• Antigravity and Al Studio

Don't treat this session casually. Ask every doubt you have. We asked a lot of questions,
understood the limitations of each tool, and even started discussing our execution strategy
immediately after learning that Claude Code had limited tokens.
Meet Your Tech Buddy:
Every team was assigned a Tech Buddy who stayed with us throughout the hackathon.
--- PAGE 5 ---
My advice? Make full use of them.
They know the environment better than anyone else and are there to help not judge. Whether it's
debugging, infrastructure issues, or understanding the provided tools, don't hesitate to ask. Also, take this
opportunity to network with them. Everyone we interacted with was incredibly friendly and supportive.
Environment Setup
Before leaving for the day, everyone had to prepare their development environment.
This included:

• Logging into the Nomura-provided AWS EC2 instance through Remote Desktop (using our own

laptops).

• Installing Python requirements.

• Installing npm/node packages.

• Uploading datasets (if required).

• Verifying that the project could run successfully.

Linux users: Boot into Windows before coming. The setup process is much smoother since the
provided environment is designed around Remote Desktop.
One Mistake That Cost Many Teams Time
If there's one thing I'd tell every future participant, it's this: Lock your versions before the hackathon.
In our Executive Summary, we had already documented all package versions and dependencies. That
preparation saved us.
Unfortunately, during setup, the EC2 machines ended up installing the latest package versions instead of
the versions we actually required. Our project depended on Python 3.12, but the environment wasn't
configured accordingly, and because of the restricted permissions, we couldn't simply install another version
ourselves. Even GitHub access was blocked, and the systems were heavily monitored, so bringing pre-built
code or downloading random packages wasn't an option.
Luckily, we had already tested everything locally using the exact same requirements file. So although the
setup couldn't be completed that evening, we knew that once the environment was fixed, we'd be up and
running in just a few minutes the next morning. Several teams lost a significant amount of time because of
compatibility issues.
Moral of the story: Before you submit your requirements file, sit with your Tech Buddy and verify every
dependency, every package version, every model version, and every environment requirement. It'll
save you hours during the hackathon.
Wrapping Up
Nomura had taken care of almost everything for us:

• Pickup & drop facility

• Lunch

--- PAGE 6 ---

• Evening high tea & refreshments

• Development infrastructure

• Tech support throughout the event

All you really needed to bring was your laptop and your preparation.
After heading home, my teammate and I quickly discussed our execution plan for the next day so we knew
exactly where to start once the hackathon began.
One last tip: Go home, finalise your strategy, and get a good night's sleep. Trust me, the next 24 hours are
going to be intense. I didn't sleep enough, and I definitely felt it the next day.

3. Grand Finale [ 7 teams from SPIT were selected for this round]

We had to report to the Nomura Powai office early in the morning. After checking in, our Tech Buddies
escorted us to our assigned rooms, and the 24-hour coding sprint officially began.
The First Few Hours
Before writing a single line of code, fix your setup first.
Since we had already planned everything during the orientation day, we spent the first few hours ensuring
our environment was working correctly. In fact, we deliberately avoided using the provided Al agents
initially, which ended up saving a good number of Claude Code tokens for later when we actually needed
them.
A couple of teams in our room spent almost half the day fixing dependency and compatibility issues, while
we were able to start development much earlier.
One lesson: Never ignore package versions. A small compatibility issue can easily cost you a
few hours in a 24-hour hackathon.
Evaluation Round 1 :
During the hackathon, every team was assigned an Evaluator who periodically reviewed the project. Think
of these evaluations as technical interviews, except instead of talking about your resume, you're defending
the product you've been building.
Our evaluator was extremely friendly, but he wanted us to justify every major decision.
Some of the topics we discussed included:

• Why we chose our overall architecture.

• How our Agentic Al workflow functioned.

• Why did we trained our adaptive learning model the way we did

• How our personalised dataset was generated and utilised.

• API choices (Claude vs Gemini) and why we used each where appropriate.

• Why we avoided a cloud-hosted RAG database and switched to a local vector-based approach.

• Scalability considerations.

• Business impact of every major feature.

--- PAGE 7 ---
Fortunately, this is where my preparation over the last three years really helped. All those personal projects,
internships, system design sessions, ML projects and understanding the math behind them and computer
science fundamentals finally came together.
One thing I realised is that if you genuinely understand your project, the evaluator doesn't have to keep
asking questions-you naturally end up answering them while explaining your thought process.
The only major feedback we received was that one of our UI components wasn't updating efficiently.
I suggested using a Cron Job to periodically refresh the data, cache the responses, and display cached
values between updates instead of querying repeatedly. The evaluator appreciated the approach and later
suggested another feature where NGOs could generate revenue using the platform.
One important piece of advice: Don't overpromise. If someone asks what you'll complete by tomorrow
morning, be realistic. Evaluators remember your commitments and compare them against your final
implementation during the next review.
Through the Night...
As the night progressed, the project slowly stopped looking like an MVP and actually started feeling like a
real product. One of the most memorable parts of the hackathon wasn't coding. It was the people.
Throughout the night, Tech Buddies, engineers, mentors, senior developers, and even members of the
KakushIN organizing committee kept visiting different rooms to see everyone's progress. Around 3 AM,
many of them came over to our desk after hearing about our project from others. Even the core managing
committee members of Kakushin 10.0 asked us if we can explain our project as they heard it from someone
that it's something unique. They appreciated our idea and even shared presentation tips for the final judging
round. One thing I'd strongly recommend is: Talk to everyone who visits your desk. Don't treat them as
judges. Treat them as mentors. Many of the questions asked during the final presentation were things we had
already discussed informally with Nomura engineers during the night. Those conversations genuinely helped
us improve both our product and our pitch. By morning, we had built everything we had planned. We
somehow managed to squeeze in barely 1-2 hours of sleep before the next evaluation.
Evaluation Round 2
The second evaluation was much smoother. We had incorporated the feedback received earlier,
demonstrated the completed MVP, explained the improvements, and showcased the final workflow. The
evaluator seemed satisfied with the progress and wished us luck for the final presentation.
Final Presentation
Once coding ended, every team prepared for the final presentation. The judging panels consisted of very
senior leaders from Nomura, and to our surprise, our presentation was attended by the Technology Head
of Nomura India. This round was less about coding and more about business. Because of all the discussions
we had throughout the hackathon-with evaluators, Tech Buddies and mentors we were already prepared
for most of the business questions. The discussion revolved around:

• Business impact.

• Scalability.

--- PAGE 8 ---

• User adoption.

• Future roadmap.

• Technical decisions.

• Practical implementation.

One thing I realised here is: You're not just building software. You're solving a business problem
through technology. That mindset completely changes how you present your project.
Results
After the presentations, we finally got some time to relax, have lunch, and wait for the results. Since our
presentation slot was towards the end, we even managed to polish our slides one last time. When the winners
were announced... our team wasn't among them. I'll be honest. That moment hurt. We had spent the last
7-10 days thinking about nothing except this hackathon. We genuinely believed we had a chance of
winning. I went home disappointed. The very next day was the PhonePe Online Assessment, but after
almost ten days away from regular DSA practice and barely any sleep, I couldn't prepare properly. I
remember sitting there wondering how I was going to restart my placement preparation from scratch. For a
couple of days, it felt like all that effort had gone unnoticed.
And then, 3-4 days later... I received a call from the TPC. I had been selected for the Nomura ITD
Internship. I still remember sitting there in complete disbelief. Out of the 14 students from SPIT who
reached the Grand Finale, 7 students were selected in total four from the winning teams and three
individual selections from three different teams. I was fortunate to be one of those three. If this
experience taught me anything, it's that luck really is a factor. You can control your preparation, your
attitude and your effort-but sometimes the final outcome isn't entirely in your hands.
A huge thank you to Aryan Tikam. This journey wouldn't have been the same without him. He was an
incredible teammate smart, dependable, and someone I could always rely on.
Final Tips

• Fix your environment before coding

• Lock dependency versions and test them beforehand.

• Use Al tools wisely don't burn all your tokens in the first few hours.

• Make full use of your Tech Buddy.

• Think about security and governance too. Some teams were asked about topics like JWT

architecture, Prompt Injection, and mitigation strategies.

• Never overcommit during evaluations.

• Understand every technology, model, API, and architectural decision in your project.

• And finally... enjoy the experience. Very few people get to spend 24 hours building alongside some

of the best engineers in the industry. Even if you don't win, you'll come back with lessons that stay
with you far longer than any trophy

• Participate in Hiring hackathons you never know what lies in the future.

7 people received the offer (Internship + Performance based PPO)
--- PAGE 9 ---

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Resume (This is where placements actually begin)

Before worrying about OAs or interviews, ask yourself one question:
"Will my resume even get shortlisted?"

• Maintain an ATS score of 70+.

• Keep your CGPA above 8.0. If possible, 8.5+ is the safest zone and makes you eligible for almost

every company.

• Tailor your resume according to the Job Description (JD) instead of sending the same resume

everywhere.

• Keep different versions of your resume (SDE, ML, etc.) ready beforehand

• Every point on your resume should be something you can explain confidently for 10-15 minutes if

needed.

• Numbers always make your resume stronger. Quantify your work wherever possible.

• Keep your resume clean, one-page, and ATS friendly.

Personally, maintaining a good CGPA and tailoring my resume helped me get shortlisted for companies like
JPMC, AUXO AI, WorkIndia, as these were all the companies that sent out the applications by then.
Though I was not allowed to sit for JPMC.

• DSA & Competitive Programming

This is probably the single most important part of placement preparation. I never stopped doing DSA, even
while working on internships, hackathons, or personal projects.

• Be consistent rather than solving hundreds of questions in one week.

• Solve LeetCode Daily and GFG POTD whenever possible.

• Follow a structured sheet like Striver A2Z.

• Give as many LeetCode Weekly/Biweekly, CodeChef Starters, and Codeforces contests as

possible.
One regret I have is that I wasn't as consistent with Competitive Programming as I was with LeetCode and
GFG. Looking back, I definitely feel doing more contests would've improved my problem-solving speed.
Remember, Interviews test your thinking process. OAs test your speed. Practice both.

• Core Subjects

Never underestimate Computer Science fundamentals. Most interviewers are more interested in how well
you understand the basics than how many frameworks you've used.
Resources I Used :

• DSA: Striver A2Z Sheet (You can also go for CSES problem set)

• OOP (Java): Kunal Kushwaha

• DBMS: Love Babbar (One Shot)

• Operating Systems: College Notes + Online PDFS

--- PAGE 10 ---

• Computer Networks: College Notes + Online PDFs

• SQL: LeetCode SQL50

For SQL, completing SQL50 is more than enough for most companies. But you can definitely find some
other resources as well online.

• Development & System Design

Projects help you get shortlisted. Fundamentals help you clear interviews. Both are equally important.

• Build projects where you actually understand every design decision. Don't build basic projects, build

something that shows your understanding of the concepts and also that you can think at scale.

• Don't just integrate an API know why you chose it over alternatives.

• Learn System Design concepts like APIs, databases, authentication, caching, scalability, queues, and

deployment.

• Al can generate code today, but companies still need engineers who can design systems, justify

trade-offs, and solve real business problems.
One thing that really helped me during KakushIN was that I had already worked on similar projects and
spent time understanding System Design instead of only focusing on implementation.
Finally..., Placements are unpredictable. Sometimes you clear every round and still don't get selected.
Sometimes you don't even expect an opportunity, and it completely changes your journey. I got rejected in
the final rounds of summer internships I really wanted. I couldn't even sit for a f

journey.prep:
Maintain a minimum 8+ CGPA with no backlogs in any subject across all the semesters.
Be confident during your interviews. Your introduction sets the tone for the entire tech interview
‚use it to highlight your strengths, guide the conversation toward your best work, and show that
you know exactly what you bring to the table. Show genuine engagement by asking thoughtful
--- PAGE 3 ---
questions which demonstrates your curiosity and interest. Don't rush your answers and take a
moment to think before responding.
Be thorough with the core concepts of OOPs, Java, C++, C, DBMS, Operating Systems.
In areas where you feel less confident, be transparent but express your willingness to learn and
grow.
It doesn't matter how many projects you include in your resume, what truly matters is how well
you understand the projects you've listed and whether you can confidently explain and answer
questions related to them. The interviewer is more interested in your clarity of thought, your grip
on fundamentals, and how you apply them.
Whenever you're asked to explain a project, start by drawing the system architecture. This helps
you walk through the entire flow clearly and shows the interviewer that you have a solid
understanding of how everything fits together and it immediately conveys that you know your
work well.
Continue practicing DSA in the language you are most comfortable with.
Feel free to contact me if you have any questions:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/anushka-kenia

1. Online Assessment [ Out of all who appeared, 38 were selected for the next round]

This was an online test conducted at college consisting of 25 questions. Among these, 5 were
SQL query based questions and the rest were MCQS. The MCQs covered questions on OOPS,
JAVA, C and C++.
For this round, I had solved SQL questions from Leetcode and had revised OOPS and JAVA
from the PPTs and ISE questions that were provided during the second semester and questions
from Sanfoundry and GeeksForGeeks.

2. Technical Interview [ 38 appeared for this round, and 19 got selected for the next]

This round lasted for about 25 minutes. The process began with the interviewer asking me to
introduce myself followed by a few questions related to my resume. As I had mentioned in
my introduction about DBMS being one of the subjects in our curriculum, he asked me many
questions regarding the same. Starting with the types of joins and demonstrating each join
with an example and then types of keys and questions on them. He then gave me 4 tables and
asked me 3 SQL queries related to them. The queries covered concepts of joins, aggregate
functions and applications of GROUP BY and HAVING clauses. He then asked me what
Object Oriented Programming Language is and then the principles of OOPS. He then asked
me to write a code in C++ to declare a list and find the second largest element. Then he asked
me questions that blended object-oriented programming (OOP) concepts with a database
--- PAGE 2 ---
schema he had provided earlier. He chose a table and asked me to create a class in C++ for
the chosen table with appropriate attributes. Instantiate objects of the class representing
sample records (rows) from that table. Store the objects in an array. Then, the interviewer
asked how I would check if two objects represent the same record. Towards the end, he just
asked me about my project (tech stack and motivation behind it) and why I had done it in
MySQL instead of MongoDB and why indexing is done in databases. No follow-up
questions were asked on the project after this.

3. Technical Interview+ HR questions [19 students appeared for this round]

This round lasted for about 45 minutes. This round started with the interviewer asking for a brief
introduction. The interviewer then moved on to questions focused heavily on my project. I
was asked to explain the project idea and my motivation behind it. The tech stack used and
why I chose it. A detailed walkthrough of the implementation and flow between frontend and
backend when a user interacts with the application. You need to be thorough with your
project. I was then asked to list all the database tables used in the project along with their
attributes. Draw an ER (Entity-Relationship) diagram, specifying the relationships between
each table. Solve two SQL queries based on the structure. He then asked me what APIs are,
and how they are used in web development and 1-2 questions on React. Then he asked me a
pattern printing code which was moderately difficult. Then he asked me 3-4 situation based
questions. How do you divide tasks within your teammates whenever working on a new
project and what do you do if one of them fails to do their task close to deadline? If you are
working in a company and write a correct but unoptimized code and the deadline is near, do
you submit it, try to improve it, or ask for help? Have you ever done something not explicitly
asked of you but went ahead with it because you felt it would add value to the application?
To conclude the interview, the interviewer asked about my role during a 4-week internship
mentioned in my resume. I explained the responsibilities I undertook, the technologies I
worked with, and how the experience helped me.
16 students were offered the position.

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Group Discussion (3 July 2026)

• Technical Interview (3 July 2026)

• HR Interview (3 July 2026)

• Final Result Declaration (3 July 2026)

The entire interview process was conducted online from the college campus due to the heavy rainfall and
red alert in Mumbai. Candidates were required to report to college, from where all interviews were
conducted virtually.
The process was highly dynamic. Different interview panels followed slightly different formats, with
interview duration, number of technical rounds, and order of shortlisting varying across candidates. Some
candidates had multiple technical interviews, while others were directly shortlisted for HR after a single
technical interview. Therefore, it is important not to compare your process with others during the day or
assume the outcome based on interview duration or the order in which candidates are called.
For the Banking role, the overall selection process was:

• 67 candidates were shortlisted after resume screening.

• 55 candidates were shortlisted after the Online Assessment.

• 29 candidates were shortlisted after the Group Discussion.

• 10 candidates shortlisted for the HR round.

• 10 internship offers rolled out for the Banking role

1. Pre-Placement Talk and Resume Shortlisting

The process began with the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), followed by registration through the official
JPMorgan Chase Careers portal. While many students treat the PPT as a formality, I would strongly
recommend attending it attentively. The session gives you a clear understanding of the different business
divisions, the responsibilities associated with each role, the internship structure, and the qualities the firm
looks for in candidates. Take notes throughout the session, as several discussion points from the PPT can
later be incorporated into your interviews and the questions you ask the interviewers. If given an
opportunity, ask thoughtful and role-specific questions instead of speaking just for the sake of visibility.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Resume shortlisting is one of the most important elimination stages of the process. For the Banking role,
your resume should demonstrate a genuine interest in finance rather than just listing certifications. I would
recommend having at least one strong finance project that you can confidently discuss in depth. Interviewers
thoroughly evaluate your understanding of every project and internship mentioned on your resume, so only
include experiences that you have personally worked on and can defend confidently. Along with finance
projects, relevant internships, case competitions, leadership positions, and certifications help create a
well-rounded profile.
Remember that interviewers often try to understand the story behind your resume rather than
simply verify its contents. If your profile spans multiple domains, be prepared to explain how
your experiences connect to your interest in finance and why you chose this role.

2. Online Assessment (67 Candidates appeared for this round)

The Online Assessment was conducted online from home on the AON platform and consisted of 45 MCQs
to be completed in 45 minutes. There was no sectional timing, allowing candidates to manage their own
time.
The paper consisted of four sections:

• Corporate Finance & Accounting (10 Questions)

• Market Awareness (10 Questions)

• Quantitative Aptitude (15 Questions)

• English (10 Questions)

• Corporate Finance & Accounting (Moderate): Tested fundamental concepts such as financial

statements, financial ratios, inflation, bonds, GDP, and basic accounting. Focus on understanding
concepts rather than memorizing definitions.

• Market Awareness (Difficult): This was the toughest section for me. Questions were based on

recent business and financial developments, making it difficult to predict. Regularly reading financial
news is far more effective than last-minute preparation.

• Quantitative Aptitude (Easy-Moderate): Similar to IndiaBix-level questions covering Profit &

Loss, Time & Work, Ratios, Probability, Permutations & Combinations, SI-CI, Mixtures, and Speed,
Time & Distance.

• English (Easy): Includes Reading Comprehension, Grammar, Vocabulary, and Sentence Correction.

Overall, it was straightforward.
Preparation
The resources that helped me the most were:

• IndiaBix for Quantitative Aptitude.

• CFI courses (Coursera) for Accounting and Corporate Finance fundamentals.

My strategy was to maximize my score in Quant, English, and Finance, as these sections are relatively
more predictable, while avoiding spending excessive time on difficult Market Awareness questions.
Out of 67 candidates, 55 were shortlisted for the Group Discussion round.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Tips

• Strengthen your accounting and finance fundamentals rather than focusing on advanced valuation

concepts.

• Practice Quant under timed conditions.

• Read financial news consistently instead of relying on last-minute preparation.

• Manage your time well; speed is just as important as accuracy.

3. Group Discussion Round (55 Candidates appeared for this round)

The shortlist for the Group Discussion was announced the night before the interviews, along with the
topic. This leaves very little preparation time, so start researching as soon as the shortlist is released.
GD Topic: "Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful share of
its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are approximately
2× longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial metrics. As the
CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
The discussion lasted around 20-25 minutes with 8-10 candidates per panel. Unlike a traditional GD, this
was moderator-driven. The moderators asked specific questions, guided the discussion, and ensured that
everyone had an opportunity to contribute.
I spoke four times, but each contribution either introduced a new perspective or built upon an existing point
rather than speaking just to increase my count.
Tips

• Focus on adding value rather than speaking the most.

• Research the topic from multiple perspectives, as moderators may ask follow-up questions.

• Don't disagree just to stand out. If you agree with someone, acknowledge their point and build

upon it. I often built on another candidate's ideas instead of contradicting them, and I believe this
demonstrated teamwork rather than competition.

• Listen actively. The moderators ensured everyone had a fair opportunity to speak, so there was no

need to interrupt or dominate the discussion.

4. Technical/Finance Interview (29 Candidates appeared for this round)

Out of 55 candidates, 29 were shortlisted for the interview round. One thing worth mentioning is that there
was no fixed interview structure. Different panels followed different formats, some candidates had one
technical interview, others had two, and a few had three. Similarly, some candidates who had only one
interview were shortlisted further, while others were eliminated after a single round. Do not compare your
process with others or assume your chances based on the number or duration of interviews.
Personally, I had one 15-minute technical interview with a Vice President. The interview was fast-paced
and focused almost entirely on finance fundamentals rather than my resume. The questions asked were:

• Tell me about yourself.

• "You look like a marketing girl. Why finance?"

• Buy Side vs Sell Side.

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Private Equity vs Venture Capital.

• Investment Banking vs Commercial Banking vs Corporate Banking.

• IPO vs FPO.

• Tata Capital IPO.

• Is the current market favourable for IPOs? How is it different from last year?

• Difference between a Merger and an Acquisition.

• Mention a recent M&A deal and explain it (I discussed L'Oréal's acquisition of Innovist).

Looking back, I realised that the interviewer wasn't looking for textbook definitions. Most questions were
followed by "why?" or "explain further," so having conceptual clarity was far more important than
memorising one-line answers. I knew many of the concepts but struggled to articulate a few of them under
pressure, which reinforced the importance of practising finance discussions aloud rather than only reading
notes.
Preparation & Tips

• Be extremely comfortable with finance fundamentals, especially:

• Buy Side vs Sell Side

PE vs VC

• Types of Banking

• IPO vs FPO

• M&A

• Financial Statements

• Financial Ratios

• Prepare your introduction well-it often determines the direction of the interview.

• Don't panic if you cannot answer a question immediately. Explain your thought process and reason

through the problem.

• Most importantly, don't judge your performance based on interview duration or compare

yourself with other candidates. I walked out convinced I had performed poorly, but eventually
received the offer.

5. HR Interview (10 Candidates appeared for this round)

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round, and everyone who reached this stage was
eventually offered the internship. My HR interview lasted approximately 15-17 minutes and was the most
relaxed conversation of the day.
Unlike the technical interview, the HR round was not a question-answer session. After asking me to
introduce myself, the interviewer made an interesting observation: "You look like a marketing girl. Why
finance?ạ
I spoke about my internships, particularly my experience working with Mastercard during my internship at
McCann Worldgroup, and how it made me realise that finance is at the core of every business decision,
ultimately leading me to pursue Corporate Finance and Investment Banking through my minor and finance
projects.
The rest of the interview was largely conversational, giving me an opportunity to ask questions and
understand the firm better.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Tips

• Treat the HR round as a conversation, not an interrogation.

• Have a clear and authentic reason for why finance and why JPMorgan.

• Prepare thoughtful questions for the interviewer. It shows genuine curiosity and leaves a strong final

impression.

• If you reach this stage, stay calm and let your personality come through. The interview is largely

about assessing cultural fit rather than testing technical knowledge.
All 10 students who gave this round were selected.

journey.prep:
The biggest thing that helped me through the process was being able to reason through problems even
when I didn't immediately see the full solution. The interviewers weren't just checking if the final answer
was perfect -- they were watching how I approached the problem, whether I could explain my thought
process, and whether I could break things down logically.

1. DSA

Focus on common patterns rather than memorizing individual questions. In particular, revise:

• Arrays and strings

• Hashing

• Binary search

• Trees

• Sorting

• Dynamic programming

• Two pointers

• Intervals

• Basic greedy problems

It also helps to practice writing code without an IDE occasionally -- several of my interview questions
had to be written on paper.

2. SQL and DBMS

Revise:

• Joins

• GROUP BY and aggregate functions

• Subqueries

• CASE statements

• Primary and foreign keys

• Normalization

• ER diagrams

• One-to-many and many-to-many relationships

• Converting ER diagrams into relational tables

The SQL questions weren't necessarily very hard, but knowing the fundamentals cold matters a lot.

3. Resume

Know everything on your resume -- don't list a technology or project you can't explain. For each project,
prepare a short walkthrough covering: Problem → Your solution → Technologies → Your contribution →
Challenges → Result. Be ready for follow-ups too -- if you mention something like Flask, MySQL, JWT, or
Redis, expect to be asked why you used it and how it works.

4. Practice explaining your thought process

Don't work on a problem silently for too long -- explain what you're thinking as you go. For example: "I
think I can use binary search here because the condition changes from good to defective only once."
This shows the interviewer you understand the underlying logic, even before you've finished writing the
code.

5. Don't panic if you make a mistake

I wasn't able to write one SQL query fully correctly in the technical interview, but I still explained my
reasoning and moved forward. If you get stuck, don't give up -- explain what you know, clarify your
assumptions, and work toward the answer.
Things I could have done better

• Prepared more thoroughly for harder DP problems -- I only passed about half the test cases on

the DP question in the online test.

• Understood many-to-many relationships better, including how to model and query them in a

relational database.

• Reasoned through the cycle-time aspect of the traffic-signal problem faster in the final round.

For future candidates, I'd suggest not preparing only the easiest DSA questions -- the assessment and
interviews can combine multiple concepts at once.
Final Advice
The overall process was fairly problem-solving oriented. I'd recommend preparing DSA and SQL
seriously, but don't neglect your resume, projects, and communication. Most importantly, don't try to
bluff when you don't know something -- explain your approach honestly and show you're willing to
reason through the problem. Demonstrating logical thinking mattered even when my final answer
wasn't perfect. On interview day: stay calm, listen to the full question before starting, clarify
requirements if needed, and explain your approach as you solve.
Good luck to everyone appearing for Wissen! All the best.

The Wissen placement process consisted of an online coding assessment followed by two interview
rounds. Around 270 students appeared for the initial assessment, roughly 40 were shortlisted for the
technical interview, and the final selection came after the subsequent interview rounds. In total, 9
students were offered the role -- 7 with Internship + Full-Time Employment, and 2 with Internship only.

1. Online Coding Assessment (HackerEarth) [~270 candidates]

The first round was an online coding assessment on HackerEarth, lasting about 2 hours, with two DSA
questions and one SQL question worth a total of around 195 marks. I scored 105 marks, and about 40
students were shortlisted for the next round -- based on the scores I saw, the effective cutoff seemed
to be around 100 marks, though it wasn't officially announced.
DSA - Tree Question
This problem asked for the longest "harmonious" path in a tree, where every node's value had to satisfy
a condition relative to the average value of its ancestors and a given K. I solved it using an iterative DFS
with a stack holding the current node, the sum of its ancestors, the ancestor count, and the current path
length. At each node, I computed the ancestor average, checked the condition, and continued into its
children -- updating the maximum path length whenever I hit a leaf. I solved this one completely.
DSA - Dynamic Programming Question
This was the tougher of the two -- selecting sites/towers based on position and profit while respecting a
minimum distance constraint, with a bonus for sites picked at a particular distance. I sorted the sites by
position and built a DP array tracking the best achievable profit up to each site, using binary search to
find the last valid site that wouldn't violate the distance constraint. I got roughly half the test cases to
pass -- this was the hardest question for me in the assessment.
SQL Question
This involved calculating the completion rate of different training courses -- joining the training course
and training result tables, grouping by course, counting total participants, counting how many scored
above 50, and computing the percentage. Results had to be sorted by completion rate descending, then
course name ascending. I solved this one fully.
Preparation Tips for This Round
Practice DSA under time pressure, especially trees, DP, binary search, and greedy/optimization
problems. Don't skip SQL -- the question wasn't especially hard, but it needed a solid grip on joins,
aggregation, conditional counting, and sorting. Also, solving two questions completely was enough to
clear this round, so it's often better to nail the easier questions than burn the whole test on one hard
problem.

2. Technical Interview [~40 candidates]

The second round was an offline technical interview, about an hour long with one interviewer, focused
on problem-solving, DSA, and SQL/database concepts. Some answers had to be written out on paper.
DSA / Problem-Solving Questions
One question involved processing email addresses -- separating name and domain, organizing the data
using a hash set, and splitting a domain's list once it crossed a certain size. I had to write this out on
paper, so explaining my logic clearly while writing mattered a lot.
Another question was based on binary search, built around a machine producing good and defective
products. In one version the sequence looked like GGGGGGDDDDDDD, and I had to efficiently find the
index of the first defective product. In a trickier version, like GGGGGDDDDDDDGGG, I had to find both
the first and last defective product. The point of the question was really about recognizing when binary
search applies instead of defaulting to a linear scan.
SQL / Database Question
I was asked to design an ER diagram for a database and convert it into a relational design, with a focus
on handling a many-to-many relationship -- I explained how this needs an intermediate/junction table
holding keys from both related entities. I was then asked to write a SQL query based on the design, and
while I didn't get it fully correct, I was able to explain my reasoning clearly. The interviewer seemed
more interested in my approach and logical thinking than a perfect answer, and I moved on to the next
round.
Preparation Tips for This Round
Focus on being comfortable with fundamentals rather than memorizing solutions, since DSA questions
often show up wrapped in real-world scenarios. Revise OOP concepts; DBMS and SQL, especially ER
diagrams, relational mapping, and many-to-many relationships; common DSA patterns like binary search
and hashing; and your resume and projects. Above all, think out loud -- even an imperfect final answer
shows the interviewer how you reason through a problem.

3. Director Round - Final Interview

The third round was an online Director Round, about an hour long with one interviewer. It opened with
some basic questions about me and my resume/projects -- the questions I personally got were fairly
basic, but candidates should be ready to go deeper, since the level of questioning can vary a lot from
person to person.
Problem-Solving Question - Traffic Signal
This one involved an intersection with a traffic signal, where I had to distribute available green-light time
across roads given constraints like minimum and maximum green-light time, total cycle time, and the
gap before a signal turns green again after turning red. It was more about problem-solving and logical
thinking than something memorizable -- I worked through it, though I got a bit stuck reasoning about
the cycle-time aspect.
Coding Question - Minimum Meeting Rooms
Given the start and end times of several meetings, I had to find the minimum number of rooms needed
so no two overlapping meetings shared a room -- written out on paper. The key idea was to find the
maximum number of meetings happening simultaneously, which gives the minimum rooms required.
Resume and Project Discussion
The interviewer asked about me and discussed my projects, though the questions I received stayed
mostly at a basic level. Even so, I'd strongly recommend knowing your projects thoroughly -- why you
picked them, your role, the tech used, database design, key features, challenges and how you solved
them, why you chose a particular technology, and how the project could be improved. A conversation
that starts basic can get deeper fast depending on your answers.
My Performance
I was able to answer everything asked of me, though I spent a bit of extra time on the cycle-time part of
the traffic-signal problem. When I asked for feedback afterward, it was mostly positive.

fundamentals, and aptitude pays off.

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:
14 July 2026 :

• Pre-Placement Talk

• Resume Shortlisting

17th July 2026 :

• Online Assessment

• Technical Interview

• HR Interview

• Result Declaration

1.
Resume Shortlisting [ 214 students were shortlisted]
The first stage for almost every company is resume shortlisting, and this is often the most unpredictable
round. My resume wasn't shortlisted for companies like UBS and AuxoAI. There can be several reasons for
this-it could be the ATS parser, your resume not aligning well with the job description, or sometimes
simply luck.
After facing a few resume rejections, I spent time improving my resume. I tailored it specifically to the job
description, quantified my achievements wherever possible, and optimized it for ATS. This increased my
ATS score to around 77. You can check your resume's ATS score on ResumeWorded-a score above 60 is
generally considered good.
One thing worth noting is that this company had an eligibility criterion of &+ CGPA, whereas many
companies usually have a cutoff of 6 or 7. My advice would be to maintain a CGPA of 8 or above if
possible, as it keeps you eligible for a larger number of opportunities.
The shortlist was released three days before the interview process, giving us enough time to prepare for
the subsequent rounds.

2. Online Assessment [ 214 students appeared ]

--- PAGE 2 ---

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA) (90 mins 8.30 am - 10am)

The first round was an Online Assessment (OA) consisting entirely of MCQS. This year, the test had three
sections: Technical (45 questions) covering Java, Python, and SQL, Aptitude (25 questions), and a newly
introduced Al section.
The Java and Python sections were primarily output-based, testing conceptual understanding rather than
direct theory. In Java, questions revolved around OOP, the Collections Framework, Records, the Optional
class, and code output prediction. Python focused on concepts like slicing, OOP, Method Resolution Order
(MRO), and output prediction. The SQL section had around 3-4 query-based questions involving joins,
subqueries, aggregate functions, and TOP/LIMIT clauses.
The newly introduced Al section consisted of basic Al-related MCQS which were slightly lengthy but
completely doable. Most questions were prompt-engineering based, where a technical prompt and multiple
Al-generated responses were provided, and you had to identify the output that best satisfied the prompt.
There were also questions where you had to spot inaccuracies or suggest corrections to Al-generated
responses. Overall, the section tested your ability to effectively interact with Al tools while also evaluating
your technical judgment. Many questions required you to identify the best Al-generated response for
programming-related prompts involving SQL, code snippets, debugging, and other technical concepts, rather
than testing theoretical knowledge of machine learning or AI.
The aptitude section was comparatively easy, with questions from topics such as Boats and Streams,
Permutations & Combinations, Probability, Stocks and Shares, and other standard quantitative aptitude
concepts. I had been practicing aptitude consistently for the last 1-2 months using IndiaBix, and I feel that
solving one timed test for each topic on the website is more than enough for placement preparation.
The marking scheme was +1 for every correct answer and -0.25 for every incorrect answer. Because the
negative marking wasn't too high, it made sense to take educated guesses when you could eliminate one or
two options. However, if you were completely unsure about a question, it was better to leave it unanswered
rather than lose marks unnecessarily.
Since Java is my primary language for DSA, the Java section wasn't much of a challenge. I revised Java
theory from TPoint Tech, which covers placement-relevant concepts very well, and used the same website to
brush up on Python topics. During the final stage of my preparation, I also used ChatGPT and Claude to
generate mock online assessments and attempted them under timed conditions. This helped me improve both
my speed and accuracy before the actual OA.

3. Technical Round [ 44 students appeared ]

Round 2: Technical Interview (45 - 60 mins)

After an anxious wait, the placement team started calling students in batches of 4-5 to the TPO cabins. The
complete shortlist had not been announced yet, but after seeing three or four batches go in, I had almost lost
hope. I even stopped revising and stepped out of the auditorium for some fresh air. Suddenly, my friends
started spam-calling me saying, "Arushi, you've been shortlisted!" I literally ran back to the TPO office,
excited and relieved.
--- PAGE 3 ---
When my turn came, I entered the room, smiled, asked, "May I come in?", and took my seat. There were two
interviewers on the panel. Having already appeared for interviews at Barclays, JPMC CR, and
WorkIndia, I was familiar with the process and had my introduction ready. However, after greeting me, one
interviewer said, "Tell us about yourself but we already know you're Arushi, a final-year student from SPIT
blah blah so, directly talk about your technical knowledge and projects" That immediately set the tone for a
purely technical interview.
I started by briefly discussing the two internships I had completed, explaining my role and the key features
I worked on. I then mentioned that I had also built several personal projects. They asked me to explain one
of them, so I chose my latest project and walked them through the problem statement, key features,
architecture, and the tech stack. They seemed satisfied with the explanation.
The interviewer then handed me a sheet containing two API endpoints:
GET /api/products/mobile/iphone
GET /api/products/laptop/dell
He explained what these endpoints did and asked me to describe the complete request flow in an
e-commerce application- from routes to controllers, services, models, database, and finally the response
returned to the client.
He then followed up with, "If tomorrow you need an endpoint for Samsung phones, will you create a new
API?" I explained that this wasn't scalable and introduced the concept of path parameters and query
parameters for building dynamic endpoints. Although I couldn't recall the exact syntax on paper, I clearly
explained the logic behind parameterized routes that can handle thousands of products through a single
endpoint. He smiled and said, "I was looking for the logic, not the syntax, " before moving on.
Next, he asked whether I knew Java. I replied that Java is my primary language for DSA. Although I
didn't have hands-on experience with Spring Boot, I confidently mentioned that I was comfortable with Java
fundamentals and could quickly adapt to Java backend development. Never say never I knew the companies
techstack had springboot so I beforehand mentioned my capability of adapting to it.
The next problem was Java-based:
Given a List<Student>, return the students with the highest marks from each department.
Before jumping into the solution, I asked a few clarifying questions about the requirements. Since the
company primarily worked with Java, I proposed using a HashMap with the department as the key and a
List<Student> as the value. I explained that while iterating through the list, if the department wasn't present,
I would create a new entry. Otherwise, I would compare the current student's marks with the highest marks
stored for that department-replacing the list if the marks were higher, adding the student if the marks were
equal, and ignoring the student otherwise.
He then asked me to write the map declaration, which I wrote as:
HashMap<String, List<Student map = new HashMap 0;
He followed up with another question: "What if I want this to be a TreeMap instead?" This gave me the
opportunity to discuss programming to interfaces and the concepts of loose coupling vs. tight coupling. I
--- PAGE 4 ---
explained that both HashMap and TreeMap implement the Map interface, so declaring the reference using
the interface makes the implementation easily replaceable. I then wrote:
Map<String, List<Student>> map = new TreeMap<>0;
Finally, he asked a DSA question on finding the length of the longest substring with unique characters. I
first explained the brute-force approach along with its time complexity and then optimized it using the
sliding window technique with a HashSet and two pointers, discussing the improved time complexity.
Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked about the biggest challenges fresh
graduates face during their initial months in the company. Both interviewers answered enthusiastically,
sharing their experiences and expectations from new hires. We had a brief but insightful conversation before
I thanked them for their time and walked out hoping for the best.

3. HR Round [21 students appeared]

Round 2: HR Interview (approx 25 mins)

The final round was an HR interview conducted by the HR Head (Asia Pacific) and the Managing
Director. The interview began on a very light and friendly note. They asked how my day had been, how the
OA went, whether it was lengthy, and made me feel comfortable before moving on to the actual questions.
They then asked me to introduce myself, followed by questions about my family, where I lived, and how I
planned to commute to the office at Goregaon. I mentioned that although I live in Navi Mumbai, I currently
stay in a PG. They asked what I would do if my parents wanted me to shift back home. I answered
positively, saying that my family has always supported my career decisions and that I believe ISS STOXX
would provide me with excellent opportunities for growth, so we would manage accordingly. One thing I
would recommend is to always answer such questions positively-the interviewer is often trying to
understand your commitment rather than looking for a perfect answer.
The conversation then shifted towards my hobbies and whether I still actively pursued them. They also
asked about my internship experience, the technologies I had worked on, my responsibilities, and the size of
my team. This gave me a chance to naturally mention that I had worked in an Agile environment using Jira
for project management.
I was also asked how I learn technologies outside my college curriculum. While answering, I mentioned that
I regularly take online courses and referred to a few Coursera certifications I had completed. I also used
this opportunity to talk about my hackathon victory, even though it wasn't directly asked. Remember, you
don't always have to wait for the interviewer to ask about your achievements-if there's a natural opening,
confidently bring them into the conversation. Lastly, they asked me about a project that had created a
meaningful impact. I spoke about my Women's Safety Application mentioned on resume, explaining the
motivation behind it and answering a few follow-up questions.
Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked them about their first six months at
ISS STOXX and what their onboarding experience had been like. The Managing Director laughed and said
that he had been with the company for so many years that he barely remembered his first six months
--- PAGE 5 ---
anymore. I smiled and mentioned that I recognized him from the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), which made
the conversation even more engaging.
The other interviewer then shared her journey at ISS STOXX, talking about how she had grown within the
organization and the experiences that shaped her career. Towards the end of her answer, she spoke about the
core values of ISS STOXX. I took that opportunity to connect my own aspirations with the company's
culture and mentioned that those values genuinely resonated with me. I also added that ISS STOXX, being
at the intersection of finance and technology, perfectly aligns with my interests and career goals,
making me feel that I truly belong here and was excited about the opportunity to contribute and learn.
I thanked both the interviewers for their time, wished them a great day, and walked out of the room with a
smile, hoping for the best.
Overall, the HR round felt more like a conversation than an interview. My biggest advice would be to be
genuine, answer confidently, and keep the conversation natural. Don't hesitate to highlight your
achievements whenever you get the opportunity, whether it's internships, certifications, hackathons, or
projects. Most importantly, keep a smile on your face throughout the interview. No matter how nervous you
feel on the inside, projecting confidence and enthusiasm leaves a lasting impression.
Later that night, the final list of 12 selected candidates was released. Seeing my name on it was a moment
of pure happiness and relief. All the hard work had finally paid off.

1. Screening Round on HackerEarth (14/08/2026)

2. Machine Coding Round (18/08/2026)

3. Technical Round 1(18/08/2026)

4. Technical Round 2 (18/08/2026)

5. Interview with the Head of Engineering (19/08/2026)

1. Screening Round on HackerEarth [ Around 40 student were shortlisted for this round]

It has been more than a month since this process was conducted so apologies in advance for any hazy details
but I'll try my best to keep it as accurate as possible. The CGPA criteria was 8.5+ while applying which was
the first major hurdle to cross ( My CGPA at the time of application was 9.28). I would assume they also
shortlisted candidates on the basis of one's resume's ATS score so make sure your resume is polished as
well. I recommend Resume Worded for calculating your resume's ATS score. From what I have seen,
anything above 60 is good but I'd recommend getting it above 70 ( The one I submitted scored 78).
As for the screening round, there were 3 coding questions:

1) A sort of non-DSA question about reverse proxies in which you are given a list of requests and are

asked to route the requests to their respective services and finally output which machine handled
which request.

2) A simple DSA question on Dynamic Programming

3) A simple DSA question using Two Pointers

Note: I don't consider myself to be that good at DSA, so when I say they were simple questions, I actually
do mean they were pretty doable. The first question was very non-typical and no one I know was able to
fully solve it (including me), so just try to pass as many test cases as possible.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Machine Coding Round | 11 candidates appeared for this round] (2 Hours )

In this round, we were asked to code a server using the framework of our choice over the duration of 2
hours. I chose Flask for its simplicity and the ease of multithreading. We were invited to a Zoom meeting for
which we were supposed to be ready for at 9am ( The actual timings were from 10:30am to 1:30am). The
entire process was conducted from home. The meeting actually began a little after 10:30 during which we
were briefed about the process and eventually were assigned our individual Zoom breakout rooms. We were
alone in our respective Zoom breakout room along with one mentor/evaluator from Edra Labs (Don't worry,
they are nice and helpful people) who provided us with the problem statement when the clock started
running. A single mentor was responsible for multiple rooms as such he was not in the room throughout the
entire coding round but you could call upon him for queries/help by using the 'Raise Hand' feature in Zoom.
Once you were done with your code, we had to roughly explain it to our assigned mentor/evaluator and
submit it as a zip on a GForm provided at the end. After this, we were allowed to leave the meeting and were
told to wait for any calls from Edra Labs.

3. Technical Round 1 (Note: From here onwards, the people from Edra Labs directly called the

participants eligible for the next round. As such, the exact number of participants for each round is
not known. It is extremely important to pay attention to your phone as they may call you at any
time after your rounds. If you are like me and keep your device on silent or DnD indefinitely,
you should toggle both off for the duration of this process.) (30 Minutes )
I got a call at around 1:37pm informing me that I have been shortlisted for this round (Note that I was done
pretty early with my machine coding round at around 12:30pm ). Another zoom meeting was scheduled for
me for this round (3:00pm - 3:30pm ) during the call itself post my approval. My interview started with the
interviewer giving his introduction and what he does over at Edra Labs. Then he asked me to introduce
myself and go through my resume. I talked about myself and the various projects I have done. We went on
to talk about the various functional and non-functional requirements of several of my projects along the lines
of - What does this do?, Why did you make it?, How many requests could it handle at once?, How would
you go on to scale it?, Why did you choose the tech stack that you did? - and so on. Several of my projects
were Al-related and happened to contain topics the interviewer was familiar with. As such, we went on a
very conversational tangent about various topics until time ran out. It was pretty enjoyable and the
interviewer felt very easy to talk to. The interview ended with him asking if I had any questions for him, to
which I only asked about the projects they work on at Edra Labs. I suppose the key takeaway here would be
to not lie on your resume. Actually do and be familiar with the projects you are mentioning on your resume
and talk about them passionately.

4. Technical Round 2(30 Minutes )

I got a call about being shortlisted for this round at around 4:17pm. I do not exactly remember when my
interview was but it was around 5pm. This interview was a bit more technical asking questions about
Computer Networks, OS, etc. (What happens when you search something?, How does a page load?, etc.).
After that, it went more of the same as the first round as we once again ended up conversing and talking
about my projects, open-source contributions, Linux and AI. Once again, it was very fun talking to the
--- PAGE 3 ---
interviewer and I felt comfortable talking with him throughout the interview. At the end, he mentioned it
was fun talking with me and used the last 5 or so minutes to ask the final question he was meant to ask
before we ended up on a tangent. It was less of a DSA question and more of a logical puzzle - Assuming a
language that can only store 2 digit integers, how would you perform addition? I was able to mostly answer
it but missed a trick about just performing 99 - x to check for overflows instead of raising an exception or a
flag and checking that. He nevertheless seemed satisfied with my solution as well and was rather excited to
talk about the solution on a whiteboard. Once again, I was asked if I had any questions, to which I asked
about the technologies used over at Edra Labs.

5. Interview with the Head of Engineering [ 4 candidates appeared for this round] (Note: This was

the final round for us. There was no HR round.) (30 Minutes )
I was informed about being shortlisted for this round on the same day but the final round was scheduled for
the next day ( 19th August 2026) at 2:00pm - 2:30pm. The issue was that I was also shortlisted for
BlackRock's process which was also happening on the same day. As luck would have it, I ended up getting
shortlisted for the final round of BlackRock as well and it got scheduled at around the same time as my Edra
Labs. Huge props to the folks over at the CCD, they managed to postpone my BlackRock interview to be at
around 4pm rather than 2pm. Allowing me to give both the interviews without sacrificing my prospects to be
in one of the companies. They were also kind enough to provide me with a cabin to give my Edra Labs
Interview in as the BlackRock process was offline. The final interview took place on schedule at 2pm. This
one was the scariest of them all as the interviewer was a senior and pretty stern. He asked me to explain the
code I wrote for the machine coding round line by line and asked detailed questions about why I did what I
did. He asked me to send parallel requests to one of my endpoints and log the times in the console. I had
forgotten how to send parallel curl requests (It's the -Z option) and asked him whether I could look up the
syntax which he allowed. I was trying to avoid the Al overview which he noticed and said I could refer to it
if I wanted. I finally managed to send the requests as he wanted (He took the opportunity to ask me a little
about bash, like why couldn't I just use && to send the parallel requests among a few other questions.
Luckily I was familiar with bash scripting and was able to answer them.). However, the logs printed suggest
the requests were off by 0.000x or so seconds. I was genuinely flummoxed. I hadn't even noticed the
difference at first and claimed that they were parallel for which he corrected me. I accepted that I hadn't
noticed it and apologized after which he went on to ask me why my code wasn't logging the same time for
each request despite being multithreaded. I genuinely had no clue and told him as such, but I also told them I
had theories as to why it may be so and presented them to him with the disclaimer that they might be
incorrect. The answer to me seemed to be natural variation and how you can't really time requests to be truly
parallel but that didn't seem like a satisfying answer, hence I also presented a few other theories. He had a
poker face throughout the interview and I honestly thought I had flunked it by this point. He ended the
interview, asking me to look into why that happened and asked if I had any questions for him. I just asked
about his role at Edra Labs. By the end of it, I had given up hopes but I also had the final BlackRock
interview to give which went extremely well.
I got a call from the CCD at 8:44pm, notifying me that I was the only candidate selected for the role. I
genuinely couldn't believe it. I completely thought I had messed up too much in the final round but ended up
landing the offer. I suppose, you should never lose out on hope. It isn't over until it is over.
--- PAGE 4 ---

journey.prep:
Looking back, I do not believe I was selected because I answered every question perfectly--I certainly did
not. There were questions where I had to think before responding, and there were moments where I felt I
could have articulated my answers better. What I believe made the difference was my strong conceptual
foundation, genuine interest in finance, structured thought process, and the ability to reason through
unfamiliar questions instead of panicking.
More importantly, I had spent the last two years deliberately building my profile around finance. Through
internships, valuation projects, case competitions, leadership experiences, and continuous self-learning, I
had gradually developed both technical knowledge and confidence. The interview simply became an
opportunity to demonstrate that journey.

1. Your Resume is Your Biggest Asset

Know every line of your resume thoroughly. Every internship, project, certification, competition, leadership
position, and even a single word or name mentioned on your resume can become the subject of detailed
questioning.
Only include experiences that you have genuinely worked on and can confidently defend.

2. Build Concepts, Don't Memorise Answers

Instead of memorising interview questions, understand the concepts deeply.
Practice explaining topics such as:
 Three Financial Statements
 Valuation
 DCF
 Comparable Company Analysis
 M&A
 Working Capital
 Corporate Finance
out loud, exactly as if you were explaining them to an interviewer.
The interviewers are evaluating your thought process, not your ability to reproduce textbook definitions.

3. Treat the Group Discussion as a Business Discussion

The objective is not to speak the most.
The objective is to contribute meaningful ideas.

Come prepared with 3-4 structured perspectives, listen carefully to others, and whenever appropriate,
acknowledge someone's point before building upon it.
This demonstrates maturity, collaboration, and professional communication.

4. Never Compare Your Journey with Others

This is probably the biggest lesson from our process.
Different candidates had:
 Different interview panels.
 Different technical questions.
 Different interview durations.
 Different numbers of technical rounds.
Some candidates had one interview.
Some had two.
Some had three.
Some finished within 15 minutes.
Others continued for much longer.
None of these factors indicated whether they would eventually be selected.
Focus only on your own preparation and performance.

5. Continue Preparing While Waiting

There can be long waiting periods between rounds.
My Technical Interview concluded at around 11:50 AM, and my HR Interview was completed by
approximately 12:20 PM. However, several other candidates continued with their technical interviews until
3:00-4:00 PM, and the final results were declared only around 5:00 PM.
Don't get distracted , just focus.

6. Never Underestimate the Online Assessment

Personally, I found the Online Assessment to be one of the most stressful stages because it is a major
elimination round and many highly capable candidates are filtered out at this stage.
Looking back, I feel I could have performed even better with more timed practice and additional preparation
for Market Awareness.

Do not assume that a strong resume alone is sufficient--the Online Assessment deserves dedicated
preparation.

7. If I Had More Time...

Looking back, there are a few things I wish I had done even better.
 I would have attempted CFA Level I before placements if my academic schedule had permitted.
 I would have tried to gain additional finance work experience, particularly through boutique
investment banks, research firms, or valuation-focused internships.
 I would have started following global financial markets even earlier and in greater depth.
Although none of these were mandatory for selection, they would have further strengthened my profile.

8. Learn AI Alongside Finance

One area that I found increasingly valuable throughout my preparation was the application of Artificial
Intelligence to finance.
During my interviews, I discussed how I had used AI tools responsibly to improve my understanding of
valuation, financial modelling, research, and market analysis. We also had discussions around Large
Language Models (LLMs), their applications, and how they can improve productivity while still requiring
strong financial judgement.

9. Stay Curious

Throughout my preparation, I realised that interviewers appreciate candidates who are genuinely curious.
Read annual reports.
Read investor presentations.
Follow major transactions.
Understand why companies merge.
Learn how businesses create value.
Do not prepare only for interviews.
Prepare to become a better finance professional.
.
