journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

● Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

● Resume Shortlisting

● Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

● Group Discussion (2 July 2026)

● Technical Interview (2 July 2026)

● HR Interview (2 July 2026)

● Final Result Declaration (2 July 2026)

The entire interview process was conducted virtually from the college campus  due to heavy rainfall and a
red alert declared in Mumbai. Although the interviews were online, all shortlisted candidates were required
to report to the college, from where the complete selection process was coordinated.
One important observation is that the interview process was highly dynamic . Different interview panels
followed slightly different formats, and there was no fixed sequence of rounds for every candidate. The
duration of interviews, number of technical rounds, and the order in which candidates were shortlisted
varied significantly across panels. While some candidates had two technical interviews before the HR round,
others were directly shortlisted for HR after a single technical interview. Therefore, do not compare your
process with that of other candidates during the day or draw conclusions based on interview duration,
the order in which candidates are called, or the number of rounds they undergo.  Each panel evaluates
candidates independently.
For our batch, approximately 54 candidates were shortlisted after the Online Assessment and were divided
into 6 Group Discussion panels, with around 9 candidates in each panel. Each GD panel was evaluated by

two interviewers. Following the GD, approximately 3-4 candidates from each panel were shortlisted for the
interview stage.
The interview stage was also divided into 6 interview panels, each comprising senior professionals from J.P.
Morgan. In my case, I was interviewed directly by a Vice President (VP) My selection process consisted of
one Technical Interview followed by one HR Interview . However, this should not be considered the
standard format, as several candidates underwent multiple technical interviews before moving to HR.
Throughout the day, the process remained flexible, and interview schedules were continuously adjusted based
on panel availability. My advice is to stay calm, avoid speculating about your chances based on others'
experiences, and remain mentally prepared for any interview format. Focus only on your own
performance, as the evaluation process differs across panels.

Selection Statistics (Banking Role)
The recruitment process for the Corporate & Investment Banking (Banking) Internship  was highly
competitive.
 275+ students applied across the Banking and Risk roles during the campus recruitment process.
 After resume screening, 67 candidates were shortlisted for the Banking role.
 55 candidates progressed to the Online Assessment stage.
 29 candidates were shortlisted for the Group Discussion round.
 10 candidates advanced to the HR Interview.
 Finally, 10 internship offers  were rolled out for the Banking role, with the internship carrying the
opportunity for a Performance-Based Pre-Placement Offer (PPO).
Overall, the selection process was highly competitive, with multiple elimination stages evaluating not only
technical knowledge and aptitude, but also communication skills, commercial awareness, structured thinking,
and overall cultural fit with the firm

Pre-Placement Talk  (300+ Candidates appeared )
The recruitment process began with the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), followed by the application through
the official J.P. Morgan Chase Careers Portal. While many students consider the PPT to be a routine
introductory session, I strongly recommend treating it as the first round of your preparation rather than a
formality.
The PPT provides valuable insights into the firm's businesses, culture, internship structure, expectations
from interns, and the specific responsibilities associated with each role. Pay close attention to the discussion,
as many of the points shared during the session can later be incorporated into your interview answers,
particularly for questions such as "Why J.P. Morgan?", "Why this role?", and "What do you expect from this
internship?"
 Take detailed notes throughout the session. Instead of relying solely on the presentation slides,
write down important points regarding J.P. Morgan's businesses, the Corporate & Investment
Banking division, the Banking role, and the qualities the firm values in its employees. I also
recommend taking screenshots of important slides for future reference.
 Understand the role in depth. Note the responsibilities, day-to-day work, required skills, and how
the Banking division fits within J.P. Morgan's overall business. This understanding will help you
tailor both your resume and your interview responses.
 Do not ask questions merely to gain visibility. During our PPT, the presenters repeatedly
encouraged students to keep their questions relevant to the role. If you genuinely have a thoughtful
question related to the internship, business, or role, ask it confidently. However, avoid asking generic
or unnecessary questions simply to be noticed.
 Pay attention to the speakers. Make a note of the names and designations of the HR
representatives and business professionals conducting the session. While the same individuals
may not necessarily interview you, referring to insights shared during the PPT demonstrates genuine
interest in the firm.
 Read the Job Description (JD) thoroughly--word by word. This is one of the most overlooked
aspects of preparation. Every requirement mentioned in the JD indicates what the firm is looking for
in a candidate. Understanding these requirements will help you refine your resume, highlight
relevant experiences, and significantly improve your chances of getting shortlisted.

 Start following financial markets well in advance. Ideally, begin reading business and financial
news at least a year before placements. Develop the habit of tracking:

o Major Mergers & Acquisitions
o IPOs
o Equity and Debt Capital Market transactions
o Global macroeconomic developments
o Interest rate decisions by major central banks
o Geopolitical events affecting financial markets
o Significant transactions advised by leading investment banks such as J.P. Morgan, Goldman
Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citi, HSBC, Barclays, and others.
This long-term preparation will not only strengthen your market awareness but also help you perform
better during Group Discussions and interviews, where commercial awareness is evaluated
extensively.
The PPT is your first opportunity to understand exactly what the firm is looking for. If you use it
effectively, it becomes much easier to align your preparation, resume, and interview answers with the
expectations of the role. Looking back, I found that several points discussed during the PPT directly helped
me answer interview questions and demonstrate a clearer understanding of both J.P. Morgan and the

2.     Resume Shortlisting (67 candidates shortlisted)

In my opinion, resume shortlisting is the most important elimination stage of the entire recruitment
process. Before you get an opportunity to demonstrate your technical knowledge, communication skills,
or market awareness, your resume must first convince the recruiters that you are a suitable fit for the role.
For our process, 67 candidates were shortlisted from the resume screening stage, making it one of the
most competitive elimination rounds.
One important observation from our recruitment process was that several candidates with exceptionally
strong profiles were not shortlisted . The exact shortlisting criteria were never disclosed  to us, and
therefore it is difficult to conclude that selection depends on any single factor such as CGPA, internships,
or certifications alone. My advice would be to focus on building the strongest and most balanced profile
possible rather than trying to optimize for one particular metric.
For the Banking role, your resume should demonstrate a consistent and genuine interest in finance rather
than simply listing finance-related certifications or buzzwords. The strongest resumes usually tell a
coherent story, where internships, projects, competitions, leadership positions, and certifications
collectively reinforce your interest in Corporate & Investment Banking.
During my preparation, I spent over two months working exclusively on my resume. It went through 8-
9 major iterations , incorporating continuous feedback from seniors, mentors, professionals working in
Investment Banking, and placement coordinators. Every revision focused on improving clarity,
quantifying impact, strengthening Investment Banking-specific terminology, and ensuring that every
bullet point reflected work I had genuinely performed. Include all the things in a numerically ,
quantifying all the things u have mentioned with IB related words
Before submitting my final resume, I also evaluated it using multiple ATS (Applicant Tracking System)
platforms, including Resume Worded, where it achieved a score of 91. While ATS scores should not be
treated as the sole indicator of resume quality, I would recommend maintaining a score of 80+ to ensure
that your resume is ATS-friendly and appropriately optimized. Equally important is ensuring that your
resume is free from grammatical, formatting, spelling, and alignment errors, as even minor mistakes
can create a poor impression or affect automated screening systems.
Although the minimum eligibility criterion for our process was a CGPA above 7 , I would strongly
recommend maintaining the highest CGPA possible throughout your academic journey. In addition to your
undergraduate performance, Class X and Class XII academic records may also be considered by
recruiters, even though the exact evaluation methodology is not disclosed. Therefore, maintaining
consistency across your academic record is always beneficial.
Your resume should ideally contain  two strong finance projects that you understand thoroughly, rather
than multiple superficial projects. Every project listed on your resume is a potential discussion topic during
the interview. Interviewers frequently ask detailed follow-up questions to assess the depth of your
understanding, so never include a project that you have not personally completed or cannot
confidently defend . It is always better to present fewer, high-quality projects than a long list of
experiences that lack substance.(I had represented 3)
Apart from projects, I strongly encourage participating in finance case competitions organised by IIMs,
IITs, and other reputed institutions. These competitions provide practical exposure to valuation, financial

modelling, M&A, corporate finance, and strategic decision-making while significantly strengthening your
resume.
Leadership is another aspect that recruiters value. Try to hold one or two meaningful Positions of
Responsibility (PORs)  where you can demonstrate measurable impact. Focus on contributing
meaningfully rather than simply collecting titles, and wherever possible, quantify your achievements.
If possible, secure at least one relevant internship or work experience before placements. While this is
not a mandatory requirement , it significantly strengthens your profile and provides valuable practical
exposure. Obtaining a finance internship can be difficult, especially initially. Personally, I faced numerous
rejections while applying through LinkedIn and cold emailing professionals, HRs, boutique investment
firms, and research firms before eventually securing an opportunity. My advice is to remain persistent
network actively, reach out to professionals, and do not be discouraged by early rejections.
Professional certifications such as the CFA Program can further strengthen your profile and demonstrate
a genuine commitment to finance. Although I was unable to attempt the examination before the recruitment
process due to time constraints, I believe that clearing CFA Level I  can positively differentiate your
profile. However, it is important to emphasize that it is not a prerequisite for selection . In our batch, 9
out of the 10 selected candidates had not completed CFA Level I , clearly indicating that recruiters
evaluate the overall quality of your profile rather than any single certification.
Finally, remember that your resume is not merely a document--it becomes the blueprint for your
interview. Every line can become the subject of detailed questioning. Build a profile that reflects genuine
interest, tailor your resume specifically for the role, eliminate every possible error, and include only
experiences that you can discuss confidently and honestly.
Remember that interviewers often try to understand the story behind your resume rather than simply verify
its contents. If your profile spans multiple domains, be prepared to explain how your experiences connect
to your interest in finance and why you chose this role.

GROUP DISCUSSION (29 STUDENTS WERE SHORTLISTED)
The shortlist for the Group Discussion (GD) was announced on the evening before the interviews, along
with the discussion topic. This left candidates with very little preparation time. My advice would be to begin
your research immediately after the shortlist is announced instead of waiting until the next morning.
Personally, I spent approximately four hours researching the topic the previous night and another one
hour revising and organising my thoughts on the morning of the interview. This preparation proved
extremely valuable, as the discussion required structured thinking rather than spontaneous opinions.
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful share of its
inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are
approximately twice as long for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, adversely
affecting financial metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
Unlike a conventional Group Discussion based on current affairs, this was a business case discussion where
candidates were expected to think like senior management and propose practical, well-reasoned business
solutions.
The discussion lasted approximately 20-25 minutes, with 8-10 candidates in each panel. It was a
moderator-driven discussion, meaning the moderators actively guided the conversation, asked follow-up
questions, and ensured that every participant had a fair opportunity to contribute. Rather than allowing

candidates to debate freely, the moderators frequently directed questions toward specific individuals and
encouraged discussion from multiple perspectives.
In my panel, I contributed four times during the discussion. Instead of speaking frequently simply to
increase my participation count, I ensured that each contribution either introduced a new perspective,
expanded upon an existing point, or proposed a practical solution. I believe this approach demonstrated
structured thinking and collaborative problem-solving rather than merely trying to dominate the discussion.
One important point to note is that candidates were not permitted to refer to written notes during the
GD. Therefore, while researching, avoid preparing lengthy scripts. Instead, focus on understanding the case
thoroughly and memorising the key ideas, frameworks, and important facts so that your responses appear
natural and conversational.
Preparation Strategy
Since the preparation window is extremely limited, I would recommend using multiple sources to
understand the problem from different perspectives. I primarily used Google and Gemini to gather
information on supply chain disruptions, global shipping, inventory management, logistics, freight costs,
inflationary pressures, and the financial implications of delayed imports. Rather than simply collecting facts,
my objective was to understand the complete business context and think like a CEO responsible for making
strategic decisions.
While researching, try to analyse the case from multiple perspectives, such as:
 Supply Chain & Logistics
 Operations & Inventory Management
 Finance & Cost Management
 Customer Experience
 Risk Management
 Procurement & Vendor Diversification
 Pricing Strategy
 International Trade & Geopolitical Risks
This broader understanding allows you to answer follow-up questions confidently and contribute meaningful
insights during the discussion.
 Treat the GD as a business discussion, not a debate. The objective is to solve the problem
collectively rather than prove that your opinion is superior.
 Focus on adding value instead of speaking the most. A few meaningful contributions are
significantly more impactful than speaking repeatedly without introducing new ideas.
 Research the topic from multiple perspectives. Moderators frequently ask follow-up questions to
evaluate the depth of your understanding.
 Build upon others' ideas whenever appropriate. You do not have to disagree simply to stand out.
If another candidate makes a good point, acknowledge it and extend the discussion further.
Demonstrating collaboration often creates a better impression than unnecessary confrontation.

 Listen actively. Since the moderators ensured that everyone had an opportunity to speak, there was
no need to interrupt or compete for speaking time.
 Maintain a structured approach. Present your thoughts logically, explaining not only what you
would do but also why you would do it and how it would affect the business.
 Remain calm and confident. The moderators are evaluating your thought process, communication
skills, business acumen, and ability to work as part of a team--not whether you arrive at the perfect
solution.
Looking back, I believe that thorough preparation, structured thinking, and collaborative participation
were the biggest factors that contributed to my performance in the Group Discussion. Rather than trying to
impress the panel by speaking the most, I focused on making every contribution meaningful, practical, and
relevant to the case. I believe this approach aligned well with what J.P. Morgan was looking for in
prospective interns. One observation from our recruitment process was that many candidates who had
performed confidently during the Group Discussion were called for their interviews relatively early in
the day. While I cannot confirm whether this was an official evaluation criterion or simply a scheduling
decision, it was a noticeable pattern during our process.
For instance, interviews across the different panels began at approximately 11:30 AM, and I received my
call for the Technical Interview at around 11:35 AM, immediately after the Group Discussion. However, I
would advise future candidates not to draw conclusions based solely on the order in which interviews
are conducted, as scheduling may vary depending on panel availability and logistics.
Irrespective of the interview order, treat the Group Discussion as one of the most important stages of the
recruitment process. Enter the discussion with 3-4 well-structured points prepared around different
aspects of the case rather than memorising complete answers. Since written notes are not allowed during the
discussion, focus on understanding the business problem thoroughly so that you can speak naturally and
confidently.
Finally, do not let anxiety affect your performance. It is natural to feel nervous before speaking, but
excessive stress often causes candidates to forget points they have already prepared. Trust your preparation,
listen carefully to the discussion, and contribute thoughtfully whenever you have something meaningful to
add. Remember that the panel is evaluating your ability to think logically, communicate effectively, and
collaborate with others, not the number of times you speak. In my experience, remaining calm and
composed helped me articulate my thoughts much more effectively than trying to force additional
contributions.

We further discussed various valuation multiples, including:
 EV / EBITDA
 EV / EBIT

 Equity Value based multiples
The interviewer then asked which valuation multiples are appropriate for different industries.
I explained that multiple selection depends on:
 Industry characteristics
 Capital structure
 Profitability
 Business model
For example, I discussed why:
 Banks are commonly valued using Price-to-Book (P/B) and Return on Equity because Enterprise
Value is not meaningful due to the nature of debt in banking institutions.
 Manufacturing companies frequently use EV/EBITDA because it allows comparison independent of
capital structure.

6. Why do we use EV/EBITDA instead of Market Capitalisation / Net Income?

This question tested conceptual understanding rather than memorisation.
The interviewer asked:
 Why EV is paired with EBITDA.
 Why P/E uses Net Income.
 Why Enterprise Value cannot be compared with Net Income.
I explained that valuation multiples should always compare like with like.
Enterprise Value represents the value attributable to both debt and equity holders, whereas EBITDA is a
pre-interest operating metric that is independent of financing decisions.
Similarly,
Market Capitalisation represents only the value attributable to equity shareholders.
Therefore,
 Enterprise Value is compared with EBITDA or EBIT.
 Market Capitalisation is compared with Net Income using the P/E multiple.
I also explained how EBITDA removes the impact of:
 Capital Structure
 Interest Expense
 Taxation
thereby enabling better comparison across companies with different financing structures.

However, do not assume that a conversational interview is an easy interview. Every response is being
evaluated carefully. The interviewer is assessing not only what you say but also how you communicate,
structure your thoughts, and whether your motivations appear genuine.
Throughout the discussion, I ensured that my answers consistently reflected the themes that J.P. Morgan had
emphasised during the Pre-Placement Talk--particularly client service, teamwork, ownership, integrity,
professionalism, and continuous learning. Rather than providing generic HR responses, I connected each
answer to the firm's values and to my own experiences, making my responses more authentic and relevant.
Tips for Future Aspirants
 Do not take the HR round lightly simply because it is conversational. This is the final stage of
evaluation, and every answer contributes to the overall assessment.
 Prepare convincing answers for "Tell me about yourself," "Why Finance?", "Why Investment
Banking?", "Why J.P. Morgan?", and "Why not MBA?"
 Understand J.P. Morgan's culture and values, particularly its emphasis on client service,
teamwork, integrity, and excellence.
 Structure every answer with examples from your own experiences rather than giving generic
responses.
 Prepare 2-3 thoughtful questions for the interviewer. This demonstrates curiosity and genuine
interest in both the role and the organisation.
 Most importantly, be authentic. The interviewer is not looking for rehearsed answers but for
candidates who communicate clearly, think logically, and genuinely align with the firm's culture.
Looking back, I believe the HR Interview was less about finding perfect answers and more about
demonstrating maturity, professionalism, and a genuine motivation to build a long-term career in Investment
Banking at J.P. Morgan
All 10 students who gave this round were selected

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Looking back, I do not believe I was selected because I answered every question perfectly--I certainly did
not. There were questions where I had to think before responding, and there were moments where I felt I
could have articulated my answers better. What I believe made the difference was my strong conceptual
foundation, genuine interest in finance, structured thought process, and the ability to reason through
unfamiliar questions instead of panicking.
More importantly, I had spent the last two years deliberately building my profile around finance. Through
internships, valuation projects, case competitions, leadership experiences, and continuous self-learning, I
had gradually developed both technical knowledge and confidence. The interview simply became an
opportunity to demonstrate that journey.

1. Your Resume is Your Biggest Asset

Know every line of your resume thoroughly. Every internship, project, certification, competition, leadership
position, and even a single word or name mentioned on your resume can become the subject of detailed
questioning.
Only include experiences that you have genuinely worked on and can confidently defend.

2. Build Concepts, Don't Memorise Answers

Instead of memorising interview questions, understand the concepts deeply.
Practice explaining topics such as:
 Three Financial Statements
 Valuation
 DCF
 Comparable Company Analysis
 M&A
 Working Capital
 Corporate Finance
out loud, exactly as if you were explaining them to an interviewer.
The interviewers are evaluating your thought process, not your ability to reproduce textbook definitions.

3. Treat the Group Discussion as a Business Discussion

The objective is not to speak the most.
The objective is to contribute meaningful ideas.

Come prepared with 3-4 structured perspectives, listen carefully to others, and whenever appropriate,
acknowledge someone's point before building upon it.
This demonstrates maturity, collaboration, and professional communication.

4. Never Compare Your Journey with Others

This is probably the biggest lesson from our process.
Different candidates had:
 Different interview panels.
 Different technical questions.
 Different interview durations.
 Different numbers of technical rounds.
Some candidates had one interview.
Some had two.
Some had three.
Some finished within 15 minutes.
Others continued for much longer.
None of these factors indicated whether they would eventually be selected.
Focus only on your own preparation and performance.

5. Continue Preparing While Waiting

There can be long waiting periods between rounds.
My Technical Interview concluded at around 11:50 AM, and my HR Interview was completed by
approximately 12:20 PM. However, several other candidates continued with their technical interviews until
3:00-4:00 PM, and the final results were declared only around 5:00 PM.
Don't get distracted , just focus.

6. Never Underestimate the Online Assessment

Personally, I found the Online Assessment to be one of the most stressful stages because it is a major
elimination round and many highly capable candidates are filtered out at this stage.
Looking back, I feel I could have performed even better with more timed practice and additional preparation
for Market Awareness.

Do not assume that a strong resume alone is sufficient--the Online Assessment deserves dedicated
preparation.

7. If I Had More Time...

Looking back, there are a few things I wish I had done even better.
 I would have attempted CFA Leve

1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Resume + Behavioural Interview)

1.  Online Assessment  [ 100+ candidates appeared for this round ]

The  Online  Assessment  (OA)  was  a  1-hour  MCQ  and  programming  test  conducted  on  the
HackerEarth  platform.  It  consisted  of  a  total  of  22  questions:  20  MCQs  based  on  mathematics  and
logical reasoning, and 2 programming questions.
The  marking  scheme  was  as  follows:  each  MCQ  carried  4  marks,  while  each  programming  question
carried  20  marks.  To  be  eligible  to  attempt  the  OA,  candidates  were  required  to  have  a  minimum
CGPA of 8.0.
The  programming  section  included  questions  of  varying  difficulty.  The  first  question  was  of
LeetCode  medium-easy  level,  involving  concepts  such  as  sorting,  greedy  algorithms,  and  the
two-pointer  approach.  The  second  question  was  of  LeetCode  medium-hard  level,  based  on  number
theory,  prefix  and  suffix  GCDs,  and  detailed  implementation  logic.  Only  a  few  candidates  were  able
to solve both programming questions successfully.
The  MCQ  section  primarily  focused  on  counting,  combinatorics,  and  probability.  Having  a  strong
foundation  in  12th-grade  combinatorics  concepts  proved  helpful,  though  revising  these  topics
beforehand would have been even more beneficial.
Overall,  the  assessment  was  well-balanced,  testing  both  analytical  reasoning  and  problem-solving
ability through a combination of conceptual and coding challenges.

2. Interview Round 1  [ 50+ candidates appeared for this round ]

This  round  was  conducted  approx  20  minutes  after  the  OA  results  came  out.  Since  this  was  my
ssssssss  second  time  (first  was  UBS)  giving  interviews  on  campus,  I  didn't  feel  very  nervous  here.  Also,  the
ssssssss  interviewers  were pretty welcoming so that helped me stay calm.
My  first  round  of  the  interview  began  with  a  series  of  logical  and  analytical  puzzles.  I  was  asked
questions  such  as  identifying  the  next  number  in  a  sequence,  the  classic  5L-3L  jug  problem,  the  two
burning  ropes  problem,  and  the  Knights  and  Knaves  logic  puzzle.  These  were  aimed  at  testing  my
problem-solving and reasoning abilities.
Following  the  puzzles,  the  discussion  moved  on  to  core  technical  topics.  I  was  asked  questions
related  to  Operating  Systems,  Data  Structures,  Java,  and  SQL.  In  SQL,  the  focus  was  on  joins  and
their different types.
From  Object-Oriented  Programming,  I  was  asked  to  explain  the  four  main  principles  of  OOP,  along
with conceptual and syntax-based questions such as what is an object.
In  Data  Structures  and  Algorithms,  I  was  tested  on  DFS  and  BFS  traversal  techniques,  the  binary
search  algorithm,  recursion,  and  graph  concepts.  I  was  also  asked  to  explain  hashing,  collisions  in
hashing,  and  methods  to  reduce  collisions.  Additionally,  I  was  asked  to  write  a  program  to  find  the
maximum element in a Binary Search Tree (BST).
Overall,  the  interview  was  comprehensive  and  balanced,  testing  both  logical  aptitude  and  technical
depth. It lasted approximately 20-25 minutes.

3. Interview Round 2  [ 10+ candidates appeared for this round]

This  round  was  conducted  at  varying  times  for  different  candidates.  In  my  case,  it  took  place
approximately  3-4  hours  after  Interview  Round  1.  It  was  a  one-on-one  discussion  with  the  Senior
Director and felt more like a professional conversation than a formal technical interview.
The  interview  began  with  the  Director  going  through  my  resume  and  asking  me  to  describe  my  best
project  and  explain  why  I  considered  it  my  best.  He  then  asked  several  in-depth  technical  questions
related  to  the  project.  Although  I  didn't  have  precise  answers  to  a  few  of  them,  I  made  sure  to
explain my thought process clearly, which the interviewer seemed satisfied with.
After  around  10  minutes  of  technical  discussion,  the  interview  gradually  transitioned  into  an
HR-style  round.  The  Director  asked  me  questions  such  as  "What  motivates  you?",  "What  frustrates
you?",  "What  are  your  goals?",  and  "What  are  your  strengths?".  It  was  evident  that  he  valued
honesty  and  self-awareness  more  than  rehearsed  or  overly  polished  answers,  so  responding  humbly
and genuinely was key.
Towards  the  end,  he  invited  me  to  ask  questions.  I  began  by  requesting  him  to  revisit  one  of  the
earlier  technical  questions  I  hadn't  answered  completely,  and  we  discussed  it  further  for  about  10
minutes.  After  that,  I  asked  him  why  he  chose  to  join  Russell  Investments  and  what  had  motivated
him  to  continue  his  journey  in  the  company.  The  conversation  concluded  on  a  pleasant  and  insightful
note.
In  the  end,  6  students  were  offered  the  Tech  Intern  role  at  Russell  Investments  from  among  the  7
shortlisted candidates (with 1 candidate being offered the Investment Research role).

1. Round 1: Resume Shortlisting [Everyone was eligible to apply so I am assuming upwards of 200]

This round was based on your resume, pay attention to the ppt to understand what they want in a candidate and what the role is about, tailor your resume not only for the technical keywords but also for what the role requires, for example, the role requires us to sit close to non-technical people and observe how they work and how we can make their lives easier by simplifying their workflows.

Here is a resume I generally used:
[Chiranjan_Resume.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ewouVKoDckSi4azyvJHJPJeIxTmxoBDd/view?usp=sharing)
v/s the one I applied with:
[Chiranjan_Resume_UBS.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1y6vLjGO-ntg3kSXHNNbX5c_WDHNjqh0J/view?usp=sharing)
They asked to put a photo on the resume, even if they don't mention it, I think it is better to do so (might be right, might be wrong).

All in all, pay attention to what you put in your resume. I highlighted how I collaborated with different people during my internships, and how they made the product better, the role was agentic so I swapped a deep learning project for one with agentic AI and which made it easier for people to log their complaints.

Basically don't stop at keyword matching for tailoring your resume, go the extra mile to reword your experiences, because that's literally the selection criteria -- Your resume.

2. Round 2 Name:  Technical interview [Only 10 students made it to this round]

We were given a take home assessment, pay attention to ppt, that will guide you how to interpret the take home assessment, and make your solution appeal better to the interviewers. The assignment was to make interfaces for a senior leader and a risk analyst based on the given dataset, the interface should make their jobs easier by allowing them to focus on exactly where they have to make a decision and how to prioritize which case/part of the process they should look at.
My interview was around the assessment itself, all the interviews were only 30 minutes, so you need to be quick, the interviewer then asked about my work, what tools I use, how I solve a problem when given one (again, pay attention to the ppt and the job description, you will understand how to answer these questions from there).
The interviewer didn't ask me if I had any questions, but I asked the interviewer if I can ask them a question, so I asked "Was there anything about this interview that would make you think that this is not a good fit?" Of course they couldn't answer directly but they did give me feedback to be quick, specially because we only had 30 minutes in the interview.

3. HR interview: [5 Of us made it to HR]

First question was "Tell me about yourself", I began by introducing myself and how I solve problems, HR was kind enough to interrupt me and correct me "Not technical, about yourself, your hobby, interests, family background".
Be yourself in HR round thats all (of course be formal and prepare for some standard HR questions as well).

4 students were offered the job.

1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Tech Interview)

All Three Rounds were conducted on the same day.

1. OA [100+ candidates appeared for this round ]

Duration: 60 minutes (Hackerearth)
Format: 20 MCQs (4 marks each) + 2 Coding Questions (20 marks each)
Tip: Before attempting MCQS, quickly read both coding questions. This helps you understand how much
time you'll need for DSA. If the coding questions are tough and time-consuming, solve them first and then
attempt MCQs.
Plan your strategy before starting the test -- decide whether you want to focus on solving the DSA questions
or aim to get maximum MCQs correct. Both paths can help you clear the OA, but with limited time, it's
almost impossible to do everything perfectly. So be clear about your approach from the beginning and stick
to it.
MCQ Section
Most questions were from Probability and Permutation & Combination, while a few were based on time and
space complexity of algorithms. I focused first on the time complexity questions as they were straightforward
and could fetch accurate marks. For probability and combinatorics, since they were lengthy and
calculation-heavy, I guessed a few remaining questions.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Coding / DSA Section
Tip: When in doubt, always start with a brute force solution.
Question 1 - Sorting + Two Pointers (Greedy Approach)
It was similar to this problem https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1090 where you can sort the array and try to
greedily pair largest value with smallest value within k and then accordingly move the pointers
Question 2 - Maximize GCD by Modifying Exactly One Element
You have an array of integers. You are allowed to change exactly one element to any value. Your goal is to
maximize the GCD of the entire array after this modification.
My initial approach was a straightforward brute force idea: for every index in the array, I assumed that
element would be replaced, and then calculated the GCD of all the remaining elements. I repeated this for all
indices and kept track of the maximum GCD obtained. This method was logically correct and helped me
pass 6-7 test cases, but it was inefficient because for every element I was recomputing the GCD of the entire
array, which resulted in a time complexity of around O(n' log n).

2. Interview Round 1[60+ candidates appeared for this round]

Tip: Make a strong first impression, be honest if you don't know something, ask for constraints and
clarifications when solving problems, and explain your answers in a simple, clear way without using
unnecessary technical jargon. Also, always ask at least one question at the end - it shows interest and
maturity.
A day before the interview, I had only revised OOPs concepts from an Apna College YouTube video and
then went to sleep. I wasn't very stressed about the interview because my intention was just to experience it,
understand where I currently stand, and prepare better for future interviews. I genuinely didn't expect to get
shortlisted and was still debating whether or not I even wanted this internship. But things turned out
differently - when the shortlisted names from the OA were announced, my name was on the list. I quickly
ran to get my resume photocopied and within minutes, I was sitting inside the interview room.
The interview started in a very unexpected way. They didn't ask for my introduction, didn't ask about my
resume or projects. Instead, they casually asked, "How did your OA go?" and immediately followed it with
a DSA question. Both interviewers were technically strong and straight to the point, which initially surprised
me, but I decided to go with the flow.
The first problem they asked was to rotate an array https://leetcode.com/problems/rotate-array/ .
I explained multiple approaches - one was using an extra array and placing elements in their new
positions, and the other was a more efficient approach using Python slicing
def rotate (arr,k):
--- PAGE 3 ---
k = k % len(arr)
return arr[-k:] + arr[:-k].
I could see from their expressions that they were satisfied with my thought process.
After that, they moved on to OOPs concepts like abstraction, polymorphism, and types of polymorphism.
Since I had revised these the night before, I could answer well. I had stopped revising at runtime
polymorphism, so for a moment I couldn't explain it. I told them honestly that I couldn't recall it clearly, and
then after they gave a small hint, it clicked and I was able to answer.
Next, they asked questions from SQL - mainly the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and which
one is executed first. I answered that WHERE is applied before grouping and filters rows, while HAVING is
applied after GROUP BY on aggregated results. I also mentioned that WHERE executes first. They then
asked me about Normalization. I explained 1NF first, and when they asked about 2NF, I took a moment,
recalled it, and then explained till 3NF. Thankfully, they didn't go into 4NF.
After that, they moved to core algorithms. They asked me to explain divide and conquer, so I explained it
using merge sort. Then they asked me to explain binary search, its time complexity (O(log n)), and what
condition must be satisfied to apply it. At first, I missed it, but then I smiled when I realized the simple
answer -- the array must be sorted.
Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. Even though I hadn't prepared any, I didn't
want to say no. So I asked, "What kind of work do you do daily, and what kind of problems do you deal
withiạiThey shared their experiences openly, and the conversation ended on a positive note. I knew from
their smile, I was going for round 2.
PS: Always keep smiling even if you don't have any answers ‚the interviewer will guide you

3. Interview Round 2 [ 20+ candidates appeared for this round]

Tip: Talk to other candidates to understand what kind of questions are being asked, but most importantly,
don't back down in the interview room. Stay confident, trust your reasoning, and keep explaining your
thought process clearly - that's what truly leaves an impression.
The second round was conducted on a rolling basis, meaning interviews were happening at different times
for different candidates. I was supposed to have mine after the lunch break, but since I didn't go anywhere
and was sitting outside, they unexpectedly called me in early. Interestingly, another person who was called
along with me had to wait for 2-3 hours before getting his turn, so I considered myself lucky to be
interviewed sooner.
Once again, there were no questions about my resume, projects, or background. They began the
conversation casually, asking how my first round went, and then jumped straight into technical questions.
The interviewer asked about my favorite data structure, to which I confidently replied, "Heaps." He
immediately followed up with, "What about Graphs?" I was honest and said, "Earlier, I used to skip the
graph problems on LeetCode POTD, but later I studied the topic thoroughly and solved over a hundred
graph problems since it's one of the most important topics in DSA." He nodded, satisfied with the response,
and moved on to the main question.
--- PAGE 4 ---
I was given a singly linked list:
1→2→3→4→5→6→7→8
and the expected output was:
7→2→5→4→3→6→1→8
The constraint was to solve it in On) time and O(1) space.
Most Similar Question : https://leetcode.com/problems/reorder-list/
At first glance, I was completely blank, but I didn't panic. I began by observing the pattern and asked a
clarifying question: "If there were an odd number of nodes, how would the pattern change?" This helped me
think aloud and show my reasoning process. I started identifying possible patterns - like reversing the odd
nodes while keeping the even nodes as they were - and simultaneously considered how to perform the
operation in-place, since using an array or another linked list wasn't allowed.
Initially, I thought of the slow and fast pointer approach, but soon realized it might not fully help here. Then
I tried dry-running the given example by moving towards the second-last node, while maintaining two
pointers - head and next - at the start, so I could manipulate pointers directly in place. The interviewer
interjected and asked if I could do it using two pointers. I paused, thought through it, and modified my
approach accordingly. Then he pushed further -- "Can you do it using just one pointer?" I smiled and said
no, explaining that one pointer was needed at the start and one at the end for proper swapping. That seemed
to satisfy them.
After a few minutes of discussion, the other interviewer, who had been mostly silent till now, looked slightly
bored and said, 'Okay, just code it.' That caught me off guard for a moment, but I composed myself and
started coding while explaining my logic step by step. I coded quickly and somewhat hastily, narrating my
thought process as I went. Thankfully, they didn't test it on additional cases, which he had initially
mentioned. Later, I found out from seniors who had cracked the same company that they had the same
interviewers and even the same question - their main goal was not to test perfection but to assess
confidence and problem-solving under pressure.
Despite the challenging question, I never let my confidence drop. Towards the end, they asked if I had any
questions for them. I asked, "What's the biggest difference you've observed between the kind of work you
do that impacts real people and what we, as students, learn in classiạiThe second interviewer, who had been
quiet most of the time, smiled and said, "That's a nice question," and answered fondly.
By that point, I was exhausted but relieved that it was over. I was surprised that the entire round consisted of
only one question - no resume, no project discussions, nothing else. Later, I learned that different panels
had different formats, but I happened to get the most technical one both times. One of the interviewers later
mentioned, "We know from your resume that you've achieved a lot - we just wanted to test your
problem-solving skills and understanding of core concepts." That line stayed with me.
PS: Don't think much about implementation problems, just do what is asked by you.

4. Interview Round 3

--- PAGE 5 ---
After completing the previous rounds, we waited until around 5:00 PM, expecting one more interview
round. However, the coordinators later announced that the shortlisted candidates for the next stage would be
declared in the evening, and the final interactions, if any, would take place the following day. Honestly, I felt
a wave of relief - I thought my interviews were over, and I had already made peace with the idea that I
wouldn't be shortlisted.
Looking at other panels where the interviews were more conversational and focused on resumes and
projects, I felt sure that my highly technical interviews might not have worked in my favor. I was simply
glad that I had given my best and wouldn't have to go through an HR round the next day.
But later that evening, the results were announced - and to my complete surprise, the names they read out
weren't for another round, but for the final internship selection. Hearing my name on that list genuinely
shocked me. It was an unexpected and wholesome moment.

1. Online Assessment [300+ People]

My strategy going into the OA was simple: I estimated that solving around 2-2.5 questions would most
likely be enough to get shortlisted. Instead of chasing every question, I focused on maximizing my score.
Knowing your limits during OA is just as important as knowing DSA.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points)
We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers (capability), plus an integer K denoting the
maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A worker can only do a task if their capability is
greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to find the minimum value of k (1 <= k <= K)
such that all tasks are assigned and no worker does more than k tasks.
Even though this was Question 1, I solved it last because this is the one with the least points. I initially
started off with sorting both the arrays and using two pointers to just greedily assign the task to the current
worker if possible either till it becomes invalid or we exceed k. This passed 9 out of 14 cases.
While implementing it, I noticed: if a particular value of k works, then every value greater than k also
works. That immediately confirmed the answer was monotonic, making it a perfect candidate for Binary
Search on the answer.
Luckily, I had solved a Binary Search problem just before, so recognizing the pattern was almost instant. I
replaced my greedy solution with a Binary Search + feasibility check and ended up passing all the test cases.
Question 2 : Network Routers and Regions (70 Points)
You are given an undirected tree with N nodes representing a network. The network consists of exactly one
central server, multiple routers, and multiple regions. The server is connected only to routers, each router is
connected to the server and one or more regions, and every region is connected to exactly one router. The
task is to determine the number of routers and regions present in the network using the given tree.
Note: Whenever you get an extremely wordy graph or tree problem, DON'T rush into coding. Spend a
minute drawing the structure on paper.
--- PAGE 2 ---
When I actually drew the tree, I understood that the "regions" they kept talking about were literally just the
leaf nodes. And since the problem clearly mentioned there is exactly one "central server" (which is basically
the root of the tree). From there, the solution became almost trivial.
Regions = Count all nodes with degree 1
Routers = N - Regions - 1
All I needed to do was calculate the degree of every node, count the leaves, and apply the formula. It passed
all the test cases.
Problem 3: Problem - 1665C - Codeforces - Tree Infection (110 Points)
You are given a rooted tree with n vertices where vertex 1 is the root. Initially, all vertices are healthy. Every
second, two operations occur in the following order:

1. Manual Infection (Spreading): You can choose exactly one healthy vertex and infect it.

2. Natural Infection (Spreading): For every infected vertex, the disease naturally spreads to exactly

one of its healthy siblings (vertices sharing the same parent).
Your goal is to find the minimum number of seconds required to infect all the vertices in the tree.
I attempted this first because this problem carried a lot of points, so I really wanted to give it the time it
deserved. Right in the start, I noticed that the time needed to infect the entire tree is monotonic, which
immediately told me I could use Binary Search on the answer.
Note: Whenever a question asks for the minimum or maximum value of something like time, days, capacity,
or cost, always stop for a second and check whether the answer space is monotonic. If it is, Binary Search
should be one of the first ideas that comes to mind.
Knowing I needed Binary Search was the easy part; the hard part was figuring out how to actually model the
tree for my check(mid) function. Initially, I kept thinking in terms of the entire tree structure, but after
dry-running a few examples, I realized I was overcomplicating things. Instead of treating it like a tree
problem, I grouped nodes based on the number of children they had and sorted those groups in descending
order.
In my check(mid) function, the greedy logic was simple: we should manually infect the largest groups first.
Because of how the time flows in the problem, group i will naturally infect mid - i nodes on its own. If a
group has more nodes than that, it means we have to step in and use extra manual injections to finish it off.
I coded it up but only passed about half of the test cases due to some annoying implementation bugs. It was
tempting to sit there and debug,but I forced myself to move on to grab points from the other questions.
Luckily, I managed to come back to it at the very end, tweaked a few things, and passed a few more cases.
Problem 4: Problem - 8C - Codeforces (120 Points)
This was the heaviest question on the OA. By the time I got here, I hardly had any time left to fully
understand the intricate details, let alone write out the code for it. I immediately recognized that the optimal
solution would require a Bitmask DP approach, but I knew I didn't have the time to implement it. Instead of
--- PAGE 3 ---
giving up, I tried writing a smart brute-force solution to target specific edge cases (like the sample test cases
provided) just to grab some partial points. Unfortunately, it didn't pass any hidden test cases, but the attempt
was worth the shot.
Takeaway: Knowing how much time to invest in each problem and to stay calm under time pressure will be
the key to your performance...

2. Technical Round 1 [26 People ]

I was in Panel 1
First we had a quick introduction and moved towards the problem
Problem 1: Maximum Points Activated with One Addition - LeetCode
To be completely honest, I started off on the wrong foot.
I proposed a simple two-hashmap approach to keep the frequencies of x and y separately, thinking I could
just pick the max frequency x and y to form a new point. As soon as I tested it out on a sample test case, I
quickly realized on my own that this new point could overlap with an existing point, giving us a wrong
answer.
Then I confirmed with the interviewer how the answer was for the question. I kept thinking out loud and
asked my interviewers for feedback. They hinted that I should try keeping x and y together. Looking at my
hashmaps and talking to them, I started drawing lines between activated points and asked, "Wait, is this
actually a graph problem?" The interviewer didn't reject it, so I dug in.
I realized it was a Connected Components problem. If we connect points that share an x or y, we just need to
find the size of the two largest components. By greedy logic, we pick a new point that connects them,
returning largest_component + second_largest
_component + 1.
I decided to use a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) approach. But then the interviewer asked me how do you
model the graph without hitting an O(N^2) worst-case complexity by checking every point against every
other point?
I had to think on my feet and looked at the two hashmaps I had dry runned earlier and it hit me. I came up
with a way to append 'y' to 'x' and 'x' to 'y' to track collisions. The interviewer liked it, and later asked how I
would reduce the edges further. I realized I could just use indices instead of storing the actual values, which
fully satisfied them.
Then I was asked to write code, they initially mentioned to consider DSU as blackbox but I still explained
to them how my find and union function would look like, and I would be using size and parent lists in the
DSU for memory. I wrote the other things quickly and considered the case of finding two max properly
which my interviewer wanted to see if I got it correct or not and then he asked me to write union function of
DSU and I wrote it quickly all the time explaining what i was doing to them to show how I normally code
just to keep conversation flowing and showcasing How I generally work.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Problem 2 : Subarrays with K Different Integers - LeetCode
I quickly explained the O(N^2) brute force and moved to the optimal sliding window approach. But during
the dry run, I messed up. Because I recognized the problem, I blindly used a standard sliding window
template, forgetting that the problem asked for exactly K, not at most K. I talked about using two loops to
calculate atMost(K) - atMost(K-1), but then tried to over-engineer it into a single loop, I even wrote the
sliding window template code properly but my interviewer asked me to dry run what I was doing and I kept
getting stuck on it.
My interviewer came in clutch again and asked me back to the two-loop approach and I quickly discussed
what I would do. This is where thinking out loud helped me because I had proposed the ways before it
helped me and I was able to complete both the questions within time.
After the interview ended my friend showed me a single loop with a three pointer approach that worked
beautifully.
Because I had put out wrong approaches out there I was able to get to the correct one in both problems and
more importantly was able to communicate better to the interviewers. Some people were able to solve
problems and had better op skills but did not get shortlisted further because of lack of communication and
the ability to pitch your solution to the interviewer clearly, what they want to see is the entire process and
not just the final solution.
They asked me for any questions and I asked them what makes you excited and thinking on your feet at
work like we have hackathons and competitions at college. The interviewer gave a detailed answer, noting
that in an organization, the focus often shifts from pure algorithm optimization like ON) vs O(2N) to
scalability, cost reduction, and impact and smiled at me. I left the interview feeling confident.
Takeaway: Keep the conversation alive and be transparent with your thought process so the interviewers
can see how you think, even if you start with the wrong approach. This gives them a chance to guide you in
the right direction. Also, try to gather as much information from them as possible, both verbally by
asking questions and non-verbally through their eye contact and facial cues

3. HM Round [9 People ]

I was immediately called for the Hiring Manager (HM) round, and we moved to a different room. He started
off by asking about the project I was most proud of. I actually hadn't included it on my resume because I was
trying to tailor it strictly to the Job Description (JD), but I went ahead and explained it anyway.
A quick tip: you don't always need to blindly follow the JD, especially when there is no ATS shortlisting
involved. I even opened the project's GitHub repository right there on the HM's laptop and showed him a
YouTube video demo I had made.
He then asked me to explain the system design of that project in detail. We had a great discussion about what
I did right, what I should have done differently, and potential improvements. At one point, he asked me,
"Why did you choose Kafka instead of RabbitMQ?" I answered honestly, saying, "Because I simply
wanted to learn Kafka." He smiled and said, "Fair enough." Then, he tested my knowledge on the history of
asynchronous programming. I recalled async/await and Promises, and he kindly walked me through how
callback functions fit into the picture.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Next, the conversation shifted when he asked, "Have you used the PhonePe app?"
I was prepared for this. I told him that while I hadn't used the app personally, I had actually integrated the
PhonePe SDK during my previous internship. This opened up a deep discussion about that integration. He
threw a lot of edge cases at me, asking how I would handle them. For example, he asked me to imagine a
scenario where a payment succeeded, but the callback URL failed and the webhook was down. I suggested
polling the server once it comes back online.
He smiled and said,
"Exactly. That's what we call Recon at PhonePe."
That was probably one of my favorite moments in the interview because it felt like my reasoning aligned
with how they handled the problem in production.
After that, he asked me what my favorite app was, which is again commonly asked in interviews. I replied
with "LeetCode," which smoothly transitioned us into a system design discussion. We designed the
architecture for taking code input from the website, running it, and returning the result. He grilled me on the
specifics: How would I send the code? How would it execute safely? I suggested using Docker containers,
and he pushed further on exactly how the container would access the code where I replied through a signed
URL from AWS S3 Blob or if we are storing code locally then we can just make the docker container access
the shared files from root OS.
Once we wrapped up the system design discussion, we moved on to a few behavioral and
teamwork-oriented questions. He first asked me how I handle conflicts within a team.
Instead of giving a generic answer, I shared an incident from one of my hackathons where our team became
frustrated after losing. Rather than letting the disappointment affect us, we sat together, analyzed what had
gone wrong, identified the areas we could improve, and converted that setback into a learning experience for
our next competition.
The discussion naturally transitioned into how we collaborate during hackathons. He asked how we manage
a shared codebase with multiple people working simultaneously.
I explained that we usually divide the project into independent modules - frontend, backend, Al, etc,so that
everyone can work in parallel with minimal dependencies. Once the individual components are ready, we
integrate everything together while resolving any integration issues as a team.
He then asked how we plan and track progress when working under tight deadlines.
I discussed how we loosely follow an Agile workflow by breaking the project into small milestones,
conducting regular check-ins, discussing blockers, and continuously evaluating whether we're on track to
finish within the available time. Finally, he pushed the discussion one level deeper.
He asked, "Even if everyone is working on separate modules, what kinds of merge conflicts do you still
expectạẠại
I talked about common integration problems such as shared schema changes, modifications to common data
structures, configuration conflicts, and API contract mismatches between different modules.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Then came something I genuinely wasn't expecting. He asked for my GitHub ID.
I assumed he simply wanted to note down my username, but instead he opened it right there. He spent a few
minutes exploring my repositories, opened my portfolio, browsed through my blog, and even looked at some
of my recent work. I was genuinely surprised but smiled because this was my strong point. He was
impressed by no. of followers,stars and the projects.
Seriously, Put your best work out there and keep it publicly visible! I also talked to him about what I am
currently working on, mentioning my deep dives into Large Language Models (LLMs) and Reinforcement
Learning (RL), and how I am actively blogging about those topics too.
When it was my turn to ask questions, I asked him about the journey from being a fresher to becoming an
Engineering Manager. He gave a very thoughtful reply, explaining that it is a gradual process. He talked
about how your understanding of code quality, design patterns, and architectural decisions (like choosing
between Kafka and RabbitMQ) evolves over time. He mentioned that his main job now is setting up the
right platform and environment for everyone on his team to fulfill their goals. While answering, he kept
using examples like, "If you were on my team, then..." which gave me a huge hint that I had done something
right. I really loved his answer.
Towards the end, he also asked about my internship at Russell Investments and whether interviewing
elsewhere was allowed. I explained that we had been given an NOC, which made us eligible to sit for
placements. Honestly, I still feel incredibly grateful that we even got this opportunity. A huge credit goes to
Aaryan and Harshav, who coordinated with both Russell HR and our TPO to make it happen.
Finally, I asked him for feedback on my interview. He told me, "You have curiosity, you have strong
technical fundamentals, and you have the drive. I think there is one more round for you as a standard
procedureạỊại
Walking out of that room, I felt something I hadn't felt after the previous round.
It wasn't a relief. It was validation.
For the first time that day, I genuinely felt that all the hackathons, side projects, blogs, GitHub repositories,
and countless hours spent exploring technologies beyond the syllabus had actually mattered.
Takeaway: Looking back, this round isn't something you can prepare for in the last month before
placements. It is the compounding of everything you do throughout your degree - participating in
hackathons, building side projects, learning computer science fundamentals, understanding why systems are
designed a certain way instead of just what they do, writing blogs, maintaining your GitHub.
Start building early. Stay curious. Understand why, not just what. Build things, share your work
publicly, and let your passion for technology show naturally during the interview.

4. Technical Round 2 [16 People ]

There was quite a long gap before Technical Round 2 started, and I used that time to think strategically
rather than just revising randomly. I noticed that the first technical round had already covered Graphs and
Greedy, but they hadn't touched Dynamic Programming or Tries two topics that PhonePe has historically
loved asking. So instead of trying to revise everything, I spent the break mentally preparing for those
specific areas.
--- PAGE 7 ---
As luck would have it, I got the same interviewer from my first technical round. He even asked another
panelist if it was okay for him to take my second round as well, and they agreed. That immediately made me
feel more comfortable because we had already built a good rapport during T1.
Problem 1 : M - Candies
Sure enough, the first question was Dynamic Programming. I started by explaining the brute-force recursive
solution that tries every possible candy distribution. From there, I pointed out the overlapping subproblems
and naturally transitioned into a memoized solution.
Note: Whenever you're discussing a DP solution in an interview, always explain these five things before
writing any code:

• State - What does dp[i][i] actually represent?

• Transition - How do we compute the current state from previously solved states?

• Base Case - What are the initial conditions that start the DP?

• Order of Evaluation -In what order should the states be computed so dependencies are already available?

• Return Value - Which DP state contains the final answer?

Interviewers care much more about your DP formulation than your syntax. I wrote all of these down on paper
and even mentioned that in Python, I could simply use the @cache decorator to memoize the recursive
function.. He liked the approach but asked me to write the iterative (bottom-up) code instead. I walked him
through how to convert my memoized function into a tabulated DP. My logic was correct, but the time
complexity was O(N.K^2). He asked me to optimize it to ON K).
This was the first time in the interview where I genuinely got stuck. I kept staring at the transition, trying to
figure out how to eliminate the inner loop. The interviewer then gave me a small but brilliant hint.
He asked me to simply expand the recurrence relation on paper.
The moment I wrote out a few consecutive DP states, the pattern immediately became obvious.
The second I wrote the expanded equation out, the pattern clicked - it was a Prefix Sum optimization! I
pointed it out, and he smiled and said, "Yes, that's exactly what we were looking for."
Problem 2: Maximum Strong Pair XOR II - LeetCode
Right on cue, here was the Trie problem. I knew immediately that we needed a Binary Trie to maximize the
XOR. But the trick was handling the strong pair condition: x - y <min(x, y).
Initially, I suggested storing the original indices inside the Trie and verifying if the condition held true while
traversing for the max XOR. The interviewer wasn't satisfied. He asked me to optimize that. I thought out
loud and suggested sorting the array first. He told me I was on the right track and asked me to open up the
mathematical condition on paper. Assuming x< y, I simplified |x - y| < x down to y< 2x.
Once we had that, I explained that we could use Binary Search to find the upper bound, but we also needed
an efficient way to remove the "stale" elements from the Trie (elements strictly less than x) as we moved
forward. He gave me a hint to think about a new function inside the Trie. I spent a lot of time here. I was
honestly struggling and eventually suggested maybe keeping a count variable at the end of the Trie nodes.
By this point, time was up. I asked him for the intended solution, and he explained that I was extremely
close: the trick is to keep a frequency count on every single node in the Trie. You increment the count while
--- PAGE 8 ---
adding a number, and subtract from the count while removing a number. That way, you know if a bit path is
still valid simply by checking if its count is greater than zero. Even though I missed that final piece of the
puzzle and couldn't code the optimal solution completely, Even though I couldn't fully implement the
optimal solution, I didn't let the interview end there.
Instead, we spent the remaining time discussing the overall algorithm, along with its Time and Space
Complexity.
Takeaway: By the time we were wrapping up, I had lost almost all my stamina, and my brain felt
completely foggy. It is absolutely crucial to stay in the zone and fight through that fatigue, especially when
T2 is your final technical round and you need to bring your A-game. I had almost lost my thinking abilities
at the very end, but my years of consistent practice and muscle memory are what ultimately carried me
across the finish line.

--- PAGE 1 ---
MAHINDRA FINANCE • DATA ANALYTICS
Mahindra Finance - Data Analytics
2 Months Summer Internship
Darsh Bajaj, CGPA: 9.3, CE
Role: Data Analytics (Open for All Branches)
Compensation: 14 Base + 2 Retention over 2 Years

Round 1: 100 MCQ Questions (Online) in 60 minutes on Yugma Platform

The first round consisted of 50 MCQS covering English Aptitude, GK and Current Affairs, Stock Market,
Basic Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, basic Machine Learning and Data Cleaning.

1. English Aptitude (Comprehension)

The English aptitude section consisted of paragraphs with multiple questions based on matching and
logical reasoning. For example, A likes B, B doesn't like C, and you had to determine who would sit next to
whom. There were also questions involving matching colours with people and similar arrangements.
This section was quite tricky because some questions were not very clearly worded. One paragraph could
have multiple questions based on the same information. There was a decent amount of this section.
Tip: Try solving these questions at the start, but as soon as you realise a question is not solvable or
is taking too much time, make a random smart guess and move ahead.

2. GK, Current Affairs & Stock Market and other basic Finance Questions

There were questions related to GK, Current Affairs and the Stock Market. For example: Which giant
payments company had their IPO listed in 2021? - Answer: Paytm.
If you trade in stock markets or have basic knowledge of the markets, some questions can be answered
through option elimination, but they do require prior knowledge.
Finance questions were related to terms in banking like withdrawals, formula of SI and CI.

3. Python & Machine Learning

The Python part was basic and mainly covered Pandas functions and related concepts. There were also
theory questions on Machine Learning, including Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning,
along with basic data cleaning concepts.

Round 2: Coding Test - Python L1 & Python Coding Assessment

No DSA was asked in this round. The assessment consisted of Python, Pandas, Matplotlib, Scikit-learn
and Seaborn basics, along with differentiation between these libraries, Data Cleaning concepts and very
basic Machine Learning questions based on supervised and unsupervised learning.
MCQs: 15 questions in total.
Coding: 2-3 simple Python coding questions.
The coding questions were very simple. They provided a function and we needed to complete it. One
question was as simple as sorting an array and one was like finding max value from an array.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Important: The function codes provided were syntactically incorrect and, in some cases, logically
incorrect as well. Therefore, even if your function logic was right, the platform would not accept the
answer. I had to rewrite the function body itself.
The shortlist for this test was based on marks, time taken to complete the test and the number of
submission attempts required to complete the function codes.

Round 3: Tech Interview (Offline)

Around 25-30 people were shortlisted for the technical interview. There were two panelists.
My panelist grilled on the Machine Learning projects mentioned on my resume and asked deeper
questions about the concepts behind the projects. He also asked basic concepts related to Machine
Learning and Data Analytics, especially Data Cleaning and related topics.

Round 4: HR Interview (Same Day, Offline)

A total of 10 people were shortlisted from the technical rounds for HR, out of which 9 received the offer.
The HR interview was relatively light. Questions were mainly about family background, resume
achievements, hobbies and general personal questions.
Tip: If you reach the HR round, stay calm and don't become too ecstatic. They paid attention to body
language and overall confidence as well.
Final Outcome
Out of the Summer Interns, all 9 of them received PPO offers after completing the internship.
Tips

1. Revise Data Science and Basic ML Concepts

Revise Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Data Cleaning, Data Preprocessing and the fundamentals of
Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning before the tests and interviews.

2. Study Your Projects in Depth

Do not prepare only what you actually implemented. Be ready for questions about the problems you faced,
their resolutions, why you selected a particular approach, what could have been done differently, limitations
and future scope.

3. Manage Time in the Tests

Some aptitude questions can consume a lot of time. If a question is becoming too difficult or
time-consuming, make a smart guess and move on.

4. Stay Calm in HR

The HR round is comparatively light. If you reach this stage, remain calm, confident and natural, while
maintaining good body language.
Contact
For any genuine questions or doubts, reach out to me on LinkedIn.
LinkedIn: https://in.linkedin.com/in/darsh-bajaj.
