Process Date: 9th July 2026 (OA), 10th July 2026 (Interviews)

Key Points:
There were 5 Rounds officially

1. Resume Shortlisting: Out of approximately 300 - 400 applicants, 159 students were

shortlisted.

2. OA: 159 students appeared for the OA, and 16 were shortlisted for the next round.

3. Technical Interview 1: 16 students were interviewed, and 8 advanced to the next

round.

4. Technical Interview 2: 8 students were interviewed, and 5 advanced to the HR round.

5. HR: 5 students appeared, and all 5 received offers.

1. Resume Shortlisting:

On Superset, the application was open from 3rd July to 6th July. Within this period, you
were supposed to submit your resume and apply through the Superset job profile. The JD
was shared with us as this, so tailor your resume according to the JD and try to include
relevant keywords, as they help improve ATS matching. Also, include relevant projects.
Since this was an AI Engineer role, try to highlight AI/ML-related projects.
Do not add unnecessary jargon or mention topics that you are not completely aware of. Just
knowing something superficially is not enough, because a single word on your resume can
lead to several interview questions, and you might end up digging your own gr ave. Be
authentic and do not add even a single false or misleading statement to your resume.
Use Jake's resume template from Overleaf, as it is the standard resume template that is
generally followed.
We received the shortlist first through individual emails on 8th July, along with the test
links for the CodeChef platform. Later, the same was announced on the TPO group, where
we came to know that 159 students had been shortlisted.

2. Online Assessment

The OA was conducted online on campus through the CodeChef platform. It consisted
of 28 questions, as shown above. Out of these, 3 were coding questions and the
remaining 25 were MCQs consisting of Aptitude and AI/ML -related questions. The
total duration of the test was 90 minutes.
Some of the MCQ topics that I can recollect are as follows:

• Quantization

• GGUF

• Hallucinations

• Finding the Time Complexity

• Prompting

• Inference

• Overfitting, Underfitting, Bias/Variance

• Types of ML and their identification, like Supervised Learning, Unsupervised

Learning, etc.

• GCD

• Context Window

• And many more similar questions related to AI/ML

If you have studied AI/ML well, then these MCQs are going to be quite easy. I had
chosen Artificial Intelligence as my Program Elective in the 6th semester. Because of
that, I studied NLP and Deep Learning, which were part of the AI elective subjects.
Also, since I belong to the CE department, Machine Learning was already a core
subject. I believe these subjects definitely helped me a lot. So, if you are planning to
apply for this role in the future, I would definitely recommend choosing AI as your
Program Elective.

I believe the only real concern would be the aptitude section, so practice enough
aptitude questions from IndiaBix. That would definitely help you a lot.
The aptitude section had a few calculation -based questions involving percentages,
puzzles like "what comes next" patterns, ratio questions, finding missing numbers,
comprehension-based questions, and choosing the correct logical flow.
I remember one question where if TIGER is written as QDFHS, then what would be
the code for FISH? It actually had a very simple solution, but it seemed confusing when
I first read it. The approach was to reverse the word first, so TIGER becomes REGIT,
and then write the previous alphabet for each character. Similarly, for FISH, reversing
it gives HSIF, and applying the same logic gives GRHE.
It was quite simple, wasn't it? But trust me, I spent almost 5 minutes straight trying to
crack this because I initially thought it was related to cryptography. I started thinking
about the cipher techniques we had studied, like Substitution, Transposition,
Monoalphabetic Cipher, Caesar Cipher, Rail Fence Cipher, and others. After trying
around 10-15 different approaches, I finally understood the pattern.
Honestly, it felt like I was just wasting my time on a single MCQ, but I don't know why
I took it as a challenge and wanted to crack it. When I finally did, it was a huge relief,
and I had a smile on my face because of that small feeling of satisfaction. S ometimes
we get completely involved in a question and spend more time than required.
However, I would not suggest spending 5 minutes on a single MCQ. Time management
in an OA is very important, and you need to maintain a balance between solving
difficult questions and moving ahead.

Next, as I mentioned earlier, there were three coding questions. I was able to solve one
coding question fully and another partially.  Each question carried 100 points, and the
score depended on the number of test cases your solution passed. So even if you are not
able to come up with the most optimized solution, don't just keep thinking about it on
paper. Dry-run the problem, write the brute-force solution if that's all you can think of,
and try to pass as many test cases as possible. Partial points are always better than
scoring zero by spending too much time searching for the perfect approach.
One more important point: a few students were not aware that we could switch between
coding questions. In previous placement cycles, some seniors had mentioned in their
interview experiences that there was no option to move back and forth between
questions. However, this time there was a navigation button at the top -right corner of
the interface. It was quite small, and a few students completely missed it until the very
end after wasting a significant amount of time on a single question.
So, definitely read previous interview experiences, but don't assume the process or
interface will be exactly the same. Many students went into the OA with that
preconceived notion and didn't even bother exploring the interface. Don't make that
mistake.
Moving on to the DSA questions.

1. The first question was quite easy. As far as I can remember, it was something like

this:
We were given a string S (of length N) and an integer K. The task was to find all
the unique characters that appeared in the string at least K times (frequency ≥ K).
The final output had to be a single string containing all such characters sorted in
ascending ASCII order. This meant that uppercase letters (A -Z) should appear
before lowercase letters (a-z), and each qualifying character had to be printed only
once.
Since N was up to 10^5, an O(N log N) approach using sort() would probably have
passed as well, but I solved it using the Counting Sort idea.
I simply maintained a fixed frequency array of size 256. I traversed the string once
to count the frequency of every character, and then iterated from index 0 to 255.
Since the array indices themselves represent ASCII values, the output automatically
came in sorted ASCII order without using any sorting function. This gave a clean
time complexity of O(N) with O(1) auxiliary space.
The core idea was very similar to problems like LeetCode 451 (Sort Characters By
Frequency) and LeetCode 242 (Valid Anagram), both of which I had already solved
from Striver's String module. Instead of using an unordered_map or calling sort(),
I simply used a fixed int cnt[256] = {0}; array.
Initially, I had taken the array size as 128 because we usually study standard ASCII.
Then I realized that using 256 would cover the extended ASCII character set as
well. It doesn't really hurt the complexity, so I changed it to 256 just to make sure
no valid character would be missed. Overall, it was a straightforward problem, and
all my test cases passed.

2. Chef and Shop

The second question taught me a really important lesson: always read the
constraints carefully before deciding on an approach.
The problem was something like this:
Chef loves shopping, and he specifically wants to buy oranges. However, he has
only (K) rubles to spend. There are (N) oranges available, where the (i) -th orange
has a cost (cost_i) and a weight (weight_i). Chef wants to buy a combination of
oranges that maximizes the total weight without exceeding his budget of (K) rubles.
We had to output the maximum possible weight for multiple test cases.
When you first read this problem, your immediate instinct is to classify it as a classic
0/1 Knapsack problem. That's exactly what I did during the OA. I implemented the
standard 1D Dynamic Programming solution where you maintain a DP array of size
money + 1 and iterate backwards to compute the maximum achievable weight.
The DP logic itself was completely correct for a standard knapsack problem, but I
completely overlooked the constraints. The budget, K, could be as large as 10⁸,
whereas the number of oranges was extremely small (N ≤ 10). Because of this, my
line vector<long long> dp(money + 1, -1); tried to allocate an enormous amount of
memory for the largest test cases, eventually resulting in a Memory Limit Exceeded

(MLE) on the final subtask. Even if memory had not been an issue, iterating up to

10⁸ for every test case would event ually have resulted in a Time Limit Exceeded

(TLE) as well.

Fortunately, the problem had partial scoring. My DP solution comfortably passed
all the smaller subtasks, so I still managed to secure 60 out of 100 points  for this
question.
The actual trick was hidden in the constraints. Since N ≤ 10, there was no need to
use Dynamic Programming at all. With only 10 oranges, there are just 2¹⁰ = 1024
possible subsets. So, the optimal solution was to generate every subset using
Bitmasking (Power Set), calculate the  total cost and total weight for each subset,
discard the ones that exceeded the budget, and keep track of the maximum weight
among the valid ones.
This solution runs in O(N × 2ᴺ) time, which is only about 10,000 operations per test
case, uses only O(1) extra space (excluding the input), and completely avoids any
dependence on the huge budget constraint of 10⁸.
This was honestly a great reminder that sometimes the constraints are more
important than the problem statement itself. Had I paid closer attention to the value
of N, I would have immediately recognized that the intended solution was based on
Bitmasking rather than Dynamic Programming.

3. The third question was honestly a bit of a heartbreak because I ran out of time just

when I had figured out the approach. The problem itself was actually quite
interesting.
We were given a shuffled set of travel itinerary cards. Each card contained a source
city, a destination city, and the travel cost between them. The traveller never visits
the same city twice. Our task was to reconstruct the original order of the journey,
print the itinerary in the correct sequence, and calculate the total cost.
My first thought was to solve it using graphs. Since no city was visited more than
once, the journey essentially formed a single path. The main challenge was finding
the starting city. I realized that every intermediate city would appear once as a
source and once as a destination, whereas the starting city would only appear as a
source and never as a destination. Once the starting city was identified, we could
simply follow the path until the end while printing the itinerary and adding the travel
cost.
Unfortunately, I had already spent a lot of time on the second question trying to
make my DP solution pass all the test cases. By the time I reached this question, I
was under a lot of time pressure. I had the complete logic in my head and had just
started implementing it when the timer ran out.
Looking back, this question taught me a bigger lesson than the algorithm itself.
Time management in OAs is extremely important. If a particular approach isn't
working, it's often better to secure partial marks, move on, and come back later if
time permits. I probably could have completed this question if I hadn't spent so
much time trying to optimize the previous one.
After the OA ended, we received the list of the 16 shortlisted students for the interview
round on the same night around 8 PM. We were then asked to report to college by 9:30
AM the next morning.

3. Interview Round 1:

The interviews were conducted in parallel, with three students being interviewed at a
time, as there were three interviewers from the company's side. This first technical
round was quite  resume intensive and focused deeply on my internship experience,
followed by my projects and core subjects like DBMS, AI, ML, Distributed Systems,
and DevOps.
Firstly, he asked me to give my introduction. Then the interview proceeded.
Here are some of the questions/topics that were asked to me.
DBMS:

• Design a database schema.

• Normalize it up to 3NF.

• Explain each Normal Form.

• What happens if we over -normalize a database? When should we stop

normalizing?

• Understanding of JOIN queries to retrieve data from the normalized tables.

• Foreign key references.

• Explain the ACID properties in detail with examples.

Then came a really interesting question.
Suppose you're given a table and asked to find its PK. How would you find it?  Seeing
this, I initially thought it was a pretty straightforward question. I said I would simply
use DESCRIBE table_name; to inspect the table structure. He then added a twist. He
said, "Suppose the engineer forgot to declare the Primary Key while creating the table."
For a few seconds, in my mind I was like, "Who does that, man? What kind of engineer
was that?" Anyways, I had to solve his mess.
My first instinct was to look for an AUTO_INCREMENT column because, in most
cases, that ends up being the Primary Key. Another possibility was the leftmost column
since that's also quite common. But then I immediately thought that this definitely
wasn't wh at he was expecting because I couldn't just keep looking at the columns
manually, and I even thought this  out loud. Right then, he added, "Exactly. What if
there are thousands or even millions of columns?"
So I picked up the pen and paper and started breaking the problem down.
A Primary Key is nothing but a column that is unique and cannot contain duplicate
values. So my goal was to identify the column that satisfied this property.
The approach I suggested was simple. First, count the total number of records in the
table. Then, count the number of distinct values in the candidate column. If both
numbers matched, then that column could be the Primary Key.
The SQL queries I suggested were:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_records
FROM table_name;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) AS unique_records
FROM table_name;
If both counts were equal, then the column contained only unique values and was a
valid candidate for the Primary Key.
Initially, the interviewer looked a little doubtful, so I explained my reasoning properly.
Once I walked him through the logic, he was convinced, appreciated the approach, and
this was my final DB question.
AI/ML
Then we had a very detailed discussion about my second project. He wanted to
understand everything in depth, right from the motivation behind the project to every
stage of the implementation. He kept asking why I chose a particular approach, what
the alternatives were, what trade-offs were involved. So one piece of advice would be
to know your projects inside out. Be prepared to justify every design decision because
interviewers can dive really deep.
Some of the AI/ML topics that were discussed are as follows:

1. LangChain

2. LangGraph

3. Vector Embeddings

4. Chunking

5. Cosine Similarity

6. BM25

7. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)

8. LLM Hallucinations

9. RAG and its drawbacks

10. AI Personas

11. Context Window

12. Agentic Workflows

13. LLMs

14. Shared state vs separate state in LangGraph

15. Prompting

DevOps
The discussion then shifted towards DevOps. Some of the topics that were asked were:

1. Terraform - complete architectural explanation and why it is needed.

2. CI/CD

3. Jenkins - he asked me to explain how I would implement a CI/CD pipeline using

Jenkins from scratch.

4. Kubernetes

5. SonarQube

6. Webhooks

7. Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

8. Microservices vs Monolithic Architecture

After discussing these topics thoroughly, my first technical interview came to an end.
The interviewer said he was done from his side and asked if I had any questions for
him.
The questions I asked were:

1. While researching about AuxoAI , I found that the company primarily works

with Fortune 500 clients. I asked whether the work is limited to these companies
or if they also cater to other industries and domains, and what kind of projects
the company generally works on.

2. I also asked, "What is the one core technology or skill that you would

recommend I focus on over the next six months before joining AuxoAI so that
I can quickly catch up with the team?"
With that, my first technical interview ended. Personally, I felt it had gone really well.
I was quite confident that I would be shortlisted for the second round, and I walked out
of the interview feeling happy and satisfied.
I left the interview room and went to the conference room, thinking I would revise a
few guesstimates and quickly go through my last -minute revision cheat sheet. At that
time, many students were still waiting for or were in the middle of their first techni cal
interview, so I assumed I would have a decent amount of time before the next round.
But, to my surprise, within just 3 to 4 minutes, I was called again for Interview 2. In
fact, I was the first one to be advanced to the second round. I didn't even get enough
time to settle down, let alone open my revision PDF. Everything happened so quickly,
which, of course, made me really happy because I knew my first interview must have
gone well.

4. Interview 2:

Interview 2 also started with the standard "Tell me about yourself."
He then asked, "Why are you interested in joining AuxoAI?"
Just like Interview 1, this round also involved a deep dive into my resume and projects.
I explained my projects in detail, and from there the discussion naturally branched into
different technical topics.
Some of the topics and questions discussed during Interview 2 were as follows:
Distributed Systems

1. Lamport Logical Clock

2. Ring Election Algorithm

3. Leader Election Algorithm

4. Load Balancing - Round Robin and other algorithms

5. Proxy Gateway

Apart from these, he also asked a few other fundamental Distributed Systems questions.
After that, he switched to Machine Learning. We had a detailed discussion on concepts
like Precision, Recall, True Positives, False Positives, and other basic ML
fundamentals.
Then he referred back to something I had mentioned while explaining my project. In
my project, I had used a cosine similarity threshold of 0.85 as a final filtering criterion.
If the cosine similarity was greater than 0.85, I considered the retrieved citations to be
valid and proceeded to the next stage; otherwise, I repeated that step.
He asked me a very simple-looking question: "Why did you choose 0.85?"
Initially, I thought explaining the logic would be straightforward, but the discussion
kept going deeper. He connected it with concepts like Precision, Recall, True Positives,
False Positives, and overall model performance. He kept asking questions like, " Why
0.85? Was it just a magical number? How did you arrive at it?"
This was probably the toughest part of my entire interview. We spent around 5 to 7
minutes discussing just this one threshold. I tried explaining my reasoning in different
ways, but he still wasn't fully convinced and kept challenging my answers from
different perspectives.
Finally, I told him that I wouldn't claim 0.85 to be some standard or universally correct
threshold. It was something I had arrived at through experimentation. I had also tried
values like 0.95, 0.7, and 0.6 before settling on 0.85 because it gave me a rea sonable
balance for my use case. Since this threshold was only acting as a final gatekeeper to
decide whether to proceed with the next stage or perform another retrieval, I chose the
value that worked best for my project based on my observations.
I also admitted that I hadn't done an exhaustive study on threshold tuning and that it
was definitely an area I wanted to explore further and improve upon.
I think this was what he was looking for. Rather than insisting that my choice was
perfect, I acknowledged the trade -offs involved and admitted that there was room for
improvement. After that, he seemed satisfied with the discussion.
He then said, "Okay, let's move on to some case study and business questions. Grab a
pen and paper; you'll need them."
And with that, he started explaining the first case study.
Problem 1:
The first case study was based on Zomato launching its services in a new city.
I don't remember the exact numbers that were given, but the problem statement included
details like the daily order volume, average order value, restaurant commission,
delivery partner payout per order, and the marketing/customer acquisition cost. My task
was to calculate whether the new city was profitable or not based on these numbers.
Initially, seeing so many numbers and variables together can feel a little overwhelming,
but if you stay calm and break the problem down step by step, it becomes quite
manageable. That is exactly what I did.
The calculations themselves were quite straightforward. It was nothing more than basic
mathematics involving percentages, profit and loss, and simple arithmetic. So don't
worry too much about the calculations. The challenge was more about interpreting the
result rather than actually computing it.
I first noted down all the revenue sources and expenses on paper. Then I calculated the
total revenue generated through orders and commissions and compared it with the
delivery costs and marketing expenses. After doing the calculations, it was quite evident
that the city was running at a significant loss because the marketing spend was much
higher than the profit being generated from operations.
The interviewer then asked me, "How would you make this city profitable?"
Initially, I suggested a few straightforward business solutions. I said we could increase
the commission charged to restaurants, improve the average order value through
minimum order requirements or targeted offers, and try to increase the total number of
orders.
Then, while looking at the sheet, I casually pointed towards the delivery partner payout
and suggested that we could reduce it.
The interviewer immediately smiled and said, "Don't even think about reducing that
innocent man's salary."
We both exchanged a smile, and then he gave me another hint. He said, "You're a
Computer Science student. Think about it from that perspective."
That one hint changed my direction of thinking.
I started looking at it from a Computer Science perspective rather than just a business
perspective. He then gave me another hint saying, "You must have surely studied the
Travelling Salesman Problem."
That was the point where everything clicked. I quickly grabbed my pen and paper and
started thinking about how the routing could actually be optimized.
We then discussed how, instead of one restaurant order being handled separately every
time, the system could pick multiple orders from the same restaurant or nearby
restaurants and deliver them together to customers in the same locality. This would
reduce unnecessary travel and improve delivery efficiency without cutting down the
delivery partner's payout.
After that, we had a brief discussion about the Travelling Salesman Problem and the
Milkman's Problem.
Once we finished discussing this case, he said, "Since we are already into the food
business, let's open our own restaurant and move on to the second problem."
And with that, we proceeded to the next case study.

Problem 2:
For the second problem, he gave very minimal information initially.
He said that we were running a restaurant business and initially our target customers
were Indian families. We had a typical family -oriented menu with items like dal, rice,
and other such dishes. Later, after analysing the market, we realized that the busi ness
model that was attracting the younger generation, with items like burgers, pizzas, and
fast food, was more profitable and had higher demand. So, we decided to change our
business model and started a second model focused on this segment.
However, instead of increasing, our revenue started dropping.  The question was, what
could be the possible reason?
I asked him for a little time and took around 20-30 seconds to think about the problem.
I was trying to understand the possible reasons in my mind while also thinking out loud.
The first thought that came to me was related to the difference in customer behaviour.
I said that since our first business model was family -oriented, we were attracting
families, and generally one family would come in a group of around 4 people on
average. However, in the second model, targeting the younger generation, the number
of customers could be much lower. Apart from birthday parties or small celebrations,
young customers might come alone or with at most one other person. So, the average
number of customers could have reduced, which could directly impact the revenue.
He agreed and said, "Okay, fair enough. This could be one reason. What else?"
Then he told me that I could ask questions if I wanted. At that point, I understood that
some information was intentionally hidden, but I wanted to first try solving it based on
my intuition before asking for any hints.
I suggested another possible reason: maybe the menu pricing strategy had changed, and
that could have impacted the revenue.  To this, he immediately said, "Let's assume
everything is the same and there is no change in the pricing."  Then he added, "Okay,
there is an IPL going on."
The moment he said IPL, I was completely confused. I was like, wait, how is my
restaurant connected with IPL? Within the next few seconds, multiple thoughts started
coming into my mind. I started thinking of different possibilities:

• Is it related to sponsorships or promotions?

• Are people watching the matches at home instead of coming to restaurants?

• Are we located near a stadium?

• Have competitor restaurants installed big screens and started IPL screenings,

attracting more customers?

• Since the younger generation is our target audience, are they easily switching to

competitors because of these offers?
I started discussing these possibilities with him, and he was calmly listening to my
thought process throughout.
Finally, I decided to continue with one of my approaches and said that maybe customer
count was declining because competitors had introduced better strategies during IPL
and were attracting our customers.
He listened to my explanation and then gave me another piece of information. He said,
"There is a queue outside your restaurant."  Again, this completely changed my
perspective.
I thought, wait, if there is already a queue outside, then customers are definitely coming.
So, customer demand is not the problem. I immediately dropped my previous
assumption about losing customers and started thinking about the queue itself.
Initially, I was even trying to connect it with some DSA concepts, but after thinking for
a minute or two, I realized the actual problem.
I told him that if there is a queue outside, it means demand is clearly present. The issue
could be that the table utilization has changed. And continuing with my first approach
that I told earlier, when families came, a single table was occupied by around four
people, leading to more orders per table. But now, when younger customers come, they
might occupy the same table with fewer people and spend more time there. Since the
number of tables is limited, the waiting queue increases, and the number of customers
being served decreases.
After explaining this approach, he immediately stopped me and said, "Perfect, perfect.
You have done really well. You have cracked almost 95% of it." He told me that this
was enough for him and that he was satisfied, so there was no need to continue solving
further.
Then he explained the remaining 5% part related to IPL. The IPL connection was not
about competitors installing screens or attracting our customers away. He smiled and
revealed that the IPL setup was actually happening inside our own restaurant. That was
the moment I was like, "Wait, what a connection that was!"
The actual issue was that customers were spending more time sitting at the table while
watching the IPL match. Since they were engaged in watching the game, they were
ordering less frequently and occupying tables for a longer duration. This slowed down
the queue processing and reduced the overall restaurant throughput.
The whole discussion ended with smiles and a positive exchange.  And I realized that
this problem was somewhat similar to concepts from Operating Systems, like CPU
scheduling, processes waiting in a ready queue, and resource utilization. The restaurant
tables were basically the limited resources, and customers were the pro cesses waiting
to use those resources.
I believe the appreciation was not just for reaching the final answer but for the way I
approached the problem. I considered multiple scenarios, kept thinking out loud, and
explored different directions instead of getting stuck on one assumption. One important
thing I learned from this case study is that during such interviews, you should always
think aloud. Even if your initial direction is not completely correct, the interviewer can
guide you with additional information and help you reach the rig ht approach. The
discussion itself is what matters.
With that, this case study also ended on a positive note. The interviewer then asked if I
had any questions for him.  In such situations, you should generally avoid saying that
you don't have any questions. You can always ask something simple related to the
company, role, team, or your transition from college to a professional environment.
So, I asked him the same question that I had asked Interviewer 1:
"What is the one core technology or skill that you would recommend I focus on over
the next six months before joining AuxoAI so that I can quickly catch up with the
team?"

After this round ended I was waiting for the Final HR interview and later on around 6
PM Round 2 results were announced and we were told HR round would be online since
the HR couldn't come offline.

5. HR Round:

This was a very relaxed round. We mostly had a normal conversation where she asked
me about the overall interview process, how my experience was, and a few general
interaction-based questions.
After that, she informed me that I had been selected and that I would be receiving both
an internship plus a full -time offer. She then explained the complete CTC breakdown
and also mentioned a clause stating that if I leave the firm within 18 months, I would
have to return the joining bonus.
We continued with some casual conversation, and she told me that the official
communication would be sent to the campus the next day since it was already quite late
(around 9:30 PM). The entire discussion lasted only about 10-15 minutes.

So yeah, that was the overall process and my experience. One final piece of advice is to keep
Parkinson's Law in mind. If you aren't familiar with it, a quick search will explain how it can
help you make more efficient progress. Once you understand this law and actually apply it, you
will see a much faster improvement in your progress instead of getting stuck for a long time on
the same thing. All the best for your upcoming processes. I will also list down the resources I
followed for my overall preparation.
I always believe in one thing: whatever happens, happens for a good reason. This was the first
company interview I gave during my placements, and luckily, I got selected in the first shot.
But that does not mean everyone will have the same journey. Everyone has their own timeline,
so never get disheartened because of any missed opportunity. Sometimes that opportunity was
just not meant to happen because something better might be waiting ahead. Always try to stay
optimistic.
Even I faced a similar situation before this. The company I appeared for before this was IDFC,
where the Online Assessment was conducted from home. Unfortunately, it was raining heavily
that day, and at the exact moment when I was giving the test, the electricity went off.
I had already completed the aptitude and CS section and solved 1 out of the 2 coding questions.
I was working on the final coding question. Although I had an inverter backup, my Wi -Fi
connection was not connected to the plug point that had inverter support. Apparently, it was
connected to the other socket, and because of that, I lost my internet connection. Due to the
strict rules of the assessment, I could not rejoin and eventually got eliminated.
The funny thing was, my mom, younger brother, and dad were more disappointed than I was.
They started blaming themselves and thinking that it happened because they had changed the
plug connection. My dad even said that I should have kept an extra data pack  as a backup on
top of my daily 2GB mobile data, so that I could have used my mobile hotspot if required. This
was mainly because the assessment involved video and screen recording, so a mobile hotspot
could have been used as an alternative connection. There were multiple regrets and "what if"
situations discussed, along with many improvement plans suggested by my family. A typical
family reaction that most of us can relate to.
But honestly, I was disappointed for hardly 5 minutes. After that, I quickly moved on, became
positive again, and started focusing on the next opportunity. However, that is how families are.
They take every failure and success personally because they genuinely care about us. They will
always be there  to support you, so always try to explain things to them and make them
understand that these things are a part of the journey. Their reaction always comes from a place
of concern and wanting the best for you.
Another thing I would suggest is always do proper research. Maintain a sheet where you track
companies, job roles, eligibility criteria, and your preferences. Sort companies based on what
aligns with your career goals and target those companies accordingly.
Placements can become very hectic because openings can come anytime. Sometimes
companies open applications 3 to 4 days before the deadline, and sometimes they open 10 to
15 days earlier. Usually, you are given only 2 to 3 days to apply through platform Superset, so
making decisions quickly becomes important.
During my placements, I did not apply to every company whose openings were available
initially, such as IDfy, JPMC, Infosys, WorkIndia, IDFC, Dolat Capital, PhonePe, AuxoAI,
and others.
What usually happens is that on a particular day, multiple companies open their applications
together along with their JDs and other details. At that point, it becomes very important to make
your choices wisely. Do not just apply everywhere because the pac kage looks good. Look at
the role, your interests, and your long-term goals.
For example, JPMC had come with a non-tech role. Even though the package was good, I did
not apply because it did not align with the career path I wanted to follow. Similarly, because
of my own preferences, I skipped some companies like WorkIndia, IDfy, and Infosys. I focused
only on companies like IDFC, PhonePe, and AuxoAI because their roles matched my interests
better.
So do your own research, understand what kind of career path you want, and then make your
decisions accordingly. Placements are a long process and require a lot of time and energy. You
cannot waste your efforts sitting for every company if you are not genu inely interested in the
role.
Also note that you will receive emails for every missed opportunity, including companies
where you were eligible but did not apply. You can do this for a maximum of 10
companies for which you are eligible but choose not to apply. If you miss 10 such
opportunities, you may get debarred from further placement processes. So, keep this
point in mind as well while making your decisions during placements.
Lastly, always stay optimistic. Every setback teaches you something. Keep improving yourself,
keep learning, and keep moving forward. Everyone has their own game to play and their own
journey to win. You just need to find your game, understand your strengths, and give your best.

Resources:

you can always search for good YouTube playlists for any subject or topic that you want to

If you have any doubts or just want to connect, feel free to reach out to me on any social media

WhatsApp has also introduced usernames, and I have reserved the same username         there as

That said, my LinkedIn DMs are always open, and I would definitely recommend using

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting (Out of 300, only 122 students were shortlisted)

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 1(03 July 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 2 (03 July 2026)

• HR Interview (03 July 2026)

• Result Declaration (03 July 2026)

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was held on 24th June at 2:00 PM. We were informed about it only a day
before, around 9:00 PM
J.P. Morgan Chase was hiring for three different roles:

• Banking (Investment Banking)

• FinTech

• Corporate Risk

The session began with an introduction to the company, followed by an overview of the three roles, their
--- PAGE 2 ---
responsibilities, and the kind of work involved. While attending the PPT, pay close attention to the skills and
qualities they emphasize, as these often reflect what they look for in candidates.
After the presentation, there was a Q&A session. This is a good opportunity to clear your doubts, but make
sure your questions are genuine and related to the presentation or the role. They do notice the students
being interactive in the session so ask good questions and interact well. Our PPT was online so it
didn't make a lot of difference but in case of offline presence it would matter more.
After the PPT, we had to register on the J.P. Morgan Chase careers website and fill out the Google Form
shared by the Training and Placement Office (TPO). We also had to submit our final resumes, so it is
important to have your resume completely ready before this stage.
I had my Resume already ready for all 3 roles, I just made minor changes to tailor better to the Job
Description. The resume shortlist was announced on 26th June at around 5:30 PM, just one day before the
online assessment.
The company does not officially disclose the criteria used for resume shortlisting, but it is generally believed
that the ATS score plays an important role. You can check your ATS score on ResumeWorded Website. My
ATS score was 80. Anything above 72 is safe.

2. Online Assessment [ 122 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Banking
MCQ Assessment - 45 Qtns - 45 Mins - 45 Marks
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounts - 10 Qtns
Section 2: Market Awareness - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Quantitative Aptitude - 15 Qtns
Section 4: English Usage - 10 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
The Online Assessment (OA) consisted of Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, and Quantitative Aptitude
questions. The quantitative section mainly covered topics like Time and Work, Trains, Permutations and
Combinations, Pipes and Cisterns, Calendars, and similar concepts. I paid more attention to Probability
as that is given a lot of weightage in aptitude tests.
The questions were of moderate to difficult difficulty and were quite time-consuming, so regular practice is
important. You can practice from websites like IndiaBix and also solve easy CAT-level aptitude questions,
as they are at a similar level. You can also refer to CareerRide (They have on youtube as well)
Depending on the TPO, this round can be conducted either online or offline. In our case, it was an online
assessment taken from home using Aon's proctoring software. We had to solve 30 questions in 45
--- PAGE 3 ---
minutes under strict online monitoring with +2/-1 negative marking.
Only 32 students were shortlisted out of 122 who appeared for the test.

3. Technical Round 1 [ 32 students were shortlisted]

• Interview Duration and Panel

My technical interview lasted for around 25 minutes and was conducted by two panelists, one of whom
was a Vice President (VP) at J.P. Morgan Chase. I was the first person to be interviewed among all
students so I wanted to put up a good start.

• The panel started with asking me to give a brief introduction about myself followed by a question

from my resume - I had mentioned Tedx in my resume so I was asked about the speaker who came
at Tedx and why did I organise this event. I was also asked about my experience at E-CELL as I
had been a part of this committee for 3+ years and what I learned here.

• Then they asked me about my projects- out of 3 projects they asked me to explain 2. Note that you

need to be thorough with each and every word in your resume. They can ask you anything
from the resume so be crystal clear. I had used ML techniques in one of the projects so I was
counter questioned on why using this method and not any other. In such cases you need to know
everything about your project- Why, What, How you did wrt technologies used/ data/ results
everything.

• They were pretty happy with my projects and the way I explained everything and then moved on to

a guesstimate puzzle. I was asked about the number of Indian marriages taking place in India
every year. Note here- they want to see your approach and how good you are at problem solving
and breaking a complex problem into smaller parts. Its fine if your final answer is not fully correct.
I explained by dividing the 12 months into 3 parts (Jan- March, April-July, Aug-Dec) and
classified the parts wrt high/low/medium no of marriages and then solved wrt to states/region wise
population to get the overall number.

• They also asked a follow up question like which industries benefit in Indian marriages to which i

firstly mentioned gold/silver as in Indian Tradition its a symbolic to give gold/silver and the
apparel/fashion industry along with event management and hospitality companies.

• Then they asked me why I want to join JPMC and why am I fit for this role to which I

mentioned about JP morgan being one of the largest financial institutions overall and the
experience and learning opportunities which I could get. They hadn't asked me anything about Risk
yet so I myself mentioned that Risk is something which every financial institution/ company needs
to mitigate whether its a bank or a company that needs to make decisions. I mentioned that I want
to help the company make important decisions through risk assessment and mentioned some of my
skills like dealing with large datasets, proficiency in SQL and Python etc. Don't talk a lot about this
unless they ask. Since they asked me at the end so i could speak but sometimes they will follow up
and grill if you mention some skills which you don't know.

• Questions I Asked the Interviewers

At the end of the interview, they asked if I had any questions. I asked, "How does an average day
look like for a person working in the Risk Management Team?" They spoke about both the roles-
The Risk Monitoring and Project Management and how they make reports, analyse data use
different tools etc.

• Overall Interview Experience

--- PAGE 4 ---
The panel wanted to see whether I genuinely understood every project mentioned on my resume
and whether I could explain it confidently. They want to see how good you are at communicating.
The most important tip here is to be completely thorough with your resume. Don't mention
anything that you don't know/ can't talk about.

4. Technical Round 2 [ 16 students were shortlisted]

• In this round the focus was more on technical skills and knowledge rather than only resume. It

started with a brief introduction about myself followed by my internship experience. I had done
an Investment Banking Internship at Avendus so I was asked to explain what I did there and what I
learnt.

• The interviewer then asked me to rank myself wrt proficiency in Python and SQL. I gave 8.5 in

both. I was then asked an SQL query related to 2 tables which I solved by using INNER JOIN.

• I was also asked some specific questions like if i have a very large dataset how will i import it if its

not happening on excel using Get Data and about a Tableau Dashboard - if the content is not
showing correctly what could be the reason for that.

• I honestly didn't know the exact answer but I answered by saying I am unable to recall the exact

library but I have used something similar in my project and then I just explained my Project. She
seemed satisfied with my way of answering. This was the catch I learnt from my IB interview on
the previous day which is to not fake anything (I will talk about it at the end of the interview
experience)

• She also asked me about which role I would prefer- Risk Monitoring or Project Management and if

I'm aware of the roles and responsibilities in the JD.

• Overall Interview Experience

This interview was much more detailed than the first one. They also looked at how I approached
problems, explained technical concepts, and communicated my thought process when faced with
unfamiliar questions.

5. HR Round [10 students were shortlisted]

• Interview Experience

The HR round was the most relaxed out of all the interviews. It started with a casual conversation where
the interviewer asked how my day had been and how I felt about the overall interview process. The
atmosphere was friendly, and it felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

• General Discussion

• The interviewer asked me about my roles and responsibilities of this role which I explained

thoroughly.

• She then asked me about my strengths and also a question about my leadership experience to

which I gave the example of my Committee involvement as the VCP of E-CELL where I
had to manage multiple tasks and take responsibility for all events, manage sponsors,
stakeholder management and ensuring Teamwork and coordination across the entire team.

• Try to give real life examples to make your answer better like I gave the example of

E-Summit with multiple events.

• Role Expectations

• The HR interviewer asked me where I stay and then asked if I would be comfortable

relocating to Bangalore to which I answered YES. (Don't be dicey here or don't sure
you aren't sure about it / not comfortable as this can have an effect on your selection)

• They also mentioned that the work could involve irregular shift timings and wanted to

--- PAGE 5 ---
know if I was comfortable with that as well. These questions were mainly to ensure that I
understood the nature of the role and was willing to adapt to its requirements.

• She asked me about why I want to join JP Morgan. Here I mentioned additionally that

my dad has also been associated with this organisation earlier and has told it's a great
learning experience. She then asked me if any other family members had been employed
here to which I said no.

• Overall Interview Experience

• This round was mainly to understand my personality and check whether I would be a good fit

for J.P. Morgan Chase's work culture. The focus was not on technical knowledge but on my
attitude, communication, and willingness to take up the role. My advice for this round is
simple-be yourself, answer honestly, and speak with confidence.
ALL THE 10 STUDENTS APPEARING FOR THE HR ROUND WERE SELECTED.
An important learning from my CIB interview

• During my CIB interview I was in the top 5-6 candidates to be selected after my round 1. I was called

for my round 2 within 5-10 minutes.

• The earlier you are called, the better your chances of selection. But in round 2 something

happened which I do regret and I feel might have been the reason for not getting a final HR call
which was answering a question by saying some ans / bluffing it even if you don't know it.

• A lot of times we try to ensure that we answer everything correctly but sometimes it's better to be

honest and just say you aren't aware of it. Even one small mistake can spoil your interview so be
aware of such things and avoid it.

• I had only prepared forCIB and after not getting it despite being so close to the final decision I was

so heartbroken and I only had half an evening left to prepare for CR. But instead of thinking about
the past I got back and clutched in half a day for my CR interview.

• Interviews are 80 % luck and only 20 % skills. Sometimes things don't go your way but remember

there's always something better waiting for you! So never stop working hard!!

Before I state the rounds of the Placement and how it went- I would first appreciate the WAY UBS
CONDUCTED THE WHOLE DRIVE-one of the best ways to select the best of the shortlisted candidates.
Rather than going the way of DSA based OA which leads to either unfair use of Al for code, or selection of
candidates who know nothing, but JUST DSA- both of which leaves behind a great developer who
KNOWS HOW TO BUILD, IDEATE, COLLABORATE; and such candidates which are a PERFECT
VIBE MATCH FOR CULTURE.
So yes, in this part- UBS genuinely made a selection process that is 100% apt for 2026 (and coming time)
where companies want a T-shaped over an I-shaped candidate profile (just search on Internet what this
--- PAGE 2 ---
means, and it would be pretty clear). Alright, with this being said, the following were the rounds conducted
by the company-

1. Company Presentation

2. Group Coding Round (More of Group Ideating, and Presentation)

3. Pen-Paper Based MCQ Round (Best decision to use Pen-Paper)

4. Technical Interview

5. HR Round

1. Group Coding Round

So, UBS had shortlisted around 50 candidates or so for the whole process based on the resume (I presume,
as the true nature of selection was not disclosed, so am assuming it was a resume screening). In this round,
we were given a Problem Statement- "How we would optimize and better the Fraud Detection System of
UBS" (they gave a sheet, which had a small dataset, and also, the Detection System of UBS means, a
simple, rule based). So, during this time, our team split the work- now I could code, as well make a good
PPT- but everyone wanted to code (lol, cause it was NAMED as a GROUP CODING round)-so I said, I
don't mind and would rather prepare the PPT along with System Design for the same.
We were said to be given 90mins, but it was just 70mins max. We made the ppt, while my teammates
worked on the coding aspect, and in midst of that, people from UBS were asking us, WHAT OUR
APPROACH WAS, WHY, and I remember, there was this UBS Employee- not so senior- he came,
listened, and then, seemed to like our idea, and gave me a tip that, we should even look for the COLUMNS
AND THE DATA THAT IS NOT HERE- thus, I really liked the advice, and even made sure, we prep for
every scenario. It's all about, presenting, knowing your solution, and backing it with tech decisions!

2. MCQ and Small Pen-Paper Based Test

After that 70mins of grind- we were told to start with the MCQ test ASAP- so, it seemed to be a bit
overwhelming, but then, the paper was simple. It was basic DSA MCQ, then Networking, a bit of OS (ig OS
was there, am not sure atp) - then there was a pseudocode based thing, a situational approach, debugging,
and stuff.
So, it rather had more focus on HOW YOU APPROACH PROBLEM and thinking, over the normal
SYNTAX FOCUSED DSA QUESTIONS. Thus, I would say, prepare core, thinking ability, and problem
solving- as this is something that is needed. Also, one thing am gonna say- NO MATTER HOW DUMB
DSA WOULD SEEM- IF A COMPANY NEEDS TT, AND YOU NEED TO JOIN A COMPANY-
WELL DSA IS THE THING YOU NEED TO GRIND (and as I said, 1 missed two good companies- all
thanks to me forgetting the Syntax and not clicking on time!)
Once this was over, they said, we had 30mins to refine the ppt and stuff before presenting. So, we spent time
refining, I explained who would say what, and why, I made counters for each of my teammates so that they
prepare for that as well, and then- we presented. The presentation was good enough- we got some good
responses- but the end was a bit sus feeling- which made me feel a bit nervous (let's not discuss that here).
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Technical Interview

Now, before the technical interview started, I was preparing for it, and was revising "TELL ME ABOUT
YOURSELF" and going through the things I wrote in my resume and preparing for it. After some time,
there was an announcement of the news of selects and my name was not there (No.34) and I was heavily
disheartened but after 4mins- my number came and I rushed to TPO (aka CCD). We sat in the TPO for
around 10mins, and then the interview started.
Now, before I tell what happened in the tech-interview, hear me out- the tech interview becomes highly
LUCK BASED on who is in your panel, what is their expertise, and are they in mood to hire or not. This is
very luck based and that's something that is not in your hands too!
So, I got Panel-2, it had the same sir who gave me the advice in Round-1 and was even there in the
Presentation round, along with another Ma'am who too seemed to have liked the way I presented. Now, it
started with a brief introduction- and then, asked about my resume. The things routed from My Hackathon
winning PS, to docker, k&s, Linux, to even the usage of Al and places where Al should and shouldn't be
used- ending it with a situational tech question of debugging an improper responding API endpoint- thus an
overall Cloud and Linux Heavy (my domain) interview, with some situational, and perspective based
questions to see what decisions would I be taking as a Dev.
This was a rather chill and a smooth round- I would say, DO NOT FAKE ON YOUR RESUME, and be
confident, and have a smile. Be honest, and give your best!

4. HR Round

This was a rather quick for me- my tech interview went well, and it was hardly Smins, when I was called for
the HR Round- and the things that HR asked me was- "Explain a Project as if you explaining to a layman"
and then, we talked about my current Intern at HERE Technologies, and how its in the same IT Park and
some general topics; followed by which, she explained the relocation and formality- and it ended (this was a
legit 10min of thing for me- so yes, nothing much here)

journey.howSecured:
In total, 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment round, 1 Technical Interview round and
1 HR round (however Managing Director was also present in the HR round and he also asked
Technical questions). The CGPA criteria was kept at 8.

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting [ Around 220 candidates]

The first round was fairly simple, resume shortlisting was done and in all fairness resume
shortlisting is very unpredictable. The best thing to do is list as many technical skills as possible
(but also learn them) because the number of technical skills is a big factor. Also check ur ats
score keep it above 70+

2. Pre-Placement Talk

The Managing Director of the Mumbai branch gave the talk, and a detailed salary breakdown
was given as well. Try to listen to it carefully so that you can ask better questions in the HR
round as it matters alot. Other than that it's ur call to ask questions or not in ppt as for my case it
did not matter however try to avoid asking stupid ai related questions only ask genuine questions
--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Online Assessment Round [ Approx 210 candidates]

This was by far the trickiest round. So this was the structure of the test
15 Java mcqs
15 Python mcqs
3 sql mcqs
10 Al output scenario based questions (this also was indirectly 5 java and 5 python based
questions)
25 Aptitude Questions
Let's discuss one by one :

1) Since Java was my primary language I focused on this section alot and solved around

12/15. Because of negative marking I was very cautious to attempt these questions.
Topics to prepare : Classes, Objects, generics, Collections framework, error handling,
Interfaces and abstract classes, enums, steams, Lamda functions.

2) I don't use python and I had only a basic understanding of python so my strategy was to

study 7-8 standard patterns which were asked from claude using all the interview
experiences. I only remember the single question of Method Resolution Order in python
. However, OOPS of python was asked well in depth. Some people mentioned that this
section was very hard so dont solely rely on it. I attempted 10/15 questions

3) This section was very standard. If you are aware of various types of aggregate functions,

window functions and CTE in sql then this section will be a breeze for you. I attempted
all the 3 questions.

4) This again as I mentioned was indirectly test java and python knowledge in a different

format. The main goal was to read the prompt properly and identify what the code is
intended to do, then you can easily find the correct option which is the correct snippet of
code . I attempted 9/10 questions .

5) This was fairly simple. Some 11th std Physics and common sense will do the trick,

however try to complete the 100 gfg puzzles I incorrectly attempted 1 question.
It was the question known as 8 identical balls where 7 have the same weight and 1 is
slightly heavier. 1 attempted 24/25 questions
So in total before the test I was aiming for 50+ questions and I answered 60/70. The
main thing was to not waste time on lengthy questions, utilising every minute and
maintaining a fairly consistent pace, not slow and not fast.

2. Technical Interview Round | 44 candidates appeared ]

Now after the mcq round the candidates were called for second round in batches of 5. This made
everyone very tense as results were announced after a while (after 1 hour). Panels were allotted
based on the OA performance (I confirmed with my senior) so panel 1,2,3 were allotted to
people who performed fairly consistently in all the sections.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Lets Jump into the interview directly :
I was very nervous and it was visible in my body language and answers, however luckily the
interviewer was an Alumni of Spit this single fact made me 10x relax and after that Introduction
was given by him and he asked for mine as well. I had prepared it in advance and It was
structured in this format Name -> Year, Branch and Cgpa -> Languages and frameworks I use
for development and Dsa > A brief overview of all my 3 projects > followed by thanking him
for patiently listening.
He first asked me for my favourite project and told me to explain it in depth. And I explained
everything related to the project from why it was made to what features it had, end to end API
life cycles of every user request and User flows for every use case. It had docker in it as well so
asked about my proficiency in docker and I answered honestly that I had working understanding
of docker however I have never used it in production and he was satisfied with it. Other then
that he was very impressed with my project explanations. Try to answer every tech stack
decision, libraries used and system design choices properly so that U wont get cross questions
related to the project.
Then He started with Core Subjects →
He directly asked me to explain the concept of OOPs so I had to started with the core problem
before OOPs and then followed by explaining Classes and Objects. Then he asked for 4 pillars
of OOPs. Again I first mentioned all 4 pillars then started explaining them one by one and I
went in a little more depth in Abstract and difference between abstract classes and interfaces
(dont forget to mention interfaces are contracts which are enforced when implemented). He was
satisfied with the OOPs then he moved to DBMS.
He first asked Full Form of ACID properties and Idk what Happened but I got froze and I got
stucked and forgot what I and D. Luckily he was chill and asked me how much Sql I know and I
answered that I have strong foundational knowledge and I can solve complex questions.
And I was then asked to write a Query to find Top 3 salaries of Employees For Each department
. This was a standard window function question. I was first using RANKO function however
then he cautioned me by asking how RANK works for ranks skips the next ranks if There are
two person with same salary so there may be a case where 3 highest earners will all have rank 1
and directly then next employee will be assigned to 4th rank. Since I answered the working
correctly he asked me, "What if he does not want to skip ranks and the next person should be
given 2nd rank. So I then explained to him how dense rank is correct for this scenario then I
completed the query.
Then He gave me a scenario of How to show a table of 1 million rows in Db i.e He was
indirectly asking me what Pagenation is . I explained to him the approach correctly but could not
--- PAGE 4 ---
answer what this concept is called as (th i just answered logically without thinking of
pagination).
Then he asked me the difference between Encryption and Hashing. Which I explained correctly
by mentioning that Hashing is irreversible and Encryption is reversible (i.e there can be 2 stages
Encryption and Decryption) . Now I also mentioned / gave examples of Private and Public key
cryptography. So he asked me for an algo which uses both public and private key and SomeHow
remembered the Diffie Hellman Key Exchange Numerical in CNS so I explained to him that algo
itself and he was impressed.
Then he asked me what RESTful apis are so again in Classic dhruv fashion I didn't remember
the fullform however I explained to Him what it meant and what it introduced. He then asked
me HTTP methods and the difference between GET and POST methods. I answered them
correctly and also said that the POST method can also be used to read data from the server,
however it is generally a bad practice. (BTW he directly asked next 3 candidates how POST
method is used to fetch data from server)
He then asked me what I know about about Queues and RabbitMQ, I honestly answered him
that I am aware about the concept however I have not used any of them for my projects. So he
skipped this section for me.
Then Came the DSA section, he first asked my current progress in DSA and I answered him
about my familiarity in Linear and Non Linear Data Structures. Now he then straightaway asked
me Least Frequently Used cache and I had no clue what it was so I told him about it and to
explain me the Problem and I then explained him what I interpreted from the question and started
thinking of what data structure can be used before anything else. I first told him hashmap will be
necessary and then Maybe a priority queue to acces the term which is least frequently used in
o(1) time. this was wrong however he told me that he needed something simple and also
mentioned that he loves simple solutions not fancy and complicated answers. Then after trying
for 2 minutes he moved on to the next question.
He then asked me how to print all elements in a linkedList in reverse without tampering the
original list and answered Stack in an instance and explained my approach within 10 seconds
then he accused me knowing this question beforehand which i laughed and defended me by
mentioning that i had learned it from striver sheet and it one of the foundational questions of
stack .
With this he concluded my interview and asked me if I had any questions:
I asked these questions -

1) How the first 3 months for an intern in ISS will look like.

--- PAGE 5 ---

2) I explained him my 3rd project then told him this project has inspired me create a new project

related to cricket and asked him to approach the data creation part for the new problem statement
and we discussed it for next 5 mins .
In total My interview lasted for around 1 hour.
I btw waited from 3 pm to 7 pm for my official confirmation for my status (got rejected or
Selected for HR

3. HR Round [22 candidates appeared]

This was according to me the easiest round of them all since The panelists were fairly tired I
knew they will not grill me if i dont keep any loose ends. Main key factor was to always keep a
Smile on your face and have a respectful tone while speaking and this helps a lot just trust me on
this
Questions asked :
Introduce yourself - Prepare a non tech style intro which includes hobbies, jee/ cet 10th 12th
marks .
Family Background - Basically to check if I have any intentions of higher studies
Explain 1 project: Explain in non technical terms and how did you came up with the idea of
project be genuine and show how curios and passionate U are about ur projects
Challenges I face in my day to day life: Just dont answer with your basic weaknesses they are
looking for it. Just respond with simple generic challenges Like I mentioned Screen Fatigue and
How college schedule is unpredictable(Multiple lab eses and ises in a single day) and How I
tackle it optimally/
--- PAGE 6 ---
As I mentioned in the start MD was also present and he asked me for my 3rd project so I
explained him in technical terms without going in much depth .He then specifically asked for
how I implemented and a feature and Why I used RAG so had to justify my reasoning and how I
implemented the feature.
Then they asked whether I had questions or not so I just answered some few company and hr
related doubts and since they both were seniors and have seen multiple generations of
programmers I asked what my generation is lacking and what things my generation should work
on. They seemed to enjoy this question and HR mam answered me in very detail and main thing
was Human Connection and lack of Offline talks.

journey.howSecured:
Resume Shortlisting (CE/CSE only) -> Online Assessment -> Technical Interview -> HR Interview

1. Online Assessment [120 candidates]

The test was held on SHL Platform at college itself.  Navigation was not allowed you can't go back that's
important to note. It was a 90 mins test divided into 4 sections,

1. Logical Reasoning 12-13mins 14Qs

2. Quantitative Aptitude 15mins 12Qs

3. DSA 45mins 2Qs

4. English Comprehension 15mins 12Qs

The questions were quite typical I got 2-3 blood relations questions, age related, direction related (if you
start from south-west move 180 degree clockwise then move 270 degree anticlockwise which direction will
your back finally face), coding-decoding, vectors (5km north then 2 km west then 3km south then 8km 5km
west what is the shortest distance from starting position ), LCM-HCF, Permutation, Divisibility( 4522 is
NOT divisible by __), Percentage, patterns, Speed-distance and Simple interest
For English part basic sentence formation checks, Synonyms, 3-4Qs on a passage.
DSA part was different for all I got extremely easy ones,

1. Check how many characters land in same position after reversing the string kinda like

palindrome. I passed all the testcases.

2. You are given an integer k,  sort the  first k  array ele ments in ascending and rest others in

descending that's it!! Again, all cases passed.
I made sure I finish the section within 5-10mins as many times when most of us get easy questions, the time
in which you complete becomes important hence do not waste time su bmit quickly and move ahead.  I think
most of them got doable questions.

2. Technical Interview [34 candidates]

Interview Prep Story
We received shortlisting at around 7.30pm and interviews were next  day at 9am but I didn't panic because I
somewhere knew that this hopefully will be last and final technical interview so I started my prep at around
9pm then slept for 3-4hrs again woke up at 3am and started with OOPs. Did around 45mins conversation with
Claude, revised everything then went for projects . I had made docs for all my projects and internship work
any possible technical or business -related cross question I was somewhat ready for it. Then did a little
DBMS/SQL revision and done… lets start with what reallyy happened…
Actual Interview
There were 4 panels I was the 3rd or 4th one, from my prep you might have seen that I didn't do DSA as such
but but but some of the panels were asking dp based question like Coin Change. I was panicking and just
prayed that I get some other panel and luck was in my favour that day. I think that I got the chillest panel.
I went in greeted them with big smile , they were quite swee t both from Senior DevOps team ig south africa
division. My interview was entirely RESUME BASED , I introduced myself first thought they would ask
about my internship work but they asked about the committee work which I didn't do so just cooked some
random story and they were impressed. We talked about this for 10-15mins I just don't know why they were
so much interested in that, it was just 2 lines in my resume.
Then we moved to my project the first project which SEO Rank tracking, I explained why it is important for
small scale businesses so he had multiple follow -up questions on this how will you market this t o a brand?
How can you guarantee them about improvement in their rankings? Almost all these questions were business
related nothing technical as such. I told him how SEO analysis would help the brands find their Target Market,
customer segmentation and so on. Just kept on talking and they liked it
One of my project had JWT since I had already made docs on such important topic I was aware on all possible
things he could ask but he just wanted surface level knowledge.
Since he was f rom DevOps side he asked that why my resume doesn't have a devops project while most of
the candidates had such projects so I told him honestly that we did make a project during our DevOps lab but
I  didn't put any efforts into it hence now I want to learn and then only if I have good confidence then only I
will mention it in my resume.  He appreciated the honesty and we moved on to last part of interview
He asked me to explain all types of Joins and w rite a query using joins so I made up my own ta bles and
explained all kinds of joins. After this he asked if I had any questions, so I asked since he was from South
Africa division did he ever visit there and can we get a chance too, then I asked how transunion is making a
platform somewhat similar to AWS or Google Cloud since this was mentioned during PPT I asked about this.
Then about a few services that transunion offers, we had discussion on that.
With this interview ended around 35-40mins. I was genuinely lucky that I got such good panel because
as I said in other panel candidates were asked to write oops code or coin change code . Try to have a
smile and be confident because you really can't predict in which direction the interview might go. I had
prepared for something else and was asked random things.. so just go with the flow.

3. HR Interview [11 candidates]

This round took place after lunch break at around 3pm, there were two panelists. I was asked with "Who
is Dishant?" so I gave my introduction as third person. Then was asked about Mini Project since that was
in a group, I was asked typical question, how did you get idea to do this? How to work as a team? Later
on, was asked about my family background, school and whether I was ok to relocate or not.
I asked her about the CSR activities that are done and that was the end.
Around 10-15mins of conversation.

At 4.45-5pm results were announced, 10 of us were selected and felicitated!!

MISTAKES YOU MUST AVOID:

1. Lying or Overstating in your resume

Please do not lie about the technical stuff as after just 1-2 follow-up questions, interviewers can easily
understand if you have deep understanding what you have written or not, if you are not 100% sure just
don't write. Each and every technology you write you must be able to back that up.

2. Don't get intimidated by the competition around you

When I saw there are so many non-tech hungry people around me , I didn't apply for JPMC thinking
that I just don't stand a chance against them but later on many people who were kinda tech heavy also
got selected. This is same thing happened in ISS's OA when I saw there are almost 300 people giving
OA I already made up my mind and didn't do well in that OA too.

3. Don't take rejections too hard

This year UBS didn't take normal OA they followed a different process and only 45 people had been
selected I thought that this opportunity was on a silver-platter hence I must get selected and I reached
till interviews but luck didn't take my side, I messed the interview very bad couldn't answer simple
OOPs questions and got rejected. That just hit me so bad that for day or two I couldn't do anything
and was just depressed and wasted lot of time.

4. You have to do more than just DSA

For few months of placement prep I was just focusing on DS A but I didn't pay much atte ntion on
OOPs, SQL, Aptitude prep and Java fundamentals . You must know java in -depth although I did my
dsa in python most of the companies expect java and sql to be the must know things.

Be ready since this year companies had a completely random shortlisting for OA most of them
wanted little to some work-ex like UBS and WorkIndia so try to do some int ernship. Also keep
your CGPA above 8 , even though can 't do anything about your 10 th ,12th score that is a lso
considered by companies and always tailor your resume according to the company's JD.

I have seen that even though you might have crossed the cgpa cutoff still your resume won't be
shortlisted so check the ATS Score to o. Since our batch was the first with increased intake no t
everyone gets shor tlisted so have a well rounded profile - cgpa, internships, projects, extra -
curricular you must have all these things.
