1. Resume Shortlist

2. Pen-Paper Test

3. Technical Interview

4. HR Interview

Resume Shortlist [313 students applied on Superset]
The company shortlisted around 116 students. I didn't make any changes to my resume for this role. My
resume was AI/ML- data science based. Use ResumeWorded, and keep ATS > 65.

2. Pen-Paper Test] [116 students appeared for this round]

1. Aptitude: 8 questions, +3 for every right answer and -1 for every wrong answer. Age problems,

speed-distance problem, basic math, profit-loss, time-work, geometry, permutation-combination.

2. Python Coding: 2 questions, total 4 marks. (no -ve marking). Find the number pattern and code it

out.
Sequence 1: 3, 6, 15, 24 .. N. so this is N^2 + 2N
Sequence 2: 2, 9, 28, 65,.. N and this is N^3 + 1

3. SQL: 4 questions, 2 marks each (no -ve marking)

3 tables were given - one for Sales, one for Region and one for Quarter.

1. Find best, worst and average sales for each salesman

2. Find second best sales

3. Rank average sales by region

--- PAGE 2 ---

4. Find count of salesmen who did no sales in a quarter

3. [Technical Round] [ 29 students were selected]

I was among the last 4-5 candidates to be called. They collected our resumes and called people randomly
instead of following the written test rankings.
Tip: Stay calm even if you're called last. You may be asked to wait, go back, or sit outside while the process
continues. Don't get frustrated - just follow the instructions. In my case, despite being among the last few
candidates, the interviewers were still fresh because there were several breaks between interviews.
The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself. I kept it short, covering my name, year, department, and
internship experience.
Tip: Tailor your introduction to the role. For SDE roles, talk about your tech stack and development
experience. For Business Analyst roles, focus on analytics, business understanding, and problem-solving.
He then asked about my internship. I explained that I worked at an early-stage startup where I collected and
analyzed data and built dashboards to answer business questions for the CFO. He also asked what the startup
did. I explained that it helped users manage household finances, bills, and budgeting using AI. When he
asked how the AI worked, I honestly told him I wasn't involved in that part but guessed it likely used
historical spending patterns, bill history, and user behavior. He didn't seem to mind.
Next, he asked what subjects we had in the previous semester (ML, Generative Al Fundamentals, Build
ChatGPT from Scratch, SPCC, and DevOps). He then asked if I had built any projects. I explained my Build
ChatGPT from Scratch project in detail, including the architecture, preprocessing pipeline, and why each
preprocessing step was necessary.
Tip: Know your projects inside out. Explain the architecture, workflow, and design decisions before the
interviewer even asks follow-up questions.
He then asked where I lived. After I answered [my location], he gave me a case study:
> Would you give a loan to a toy retailer from [my location]?
I first clarified a few details - the exact shop location, loan history, and whether there was a guarantor. I then
explained that I would evaluate the retailer's CIBIL score, income stability, repayment history, existing
loans, EMI record, and the guarantor's financial stability.
The interviewer then asked me to assume there was no guarantor and that the shop was in a well-known
market, "X." I estimated the retailer's income based on daily sales. My initial estimates were too high, and
the interviewer challenged me to consider transportation costs, procurement costs, and profit margins. Atter
revising my assumptions, I concluded that the retailer's actual income would be too low to comfortably
sustain the business and repay the loan, so I wouldn't approve the loan. The interviewer seemed happy with
my approach and reasoning.
He then asked whether I had done any traditional ML projects. I explained one from my third semester,
although it wasn't on my resume anymore. Since it had been over two years, I couldn't recall every detail, so
I admitted that honestly. He didn't seem to mind.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Towards the end, he asked whether I planned to pursue a Master's. I said no because I wanted to gain
industry experience first and understand the kind of work I enjoyed before making that decision. He also
asked why I wanted this role, and I explained that I wanted to explore the business side after working in
analytics during my internship and because I found business problem-solving more interesting.
Finally, he asked whether I had attended the PPT. This was probably to check whether I had paid attention. I
said yes, and he asked what I liked about it and whether I had any questions. I asked about the company's
three-year growth plan and responsibilities at each stage, and also about how they were using Al internally.
He answered both questions, and once I had no further doubts, he ended the interview by saying, "That's it.
Thank you for comingại
4.
[HR Round] [ 11 students were selected ]
I was the Sth/6th person to be interviewed. My panel consisted of the HR and two other interviewers. I
noticed that they had my pen-and-paper test answer sheet and scores with them. There was also an additional
score from my first-round interview written at the top.
They asked me to introduce myself again. This round was much more relaxed - the interviewers were
smiling and joking throughout the conversation.
The main question was a case study:
> How would you increase Zomato's profits? (Assume Blinkit is not included.)
I regained my composure and came up with several innovative as well as standard ideas covering customers,
delivery partners, and the business.
They then asked me to group my ideas into categories such as customer retention, improving existing
operations, and new business strategies, which I did successfully.
The HR then asked, "What's the first thing you would do if you were given a large dataset?"
I first clarified the objective - whether I was trying to increase profits, acquire new customers, or detect
anomalies. She asked me to continue with the profit objective. I said I would group orders by pincode,
identify peak-hour demand, and allocate more delivery partners to high-demand areas.
She then challenged my approach by asking, "Those areas are already profitable. What would you do for the
ones at the bottom of the list?" I replied that I would focus on those underperforming areas and apply the
strategies I had proposed earlier to improve demand and operational efficiency. She smiled, which made me
feel I was on the right track.
Towards the end, they asked where I lived and how many members were there in my family. Finally, they
asked if I had any questions.
I had already asked most of my questions in the first round, so I made the mistake of asking how I had
performed.
Tip: Avoid asking this. It can give the impression that you're looking for feedback to use in future
interviews. Thankfully, they were very friendly and simply said that I had done well since I had reached the
second round, and that the final decision would be communicated through the TPO.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Result: Out of all the candidates interviewed, 5 students were offered the job.
Motivation:
I enjoy AI/ML - Data related work but most companies that come in the beginning of the placement season
do not offer such roles. So, if you're doing AI/ML - data related projects, then be ready for a bunch of
rejections initially. In general, SDE people get placed before and with higher packages. So, choose wisely.
Also, with the rapid progression of AI, I am not sure which roles will last so just check the job market
requirements before choosing a particular side. Be ready to adapt.
I did minors in finance and strategic management which helped me a lot! I was able to land a somewhat
non-technical role because of this and quick thinking, problem solving attitude.
Resume shortlisting is sometimes random but mostly if your CGPA is above 9 and you have good projects,
you stand a good chance of getting shortlisted. Also, don't just say "IDK", say - "I can't seem to get to the
answer, can you give me a hint?"
Keep smiling, don't look nervous/serious/angry/frustrated. It's a long process.
"Comparison is the thief of joy" - Idk who
So, don't compare yourself with others. Everything happens for a reason and you can build from there.
Kabhi na kbahi kuch toh accha hoga, law of averages hai.

journey.prep:
-

• Try to begin or close the discussion if possible since they draw the attention of the moderator and

you can give a quick brief/conclusion on the topic without going too deep in.

• You have to choose a side - Pros, Cons or Neutral. Once you have chosen a side you have to stick to

it. You can't change your mind in the middle.

• If you feel you don't have any knowledge on the topic then it's okay to let a few people speak as it

will allow you to gather some info and you can then think of a point or you could agree/disagree with
someone's opinion. DO NOT DOMINATE THE DISCUSSION.

• Ensure that you speak 2-3 times during the discussion. If you have spoken more than that, then you

could allow someone else to speak who hasn't spoken at all. That shows the moderator that you
include everyone into the conversation and consider everyone's opinion.

4. Business Round

19 people were shortlisted for this round and I was the first to interview. The interview was online on zoom
with two people from JPMC. The interview lasted for 40-45 minutes. First I wished both the interviewers
Good Morning and asked them how they were doing. Following are the questions asked during the
interview:-

1. Tell me about yourself.

2. Tell me about a project from your resume.

3. In this project what were the challenges you faced and how did you resolve them?

4. Since the project I explained was an agentic Al project they asked me to explain the graph structure

and what LLM i used for the agents and why. Also they asked the latency and cost factors.

5. If you are given a dataset how would you analyze it and what tools would you use? Tell the entire

process

6. Tell me about a time you were on a project and you had no experience with that field or the tools

used for it? What did you do?

7. Have you used Al tools like Github Copilot, Claude Code, etc.

8. How do you write a good prompt for Claude?

9. Do you have any experience with python, alteryx, etc.

--- PAGE 3 ---

10. Do you know how to make Al agents?

11. Why should we hire you?

5. HR Round

8 people were shortlisted for the HR interview. This was the most chill round which lasted for 15-20 minutes
and I was asked easy and casual questions like:-

1. Tell me about yourself besides what's on your resume.

2. Where do you live and where are you originally from?

3. Tell me about a time when a team member was sidelined/overshadowed by others and their opinions

were not considered in the decision making process? What did you do and how did you solve this?

4. Tell me about a time when an argument broke out between team members. How did you approach

this situation and solve it?

5. Tell me about a weakness that you think you have.

6. Where do you see yourself in five years?

Out of the 8 people, 7 were finally selected and I was among them !!!.

Useful Tips:

• Know your resume thoroughly. [MOST IMPORTANT] Every project, technology, and skill

mentioned on your resume can lead to follow-up questions. Be prepared to explain your project's
architecture, the challenges you faced, the decisions you made, and the reasoning behind them. Your
resume is your selling point. You have to pitch them your skills and experiences!!!

• Based on what I've seen in this year's placement cycle, DSA isn't as important as it used to be. More

emphasis is on Al concepts and Al tools and how you have used them in your projects. I suggest
solving only easy and medium questions in DSA (unless you want to give FAANG interviews!) .
Agentic AI, GenAl, Claude Code,etc. are what companies are interested in these days!

• Internships are something that will favour you in an interview as it gives you something to talk about

and show that yes, this person does have some corporate experience. So I suggest doing at least 1
internship before placements.

• Based on the rapidly changing job market, I suggest not preparing for just ONE role. Rather its good

to have both tech and non-tech experience since you never know what you will end up doing.
Hence, don't limit yourself to one role. Explore everything !!!!! (preferably in 3rd year itself since it
gives you time and options to decide.....)
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Practice aptitude regularly. The Online Assessments are highly competitive and often the most

difficult round, so solve questions under timed conditions to improve both speed and accuracy. For
Aptitude, IndiaBix website (https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/) is the best and CareerRide youtube
channel.

• For Interviews:-

a. Prepare a strong self-introduction: It sets the tone for the interview and often determines
the direction of the discussion.
b. Understand the role, not just the company: Read about JPMorgan Chase, the role offered,
and the different teams discussed during the Pre-Placement Talk. Paying attention during the
PPT can be helpful during interviews. Bringing a few points up from the PPT into the GD or
interview surprises interviewers !!!!
c. Focus on your thought process: Interviewers are more interested in how you approach a
problem than in memorized answers.
d. Be brutally honest, no lies: If you don't know an answer, admit it confidently instead of
guessing. Interviewers appreciate honesty and will move on to the next question.
e. Ask meaningful questions: Prepare one or two questions for the interviewers. It
demonstrates genuine curiosity about the role and the organization.
f. Stay calm: Confidence comes from preparation and interviews become much easier when
you treat them as discussions rather than interrogations. Imagine you know them beforehand
and they are your friend (but don't get too casual and friendly, formality also has to be
maintained!)

• Topics Worth Revising before interviews

a. Python fundamentals, pandas, and data cleaning
b. SQL queries, joins, aggregations, and subqueries
c. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and data visualisation
d. Basic statistics and analytical reasoning
e. Machine learning fundamentals, if mentioned on your resume
f. Al agents, LLMS, RAG, and prompt engineering,
g. Project architecture, technology choices, limitations, latency, and cost
h. Group discussion topics related to Al, automation, remote work, and digital payments
i. Behavioural questions on teamwork, conflict resolution, leadership, and adaptability

• The placement process is grueling and competitive. It eats you up and starts affecting your attitude

and behaviour. I interviewed for 7 companies before JPMC and i had given up also but everyday you
have to keep moving forward despite the past. I never expected to get placed at JPMC and I had no
hopes going into the process as well. But I was determined to give my best despite the results and
voila!! I cracked it. So bottom line NEVER GIVE UP NO MATTER WHAT. Believe in yourself
and keep moving forward. Preparation and determination will always open doors for you and make
opportunities run towards you !!!!!
--- PAGE 5 ---
I hope this interview experience helps you prepare for the Corporate Analyst Development Program at
JP Morgan Chase. The questions and recruitment process may vary, but I hope my experience gives you a
useful starting point.

In case of any further doubts, you can refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.
ALL THE BEST !!!!!

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (25 September 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting (28 September 2026)

• Group Discussion Round (29 September 2026)

• Business Round (29 September 2026)

• HR Round (29 September 2026)

1. Pre-Placement Talk

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was held on 25th September at 4:00 PM. We were informed about this a day
earlier at 10pm. The session began with an introduction to the company, what they do, how they work, etc.
After that they spoke about the program and what they are looking for in candidates. After that a person who
was currently enrolled in the program spoke about her experience in the program and in JPMC. Following
this, at the end, there was a Q & A session for students to ask their doubts. Make sure to ask good questions
with regards to the role or the presentation. Finally, they urged the students to apply for the role on the
company website as well before applying on superset app.

2. Resume Shortlisting

The first round in any placement process is always resume shortlisting and JPMC has some strict criteria.
The eligibility criteria before they even look at the resume is 80% in 12th. So if you have a score lower
than that then you are out. Next they look at your resume and make sure the resume is tailored to the JD
they send. Tell ChatGPT to extract the keywords from the JD and put it in your resume only if you have
worked with that technology or you have that skill. Next put your resume in an ATS score checker, a
--- PAGE 2 ---
website like resumeWorded is good. Always make sure you have an ATS score above 70, that is more
than enough for all companies. In this process, 81 people were shortlisted for the further rounds.

in a room in college so that we could be monitored. There were 5-6 groups with 13-15 students in each
group. The topic given to us wasạiIs it a good idea to make Work From Home permanent for select
roles?". Next we were given 2 mins to prepare content and then the moderator began the discussion.

The online assessment was conducted on Coderbyte sharp at 8:30 AM. It was divided into four distinct
sections, testing programming, machine learning, databases, and fundamental concepts.
Section 1: Python Programming
Implementation of basic Bubble Sort strictly from scratch without using . sort () or built-in functions.
Section 2: Machine Learning Notebook
A single code file containing 4 blank snippets where you had to write the implementation logic. This
covered end-to-end data tasks including Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), missing value handling and
preprocessing, aggregation, and basic model setup using pandas and scikit-learn.
Section 3: SQL
A straightforward database query focusing on joining two tables and filtering aggregated data.
Section 4: Technical MCQs
Multiple-choice questions testing core machine learning intuition, standard Python syntax, and CS
fundamentals.
Points to Remember:
Manage your time well across coding and MCQS. Keep basic pandas transformations and array
manipulation logic right at your fingertips so you don't waste time looking up trivial syntax. Around 24
students were shortlisted for the next stage.

2. [Group Discussion Round] [24 Candidates Shortlisted]

The shortlisted students were divided into 3 groups of 8 students each. The discussion lasted for around 40
minutes per group.
The panel was very warm, polite, and receptive. This was not an aggressive debate round; they were
genuinely observing how structured your thoughts were, how clearly you communicated, and whether you
--- PAGE 2 ---
could build meaningfully upon points made by your peers. Active listening, avoiding talking over others,
and summarizing logically went a long way here. 8 candidates were shortlisted for the interview rounds.

3. [Technical Interview Round] [8 Candidates Shortlisted]

Duration was around 45 to 50 minutes. I was the very first candidate scheduled for the interview slot.
The interview started with a self-introduction where I walked them through my academic background, prior
internships, and core technical stack before steering toward my primary domain: Al and Deep Learning.
Project Deep Dive:
The panel spent nearly 20 solid minutes grilling me on my AI and deep learning projects. They went deep
into architectural choices and theoretical foundations. They questioned me thoroughly on convolutional
layers in CNNS, feature mapping, Vision Transformers (VIT), and attention mechanisms. For Generative
Adversarial Networks (GANs), they asked what exact architecture variant I used, why I chose it, and how
the generator-discriminator loss balance was maintained. They also demanded exact mathematical formulas
for evaluation metrics and pressed me on the precise performance numbers and benchmark scores my model
achieved
Live Coding:I was given an algorithmic coding problem to implement Insertion Sort from scratch. Once
implemented, they added a follow-up variation asking to retrieve the second largest element from the
structure. Scenario-Based ML: They presented practical, real-world machine learning problem statements
requiring structured logical reasoning, data handling strategies, and architectural decisions under real
constraints.
Points to Remember:
Own every single line on your resume. If you mention high-level architectures like Transformers or GANS,
be prepared to explain the underlying math, loss functions, hyperparameter choices, and exact benchmark
figures. Also, talk through your code out loud while implementing live algorithmic problems.

4. [HR Round] [Shortlisted Candidates]

The HR round lasted about 20 to 30 minutes. It was very calm, friendly, and conversational. Questions were
centered around: My personal background and journey into tech, my long-term career vision and aspirations,
my core strengths and genuine weaknesses, backed by real academic and project experiences, situational
questions on handling workplace pressure, team dynamics, and adaptability. Be genuine, grounded, and clear
about your motivations. Frame your weaknesses alongside the concrete actions you are taking to improve
them.
The final results were announced on the same evening. 2 students were selected for the role, and I was
fortunate to be one of them.
--- PAGE 3 ---

From the start of the placement season my target was non-tech companies, this didn't mean that I did not
apply for tech companies. You never know, an opportunity can appear out of thin air and you must be ready
to grab it. So keep applying and not losing hope. The entire process can be stressful and unpredictable, but
rest assured that you will have multiple but limited opportunities. You just have to be brave enough to apply
and give it your best shot each and every time. I got dropped in the very last round of two companies which
were also very good opportunities but there was something better planned for me. So staying at it is a must!
Here are a few tips to prepare for non tech companies:
Note: I am considering data analyst roles as non-tech too
Keep your Aptitude strong and this is by far non-negotiable. Practice a variety of problems, time yourself
and keep working on speed. You can use IndiaBIX and can practice CAT pyqs for a greater difficulty. Give
timed tests if possible, you can find these too on IndiaBIX.
Practice Business Case Studies thoroughly and visualize how you will answer such problems in an
interview.
--- PAGE 4 ---
These books might help:
por [IIMI 2023-24.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wz_Kg1WBYoDivEf4bnByCSNhq2sMS-rp/view?usp=drive_link)

Por [6.-Wharton-Casebook-2017.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b8E2xfixgawxUEdVq3sbSFA5Lz0TptcJ/view?usp=drive_link)

Practice Guesstimates: have a few guesstimates already prepared based on your resume (e.g my resume had
a project based on data analysis of amazon so prepare a guesstimate on how many deliveries amazon makes
in a day in mumbai) apart from that practice guestimates in general. You must know a few numbers like the
population of India/Maharashtra/Mumbai, age wise percentage breakdown, land area in sq km of mumbai,
etc. This book might help
PoF [Guesstimates-Book-Volume-1.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1sdgPLrCbGrqlC-_opkyhvnIdvUuj1g6b/view?usp=drive_link)
Practice Puzzles from geeks for geeks, they are genuinely interesting so you can go through them during
your commute/free time and discuss them with your friends.
Learn Python and its libraries, I learnt it while working on my projects but knowing a couple of libraries in
and out comes in handy (numpy, pandas etc)
Practice SQL problems, learn the basics and solve the Leetcode SQL50. Don't go for very complex queries;
anything above 10-12 line queries is not necessary.
Prepare overall for your GDs, participate in mock GDs held by the TPO and learn how to be articulate.
Know Your Resume in and out, if asked anything from it you must be able to fluently speak on it for at least
2 minutes.
As I mentioned earlier make a conscious effort on preparing good questions for your interviewers as they

2. Resume Shortlisting

Pre-Placement Talk (Online) - 25th September 2026
The Pre-Placement Talk is the best place to get to know about the role you are applying for apart from the
Job Description. There were multiple presenters that day and explained everything thoroughly which
included what the job role is, what they expect from a candidate, the pay and finally the entire hiring
process. I feel when it comes to JPMC or any other company for that matter, it is important to religiously
attend the pre placement talk as sometimes they do ask in interviews (they didn't in this case) about what
was discussed in the pre placement talk or who were the presenters of the talk etc. Be active especially in an
online setting keep your camera on, ask doubts only if you genuinely have any.

1. Resume Shortlisting [Approx. 200 students]

It is very difficult to exactly point out the Dos and Don'ts for the resume shortlisting as it seems to be a bit
random. However some good practices are having a single page resume and having an ATS score of 70 or
above. Your CGPA and 12th scores matter a lot for specific companies so ensure they are mentioned
correctly. My goal in maintaining my CGPA was to be 8.00+ but I feel with increasing resume shortlisting
for many companies being 8.5+ is safer. Most Importantly you must have projects that align with the role
also your skills section should be role based. For the CADP role I had put up 3 projects, 2 data analysis
projects and 1 Business Analysis project (DCF modelling). I have attached the resume I had applied with
below:
Port [JPMC_HHG_CADP.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1NmAAfSizhpDVGASXFnT8-0VV0aFQl3hH/view?usp=sharing)
--- PAGE 2 ---
Note:- They mentioned in the pre-placement talk that this is not a finance heavy role and it is okay if you do
not have a lot of finance knowledge, but again it always comes in handy to know the basics if you are
applying for a bank.

2. Group Discussion (online) [76 Students ]

Groups of 12 people were made and there were 2 panels. Topics were not given beforehand, instead the
topics were given on the spot and we were given 2 minutes to think and start the discussion. The topic for
my group was "Are digital payments secure in India and are they helping us grow towards a healthy
cashless economằ We were allotted 15 minutes for the discussion. Some key points to remember are, do
not talk too less or even too much. 3 entries are more than enough excluding the intro and/or conclusion.
The major issue in this round since it was online was to get a turn to speak, as when one person finished
their point many would unmute and start speaking which lead to a lot of cross talk and unprofessionalism, be
patient but not passive. When you speak, ensure your points are unique and assertively conveyed. Do not
argue with anyone and try to constructively build from a point someone else has mentioned which has
similar meaning to your point. This doesn't mean that you always have to speak following others line of
thought, feel free to give your own unique ideas just ensure you do not sway off topic.

3. ¡Business Round (Interview round 1) | 19 Students ]

The interview started with a classic "walk us through your profile." My biggest takeaway here is to have a
compelling introduction prepared beforehand don't just wing it. Keep it engaging and ensure it provides a
strong gist of your resume. When asked about my approach to understanding clients as a new intern, I
emphasized the importance of internal communication. I mentioned that I would first talk to colleagues and
teammates to understand who the client is and gauge their expectations, ensuring I follow the proper chain
of command before initiating any direct contact.
We then moved to technical discussions, where I was asked to explain a project I was most comfortable
with. I detailed my data pipeline project since I was very thorough with its architecture. When they asked
who the project benefited, I was initially a bit unsure but honestly stated it was primarily a skill-building
exercise for me. However, I made sure to acknowledge how crucial it is to understand the real-world
business application of any project. Following this, they presented a scenario about using Al to summarize a
peer meeting and gauge audience expectations. I asked them to elaborate on the question first for clarity.
Once clear, I suggested deploying a live meeting recorder that notes discussion points, assigns weights based
on predefined criteria and time spent on topics, and generates a real-time summary by the end.
The behavioral questions tested practical decision-making and time management. When asked about a time I
considered a shortcut, I shared an instance from a case study competition. With less than an hour to the
deadline, we had five slides done and three pending. We considered using Al to instantly generate the
remaining three, but the output lacked consistency and quality. Instead of forcing eight mediocre slides, we
adapted and strongly concluded our presentation on the sixth slide itself. Finally, for a scenario involving
clashing deadlines between a manager's project and a client's last-minute modification, my approach focused
on transparency and delegation. I explained that I would politely inform the client that late changes are
challenging, assess the magnitude of their request, and either implement it fully (if small) or partially (if
large) to keep them satisfied. To manage the clashing internal deadline, I would temporarily delegate parts of
the manager's task to teammates to ensure both deliverables stay on track.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Most importantly: Ask very good and unique questions to your interviewers. I asked two questions at
the end of my interview. I say it is important because good questions can take an interview from
mediocre to a great right at the very end.

4. HR Round (Interview round 2) [ 8 Students ]

The HR round focused on cultural fit, personal values, and basic logistics. When asked to share something
not on my resume, I steered the conversation toward my sports background. I explained how my experience
in sports has shaped me into a collaborative team player and honed my ability to make difficult, real-time
decisions- qualities that directly translate to a fast-paced work environment. Later, they asked a behavioral
question on what "doing the right thing" means to me. I answered that it means upholding my own morals
and the ethics of the institution I represent, ensuring that I don't hurt anyone in the process of achieving
goals.
They also tested my communication approach by asking how I would explain a technical concept to a
non-technical audience. I pitched the idea of gamified learning, explaining that turning a complex concept
into a game makes the learning process much easier, relatable, and fun. For the standard logistical questions
regarding my willingness to relocate and my comfort with working across different time shifts, I kept it
straightforward and answered yes to both.
The googly of the round was when they asked what one thing would persuade me to quit this job for another
offer. I took a moment to genuinely think about it before answering. Ultimately, I chose to be honest and told
them that, at this point, I couldn't think of anything that would make me want to leave.
Again, I asked a couple of questions to conclude the interview.
7 students were offered the job

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting (Out of 300, only 122 students were shortlisted)

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 1(03 July 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 2 (03 July 2026)

• HR Interview (03 July 2026)

• Result Declaration (03 July 2026)

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was held on 24th June at 2:00 PM. We were informed about it only a day
before, around 9:00 PM
J.P. Morgan Chase was hiring for three different roles:

• Banking (Investment Banking)

• FinTech

• Corporate Risk

--- PAGE 2 ---
The session began with an introduction to the company, followed by an overview of the three roles, their
responsibilities, and the kind of work involved. While attending the PPT, pay close attention to the skills and
qualities they emphasize, as these often reflect what they look for in candidates.
After the presentation, there was a Q&A session. This is a good opportunity to clear your doubts, but make
sure your questions are genuine and related to the presentation or the role. Avoid asking questions just to
get noticed or because everyone else is asking.
After the PPT, we had to register on the J.P. Morgan Chase careers website and fill out the Google Form
shared by the Training and Placement Office (TPO). We also had to submit our final resumes, so it is
important to have your resume completely ready before this stage. The resume shortlist was announced on
26th June at around 5:30 PM, just one day before the online assessment.
The company does not officially disclose the criteria used for resume shortlisting, but it is generally believed
that the ATS score plays an important role. Make sure your resume aligns with the job description of each
role. Before submitting your resume, check it on multiple ATS evaluation websites such as Enhancv and
Resume Worded. Since different platforms calculate ATS scores differently, comparing results from two or
three websites gives a better idea of how your resume might perform. A score of around 72 or higher is
generally considered a good ATS score, although there is no official cutoff.

2. Online Assessment [ 122 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Banking
MCQ Assessment - 45 Qtns - 45 Mins - 45 Marks
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounts - 10 Qtns
Section 2: Market Awareness - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Quantitative Aptitude - 15 Qtns
Section 4: English Usage - 10 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
The Online Assessment (OA) consisted of Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, and Quantitative Aptitude
questions. The quantitative section mainly covered topics like Time and Work, Trains, Permutations and
Combinations, Pipes and Cisterns, Calendars, and similar concepts.
The questions were of moderate to difficult difficulty and were quite time-consuming, so regular practice is
important. You can practice from websites like IndiaBix and also solve easy CAT-level aptitude questions,
as they are at a similar level.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Depending on the TPO, this round can be conducted either online or offline. In our case, it was an online
assessment taken from home using Aon's proctoring software. We had to solve 30 questions in 45
minutes under strict online monitoring with +2/-1 negative marking.
Do not underestimate this round. It had the highest elimination, with only 32 students shortlisted out of
122 who appeared for the test.

3. Technical Round 1[32 students were shortlisted]

• Interview Duration and Panel

My technical interview lasted for around 20 minutes and was conducted by two panelists, one of
whom was a Vice President (VP) at J.P. Morgan Chase. The interview was very conversational, and
almost all the questions were based on my resume and the projects I had mentioned.

• DCF Valuation Project

The discussion started with my Discounted Cash Flow DCF) valuation project on Apple (AAPL).
They asked me to explain the complete valuation process, the assumptions I had used, and how I
arrived at the final valuation. Since I had also included a Monte Carlo Risk Model in the project, they
spent some time asking how I built it, why I used it, and what insights it provided. They also tested
my fundamentals by asking basic finance concepts such as the difference between Enterprise Value
and Equity Value.

• Case Study on Financial Crises

My next project was a case study covering Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank, and Credit Suisse.
The panel asked me to explain the Lehman Brothers crisis in detail, identify the type of risk
involved, and describe the Subprime Mortgage Crisis. They were interested in understanding
whether I knew not just what happened, but also why it happened and how it eventually led to
Lehman Brothers' collapse.

• Python Prediction Model

They then moved to my Python-based prediction model. I was first asked to give an overview of the
project, after which the discussion focused on the technical aspects. They asked me about the data
cleaning process, the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) I performed, and the different Python
libraries I used. I explained each library, why I chose it, and how it contributed to building the final
model.

• HR and Behavioral Questions

Since one of the interviewers was a VP, the interview also included a few HR questions. They asked
me about my strengths and weaknesses, and why I believed I was the best fit for the role. These
questions were aimed at understanding my personality, confidence, and how well I understood my
own profile. I had also added about E-Cell and the different speakers we had hosted, so one of the
questions was which speaker I liked the most and why.

• Questions I Asked the Interviewers

At the end of the interview, they asked if I had any questions. I askedạẠIf you select me today, what
should I work on during the next six months and throughout my internship so that I am better
prepared and you feel selecting me was the right decision?" They appreciated the question and
advised me to focus on AI and automation tools, as these are becoming increasingly important in the
industry.

• Overall Interview Experience

Looking back, the interview was less about solving difficult technical questions and more about
--- PAGE 4 ---
understanding what I had actually worked on. The panel wanted to see whether I genuinely
understood every project mentioned on my resume and whether I could explain it confidently. They
also evaluated if my skills, experience, and personality were a good fit for roles within Corporate
Risk, such as Middle Office & Reporting, Risk Controller, Project Management, and Data Analysis.

4. Technical Round 2 [ 16 students were shortlisted ]

• Interview Duration and Focus

This interview also lasted for around 20 minutes and was completely based on my resume.
Compared to the first technical interview, this round was more detailed, with the interviewers
focusing on specific parts of my projects and asking deeper follow-up questions to test my
understanding.

• DCF Valuation Project

The interview started with my DCF valuation project. They asked me about the different risk
metrics I had used and how I monitored them. I explained that I had tracked various financial ratios
and margins and used a RAG (Red-Amber-Green) system with predefined thresholds to identify
potential risks. I also gave a practical example to make my explanation clearer. They again asked
about the Monte Carlo Simulation, specifically how I had built it in Excel and which functions I
had used to generate the simulation.

• Case Study on Financial Crises

They once again discussed my case study on Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank, and Credit
Suisse. This time, the focus was on why the Lehman Brothers collapse triggered a global
financial crisis. They wanted to understand whether I could explain the chain of events and the
broader impact on the financial system.

• Python Prediction Model

The discussion then moved to my Python prediction model. They asked how I had performed
feature engineering, why I created those features, and how they improved the model. They also
revisited the data cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) steps. Based on my answers,
they gave me a scenario-based problem and asked how I would solve it using Python, including the
code and the syntax I would use.

• SQL Questions

After Python, they asked me a basic SQL question on the difference between WHERE and HAVING. I
answered it confidently and correctly, and since they were satisfied with my explanation, they did not
ask any further SQL questions.

• Tableau Discussion

They then asked about my experience with Tableau. I explained that I had practiced using a few
datasets and created dashboards to learn the tool. They followed this up by asking the difference
between Measures and Dimensions in Tableau. Initially, I wasn't sure of the answer, so I politely
asked for some clarification. They explained it using an example, which helped me understand the
question, and I was then able to answer it correctly.

• Puzzle Round

I was also given a logical puzzle involving water jars. The question was how to measure 4 litres
using a 5-litre and a 3-litre jar. They were more interested in my thought process and approach
than just the final answer.

• Questions I Asked the Interviewers

At the end, I was again given an opportunity to ask a question. I asked, "Which department do you
work in, and how has your journey there shaped your personal and professional experience?" The
--- PAGE 5 ---
interviewers genuinely appreciated the question and spent nearly 2-3 minutes talking about their
own experiences and career journey. It turned into a very natural conversation and ended the
interview on a positive note.

• Overall Interview Experience

This interview was much more detailed than the first one. The interviewers carefully tested whether I
genuinely understood every project listed on my resume rather than simply memorizing the content.
They also looked at how I approached problems, explained technical concepts, and communicated
my thought process when faced with unfamiliar questions.

5. HR Round [10 students were shortlisted ]

• Interview Experience

The HR round was the most relaxed out of all the interviews. It started with a casual conversation
where the interviewer asked how my day had been and how I felt about the overall interview process.
The atmosphere was friendly, and it felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

• General Discussion

The interviewer asked me about my hobbies and interests to get to know me better. They also asked
whether I had spoken to any seniors who had interned or worked at J.P. Morgan Chase and what I
knew about the internship experience. I told them that I had interacted with a few seniors and shared
the insights they had given me about the internship and the kind of work involved. This showed that
I am eager to join and prepared for what the internship will demand.

• Why I Was a Good Fit

One of the main questions was why I believed I was the best suited for the role. I answered that I
genuinely enjoy finance and risk management because of my Corporate Finance and Investment
Banking minor. At the same time, I also enjoy coding and working with real-world data. Since this
role combined both finance and technology, I felt it matched my interests and skills well. The
interviewer seemed to really like this answer.

• Role Expectations

The HR interviewer clearly explained that the Corporate Risk role would be based entirely in
Bengaluru and asked whether I was comfortable relocating. They also mentioned that the work
could involve irregular shift timings and wanted to know if I was comfortable with that as well.
These questions were mainly to ensure that I understood the nature of the role and was willing to
adapt to its requirements.

• Overall Interview Experience

This round was mainly to understand my personality and check whether I would be a good fit for J.P.
Morgan Chase's work culture. The focus was not on technical knowledge but on my attitude,
communication, and willingness to take up the role. My advice for this round is simple-be
yourself, answer honestly, and speak with confidence.
ALL THE 10 STUDENTS APPEARING FOR THE HR ROUND WERE SELECTED.
ALSO NOTE THAT JPMC CAN AND DOES REMOVE STUDENTS FROM THE HR ROUND AS
WELL. SO BE PREPARED AND DO NOT TAKE IT LIGHTLY.
--- PAGE 6 ---

(OA, Tech interview 1 and Tech interview 2 so all in all 3 rounds)
Pre OA shortlisting
Eligibility Criteria mainly was 7.5 cgpa, they even asked for internships, work experience, lol also my

journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting

The first stage was resume-based shortlisting. Although the exact criteria are not known, having at least one
project related to AI/ML can be helpful. Try to maintain a CGPA of 8.5+, as the competition and number of
applicants are increasing, making academics an important factor in shortlisting.
Having internships of at least 3 months can also improve your chances. For Auxo Al specifically, an
internship is more useful if it is related to AI/ML, as domain-relevant experience is likely to carry more
value.
150 students were shortlisted for OA

2. OA [150 students]

The OA was of 1.5 hours and had 28 questions: 25 MCQs and 3 coding questions. The MCQS were quite
easy and were mainly based on basic ML concepts, along with some LLM-related questions and
aptitude. Questions covered topics like overfitting, tokens, embeddings, etc. The concepts covered in
ML, DL and NLP subjects were enough to solve these questions.
Coding Questions:-

1. The first coding question was based on strings and frequency. Given a string and an integer k, we had

to return only the characters whose frequency was greater than or equal to k, arranged in decreasing
order of frequency. Characters with the same frequency had to be sorted lexicographically and it also
contained both upper and lower case characters.
Example: s = "mississippi", k =2 → Output: isp.
Solved all the test cases
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. You are given a budget of k kibbles and an array of oranges. Each orange is represented by a pair

(cost, weight), where cost is the price of the orange and weight is its weight. Find the maximum
possible total weight of oranges that can be bought without the total cost exceeding k.
Example:- k=10
Oranges = I (4, 5), (5, 6), (3, 4), (6, 8) ]
Output= 13
It was a simple 0/1 knapsack problem
I was not able to clear only 1 test case of this question because i did not get time to write the
tabulation approach.

3. This question was tricky and tough. The question was based on a person who had planned a trip to

different cities and made postcards for each place, but the postcards got jumbled. We had to find the
correct order in which the cities were to be visited, given that no city was visited twice.
On reading the question, it seemed like a topological sort or BFS/DFS problem. We had to try
finding the starting city and then determine the order in which all the cities could be visited. A travel
cost was also given between two cities.
The difficult part was that the input consisted of city names, and the output required the ordered list
of cities along with the total travel cost.
Example:- Input:- [
("Lucerne", "Interlaken", 80),
("Zurich", "Lucerne", 50),
("Interlaken", "Zermatt", 120),
("Zermatt", "Geneva", 150)
Output:-
Order of cities:
Total Cost:
400
The sample test case were cleared but no hidden test case were solved for this question.
The question is easy but handling string names is tough because it requires mapping of names to
integers and vice versa.
The OA was conducted on the CodeChef platform. The errors shown for the coding questions were not very
descriptive, which made it difficult to understand and debug the code. Also, some candidates mentioned that
they were able to solve the second question using only memoization, so there is a possibility that the test
cases or questions may have varied between candidates.

3. Interview 1 [15 Students]

There were 15 students for the first interview round. We were given different interview slots, but due to
delays, the interviews started around 11 AM. There were 3 interview panels, and since they were running
short on time, after around 3 interviews, 2 panels started conducting the second round of interviews while
the remaining panel continued with the first round. I was then moved to another panel and ended up being
second last to give the first round interview, which was after lunch.
The interview started with "Introduce yourself, and the interviewer had my resume open on their laptop. He
then started asking questions about my projects and internships. I was asked to explain my projects and what
I had worked on during my internship. From the explanations, the interviewer picked specific topics and
started asking questions related to them. Since I had a project based on RAG, I was asked about the
complete RAG flow and some related concepts.
After covering my projects and internship, the interviewer started testing my knowledge of ML, NLP and
DL concepts. Questions were asked about Lasso and Ridge Regression, Ensemble Learning, Random Forest,
validation and testing, K-Fold Cross Validation, tokens, embeddings, RNN, LSTM, GRU, Transformers,
Attention Mechanism, and other related concepts. Most questions were focused on what these concepts are
and their general working.
I was also asked some SQL and DBMS questions, including joins, primary and foreign keys, CTES, and
normalization (INF, 2NF and 3NF). At the end, the interviewer asked if I had any questions.
Almost all questions were answered to the satisfaction of interviewer but in some questions there were some
terms that i could not recall but overall the interview was good.
This interview was around 45 minutes long.
Tip:- For interview know your resume well. Be prepared for any type of questions here. They will not leave
any topic from your resume. If you have mentioned some technology they will ask questions on it for sure.
Out of the 15 students, 8 students were selected for the next round.

4. Interview 2 [ 8 Students]

This was a technical interview, but the interviewer also included several case-study and problem-solving
questions. The interview started with an introduction, followed by a discussion about my projects. One of
my projects was skipped because my teammate had already explained it in detail during Round 1, so we
briefly discussed my other projects similar to the previous round.
I was then asked to explain TF-IDF which i was able to explain. Then i was asked about knowledge graphs
but for this i could not answer properly.
The interview then moved to case studies. We had some fun conversation about what type of questions he
should ask, and when I said he should ask something that would get me selected, he jokingly replied that he
would give me a tougher question.
--- PAGE 4 ---
The first case study was based on Zomato entering a new Tier-2 city. The expected daily orders were 10,000,
with an average order value of 7300. Restaurants gave 20% of the order value to Zomato as commission,
Zomato paid 350 per delivery to the delivery partner, and there was a fixed daily cost of <2,00,000. I had to
determine whether the business would be profitable and suggest ways to make it profitable. It involved a
simple calculation followed by an open-ended discussion about what could be changed to improve
profitability. I started with we can take like a platform fee of like Rs.10 this will make the business break
even and then i told we can pitch restaurants that we can provide them special marketing and we would
charge them 23% commission. Then I also said that we could not reduce the delivery cost but if we would
club the delivery of the same localities in that way we could reduce the cost. Since this was relatively
straightforward, I completed it quickly.
The interviewer then gave me another case study where a company's profit margin had suddenly decreased,
even though it had been gradually increasing before. I was asked to identify possible reasons for the sudden
drop. I initially suggested several possibilities such as increased competition, higher commissions, raw
material costs, import/export duties, labour costs and operational costs. However, these were not the
expected answer because none of these factors had changed.
During the discussion, he noticed my surname, Zaveri, and asked whether my family was involved in the
jewellery business. When I mentioned that I come from a business family, he jokingly said that I should be
able to solve the question and he will not help me with this question.
After I gave several more possibilities, he provided an important hint: the company's revenue had actually
increased during the period when the profit margin decreased. Based on this, we discussed the possible
reasons, and I eventually arrived at the expected answer: increased marketing expenditure. The additional
marketing cost reduced the profit margin, while the increased marketing also helped increase the company's
revenue. I was clear that the profit margin reduced suddenly so there would be a change in costing or some
extra expenditure and it was clear that cost of materials and other things are the same so i had to think of all
the expenditures that could have increased.
The interview ended with the interviewer asking if I had any questions.
This interview was around 45-50 minutes long.

5. HR Round [5 Students]

This was not an interview round, here the hr personally called and gave results.
After around 6:00 pm all the Round 2 interviews were completed, we were informed that 5 students had
been selected for the HR round. We were told that the HR round would be conducted online, so we were
asked to go home and were asked to be available around 7:30 PM.
Later, we came to know that it would actually be a phone call rather than a video interview. Based on
previous interview experiences, I expected it to be a normal conversation, but I still went through some
common HR questions while waiting.
After a long wait, I finally received the call around 9:30 PM. The HR informed me that I had been selected
for the internship and the full-time opportunity afterwards and then explained the compensation breakdown

All 5 of them were selected for the internship and full time offer.

Placement Process:

There were three rounds in total. The eligibility criteria were open to students from all branches with a CGPA of 7.5 or above. The entire process was conducted virtually.
There were two roles: Software Engineering and Aladdin Data, and I applied for both. The interviews were conducted through Webex, although candidates were required to attend them from the TPO office. It was a pool campus placement process, with students participating from several other colleges as well, including NIT Agartala, Manipal University Jaipur, and others.

1. Online Assessment [Around 280 people appeared for this round]

Everyone who met the eligibility criteria received the OA link via email one day before the assessment. There were seven sections in total: Basic Coding, Advanced Coding,Basic Design Patterns, Advanced Design Patterns, DBMS, Aptitude, AI and Reasoning
Each section was timed separately. Once a section was started, it could not be skipped or revisited until the allotted time was over or the section was submitted.
Since we received the OA link a day in advance and could see the section names, I prepared Design Patterns thoroughly because I had not studied them much before. The MCQs covered all 23 Gang of Four design patterns.
For Basic Coding, I received a Java and OOP-based question. The problem involved a list of baggage items with their destinations, where the bags had to be grouped by destination. If there were 10 or fewer bags, they had to be processed sequentially. If there were more than 10, the list had to be divided into two parts, processed in parallel using Fork/Join, and then the results had to be merged in right-to-left order.
Since Java is my primary language, I was able to solve it within the allotted 40 minutes.
For Advanced Coding, I received a Selenium-based debugging question. The codebase was fairly large, and it took me some time to understand the existing code and the problem. Since the section had a 15-minute limit, I was unable to solve the question.
The DBMS section was easy to moderate. It covered joins, keys, SQL queries, ACID properties, and general database concepts involving technologies such as PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Oracle.
The Aptitude section was moderate to difficult, with questions on permutation and combination, ratios and proportions, percentages, family relationships, seating arrangements, and similar topics.
The AI and Reasoning section was comparatively easier and could largely be approached using basic logical reasoning and common sense.
The coding questions varied across candidates. Some candidates received two DSA questions, while others received combinations involving OOP, debugging, or other coding concepts.

2. Technical Round 1 [ 28 students for SDE and 9 for Aladdin Data]

I received a call from HR at around 7:30 AM informing me that my interview was scheduled for 9:30 AM.
There were two panelists, and the interview started with them asking me how my day was going. I asked them the same. They then asked me to introduce myself and asked about my minor in Banking Technology from Barclays. I explained how the course developed my interest in the finance industry. I was also asked about my opinion on AI-based projects and whether I would be open to working on them.
The interview then moved to a DSA question. I was asked to share my screen and open Notepad. The interviewer gave me a string (consisting of lowercase letters and brackets) . I was supposed to reverse the string whenever I encountered a matching pair of brackets till there were no brackets left, (basically valid parenthesis but with a twist). I was asked to write the code and explain the dry run as well. I initially approached the problem recursively, and then optimized the solution using a stack.
After this, I was asked how comfortable I was with Java and Python. I mentioned that Java is my primary language and that I know the basics of Python. Since my solution involved Strings, the discussion then moved into Strings in Java. I was asked several questions, including:

● Why did you use StringBuilder?

● What do mutable and immutable mean?

● Why are Strings immutable in Java?

● What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer?

● When would you use StringBuilder and when would you use StringBuffer?

● How are Strings stored internally in Java? Can you give an example?

I was able to answer all of these questions.
The interviewer then moved on to SQL. I was asked about the difference between the WHERE and HAVING clauses. I explained what each clause does and gave an example. I also mentioned that HAVING can be used without GROUP BY, so the interviewer asked me to explain this with an example. I was then asked about the difference between a Primary Key and a UNIQUE constraint. The interviewer followed up with a conceptual question: if we can simply use UNIQUE along with NOT NULL, what would happen if there were no Primary Keys, and why do we need Primary Keys in the first place?
The discussion then moved to my projects. I was asked to give an overall explanation of my projects and was asked why I had chosen particular technologies or methodologies for them.
I was also asked about my internship experience, including what I worked on and what I learned from it.
Throughout the interview, there were also behavioral questions, including questions about my future plans, positions of responsibility, and how I respond to feedback.
At the end of the interview, I was asked whether I had any questions for them. I asked about their work experience at BlackRock and the types of projects they work on.
I initially felt that my interview had not gone particularly well because the interviewer maintained a very concise communication style and often responded briefly after my answers. The interview lasted around 35 minutes. However, shortly afterward, I received a call from HR informing me that I had been shortlisted for the next round.
The first technical round was quite different for different candidates. Some candidates were asked two three DSA questions, while others were asked questions related to React/Next.js or had a more HR-oriented discussion.

3. Techno HR [ Around 18 ]

This round was different for everyone as well. For some candidates, it was purely HR-focused, for some it was more technical, while others had a mix of both.
The interviewer started by asking how my previous round went. He then introduced himself and explained what he does at BlackRock. After that, he asked me to introduce myself.
He then asked me to explain my favorite project in depth : why it was my favorite, what the project was about, what motivated me to build it, and what problems I faced while working on it. I chose my DevOps project, which also involved system design concepts.
He then asked me to explain a particular bug I had faced and how I solved it. This discussion eventually led to me explaining my entire CI/CD pipeline in depth.
We also had a discussion around Redis, since I had used it in my project. From the way the questions were framed, I felt that he was particularly interested in understanding how I approach a problem and make technical decisions, rather than simply testing whether I knew the technology.
He then asked me: "If you could add ONE feature to this project, what would it be and why?"
The discussion then moved to my internship experience. He asked me how I handled feedback from clients, how I managed deadlines, and how I had optimized my project.
I was also asked: "What is one use of AI in your life that you are really proud of?"
Another interesting part of the interview was a discussion around core values. I was asked to name three core values I had learned during college and whether those values were already present in me before I joined college. I was also asked about a situation where I had failed badly, made a comeback, and what I learned from that experience. I discussed one of my hackathon experiences for this question.
Towards the end, the interviewer asked me if I had any questions for him. Since he had mentioned at the beginning that he had been working at BlackRock for around 14 years, I asked him: "What are three core values that you have personally learned during your time at BlackRock?" He really liked the question, and we had a good discussion around it. I then asked him what would be expected of me during the first few months if I were to join as an intern.
The round lasted around 50 minutes. One interesting thing about the process was that after the interviews of all the initially shortlisted candidates were completed, they also started calling waitlisted candidates for Round 1 for SDE role
Altogether 8 people were offered the job ( 7 SDE+1 aladdin data)

1. Online Assessment [ 320+ students appeared for this round]

Based on my experience, this year's PhonePe OA was much tougher and felt like a true PhonePe-level
assessment than the previous years, so don't assume the difficulty level will be the same just because earlier
OAs were considered easy. The questions required strong problem-solving skills and good implementation
under time pressure. According to me, the technical interview questions were actually much easier than the
OA. So, make sure you prepare well for the online assessment, as clearing it is probably the hardest step in
the entire interview process.
The OA was of total 350 points
Question 1: Task Assignment (50 Points)
We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers (capability),plus an integer K denoting the
maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A worker can only do a task if their capability is
greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to minimize the maximum number of tasks that
each worker could do and we have to complete each and every task after assigning a max fixed number of
tasks to any worker. We can to output max tasks completed and max number of tasks assigned to any worker
Initially, I misunderstood the problem and completely missed the condition to minimize the maximum
number of tasks assigned to any worker. So, I used a greedy approach by sorting both arrays and assigning
tasks using two pointers, which passed 9/14 test cases. After spending around 10 minutes on it, I moved on
to the other question instead of getting stuck. This is something I'd recommend if you're stuck, solve the next
questions first and come back later. In the last few minutes, I reread the problem carefully and realized the
intended approach was Binary Search on the Answer combined with a feasibility check using two pointers.
Unfortunately, there wasn't enough time left to implement it completely. The biggest takeaway is to read the
problem statement carefully before jumping into a solution.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Question 2 : Network Routers and Regions (70 Points)
You are given an undirected tree with N nodes representing a network. The network consists of exactly one
central server, multiple routers, and multiple regions. The server is connected only to routers, each router
is connected to the server and one or more regions, and every region is connected to exactly one router. The
task is to determine the number of routers and regions present in the network using the given tree.
This was a tricky problem because understanding the statement was the hardest part. Once I understood the
network structure, the solution became quite straightforward. The key observation was that every region is a
leaf node, so it has a degree of 1. The server is the only node connected directly to all the routers and never
to any region, while each router is connected to the server and one or more regions. So, I first calculated the
degree of every node. Then, for each node, I counted how many of its adjacent nodes had degree 1. The
node whose neighbors represented all the leaf nodes while the remaining neighbors acted as routers was
identified as the server. Once the server was found, the number of routers was simply the number of its
neighbors, and the number of regions was obtained by counting all the degree-1 nodes connected through
those routers.
I was able to solve this problem completely
Question 3 : Codeforces 1665C (110 Points)
This was a Codeforces problem with the statement slightly reframed. If you've seen the original problem
before, you'll recognize it immediately. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to recall the exact approach during the

came up with a heuristic based on counting the number of children of each node and performing a simple

journey.prep:
Placements are not purely skill-based; luck, timing and the particular interview panel can also play a role.
So, as niche as it may sound, don't let a rejection define your preparation. Keep improving and stay
consistent.
Resources:

• DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet - one of the most structured resources for placement preparation.

Focus on understanding concepts and solving the more frequently asked data structures and their
problems (Strings, Stacks, Queues, LinkedLists) at least once (Please note: Every company usually
has topics that they tend to ask more on, so do your research thoroughly and try covering the other
topics if needed).
https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z/

• SQL: LeetCode SQL 50 - Repeat questions you struggle with and understand multiple approaches.

https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

• Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel for Java and OOP fundamentals.

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL9gnSGHSqcno1G3XjUbwzXHL8_EttOuKk

• Core CS: GeeksforGeeks for OOP, DBMS, OS and Computer Networks concepts and practice.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/interview-experiences/technical-interview-preparation/

• System Design: Gaurav Sen's content + ChatGPT/Claude for explanations and interview-style

practice.

• Aptitude: IndiaBIX, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

• Puzzles: GeeksforGeeks' interview puzzles, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

Interview-Day Tips:

• Know your resume thoroughly. Anything written on it can be questioned, so understand every

technology, tool and project you mention.

• Know your projects end-to-end: schema/database design, backend structure, APIs, architecture,

your contribution, limitations and possible improvements.

• Be strong in fundamentals: You don't need to know everything, but the fundamentals of every

technology on your resume should be clear.

• Prepare for follow-ups: Interviewers may keep changing the conditions of a scenario, so understand

your reasoning rather than memorizing answers.

• CGPA: 8+ is a decent position, while 8.5+ is preferable where companies have academic cutoffs.

• Prepare for HR and behavioural questions as well. Technical preparation alone is not enough. Be

ready for questions about your strengths, weaknesses, leadership experiences, failures, career goals,
and situational judgement. Answer smartly but honestly; don't try to give the answer you think the
interviewer wants to hear. Keep your responses genuine and support them with real examples from
your experiences.
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Don't lose confidence after rejection: BlackRock was the 18th company I encountered during

placements. I had previously been shortlisted by two companies but was rejected by HR in the final
rounds in both. I kept preparing and eventually got this opportunity.

• Don't convince yourself that you're underprepared: You will never feel completely prepared.

Trust your preparation and focus on the interview in front of you.

• Stay calm and patient. Take a few seconds to think before answering difficult questions and explain

your reasoning clearly.

• Sleep properly: I had only around 1.5 hours of sleep before my interview day, and it definitely

affected how calmly I handled the long day. As funny as it might sound, get adequate sleep the day
before interviews at least, and keep your setup ready beforehand.
Finally, positivity, patience and consistency are key. Placement season can be stressful and unpredictable,
so keep learning from every interview and don't compare your progress with others. Wishing everyone all
the best!!

Whatsapp: 8879782190
