1) Pre-placement Talk

2) Online Assessment

3) Technical Interview

4) HR Round

The pre-placement talk was conducted online on Webex platform. Since it was a pool campus placement
process, the online meeting had over 4000 students from colleges all over India. Every company shares
important pointers about the company and the roles they are hiring for that might be useful for later
interview rounds, so make sure to pay attention and note down a few important points (or any questions that
could be asked based on the preplacement talk in the interviews). BlackRock was hiring for 2 roles, namely
Software Engineering and Aladdin Data. We were asked to choose our preference and/or apply to both roles
(I applied for both roles). The eligibility criteria was open to students of all branches with a CGPA of 7.5 or
above. There was no apparent resume based shortlisting done for the Online Assessment.

1. Online Assessment [Around 285 students appeared for this round]

Everyone who had applied for either of the roles received the HackerRank test link on their email IDs a
day prior to the assessment. The duration of the test was 95 minutes, consisting of 7 timed sections, which
were as follows:
a) Coding (Advanced programming fundamentals) - 1 Question, 40 minutes
b) Coding (Basic programming) - 1 Question, 15 minutes
c) Design Pattern (Advanced) - 15 questions, 6 minutes
d) Design Pattern (Basic) - 15 questions, 4 minutes
e) Fundamental Al and Cloud concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
f) DB Concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
--- PAGE 2 ---
g) Aptitude - 15 questions, 10 minutes
The sections were timed, and once the timer ends, you are automatically moved to the next section. (Please
note, for the coding sections, the code is not auto-submitted, so please make sure you submit the code
before the timer ends).
For the Coding (Advanced) section, I received a question that involved an airport baggage-handling system
where each baggage item had a name and a destination. The objective was to group the baggage items by
destination and return the results in the required sorted order, while using Java's Fork/Join framework. I
implemented this using a RecursiveTask that returns a Map<String, List<Baggageltem. The baggage list
was recursively divided into two ranges until reaching a single-item base case, where the item was added to
a map under its destination.
For the recursive steps, I used fork to execute one half asynchronously, processed the other half directly,
and then used join to retrieve the first half's result. The two maps were then merged by combining baggage
lists belonging to the same destination using computelfAbsent. After merging, the baggage lists for each
destination were sorted by baggage name. One key detail was treating the end index as exclusive, which
ensured that the recursive ranges were handled correctly without index-out-of-bounds errors. I was able to
pass 7 out of 15 test cases with this approach.
For the Basic Coding section, I received a Selenium-based debugging question where I had to automate a
3-step verification flow that captures and persists HTML page source only when encountering a failure page.
It took me some time to thoroughly understand the existing codebase and requirements, so I was only able to
implement the input validation and Step 1 flow before running out of time.
The Design Pattern sections were based on basic LLD and related concepts, which I prepared for using
ChatGPT and Claude a day before the assessment and it fairly sufficed for the level of questions asked. The
Fundamental AI and Cloud concepts section consisted of questions based on mainly AWS and basic
questions of AI and ML. The DB concepts section consisted of questions based on ACID properties,
basic queries for transactions and fundamentals of DBMS (Please note: Oracle based questions were
also asked, which was slightly different as other OAs do not usually ask these, but they could be attempted
by option elimination and common knowledge). The Aptitude section was comparatively easier, but time
consuming, so time management was a key factor in attempting this section.
The interview shortlist and waitlist for both the roles were released on 18th August around 6 PM, 28
students shortlisted and 10 students waitlisted for the Software Engineering role, and 8 students shortlisted
and 6 students waitlisted for the Aladdin Data role. I was among the shortlisted candidates for SDE.

2. Technical Interview 1 [Around 38 students appeared for this round for SDE]

The interviews were conducted virtually through Webex on our personal laptops, but we were asked to
report to TPO at 8:30 AM for the same. Some students received the interview meeting links a night
before the interviews followed by a call from the HR confirming their slot and timing of interview. I
received my meeting link at around 9 AM, followed by a call from the HR mentioning that my interview
is scheduled for 9:30 AM, and that I will receive a call stating when to join the meeting. Make sure that
your laptop is connected to a stable internet connection as it helps you to remain calm during the
interview and avoid any technical glitches during the interview. Upon receiving the second call, I
immediately ran into some setup issues which made me delay joining the meeting, which I apologized
for upon joining the meeting.
--- PAGE 3 ---
There were two interviewers who warmly welcomed me and began by asking how I was feeling. This helped
ease some of the initial nervousness. They then asked me to briefly introduce myself. I gave a semi-formal,
resume-based introduction, while also mentioning some of my hobbies and personal interests to make the
introduction more conversational.
The interviewer then quickly moved into a technical, scenario-based question. He asked me to imagine a
situation where a client's payment gateway service had gone down in production and I was working as part
of a team of three developers. He asked what my approach would be to resolving the issue and, more
importantly, why I would choose that approach. I explained that my first priority would be to get the basic
functionality back online through a temporary patch or workaround, while simultaneously investigating
the underlying issue. I explained that in a production environment, restoring service is extremely important
for both the client and the organization. A temporary fix would not only restore essential functionality but
would also give the team additional time to investigate the root cause and develop and test a proper
permanent solution without keeping the entire service down.
The interviewer then spent a significant portion of the interview grilling me on this approach and
introducing additional constraints to the scenario. For instance, he asked how my approach would change if
the payment gateway was handling a very large number of transactions and a faulty fix could potentially
have a much greater impact. I calmly defended my reasoning while adapting it to each new condition he
introduced. I emphasized that the patch would not simply be pushed directly into production; it would first
need to go through appropriate testing, including multiple test cases and validation of edge cases, before
deployment.
The discussion then moved towards accountability. I was asked whether I would take responsibility if the
system still failed after implementing my proposed solution and customers suffered financial losses as a
result. I responded that, when working as a team, a solution should ideally be reviewed and challenged by
the other team members as well, which significantly reduces the possibility of overlooking an error.
However, if the solution ultimately failed despite these checks, I would take accountability for my decision,
particularly because I was the person who had proposed the approach. The interviewers seemed satisfied
with this response. I was also asked how I would handle the situation if the other two members of my team
did not agree with the idea of implementing a patch. I explained that I would first clearly communicate
my reasoning and the advantages of the approach, while also giving them an opportunity to explain their
concerns. Rather than forcing my approach on the team, I would compare the pros and cons of both
alternatives and try to arrive at a mutually agreed solution based on what would be safest and most
beneficial for the client and the system.
The second interviewer then shifted the discussion towards one of my projects, my regulatory compliance
platform. He asked me about the specific components I had implemented, how I had implemented them,
and some of the technical decisions I had made while developing the project. He then posed a hypothetical
question about how I would modify the system if, instead of building and maintaining my own RAG
model, I had to integrate an existing LLM.
I explained that one of the simplest approaches would be to integrate an LLM through an API using an
API key. However, I also pointed out that for a regulatory compliance platform, simply integrating an
external LLM would raise important concerns around data security, privacy, and the handling of
potentially sensitive information. This led to a few follow-up questions where I discussed how I would
approach these concerns and what factors I would consider before selecting such an integration.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Towards the end of the interview, the interviewers asked if I had any questions for them. I asked them to
briefly introduce themselves and share how their experience at BlackRock had helped them grow, both
personally and professionally. They answered the question very sincerely and shared their own
experiences and perspectives, which made the closing part of the interview quite conversational.
The interview ended on a positive note, with the interviewers asking me to stay calm and wait for
communication from HR regarding the next round, should I be selected. The interview lasted for around 50
minutes, upon which I encountered probably the toughest part of the entire process - the waiting for the call
from HR regarding the next round.

3. HR interview [Around 18 students appeared for this round]

I finished my first interview around 10:20 AM. Since some students had started receiving calls for the
second round within 10-15 minutes of their first interview, I was initially stressed when I did not receive
any communication. I tried to remain calm and waited. Finally, around 3:10 PM, I received an email with the
meeting link for the second round, followed by a call from HR asking me to join as soon as possible. I
quickly composed myself and joined the interview.
This round had only one interviewer, who started by asking how my first round had gone and how I was
feeling. He then asked for my introduction, after which he went through my resume in detail. He focused
mainly on my Al-powered regulatory compliance platform project. He asked how we came up with the
idea, the complete project pipeline, the technologies used, and my specific contribution. I explained the
technical implementation of the document ingestion pipeline and the knowledge graph component,
including how we used graph databases to represent the information.
The discussion then moved to my leadership experience as Chairperson. He asked how I had created an
impact in the role. I explained that I primarily focused on improving communication and coordination
between different teams, as miscommunication often affects the outcome of large initiatives. I also
emphasized long-term planning, which helped avoid last-minute issues. He asked a few follow-up questions
about how the experience helped me personally and professionally.
He then asked a more reflective question: if I could go back to my first year, what would I change? I asked
for a minute to think and answered that I would have said 'yes' to more opportunities, both socially, such as
making more friends and being open to new experiences, and technically, by participating in more projects
and activities that could have given me greater exposure. He also asked what I felt was currently lacking in
my resume. I mentioned that since BlackRock is a fintech company and Java is widely used for backend
development in financial services, I would like to strengthen my Java and Java-based development
framework skills further.
At the end, he asked if I had any questions. I asked for a brief introduction about himself and then asked
what a typical day for a software engineering intern at BlackRock looks like. He answered both
questions and gave me a better understanding of the internship experience. The interview lasted
approximately 20-25 minutes and was more techno-HR than pure HR, largely focused on my projects,
leadership experience, technical understanding, and self-awareness.
Finally, the results were declared the next day, and 7 students got the offer for the Software Engineering
role and 1 student for the Aladdin Data Role (total 8 students were selected).
--- PAGE 5 ---

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Placements are not purely skill-based; luck, timing and the particular interview panel can also play a role.
So, as niche as it may sound, don't let a rejection define your preparation. Keep improving and stay
consistent.
Resources:

• DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet - one of the most structured resources for placement preparation.

Focus on understanding concepts and solving the more frequently asked data structures and their
problems (Strings, Stacks, Queues, LinkedLists) at least once (Please note: Every company usually
has topics that they tend to ask more on, so do your research thoroughly and try covering the other
topics if needed).
https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z/

• SQL: LeetCode SQL 50 - Repeat questions you struggle with and understand multiple approaches.

https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

• Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel for Java and OOP fundamentals.

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL9gnSGHSqcno1G3XjUbwzXHL8_EttOuKk

• Core CS: GeeksforGeeks for OOP, DBMS, OS and Computer Networks concepts and practice.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/interview-experiences/technical-interview-preparation/

• System Design: Gaurav Sen's content + ChatGPT/Claude for explanations and interview-style

practice.

• Aptitude: IndiaBIX, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

• Puzzles: GeeksforGeeks' interview puzzles, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

Interview-Day Tips:

• Know your resume thoroughly. Anything written on it can be questioned, so understand every

technology, tool and project you mention.

• Know your projects end-to-end: schema/database design, backend structure, APIs, architecture,

your contribution, limitations and possible improvements.

• Be strong in fundamentals: You don't need to know everything, but the fundamentals of every

technology on your resume should be clear.

• Prepare for follow-ups: Interviewers may keep changing the conditions of a scenario, so understand

your reasoning rather than memorizing answers.

• CGPA: 8+ is a decent position, while 8.5+ is preferable where companies have academic cutoffs.

• Prepare for HR and behavioural questions as well. Technical preparation alone is not enough. Be

ready for questions about your strengths, weaknesses, leadership experiences, failures, career goals,
and situational judgement. Answer smartly but honestly; don't try to give the answer you think the
interviewer wants to hear. Keep your responses genuine and support them with real examples from
your experiences.
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Don't lose confidence after rejection: BlackRock was the 18th company I encountered during

placements. I had previously been shortlisted by two companies but was rejected by HR in the final
rounds in both. I kept preparing and eventually got this opportunity.

• Don't convince yourself that you're underprepared: You will never feel completely prepared.

Trust your preparation and focus on the interview in front of you.

• Stay calm and patient. Take a few seconds to think before answering difficult questions and explain

your reasoning clearly.

• Sleep properly: I had only around 1.5 hours of sleep before my interview day, and it definitely

affected how calmly I handled the long day. As funny as it might sound, get adequate sleep the day
before interviews at least, and keep your setup ready beforehand.
Finally, positivity, patience and consistency are key. Placement season can be stressful and unpredictable,
so keep learning from ev

• Online Assessment

• Tech Round 1

• Techno HR round( Tech + HR)

Round 1: Online Assessment (MCQ Test)

Around 220+ students appeared for the assessment.
A Google Form was shared, and we were given 90 minutes to complete 4 sections.

1. Java (Approx. 15 Questions)

This section was conceptual and fairly tricky, not just direct syntax questions.
Topics to prepare:

• Method Overriding vs Overloading

• Collection Framework

• Optional

• String vs StringBuilder

• Internal working of Java collections and objects

• Edge cases in OOP concepts

--- PAGE 2 ---
I would recommend understanding why things work instead of only memorizing
definitions.

2. Python (Approx. 15 Questions)

This was also tricky and focused on Python internals.
Important topics:

• Object creation using __new_- () and __init__ ()

• Mutable vs Immutable objects

• Default mutable arguments in functions

• with statement and Context Managers

• Object references and memory behavior

• Function argument evaluation

• Basic Python internals

Many questions tested concepts that are often skipped during normal interview
preparation.

3. SQL (Approx. 5 Questions)

This section was relatively easy.
Questions mainly involved:

• Choosing the correct SQL statement for a given scenario

• Basic SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, filtering, and aggregate functions

4. AI-Generated Mistakes (Approx. 15 Questions)

This section was interesting.
You were given Al-generated solutions (mostly SQL or programming-related) and had to
identify:

• Logical mistakes

• Incorrect approaches

• Better or optimized solutions

• Whether the generated answer actually solved the problem

Reading the problem carefully was more important than writing code.
--- PAGE 3 ---

5. Aptitude (Approx. 30 Questions)

Overall, this section was easy.
Topics included:

• Quantitative Aptitude

• Logical Reasoning

• Basic Verbal Ability

Around 4-5 questions were slightly tricky, but the rest were straightforward. Preparing
from CareerRide or practicing aptitude questions with ChatGPT should be sufficient.
Marking Scheme

• +1 for every correct answer

• -0.25 for every incorrect answer

So, avoid random guessing.
My Experience
I finished the paper with around 10 minutes remaining.
Overall, I found the assessment manageable, but only if your concepts are strong. The
technical questions were designed to test internal working and edge cases, not just
surface-level knowledge.
I could not confidently solve around 4-5 tricky puzzle/strategy questions, and because
of the negative marking, I avoided making blind guesses.
Preparation Tips

• Focus on conceptual understanding rather than memorizing answers.

• Revise Java and Python internals.

• Practice SQL scenario-based MCQs.

• Learn to identify mistakes in Al-generated code and optimized approaches.

• Practice aptitude regularly.

2. Round 2: Technical Interview 1

Around 49 candidates were shortlisted for this round.
--- PAGE 4 ---
The interview process started about 2 hours after the online assessment. My test ended
around 10:00 AM, and I was called for the interview around 12:00 PM.
Initially, I was nervous, but the interviewers were very friendly and made the
environment comfortable.
Interview Flow
They first asked me to introduce myself and then went through my resume.
The discussion quickly shifted to system/API design rather than coding.
Question 1: Design a Student API
They gave a simple API:
GET /students
and asked:
"How would you design the complete flow from receiving the request until
returning the responseạẠại
They expected the entire backend flow, including:

• Controller

• Request handling

• Validation

• Service layer

• Repository/DAO layer

• Database interaction

• Returning the response

I explained the architecture as:
Client
Controller
Validation
--- PAGE 5 ---
Service
Repository
Database
Response DTO
lightweight.
I also discussed where validations should happen and how the controller should remain
Follow-up Question
They then asked:
"Suppose you want to edit a student. What API would you design?"
I answered:
PATCH /students/{id}
where:

• The student is first fetched using the ID.

• If not found, return an appropriate error.

• Otherwise, validate the input, update the fields, save the entity, and return the

updated response.
Question 2: Department-wise Top Scorer
Next, they changed the problem.
--- PAGE 6 ---
They asked me to design a data structure and API to store the top-scoring student of
each department.
I suggested using:
Map<Department, Student>
since only the top student per department needs to be stored.
(Initially, I said Map<Department, List<Student>>,after understanding the
requirement was only the highest scorer but tie could be possible, so list of Student per
department is sufficient.)
They then asked:
'How would you insert students into this data structure?
I explained the algorithm:

• Iterate through each student.

• Check whether the department already exists in the map.

• If it does not exist, insert the student.

• If it exists, compare marks with the current top scorer.

• Replace the stored student if the current student has higher marks.

Time Complexity:

• O(n), since each student is processed exactly once.

The interviewers seemed satisfied with the explanation, and we discussed the approach
for around 20 minutes.
Overall Experience
The interview was more focused on:

• API design

• Object-oriented thinking

• Backend architecture

• Choosing appropriate data structures

• Explaining your reasoning clearly

There was very little emphasis on writing code. They were more interested in how you
think through a backend design problem.
--- PAGE 7 ---
The duration varies by panel. Mine lasted around 20 minutes, while some candidates had
interviews close to an hour.
I received my Technical Round 2 interview slot at around 2:00 PM.

3. Round 3: Technical + HR Interview

Around 19 candidates were shortlisted for the final round.
My interview was conducted by Dipesh Sir and Jyoti Ma'am. I remembered both of
them from the pre-placement talk (PPT), which made the interaction feel a little familiar.
The interview started on a very friendly note.
They first asked:
"How has your day been?"
Instead of giving a generic answer like "good' or "nice," I replied that it had been
rocking.
They smiled and asked,
"Why rocking?"
I explained that I had cleared every stage so far and had now reached the final interview,
so the day was definitely going in my favour. They appreciated the positive response, and
it helped create a relaxed atmosphere.
Introduction
I gave my introduction, after which they asked:

• Why ISS STOXX?

• Tell us about your internship.

• You have been interning for almost two years. What kind of work have you done?

• You are also pursuing the IIT Madras BS degree. How do you manage both

college and your internship?

• Did you find today's MCQ round easy or difficult?

The discussion then shifted towards my projects.
Mini Project Discussion
--- PAGE 8 ---
Dipesh Sir directly asked me to explain one of my projects.
I talked about our online proctoring system, where we used:

• Webcam monitoring

• TensorFlow.js

• Browser-based Al inference

• COCO-SSD object detection

They asked several follow-up questions.
Why Tensor Flow.js?
They wanted to know why we chose browser-based inference instead of running
everything on a centralized server.
I explained that if 200+ students were taking an exam simultaneously, sending every
webcam frame to the server would:

• Create significant infrastructure costs.

• Increase server load.

• Introduce latency.

• Make scaling difficult.

Running inference directly in the browser distributes the computation to each candidate's
device, reducing backend infrastructure requirements while providing real-time detection.
They seemed satisfied with this reasoning.
Product Design Questions
They continued with practical design questions such as:

• How would you decide the confidence threshold for object detection?

• At what confidence percentage should a student be flagged?

• Should every detection trigger a warning?

• How would you implement fullscreen detection?

• What other anti-cheating mechanisms would you include?

The discussion was less about coding and more about product thinking and design
decisions.
Internship Discussion
--- PAGE 9 ---
Next, they asked about my internship project (xresume.ai).
Topics discussed included:

• Overall architecture

• Resume parsing workflow

• Technologies used

• LangChain integration

• End-to-end workflow

• Problems I faced during development

• Improvements 1 suggested to the product

• Challenges while deploying and maintaining the system

They also asked how I generally approach solving difficult engineering problems and
whether I had encountered situations where I was initially stuck but eventually found a
solution.
Questions I Asked
At the end of both Technical Round 1 and the final interview, I asked a question that led
to some of the most interesting conversations of the day.
Instead of asking about work-life balance or company culture, I asked:
"Can you share an incident or a project at ISS STOXX where you felt you
had done something extraordinary for the company-something that made
you feel proud of your contribution?"
(In Hindi, it: "ISS STOXX mein aisa kya kiya jiske liye aapko laga ki 'haan, maine
company ke liye kuch khaas kiya haiạ)
The interviewers genuinely appreciated the question.
One of them even smiled and said:
"My Boss should have asked this question, and was very difficult"
They then shared memorable experiences from their time at ISS STOXX.
One interviewer spoke about a critical project where senior leadership was considering
shutting it down because of various challenges. Instead of giving up, he and his team
prepared a detailed proposal, presented their vision to the leadership, convinced them to
continue investing in the project, and successfully turned it around. He explained how
--- PAGE 10 ---
leading the team through that period and seeing the project succeed was one of the
proudest moments of his career at ISS STOXX.
Hearing stories like these gave me a much better understanding of the ownership,
leadership, and impact engineers can have within the company than any standard answer
about company culture could.
Overall, the interview felt more like a technical discussion than an interrogation. The
interviewers were approachable, encouraged conversation, and genuinely wanted to
understand my thought process rather than just test technical knowledge.
My Advice

• Be honest and conversational rather than giving rehearsed answers.

• Be prepared to explain every project on your resume in depth.

• Justify your design decisions with logical reasoning and trade-offs.

• Think from a product and scalability perspective, not only from an

implementation perspective.

• Ask thoughtful questions at the end. A good conversation with the interviewers

leaves a lasting impression.
Overall, it was one of the most enjoyable interview experiences I've had.
[In total 12 were given]
Can be ignored (for knowledge purpose)
Reflections, Preparation Strategy, and Advice for Future Candidates
Looking back at my placement journey, I believe getting selected was the result of consistent
preparation over a long period rather than preparation for a single interview. Before receiving
this offer, I had gone through multiple placement processes where I reached the later stages but
did not convert the opportunity. Those experiences helped me identify my weak areas and
improve them before the ISS STOXX process.
What Worked Well

1. Strong understanding instead of memorization

--- PAGE 11 ---
For technical preparation, I focused on understanding concepts rather than memorizing interview
answers. During the online assessment, many Java and Python questions tested language
internals and edge cases instead of syntax. Similarly, the interviews emphasized reasoning, API
design, scalability, and trade-offs rather than writing large amounts of code.

2. Knowing every project in depth

I made sure I could explain every project on my resume end-to-end:

• The problem it solved

• Why specific technologies were chosen

• Alternative approaches considered

• Design decisions and trade-offs

• Challenges faced

• Improvements I would make today

Whenever interviewers asked follow-up questions, I tried to justify every technical decision with
reasoning instead of simply stating what I had implemented.

3. Drawing from real internship experience

My internship gave me practical examples to discuss instead of only theoretical knowledge. I
could explain how APIs were designed, how production issues were handled, how features
evolved over time, and how engineering decisions were made while balancing scalability,
maintainability, and business requirements.

4. Treating interviews as discussions

I tried to keep the interviews conversational rather than reciting prepared answers. When asked
how my day was going, I responded naturally instead of giving a generic reply, which helped
establish a comfortable interaction from the beginning.
Throughout the interviews, I explained my thought process while solving problems instead of
rushing to an answer.

5. Asking thoughtful questions

At the end of each interview, I asked questions that went beyond standard topics like work-life
balance or salary.
For example, I asked the interviewers to share a moment at ISS STOXX where they felt they had
made a significant impact on the company. This led to meaningful conversations about
--- PAGE 12 ---
ownership, leadership, and engineering culture and helped build a genuine connection with the
interviewers.
Areas Where I Could Have Performed Better
Although the overall process went well, there were areas where I could have improved.

• During the online assessment, I found a few Java and Python language-internals

questions challenging. I realized that revising only common interview topics is not
always enough; understanding how the language works internally is equally important.

• There were a few logic and puzzle-based aptitude questions where I was not completely

confident. Because of negative marking, I chose not to guess. Practicing more standard
puzzle patterns beforehand would have helped.

• In one of the design discussions, I initially suggested a broader data structure before

refining it after understanding the exact requirement. This reminded me of the importance
of clarifying requirements before proposing a solution.

• There were moments where I could have communicated my ideas more concisely. While

thinking aloud is useful, structuring the explanation before speaking makes answers
easier for interviewers to follow.
Lessons from Previous Rejections
This was not my first interview process.
In earlier placement opportunities, including companies where I reached the later stages but was
not selected, I realized that reaching the final rounds does not guarantee an offer. Instead of
treating those outcomes as failures, I used them to identify gaps in my preparation.
Those experiences helped me:

• improve the depth of my project explanations,

• become more confident during technical discussions,

• learn to justify engineering decisions with clear reasoning,

• and approach interviews with a calmer mindset.

Every interview-whether successful or not-became valuable preparation for the next one.
General Tips for Candidates

• Read every line of your resume carefully. Anything you mention is fair game for

discussion.

• Focus on understanding concepts instead of memorizing answers.

--- PAGE 13 ---

• Be able to explain the reasoning behind every design decision.

• If you do not know something, admit it honestly rather than trying to bluff.

• Clarify requirements before jumping into a solution.

• While solving problems, explain your thought process clearly.

• During system or API design questions, discuss validation, error handling, scalability,

and maintainability instead of only the happy path.

• Keep a positive attitude throughout the interview. Interviewers often evaluate

communication and collaboration skills alongside technical ability.

• Ask thoughtful questions at the end. It demonstrates curiosity and genuine interest in the

company.
Final Thoughts
The biggest takeaway from this journey is that placement preparation is cumulative. The
concepts learned, projects built, internship experience gained, and even previous interview
rejections all contributed to this opportunity.
Treat every interview as a learning experience. Even if an interview does not result in an offer,
the lessons you gain often become the reason you succeed in the next one.
Wishing everyone the very best for their placements!

You need to be patient. At the start of the season, I was able to clear the PhonePe OA, and got rejected
during my HM Round. I was unable to get my resume shortlisted for companies like WorkIndia, Nomura,
UBS. Failed to clear the IDFC and ISS OA. Futures First was very aptitude based and could not clear that
as well. I managed to reach the GD for the JPMC(non tech) role. I focused on non-tech for a few days, just
for that process, but could not reach the interviews.

very little time to mentally prepare for the next one. Even though the Edra result hadn't come out yet, I was
sure I wasn't getting another round, so gave up hopes for that.
Talk to friends and family, don't bottle it up. There will be lows but keep putting in genuine efforts and the
result will show.

This was a pool process, I honestly did not sit for the PPT and later came to know that 4k+ students were
attending it(including some NITs, VIT and SPIT)! BlackRock came for 2 roles: Software Engineering and
Aladdin Data, we were asked to choose our preference (you could choose both).
The process usually includes an OA, followed by 2 interviews, which are held online on the Webex Platform
and to be attended from the TPO. The GPA cutoff was set to 7.5, also while registering on Superset, they
asked for any professional qualifications, I do not have any, but also I have no idea how much weightage

1. Online Assessment

Technical Round 1[28 Shortlist + 10 Waitlist]
Interviews were held online from the TPO office, on the Webex platform. Please make sure you have your
laptop, webcam, mic, internet connection working before the process. I received a call at around 9:30 that
my interview would be scheduled at 10:30. They will tell you when to join the interview, do not barge into
the meeting.
A thing to keep in mind is that there were many panels running in parallel. Each had a different style of
questioning, some focusing more on projects, others more so on Java and DS. There is not much you can do
in such cases other than prepare / ask other people who got alloted the same panel, but this isn't in your hand
and just do your best and prepare.
I got the call to join only at around 11, so I joined the call. Be proactive here and turn on your camera
without being asked and greet them. They started off by introducing themselves and then asked me to do so
as well, however funny enough they did not want me to get into much details, and keep it very simple. I
however had a small network issue just this moment and heard that they wanted me to go into detail.
I went on for around 5 mins before they interrupted me, and told me that they did not want much detail, at
which point I realized the blunder I had made, I apologized and explained but they were very chill about it
and started their line of questioning.
They mainly focused on projects, on the problem I tried to solve and how I did it. Make sure that you can
defend each decision and explain each concept mentioned on your resume. They just wanted to know the
tech stack I used and how data got passed around the system.
My project had a bit of scraping involved, and during my explanation I said very very casually "unki API
bohot slow hai_ to which they started laughing. I still don't know why I said it in such a way, but it led to a
discussion where they asked me what I would do to make it faster. This led to a discussion on scalability and
caching.
They asked me how this slowness is measured, I was aware of terms like p99,95 latency and said so.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Other questions were still very project dependent, like explain rate limiting (I had nginx mentioned so), why
Base62 Encoding instead of hashing, high level overview of the services and how to further scale them.
The interviewers finally allowed me to ask them a few questions. Prepare 2-3 good questions, look at what
the company does and make it seem as if you are really interested in what they do and want to join the
company. I asked something very basic first to which they again laughed and said "we've been asked this
before" but gladly answered.
Next I asked something like "How much financial awareness is required to be an analyst at BlackRock?"
They were very enthusiastic to answer this, and I asked this directly as previous year interviewers directly
asked the candidates how much they know, so again a good way to show that you researched about the role.
My interview only went on for around 20-25 mins, which I felt was very short and I truly believed that I was
done for the day. Others had rounds which started before mine and ended after mine, even during the
interview I was taken aback when they ended the round in such a short amount of time, but I kept it together
and gave it my best.
However, within 30 mins of my round finishing, I got the call that my 2nd round was scheduled at 1pm.
Note: Do not compare your process to others, each panel has its own way to ask, many were even asked HR
questions along with tech in their 1st round like if they would relocate.

3. Technical Round 2 [15/16 for SDE + 3/4 for Data ]

This round was again very technical, started off in a similar fashion with their introduction and then mine.
After my introduction, they started their line of questioning, mostly based on my projects, tech stack, and
what problem I was trying to solve.
Also if you used X in your project, be prepared to explain why you used X and why you would not use X.
Be aware of the fact that Y and Z also could have been used, but why you chose not to, or if you would but
were unable to implement. It is important that they understand your line of reasoning and how you would
approach a new problem. They indirectly asked me this : "what would you have done differently if you were
to build this again".
This round was again very project dependent and so it is necessary to know what you have done and written
on your resume.
They then asked me a simple DSA question:
Given a list of N integers, where each element from 1 to N occurs exactly 1.
You need to sort this list.
Note that you need to share your screen and pseudo/code on notepad.
I explained the brute and then explained how it could be reduced to cycle sort. Keep in mind that it should
not appear as if you have learnt the solution. Be very proactive here, note down the question, literally type it
out, take sample input and simulate the operation and get to the answer.
Also when asked to code, go with good quality of code and don't use random variable names.
Next they asked me: Given a 2D array of N*3, sort the vector on the basis of the internal sum in ASC.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Example : [[1,2,4] , [1,1,1]] > [[1,1,1] , [1,2,4]]
I straightaway jumped to using a comparator for this and they seemed to be happy with the approach.
Finally, maybe just because i was writing the full code, they asked me something like : " how would you do
something like stack<I can put any data type here>"
I struggled with this, and said something like maybe custom structs, but then they straight away asked me if
I was aware of Generics and Templates in C++.
I mentioned yes, I had used it before for implementing policy based structures where I mentioned both avl
and rb tree here, i wasn't sure myself how it was internally implemented but just wanted to prove that I
wasn't bluffing and had actually used them.
They immediately caught on that I wasn't too sure about their difference and asked me, I could explain AVL
but for RB trees I just simply said that the nodes were coloured and had a set of rules.
Not too sure whether they were satisfied or not, I could barely see or hear them both. Finally I asked them
something like " what do you love about your job at BlackRock? / what is the most exciting part of your
dayi
My round went on for around 45 mins. BlackRock generally only conducts 2 rounds, so from this point
onwards it was just a waiting game, results usually arriving only on the next day.
There is no point in overthinking the results, jo hoga wo hoga, and leave it at that, focus on the next
company and learn from the mistakes you made before.
Results arrived at around 12 pm the next day.
Finally, 7 students were shortlisted for SDE and 1 for Aladdin Data.

journey.prep:
Don't measure your preparation against what everyone else around you is doing. Some people swear by
Striver's Sheet, some by pure competitive programming, some by hundreds of LeetCode questions - find what
actually helps you understand a concept rather than memorize it, and stick with that. It's completely fine to
start late, solve fewer questions, or skip a "must-do" resource, as long as you genuinely understand what you've
learned and know exactly where and how to apply it.

1. Be honest when you don't know something. If you're asked something you genuinely don't remember or

don't know, say so clearly instead of guessing or making something up. Interviewers notice and generally
respect honesty far more than a shaky, incorrect answer.

2. Know your resume and your projects inside out. Be ready to explain the "why" behind every technical

decision in your projects, not just the "what". Counter-questions are far easier to handle when you've actually
built the thing yourself and understand it end to end.

3. Don't ignore the basics - SQL, joins, and core concepts. Even in a data-focused or backend-adjacent role,

expect fairly direct questions on SQL fundamentals like joins and stored procedures, so keep these fresh.

4. Stay calm through multiple rounds and pen-and-paper style tests. If a round is unusual - like a pen and

paper test that later feeds into your interview questions - treat it seriously and think through your approach
properly, since it may well resurface later.

5. Be yourself in HR rounds. HR rounds are as much about how you communicate and handle pressure as they

are about your answers. Being honest about past rejections and what you learned from them tends to land far
better than pretending everything has gone smoothly.

In case of any further doubts, feel free to reach out, and you can also refer to the past interview experiences
shared by TPO.
journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment (DoSelect, from home) - 22nd August

This was a standard online round conducted remotely. Around 50 candidates were shortlisted from this round
to move ahead in the process.

2. Pen and Paper Test [All 50 shortlisted candidates] - 27th August

Before the interviews began, we were made to sit for an in-person pen and paper test. This was interesting
because our answers here were later picked apart and questioned directly in the interview - so it wasn't just a
filter, it fed straight into the next round. There were 3 questions:
Problem 1: You were given a string made up of lowercase letters, uppercase letters, numbers, and special
characters. The task was to strip out all the numbers, special characters, and spaces, and then check whether
the remaining string was a palindrome or not (uppercase and lowercase versions of a letter were to be treated
as the same character).
Problem 2: You were given a string made up of vowels and consonants, and had to check it against three
constraints - the string could not contain more than 3 continuous vowels, could not contain more than 5
continuous consonants, and the total length of the string had to be less than or equal to 8. (I don't remember
the exact constraints word for word, but this was the gist.)
Example: input "abei??gh" -> output True
Problem 3: You were given an N x N matrix, and had to find how many smaller square sub-matrices could be
formed from it. For example, a 3x3 matrix can form 14 squares in total - nine 1x1 squares, four 2x2 squares, and
one 3x3 square, adding up to 14.
Some candidates were also asked to optimize the approach they had written down for these questions, so it's
worth thinking about the time and space complexity even for a pen-and-paper round.

3. Technical Interview [All 50 who cleared the pen and paper test]

My interview slot came up quite late in the day. In the interview, they went back over the pen and paper test
questions I had answered - asking me to explain my approach, pointing out what could be wrong with it, and
giving me small variations of the same questions to solve on the spot.
The interviewer then asked me to introduce myself and describe all my projects in detail. After listening to my
introduction, he picked two of my projects and asked me to explain them further - why I had used whatever
technology or approach I mentioned, and how it actually affected the problem it was solving. I answered each
project in three parts: why I made the project, how it helped me, and how I built it using everything I knew.
Make sure you know your resume thoroughly, because there were a few counter-questions along the way, and I
was able to handle all of them comfortably since I had built each project myself. We then moved to the second
project, which I explained in a similar structured way.
After the projects, he moved on to SQL. He asked me what LEAD and LAG were, followed by questions on joins -
self join, left join, inner join, and so on. Then he asked me what stored procedures in SQL were. I wasn't sure
about this one, so I was upfront and told him I knew the term but couldn't recall the exact definition, and asked
if he could give me an example that might jog my memory. He said not to worry about it and moved on to the
next question.
He then asked me what an MCP server was. I told him honestly that I didn't know the exact technical definition,
but explained it as best I understood it - that MCP servers are like functions or tools of an application that an AI
can use directly, letting it make changes within that application on the user's behalf. I gave him an example
from my own experience, where I had used Claude's Fusion 360 plugin to generate a design for me - it didn't
come out exactly as I wanted, but it was clearly doing part of the work for me.
When he asked if I had any questions, I asked him to describe what a typical day at Revvity looks like, and what
someone should do to prepare before joining.

4. HR Round

After some time, I was called back directly for the HR round. Usually the process has two technical rounds
followed by HR, but in my case I was moved straight to HR after this one technical round. The HR round was
fairly relaxed - he asked basic things like whether I'd be comfortable coming in to that location, about my family
background, and what kind of roles I preferred. He was very supportive throughout, and even when I made
small mistakes, he was patient and helped me through them - the overall atmosphere was friendly.
He then asked me to explain one of my projects again, which I did, followed by which role I would prefer and
why, and which programming language I preferred and why not another one - I got the sense he was testing
how I respond under a bit of pressure rather than looking for a "correct" answer. The conversation flowed well
after that, and we had a good discussion where he also asked about my previous rejections - what mistakes I
felt I had made, and how I worked on overcoming them. These were all fairly basic, conversational questions
overall.
Results were announced 4 days later, on 31st August, and I was selected for the Data Engineer role at Revvity.

journey.prep:
The placement process is no less than being in a hellhole for 4 months. It drains you physically and
mentally. There were countless times that I wasn't shortlisted for OA or interview even after fulfilling all
the requirements. After 2 months I realised that skills have their own place but won't matter if luck isn't
by your side. I have been rejected after giving a great interview. You may feel the interview was great
but after realising you weren't shortlisted you will doubt yourself and that is a rabbit hole you don't want
to go down.
You may see many undeserving people get placed before you or getting placed without breaking sweat
while you struggle to even get shortlisted for OA.
But IT IS WHAT IT IS that is the only thing that will get you by.
I won't say don't get disheartened because you will be, countless times but you have to work
nevertheless.
All the best

1. Resume Shortlisting

2. Online Assessment

3. Pre-Placement Talk

4. Group Discussion

5. Technical + HR Interview

Prep-placement talk GD and Interview all took place on 30/09/2026

1. Resume Shortlisting [~200 students had applied]

Since the role at Colgate-Palmolive was IT-focused, I tailored my resume to highlight projects and skills
relevant to the job description. I included my Al based and full stack apps to demonstrate my experience
with software development, databases, backend systems, APIs, and Al integration. I also highlighted my
technical skills in Python, SQL, and web technologies, along with my ability to learn new tools and solve
real-world problems.
I recommend keeping your resume to one page, ensuring it is ATS-friendly, and tailoring it to the company's
JD rather than using a generic resume. You can use tools like ResumeWorded to assess your resume and
identify areas for improvement. Mind it that this is for cross-checking your resume, don't waste time
tailoring it to perfection.
Academic performance, including 12th-grade marks and CGPA, can also influence shortlisting, depending
on the company's eligibility criteria. Meeting the required cutoffs can be an advantage, but selection also
depends on your projects, technical skills, resume relevance, and the overall applicant pool. Sometimes,
shortlisting can be unpredictable, so keep improving your resume and applying consistently.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [ 30 students ]

The OA was from home at 4-5 pm, MCQ format and of 30 questions.
The OA covered DSA (binary trees, sorting algorithms, and Minimum Spanning Tree using Prim's
algorithm), Operating Systems (disk scheduling, CPU scheduling using SJF, and inode structures), and
DBMS (functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, and normalization forms such as 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and
BCNF). It also included Computer Networks, focusing on the OSI model and the Presentation Layer, along
with C++ programming concepts such as destructors, global and local variables, object creation, and output
tracing.

3. Group Discussion [ 30 students ]

3 groups of 10 people
My topic was 'Are exams right way to assess someone's intelligence'
The discussion lasted about 20 min where last 3 min where given to conclude your points
Always try to initiate the discussion or be in the first 3 people to start the discussion to catch the
panelists attention.
2 mins time is given beforehand to jot down the points before the discussion.
Write brief bullet points and pros and cons and do not pick a side as it is a discussion and not a
debate.

4. Technical + Hr Interview [15 students ]

I was the first one to give the interview so I had no idea what type of questions were asked by the panelists.
There were two panelists
The interview started with a brief introduction and a walkthrough of my resume. Towards the end of my
introduction i stated that would you like me to elaborate on one of my projects technicalities, setting the tone
of the interview in my favour.
They asked surface level questions on each of my projects and then deep-dived into one of my projects.
I was asked if the database was static or dynamic if static what changes would you make, if i want to migrate
the data, how would I do it safely without causing a downtime issue.
I was asked how would you design a website where many students are filling a form and high traffic
shouldn't affect the web app.
Then i was asked if i click on a login button what happens in the backend behind the scenes in depth.
After a while I was comfortable with the panelists and was confident with my answers. Then they asked
behavioral questions like if a team mate is calling sick with a deadline for your project how would you
handle the situation.
And if a project cannot be completed before the deadline what measures would you take.
They also asked me about why you chose this branch and why not CSE/CE.
--- PAGE 3 ---
The key to a good interview is to remain composed before you answer. I know it's better said than done, but
as I had given 2 interviews and a group discussion before this company I was aware of the body language,
tone and familiarity with the interview room. Never use negative words like not, no, I am not aware etc.
Always use positive alternatives like I am yet to explore this area, I am yet to have hands-on experience in
this technicality etc.
Do not get excited if you know the answer to a question, take a pause, assess your thoughts and start from
the basics and stretch it with all the technicalities you are aware of and relate it with your resume. As you
can see I have implemented this in my XYZ project. It makes an impression that you have practical
experience of the question asked
In the end I asked them a questions:
In the pre placement talk it was mentioned that there is In job posting and interns get to experience a
variety of roles.
What would you expect a 6 month intern to be like? As in do you expect him to master a specific
stack or get as much experience and explore a variety of stacks.
We were under the impression that an HR round was going to take place but the results were announced at
3:00 pm 8 out of 15 people were offered the internship.

specifically asked about proficiency in Excel and PowerPoint features such as Pivot Tables,
VLOOKUP, Conditional Formatting, etc., I used the two days before the process to quickly brush up
on these functions.

trying to bluff your way through. I did not know a concept related to the various types of testing and
which one would best fit the use case given by them during my interview so I mentioned the 3 types
I knew, what they meant and said that I would read about them further to gain knowledge.

The first stage was resume shortlisting, followed by three rounds: Group Discussion, Business Round
(Interview 1), and HR Round (Interview 2). All the 3 rounds were held in an online zoom meeting.
For this particular role, your resume can include both technical and non-technical projects or internships, but
make sure you are thoroughly familiar with everything you mention. Try highlighting relevant skills such as
Advanced Excel, Power BI, or similar tools that align with the role requirements. The 3 core domains were:
project management, process improvisation and intelligent analytics - read about them from the job
description and gain basic knowledge about them. Lastly, ensure your academic scores, particularly 10th,
12th and CGPA, meet the 75%+ or 7.5+ CGPA safety benchmark.
You can check your ATS score using Resume Worded (60-70 is a good range).

1. [Group Discussion] [77 students were selected after the resume shortlisting]

Each group had 12 participants and was given around 15-20 minutes to discuss the topic and arrive at a
conclusion. My group was given the topic "Mobile Wallets - Advantages and Disadvantages." The topic
was relevant to recent developments around MDR charges on UPI for vendors and other initiatives
promoting digital transactions. Another group was given "Work From Home vs Offline Work." Hence, it is
advisable to stay updated with current and trending topics such as Al replacing manual work, digital
payments, changing workplace trends, etc., since the topic is given on the spot with no preparation time.
If you are strong with content but face communication issues, make good use of the mock GD sessions
conducted by the college. Focus on speaking fewer but valuable points, while also being an active listener
and building on others' arguments rather than trying to dominate the discussion.

2. [Business Round] [ 19 students were selected for this interview and divided into 2 panels]

Most interviews begin with the standard question "Introduce yourself", so prepare this well and highlight
your key skills, experiences and achievements. Follow-up questions are often based on your introduction, so
know your resume thoroughly-anything mentioned can be questioned. I was asked about the case
competitions I had won and even about leverage and D/E ratio since it was mentioned in my resume.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Apart from resume-based questions, I was asked about current topics such as "What is your view on MDR
charges? Are they necessary?" and "What is the impact of the Make in India initiative on you as a youth?" I
was also asked situational questions, such as whether, as a JPMC manager, I would reduce a team from 20 to
2 after implementing an Al system with 98% accuracy, and if not, how I would justify the investment.
Hence, prepare for situational and decision-making questions as well.
Finally, if you mention Excel, Python or Power BI on your resume, be prepared for basic questions such as
syntax and implementation of VLOOKUP, handling null values in Python, etc. In case you prepared only for
non tech roles and do not know the python syntax tell them that you do not code or do dsa but focus on
finance, case studies, power bi and related stuff and give evidence for the same projects/internships (they
will divert the question in that direction and its better than saying i dont know or a wrong answer)

3. HR Round] [8 candidates were selected for this round]

In this round, your presence of mind, interpersonal skills and confidence are tested, so it is important to
remain attentive, composed and confident throughout. You may be asked to introduce yourself again or
share something about yourself that is not mentioned on your resume. Questions like "Why this role?" and
"Why do you want to work at this company?" are common, along with situational questions based on your
resume. For example, since I was the Vice President of a Rotaract Club, I was asked about a situation where
I had a disagreement with another club member and how I handled it. Towards the end of the interview you
will be asked if you have any questions for them - you can ask any valuable question or something you are
genuinely interested to know like the work culture there, whether they encourage interns and employees to
pursue CFA levels or an equivalent course, what qualities should a good intern possess to progress, etc.
Overall, show genuine interest in the company and role, communicate clearly, and maintain a professional
attitude throughout the interview.

customSections.content:
1. Read the JD carefully: I went through the JD and application form thoroughly. Since the form

specifically asked about proficiency in Excel and PowerPoint features such as Pivot Tables,
VLOOKUP, Conditional Formatting, etc., I used the two days before the process to quickly brush up
on these functions.

2. Know your resume: Be thorough with everything mentioned on your resume, including projects,

internships, skills and achievements, as follow-up questions can come from any section.

3. Stay updated: I went through recent and trending topics to prepare for the GD, especially topics

related to business, technology, AI, the economy and current events. Also ensure you have read
about the company you have applied to - for example its CEO and its core values.

4. Be honest when unsure: There may be questions where you are not completely sure of the answer.

In such cases, first share whatever you know that is relevant, and if you genuinely do not know the
exact answer, be honest about it and mention that you would read up on the topic. It is better than
trying to bluff your way through. I did not know a concept related to the various types of testing and
which one would best fit the use case given by them during my interview so I mentioned the 3 types
I knew, what they meant and said that I would read about them further to gain knowledge.
Be patient, calm and stay positive! For any queries do reach out - https://www.linkedin.com/in/krisha
