O.
Pre Placement Talk
You should be here with all ears. Note down all the important points, names of people who
came and presented, and everything that you think that you can ask during the interview
when the interviewer is going to ask you if you have any questions for them. Use this advice
for all the processes. Don't do this just for the sake of doing it. It's a good practice to be
attentive in general and have information about all companies. You can also ask questions at
the end of PPT if they let you. Don't ask silly and illogical questions (e.g. how many students
they are going to hire, anything about their internal policies, anything controversial). You can
stand out here but try to stand out in a good way

1. Online Assessment: 3 Sections (Around 165 People)

1. Aptitude - 20 mins

2. Core CS fundamentals - 30 mins

3. Coding Section - 40 mins

* The Aptitude section was among the most challenging parts of the assessment. It

consisted of 15 questions to be completed in 20 minutes, and the use of calculators was
not permitted. The section included a mix of quantitative aptitude and logical
reasoning problems. Topics covered included Time and Work, Cubes (opposite faces
and cube orientation), Mixtures and Alligations, Mean and Variance, Probability, and
a CAT-style DILR arrangement set. There were also sequence- and ordering-based
--- PAGE 2 ---
puzzles similar to those found in banking aptitude exams, where a single puzzle was
followed by multiple sub-questions. Overall, the difficulty level of this section was
moderate to difficult, with the strict time limit making it particularly demanding. A good
resource for preparation is IndiaBIX for quantitative aptitude practice, along with
banking-style puzzle sets such as sequence and arrangement questions.

* The Core CS Fundamentals section primarily consisted of MCQS covering code

snippets, flowcharts, DBMS, Operating Systems, SQL, OOPS, and basic software
engineering concepts. The overall difficulty level ranged from easy to moderate for
candidates with a strong grasp of core subjects, though several questions had closely
related options that could be confusing. A significant number of questions required
analyzing code snippets and flowcharts to determine the output or behavior of the
program. Some of these involved recursive functions, requiring careful tracing of
execution. Questions related to code snippets of confusing pre and post increments
were also there. The section also included conceptual OOPs questions, such as method
overriding, whether static methods can be overridden, object interactions, and message
passing. Additionally, there were questions comparing SOAP and REST APIs, where
candidates had to identify incorrect statements or distinguish between their
characteristics. Overall, the section tested conceptual understanding rather than
memorization, with an emphasis on reasoning through code and applying core computer
science principles. GFG for preparation of CS fundamentals. Sanfoundary and Indiabix
for output-based questions.

* The DSA section consisted of two coding questions of medium difficulty.

Question 1:
The first problem involved two integers, X and Y.
Starting with the number X, you had to form new
numbers by appending digits to its end and
determine the smallest such number that
is
divisible by Y. The challenge was to efficiently
search for the minimum valid number while
preserving the original prefix.
FUNCTION smallestNumber(x, y)
// If x itself is divisible by y
IF x MOD Y = 0 THEN
RETURN x
END IF
base + x
WHILE TRUE DO
// Append one zero to x
base + base × 10
remainder + base MOD y
Pseudo-code:
IF remainder = 0 THEN
minAdded + 0
ELSE
minAdded + y - remainder
END IF
// Check if the required addition fits within
// the current number of appended digits
IF minAdded < (base / x) THEN
RETURN base + minAdded
END IF
END WHILE
END FUNCTION
--- PAGE 3 ---
Question 2:
The second problem was a classic 2D Dynamic Programming question on matrices. Given a
grid of integers, the objective was to find the maximum path sum from the top-left cell to the
bottom-right cell while moving only in the allowed directions (typically right and down). It was
essentially a variation of the standard matrix path DP problem, with the optimization criterion
changed from minimizing the path sum to maximizing it. Similar Problem of leetcode
Pseudo-code:
FUNCTION getMaxValue (values, m, n)
CREATE 2D array dp[m][n]
// Initialize first cell
// Fill first row
FOR j + 1 TO n - 1 DO
END FOR
// Fill first column
FOR i + 1 TO m - 1 DO
dp[i][0] + dp[i - 1][0] + values[i][0]
END FOR
// Fill remaining cells
FOR i + 1 TO m - 1 DO
FOR j + 1 TO n - 1 DO
dp[i][i] + MAX(dp[i - 1][i], d[i][j - 1]) + values [i][i]
END FOR
END FOR
RETURN dp[m - 1][n - 1]
END FUNCTION
MAIN
INPUT m, n
CREATE matrix values[m][n]
FOR i + 0 TO m - 1 DO
FOR j + 0 TO n - 1 DO
INPUT values [i][]]
END FOR
END FOR
answer + getMaxValue(values, m, n)
OUTPUT answer
END MAIN
Overall, the coding section focused on problem-solving ability and familiarity with common
DSA patterns, particularly number manipulation and dynamic programming.
Sources for DSA preparation are mentioned in the end.

2. Technical Interview 1 (L1) (48 candidates )

I entered the room, greeted both interviewers, and after intro of both sides was immediately
given a DSA problem.
The coding question was to count the number of palindromic substrings in a given string. The
problem itself was fairly straightforward, but due to the pressure of the interview, I could only
come up with the brute-force approach. I wasn't able to derive the optimal solution during the
--- PAGE 4 ---
interview, even though it uses a standard optimization technique. Looking back, it was a
reminder that interview pressure can affect even familiar problems.
After the coding question, the discussion shifted almost entirely to core computer science
fundamentals, with a strong focus on Object-Oriented Programming in both C++ and Java.
Some of the topics discussed included:

• Different types of inheritance and their use cases

• Hierarchical vs. multilevel inheritance

• Virtual functions

• Interfaces

• Multiple inheritance in C++ and how Java handles it differently

• Destructors- what they are, why they are needed, and when they are invoked

One interesting question was whether a virtual constructor can be overridden. I wasn't
completely sure of the answer, so instead of guessing confidently, I explained my reasoning and
thought through the problem aloud.
One thing I learned from this interview is that it's perfectly acceptable to admit when you don't
know something, provided you genuinely try to reason about it. Interviewers often appreciate
seeing your thought process rather than hearing a memorized answer.
Meanwhile, the second interviewer started going through my resume.
Since I had listed React, Node.js, and Express in my projects, he asked several questions related
to them:

• Is Node.js single-threaded?

• How does the Event Loop work?

I remembered the basics of the Event Loop and explained them to the best of my ability.
The first interviewer then switched to Operating Systems and asked questions on:

• Concurrency

• Deadlocks

• Banker's Algorithm

--- PAGE 5 ---
After that, the second interviewer noticed Git and GitHub on my resume and asked about the
difference between Git Merge and Git Rebase, along with when each should be used. I
answered based on my understanding and practical usage, although I'm still not entirely sure
whether my explanation matched what they expected.
The entire interview lasted only about 40-45 minutes. Shortly after it ended, I received a message
asking me to be ready for the Level 2 interview which happened 2-3 hrs later.
Key Takeaways
The biggest lesson from this interview was that not solving the coding question optimally did not
immediately eliminate me. While DSA was important, the interview quickly shifted toward
evaluating my understanding of core CS concepts. It felt like the interviewers were testing not
only my technical knowledge but also how I handled pressure and responded when I encountered
unfamiliar questions.
For preparation, I would strongly recommend thoroughly revising:

• Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

• Operating Systems (OS)

• Database Management Systems (DBMS)

• SQL

• Computer Networks (CN)

A quick and effective revision strategy is to search for "<subject> interview questions GFG"
(for example, OOP interview questions GFG or DBMS interview questions GFG) and work
through those lists.
Don't limit your preparation to only core CS subjects. Review every language, framework, and
technology mentioned on your resume, because interviewers often ask questions directly from
your listed skills. For example, if your resume includes Java, C++, Python, JavaScript,
TypeScript, React, Node js, Express, MongoDB, SQL, DBMS, OS, OOP, or Computer
Networks, be prepared to answer conceptual questions about each of them.
In my case, I had revised OOP particularly well, and fortunately, a significant portion of the
interview revolved around those concepts.

3. Technical Interview 2 (L2) (20 candidates )

Unlike the first round, there were no introductions from the interviewers, and they didn't ask me
to introduce myself either. I simply greeted them, asked how they were doing, and we got
straight into the interview.
--- PAGE 6 ---
This round was heavily focused on my projects and SQL.
The interviewer started with my Job Portal project, particularly the Role-Based Access Control

(RBAC) implementation. He asked me to explain how I had implemented different user roles and

permissions. From there, the discussion became very detailed. He asked about almost every API
I had built, what each endpoint did, and how access was controlled for different users. He also
questioned how I was using access tokens and authorization throughout the application.
The discussion on RBAC alone lasted around 15 minutes. While I was explaining my
implementation, the interviewer kept counter-questioning almost every statement I made. At
times, it felt as if he wasn't convinced or didn't fully understand what I was trying to explain. I
had to explain the same concept in different ways nearly five or six times.
One important lesson I learned from this experience is not to panic when interviewers keep
challenging your answers. They may simply be testing how well you understand your own
project and whether you can defend your implementation under pressure. Throughout the
discussion, I stayed calm and remained consistent with my explanation instead of changing my
answer every time I was questioned. Eventually, I was able to communicate my implementation
clearly. Although I couldn't really tell whether the interviewer was completely satisfied, I was
confident that I had explained exactly how my project worked.
The discussion then shifted to my second project. Since it was relatively simple, the interviewer
asked me to explain all of its major functionalities and how each feature worked internally. I
walked them through the complete flow in detail.
The second interviewer then focused on the technologies mentioned in my resume. She asked
questions about several project-related technologies, including:

• JWT

• Cloudinary

• Multer

Most of the discussion revolved around JWT. She asked me about the structure of a JWT token,
its three components, how authentication works using JWT, and the complete request-response
flow.
Towards the end of the interview, I was asked to write an SQL query.
The question was based on two tables: Employee and Department. I had to write a query to
display the employee name along with the corresponding department name for the employee(s)
--- PAGE 7 ---
who received the maximum salary in the previous year. The interviewer specifically mentioned
using SQL date functions to determine the previous year.
SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_ name
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d
ON e.department id = d.department_id
WHERE YEAR(e.salary_date) = YEAR(CURDATEO) - 1
AND e.salary = (
SELECT MAX(salary)
FROM Employee
WHERE YEAR(salary_date) = YEAR(CURDATEO) - 1
The interview concluded after the SQL question. Before leaving, I asked both interviewers for
their names and thanked them for their time.
Key Takeaways
This round reinforced the importance of knowing your projects inside out. If a technology or
feature is mentioned on your resume, be prepared to explain not just what it does, but also why
you chose it, how you implemented it, possible alternatives, and how the complete flow works.
Another important observation was that interviewers may intentionally challenge your
explanations repeatedly. Staying calm, reasoning through your answers, and confidently
defending your implementation leaves a much better impression than changing your explanation
under pressure.
Finally, revise SQL thoroughly. Be comfortable with:

• Joins

• Aggregate functions

• Subqueries

• GROUP BY and HAVING

• Date functions

• Basic optimization concepts

A single SQL query can become an in-depth discussion if the interviewer asks follow-up
questions about your approach. This round lasted for 40-50 minutes.
--- PAGE 8 ---

4. HR Round (10 students appeared for this round)

I was called for the HR round about 15-20 minutes after my previous interview.
The interviewer began by introducing herself and then asked me to introduce myself. I hadn't
planned anything special for this question, but instead of giving a standard introduction, I spoke
honestly about my journey. I talked about moving from my hometown to Mumbai, how the city
had changed me as a person, and the experiences that shaped me over the last three years of
college. I also spoke about the responsibilities I had taken up through various committees,
events, and extracurricular activities.
To my surprise, she seemed genuinely interested in my story and kept listening attentively
instead of interrupting with follow-up questions.
She then asked whether I planned to return to my hometown in the near future. I understood that
she was trying to assess my willingness to relocate, so I answered that I was open to working
wherever the company required me.
The conversation then moved to behavioral questions.
She asked me to describe a situation where I had resolved a conflict within a team. I shared one
of my experiences from my committee work, explaining the situation, how I handled it, and the
outcome. She even asked whether the incident had actually happened, to which I replied that it
was a real experience.
Another interesting question she asked was:
"Suppose your manager is extremely busy and doesn't assign you any work for 20-25 days. What
would you doẠạ
There wasn't a single correct answer to this question. It felt more like they wanted to understand
my attitude in such a situation. Rather than saying I would sit idle or become frustrated, I
explained that I would first try to understand the team's priorities, explore the existing codebase
or documentation, learn independently, and proactively reach out to my manager or teammates to
ask if I could contribute anywhere. The idea was to show initiative instead of waiting passively
for work to be assigned.
Soon after that, she informed me that the round had to end because I had been shortlisted for the
next round.
Before concluding, she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked about the most common
challenges she had observed while working with freshers and interns. Interestingly, she said that
--- PAGE 9 ---
the very scenarios she had asked me about-such as relocation flexibility and how someone reacts
when they are temporarily not assigned work-were among the common issues they encountered.
After the discussion, she personally escorted me to another room, where my Level 3 interview
was scheduled virtually with a senior employee from the company. I waited for around 10
minutes before the interviewer joined the Google Meet.
Key Takeaways
This round was much more about personality, communication, and attitude than technical
knowledge. The interviewer seemed interested in understanding how I think, whether I can adapt
to new situations, and how I would behave in a professional environment.
My advice would be:

• Be genuine during your introduction instead of trying to recite a memorized script.

• Use real experiences while answering behavioral questions.

• Show ownership and initiative in hypothetical workplace scenarios.

• Demonstrate flexibility regarding relocation and work assignments if you're comfortable

with them.

• Always ask at least one thoughtful question at the end of the interview-it leaves a positive

impression and often provides useful insights about the role and the company.

5. Technical Interview 3 (L3) (10 candidates )

The final interview was conducted virtually over Microsoft Teams with a senior engineer from
the company.
The discussion once again revolved around my projects. The interviewer started with my Job
Portal project and asked me to explain the Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) implementation.
While discussing it, he pointed out a limitation in my design. I had implemented RBAC using
different APIs for different user roles. He explained that this approach would not scale well in a
real-world application with a large number of roles, as creating and maintaining separate APIs
for every role would become difficult.
At that moment, I didn't have the ideal solution. Instead of staying silent, I tried to reason
through the problem and suggested an approach that was closer to how it could be solved in
practice. Although my answer wasn't perfect, it was enough for us to move on to the next topic.
--- PAGE 10 ---
The interviewer then switched to my second project, which used SQLite. He asked me about the
database schema, the tables I had created, the relationships between them, and how the data
flowed throughout the application. Most of the discussion focused on understanding whether I
genuinely knew the internals of my own project.
Towards the end of the interview, he asked me to write a simple SQL query.
The problem consisted of two tables-Student and Department. I had to return the student names
along with their department names, but only for students belonging to the IT and CS
departments.
SELECT s.student_name, d.department_name
FROM Student s
JOIN Department d
ON s.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE d.department_ name IN ('IT", 'CS');
The interview ended shortly after the SQL question.
Key Takeaways
This round reinforced an important lesson: know the design decisions behind your projects, not
just the implementation. The interviewer wasn't trying to find mistakes in my project-he
wanted to understand whether I had thought about scalability and how I would improve my
design when faced with real-world constraints.
If you don't know the perfect answer, don't panic. Explain your reasoning, discuss possible
alternatives, and show that you can think through the problem logically. Interviewers often value
your approach to problem-solving as much as the final answer itself.
Finally, make sure you are comfortable with writing basic SQL queries involving JOINs,
filtering, and multiple tables, as these are frequently asked even in project-based interviews.
This round lasted for 40-45 minutes.
| 8 students received the offer.]
--- PAGE 11 ---
Must read
Placement season was one of the most challenging phases for me.
When it started, I got rejected from the JPMorgan Chase FinTech role, then PhonePe, and I
couldn't even make it into the WorkIndia process. Every day I was coming to college either for
an online assessment or an interview. In most companies I reached the last round, only to face
another rejection. It was discouraging, and after every rejection it became harder to get up the
next morning and prepare with the same energy.
But I kept trying.
Looking back, I don't regret anything I did for my preparation. Yes, I was constantly stressed and
anxious, sometimes overthinking every small thing. That pressure made me more attentive and
pushed me to prepare better. At the same time, I learned that you shouldn't let stress take over
your preparation. Use it as motivation, not as something that controls you.
Every rejection taught me something valuable that eventually helped me crack IDFC First Bank
JPMorgan made me realize that I needed a much stronger understanding of my projects and CS
fundamentals. PhonePe exposed the gaps in my DSA preparation. Instead of treating those
interviews as failures, I treated them as feedback.
One mistake I made was stopping DSA practice almost two months before placements. I was
going through a difficult phase personally and wasn't in the right state of mind to prepare. I only
started studying seriously once companies had already started visiting campus. It was extremely
difficult to catch up, and I would never recommend doing what I did.
No matter what is happening in your life, placement season is an opportunity you cannot afford
to ignore. Even if you feel overwhelmed, even if you feel like giving up, you still have to show
up for yourself. No one else can prepare on your behalf. It's just a matter of a few months, but
those months can shape the beginning of your career.
Work hard. Study consistently. Put in the effort every single day.
If you're consistent, the workload never becomes overwhelming. DSA is not something you can
master or revise in a day. I had already studied it before, yet I still couldn't revise everything
during placements. The same applies to CS fundamentals, projects, SQL, operating systems,
DBMS, computer networks, and everything else on your resume.
Know your resume inside out. If someone points to any line on it, you should be able to explain
it confidently, discuss the design decisions you made, the alternatives you considered, and the
--- PAGE 12 ---
challenges you faced. There should never be a point on your resume that surprises you in an
interview.
Start preparing early so that when placement season begins, you are improving-not rushing.
And finally, don't lose hope because of rejections.
I know how painful they feel. I questioned myself after every rejection. But every interview
made me better than I was before. If I had been selected in one of the earlier companies, I might
never have learned the lessons that helped me succeed later.
Your job is not to predict when you'll get your offer or which company it will be. Your job is
simply to prepare, learn from every experience, and give your best every single time.
The right opportunity will come. When it does, all the preparation, all the rejections, and all the
difficult days will finally make sense.
# Backstory (read only if you have time. Has nothing to do with interview prep. Fun tho)
Even after all my interview rounds were over before almost everyone else's, my result still wasn't
announced.
The first list of selected candidates came out, and my name wasn't on it.
I can't even explain how stressed I was. I was already emotionally drained after multiple
rejections, and at that moment I genuinely felt like I couldn't handle another one. Later I found
out that there were two L3 interview panels, and the results from my panel were still pending.
But at that time, I had no idea. All I knew was that everyone else seemed to be getting their
results while I was still waiting.
Then came one of the most embarrassing moments of the placement season.
Our TPC, Apurv Jaiswal, started announcing a few names. He was actually reading out the
names of students whose results were still pending, but he didn't mention that before starting. We
had already been waiting for hours, so my brain immediately assumed he was announcing the
final selected candidates.
The moment I heard my name, I completely believed I had been selected.
I started crying right there.
For a few seconds, I thought the dream had finally come true... only to realize those weren't the
final results. Safe to say, I'll never forget that moment.
Eventually, we were told to go home and that the final results would be declared the next day. I
was convinced there was no way I was going to sleep that night.
Then another legend stepped in.
Samudra Banerjee called me. The first thing he said was, "Bad news..."
My heart absolutely sank.
--- PAGE 13 ---
He paused for a second and then said,i...you can't sit for tomorrow's process because you're
selected in IDFCại
I don't even remember what happened after that. I was literally jumping around the house.
After everything-the preparation, the anxiety, the interviews, the waiting, and the rejections-that
phone call made every bit of it worth it.
A huge shoutout to Apurv Jaiswal, Samudra Banerjee, and the entire TPC team. We often only
see the announcements, but there's a tremendous amount of work happening behind the scenes to
coordinate companies, schedules, interviews, and communication. They put in a lot of effort to
make the placement process as smooth as possible for everyone, and they truly deserve the
appreciation.

• I would say your frontend is very important but since our solution was WhatsApp we had to focus

more on the backend, though we ended up integrating a lot of features that we deemed hard to finish
like voice-to-voice workflows, image-to-text processing, etc..

• One of our main features broke down within the last 15 minutes of the submission deadline and even

Claude Code was not able to fix it, likely because it wasn't aware of the latest documentation. So we
had to read the official documentation and make changes which proved beneficial as this was the
flow that the judges really liked. So always stay updated with the latest documentation as Al can
only help to a certain extent.

• Know your dependencies in advance as you are not allowed to download anything on the hackathon

day

• Your ideation matters a lot since solutions with unique ideas were the ones who actually won.

(Second prize went to the team which incorporated Telegram, and Third prize went to the team
which incorporated financial literacy through the medium of reels!)

• Try not to be too overwhelmed during the presentation. Let your project do the work and explain

how it works. If you get stuck on a feature, do not panic and simply move on.

• The most important thing that you need to know before applying is to get your priorities straight

since if the dates of the hackathon clash with another company's process, you would not be allowed
to sit for it. In our case, our dates collided with JPMC's OA and Interviews and we were not allowed
to sit for it.

• One of the most underestimated factors in placements is luck. It genuinely plays a significant role

throughout the process. So, if you are not getting shortlisted or are unable to clear interviews, don't
get discouraged. Stay confident, keep learning, and continue giving your best. If not this company,
then the next one could be the opportunity you're waiting for

Important Dates

• Round 1 (Executive Summary): 4th - 11th June

• Round 2 (In-Person Presentation): 22nd June

• Round 3 (Hackathon): 3rd - 4th July

ROUND 1- Executive Summary

Getting Shortlisted in Round 1 and Round 2 is extremely difficult.
In this round, we were given a problem statement and asked to submit a two-page executive
summary. The summary had to include sections such as:

• About Us

• Brief Understanding of the Problem Statement

• Proposed Solution

• Dependencies and Tech Stack

Everyone has access to LLMs, so most teams end up researching similar ideas and proposing similar
solutions. This makes it difficult to stand out. I would recommend thinking outside the box and coming up
with an idea that genuinely catches their attention. For example, our problem statement was about improving
financial access for underprivileged people. While most teams focused on building websites or mobile
applications, we decided to leverage WhatsApp, an app already used by millions across India. This became
our biggest USP
Your summary should contain well-defined and concise points. Including diagrams or UI mockups is an
added advantage, as they demonstrate clarity of thought and a better understanding of your solution.

ROUND 2: Presentation Pitch

--- PAGE 2 ---
26 teams were selected from our college for this round. We were required to prepare a presentation and pitch
it to the Nomura panel at our college. The format consisted of a 10-minute presentation followed by a
5-minute Q&A session. (The timings are quite strict so adhere to the time limit)
This was honestly the most nerve-racking round because we finished our presentation the night before the
pitch.
Make your PPT descriptive with more images than text. One of the biggest reasons we finished our PPT so
late was because it was initially too text-heavy, and we later had to redesign several slides by replacing text
with visuals.
The one thing I would recommend is adding User Journeys to your PPT so as to show the judges how the
user would actually go through while using your solution.
My teammate and I started with a skit to catch the attention which directly correlated with our USP.
Be sure to know your solution inside out as the questions can be asked for any feature or any point. We were
asked about data security and the working of our features.
Memorizing your presentation script usually never works as I forgot mine halfway through the presentation,
but since I knew the solution I was able to explain and answer the judges' questions.
Our panel had 3 judges. Highlight key features (USPS) and keep the judges engaged, as they'll hear many
similar solutions.
Be sure to use the feedback of the judges in your final hackathon.

ROUND 3: Final Hackathon

7 teams were shortlisted from our college and around 30 teams participated in the hackathon overall
This was probably the most memorable and exciting round.
The hackathon was held on 3rd and 4th July. We were asked to visit the Nomura office on 2nd July for tech
setup. Pick-up and Drop-off for all three days are provided by Nomura!
You would most probably be working on your own laptops which would be connected to their AWS instance
so that no one can access pre-written codes and have to start afresh.
We were provided with Claude Code for development. We were also allowed to use APIS, provided they
were free and did not require paid API keys. Access to all other LLMs was blocked.
Each team is assigned a mentor who plays a very crucial role in the hackathon as they would help you solve
difficulties while evaluating your performance.
The hackathon was an incredible experience. Everyone at Nomura was extremely supportive and
welcoming. Every aspect of the event was thoughtfully planned, from food and refreshments to resting areas
and recreational activities. It was probably the most well-organized hackathon I have ever seen. A late-night
pizza party, along with plenty of snacks and energy drinks, kept everyone going, although we were too
anxious to eat much
There were no difficulties faced during the hackathon process other than the installation of our specified
python version which was later resolved.
I would recommend being well-versed in both the financial and technical aspects of your solution. Since the
evaluation panels are randomly assigned, you may face judges with either a technical or a financial
background, so you should be prepared to answer questions from both perspectives
--- PAGE 3 ---

This was a pretty straight forward and simple round consisting of 50 marks. It had 10 MCQS, 3 Debugging

root node; some question around SQL Injection; What converts domain name to IP addr? (Ans: DNS)

provide a fix for it. This was quite intuitive and doable.
Pseudocode: An array was given and asked to write a pseudocode to find the maximum unique element.

calculation based - on which day maximum errors were found? etc
Situation: The server is facing a downtime during the month end and duplicate entries are stored. The
response time is huge. How will you solve this problem? (I proposed to scale the server by adding a load

[ List down the rounds that were conducted and any specific information related to it ]

1.    Online Assessment:  [149 Candidates appeared]

The Online Assessment was conducted on HackerEarth platform. It consisted of 20 MCQs and 5 SQL
questions. Surprisingly, there were no DSA based coding questions. 20 MCQs were easy to test the
understanding of basics of Java, C++ and SQL, along with a few easy logical questions in the form of code
behaviour/output. Next, 5 SQL questions were also ea sy, they tested your basic SQL syntax knowledge and
there was minimal usage of joins to solve the questions.
The round was of 45 minutes overall. The questions were relatively easy, especially the MCQs, it was
basically a race against time, how quickly you can solve all the questions. A total of 38 students were selected
for the interview round.
For the MCQs, I had prepared using GeeksForGeeks and solved Leetcode and Codeforces problems to
build my logic and problem-solving ability. I had practiced the SQL 50 problems from Leetcode for the SQL
questions, as well as websites like SQLZoo and W3Schools.

2. Interview Round 1:    [38 candidates appeared]

After the shortlisted candidates list came, we were told that the interviews would be held 2 days later.
As we didn't have much time, so being prepared early on is the key. All shortlisted candidates were called
at 8 in the morning for pre placement talk, which eventually began at 9 , where the directors explained
many important and key things about the company, internship and about the interview process. I would
recommend to listen to the presentation attentively and note down the relevant points as well as the names
of the Directors, as it might help you later on.

There were 6 panelists and the interview was one-to-one. I was the third candidate in my panelist.

When I entered the interview room, the interviewer asked to introduce myself and took a moment to read
my resume. He asked some basic questions about my projects, its feasibility, how many of them were
individual or done in groups, etc. He also asked few basic HR type questions also. Next, he dived into my
projects and asked me to explain anyone whichever I liked in complete detail. He cross -questioned me
based on certain features which I answered. He told me to write down the code whatever I remember. I
had done my project in Python, so I tried to recall the syntax and wrote down the basic ones which I know
of the back of my mind. He kept on asking me particular questions about me code, projects because of
which I was distracted from writing the code and made some mistakes while answering. But I pulled
myself and covered it up to my ability.

After this, he asked few questions about my skills, on Java, C++, and asked me what my preferred
language was. My go to language was C++, so he asked me difference between NULL, 0, undefined and
pointers and pointers exception. He wrote pieces of  code (of strings) in C++ and asked me to state the
output in each case. I was told to explain time and space complexity and give the same of a piece of code
he showed in his laptop. He questioned me about DBMS Joins and I explained them verbally and using
Venn diagrams as well. At last, he gave me two tables on paper and asked me to perform full outer join
and give the correct output.

3. Interview Round 2    [19 candidates selected]

This interview was taken by the senior person who gave the talk at the start of the day , he took few
moments to look at my resume and asked me to explain any project or any problem which I would like to
share. I explained my AIML project on the resume as well as the purpose and intention behind the resume.
He asked me things about the dataset features, how I cleaned it, which features were important and how I
decided them, which model gave the better result and how I deduced that and similar questions. I answered
as per the question and he cross -questioned me based on my answer. He told me to explain one specific
project on my resume, I explained it and the same process went on where he cross-questioned some aspect
or the other. The interviewer migh t or might not agree or validate your answer, so do not wait for any
positive response and just answer to the best of your knowledge.

[Finally 16 Students were selected for the Internship]

1. Resume Shortlisting

Out of all the applications received, 67 students were shortlisted for the next round, the Online Assessment
(OA). This stage is often underestimated, and your resume plays a crucial role in securing a shortlist.
Take your time to build your resume and follow a clean, professional, and consistent format. Carefully check
for formatting issues, grammatical errors, and spelling mistakes before submitting. A good ATS score alone
does not guarantee a shortlist; the overall quality and relevance of your profile matter significantly.
Although the minimum CGPA criterion specified by the company was 7.0, it is advisable to maintain a
CGPA of at least 8.0 to remain competitive.
For your resume, try to include:

• One or two finance-related projects, preferably including a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) valuation

project.

• At least one FinTech or data analytics project that demonstrates technical and analytical skills.

• Relevant internship experience and positions of responsibility.

• Participation in case competitions, especially if you were a finalist or winner.

• Certifications relevant to finance, analytics, or technology.

Wherever possible, quantify your achievements by including meaningful numbers and measurable impact.
Tailor the skills section of your resume according to the job description provided by the company and
highlight the skills most relevant to the role.
Once the company shares the registration link after the PPT, make sure to submit your application as early as
possible.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assesment [67 students were selected]

The Online Assessment (OA) consists of 45 multiple-choice questions (MCQS), with 1 mark awarded for
each correct answer. The section-wise breakdown is as follows:

• 10 Questions: Corporate Finance and Accounting

These are primarily basic finance and accounting concepts. If you have prepared well for finance
fundamentals, this section should be manageable.

• 10 Questions: Market Awareness

Stay updated with current affairs, business news, recent mergers and acquisitions (M&As), and
major developments in the financial markets, as questions can be asked from a wide range of topics.

• 15 Questions: Quantitative Aptitude

The questions are generally easy and doable, but the section is time-constrained. Practising under
timed conditions is highly recommended. I used IndiaBIX for preparation, which I found quite
helpful.

• 10 Questions: English

This section is relatively straightforward. If your fundamentals in grammar, vocabulary, and reading
comprehension are clear, you should not face any major difficulties.
The OA is an important stage of the selection process, so start your preparation well in advance. Also, there
is no negative marking for CIB (Banking), so make sure to attempt all the questions, even if you are
unsure of some answers.
Out of 67 students 56 went for Group Discussion

3. Group Discussion [56 students were selected]

The GD topic and shortlist were shared just one day prior, at around 9:00 PM, so don't lose hope if you
haven't received an update yet-keep preparing and stay patient.
GD Topic:
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful share of its
inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are approximately 2x
longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial metrics. As the
CEO, how would you tackle this situationạ
We were divided into 6 panels, with each panel consisting of around 9 students. Approximately 20 minutes
were allocated for the GD. However, this was not a traditional group discussion. The discussion was
conducted more like a Q&A session, where we were asked specific questions and were expected to share our
views only on those questions.
Therefore, it is important to:

• Understand the GD topic in depth and research it thoroughly.

• Think about possible subtopics and follow-up questions that may arise from the main topic.

• Stay updated on current affairs and business trends related to the topic.

A few tips for the GD:
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Try to speak at least 2-3 times during the discussion.

• Ensure that all your points remain relevant to the topic being discussed.

• Be clear, structured, and confident while presenting your views.

• Avoid using heavy jargon unless you fully understand its meaning and can use it appropriately.

• Listen carefully to others, be respectful, and maintain a civil discussion.

• Do not try to dominate the conversation; evaluators value quality of inputs and collaborative

behaviour more than the quantity of speaking time.
Remember, the evaluators are looking not only at your knowledge but also at your clarity of thought,
confidence, communication skills, and ability to think under pressure.
28 students were selected for the interview

4. Technical Round [28 students were selected]

The shortlist for the interview was released quite quickly after the GD round.
The interview was primarily focused on the resume, so make sure you know every point on your resume
thoroughly. Be prepared to answer questions on your projects, internships, positions of responsibility,
certifications, and any achievements that you have mentioned.
Apart from your resume, the interviews also tested general financial knowledge. Some commonly asked
topics included:

• How to value a company

• Valuation methodologies and valuation multiples

• Macroeconomic concepts such as the repo rate and its impact

• Puzzles and guesstimates

• Basic accounting and finance concepts

The questions varied significantly across panels, and every panel seemed to have a different approach.
Therefore, it is difficult to predict the exact questions that will be asked. The best strategy is to have a strong
grasp of your resume and a solid understanding of finance fundamentals.
The interview process was also quite uncertain and dynamic. Some candidates had to go through three
technical rounds, while others had only one interview round before receiving a decision. Hence, be patient
throughout the process and do not lose hope if your process differs from that of others. Focus on your
preparation and trust the process.

4. HR Round students students were selected]

The HR round was very relaxed and felt more like a casual conversation than a formal interview. The key is
to stay confident, communicate clearly, and showcase your personality while aligning your answers with
JPMC's core values.
Some of the questions that were asked included:

1. Tell me about yourself and why you want to pursue a career in finance.

2. A detailed discussion on one of the projects mentioned on my resume.

3. What is one thing you liked about JPMC from the Pre-Placement Presentation (PPT)?

--- PAGE 4 ---

4. Do you have any questions for me?

The questions can vary from panel to panel, but overall, the HR round is primarily aimed at understanding
your motivations, communication skills, and cultural fit for the firm.
A few tips for the HR round:

• Be genuine and conversational rather than sounding overly rehearsed.

• Have a clear answer for "Why Finance?" and "Why JPMC?"

• Know your resume and projects well, as they may ask you to elaborate on any point you have

mentioned.

• Read about JPMC's values, culture, and ethics beforehand and try to reflect them naturally in your

answers.

• Go through the job description (JD) carefully and understand the qualities the firm is looking for.

For example, the JD for this role placed significant emphasis on team collaboration, so I
consciously highlighted instances where I worked effectively in teams and incorporated this point
into my answers.

• Prepare a few thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer at the end.

• Stay calm, smile, and treat the interaction as a normal conversation.

Overall, the HR round was very chill and was more about getting to know you as a person than testing your
technical knowledge.
10 students were selected for CIB banking role

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following rounds:

1. Online Assessment (MCQ Test)

2. Technical Interview

3. Techno-HR Interview (Technical + HR)

Resume Shortlisting | 214 students were shortlisted]
The first stage of the recruitment process was resume shortlisting. While the exact shortlisting criteria were
not disclosed, I believe my academic performance, relevant projects, and an ATS-optimized resume played
an important role in getting shortlisted.
I maintained a CGPA above 8.7 throughout engineering, which met the company's eligibility criteria of 8+
CGPA. I would strongly recommend maintaining a CGPA above 8 (preferably above 9), as it keeps you
eligible for a larger number of placement opportunities. Before the placement season, I optimized my
resume using Resume Worded, where it achieved an ATS score of approximately 83. (A score above 70
would help you get shortlisted for most of the companies) I also ensured that the resume was concise, one
page long, included quantified achievements, and highlighted projects relevant to software engineering.
My advice would be to regularly improve your resume, keep it ATS-friendly, tailor it wherever possible to
the job profile, and be prepared to justify every point mentioned during the interview. (Do not mention any
technical skill on your resume unless you are confident discussing it in depth during the interview.)

1. Online Assessment 214 students appeared for the test ]

The first round was an offline on-campus Online Assessment conducted through Google Forms. The
assessment was held from 8:30 AM to 10:00 AM (90 minutes) and consisted of approximately 70
multiple-choice questions.
Marking Scheme

• +1 for every correct answer

• -0.25 for every incorrect answer

--- PAGE 2 ---
Since negative marking was involved, accuracy was much more important than attempting every question.
My strategy was to attempt only those questions where I was reasonably confident instead of making
random guesses.
The assessment consisted of five sections:

• Java

• Python

• SQL

• Al-based Code Review / AI Output Evaluation

• Aptitude

Java (Approximately 15 Questions)
Java was my primary programming language, so I spent a significant amount of time preparing for this
section. The questions were primarily output-based and conceptual rather than definition-based. Instead of
asking direct theoretical questions, the assessment tested whether the candidate truly understood the internal
working of Java.
The important topics included:

• Object-Oriented Programming concepts

• Method Overloading and Method Overriding

• Collections Framework

Generics and Wildcards
Optional Class

• String vs StringBuilder

• Exception Handling

• Lambda Expressions and Streams

• Access Modifiers

• Interfaces and Abstract Classes

• Code Output Prediction

Several questions contained subtle edge cases where a small conceptual misunderstanding could easily lead
to an incorrect answer. My recommendation would be to understand why a particular output is produced
rather than memorizing definitions, as most questions tested conceptual understanding instead of factual
knowledge.
Python (Approximately 15 Questions)
Although Python was not my primary programming language, the questions mainly focused on conceptual
understanding and output prediction.
The important topics included:

• Object-Oriented Programming

• Method Resolution Order (MRO)

• Mutable vs Immutable Objects

• Object References

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy

• Function Behaviour

• Lists, Dictionaries and Sets

• Basic Python Internals

Many questions revolved around Python-specific behaviors that are commonly overlooked during interview
preparation. Since I was comparatively less comfortable with Python, I focused on attempting only those
questions where I was confident, which helped avoid unnecessary negative marking.
SQL (3 Questions)
This was the shortest and comparatively easiest section of the assessment. The questions were
scenario-based, where a problem statement was provided and candidates had to identify the most appropriate
SQL query among multiple options.
The topics primarily included:

• SELECT Statements

• JOINs

• Aggregate Functions

• GROUP BY

• HAVING Clause

• Filtering Conditions

I had completed the LeetCode SQL 50 before the assessment, which covered almost every concept required
for this round. As a result, I was confident in this section and attempted all the SQL questions. For future
candidates, I would strongly recommend completing the LeetCode SQL 50 questions, as they provide
sufficient practice for assessments of this level.
Al-Based Code Review / AI Output Evaluation (Approximately 10 Questions)
This was one of the most interesting and unique sections of the assessment. Instead of testing theoretical
Artificial Intelligence concepts, the section evaluated whether candidates could critically analyse
Al-generated responses. Each question presented a prompt along with one or more Al-generated solutions.
Candidates had to determine whether the generated response was correct or identify logical flaws and
choose the most appropriate alternative.
The questions mainly tested:

• Identifying logical mistakes in Al-generated code

• Selecting the most accurate Al-generated solution

• Recognising incorrect programming approaches

• Reviewing Al-generated SQL and programming snippets

• Understanding whether the generated output actually satisfied the given prompt

Aptitude (25 Questions)
The aptitude section was comparatively straightforward and highly scoring. The questions covered standard
quantitative aptitude topics such as:
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Time, Speed and Distance

• Work and Time

• Profit and Loss

• Simple Interest

• Probability

• Geometry

• Ratios and Proportions

• Logical Reasoning

• Scalar and Vector Concepts

• Minimum Weighing Problems (Ball Puzzle)

• Basic Quantitative Aptitude

Most of these questions were very similar to those available on IndiaBIX, and regular practice from the
platform was sufficient.
Out of 25 aptitude questions, I attempted 21, choosing accuracy over quantity because of the negative
marking. Since I was confident about the questions I attempted, I preferred leaving uncertain questions
unanswered rather than risking unnecessary deductions. I would strongly recommend solving IndiaBIX
topic-wise before the placement season begins, as aptitude plays a significant role in many company
assessments and is often underestimated by students.
Overall, I attempted 55-60 questions during the Online Assessment while ensuring that I attempted only
those questions where I was reasonably confident. Rather than trying to maximise the number of attempts,
my focus was on maintaining accuracy throughout the assessment because of the negative marking.

2. Technical Interview [ 44 students were shortlisted]

The technical interview lasted around 30-35 minutes and was primarily based on my resume, Java
fundamentals, React, and project discussions.
The interview began with a self-introduction. During my introduction, I mentioned one of my React projects

(ToyStation) and that it was deployed. The interviewers immediately opened the website on their own

laptop and started exploring it themselves. They clicked through different pages, asked how various features
were implemented and questioned my technology choices. This taught me that if you mention a deployed
project, be prepared for the interviewer to open it live and ask questions from any part of the
application.
One of the first questions was whether the project was Al-generated. I honestly explained that Al had
assisted in development but that I clearly understood the implementation and could explain every technical
decision. The interviewers emphasized that using Al is completely acceptable, provided you understand the
code and can debug or extend it independently.
The discussion then moved towards React and frontend development. Some of the questions asked were:

• How would you persist a field (such as age) across multiple pages in React?

• Why did you choose TypeScript instead of JavaScript?

• Why did you use Tailwind CSS?

• Which parts of the project were implemented by you and which were Al-assisted?

--- PAGE 5 ---
The next part of the interview focused on Java. The interviewers displayed multiple code snippets on their
laptop and asked me to predict the output. They also modified the snippets during the interview to test my
understanding of different scenarios.
The major topics covered were:

• Exception Handling (try-catch-finally)

• Collections Framework

• Java Streams

• Output Prediction

• Edge cases involving Stream terminal operations

Towards the end of the interview, I noticed that my project, which was highly relevant to ISS STOXX's ESG
domain, had not been discussed. Before leaving, I politely requested a few additional minutes to explain the
project. The interviewers asked questions related to ESG, RAG, hallucination reduction, and the overall
architecture of the solution. They challenged several of my answers to understand my thought process, but I
remained calm and justified my design decisions confidently.
Preparation & Suggestions

• Be prepared to explain every project on your resume in depth.

• If a project is deployed, expect the interviewer to open it live and ask questions from any page or

feature.

• Be honest about using Al tools. Interviewers care more about your understanding than whether Al

was used.

• Revise Java thoroughly, especially Exception Handling, Collections, Streams, and output-based

questions.

• Stay calm if interviewers challenge your answers they are often evaluating your reasoning rather than

expecting perfect answers.

• If an important project is not discussed, politely ask if you can explain it. It demonstrates confidence,

communication skills, and genuine interest.

3. HR Interview [ 20 students were shortlisted]

After the technical interviews, the shortlisted candidates for the final round were announced. Since many
candidates were being rejected in my technical interview panel, I was initially unsure about my
pertormance. However, when my name was announced for the final round, it was a huge confidence boost.
The final round lasted around 25-30 minutes and was conducted by the Managing Director and the HR
Head. It was a combination of technical discussion and HR questions.
The interview began with basic HR questions about my family background, hometown, and whether I would
be comfortable working from the Mumbai office five days a week.
The discussion then shifted to my internship experience. I was asked to explain my role during my NET
internship, the projects I worked on, how I handled deadlines, and a situation where I received constructive
feedback on my work. I answered these questions using the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
approach, explaining how I improved after receiving feedback and the importance of writing maintainable
production-quality code.
--- PAGE 6 ---
The HR also asked about my hobbies and interests. The Managing Director then took over the discussion and
asked me to explain my project in detail. The discussion focused on:

• Overall project architecture

• Why I chose RAG

• How hallucinations were reduced

• How the chatbot retrieved relevant ESG information

Compared to the technical interview, I was much more confident while explaining the project and was able
to answer the follow-up questions calmly. Towards the end of the interview, I was asked whether I would be
comfortable working with technologies outside my current skill set, such as NET. I explained that I enjoy
learning new technologies and would be happy to contribute to any team where I could learn and grow.
Finally, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I asked "What does a typical day in the life of an
intern at ISS STOXX look like?" The interviewers explained the work culture, mentorship, and
collaborative environment, which gave me a positive impression of the company.
Preparation & Suggestions

• Prepare your internship experience thoroughly, including your contributions, challenges, and

learnings.

• Keep at least 2-3 STAR-based stories ready for common HR questions on teamwork, deadlines,

conflict, and feedback.

• Be honest about your strengths, weaknesses, and learning experiences.

• Show enthusiasm towards learning new technologies instead of limiting yourself to a specific tech

stack.

• Always ask at least one thoughtful question at the end of the interview, as it reflects genuine interest

in the role and the organization.
Later that evening, the final list of 12 selected candidates was released. Seeing my name on it was a
moment of immense happiness and relief, and it felt rewarding to see all the hard work finally pay
off. Approximately a week later, the company released another list, selecting 3 additional
candidates, taking the total number of offers to 15.

Online Interviews from college - [03/07/2026]

4. Technical Interview Round 1

5. Technical Interview Round 2

1.
[Pre Placement Talk]
This session was conducted online. The speakers introduced themselves, explained the different roles
offered by JPMorgan Chase, and discussed the work culture, expectations, and hiring process. One
suggestion I'd give is to note down the names and roles of the presenters, because there is a possibility that
one of them may appear in your interview panel. It also helps in making the interview feel more familiar.
Pay close attention during the presentation because interviewers sometimes ask questions related to the
company, business areas, or the role, and many of these are explained during the PPT itself.
Regarding asking questions, I personally don't think it has a major impact on your selection. However, if you
do ask something, ensure that it is relevant and thoughtful rather than asking just for the sake of asking.

2. Resume Shortisting.

In my opinion, this was the most important stage of the entire process.
Everything that happened during the interviews revolved around my resume. Almost every technical
question was asked based on the skills, projects, and experiences that I had mentioned.
My biggest advice is:
--- PAGE 2 ---
Tailor your resume according to the Job Description instead of trying to showcase every
project you've ever built.
For this role, there were multiple business areas such as:

• Risk Reporting

• Risk Controllers

• Middle Office

• Data Analytics / Intelligent Solutions

Among these, I felt the Data Analytics track aligned best with my background.
To strengthen my profile, I created a Business Analytics Dashboard project before the interviews because it
directly matched the responsibilities mentioned in the JD. I intentionally kept its description general enough
to discuss comfortably during interviews while still making it relevant.
I also added a few skills such as Excel and Power BI even though I wasn't highly proficient in them at that
time. Since they were explicitly mentioned in the JD, I made sure to learn the basics thoroughly before the
interview through YouTube tutorials and practice.
Important Advice

• Do not add skills just to fill space.

• If you mention something on your resume, be prepared to explain it confidently.

• Interviewers can ask questions from any single word on your resume.

3. [Online Assessment] [ 122 Candidates Appeared ]

The Online Assessment was conducted from home through the AON Assessment Platform.
The company specifically instructed us to sit in a quiet environment with minimal background disturbance.
The assessment mainly consisted of Verbal Ability, Quantitative Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, Number
series, Overall difficulty: Easy to Medium
Initially, we were informed that pen and paper would not be allowed, but later permission was granted.
Since time was limited,

• I first completed Verbal and Logical Reasoning.

• I kept Quantitative Aptitude for the end because calculations generally take more time.

• No calculator was allowed.

One small tip: During online proctored assessments, try to keep your focus on the screen. Even before using
my rough sheet, I showed both the pen and paper to the webcam to avoid unnecessary suspicion.

4. [Technical Interview Round 1] [ 32 Candidates Shortlisted]

Duration: Approximately 20-25 minutes, Panel: 2 Interviewers
--- PAGE 3 ---
The interview started with brief introductions from the panel, followed by,"Tell us about yourself." I kept my
introduction concise by mentioning Diploma, Current degree, Areas of interest, Internship experience. Since
this round felt technical, I skipped hobbies and focused only on my academic and professional background.
The questions I remember are:

1. Tell me about yourself.

2. Walk me through your projects.

3. You mentioned using an LLM in your project. How did you prevent hallucinations?

• I explained the use of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide context-aware

responses.

4. Explain SQL Joins.

5. What do you know about Excel? Where have you used it?

6. Since Power BI and Tableau were mentioned on my resume, they asked about my experience with

them.

• I honestly told them I did not have hands-on experience but had worked extensively with

Zoho Analytics, which serves a similar purpose. I then explained my Business Analytics
Dashboard project.

7. Explain Data Cleaning and Data Preprocessing.

8. How do you remove duplicates in Python?

9. Explain Encapsulation and Abstraction along with their differences.

This question is memorable because I panicked a little
*. Initially, I mistakenly explained dropna () for
removing null values. The interviewer clarified that she was asking about duplicates. Then, due to
nervousness, I switched to explaining duplicate removal in Excel! After taking a deep breath, I finally
answered correctly using drop_duplicatesO
Towards the end, the interviewers explained the role in detail and asked if I had any questions. I asked, "I
recently read that J.P. Morgan has been investing heavily in AI. How is Al currently being used within this
roleại
This led to a good discussion and left a positive ending to the interview.

5. [Technical Interview Round 2 ] [ 16 Candidates Shortlisted]

Duration: Around 20 minutes, Panel: 2 Interviewers
This interview was much more conversational. It had been raining heavily that day, and the panel started
with a casual discussion about the weather before moving into technical questions, they asked me to "Walk
us through your resume." Initially, I only introduced myself. One interviewer smiled and said, "Walk us
through your projects as well." After explaining each project briefly, they asked:
Questions

1. Write a Python program to find the maximum element in a list. I honestly didn't expect live coding,

since screen sharing would consume time, I verbally explained:

• Using max ()

• Sorting the list

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Iterating through the list while maintaining the current maximum

2. Explain the different types of Risk.

3. What does JPMorgan Chase do?

4. How does a bank earn profit?

5. Multiple follow-up questions related to Risk Management and JPMorgan.

6. Surprisingly, they also asked an HR question: Tell us your three strengths and three weaknesses.

My suggestion for this round, learn the basics of Risks, its types and management, along with famous
examples such as Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank, Harshad Mehta Scam. Explaining concepts using
real-life events makes your answers much stronger.

5. ¡HR Interview] [ 10 Candidates Shortlisted]

This was the most relaxed round. The interview began with casual questions like "How has your day been?".
Then she moved towards role-specific HR questions. Some questions I remember:

• You've lived in Mumbai all your life. Are you comfortable relocating to Bengaluru?

• Are you comfortable working in rotational or night shifts?

• Why this role?

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

Unlike traditional HR interviews, there were very few generic HR questions. Most questions focused on
your motivation, company values, role expectations, adaptability

In total, 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment round, 1 Technical Interview round and 1 HR
round(I felt it more to be techno-HR). The CGPA criteria was kept at 8 and they followed it throughout in
my knowledge, so preferable to keep it above 8 and 8.5 if possible (Mine was 8.56).

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting [ Approx 210 candidates]

ISS-STOXX requires a photo on their resume so I made it accordingly. Tailor your resume to the JD it really
helps, keep only those projects and tech stack that you can talk about for hours, don't fill it unnecessarily it
only creates holes that they can poke in the interview rounds. Use resumeworded or enhancv for ATS score
checking, keep it above 60 preferably 70, mine was 65 but I think that was a factor of rejection in some
shortlistings.
--- PAGE 2 ---
2.
Pre-Placement Talk
They took the PPT online at around 3:00 PM. I always made it a point to note down the names of the
speakers, important points, their values, anything that could help me talk or indicate that I was paying
attention during it, it shows interest as well so I'd suggest you'd do the same. Previous interview
experiences noted they were asked the names of the speakers in the HR round so it is important.

3. Online Assessment Round [ Approx 210 candidates]

The OA round was conducted offline on-campus, the test ran from 8:30 AM to 10:00 AM. The format of the
test was changed slightly this year; 70 questions were to be solved in 90 minutes on google forms. 15 Java
output, 15 python output, 3 SQL, 12 Al proficiency, 25 Aptitude. Correct answers awarded +1 and wrong
gave -0.25.
Java section included a lot of Streams fundamentals like Collectors.groupingBy)) output type (and basic
stream filter and mapping problems like from a list = [1, 5, 7, 9, 3, 8], take only those numbers greater than
3 and square them and print the output), wildcards and generics knowledge (List<? extends Number> and
List<? super Integer> type questions), static methods and variables, polymorphism, String concepts (one
where s = "Hello"; s.concat(" World"); print(s);), Inheritance and Exception handling. Overall it was doable
if prep was targeted on this.
Python section was overall doable (even though I primarily use Java, the concepts transfer here as well).
Some questions on MRO, Multiple inheritance handling, use of namedtuples and @dataclass, difference
between _init
_ and exec, exceptions, etc. It was very similar to java outputs but some python quirks were
tested.
SQL section was easy to moderate, with question on UPDATE, DELETE and one SELECT query, all were
well defined on what to do with 4 query options for each with minimal differences but easy to spot if enough
practice done beforehand (Even tho I had dbms trauma at one time I did it)
Al Proficiency was something new this time, but the questions were easy to moderate with questions like the
Al generated this data schema or this Java snippet, these issues are popping up, choose one of the alternate
code or maintain that original code is correct. And some general questions I couldn't recollect like vector
DB and also a vector addition one where a triangle where AB + BC = AC property applied and we had to
choose the wrong equation out of 4. Overall nothing Al heavy instead it was to check if we can review and
identify issues in the code it generated so more like good knowledge of SQL and Java code.
Aptitude was easy to moderate with questions on permutations and combinations (balls w/o replacement),
bayes theorem, river problems, train and pole, etc. Standard problems on IndiaBIX nothing too out of scope.
I attempted around 55 / 70 questions and I assume I got 48-50 correct answers at minimum.
--- PAGE 3 ---

2. Technical Interview Round [ 44 candidates appeared ]

We were shortly given the shortlist and funnily enough it was the same number as last year. I was 3rd on my
panel which helped me for sure compared to being near the end of the list. I still maintain that luck plays a
pretty big role for which panel you get. Some of my friends got a panel where they asked 3-4 Java output
questions and asked them to explain it and ended the interview in 10-15 minutes, and a lot of candidates
were rejected in that time as well.
I went for my interview at 12 noon and greeted the interviewer after I went in. He had already asked for my
resume beforehand and went through it before I went in so it wasn't spontaneous. I wasn't asked for my
proper introduction but he asked how my OA round went, how would I assess how I performed, to which I
replied that it was definitely the best one I had given yet, all the questions were challenging but doable
because of my prep which felt satisfying. I was asked to take one project, go super deep into it, explain what
I did, it's architecture, basically whatever I want to talk about it.
I chose my GSoC project and started with the problem statement with how OpenMRS (my org) consisted of
about 800+ different API endpoints and how it was tough to document all the changes (Additions /
Deletions) that occurred so a new developer may understand what is the correct way to process it. He
interrupted me here and asked me what is an API, what are REST APIS in particular and what do their
different types mean. When I answered each method had a specific purpose he put me in a scenario where I
am designing an API where I have to take in a very very large input from the user, say for example a RAG
pipeline where the input is a 1000 lines so how would I exactly send it to the backend? I answered that GET
is the ideal method since it is the endpoint that returns a response, but I was fuzzy on the specifics on how
exactly big responses are passed. I said chunking might be an option which he didn't really like, I answered
back saying yes since the requests are not guaranteed to be ordered, it might fail so a chunk would disappear
etc. He asked me whether we can use a POST method for this purpose, to which I answered that it's a
workaround and not the ideal use of it. He told me to answer CAN we before moving onto SHOULD we? I
said yes it should be possible as we can fill in the fields with whatever input we get and send it to the
backend. But I was still kind of stuck on what he was asking but I came around. He asked me how exactly
but I wasn't able to pinpoint what he expected so we moved ahead.
He started with a DSA question asking me whether I knew about the fizzbuzz problem which I had heard the
name of but did not know the specifics which made him happy. I was given a list of numbers from 0 to 100,
if the number was divisible by 3, print 'fizz', if it was divisible by 5, print 'buzz', if it was divisible by both
then print 'fizzbuzz'. He wanted me to write it in any language but it should be clean and simple, not
complicated at all. He hated it. So I made a class and main function in Java and wrote a basic for loop from
O to 100 and suggested 3 if else conditions starting with the both divisible case and moving onto others. This
was the tricky part that he did not want me to use the both divisible if condition. I sat there and thought
about alternatives but I just couldn't. I kept trying and suggested an approach where I use a 2nd for loop to
go through the multiples first then go to the other ones which he rejected. Eventually he gave me a micro
hint to write the output for 3, 5 and 15 and observe it carefully. Then it clicked for me to use a StringBuilder
where if i % 3 then append fizz, if i % 5 then append buzz and print the string if it's not empty. He was
satisfied and moved onto the next problem.
I was given a singly linked list with a 100 nodes and I had to print the values of the nodes in reverse without
changing the input linked list in any way. He again iterated he liked simple not complicated and I should
keep it in mind. I suggested a way where we take a list, iterate through the linked list and adding values and
--- PAGE 4 ---
reversing the list in the end or backwards for loop whatever he wants. He asked me to think of more
approaches so I asked him if I should explore making a dummy linked list which he rejected. I suggested
using a stack, and with his reaction I understood that's what he wanted from me and he asked me how
exactly I would use it. Then he asked me to think more and I suggested using a deque which was the same
so I kept on thinking but couldn't think more. I came home and looked at it, and understood he wanted a
recursion approach which did not click for me but it's alright.
I was asked how good I was with DBMS for which I said I'm decent. He asked me the difference between
PRIMARY and UNIQUE keywords which I answered. I was then asked a query on an Employee table with
attributes of name, dept, age and salary to get the 2nd highest salary where the age is between 15 and 25 and
asked me to write the query. I wrote SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE age BETWEEN 15 AND 25
ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1; He read it, accepted it and we moved ahead.
He was also interested in knowing why java and go and why not some other language where I told him
language did not matter for me, I look at the requirements and decide accordingly, like I would use python
for ai projects because of vast library support, go for concurrency like my HTTP server project since I
wanted to understand how it worked which he appreciated and initially I only used what I knew but I don't
do that anymore.
We moved onto my projects and he asked me about kafka and how I used it in my project, I made a small
diagram showing my flow and showed him that kafka was ingestion intended and not user facing so I don't
have to wait for http requests to end and could do it async and made it for future features of notifs and email
services as well. I justified why I did not use rabbitmq and he asked me if we really need kafka then? We
could have a column or table in postgres where we handle it somehow but I told him the ease of doing it in
kafka made me choose this approach.
He asked me about redis and what is redis based distributed deduplication. I explained to him how redis puts
a lock on a request so multiple requests for the same thing do not go out. He asked me what if the request
failed then it would fail for everyone right? In the moment I told him yes it's a weakness but it's something I
could do like retry it afterwards.
One thing I'll mention was he was particularly happy that I used Golang and not python just for the sake of
everyone using it, because he worked entirely on go and it really made an impact on him. So in the end I
asked what was his role in the company and to elaborate on it for which he told me he worked on the
platforms team so managing the k8s which he told me were 300ish pods active. And he managed everything
cloud wise which was on prem but they partnered with google recently for ai purposes and cloud as well so
that's going on. I asked him about the open source summit and his thoughts on it so I could share some
interests that way. It really felt so natural talking to him and he was very knowledgeable for sure. GSoC
played a really big part in this round as he was aware of open source and it gave me a very big edge.

3. HR Round [19 candidates appeared]

My HR round started at around 3:30 PM, where it was taken by the MD and the HR head of ISS STOXX
The madam introduced herself and then proceeded to ask me about my hobbies, whether I'm planning to
watch odyssey, and asked me my favorite Nolan movies and I named a couple like the prestige and
--- PAGE 5 ---
oppenheimer etc. She asked me what else are you interested in, I said I follow everything so she asked me
my thoughts about the england vs argentina world cup semis.
She then asked me why I chose Computer Engineering, my biggest achievement yet where I referred to my
GSoC experience again and went very deep on how I prepped for it, submitted a proposal and worked on
such a great real world experience. She was very interested and asked me how it worked and I told her the
whole process about open source orgs and what they needed and how google provides stipend to new
contributors. Then the sir chimed in and asked me about how I chose this particular project, I told him I went
through each org and how they worked, and then I came to proposals where I researched on each one and
saw which one I could do naturally where ideas came so that's how. He asked me why I used a maven plugin
for example and if the org had asked me to use it. I was asked what was a mistake or difficulty that I had
faced during the project phase for which I described a real incident where I was not notifying my mentors
about my daily progress due to breakthroughs happening every 3-4 days not daily, but I worked on that habit
and learnt to show my work in a better way.
Throughout the round I focused on showcasing how much I value the non-coding parts. I highlighted that
the most important part of the project was not the coding phase but the architecture design and planning
phase where I spent a month since I needed a strong foundation. Also that documentation was really
essential as just creating a project was not useful but deep description really helps other developers to
continue maintaining it which is much more important.
They noticed that python was missing from my resume and asked why Al projects were omitted for which I
told him I explored Al as well where my mini and major projects are both Al domains showing I'm not just
one dimensional. It was just preference and I could adapt to anything that was given to me. He asked me
what if I was put in the backend domain or frontend would I have a preference? I answered that I have learnt
how to adapt to anything in the past 3 years so I could work with anything, language did not matter if the
fundamentals are clear which they liked.
They asked me what my family members did, where I lived and how would I travel to their office where I
told them I'm used to coming to college and it's the same route so completely doable. She also asked me why
I didn't go into the navy like my dad for which I said I don't like complacency and a government job felt like
that so didn't go there.
In the end they asked me if I had any questions for which I told them I really liked what my previous
interviewer did and can I put a preference to work under them for which they told me I'll go through
training, assessment after which if requirements exist then sure but they can't guarantee anything. I also
asked them about their products of esg and corporate governance and do they see a meaningful difference
between them for which the guy answered they're different domains and they do answer different questions
even though they're both governance.
Out of the 19 candidates, 12 were offered the role. Honestly it came to fine margins here because everyone's
HR went well so it's a shame.
