Stay Calm and Confident: Even when things seemed chaotic or rushed (e.g., back-to-back interviews with
little prep time), remaining calm and composed helped me think clearly and perform better.
Be Ready for Variability: The process can be unpredictable, with interview sequences or timings changing at
the last minute. Be flexible and adapt quickly.
Keep All Documents Ready: Arrive with your resume, laptop, and a notebook. Take notes during company
presentations; you may be able to reference these during interviews.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Don't Be Discouraged by Tricky Questions: Some questions may be designed to test your composure rather
than your technical skills. Answer honestly, and don't be afraid to admit when you don't know something.
Prioritize Rest Before the Interview: Try to get enough sleep, especially after intense last-minute
preparation, so you're fresh for the interview day.
Practice Explaining Projects Clearly: Practice talking about your projects in depth, including technical
implementation details (like naming database tables/columns and writing queries), as this is a common focus
area.
journey.howSecured:
First, there was an OA round. Then the second round was a technical interview round lasting around 35-40 minutes.
The third round was also a technical round. There was no HR round this time.

1. Round 1(OA): 128 Candidates appeared for these round

This round was 45 minutes long and consisted of 20 MCQ questions and 5 SQL queries that you had to execute and
submit. For this round, the first 18 questions were on JAVA, C, and C++ concepts. Study OOPS concepts as they are
essential for this round as well as the second round. Also practice OOPS questions in both JAVA and C++ languages.
Then practice questions where you have to predict the output. You can practice these types of questions on GFG. I
strongly suggest studying JAVA, OOPS, and C++ from the InterviewBit website as it helped me a lot. The next 2
questions were on MySQL and DBMS concepts, so for these I also suggest studying from InterviewBit. For the 5 SQL
queries, practice the TOP 50 SQL questions from Leetcode-they will be more than enough. I solved about 45-46 of
the Top 50 questions the night before the OA, as we learned about the OA pattern only one day before the test. The 5
SQL queries carried the highest weightage in the OA, so give them high priority. I was able to solve all 5 queries and
scored the 2nd highest in the entire OA test. The OA results came the next day in the afternoon, and 38 students were
selected for interviews scheduled for 29/07/2025-giving us only 1.5 days to prepare for the second round.

2. Round 2 38 students were selected

All 38 selected students were asked to arrive at 8 o'clock in the morning with their resumes and laptops, dressed in
formals. First, a PPT presentation was held at 9 o'clock by the Barclays Director. Take a notebook with you and try to
note all the Barclays representatives' names as it will be helpful, and also note the points presented in the PPT that you
think are important. Then the first technical interview started at 10:30 AM. We were called in batches of 6 students as
there were 6 panelists, and my interview started at 11:10 AM. When I entered the panelist's room, he didn't introduce
himself nor ask for my introduction-he just took my resume and read it for 2-3 minutes, then asked me directly to
describe one of my projects, so I started describing my project. After I described my project, he asked about some
legal aspects of one of the features. This was just a tricky question designed to lower your confidence. Don't fall for
these types of questions-answer honestly and confidently with what you know, and if you don't know something, just
say no. They won't deduct marks for these types of questions as they only test your confidence. Then he asked 2
normal HR-based questions like what I had done when I encountered a bug in projects, and asked me to describe a
time when I collaborated with a team and how I managed effective communication among team members. After
hearing my answer, he asked me what I would do if I were a team project leader managing 53 people when they all
start working on the project. Then he asked me to describe what GitHub is. Next, he gave me the first coding question,
which I had to solve: swap two numbers without using a third variable. After that, he gave me 2 pattern printing
--- PAGE 2 ---
questions using stars (*) with the constraint that I could only use two for loops and not more than that. I initially
struggled with the second question, but after thinking for about 5 minutes, I was able to solve it. While writing the
solution, explain to the interviewer how you are solving it and what your approach is, as they want to see your thought
process rather than just the correct solution. After this, he said my interview was done and asked me to leave. (He
didn't ask if I had any questions, so I left.)
3.
Round 3 Name 19 were selected
For the second round, things were a bit chaotic for me. My first round finished around 11:40 AM, after which we were
told to sit in room 205 and not interact with each other. About 10-15 minutes after I finished, someone came into the
room and told me I was being called to the TPO office with my resume. I rushed to the office and was surprised to
learn that my second interview was starting immediately-especially since more than half of the people still hadn't
finished their first round, and no one else had been called for their second interview yet. They asked me to wait for 5
minutes because my interviewer wasn't there yet, so I began preparing. I thought it might be an HR round, so I asked
the TPC staff who would interview me, and they said it would be the Director himself. I was a bit panicked, but soon
the Director arrived and my second interview started at 12:00.
Just like the previous round, he didn't ask me to introduce myself. He reviewed my resume for about 2 minutes and
then asked me to describe one of my projects. It turned out to be the same project I'd discussed in the first round. Since
it was mostly a MySQL project, he asked me to name all the tables, then the column names for each table, and then
about the features I implemented and how I implemented both the backend and frontend. He also asked me to write an
SQL query related to my project and whether I had implemented a specific feature; I honestly told him no. Always be
truthful-interviewers are very experienced and can tell if you're not being honest. Check out the RISES principles on
the Barclays page: one of the principles is Integrity-be honest with them and with others as well.
He spent almost 30 minutes asking about that one project. Then, he asked if I had any favorite project I'd like to talk
about. I described my latest project, and he asked one basic question about it. After that, the interview wrapped up and
he asked if I had any questions for him-I asked a question I had prepared beforehand. Always prepare thoughtful
questions to ask the interviewer and avoid anything trivial.
My interview ended around 12:50, and I was told to return to room 205. Up to that point, I was the only person who
had completed the second interview, which made me happy but also anxious because I hadn't had any preparation
time. The official second interviews for the other candidates didn't begin until after 2 PM, and results for round 1 were
announced around 4 PM. I know it all seemed quite chaotic, but try to stay calm-this kind of thing happens a lot. At
7 PM, round two officially finished. I had to wait for around 7 hours just to hear the result, and by 6 PM, I was getting
impatient and panicky because there were no updates for hours. Take my advice: remain calm and don't panic, even
though I know it's hard. Staying calm and confident really helps in these situations because unexpected things can
happen to anyone.
At 7:30, they started calling the names of candidates (from the 19 students left) and told us to sit in a room. Then, they
played a bit of a prank on us before telling us that we were all selected. It was one of the best moments of my life and
made all the waiting worth it.
A total of 16 students were selected for the Summer Internship

The Wissen Technologies placement process consisted of an Online Assessment (OA) followed by two
rounds of interviews. The OA was conducted on 31 July 2026, both interview rounds were conducted on 1st
Aug 2026, and the final result was announced on 3 August 2026.
The overall process was:

1. Online Assessment (OA) - 31/07/2026

2. Technical Interview - 1/08/2026

3. Director Round - 1/08/2026

1. Online Assessment (OA) | No of candidates who appeared for this round]

The Online Assessment was conducted on 31 July 2026. All eligible candidates were allowed to sit for
the OA. The assessment consisted of:

• 2 DSA coding questions

• 1 SQL question

• 5 MCQs

DSA Questions
The first DSA question was based on Dynamic Programming (DP). The second DSA question was based on
a Binary Tree. Both questions required understanding the underlying concept rather than simply
implementing a standard algorithm. Therefore, it is important to be comfortable with the fundamentals of
DSA and be able to identify which data structure or algorithm is appropriate for a given problem.
SQL Question
There was one SQL question based on:
--- PAGE 2 ---

• CTE (Common Table Expressions)

• GROUP BY

The question required understanding how to structure a query using a CTE and then perform aggregation
using GROUP BY.
There were 5 MCQS. The questions included:

• Finding the output of a given piece of code

• Aptitude-based questions

• Programming/technical concepts

Preparation Suggestions
For coding preparation, practicing medium-level problems on LeetCode, or similar platforms is useful.
Along with solving problems, focus on understanding the approach and complexity rather than memorizing
solutions.
For SQL, practice do solve sql 50

2. Technical Interview (40 candidates appeared)

The first interview round was a Technical Interview and was conducted on 1 Aug 2026. The interviewer
focused primarily on Data Structures, Database Design, SQL and choosing appropriate data structures for a
given problem. The interview consisted of three major sections.
Question 1 - DSA Array List / Bucket Formation
The interviewer first gave a problem involving a list of numbers:
[1000, 2000, 500, 2500, 3000]
The requirement was to create buckets such that the sum of the elements in each bucket is not more than
5000.
The resulting buckets were:
[[1000, 2000, 500], [2500], [3000]]
The interviewer then asked a follow-up question. If a bucket contains 3 or more elements and all the
elements are divisible by both 5 and 10, then that bucket should be split into individual elements.
For example:
[1000, 2000, 500]
contains three elements and all of them are divisible by 5 and 10, so it should be split into:
[11000], [2000], [500], [2500], [30001]
Question 2 - Database Schema Design
The interviewer then gave a database-design scenario involving:

• Actors

• Films

• Multiple sequels for each film

• Actors appearing in multiple films

--- PAGE 3 ---

• IMDb ratings for films/sequels

The task was to design an appropriate relational database schema.
I designed separate tables for:

• Actor

• Film

• Cast/Actor-Film Mapping

• Sequel

The mapping table handled the many-to-many relationship between actors and films, while the
sequel-related table maintained the relationship between a film and its sequels. The interviewer then asked
me to write SQL queries based on the schema I had designed. He also asked several follow-up questions
about my database design, including why I had created the tables in that particular way and how the
relationships between the entities were being maintained.
Question 3 - Choosing the Appropriate Data Structure
The interviewer then gave a scenario involving logs with timestamps. The question was essentially about
how to efficiently access logs corresponding to a particular timestamp. The appropriate data structure
discussed was a B-Tree, because it provides efficient searching and indexing, with operations typically
taking O(log n) time. The discussion also involved the idea of organizing/indexing the log data so that a
specific timestamp could be accessed efficiently rather than scanning all the logs.
Preparation Suggestions
For this round, I would strongly recommend revising:

• Arrays and ArrayLists

• HashMap and HashSet

• Trees

• B-Trees / database indexing

• Time and space complexity

• SQL

• DBMS

3. Director Round (16 candidates appeared for this round)

The second and final interview was a Director Round. This round lasted significantly longer and was more
like a technical discussion combined with resume discussion rather than a traditional question-and-answer
interview. The interviewer first asked me to walk through my resume. He asked about my work experience at
Adhyayan Classes, where I had taught students and also worked on developing a portfolio website for the
classes. I explained that I had developed and hosted the website and mentioned the technology/deployment
setup, including Vercel, Render, GoDaddy domain. The interviewer was particularly interested in the fact that
I had worked with the GoDaddy domain and deployment process, which led to further discussion about the
project. The interviewer then moved to my project section and asked about my project PeerMint. One of the
major discussions was around JWT authentication.
He asked about:

• What JWT is

--- PAGE 4 ---

• How JWT works

• Different ways of storing JWTs

• Advantages and disadvantages of different storage methods

• Security concerns

• CSRF

• XSS

• How different attacks can affect authentication systems

The questions were not limited to definitions. The interviewer focused on understanding whether I knew
why a particular approach should be used and what its security implications were. The interviewer then
asked about REST APIs and whether I knew about any alternatives. I discussed REST and also mentioned
GraphQL. The interviewer also asked me to explain DNS resolution. This required explaining what happens
when a user enters a domain name and how the domain gets resolved to the corresponding IP address. The
interviewer then moved to my third project and asked me to explain RAG (Retrieval-Augmented
Generation). I explained the complete pipeline starting from the basics, including What RAG is, Document
processing, Chunking, Embeddings, Vector representations, Vector search, Retrieval, Passing retrieved
context to the LLM, Generation of the final response, pgvector and its role in storing/searching vector
embeddings. The interviewer asked questions throughout the explanation, so it was important to understand
every component rather than simply knowing the definition of RAG.
The interviewer then asked me about my favorite programming language. I answered Java. He then asked
me to design and write a Cab Booking System in Java on paper. I was expected to write the solution with
proper Classes, Objects, Data structures, Methods, Java syntax, Appropriate data structures.
The interviewer continuously monitored my approach and asked follow-up questions while I was writing the
solution. For example, when I initially considered a particular approach, he asked whether a HashMap could
be used to achieve faster access. This tested whether I could evaluate and improve my design while solving
the problem. The interviewer then asked me to write a function that would return the cars near a user's
current location in sorted order, along with the time required for each car to reach the user.
I represented the input conceptually as:
getCars(Car[ll] cars, int[]I] grid)
The Car[][] matrix represented the locations of cars.

• If a car was present at a particular cell, the cell contained a Car object.

• If no car was present, the cell contained null.

The int[]I] grid contained the time required to reach each corresponding cell.
For example, if:
grid[1][]] = 12
then reaching cell (1,1) would require 12 minutes.
The task was to determine the cars relevant to the user's current location (x,y) and return them along with the
corresponding time required to reach the user.
I used a structure conceptually represented as:
HashMap<Car, Integer>
where the Car represented the vehicle and the integer represented the estimated time required to reach the
user's location. The interviewer also asked follow-up questions about the approach and the data structures
--- PAGE 5 ---
being used. I wrote the solution on approximately three pages of paper, including the class structure,
methods, data structures and algorithm. The interviewer continuously interrupted with questions and
suggestions, so the round tested not only coding ability but also the ability to think, adapt and improve a
solution while being questioned. This round was considerably different from the first technical interview. It
was more of a discussion and problem-solving round.

Placement opportunity at Wissen Technologies. Finally 9 candidates were offered the job

Overall 5 rounds were conducted, all in a single day. All interviews were conducted online, but from
college. Their HR communicated everything and coordinated the whole process via a WhatsApp group. In
general, try to have a good grasp of basic debugging and schema design, along with core CS fundamentals.
Resume Shortlisting: Initial shortlisting was based on resume. While applying on Superset, they had also
asked specifically about your internship experience. It's not confirmed but candidates having no internship
experience were not selected so that was the distinguishing criterion. Many people must have applied, but
around 100 were shortlisted, with the list being shared a day prior.

1. Rapid Fire MCQ Round (101 students appeared for this round) - 10 minutes

It was very frantic as expected from its name. There were around 50 multiple choice questions related to
core CS fundamentals, basic programming languages and related concepts like OOPS (including loads of
Python). It contained technical questions on Java, Python and C++, like determining the time complexity,
space complexity and output of code snippets, some questions on basic OS and CCN like deadlocks and
DNS, some Github commands like listing all branches, stash and pop, some questions on prefix and postfix
increment operators and some basic data structure questions like which data structure is LIFO, FIFO etc. We
were sent a Google Forms link in our mail at around 10 am and had to submit it in around 10-12 minutes.
The only constraint was time since many questions weren't necessarily straightforward and needed some
time to think. I believe it was expected to properly solve around 20-25 questions and if possible, mark all
other questions as let's say B since there was no negative marking. We had been asked to attempt as much as
possible since it was designed to be fast paced and clumsy.

2. APT Debugging Round (52 students appeared for this round) - 30 minutes

We were split in 4 slots each having 13 students. It's unclear whether shortlisting order was based on the
previous round's results but it's obviously more beneficial to be placed in the earlier slots or panels. We were
sent the shortlists and G-Meet links for each candidate which we had to join from any room in the TPO.
There were 2 interviewers in it. They asked to choose any language of choice from Django, Golang, FastAPI
or Node. I chose Django. This is because I had read the previous year's interview experience and both the
selected candidates had chosen Django so I had more clue in general about what to expect. (obviously any
language works and it's not compulsory to choose Django only). I had read all basic frameworks, file
structures, common errors etc in this language a day before. Then the interviewer sent a link to a small
existing Django codebase containing an Attendance Tracker project, with a README file containing
instructions on what was to be performed. To my surprise, the same scenario and the project had been asked
to me which was also asked in the previous year. So obviously I was very fortunate since I knew beforehand
about the bugs and their solutions. Initially, while starting the server, there were 2 bugs that were required to
--- PAGE 2 ---
be fixed. One bug was in the models.py, a syntax error in the choices parameter passed to a
models. CharField.
Expected syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices-[('active', 'Status active'), ('inactive',
'Status inactive')])
Given syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices=['active', 'inactive])
The second bug was in the views.py, another syntax error in which the key of a python dictionary was being
accessed incorrectly.
Expected syntax: [s['name"] for s in students]
Given syntax: [s.name for s in students]
Both interviewers were very helpful and it's advisable to constantly communicate your thought process with
them. They will guide you for sure instead of an awkward silence. I remember there was some issue related
with permission viewing in settings.py file but they explicitly told me to allow * in hosts.
After fixing the errors, I started the server. Then, I was asked to implement an API endpoint to mark a
student's attendance. Time was running out so I explained my basic thoughts (like unique together
constraint, ORM, why to create a foreign key in a separate table etc). Note that they will also ask lots of
conceptual questions about the language so just debugging won't do. For example, they asked me many
basic questions in general (for example, why do we do makemigrations before migrate). Not many people
could start the server itself so I knew that I was progressing to the next round. Obviously, it's not expected to
know the syntax or actual code of the language, we were allowed to use Google (including that Al mode
which automatically opens on searching anything). They cared about overall approach and thought process
more than actual debugging or coding. Also it had been noticed that people in the subsequent slots were
asked much deeper conceptual questions since it was assumed that they already knew the bugs of their
respective language from the previous rounds' candidates so it was a bit of a disadvantage for them. Most
people had chosen Node or FastAPI. I think that debugging was sufficient to proceed to further rounds, API
writing was additional but no one could completely finish that due to time constraints. Overall the whole
process started around 10.30 and we were given further shortlists at around 3 pm. (I think 2-3 students were
given a choice of app development in this round as well due to their resumes but they chose debugging only)

3. DSA and Schema Design (16 students appeared for this round) - 75 minutes

Last year, they were separate rounds but this time, they were merged in 1. We were sent the shortlist at
around 3 and split into 2 slots of 8 panels. (I don't think it's a coincidence that all the final selected students
were from slot 1 in this round). Again, each panel had 2 interviewers. They were very friendly, made me
comfortable, asked for basic introduction and started with the DSA question. I was asked to open a Google
Docs and try to communicate my thought process from there. My question was a bit ambiguous and open
-ended. It was to design a class for shuffling n songs when each song can be repeated after at least k other
songs. I asked lots of clarifying questions about the problem. The intended solution was to use a queue (to
keep track of order) and a set (for checking duplicates in k songs). I couldn't exactly reach it but explained
my thought process as clearly as I could. They asked lots of other basic related questions like time
complexity, pros and cons of the provided solution etc. The discussion lasted around 30 minutes and they
were generally very helpful and responsive. The schema design followed next. It was a pretty basic problem
around a ticket booking system. They dwelled deep into types of attributes, entities, relationships etc (basic
ER diagram intricacies). They also expected some low level code connecting classes and their objects,
which I couldn't implement properly. All in all, again they were more interested in the thought process,
approach and communication clarity rather than actual coding. Other DSA problems asked were standard
like Trapping Rainwater, multi source BFS etc. The schema design is relatively easier for everyone. The
--- PAGE 3 ---
round ended with me asking some questions regarding scamming by employers in the app and how do they
monitor it and about legal compliances being a startup.

4. HR and Culture Fit Round (6 students appeared for this round) - 30 minutes each

Immediately after my interview, I got a call from their HR about scheduling the further interviews and was
sent the Meet link along with the time. Both interviews were very chill honestly. They asked me to be
myself and not fake anything for the sake of 'cracking' the interview. Standard questions were asked like the
highest moments in life, the lowest ones, best projects, hackathon experiences, college experiences, daily
routine, explaining 1 project to a 5 year-old etc. Questions like comfort regarding relocating to Bangalore
and working in a high pace environment with less 'work-life balance' were also asked. Overall, it was just a
friendly and honest talk regarding compatibility of the company and the candidate. Basic questions from
resumes like minor degree, motivation to do engineering and the trends of AI were also discussed. Both
rounds felt more personal and absolutely non-technical. So all in all, just be yourself here, maintain some
basic confidence and stay as honest as you can.
Overall the whole process ended around 8 pm (special mention to TPCs as well who were also very helpful
and patient throughout the day). We got the result the next day around 6 pm. 5 students were given the offer
finally.

Process Date: 9th July (OA), 10th July 2026 (Interviews)

Preparation Tips

• During the months of June-July, I used to pick one topic each day and revise all the

problems from Striver's Sheet under that topic. (Try not to look at the solution
immediately. First, attempt to come up with the brute-force approach, then improve it
step by step until you reach the optimal solution).

• If you're starting your preparation late, don't panic. Focus on giving your best instead of

worrying about the time left. Divide your day into DSA, core subjects (DBMS, OS, CN,
OOPS, SQL, etc.), and aptitude so that you make consistent progress in all areas.

• One common mistake I see is that people spend most of their time watching DSA videos

instead of solving problems themselves. Watching solutions alone won't significantly
improve your problem-solving skills because, during interviews and OAs, you'll need
to come up with the approach on your own. Instead, use Al or YouTube to find important
problems under each topic, and then make sure you solve those problems completely by
yourself. For the remaining questions, it's fine to read the solution or watch an
explanation to cover more topics efficiently.(Read the interview experiences of
companies which visit campus and accordingly make a list of topics which should be
prioritized first)

• Internships definitely help, as interviewers often spend a significant amount of time

discussing your work experience. However, don't worry if you don't have one. In that
case, make sure your projects are strong enough to demonstrate your technical skills and
problem-solving ability.

• Prepare concise notes in advance. Before the placement season starts, make short

revision notes for every subject. They become extremely useful before OAs and
interviews when you don't have time to go through entire resources again.

• Maintain a separate aptitude formula sheet. Keep all important formulas and

commonly used concepts in one place so that you can revise them quickly before an OA.

• For SDE projects, Be prepared to explain:

• Database schema

--- PAGE 2 ---

• REST APIs and their purpose

• Why you chose your tech stack

• Why you selected a particular database

• Challenges faced during development

• Fallback mechanisms and error handling

• Possible improvements if you had to redesign the system

• For ML projects: Be prepared to explain your dataset, model architecture, training

pipeline, loss function, optimizer, evaluation metrics, hyperparameters, and why you
chose your approach over alternative methods.
Auxo Al Process:

1. Resume Shortlisting

The process started with resume shortlisting. Although I don't know the exact number of
applicants, there was a good amount of competition. My advice would be to tailor your resume
according to the job description. Since this was an AI Engineer role, I had included two AI/ML
projects and one SDE project on my resume .Based on my experience, I would recommend
prioritizing AI/ML based projects on your resume if you're applying for this role, as they
significantly increase your chances of getting shortlisted. Also make sure your ATS score is at
least 70. (Adding quantifiable metrics no of users using your platform, ML project results etc)
helps increase your ATS score).
Results: 150 students moved forward to the Online Assessment.

2. Online Assessment (150 students appeared)

This year, the OA duration was 90 minutes and consisted of:

• 25 MCQs

• 3 Coding Questions

The assessment was conducted offline on CodeChef (Java was available this year).
MCQs
I found the MCQs to be fairly easy. They were a mix of Machine Learning, LLMs, and
Aptitude.
Some of the ML/LLM topics included:

• What is a token?

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Context window/context size

• Overfitting

• Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning

• General Al concepts

The aptitude section mainly consisted of:

• Analogies

• Coding-Decoding

• Ratio & Proportion

• Basic logical reasoning

Overall, if you have a good understanding of basic ML concepts and practice aptitude
beforehand, the MCQ section is quite manageable.
Coding Questions
Q1. Frequency-Based String Filtering
You are given a string and an integer k. Return a new string containing only the characters whose
frequency is greater than or equal to k, arranged in sorted order.
This was a fairly straightforward problem and could be solved using a TreeMap (or HashMap +
sorting).
Q2. Maximum Weight within Budget
A person has k kibbles to spend, and you're given an array of (cost, weight) pairs for oranges.
The task was to find the maximum total weight of oranges that could be purchased without
exceeding the budget.
This is essentially a 0/1 Knapsack problem.
I solved it using 2D Dynamic Programming.
Q3. Reconstruct Travel Route
A person had notes for a trip in the format:
Mumbai Goa 500
Goa Bangalore 600
Bangalore Chennai 400
The notes had become shuffled, and we had to reconstruct the correct travel sequence and
--- PAGE 4 ---
calculate the total travel cost.
Unfortunately, I couldn't attempt this question due to lack of time.
I was able to solve 2 coding questions completely.
From what I observed, everyone who had solved 2 coding questions completely was shortlisted
for the next round.
Additional Points for the OA

• I would recommend attempting the assessment on Google Chrome. I initially used

Firefox, but I experienced a few minor issues with the platform. Chrome seemed to work
more smoothly.

• Unlike platforms like LeetCode, you need to write the complete code yourself, including

taking input from standard input and printing the output in the required format.

• Also check the network connectivity beforehand. Once you start the test and if there is

any network lag you won't be able to change the network so it's better to test it before the
exam.
15 students were shortlisted for the technical interviews.
We got the list of shortlisted students at around 8PM and the next day from 10 AM interviews
were going to start.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (15 students appeared)(40-45 mins)

The interview started with a brief introduction, after which the interviewer immediately started
discussing my resume. They covered all three of my projects during the interview.
Project Discussion :
The majority of the interview was centered around my ML projects.
Federated Learning Project
The interviewer wasn't familiar with the concept of Federated Learning, so I first explained the
complete idea, why it is used, and how it differs from traditional centralized learning.
Since I had mentioned using a Reinforcement Learning (RL) Agent in my project, they went
deeper into that and asked:

• Why did you use Reinforcement Learning?

• How does the RL agent work?

--- PAGE 5 ---

• Explain the complete RL loop used in the project

• How does the agent improve over time?

SDE Project
From my backend project, they asked questions like:

• Role of Redis in my project

• Difference between Docker and Virtual Machines

• Working of Kubernetes

Small Language Model (SLM) Project
For my SLM project, they asked:

• What was the dataset format?

• Which model did you use?

• Number of model parameters

• Overall training pipeline

• What is Perplexity?

• Why did I use Mixed Precision Training?

Internship Experience
Since I had two internships on my resume, they also asked me to explain both.
For my AI Engineering Internship, they asked about the Al systems and automation solutions I
had worked on, what were the hurdles faced while development, and what security constraints
were used.
For my SDE Internship, they asked me to give a high-level overview of the projects, my
responsibilities, and the technologies I used.
SQL Questions
Towards the end, I was asked a few SQL questions, including:

• Types of JOINs

• Primary Key vs Foreign Key

• GROUP BY

• PARTITION BY

At the end of the interview, when the interviewer asked if I had any questions, I had a technical
discussion based on the work I was currently doing.
--- PAGE 6 ---
I was working on an Agentic Al project at the time, so towards the end of the interview, I asked
the interviewer how their team handles hallucinations and error propagation in multi-agent
workflows, where incorrect outputs from one agent can affect all downstream agents. This led to
a very interesting technical discussion. The interviewer first asked me to explain my project in
more detail, after which he shared some of the techniques their team follows to improve
reliability. Based on his explanation, I asked a few follow-up questions.
My Advice: Be prepared to justify every single technology, model, library, and term you
mention on your resume.
Even if you've worked with any LLM APIs, know exactly:

• Which model you used

• Why did you choose that model

• Whether it was an API-based or open-source model.

• If it's an open-source model, know its approximate number of parameters, architecture,

and why it suited your use case.
The same applies to ML projects. If you've mentioned a model or algorithm, be prepared to
explain:

• Dataset

• Model architecture

• Loss function (with intuition and formula)

• Optimizer (with intuition and formula)

• Evaluation metrics

• Learning rate scheduler

• Training pipeline

• Hyperparameters

• Why did you select that particular approach over alternatives

Also one of the panelists was from a consulting background. So he was asking a little tough
guesstimates in 1st round itself so be prepared for it.

4. Technical + Business Round (8 students appeared) (30-40 mins)

Instead of asking questions from multiple projects, the interviewer picked one of my Al
Engineering internship projects and went into great depth.
The interviewer first asked me to explain my project from start to finish.
After that, they asked several follow-up questions, including:

• The complete end-to-end workflow of the system.

--- PAGE 7 ---

• Why I designed the architecture the way I did.

• What fallback mechanisms I had implemented if one component failed.

• The major challenges I faced while building the system.

• How I identified those issues and the approach I took to solve them.

The discussion was less about definitions and more about understanding how I think while
building production AI systems.
The interviewer then moved to my ML projects.
For my projects, he asked me to justify almost every important design choice(Optimization
technique, loss function etc).
Then for my SLM project, they asked questions about the model architecture, such as:

• How positional embeddings are added.

• Where were the positional embeddings introduced in the model.

• What are positional embeddings initialized as in the pipeline

• Overall transformer flow.

• Training pipeline.

Guesstimate:
Towards the end, I was given a business case study.
The interviewer asked:
"Suppose you are the founder of Uber. You want to introduce a new pricing model
where every driver is paid ?X per kilometre. How would you determine the value of
X such that existing Uber drivers are satisfied with their earnings while also making
the platform attractive enough for drivers working with competing companies to
switch to Uber?"
This wasn't a mathematics question with a single correct answer. The interviewer wanted to
understand my approach. Also all the details won't be given to you at the start. It's important
to ask the right questions as you are moving towards the answer.
At the end of the interview, I asked him : What metrics does AuxoAl use to evaluate the quality
of responses generated by Al models and When a client approaches AuxoAl with a problem,
how do you determine whether investing in an Al solution is actually worthwhile, More
specifically, how do you measure the ROI or business impact of the AI system after it's deployed.
At the end of the day at around 6 PM when all round 2 interviews were finished, we were
informed that 5 candidates had been selected for an HR interview which is going to be online
later that evening.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Later that evening, instead of conducting a separate HR round, the company directly informed all
the shortlisted candidates that we had been selected.
Resources

• SQL: I had practiced SQL 50 on leetcode. For revising SQL concepts quickly, I found

Apna College's SQL One Shot to be helpful (Also make sure you make good notes to
revise before interviews ).

• DSA: I primarily used Striver's DSA Sheet along with NeetCode for preparation.

Although Striver's sheet itself covers almost every important DSA concept, NeetCode is a
great supplementary resource for additional practice and explanations. (For Auxo I feel
Striver's sheet is more than enough)

• Aptitude: I had practiced from IndiaBix and Code Step By Step YT channel

• Guesstimates: Be sure to prepare guesstimates thoroughly. There are plenty of good

You Tube videos that explain the approach to solving them.

• ML : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/machine-learning/. And for

reading in detail about transformers and all I prefer reading blogs on Medium they
provide content in depth.

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 1(03 July 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 2 (03 July 2026)

• HR Interview (03 July 2026)

• Result Declaration (03 July 2026)

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The PPT, held on 24th June, covered the three open roles - Banking, FinTech, and Corporate
Risk along with the responsibilities and skill sets expected for each. This session is worth taking
seriously: several interview questions later circled back to points discussed here, and referencing
it shows genuine interest in the role. I took detailed notes, which helped me a lot in later rounds.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [122 Candidates Appeared ]

The Online Assessment was conducted on the AON platform from home and consisted of 30
questions to be completed in 45 minutes with negative marking (+2/-1).
Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Banking
MCQ Assessment - 45 Qtns - 45 Mins - 45 Marks
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounts - 10 Qtns
Section 2: Market Awareness - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Quantitative Aptitude - 15 Qtns
Section 4: English Usage - 10 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
It included Quantitative Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, and basic analytical questions and
was conducted online through AON's proctored platform.
The quantitative section covered topics such as Time & Work, Trains, Pipes & Cisterns,
Permutations & Combinations, Calendars, Percentages, and Profit & Loss. While the
concepts were manageable, the biggest challenge was completing the paper within the time limit.

2. Technical Interview Round 1[32 Students appeared for this round]

Around 32 candidates were shortlisted for the first technical interview. The interviews were
conducted across 7 panels, each consisting of two interviewers. My interview lasted
approximately 25 minutes and was almost entirely resume-driven.
The interview began with "Tell me about yourself." I would strongly recommend preparing this
answer well, as it sets the direction of the interview. My introduction focused on my interests in
finance, analytics, technology, and leadership, which naturally guided the discussion towards
my strengths.
--- PAGE 3 ---
The panel then asked me to walk them through my resume, beginning with my internships.
Research Internship - SPJIMR
We discussed my research on greenwashing, where I explained the concept, my role in
conducting literature reviews and stakeholder outreach, and the risks associated with misleading
sustainability claims. This led to a discussion on different types of risks, including Credit,
Market, Operational, Liquidity, Compliance, Reputational, and Regulatory Risk, along
with real-world examples.
Web Development Internship
Next, the interviewers discussed my internship at the SWIS Foundation, focusing on the
challenges I faced while redesigning the website, the REST APIS I integrated, backend
automation, and my overall problem-solving approach.
Projects
The interviewers spent the majority of the interview discussing my projects.
Financial Modeling & Valuation (DCF)
They first asked about my DCF Valuation project.
Some of the questions included:

• Why would you use EV/EBITDA instead of a P/E multiple?

• Why are EV-based multiples generally preferred while comparing peer FMCG

companies?

• What conclusions did you derive from your valuation?

The discussion revolved around valuation methodologies, peer comparison, and understanding
the assumptions behind financial models rather than simply memorizing formulas.
InvoSmart - GST Billing & Accounting Platform
They then moved to my InvoSmart project and asked me to explain the complete workflow.
The discussion included:

• OCR-based bill extraction.

• GST and non-GST invoicing.

• Why PostgreSQL was chosen.

• Tally-compatible journal exports.

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Backend architecture.

• APIs used for automation.

The interviewers wanted to understand how each component fit together to solve a practical
business problem rather than testing framework-specific knowledge.
Banking Stock Market Analysis Dashboard
This project generated the most discussion.
I explained how I analyzed 25,000+ trading records across five NSE-listed banks using Power
BI and DAX.
The interviewers asked:

• On what basis did you calculate the performance of each bank?

• Which financial metrics did you compare?

• How did you evaluate risk and return?

• What conclusions did you draw from your analysis?

I explained that the dashboard primarily analyzed stock performance using opening price,
closing price, daily price movement, trading volume, returns, volatility, and consistency of
stock performance over time. I also described how interactive visualizations helped compare
different banks on multiple parameters, making it easier to identify trends, relative stability, and
risk-return characteristics.
Case Competitions & Risk Management
The discussion then shifted to my national case competition experiences, including CRED's IPO
strategy, Greenko's sustainability initiatives, and an inclusivity-focused business strategy,
where the interviewers were interested in my approach to solving business problems.
Since I had mentioned risk mitigation, they further asked about different risk mitigation
strategies, Basel Accords, and how regulations evolved after the 2008 Global Financial Crisis.
I supported my answers using real-world banking examples.
Why JPMorgan Chase?
Towards the end, they asked:

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

• Apart from being one of the world's largest investment banks, what do you know about

the company?
--- PAGE 5 ---
Questions for the Interviewers
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions.
I asked: "If I were selected for this internship, what skills or areas should I focus on before
joining so that I can contribute effectively from Day One? Also, are there any areas where
you think candidates typically need improvement for this roleại
2.
Technical Interview Round 2 [ 16 Students appeared for this round]
Duration: Approximately 25-30 minutes
Panel: 2 Interviewers
The second technical interview was significantly more in-depth than the first. While Round 1
focused on understanding my experiences, this round tested my technical knowledge and the
reasoning behind every project on my resume. Almost every answer was followed by multiple
follow-up questions, making it a highly interactive discussion.
The interview began with "Tell us about yourself" and "Walk us through your resume," after
which the discussion moved into technical concepts.
Technical Fundamentals
Since several of my projects involved data analytics and machine learning, the interviewers
asked me about my technical stack and programming experience.
They first asked me about my primary programming language, followed by questions on my
proficiency in Python and SQL. Instead of simply asking me to rate my skills, they wanted me
to justify my ratings with examples of projects where I had applied them.
The discussion then covered SQL queries and joins, their use cases, and practical applications.
They also asked me to explain the complete machine learning pipeline, from data preprocessing
and EDA to feature engineering, model selection, evaluation, visualization, and the Python
libraries used throughout the workflow.
Financial Modeling
The panel then revisited my DCF Valuation project, but this time the discussion was
significantly more detailed.
Some of the topics covered included:
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Assumptions used while building the model

• Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)

• Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)

• Beta

• Peer company selection

• Valuation multiples

• Final investment conclusion

Rather than checking whether I remembered formulas, the interviewers wanted to understand
why I had made certain assumptions and whether I could defend my conclusions logically.
Al & Agent-Based Systems
One of the interviewers asked whether I had worked on any Al/agent-based systems. Although
this project was not mentioned on my resume, it turned into one of the most engaging
discussions of the interview.
I explained that the system consisted of:

• A three-tier Al architecture

• Seven specialized Al agents

• A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) layer

• An LLM layer using Grok, with the output of each layer acting as the input for the next

Next, instead of discussing only the architecture, the interviewer wanted to understand why we
built the project. I explained that:

• The idea originated from challenges I encountered during my web development

internship.

• We identified repetitive workflows that could be automated intelligently.

• This led us to design an Al-powered solution capable of handling complex tasks in a

structured manner.
Further in the interview, I was asked: "Tell us about a situation where you tried everything to
solve a problem, but nothing worked. What did you doạ
I answered that when every possible solution has been explored, it's important to escalate the
problem to someone with greater expertise rather than wasting time. I illustrated this with
my Al project, where our faculty mentor suggested adding an additional LLM layer, which
significantly improved the system's performance.
Banking Dashboard & Analytics
--- PAGE 7 ---
The discussion then shifted to my Banking Stock Market Analysis Dashboard, where the
interviewers asked about my experience with Power BI, Tableau, and Alteryx.

• I explained that I had worked extensively with Power BI and gained hands-on experience

with Tableau through my Business Data Analytics coursework.

• Since I hadn't worked with Alteryx, I answered honestly and mentioned that I had

already started exploring it and was eager to learn it before joining.
Later in the interview, I was asked, "Can you tell us about something that isn't on your
resume?" I spoke about PYQ Space, an HMI project my teammate and I built.

• Web scraped the college's DSpace repository and built a user-friendly platform for

accessing PYQs.

• The project was supported by our HOD, who helped facilitate its rollout across the

college.

• It received 5,000+ views, 200+ registered users, was widely used during exams, and our

team received certificates for the initiative.
Leadership Experience
The interviewers also discussed my leadership experience, focusing less on my responsibilities
and more on how I handled real-world challenges, including:

• Managing teams with different opinions

• Resolving conflicts and meeting tight deadlines

• Taking ownership under pressure

The discussion was aimed at understanding my decision-making, communication, and leadership
style.
Understanding the Role
Towards the latter half of the interview, one of the interviewers asked: "If selected, which
Corporate Risk function or team would you prefer to work in, and whyại
This was one question I had specifically prepared for after carefully attending the
Pre-Placement Talk (PPT). During the session, different leaders from JPMorgan Chase spoke
about the various functions within Corporate Risk, explaining their responsibilities, the type of
work involved, and the skills required for each team. Paying close attention during the PPT
proved extremely valuable, as it gave me a much clearer understanding of the role beyond the
job description. The interviewers appreciated that my answer reflected a genuine understanding
of the role and how it aligned with my background and long-term career goals.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Closing Discussion
Towards the end of the interview, the conversation then became more HR-focused.
Some of the questions included:

• Tell us about your hobbies.

• How do you manage stress during challenging situations?

• How do you feel about relocating to Bengaluru?

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

• Do you have any questions for us?

I once again asked: "If I'm selected for this internship, what skills or areas would you
recommend I focus on before joining so that I can contribute effectively from Day One?ạ

3. HR Interview [10 Students appeared for this round]

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round. This was the most relaxed interview of
the day and lasted approximately 15-17 minutes. Unlike the technical rounds, the discussion
focused on my personality, communication skills, values, and overall fit for JPMorgan Chase.
The interview began with a casual conversation about how my day had been before moving on to
questions about my interests, career goals, and understanding of the Corporate Risk role.
Some of the questions I was asked included:

• Tell me about yourself.

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

• Why do you think you're a good fit for Corporate Risk?

• Have you interacted with any seniors working at JPMorgan Chase?

• Tell me about a time when you witnessed something unethical or wrong. How did you

handle it?

• Are you comfortable relocating to Bengaluru?

• Are you comfortable working flexible or extended hours if required?

The HR interviews concluded at around 4:45 PM. We then waited anxiously on campus until
around 6:00 PM, when we were informed that the results would be announced online. After
what felt like the longest wait of the day, the final results were declared at 7:49 PM.
ALL THE 10 STUDENTS APPEARING FOR THE HR ROUND WERE SELECTED.
--- PAGE 9 ---

1. Pre placement talk

2. Resume Shortlisting

4. Technical Interview

5. Hr Interview

Before starting with everything I first want to say that you will hear alot of people saying that LUCK
matters alot during placement season. I personally feel it's not always about luck but also about timing.
When your luck and timing aligns, that is the day you achieve everything that you have ever wished for.
So till then keep your head down, do your work and become that best version of yourself! :)
If you are from EXTC - I have listed the names of the company that didnt allow extc to sit for
placements. Some companies might allow EXTC students to participate during your placement
season, but it's good to be prepared.
Pre-placement talk - 25th September
For this all I can say is just listen to what the speakers are saying and personally I never once raised
my hand to ask a question during any of the PPT sessions because I never felt the need to. But for
some people it works. So always ask genuine questions if you have any and don't ask just for the sake
of asking . The interviewers might hardly remember your name as they interact with so many people
on a daily basis.
If you feel you have good questions then keep them for the interviews as interviewers might like your
questions and they might remember you.
Always take screenshots so during the interviews you can refer and ask questions.
Also keep in mind that this role is a 2-year rotational program after your internship. During those 2
years you will have 3 rotations each of 8 months and then you will be promoted to ASSOCIATE role at
JP Morgan ( got this from one of our alumni, they don't mention this during the talk). The 6 months
internship stipend will be 60k . The ctc for the two years was not disclosed . But it will be the same as
other roles offered by jpmc (found this also from the seniors:)).
--- PAGE 2 ---
Resume Shortlisting [around 200 students who were unplaced]
My resume for JPMC - por [Navya_Sinha_JPMC.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1c6driT6Zb7uVfMQrye36hA2Bqe_eH3U8/view?usp=sharing)
My SDE resume -
Por [Navya_Sinha_SDE (2).pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hh49TH_qGiwizLupMSB-3TTN62m7_cCb/view?usp=sharing)
Since the role had analytics in it, I added 2 data analytics projects and one DCF valuation and one ml
project. The shortlisting was mainly on the basis of 12th std marks and your CGPA. If you have 1-2
semesters left try to keep your pointer above 8 because most of the companies have this criteria. Try
to keep your ATS score above 75. Keep altering your resume according to the requirements of the
company and ATS score increases if you add numbers, So try to add a few metrics around your
resume.
We received the list of shortlisted candidates around 7pm, before the day of interviews.

2. Group Discussion- 29th September [approx 75 students ]

6 groups were made each of around 12-13 students.
Our topic was - Mobile Wallet (Pros and cons)
Some more topics that I got from my friends - Work From home (beneficial or not), UPI payments.
The GD was conducted in online mode and we weren't given any time for the prep. So as soon as the
topic is given make sure you unmute yourself and start speaking. Also there wasn't a thing like raising
your hands and then the speaker lets you speak, so everyone will try to speak together, make sure you
stop whenever someone else is speaking and if you have a valid point then continue so that the person
in front stops (it's kinda messy but it works).
Always give some examples relating the topic to your own personal experience.
Speaking 2-3 times is more than enough and always keep nodding your head when someone else is
speaking (this shows you are paying attention).
Always try to be among the first 3 people who start the discussion. This creates a good impression.

3. Technical Interview [19 students ]

My interview started after the lunch break around 2 pm. There were 2 panels and in every panel
there were 2 panelists. The panelists made me comfortable by asking "did i have my lunch" and
greeted me. One important thing to remember for any interview is to keep smiling. Have a small
smile on your face ALWAYS. I cannot stress on how much it tells about your confidence to the
interviewer.
The round started by them introducing themselves and asking me for my introduction.
Now I wanted my introduction to be unique so that they actually listen to me rather than just
looking at my resume. I gave my introduction like -ạI am Navya Sinha, currently an extc student at
spit minor in blah blah", then i said "from the first year of my college everyone around me started
doing courses in tech and due to peer pressure even i started focusing on my technical skills and
that's how I landed up an internship at XYZ company" then talking about my internship and what I
did there. (Both the interviewers smiled when I said it like this).
--- PAGE 3 ---
Make everything in your resume like a story. Example for extracurricular activities - "Apart from
academics major part of my college life has been about teamwork and leadership and hence i
served as VCS in student's Council...." This creates a better impression than just saying "I interned
at this company" and "I was also VCS in the student's council".
After my introduction, one of them directly asked me to explain a particular project and what i did
, why i did, was it even necessary. Make sure to know each and every word in your resume and
justify how your project was actually needed.
My webscrapping project was the one that caught their attention and it was basically about
automation (Since automation is the work that we might do during our internship)
So he asked me every question possible.
I was also asked for counting the number of null values which python function I used
(df.isnull.sum()
Then they asked me

• What is non-controlling interest?

• What is the credit conversion cycle?

• What is meant by assets and liabilities in terms of credit conversion cycle? (Amounts receivable

and payable, and which comes under what)

• What is meant by deferred revenue? Does it come under current or non current liabilities?

• Explain me the steps involved in a company going public (basically non disclosure agreement,

due diligence, how sebi works, roadshows etc)
They were quite impressed that I knew the answers since it was analytics role, then they asked me
situational questions

• If your senior manager takes the credit for all the work that is done by you and your team how

would you react?

• What are your strengths and weaknesses? (Always try to answer these questions honestly and

in weaknesses mention how you are overcoming it)

• If one of your team members is overshadowed and is an introvert how would you help him

open up and share his ideas?
(In situational based questions try your best to relate it to the real world as if it has happened with you
and how you tackled the problem).
For JPMC REMEMBER TO ANSWER IN SUCH A WAY THAT YOU PUT CLIENTS FIRST AND AT TOP
PRIORITY.
Then the worst nightmare of my life.
My interviewer said "Since you are from EXTC, tell me something about the semiconductor industry"
OMG my jaw dropped when he asked me this question. (Lets be serious nobody expects this) I still
smiled and started saying anything that came to my mind, I can't even remember it clearly, but I said
something about taiwan, Gpt astra came and now pobs can also be designed blah blah ...
Then as I was saying something he stopped and asked "So are you saying that there won't be jobs
when the semiconductor industry booms? " At this point I knew I had to say something crazy so that
he would stop asking me about this topic. I gathered all the confidence I had and explained "I am not
saying it won't create jobs, All I am saying is it won't create entry level jobs and freshers would be
--- PAGE 4 ---
expected to know more than usual as Al can now do all the basic tasks for which interns were

1. Resume Shortlisting [313 Students Appeared]

This year, many companies began their recruitment process with resume shortlisting, probably because our
batch size was larger. From what I observed, CGPA played a significant role in the initial screening. A
CGPA of 8.5+ is generally a safe benchmark for getting shortlisted in the early phase of placements,
although this can vary across companies.
One of the biggest mistakes students make is submitting the same resume everywhere. Tailoring your
resume according to the job description is essential. I personally maintained different versions of my resume
and tweaked them based on the role I was applying for. I mainly used Claude to rephrase bullet points and
present my existing work in a way that aligned better with the JD.
If you're targeting different roles (SDE, Data Analyst, AI/ML, etc.), try to build projects relevant to each
domain and include the 2-3 projects that align most closely with the specific role in the resume you submit.
Also, don't overlook your minors, positions of responsibility (PORS), leadership experiences, certifications,
and achievements if they're relevant. In my case, pursuing a Management Minor proved to be very
beneficial. It not only strengthened my resume for a Business Analyst role but also gave the interviewers an
interesting topic to discuss, helping steer the conversation toward an area where I was comfortable.
One piece of advice I'd definitely give is don't list skills or technologies just for the sake of filling up your
resume. If you've mentioned something in your skills section, be prepared for the interviewer to dive deep
into it. It's completely fine to have a shorter skills section, but make sure everything you mention is
something you're genuinely comfortable explaining. A resume should create confidence, not unnecessary
pressure during the interview.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Pen & Paper Test [116 Students Appeared]

The pen-and-paper test lasted 75 minutes and was divided into two sections. One important thing to note is
that both sections had individual cutoffs.
Section 1: Aptitude (24 Marks)
The first section consisted of 8 aptitude MCQS, with a marking scheme of +3 for every correct answer and
-1 for every incorrect answer. The questions were fairly straightforward and covered topics such as:

• Time and Work

• Speed, Time and Distance

• Profit and Loss

• Basic Mathematics

• Age-based problems

• Permutation & Combinations

I found this section to be relatively easy. Even if you weren't able to directly solve a question, most of them
could be answered using option substitution or the elimination method, so don't spend too much time stuck
on a single question.
Section 2: Coding + SQL (12 Marks)
This section had two pattern-based coding questions, where we had to write either Python code or
pseudocode to find the sum of the series.
The series were:

1. 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ... (1 mark)

2. 2, 9, 28, 65, 126, ... (3 marks)

The test also included four SQL questions (2 marks each). They were all based on common analytical
queries and mainly tested your understanding of aggregation, ranking, and grouping.
The questions were:

1. Find the best, worst, and average sales for each salesperson.

2. Find the second-highest sale made by each salesperson.

3. Rank the regions based on their average sales.

4. Count the number of salespeople who made no sales in each quarter.

Overall, I felt this round was quite manageable if you have a decent grasp of aptitude and SQL. My advice
would be to practice SQL beyond just basic queries, be comfortable with GROUP BY, aggregate functions,
CASE WHEN, subqueries/CTEs, and window functions like RANKO and DENSE_RANKO. For the coding
part, don't overthink it, being able to recognize number patterns is more than enough.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. HR Round [This was an extra interview taken on spot only for about 3-4 candidates not all]

This round was a little unexpected. While everyone else was waiting for or attending their technical
interviews, I was suddenly called for the HR round first. It caught me by surprise, but the interview itself
was very relaxed and lasted around 5-7 minutes.
The HR started with some basic questions to understand my motivation for applying. Some of the questions
I was asked were:

• Tell me about yourself.

• Why did you apply for the Business Analyst role?

• What do you know about the role?

• What does InCred do?

My advice would be to spend 15-20 minutes researching the company before the interview. Know what
InCred does, its major products/services, and why you're interested in working there. Along with that, be
clear about why you're interested in becoming a Business Analyst, what responsibilities the role involves,
and how your background aligns with it. Since the round is conversational, answer honestly and confidently
instead of trying to give rehearsed responses.

4. Technical Interview 29 Students Appeared]

The technical round started with a brief introduction, where I was asked to introduce myself and walk
through my background. Since the interviewer had my resume in front of her, the discussion quickly shifted
to my projects and the technologies I had used.
The first few questions were based on my project. Some of the questions I was asked were:

• Explain the difference between Random Forest and XGBoost.

• When would you prefer Random Forest over XGBoost and vice versa?

• Which model takes longer to train and why?

• Do you know what SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) is?

• If not SHAP, what other techniques can be used to determine feature importance?

The interviewer was more interested in understanding my thought process than hearing textbook definitions.
The interview then shifted to business case studies.
Case Study 1
I was given the following scenario:
A D-Mart store has a ground floor that sells groceries and daily essentials and a first
floor that sells apparel and clothing. Currently, 80% of the sales come from the ground
floor and only 20% from the first floor. How would you increase the sales split to 70:30?
The interviewer gave me a few minutes to think before answering.
--- PAGE 4 ---
For questions like these, don't jump to the first solution that comes to your mind. Try to think from multiple
perspectives. I structured my answer around factors such as:

• Demographic factors (age groups, families, students, etc.)

• Geographic factors (store location, nearby residential/commercial areas)

• Behavioural factors (shopping patterns, purchase history)

• Psychographic factors (lifestyle, preferences, fashion trends)

• Store layout and customer journey

• Promotions, discounts, loyalty programs, and bundling offers

The interviewer wasn't expecting one perfect answer. Instead, she wanted to see how broadly and logically I
could think about the problem.
Case Study 2
The second case was from the lending domain.
Suppose a person earns 225,000 per month, and you have access to all the non-personal
SMS messages received on their phone. How would you decide whether this person
should be granted a loan?
The first thing I did was ask a few clarifying questions instead of making assumptions. For example:

• Is the person a salaried employee or self-employed?

• Is the employment permanent or contractual?

• Which city or location does the person belong to?

• Are there any existing loans or EMIs?

The interviewer appreciated asking relevant questions before proposing a solution.
I then discussed how the SMS data could be used to extract useful signals, such as:

• Credit card payment behaviour

• Utility bill payments

• Spending patterns across different categories

• Transaction frequency

You could also suggest that Machine Learning or NLP could be used to categorize SMS messages and build
spending and repayment profiles to assist in the credit decision.
Overall, these case studies were testing how creatively I could think, how structured my approach was, and
whether I considered multiple perspectives before arriving at a solution.
Towards the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions for the interviewer. I genuinely think
this is one of the most underrated parts of any interview. It's your opportunity to show that you're not just
looking for a job, but that you're genuinely interested in this role and this company.
--- PAGE 5 ---
I asked two questions:

1. "If I were selected for this role, what skills or technologies would I primarily be working with?

Since I have around five months before joining, I'd like to use that time to prepare so that I can
contribute from Day 1ạ
I feel this question reflected my willingness to learn and showed that I was already thinking about
how I could add value once I joined.

2. "You've been with InCred for quite some time. How have you seen yourself evolve over the

years?"
This led to a really interesting conversation. The interviewer was very warm and shared her own
journey from graduating with a B.Tech from VJTI to growing within the company over the years and
eventually becoming a Vice President.
The interview ended on a very positive and warm note. My biggest takeaway is to never waste the
opportunity to ask questions. Instead of asking something you could easily find on Google, ask questions
that reflect curiosity, enthusiasm, and a genuine interest in the role. A good conversation at the end can leave
a lasting impression just as much as your answers throughout the interview.
My Advice
If you're preparing for a Business Analyst interview, don't focus only on technical concepts. Practice solving
open-ended business problems. Whenever you're given a case:

• Spend a minute structuring your thoughts.

• Ask clarifying questions instead of making assumptions.

• Break the problem into different dimensions.

• Explain your reasoning clearly.

• Don't stop after one solution, explore multiple possibilities.

A structured thought process is often valued more than arriving at the "perfect" answer.

5. Case Study Round [11 Students Appeared]

The final round was the Case Study Round and, just like the technical interview, it began with a brief
introduction. One of the interviewers found my major project interesting, so we spent a few minutes
discussing it in detail. He asked several follow-up questions to understand my approach, the challenges I
faced, and the decisions I made while building it.
After that, I was given the following business case:
Assume you are the CEO of Air India. The company is currently running at a loss. How
would you turn it into a profitable business?
I was given a few minutes to think about the problem. Before I started answering, the interviewer clarified
that he wanted me to structure my response by focusing on:

• How would you reduce costs?

• How would you increase revenue?

• Consider both short-term and long-term strategies.

--- PAGE 6 ---
I found this clarification very helpful because it gave me a framework to organize my thoughts.
Some of the points I discussed were:

• Analyze the relationship between routes, demand, and travel timings to optimize flight scheduling

and maximize seat occupancy.

• Reduce the number of low-occupancy flights and focus on routes with consistently high demand.

• Partner with reliable third-party vendors for services such as fuel procurement, catering, and ground

operations wherever it is cost-effective.

• Optimize fleet utilization by rotating aircraft based on maintenance schedules and route requirements

instead of keeping aircraft idle.

• Hire and train young technicians, reducing hiring costs while creating a strong long-term workforce

through career development opportunities.

• Introduce or strengthen customer loyalty programs and premium lounge access to improve customer

retention and encourage repeat travel.
They were more interested in seeing whether I could balance both cost optimization and revenue generation.
Towards the end of the interview, I again made sure to ask a question:
"When selected candidates are assigned to teams, is the allocation based purely on
business requirements, or are the candidates' interests and preferences also taken into
considerationẠạ
The interviewer explained how team allocation generally works within the organization, after which they
informed me that the results would be announced soon.
My Advice
For case study rounds, don't rush to answer immediately. Spend a minute understanding the objective and, if
needed, ask clarifying questions. Then structure your response into clear buckets (for example, cost
reduction vs. revenue growth, short-term vs. long-term). Interviewers are usually evaluating your
problem-solving approach, business acumen, and structured thinking. Even if you can't think of the "best"
answer, presenting multiple logical perspectives will leave a much stronger impression.
5 students were offered the job, including me :)
--- PAGE 7 ---
Don't get attached to opportunities that aren't yours yet. Prepare sincerely, give every company your best,
learn from every rejection, and move on. Every bit of effort compounds, even if you can't see it immediately.
One day, those efforts will come together in ways you never expected.
There's a verse from the Bhagavad Gita that I kept coming back to during placements:
"You have a right to perform your duty, but never to the fruits of your actions. Do not let the results of your
actions be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction."
This verse reminded me to focus on what I could control - my preparation, my consistency, and my attitude
and let go of everything else.
So keep showing up. Keep preparing. Trust your timing. Trust the process.
Good things have a way of finding those who don't give up.
All the best! You've got this.

journey.prep:
Learn the Patterns through High-Volume Practice: Consistency is everything. Make it a daily habit to
solve the CSES Problem Set, participate in Codeforces and CodeChef contests, and grind LeetCode. Lock
down the standard variations of foundational problems then study the variations.
Compete Offline: Participate in as many offline competitive programming contests as possible. Competing
in person drastically boosts your confidence, sharpens your focus, and perfectly simulates the
nerve-wracking environment of an actual physical interview.
Build High-Effort, Unique Projects: Avoid generic, copy-pasted CRUD applications. Spend 3 to 4 months
deeply engineering unique projects. You must know every single aspect of the architecture, from the
database schema to the actual production deployment.
Prioritize System Design: Development isn't just about writing code; it is about scaling it. Focus heavily on
system design concepts. Understand load balancing, caching, and the tradeoffs between consistency and
availability in distributed systems. You will be tested on how your projects handle scale.
Collaborate and Mentor: Do competitive programming and software development in groups. Discussing
complex game dev algorithms with a peer or breaking down CP mindsets for junior engineering students
forces you to articulate your technical logic clearly. If you can explain it to a peer, you can explain it to an
interviewer.
If you have any doubts, feel free to connect with me:-
https://www.linkedin.com/in/nikhil-vishwakarma-074675295/
