On Sth July, 2026 we were asked to report around 2:40 for the PPT(Pre Placement Talk) followed by OA at
4:30 . Be attentive in the PPT.

1. Online Assessment [ Around 300+ candidate appeared for this round] (conducted on 5th July, 4:30

PM)
There were 4 questions for this round having 50-70-110-120 points respectively and a total of 90 Minutes
(1Hr 30 Min).
The questions of the OA are a bit more difficult than the previous years. I was idle for 15 minutes before
starting and understanding the question and coding the questions like before the starting attempting the
question.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points)
Problem Statement:
You are given an array tasks of size M representing the difficulty levels of various tasks, and an array
workers of size N representing the capabilities of available workers. You are also given an integer K, which
denotes the absolute maximum number of tasks any single worker is allowed to perform.
A worker can only be assigned to a task if their capability is greater than or equal to the task's difficulty
(workers [1] >= tasks [j]).
N<=2e5 , M<=2e5 , k<=1e3
Your goal is to perform a two-step optimization:
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Find the maximum possible number of tasks that can be completed using the given workers,

assuming each worker can do up to K tasks.

2. Find the minimum value of k (0<=k<=K) such that the exact same maximum number of tasks can

still be completed without any single worker exceeding k assigned tasks.
After drawing the diagram I just realized that it is just a sorting and greedy approach and then binary search
on the answer, so I coded it and forgot the edge case of k=0 after adding that got AC in that question
completely.
Problem 2: Network Routers and Regions (70 Points)
Problem Statement: You are given a network topology represented as an unweighted tree data structure
consisting of N nodes and N-1 edges.
The network contains three distinct types of components:

1. Exactly one central server.

2. Multiple routers.

3. Multiple regions.

The connections within the network adhere strictly to the following rules:

• The central server connects only to routers.

• A router connects to the central server and to one or more regions.

• A region connects to exactly one router.

Minimum of both is 2.
Given the edges of this tree, your task is to write a program that determines the total number of routers and
the total number of regions in the network.
Initially, I misread the question (assuming node 1 was always the root, which wasn't mentioned). Once I
cleared that confusion, I realized it was a straightforward brute-force problem. If you know how to calculate
the size of a subtree, it becomes super easy. I just brute-forced all nodes as a potential root and checked if its
size was >= 2 and if each subtree size minus 1 was >=2. It passed all test cases.
Problem 3: Codeforces 1665C - Tree Infection (110 Points)
Problem Statement:
You are given a rooted tree with n vertices where vertex 1 is the root. Initially, all vertices are healthy. Every
second, two operations occur in the following order:

1. Manual Infection (Spreading): You can choose exactly one healthy vertex and infect it.

Natural Infection (Spreading): For every infected vertex, the disease naturally spreads to exactly
one of its healthy siblings (vertices sharing the same parent).
Your goal is to find the minimum number of seconds required to infect all the vertices in the tree.
--- PAGE 3 ---
When I first read this, my mind immediately jumped to Tree DP. I spent about 10 minutes trying to figure
out the states and transitions before deciding to move on to the 4th question. Not attempted for the partial
scores forgot about that you should try for that.
Problem 4: Codeforces 8C - Looking for Order (120 Points)
Problem Statement:
You start at a fixed base coordinate (the chest) and need to collect N objects (relics) scattered at various 2D
coordinates. You have a carrying capacity constraint: you can carry a maximum of 2 relics at a time before
you must return to the base to drop them off.
Your goal is twofold:

1. Find the minimum total distance traveled to collect all N relics and return to the base.

2. Explicitly print the sequence of steps (the optimal path) taken to achieve this minimum distance.

Input Format:

• The first line contains the base coordinates X_0, Y_O.

• The second line contains an integer N (1 <N<= 24), the number of relics.

• The next N lines contain the X, Y coordinates of each relic.

Output Format:

• The first line should print the minimum total distance.

• The second line should print the sequence of indices visited (with $O$ representing the base).

As soon as I read the problem, the N<=24 constraint and the traversal nature immediately gave it away as
Bitmask DP. Having grinded through similar city traversal and graph DP problems on CSES, the state
definition was clear to me: let dp[mask] be the minimum distance to collect the subset of relics represented
by the active bits in the mask.
I got the core logic half-right, but I completely messed up on two fronts: handling the 2-relic collection limit
optimally and printing the actual path.
Looking back, if I had approached it more calmly instead of panicking over the complexity, I definitely
could have written a less optimal solution just to extract some partial points.
Online Assessment Results & Shortlist:
Overall, I scored 120 out of 350 points in the OA. We received the shortlist results around 10:00 PM that
same night. Roughly 26 people were selected for the technical rounds, which were scheduled to begin at
9:00 AM the following morning.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Key Takeaways & Tips for the OA:

• Stay Calm & Read Thoroughly: Read every question calmly. The key is to map the OA question to

patterns or similar questions you have solved in the past.

• Volume of Practice Matters: To successfully relate OA questions to known patterns, you need a

strong foundation. You have to solve a large volume of problems first.

• Consistency Pays Off: Honestly, if you have consistently practiced CP or done rigorous DSA for

about a year, clearing the OA and securing an interview is very doable. Focus on extracting partial
points whenever you are stuck!

1. Technical Round 1(6th ,july) [26 people appeared ][Duration: 50-60 mins]

We were asked to come at around 9:00 AM the next day. They called us in the order of how we finished in
the OA. I was in the second batch of students.
There were 10 panels so there were 3 batches for this round. I was in batch 2. I was asked for the following
problems.
Problem 1: LeetCode 827 - Making A Large Island
https://leetcode.com/problems/making-a-large-island/description/

• I took about a minute to structure my thoughts and then spent 3-4 minutes conveying my approach

and covering all the edge cases. (Honestly, my rigorous practice with CSES graph problems really
paid off here; I didn't even realize this was classified as a "Hard" problem until later).

• I first proposed a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) method: track the size of every connected component of

1s. Then, iterate through every 0, temporarily treat it as a 1, use a set to fetch the unique parent IDs
of its neighboring components, and sum their sizes plus one.

• The interviewer then asked if I could achieve this using DFS instead of DSU. I explained that the

core logic remains exactly the same-we can just use standard DFS or BFS to traverse the matrix,
explicitly marking each component with a unique Parent ID and storing its size in an array or map.

• He was visibly impressed with my speed and clarity. He then asked me to write the complete code,

which took me about 15-20 minutes.
Problem 2 :- LeetCode 3203 - Find Minimum Diameter After Merging Two Trees
https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-diameter-after-merging-two-trees/description/

• I started by doing some manual casework. I mathematically proved to the interviewer that picking

any node other than a node on the diameter to connect the two trees will always yield a sub-optimal
maximum distance.

• He was convinced by this initial proof. After receiving one minor hint from him, I further proved that

the optimal connection point on the diameter is exactly its middle node (the center).

• Once the logic was locked in, I explained the standard 2-BFS method for calculating the diameter of

a tree and proceeded to write the code.
This round lasted for me around 50mins - 60 mins.
--- PAGE 5 ---
From every slot of panels 3 students were asked to give HM round first. From the 10 people in my panel, 3
students including me were asked to give HM round first.

2. Hiring Manager (HM) Round _[6(after T1) + 3 (after T2) ][Duration: ~1 hr 45 mins]

• The round started in the afternoon, just 15 min after my T1, and was, without a doubt, the toughest

of all three rounds. It kicked off with a standard introduction, followed by a deep dive into my past
work experience and internships.

• I have three highly unique and strong projects on my resume. The interviewer started by asking

about the first two smaller projects. I explained the core problems they solved and my initial
motivations for building them.

• The "Vegha" Deep Dive: Once we moved to my third project, Vegha, the intensity skyrocketed. We

spent a solid 40 minutes discussing this single project. The interviewer grilled me on the actual
production deployment, the architecture, and exactly how I solved specific technical bottlenecks.
This wasn't just a surface-level summary; he wanted to know the engineering reality behind the code.

• Throughout this entire project discussion, behavioral and technical questions were seamlessly mixed

together. I had to defend my technical choices while demonstrating how I handle challenges, making
it an exhausting but engaging conversation.
The System Design Pitch (E-Commerce Startup):

• Next, he asked me to imagine I was launching an E-Commerce startup and to design the

system for it, including browsing, ordering, and third-party delivery integration(3r party).

• Phase 1 (Initial Launch): I had to design the architecture to support 10,000 visitors and 100

actual buyers, assuming all sales were restricted exclusively to my own website.

• Phase 2 (Scaling Up): He then introduced new constraints. What happens when the customer

base rapidly increases? How do we scale the system when we integrate third-party platforms
like Amazon and Flipkart into our sales pipeline?

• Phase 3 (Architecture Evolution): We discussed the necessary architectural changes to

handle this distributed scale. I had to build out the evolving system design on the spot,
incorporating caching layers, load balancing, and data consistency across multiple platforms.

Tips:

• Deployment Matters: It is not enough to just build a project locally. You must know the ins

and outs of how your project is actually deployed and how it behaves in a production
environment.

• System Design is Dynamic: Don't just memorize standard system design templates (like

"Design Twitter"). Be ready to apply scalable architecture concepts (like caching and
third-party API integration) to your own ideas on the fly.

• Know Your Story: Because behavioral questions are mixed directly into technical

explanations, practice explaining why you built something, not just how.

• Be 100% Genuine in the HM Round: The Hiring Manager will strip away the fluff and test

the engineering reality behind your resume. Be completely truthful about what you built,
what failed, and what your specific role was. If you bluff about a technical bottleneck, a
seasoned Engineering Manager will catch it immediately.
--- PAGE 6 ---

3. Technical Round 2 | 13(after T1) + 3 (after HM) ][Duration: 60-70 mins]

I was one of 3 student who cleared the T1 and HM
Problem 1 : -
Similar to the solution of this problem - https://codeforces.com/contest/2236/problem/F2
In that problem distributing the prime
The Problem: We were given an array of N children, each with a different maximum candy limit, and K
candies to distribute. We needed to find the number of ways to distribute all K candies without exceeding
any child's maximum limit.
The Process: I read the problem and instantly related it to a similar distribution problem I had solved
recently in a Codeforces Div3 (Problem F2). Within the first two minutes, I laid out my initial observation:
if all children had infinite capacities, this would be a simple "Stars and Bars" (or Beggar's Method)
combinatorics problem.
However, because the limits varied, the combinatorics approach (Inclusion-Exclusion) would get too
complex, so I pivoted to Dynamic Programming. I started by writing out the pure recursive relation, then
converted it into a tabulation state.
Once the O(NK^2) transition was clear, I applied a prefix-sum optimization to bring the complexity down.
To push the envelope, I briefly discussed how this could theoretically be optimized even further using
Generating Functions.
I coded the full recursive approach and then wrote out the optimized tabulation loops. The interviewer was
highly satisfied with how I evolved the solution step-by-step.
Problem 2:- Maximum Strong Pair XOR II (LeetCode 2935)
https://eetcode.com/problems/maximum-strong-pair-xor-ii/description/
The Process: This one took me a bit more time. I started by mathematically deriving the valid range for the
pairs. Assuming x <= y, I simplified the strong pair condition down to y <=2x (meaning for a fixed y, x must
be in the range [ceil[y/2],y]). I proved this derivation to the interviewer to ensure we were on the same page.
Once the math was locked in, I figured out it required a Bit Trie. The standard optimal solution here involves
a sliding window over sorted elements, but that didn't click for me in the moment.
Instead, I came up with an alternative: I treated it almost like a Digit DP problem. I wrote a custom walk on
the Trie where I maintained the lower bound of ceil (y/2). When searching for the maximum opposite bit for
y, my search function explicitly verified if a valid index existed strictly within the [y/2, y] range down that
specific Trie path.
I partially coded my custom Bit Trie structure and the specialized search function. Like I was running out of
time so the coding part was a bit messy.
I was the last one to finish this round.
--- PAGE 7 ---
Results were announced
2 of us got internship +fte
And 4 including me got internship + performance based full time

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Learn the Patterns through High-Volume Practice: Consistency is everything. Make it a daily habit to
solve the CSES Problem Set, participate in Codeforces and CodeChef contests, and grind LeetCode. Lock
down the standard variations of foundational problems then study the variations.
Compete Offline: Participate in as many offline competitive programming contests as possible. Competing
in person drastically boosts your confidence, sharpens your focus, and perfectly simulates the
nerve-wracking environment of an actual physical interview.
Build High-Effort, Unique Projects: Avoid generic, copy-pasted CRUD applications. Spend 3 to 4 months
deeply engineering unique projects. You must know every single aspect of the architecture, from the
database schema to the actual production deployment.
Prioritize System Design: Development isn't just about writing code; it is about scaling it. Focus heavily on
system design concepts. Understand load balancing, caching, and the tradeoffs between consistency and
availability in distributed systems. You will be tested on how your projects handle scale.
Collaborate and Mentor: Do competitive programming and software development in groups. Discussing
complex game dev algorithms with a peer or breaking down CP mindsets for junior engineering students
forces you to articulate your technical logic clearly. If you can explain it to a peer, you can explain it to an
interviewer.
If you have any doubts, feel free to connect with me:-

journey.prep:
DSA should be your top priority. I personally referred to Striver's content and the TLE Eliminators course,
which helped me a lot. You can even find these courses for free on Telegram. Practice DSA every single day
and participate in as many contests as you can on LeetCode, CodeChef, and Codeforces. Contests really help
you get used to solving problems within a time limit.
If you're good at DSA, you'll be able to clear the OA rounds of most companies. Before Auxo Al, I had
already cleared the OAs for PhonePe and IDFC, and I learned a lot from the mistakes I made during those
interview processes.
Before your interviews, prepare your introduction and project explanations really well. Focus on your
strengths and use the breadcrumb strategy while answering questions. For example, while explaining
chunking in my RAG pipeline, I connected it to the concept of the cross-attention mechanism while
discussing how overlapping chunks can improve retrieval quality. This naturally sparked a discussion about
cross-attention, and since I was comfortable with the topic, I was able to explain it confidently.
Also, don't give generic interview answers. Research about the company and the role beforehand. Be ready
with a short story about why you're a good fit, even if your resume isn't perfectly aligned with the role.
Interviewers often care more about your analytical thinking and problem-solving approach.
One thing that's really important is keeping your CGPA above 8. It matters for shortlisting at many elite
companies.
And finally, luck is definitely a part of the placement process, but that's something you can't control. Just
keep working hard, focus on what you can improve, and enjoy the journey. Placements often come when
you least expect them.
All the very best!

journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting

Although I didn't know the exact shortlisting criteria, around 150 students were shortlisted in this round.
From my experience, one thing that likely helped was having a resume that closely matched the job
description. So, I'd recommend including the skills, tools, and programming languages mentioned in the JD
to improve your chances of getting shortlisted.
Resume Tips:

1. Since this was an AI/ML role, I'd recommend having AI/ML-related projects on your resume. All

three projects on my resume were based on AI/ML, which aligned well with the role.

2. Try to include your model accuracy, performance metrics for your projects. It makes your projects

look more impactful and can also help improve your ATS score.

3. Internship experience is always an advantage during placements. If possible, complete an internship

before the placement season begins. Although I did not have internship experience, my projects were
closely aligned with the job description.

2. Online Assessment (150 students appeared)

The online assessment was conducted on campus and lasted 90 minutes. It consisted of 25 MCQS and 3
DSA coding questions.
The MCQs covered basic AI/ML concepts such as:

• Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning

• Overfitting

• Tokens in LLMs

• Context Window

--- PAGE 2 ---

• Model weight storage formats

There were also a few aptitude questions on topics like Analogies, Coding-Decoding, Ratio & Proportion,
and Basic Logical Reasoning. Overall, the MCQs were fairly easy if you had a good understanding of basic
Al/ML concepts and had practiced aptitude questions beforehand.
The coding section consisted of the following problems:
Q1. Basic String Sorting
Given a string and you have to return a new string where the characters are sorted based on their frequency.
Q2. Maximum weight within Budget
You were given an array of (cost,weights) pairs representing oranges. The task was to find the maximum
total weight of oranges that could be purchased without exceeding the given budget. This was a standard 0/1
Knapsack problem.
Q3. Reconstruct Travel Route
You were given shuffled travel records in the format:
Mumbai Goa 500
Goa Bangalore 600
Bangalore Chennai 400
The task was to reconstruct the correct travel route and calculate the total travel cost.
I was able to solve 2 coding questions completely, and since the MCQS were quite straightforward, the test
went well overall. From what I observed, most students who solved 2 or more coding questions were
shortlisted for the interview rounds. In the end, 15 students were selected for interviews.

3. Technical Interview Round 1(15 students appeared)

The interview started with my introduction. After that, the interviewer picked one of my agentic Al projects
from my resume and asked me to explain it. I gave a brief overview covering all the major functionalities.
Then he started asking about the role of each agent, what tools I was using, the API endpoints in the project,
and how I had implemented one of the core functionalities. After I explained it, he asked how I could
optimize that implementation. We had a good discussion about different optimization approaches and how I
would go about implementing them.
Next, he moved on to my second project. I gave a brief introduction, and since I mentioned that it used
RAG, he started asking RAG-related questions. He asked how I was collecting data for the RAG pipeline,
how I had implemented it, how I would decide the right chunk size, and how I was retrieving context from
the vector database for the LLM.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After that, he asked how I could optimize the RAG pipeline. I mentioned things like reranking, metadata
filtering, and using different retrievers. He then asked how I would actually implement those optimizations
and how libraries like LangChain handle them internally. We also discussed common problems in RAG
systems and possible solutions.
After that, he wrapped up the interview. Before leaving, I asked him how Auxo Al handles hallucinations in
LLMs. He explained their approach and how they work on reducing hallucinations. It turned into a really
interesting discussion.
A few tips from my experience:

• Be confident while answering your questions.

• If you don't know something, it's completely fine to say you don't know. After that, you can share

how you would approach the problem or what you think the solution might be instead of making up
an answer.

• Whatever technologies you mention on your resume, make sure you know them well because most

of the questions will come from your own projects and tech stack.

• It's perfectly okay if your resume isn't packed with every possible technology. A smaller resume that

you can confidently defend is much better than a long one where you struggle to answer questions.

• I wasn't confident about deep learning, so I didn't include it on my resume. Highlight your strengths

instead, and even in your introduction, focus on the areas you're most comfortable with.

4. Technical + Business Round (8 students appeared)

The second interview round also started with a brief introduction. Since the interviewer came from a
consulting background, he wasn't focused on asking very deep technical questions.
He started with one of my projects and asked why I chose that particular tech stack, what functionalities the
project had, and what challenges I faced while building it. There was one technology he didn't understand
why I had used that particular technology in the project, so I explained the problem I was trying to solve and
how that technology helped address it. He seemed satisfied with my explanation. We had a similar
discussion about my second project as well.
After that, we moved on to the case study. He gave me a scenario where there was a restaurant outside my
college that originally served Indian food. The owner's son took over and completely changed the menu to
fast food. Students loved the new menu, there was always a long queue outside the restaurant, but
surprisingly, the restaurant's revenue had started decreasing.
I was asked to act as an analyst and analyze the situation. He gave me a few minutes to think, and then we
discussed my approach. I suggested multiple possible reasons, and he kept correcting my thought process.
Eventually, with a hint I arrived at the answer he was looking for. He then asked how I would increase the
restaurant's revenue. I answered using a real-life example that I had seen, and he seemed happy with my
response.
The interview ended with me asking him about his career journey and one of the services offered by Auxo
AI. We had a nice discussion before wrapping up.
--- PAGE 4 ---
After all the interviews were over, we were informed that five candidates had been shortlisted for an online
HR interview later that evening.
However, instead of conducting a separate HR round, the company directly informed all the shortlisted
candidates that we had been selected.

My placement journey involved applying to around 46 companies on Superset and appearing for 40+ online
assessments. What helped me most was learning from every OA and interview. I used to maintain a record
of the questions asked in previous interviews, identify my weak areas, and work on them before the next
opportunity.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Revise DSA, know your resume and projects thoroughly, and practise under time limits. I could have done
better in prompt engineering and time management, so always practise writing precise prompts and submit
at least a minute before the deadline.

others; keep learning from every OA and interview, work on your weak areas, and keep applying. You may
face many rejections, but consistency and improvement really matter.
journey.howSecured:
A. At Home:
a. Communication Test (28th Sept 2026, retest on 1st Oct 2026)
b. Final Assessment Test (28th Sept 2026)
B. At College:
a. Online test (8th Oct 2026)
b. Interview (8th Oct 2026)
1.
Communication Test [Everyone gave the test]
The communication test was conducted from home on 28 September 2026, with a retest on 1 October
because few candidates couldn't access the previous one. It had 29 questions divided into five sections.

1. Reading Comprehension: Passage-based MCQs testing understanding, inference, and reasoning. One

passage discussed Universal Basic Income (UBI) trials in Finland and Kenya.
Example questions:

• What is the main purpose of the passage?

• What did the Finnish trial reveal about employment and well-being?

• Why can't these trials establish whether UBI would work at a national scale?

2. Listening Comprehension: Audio-based questions testing understanding of details, speaker intentions, and

emotions.
Example: How does a business owner feel about no longer knowing every customer personally? (the ans
was in the audio, just listen properly)

3. Spoken Communication: Timed video responses on personal experiences and workplace situations.

Example questions:

• Describe someone who influenced your career positively.

• Would you prefer giving difficult feedback face-to-face or in writing?

--- PAGE 2 ---
For the career question, I spoke about my NCC senior who trained me for AIVSC 2025 and helped me
develop discipline and perform under pressure. I connected this guidance to my achievement of becoming
Best Pilot of AIVSC 2025.

4. Business Communication Writing: Workplace messages and longer opinion-based writing tasks.

Example questions:

• Write a message explaining that your car is unavailable for a shared lift and request someone to

cover your turn.

• Inform your team about a change from approach A to approach B.

• Should cities charge drivers to enter busy areas during peak hours?

• Should regular meetings be limited to 30 minutes?

5. Grammar and Sentence Correction: MCQs on subject-verb agreement, relative pronouns, sentence

structure, and parallel construction.
Examples included choosing between has been and other verb forms, correcting sentences involving
"neither...nor," and selecting grammatically correct phrases.
Preparation Tips

• Practise passage-based questions and answer strictly from the given text.

• For speaking, use a simple structure: answer, reason, example, and conclusion.

• For writing, follow the word limit and keep the tone natural and professional.

• Revise basic grammar rules and read each sentence carefully before selecting an option.

2. Final Assessment Test [Everyone gave the test]

This round was conducted from home on 28 September 2026. It mainly tested hand-eye coordination, quick
thinking, attention, and memory retention through interactive games.
One task involved observing several balls on a screen, including one ball of a different colour. A
matching-figure question followed, requiring a True/False response. This pattern repeated three or four
times, after which I had to select the coloured balls in the sequence in which they had appeared.
Preparation and tips:

• Practise visual memory, pattern recognition, and quick decision-making games.

• Pay attention to the sequence of objects and colours, not just their individual appearance.

• Stay focused throughout the task, as information from earlier screens may be needed later.

• Accuracy is important, but you must also respond within the available time.

--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Online Assessment [77 shortlisted candidates]

The online assessment was conducted at college on 8 October 2026. It had four rounds, with different time
limits and problem-solving requirements. At the beginning, we had to select a technology/language option,
such as React or Node.js, which was relevant to the later Al debugging and function-development questions.

Round 1: Basic DSA - 30 minutes

This was a basic data structures and algorithms coding question. I found it relatively easy and completed it
in around 15 minutes, with all test cases passing.
Tip: Focus on correctness first, consider edge cases, and use the remaining time to verify the solution.

Round 2: Prompt Engineering - 15 minutes

We were given a problem and had to write a complete prompt for an Al system to generate the required
solution. The generated code was not visible, and we could not directly inspect which test cases were failing.
The question text also could not be copied, although the test cases were copyable.
Initially, I wrote two prompts explaining the expected answer in my own words, but no test cases passed. I
then added the implementation approach, explaining that a dictionary should be used to store values and
retrieve them as required. This improved the result, and 5 out of 6 test cases passed before time ran out.
Tip: A prompt should describe not only the expected output but also the implementation logic, constraints,
edge cases, and expected behaviour.

Round 3: AI Debugging - 35 minutes

A complete website (frontend + backend) with a faulty feature was provided, along with an Al assistant. The
assistant gave hints about dependencies and possible issues rather than directly supplying the answer. Direct
questions asking it to solve the evaluation problem were restricted.
This I was not able to complete.
Tip: Understand the existing code flow, inspect the relevant components and dependencies, reproduce the
issue, and use Al hints to guide debugging rather than depending on it to generate the entire fix.

Round 4: AI Function Development - 30 minutes

This round provided frontend and backend code and required adding the functionality described in the
problem statement. I was able to implement the main functionality, but the implementation was only partial
by the end of the round.
Tip: Read the complete requirements first, identify the essential functionality, and prioritise a working
end-to-end implementation before spending time on additional details.
Important:
I submitted the first question with sufficient time remaining, and it displayed a green tick. For the second
and third questions, I attempted submission in the final 10 seconds, but errors appeared and the green tick
--- PAGE 4 ---
was not displayed. I was unsure whether the code had been submitted automatically, so I checked with HR,
who said they would verify it with the technical team.
My strongest advice is to submit every question at least one minute before the deadline. Wait for the
submission confirmation or green tick rather than assuming the code has been saved. Reserve the final
minutes for submission and verification.

4. Interview [6 shortlisted candidates]

The final round was a technical-cum-HR interview based mainly on my resume, projects, internship,
technical skills, and workplace scenarios.
Questions asked

• Tell me about yourself. I introduced myself and summarised my technical background and

experience.

• Give a brief overview of your projects. I explained the projects listed on my resume.

• What are you doing in your AI/ML internship at NeoSkillz? What difficulties did you face? I

discussed my internship project and the challenges involved in building it.

• What is the difference between REST APIs and FastAPI? Which is more secure?

• A team has a very close deadline. Three members are capable but overloaded, while the fourth

member is struggling. What would you do?
I explained that I would prioritise the critical work first, then help the struggling teammate. Rather than
making one person responsible for all the extra support, each team member could help in turns so that
nobody's own work was neglected. I would also share useful resources, references, and Al tools to help the
teammate complete their tasks.

• Why should we hire you? I gave my prepared answer, highlighting my technical skills, learning

ability, and project experience.

• What do you know about Capgemini? I answered based on my understanding of the company.

Finally 4 candidates were selected for the final offer, results were announced on 16th Oct. (Actually there
were 5 names but 1 of us got another company before this result).

1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Resume + Behavioural Interview)

1. Online Assessment | 100+ candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted on campus, there were 22 questions, 20 of them were Math, puzzles and other
questions. The last 2 were questions on programming. 8 CGPA was required as a minimum to give the test.
The marking scheme was as follows: each MCQ carried 4 marks, while each programming question
carried 20 marks. The OA was conducted on hacker earth platform.
The programming section included questions of mainly two difficulties. All candidates had the same
programming questions in the same order. The first question was of LC easy level, involving mainly the
concept of two-pointer approach. The second question was of LC medium-hard level, based on number
theory, and detailed implementation logic.
I managed to solve the first question but was unable to solve the second question in time. The marks were
allotted on the test cases basis. Two of the test cases were visible while the rest weren't visible. Most of the
OA questions were based on ratios and similar questions.

2. Interview Round 1 50+ candidates appeared for this round

The interview round occurred roughly 4 hours after the OA, this was caused by the entire process being
taken on the same day. There were multiple panels and I was one of the last set of candidates who were
selected for the interview.
It began with me introducing myself, after that I was asked questions about various topics ranging from OS,
normal forms in databases, computer networking etc. I was also asked to write down the solution to a
problem that consists of sorting two already sorted arrays.
I was also asked OOP questions mainly to explain concepts like encapsulation, abstraction, polymorphism
and message passing. Later I was also asked questions based on my projects and the way in which I
implemented them. Lastly I thanked the interviewers and made sure to shake their hands.
--- PAGE 2 ---
My interview lasted around 20 min and was conclusive but also relatively easy.

3. Interview Round 2[10+ candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted at varying times for different candidates. In my case, it took place almost
immediately after Interview Round 1. It was a one-on-one discussion with the Senior Director and didn't
feel much like an interview.
This round began with asking me to explain my role in any one project mentioned in my resume. He also
allowed me to go on about the setting and the experience. I explained about 3-4 in detail and acted confident
about it. There were very few counter-questions asked to me, much more of an HR style round.
After that there were basic HR questions like 'why do you want to join the company?,what motivates
you?' and 'what are some of your weaknesses?'. I managed to answer them with confidence while also
being humble in pointing out my weaknesses.
The interview came to a relatively faster halt as I was basically the last person they interviewed, after which
I made sure to ask some questions about the role and other questions to leave a good impression that I was
genuinely interested in the role. I feel like that is mainly what helped me.
What could have been improved was my starting portion of the interview which felt dry and less engaging as
I was relatively exhausted from the long process, in fact it began with him apologizing for the long process.
I should have shown more energy and enthusiasm, but I managed to come back up later on.
In the end, 6 students were offered the Tech Intern role at Russell Investments from among the 7
shortlisted candidates (with 1 candidate being offered the Investment Research role).

journey.prep:
Prepare in advance for placements. Very few companies come specifically for ML roles so generally most
people don't prepare for this in advance, even I prepared for SDE role only ‚all the ML/AI knowledge I have
is from second year and projects and not just before placement studies.
Also don't be demotivated by rejections. I have been rejected in my second year for internships at Barclays
and Russel investments(last round) interviews. In placement month I was rejected from JPMC and ISS
Stoxx HR round(15 out of 20 selected). One thing that is really important is that you take each opportunity
very seriously especially the HR round because rejection in the last round hurts very much. Nonetheless keep
trying, don't stress and most importantly don't be jealous of others because placements is a lot about luck so
don't compare yourself to anyone else. During placements try to learn everything from projects to System
design to DSA to AI/ML.

Tips:

CGPA does matter so if possible try to maintain as high as you can (don't follow 8+ or 8.5+, aim for 9+ this
will help in shortlisting you for OA because in many companies OA hidden criteria is CGPA)
Focus on yourself only, take rejections as a chance to improve. After my rejection I had 2 weeks where I
literally learned everything needed to my best capacity so that whenever given the next chance I am so
prepared to get it. (Don't look around at others as competition just focus on yourself).

2-3 sections of MCQS across sections like english, coding fundamentals, aptitude, this time a little bit of ai
based questions were also asked. The mcqs were quite easy and doable just time management was needed as
90mins for around 95 questions(including 3 DSA) so the OA needed to be completed at very fast speed
I was confident in DSA so I very quickly did the mcqs and gave myself 50mins for DSA in which i managed
to solve 2 questions entirely
Then next section had 3 DSA questions(each person had different set of questions)
1)house robber variation- given array of values (1 indexed array)
You can select an element at index i and then you can select element at index j only if j%i=-0
So if index 1 then any index allowed if index 2 then only 4,6,8 and so on..
This question i was able to solve and the recursive solution was enough to pass all the test cases no need of
memoization
--- PAGE 2 ---

2) Some extremely difficult question. Like given n vertices of a polygon as coordinates, sort in anticlockwise

order and then find area of the polygon( no formula or anything given)
This i skipped entirely
3)given an array of elements choose a subarray such that the OR of elements of the subarray is equal to the
OR of elements of the remaining array
For this question i provided a brute force solution (iterate over all subarrays compute OR and another loop
for OR of the array excluding current subaary and then just match both results)
TIP: solve questions with brute force at least to pass most of the test cases and then if time permits go for
optimal approach
Practice DP in advance because such questions can be solved in pressure only with lots of practice in
advance(Focus on arrays all variations(2 pointer,sliding window,prefix sum+hashmap,binaryh search all
types) and DP ‚trees and graphs only if time permits)

company but students were allowed to switch to another role in the interview round. Most students solved
one/two DSA were shortlisted for FE and MLE role ,for BA some people solved 1 or partial question)

like I had an anomaly detection model so he asked about why this model,alternatives,exact input
features, why embeddings made? which transformer used?

and collaborative filtering. He tried to ask 1-2 random questions like the full form of TFIDF which i had
used in the project(generally 1-2 specific questions are asked so that they can judge if you actually did
the project or not). So make sure you know your project perfectly along with all the tech stack and
justification of why that tech stack.
At the end of the round I asked the interviewer a few questions like
What qualities/skills do you expect from a fresher candidate, In an MLE role will we get to deploy
models or only build them. Also the career progression as MLE in two-five years.

3. Vibe coding round: approximately 15-18 people in total (4MLE 9 FE)

This was a non elimination round so all people had to give the next round by default.
We had to share our screen on unstop,the interviewers could view whatever we were doing on screen.
Any ai tools were allowed and we were given a simple problem statement and 90 minutes to complete
I used antigravity to make the project it took only 20mins even with errors)
--- PAGE 3 ---
The remaining time I took to understand the project,see all the api routes, DB schema and details about react
hooks used(because mainly frontend was only required). We had to upload the project on github and
paste the link in unstop.

journey.prep:
You probably won't be the best in everything, which they expect, but try to balance everything (including
your soft skills) better - that's what they are looking for.

• Only put what you can explain to the last detail on your resume. It's fine if it's a bit empty, don't

mention things you don't know.

• Make sure to take notice of what the company is looking for as well. If your strengths match with the

company's interest, you have a better chance.

• Be honest, always. Mention your weaknesses beforehand. If you don't know any concept or tool,

admit it before you are caught.

• Always show a learner attitude. They aren't looking for someone who knows more stuff, they're

looking for someone who is willing to learn and work with them.

• Try to ask questions. Questions on how you could work on your weaknesses and suggestions based

on their experience could show your learner attitude and make you stand out a bit.

• Think of the interview as a discussion rather than a Q&A session. Your interactiveness is important,

questioning the interviewer and discussing certain scenarios gets them a bit more inclined to work
with you rather than the rest.

• Avoid having expectations. As your expectations rise, so does your anxiousness thinking about

what's at stake and the pain if you aren't selected. This could weaken your confidence.
So, just be thorough with your resume, know that it's okay to not know stuff, be interactive and confident,
and most importantly, be calm, composed and think of this as just one of the many opportunities coming
your way. :)

). He then asked me about my

challenges faced, and possible improvements, as questions can be asked on any of them.

Cash Flow Statement), how they are linked, and concepts like IPOs. Although these were not asked
in my interview, it is better to be prepared since a few interviewers were common for both
Investment Banking and FinTech roles.

India, RBI Governor, SBI Chairman, and other important institutions.

incorrectly, don't dwell on them during the interview. Stay composed, focus on the next question, and give
your best throughout the process.

1. Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

2. Resume Shortlisting

3. Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

4. 2 Technical Interviews (2 July 2026)

5. HR Interview (2 July 2026)

6. Final Result Declaration (2 July 2026)

For the Banking FinTech role, candidates shortlisted after the Online Assessment (OA) were invited directly
to Technical Round 1, unlike the Investment Banking (IB) role, where a Group Discussion (GD) was
conducted after the OA. The selection process for the Banking FinTech role consisted of OA → Technical
Round 1 → Technical Round 2 → HR Interview.

1. Resume Shortlisting

The first and foremost stage of the selection process was the Resume Shortlisting round. I don't have the
exact number of applicants, but I assume that most students preparing for tech roles who were open to
working in a full-time non-tech role after the internship had applied for this role.
Out of the resume shortlisting, only 34 candidates were shortlisted for the Online Assessment (OA).

2. Online Assessment [ 34 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
--- PAGE 2 ---
Out of the three sections in Paper 1, the Probability section was the toughest of all. Going through JEE-level
probability and the probability topics studied in engineering might prepare you for this section, but it is still
very calculation-heavy, and time management became a crucial factor.
The next section was Logical Reasoning, which contained medium-level aptitude questions. One can expect
relatively straightforward questions on topics such as probability, mathematics, speed, distance, time &
work, profit & loss, etc.
The Coding MCQ section consisted of code snippets where you had to select the correct output. The
questions were of medium difficulty, similar to those covered in the PSIPL course, and all the questions
were based on the C programming language.
The last paper was English Usage, and the questions were of an easy level. They were based on vocabulary,
reading comprehension, grammar, etc.
Out of this round, only 9 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

3. Tech Round 1[9 candidates appeared for this round]

The candidates shortlisted for Technical Round 1 were divided into two panels consisting of 4 and 5
candidates, respectively. I was the second candidate in the first panel. My panel consisted of two
interviewers.
The interview started with a brief introduction of myself and was broadly divided into four parts.
Technical:
This section started with the interviewer asking me about the four pillars of Object-Oriented
Programming (OOP) and explaining what each of them meant.
Next, he asked me what a palindrome is and how I would determine whether a given string/number is a
palindrome.
He then wanted to know my approach to printing an inverted triangle using stars/dots.
The discussion then shifted to Python and data structures in Python. I was asked about the differences
between lists, tuples, and sets, along with their respective use cases.
I was able to comfortably answer all these questions, which led us to the next section.
Quant:
This part of the interview felt more like a rapid-fire round.
The interviewer first asked me to calculate 95 × 95 very quickly. I started calculating it normally, but he
asked me to answer without doing the calculations. I answered 9975 (1002 - 52), which was obviously
incorrect. There are shortcut tricks for such calculations, but they didn't strike me at that moment.
Next, he asked me what the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand would be at 6:30. I started
explaining my approach, but he asked me to directly give the answer, which I did correctly.
--- PAGE 3 ---
To conclude this section, he asked me the classic 3 ants on a triangle puzzle, which I was able to answer
within 5 seconds.
General Knowledge:
The second interviewer asked me who the President of India was, which I answered correctly.
She then wanted to test my knowledge of current affairs and asked me about the current US-Iran conflict.
I honestly admitted that because of placement preparation, I hadn't been able to keep up with the latest
developments. However, I spoke about the major events that had taken place during the previous week.
Non-Technical:
In this section, I was asked about the SENSEX and NIFTY 50. I explained whatever I knew about these
indices, including the previous day's closing price.
The interviewer then asked me to name five companies from the NIFTY 50. Since I wasn't sure about the
NIFTY 50 constituents, I honestly told them that I was more familiar with the companies in the SENSEX
and proceeded to list a few of them.
The interview concluded with me asking the interviewers a question regarding their day-to-day work and
responsibilities at the firm.
Out of this round, 3 candidates were shortlisted for Technical Round 2.

4. Tech Round 2 [ 3 candidates appeared for this round]

This round consisted of a single panel with one interviewer.
The interviewer did not ask me to introduce myself. Instead, he asked me to walk him through my resume.
While discussing my resume, he stopped at one of my projects and asked me to describe it in detail, which I
was able to do comfortably.
Next, he gave me a problem statement and asked me to think for a minute before coming up with a suitable
framework. The problem statement revolved around automating the research process, extracting insights,
and sending weekly reports to bankers. I proposed a pipeline consisting of web scraping, LLM calls for
extracting insights, and generating reports and presentations using Python scripts. I also explained which
Python libraries I would use for each part of the pipeline. This was followed by a discussion on VBA and
where it could be useful in such workflows.
Next, the interviewer asked me a guesstimate question, where more than the final answer, the approach and
thought process behind arriving at the answer mattered. Since I was familiar with such questions, I was able
to structure my answer well, and the interviewer seemed satisfied with my approach.
The interview concluded with a discussion about JPMC's in-house LLMs and how they were developed.
Out of this round, only 2 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round.

4. HR Round [ 2 candidates appeared for this round]

The HR panel consisted of two interviewers. The interview started with a brief introduction of myself.
--- PAGE 4 ---
They first asked me about my SPJIMR Management Minor, specifically whether it was something I was
pursuing in addition to my degree or if it was a part of my curriculum. I explained how our college offers
multiple minor programs, out of which students can choose one, along with the shortlisting criteria for the
same.
The interviewer was curious about my interest in finance, considering that I was pursuing a Bachelor's in
Computer Engineering. I answered that being a part of E-Cell exposed me to several non-technical domains,
which eventually led me to participate in case competitions. These experiences significantly strengthened
my interest in finance and management.
The interviewer then asked me to mention two key insights from the firm's Pre-Placement Talk (PPT). I was
able to recall and explain the points that I had noted during the session.
Finally, when I was allowed to ask a question, I asked about the role of HR in the organization and how they
coordinate different departments within the firm.
After the HR round, 2 candidates were finally selected and offered the role.

the condition. (I converted num to string, added the char, converted back to num)
Was able to pass 11/12 test cases.
Q2:
This question was similar to  https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-path-sum/

1. [Technical Round 1]  [48 people appeared for this round ]

Lists?  What  to  use  if  I  want  to  insert  an  element  in  constant  time?  Which  is  faster  for  searching
an  element?  He  then  gave  me  a  pattern  printing  question  (basically,  print  a  diamond,  using  the  *

further  optimize  it.  He  then  asked,  what  happens  when  you  type  a  URL  on  the  browser  and  hit
enter? What is TCP? What is UDP? Give an example when you could use UDP.
Objects,  Garbage  collection,  ThreadSafe,  method  overloading  and  overriding,  constructor
overloading,  pass  by  value,  pass  by  reference  in  Java.  Exception  Handling,  what  is  it?  Difference
between  'throw'  and  'throws'?  Do  you  have  multiple  inheritance  in  Java?  What  happens  when  2
interfaces have the same method definition? (wasn't able to answer the last one)
Then,  the  interviewer  gave  me  a  case  to  design  a  basic  library  DBMS.  Highlight  the  entities,
attributes,  why,  with  constraints  (PK  /  FK  /  NOT  NULL  etc).  I  explained  the  purpose  of  each  table
and entity, why they were needed, and how they would be used in the overall system.
He  then  asked  a  few  SQL  queries  to  be  performed  on  the  same  tables  that  I  had  designed.
These  were  quite  simple,  just  2  queries  -  one  using  GROUP  BY  +  HAVING  and  second  using
UNION.  He  asked  about  SQL  vs  NoSQL.  What  are  the  different  kinds  of  databases  I  am  aware
of? Any examples for graph databases? (Facebook friends network)
Make  sure  you  explain  your  approach  from  scratch,  think  out  loud  ,  don't  just  jump  and  say  "this  is
the  answer"  Approach  >  Answer  .  Ask  questions  if  you  are  not  sure,  I  blanked  out  in  between
once,  while  he  was  asking  a  question.  So,  I  politely  requested  if  he  could  repeat  it.  Although  this
shouldn't happen but yeah make it sound like you are trying to clarify the question.
He  then  asked  questions  about  OS  -  Processes  vs  Threads,  do  processes  share  memory?  Do
threads  share  memory?  What  is  a  deadlock?  What  is  virtual  memory?  Why  do  you  need  it?  How
to resolve deadlocks?
I  was  able  to  answer  all  but  2  or  3  questions  where  I  mentioned  "I  am  not  sure  about  this,  but  I'll
look into it"  .
The round ended on a positive note with me asking them 2 questions :

-  How does banking work via calls? (Something related to IVR as they mentioned)

-  What do you expect from freshers?

Other  students  were  asked  easy-medium  DSA  questions(eg:  Longest  palindromic  substring,
Valid parentheses, find the repeating number, basic tree traversals - these are what I can recall)
Port numbers of various web services (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Mongo, Docker, http etc),
In  depth  Java  questions(really  deep).  Honestly,  this  depends  quite  a  lot  on  your  panel  but  overall
DBMS schema+DSA+Computer Fundamentals to a basic understanding level was consistent.
For  this  round,  just  have  clarity  with  the  concepts  and  your  answers.  Be  calm  and  don't  show
evident  confusion  on  your  face  at  any  point.  Be  loud  and  clear.  Don't  murmur.  Also  I'd  highly
suggest,  do  not  give  direct  answers  or  one  liners.  For  instance,  'throw'  vs  'throws'  can  be
answered  in  one  line.  But  try  to  first  give  a  gist  about  exceptions,  then  use  scenarios/examples
to  support  your  answer.  This  does  2  things  -  shows  clear  understanding  of  the  topic,  and  eats  up
more  time  in  the  interview.  Try  to  'control'  the  interview,  although  I'm  using  a  strong  word  here  but
basically learn to speak a bit more.

2. [Technical Round 2]  [20 people appeared for this round ]

This  round  was  again  conducted  by  two  interviewers  and  lasted  about  40-45  minutes.  It  began
with  my  introduction,  followed  by  a  deep  dive  into  RAG,  what  it  is,  how  it  works  under  the  hood,
and  an  explanation  using  an  example.  I  was  also  asked  about  the  vector  database  I  had  used.
Next,  I  was  asked  about  my  favorite  subject.  I  answered  DBMS  and  explained  why,  using
examples  from  my  projects  to  show  how  databases  helped  me  build  a  stronger  practical
understanding  than  subjects  like  OS  or  Computer  Networks.  I  also  emphasized  that  I  believe
every core subject is equally important in engineering and software development.
He  then  looked  at  'ETL  Pipeline'  that  I  mentioned  in  my  internship  points,  and  asked  me  to
explain  it  clearly,  "what  is  ETL?  Explain  it  to  your  Mom."  I  explained  my  internship  project  and  the
project  lifecycle.  He  later  got  confused  why  Barclays  is  mentioned  as  an  education  field,  I
explained  everything  about  MDMs  and  what  this  minor  was  about.  He  then  told  me  to  print  a
christmas tree(using *), something like this:
I  divided  the  problem  into  two  independent  parts:  the  triangular  canopy  and  the  rectangular  trunk.
For  the  canopy,  each  row  has  N  -  i  leading  spaces  and  2*i  -  1  stars,  producing  a  centered
isosceles  triangle.  After  printing  all  N  rows,  I  printed  a  centered  trunk  by  calculating  its  width  and
left padding. He followed up by asking the TC and SC.
Another  question,  which  was  pretty  random,  but  worked  well  in  my  favour  (maybe  because  I  was
able  to  answer  this  in  3-4  seconds)  was,  he  asked  me  to  "Find  12%  of  730".  Just  multiplied
12*73,  which  was  876  and  divided  that  by  10.  He  asked  me  to  iterate  my  approach  loudly  later.
Nothing  major,  I  guess.  Maybe  they  were  just  testing  whether  I'd  get  stressed  on  getting  a
sudden mental math question.
The  next  question  was  "Explain  different  problems  that  can  arise  after  you  push  a  project",  so  I
took  example  of  my  Flash  sale  order  manager  project,  and  explained  how  I  first  used  MySQL  for
the  entire  thing  but  it  resulted  in  dropping  orders  due  to  heavy  traffic  on  server  (multiple  POST
requests  hitting  at  the  same  instant).  To  solve  this  problem,  I  used  a  Redis  queue  and  a  worker
service  which  helps  maintain  the  order  and  consistency  in  the  order  count.  Although  this  was
slightly  off  wrt  the  question,  I  intended  to  leave  an  impression  that  I  have  studied  design  concepts
and implemented them in my project.
The round concluded, again on a positive note, with me asking 2 questions to the interviewers:

-  "This  might  sound  a  bit  crazy,  but  since  IDFC  is  trying  to  expand  its  reach  in  tier  2,3  cities

in India, is there any solution where you can have offline payments? Just curious"

-  What  do  you  suggest  one  should  focus  on  in  the  next  6  months  before  joining  the

company?
Within  five  minutes,  I  was  shortlisted  for  the  next  round.  The  HR  then  requested  my  email  ID
from the TPC to send the meet link for the virtual L3 interview.

3. [HR Round]  [ 10 students appeared for this round ]

This  was  more  of  a  casual  conversation  that  lasted  for  around  10  minutes.  The  point  of  this
round  is  to  judge  you  as  a  person  and  the  character  that  you  bring  to  the  table.  I  was  asked  the
typical  "Why  do  you  want  to  join  IDFC?".  Further  questions  -  Why  not  a  tech  company  and  a
bank  instead?  What  is  your  favourite  app  you  have  on  your  mobile  phone  and  why?  Do  you  use
any  banking  apps?  What  is  that  one  feature/characteristic  that  you  would  want  the  mobile
banking  app  to  have?  What  if  you  are  assigned  a  project  where  you  do  not  like  the  technologies
being  used,  or  the  project  itself?  Where  are  you  from?  Where  are  your  parents  from?  Are  you
comfortable with relocating to any other location?
The  round  concluded  by  me  asking  a  question  to  the  HR  representative,  "What  do  you  expect
from interns?"
Some  candidates  had  their  HR  round  before  the  L3  interview,  while  others  had  the  L3  interview
first.  The  L3  interview  was  scheduled  within  a  fixed  time  window  for  each  candidate,  and  the
invitation  email  included  a  Microsoft  Teams  meeting  link  along  with  our  resume  for  the  senior
manager to review.

4. [Technical Round 3]  [10 students appeared for this round ]

This  round  was  conducted  virtually  by  a  senior  manager  on  Microsoft  Teams  and  focused
primarily  on  my  resume  and  projects.  After  a  brief  introduction,  the  interviewer  noticed  my  Minor
in  Banking  Technology  and  asked  about  it.  I  highlighted  topics  such  as  BFSI,  Agile/Scrum,  and
Enterprise  Risk  Management,  and  mentioned  that  we'd  be  working  on  a  related  project  in  the
upcoming semester.
He  then  directly  picked  my  first  project.  He  asked  me  specific  concepts  and  their
implementation,  one  by  one,  for  each  project.  He  asked  questions  like  "Why  did  you  use  Redis",
"What  is  NGINX  and  how  is  it  balancing  the  load",  "Explain  the  CI/CD  Pipeline  you've  created  in
your project".
My  second  project  was  based  on  NLP  and  RAG.  He  asked  me  how  RAG  works,  do  you  need  an
LLM  layer  or  not  for  the  RAG  Pipeline?  What  would  happen  without  it?  With  it?  What  is  the  vector
DB  you  have  used?  Why  have  you  used  MongoDB?  (to  store  the  files),  but  why?  U  just  need  to
chunk  and  store  the  embeddings  right?  I  answered,  for  file  history  that  can  be  accessed  on  the
user  profile.  For  the  third  project,  he  just  asked  me  to  explain  the  authentication  flow  in  the
project.
He  then  gave  me  2  tables-  orders1  and  orders2,  and  then  asked  me  to  write  a  SQL  query  to  find
the maximum amount from both the order tables, which can be solved using UNION.
SELECT MAX(amount) AS max_amount
FROM (
SELECT amount FROM orders1
UNION ALL
SELECT amount FROM orders2
) AS all_orders;
The  round  concluded  with  me  asking  him  how  his  journey  at  IDFC  was,  and  how  he  has  grown
professionally.  Also  one  advice  that  would  help  me  become  a  better  fit  and  better  engineer
overall.  He  gave  some  good  insights.  I  was  the  last  person  to  give  this  round  and  come  out  of  the
TPO. It ended at 9:40pm lasting about half an hour.
The  final  results  were  announced  at  10:40  PM,  when  I  was  on  my  way  home.  My  phone  started
ringing,  notifications  started  flooding  in.  Everything  changed  in  an  instant,  leaving  a  moment  and
feeling that was difficult to process and explain.
At  one  point,  the  previous  day,  I  didn't  feel  confident  I  would  make  it  past  even  R1,  as  I  was  quite
exhausted  after  PhonePe  and  WorkIndia  and  had  not  revised  anything.  But,  things  started  turning
out  well  at  every  stage,  and  I'd  just  say  this  ki  "jis  din  tumhara  placement  hona  hai,  uss  din
pakka  ho  ke  rahega."  It's  a  fact  that  you  cannot  change,  you'll  have  to  personally  withdraw  from
the process to prove this otherwise.
[ 8 students received the offer at the end, including me.]
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A little background about my placement journey that I would like to share,
I  wasn't  able  to  clear  the  OAs  for  JPMC  CFG,  Barclays'  and  UBS'  and  Mahindra  Finance
Summer  internships.  I  reached  the  Interview  R1  for  Russell  Investments  but  did  not  make  it
further.  It  did  hurt  a  bit  after  every  rejection,  but  every  experience  was  a  stepping  stone.  It  is
important  to  acknowledge  things  are  not  in  our  hands  all  the  time.  Now  that  I  look  back,  had  I
cracked  Barclays  SI  last  year,  I  would  not  have  got  this  opportunity.  There's  always  a  better
opportunity  ahead.  Keep  your  head  high  and  just  keep  working  towards  your  goal,  is  what  I  have
learnt over these 1.5 years.
Over  time  you'll  realise,  luck  plays  a  huge  role  in  placements.  You  might  be  the  best  candidate  in
terms  of  preparation,  but  you  might  not  get  an  OA  shortlist  (it  happens,  IDFC  shortlists  before  the
OA  round  were  kinda  random).  You  might  miss  the  interview  shortlist,  for  whatever  reasons
(again,  it  happens  more  often  than  you  would  imagine).  Your  selection  depends  on  the  interview
you  give  which  depends  on  the  kind  of  panel  you  get,  at  every  stage.  There's  at  least  a  50-60%
luck  factor  involved  in  placements,  which  is  not  in  our  control.  What  is  in  our  hands  is  our
preparation  and  our  temperament.  Focus  on  what  you  can  control.  Don't  leave  any  room  for
regrets.

journey.prep:
• Know your resume inside out you should be able to explain every single word you've written on it,

since interviewers often dig deep into whatever you mention.

• Be presentable and work on your communication skills, as they matter just as much as your technical

knowledge.

• Stay confident throughout, but don't try to bluff your way through something you don't know it's

better to admit you're unaware of a topic than to talk unnecessarily around it.

• Try to genuinely convince the panel why you're the right fit for the role, rather than just answering

questions mechanically.

• For aptitude preparation, practicing questions from IndiaBix helped a lot, and following the YouTube

series by CareerRide.com is also a good way to build speed and accuracy.
Since I came from a technical background, my core strength was in tech, but having a minor in Financial
Strategy and Management gave me a decent grasp of financial concepts. If you come from a technical
background, don't worry about having extensive finance knowledge, as only a basic understanding is
generally expected. However, I would recommend completing a few introductory courses from the
Corporate Finance Institute (CFI) before the interviews. They provide a good foundation and can help you
answer finance-related questions more confidently.
--- PAGE 4 ---

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk - 24 June 2026

• Resume Shortlisting

• Online Assessment - 27 June 2026

• Technical Interview Round 1 - 03 July 2026

• Technical Interview Round 2 - 03 July 2026

• HR Interview - 03 July 2026

• Result Declaration - 03 July 2026

Because it was raining heavily in Mumbai and there was a red alert, all interviews were held online instead
of in person. But students who got shortlisted still had to come to college and give their online interviews
from there.

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The process began with an online Pre-Placement Talk on 24 June 2026. In this session, the company talked
about itself, its different teams, the Corporate Risk team, the internship program, and what kind of
candidates they usually look for.
My tip: listen carefully during this talk, because it helps you later in the process. Take some notes, and if you
get a chance during Q&A, ask good questions.
After the talk, candidates had to apply through the JPMorgan Chase Careers Portal, using the link given by
the TPO. The company then checked these applications to shortlist candidates.
Students who were shortlisted for the Online Assessment got to know on 26 June 2026, around 5:30 PM.

2. Online Assessment (122 shortlisted candidates)

The Online Assessment took place on 27 June 2026 in a remote, proctored format, with candidates taking
the test from home under continuous webcam surveillance. The exam lasted 45 minutes. Rough sheets were
permitted for calculations, provided they stayed visible within the camera frame at all times.
--- PAGE 2 ---
The paper consisted of 30 multiple-choice questions in total, with a marking scheme of +2 for each correct
answer and a penalty of -1 for each incorrect one. Of these, 27 questions belonged to the Quantitative
Aptitude section, while the remaining 3 covered Probability, Permutation & Combination.
The Quantitative Aptitude questions were drawn from standard topics such as Profit & Loss, Time & Work,
Time, Speed & Distance, Ratios, Train-related problems, and other foundational aptitude concepts. The
paper was rated moderate in difficulty overall, and managing time wisely across the 45-minute window was
essential to scoring well.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (32 shortlisted candidates)

The shortlist for this round came out on 2 July 2026, around 8:30 PM, with 32 candidates making it through
from the Online Assessment. Due to the weather situation in Mumbai, interviews were held online from the
college campus, with multiple panels running in parallel.
My round lasted about 20 minutes and began with a quick self-introduction, followed by a brief explanation
of one of my projects. Since I had built a DCF valuation model as part of it, the panel asked me to walk
through the formulas and terms I'd mentioned in my resume. As my project also involved some ML work,
they followed up by asking how I had integrated the ML pipeline. From there, the conversation shifted to a
more conceptual question on how risk affects banks and financial firms, which I answered by explaining the
different types of risk and their impact. The panel then lightened up a bit, asking about my hobbies, followed
by why I was interested in a non-tech role despite my technical background, and the standard why-JPMC
question. Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions, so I asked about the Al tools they've recently
started using and the workflow followed within the Corporate Risk team.
Overall, this round was essentially about convincing the panel why I was the right fit for the role.
Around 15 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (15 shortlisted candidates)

This round was again resume-based but went deeper into financial concepts, testing both my technical
grounding and critical thinking. The questions asked were:

• A quick self-introduction to start off

• A detailed walkthrough of my DCF model explaining the entire workflow, how each calculation was

done, the formulas used, and what they meant

• A brief overview of my ML project

• A short explanation of another project that combined tech and finance elements

• Whether I knew any financial ratios, along with a detailed explanation of one of my choice

• Questions on my Excel skills though not mentioned on my resume, I explained I had used it while

building my DCF model and had working knowledge of the basics

• The why-non-tech question again, which I answered by mentioning my minor in Financial Strategy

and Management, and my interest in solving real-world problems rather than just writing generic
code

• Details about a committee I had mentioned on my resume what my role involved and how I

approached it

• A casual question about my hobbies, where I mentioned painting, followed by a scenario-based

question on how I'd use a website to encourage more people to take up painting
--- PAGE 3 ---

• A guesstimate question assuming Mumbai has a population of 2 crore, how would I estimate the

number of cars running daily in the city

• A general awareness question on what I knew about JPMC

Overall, this round was more about testing how I think and how I apply that thinking to real situations.

5. HR Interview (10 shortlisted candidates)

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for this final round, which was much more conversational and
relaxed compared to the earlier rounds. The questions asked were:

• A quick self-introduction

• Location preference, along with details about shift timings and cab facilities provided by the

company

• A situational question whether I had ever faced a moment in life where I was asked to do something

wrong, and how I responded to it
This round was largely focused on understanding my location preference and getting a sense of my
personality and values rather than testing technical knowledge.
The HR interviews wrapped up by around 4:45 PM. Following this, we stayed back on campus until roughly
6:15 PM, when we were told that results would be shared online. The final outcome was announced
sometime between 7:50 and 8:00 PM, and all 10 candidates who appeared for the HR round were offered
internships.

journey.howSecured:
Everyone had applied for the role via Superset, and out of everyone that applied, 27 people were
shortlisted. Our best guess at the time was that they had selected candidates based on our pointers, since
everyone that was shortlisted had a high pointer. Mine was 9.27.
For the 27 shortlisted candidates, we were told that we would have Group Discussions (GDs) and then
interviews.
Group Discussion (GD) [27 people appeared, 7 shortlisted for next round]
We were divided into 3 groups for the GD, and my group had 8 people. Each group was given different
topics:

- T1: "Will Al replace software engineers in 10 years?"

- T2 (My topic): "Does data privacy seem far-fetched in today's era?"

- T3: "Should the government regulate AI?"

The time given for the GD was 2 minutes to prepare, 8 minutes to speak, and 2 minutes to conclude. I was
the first one to speak, meaning I started the discussion. Later, I was able to make one more point. There
were 2 people in my group who did not get an opportunity to speak a single point. So, try to be careful
here-given how short the time is, make sure to make at least 2 points.
After the GD, 7 people were shortlisted for the interviews.
Technical Round - 1[7 people appeared, 3 people moved for next round]
I was the 2nd person to be interviewed. They started by scanning my resume and asked which project I
would like to discuss in detail. I said I would like to discuss my UPI Analytics project because it closely
aligns with the role (which involves analytics) and it has a finance element to it as well.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Now, I did not just discuss the project verbally; instead, I showed them the live hosted project via my site.

- My site: https://prasadgade.dev/

- Project 1 showed: https://upi-analytics.streamlit.app/

Initially, the project did not open on their laptop due to a firewall blocking it, but the second interviewer
pulled up his phone and saw the project. I got lucky here that he took the effort to open it on his phone.
Then, we discussed the project for about 5 minutes.
Later, the conversation switched to Python coding. Since this was an analytics role and the company uses
Python, knowing Pandas and NumPy was a must. I will be honest: I am very well aware of how NumPy
and Pandas work, but I did not know all the exact syntax. Here were the questions and how they went:

- Write a Pandas query to find department-wise mean salary: I was able to write this one.

- What is the difference between concat and merge in a dataframe? I was able to explain the function, but

I got the syntax wrong, and I was informed by the panel right there that I got it incorrect.

- What is a lambda function and write one example: I was able to do this.

- What is list append vs. list extend? I was a bit hesitant initially but was able to answer.

- Aggregate vs. Transform in Pandas: I got this correct.

- Add one column named 'average salary' to each row (similar to a window function and partition in

SQL): I did not know how to do it in Python, so I asked them if I could write it in SQL. They said no, it's
alright.
I was also asked one DSA question:

- How to find if a Linked List has a cycle: I knew this question from the Neetcode 150 sheet, so I

immediately told them the Fast and Slow pointer approach. Understanding that I knew the approach, they
asked me to write the pseudocode, which I was able to do. Then they asked if there were any other
approaches I could think of. I said yes, using a Hash Set to keep track of nodes and then returning cycle if
we have seen the node previously.
They then asked if I had any questions for them. During the intro, one of the interviewers had mentioned
that he was just 2 batches senior to us from DY Patil college. So, I asked him how the transition has been
at Nomura from a student to an employee. I don't know if I got brownie points for the question or not, but
that ended Tech Round 1.
As we were waiting outside, me and 3 other students were told that we were selected for the next rounds
(Tech Round 2 and HR). These rounds happened in parallel, meaning while I was giving Tech Round 2,
another candidate was giving their HR round.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Technical Round - 2 3 people appeared
This round started with him asking for my introduction. Then we started talking about my first internship
(which I did during my diploma). It was a data analytics internship where I learned Power BI, so I
discussed that.
Later, he asked about an experience on my resume: Independent AI & Software Developer for a
Confidential Client (NDA-Protected). Since this is NDA protected, I told him clearly that I would not be
able to discuss the details about the client or what the product is, but I could talk about the engineering
methodologies, tools, and frameworks I used. I then went on to explain all the technicalities behind it.
Then came a series of behavioral/situational questions:

- Why Nomura / Why this role? I talked about how Nomura is one of the leading

institutes in finance, and since this is an analytics role, my entire profile aligns with it (my projects, my
internship, etc.).

- What do you know about the role and where did you study it from? I shared the info about the role and

said I studied it online and from LLMs. He asked if I talked to someone in person for guidance about the
role, to which I honestly said no.

- "Assume a senior of yours gives you work which you have 0 knowledge about and you have to submit

in 2-3 hours. What will you do?" I said initially I would talk to the senior if they are available to clear my
doubts; otherwise, I would do research on my own using the internet and LLMS. I also gave an example
of a past experience where I was in the exact same situation and had to figure things out on my own.

- Do you like what you work on? What drives you? What will get you to get up on a Monday and start

working? I answered about my interest in data analytics, ML, and the joy I get when I automate tasks with
machines.
Then he moved to my exposure in finance:

- I mentioned I am doing a management minor where I had some exposure to finance.

- He asked me a financial term. I don't even remember what it was, but I honestly said, "Sir, I am not

aware of it."

- What are your goals wrt your career? A pretty standard question.
