geopolitics and government financial policies.
Then he went back to behavioral:
--- PAGE 4 ---

- Describe yourself in 3 words: I said Integrity, Empathy, and Hardworking.

- How can you say that you have empathy? Here, I was able to showcase my portfolio

(https://prasadgade.dev). I explained the whole philosophy of why I made my site and how it is structured
for different users (technical users as well as non-tech users like my parents and friends). This showed
how I put myself in others' shoes.
The Risk: After this, he asked, "Do you have any questions for me?" At this point, having fumbled the
two finance questions, I decided to take a huge risk and asked him: "Will there be any reason that you will
not hire me today?ạ"i
(Note: This question could have backfired very badly!! I took the chance, but do this at your own risk).
To this, he said, "Yeah, there could be several reasons for not selecting you. We might get a better
candidate, or another candidate might have a better passion for finance than youại
This actually worked out to my luck, because I used his answer to extend the conversation back into my
finance project (https://upi-analytics.streamlit.app/). I explained how this project proved my interest and
passion for finance. I shared a few insights from my analytics,
like:

1. Did you know that despite being the financial capital of India, Mumbai is not 1st in terms of UPI

payments, rather Pune is? (He was genuinely surprised and intrigued by this).

2. The average amount of transactions reduces during the festive season. (You would think the opposite

should happen, right? But the data says otherwise).
I was able to thoroughly explain both insights, and he seemed very happy. Remember, my interview was
technically over, but because I asked that bold question at the end, I was able to extend the conversation.
He then casually asked about my family background, where I am originally from, how the change from
Nashik to Mumbai has been, what my day looks like when I'm free, and my hobbies.
HR Round [3 people appeared - finally 1 selected]

- Where are you from?

- Tell me something famous about Nashik.

- What do you love more, Nashik or Mumbai, and why?

- What are your hobbies?

--- PAGE 5 ---

- Favorite IPL team? (I said CSK).

- Why CSK? Shouldn't MSD retire? My Answer: Obviously, this was a light-hearted question, but I was

able to turn this into an HR-style answer. I said I admire MSD due to his leadership qualities and his
down-to-earth attitude. I quoted a line MSD once said: "I do not want people to remember me as a good
cricketer, rather I want them to remember me as a good personẠạ

- Name one emerging player from the IPL you think would do wonders for TeamIndia.

- Talk about my experience as an Independent Al & Software Developer. (We had a similar conversation

about this experience as in the previous round).

- Tricky Question: "Because of Al, companies are removing freshers despite that, you were able to get

this role as an Independent AI Developer. What is your take on this?"
After this, we were sitting in the top office lobby. One thing to note here is that only 3 people were given
a chance for the HR and Tech 2 rounds. They did not even consider the rest of the people who had their
Round 1 interview, maybe because they had already found their candidates. I got lucky because I was the
2nd to be interviewed overall.
Then the TPC came outside and told me I was selected!
Now surprisingly Nomura only selected one person as opposed to previous years. So yeah happy and
humble to be selected.
My Placement Journey (Rejections before Success)
My journey actually started in my 3rd year when BNY came for summer interns. I was shortlisted for the
OA, gave Interview 1 and Interview 2. But in the end, I was kept on a waiting list, which left me
incredibly disheartened.
When our actual placement season started in July 2026:

- First was JPMC. The roles were non-tech, so I did not apply (even though the CTC was very good).

- Applied for IDFC First Bank > Could not clear the OA.

- Applied for PhonePe > Could not clear the OA.

- Applied for WorkIndia -> Resume was not shortlisted.

- Applied for AUXO AI -> Could not clear the OA.

- Applied for UBS -> Was not able to land an interview.

I faced all these rejections. The UBS process and Nomura process were on consecutive days. After getting
rejected by UBS, I was feeling very disappointed. The next day I had the Nomura process. I talked to a

--- PAGE 6 ---
Let me tell you, the placement process does involve luck. So do not worry if you don't get placed early.
You just have to crack one company, not every company. I always kept telling myself one thing: "The
question is not IF I will get placed. The question is WHEN I will get placed." Do not doubt yourself. It is
just a matter of time before you get things right.

strongly recommend is maintaining a balance between tech and non tech preparation. For me, non
tech was more of a fallback option because I had already invested enough time in technical
preparation through DSA, CP, and projects. That gave me the confidence to apply for both types of
roles instead of depending entirely on one. Keep practicing DSA, build a few good projects, and have

shortlisted.

Most of the questions were of easy to medium difficulty, but don't take this round lightly because a large

level questions and mainly covered topics such as Permutation and Combination, Time and Work, Pipes and
Cisterns, Calendars, and similar concepts. The second section focused on Data Interpretation and Logical
Reasoning.
For preparation, I would recommend practicing aptitude questions on IndiaBix and following the Career
Ride aptitude playlist, as both are useful resources for building speed and accuracy.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Technical Round 1 [ Close to 33]

The names of the shortlisted candidates for the CR role were released almost two days before the interview.
However, for the CIB and FinTech roles, the shortlist was announced only a day before the interview. My
advice is to start your preparation early because you may not get enough time between the shortlist
announcement and the interview.
Because of heavy rains, the interview was conducted online from the college campus.
Some key points from my interview experience:

• The interview was entirely based on my resume.

• My panel consisted of two interviewers from the risk team. If the interviewers don't introduce

themselves, politely ask for their names and remember them. It leaves a good impression.

• The interview began with my introduction. I spoke about my finance minor, case competitions,

Python, and data analytics experience. Your introduction is very important because it often sets the
direction for the rest of the interview.

• I had mentioned an M& A focused case competition presentation in my projects and had also

completed the CFI Accounting Fundamentals course. Based on this, I was asked finance related
questions such as:

• Why did you use the Precedent Transactions model instead of the DCF model?

• How do changes in depreciation and tax rates affect the balance sheet?

• One of my hackathon projects involved using an LLM with RAG. The discussion revolved around:

• What problem was the project solving?

• Why did you choose to build it?

o How did the overall solution work?

• I was also asked about the tools and technologies relevant to the role. Since I had studied the job

description carefully and spoken to a few seniors beforehand, I discussed tools such as Power BI,
Tableau, Alteryx, Python, and the libraries I had used.

• Towards the end, they asked how Al is impacting the banking industry and the job market. To which

I told them everything is an abstraction. Earlier we used to have assembly now we have Al and stuff.

• They also asked which track from the job description I would like to join as an intern. Pay close

attention to the PPT and the JD because this is a common discussion point. Asking thoughtful
questions related to them also creates a positive impression.

• The round ended with me asking them a question about the tracks, how do they use ai and stuff in

their workflows.
Overall the interview lasted around 25 minutes and was quite conversational. Personally I found it to be a
relaxed experience. In fact, the day before the interview I was busy solving Codeforces and LeetCode
problems for the PhonePe OA that was scheduled the following day.
One important piece of advice is to know your resume inside out. Every project, course, skill, and
achievement you mention is fair game. While my interview focused mainly on data analytics, finance and
projects, some of my friends were asked core technical subjects such as Object Oriented Programming &
SQL.
If you're mentioning numbers on your resume then you should be ble to justify them.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Technical Round 1 [ Close to 10-12]

Just like the previous round, this interview was heavily focused on my resume, so make sure you know
every single point you've mentioned.
Some of the topics discussed during my interview were:

• Be prepared to explain every number, assumption, and result in your projects. For example, I had

built a DCF model for CDSL, so I was asked about the assumptions I had made, the numbers I had
used, and concepts such as WACC and CAPM.

• I was asked about my Python and data analytics experience and whether I was comfortable using

Python. I answered honestly by saying that C++ is my primary programming language because of
competitive programming. I am comfortable solving DSA problems in Python as well, but for my
projects I have also relied on Al assistants and official documentation whenever required.

• The interviewer then asked about my understanding of the role and my knowledge of risk and credit

since I had completed the Coursera course Introduction to Risk and Credit. I explained that the role is
a combination of data analysis, reporting, and stakeholder communication. I had a good
understanding of the role because I had spoken with seniors who were already working in the same
department.

• To explain my understanding of risk, I discussed real world examples such as the recent issues faced

by HDFC Bank, the collapse of Lehman Brothers, and the Credit Suisse crisis. I also spoke about
how JPMorgan Chase acquired Bear Stearns and Washington Mutual during the 2008 financial crisis
to help stabilize the financial system.

• We further discussed Basel norms and a few important banking ratios such as the Capital Adequacy

Ratio (CAR) and the Leverage Ratio (LR), including how these metrics are used to assess the
financial health of banks.

• Towards the end, I was asked to rate my proficiency in Python and Tableau on a scale of 1 to 10. I

honestly rated myself around 7.5 to 8 because I had used both tools in multiple case studies and as
part of my Business Analytics with Python coursework.
The interview concluded with me asking the interviewer a question.
Overall, this round lasted for about 25 minutes. It was technical but conversational, and once again the
discussion revolved almost entirely around my resume. My biggest advice would be to thoroughly
understand every project, course, certification, and skill you've mentioned because the interviewers can dive
deep into any of them.

3. HR Round [ close to 10 people]

This was the shortest and the most relaxed round of the entire process. The interview lasted for only about
10 minutes.
The interview started with a brief introduction where I spoke about myself, where I am from, and how
pursuing a Finance minor sparked my interest in the finance domain.
The questions asked were mostly HR and role related, including:
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Tell me about yourself.

• How do you think a typical day at jpmc would look for you in this role?

• Are you comfortable working afternoon or night shifts if required?

• Are you willing to relocate to Bangalore?

Overall, the conversation was very casual and focused on understanding my interest in the role, my
expectations, and whether I was a good cultural fit for the team. There were no technical questions in this
round, and it concluded within 10 minutes.
Results were announced almost 3 hours after the HR round around 8:30PM.
Everyone who appeared for this round was selected for the role.

7th August, 2026

Internship Stipend: €25,000 per month

Location: Pune / Bangalore / Chennai / Hyderabad

CTC: <8,50,000 + 21,00,000 joining bonus

1. Resume Shortlisting (121 candidates shortlisted)

least 70 on https://resumeworded.com/

2. TransUnion PPT

asked "What were your two biggest takeaways from the PPT?" So make sure you understand what
TransUnion does, what they emphasized during the presentation, and what interests you about the
company.

3. Online Assessment (121 candidates appeared)

This was conducted after the PPT on the day itself and consisted of English, Logical Aptitude,
Quantitative Aptitude and 2 Coding Questions. Each of these sections were timed so speed is critical.
English was based on Grammar, Vocabulary, Reading comprehension, Understanding the main idea
of a passage
Logical Aptitude included Number series, Odd one out, Pattern-based questions, Basic logical
reasoning. I practised aptitude using ChatGPT by asking it to give me the important formulas and
then quiz me with difficult questions. If you have time, do practise from IndiaBix as well; they have
good-level questions.
Quantitative Aptitude included Ratios and proportions, Simple interest, Time and work, speed and
distance, Percentages, Basic arithmetic as far as I remember.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Coding : (2 Q's in 45 min) I got two very easy coding questions, both based on arrays/strings. One
question involved removing vowels from a string. The other was a basic array-based problem.
However, the coding questions are shuffled between candidates, so your experience can be very
different. Some students may get two easy questions, while others may get a more difficult one. So
don't prepare assuming that the coding round will be easy.

4. Shortlisting (34 candidates shortlisted)

The OA results came out at around 8 PM, and the interviews were scheduled for the next morning.
This meant there was very little time between getting shortlisted and the interview. I ended up
studying almost the entire night and got around 3.5 hours of sleep.
If you get shortlisted late at night and have an interview the next morning, you should ideally only
need to revise, not learn everything from scratch.
The night before, focus on: Resume → Projects → Core CS → SQL → DSA → Company
Also, practise speaking your answers out loud as if you're answering the interviewer. This really
helped me with my communication, especially because I tend to get anxious. It helps you structure
your thoughts and stay calm during the actual interview.

5. Technical Interview (34 candidates appeared)

The interview experience can vary a lot depending on the panel. In my case, the interview focused
heavily on projects. I was asked if I could demonstrate my projects live, show my GitHub
repositories, and explain my code and database schema.
At one point, they asked me to open specific files from my code, so know your project directory
structure and where things are. Be ready to open VS Code and demonstrate your project. So for
the projects on your resume:

* Know your project structure and code at a basic level.

*
Understand your database/schema.

* He prepared to explain chalenges and how you solved them.

Know why you chose your technologies/ why not other tech stacks
You don't need to know every line of code, but you should genuinely understand what you have
built. Other candidates were asked more technical questions, including DSA, SQL and Core CS. So
prepare for all three areas.
And if you don't know the answer to something, don't panic or try to make up an answer. Just be
honest and say that you're not sure about it right now, but you'd look into it after the interview. It's
completely okay to not know everything, they don't expect you to.
--- PAGE 3 ---

6. HR Interview (11 candidates shortlisted)

The HR round was more conversational. I was asked:

* Whether I was comfortable with relocation

* How do vou handle Team conflicts / working with people

For the team conflict question, I answered with a story. You can use an incident from your own life
that shows how you handled a disagreement and reached a solution.
Using the STAR framework can make your answer much more memorable and impactful. Generic
answers like "I communicate with my teammates and resolve conflicts" don't really tell the
interviewer anything about you, whereas a real story gives them something to remember. This also
works well for other HR questions like "Tell me about a challenge," "Tell me about a time you failed,"
"Tell me about a time you showed leadership," etc.
The main thing they seemed to evaluate was how you communicate, how confidently you
present yourself, and whether you genuinely want to learn and work with the company. So
don't try to sound overly rehearsed. Be authentic and confident.
Finally 10 candidates were shortlisted for TransUnion!
Useful Resources & Prep Tips
Projects: I used AntiGravity as my mock interviewer. Give it each project and ask it to explain the
codebase, architecture, database, tech choices, challenges, and ask follow-up questions.
SQL: https://eetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-5Q/ is useful, but you can start by asking ChatGPT to
create sample tables and practise basics like SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY and HAVING and then move
to SQL50
DSA: Practice LeetCode or Striver's A2Z Sheet. Also practise taking input and producing output for
complete Java programs, not just LeetCode functions.
Puzzles: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzles/ has good puzzles. I always kept a
puzzle tab open and solved one whenever I needed a break from studying.
OOPS : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/java-interview-questions/
--- PAGE 4 ---
My Advice :)
One thing that really helped me find my weak points was practising interviews with my friends.
It's very different from studying a question and actually having to answer it when someone is sitting
in front of you. Practice introducing yourself & don't make it too generic. Try to say something about
yourself that isn't already on your resume instead of just describing your projects. When you're
asked to explain your projects, practise a 1-2 minute explanation for each one: what it is, why you
made it, what features you're proud of, what you contributed, etc.
Also practise answering HR questions and thinking aloud while solving technical questions. These
things become much easier when you've actually said them out loud before.
And honestly, placement is going to happen on one random day when you least expect it.
Until then, you might constantly have that feeling of uncertainty "When am I going to get placed?
What if I don't?" I had the same feeling, and I genuinely did not expect to get placed on the day I got
placed at TransUnion. It just happened.
So don't spend too much time worrying about the future. Keep preparing and keep going.
And if you don't get selected somewhere even if you make it all the way to the interview round and
then get rejected, allow yourself a few days to feel bad about it. It hurts, and that's completely okay.
Then get back up and start preparing for the next company.
Give every opportunity your 100%, but don't let one rejection define you.
The right opportunity will find you. Keep putting in the work, trust the process, and don't
give up. You might be closer than you think!!
If anything, feel free to reach out to me at : Linkedin- Rachel Fernandes

journey.prep:
• Listen to the Clues: The single most impactful thing I did was pay close attention to the

pre-interview presentation. Hearing that Barclays was exploring GenAl allowed me to tailor my
entire interview narrative around it. I also followed up on advice from seniors, which prepared me
for broad DBMS questions beyond what was on my resume.

• Don't Just Prepare Your Resume, Prepare Beyond It: My first interview was almost entirely about

cloud architecture, a topic not on my resume. They don't just want to know what you've done; they
want to know how you think. Be ready to tackle problems you've never seen before by reasoning
from first principles.
Targeted Practice for the OA:

• For the OA, time is your biggest enemy. I highly recommend practicing a large volume of MCQs

from platforms like GeeksforGeeks or Indiabix to get your speed up.

• I used a simple SQL Cheatsheet for last-minute revision. It's perfect for recalling syntax under

pressure.

• My advice: Talk to people who have recently taken the company's test. Patterns and concepts are

very likely to repeat.

• Know Your Projects Inside and Out: For the director's round, I strategically chose my SIH project

because I knew it had more talking points than my ISRO internship, which he had already read
about. You should have a "go-to" project that you can discuss from a high-level, feature-rich
perspective.
On the Day of the Interview

• Answer Every Question: My rule was to attempt an answer for everything unless I was completely

blank. When asked to code a 'fail-safe' architecture in Java, I was honest about my limitations but
immediately pivoted to reasoning through it in Python. This shows you're a problem-solver, not just
a fact-reciter.

• Navigate Disagreements with Grace: When the director disagreed with a feature, I didn't say, "You're

wrong." I validated his point and then explained my team's rationale. A great phrase to use is: "That's
a very valid point, and we did consider that. Our thinking for this approach was..." This shows
confidence without being confrontational.

• Ask Insightful Questions: When it's your turn to ask questions, make them count. I asked about

Barclays' data security on AWS, which showed I was listening. Asking for direct feedback, while
bold, also demonstrates a growth mindset.
Where I Could Have Done Better:
--- PAGE 5 ---

• Don't Put It On Your Resume If You Can't Defend It: The most direct feedback I received was to

remove Java from my resume. I had only coursework-level knowledge, and it showed. If a
technology is listed, be prepared for a deep dive. I should have either removed it or prepared for it
much more thoroughly.

• Build a Small Full-Stack Project: My lack of hands-on deployment experience was a clear gap. Even

building a simple web application and deploying it on a free-tier cloud service would have given me
a much stronger foundation for the cloud architecture questions.

• Time Management in the OA: I genuinely struggled with the clock during the online assessment. I

should have done more timed mock tests to better simulate the high-pressure environment. My
advice stands: do the SQL part first.
In case of any doubts you can contact me using the contact details in my resume and refer my discussions if
required:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/14CaoHGf9SnePWi2dMyateyJ-EVXamYBl/view?usp=sharing

There we 3 parts of the process:-

1. Online Assessment (OA)

2. Technical Interview Round 1

3. Interview Round 2

1.
Online Assessment (OA) (No. of candidates:

149) (Date: 27/07/25) (Time: 45 mins)

The initial stage of the process was an online assessment hosted on the HackerEarth platform, which was a
sprint against the clock. The test was composed of 20 Multiple Choice Questions and 5 SQL queries.
The MCQS were designed to evaluate our grasp of fundamental concepts in Java, C++, and C#. A few of
these were logical questions where we had to predict the output of a given code snippet. The 5 SQL queries,
on the other hand, seemed straightforward but required the use of less mainstream functions like type casting
and the || operator. While I had braced myself for complex Data Structures and Algorithms questions, partly
through some last-minute trick-sharing sessions with friends (a method I wouldn't necessarily recommend),
the assessment surprisingly did not include any.
For me, the single biggest challenge was time management; I genuinely struggled to pace myself effectively.
Based on my experience, I would strongly recommend that future candidates attempt the SQL questions first
before moving on to the MCQs.
In terms of preparation, my main advice is to practice as many MCQS as possible. In a test with such a tight
time limit, your final score is heavily dependent on them. For SQL, a good cheatsheet was invaluable for a
quick revision. Lastly, I'd suggest connecting with individuals who have recently taken the company's OA;
there's a high chance the core concepts and pattern will be similar. Speed and accuracy were the deciding
factors, and 38 candidates, including myself, advanced to the interview rounds.

2. Technical Interview Round 1 (No. of candidates:

38) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 1 hour 10 mins)

--- PAGE 2 ---
After we assembled in the auditorium, the Barclays team gave a presentation about their work and
culture. I paid close attention, as this proved invaluable. They mentioned that they were beginning to
explore Generative Al, a key detail that was also confirmed by a few seniors I had spoken with.
My interview began with a discussion of my resume. Armed with the knowledge of Barclays' new focus,
I strategically highlighted the Generative Al components within my existing projects, discussing their
underlying architectures. After about 20 minutes of this targeted discussion, the interviewer seemed
convinced of my understanding and posed a significant challenge based on our conversation: "If we
wanted to deploy a project with these capabilities at Barclays, how would you do it?"
This is where the interview took an unexpected turn into cloud architecture design. Drawing from the
morning presentation, I noted that we would host it on AWS. Despite my resume having no mention of
cloud deployment, I was asked to design a complete, resilient architecture from scratch, specifying
regions and availability zones to ensure high availability.
The challenge peaked when I was asked to code a 'fail-safe' architecture that could self-heal from server
issues. The interviewer requested the code in Java, but I explained that Python was my core language
and asked if I could use it instead, which he allowed. The entire exercise was done with pen and paper,
so definitely be prepared for that. My core strategy was to answer every question unless I was
completely unaware of the topic. I was transparent about not having direct deployment experience but
then immediately attempted to reason through a logical solution for every problem posed. This included
troubleshooting specific issues like the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and "CUDA out of memory"
errors.
Following the intense architecture discussion, he asked two specific Java questions: one on calling a
function without public static void main, and another describing the JRE, JDK, and JVM. I answered,
again noting that Python was my area of expertise. The interview then shifted to DBMS. Although my
resume only lists MySQL, I was prepared for broader questions on topics like horizontal vs. vertical
scaling, the CAP theorem, SQL vs. NoSQL databases, and ACID properties, all of which I answered
confidently.
When I asked for feedback, the interviewer was candid. He praised my problem-solving but wryly
suggested I remove Java from my resume!
Key Takeaways from my experience:

• Pay close attention to pre-interview presentations and talk to seniors; they contain valuable clues

about a company's focus.

• Make an attempt to answer every question. However, this doesn't mean providing incorrect answers.

If you're unsure about something, acknowledge it honestly and explain that, based on your
knowledge, the issue might be approached or solved in a particular logical way. Unless you are
completely blank on a topic, always try to reason through a solution. This showcases your thought
process. [Do not answer wrong things]

• Be prepared to go far beyond what's on your resume. Interviewers test your ability to reason, not just

recite.

• It's okay to request coding in your preferred language, but be ready for pen-and-paper rounds.

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Honesty is the best policy. It's better to admit a lack of experience and then attempt a logical solution

than to feign expertise.

3. Interview Round 2 (No. of candidates:

19) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 45 mins)

The second and final interview was with one of the company's directors, and it felt like a conversation
designed to see how I think, rather than just what I know.
As the interview began, I noticed the director had already thoroughly read the description of my 7-month
ISRO internship on my resume. Instead of repeating what he already knew, I made a strategic choice to
discuss my Smart India Hackathon (SIH) winning project when he asked me to talk about a project I was
passionate about. My reasoning was that the SIH project was architecturally diverse, offering more
avenues for a broad, high-level discussion.
This turned out to be the right move. The director was more interested in the 'why' than the 'how'. We
discussed the high-level architecture, the project's features, and its potential impact, rather than granular
implementation details. It felt like a hybrid HR-technical round where he was gauging my product sense
and communication skills.
Pleased with the discussion, he then asked me to choose one more project to talk about. The
conversation followed a similar high-level pattern, but a crucial moment arose when we had a friendly
disagreement about one of my project's features. This is a delicate situation, and my approach was to
never directly state that a director is wrong. I handled it by saying: "Yes sir, you have pointed out a very
valid concern. It's something our team also thought about. However, we intentionally designed it this
way because we wanted users to have a specific kind of experience, which we feel is still very helpful."
When he suggested an alternative use for my Al agent, I acknowledged its potential by agreeing that his
idea was partially applicable. This approach keeps the conversation collaborative and shows that you are
confident in your decisions but also respectful of other viewpoints.
The interview concluded with him asking about the team size for my projects and if I had any questions.
Overall, it was a mature conversation where both parties were learning about each other. Ultimately, 16
of us were selected for the internship.
Key Takeaways from my experience:

• Be Strategic in Project Selection: Don't just pick your longest or most complex project. Choose one

that allows for a broad discussion and, if you can, one the interviewer hasn't already deeply read
about. Read the room.

• Know Your Audience: A conversation with a director will likely be about high-level impact and

architecture. Focus on the "what" and "why" more than the minute details of the "ho% &

• Navigate Disagreements Gracefully: Never say "you're wrong." Acknowledge their perspective,

validate their point, and then calmly explain your team's rationale. It shows maturity and confidence.
Finally 16 candidates were offered the internship.
--- PAGE 4 ---

Looking back, my selection was a result of a combination of targeted preparation, strategic thinking during
the interviews, and a bit of luck. Here's a breakdown of what worked for me and what I could have done
better.
Preparation and Strategy:

• Listen to the Clues: The single most impactful thing I did was pay close attention to the

pre-interview presentation. Hearing that Barclays was exploring GenAl allowed me to tailor my
entire interview narrative around it. I also followed up on advice from seniors, which prepared me
for broad DBMS questions beyond what was on my resume.

• Don't Just Prepare Your Resume, Prepare Beyond It: My first interview was almost entirely about

cloud architecture, a topic not on my resume. They don't just want to know what you've done; they
want to know how you think. Be ready to tackle problems you've never seen before by reasoning
from first principles.
Targeted Practice for the OA:

• For the OA, time is your biggest enemy. I highly recommend practicing a large volume of MCQs

from platforms like GeeksforGeeks or Indiabix to get your speed up.

• I used a simple SQL Cheatsheet for last-minute revision. It's perfect for recalling syntax under

pressure.

• My advice: Talk to people who have recently taken the company's test. Patterns and concepts are

very likely to repeat.

• Know Your Projects Inside and Out: For the director's round, I strategically chose my SIH project

because I knew it had more talking points than my ISRO internship, which he had already read
about. You should have a "go-to" project that you can discuss from a high-level, feature-rich
perspective.
On the Day of the Interview

• Answer Every Question: My rule was to attempt an answer for everything unless I was completely

blank. When asked to code a 'fail-safe' architecture in Java, I was honest about my limitations but
immediately pivoted to reasoning through it in Python. This shows you're a problem-solver, not just
a fact-reciter.

• Navigate Disagreements with Grace: When the director disagreed with a feature, I didn't say, "You're

wrong." I validated his point and then explained my team's rationale. A great phrase to use is: "That's
a very valid point, and we did consider that. Our thinking for this approach was..." This shows
confidence without being confrontational.

• Ask Insightful Questions: When it's your turn to ask questions, make them count. I asked about

Barclays' data security on AWS, which showed I was listening. Asking for direct feedback, while
bold, also demonstrates a growth mindset.
Where I Could Have Done Better:
--- PAGE 5 ---

• Don't Put It On Your Resume If You Can't Defend It: The most direct feedback I received was to

remove Java from my resume. I had only coursework-level knowledge, and it showed. If a

much more thoroughly.

building a simple web application and deploying it on a free-tier cloud service would have given me
a much stronger foundation for the cloud architecture questions.

• Time Management in the OA: I genuinely struggled with the clock during the online assessment. I

should have done more timed mock tests to better simulate the high-pressure environment. My
advice stands: do the SQL part first.

--- PAGE 3 ---

1. Only Add What You Know to Your Resume

Your resume is the foundation of your interview - don't treat it like a wishlist. Only include technologies,
languages, and tools you're actually comfortable with. Interviewers often pick up on one small keyword and
dive deep into it. If you're not confident in what you've written, it can create a negative impression. It's
better to showcase fewer things and answer strongly than to list a lot and struggle during questioning.

2. Be Thorough with Your Projects

Expect to be grilled on your projects -- not just what they do, but how they do it. Be prepared to explain
your project's architecture, tools used, problem-solving approach, and even alternatives you considered.
Interviewers love to see ownership and clarity. A shallow understanding of your own work is a red flag, so
revise your code, flow, and logic before the interview.

3. Understand the Tools, Not Just Use Them

It's not enough to implement tools like JWT, MongoDB, or OAuth - you need to understand how they
work under the hood. Interviewers may ask why you chose a certain tool, how it functions internally, and
what its limitations are. This shows depth and maturity in your technical decisions. Learn the why and how,
not just the what.

1. Online Assessment (OA) (No. of candidates:

149) (Date: 27/07/25) (Time: 45 mins)

The first stage of the process was an online assessment conducted on the HackerEarth platform - a true
race against time. It consisted of 20 multiple-choice questions (MCQS) and 5 SQL query-based tasks. The
MCQS tested our understanding of core concepts in Java, C++, and C#, with several logical problems
requiring us to predict the output of given code snippets.
The SQL questions, though appearing simple at first glance, involved lesser-known elements like type
casting and the use of the | | operator. While I had prepared extensively for complex Data Structures and
Algorithms problems - even joining some last-minute "trick-exchange" sessions with friends (which I
wouldn't particularly endorse) -- to my surprise, the test didn't include any.
Personally, the biggest hurdle was time management. I found it genuinely difficult to maintain a steady pace
throughout. Based on that, I would highly recommend tackling the SQL queries first, then moving on to the
MCQs.
As for preparation, practicing a wide variety of MCQS is crucial - given the strict time limit, your score
will largely depend on how quickly and accurately you can solve them. For SQL, having a reliable
cheatsheet helped me revise important functions quickly. Lastly, try to connect with peers who have recently
taken the company's online assessment - the core patterns and concepts are often repeated. In the end, it
came down to speed and precision, and 38 of us, including myself, moved on to the interview stage.

crashes. Although the interviewer initially asked for Java, I clarified that Python was my primary language
and got permission to use that instead. The entire coding task was done on pen and paper, so being
comfortable with that format really helped.
Throughout the interview, I made sure to attempt every question unless I was completely unfamiliar with the
topic. I was transparent about areas where I lacked experience but always tried to reason through possible

journey.prep:
1. Start as early as you can, but if you're late, START anyway.

Don't wait for the "perfect time" to begin. I started DSA and computer fundamentals around
July-December, but I wasn't consistent initially. What mattered was that I eventually realised I needed to
take it seriously and started grinding consistently. Even if you think you're late, it's not over. Start from
wherever you are and be smart about what you cover. You don't have to learn everything; you need to learn
the right things for the roles you are targeting.

2. Be ready to change your plan.

Initially, I was almost certain that I wanted to go into non-tech roles. But after seeing the experiences of
some of my seniors, I realised I should also prepare for SDE roles. I had already been doing some DSA and
computer fundamentals from July to December, but not consistently. Then I made a major decision: I
dropped Finance preparation, even though I had been preparing for it for almost two years. I felt that with
my existing preparation, I could revise Finance in a month if needed. For the next six months, I completely
tocused on DSA and computer fundamentals. I also gave around 12-15 mock interviews to seniors and
professionals. And trust me, there was a point where I genuinely questioned whether I was even prepared.
I had set myself a target to complete DSA before March. During one mock interview around that time, I
couldn't even write basic syntax properly. LeetCode and actually sitting in front of a blank compiler are two
very different experiences, and that blank screen can be scary.
So, I started again.
From March onwards, I practised writing code from scratch, worked on my logic, and gradually became
comfortable with solving problems without relying on an online platform. I also want to clarify that I didn't
--- PAGE 10 ---
prepare every hard DSA topic. My target was to prepare DSA up to the level required for placement
interviews. Be strategic about your preparation instead of trying to master everything.

3. Don't completely depend on Finance roles.

If you're planning to rely mainly on Finance roles, first understand your college's placement scenario. Check
how many companies actually visit your campus for the specific role you're targeting. Companies like JP,
KPMG, GEP, OMP, etc. may visit, but you need to understand whether there are enough opportunities for
you. Don't build your entire placement strategy around a role without checking the actual opportunities
available on campus.

4. Sometimes taking a risk is worth it.

Taking a risk doesn't always work out, but sometimes it can completely change your outcome. I had actually
made a personal rule for myself: I would take risks during the first two months of placements, and after that,
I wouldn't. This decision was based on my understanding of my own situation and how the placement
season was progressing. The point is not to blindly take risks. Understand your situation, assess what you
have to lose, and then decide.

5. Surround yourself with the right people.

This made a huge difference in my journey. Surround yourself with people who believe in you, push you to
do better, and have a positive impact on you. Good friends can completely change how you approach
stressful situations. My friends helped me with preparation, revisions, mock interviews, notes, and
sometimes simply by reminding me that I was capable of doing it. Your preparation is yours, but the people
around you can make the journey much easier.

6. Learn from your previous mistakes.

Before BlackRock, I had already reached some of the final rounds/T2 rounds at JP and ISS. And honestly, I
made mistakes there. Looking back, those experiences taught me a lot about what I was doing wrong, what I
needed to improve, and how I should approach interviews differently,JP was the first company that came
to our campus, and I made it through the Technical Round 1. Unfortunately, I wasn't selected for the HR
round. Honestly, I still don't know exactly what went wrong. I felt that most of the technical answers I gave
were correct, so maybe the issue was my communication or the way I presented my answers. There are also
so many factors during an interview-what time you're scheduled, the interviewer's mood, how the
conversation flows, and, of course, your own performance. "I was the last person to be interviewed, and my
interviewer had joined through his phone. I still don't know what went wrong, and perhaps I simply didn't
communicate as well as I could havei Maybe that played a role, maybe it didn't. I'll never really know. But
JP definitely broke my heart a little. It was the first company, I had put in a lot of effort, and I couldn't move
on from the rejection easily. I was still thinking about it when ISS came around.
For ISS, I had to almost start from square zero. I had spent about a month preparing heavily for Finance,
and in the process, I had lost some of my grip on technical concepts. I was stressed and honestly struggling
to get back into the flow. My school friends, and college, especially Nidhi and Asmiya, supported me a lot
during this phase and helped me get back on track.
Then came my ISS interview, where I made another very simple mistake. I was asked about polymorphism,
a concept I had studied before, but I completely blanked out and couldn't explain it properly. That moment
--- PAGE 11 ---
taught me something important: knowing something and being able to communicate it under pressure
are two completely different things. After that, I started giving mock interviews continuously. I practised
explaining concepts out loud, solving problems while someone was watching, and getting comfortable with
the pressure of being questioned.
Slowly, I stopped feeling anxious during interviews and became much more comfortable communicating my
thoughts. Looking back, JP and ISS were not failures. They were probably the practice rounds I needed
before BlackRock. Every interview showed me something I needed to fix. By the time BlackRock came
around, I wasn't just technically better,I was much better at communicating what I knew under stress and
anxiety.

7. Don't Prepare for Placements - Prepare for the Role

Once you know the kind of role you want, work backwards from it. For SDE, I focused on DSA + computer
fundamentals + my resume rather than trying to study every possible CS topic. The goal isn't to know
everything. The goal is to be interview-ready for the role you are targeting.

8. Your Resume Can Decide the Direction of Your Interview

Never put something on your resume just because it sounds impressive. If you mention AWS, Oracle, AI,
Azure, React, Java, SQL, etc., assume the interviewer can ask you anything about it. Before every interview,
go through your resume line by line and ask yourself: "If I were the interviewer, what could I ask about
this?" Prepare those answers

9. Mock Interviews Are NOT Optional

LeetCode can teach you how to solve problems. Mock interviews teach you how to solve problems while
someone is watching you. Give mocks to seniors, friends, professionals-anyone who can question you
seriously. And don't just ask them, "How was my interview?"
Ask:

• Where did I hesitate?

• Was my explanation clear?

• Did I communicate my thought process?

• Did I speak too much?

• Did I speak too little?

• Where did I lose confidence?

• What would make my answer stronger?

That feedback is gold.

10. Practise on a Blank Compiler

This one genuinely matters. Solving on LeetCode and solving on a completely blank screen are very
different experiences. Before interviews, practise writing code from scratch without autocomplete or
familiar platform support. Even basic syntax can suddenly disappear when you're under pressure.
You don't want your first blank-compiler experience to be during the actual interview.
--- PAGE 12 ---

11. Don't Memorise Answers -Understand the "Why?

For every technology, project, or concept on your resume, know three things:
What is it? Why did I use it? How did I use it?
And preferably a fourth:
Why this instead of an alternative?
This helped me tremendously when interviewers started asking about my tech stack and its competitors.

12. Learn How to Say "I Don't Know"

This is an underrated interview skill. If you genuinely don't know something, don't start making things up.
You can simply say:
"I'm not completely sure about that, but based on my understanding..."
Or:
"I don't remember the exact details right now, but I have worked with this concept in..."
Honesty + whatever knowledge you actually have is much better than confidently giving a wrong answer.

13. Don't Let One Rejection Ruin the Next Interview

This was something I personally struggled with after JP. You can spend days thinking:
"What did I do wrong?"
"Why did they reject me?"
"Maybe I'm not good enough."
But eventually, you have to close that tab in your head.
Also be ready for your interview schedule in the next 10-12hrs. For some companies you literally get the
shortlist this prior.
The next company doesn't know what happened in your previous interview. Walk into every new
interview as a fresh opportunity.

14. Prepare Your "Why This Company?" Before Every Interview

Don't give a generic:
"BlackRock is a reputed company and I want to grow professionally."
Research the company, understand the role, and connect it to your own interests and experience. For
BlackRock, I was able to connect my answer with the principles they had discussed during the PPT. That
made my answer much more relevant.
--- PAGE 13 ---

15. Keep a Placement Journal

This is something I wish more students did. After every interview, immediately write down:

• Questions asked

• Questions you couldn't answer

• Topics you struggled with

• Questions that surprised you

• What you could have communicated better

• What the interviewer focused on

After 5-6 interviews, you'll start seeing patterns. Your placement preparation then becomes much more
targeted.

16. Don't Compare Your Timeline With Someone Else's

Someone might get shortlisted before you. Someone might get an offer in the first month. Someone might
get rejected from five companies and crack the sixth. Someone might get an easier interviewer. Someone
might get a tougher one. Placement season is not a race with one fixed timeline.
Focus on improving between every interview.

17. Take Care of Your Mind During Placement Season

This one is personal but important. Placement season can mess with your confidence because every few
days you're either celebrating someone else's offer or dealing with your own rejection.
Don't let your entire self-worth become:
"I got placed / I didn't get placed."
You're still the same person before and after an interview. Prepare seriously. Give it everything. But don't
destroy yourself over one result.

18. And Finally ,Don't Give Up Too Early

You genuinely never know which interview will work out. You can be rejected after reaching a final round.
You can be waitlisted and still get interviewed. You can have an interview you think went terribly and still
move ahead. And you can spend six hours thinking you've been rejected... only to get the HR call.
So stay in the game.
You don't need every company to say yes. You just need one company to say yes.
If you have any questions, please feel free to reach out on:
Whatsapp: 7558596840
--- PAGE 14 ---
Resume: Tulsi BlackRock

BR_PPT_NOTES (Credits:Ronit Sonawane)
BlackRock was hiring for two roles:

• Software Engineering

• Aladdin Data

Candidates could choose their preferred role or apply for both. I applied for both roles.
Eligibility & Shortlisting
The eligibility criteria was quite straightforward:

• Students from all branches were eligible.

• Minimum CGPA: 7.5 (For safer side keep your CGPA above 8)

• There was no apparent resume-based shortlisting for the Online Assessment.

So, if you met the eligibility criteria, you had a good opportunity to directly attempt the OA and prove
yourself through the selection process.

1. Online Assesment [Around 285 students appeared for this round]

Everyone who applied for either of the two roles received the HackerRank assessment link via email one
day before the test.
The assessment was 95 minutes long and was divided into 7 timed sections. Each section tested a different
skill, so managing time was just as important as solving the questions correctly.
The sections were:
a) Coding (Advanced programming fundamentals) - 1 Question, 40 minutes
b) Coding (Basic programming) - 1 Question, 15 minutes
c) Design Pattern (Advanced) - 15 questions, 6 minutes
d) Design Pattern (Basic) - 15 questions, 4 minutes
e) Fundamental Al and Cloud concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
f) DB Concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
g) Aptitude - 15 questions, 10 minutes
BlackRock usually gives enough time to prepare between the OA and interviews so make sure you utilize it
very carefully, also put the name of company and add "gfg interview on campus experience", usually you
get to know questions or OA patterns if companies don't mention them. (we had a very different pattern than
all the previous years, and being honest and the research done it was noticed that since 2-3 years similar OA
questions were appeared in OA, except this year)
I will add few website links, from where you might get company specific OA questions:
--- PAGE 3 ---
https://oavoservice.com/en/articles/blackrock-oa-guide-question-types-real-questions-2026(credits:Nidhi
Patel)
Few more I found:
https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/mobile/folders/1c2wIdukwLZCYtb8wIA2-T7bkqZ86xfsa
https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/mobile/folders/16SUOj1gcmi1gqb-y8sbLig6ZdbAtBuyX
https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/mobile/folders/1L4jLM31W-qkvqel3aSK7_ZYFCgFPmJSq/11bKpCEhP
7woxWyVQh3Rm xi1tMadSpR5?sort=13&direction=a
The sections were strictly timed, and once the timer ended, you were automatically moved to the next
section.
Important: In the coding sections, the code is not submitted automatically when the timer ends. Make
sure to submit your code before the timer runs out, otherwise your solution may not be considered.
My coding question was based on a tree height minimization problem. I was given a tree and a maximum
number of operations, where an operation could be used to move a node closer to the root. The goal was to
find the minimum possible height of the tree after performing at most the given number of operations.
I solved it using binary search on the answer. For each possible height, I used a bottom-up greedy
approach on the rooted tree to check whether that height could be achieved within the allowed number of
operations.
The Design Pattern sections focused mainly on basic LLD (Low-Level Design) and related concepts. I
prepared for these just one day before the assessment using ChatGPT and Claude, and honestly, that
preparation was enough for the level of questions asked.
The Fundamental Al & Cloud Concepts section mainly covered AWS fundamentals along with basic
AI/ML concepts.
The DB Concepts section focused on:

• ACID properties

• Basic transaction-related queries

• DBMS fundamentals

• Some Oracle-based questions

The Oracle questions were slightly unexpected since they are not commonly seen in other OAs. However,
most could still be attempted using option elimination and basic knowledge.
The Aptitude section was comparatively easier, but it was time-consuming. So, managing time efficiently
was crucial to attempting all the questions.

• 8 students shortlisted

• 6 students waitlisted

I was shortlisted for the Software Engineering role, which meant it was time to prepare for the interview
rounds (Even though I was shortlisted for another company a very dicey thing to do, as EXTC
struggled a lot to get shortlisted, I decided to take a risk and go for BlackRock. Sometimes, taking a
risk can leave you with regret-but sometimes, you win so big that you're left with nothing to regret.
So, when you believe in yourself, take the leap.)

2. Technical Interview 1 [Around 38 students appeared for this round for SDE]

It's a rare scenario, but yes, waitlisted candidates did get a chance to appear for the interviews. In fact,
there were candidates who eventually made it to the final shortlist after initially being waitlisted. So, if
you find yourself on the waitlist, don't lose hope. It takes immense patience and calmness to get through
such a situation, but sometimes, staying in the game is all it takes for the opportunity to come your way.
My panel number was 19 (it was going all over India, later after interview i got to know my panelists
were from bangalore), and the interviews had started from 9:00 AM. Mine was scheduled for 9:30 AM.
That morning, we also received a confirmation call and were specifically instructed not to join the Webex
meeting until the HR asked us to. We were asked to bring our laptops, and the interviews were conducted
on Webex.
The 9:30 AM Moment
I reached the venue, settled myself, took a breath, and joined the meeting. I wasn't extremely nervous, but I
wasn't overconfident either. I was simply in the mindset:
"I want this. Somehow, I'm going to make it happen."
As soon as I joined, I immediately noted down the names of my interviewers. This might sound like a tiny
thing, but remember your panelists' names. If you make it to the next round, being able to address them
by name can make the interaction much more personal and confident.
They said, "Hi."
I replied with a "Good morning."
And then...
Silence.
--- PAGE 5 ---
LOL.
At that point, I realised, Okay, someone has to start this. So I took the initiative and started with my
introduction(make sure you prepare this very well.)
The first question was:
"Why Software Engineering when your branch is EXTC?
Luckily, I was very well prepared for this question, so I was able to explain my transition towards
software and why I wanted to pursue SDE. The answer seemed to satisfy them, and we moved ahead.
Internship
The interviewer then started asking questions about my internship and tech stack. They went quite deep
into what I had worked on, including questions around Azure Data Factory (ADF) and specifically:
"How did you initialise Azure Data Factory? What exactly did you do?"
Here, one important lesson came up "Drive the Interview" I deliberately explained the overview first
instead of dumping every technical detail I knew. Why? Because if you tell the interviewer absolutely
everything at once, you are essentially giving them a list of things to question you on. They can easily pick
one tiny detail and take you somewhere completely unexpected. So, don't hide things or lie, but structure
your answers intelligently. Give enough information to demonstrate your understanding, and then let the
interviewer decide where to go deeper. In my case, the interviewer had already grilled me quite a bit on
ADF, so eventually we moved to another project.
During the pre-placement presentation, BlackRock had placed considerable emphasis on Al-driven
solutions. I had already researched this beforehand and had Al-based projects on my resume, including
Oracle-based AI/GenAl solutions. I also had a minor focused on AI for Non-CS students, which helped me
here. This gave me an advantage because I could confidently discuss the concepts and projects I had actually
worked on. And this brings me to one of the biggest lessons from my interview:
Know your resume inside out.
I had maintained a separate Google Doc containing everything on my resume and prepared possible
questions for each section:

• Education: What did you actually learn/do during your degree?

• Internship: What was your contribution?

• Projects: Why did you build it? How does it work?

• Certifications: What did you learn from them?

• Tech Stack: Why this technology? Why not another?

• AI/Cloud/DB: What concepts did you actually use?

If you don't have time to revise an entire certification, at least take a screenshot of its contents/index
and ask ChatGPT to summarise the course for you. The interviewer even asked me about competitors to
the technologies in my tech stack and why I had chosen a particular technology over its alternatives.
--- PAGE 6 ---
So, once again: Your resume is not a piece of paper. It is your interview syllabus. After the project
discussion, I was asked 3 DSA questions. All three were around the easy-to-medium level.
Question 1 - Even and Odd Indices
The first problem was related to ensuring that even indices contain even numbers and odd contains odd
numbers. The interviewer explained the problem, but didn't initially provide an example.
Instead of immediately jumping into the solution, I asked:

• "Can I write down my logic on paper?"

• "Could you give me an example?"

• "Can I have a little time to think?"

• "Could you provide some edge cases?"

And here's another important lesson:
Communication is part of DSA.
I knew the solution, but normally I would approach a problem through brute force → better →
optimal. However, the interviewer specifically told me that I should directly provide the optimized
approach. So I adapted. I opened Notepad and started writing the code...
And then they stopped me:
"Please don't code. Can you explain the approach first?"
So I switched gears, took the example they provided, dry-ran my approach, and explained the logic
step-by-step. That worked. Remember: Solving DSA questions is only half the job. If you can't
communicate your approach clearly, all those questions and patterns you've practised won't help much.
You should be able to transfer your logical thinking to the interviewer clearly and confidently.
And please, start taking communication and soft skills seriously. Otherwise, you might genuinely regret
it later. I've seen people who are technically brilliant but struggle during HR rounds, GDS, or simply
communicating their thoughts. And honestly, that hurts, because you worked so hard to build the
knowledge, only to lose an opportunity because you couldn't communicate it properly. Don't let all that
hard work go to waste. Work on your communication alongside your technical skills. Trust me, you
don't want to reach the end and think, "I knew it all... I just couldn't express it." and end up in tears.
The other two questions were related to removing duplicates and anagrams. I followed a similar
approach, understand the problem, clarify the requirements, think through edge cases, and then explain the
solution.
And yes, even if you don't know a term like "anagram", simply ask. There is absolutely nothing wrong
with saying:
"Could you please explain what you mean by anagram?"
The interviewer isn't sitting there trying to defeat you. They're trying to evaluate whether you can solve
problems and communicate your thought process.
--- PAGE 7 ---
Towards the end, they started asking about my Oracle certifications and an AWS certification. Here, I
chose honesty. For AWS, I admitted that I didn't remember every detail of the certification, but I could
confidently talk about the services and concepts I had actually worked with, including SageMaker. You
don't need to pretend that you remember every single thing you've ever studied. Be honest, but
demonstrate what you actually know.
I was also asked:
"Why BlackRock?»
This was another question where the Pre-Placement Talk helped me. I referred to the five principles they
had highlighted during the PPT and connected them with why I wanted to join BlackRock. This is exactly
why I recommend paying attention during the pre-placement presentation. Sometimes the answers you
need are literally given to you beforehand.
Finally, they asked:
"Do you have any questions for us?"
Always have a question ready.
I asked "Could you tell me a little about the kind of projects the team is currently working on and the
technologies or tech stack I would get an opportunity to work with in this roleạThis not only keeps
the conversation going, but also shows that you're genuinely interested in the actual work you would be
doing. And with that, Round 1 was over. The interviewer ended with "all the best for further
interviewsạẠạ
The interviewer is not your opponent. Your job is not to know everything. Your job is to show
that you can learn, think, solve problems, and communicate.
The interview lasted around 45 minutes. And honestly, luck plays a small but real role too. Luck
does play a small role,you can't control your panelist, the questions you get, or the timing of your
interview. But preparation decides how well you handle whatever comes your way. I had friends
whose first round was HR(and very little TECH), and all of them made it to the second round. On
the other hand, I knew people who were asked some really tough DSA questions, answered them
well, and still didn't make it to the next round. So yes, you can't control everything. You can only
control your preparation, communication, and how you handle whatever comes your way. Prepare
for the worst, hope for the best, and make the most of the panel you get.
And then came the longest 6 hours of my entire life.
Honestly, I was pretty heartbroken. I felt I had given the interview a really good shot, but I still hadn't
received the HR call while everyone else had already finished their interviews.
At that point, my brain started overthinking everything.
"Okay... maybe the interviewer cooked me."
"Maybe that was their way of saying, 'All the best for your other companies.'
--- PAGE 8 ---
I had almost started convincing myself that it was over. But sometimes, the process is not as
straightforward as you think it is.
Tech Interview 2 [19 including both roles]
So finally, I got the HR call. I joined the Webex meeting and honestly, the drama had already started. The
interviewer was casually sitting there, scrolling through his phone, while I was thinking, "Okay, how do I
tell him I actually got the HR round?" I finally interrupted and said, "Hey, am I audible?" No response. My
anxiety level went up instantly. I repeated myself, and this time he noticed. He said hi and then casually
asked, "How are you? Did you have your lunch?"
After answering that, he asked, "How have you been doing while waiting for this call?" I answered
honestly, Honestly, the longest 6 hours of my life, I must say." He then asked which college I was from, and
I told him SPIT.
He then asked me, "What is one thing you liked about yourself during the interview, one thing you
didn't like, and what would you improve?i I started by mentioning my panelists from the previous round,
Riya Ma'am and Kalvi Sir, and then explained what I thought went well, what I could have done better, and
what I would improve. This was a good reminder that HR rounds are also about self-awareness. You don't
always need a perfect answer; you need to show that you understand yourself and are willing to improve.
Next, he asked me to give an informal introduction. I made sure it wasn't just the usual name, college, and
branch introduction. I included my hobbies, interests, and a little about myself beyond academics. He then
asked me to walk him through my resume, which I did. From there, we moved to my internship. He asked
what I had worked on, whether it was remote, and then started asking about my tech stack.
At this point, I noticed a very interesting pattern. Whatever I ended my answer with became his next
question. For example, I mentioned that I had worked in an Agile team, and immediately he asked, "What
do you mean by Agile?" Once I noticed this pattern, I started using it to my advantage. I consciously tried
to end my answers with topics I was confident discussing. You should never lie or deliberately mislead an
interviewer, but if you understand the direction of the conversation, you can definitely communicate your
answers strategically and help drive the interview.
He then asked me to choose one of my projects. I picked my first project and was asked to share my screen
and explain its tech stack. He then asked why I had chosen that particular tech stack, what its alternatives
were, and what competitors existed. I had prepared six tech stack beforehand, so I was able to answer those
questions confidently.
Then came a quick rapid-fire round on DBMS, SQL, and related concepts. Again, the same pattern
continued: whatever I mentioned often became the next question. So I made sure I ended my answers with
concepts I was comfortable discussing. A huge shoutout to Shahid, who helped me identify the important
topics I needed to study, and to Vikrant, who sat with me for two hours the day before the interview and
revised some of the most important DBMS topics with me.
This is something I genuinely want to highlight: have good friends. The kind of friends who show up when
you need them. My placement journey was honestly a roller coaster, and Thad Sarthak who helped me with
PPT preparation, notes, Claude-ready PDFs, last-minute revisions, and random doubts. My ex-roommate
--- PAGE 9 ---
also deserves a special mention because she would regularly check on me, especially after companies I
really wanted didn't work out. You may prepare individually, but you don't have to go through the journey
alone.
The interviewer then asked me about relocation, and I was completely comfortable with it. I said yes.
Finally, he asked, "Do you have any questions for me?" I asked him about his experience at BlackRock and
what life was like for him there. I wanted to understand the person behind the role and the actual work
environment, rather than just asking something for the sake of asking.
Throughout the interview, I also noticed that many of my answers naturally connected back to the five
principles of BlackRock that they had highlighted during the Pre-Placement Talk. This is another reason
why I keep stressing the importance of paying attention during the PPT. Those small details can come back
and help you when you least expect them.
After everything, from the OA, the first interview, the six-hour wait, and finally this conversation, I was left
with one thought: maybe the delay wasn't a rejection. Maybe it was just another part of the story.
Sometimes, you don't understand why things happen when they do. But when you finally look back, you
realise that maybe everything happened for a reason. And the next day i got to know i m Selected!!!

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Start as early as you can, but if you're late, START anyway.

Don't wait for the "perfect time" to begin. I started DSA and computer fundamentals around
July-December, but I wasn't consistent initially. What mattered was that I eventually realised I needed to
take it seriously and started grinding consistently. Even if you think you're late, it's not over. Start from
wherever you are and be smart about what you cover. You don't have to learn everything; you need to learn
the right things for the roles you are targeting.

2. Be ready to change your plan.

Initially, I was almost certain that I wanted to go into non-tech roles. But after seeing the experiences of
some of my seniors, I realised I should also prepare for SDE roles. I had already been doing some DSA and
computer fundamentals from July to December, but not consistently. Then I made a major decision: I
dropped Finance preparation, even though I had been preparing for it for almost two years. I felt that with
my existing preparation, I could revise Finance in a month if needed. For the next six months, I completely
tocused on DSA and computer fundamentals. I also gave around 12-15 mock interviews to seniors and
professionals. And trust me, there was a point where I genuinely questioned whether I was even prepared.
I had set myself a target to complete DSA before March. During one mock interview around that time, I
couldn't even write basic syntax properly. LeetCode and actually sitting in front of a blank compiler are two
very different experiences, and that blank screen can be scary.
So, I started again.
From March onwards, I practised writing code from scratch, worked on my logic, and gradually became
comfortable with solving problems without relying on an online platform. I also want to clarify that I didn't
--- PAGE 10 ---
prepare every hard DSA topic. My target was to prepare DSA up to the level required for placement
interviews. Be strategic about your preparation instead of trying to master everything.

3. Don't completely depend on Finance roles.

If you're planning to rely mainly on Finance roles, first understand your college's placement scenario. Check
how many companies actually visit your campus for the specific role you're targeting. Companies like JP,
KPMG, GEP, OMP, etc. may visit, but you need to understand whether there are enough opportunities for
you. Don't build your entire placement strategy around a role without checking the actual opportunities
available on campus.

4. Sometimes taking a risk is worth it.

Taking a risk doesn't always work out, but sometimes it can completely change your outcome. I had actually
made a personal rule for myself: I would take risks during the first two months of placements, and after that,
I wouldn't. This decision was based on my understanding of my own situation and how the placement
season was progressing. The point is not to blindly take risks. Understand your situation, assess what you
have to lose, and then decide.

5. Surround yourself with the right people.

This made a huge difference in my journey. Surround yourself with people who believe in you, push you to
do better, and have a positive impact on you. Good friends can completely change how you approach
stressful situations. My friends helped me with preparation, revisions, mock interviews, notes, and
sometimes simply by reminding me that I was capable of doing it. Your preparation is yours, but the people
around you can make the journey much easier.

1. Resume Shortlisting

I never had an idea of how many students there were for any company or any round, so sorry, I can't provide you with the exact numbers.
Also, one of the most important things I want to tell you is: don't ever blame your resume, your skills, the TPO, or the company for not getting shortlisted. Many companies, and even the TPO, say that they shortlist on the basis of resumes, but from my experience, the process can sometimes feel random. It totally depends on your luck as well.
My roommates also had remarkable resumes, but they weren't even selected for Revvity and Infosys, and no one gives a clarification on this.
My name was also not there in the initial resume shortlist. In the evening, they sent a list in the group that had 6 names, and mine was there in it. The TPO said that we were also shortlisted and told us to join the Revvity process group.

2. Online Assessment

On 22nd August, they had the Online Assessment. The test was actually crazy. It was not hard, but the questions were from multiple domains.
Some questions were from Angular, some were from React, some Java questions were also there, and there were some aptitude questions.
Overall, the test was medium, but the questions they asked were from technologies that don't really connect with each other.
The DSA question was pretty easy. The question was something like this:
1 coding question: A string was given containing alphabets, and we were supposed to compress the string.
For example:
aaaabbbcdeee
would become:
4a3bcd3e
The test duration was 1 hour. Don't be afraid of the test. The test was conducted online.

3. Interviews

48 students were selected for interviews.
A. Physical Pen-and-Paper Test
Even though the company had told us that there would be direct interviews, they took a physical pen-and-paper test.
We had to write code on paper. They had told us it would be a 45-minute test, but it went up to 1 hour.
There were 3 questions.

1. Palindrome String

We had to check if a string was a palindrome or not, but there was a catch: we had to ignore all special characters, symbols, and whitespaces.
We also had to consider small and capital letters as equal, i.e., a and A are equal.
For example, a string like a*bA would be considered a palindrome since we had to ignore the special character * and consider a and A equal.

2. Good or Bad String

If more than three consonants or more than five vowels come serially, one after another, then it is a bad string; otherwise, it is a good string.
But the catch is that there will be question marks in the string. You can place anything in place of the question mark, either a vowel or a consonant, and then you have to calculate whether it is a good or bad string.
For example, consider:
aei??
The ? can be replaced by either a vowel or a consonant. You have to determine whether the string can be made a good string based on the possible replacements.

3. Number of Squares in an N × N Square

We were given an N × N square. We had to calculate how many maximum squares are possible in that square.
Suppose there is a 3 × 3 square. Then there will be:
9 squares of 1 × 1
4 squares of 2 × 2
1 square of 3 × 3
So, the total number of squares possible is:
9 + 4 + 1 = 14
All the questions were pretty easy, and it is important to solve all of them ASAP. I have mentioned the reason behind this ahead in the

1. Online Assessment: [128 candidates appeared]

The round lasted 45 minutes and consisted of MCQs and SQL queries.
The MCQS focused on Java, OOPs, and C. I had asked my seniors about the topics covered previously and,
since these subjects were part of my coursework, I prepared for them accordingly.
Out of the 5 SQL questions, I was only able to submit 3 due to a server issue, but my MCQ section went
well overall.
Interestingly, there was no DSA round this time, which was surprising since DSA is usually a part of online
assessments and was included in the previous year. It's possible that next year's OA might include DSA
again.

2. Technical round [ 38 candidates appeared ]

The interview process took place on the same day as the placement round.
There were two separate interview panels, one for full-time roles and another for internship candidates. My
turn came after the lunch break, around 2 PM.
The interview began with a general introduction. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, and then
reviewed my resume, noting down my listed skills. He proceeded to ask questions related to my projects and
the technologies I had mentioned.
The technical discussion started with Python. I was asked how Python differs from other programming
languages, along with the advantages and disadvantages of this difference. He followed up with:

• Why has Python gained popularity so quickly?

• What are its primary use cases?

Since I had mentioned Pandas as a skill, the interviewer asked basic questions such as:
--- PAGE 2 ---

• What is Pandas used for?

• What advantages does it offer over SQL or other systems?

He then gave me a scenario: If we have three databases in different formats - SOL, CSV, and another - is
it possible to merge and analyze them using Pandas?
Next, we moved on to REST APIs whether I had used them in any of my projects and how.
The discussion then shifted to DBMS and SQL.
He asked me to explain normalization. He then created three tables and asked me to write queries involving
JOINs, aggregation, and time-based functions. I managed to solve them partially.
Finally, we talked about Scikit-learn. He asked which models I had used in my ML projects and what the
differences were between them.
At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions. I asked about the career path an intern or a new
recruit could expect at Barclays.
The round lasted for about 50 minutes.

3. HR Round [19 candidates appeared]

My second-round interview was scheduled around 4 PM. Before going in, I'd heard from a few people who
had already been interviewed that this round was pretty technical and heavily focused on your projects --
like deep dives into how your ML models work and even writing Javascript code. So I spent most of my
prep time reviewing my own project code and making sure I had a solid grasp of every decision I'd made.
When I finally got called in, I found out that my interview was being taken by someone from the full-time
engineering panel. He started by scanning through my resume and then moved straight to project-related
questions.
He asked whether the projects were solo or team efforts, what kind of challenges I faced, how I resolved
them, and whether I'd taken help from professors or peers. Later I realized these were soft skill checks in
disguise, basically trying to see how well I collaborate and whether I'm someone who can work in a team.
There was also a question about whether I had to make any tough decisions during development. I brought
up a time when I had to pick between improving an existing feature or building a new one. But the
interviewer felt that this was more of a common trade-off rather than a genuinely difficult call, though he did
mention that perspectives can differ, to which I replied that in the context of the project it was a pretty big
decision.
He then shifted to another one of my projects. He asked what made me build it, what I expected out of it,
and whether I had made any major mistakes along the way. I explained that I usually work in small iterations
and fix bugs as they come up, which is like Agile methodology, but I forgot to use the term during the
interview.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I also shared the motivation behind the project, it came from a real problem I faced at a conference. That
part led to a mini discussion on whether I had shared the app with others, how I would go about doing that,
and why I hadn't already.
There was quite a bit of back-and-forth, and looking back, I think some of the questions were a bit repetitive
on purpose, probably to test my patience and see if I mess up or contradict myself.
The interview ended up lasting more than an hour.
