Resources and tips:

• Do relevant CFI courses on Finance and Risk from Coursera.

• Practice aptitude from Career Ride (Youtube) and IndiaBix regularly - please don't let this be the

cause of elimination from any company.

• Regularly read news from newspapers or from apps like TOI, The Economic Times or The Hindu - I

made a habit to read news daily from the start of my 6th semester while travelling.

• Read about relevant case studies related to risk mishaps like Global Financial Crisis of 2008,

Lehman Brothers, SVB, Credit Suisse, HDFC bank etc - you can include them in your answers if
you're confident enough. Sometimes, these topics can be asked by the interviewer too (I was asked
about Lehman Brothers in my JPMC CR round 2).

• Read and learn deeply about types of risks, their metrics, how the bank manages that kind of risk,

relevance to the role - I used ChatGPT and YouTube to study about these topics in great depth.

• Prepare about financial ratios and ratios important for a bank.

• Learn about derivatives and greeks.

• Revise Python and SQL.

• Try to make unique and tailored projects according to the role - it was one of the things that

impressed the interviewers most in my case.

• Also, go through the 100 puzzles from GFG and guesstimates as they can be asked (well they

weren't asked in CTC interview, but are asked frequently for CIB and CR interviews, and also in
other companies).

• In interviews, you can always write on the sheet provided to clearly communicate your thoughts.

My personal experience :)
Even though I had a tech background where I used to do DSA regularly, did an internship as an SDE intern,
and participated in hacks, I've always had this inclination towards finance and wanted to work in JPMC, I
was always so fascinated by it. I liked participating in case studies from my 1st year itself. Even though it
felt like an unreachable dream at the moment, I started doing CFI courses in my 6th semester alongside my
--- PAGE 6 ---
tech routine, and my minor in Financial and Strategic Management helped me as well - needless to say - it
was hectic as hell. But I kept on studying.
In July, JPMC came for the CIB and CR roles. Initially, I had just prepared for the CIB role, but
unfortunately, I could only reach till the 1st round. Then, I had my CR interview the next day, but I got
eliminated after the 2nd round. I was really heartbroken since I got rejected by JPMC for 2 consecutive days
and gave up on it.
Heartbroken, I resumed preparing for tech roles. I got rejected by companies for a whole month - sometimes
I knew the reason why I didn't get ahead, and sometimes I didn't even realise why. At first, I used to get
really anxious, sad and tense daily, but then over time, I just surrendered my fate to God and kept on
working hard and studying regularly.
Obviously, I took a break from finance since I was prepping for tech roles. But then, out of nowhere, JPMC
announced it is coming back for a completely new role. It felt like a second chance at redeeming myself.
From that day onwards, I started preparing for it, deep dived into the JD, prepared tailored projects for the
role, learned about different types of risks and their metrics, historic case studies, revised finance concepts
and also did mock interviews with Claude and GPT - do it with your friends too.
Finally, I would just like to say that you might feel depressed and overwhelmed when you see your friends
and peers get placed, but I would stress on this - LUCK plays a very important factor. But, Luck can only
help you in things like getting a good panel, getting easier questions in OAs etc., other than that, you always
need to be prepared to jump and take the opportunity that comes your way - so don't ponder much on things
like why isn't luck on my side etc and just keep on grinding and studying hard - because the day Luck is on
your side, it's your job to shine the brightest!!
All the best guys, keep faith in yourselves and stay resilient, you can do it!!

Round 4: Technical Interview 1 - 11/8/2026

Round 5 : Technical Interview 2 - 11/8/2026

Round 6: HR Interview - 11/8/2026

1. Resume Shortlisting | 250+ students applied approximately]

Since the role was open to all branches, there might be 250 or 300+ resume applicants. One consistent thing
I noticed across both JPMC CIB and JPMC CTC roles were, people who had 12th marks below 80%, got
out in this round itself. Apart from this, make sure to at least have your CGPA above 7.5, but preferably try
to keep it above 8 for other companies as well.
Tailor your resume according to the role- try to align your projects as closely to the role as possible, try to
make some projects related to risk and finance, include relevant courses and certifications, put keywords
according to the JD and ofc don't mention anything you won't be able to justify as ANY of the keywords or
anything you put in the resume can be asked in the interview.
Lastly, make sure to have a good ATS score above 70 of your resume on Resume Worded.
We had to apply both on superset and JPMC website, so try to fill out the application as soon as possible.
There were some people who filled the application late and didn't get shortlisted for the test, as JPMC
reviews applications on a rolling basis.

2. Online Test [ 120 students shortlisted for the online test ]

--- PAGE 2 ---
The online test was from home. The pattern was the same as the CIB test. There were 4 sections, no negative
marking and total 45 questions in 45 mins of total 45 marks.
Section 1 - Corporate Finance and Financial Account (10 gs) - Basic finance questions based on ratios,
gross profit, profit and loss.
Section 2 - Market Awareness (10 gs) - Included questions on current affairs, budget, recent laws on taxes
and finances, and some basic macroeconomics logical questions. Make sure to regularly read the news.
Section 3 - Quantitative Aptitude (15 gs) - The most time consuming section. The questions were of
medium level based on topics like probability, cards, PNC, speed, profit loss, percentage etc.
Section 4 - English Usage (10 gs) - Easiest section. Basic grammar based fill in the blanks, comprehension
type questions, order the sentences type qs, and two bar graph based questions.

3. Group Discussion Round [ 29 students appeared for the GD]

The shortlisted candidates list came one night before the interviews around 9 pm.
A GD round was declared the night before. No topic was given for the GD, unlike the CIB role where a
topic is mostly given beforehand.
The rounds began at around 10.30 am the next day. There were 4 groups made with 7 - 8 people in each
group and 2 panels in total - so each panel conducted 2 GDs.
Each group was given a different topic. In my group, there were 7 people. The topic given to us was - "Is AI
making college degrees less relevant and valuable?"
Try to speak as soon as possible, as in that way, you can put the unique points forward first. I spoke second
in the GD. Make sure to speak confidently, try to use real life examples and numbers or stats if possible to
back your points. Don't try to interrupt or overpower others, and even if you disagree with someone, do it
politely. (4 people got selected for the next round from my group)

4. Interview Round 1[14 people appeared for this round]

Since there were 2 panels, each panel interviewed 7 students.
Through other students, I came to know that my panel was grilling hard based on the resume, so I kept on
revising my projects until my chance came.
(I'll try to keep my experience as detailed as possible to help you guys - my round lasted for about 40-45
mins so it's gonna be pretty longg !!)
My chance came just after the lunch break, and I entered confidently with a smile on my face and greeted
the interviewers (a sir and a ma'am) and shook their hands - this always sets a good impression from the
start!
They introduced themselves and asked how I was feeling, how was the GD and then asked me for my
introduction. Make sure to have an interesting and a story like introduction which could justify why being an
engineering student, you wanna go into finance and risk dept.
I was then asked about my first project on credit risk analysis, how did I make it, from where did I get the
idea (sir seemed very interested in the project), since he knew obviously things like these aren't taught to us
--- PAGE 3 ---
in college, so he wanted to know from WHERE did I think about this project- to which I replied that I went
for a case study in another college and made some friends there and asked them about the topics being
taught to them in finance and took an interest in risk related topics, so I asked them for materials and made
this project with the help of Al after learning the concepts. Things like these also help them understand that
you have good communication and interpersonal skills. I was then asked for a deep dive into the project. The
interviewers seemed impressed and mentioned that my project was very identical to the work people
actually do in credit risk.
Similarly, sir asked me about my 2nd project - which was based on portfolio risk analysis using Modern
Portfolio Theory. I was asked about the aim and overview of the project - I supported my answers by making
the Risk vs Return graph of my project on a sheet and explained the figure in great detail. The interviewers
seemed satisfied with my explanations.
Then ma'am went through my skills section and asked whether I knew about financial statements and asked
"Which statement should a bank see of a company before giving out a loan to them" - I then talked about
the 3 financial statements, how they connect, how the answer should be cash flow statement and not the PnL
statement as CF statement shows the actual liquidity, then threw in some concepts about how a company can
be solvent but illiquid etc. It's important to throw in some extra things you know related to the questions
asked as they always help you out!
I was then asked if I followed the markets, I said at a macroeconomic level, yes. Then I was asked how the
war is affecting the economy, repo rates, inflation, role of RBI etc. I then asked them if I could also explain
how change in interest rates affect banks, to which they happily replied "Sure!', so I talked about Asset
Liability Management and the scenarios when assets reprice faster than liabilities and vice versa and what
effect they have on the NII in the short term, then I was asked some follow up questions as well.
Then I was asked to explain any one kind of risk. I took up market risk, coz my project already included
credit risk, and explained what market risk is, how it can affect banks, metrics of market risk like VaR and
ES.
Then, I was asked if I knew about derivatives- to which I said yes, and then I was asked about options. So I
explained what options are, call and put options with examples. This led on to a conversation on Greeks.
Then sir asked me, what experience I have in tech, to which I replied that I have experience in development,
my primary language is Java in which I do DSA and I talked about my internship as an SDE intern where I
had to work with a completely new tech stack in NEXT/NEST Js. So then I talked about how the tech stacks
don't matter if we know the underlying concepts clearly. Then I said that I know Python at a medium level
since I don't code in it regularly, as my primary language is Java, then talked about how most of the
concepts are pretty similar with some differences such as in OOPS, to which ma'am quickly asked me to
explain the difference in Java and Python OOPS so I talked about multiple inheritance, diamond problem,
MRO in python etc. I was also asked about the difference between linear and logistic regression.
Then sir asked me, how did I take an interest in finance, on which I talked about my background that I've
always had this balance between tech and finance since my cousins are all in tech and my father is an MBA
graduate, how I started doing case study competitions from my 1st year and gradually learned more and
more about finance by taking up my minor in Financial and Strategic Management and through some CFI
Courses. I also talked about how hectic my 6th semester had become due to daily DSA, dev, my internship,
--- PAGE 4 ---
college and finance courses all at once, but I learned how to manage my time. I talked about how my parents
trade in stock markets and lightened the convo by bringing in how my parents get sad if they don't get
allotted any IPO and talked about some recent IPOs and the interviewers smiled and shook their heads as
well.
At the end I was asked where I lived. Then I asked them questions about the AI tools being used in JPMC
and how they make work easier for the employees and how the risk team helps the main IB and front office
teams.

5. Interview Round 2 [6 people appeared for this round]

This round was stricter and harder than the previous round, as in this round, most of the questions were
scenario based and not resume based, as they wanted to know if we understood concepts clearly. There were
2 interviewers, a sir and a ma'am. I was first asked why I wanted this role.
Then ma'am grilled me on liquidity risk, so I talked about liquidity risk, how it's important to a bank, ratios
like LCR and NSFR, on which I was further grilled on the ratios and topics like High Quality Liquid Assets,
where they are present in a bank's balance sheet etc.
Then I was asked which type of risk is the most relevant in today's time, I related it to the geopolitical
scenario and said Market Risk and Interest Rate Risk and explained the reasons why.
The next question was - "If I were to take a bond from the Mumbai Airport, what factors would I assess
before taking itạ so I talked about secured bonds, interest rate factors, yield etc.
Then sir asked me to do a deep dive into my DCF Project. Be sure to explain it deeply from start to finish in
this manner:

• what the company is about

• how their balance sheets are, is it a cash heavy, loan heavy company

• how you made the assumptions for projections for the components of FCFF, explain the components

too and what they tell you about the company, for example what a negative WC would tell you about
the company etc, then arrive at the FCFF

• then talk about the whole derivation process of Cost Of Debt, Cost of Equity - talk about how you

got the beta, what you infer from it, CAPM model - then arrive on WACC

• then arrive at Enterprise Value, Equity Value, Intrinsic Price of share derived in your model vs the

actual share price and your recommendation for the share and why.
You should be able to talk about the whole flow of DCF while explaining and justifying your steps and
talking about the formulae used, in a very clear and orderly manner.
I was then asked if I knew about Comparables method of valuation, so I explained about that method, then I
talked about ratios like P/E, EV/EBITDA etc. and how different types of companies would use different
kinds of ratios based on their profitability. I was then asked about EBITDA, debt related ratios like
Debt/EBITDA, D/E etc.
I was then asked about a case study of mine where we won first place and what we did in it.
--- PAGE 5 ---
The interview ended with me asking them questions like "What skills should I learn so that I become the
best version of myself while joining JPMC if I get selectediằ

6. HR Round [ 3 people appeared for this round]

This round was pretty chill and relaxing, the HR ma'am was very sweet and asked me how my previous
rounds were, why this role, why JPMC, as being a CSE student, I could've gotten some other tech company
as well, and how my interest in finance grew. Then I was asked a scenario based question, "Tell me about a
time where you made a mistake and you had to apologize for itẠạThen I was asked questions like where I
lived, if my schooling and everything was done in Mumbai itself etc. The interview ended with HR ma'am
saying "All the best, results would be declared at the EOD."
About an hour after the HR Rounds, the result was announced and 2 people got selected for the role.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Resources and tips:

• Do relevant CFI courses on Finance and Risk from Coursera.

• Practice aptitude from Career Ride (Youtube) and IndiaBix regularly - please don't let this be the

cause of elimination from any company.

• Regularly read news from newspapers or from apps like TOI, The Economic Times or The Hindu - I

made a habit to read news daily from the start of my 6th semester while travelling.

• Read about relevant case studies related to risk mishaps like Global Financial Crisis of 2008,

Lehman Brothers, SVB, Credit Suisse, HDFC bank etc - you can include them in your answers if
you're confident enough. Sometimes, these topics can be asked by the interviewer too (I was asked
about Lehman Brothers in my JPMC CR round 2).

• Read and learn deeply about types of risks, their metrics, how the bank manages that kind of risk,

relevance to the role - I used ChatGPT and YouTube to study about these topics in great depth.

• Prepare about financial ratios and ratios important for a bank.

• Learn about derivatives and greeks.

• Revise Python and SQL.

• Try to make unique and tailored projects according to the role - it was one of the things that

impressed the interviewers most in my case.

• Also, go through the 100 puzzles from GFG and guesstimates as they can be asked (well they

weren't asked in CTC interview, but are asked frequently for CIB and CR interviews, and also in
other companies).

• In interviews, you can always write on the sheet provided to clearly communicate your thoughts.

My personal experience :)
Even though I had a tech background where I used to do DSA regularly, did an internship as an SDE intern,
and participated in hacks, I've always had this inclination towards finance and wanted to work in JPMC, I
was always so fascinated by it. I liked participating in case studies from my 1st year itself. Even though it
felt like an unreachable dream at the moment, I started doing CFI courses in my 6th semester alongside my
--- PAGE 6 ---
tech routine, and my minor in Financial and Strategic Management helped me as well - needless to say - it
was hectic as hell. But I kept on studying.
In July, JPMC came for the CIB and CR roles. Initially, I had just prepared for the CIB role, but
unfortunately, I could only reach till the 1st round. Then, I had my CR interview the next day, but I got
eliminated after the 2nd round. I was really heartbroken since I got rejected by JPMC for 2 consecutive days
and gave up on it.
Heartbroken, I resumed preparing for tech roles. I got rejected by companies for a whole month - sometimes
I knew the reason why I didn't get ahead, and sometimes I didn't even realise why. At first, I used to get
really anxious, sad and tense daily, but then over time, I just surrendered my fate to God and kept on
working hard and studying regularly.
Obviously, I took a break from finance since I was prepping for tech roles. But then, out of nowhere, JPMC
announced it is coming back for a completely new role. It felt like a second chance at redeeming myself.
From that day onwards, I started preparing for it, deep dived into the JD, prepared tailored projects for the
role, learned about different types of risks and their metrics, historic case studies, revised finance concepts
and also did mock interviews with Claude and GPT - do it with your friends too.
Finally, I would just like to say that you might feel depressed and overwhelmed when you see your friends
and peers get placed, but I would stress on this -

it works at the end, you work on daily basis for all the products from business requirements,

Who are you Rehan?
(i didnt hear what he said at the start i just listen to the last line and answered) i love be stressed out, and
code is already a commodity, data analysis will also be the same every soon. So you will be valued for

im the 3rd one

For which i got the remark "That was the best answer to that question I've received."

Pitch so good that you get "So I might not be your target audience, but I'm also sold on the idea."

At the end i asked him questions about the UBS why UBS over HFT. i tried to hit him personally as well as

3. HR round 5 peps were there. 4 got the offer

journey.prep:
• The most important thing to remember is that there is always a luck factor involved in these

processes - you might have done everything right but sometimes it just is not your day. You can
either sulk and waste your time or try to learn from your mistakes, get an outside perspective and
keep on learning.

• They do not expect us to know much about finance but they will grill you every chance they get. So

even if you are not able to answer certain questions, don't lose confidence.

• I thought my 2nd and 3rd interviews went terrible but I still got shortlisted.

• Make sure you start reading Newspapers well in advance, news related to M&As and IPOs.

--- PAGE 7 ---

• Follow the market for prices of SENSEX, NIFTY, Trent crude price, Gold, Silver a day before the

interviews as well.

• Have 1 IPO in mind that is upcoming, well researched and understood in advance.

• Even if you don't know the answer, try explaining your thought process. They help you reach the

answer and judge how you are interacting with them more than what you are answering.

• Keep certain answers ready: Introduce yourself, walk me through your resume, project

explanations, strengths and weaknesses, challenges faced, financial statements, overall market
scenarios, trends you noticed in the markets, why IB.

• After getting the GD topic, do as much research as you can, make notes and prepare thoroughly. You

will feel the most tensed while going to give the GD, if that goes well then you will be confident
throughout.

• Always keep a smile on your face and be polite. If you have any other doubts, feel free to reach me.

• Be humble and show curiosity and eagerness to learn. Don't let the interviewer think you are

arrogant or a know-it-all.

• Make a lot of projects - it is the BEST way to learn new concepts and it will allow you to pick and

choose appropriate projects for each company to ensure you can put your best foot forward

• The shortlist names are usually revealed just 15/16 hours before the interview or test, so you need to

prepare without worrying about the results.

• Practice generic HR questions - What are your short term and long term plans, plans for further

studies (always SAY NO), etc - I will try to give an ideal response and in detailed answer in the doc
attached above.

• Talk to your seniors in your target company, talk to people already working in your target industry,

and talk to your TPCs, all of them can give you great insights and guidance not just for your
placements but for your future career.
Feel free to reach out to me LinkedIn
ALL THE BEST!
journey.howSecured:
The pre-placement talk was scheduled online on 24th June. Try to ask questions and give answers if you
can. They ask questions like any specific major IPO or M&A deal that occurred within the last 2 years.

1. Resume Screening: Deadline 26th June

2. Online Aptitude Test: 27th June

3. Group Discussion (Online)

4. Interview round 1 (Online)

5. Interview round 2 (Online)

6. Interview round 3 (Online)

7. HR round (Online)

Rounds 3-6 were scheduled on 2nd July.
Just a general heads-up: the number of interview rounds is completely random. I had to go through three
finance interview rounds, while some candidates had only one. So don't be surprised if your interview
process differs from someone else's.

1. Resume Screening

We had to submit all details and resume via the JPMC portal. You are also allowed to attach a cover letter,
although not mandatory, do submit one.

• Use the latex template and add only things you are confident about. Keep it single column, one page.

• You will need around 5 to 6 copies of your resume as your panel may have more than one

interviewer.
67 students were shortlisted for the next round.

2. Online Aptitude Test

The test window was 10:30-11:00 am and the duration was 45 mins. It had 4 sections, with no negative
marking and navigation was allowed.

• Basics of Finance and Accounting : 10 questions

• Market awareness: 10 questions. Questions were not necessarily finance based but general current

affairs.
--- PAGE 2 ---

• Quantitative Aptitude : 15 questions.

Questions based on Profit and Loss, Workers and Time, AP GP, Probability, etc. (Normal Aptitude
questions), CAT level.

• Verbal Skills : 10 questions.

Passage based, rearranging, standard questions.
The test was lengthy so try to attempt things you know and equal parts from all sections.
56 students were shortlisted. The result was announced less than a day before the interview so be prepared.

3. Group Discussion | 56 selected students were divided into 6 panels of 9/10 each. We had Around 30

mins]
The GD topic was revealed on 1st July, just one day before the process:
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a significant portion
of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times have
doubled tor approximately two months, and shipping costs have increased, negatively impacting
financial metrics. As the CEO of the company, how would you tackle this situation?"
A few important things about the GD:

• No notes or reference material were allowed during the discussion.

• There were 2 panelists observing the GD.

• Instead of a free-flowing discussion throughout, the panelists introduced different situations one after

another, and the group discussed each before moving to the next.
The situations included questions such as:

1. Should the company increase the prices of its best-selling products to offset the higher shipping

costs?

2. If the entire disruption were resolved overnight, what would be the first thing you would do as the

CEO?

3. How to approach while keeping in mind the on paper losses?

Tips for the GD

• Aim to speak in at least 2-3 of the situations.

• Quality matters far more than quantity. You do not need to speak for a long time if your points ar

well-structured and relevant.

• Wherever possible, support your arguments with numbers, percentages, or business metrics. This

makes your points more credible.

• Try to make unique, insightful points that others can build upon. A good indicator of a strong

contribution is when other participants reference your point before adding their own perspective.
Finally, GD performance influences your interview order. Candidates who performed better were generally
scheduled for interviews earlier. I was the first person called for Round 1 after the GD. The overall process
is quite lengthy, so don't lose patience while waiting for your turn.
28 students were shortlisted for round 1
--- PAGE 3 ---

4. Interview Round 1 [ My round lasted for about 40 mins]

There were 6 interview panels, and my interview was scheduled first in my panel.
The interview began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself. Make sure you have answers to the
standard HR questions prepared, as I was asked to introduce myself in every interview round.
The discussion then progressed as follows:

• She asked me what I thought my role would involve.

• She moved on to the stock market, asking about Sensex and Nifty. Make sure you know the previous

day's closing values for both indices.

• She asked whether I invest personally and which sectors I would invest in, along with the reasoning

behind my choices.

• Next, she asked about the RBI, its monetary policies, inflation, and the current RBI Governor.

Tip: If you don't know the answer, don't guess. It's better to admit that you haven't read about
it than to give incorrect information.

• She then shifted to financial statements:

o Explain the link between the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement.

• She gave a scenario: "If depreciation expense is overstated by 710, how would it impact all

three financial statementsạẠạ

• She also asked about recent trends in the financial markets, so stay updated with current business and

economic news.

• She asked me why IB?

The interview concluded with a few analytical and puzzle-based questions, including:

• An average speed problem

• The classic water jug puzzle

• Finding the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at a given time.

Always end the interview by asking a thoughtful question. Don't waste the opportunity by asking generic or
easily searchable questions. Instead, ask something that demonstrates genuine curiosity about the role or the
team. A strong closing question can leave a positive final impression.

5. Interview Round 2 [ This round was for 15-20 mins]

I was called for Round 2 approximately 45 minutes after completing Round 1.
This round had one panelist. The interview began with the usual "Introduce yourself" question, followed by
a few questions based on my resume.
The interviewer then shifted to core finance concepts, focusing primarily on valuation:
Explain Enterprise Value (EV) and Equity Value.
What is the difference between Enterprise Value and Equity Value?
How do you calculate each of them?

• When is Enterprise Value preferred over Equity Value, and vice versa?

He also asked me about several valuation ratios, including:

• P/E (Price-to-Earnings) Ratio

• EV/EBITDA

For each ratio, he expected me to explain:
--- PAGE 4 ---

• What the ratio represents.

• Why is it used?

• What insights it provides about a company.

• In which situations it is most useful.

He then gave me a valuation case study. He provided the market capitalization and P/E ratio of two
companies and asked me to calculate the combined P/E ratio after the two companies merged.
I wasn't able to solve it immediately, but I explained my thought process and approach at every step.
Whenever I got stuck, the interviewer provided small hints, and using those inputs I was able to work
through the problem and arrive at the correct answer.

6. Interview Round 3 [ This round was for 20-25 mins]

I was called for Round 3 approximately 45 minutes after completing Round 2. There was one panelist for
this interview. The interviewer started by asking me how the overall interview process had been. Keep your
response positive and professional. Throughout the interview, maintain good eye contact, smile naturally
when appropriate, and stay confident.
The discussion then moved into valuation concepts:

• Enterprise Value (EV) and how it is affected by debt and cash.

• Why debt is added and cash is subtracted while calculating Enterprise Value.

• FCFF (Free Cash Flow to the Firm):

• What it is.

• The formula used to calculate it.

• Why FCFF is used for Enterprise Value valuation.

• Difference between FCFF AND FCFE.

• Why do we need both Enterprise Value and Equity Value instead of just one valuation metric?

• EV/EBITDA:

• Why is EBITDA used in the denominator?

• Why Net Income is not used instead.

The interviewer was particularly interested in how I arrived at my answers, not just the final response. Even
if you're unsure, explain your reasoning and thought process clearly. Interviewers often provide hints if they
see you're approaching the problem logically.
My Round 2 and Round 3 interviews did not go as well as I had hoped, but I was still shortlisted. One
interview rarely determines the final outcome, so don't lose confidence if you feel you've made a few
mistakes. Stay calm, composed, and positive throughout the process.
At the end of the interview, I asked a few questions about:

• The company's growth opportunities.

• Career progression within the organization.

• The kind of work and learning opportunities available for new hires.

10 people were selected for the HR round.
--- PAGE 5 ---

7. HR Round [ Around 10 mins ]

This was the easiest round of the process. There was one interviewer, and the discussion was largely
HR-focused. The interview started with the standard "Introduce yourself" question, followed by:

• Why Investment Banking despite having a Software Engineering background?

• Do you plan to pursue higher studies or any professional certifications in the future?

• What would your plan be if you were not selected for this role?

For questions about your future plans, it's important to demonstrate a strong commitment to a career in
finance. Even if you have long-term plans for higher studies, avoid giving the impression that this role is
only a temporary stop. Instead, communicate that you genuinely want to build your career in finance and are
excited about the opportunity the company offers.
Throughout the conversation, make it clear that:

• You have a genuine interest in finance.

• You are eager to learn and grow within the organization.

• You see yourself building a long-term career with the firm.

At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I asked about:

• Growth opportunities within the organization and what differentiates employees who progress

quickly.

• The role of HR in the recruitment and employee development process, and how HR collaborates with

different business teams throughout an employee's journey.
These questions led to a good discussion and helped end the interview on a positive note.
The process on the 2nd started around 9 and we got the results by 5 pm. 10 students were selected for the
Banking role.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• The most important thing to remember is that there is always a luck factor involved in these

processes - you might have done everything right but sometimes it just is not your day. You can
either sulk and waste your time or try to learn from your mistakes, get an outside perspective and
keep on learning.

• They do not expect us to know much about finance but they will grill you every chance they get. So

even if you are not able to answer certain questions, don't lose confidence.

• I thought my 2nd and 3rd interviews went terrible but I still got shortlisted.

• Make sure you start reading Newspapers well in advance, news related to M&As and IPOs.

--- PAGE 7 ---

• Follow the market for prices of SENSEX, NIFTY, Trent crude price, Gold, Silver a day before the

interviews as well.

• Have 1 IPO in mind that is upcoming, well researched and understood in advance.

• Even if you don't know the answer, try explaining your thought process. They help you reach the

answer and judge how you are interacting with them more than what you are answering.

• Keep certain answers ready: Introduce yourself, walk me through your resume, project

explanations, strengths and weaknesses, challenges faced, financial statements, overall market
scenarios, trends you noticed in the markets, why IB.

• After getting the GD topic, do as much research as you can, make notes and prepare thoroughly. You

will feel the most tensed while going to give the GD, if that goes well then you will be confident
throughout.

• Always keep a smile on your face and be polite. If you have any other doubts, feel free to reach me.

• Be humble and show curiosity and eagerness to learn. Don't let the interviewer think you are

arrogant or a know-it-all.

• Make a lot of projects - it is the BEST way to learn new concepts and it will allow you to pick and

choose appropriate projects for each company to ensure you can put your best foot forward

• The shortlist names are usually revealed just 15/16 hours before the interview or test, so you need to

prepare without worrying about the results.

• Practice generic HR questions - What are your short term and long term plans, plans for further

studies (always SAY NO), etc - I will try to give an ideal response and in detailed answer in the doc
attached above.

• Talk to your seniors in your target company, talk to people already working in your target industry,

and talk to your TPCs, all of them can give you great insights and guidance not just for your
placements but for your future career.
Feel free to reach out to me LinkedIn

Rounds:

1. Resume Shortlisting

2. Online Assessment

3. Technical Interview

4. HR Interview

1. Resume Shortlisting

Resume shortlisting was done based on CGPA. Approximately the first 115 applicants were shortlisted for
the Online Assessment (OA).
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [110-115 students]

The assessment consisted of four sections:

1. Logical Reasoning:

This section consisted of questions based on patterns, blood relations, coding-decoding, seating
arrangements, etc. The questions were not very difficult, but speed and accuracy were important. There were
15 questions to be solved in 15 minutes. I would recommend aiming for a high score in this section.

2. Aptitude:

There were 12 questions to be solved in 15 minutes. Questions were based on topics such as speed-distance,
ratios, profit and loss, probability, etc. I would recommend practising aptitude questions from IndiaBix, as
similar types of questions are commonly asked in OAs. Speed and accuracy are again very important here.

3. Coding:

The coding section had 45 minutes and consisted of 2 questions.
One important thing I noticed was that the difficulty of the coding questions varied significantly from person
to person. Some students received two relatively easy questions, while others received a combination of an
easy and a medium/hard question. Therefore, the difficulty of the questions you get can have a significant
impact on your performance.
For me, the first question was relatively easy, and I was able to pass all the test cases. The second question
was harder, and I was able to pass only 5/12 test cases. (At this point, I thought I probably wouldn't make it
to the interviews, but never say never! :)
The questions were based on arrays, strings, hashmaps, binary search, greedy algorithms and DP.

4. Verbal Reasoning:

This was the easiest section for me. It had 12 questions with 15 minutes to solve them. The questions
included reading comprehension, grammatical errors and similar verbal reasoning concepts.

3. Technical Interview [34 candidates ]

I was the first candidate on my panel and my interview started at approximately 10:00 am.
Here again the questions and difficulty level vary across panels. All the panels had 2 panelists.
Firstly, they asked me to introduce myself (keep this script ready). I highlighted one backend heavy project,
my app dev internship and talked about the research paper I had published. I think the direction of the
interview and the questions that follow are influenced by your introduction. So prepare your intro
accordingly.
After the intro, they picked the first project and told me to explain the schema and asked in brief about how I
had implemented some of the functionalities. They asked me why I had used MongoDB and not SQL
database (Design choices are often questioned in interviews, so keep such answers ready). Then they asked
me when we should use SQL related databases and when to use NoSQL with one example each.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After this they asked me to write 3 SQL queries. The first two I got correct, then he twisted the third
question a little. I explained to him my approach but I was not able to write the whole query correctly. (Just
tell whatever you know instead of being silent).
He then asked me a DSA question similar to the Coin Change DP problem on LeetCode, but here he wanted
to know how many coins of each denomination were used. I was not able to come up with the DP solution
for this, so I asked if I could explain the greedy approach instead. He told me to write the code on paper and
then he gave me a sample input and told me to dry run the code on that input.
(Be ready to write codes on paper, I was asked to write code on paper in one other interview too).
He was satisfied with that approach and explanation.
Then he asked me about JWT tokens, how they are generated, how they are renewed, their significance etc.
After this he told me to talk about my research paper, what was unique, how did I implement that etc.
I was asked about the difference between ML and DL.
He then asked me to explain 4 pillars of oops with examples for each.
Lastly he asked me about my Barclays minors and 10th and 12th percentages.
He asked me if I had any questions for them to which I asked what technologies do I need to equip myself
with if I were to work at TransUnion. The technical interview thereby concluded on this note.

4. HR Interview [11 candidates ]

I was called for the HR interview 20-30 minutes after my technical interview. There were 2 panelists here
too. They asked me to introduce myself. After this they asked me what TransUnion exactly does. I had
expected this question to be asked and had looked up for it before. I explained it in detail, and she
appreciated my answer.
Then she asked me to walk through any two of my projects, but without going into the technical details. She
wanted to know things like the motivation behind the projects and how I approached implementing them.
Then she asked which of these projects I had done alone and which I had done in groups. She asked me for
the two projects that I had talked about earlier, what one thing would I handle/implement differently if I got
the opportunity to go back and re-do them.
Then she asked me about my two weaknesses. I mentioned them and how I am trying to overcome them as
well.
She then asked me if I would not have been an engineer, what I would have been. I personally felt this was
an interesting question cause as a child I had always thought of becoming a doctor. I told her how and why
at the last moment I decided to take PCM instead of PCB after 10th standard. Again this answer was
elaborate as it came from a personal experience (She seemed to like it :)
She then asked me situational questions like how will I handle friction between team members, how would I
solve conflicts, how would I prioritize projects if multiple deadlines were approaching etc.

She concluded the interview by asking about my family background and whether I had any questions for
them.

The Wissen placement process consisted of an online coding assessment followed by two
rounds of interviews. Approximately 270 students appeared for the initial assessment, out of
which around 40 were shortlisted for the technical interview. Following the subsequent interview
rounds, 9 students were ultimately selected - 7 received Internship + Full-Time Employment
offers, while 2 received Internship-only offers.
Online Assessment: (~270 candidates) There were 8 questions in total → 5 MCQS covering
general aptitude, OS, and OOPs concepts, 2 DSA questions, and 1 SQL question.

• A) Ancestory: Find the max length path from root to leaf such that for every node in the

path, abs(avg of values of ancestors of node - value of curr node) ≤ k. Input given as n,
value, leftchild], rightchild[], k.

• B) Sandbar: Given a position array xI and prize array PI], once you take the prize at a

position you can't take another within distance d -i ≤ d based on positions, not indices).
If you take a pair exactly at j-i = d+1 after claiming i, you get a bonus b. Find the max
prize obtainable.
I managed to solve correctly all 5 MCQs and one of the DSA questions (Ancestory).
Interview Round 1 (40 candidates) (1 hr 30 min):
This round was honestly quite manageable by anyone with a bit of DSA experience could clear
it without much trouble. We started with a walk-through of my resume along with a few standard
questions, which took about 10 minutes. From there, the interviewer moved into DSA and asked
which language I was most comfortable with - I said C++. The format was old-school: explain
my approach first, then code it out on paper with strict syntax, taking care of input and output.
The first problem involved an array of G's and B's (like G,G,G,B,B,B,B) where I had to find the
first and last B, both when the array was sorted and when it wasn't. Next was a sorted array of
random numbers where I had to print all numbers between 120 and 150 using binary search.
After that came a question involving a vector of social media posts, where I had to count the
number of hashtags in each post and return the posts) with the highest count (accounting for
--- PAGE 2 ---
ties), and then figure out which hashtag was used most across all the posts - an
unordered_map handled this nicely.
The one genuinely tricky question in this round was a system design-style problem: designing
the "top k searches" feature you often see on e-commerce sites, like when you tap the search
bar and see your 3 most recent searches. The expected answer was a doubly linked list
combined with a hashmap, and I was able to explain and code this correctly.
Following that, the interviewer shifted to SQL and asked me to draw an ER diagram for a
scenario: an actor works in many movies/shows, a movie/show can have multiple actors, and a
film can have several sequels - with each sequel having a different IMDB number despite
belonging to the same film. I had to mark primary and foreign keys and define the relationships.
My diagram held up well, and as a follow-up, the interviewer asked me to write a SQL query to
find movies with only one actor, my soln was a simple GROUP BY on actor-film entity with a
COUNT = 1 condition.
Toward the end, I got the chance to ask my own questions, so I asked about the internship's
training process and the overall work culture, and they were happy to answer in detail.
Interview Round 2 (45 min):
This round was conducted by the company's Executive Director, whereas the previous round
had been taken by a junior developer.
This round had just one DSA question, a traffic light scheduling problem. The premise: a
traffic signal only exists if it connects two or more roads. You're given an array representing
average vehicle traffic at each road (e.g., [100, 20, 110, 0]) along with a total cycle time t (say,
120 seconds). Within this cycle, each signal must turn green exactly once, in the order of the
roads, with each green phase lasting a minimum of 10 seconds and a maximum of 60 seconds.
The goal is to distribute the signal timings to minimize overall vehicle wait time, and the cycle
then repeats. The output should be an array representing the schedule. This is essentially the
same as a LeetCode discussion question on traffic signal management. I got this one right, it
mostly came down to applying ratio and proportion logic while handling edge cases around the
10s/60s bounds.
Next came an OOP design question that had me confused. I was asked to design the class
structure for how an air conditioner works, covering components like the temperature sensor,
condenser, and fan, and how these objects would interact with each other. If you're preparing for
this company, it's worth practicing this style of "given an application, design the classes"
question.
The conversation then moved toward Al, since I mentioned I'd completed a GenAl course with
Vizura and had built a small language model (SLM) on my own. This opened up a broader
discussion, the interviewer asked what RAG is, the difference between an LLM and an agent,
what an Al harness and guardrails are, and how agents retain context across a conversation. I
--- PAGE 3 ---
leaned on real-lite examples while explaining these, which the interviewer seemed to
appreciate.
When it was my turn to ask questions, I asked about growth opportunities for freshers at Wissen
and how they use Al internally, and got a thorough answer about the agents they've built and
how they're integrated. My advice here would be to genuinely show curiosity about the role and
the process during these conversations, it tends to come through positively.
Ultimately, I was offered an Internship + FTE.

There were a total of 6 rounds of shortlisting(resume shortlist, rapid fire MCQs and 4 rounds of interview).
All rounds of interviews were conducted online as the company staff was in Bangalore.

1. Round 1: Resume shortlisting (more than 200 candidates appeared for this round)

A resume with work experience is preferred during shortlisting. Try to include an unpaid internship, it will
help basically everywhere. Along with this, it is highly recommended to be honest with your projects. DO
NOT lie about them. Though I wasn't asked much about them, many candidates struggle to explain the
details of their projects in general, leading to a bad impression. Maintain a CGPA of more than 8.5 or at least
8 as in many cases, it is the first criteria during shortlisting.
Nearly half of the students were selected for the process.

2. Round 2: Rapid fire MCQ (101 candidates appeared for this round)

The rounds were held in the college from here on. In this particular round, we were expected to complete 50
MCQs in under 10 minutes. The questions were on basic C, Java and Python along with core CS subjects
like Computer Networks, OS, DBMS, etc. No one completes it all. Just keep marking answers without
thinking much(even if you don't know the answer). Make sure you submit it on time.

3. Round 3: API Debugging Round (52 candidates appeared in this round)

The interview officially begins here. We were given a google meet link. We joined it from the TPO cabins.
The interviewer asked me to introduce myself. He then got straight to the point and gave me a list of options
for the round. I selected Nodejs as nearly all my development projects use this. After that he pasted a link in
the chat section. It was like VS Code inside the browser. It has a bunch of folders consisting of code for a
web application in nodejs(backend only obviously) and a jupyter notebook for testing API. In this round,
you are expected to:
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Debug what is wrong with the currently written APIs(syntax and other errors)

2. Create a new API for a different purpose.

The application was for student attendance as far as I remember. I was asked to check why the API made for
creating a new student was not working as intended. You will have to search through the files for finding the
syntax error. It was a normal JS syntax error where an object was passed as a parameter where boolean was
expected. I corrected the code. He then asked what was actually wrong, which I explained.
It is highly advisable to KEEP TALKING. Do not go blank if you can't see the error right away. Ask the
interviewer for hints. Ask questions on what this particular section of code does. Ask for clarifications. I
took some time but was able to identify the syntax errors in both APIs.
After that, he asked me to write a code for an API. I would rate that question moderately difficult as it
involved some logic. I was not able to code but I told my approach and he was like "Okay, time's up!".
It lasted for about 1 hour. Before leaving, he asked me if I had any questions about the company. I came
prepared for this moment. I asked, "Did you encounter a situation during your time at WorkIndia where you
learned a completely new technology from scratchạ
ẠạiHe answered firmly, giving some examples.
It took some time to get results. We were waiting while discussing what we were asked. 16 students were
selected for the next round.

4. Round 4: DSA & Database Round (16 candidates appeared in this round)

This round started almost in the evening. The interviewer again asked me to introduce myself. He then asked
me to open a google doc page. He started dictating the DSA question which was as follows:
You are given a n * n matrix with values 0, 1 and 2.
0 -> Empty cell
1 -> Wall
2 -> Power cell
In 1 second, a power cell(2) can transform the empty cells around it to power cells. Calculate the time to
convert all empty cells to power cells, return -1 if not possible.
It was a classic, Striver style graph traversal question. I explained both the BFS and DFS approach. He
asked me to write a pseudocode in the doc, which I did.
As I was explaining my code, he was satisfied with my answer. He asked me, "Do you like DSA? Personally
I don't like it that much'. I still don't know whether it was a trick question or not but I said, "I like DSA
decent enough, I like System Design more than this!" He then started with the database design question.
It was a classic question of schema design for an ola/uber like app. This was more of an open ended
discussion after I suggested what the basic tables will look like.
Now the question part, I again asked the same question as the previous round. Along with that, I also asked a
question about CI/CD pipelines(I suggest preparing for more than one question).
It was a chill conversation which also lasted for about an hour.

5. Round 5: HR Round (6 candidates appeared in this round)

--- PAGE 3 ---
As I went downstairs after completing the DSA round, I almost immediately got a call from HR for this
round, which was scheduled 30 minutes later. It was full of classic HR questions, talking about family,
hackathons, projects, priorities, deadlines, etc. It lasted for about 20 minutes.

6. Round 6; Culture Fit Round (6 candidates appeared in this round)

Honestly, this was the most challenging round which I wasn't expecting at all! He started with a completely
random hypothesis, "What will you do if I give you 100 crores, right now?" I tried to answer from this
perspective of finance, since I have some finance background. He said he isn't expecting that, he wants to
know what value will I generate from than 100 crores for the community. Since I was watching some reels
about the data center water issues in the past few days, I immediately suggested researching data centers to
solve this issue. We had a 5-minute quick conversation and he said we're good.
The results didn't come until the next day, 5 students were selected for the role, I was one of them.

customSections.content:
1. DSA is still the king, CP(Codeforces, Codechef) is very helpful but not necessary.

2. Striver's A2Z series is highly recommended for complete DSA practice. Solving 3 questions a day

takes around 5 months to complete, so get started NOW!

3. Periodically revise your core CS subjects, as they will be asked in almost every OA.

4. Practice aptitude tests in Indiabix.com.

5. Practice giving interviews in front of a mirror or in your mind.

6. Do not underestimate DBMS. It is just as important as DSA. Understand the possible database

designs of popular apps like Ola/Uber, Netflix, Google, Amazon, YouTube, etc.

7. Regular practice SQL along with DSA.

8. Keep participating in hackathons, you may get your best projects from one of your hackathons.

9. An unpaid internship or any work experience gives a tremendous boost to your resume.

10. Be familiar with OOPs concepts.

11. Keep talking during interviews, ask questions, seek clarifications, be confident in your answer.

My Resume for reference:
Por [ShivenShuklaMLResume.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1V3ZgbQwO0u1JClJPatuYJjM0SI4MF94O/view?usp=sharing)
Feel free to contact,
Phone: 8591572172
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/shiven-shukla-1b2065290/
Placement season can be exhausting, discouraging, draining as well as luck-dependent. Managing stress
while working on yourself continuously is of utmost importance. Take it one step at a time.
Remember,
"God's plan is like a beautiful tapestry, and the tragedy of being human is that we only get to see it from
the back. With all its ragged threads and muddy colors. We only get to see a hint of the true beauty on

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Try to have at least 1 entry for each new sub-topic, and make sure your body language is

positive and confident.

• It's okay if you haven't got a chance to speak, the moderators will ask you about your

opinion, and give you a chance to speak.

• Everyone can and will have similar points and example, try to have a unique and different

angle to the same topic (ex. Some political viewpoint, or view from a manager/CEO
which mattered in our topic... for this try discussing the same with relatives, friends in
finance). This had given me an edge.

• Try using good examples, or numbers to back the points you make, please make it

relevant to the sub-topic in discussion.

5. Interview Round 1 [29 students were shortlisted for this round]

Before the interview rounds, one thing to keep in mind is that there is no fixed interview
structure. Some candidates had only one interview, while others went through two or even three
rounds. The process varies from person to person, so don't compare your process with others.
Stay patient, trust the process, and focus on giving your best in each round.
There were 6 interview panels, and my interview was scheduled last in my panel.
My first interview lasted around 45-50 minutes. During the interview, I faced network issues on
many occasions-once while the interviewer was asking a question and another time while I was
answering. I remained calm, politely informed the interviewer whenever the connection was
interrupted, and resumed the conversation once it was resolved. If you face a similar situation,
make sure to immediately inform both the interviewer and the TPO. Handling such situations
professionally leaves a much better impression than panicking.
Questions asked:

1. Tell me about yourself.

2. What do you expect your responsibilities to be if you're selected for the CIB

R&A Banking role?

3. Explain the three financial statements, how they are linked, and the impact of a

$10 decrease in depreciation across all three statements.

4. What is working capital? Explain its components and how changes in each

component affect cash flow.

5. Do you actively follow or invest in the financial markets? What sectors do you

track and why?

6. What are the Nifty 50 and Sensex? How are they calculated, what are their

current values, and what has been the recent trend in these indices?

7. What is the Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate? What are their current values?

8. Why does the RBI increase or decrease the repo rate?

--- PAGE 5 ---

9. How does the government/RBI use the repo rate to control inflation and support

economic growth?

10. How has the RBI used the repo rate in response to recent geopolitical and

economic events?

11. What is valuation? Explain the different valuation methods.

12. Explain what is meant by Enterprise Value and Equity Value. Formula. Why do

we add debt and subtract cash to find EV.

13. Among the three commonly used valuation methods, which one do you think

provides the most realistic valuation, and why?

14. What is FCFF, how is it calculated? Why Net Profit isn't used to calculate the

Enterprise Value.

15. How is the discount rate calculated? Have you heard of WACC. Can it be used to

calculate FCFE?

16. Mental Math Qns: (do without pen paper)

• Find the total number of squares on a chess board(8x8)

• 67*73 (wanted the final answer)

Any questions? At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I
asked about:

• The career progression and growth opportunities for a fresher joining the CIB Banking

role.

• How is Al being used in the day-to-day workflow at JPMorgan Chase, and do analysts in

this role get to use tools such as SQL and Power BI?

• What are the primary sources of data that analysts work with in this role?

(Prepare 3-4 questions beforehand, and frame it in an interesting way, shouldn't be a
forced question)

6. Interview Round 2

I was called for this round immediately after Round 1, so I would recommend staying near the
TPO throughout the recruitment process. Although I was informed that it would be an HR round,
it turned out to be another interview round instead. So, be prepared for any type of interview,
regardless of what the round is called. This round lasted around 15-20 minutes and was
conducted by a single panelist. At the beginning, the interviewer mentioned that the interview
would be fast-paced and that he might interrupt me while I was answering to save time, so I
shouldn't take it personally. He also made it clear that he would be tough, and the interview
reflected that.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Most of the questions were based on my responses, with each answer leading to several
follow-up questions. The interviewer asked a few trick questions, repeatedly asked "Are you sure
about that?" "Do you want to try again?", and even explored topics I had admitted I wasn't
familiar with. The aim was to assess both my understanding of investment banking concepts and
how I handled pressure. My advice would be to stay honest and maintain a learning
attitude don't pretend to know something you don't, as interviewers love to grill on it.
Questions asked:

1. Introduce yourself

2. What do you think investment bankers do apart from investment banking?

3. What is the difference between buy side and sell side?

4. What are PE firms and VC? What's the difference between them? Give 2

examples

5. Do you invest in stock markets? (to which I stated no, but I follow it regularly)

6. What sector do you think will grow in the near future? Why?

7. Tell me 2 stocks of that Sector(I had said Pharma) and their PE ratios?

8. What is PE ratio? Should it be high or low? (trick question... are you sure)

9. Gave a hypothetical situation of 2 companies one having PE 5 and other 10,

which would you choose to invest in? How to check if stock is undervalued /
overvalued

10. Can you explain what an IPO is? Why does a company opt to go public?

11. Could you walk me through the key steps involved in the IPO process?

12. Tell me about one recent IPO you have followed closely. What was your analysis

or takeaway from it? (I told him about the upcoming Jio IPO in depth)

13. During the IPO book-building process, if investors bid at $10, $15, and $20,

which price would the company ideally choose as the issue price, and why? Does
the stock usually list at the same price?

14. Have you heard of the Greenshoe option? (I had read about this, but didn't know

it in depth, so I told him whatever I knew and an example when it is used)
That was the end of the interview. I wasn't able to answer some of the questions, and whenever I
didn't know something (for example, whether a higher or lower P/E ratio is preferred), I was
honest about it and said I would read more about it instead of guessing. The interviewer
remained very serious throughout the interview and simply asked me to leave once it ended.
Since the interview lasted only about 15 minutes, I walked out feeling that I had fumbled a few
questions and wasn't very confident about my chances of getting through.

7. HR Round

--- PAGE 7 ---
This round took place almost 2 hours after Round 2. By then, I was completely exhausted and
had almost convinced myself that I should start focusing on other companies, as I felt Round 2
hadn't gone well. The TPO then called out the names of 8 shortlisted students and asked us to
come inside. We weren't told whether it was another interview round or the HR round, so there
was a bit of uncertainty until we entered.
There were two interview panels, and I was the second candidate in my panel. The interview
lasted around 10 minutes and felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.
The interviewer was very friendly and immediately recognized me from the Pre-Placement Talk.
He asked, "You're the one who was asking and answering questions during the PPT, right? You
seem quite excited about this opportunity. " That instantly boosted my confidence.
He started by asking how my day had been and how I felt about the recruitment process so far.
We then moved on to a few standard questions, including Tell me about yourself," "Why
Finance?", "Why JPMC?", along with questions about my family and where I live.
He was also curious about the volunteering work I had done as part of my second-year
community project. We discussed the impact of the initiative and what I had learned from the
experience. Towards the end, he asked about the Minors in Finance and Strategic
Management mentioned on my resume and how they had sparked my interest in the field of
finance. He also asked about my future plans. In the end again I was asked if I had any questions
so keep 1-2 hr related questions also ready.
Although many people consider the HR round to be the easiest, don't take it lightly. Try to frame
your answers around the following points:

• Show a genuine interest in finance and a willingness to learn and explore the field.

• You know about the Company and have well-researched about it and the roles being

offered. So, be attentive during the pre-placement talk and also read about JPMC's
mission, vision, goals, and values from their website.

• Highlight your extracurricular activities and leadership experiences to demonstrate that

you can work well in teams and handle responsibilities. Use examples from your
committee or other leadership roles wherever possible.

• If asked about higher studies say NO. Instead, mention that you would first like to gain

practical experience in finance, build a strong foundation, and pursue professional
certifications such as CFA.
10 students were offered the role.

Useful Tips:

--- PAGE 8 ---

• Start preparing for finance at least by the beginning of 6th semester. The earlier, the

better. At the same time, keep doing tech side-by-side.

• Build your basics well. Knowing fewer topics in depth is much better than knowing many

things superficially. Remember that the interviewers know you're from an engineering
background, so they don't expect you to know everything.

• Your introduction guides the entire interview. Make it unique and interesting so the

interviewer wants to know more about you.

• Don't take the PPT or resume shortlisting lightly. They are a very important part of the

process.

• Start building your finance base carly by taking up finance minors, certifications, or

case study competitions. Winning doesn't matter-the exposure and learning do.

• Have something apart from academics on your resume, whether it's committee work,

leadership roles, sports, or any hobby you genuinely enjoy. It always adds value.

• Maintain a decent CGPA. From what I observed, 8+ generally works well, and JPMC

also seemed to consider 10th and 12th scores during shortlisting.

• Be very thorough with your resume. Know every small detail mentioned in it, as many

interview questions come directly from there.

• Always keep a smile on your face, no matter how the interview is going. Stay positive,

trust your preparation, and give your best.
For me, what carried me through the entire process was confidence and a positive attitude. I had
decided from the very beginning that I would give it my best. I was actively involved during the
PPT by answering and asking questions, and I feel that confidence stayed with me throughout the
interviews. I also believe my committee experience and leadership roles played a big part.
Interacting with juniors, faculty, sponsors, and other stakeholders taught me how to communicate
with people and stay confident in conversations.
Finally, the placement process is mentally exhausting and full of ups and downs. In the end, it
comes down to hard work and a bit of luck. You can't control luck, but you can control your
preparation. Your efforts are never in vain-they always teach you something and
eventually pay off. Keep working hard, stay patient, and your opportunity will come.

1. Pre-Placement Talk [open to all]

The recruitment process begins with the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), where senior leaders from
CIB, Risk, and HR introduce the company, explain the roles being offered, and provide an
overview of the recruitment process and expectations.
Although many candidates treat it as a formality, it is a valuable opportunity to learn about the
company and make a positive first impression. Stay attentive throughout, participate whenever
appropriate, and ask thoughtful, role-related questions during the Q&A instead of generic ones
like CTC or the number of candidates being hired.
In my case, the HR representative who conducted the PPT was also one of my interviewers. He
remembered my participation during the session, and it helped establish a positive rapport at the
--- PAGE 2 ---
start of the interview. So, don't underestimate the PPT-it can give you an advantage even before
the actual interview rounds begin.

2. Resume Screening

Candidates need to submit their applications on both the JPMC Careers Portal and the Google
Form shared by the TPO. It is advisable to apply as early as possible. While applying on the
JPMC portal, you'll be asked to upload your resume and have the option to attach a cover letter.
Although optional, I would recommend including one.
As communicated by the TPO, While the stated eligibility was a 7+ CGPA, I would recommend
maintaining a CGPA of 8.0-8.5 or above to be on the safer side, as shortlisting can be
competitive. Based on previous years' trends, having a strong academic record (especially in 10th
and 12th - 80%+) and meaningful achievements outside academics can further strengthen your
profile. Publications, research work, leadership roles, and certifications such as CFA Level I
are also viewed positively, though don't guarantee a shortlist.
Resume Tips:

• Follow a latex template - Resume. Keep it single-column and try to minimise

white-spaces as much as you can (remove the lines having just 1-2 words...optimise
whitespace)

• Target a 80+ ATS Score. (Link - https://resumeworded.com/)

• Include your 10th and 12th marks in the Education section, especially if they are strong.

• Keep the sections in a logical order: Education → Work Experience → Positions of

Responsibility → Projects/Publications → Achievements/Extra-curriculars → Skills.

• Tailor your resume to the job description by incorporating relevant keywords and

highlighting impactful achievements.
67 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

3. Online Aptitude Test

The test window was 10:30-11:00 am and the duration was 45 mins. It had 4 sections, with no
negative marking and navigation was allowed.

• Basics of Finance and Accounting : 10 questions

3 financial statements, ratios, Depreciation, effect of changes in line items on all 3 statements,
dividend yield, and basic corporate finance

• Market awareness: 10 questions. Questions were not necessarily finance based but general

current affairs.

• Quantitative Aptitude: 15 questions.

--- PAGE 3 ---
Questions based on Profit and Loss, Workers and Time, AP GP HP, Probability, etc. (Normal
Aptitude questions).

• Verbal Skills: 10 questions.

Passage based, rearranging, standard questions.
The test was lengthy so try to attempt things you know and equal parts from all sections rather
than acing one section. Check for negative marking, generally the Risk role carries -1 marking
for wrong answer.
55 students were shortlisted. The result was announced only a day before the interview, so even
if test was bad, don't stop preparing there's always a chance.

Tips:

• Practice aptitude questions from IndiaBIX. Cover all major topics first, then switch to

timed mock tests, as speed and accuracy are equally important.

• For aptitude concepts, I found this playlist very helpful: CareerRide. It covers most of

the commonly tested topics.

• Build the habit of following business and financial news. I used Finshots Daily and

Zerodha AfterMarket Report podcasts. This helps not only in the current affairs section
but also during interviews.

• Keep your accounting fundamentals & corporate finance basics clear, especially the

three financial statements and financial ratios.

4. Group Discussion

[55 students were shortlisted for this round]
The results were announced on 1st July, one day prior at approx 8pm, which was just one
day prior to the process. The topic for the GD was also given late at night at approx 9pm.
GD Topic -
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful
share of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead
times are approximately 2x longer for around two months, and shipping costs have
increased, affecting financial metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
Due to heavy rains, we were informed that rest of the process will be held online [online
through campus, conducted on zoom.]
We were called at 8:15 am for the GD, and 55 students were divided into 6 groups of
9-10 candidates. In my panel there were a total of 3 panelists, one was the moderator, and
introduced new sub-topics and questions, the rest panelists were seen to make notes and
judge body language, and points you make.

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 1 (03 July 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 2 (03 July 2026)

• HR Interview (03 July 2026)

• Result Declaration (03 July 2026)

The entire interview process was conducted online due to heavy rainfall and the red alert in Mumbai.
However, all students were required to report to the college campus and appear for the online interviews
from there.

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The process began with a Pre-Placement Talk conducted on 24 June 2026. This round is often
underestimated, but I believe it plays a very important role. The speakers explained the company's culture,
lines of business, Corporate Risk division, internship structure and expectations from candidates.
My suggestion is to attend the session with complete attention. Do not join just for attendance. Take notes
throughout the session because many points discussed during the PPT become useful while preparing for
interviews after the shortlist is announced. Ask genuine and relevant questions if you have any. Avoid asking
repetitive questions merely to get noticed.
Candidates also had to register through the official JPMorgan Chase careers portal using the link shared by
the TPO. Resume shortlisting was done based on this application.
The shortlisted candidates for the Online Assessment were announced on 26 June 2026 at around 5:30 PM.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment (122 shortlisted candidates)

The Online Assessment was conducted on 27 June 2026 from home on a proctored platform.
The platform monitored eye movement, hand movements and general activity through the webcam.
Therefore, avoid attempting to deceive the proctoring software. You may use rough sheets for calculations,
but ensure that your face remains visible to the camera throughout the assessment.
The test consisted of 30 questions with a +2/-1 marking scheme.

• 27 Questions: Quantitative Aptitude

• 3 Questions: Probability and Permutation & Combination

The quantitative section mainly covered: Profit & Loss, Time, Speed & Distance, Work & Time, Ratios
Train Problems, Basic Quantitative Aptitude. The questions were of MBA aptitude level but were
manageable with proper practice. Time management was the biggest challenge.

3. Technical Interview Round 1(32 shortlisted candidates)

The interview shortlist was released on 2 July 2026 at around 8.30 pm.32 candidates were shortlisted for the
first interview. Due to the weather conditions, interviews were conducted online from the college campus.
There were multiple interview panels conducting interviews simultaneously.
This round mainly focused on my resume and getting to know me as a candidate.
Some of the questions asked were:

• Tell me about yourself.

• Walk me through your resume.

• Explain your projects.

• Why did you choose Electronics & Telecommunication instead of Computer Science?

• Questions based on my skills and certifications.

• Discussion around my interests and experiences.

The biggest takeaway from this round was that confidence matters only when it is backed by knowledge.
They can easily identify whether you genuinely know your work or are simply trying to impress them.
Around 15 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (15 shortlisted candidates)

The second round was comparatively more technical and involved deeper discussions. Unlike the first round,
where the interviewers tried to understand my profile, this round focused on verifying my knowledge. Most
questions revolved around my projects. Since I had personally worked on them, explaining the
implementation, challenges and learnings was comfortable.
The interviewers also asked follow-up questions based on my answers to assess whether I genuinely
understood the concepts. This round reinforced an important lesson: if you have genuinely built your
projects yourself, there is nothing to fear. Simply explain your work honestly and confidently. You can ask
them any sensible question if you wish to do so.
--- PAGE 3 ---

5. HR Interview (10 shortlisted candidates)

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round. This was the most comfortable interview of the
day. The discussion focused more on personality, professionalism and flexibility rather than technical
knowledge. Some questions included:

• Preferred work location.

• Willingness to relocate.

• Comfort with working hours.

• General discussion about my interests and career goals.

The HR was mainly trying to understand whether I would be a good fit for the organisation. My advice is to
be yourself. There is no need to create artificial answers. Honest and thoughtful responses create a much
better impression.
The HR interviews concluded at around 4:45 PM. We waited on campus until around 6:15 PM, after which
we were informed that the results would be announced online. The final results were declared at around
7:50-8:00 PM, and all 10 HR candidates received internship offers.
Resume Suggestions

• Keep your resume to one page.

• Mention only what you can confidently explain.

• Be thorough with every project, skill and certification.

• Focus on gaining knowledge rather than collecting certificates.

Online Assessment Tips

• Revise aptitude concepts and manage time well during the test.

• Avoid guessing due to the +2/-1 marking scheme.

Interview Tips

• Know your resume thoroughly. Be honest if you don't know an answer.

• Maintain eye contact, smile naturally and communicate confidently.

• Speak slowly, think before answering and be prepared for cross-questions.
