1) The months leading up to the placement (January to June End) is extremely crucial for learning new

skills and sharpening your problem solving skills. However, the moment companies start coming in
the start of July, it becomes very important for you to stop learning new things and just revise the
things you have learnt in these past weeks/months. This is crucial as this will prevent you from being
overwhelmed and make you more confident for the OAs and Interviews.

2) Although, it is appreciable to be ambitious. I would not recommend skipping applying to companies

due to less CTC/Salary. Having location preference is fine but if the role the company offers aligns
with your interests, DO NOT skip it. At least try to get an OA or Interview Experience out of it.
Lastly, instead of sharing resources that you already know of. I would like to share the analysis of my
shortcomings in the previous companies that could help you get placed earlier and with better packages.

1) JP - Didn't Apply

2) IDFC - Applied but couldn't get myself registered due to some technical error

3) PhonePe - Couldn't make it to the interview. Solved 1 problem completely and 1 partially.

The OA in total had 4 questions having 50,70,110 and 120 points respectively. My total score was
89(70+19).
Moral: Rome was not built in a Day. I tried to do my very best by learning concepts and practicing
questions that I had never seen just one day before the OA. This is not how one can reach the
interview where people reach by months of grinding. I would advise to read Interview experiences of
PhonePe or get in touch with the seniors who are placed to get genuine roadmaps.
WorkIndia and AuxoAl - Applied but resume didn't get shortlisted

5) UBS and Nomura - Applied but resume didn't get shortlisted + CGPA was a factor, it was observed

that only the people who had approx 8.8+ could reach the offline rounds for both (I might be
wrong).
Either way, these 4 companies made me realise my mistake and led me to change the resume
completely for my upcoming companies. Please do not repeat this mistake, keep your CGPA the
best you can and get your resume proof read by seniors/mentors and also have an ATS score above
70.

6) ISS - Could not clear OA. Made me realise that grinding DSA is not enough. Core subjects have to

be respected and revised on a daily basis. The OA was conducted on Google Form and it was all
MCQs with a +1 for correct answer and -0.25 for wrong answer.

7) Dolat Capital - Could not clear OA. This was one particularly disheartening as the OA questions

were pretty straightforward and this was my 3rd failure after PhonePe and ISS. It had 3 coding
questions and 6 MCQs.

8) Infosys - I absolutely have no words for this. It was the first time where I could not even pass a

single test case in any question. The questions asked over here are completely different and
traditional DSA practice might/might not help. It is not as difficult as compared to the ones asked in
CP contests but the questions were lengthy and required prior practice. If you are seriously targeting
this company then make sure to dedicate and modify your preparation a little bit.

9) Incred - Resume didn't get shortlisted. Wasn't really keen on the business analyst role anyways.

--- PAGE 6 ---

10) IDfy - The first company for which I could clear the OA and reach Interview. The OA had 1 SQL

query and 4 Coding Questions to be done in 90 minutes. After solving the SQL in 10 minutes, I
proceeded to apply a brute force solution to ¼ questions where I was able to pass 8, 10 and 7 test
cases respectively out of 15. For the 4th question, I couldn't think of even a brute force approach
and hence I hard coded the given test cases to get some points. Luckily enough, even for the hidden
test cases the output was visible even if the input wasn't. This helped me pass 5/15 test cases in that
question too. This OA made me realise that even if I don't have the best solution in that heat of the
moment with a little presence of mind and smartness I can clear OAs.
As far as the Interview experience is concerned, the first round was pretty straightforward asking questions
in and around my projects. Even the core subjects' questions revolved around CCN (TCP vs IP and DNS)
which I was very comfortable with. Lastly the DSA that was asked was binary search on sorted array and
then binary search on rotated sorted array. This round helped me build confidence for my future placement
processes.
The second and the final round of this process was again a Tech round and not a HR one. This one was
particularly humbling as this was where the interviewer picked a ML project from my resume where he was
sure that I had not created a Database and asked me to design my schema in front of him on the spot.
Although I had prepared my projects inside out, I was not ready for a question that challenged me to think
and discuss on the spot. I created and modified tables, relationships and constraints as per the interviewers'
needs and still after each modification he didn't look happy. After a point I was just panicked, frustrated and
all given up. This interview experience made me promise myself that even after I get placed, I would never
stop learning and always make designs on my own without being dependent on AI.
I strongly advise you all to study system design extensively along with DSA/CP and even if there is less
time available I would recommend you to develop your thinking so you can at least be able to make
schemas.

11) Wissen - Disappointing performance. Although I was able to solve the SQL query and MCQ

correctly. For the DSA questions I was only able to pass the given test cases in one question and
given+2 extra in another one. This one broke my confidence as the question didn't feel very tough
upon upsolving.
journey.howSecured:
The placement process began with a shortlist of 121 students. Although the criteria were undisclosed, it
seemed that a CGPA above 8.0 was required.
A CGPA above 8.0 would suffice the cutoff of most companies but I would still recommend you to push to
8.5+ if possible. My CGPA was 8.19 as of the end of 6th Semester.
The PrePlacement Talk was held on 6th August at roughly 12:30PM. Sitting for each PrePlacement Talk is
almost a compulsion and I would highly recommend you to take notes of the company's products, the
company's values and the people who are presenting the talk along with their roles in the company.

1. [Online Assessment] [ 121 Candidates ]

The Online Assessment was divided into 4 sections namely Logical Reasoning, Quantitative Aptitude,
Coding and Verbal Ability ( the section names might be a bit different).
Logical Reasoning: This section consisted of 15 questions to be done in 15 minutes from topics like
coding-decoding (example: AQPR -> BRQS then what is SQOK), directions (example: if you face the
south-east direction then rotate 90degree clockwise and then 180 degree anti clockwise. what direction
would you be facing) and a few blood relations questions.
Quantitative Aptitude: This section consisted of 12 questions to be done in 15 minutes and topics included,
Ratio and proportion, profit/loss and percentage increase/decrease. This section was quite simple and
intuitive.
Coding Section: This section consisted of 2 questions to be done in 45 minutes.
The questions were random for all candidates and even though the majority of them had both easy questions
it becomes crucial to not miss out on any topic as you could unfortunately be one of those candidates who
receive one easy and one medium/tough question.
--- PAGE 2 ---
My questions were

1) The input array was called the product IDs and we were required to return the quantity of products

sold which was defined as the sum of digits of product ID
Input array = [54 13 511 982 20]
Output array = [9 4 7 19 2]
I iterated through the input array, calculating the sum of the digits using a while(n>O) loop and the
pushing back the sum into the answer vector.

2) Sort the digits till kth position in descending order and the rest in ascending order

Input:
K=3
Array: 13 6 8 2 3 5 4
Output : 63123458
Here I made two temporary vectors, one till the kth number and another one from the k+ 1st number till the
end. Sorted the first temporary vector in descending order and the second vector in ascending order. At last I
pushed back values from both the vectors into the answer vector.
Upon thinking about the question after reaching home, I realised that those 3 extra vectors were kind of
unnecessary and I could have done something like
sort(arr.rend() - k, arr.rend();
sort(arr.begin() + k, arr.endO);
Both these questions were Leetcode style (the main function and parameters were already defined, and you
just had to return the answer vector from your defined function to the main function).
I was able to pass all test cases in both the questions.
Verbal Ability: This section consisted of questions such as 'what part of the sentence is grammatically
incorrect' and paragraph based questions to test your comprehension skills.
--- PAGE 3 ---
2.
[Tech Interview] [ 34 Candidates were selected for Interviews]
The Interviews were scheduled a day after the PPT and OA day(7th August). The shortlist arrived on the 6th
August at 7:45 PM leaving less time for preparation. I prioritized revising my projects section on the
resume as I knew it had been my weak point all along. Even after prioritizing the majority of time
towards projects, I took an hour to brush upon my core subjects and DSA. It is very important for you
to cover all things and be balanced even in your last minute preparation.
I was 21st on the 34 person shortlist they had arranged the list CGPA wise) and my turn to interview came
at 1:00PM. Luckily enough, as soon as I was about to enter, all the panelists called for a lunch break
and it was announced that the interviews would resume at 2:00PM. This gave me time to have some
food and get energized before my turn.
Upon returning from lunch break, I was the first person to get interviewed. I greeted the panelists with a firm
handshake and then they asked me to introduce myself. My introduction was pretty dull as I only
mentioned my name, branch and college (I strongly discourage you to do this and I would suggest you
to be ready with a strong and confident introduction).
The interview started with basic questions on Java OOPS where they asked me about the 4 Pillars.
Upon describing each pillar to them, they asked me to write the code for Polymorphism and Encapsulation
on paper. For the polymorphism part, I wrote code for both method overloading and method overriding.
As far as the encapsulation part is concerned, I created a private variable in my class and wrote public getter
and setter methods for the same.
Then the panelists asked me what is the use of Stack in Java. I panickingly replied that during recursion an
internal stack is used. Now that I think about it, the answer they expected might have been that Stack
Memory is used to store Primitives and Object References. As I had spilled out the word recursion, the
interviewer then asked me to explain it and write down an example using recursion. I chose the simplest
example, factorial and explained to them the thought process as I wrote the base case and the recursive
equation.
The interviewer then asked me if I remember the question I received in my OA and my solution to it. To
which I replied yes and explained the logic. He then asked me to write down the code on paper.
(Important thing to note is that even though you don't remember the question it's fine as they have it on
their laptops. I was lucky enough to receive easy questions and solve them completely but it is better to
be honest with the Interviewer in case you were able to pass only a handful of test cases by brute torce or
some hardcoding as he MIGHT have your solution on his laptop too).
The conversation then shifted to DBMS where I was asked to explain Cardinality (1-1, 1-N, M-N) using
examples of my choice. I can't exactly recall what example I had chosen but it was a simple one using
Students, Teachers, Courses etc. Then the topic shifted to Normalization where again I was allowed to
take example tables of my choice and apply normalization on it. Luckily the interviewer stopped me
after I was done applying 2NF as I was anyways not very comfortable with the higher normal forms.
Then I was asked a SQL query where I had to find the total number of employees. They told me to assume
the tables, columns and constraints as per my need and just provide them with the final query.
--- PAGE 4 ---
I wrote something like :
SELECT d.department name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS total
_employees
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON e. department_id = d.department id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department name;
After writing this query , I was asked about types of joins and the differences. At last the SQL section of the
interview ended with them asking me what Stored Procedures were and the advantages of using them.
At the very end of the Interview one of the interviewers asked me how good I was at solving puzzles to
which I replied that I am not the best but I do enjoy solving them with my friends on a regular basis.
To which he asked me a very simple question:
There are 3 temples and 2 ponds. At the very beginning I had x flowers. I visit each temple sequentially and
at each temple I place y flowers. After the first and second temple visit I also take a dip in the pond
where my remaining flowers get doubled. After repeating this process when I placeiy flowers' in the
third temple, I have nothing left. What is the value of x and y.
I explained systematically how my count of flowers are affected by each temple visit and pond dip.
i) After the first temple visit my remaining flowers: x-y
il) After first pond dip : 2(x-y) = 2x-2y
iii) After second temple visit : 2x-2y -y = 2x-3y
iv) After second pond dip : 2(2x-3y) = 4x-6y
v) After third temple : 4x-6y -y = 4x-7y
vi) 4x-7y=0. Therefore, x = 7 and y = 4.
Then the interviewer just asked me to substitute these values into the problem and dry run through it.
Lastly before leaving the Interview I asked the interviewer their names and their Roles at the company.

3. ¡HR Interviewl [ 11 Candidates appeared for this Round]

The interviewers greeted me by introducing themselves and then asked for my introduction. This time along
with my name and department, I shared about my hobbies and interests. Then they proceeded to ask me
one small question on my project (it was not technical at all, so no need to worry). After that one of the
interviewers said even though my project has Development and ML, it lacks Al. She asked me why this
is the case and whether or not I feel any fear of missing out' due to the lack of Al projects and skills.
Then she asked me whether or not I use Al in daily life tasks and if Yes then for what tasks. I was then
asked about how I would deal with a teammate/colleague who is never doing his part of the work in the
project. I was then asked what TransUnion does and what is CIBIL. The topic then shifted towards my
residence, my family and my thoughts on relocation. Lastly one of the interviewers observed that I had
mentioned my GATE AIR on the resume. She asked if I had any plans to pursue a masters. I clarified
that I had appeared for the examination just to assess my knowledge on a national level and I had no
plans to pursue a masters degree as of now. (I would still recommend not putting any such thing on your
resume).
I was then asked the interviewer's name from Round 1 which I could not recall. Lastly before leaving I
asked the HR about the Extra curricular and CSR activities at TransUnion.
10 Candidates were offered the Job.
--- PAGE 5 ---

Placement Process:

1. Pre - Placement Talk: 24th June '26

2. Resume Screening: 26th July '26

3. Online Aptitude Test: 27th July '26

Further Rounds took place offline on the 3rd of July '26-

4. Group Discussion

5. Interviews

A) Technical Interview Round (1-4)
B)HR Round

--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Pre-Placement Talk [X]

• Participate actively, but avoid repeating points others have already made.

• Ask meaningful, role-specific questions don't ask questions just for the sake of speaking (e.g.,

"How many people are you hiring?").

• Focus on understanding the role, responsibilities, career growth, team structure, training, and

relocation requirements (if applicable).

• HR may also ask questions based on the PPT, such as: "What are two things you liked about the

pre-placement talk?" (I was asked this question in HR round)

• Maintain professional etiquette throughout the session.

Key Takeaway: Use the PPT to learn about the role and company and location of job.

2. Resume Shortlisting [X → 67]

Your resume is one of the most important parts of the selection process. Start early and tailor it to the role
you are applying for.

• Keep it to one page and use a single-column LaTeX format.

• Optimize for ATS; check your resume on ResumeWorded (aim for a good ATS score).

• Include relevant projects, internships, coursework, achievements, and case competitions.

• For finance roles, add 1-2 strong finance projects and relevant finance certifications.

• You can make small role-specific changes to your resume before interviews.

• Use format Resume

"Walk me through your resume", " What was your job role and overall internship experience" (I was
asked these questions in Technical round)
Key Takeaway: You will be asked questions based on your resume so make it so that it steers the interview
towards your strengths and away from your weaknesses.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Online Aptitude Test [67→55]

• Format: 45 MCQs, 45 minutes (1 mark each). Speed and accuracy are crucial.

Sections:

• Corporate Finance & Accounting (10): Inflation, repo rate, financial statements, financial ratios,

bonds, GDP, and basic accounting concepts.

• Market Awareness (10): Current affairs in finance and business. Stay updated with financial news,

but expect some unpredictable questions.

• Quantitative Aptitude (15): AP/GP, Probability, Permutations & Combinations, Ratios, Profit &

Loss, Time & Work, Speed-Time-Distance, Mixtures, SI/CI (IndiaBix-level).

• English (10): Reading comprehension, grammar, sentence correction, vocabulary, and a few data

interpretation (bar/pie chart) questions.
Preparation Tips:

• Maximize your score in Quant, English, and Finance, as they are more predictable.

• Focus on finance and accounting fundamentals rather than advanced valuation topics.

• Practice Quant under strict time limits to improve speed and accuracy.

Key Takeaway: Completely Finish Indiabix.com, get basics of financial ratios, interest rates, bonds strong
and read key happenings ie. which manufacturing plants are inaugurated recently etc.

4. Group Discussion [ 55 → 29]

The topic for the group discussion was revealed on 2nd July around 8pm and the next day we had to report
around 8:30 am so make sure to do your research prior to the d-day.
G.D. Topic: "Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful
share of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are
approximately 2x longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial
metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situationại

• Format: Around 9 students per panel. This is not a traditional GD the moderator asks specific

questions, and the discussion evolves around those questions with follow-up prompts.

• Research the main topic and its possible subtopics, as follow-up questions are common.

• You will typically get to speak only 2-3 times, so make each opportunity count. Aim for 30-45

second responses with 2-3 relevant points each.

• Avoid memorized or rigid viewpoints. Be open to changing your stance as the discussion progresses.

• Don't interrupt or dominate the conversation. Agree when appropriate, disagree respectfully when

you have a valid reason, and build on others' points.

• Support your arguments with facts, examples, or insights from reputed sources (e.g., BCG,

McKinsey, World Bank, RBI) when relevant.

• Stay calm, humble, and articulate. Quality of contribution matters far more than speaking the most.

Key Takeaways: 2-3 Short 30s bursts of quality information in a calm and humble way should do the trick.
Think of unique points and not the plain simple stuff.
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Interviews [29 → 10]

A) Technical Interview [10 minutes]
Please refer to other experiences for non resume-oriented interview styles,
My technical interview was almost entirely resume-driven, with most of the discussion centered around my
internship in Portfolio Management. The interviewer was less interested in definitions and more interested
in whether I could think like someone actually working in the role.

• Be prepared to explain every line of your resume in detail. Expect follow-up questions on what you

did, why you did it, how you did it, and why you chose a particular approach.

• Use proper financial terminology and clearly communicate the objective, methodology, and outcome

of your work.
My Interview Experience
After asking me to explain my Portfolio Management internship, the interviewer said:
"Suppose you are my portfolio manager. What would you do?"
From there, the interview became a live portfolio construction exercise.

• I first assessed the client's risk profile, investment horizon, and objectives before recommending an

investment strategy.

• Based on the assumed risk appetite, I proposed an equity allocation across major Indian sectors

(Banking & Financial Services, IT, Pharma, FMCG, Capital Goods, Auto, Energy, Defence etc.).

• For every sector allocation, he asked:

• Why this sector?

• Why not allocate more or less?

• What macroeconomic or industry factors support your decision?

• Once he was satisfied with the sector allocation, he went one level deeper.

• He then asked me to recommend 3 specific stocks (My ans included one pre-ipo stock) and justify

every choice using company fundamentals, growth prospects, competitive positioning, valuations,
and overall investment thesis.

• Throughout the discussion, he continuously challenged my assumptions and asked me to defend my

reasoning rather than simply state an answer.
A fortunate aspect of my interview was that 2 of the stocks I recommended had gained around 4% during
the trading session (the interview was around 2:30 PM, with about an hour left before market close). While
this was because i'd looked at them one night prior, a large coincident, it strengthened the credibility of my
recommendations and led to further discussion on why I had selected those companies.
Preparation Tips

• Know every project and internship on your resume in depth.

• If you mention portfolio management or equity research, be ready to discuss:

• Asset allocation

• Sector allocation

• Stock selection

• Risk profiling

• Portfolio construction

Current market outlook

• Investment rationale using financial terminology

--- PAGE 5 ---

• Expect interviewers to keep asking "Why?" until they understand your complete thought process.

Key Takeaway: Technical interviews are often practical rather than theoretical. Your ability to justify
decisions with structured reasoning is far more important than simply knowing finance concepts.
A small observation from my experience: almost everyone around me had 2-4 technical interviews, each
lasting 20-30 minutes, whereas I had only one technical interview that lasted about 10 minutes, and I
was among the last candidates to be interviewed. At the time, it was easy to overthink this, but it turned out
fine. Don't judge your chances based on interview length or compare yourself with others. My only
objective throughout the interview was to have a genuine finance conversation, explain my thought
process honestly, and learn wherever possible and that mindset helped me stay calm and perform
naturally.
B) HR Interview [15 minutes]
The HR interview was conversational and relaxed. Stay calm, be genuine, and avoid saying anything
inaccurate or contradictory.

• Expect questions based on your resume, including activities beyond academics. For example, I was

asked about my marketing gigs and other extracurricular experiences.

• Most candidates who reach this stage are typically being evaluated for fit rather than technical

ability, so enjoy the conversation and let your personality come through.
10 students were shortlisted for the Banking role.
Not getting selected immediately doesn't mean it's over-another 10 students were shortlisted for the CR
role the next day from the separate candidate list for CR role.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Resources (I personally have used all of the below resources):
Resume

• ResumeWorded (ATS check)

• Resume(LaTeX resumes)

Online Assessment

• IndiaBix (Quant)

• Investopedia (Current Affairs)

Corporate Finance Institute (CHI) (Accounting & Corporate Finance)

• Indian Economy for UPSC | Introduction- Basics of Economics | Lec 01 | StudyIQ INdian

Economy)
Group Discussion

• Financial news: Mint, The Economic Times, Business Standard, Bloomberg

• AI LLMS

• Mock interviews with friends to understand what points people put forth

Technical & HR Interviews

• Forage Virtual Experience Programs

• Company Annual Reports & Investor Presentations

• Revise your resume line-by-line and stay updated with current affairs.

Current Affairs

• https://affairscloud.com/

• CNBC news especially at 3:30

Financial Accounting Fundamentals:

• If you're taking FSM (Financial Services Management), pay attention in class. The subject

provides an excellent foundation for finance interviews, and a significant proportion of the
selected candidates in our batch had taken FSM.
Resources given by my seniors (not completely used by me but very useful): Non TechPrepList
--- PAGE 7 ---
Final Tips

• A CGPA above 8 is always helpful, but don't get discouraged if yours is lower.

• Take the GD seriously-it's often one of the biggest differentiators.

• Start building your profile early through internships, projects, certifications, and case

competitions.

• If you don't have an internship, compensate with a strong finance project that demonstrates practical

skills.

• Be confident with finance fundamentals; interviewers value clear basics over advanced knowledge.

• Read financial news consistently, not just a few days before the interview.

• Be polite, professional, and dress formally (light shirt, dark trousers; a suit/tie is perfectly

appropriate).

• Network with other aspirants(always grateful for my friend Nitya's inputs) -- you'll learn a lot by

preparing together.

• Stay humble throughout the process and don't judge your chances until the results are out.

Have fun with finance!!!
As someone who came from a tech-first background, I went into the interview simply hoping to have a
great finance conversation and learn from the interviewer. That genuine curiosity helped me stay
relaxed, think clearly, and, I believe, made a stronger impression than trying to sound perfect.
This is your journey, and your experience will be different from everyone else's. Keep learning, keep
improving, and give your best every single day.
Focus on the effort, not the outcome. Control what you can, trust the process, and let the results take
care of themselves.
I'm always excited to have a good conversation about finance, markets, investing, or careers- whether it's to
exchange ideas, learn something new, or help however I can.
Feel free to reach out to me anytime in uni or on Whatsapp if you have any questions or just want to talk
finance.
Wishing you all the very best!

performance on the MCQs was enough to advance.

Java, C++, and OOPs concepts, I went through GeeksforGeeks articles and used ChatGPT to clear

Overall, 40 candidates were shortlisted for Technical Interview 1 out of 120.

∼40 mins)
The round started directly with my technical introduction, where I highlighted my full-stack de-
velopment experience, my competitive programming background (mentioning a CP contest victory

journey.prep:
• Practice and study aptitude, general knowledge, and HR questions, and work on your speaking and

communication skills. These are important for both tech and non-tech roles, but they matter even
more for non-tech roles, so don't neglect them.

• Don't lose confidence because of early rejections. I wasn't shortlisted for JPMC, InCred, and a few

other non-tech roles before this, which was upsetting since I felt I was genuinely skilled for non-tech
profiles, and at one point I felt like giving up. This opportunity came about a month into the
placement cycle - it was the first company that shortlisted me, and I got selected directly. So trust
your skills, stay patient, and don't give up after a few setbacks.

• Keep your CGPA in mind -- aim for a minimum of 7, and preferably 7.5 or above, so you don't miss

out on eligibility for any companies. Mine was 7.26 after the 6th semester.

• In GDs, take the initiative to speak early, organize your points logically, and stay updated on general

knowledge and current affairs.

• Always communicate politely and respectfully, regardless of the round -- panels notice how you

interact, not just what you say.

• Expect interviewers to apply pressure or push back on correct answers to test your composure

stay calm, stick to your reasoning, and don't second-guess yourself unnecessarily.

• If interviewers try to discourage you from the role or the company, treat it as a test of your

conviction, and use it as a chance to reaffirm why you're a strong fit.
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Above all, confidence is the common thread across every round - carry it through the GD, the

aptitude and technical rounds, and the HR round alike.
Feel free to reach out to me on LinkedIn for any doubts. All the best!
In case of any further doubts, you can also refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.

The process began with an online test that all 233 candidates appeared for, out of which 44 were shortlisted
for the Business Analyst role. The test was 90 minutes long and included aptitude questions, technical
MCQS, and 3 coding questions. During the pre-placement talk, the company had specifically advised
candidates to focus on aptitude for the Business Analyst profile. Keeping that in mind, I concentrated on the
aptitude and technical MCQ sections and completed them in about 30 minutes, and chose not to attempt the
coding questions at all.

Tips: Pay close attention to the pre-placement talk, as companies often hint at what they prioritize in the test.

For a Business Analyst role, that was clearly aptitude. Being efficient with your time matters more than
attempting every section; I finished the aptitude and MCQ portions quickly and didn't waste time on the
coding questions, since they weren't a priority for this profile. Focus your prep and your test-time effort on
what's actually relevant to the role you're targeting.

1. Group Discussion (GD) [233 candidates appeared]

The process began with a Group Discussion round for the Business Analyst role. Out of the 233 students
who appeared, 44 were shortlisted after the GD, and of those, 19 candidates were selected to move on to the
next round.

Tips: Try to initiate the discussion, as it creates a strong first impression. Structure your points clearly and

cover the key aspects of the topic rather than speaking at length without substance. Keep basic general
knowledge updated, since GD topics can draw on current affairs. Most importantly, stay polite and
respectful while communicating - interrupting others or being aggressive can count against you even if
your points are good.

2. Interview Round 1[19 candidates appeared, roughly 10-12 selected]

Of the 19 candidates who cleared the GD, around 10-12 advanced from this round. Since my interview slot
was scheduled quite late in the day, I was interviewed virtually instead of in person. The round focused on
general aptitude and guesstimate questions, and the panel also went through my resume in detail, asking
questions about the projects and experiences listed on it.
--- PAGE 2 ---

Tips: Brush up on quantitative aptitude and practice a structured approach to guesstimates (state assumptions

clearly, break the problem down, and sanity-check your final number). Be ready to explain every line on
your resume, since interviewers often probe deeper into whatever you mention.

3. Interview Round 2[10-12 candidates appeared, 7 selected]

Out of the 10-12 candidates who appeared, 7 advanced from this round. This interview involved an in-depth
discussion of my resume, including detailed questions on all my projects and internships, along with some
math-based questions. The biggest challenge in this round was handling the pressure the interviewer
deliberately applied - even when I gave the correct answer, the interviewer kept asking me to recheck it,
seemingly to test how I would react.

Tips: Stay confident and stick to your answer once you're sure it's correct, even if the interviewer pushes

back repeatedly - this is often a deliberate pressure test rather than a sign that you're wrong. Interviewers
may also try to talk you out of joining the company or downplay the role; treat this as another test and use it
as an opportunity to convince them why you're a strong fit, rather than getting discouraged.

4. HR Round [7 candidates appeared, 6 selected]

Of the 7 candidates who reached this stage, 6 were finally selected. The HR round varied from candidate to
candidate; in my case, the discussion was centered around my family background.

Tips: Be genuine and comfortable discussing personal background questions. As with the earlier rounds,

staying confident and consistently conveying that you are a good fit for the company goes a long way in this
round as well.
6 out of 233 students were finally offered the job.

journey.prep:
1. Practice DSA thoroughly: Follow Striver's DSA Sheet and practice regularly on LeetCode to

build strong problem-solving skills and familiarity with common DSA patterns.

2. Practice SQL: Use LeetCode SQL 50 to practice important SQL concepts and commonly asked

query patterns.

3. Build diverse projects: Have good-quality projects in both Web/App Development and AI/ML.

This makes your profile more versatile and prepares you for both SDE and AI/ML-oriented roles.

4. Practice Aptitude and Verbal Ability: Use resources such as IndiaBix and GeeksforGeeks

(GFG) to practice quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, and verbal ability questions commonly

asked in OAs.

5. Practice Puzzles and Guesstimates: Solve puzzles on GFG and practice guesstimation questions

through YouTube to improve your analytical and structured problem-solving skills.

6. Learn AI/ML systematically: Make use of popular AI/ML courses on Udemy and Coursera to

build strong conceptual foundations and understand practical applications.

7. Take Mock Interviews: Practice mock interviews using ChatGPT and Gemini. Ask them to

simulate technical, HR, behavioural, and role-specific interviews, and use their feedback to identify
and improve your weak areas.

8. Participate in Hackathons, Case Studies, and Research: Take part in hackathons, case study

competitions, and research projects or publish research papers to gain practical exposure to
real-world problems. These experiences help you develop problem-solving, teamwork, and
presentation skills while also strengthening your resume
My Failures
Looking back, these rejections were not just setbacks but a collection of experiences that gradually helped
me understand what different companies look for. Some rejections were because of clear skill gaps, while
others were simply situations where I felt that luck or circumstances played a role. I have tried to document
each experience honestly so that someone going through a similar placement process can learn from them.
--- PAGE 5 ---

1. JPMC - CIB

JPMC CIB was the first company to visit our campus. I cleared the OA, after which the GD was
conducted online. However, it was not a traditional GD; it was more of a group question-and-answer
discussion. Despite raising my hand multiple times, I did not get many opportunities to speak, and the
discussion also went somewhat off-topic from what I had expected. I also felt that I did not have sufficient
knowledge about some of the topics being discussed. Lesson learnt: Be proactive and speak whenever you
get an opportunity, and for JPMC CIB in particular, have a strong understanding of current affairs,
economics, finance, and business news.

2. WorkIndia

The WorkIndia OA consisted of 50 MCQS covering CS fundamentals such as Data Structures,
Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and DBMS, with the primary focus being on accuracy and
speed. I cleared it and moved to a debugging interview, where I was able to solve 1 out of 2 questions,
although I needed multiple hints. However, the interviewer was impressed by my SLM project and asked
me several questions about LLM development and system design, which I believe helped me reach the next
round. The following round consisted of DSA and schema design; I answered the schema design question
well, but the DSA problem was a difficult Graph DFS + DP question that I could not solve. Lesson learnt:
I needed to put significantly more effort into DSA, particularly advanced problem-solving patterns.

3. IDFC FIRST Bank

I cleared the IDFC FIRST OA, which consisted of CS fundamentals, aptitude, and two easy-to-medium
DSA questions. In the first technical interview, I was able to solve both DSA questions given to me.
However, I struggled with a situational question based on Object-Oriented Design, which ultimately
became the weak point in my interview. This experience made me realise that being comfortable with DSA
alone is not enough for technical interviews, especially when companies also evaluate design thinking and
problem-solving. Lesson learnt: I needed to strengthen my understanding of System Design and
Object-Oriented Design, particularly how to approach open-ended design situations.

4. UBS

The UBS process began with resume shortlisting, where 51 students were selected. I could not identify any
specific pattern based on CGPA or particular skills, so I considered myself fortunate to have been
shortlisted. The first round combined a technical case study and a pen-and-paper technical test. We were
given a problem statement, asked to develop a solution, prepare a PPT, and present it within approximately
1.5 hours. From each group, around 2-3 students progressed to the technical interview, and it appeared that
candidates who took the lead and spoke more were more likely to be selected; the pen-and-paper test did not
seem to play a major role. Lesson learnt: In group-based selection processes, take initiative and make sure
you communicate the parts of your solution that are most important from the evaluator's perspective.

5. Nomura -- GM Role

For Nomura's GM role, the initial shortlisting was based on CGPA and resume, with only 27 students
selected for the GD; most selected candidates had a CGPA above 9. I managed to clear the GD, after which
only 7 candidates were shortlisted for interviews. During the interviews, we realised that the primary focus
was on Pandas queries. Since SQL was my stronger database/querying skill, I spent the 1-2 hours before
--- PAGE 6 ---
the interview learning as much Pandas as I could. I was able to answer most of the questions but missed a
few, and ultimately only one candidate was selected. Lesson learnt: Go through the JD carefully and
identify the specific skills the company is likely to test, even if they are not currently your strongest skills.

6. ISS STOXX

ISS STOXX was one of the first processes where there was no major resume-based shortlisting, and
students from branches such as EXTC and MCA were also eligible. Around 300 candidates appeared for
the OA, which consisted of MCQs on Java, Python, Aptitude, and SQL, along with negative marking. I
cleared the OA, and around 40-45 candidates were shortlisted for interviews. The panel interviewing me
consisted of around 15-16 candidates, and I was asked approximately 8-10 Java code-output questions. I
was able to answer around 6-7 correctly, but I was still rejected at this stage. Lesson learnt: Even when
your overall preparation is good, interviews can sometimes be heavily dependent on a particular technical
area, so I needed to strengthen my depth in Java.

7. InCred

The InCred process began with resume shortlisting, followed by an OA consisting of Python coding
questions, SQL queries, and aptitude MCQS with negative marking, with a sectional cutoff for cach
section. I cleared the OA and reached the interview, where the interviewer went through my resume, asked
questions about my projects, and also gave me a guesstimate. I was not able to answer the guesstimate as
accurately as I would have liked. More importantly, after looking at my resume, the interviewer felt that my
profile was better suited to an AIML or SDE role rather than the Business Analyst role that InCred was
offering. Lesson learnt: Either tailor your resume to the role you are applying for or, if the role is
significantly different from your interests and profile, reconsider whether it is the right opportunity to
pursue.

8. BlackRock

After a relatively long gap, my next interview process was with BlackRock. The OA consisted of two
coding questions - one DSA and one debugging question - along with MCQs, and the assessment also
included an Al assistant. I believe the shortlisting may have been based on an aggregate of CGPA and test
performance, and I was selected for the SDE interview. During the interview, I was asked to explain one of
my projects, which was heavily focused on Al/ML. I explained it to the best of my ability, but I felt that one
of the interviewers, whose background was more in frontend and backend development, found some
aspects of the project difficult to relate to. I was also asked a DSA question, which I solved, although my
approach was not the most optimal. Lesson learnt: I needed to diversify my resume and have at least one
strong app-development or web-development project, since many companies visit campus primarily for
SDE roles.

9. Mastercard

I cleared the Mastercard OA, which I found to be quite difficult. I was able to solve only around 4/12 test
cases for each of the two DSA questions, yet I was still shortlisted, with 9 candidates eventually selected
for interviews held at Cummins College, Pune. The first round was a GD in which nobody was eliminated,
followed by a technical interview that lasted almost an hour and covered everything from DSA and my
cybersecurity research paper to basic AI/ML and in-depth Java concepts. I cleared this round, but in the
second technical interview I faced situational questions and detailed questions on caching, a topic I was
--- PAGE 7 ---
not sufficiently familiar with. Lesson learnt: I needed a much deeper understanding of System Design
concepts, rather than preparing only the commonly asked fundamentals.

10. JPMC - CADP Internship

The CADP Internship process at JPMC was probably the most disappointing rejection for me. Around 72
students were shortlisted for the GD based on their resumes, and after the GD, 19 candidates were
selected for interviews, including me. The interview focused primarily on situational and behavioural
questions; I was also asked to explain one of my projects, but there were no significant cross-questions on
it. I was subsequently selected for the HR round, which was again largely behavioural, and no major
technical skills were assessed throughout the process. Out of the 8 candidates who reached the HR round,
7 received offers and I was the only one who was rejected. Lesson learnt: Honestly, there was no
specific technical lesson here - it was simply a very difficult rejection to process, and at times, bad luck
and circumstances are also part of the placement process.

11. Other Attempts

Apart from these 10 major interview processes, I also appeared for companies such as Auxo AL, Wissen,
TransUnion, HSBC, and others, where I could not progress beyond the OA. Some of these assessments
had difficult DSA questions, while others tested skills or formats that I had not anticipated. For example, the
HSBC assessment included a behavioural test, which was something I had not expected; out of
approximately 58 candidates, only 9 progressed to the next round. These experiences reinforced the
importance of being prepared for a wide variety of assessment formats rather than focusing exclusively on
technical coding questions. Lesson learnt: You cannot predict every company's OA, so building a broad
preparation base and being adaptable is extremely important.
In case of any further doubts, feel free to reach out to me on Linkedin

1) Resume shortlisting - 30/9/26

2) Functional interview - 1/10/26

3) HR interview - 1/10/26

1.
[Resume Shortlisting] [ 150-200 students appeared for this round]
The first round was resume shortlisting. All B.Tech students with no active backlogs were eligible to
apply. There was no Online Assessment (OA) for this process.
The shortlisting was primarily based on the relevance of the candidate's internship experience and projects
in the AI/ML domain, as the role was more aligned with an AI/ML Engineer profile rather than a
traditional SDE role. Having two AIML projects along with relevant internship experience helped me
stand out and clear this round.
However, resume shortlisting can sometimes be quite unpredictable and may depend on several factors
beyond the candidate's control. In my experience, there is also an element of luck involved, especially when
a large number of students apply for a limited number of positions. Therefore, while having relevant projects
and experience certainly helps, getting shortlisted is not always a direct reflection of the strength of one's
resume.
Ultimately, 15 students were shortlisted for the Functional Interview round.

2. [Functional Interview] [15 candidates appeared for this round]

The functional interview began with a brief self-introduction, after which the interviewer candidly asked
me whether I was related to Kailash Kher. The interview was then entirely focused on Generative Al,
Large Language Models (LLMs), and my AI/ML projects.
The interviewer first asked me about the dot product, including what it is and why it is important in the
context of machine learning and LLMs. He then asked me to explain the Transformer architecture in brief
and discuss the key differences between BERT and GPT. This was followed by questions on orthogonal
vectors and cosine similarity.
One of the more interesting questions was about how an LLM handles repeated prompts. He gave the
example of asking an LLM to "List different designations." The model initially provides a set of
designations, but when prompted again with "Give more," it generates additional designations instead of
simply repeating the previous ones. He asked me how this works internally.
I was not completely certain about the exact mechanism, so I explained my understanding in terms of
next-token prediction and semantic similarity using concepts such as cosine similarity. The interviewer
was satisfied with my reasoning but then explained the exact mechanism to me. He then asked me about
--- PAGE 3 ---
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and their architecture. I was able to explain the different
components of a CNN and relate them to the practical work I had done during my internship, where I had
worked with CNNs as part of my project.
The interviewer then asked me to explain one of my projects, an Al-powered Legal Intelligence Tool.
While discussing the project, he asked several questions related to the technical choices I had made,
including:

• Why did you use Sentence-BERT (SBERT)?

• Why was SHAP Explainable AI required in the project?

• What are adapters in LoRA?

I explained the architecture and the reasoning behind each of these choices based on how they were
implemented in my project.
Towards the end of the interview, I asked the interviewer about the exact nature of the role at Axis, since
the job description covered a wide range of technologies, including AI/ML, cloud, frontend, and backend
development. He clarified that the role would primarily involve AIML application development, which
gave me a much clearer understanding of the position.
Overall, the interview was strongly focused on Generative AI and LLM fundamentals. My Program
Elective of Vizuara is the main cause I was aware of these concepts. 4 candidates were selected for the HR
Round.

3. [HR Interview] [4 candidates were selected for this round]

The HR interview began with questions that were more focused on getting to know me beyond my resume
and technical background. She first asked me to talk about myself, including my hobbies and interests,
and deliberately stayed away from technical questions.
She then asked me about where I stay in Mumbai and whether I would be comfortable travelling to
Lower Parel for work. My suggestion for such questions is to always answer positively and show that you
are comfortable with the practical requirements of the role, unless you genuinely have a constraint that
would prevent you from doing so.
The most important part of the HR interview was a discussion about my family background, which lasted
for almost five minutes. I mentioned that both my parents are engineers and currently work at MNCs. She
then followed up by asking a very direct question:
"If your parents are already working at MNCs, why Axis and not those companies?"
I explained that I have always wanted to build my career in the FinTech domain, and that the role at Axis
particularly interested me because it was focused on AIML application development, which strongly
aligns with my interests and the kind of work I want to pursue.
I also explained the difference between the nature of work at a typical service-based organisation and the
role I was interviewing for. I mentioned that if I joined an organisation similar to where my parents work, I
could potentially be assigned to projects across a wide range of technologies depending on the project
--- PAGE 4 ---
requirements - from frontend development and backend development to cloud and AI/ML. In contrast,
the Axis role offered me an opportunity to work specifically in an AIML-focused role within the Fin Tech
domain, which was much closer to my career interests.
This seemed to convince her that my interest in Axis was genuine and driven by the nature of the role
rather than simply the company name or the compensation. The interview ended shortly afterwards.
My biggest takeaway from the HR round: Be very clear about why you want this particular company
and this particular role. HR questions may appear simple, but follow-up questions can quickly test
whether your motivation is genuine and consistent with what you have mentioned throughout the interview.
The results were announced the next day. Out of the 4 candidates who appeared for the HR round, I was
the only candidate who received an offer.

journey.prep:
Have faith in God and trust the process. Even if things don't go as planned-like not getting a
summer internship-I know how discouraging it can feel. I was selected for the JPMC Code
--- PAGE 9 ---
for Good Hackathon but didn't receive the internship afterward, and it was definitely
disappointing.
Instead of dwelling on the past, keep moving forward. Stay consistent in your efforts, maintain
a positive mindset, and believe in your abilities. Every experience, whether it feels like a
success or a setback, teaches you something valuable and brings you one step closer to your
goal. Keep learning, keep improving, and trust that the right opportunity will come.

1. Be consistent with DSA practice.

I didn't do competitive programming at all, but I was very consistent with solving DSA problems on
platforms like LeetCode, GeeksforGeeks, and Coding Ninjas. Try to solve DSA problems every day because
it's a skill that takes time to develop. Don't get discouraged if you're unable to solve a problem immediately.
Spend enough time thinking about it first, and only look at the solution if you're genuinely stuck. After
understanding the solution, solve more problems on the same concept to strengthen your understanding. I
would also recommend exploring competitive programming, as it significantly improves your ability to
solve complex problems under time constraints.

2. Don't avoid hard problems.

Practice LeetCode Hard problems even if they seem intimidating at first. With consistent effort, you'll
gradually become comfortable solving them. During your practice, get into the habit of thinking out
loud consider multiple approaches, explain why one is better than another, and work towards the most

journey.howSecured:
So the whole process was conducted in 2 days span with OA being on 5th July while on 6th July all the
interviews were conducted.
Online Assessment | Around 310 candidates appeared for this round] - 5th July
So basically there are 4 DSA questions asked in this round with a time limit of 1 hr 30 mins. All questions
had different marks weightage and the testcases also had different marks allocated to them based on how
tricky that testcase was.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points) We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers
(capability),plus an integer K denoting the maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A
worker can only do a task if their capability is greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to
find the minimum value of k(1 <= k <= K) such that all tasks are assigned and no worker does more than k
tasks.
The question was similar to this but framed a bit differently. Each project had a skill level, and each
employee also had a skill level. An employee with a skill greater than or equal to a project's skill level could
perform that project and could take at most k projects. We had to return two integers: the maximum number
of projects allocated to any employee and the total number of projects assigned at the end.
I started by implementing the brute force approach. I sorted both arrays and assigned projects to employees
until an employee had reached either their skill limit or the maximum number of projects they could be
assigned. With this approach, I was able to pass around 9 out of 13 test cases, scoring around 30/50. Seeing
this, I moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Problem 2: (110 marks) The question was as follows: we were given a 1-rooted tree, and at every second,
we could do one of the following two operations:

1. Manually turn on a node.

2. If a parent node had one of its child nodes turned on, then it could automatically turn on its other

child node.
We had to return the minimum time required to turn on all the nodes. The nodes were numbered from 1 to N,
and a parent array was given that represented the connection between each node and its parent.
I approached this question by using a map to store the count of children for each node. Later, I realized that
the problem essentially became one of handling groups of children, where if one child in a group was turned
on manually, the remaining children in that group could be turned on automatically in the following seconds.
So, I used a variable totDistinct to represent the number of nodes that had to be turned on manually. I
also maintained an array containing the sizes of the children groups in descending order, along with a free
variable. Whenever a node was turned on manually, I increased the free variable by the size of the next
element in the children group array, representing the additional children that could now be turned on
automatically.
Then, I ran a loop with ind from 0 to n. If there were free available children, I increased ind by 2;
otherwise, I manually turned on a node, so ind increased by only 1. The answer was the number of times
this loop was executed.
So by this approach i was able to pass around 12/22 testcases and got a score of 60/110 in this question and i
moved onto next question.
Problem 3: Network Routers and Regions (70 Points) You are given a tree of N nodes and N-1 edges.
The network has exactly one central server, several routers, and multiple regions. The server connects only
to routers, routers connect to the server and one or more regions, and regions connect to exactly one router.
We had to determine the number of routers and regions.
I approached this question by calculating the indegrees of all the nodes. A leaf node would always have an
indegree of 1, while a router node would have an indegree greater than 1. (The edge case I may have missed
was that the root node's indegree could also be equal to indegree of router.).
I maintained a map of each node to its indegree. The number of routers would be the largest distinct count of
nodes having the same indegree greater than 1, which became my first answer. The second answer would be
the number of leaf nodes divided by the number of routers.
With this approach, I was able to pass around 8 out of 13 test cases, scoring 40/70.
Problem 4: (120 points) I didn't attempt this question because I was almost out of time, and it was quite
difficult. From my understanding, the question was as follows:
We were given a set of 2D coordinates representing items. A person was standing at a fixed coordinate
where a treasure chest was located. In a single trip, the person could pick up at most two items from the
--- PAGE 3 ---
given coordinates, return to the treasure chest, and place the items back. The time taken to travel between
coordinates was the Euclidean distance.
We had to return the minimum possible time required to collect all the items and also print the path taken.
This was my understanding of the question.

Tips: The OA is largely about how well you can perform under limited time and immense pressure. You

should be prepared to solve questions as quickly as possible. Even if you are only able to solve a question
partially, it is still worth attempting. I solved three questions partially, and later found out that many other
students weren't even able to solve that much.
My suggestion would be to first go through all the questions and then attempt the ones you find easier than
the others. Try to implement any approach that comes to mind, even if it is a simple brute-force solution, as
it may still pass a few test cases and earn you partial marks.
Most importantly, stay calm and confident-don't panic under pressure, as that can affect both your
thinking and your speed.

2. Technical Round 1 [26 people appeared][1 hr]

The format of the technical round was usually as follows: you were given two DSA questions, one at a time,
with a difficulty level comparable to LeetCode Hard problems. You first had to explain your approach to the
interviewer. If your approach was close to the optimal solution, the interviewer would then ask you to write
the code on paper and explain it in detail, along with its time and space complexity.
The interview calls were most likely scheduled based on the OA rankings. I was the first student in the
second batch, and each batch consisted of around 10 students.
Problem 1-https://leetcode.com/problems/making-a-large-island/
As soon as the interviewer started explaining the question, I knew that the optimal solution was to use a
Disjoint Set (DSU). So, without wasting any time, I directly explained the optimal approach. He told me that
it was correct and asked me to write the code on paper. While writing the code, I made sure to speak out
loud and explain whatever I was writing.
The optimal solution was to first traverse the entire grid. For every land cell, if there was another land cell in
any of the four directions (up, down, left, or right), I performed a union by size operation between them.
After completing this traversal, I traversed the grid again. Whenever I encountered a water cell, I checked all
four directions for adjacent land cells. If those land cells belonged to different islands, I added their sizes to a
temporary variable tmp. I then updated the answer as max (ans, tmp + 1).
Later, the interviewer asked me to write the code for the Disjoint Set class as well, which I did. He then
asked me to think of any edge cases that I might have missed. One edge case was when all the cells were
water, which I had already handled by initializing ans to 1. Another edge case was when there was no water
--- PAGE 4 ---
cell in the grid. I had missed this test case initially, but after he pointed it out, I explained how I would
handle it.
He seemed satisfied with my approach, and then we moved on to the next question.
Problem 2 - https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-diameter-after-merging-two-trees/description/
I initially approached this question by explaining the brute-force solution. I said that I would use
Floyd-Warshall's algorithm to compute a matrix containing the shortest distances between every pair of
vertices. Then, I would choose the vertex with the minimum maximum distance from all other vertices in
each tree, connect those two vertices, and finally compute the diameter of the resulting tree.
The interviewer then asked me to optimize the solution. I struggled for a while to come up with a better
approach, but I kept explaining my thought process out loud. After giving me a few hints, I was able to
derive the optimal solution. I explained that I would first find the diameters of the first and second trees. The
resulting diameter would then be:
max (d1, d2, r1 + r2 + 1)
where r1 and r2 are the radii of the two trees, computed as the ceiling of d1 / 2 and d2/2, respectively. I
then wrote the pseudocode for this approach and explained it to the interviewer.
Later, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. Make sure to ask a few thoughtful questions, as this
shows your curiosity and genuine interest in joining the company. Try to ask questions related to the
interviewer's domain of work.

Tips:

Think out loud throughout the interview. Clearly explain what you are currently thinking, even if you are
unsure of the answer. The interviewer wants to understand your problem-solving process and see that you
are making a genuine effort to reach the solution. If they see that you are approaching the problem in the
right direction, they may even give you hints to help you arrive at the optimal solution.

3. Technical Round 2 [13 people appeared]

Six people were directly selected for the Hiring Manager (HM) round (out of which only three were allowed
to proceed to Technical Round 2), while the remaining 10 candidates, including me, first had to go through
Technical Round 2.
Problem 1:
The question involved an array children, where each element represented the maximum number of
candies a child could receive. There were a total of m candies, and we had to return the number of ways to
distribute all the candies among the children such that every candy was distributed and no candies remained.
--- PAGE 5 ---
I told the interviewers that it was a Dynamic Programming (DP) problem. They then asked me to explain the
solution by directly deriving the tabulation approach with a dry run. However, I wasn't able to construct the
DP table directly. Instead, I explained my thought process in sequence, starting from the backtracking
approach, then memoization, and finally tabulation.
For some reason, they still didn't fully understand my approach, so I drew the entire recursion tree and
demonstrated the overlapping subproblems. Even then, they weren't completely convinced. They were
actually looking for a more optimized solution using prefix sums (although, from what I heard later, most
students were unable to solve it using that approach).
I then wrote the code for my DP approach. By this time, a significant amount of the interview had already
been spent on this question, so the interviewer asked whether I wanted to continue trying to find the optimal
solution or move on to the next question. Without wasting more time, I chose to proceed to the next
question.
Problem 2: maximum-strong-pair-xor-ii
I first explained the brute-force solution for the problem by checking all possible pairs that satisfied the
given condition and returning the maximum XOR among those pairs. The time complexity of this approach
was O(n').
The interviewers then asked me to optimize it. I explained that I would first sort the given array and then use
a two-pointer approach along with a Trie. I would keep increasing the right pointer until the given condition
was violated. While moving the right pointer, I would insert each number into the Trie (from the most
significant bit to the least significant bit, i.e., 32 bits).
Whenever the condition was violated for the first time, I would find the maximum XOR of the element at
the left pointer with the numbers currently present in the Trie. Then, I would keep moving the left pointer
until the condition was satisfied again, removing the corresponding numbers from the Trie as I moved it.
This was the optimal approach. The interviewers then asked me to write the complete code in detail, which I
did, while explaining each part of the implementation as I wrote it.
So the time complexity became Onlogn)
Then, they suggested that we revisit the first question. After a lengthy discussion, we agreed on a solution
with a time complexity of O(n × k × k).
Once we finished discussing the coding questions, I asked them a few questions about their line of work and
the kind of projects their team works on.
After the interview was over, I realized that it had lasted for almost 1 hour and 45 minutes.

Tips:

The duration of interviews can vary, so don't worry if your interview lasts much longer than others. A longer
interview does not necessarily indicate anything negative.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Also, even if you get stuck at some point or the interviewer says that a part of your code is incorrect, don't
immediately assume that you are wrong. If you genuinely believe your logic is correct, be confident and
explain your reasoning by dry-running your code on a few different test cases. This happened to me during
this interview, and it helped clarify my approach.
Finally, never stop trying to reach the optimal solution. Even if you don't arrive at it immediately, keep
explaining your thought process and refining your approach. Interviewers often value your problem-solving
process just as much as the final answer.
4 Hiring Manager Round [Around 9 people appeared for this round] [Around 1 hr 15 mins ]
This round was taken by a Senior Engineer. It started with him giving a brief introduction about himself,
after which he asked me to introduce myself as well. He interrupted my introduction midway and directly
opened my GitHub account, which was quite a surprise for me because, based on previous years' interview
experiences, this had never happened.
He then asked me which project on my GitHub was my favorite. I pointed to one of my hackathon projects.
He opened that repository and asked me about my role and my teammates' roles in the project. I clearly
explained that I had worked on the backend and Al/ML along with one other teammate, while the other two
teammates handled the frontend.
He then opened the backend folder of my project and asked me to explain the purpose of each folder. I
explained that I had written the backend in a modular way:

• controllers - contained the main business logic.

• db - handled the database connection.

• middlewares - contained all middleware functions.

• models - defined all the database models.

• routes - contained all the API routes.

• services - included reusable or recurring service logic.

• utils - contained utility functions.

• app-js - configured the main application, middleware, and API routes before passing them to the

route modules.

• index.js - served as the entry point of the application, where the server was started and the port was

configured
I explained all of this to demonstrate how I had structured the backend.
He then opened index. js and asked me what CORS was and why it was used, which I answered. After
that, he noticed that I had hardcoded the allowedOrigins inside the CORS configuration and asked me
why I had done that. I honestly told him that since it was a hackathon project, my teammates and I had
hardcoded the list of allowed URLs. However, in a professional environment, I would usually keep such
values in environment variables so they could be configured through env files. The interviewer
appreciated this answer and was very friendly and understanding, considering it was a hackathon project.
Later, he opened the controllers folder, randomly selected one of the files, and asked me to explain the
complete flow of how that function was invoked in the backend. I started by showing him how the request
first reached app. js, then how it was forwarded to the appropriate route file inside the routes folder,
--- PAGE 7 ---
and finally how that route invoked the corresponding controller function. From this discussion, he got a
good idea that I had a strong understanding of the code I had written.
He then asked me about Git branching strategies. I told him that it completely depends on the application
and its scale. Branches can be created based on different modules, individual features, or even assigned to
different developers working on the project.
Finally, he asked me how I would resolve merge conflicts. I explained that one approach is to use git rebase,
and another is to resolve the conflicts manually using a merge editor by selecting the required portions of
code before completing the merge.
He then shifted the conversation to my internship and asked me what exactly I had worked on there. After
that, he asked me to explain JWT in detail and even provided me with a paper and pen to illustrate it.
I explained that a JWT consists of three parts: the header, the payload, and the signature. The header
contains the token type and the signing algorithm, the payload contains basic user information and claims,
and the signature stores the hashed value of the header and payload generated using a secret key.
While I was explaining, he asked me a few follow-up questions in between to test my understanding, all of
which I was able to answer.
I then explained the complete authentication flow. When a client logs in, the server first verifies the user's
credentials. If the user is authenticated, the server creates a JWT using a secret key and sends it to the client,
where it is typically stored as an HTTP-only cookie to help prevent XSS attacks.
Whenever the client sends a request to a protected endpoint, the JWT is sent along with the request as a
Bearer token. The server then verifies the token by again hashing the header and payload using the same
secret key and comparing the result with the signature present in the JWT. If the signature matches, the
token is considered valid, and the server authorizes the user and serves the requested resource.
I explained this entire flow in detail using the paper, and the interviewer seemed satisfied with my
explanation.
He then asked me to draw the high-level system design of the project I had worked on during my internship.
I drew the complete architecture in detail and explained every component, along with why I had chosen a
particular technology or design decision over other alternatives. While I was explaining the architecture, he
asked me several follow-up questions related to SQL vs. NoSQL databases and many other system design
concepts, all of which we discussed in detail.
Later, he asked me about async and await in JavaScript. I explained that JavaScript is a single-threaded
language, so if a long-running synchronous function blocks the main thread, it can affect the responsiveness
and overall performance of the application. async and await are used to handle asynchronous operations
in a cleaner and more readable way, allowing the event loop to continue processing other tasks while waiting
for an operation to complete.
He then asked what was used before async/await in JavaScript. What was used before that which was
Promises and before that which was callbacks.
--- PAGE 8 ---
At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions for him. I made sure to ask a few thoughtful
questions about his experience working at PhonePe, the team's culture, and the kind of work they do.
Some of the questions I asked included:

• How has your growth journey been at PhonePe, and what does the typical growth curve look like for

a new joiner!

• Given that PhonePe processes tens of millions of transactions every day, how do you approach

testing and staging for payment-critical services? Do you rely more on shadow traffic, canary
deployments, feature flags, or other strategies?

• I also asked a few other questions related to the team's day-to-day work, engineering practices, and

the technologies they use.
The interviewer appreciated my curiosity, and we had a good discussion around these topics before
concluding the interview.
Lips:
Always be thoroughly prepared for everything mentioned on your resume, as interviewers can ask questions
on any detail you include.
Be honest in your responses. If you haven't explored a particular technology deeply, it's better to admit it
rather than attempting to give incorrect or fabricated answers.
Stay prepared for unexpected situations. For instance, interviewers may review your project code directly
from GitHub. Even if you're not fully prepared for that, maintaining calmness and confidence can help you
navigate such questions effectively.
Focus on building meaningful projects where you have a strong understanding of the implementation. Be
ready to answer in-depth questions about every aspect of those projects, including the technologies used,
design decisions, and challenges faced.
Results were announced
2 of us got internship + fte
And 4 including me got internship + performance based full time

summer internship-I know how discouraging it can feel. I was selected for the JPMC Code

a positive mindset, and believe in your abilities. Every experience, whether it feels like a
success or a setback, teaches you something valuable and brings you one step closer to your
goal. Keep learning, keep improving, and trust that the right opportunity will come.

platforms like LeetCode, GeeksforGeeks, and Coding Ninjas. Try to solve DSA problems every day because
it's a skill that takes time to develop. Don't get discouraged if you're unable to solve a problem immediately.

understanding the solution, solve more problems on the same concept to strengthen your understanding. I
would also recommend exploring competitive programming, as it significantly improves your ability to
solve complex problems under time constraints.

gradually become comfortable solving them. During your practice, get into the habit of thinking out

journey.prep:
There will be times when you feel you are doing everything right, yet nothing seems to go in your favour. I
went through this too, whether it was not getting shortlisted, not clearing an OA, or not making it through an
interview. These situations can be disheartening, and you may even start doubting your decisions. But what
is done is done, and you cannot change the past. Accept it, learn from your mistakes, and keep moving
forward. That is the best thing you can do.
Make sure you surround yourself with people who motivate you but also show you the mirror when you are
wrong. Having people who support you while being honest with you is extremely important. I am grateful to
have had a wonderful group of friends and my parents supporting me throughout this journey.
The waiting period can sometimes be long, and the uncertainty can be frustrating. But stay persistent, trust
the process, and keep improving yourself. Whatever you do, do it with complete honesty and give it your
best. Things may not always work out when you expect them to, but every experience teaches you
something valuable.
