Pre-Placement Talk (25th September) (online):
Be attentive during the meeting and listen carefully to role-specific discussions and the information shared
by the team. This will help you understand the role better and prepare relevant questions for the interview. It
is also recommended to note down the names of the speakers and HR representatives, as you might be asked
about them during the interview( not mandatory but recommended).
Take screenshots of important slides whenever required so you can refer to them later. If you get an
opportunity to ask questions, ask something genuine that you are actually curious about. Avoid asking
questions just for the sake of it or using GPT-generated questions without understanding them. A thoughtful,
relevant question is always better than a forced one.
--- PAGE 2 ---
1.
Resume Shortlisting [~200 students had applied]
Por Soham Jadhav Resume_JPMC.pdf
Since this was an analytical role, I included two data analytics projects, a DCF valuation project, and a
Power BI project. I also added a technical AI/ML project, as I was comfortable with that domain. Keep your
resume to a single page, aim for an ATS score of 75+(ResumeWorded can be used to check ats score), and
tailor it according to the company's job description (JD).
Your 12th-grade percentage and CGPA can play a significant role in shortlisting, as many companies have
eligibility criteria such as 80%+ in 12th and an 8+ CGPA. If you meet these requirements, that can be an
advantage. However, at the end of the day, shortlisting also depends on several factors, and luck plays a
major role in whether your resume gets selected and at times it is a bit random too, but keep going.

2. Group Discussion [ 76 students ]

Six groups of around 12-13 candidates were formed, each with a different GD topic. My panel discussed
"Should organisations opt for work from home for selected roles?" (topic given on spot) Another panel
discussed digital payments and India's transition towards a cashless economy. The GD was conducted on
Zoom (from college campus) for around 20 minutes, with one minute to think and note down points.
However, candidates in my panel started speaking almost immediately.
Starting or concluding the GD is a plus. I spoke third and got three opportunities to put forward my points,
either continuing the discussion or presenting a positive counter-argument. Since there was no raise-hand
option, we had to find our own opportunities to speak. Be mindful of when to interrupt and when to let
others finish, ensuring your points are relevant and constructive.

3. Business Round (Technical Round) | 19 students]

My interview was scheduled for around 12:30 PM. There were two panels, each consisting of two
interviewers, on the Zoom call.
The interview started with me greeting the interviewers, followed by a short and crisp self-introduction.
They then moved on to the projects mentioned in my resume.
Since DCF valuation was the first project on my resume, the first question was: "What is DCF?"
They asked a few basic questions about DCF, and I explained what I had done, how I approached the
valuation, and what my analysis concluded.
The obvious follow-up questions were:

• Why did you choose DCF instead of other valuation methods?

• What made you interested in studying finance when you had initially been inclined towards

technology?

• When did you start preparing for finance?

--- PAGE 3 ---
They then asked about my technical project, including what I had built, how I implemented it, and which
technologies I had used. I explained the complete project workflow, its implementation, and the target
audience it was designed for.
The interviewer seemed satisfied with my explanation, after which the other interviewer moved on to
situational and general questions to understand my thought process and point of view.

1. If you are working in a team and the other members are not contributing, what would you do? How

would you handle their responsibilities? The interviewer followed up by asking what I would do if
they still failed to coordinate even after I had helped them.

2. What would you do if your manager disclosed sensitive information publicly or used it for personal

benefit? I had recently read about a similar case, so I supported my answer with that example.

3. What is the difference between chip design and chip development? I wasn't fully aware of the

technical details, and the interviewer also seemed to be exploring the topic. I tried to support my
answer with another example, which helped keep the discussion going.

4. Given the current situation, should the Indian government invest more in technology, considering

that many Indian companies primarily provide services to multinational corporations?
At the end, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I asked three:

1. A question about the role and its responsibilities.

2. How the growth and learning curve at JPMorgan Chase would look for someone joining this role.

3. If I received an offer, what standout qualities would they expect from an intern to help them perform

well and become a stronger prospect for the company? I was advised to ask this question during the
HR round if I progressed further.

4. HR Round [ 8 students ]

I was called for the HR round at around 4 PM, after a long wait. The interview was relatively short, lasting
approximately 15 minutes.
The HR introduced herself and asked me to introduce myself. After greeting her, I gave my introduction.
She then asked me to "Tell me something outside your resume." I spoke about my hobbies and shared a
little more about myself.
The HR asked a few questions to understand my personality, teamwork, and approach to challenges.

1. Tell me about a time you faced obstacles while working on something and how you tackled them. I

framed my answer in a way that also showcased my interest in finance.

2. If a teammate wants to contribute but feels left out, how would you handle the situation? I used an

example from one of my hackathons to explain my approach.

3. How have you handled a situation where you disagreed with a teammate? I shared another relevant

example to explain how I approached the disagreement.

4. What attracted you to this role?

5. Do you currently have any offers?

6. Would you be comfortable relocating for the job, and would you be comfortable with the job

requirements?
--- PAGE 4 ---
I tried to keep the conversation playful, friendly, and positive throughout the interview.
Towards the end, I asked two questions:

1. JPMorgan Chase has a strong legacy and established policies, ethics, and values. How does the

organisation ensure these principles are upheld in everyday work?

2. If selected, would I get opportunities to explore domains beyond the three verticals mentioned

earlier?
At around 8pm the final results were out and 7 students were selected out of 8.

customSections.content:
There will be times when you feel you are doing everything right, yet nothing seems to go in your favour. I
went through this too, whether it was not getting shortlisted, not clearing an OA, or not making it through an
interview. These situations can be disheartening, and you may even start doubting your decisions. But what
is done is done, and you cannot change the past. Accept it, learn from your mistakes, and keep moving
forward. That is the best thing you can do.
Make sure you surround yourself with people who motivate you but also show you the mirror when you are
wrong. Having people who support you while being honest with you is extremely important. I am grateful to
have had a wonderful group of friends and my parents supporting me throughout this journey.
The waiting period can sometimes be long, and the uncertainty can be frustrating. But stay persistent, trust
the process, and keep improving yourself. Whatever you do, do it with complete honesty and give it your
best. Things may not always work out when you expect them to, but every experience teaches you
something valuable.

1. English Assessment round (from home)

2. Cognitive Assessment round (from home)

3. Technical Assessment (on campus)

4. Technical Interview (on campus)

1.
English Assessment [ 170+ students gave the test ]
This round was purely based on grammar, writing skills, listening skills, speaking skills, and
decision-making. The assessment consisted of multiple sections, each testing a different skill.
The first 10 questions were behavioural and situational judgment questions. These were not necessarily
related to workplace behaviour but focused more on general decision-making in different situations. For
example, one question described a situation where two countries were at war and asked what you would do.
The options included taking one side, negotiating between the countries, or appealing for peace. I do not
remember the exact wording or all the options.
The next section was listening comprehension. We were given a short audio clip of approximately 20
seconds, which we had to listen to carefully and answer four questions based on the audio.
The following section was reading comprehension, where a paragraph was provided, followed by five
questions based on the information in it.
The next section was the speaking assessment through video questions. We were given two questions and
had to record our answers. Everyone received different questions. I was asked, "How does a typical day
differ between working from home (WFH) and working from the office (WFO)? Does this affect team
collaboration and communication?" and "Tell me about a technology you use every day, what you use it for,
and why." Some of my friends received questions such as "Tell me something about your friend."
The next section tested grammar and sentence correction. Each question contained a sentence with an
underlined portion, and we had to choose the option that best replaced the underlined part while maintaining
grammatical correctness. There were 10 questions in this section.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Lastly, there were four email-writing questions. Each question described a particular situation and
specified the points that had to be included in the email, along with the tone to be used. For example, one
question asked us to write a polite email to our landlord about a leak in the rented house while highlighting
the urgency of the issue. Another asked us to write an email to a client informing them that the project
deadline was being extended or delayed. I do not remember the other two questions exactly.
This was a easy round

2. Cognitive Assessment (All those who gave english assessment)

This round was conducted on the same day, approximately two hours after the English assessment. It
consisted of five sections and was quite tiring. The assessment included puzzles, some behavioural
questions, and tasks where we had to remember the sequence of dots while being interrupted by other
questions. I do not clearly remember all five sections.
The last section was particularly time-consuming and consisted of 100 questions. Each question described a
situation, and we had to respond using a slider with options ranging from Strongly Disagree, Disagree,
Neutral, Agree, and Strongly Agree.
The assessment also had technical issues, as only five questions appeared on each page and the questions
loaded very slowly. In some cases, it took approximately 10 minutes for the questions on a page to load
Despite these delays and the lengthy assessment, I was eventually able to complete the round.
The English assessment retest was also conducted for everyone who needed it because some candidates
had experienced problems during the initial assessment. However, the cognitive assessment retest was
conducted only for candidates who had faced issues during their original test, rather than for everyone.

3. Technical Assessment (77 students shortlisted for this round)

This round was conducted on campus, with representatives from the company present at the venue. We
were instructed to arrive by 7:45 AM, as the assessment was scheduled to begin at 9:00 AM sharp. Before
starting the test, our Aadhaar cards were verified to unlock access to the assessment. The company
representatives then gave us a brief introduction to the company and explained the assessment process.
On the first page of the assessment, we had to select one of five frameworks: React, Django, Flask,
Node.js, or Spring Boot. I selected Spring Boot because I was more confident in it than the other options.
My advice would be to choose the framework you know best rather than selecting one simply because
it seems easier. I saw some candidates choose React because it was a frontend framework and seemed easy
to them, even though they were not thoroughly familiar with it.
The assessment consisted of four sections, each with a fixed time limit.
The first section was DSA (25 minutes). However, I would not describe the questions as typical DSA
problems. They were relatively easy if you were confident with programming language syntax, array
--- PAGE 3 ---
manipulation, and accessing data structures. My question was related to product management. I was given
an array of products, each containing an ID, name, and price, along with a queries array in the form [type,
value]. There were three types of queries: the first required finding products with prices greater than the
given value, the second required finding products with prices lower than the given value, and the third
required finding products whose IDs were smaller than the given value. For each query, we had to print the
names of all products satisfying the specified condition. Everyone received different questions in this
section.
The second section was Prompt Engineering (15 minutes). We were given a situation in which we had to
retrieve logs for the endpoint with the highest number of errors, following a specific output format. Our task
was to write a prompt that would make the Al generate the desired output. The test cases would pass if the
prompt correctly captured the requirements and produced the expected result. This question was common to
everyone, although some of my friends were unable to pass all the test cases.
The third section was Debugging (30 minutes). We were given a buggy application based on the framework
we had selected at the beginning of the assessment. An Al assistant was available to help us, but it did not
directly provide the complete solution. My suggestion would be to ask the Al assistant general questions
about the codebase and the flow of execution rather than immediately asking it to fix the bug. I started
by asking which files handled the relevant logic, including the controller, entity, and repository. Once I
understood the structure, I began debugging the application. I was able to pass only two test cases. The
number of test cases varied depending on the selected framework.
The final section was Feature Development (40 minutes), which I found to be the toughest part of the
assessment. We were given a feature to implement in the application, and the implementation was evaluated
using test cases. In my case, there were six test cases, but I was able to pass only one by the end of the
allotted time.

4. Technical interview (only 6 students were shortlisted for interviews)

There were three interview panels, and the interviewers arrived later in the day rather than being present
during the morning assessment. I was the second candidate to be interviewed in my panel.
When I entered the room, the interviewer initiated a handshake, introduced himself by name, and I
introduced myself as well. He did not ask me for a formal self-introduction and instead took a quick look at
my resume before starting the interview.
He first asked me whether I wanted to become a Data Engineer or a Cloud Engineer. I replied that I was
comfortable with both roles and that my skills, projects, and experience aligned with both. He then asked me
what I understood by the role of a Data Engineer and what a Data Engineer actually does. Following that, he
asked me to rate my proficiency in Python.
Next, he asked me to design a complete data engineering pipeline. I began by explaining the data source,
how the data would be collected, and where it would be stored. The interviewer challenged my approach
several times with follow-up questions. For example, he asked how I would handle millions of rows of data.
I suggested processing the data in chunks and using object storage such as AWS S3. He then asked me
questions about AWS S3, which I was able to answer because I had used it in one of my projects. However, I
could not complete the entire pipeline before he moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 4 ---
He then asked whether I knew MySQL and PostgreSQL, as both were mentioned on my resume. After that,
he asked me about the difference between OLAP and OLTP. I was not familiar with these terms and
admitted that I did not know the answer. I genuinely thought I had lost the interview at this point.
He then asked me to design a database schema for DMart. I created an ER diagram and explained the
entities and their relationships. He asked how the tables were related in terms of primary keys and foreign
keys. He also asked me about fact tables and dimension tables, but I was unfamiliar with those specific
terminologies at the time.
The interviewer then moved on to object-oriented programming (OOP) and asked why we needed it,
followed by a question about the four pillars of OOP. After that, he asked why Git, GitHub, and GitLab were
mentioned on my resume and why we needed them. I explained their purpose and how they were used.
He then presented a practical scenario: could I merge my code directly if I did not have the necessary
permissions? I replied that I would raise a pull request, and a maintainer or supervisor would review it. If
everything was correct and the CI pipeline had passed all the tests, the authorized person could merge the
code. He followed up by asking whether we could merge the code directly if doing so would make it live. I
explained the concept of blue-green deployment in response, and he seemed satisfied with my answer.
After that, he asked me about one of my projects but did not go into much technical detail. He was mainly
interested in a general overview.
The next topic was SDLC and its stakeholders. He asked who the stakeholders in the software
development life cycle were, and I mentioned clients, the business team, the project manager, and the
development team.
He then gave me a situational question. He asked me to imagine that I had become good friends with a client
and that the client was now asking me to implement an additional feature. I fumbled a little while answering
this question. I initially said that I would conduct a proper risk analysis of the proposed feature and identify
the modules that would be affected. The interviewer then asked whether I would implement the feature for
free. I replied that I would inform the client that the additional feature would incur extra costs and could
push the project deadline forward. He then asked whether I needed to inform the project manager as well. I
agreed that the project manager would need to be kept in the loop throughout the process. I felt that I had not
handled this question as confidently as I could have.
Towards the end of the interview, the interviewer asked me whether there was anything he should have
asked me but had not. I took this opportunity to bring up my final-year major project, which he had not
asked about earlier, and gave him an explanation of the project.
The interview ended with another handshake, and I left the room. We had expected an HR interview to
follow, but no further interview took place. Instead, we were asked to leave for the day.
The results were announced approximately one week later, and fortunately, I was selected for the final
offer! In total, 5 candidates were selected. However, one of the selected candidates had already accepted an
offer from another company and therefore could not accept this offer.
--- PAGE 5 ---

Application → Resume Shortlisting → Culture Aptitude Test & Cognitive Ability Test (AON) → Technical
Interview → HR Interview → Offer
Around 200 students appeared for the initial selection process . The process began with submitting an
application through Superset, followed by registration on the UBS career portal. After completing the
application, applicants received two assessment links: the Culture Aptitude Test and the Cognitive Ability
Test. The Culture Aptitude Test consisted of around 16-18 scenario -based questions , where we had to
choose how we would respond to different workplace situations. The Cognitive Ability Test consisted of two
sections: verbal reasoning, where we had to read short passages and answer questions based on them, and a
cognitive/pattern-based section , where we had to identify and match different patterns or figures. After
completing both assessments, the candidates were further shortlisted, and 10 candidates were selected for
the Interview round. We Received results on 9/09/2026 about the shortlisting.

1. Technical Round [10 Candidates]

For the technical round, on 10 September 2026 , we were given a problem statement along with a dataset
containing around 1,000 entries. We were asked to build an AI-based solution and submit both an HTML
file containing the solution and a supporting PPT . The deadline for submission was 2:00 PM on 11
September, giving us roughly a day to understand the problem, analyze the dataset, develop the solution and
prepare the presentation. While working on the assignment, I tried to align my solution with the job
description, particularly by incorporating elements related to AI, automation and the kind of work expected
from the Agentic Automation team. Before the interview, I also researched the professional backgrounds of
the senior manager, other interviewers and the HR representative, so that I could better understand their
work and have a more meaningful conversation during the interview.
My technical interview was scheduled on 11 September at around 6:30 PM , as the panel included
interviewers working with the US team. I started with a brief introduction and then walked the interviewers
through my solution, explaining my approach, reasoning and the additional elements I had incorporated. The
senior manager particularly appreciated the way I approached and explained the solution and mentioned that

my reasoning and walkthrough were very strong. He even told me that he was "scoring me in the top," which
was a really encouraging moment for me. What I particularly enjoyed was that the interview did not feel very
formal or intimidating. The interviewers were extremely friendly, and the entire discussion was quite
casual, interactive and even had a few funny moments.  Rather than simply asking rapid -fire technical
questions, they were interested in understanding my thought process and discussing the solution with me. The
entire technical interview lasted around 30 minutes.
Towards the end, I was given an opportunity to ask questions. I asked one question about the work culture
at UBS and what it was like working within the organization. I also asked the interviewer a more casual
question: "How was your weekend?"  He had actually asked me the same question at the beginning of the
interview, so I thought of asking it back at the end. He was quite happy with the question and shared that he
had actually spent part of his weekend working on a project. That small interaction made the conversation feel
much more natural and genuine. Overall, it was a very positive and memorable interview experience , not
only because of the technical discussion and feedback on my solution, but also because of how comfortable
and approachable the interviewers were throughout the interaction.

2. HR Round [5 Candidates]

After the technical interviews on 11 September , only five candidates were shortlisted for the HR
round. We received the shortlist notification on the morning of 12 September at around 9:00 AM, and
the HR interview was scheduled for around 11:00 AM the same day. The HR interview was very Short
and lasted only around 5-6 minutes. Interestingly, the HR interviewer had also been present during my
technical interview and had been taking notes on my solution and my approach. She mentioned that the
senior manager was very happy with my solution and had rated my performance highly , so the HR
discussion was relatively short. She mainly asked me about my background, my understanding of the work
culture at UBS , and how I viewed the internship opportunity. She also explained a little about the
internship, the work environment and what I could expect from the role. Towards the end, she asked if I
had any questions. I asked her, from an HR perspective, what value and growth opportunities UBS
provides to students joining the company, and she explained how the organization supports employees
and their development. Overall, the HR round was very conversational and comfortable. The interview
was scheduled in the 11:00-11:15 AM window, but my actual discussion lasted only a few minutes. The
final results were announced at around 1:00 PM on the same day, and I was extremely happy to see my
name among the selected candidates.
4 students were offered the role and I was one of them.
Tips for the Interview:

1. Stay Calm: Interviews can be nerve-wracking, but your ability to think clearly under pressure is just

as important as your technical knowledge.

2. Know Your Projects Well: Be prepared to explain not only what you built, but also why you made

specific technical decisions and be ready to confidently justify your choices.

3. Think Out Loud: Avoid going completely silent while solving a problem. Share your thought process

with the interviewerit helps keep the conversation engaging and demonstrates how you approach
challenges.

4. Be Honest When You're Stuck:  It is completely fine to ask for a hint or admit that you are unsure

about something. What matters is how you approach the problem and respond to the situation.

5. Understand Your Resume Thoroughly: Be ready to discuss anything you have mentioned on your

resume, including your projects, technologies, internships and achievements.

6. Focus on the "Why": Don't just explain the implementation. Be prepared to discuss why you chose

a particular approach, technology or architecture and what alternatives you considered.

7. Tailor Your Resume to the Job Role: This is extremely important. Before applying, carefully read

the job description and make sure your resume highlights the skills, projects, technologies, and
experiences most relevant to the role. Avoid using the exact same resume for every position. A well
tailored resume makes it easier for the interviewer to see why your profile is a good match for the
specific role.
Resources I Followed

1. DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet

2. SQL: SQL 50

3. DBMS: Complete DBMS in 1 Video (With Notes) | For Placement Interviews

4. OOPs: GeeksforGeeks

5. Operating Systems & Computer Networks: GeeksforGeeks

6. CS Fundamentals Practice: GeeksforGeeks and InterviewBit for practicing recently asked

interview questions and strengthening core concepts.

Final thoughts:
Every interview I had before UBS, including IDFC FIRST Bank, ISS STOXX, J.P. Morgan, Quantiphi ,
and many others, taught me something new. Each experience helped me become more comfortable with
interviews and gave me a better understanding of the kind of work I wanted to pursue. At the time, not
receiving an offer was definitely disappointing, even though every interview itself was a great learning
experience. But after getting selected at UBS, I genuinely felt grateful that those earlier opportunities did
not work out. When I understood the role at UBS, I realized that this was the kind of work I ha d actually
been looking for. It made me believe even more that sometimes things do not work out for a reason. We
may not understand it at the time, but the right opportunity can eventually come along. In the end, I believe
our job is simply to keep trying,  keep learning, and keep moving forward. The rest, in many ways, is
destiny.
If you have any specific questions, please feel free to reach out on: LinkedIn
All the best for your placements!

1. Resume Shortlisting

2. OA

3. Technical round

4. HIR

1. Resume Shortlisting (200+ candidates)

Maintain a GPA above 8 (I will personally recommend to keep it above 9, as it opens many doors).
Check the ATS score from Resume Worded. Mine was 65.

2. OA (200+ students)

Marking Scheme: +1 for correct, -0.25 for wrong
The Online Assessment consisted of around 70 questions with 90 minutes divided into the following
sections:

• Java: 17 Questions

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Python: 18 Questions

• SQL: 3-4 Questions

• LLM / AI Basics: 5-10 Questions

• Aptitude: 30 Questions

Java (17 Questions)
The Java section required a strong understanding of core Java concepts, especially Object-Oriented
Programming. Most of the questions were guess-the-output type questions, where understanding the
internal behavior of Java was far more important than simply remembering definitions.
The questions revolved around topics such as:
OOP concepts, Generics, Lambda Expressions, Method References, Pass-by-value vs Pass-by-reference,
Overriding hashCode () and equals () , Collections Framework, Access Modifiers
I would highly recommend practicing Java MCQs from Exam Veda and Sanfoundry.
Apart from these resources, one preparation strategy that helped me a lot was using ChatGPT to generate
tricky edge-case MCQS. Instead of asking generic questions, ask it to create questions that intentionally
include common traps and edge cases. These are the kinds of scenarios that are often tested in MCQs.
Python (18 Questions)
Similar to Java, the Python section also consisted primarily of guess-the-output questions.
The important topics included:
Dictionaries, Sets, Lists, Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy, Copying in 1D and 2D Lists, Object Referencing,
Various edge cases involving mutable and immutable objects
A lot of questions tested whether you truly understood how Python handles references and object copying
rather than just knowing the syntax. I would again recommend practicing edge cases separately, as they can
be quite tricky. Use GPT, prompt well.
SQL (3-4 Questions)
The SQL section wasn't based on writing lengthy queries. Instead, they described a particular operation that
needed to be performed and asked which SQL query would be the most appropriate.
Some of the important topics included:
Subqueries, GROUP BY, HAVING, Aggregate Functions
For preparation, I would recommend first completing the 70 SQL questions from SQL Practice, followed
by the Top 50 SQL Questions on LeetCode. Together, these should cover almost everything required for
this level of assessment.
--- PAGE 4 ---
LLM / AI Basics (5-10 Questions)
The LLM/Al section mainly focused on basic concepts and current trends.
Preparing this section doesn't require an in-depth understanding of Machine Learning. Simply use ChatGPT
to understand the currently trending AI topics and revise the basic concepts around Large Language Models,
Generative Al, and related terminology. That should be more than sufficient.
Aptitude (30 Questions)
Believe me, this is the most scoring section of the entire assessment.
For Java and Python, you either know the concept or you don't. If you're unsure about a question, don't
spend too much time thinking about it. Solve it if you're confident; otherwise, skip it and preserve your time
for the aptitude section.
I genuinely believe that attempting 25+ aptitude questions is achievable if you have practiced IndiaBix
thoroughly.
The questions were from topics such as:
Upstream & Downstream, Time, Speed & Distance, Permutations & Combinations (for example, committee
formation involving x men and y women), Basic One-Dimensional Kinematics, Probability (make sure you
understand Bayes' Theorem), Work & Time, Fractions, Averages.
I also have some actual aptitude questions that appeared in the assessment. I've attached the link below for
reference:

• Aptitude questions (link)

(ADVICE): To master aptitude, I would strongly recommend solving IndiaBix thoroughly. If you already
have a natural aptitude for solving these problems, that should be sufficient. Otherwise, you can refer to R.S.
Aggarwal's Quantitative Aptitude book or CareerRide(YT) to learn faster solving techniques and
shortcuts.
One thing I strongly feel is that aptitude is highly underrated. Everyone talks about DSA/ CP, but very
few people emphasize aptitude. While DSA is undoubtedly important, aptitude is equally important because
the majority of companies include it in their OAs.
My advice would be to start preparing for aptitude as early as possible. Once you become comfortable with
it, you'll be able to focus entirely on projects, DSA, core CS subjects, and interview preparation during the
later stages of the placement season instead of worrying about aptitude at the last moment.
--- PAGE 5 ---

3. Technical round (44 candidates)

The Technical Interview began with a very common question:
"Tell me about yourself."
Don't worry-I have shared the framework that I used to answer this question later in this document.
The interviewer then asked me to explain one project of my choice. The discussion wasn't limited to just
the project's objective. They went into considerable depth and asked about:

• The aim and objective of the project.

• The complete tech stack used.

• The justification behind choosing every technology.

• Alternative technologies that could have been used and why I didn't choose them.

I would strongly recommend preparing your projects thoroughly. Apart from knowing the implementation,
make sure you're able to justify your technology choices. Be prepared to discuss topics such as scalability,
future enhancements, possible optimizations, and why your chosen architecture is suitable for the given
problem statement. These are very common follow-up questions.
The interview then shifted towards Java fundamentals.
I was asked about the different access modifiers in Java, followed by another question on which access
modifiers can be applied to constructors.
I was confident that public, private, and default constructors are allowed. However, I wasn't completely
sure about protected. Instead of guessing, I honestly conveyed that I wasn't entirely sure about that
particular modifier.
Always admit when you're unsure rather than confidently giving an incorrect answer. Interviewers generally
appreciate honesty over bluffing.
Then he asked me to input 2 complex numbers and show the addition of them.
My response:

• Complex Number addition (link)

Then he asked me to write a solution where I need to print from 1 to 10 in any language of my choice, but
without using any loop.
I couldn't think of any other solution. I froze. I asked for a hint, when he answered, RECURSION!!
Again, it was a very simple answer but I couldn't think in that direction, anyways, now that I knew, I wrote
the solution and explained the flow of execution with a dry run.
E [Recursion](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Q6fofcUy70U8y8tKWBlFeag42RDwHCo-UeaWNBHBtKc/edit?usp=drive_link)
The interviewer then asked me a puzzle, given 3 jugs, 12, 8 and 5 litres, with the 12 one completely filled,
and rest empty, how do I measure 6 L exactly, which unfortunately I couldn't solve completely.
Never say "I don't know" or "I can't solve it' immediately. Keep thinking, communicate your thought
process, and if you get stuck, politely ask for a hint. Once the interviewer provides a hint, continue building
--- PAGE 6 ---
upon it and try solving the problem yourself. Showing your problem-solving approach is often just as
important as arriving at the correct answer.
At this point, I genuinely felt that my interview had gone terribly. I was convinced that I wouldn't get
shortlisted. I had almost lost all hope and even thought of going home. Thankfully, my friends encouraged
me to stay back and not lose hope.
A little while later, completely out of nowhere, I saw my name in the shortlist for the next round!!!
Learning: Never judge your own interview performance. Many times, the interviewers evaluate far more
than just whether you solved every question correctly. Your communication, honesty, approach towards
problems, and willingness to learn also play a significant role in the overall evaluation.

4. HR Round (19 candidates)

Compared to the technical round, the HR interview was much more conversational and comfortable.
The interviewers started by asking me about my background, where I stay, my daily commute, and some
general questions about myself.
The discussion then moved towards my project experiences.
One interesting question they asked was:
"Can you tell us about a situation where you made a decision during a project and later realized it
wasn't the right decisionại
Whenever you're answering such behavioral questions, make sure you always end your answer on a
positive note. The interviewer is less interested in the mistake itself and more interested in what you learned
from it. Also, try to relate your answer back to software engineering whenever possible.
The example I shared was from one of my hackathon projects.
Initially, we implemented session-based authentication because it was quick to set up. However, as the
project progressed, we realized that it had scalability limitations. After evaluating the trade-offs, we
migrated the entire authentication system to JWT-based authentication.
I concluded my answer by saying that not every decision we take will be correct. What's important is
accepting the mistake, learning from it, and being willing to rework the solution from scratch if necessary.
After all, quality is always more important than simply finishing quickly.
--- PAGE 7 ---
(ADVICE):

• Never answer in just one or two words. Always respond in complete, professional sentences.

• Whenever you're discussing failures, disagreements, or mistakes, always conclude by explaining

what you learned from the experience.

• Try to remember the names of your panelists.

• Finally, don't leave the interview without asking meaningful questions. Some good questions you can

ask are:

• How is Al being adopted within ISS?

• What does a typical day look like for an intern at ISS?

• What kind of learning opportunities can freshers expect during the internship?

These questions show genuine curiosity about the role and the company, and help leave a positive final
impression on the interviewers.
Finally 12 were offered the role, I was one of them.

journey.prep:
●       Resume & ATS score: Keep your ATS score at 85+ (ideally 87+). If you lack internship experience, be prepared to go through multiple resume drafts and iterations to get there -- it's a necessary step and directly impacts your shortlisting chances.

●       DSA + MCQs: Practice as much as possible. Look at past interview experiences to identify the topics companies tend to focus on. A higher MCQ/DSA score meaningfully improves your chances of being shortlisted for later rounds.

●       Know your resume in depth: Be ready to explain every skill, project, and line on your resume -- including the reasoning behind specific architectural or design decisions you made.

●       Behavioral questions: Prepare for these in advance. Practicing mock questions with friends or siblings helps a lot.

●       Research the company: Pay close attention to the company's introductory presentation -- you may be asked direct questions based on it.

●       Case study / group presentation rounds: Understand your proposed solution deeply and be ready to defend architectural choices under cross-questioning. Don't let a large panel or crowd intimidate you -- nervousness was the main reason several of my teammates didn't perform as well as they could have.

●       Stay calm: Treat the interview like a normal conversation rather than a high-pressure evaluation -- it genuinely helps manage nerves and adrenaline.

Overall, don't only focus on what went well -- reflect honestly on areas you could have handled better (for me, that was not paying enough attention to the company PPT beforehand). This kind of honest reflection helps future candidates avoid the same mistakes.

journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting  (153 candidates appeared)

153 students applied for this role, out of which only 51 were shortlisted for the next round. One of the biggest factors behind getting shortlisted is the ATS (Applicant Tracking System) score of your resume -- mine was 87. There are several websites available to check your ATS score; I'd recommend aiming for at least 85+, though anything above that only improves your chances.
I did not have any internship experience, so I had to go through many rounds of prompting and multiple resume drafts to push my ATS score up. It took effort, but I believe optimizing your resume this way is a necessary step to clear this round -- a score of 85+ should reliably get you shortlisted.

2. MCQ Test + Group Case Study Presentation

This round was originally supposed to follow the sequence: MCQ test (pen and paper) → group coding task. However, since the recruiters arrived late, we were asked to work on our group presentations first while the test was being set up.
We were divided into groups of 7 and given a problem statement: the current fraud detection system is rule-based, and we had to propose how it could be improved using an AI/ML-based (or any other) solution that is more scalable and effective at detecting fraud in transactions than a purely rule-based system. Each group was also given a set of 4+4 guiding questions to structure the answer around. We were given 1 hour to prepare a solution and design as a group before the MCQ test.
After the hour was up, we were seated two seats apart and given the MCQ test, which had three sections:

●       Section 1: Basic Python/SQL/DSA MCQs -- 10 questions.

●       Section 2: Code-snippet based questions -- we were given a code snippet, asked to explain its intended behavior, and how we would modify it to produce the correct output. There were 4 such questions, 5 marks each.

●       Section 3: A simple DSA coding question -- write a function that takes an array as a parameter and prints the top 3 unique elements (duplicates excluded). This was easily solvable using a hash map.

After the test, the presentation round began. There were 2 panels of judges (6 judges each), and only 7-8 teams in total, split across the two panels. My team had already divided the presentation into parts, which made things easier. We had built a multi-agent AI solution for fraud detection, and since we had some spare time, we generated supporting visuals and put together a PPT (using AI tools) to present our design.
There was no strict time limit -- we were told to aim for around 15 minutes, but it wasn't enforced strictly. During the presentation, I noticed that most of my teammates got nervous in front of the large panel and didn't present as clearly as expected; ultimately only two of us -- myself included -- were able to present confidently and clearly.
The judges seemed to notice who understood the solution well and specifically directed architecture-related cross-questions toward the less confident team members instead of letting the same one or two people answer everything. Judges from the other panel also walked in during our presentation and cross-questioned us, pointing out a few flaws in our system that we had to address on the spot.
In the end, only two people from my group of 7 -- myself and one other teammate -- presented and answered well, and both of us were selected to move forward. My advice for this round: understand your proposed solution thoroughly and be ready to justify every architectural decision. Most importantly, don't let a large panel of judges intimidate or demotivate you.
The shortlist for the interview round was based on a combination of the MCQ score and the presentation, though the presentation seemed to carry more weight since the MCQs were relatively easy. Around 2-3 candidates from each team were shortlisted -- 20 candidates in total moved on to interviews, and these began very shortly after the shortlist was announced.

3. [ Technical Interview] [ 20 people ]

My interview slot came up first, right after the shortlist was announced. I was fairly calm going in, having already interviewed (and been rejected) at a few other companies like Barclays, Auxo, and Russell -- each of those experiences had taught me what to prepare better for. My approach was to imagine the panel as friends and treat it like a normal conversation rather than a high-stakes interview.
The panel had two interviewers -- one technical and one HR -- though they didn't introduce themselves, so I inferred their roles from the questions they asked. It began with the standard "tell me about yourself."

●       I was asked to elaborate on the hackathons mentioned on my resume (an offline hackathon at Meta in Bangalore that required clearing qualifying rounds, and one at Amazon). I spoke about the Meta hackathon and the projects I built there.

●       Since most of my resume projects were AI-related, I was asked whether I'd be okay if I wasn't placed in an AI-specific role. I said I would be completely fine with it, since any role would be a learning experience.

●       I was asked why I was so inclined toward AI. I had prepared for this -- I answered with how, back in 2012, a lot of what seemed like science fiction is real today, and what bridges that gap is engineers building it.

●       I was asked to name the two skills I was most confident in. I said Python and JavaScript.

●       I was then asked to write code to reverse a string in Python. I directly wrote the most optimal solution I could think of, which they seemed to appreciate.

●       When asked about SQL, I was asked to write a query to reverse a string in SQL. I honestly said I didn't know how, but mentioned I was comfortable with relational tables, joins, and general SQL concepts. They seemed fine with the honest answer.

●       The last question from the HR side was, "Give me one reason why UBS?" I hadn't paid close attention to the company's introductory presentation, so my answer was fairly generic -- but it was good enough. My advice: pay attention to the company's PPT/introduction session so you have a specific, well-informed answer ready for this.

The interview wrapped up after this, and I was called back for the next (HR) round about 30-45 minutes later.

4. HR Round [10 people  were shortlisted ]

This round was much shorter and largely non-technical:

●       I was asked to explain my role in one of my projects in very simple, non-technical language, since the interviewer didn't have a technical background.

●       I was asked to choose between learning a new skill every day versus becoming a subject matter expert in one field. I chose learning something new every day, and explained how it helps me grow and think more creatively.

●       We discussed the Pune/Hyderabad location, the compensation package, and the expectation to relocate.

●       I was asked a few questions about my family background -- mainly to understand my personal situation.

●       Finally, I was asked if I had any questions for them, and the round ended there.

Initially they selected only 9/10 people but then after 2 weeks they said they have reconsidered and that they wanted to give the ppo to all the 10 people.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
●       Resume & ATS score: Keep your ATS score at 85+ (ideally 87+). If you lack internship experience, be prepared to go through multiple resume drafts and iterations to get there -- it's a necessary step and directly impacts your shortlisting chances.

●       DSA + MCQs: Practice as much as possible. Look at past interview experiences to identify the topics companies tend to focus on. A higher MCQ/DSA score meaningfully improves your chances of being shortlisted for later rounds.

●       Know your resume in depth: Be ready to explain every skill, project, and line on your resume -- including the reasoning behind specific architectural or design decisions you made.

●       Behavioral questions: Prepare for these in advance. Practicing mock questions with friends or siblings helps a lot.

●       Research the company: Pay close attention to the company's introductory presentation -- you may be asked direct questions based on it.

●       Case study / group presentation rounds: Understand your proposed solution deeply and be ready to defend architectural choices under cross-questioning. Don't let a large panel or crowd intimidate you -- nervousness was the main reason several of my teammates didn't perform as well as they could have.

●       Stay calm: Treat the interview like a normal conversation rather than a high-pressure evaluation -- it genuinely helps manage nerves and adrenaline.

Overall, don't only focus on what went well -- reflect honestly on areas you could have handled better (for me, that was not paying enough attention to the company PPT beforehand). This kind of honest reflection helps future candidates avoid the same mistakes.

journey.howSecured:
First of all, let me say ki placement is purely based on Hardwork + Luck , the luck part is not in ur hand, however u can max out the hardwork part!!
Keep on trying for all companies without being choosy, u never know what u might end up with !!
In terms of the placement process for ISS Stoxx ,It had a total of 3 rounds
(OA , Technical Round , HM round)
OA (All MCQ) -> 15 java + 15 python + 3 sql + 12 ai + 25 aptitude based
Note -> mcqs had -ve marking of 0.25 !!
Than were Technical Round & than HM round

1. Online Assessment -> [ Around 215 students had appeared for this round ]

There were 2 Categories in this test i.e Technical and Aptitude questions (45 questions each),and note that there was -ve marking as well of 0.25 marks and a total of 90 minutes for OA
For Technical Questions -> Most questions for java were based on OOPS, deep/shallow copy based,exception handling , collections,threads,java streams,pass by reference or value, interfaces and abstract classes, for python they were mainly based on OOP ,Inheritance, MRO ,List comprehensions, Slicing, Dictionaries ,Sets ,Copy vs deepcopy , now for the sql part ,it was comparatively easier, based on group by having , get nth highest salary , and the ai part was based on some code in java or py ,where most questions asked to detect the mistake or code smells
For Aptitude Questions -> It was pretty simple but lengthy (this was unexpectedly more difficult than i thought)
It contained ->Stocks & Shares ,Probability,Speed, Time & Distance, Boats & Streams , Profit & Loss , Simple & Compound Interest, Trains, Percentage, Ratio & Proportion,Clock,Height & Distance (Trigonometry)
Here remember to practice Stocks and Shares, since its the only extra topic asked here compared to other company OAs
The best daddy resource is Sanfoundry, Sandfoundary_java & Sandfoundary_py
it consists of 1k python and 1k java MCQs, however i recommend to try only 300-400 questions based on relevancy to this OA and on top of that u can practice extra on Indiabix
For sql, since here sql is comparatively simpler,refer geeksforgeeks playlist 20 vids or SQL50 if u want more practice
And finally for Aptitude , Indiabix_apti shd be more than enough
If u complete all these mentioned resources, u shd be good to go!!
Personally for me , i found aptitude very time consuming and difficult and the rest was easy to medium And learn to manage ur time properly since each question weighs the same leave any Q which u are not sure about or might consume too much time, i learned it the hard way!
I was able to solve 13-14 questions from Java and Py section , and all 3 for sql , for ai i solved roughly 8, For aptitude i was only able to solve 15-16 questions
At the end of this round, 45 candidates were selected

2. Technical Interview [45 students appeared for the interview]

This round had a total of 6 panels, all interviewing in parallel
The interview started with Me introducing myself, and immediately, interviewer asked me about my dsa and dev language , i said in terms of DSA i prefer java and for dev i work with JS,
So he started asking me questions inDepth Java, it started with him telling me to make a object arraylist which will be first made than at index i , that particular object must be removed, pretty simple
Than he started by asking, lets say if i have a string s = "abc" and i have a line like s.replace("xyz") than if i print s, will it print the Original string, i said yes and than explained about String pool and pass by reference V/S by value and explained that string is an immutable class, based on that he asked me a follow up question to write down a class ,where everything is immutable (use private+final) ,
and then he asked me about the classic integer pool cache question of Integer class , like Integer a=128 wala question ,search it up on google/gpt , these type of questions are based on java pools
After that he moved on and asked about .equals() v/s == in java ,i explained it in depth regarding recursive content checking in .equals() and reference checking in ==
Then we moved on to Exception handling , where he asked me about the main two classes in error handling mechanism, which are Error class and Exception class, and asked about when to use which class, and what are the different subclasses within the Exception and error class, after that he gave a faulty try catch final block and asked me to fix ,it was just that the different catch blocks were arranged randomly and not to their hierarchy in exception class, where according to the Exception class, the most abstractive (uppermost) class shd be at the last catch and the subclasses within that uppermost class must come before it when writing catch (so bottom-up) , and asked me about a real life use case where i needed to write finally, like in production why do we even need finally , if code is faulty ,catch handles it ,if not, try works , he asked why use finally??
He asked when making dev projects in JS, what do u use for async and await, i said i am used to handling such async reqs using the library async-handler so i didnt have much exp with try catch finally in JS
Than he asked me about JVM,JRE and JDK ,after that he asked me about creation of two objects with different content in it , say name is an variable within that class, so two classes with 2 different names, than how do i return true for a statement like obj1.equals(obj2) , this was the only question where i found myself, questioning myself ,i thought for a minute and i told him that i know that this is something related or something to do with reference ,but i cannot get the keyword which i can add to return true instead of false , since he said u cannot change the obj or the reference of it, u have to add something in this "obj1.equals(obj2)" same statement to make it return true, later i admitted i am unable to solve this !
Than he started checking my resume (skills section),first he asked me a lil bit about my projects and internship and what tech stack i used, i think he found none relevant to his Professional Experience ,so than he asked a few sdlc based questions so i mentioned during my internship we worked on JEERA and how we operated thro it , and asked me a few questions regarding state space in langGraph and orchestration and how it works on crew ai
Later he moved on to sql , he asked me 1 group by having question and a simple subquery of returning 2nd smallest salary , than he asked a sql question where i have 2 existing tables in my db , namely employee and Employee , and if i run select * from EMPLOYEE, will it run ? i said no , and explained how sql is case sensitive , than he asked a follow up question,that what shd u add in this select query to not get an error , at that moment i thought to myself saying add a comment in front of select will be stupid to answer for such a highly framed question, i tried everything i knew, but the question said to not update or remove anything, only add !! i admitted idk the answer for it. Later, now that i have check all resources, the answer was indeed add a comment :) lols, i would recommend whatever u think of , just say it out loud , dont think for a complex path how much soever u have practiced, try the most simple and logical approach first
Than he asked me if i know and have used JAVA Collections, i replied affirmatively,than he told me to draw the collection interfaces and classes and asked a few question about it and asked what is a better coding practice to write ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>() OR List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(), here explain that on the referrer side (LHS) rather than referring to the class itself refer to the uppermost interface in Collections,so in future u can change a ArrayList to a LinkedList or to any other DS,based on requirement!
He than asked me to write a thread using Runnable in java and than asked follow up regarding thread vs process and asked deadlocks and their prevention algo along with the 4 conditions which must be true for a deadlock to occur, I wasn't asked much on core subjects!
There are probably a few questions which i dont remember , but i have covered the major ones,which i found interesting and still remember , probably there were a few simple questions on oops , interface and abstract default methods, super and new keyword and diamond problem in java
Some tips i think will help -> Stay confident throughout the interview, back urself with whatever u have studied, JAVA is something u absolutely need to master for this process in general for this process i.e OA+technical round, learn OOPS in depth from geeksforgeeks it has 3 sheets on OOPS , for everything else again refer sanfoundary , Sandfoundary_java -> Great source to brush up and learn new concepts ,but for oops refer the geeksforgeeks
Keep a smile always, and dont overcomplicate stuff when explaining, only speak what u know, be honest and in times where u for sure dont know the answer -> reflect it to the interviewer, and in cases where it is a lil bit fuzzy , say i will look into it and try it for some time until correct and also dont hesitate to ask for hints ,
Always when solving a question follow the "Think out Loud" method , i found it very very useful!!
My interview finished after 1 hr ,compared to others who had theirs finished within 30mins, however irrespective of time i was confident that i will pass to the next round as the interviewer seemed happy !
Also at the end he asked me if i had any questions , and i asked about worklife balance for interns vs senior engg and how was his initial weeks in this company , and how will be the interns integrated into the current projects.

3. HM Round [ 21 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was a very simple and easy round, it was like talking to a friend (keep it formal tho), where i started with my introduction and was asked about my internships , my best project, and what are the weaknesses that u encountered during building stage and what are ur strengths, how do ur friends describe u, describe urself in 3 words, then asked me about my hobbies, i replied with football and then we talked about my career as a football player and i got asked why didnt i apply for nationals ,and i replied honestly with i was simply not good enough :) hahahahaa. Than she asked why do u think is indian football federation failing as a system and than i talked about unavailable infrastructure and money cycle for football,there is a huge market for football viewers yet no revenue generation and so on , later she asked about my family bg, and than Managerial Director (MD) asked me about my projects (give a high level view), tip->dont go on rambling about ur project
and then asked me about why i didnt join my fathers field which was IT as well, than she asked me about the worst day in my internship exp

Tips : Dont prepare too much for this round, the more u prepare the more it seems for HR that u r robotic and lying ,keep it natural and honest ,and in between talks and gaps maintain a smile,and keep the environment formal throughout the interview,and if possible crack a joke or two (usually not advisable but i did so) so that the build up decreases and also maintain a personality that u r always ready to learn adapt and excited to join a MNC as big as this, do prepare the already known stuff like best projects , the intro for it , the weaknesses and what u learned from

In the end i was told to ask any questions,and i asked how does a successful intern look like at iss stoxx, and what do my next line manager expect from me :)
Also another thing i learned is never say anything negative, keep the tone +ve, like for example say all -ve stuff than add "but in the long run , i learned from it things like blah blah blah " Also i ended the interview by making a joke about them SACRIFICING their dinner for us students, and hr joyfully corrected me, saying POSTPONED never sacrificed :) hahahaha
Also i was the 4th last for the interview ,so it was around 9pm when my interview started and the Company staff had very less time so they decided to give all next candidates only 15 mins each (compared to 1 hr for each student before me ), so i thought to myself that i was already at a disadvantage .
The duration of my interview was just 20 mins , whereas compared to all other students (1 hr),even tho my round went well, i had already fixated my mind that i had been rejected that day because of past rejections from UBS & WorkIndia, and while going home, i was counting and noting down all of the
mistakes that i made during HR and technical ,all of this to later find out at around 10:30 night that i was selected :), much love ;)
A total of 12 students were selected for i+p in the end !

journey.prep:
• Aim to keep your CGPA above 8.5. A 9+ CGPA is generally the safest zone for meeting eligibility

criteria across most companies.

• Before applying to any company, share your resume and the Job Description with ChatGPT and ask

for a resume match analysis. Alternatively, you can use Resume Worded and aim for a score of 70+.

• Stay active on your TPO WhatsApp group and Superset. Check them once a week and don't miss any

placement opportunity.

• Practice OA using IndiaBix, Sanfoundry, Career Ride and make use of Chatgpt and Claude to

generate tougher questions. Focus on understanding concepts instead of memorizing formulas.
Strong OA performance often helps you get an earlier interview slot.
(Lang - specific question, SQL, (OS+CCN rarely) , aptitude, DSA)

• For DSA, prepare thoroughly. Being comfortable with Trees and Graphs is usually sufficient for

many companies, but it's best to complete the entire DSA and DAA syllabus to maximize your
chances.

• Know your resume inside out. Be prepared to explain every project, skill, technology, and term

you've mentioned. Interviewers may also ask questions beyond your resume. In my experience, until
the ISS interview, my resume was rarely discussed, the questions were mostly from core subjects and
concepts I had studied during college end-semester exam preparation.

• DSA : https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z, Daily Leetcode

• GFG puzzles: Top 100 Puzzles Asked In Interviews - GeeksforGeeks

• DP : Aditya Verma playlist

OOPs: Kunal Kushwala

• OS + CCN + DBMS : Gate Smashers (Watched during ESE)

LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/vaishnavi-lakade-039529290/

journey.howSecured:
Total 3 rounds were conducted: Online Assessment, a Technical Interview, and an HR Interview, although
the HR round was more of a techno-HR interview. The min CGPA req was 8.0. The application process
was open around 9th July I guess, and remained open until approx 11:00 AM the following day. Candidates
were also instructed to attach their latest photo to their resume.

1. Resume Shortlisting [All Eligible Candidates applied]

We were informed around 7th July to keep our resumes with a photo attached at the left corner. At that
time, my primary focus was on preparing for the AuxoAl interview, so I postponed the task of updating my
resume with the photo. A day before my AuxoAl interview, the ISS STOXX application opened on
Superset, with the resume submission deadline set for 11:00 AM the next day. That day was particularly
hectic. After completing the AuxoAl assessment, I returned home and had to prepare for the AuxoAl
technical interview. At the same time, I also had the UBS 2 online test to be completed by EOD, which itself
took about an hour. Because of these commitments, I couldn't get around to adding the photo to my resume.
--- PAGE 2 ---
The next morning, with only about an hour left before the submission deadline of ISS, I submitted my
resume without the photograph. Later, after facing rejections from AuxoAI, UBS, and Nomura, I was feeling
a little dejected and was concerned that the missing photograph might affect my chances of getting
shortlisted for the OA. Fortunately, I was shortlisted for the OA, which was released just a day before the
PPT. My resume had an ATS score of around 70. For the on-ground rounds, I used the same resume after
with a photo attached.

2. Pre-Placement Talk [Approx 200 students]

The PPT was conducted online at around 3:30 PM and lasted until approximately 5:00 PM. I note down the
names of the speakers, important points discussed, and examples shared during the session. I would suggest
doing the same, as in previous interview experiences, candidates were asked about the names of the
speakers and key points from the PPT during the HR round. It is also advisable to join at least 10
minutes before the scheduled time, which helps avoid any last-minute issues or not being admitted by the
host. Also I did not ask any questions during the PPT, it is always better to ask at least one relevant
question related to the PPT discussion, as it shows curiosity and active participation.

2. Online Assessment Round [Approx 200 students]

The first round was an Online Assessment (OA) consisting of MCQS. The marking scheme was +1 for
every correct answer and -0.25 for every incorrect answer, so avoid random guessing. If you are
completely unsure about a question, it is often better to leave it unanswered rather than lose marks.
The assessment was scheduled to begin at 8:30 AM, so make sure to reach at least 30 minutes early. We
were instructed to use the college PCs, but I highly recommend carrying your own laptop as a backup
in case of any technical issues. In my allotted room, there was one TPC coordinator and one HR
representative from ISS STOXX. Both were extremely helpful throughout the process. If you face any issue
while accessing the Google Form, politely inform them instead of panicking.
The OA had three sections:
Technical (45 Questions) - Java, Python, and SQL
Aptitude (25 Questions)
AI Section (newly introduced this year)
I started with the Java and Python questions since they were mostly conceptual and theory-based. After that,
I solved the Aptitude section. I intentionally kept the AI section for the end because the questions contained
long prompts and code snippets, making them more time-consuming to read.
JAVA
It was of easy to medium difficulty if your concepts were clear. The questions mainly covered:
OOP concepts, Streams API (filter, forEach), Lambda expressions , String concatenation
Generics, Collections Framework, Records, Optional class, Access Modifiers, Overriding equals) and
hashCodeO, Code output prediction
My Prep : I used ChatGPT to generate medium-to-hard conceptual MCQS from these topics. Practicing
those questions made this section feel quite manageable during the actual OA.
Python
Most questions were based on conceptual understanding and output prediction. Important topics included:
--- PAGE 3 ---
Dictionaries, Sets, Lists, Mutable vs Immutable objects, Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy, Copying in 1D
and 2D Lists, Object Referencing,
new_O vs_init_0 (2 questions), await and asynchronous
programming, Method Resolution Order (MRO), Output-based coding questions
My Prep : Practiced by asking ChatGPT to generate medium-to-hard conceptual questions from these topics.
SQL
The SQL section was relatively straightforward. Questions were based on:
Joins, Subqueries , Aggregate Functions, GROUP BY and HAVING, TOP / LIMIT, output prediction
Preparation Resources: LeetCode Top 50 SQL Problems and ChatGPT-generated SQL practice questions
AI Section
This was a newly introduced section and was probably the most time-consuming due to the lengthy prompts.
Most questions focused on Prompt Engineering. A technical prompt along with multiple Al-generated
responses was provided, and you had to choose the response that best satisfied the prompt.
Identifying incorrect Al-generated responses
Programming-related prompts involving SQL, debugging, and code generation
Evaluating different Al outputs
Basic AI concepts such as Sparse vs Dense Vectors
Although I did not prepare specifically for this section beforehand, I found it completely doable. The biggest
challenge was the amount of reading required because many prompts and code snippets were quite long.
Recommendation: Attempt this section towards the end so that lengthy reading does not consume valuable
time meant for easier sections.
Aptitude
I had been practicing aptitude regularly for about a month before every company OA. I solved questions
from the first 1-2 pgs on IndiaBIX and also used ChatGPT to generate higher-difficulty quantitative aptitude
questions. Topics asked in this OA included:
Boats and Streams, Permutations & Combinations, Probability, Stocks and Shares, LCM, Sets,
Arrangements, Linear Programming (objective function maximization), Statistics (Normal Distribution)
There were also several well-known logical puzzles, including:
100 Lockers Problem, 8 balls puzzle (same which was asked in russel they gave me vague statement)
101 Coins Nim Game where you could choose 1 or 2 or 3 coins. 2 player game, last to pick loses.
50 Prisoners and 50 Boxes Problem.
Overall, I would rate the OA as medium in difficulty. The time provided was sufficient if you managed it
well. I was able to complete all the sections with around 15 minutes remaining, which gave me enough time
to revisit unmarked questions. Keep an eye on the timer to avoid submitting at the very last moment.

3. Technical Interview Round [ 44 students appeared]

The OA ended around 10:15 AM. Around 11:30 AM, the TPO started sharing the shortlisted students' names
on the TPO group, but my name was not announced initially. Later, around 12:30 PM, an Excel sheet was
shared, and I saw that my name was second last in my panel. The first thing I felt was relief and gratitude
that my name appeared after the OA round. I believe the shortlist was probably based on a combination of
CGPA and OA performance (not confirmed though).
--- PAGE 4 ---
While waiting for my turn, I started revising Java concepts. Along with that, I was also listening to the
questions being asked in other panels to understand the interview pattern. I noticed that my Panel 6 was
conducting interviews quite quickly, with many interviews lasting around 10-20 minutes. I also observed
that some candidates were getting rejected shortly after their interviews, which made me slightly
nervous. However, I continued revising topics like Java Streams, equalsO, previous year interview
questions, and the questions being asked to current candidates.
Around 3:00 PM, my interview was scheduled. I entered the room, greeted the interviewers, and handed
over my resume to both panel members. My panel consisted of two interviewers. They started with a brief
introduction. Since I knew the panel was conducting interviews quickly, I kept my introduction concise. I
covered:

• My educational background (SPIT + SPJMR Minor with CGPA)

• My interests backend and ML

• Project names with brief descriptions

• extracurricular activities

Then one interviewer asked an HR-related question: "Where do you see yourself in 2 years?"
After that, he noticed that I had mentioned a Teaching Assistant role for DBMS and asked whether I was
comfortable with SQL and database concepts. I confidently said yes. He then asked: Difference between
INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. I was able to answer that properly with examples. Next, one of the
interviewers drew this table and asked me to predict the expected output. I solved it correctly.
Table 1
