Then he noticed Redis mentioned in my tools section and asked whether Redis is single-threaded or
multi-threaded. I answered that it is single-threaded and explained the reasoning behind it. Till this point, I
felt the interview was going well and that I had handled most questions confidently.
After that, he moved towards language-based questions. He asked whether I knew Java. Since my primary
language is C++, I honestly mentioned that I understand Java code but am more comfortable with C++. He
then asked a Java Stream-related question reuse operation from GFG, a theoretical MCQ-based
concept. I didn't know, so instead of guessing, I suggested that I know high-level understanding of Java
Streams.
Then he moved directly to the next Java question which was based on OOP concepts. Due to the previous
question, I was slightly underconfident, but I still worked through it and gave the output. After that, the
--- PAGE 5 ---
interviewer said that my interview was complete. I was a little surprised because the interview had ended
earlier than expected. I thanked both interviewers and left.
Later, I realized that I had forgotten to ask them a follow-up question at the end. Since I had not answered =
Java-specific questions, while many Java-focused candidates were having 30-minute interviews and
answering several questions, I felt uncertain. I packed my bag and waited near the TPO area for the final
selection update. Unexpectedly, my name appeared in the selected candidates list. I was genuinely surprised
and grateful. What surprised me even more was that some candidates who answered 8-9 questions and had
longer interviews than me were not selected by the same panel.
This experience taught me that interviews are not only about the number of questions answered but also
about the quality of answers, confidence, honesty, and overall interaction with the panel. Also, try to add
some hints or share whatever you know about the topic instead of directly saying "I don't know."
Even if you are not completely sure about the answer, explaining your understanding or approach shows
your thought process and willingness to engage with the question.

4. HR Round [ 19 students appeared]

I was called for the HR round around 4:00 PM. Until then, I was revising some HR questions that I had
already prepared for myself and also going through company-specific questions. When I was entering the
cabin, I noticed that the interviewers were quite exhausted and were about to inform the TPO that they
needed a break. However, after seeing me, they decided to complete my HR round first and then take their
break. I was grateful for that and thanked them before handing over my resume. As expected, they were the
same people who had interacted with us during the PPT session.
The round started with a brief introduction, followed by a question about my overall day and placement
process experience. I replied that it was a great experience but equally exhaustive due to the rounds and
waiting time. They then asked about the difficulty level of the OA. I mentioned that it was moderate to
hard, but the time was sufficient enough to complete the paper comfortably. After that, they asked some
background-related questions, including: My family background and what my family members do and
my location. I told them that I am from Vashi and had already travelled to college regularly for the past three
years, so commuting would not be an issue. I also mentioned that I have alternative routes apart from trains,
which made the travel manageable. Then they asked about whether I have been given feedback from
professor or friend and how I improved that. They then asked about my interests. The discussion
moved towards my SPJIMR course experience. They asked what I had learned through the program
and how it differs from students who had taken other company-specific courses like Barclays and
Finance. I explained the broader learning experience and how SPJIMR helped me develop a more holistic
perspective. After that, they moved to my resume and asked about topics I had learned beyond the
academic curriculum. I tried to show genuine curiosity towards exploring concepts outside the syllabus.
They then asked me to explain one of my projects in layman terms. I explained the project in a way that
was understandable from a non-technical perspective. Till now all these questions were asked by HR and she
was noting it down in her laptop.
After this, the other interviewer took over and asked technical questions related to my project. Since
my project was based on a Small Language Model, he asked about terms mentioned in my resume, such as
attention mechanisms and decoder-only transformers. These concepts were relatively new to him, so I
explained them using real-world examples while ensuring that the technical essence was maintained. The
discussion then shifted towards SPJIMR and whether I would consider pursuing an MBA in the
--- PAGE 6 ---
future. I explained that the management exposure I received helped me understand how to make
informed decisions, and that having business insights alongside technical knowledge is valuable in
today's era. I felt that this answer aligned well with their expectations.
Finally, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked follow-up questions to both interviewers, which
helped end the conversation on a positive note.
[ 12 were offered the role, though everyone's HR round went well O]
[3 more students were selected after a week, so a total of 15 students were offered the role.]
My Placement Journey:
During the internship season, I couldn't clear the OAs for Trilogy, Barclays, UBS GOTO Internship,
and Mahindra Finance.
JPMC CFG Summer intern: only way that jpmc hire for tech roles
The OA difficulty was easy to medium: Rotating array/problem and String-based problem.
I solved almost both questions and received the Al interview link the following week.
One thing I noticed was that I attempted both tests on the last day. I followed the same strategy this year
for the CFG Software Engineer role and again received a comparatively easier version. Although our team
performed well during the CFG Hackathon, I wasn't selected for the internship. Looking back, one possible
reason could be that my strongest backend skills were in Python (FastAPI), while my team primarily
preferred JavaScript, which limited my ability to contribute at my full potential and this yr CFG didnt
happen
Russell Investments: first company where I cleared the OA. The entire process happened in a single day:
OA + Technical + HR
The shortlisted candidates were announced in batches throughout the day. Since nothing was announced for
several hours, I assumed I had been rejected and stopped revising. Around 4 PM, I was unexpectedly called
for Technical Round 1 and I couldn't clear. One important lesson I learned: Never stop preparing until you
receive an official rejection from that company.
Now placement season,
JPMC FinTech Role: I applied because the role matched my profile well: it required Python, SQL, and
problem-solving skills. Unfortunately, I couldn't clear the OA. The questions felt extremely difficult (almost
CAT-level aptitude), and the proctoring was very strict. Even looking down while writing on paper triggered
"Face not detected" warnings, making it difficult to solve longer questions comfortably.
PhonePe: The OA was heavily focused on DSA problems(Binary Search + Graph + DP). I couldn't clear it.
AuxoAl: The shortlist was largely based on CGPA, Class 10 and 12 marks, and OA performance.
The MCQs were straightforward for almost everyone. The coding section had three questions, and I solved
around 1.5. During the interview, I experienced anxiety because it had been a long time since my previous
interview. I also couldn't revise properly that day, and my interview was scheduled in the last slot (around 4
PM) putting me in waitlist. The interview was with a consulting guy so focused on guesstimates and
business reasoning.
Some questions included: Travelling salesperson scenario, Profit and loss calculations Restaurant revenue
estimation, Pizza sales on a Saturday night, Car pricing, What is attention? SLM vs LLM. Unfortunately, I
wasn't selected.
UBS :
--- PAGE 7 ---
It consisted of multiple stages. Complete the UBS 2 test on that day itself increases the early shortlist.
OA (Pen and Paper): Easy SQL questions, Predict/correct output, Basic system design and performance
failure scenarios
Group Assessment: The key takeaway was that they were more interested in thought process and
communication than implementation. Speaking up, contributing ideas, and collaborating effectively
mattered much more than arriving at the perfect technical solution. Btw they didnt need technical
implementation.
Interview: It started with an intro and brief about a project. Then moved to technical questions which
covered:
SQL Outer Joins, CAP Theorem, Git Pull vs Git Fetch, Caching layer in a Legal Al system, Handling
production failures, Monolithic vs Microservices, Redis vs Redis Cluster, Docker, Kubernetes And in
technical also asked some HR questions like:
What are your master's plans?
What would you do if you're assigned work that doesn't excite you?

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Aim to keep your CGPA above 8.5. A 9+ CGPA is generally the safest zone for meeting eligibility

criteria across most companies.

• Before applying to any company, share your resume and the Job Description with ChatGPT and ask

for a resume match analysis. Alternatively, you can use Resume Worded and aim for a score of 70+.

• Stay active on your TPO WhatsApp group and Superset. Check them once a week and don't miss any

placement opportunity.

• Practice OA using IndiaBix, Sanfoundry, Career Ride and make use of Chatgpt and Claude to

generate tougher questions. Focus on understanding concepts instead of memorizing formulas.
Strong OA performance often helps you get an earlier interview slot.
(Lang - specific question, SQL, (OS+CCN rarely) , aptitude, DSA)

• For DSA, prepare thoroughly. Being comfortable with Trees and Graphs is usually sufficient for

many companies, but it's best to complete the entire DSA and DAA syllabus to maximize your
chances.

• Know your resume inside out. Be prepared to explain every project, skill, technology, and term

you've mentioned. Interviewers may also ask questions beyond your resume. In my experience, until
the ISS interview, my resume was rarely discussed, the questions were mostly from core subjects and
concepts I had studied during college end-semester exam preparation.

• DSA : https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z, Daily Leetcode

• GFG puzzles: Top 100 Puzzles Asked In Interviews - GeeksforGeeks

• DP : Aditya Verma playlist

OOPs: Kunal Kushwala

• OS + CCN + DBMS : Gate Smashers (Watched during ESE)

Mobile: +91 9321327417 (more preferred)
LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/vaishnavi-lakade-039529290/
ALL THE BEST !

journey.howSecured:
Rounds:

1. Resume Shortlisting

2. Online Assessment

3. Technical Interview

4. HR Interview

1. Resume Shortlisting

The process began with resume shortlisting. It was mostly done on the basis of CGPA. I would
advise to maintain a CGPA of at least 8.0 or 8.5 to get shortlisted in most companies. Also tailor
your resume according to JD. Around 121 students were shortlisted after this round.

2. Online Assessment [121 students ]

There were four sections in this round: Logical reasoning, Quantitative aptitude, Coding, Verbal
ability. Each section was timed.
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Logical reasoning: 15 questions were to be solved in 15 mins. Fairly straightforward

questions like direction, age, decoding names, etc. were asked.

2. Quantitative Aptitude: Ratio-proportion based, mixtures, work and time type of

questions were asked. 15 mins were allotted to this section. You get approximately 1min
to solve each question, calculators were not allowed in this section and most other OAs
that I had appeared. Therefore, practice solving aptitude questions under time constraints.

3. Coding Section: 45 mins were given to this section. I had 2 easy questions so I could

complete it within 15 mins and pass all the test cases.

1. Remove vowels from a given string.

2. Given an array of numbers. Initially amount-0 add the number from array to amount if

that number is divisible by x.
Some of the applicants had also got questions where they had to use HashMaps, Priority
Queue and other data structures. DSA was asked in almost all the companies so do not
skip it!!

4. Verbal Ability: In this section simple english vocabulary questions like synonyms,

antonyms, grammar based questions like what is correct sentence for the given
sentence,etc. There were also paragraph based questions.
Solving standard IndiaBix questions was enough for logical, quantitative and verbal section. I
had also referred to career ride youtube channel for preparing aptitude.

3. Technical Interview [ 35 students ]

The shortlist for interviews arrived on 6th August in the evening. We had interviews the next day
at around 10 AM. There were 2 interviewers in each panel. My interview lasted for around
20-30mins. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself. The introduction is important as it
can decide what the interviewer will ask. Highlight your strengths in introduction. The
interviewer asked me if I was comfortable with JAVA. Java was my primary language so I
said yes. They asked me about OOP. I explained OOP highlighting examples in short. Then I
was asked about 4 pillars of OOP: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance.
Then I was asked to implement each of these four in code. I was also asked to implement
runtime polymorphism. Difference between compile time polymorphism and runtime
polymorphism and how compile time polymorphism internally works. Then they moved to
SQL. They asked me to write a query for finding 2nd highest marks in the students table.
This was a pretty easy question. I answered with 2 approaches. Then they asked me what
normalization is, what are relations in tables (1to 1, 1 to many, etc.). I was asked to draw
tables and establish many to many relation in it. So I created a students table, course and
enrolls table. Then they looked at my resume and asked me about different databases I had
--- PAGE 3 ---
used. (I had used Pinecone, MongoDB, PostgreSQL and Redis in my resume). I was asked
why and how I used them in my projects and what is the difference between them. I was also
asked to write MongoDB schema I had used in my project and sample queries in MongoDB.
I could draw the schema (in BSON format) but I had completely forgotten about the query
syntax. I told them I could not recollect the syntax. Then they asked if I would be willing to
relocate as they had no office in Mumbai. I said yes. Then they asked if I had any questions
for them. I asked them what was the biggest challenge they encountered in a project at
Transunion. They said it was handling massive data. This was the end of the interview.
Useful Tip:

1. Don't miss these topics at any cost as they will be asked in almost all companies: OOPs,

SQL, Aptitude, DSA.

2. Know every line of your resume. You should have a justification for why you used a

given tool in your project.

3. It's ok to not know something in an interview. If you don't know something, accept it.

4. Your selection also depends on what interview panel you get, so luck is involved. Give

your best in every interview!

5. No tool is better than ChatGPT when it comes to revising for an interview. You can

prepare for your projects, HR questions, MCQS using ChatGPT.

4. HR Interview [11 students]

I was called for the HR round at around 1:30 PM. There were 3 interviewers in my panel. The
interview began with a warm greeting. The HR asked me to introduce myself. She went through
my resume and particularly liked the name I had given to my project: "PyscheLens. She asked
me why I gave this name and why it is important to give meaningful names to projects. I was
also asked to explain this project. I answered it in the form of a story and the interviewer was
very impressed. Then she asked me about the group projects on my resume and how we divided
the work among ourselves. Then the interviewer asked me about my family, if I had any plans
for higher studies. Then she asked me if I was willing to relocate. Finally they asked me if I had
any questions. I asked them what growth at TranUnion looks like and what I should prepare if I
get selected. The interview lasted for about 15 mins. 10 students were selected after this round
and I was one of them.

1. Use the STAR method to answer situation based questions.

2. Try to explain your projects to HR in the form of a story.

3. Do ask questions at the end. It shows that you are curious about the company.

--- PAGE 4 ---
Lastly, I would say that the placement journey is not easy. There will be days when you prepare
your heart out and still receive a rejection. After a few rejections, you may start questioning
yourself, your preparation, your abilities, and even whether you will get placed at all. I know this
feeling because I have been there too. But remember, those difficult moments are also the
moments when you are being tested. They are teaching you patience, resilience, and the ability to
keep going even when you don't have any guarantee that things will work out. So, do not give
up. Believe in the preparation you have put in. Believe in the skills you have built. And most
importantly, believe that one rejection cannot decide your future. I got my TransUnion offer at a
time when I expected it the least. I had already experienced enough rejection to feel exhausted,
and I wasn't even expecting this opportunity to work out. But sometimes, life surprises you when
you have almost stopped expecting it to. So keep applying. Keep preparing. Keep learning from
every interview. Keep grinding, even on the days when you don't feel like it. You never know
which opportunity will finally be the one that changes everything. And when things don't happen
according to your plan, trust the process. What God has planned for you is good, often better
than what you could have planned for yourself. Sometimes the door you desperately want to
open doesn't, because there is another door waiting for you that you couldn't see yet. So don't let
rejection make you believe that you are not capable. Your journey is different, your timing is
different, and that's okay.
Keep faith. Keep working. Keep showing up. Your opportunity will come.
If you ever need any guidance regarding placements, interviews, resumes, or preparation, please
feel free to reach out to me at
Contact: 7709341361
LinkedIn: Valencia Dmonte

The placement process was quite different from that of other companies visiting our campus. Since
Capgemini was visiting our campus for the first time, we had no idea what to expect. Moreover, we noticed
that the company had changed the test format this year, so practising previous years' questions was not very
useful, TBH.
PROCESS:

1) English Communication Test (28th Sept 2026, retest on 1st Oct 2026) (both from home)

2) Assessment Test (28th Sept 2026) (from home)

3) Brief Presentation ( 8th Oct 2026)( from college)

4) Online Assessment (8th Oct 2026) (from college)

5) Interview (8th Oct 2026) (from college)

1. [English Communication Test] [Everyone who applied were eligible ]

This test was conducted twice and in both times there was slight change in the format of the test and yeah
the change was not that good. The test that happened on 28th Sept there were technical issues faced by many
in our colleges so due to which a retest was conducted. The test duration was just 1 hour so managing time
was the key, since there were a lot of things to be covered in the given time but the test difficulty was from
easy to medium but it was lengthy.
The test format was:
1 Reading Comprehension: A reading comprehension passage was provided, similar to the ones we
encounter in board exams, followed by five MCQS. However, the passage was quite long and contained
--- PAGE 2 ---
some filler and fancy words. Make sure that even if you don't understand these words, you can at least
understand the overall context of the sentence.
My passage was about a research study involving time-zone-based clocks, and five MCQs were asked based
on it.
2 Email Writing: There were 2 email that we had to write, one was formal and the other was informal (it
wasn't mentioned but since you all have given boards you will understand automatically)
I had written email in the these format:
Subject:
Para 1 : Intro
Para2: Conveying what is asked
Para 3 : Conclusion
Regards/Thanking you
Name
This was the format I used. Make sure you manage your time wisely, as a word limit was specified for each
email, and your response had to stay within that limit. Also, make sure you write naturally and don't use any
external tools, as the test instructions included a disclaimer stating that submissions would be checked for
plagiarism.
3 Listening Comprehension: Around 2 or 3 questions were there where an audio would be played and based
on that audio you have to answer the mcq question, pretty straightforward and easy section
4 MCQ: Eight standard grammar-based MCQs were asked. Most required us to identify the grammatically
correct sentence or choose the correct tense or verb.
This section was easy, but make sure you understand that sounding correct and being grammatically correct
are two different things. Don't make the same mistake I did! I realised my error when I rechecked my
selected answer.
5 Essay Writing: This section was not present in the original test. However, during the retest, two MCQs
were removed and this section was added. We had to write two essays: one of around 100-200 words and
another of around 300-400 words.
Note: The disclaimer about plagiarism was also included here
You must attempt the test smartly because mcq's are quick to wrap up, so I finished mcq and then I
attempted email as both were of 10 marks each and afterwards I attempted essay because each essay was of
just 1 marks only lol.
--- PAGE 3 ---

2. [Aptitude Assessment] [ Everyone who filled the form]

This is not the regular aptitude which you give in the other company's OA, this was completely different
one, it had around 6 to 7 sections and each section had its own time limit. It was conducted on the AON
platform.
It was not tough but it was based on pure memory retention and it's last section was just normal hr
questions.
Few Questions that I can recollect are:

• One section showed multiple balls in different frames. In each frame, a particular ball would

light up, and at the end, we had to identify the order in which the balls had lit up.

• One entire section was like a game involving multiple blocks, a ball, and a hole. We had to

move the ball into the hole using the minimum number of moves by rearranging the blocks.

• There were some other memory-retention games and true-or-false questions, such as

identifying whether a pattern was symmetrical.
The last section was untimed and consisted of HR-related questions. Each question presented two opposing
options, and we had to choose which side we preferred. We could select either extreme or a slightly
moderate option on either side. However, we couldn't remain neutral by choosing the middle; we had to
answer every question.
Many students encountered errors during this test, and I was one of them. For some reason, the particular
error I faced did not seem to affect anyone else. I had already completed three sections, so I was afraid to
refresh the page. However, the error persisted for almost 1.5 hours, so I eventually logged out and logged
back in.
To my surprise, I was able to complete the remaining sections. There was a specific time window during
which we were allowed to log in. Surprisingly, I was able to log in even after closing the application
following the 1.5-hour error, while some other students were unable to do so. I would consider myself lucky
in this situation.
A retest was conducted for the specific group of students who had been unable to complete the test.

3. [Online Assessment] [ 77 were shortlist ]

Before this round, at 8 a.m., we attended a brief presentation about the company, followed by a briefing
about the test. The interview was scheduled to take place on the same day.
The online assessment was conducted on HackerEarth through Superset. It consisted of four rounds, each
with different time limits and problem-solving requirements.
At the beginning, we had to select a technology or language option, such as React, Node.js, Django, or
Spring Boot. This selection determined the framework used in the subsequent Al debugging and
function-development questions.
--- PAGE 4 ---

Round 1: Basic DSA - 30 minutes

I received a HashMap question that was simple but somewhat tedious. I had to use three HashMaps to solve
it. Initially, I was unable to pass all the test cases, but eventually, I managed to clear them all.
When you are unable to pass some test cases, you might become anxious. During such moments, it is
important to stay calm so that you can identify the bug and fix it.
The question involved domain names and request IDs. Another table contained queries being sent to those
domain names through router IDs. We had to count the number of requests received by each domain through
the respective router IDs. I cannot recall the exact question, but it involved counting requests, updating the
counts, and returning a list of lists.
Other candidates also received questions related to hashing, so no DP or graph questions were asked.

Round 2: Prompt Engineering - 15 minutes

We were given a problem statement and had to write a prompt that would be passed to an Al assistant. The
Al would then generate a solution, and we had to ensure that it passed the test cases. This section was
essentially designed to test whether we could write an effective prompt within a short time, especially since
the expected output had to follow a specific format. I was able to pass all the test cases.

Round 3: AI Debugging - 35 minutes

We were given a buggy application based on the framework we had selected at the beginning of the
assessment. An Al assistant was available to help us, but it did not directly provide the complete solution.
My suggestion would be to ask the Al assistant general questions about the codebase and the flow of
execution rather than immediately asking it to fix the bug.
I started by asking which files handled the relevant logic, including the controller, entity, and repository.
However, since it had been a long time since I had independently debugged a development project, I was
unable to pass even a single test case.
Eventually, even the Al assistant started providing generic explanations instead of answers specific to the
given codebase.

Round 4: AI Function Development - 30 minutes

The same repository that we had been given for debugging was used for the feature-development round. We
had to implement a new feature, and after several attempts, I managed to pass one test case.
An Al assistant was provided for this round as well, and it worked similarly to the one provided during the
debugging round.
--- PAGE 5 ---
4 [Interview] [ Only 6 were shortlist ]
There was only one interview round, which was entirely technical; there was no separate HR interview.
There were three panels, and each panel interviewed two candidates.
I was the last person to be interviewed by my panel. I was not particularly nervous because I had attended a
few interviews before and had also participated in mock interviews. When I realised that I was about to be
called in, I took a sip of water to clear my throat and took a deep breath. I knocked on the door and asked,
'May I come in, sir?
He welcomed me with a smile and asked me to take a seat. He asked for my resume and invited me to
introduce myself. He then examined my resume very closely. I had completed a two-month remote
internship, and he commented that two months was too short and that I should have worked for a longer
period. Before I could explain the circumstances, he started reviewing the projects listed on my resume. He
asked about their tech stacks and functionality while I explained them.
Meanwhile, I was wondering whether the comment about my internship had created a bad impression.
However, I focused on making the most of the remaining interview time. He then explained the interview
structure: I had to draw the architectures of all three projects on paper, explain them, and then discuss my
internship.
Make sure you know your projects inside out. If you cannot answer questions about your own projects, it
creates a very bad impression, so avoid making this mistake. Along with preparing your introduction, make
sure you understand how you would scale your projects.
I took my time explaining each component and covered everything I could about the projects, including the
motivation behind building them. Make sure you keep explaining things even when the interviewer asks you
to draw or write something. For example, while drawing the architecture, I explained what happened after
each request and how the different components interacted. After I had finished explaining my second project,
he stopped me and said that was enough for the day. He then told me that the interview was over.
At that point, I was confused about why he had stopped me even though he had said that I would be
explaining all my projects and discussing my internship. I wondered whether I had not performed well
enough. However, he then asked whether I had any questions for him.
I ended up asking him four questions about his role, his experience at Capgemini, and whether freshers were
given live projects. Before asking my final question, I said, "Sir, this is the last question I wanted to ask
you." He laughed and said that I could ask as many questions as I wanted.
I was still not entirely satisfied with my interview performance. However, before leaving the room, I
thanked him for giving me the opportunity. We shook hands, and he said, "If everything goes well, I'll see
you once your semester is done." This was like a huge relief for me.
The result was declared eight days after the interview, and I had finally secured a placement! A total of four
students received offers. Initially, five students had been selected, but one of them accepted an offer from
another company.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Useful Tip and My Placement Story:
FIRST THING LET ME TELL YOU VERY HONESTLY, THE PLACEMENT PROCESS IS NOT
VAGUE, BUT EXTREMELY VAGUE, AND LUCK PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE.
Sometimes, you won't even understand why things are happening the way they are. Then, suddenly, the next
day, you might find yourself placed.
Do not compare anyone's journey with yours because your path is completely different. Sometimes when
you look around you will see people getting placed and you are still fighting yourself everyday to secure a
placement but trust me that too shall pass dont worry. I had two or three friend groups, and in all of them, I
was the only one left to get placed. The rest of my friends had secured placements during the initial months
of the placement season.
Placements started in early June, with the first company visiting our campus. I wanted to get placed before
college reopened, but unfortunately, I couldn't. Once college started, I wanted to get placed before the
mid-semester exams, but that didn't happen either. Then, I hoped to get placed before Ganesh Chaturthi, but
I was still unsuccessful. Eventually, I stopped having expectations and started believing that whatever
happened would ultimately be good for me. Finally, I got placed during Navratri, which I consider very
auspicious.
I interviewed with Dolat Capital, where candidates with strong C++ skills were required. I had studied C++
for just one day before the interview, yet I cleared almost two interview rounds before being rejected in the
second technical round because I lacked experience with C++. My primary language is Java. After that, I
was rejected in the final round at Edra Labs. Then came Capgemini, where I finally secured a placement.
I started learning DSA after completing my second year. Although I started late, I was fairly confident in my
DSA skills because I remained consistent. Many people will suggest that you try competitive programming. I
tried it too, but I wasn't motivated enough to continue, so I stuck to LeetCode, which I honestly believe is
sufficient for placements.
Since I started DSA late, I missed opportunities in my second year when companies hired students for
internships that could lead to PPOs . Therefore, I would advise you to start DSA in your second year itself.
By then, you will already have a foundation in coding from your first year. However, even if you start late,
as I did, don't worry. Just stay consistent. Despite starting late, I was able to solve more questions than many
other candidates.
For the Dev part I would say that try taking parts in hackathon because the projects you build there are some
real life problems and companies love candidates who understand real world problems and are eager to solve

I was unable to clear the OAs of several companies, which was very disheartening. Trust me, I know how it
feels. However, don't let small rejections undermine your confidence in your skills. Even if you feel
vulnerable, take a break of two or three hours if needed, and then get back in the game.
Mock interviews will help you a lot, so try to participate in as many as possible. During the placement
process, you may be assigned mentors who are already working in the industry. They are there to guide you,
and if you ask them, they may even conduct mock interviews for you. I participated in almost three mock
interviews.

themselves and can give you advice that no one else probably can.

journey.prep:
An interview is not just about how much you know, but also about how well you can communicate and
display what you know. You can have strong technical knowledge, but if you are nervous, unable to explain
your thought process, or try to give answers you think the interviewer wants to hear, it may not come across
properly. That is why I would suggest focusing on the non-technical aspects of interviews as well. These are
just as important as technical preparation and can make a big difference in how your interview goes.
I have listed the non-technical tips first because I genuinely think they are important, followed by the
technical preparation that helped me.
Non Technical Tips :

• Be confident during the interview. It is completely okay to not know everything, and it is okay to

make mistakes. Accept them, learn from them, and move on. Don't let one mistake affect the rest of
the interview.

• Remember that the interviewers are not your enemies. They are generally very helpful, so don't

hesitate to ask for hints or clarify your doubts. Knowledge is important, but that is not the only thing
--- PAGE 6 ---
they are looking for. Your willingness to learn, passion for what you do, and readiness to explore
new things matter a lot as well.

• If you feel that the interviewer is taking the conversation in a direction where you don't have much

knowledge, be honest about it. You can also ask if you can discuss another topic or project that you
are more confident about. One of my friends did exactly this. After feeling that her interview had not
gone well, she asked the interviewers if she could talk about one of her projects instead. They
allowed her to do so, and she ended up getting selected.

• Don't claim to know things that you don't. Be confident about what you actually know. Sometimes

interviewers may intentionally question your answer or make you feel like you are wrong to see how
you react, so don't immediately doubt yourself if you are confident in your answer.

• Be honest and real with the interviewer. Don't try to suck up to them or give what you think is the

"perfect" answer just because you think that is what they want to hear. Let them understand who you
actually are.

• Don't be nervous and overthink the interview. Just prepare well, give it your best, and move on. You

will get what's meant for you.

• Don't get too attached to one particular company. The placement process can be very unpredictable,

and constantly worrying about one company can become an unnecessary mental distraction. Focus
on each opportunity as it comes and keep moving forward.
Technical Tips :
You probably already know the basic resources for DSA and interview preparation, but I am attaching my
notes and some resources as well, just in case they are useful. My biggest suggestion is to stick to one good
source and complete it properly. Don't try to cover every resource available online because you will mostly
end up wasting time switching between them.

• For DSA, unless you are specifically aiming for companies like PhonePe, Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet

is more than enough for most companies. Try to finish it at least 2 months before the placement
process starts. After that, focus on solving random questions, revising concepts, and getting
comfortable with problems you haven't seen before.

• Know your resume inside out. Don't fake anything or add things just because they look good. Be

realistic about what you know. You should be able to explain even the smallest details of every
project, internship, or experience mentioned on your resume.

• Don't put every technology you have ever touched under your skills. Mention things you have

actually worked with and have at least some confidence in. Interviewers can easily pick something
from your skills and start asking questions about it.

• Be ready to explain why you chose the technologies and frameworks used in your projects. Don't just

know how to use something - understand why you chose it over other options and what problem it
solved.

• Make sure your CS fundamentals are strong. At the very least, revise DBMS, Computer Networks,

OOPs, and Operating Systems. These basics come up frequently in technical interviews.

• Practical experience is much more useful than only having bookish knowledge. Get your hands dirty

and actually build things. If you don't have good projects, build something. It really doesn't take that
much time these days to make a decent project, and the experience you get from building and
debugging something yourself is much more valuable.

• Be prepared for basic system design as well. You don't necessarily need to know advanced system

design for every company, but you should understand how to break down a system into components
and explain the decisions you make.
--- PAGE 7 ---

• Practice SQL properly. I would recommend doing LeetCode's SQL 50. Make sure you actually

understand the queries instead of just memorising solutions.

• Keep C++ or Java as your primary programming language for DSA and interviews. Pick one and

become comfortable enough that you can focus on the problem rather than struggling with the
language syntax during the interview.
The overall goal should be to finish your main preparation well before placements start. Once the basics are
covered, use the remaining time to practise, revise, and improve your problem-solving rather than constantly
starting new resources.
I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work." - Thomas Edison
Yes, you've seen this quote in college, and so have I. It was written on one of the doors in college, and for
some reason, it really stuck with me. A lot of what I have learned throughout college has come from failing,
making mistakes, trying again, and figuring out what works. I genuinely believe that failing is one of the
best ways to learn.
So don't be afraid of getting things wrong. Try things, make mistakes, learn from them, and keep going.

journey.howSecured:
Resume shortlisting was the first stage of the process, with around 100 students selected for the interviews.
Having good project experience and a strong resume seems to be preferred, so it is important to highlight
relevant projects, internships, technical skills, and any practical experience clearly.

• Round 1 - Rapid-fire MCQ round covering programming, CS fundamentals, and basic coding

concepts under a strict time limit.

• Round 2 - API debugging round focused on debugging, backend concepts, and implementing a new

API module.

• Round 3 - DSA and schema design round covering problem-solving, optimisation, database design,

and system concepts.

• Round 4 - HR round focused on background, projects, work culture, and work-life balance.

• Round 5 - Culture fit round focused on situational questions, decision-making, motivation, career

goals, and workplace expectations.

1. Rapid Fire MCQ Round - (around 100 students appeared) - 10 minutes - 10:00 AM

Round 1 was a rapid-fire MCQ round conducted through Google Forms. There were around 60 questions to
be attempted in just 10 minutes. The questions were mainly code-based and covered C++, Java, and Python,
with basic loops, conditions, and output-based questions. There were also questions on CS fundamentals like
OS, OOPS, Computer Networks, and basic data structures and their working. Overall, the questions were
quite easy and focused mostly on basic concepts.
The main challenge was the time limit. There were a lot of questions, so the key was to move quickly and
not spend too much time on any single question. When the timer was close to ending, I had not even reached
one-third of the questions. So, don't overthink the questions. There will be many easy ones that you can
answer immediately without spending much time. I think I was able to attempt around 20 questions.

2. APL Debugging Round - (52 students) - 30 minutes - 11:30 AM

Round 2 was an API debugging round. There were multiple options for the tech stack, including Django,
FastAPI, Node.js, and I think Go. There were 4 slots with multiple panels, and I was in the 1st slot. The
interview was conducted on Google Meet, and I joined from the conference room opposite the TPO. There
were 2 interviewers, both SDE 2s.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Most of my latest projects are built using FastAPI, but I chose Node.js for this round because I feel it is
easier to work with and has fewer complications. It was also the technology I started my backend journey
with, so I was more comfortable with it.
They shared a link that gave access to a VS Code environment. The project was something like a student
records management system, and there was a README file with all the instructions. They first asked me to
run the server. It did not start properly, so I had to debug it. I immediately found the first bug: the config was
not declared correctly. It needed to be declared using const and then exported. I was not completely sure
about the exact syntax, so they allowed me to Google it.
The next bug was in the get students route. The route was supposed to return all students, but it was
returning only one student by ID. I checked the type of data being returned from the route and noticed that it
was an object instead of an array. I fixed it so that the route returned an array containing all the students.
After that, they asked me to create a new module for marking student attendance date-wise. I first explained
my approach and then copied the existing student module files and started making the required changes.
They seemed satisfied with my approach and understanding of the code. They then asked how I would check
whether a student had already been marked for a particular day and prevent duplicate attendance. I
suggested keeping the student ID and date together as a primary key, so duplicate entries for the same
student and date would not be allowed. They were satisfied with the answer.
I was almost done writing the code when the time was about to end. They asked me where I would register
the new route after completing the module. I was able to point out the exact file and explain how I would
register it. They said okay and then asked if I had any questions.
I asked them what the company was doing to compete with platforms like Naukri and Indeed. They
explained that WorkIndia targets a different audience, mainly focusing on blue-collar jobs. After that, the
interview ended.
After the round, I got to know that this was the exact same question that had been asked the previous year as
well. I had no idea about this during the interview, so I just solved it normally based on my understanding.
So, if you can, it is better to prepare for questions from previous years as well.
One important thing I would suggest is to just keep talking and don't get tensed. The interviewers are very
helpful, so don't hesitate to ask for hints if you get stuck. It is completely fine to ask. The round is more
about your concepts and approach than remembering the exact syntax.

3. DSA and Schema Design - (16 students) - 40 minutes - 4:20 PM

Round 3 was a DSA and schema design round. There were 16 students split into 2 slots. I think the students
in the 1st slot were the preferred candidates because they were fast-tracked, while students from the other
slot were eliminated. I was in the 1st slot. We were told to go for lunch and come back by around 3:30. The
results were announced by around 4. Google Meet links were sent and we joined from the interview rooms
in the TPO. Some people started around 4:10, while my interview started around 4:20 because they were
still figuring out the rooms.
There was a single interviewer. I think he was an SDE 3. He first introduced himself and then asked me to
introduce myself. After that, he asked me to share my screen and shared a Google Doc with me. The
document had 2 questions, and he asked me to attempt the first one.
--- PAGE 3 ---
The first
question
was
based
on
the Trapping Rain Water problem:
https://leetcode.com/problems/trapping-rain-water/description/. The way it was initially explained was a
little unclear to me, so I asked a few questions and used examples to clear my doubts. I first explained the
brute force approach, where I would find the previous greater element (PGE) and next greater element

(NGE) for every element using loops. This would take ON?) time. He asked how I understood that I needed

to find the PGE and NGE for every element, and I explained that these values determine the level of water
that can be stored above each position.
I then moved to a better approach where I would pre-calculate the PGE and NGE information and then use it
to calculate the water height. This takes O(2N) time and ON) space. He asked me to write the pseudocode
on the Google Doc.
Then he asked if I could optimise it further. I explained how I could combine the PGE and NGE process into
a single iteration and calculate the heights while popping elements from the stack. This gives ON) time and
ON) space. He asked me to make the necessary changes to my code.
He then asked if there was any further optimization possible. I initially couldn't remember it, but then the
two-pointer approach struck me. I explained that I could keep left and right pointers and move them towards
the centre while calculating the trapped water. This gives ON) time and O(1) extra space. For anyone
preparing, the two-pointer approach is worth understanding properly. There is a good explanation of it by
Striver here: https://youtu.be/1_5VuquLbXg.
I fumbled a little while writing the final code, but I started working through examples while coding, and the
interviewer understood that I had the approach right. He said okay and moved on. There were 2 questions in
the document, but he did not ask me the second one. By around 4:40, the DSA part was done.
After that, we moved on to schema design. He shared another document with a scenario for a food delivery
platform similar to Swiggy. The requirements were to store restaurant information, their menus, customer
details, and orders. I also had to account for cases where multiple restaurants operate from the same physical
location, like cloud kitchens.
I started by listing out the different entities and then defined the relationships between them. I also added the
appropriate primary and foreign keys, including composite keys wherever required. He seemed pretty
satisfied with the design.
He then made the problem slightly more complicated by saying that an order could contain items from more
than one restaurant and involve multiple drivers. I made the necessary changes to keep the design as
decoupled as possible and avoid storing repeated or redundant information. The idea was to structure the
relationships properly rather than duplicating the same information across multiple tables.
He then asked how I would implement a driver tracking system. This felt more like a system design question
than a schema design question. I explained that instead of continuously polling the server, I would use
WebSockets to maintain a connection and push location updates to the customer regularly. He was satisfied
with the answer.
He then asked if I had any questions. I asked him about his experience working at the company, and after
that the interview ended. I was out by around 5.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Overall, this round was quite fast for me. It took around 40 minutes, while some of my friends' interviews
lasted around 70-90 minutes.
The key for this round was to keep speaking and explain whatever I was thinking. In DSA, always start with
the brute force solution and then work your way towards the optimised solution. In schema design, don't be
afraid to make changes if you realise something needs to be changed. Try to keep the design decoupled and
avoid redundant information. If you make a mistake carly in the schema, you can get trapped when the
interviewer starts adding more complications to the problem.
Most importantly, be very open with the interviewer and don't hesitate to ask questions or clarify your
doubts.

4. HR Round - (6 students) - 40 minutes - 5:15 PM

Around 5 minutes after my DSA and schema design round, I got a call from HR saying that I was moving to
the HR round. I was asked to join at 5:15.
The interview started around 5:20 and was mostly like a casual conversation. He first introduced himself and
then asked me to introduce myself. He also asked me about my favourite project. I talked about the project
that had helped me win the SE Hack. I explained the full story of how it started as a challenge that my team
decided to take up, even though we had zero knowledge about the topic, and how we managed to figure
everything out and crack it that night.
The questions were mostly basic and nothing out of the box. By around 5:40, the main interview was done
and he asked me if I had any questions. I asked about the work-life balance and work culture. He was honest
and said that the work can be a little fast-paced. He also explained why some deployments are done at night,
which can sometimes cause work to extend late.
We ended up talking about this for around 20 minutes, and the interview finally ended at around 6.

5. Culture Fit Round - (6 students) - 50 minutes - 6:15 PM

In the previous year, the HR round was the last round, so I thought my interview process was over. However,
around 5 minutes after my HR round, I got another call from HR saying that I was selected for the Culture
Fit round and had to join by 6:15.
The interview was with a single interviewer. I introduced myself and then he introduced himself. He had
been working for around 7 years. He started the conversation by explaining that WorkIndia is a fast-paced
environment and that things can sometimes get hectic. He asked if I would be comfortable handling that
kind of environment. I was honest and said that I don't mind putting in extra hours when required, as long as
I could expect some relief or flexibility in the following days.
He then asked me a few situation-based questions. For example, he gave different projects with different
conditions, where one could bring in a lot of money but was still under development, while another was
ready to ship but had lower returns. There were around 3-4 such conditions, and I had to choose which one I
would prioritise and explain why. In these kinds of questions, I don't think there is always a single right
answer. They are more about understanding how you think, how you prioritise things, and how you handle
different situations while also respecting decisions made by your seniors. He also asked what I would do if I
disagreed with my manager.
--- PAGE 5 ---
He also asked me about some of my highs and lows during college and the experiences that shaped me. I
answered honestly and explained the things that I felt had been the most important experiences for me
throughout college.
I then asked him about the learning curve at WorkIndia and what kind of projects I could expect to work on.
I was particularly interested in ML since I enjoy working on it and already had some experience in the area
He explained some of the different types of projects happening at the company and said there was scope to
work across different domains.
He was curious about why I specifically asked about the projects and what motivates me. I was honest and
said that both technical growth and financial growth motivate me. Since I had mentioned freelance projects
on my resume, he asked whether I had earned from them and whether financial growth was an important
factor for me. I explained that I had worked on those projects alongside college, mostly during my free time,
and that they gave me an opportunity to learn a lot while also earning some money on the side.
The conversation then became more personal, and he asked whether I had specific things in mind that
motivated me to earn. I said that I obviously had things I wanted to do, like travelling, buying vehicles and
getting some of the things I wanted, while also becoming financially independent and not having to rely on
my parents for everything. He then asked where I saw myself in 5 years.
Overall, this round did not really feel like a formal interview. It was more like a chill conversation where
both of us were asking questions and getting to know each other.
My main advice would be to not try too hard to say what you think the interviewer wants to hear. Be
prepared for the usual HR questions, but be honest and be yourself. Apart from helping you get through the
interview, it also helps you understand whether the company and its work environment are actually a good
fit for you.
I was the first person to have all my rounds completed, at around 7 PM. There were still people in their HR
and DSA rounds when I finished. The results were announced the next day at around 6 PM, and 5 students
were selected.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Vedant Agarwal
Computer Engineering

Company: J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. (JPMC)

Job Profile: Corporate & Investment Banking (CIB)

1. Resume Shortlisting

The first round was resume shortlisting. Although JPMC never disclosed the exact criteria, from what we
observed, factors like your Class 10 and 12 marks (there seemed to be an unofficial 80% cutoff), CGPA,
relevant projects, internships, certifications (I had completed CFA Level I), and the overall quality of your
resume all seemed to matter.
Preparation

• Tailor your resume according to the role you're applying for.

• Make sure you're comfortable explaining every single point on your resume.

Tips

• Keep your resume clean, concise, and free of grammatical or formatting mistakes.

• Check your ATS score using Resume Worded. Don't stress too much about the score though-I

know people with scores around 60-70 who still got shortlisted.

• Don't add skills or projects just to fill space. If it's on your resume, be prepared to talk about it in

detail.

2. Online Assessment (From Home)

Duration: 45 minutes
The test consisted of:

• Basics of Finance & Accounting (10 questions): Financial ratios and basic corporate finance.

• Market Awareness (10 questions): These weren't necessarily finance-based. Many were simply

current affairs and business news. (Few questions were very random so do not worry about them. For
eg, i had a question "What is the duration of long crops according to Kisan Credit Scheme")

• Quantitative Aptitude (15 questions): I practiced from IndiaBix → General Aptitude → Arithmetic

Aptitude, which was more than enough.

• Verbal Skills (10 questions): Sentence arrangement, grammar, graphs, averages, and similar

questions.
Preparation

• Revise your finance fundamentals.

• Stay updated with current affairs and business news. I personally read The Economic Times daily for

about a month before the test.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Tips

• Time management is really important, especially in the Quant section since some questions can be

lengthy.

• If you're stuck on a question, move on and come back later instead of wasting too much time.

3. Group Discussion (Online - Zoom)

The GD topic was shared a day before, so everyone had enough time to prepare. On the day of the interview,
we were divided into panels of around 6-7 students each.
My Experience
Our panel wasn't a traditional GD where everyone keeps jumping in. The panelists asked questions, we had
to raise our hands on Zoom, and they picked people to answer. They also made sure everyone got a chance
to speak at least once.
I spoke twice, for around 30 seconds each time. Since everyone gets the topic beforehand, most people end
up preparing using the same resources (and ofc ChatGPT), so naturally a lot of the content overlaps. I'd
suggest trying to speak within the first two or three people so your points haven't already been covered.
From what I telt, they weren't really checking whether your content was unique-they were looking at how
well you listened to others, whether you could build on someone else's point, and how confidently and
clearly you presented your ideas. If you know the answer to a question, raise your hand confidently. At the
same time, don't interrupt others or try to dominate the discussion-it leaves a bad impression.
Tips

• Focus on making meaningful points instead of speaking the most.

• Listen carefully to what others are saying and build on their ideas whenever possible.

• Stay calm and communicate clearly.

4. Technical Interview

My technical interview was actually much shorter than many other candidates. (around 10 minutes)
Questions Asked

• Walk me through your resume.

• What's the difference between Investment Banking and Commercial Banking?

• How do Investment Banks earn fees?

• Guesstimate: Assume India has a population of 1,000 people and you're the only supplier of TVs.

Nobody currently owns a TV. Estimate how many TVs you would sell.
Preparation
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Revise everything you've mentioned on your resume.

• Be ready to explain your projects in detail.

Tips

• If you don't know an answer, don't panic. Just explain your thought process they're often more

interested in how you think than whether you reach the perfect answer.

• Ask at least one question at the end. Since I had completed CFA Level I, I asked about the CFA

culture at JPMC and whether employees are encouraged to pursue the higher levels while working.
S. HR Interview
The HR interview was much more conversational than the technical one.
Questions Asked

• Tell me about yourself.

• Tell me about your family background.

• If you were the interviewer, what three qualities would you look for in a candidate?

• How do you handle a conflict?

• Explain the case study competition that you won.

Preparation

• Prepare the common HR questions beforehand.

• Read about the company, its values, and any recent news.

Tips

• Be genuine. Don't try to give textbook answers.

• Wherever possible, support your answers with examples from your own experiences.

• Prepare a couple of questions for the interviewer. I built on the question I'd asked during the

technical interview and asked why JPMC reimburses CFA exam fees for employees who clear the
exams while working there. It turned into a nice conversation.
Useful Tips

• The waiting time between rounds can honestly be more stressful than the interviews themselves. Try

to keep yourself busy by watching something or keep revising. In my case, the waiting time
throughout the day was longer than all my interviews combined, so I ended up watching Suits to take
my mind off the anxiety.

• Personally, I prepared for the following questions as well:

o any recent IPO, MnA, stock you would recommend

• JPMC share price, JPMC full form, JPMC values

o Current NIFTY, SENSEX, gold, silver, brent oil prices
--- PAGE 4 ---

• All current RBI and US-Fed rates (repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, MCLR, inflation targets -

just check them on the RBI official website)

• Foreign exchange rates (US-INR, EUR-INR)

• Know your resume inside out.

• Don't lose confidence if one round doesn't go exactly how you expected.

• Lastly, just be polite, humble, and communicate your thoughts clearly. That goes a long way.

Useful Links:

* [VedantAgarwal_Resume.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1fp8GkOCDJVb4FkqR41yrpTI8jZMfvRxR/view?usp=drive_link)

1. OA

2. Level 1 Technical Interview

3. Level 2 Technical Interview

4. Level 3 Technical Interview

5. HR/Cultural Fit Round

Eligibility Criteria:
CGPA > 6.75, 10th & 12th > 60%, EXTC not allowed
My Resume.
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. OA [165 Candidates were shortlisted based on the company's internal criteria]

Consisted of 3 Sections:-

1. Aptitude (15 questions, 20 mins)

There were all sorts of questions on stats, probability, reading paragraph and answering questions. There
were also visual imagination questions, like suppose if I break a cube open on each of its edges, how will
that look. Each side of the cube had a unique design.
I didn't practice aptitude at all as I didn't have time. You should definitely practice, because the
questions might be easy, but doing them in the time limit is challenging. Maine khudne 4 questions thoke
the. I have read from the interview experience of my seniors that IndiaBix is a pretty good platform for
aptitude, I never opened it though.

2. Core + Other general CS questions (25 questions, 30 mins)

DBMS, OS, OOPs questions were there. Also there were questions on types of APIs, flowchart was
given and you had to tell the output, some mutex/locking code was given and you had to predict the
output.

3. DSA (2 questions, 40 minutes)

Q.1 Literally the same question, just in a story form
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/maximize-path-sum-from-top-left-cell-to-all-other-cells-of-a-given-
matrix/
Other similar questions to practice
https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-path-sum/description/
https://leetcode.com/problems/unique-paths/
https://leetcode.com/problems/unique-paths-ii/
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/problems/gold-mine-problem2608/1
Q. 2
A positive integer N is said to begin with X if the decimal representation of N starts with the decimal
representation of X. Given two positive integers X and Y, find the smallest positive integer that begins
with X and is divisible by Y. If X is already divisible by Y, then X itself is the answer.
Example:
Input:
50 3
Output:
501 3
Explanation:
Numbers beginning with 50 are:
50, 500, 501, 502, ....
The first one divisible by 3 is 501.
Similar pattern practice questions
https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/260/A
https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/490/C
--- PAGE 3 ---
Now comes the interview section. I wouldn't recommend doing what I did. I raw-dogged the entire
interview process. I never gave a mock interview, didn't even prepare a self-introduction, and simply
walked in and spoke whatever came to my mind. I was completely frank from start to finish in every
round. Even for the HR round, I didn't prepare answers for the common questions, I just answered
honestly based on what I genuinely felt and thought.
I hadn't touched DBMS and OOPs since third semester. So whenever I got the chance to overkill my
answers during the interview, I did it to compensate for the fact that I wasn't very confident in these
subjects. Thankfully, I was asked DBMS and OOPs questions only in the first round, so again, luck
played its role. For eg. One of the questions I was asked in one of the tech rounds was, how do you
automate infrastructure provisioning. Explained the entire architecture of Terraform, the files (main.tf,
variables.tf,
outputs.tf, providers.tf, terraform.tfstate, .terraform.lock.hcl ...etc),
commands,
Idempotency, etc.
I also noticed that the interviewers in L1 were expecting a simpler, high-level understanding of the
technologies mentioned on my resume, particularly Cloud and DevOps. The reason I went into so much
depth was that I had a strong understanding of these technologies, especially at the operating systems
and networking level. However, this approach can easily backfire if you don't know significantly more
than what you've already explained. It was a high-risk, high-reward strategy.

2. L1 Tech Round [40 students were initially shortlisted, 10 more were added after a day of the initial

shortlisting, so 50]
First, I was asked to introduce myself.
OS:- What is Thrashing? What is Paging? What is the difference between Thread and Process
(overkilled, explained the types of threads, task_struct,... etc).
CCN:- What is the difference between TCP and UDP (overkilled, explained QUIC in detail too), What
are the use cases? What are the OSI layers?
DBMS:- Design a student management system, they kept adding the requirements as I was designing.
After the final design, they asked me to write a query to fetch all the students who have never failed and
have CGPA > 8.
OOPS:- As I didn't have Java in my resume, they asked very basic questions. What are the 4 OOPs
principles? What is multilevel Inheritance(I was not able to answer this)?
Cloud & Devops:- Architecture of K8S, How do you ensure that a minimum number of pods are always
up? HPA, what is Ingress in K8S(I was not able to answer this)? How do you automate infrastructure
provisioning(overkilled)?
GoLang: - What is the difference between slice and string(overkilled, explained the underlying structure
of a slice and array, then string)? What are goroutines(overkilled, explained the entire GMP model)?
DSA:- https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-substring-without-repeating-characters/description/
Gave 2 approaches, first using map and then a slice of 128 size, map lookup time is O(1) but still
hashing and resolving the collisions takes time.
--- PAGE 4 ---

3. L2 Tech Round [22 students were shortlisted for this round ]

This round was mainly focused on my projects, so I'll only mention the parts that weren't
project-specific. While answering questions about my projects, I was cut off 2-3 times because I was
going a little too deep into the explanations. During the interview, I was asked about my hobbies and my
favourite sport. I said Table Tennis, and we ended up having a brief conversation about it. I was also
asked about the motivation behind one of my projects, so I explained the entire story behind it.
To start, I was asked which question from the previous round I had been unable to answer. I said I
couldn't recall what Kubernetes Ingress was. He then asked me to explain it, and I answered. This was
followed by a question on reverse proxy and forward proxy (overkilled it). Based on my answer, he
asked where TLS operates in the OSI model (overkilled it again by explaining the entire packet lifecycle
along with the OSI layers). After that, I was asked to introduce myself.
The remaining questions were: What is Blockchain? Explain it as if you were explaining it to someone
with no technical background. Explain RSA (I wasn't able to recall it properly, but I said whatever I
could). What is the difference between hashing and encryption? (overkilled it). What is Event-Driven
Architecture? (overkilled it). The last question was to write an API template for one of my project's
functions/features. I didn't really understand what he meant. I asked him 3-4 times whether he wanted
me to write code or draw a diagram, but I still couldn't understand what he was expecting. In the end, he
simply asked me to write a cURL request and then asked where the API key would be passed in the
request.
After that, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked three questions, all of which were based on
points covered in the company's presentation and their projects.

4. L3 Tech Round [10 Students were shortlisted for this round]

This round was conducted online by a very senior engineer. I felt that this round went quite bad, I was
traumatized. So I don't remember much of what happened in this round. It lasted 20 mins, I'll just write
what little I do.
I was first asked to introduce myself. Then I was asked how Go differs from Java, followed by several
follow-up traumatizing questions on Java (probably because I hadn't prepared Java at all). After that, I
was asked about my favourite engineering subjects, and I answered Cloud Computing and Physics. This
led to follow-up questions on cloud and on-premise infrastructure, the cost of running each, which one
would be a better choice in different scenarios, and related topics. I was then asked why a company
needs a DevOps engineer, followed by several cross-questions based on my response.
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I asked the same 2/3 questions that I had
asked in L2, along with one new additional question.
--- PAGE 5 ---

5. HR/Cultural Fit Round [The same 10 students gave this round]

This round was conducted about 5 minutes after my L3 interview. The first question I was asked was
how my previous interview rounds had gone. I answered honestly, and after that, we had a casual
conversation on a variety of topics. This round lasted for around 20-25 minutes. The HR-related
questions that I remember are listed below:-

1. If your manager constantly micromanages you, for example, asking for updates every 10 minutes and

not trusting you, what would you do? I first asked whether the manager had always been like that or had
become that way after I made a mistake. The interviewer replied that the manager had always been like
that. She also mentioned that the manager belonged to the Boomer generation, she (the interviewer) was
a Millennial, and I was Gen Z, so there could be differences in ideologies and work styles.

2. Suppose you have a strict deadline to deliver an application to a client, but a few days before the

deadline, you realize that the product cannot be delivered on time. What would you do?

3. What are your future plans and long-term goals?

4. You probably have an account with another bank. If you could change one feature of that bank, what

would it be?

5. Have you ever been in a situation where one of your teammates simply wouldn't listen while working

on a team? If yes, how did you handle it?

6. Why do you want to join us? What do you like about us? What motivates you?

After all the interviews were over, I called home and told them that it was over for me because of how
badly I felt my L3 had gone. About 20 minutes later, I found out that the first four shortlisted candidates
had been selected. Another 10 minutes later, those four candidates were called to Room 105 by the Head
HR, and I was one of them. She informed us that we had been selected. Later, I came to know that I was
the first shortlisted candidate, which was completely unbelievable given how I thought my L3 had gone.
The interviews concluded around 21:40, and everyone had left by 21:50 PM. The next four selected
candidates were announced online at around 22:30 PM.

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk - 24 June 2026

• Resume Shortlisting

• Online Assessment - 27 June 2026

• Technical Interview Round 1 - 03 July 2026

• Technical Interview Round 2 - 03 July 2026

• HR Interview - 03 July 2026

• Result Declaration - 03 July 2026

1. Pre-Placement Talk and Resume shortlisting

The recruitment process started with an online Pre-Placement Talk conducted on 24 June 2026. During the
session, the company provided an overview of its organization, various teams, the Corporate Risk team, the
internship opportunity, and the qualities and skills they generally seek in candidates.
My Tip: Pay close attention during the pre-placement session, as the information shared can be useful
throughout the selection process. It is a good idea to note down important points and, if there is a Q&A
session, make use of the opportunity to ask relevant and thoughtful questions.
Following the session, interested students were required to submit their applications through the JPMorgan
Chase Careers Portal using the link shared by the TPO. The submitted applications were then reviewed by
the company as part of the initial shortlisting process.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Candidates who were selected for the Online Assessment were informed about their shortlisting on 26 June
2026 at approximately 5:30 PM.

2. Online Assessment (122 shortlisted candidates)

Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
(The photo provided by ced before test)
The Online Assessment was conducted from home on 27 June 2026 using a company-designated proctored
platform. The assessment was remotely monitored through continuous video recording, while the screen was
locked to ensure that candidates could focus solely on the test. Tab switching and access to other
applications or browser windows were restricted throughout the assessment.
The test consisted of 30 questions with a +2/-1 marking scheme.

• 27 Questions: Quantitative Aptitude

• 3 Questions: Probability and Permutation & Combination

The aptitude section consisted of questions ranging from easy to moderate difficulty, with some questions
requiring a level of understanding comparable to basic CFA concepts. The questions were not extremely
difficult, but having a strong grasp of fundamental concepts was important for maintaining both speed and
accuracy.
For preparation, I referred to resources such as IndiaBix and BodhiPrep. I also followed the CareerRide
YouTube channel, which helped me strengthen my fundamentals and improve my approach to solving
aptitude questions efficiently.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 | 32 Students appeared for this round]

The interviews were conducted across 7 panels, each consisting of two interviewers. My interview lasted
approximately 20-25 minutes.
The interview started with "Tell me about yourself." I had prepared a 2-3 minute introduction covering my
background, skills, projects, achievements, and key points from my resume.
The first technical question was unexpectedly about Al-whether I knew about it, had used it, and had
worked on any Al-related projects. Since I had mentioned an Al project on my resume, I was able to explain
--- PAGE 3 ---
it confidently. I was then given a practical scenario: how AI could help employees or HR teams manage a
large number of emails and ensure that important emails are not missed. I could answer this well
because I had recently worked on a similar project. Even without prior experience, I would recommend
thinking through such real-world problems logically and explaining the system design clearly.
The next panelist asked system design questions, including how I would design a matrimonial website and
the architecture of an ATM system. Since I had listed Java in my technical skills, I was also asked questions
on Java fundamentals. I was asked some basic questions on python on the libraries that I used in my projects
and questions like why this specific library and not the other one.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 [15 shortlisted candidates]

My interview for this round lasted around 22 minutes. It started with a brief introduction, after which I was
asked detailed questions about my internship, including:

• What exactly did you work on during your internship?

• Explain the complete architecture of the project.

• Why did you choose a particular technology/system for the backend?

• How did you implement the frontend?

Since I had completed a Software Development internship, the interviewer focused on understanding both
my technical contribution and the reasoning behind the technologies I used.
I was then asked to write a SQL query, which was LeetCode Medium SQL problem. After that, I was
given a Python-based problem involving how to open and process a large Excel file of more than 10 GB,I
was aksed to write a code for it on pen and paper.
The interview then moved to my projects. I was asked to explain each project in detail. One of my Data
Analytics projects, Job Market Analysis, particularly caught the interviewer's attention. I was asked what
technologies and libraries I had used, why I had selected them, and to walk through the entire project step by
step. I was also asked about the errors or challenges I encountered during development and how I identified
and solved them.
Another important question was why, as an Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering student, I
had chosen to apply for this role. (EXTC students should be prepared for questions like this).
Towards the end, I was asked if I had any questions for the interviewers. I believe it is always a good
practice to ask relevant and thoughtful questions, as it shows genuine interest in the role and the
organization, so I made sure to ask a question as well.

5. HR Interview (10 shortlisted candidates)

The final HR round had around 10 shortlisted candidates and was easily the most relaxed and informal
interaction of the entire selection process. It began with a short introduction, followed by a conversation
focused mainly on my willingness to relocate and my overall personality and suitability for the role.
The HR also discussed practical aspects of the job, including shift timings, working hours, and whether I
would be comfortable working longer shifts. Unlike the earlier rounds, there was little emphasis on
--- PAGE 4 ---
technical questions, with the conversation primarily aimed at understanding the candidate on a personal and
professional level.
The HR interviews concluded at around 5:00 PM, and the final results were announced between 7:50 and
8:00 PM.
All 10 candidates who appeared for the HR round were selected and received internship offers.
