journey.prep:
1. Keep your options open. I initially intended to sit only for pure technical roles and had been

extensively preparing for them. At the same time, I was always open to exploring other
opportunities. I hadn't specifically prepared for non-tech roles, but unless it's a complete no-no for
you, I'd definitely recommend sitting for JPMC. It's one of the best opportunities we get on campus.

2. Understand the role and its progression. Do note that this Fintech role eventually transitions into a

Junior Analyst role after receiving a PPO. Keep the long-term progression of the role in mind and
decide accordingly before applying.

3. Use the few minutes before the interview wisely. Since our interviews were online, we got a

minute or two before joining the Zoom meeting. I used that time to calm myself down and gather my
thoughts. It often gets quite chaotic outside the TPO, so taking a moment to settle yourself before the
interview really helps.

4. Be yourself during the interview. Speak naturally instead of trying to fit in technical jargon

wherever possible. Using buzzwords without fully understanding them can land you in trouble if the
interviewer decides to explore them in depth.

5. Learn to breadcrumb the interviewer. At the same time, you can subtly guide the direction of the

interview. For example, DCF valuation is something that would normally be expected on the resume
of a Banking candidate rather than a Fintech one. I intentionally built a project around automating
that workflow and prepared every concept related to it thoroughly. This allowed me to steer parts of
the interview towards topics I was comfortable with. Breadcrumbing simply means introducing a
concept or technical term in your answers that is likely to catch the interviewer's attention and
naturally lead the next question in that direction.

6. Never judge your interview yourself. After my first technical interview, I genuinely wasn't

confident about my chances. Although I answered most of the questions, I found the interviewer
quite intimidating and he hardly gave away any reactions. He smiled only towards the very end when
I asked him about his journey at JPMC. At one point, he even thought I was using a calculator during
a mental math question, whereas I was just making calculations on paper. I had to show him my desk
to reassure him, and that was probably the second time he smiled. The rest of the interview was
completely poker-faced, so I walked out thinking I hadn't done well.

7. Make use of the time between rounds. While waiting, I had already started looking at other

opportunities on Superset, assuming I wouldn't make it through. Then, out of nowhere, I received a
call asking me to be ready for the next round. That experience taught me never to assume the
outcome of an interview. The time between rounds is extremely valuable. Use it to revise your
concepts instead of overthinking what went wrong.

8. Prepare good questions for the interviewer. Have at least 2-3 thoughtful questions ready. Avoid

asking the usual generic questions that interviewers hear all the time. Listen carefully to their
responses and ask meaningful follow-up questions based on what they say. It turns the interview into
a genuine conversation and leaves a much better impression.

9. Smile and tell stories during the HR interview. For the HR round, keep the widest smile possible

on your face. Try to answer questions using small anecdotes or experiences rather than giving
one-line responses. Stories make your answers more memorable, authentic, and convincing.

10. Get enough sleep before the interview day. We received the interview shortlist quite late the

previous evening, and I ended up pulling an all-nighter preparing for the interviews. Looking
back, I wouldn't recommend doing the same. The interview process is long, mentally
demanding, and can be quite exhausting, so getting a good night's sleep beforehand will help
you stay focused, think more clearly, and perform consistently throughout the day.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Final Thoughts
As we all know, a significant amount of luck is involved in the placement process. There are only so many
things that are within our control. What we can control is the effort we put into every opportunity that comes
our way. There will be times when shortlists feel unfair. There will be moments when you genuinely believe
you did everything right but still don't get the outcome you hoped for. That's a part of placements, and
almost everyone experiences it at some point.
The important thing is to never let one result define the rest of your placement season. Pick yourself up,
learn whatever you can from the experience, and move on to the next opportunity with the same enthusiasm.
Every interview teaches you something, and often the preparation you do for one company ends up helping
you crack another.
During this phase, surround yourself with the right people. The placement season can be mentally
exhausting, and having roommates, friends, seniors, and family who genuinely support you makes a huge
difference. Celebrate each other's successes, help one another prepare, and remember that everyone is
fighting their own battle.
Finally, enjoy the process.
Give every opportunity your best, stay curious, and trust that the Jigsaw will fall into place.
"Reach for the stars, so if you fall, you land on a cloud."
~ Kanye West - Homecoming (02:071
All the very best!

1. Pre-Placement Talk

2. Resume Shortlisting

3. Online Assessment

4. Technical Interview 1

5. Technical Interview 2

6. HR Interview

1. Resume Shortlisting [ 400+ appeared for this round]

The resume shortlisting for this role is quite rigorous, as comparatively fewer candidates are selected than
for other roles offered by the company. It is important to tailor your resume according to the job description,
focusing on relevant keywords, technologies, and projects that demonstrate automation and problem-solving
skills. For this role in particular, a strong academic profile is beneficial. While there is no official cutoff,
having a good CGPA along with consistently strong academic performance in 10th and 12th grade
(generally 80%+) appears to strengthen your chances of getting shortlisted.
Your resume should highlight relevant coursework, internships or work experience, certifications,
achievements, and positions of responsibility, which includes leadership roles in college committees or
organizations.
Since this is a Fintech role, including at least one finance-related project is highly recommended as it reflects
genuine interest in the domain. Personally, I took an extreme approach by keeping all my projects centered
around Fintech, machine learning, and automation, but a combination of finance-focused and technically
strong system design projects works equally well. Most importantly, include only those projects that you can
confidently explain end-to-end. For this role, interviewers place significant emphasis on concepts such as
data sourcing, data quality, data handling, analytics, visualization, and automation, so having a clear
understanding of these fundamentals is essential.
We got the final shortlist for OA a day before the test.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [ 34 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
The Online Assessment was another crucial elimination stage, with only around one-third of the candidates
progressing to the interview rounds. The test was conducted online from home and consisted of two separate
MCQ-based assessments.
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment (40 Questions | 60 Minutes)

• Section 1 & 2 - Quantitative Aptitude, Probability and Logical Reasoning (28 Questions):

These sections required proper problem-solving rather than direct formula application. The questions
covered topics such as Probability, Permutations & Combinations, Speed, Time & Distance, Time &
Work, Pipes & Cisterns, Percentages, Profit & Loss, Ratios, Averages, Number Systems, Logical
Reasoning, Blood Relations, Seating Arrangements, Syllogisms, Coding-Decoding, Pattern
Recognition, and Analytical Reasoning. A strong aptitude foundation and familiarity with common
solving techniques significantly helped in managing time.

• Section 3 - Coding MCQs (12 Questions): This section did not involve writing code but instead

tested programming fundamentals through code snippets. Questions included predicting the output of
programs, completing missing parts of code, recursion-based output questions, basic data structures,
arrays, strings, functions, loops, and language fundamentals. Some recursion questions were fairly
tricky and required careful dry runs before selecting an answer.
Paper 2: English Usage (10 Questions | 10 Minutes)
The second assessment was entirely English-based and comparatively easier. It included a short reading
comprehension passage followed by questions based on it, along with MCQs covering vocabulary, grammar,
subject-verb agreement, sentence correction, sentence arrangement, and ordering sentences to form a
coherent paragraph or story.
Overall, the first assessment was not as straightforward as it may initially appear and required strong
aptitude and logical reasoning skills. It is important to prepare Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning
seriously, as knowing standard solving patterns and shortcuts can make a significant difference. The coding
section also demanded patience, especially for recursion and output-based questions. For preparation,
platforms such as IndiaBIX and PrepInsta are more than sufficient, while the CareerRide Quantitative
Aptitude YouTube channel is widely used for conceptual understanding and practice. The English
assessment, on the other hand, was relatively easy and should not pose much difficulty with basic
preparation.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Technical Interview 1[9 candidates appeared for this round]

The interviews were scheduled for the very next morning, and all shortlisted candidates were asked to report
to the campus by 8:30 AM. Due to heavy rainfall, the interviews were conducted in online mode. There
were two interview panels, and my panel consisted of five candidates. The interview lasted for
approximately 30 minutes.
My interviewer was extremely interactive but equally intimidating. Interestingly, there was no formal
introduction; he immediately began by asking whether I had spoken to any seniors about the role and the
company. I would recommend doing so beforehand, as it demonstrates genuine interest and initiative in
understanding the role. I mentioned a senior I had interacted with, after which the interviewer questioned me
in detail about my understanding of the role based on those conversations. The discussion eventually became
two-sided when I asked him about the role and his day-to-day responsibilities, leading to an engaging
conversation.
The interviewer then shifted his focus to one of my projects that involved DCF valuation and the automation
of an equity research analyst's workflow. Since I anticipated questions on this topic, I had prepared
thoroughly. We discussed intrinsic valuation, discounted cash flows, WACC, its calculation, and the
reasoning behind each component. He then moved beyond finance concepts and explored the technical
implementation of the project, asking about the end-to-end workflow, data sourcing, the financial APIs used,
how the data was stored in a structured format, how financial ratios were computed, and how the final
valuation and peer benchmarking were performed.
One interesting discussion revolved around handling live market data. The interviewer pointed out that stock
prices are constantly changing and wanted to know how my system handled this challenge. I explained that
instead of continuously querying APIS, the application monitored rolling Z-score anomalies and refreshed
market data only when a significant deviation was detected, thereby optimizing API usage while ensuring
fresh data for valuation. He seemed satisfied with this approach.
Towards the end, he presented a practical scenario: given an Excel sheet containing financial data for peer
companies in the same sector, how would I build a complete analytics pipeline and an interactive dashboard
to generate meaningful insights? He expected a detailed end-to-end technology stack and implementation
workflow, and he cross-questioned the choice of every technology I suggested, making it important to justify
each design decision rather than simply naming tools.
The interview concluded with a few mental aptitude and reasoning questions, including calculations such as
102 × 98 mentally and finding the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock. For such questions,
it is important to think out loud and keep the interviewer involved throughout your reasoning process.
Explaining your approach often matters just as much as arriving at the correct answer, as it gives the
interviewer confidence in your analytical thinking. I concluded the interview by asking the interviewer about
his journey at the company and his experience working in the role, which led to a pleasant closing
conversation.
Out of the five candidates in my panel, two were shortlisted for the next round, while one candidate
progressed from the second panel, making a total of three candidates selected for Technical Interview
2.
--- PAGE 4 ---

4. Technical Interview 2 [ 3 candidates appeared for this round ]

The second technical interview was conducted next and I was the last candidate to be interviewed. The
interviewer was at a senior position and began by introducing himself in detail before asking me to introduce
myself and walk him through my resume. It is advisable to have a well-structured introduction prepared, as I
covered my coursework, internship, ongoing rescarch publication plans, and finally my projects. Rather than
simply listing them, I explained the motivation behind each project, the problem it aimed to solve, and the
journey that led me to build it.
The interviewer then focused on my multi-agent financial intelligence platform. He questioned why I had
chosen a multi-agent architecture instead of using a single large language model for the entire workflow. I
explained that the system was designed with specialized agents, each responsible for a specific task, closely
resembling how an actual equity research team operates. By performing stage-wise inference with dedicated
agents, human-in-the-loop validation, and specialized responsibilities, the system produces more reliable and
explainable results than relying on a single prompt handled by one large model. This discussion revolved
more around architectural decision-making than the implementation itself.
He then shifted to understanding my motivation for applying to the role. Since I come from a Computer
Science background and had completed a technical internship, he asked why I wanted to pursue a Fintech
role instead of a traditional software engineering position. This is a question worth preparing for, as the
interviewer expects a genuine and convincing answer. I explained my long-standing interest in the
intersection of finance and technology, highlighting how most of my projects revolved around financial
analytics, automation, and decision support. As a follow-up, he asked why I had not opted for a pure finance
or investment banking role if finance interested me so much. It is equally important to have a clear answer
for this question, explaining why the blend of technology and finance aligns better with your interests than a
purely finance-oriented role.
The interview also included a guesstimate question. I was asked to assume that the population of India was
1,000 people and estimate how many of them would have worn a tie at least once in their lifetime. For such
questions, the interviewer is not interested in the final number but rather in the structure of your thinking. I
was given time to think and explained the assumptions, segmentation, ratios, and factors I would consider
before arriving at an estimate. Throughout the process, I kept communicating my reasoning to the
interviewer, who even challenged one of my assumptions by asking whether gender should influence the
estimate. Once I had laid out a logical approach, he was satisfied and did not ask me to compute the final
value.
Towards the end of the interview, we discussed my internship in detail, including the work I had carried out,
the research aspects involved, and the publication that was currently in progress. This was followed by an
insightful discussion about the team's work culture. The interviewer mentioned that the role was not a
conventional 9-to-5 job and could be demanding at times, but he also emphasized that the team maintained a
healthy, collaborative environment with ample opportunities for learning and professional growth.
I concluded the interview by asking a few questions of my own regarding the technologies used within the
team, the nature of the work, and his personal journey at the company. This made for a positive and
engaging end to the discussion.
2 candidates were selected for the next round.
--- PAGE 5 ---

5. HR Interview [ 2 candidates appeared for this round]

The HR interview was the most relaxed round of the process and was primarily focused on assessing
whether you would be a good cultural fit for the team. My panel consisted of two interviewers from the HR
and Early Talent teams. They began by introducing themselves, after which I introduced myself. It is
advisable to slightly modify your introduction for this round by placing greater emphasis on your previous
work experience, leadership positions, extracurricular responsibilities, and personal interests rather than
diving deep into technical details.
The interview began on a light-hearted note when they asked how my day had been. I replied, "Exciting, to
say the least," and followed it up with a brief anecdote, which made both interviewers laugh and instantly
broke the ice.
One of the first questions was about my key takeaway from the pre-placement presentation (PPT). It is a
good idea to pay close attention during the session and make brief notes, as questions related to it can be
asked. I also referred to one of the speakers by name while answering, which reflected that I had been
attentive throughout the presentation.
The interviewers then walked through my resume and noticed that I had a Computer Science degree, a minor
in UI/UX, a machine learning internship, and was now interviewing for a Fintech role. They wanted to
understand the reasoning behind this journey. I explained that I enjoy exploring interdisciplinary domains
and have always been interested in applying technology to solve problems in different fields. I supported
this by discussing how my projects consistently revolved around the intersection of finance, automation, and
software engineering, which naturally led me to pursue this role. The conversation then shifted to my
positions of responsibility, where we discussed the leadership experiences I had gained through college
committees. They also took an interest in my hobbies, particularly music and the instruments I play, making
the discussion much more conversational than evaluative.
Towards the end, I asked a few questions about the internship onboarding process, the learning curve for
new joiners, and the opportunities available for growth within the organization. I also asked both
interviewers about their individual journeys at the company, following which they shared their experiences
and spoke about the collaborative work culture within the team. The conversation ended on a very positive
and engaging note, making it a comfortable conclusion to the interview process.
After the HR interview, we had to wait for the Banking role interviews to conclude before the results could
be announced. Our interviews were wrapped up by the afternoon, so it was a long wait until the evening.
Finally, the entire CCD team gathered to announce the results. It was a tense yet unforgettable moment, with
everyone anxiously waiting to hear their names.
2 candidates were offered the role.
Resources:

1. Resume

Make sure to align it with the JD.
Follow the standard: Jake's Resume Template.
Check ATS scores using: ResumeWorded.
--- PAGE 6 ---

2. Online Assessment

Complete aptitude, quant and reasoning practice can be done on websites like: India Bix, PrepInsta.
You can also follow Career Ride's YT playlist, if you prefer videos.

3. Technical Interviews

Know your projects inside out. This is probably the biggest takeaway for this role. Be ready to
explain everything from the overall workflow to why you chose a particular technology. The team
also uses tools like Selenium, VBA, and Alteryx extensively for automation-related tasks. If you
mention any of these on your resume, expect questions on them, so only include them if you're
comfortable discussing them in detail. OOPS concepts and python were also asked to other
candidates.
Prepare computer fundamentals well using GFG and InterviewBit, just in case.
For System Design:

1. HLD: Follow Gaurav Sen's playlist.

2. LLD: code WithAryan.

Note: For this role specifically, in depth system design knowledge is not a necessity. You should just
make sure that you can justify the design of your projects well with all its strengths and trade-offs.

4. Finance

For this role, you are not expected to know corporate finance inside out. What matters is that you
have a solid understanding of the financial concepts you have explicitly mentioned in your resume or
used in your projects. Be prepared to explain every financial metric, model, and term you have
included, along with the reasoning behind using them.
My biggest piece of advice is to make ChatGPT your friend throughout your preparation. If you're
relatively new to finance, don't hesitate to ask it to break down concepts to the simplest possible
level. Keep asking follow-up questions until you truly understand the "why" behind each concept. I
followed the same approach for my entire financial preparation, using it to build my understanding
from first principles, and it proved to be immensely helpful during the interviews.
Additionally, do prepare the basics of the financial markets, as a few candidates were asked simple
conceptual questions on terms such as NIFTY 50, BSE Sensex, NSE, NASDAQ, and other
fundamental market definitions. A basic understanding of these topics is more than sufficient.

5. Puzzles and Guesstimates

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Keep your options open. I initially intended to sit only for pure technical roles and had been

extensively preparing for them. At the same time, I was always open to exploring other
opportunities. I hadn't specifically prepared for non-tech roles, but unless it's a complete no-no for
you, I'd definitely recommend sitting for JPMC. It's one of the best opportunities we get on campus.

2. Understand the role and its progression. Do note that this Fintech role eventually transitions into a

Junior Analyst role after receiving a PPO. Keep the long-term progression of the role in mind and
decide accordingly before applying.

3. Use the few minutes before the interview wisely. Since our interviews were online, we got a

minute or two before joining the Zoom meeting. I used that time to calm myself down and gather my
thoughts. It often gets quite chaotic outside the TPO, so taking a moment to settle yourself before the
interview really helps.

4. Be yourself during the interview. Speak naturally instead of trying to fit in technical jargon

wherever possible. Using buzzwords without fully understanding them can land you in trouble if the
interviewer decides to explore them in depth.

5. Learn to breadcrumb the interviewer. At the same time, you can subtly guide the direction of the

interview. For example, DCF valuation is something that would normally be expected on the resume
of a Banking candidate rather than a Fintech one. I intentionally built a project around automating
that workflow and prepared every concept related to it thoroughly. This allowed me to steer parts of
the interview towards topics I was comfortable with. Breadcrumbing simply means introducing a
concept or technical term in your answers that is likely to catch the interviewer's attention and
naturally lead the next question in that direction.

6. Never judge your interview yourself. After my first technical interview, I genuinely wasn't

confident about my chances. Although I answered most of the questions, I found the interviewer
quite intimidating and he hardly gave away any reactions. He smiled only towards the very end when
I asked him about his journey at JPMC. At one point, he even thought I was using a calculator during
a mental math question, whereas I was just making calculations on paper. I had to show him my desk
to reassure him, and that was probably the second time he smiled. The rest of the interview was
completely poker-faced, so I walked out thinking I hadn't done well.

7. Make use of the time between rounds. While waiting, I had already started looking at other

opportunities on Superset, assuming I wouldn't make it through. Then, out of nowhere, I received a
call asking me to be ready for the next round. That experience taught me never to assume the
outcome of an interview. The time between rounds is extremely valuable. Use it to revise your
concepts instead of overthinking what went wrong.

8. Prepare good questions for the interviewer. Have at least 2-3 thoughtful questions ready. Avoid

asking the usual generic questions that interviewers hear all the time. Listen carefully to their
responses and ask meaningful follow-up questions based on what they say. It turns the interview into
a genuine conversation and leaves a much better impression.

9. Smile and tell stories during the HR interview. For the HR round, keep the widest smile possible

on your face. Try to answer questions using small anecdotes or experiences rather than giving
one-line resp

My solutions to questions in Technical Interview 1:

(1) To calculate the maximum attendance frequency for a student, first determine the college's total

weekly "student-day" capacity by multiplying its simultaneous class capacity (number of classes *
capacity per class) by the number of operational days per week. Next, sum the total number of
unique students across all years. Finally, divide the total weekly "student-day" capacity by the total
number of unique students. This quotient represents the average maximum attendance frequency per
student if the college fully utilizes its available capacity to maximize student presence throughout the
week.
Given the college has 4 classes with a capacity of 200 each, its total simultaneous capacity is 800
students. Over a 5-day week, the college can therefore accommodate a total of 800 students/day×5
days/week=4000 "student-days" per week. With year strengths of 600, 400, 300, and 200, the total
number of unique students is 1500. To find the maximum attendance frequency per student if all
available capacity is utilized, we divide the total weekly student-day capacity by the total number of
students: 4000 student-days/week/1500 students~2.67 attendances per student per week. This
implies, on average, students can attend classes approximately 2 to 3 days per week to fully utilize
the college's capacity.

(2) Primarily, order of numbers doesn't matter in addition or multiplication of two numbers. Next, if we

have to retrieve a value associated with some other value, hashmap or simply map is the fastest way
(O(1)) to do so. So we can build a top level hashmap consisting of operators as keys. Below them we
will have a hashmap, having a pair of numbers as the key and their operation as the value. For
addition and multiplication, we have to store both the pairs (a,b) and (ba)) for optimization.

1. Online Assessment

149) (Date: 27/07/25) (Time: 45 mins)

The OA was conducted on HackerEarth platform. It consisted of 20 MCQs and 5 SQL questions.
Weirdly, there were no DSA based coding questions. 20 MCQs were easy to test the understanding of basics
of Java, C++ and SQL, along with a few easy logical questions in the form of code behaviour / output. Next,
5 SQL questions were also easy if all the basic syntax (LIKE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, Aggregate
functions, Wildcards, etc.) are known.
I prepared for SQL through the w3schools website (https://www.w3schools.com/sql). They have
covered everything needed. Even though DSA questions weren't asked, solving them helped in the MCQs
section.
Overall, I think it was more of a test against time, as all questions were solvable with basic
understanding of concepts, but who did it faster made it to the next round. 38 candidates were shortlisted for
the next round through this round.

2. Technical Interview - 1

(No. of candidates:

38) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 30 mins)

Candidates assembled in the auditorium at 8 am for the presentation from the Barclays team. It was
important in terms of understanding culture and expectations of panelists.
My interview began with an introduction, where I described my technical skills and interests in
Competitive programming and Deep Learning. After reviewing my resume, the first question was about my
work at ISRO as an AI ML research intern. After describing my role and responsibilities, there weren't any
technical questions based on my work at internship. Next, the interviewer started asking about OOPS
concepts, which I felt were more relevant to Java OOPS. The questions included concepts like inheritance,
overloading, overriding, static, etc. Next on I was held with pen and paper, and had to come up with pseudo
code for 4 DSA like questions. The first two were easy, the next 2 were interesting based on real world
situations. Let me describe the 3rd and 4th questions. (1) We have to give the frequency (max attendance
possible) of a student in a college which has 4 classes with a capacity of 200 each, each year has the strength
--- PAGE 2 ---
of 600, 400, 300, 200 respectively. The college is operational for 5 days a week. (Try to think on your own,
else refer to my solution in the end). (2) The last question was about server optimization, where we had
simple function taking 2 integers and an operator (+, -, *, /) as input, if we had already calculated the
answer once, we should directly retrieve it from the database, else calculate and store it in the database. How
will you achieve it and which data structure will you use? (Try to think on your own, else refer to my
solution in the end).
Next, he moved towards SQL. Initial questions were easy, then he asked me to get the names of
employees with the second highest salary from the employees table, which I did using subqueries. But then
he asked me to achieve this without using sub queries, which i failed to do (Actual solution was to use
LIMIT and OFFSET). Next, he asked me if I knew React, I answered I know the basics but haven't built any
major project using it, so he skipped it. He asked me about git merge and git rebase. I have used and hence
answered about git merge being simply merging branches, but I wasn't sure about git rebase which I failed to
answer properly. Next, he ended the interview asking some HR questions, specifically about mistakes I
made during my recent ISRO internship, any help I requested from colleagues and about solving idea
clashes in a team.
Overall, it was a test of basic and core concepts across domains. 19 candidates were selected for the
next round, eliminating the remaining 19.

3. Technical Interview - 2

(No. of candidates:

19) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 15 mins)

The second round focused more on my roles in projects on my resume and my personal favourite
ones. The interview was conducted by one of the directors. He skimmed through the resume and asked me to
describe the project that I was closest to. I have worked on Precipitation Nowcasting using a modified Latent
Diffusion model for 7 months at ISRO and hence I was able to explain it with enough technical details.
Next, he asked if there is any other project I would like to describe. I briefed about the SIH winning project
which was about Deepfake Detection, and described the secondary SIH project in great detail, which was
about optimizing city traffic flow using Deep Reinforcement Learning and minimal hardware costs.
Next, he concluded by asking the number of people on the team in the described projects and asked
me if I had any questions. I had one concern about Barclays storing their data on AWS servers, which he
cleared explaining the security layers applied on them and the cost benefits of using AWS specifically.
Overall, it felt like both the technical and HR round, where both the parties had to know each other
better. 16 candidates were finally selected for the summer internship.

There were three rounds in total. The eligibility criteria were open to students from all branches with a
CGPA of 7.5 or above. The entire process was conducted virtually.
There were two roles: Software Engineering and Aladdin Data, and I applied for both. The interviews were
conducted through Webex, although candidates were required to attend them from the TPO office.
It was a pool campus placement process, with students participating from several other colleges as well,
including NIT Agartala, Manipal University Jaipur, and others.

1. Online Assessment [Around 280 people appeared for this round]

Everyone who met the eligibility criteria received the OA link via email one day before the assessment.
There were seven sections in total: Basic Coding, Advanced Coding,Basic Design Patterns, Advanced
Design Patterns, DBMS, Aptitude, Al and Reasoning
Each section was timed separately. Once a section was started, it could not be skipped or revisited until the
allotted time was over or the section was submitted.
Since we received the OA link a day in advance and could see the section names, I prepared Design
Patterns thoroughly because I had not studied them much before. The MCQs covered all 23 Gang of Four
design patterns.
For Basic Coding, I received a Java and OOP-based question. The problem involved a list of baggage items
with their destinations, where the bags had to be grouped by destination. If there were 10 or fewer bags, they
had to be processed sequentially. If there were more than 10, the list had to be divided into two parts,
processed in parallel using Fork/Join, and then the results had to be merged in right-to-left order.
Since Java is my primary language, I was able to solve it within the allotted 40 minutes.
For Advanced Coding, I received a Selenium-based debugging question. The codebase was fairly large,
and it took me some time to understand the existing code and the problem. Since the section had a 15-minute
limit, I was unable to solve the question.
The DBMS section was easy to moderate. It covered joins, keys, SQL queries, ACID properties, and general
database concepts involving technologies such as PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Oracle.
The Aptitude section was moderate to difficult, with questions on permutation and combination, ratios and
proportions, percentages, family relationships, seating arrangements, and similar topics.
--- PAGE 2 ---
The Al and Reasoning section was comparatively easier and could largely be approached using basic logical
reasoning and common sense.
The coding questions varied across candidates. Some candidates received two DSA questions, while others
received combinations involving OOP, debugging, or other coding concepts.

2. Technical Round 1[28 students for SDE and 9 for Aladdin Data]

1 received a call from HR at around 7:30 AM informing me that my interview was scheduled for 9:30 AM.
There were two panelists, and the interview started with them asking me how my day was going. I asked
them the same. They then asked me to introduce myself and asked about my minor in Banking Technology
from Barclays. I explained how the course developed my interest in the finance industry. I was also asked
about my opinion on Al-based projects and whether I would be open to working on them.
The interview then moved to a DSA question. I was asked to share my screen and open Notepad. The
interviewer gave me a string (consisting of lowercase letters and brackets) . I was supposed to reverse the
string whenever I encountered a matching pair of brackets till there were no brackets left, (basically valid
parenthesis but with a twist). I was asked to write the code and explain the dry run as well. I initially
approached the problem recursively, and then optimized the solution using a stack.
After this, I was asked how comfortable I was with Java and Python. I mentioned that Java is my primary
language and that I know the basics of Python. Since my solution involved Strings, the discussion then
moved into Strings in Java. I was asked several questions, including:

• Why did you use StringBuilder?

• What do mutable and immutable mean?

• Why are Strings immutable in Java?

• What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer?

• When would you use StringBuilder and when would you use StringBuffer?

• How are Strings stored internally in Java? Can you give an example?

I was able to answer all of these questions.
The interviewer then moved on to SQL. I was asked about the difference between the WHERE and
HAVING clauses. I explained what each clause does and gave an example. I also mentioned that HAVING
can be used without GROUP BY, so the interviewer asked me to explain this with an example. I was then
asked about the difference between a Primary Key and a UNIQUE constraint. The interviewer followed
up with a conceptual question: if we can simply use UNIQUE along with NOT NULL, what would happen
if there were no Primary Keys, and why do we need Primary Keys in the first place?
The discussion then moved to my projects. I was asked to give an overall explanation of my projects and
was asked why I had chosen particular technologies or methodologies for them.
I was also asked about my internship experience, including what I worked on and what I learned from it.
Throughout the interview, there were also behavioral questions, including questions about my future plans,
positions of responsibility, and how I respond to feedback.
At the end of the interview, I was asked whether I had any questions for them. I asked about their work
experience at BlackRock and the types of projects they work on.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I initially felt that my interview had not gone particularly well because the interviewer maintained a very
concise communication style and often responded briefly after my answers. The interview lasted around 35
minutes. However, shortly afterward, I received a call from HR informing me that I had been shortlisted for
the next round.
The first technical round was quite different for different candidates. Some candidates were asked two three
DSA questions, while others were asked questions related to React/Next.js or had a more HR-oriented
discussion.

3. Techno HR [ Around 18 ]

This round was different for everyone as well. For some candidates, it was purely HR-focused, for some it
was more technical, while others had a mix of both.
The interviewer started by asking how my previous round went. He then introduced himself and explained
what he does at BlackRock. After that, he asked me to introduce myself.
He then asked me to explain my favorite project in depth: why it was my favorite, what the project was
about, what motivated me to build it, and what problems I faced while working on it. I chose my DevOps
project, which also involved system design concepts.
He then asked me to explain a particular bug I had faced and how I solved it. This discussion eventually
led to me explaining my entire CI/CD pipeline in depth.
We also had a discussion around Redis, since I had used it in my project. From the way the questions were
framed, I felt that he was particularly interested in understanding how I approach a problem and make
technical decisions, rather than simply testing whether I knew the technology.
He then asked me: "If you could add ONE feature to this project, what would it be and why?"
The discussion then moved to my internship experience. He asked me how I handled feedback from
clients, how I managed deadlines, and how I had optimized my project.
I was also asked: "What is one use of AI in your life that you are really proud of?"
Another interesting part of the interview was a discussion around core values. I was asked to name three
core values I had learned during college and whether those values were already present in me before I
joined college. I was also asked about a situation where I had failed badly, made a comeback, and what I
learned from that experience. I discussed one of my hackathon experiences for this question.
Towards the end, the interviewer asked me if I had any questions for him. Since he had mentioned at the
beginning that he had been working at BlackRock for around 14 years, I asked him: "What are three core
values that you have personally learned during your time at BlackRock?" He really liked the question,
and we had a good discussion around it. I then asked him what would be expected of me during the first
few months if I were to join as an intern.
The round lasted around 50 minutes. One interesting thing about the process was that after the interviews of
all the initially shortlisted candidates were completed, they also started calling waitlisted candidates for
Round 1 for SDE role
--- PAGE 4 ---
Altogether 8 people were offered the job (7 SDE+1 aladdin data)
Resources:

• I started participating in LeetCode contests in my 6th semester, but I would suggest starting as carly

as possible. Contests helped me become comfortable solving problems under pressure and also
helped me deal with OA anxiety.

• I solved NeetCode 150 first and then moved on to complete NeetCode 250.

• LeetCode SQL 50 is MUST!!!!!!

• Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel.

• Core subjects: Academic notes, ChatGPT, and GeeksforGeeks(literally best)

• Aptitude: IndiaBix.

• DSA: Kunal Kushwaha and Nikhil Lohia's YouTube channels.

• I used to randomly read Medium articles during travel on technology and interview experiences.

This helped me stay in touch with recent technical concepts.
My fav article-
https://medium.com/@shivambhadani/system-design-for-beginners-everything-you-need-in-one-art
icle-c74eb702540b

• Know your resume inside out- every word. Be prepared to explain anything you have mentioned,

and don't mention technologies that you cannot confidently explain.

• Know your projects thoroughly. You should understand your projects, the decisions behind them,

and the different scenarios that can arise. Don't blindly build projects using Al without understanding
them in depth. Even if it is a group project, try to understand the entire project and not just the part
you personally implemented.

• An internship can definitely be beneficial, but if you haven't done one, don't let that discourage

you. Keep working on your skills, projects, and fundamentals.

• Try to maintain a CGPA of 8+. Personally, I would consider 8.5+ to be a safer target for keeping

MOST opportunities open. ( i missed few companies with a cgpa of 8.39)

• Participate in hackathons. Don't get demotivated if you don't win. The experience of building,

collaborating, and solving problems under time constraints is valuable in itself.

• Puzzles and CS fundamentals MCQS: GeeksforGeeks.

• If you get rejected from an interview, start working on the areas that went wrong as soon as

possible- ideally the same day or the next day.

• Before the interview go through the company website especially their values/principles, tailor your

answers accordingly. You can also take notes during PPT as they might ask stuff from that.
MOST IMPORTANTLY:
Don't ever feel that you are not prepared for an interview, you can never be fully prepared lol. I was asked
way less than what I had prepared, I kept myself up till Sam and just got 2 hrs sleep before the interview, pis
avoid this. Whatever you have studied, just answer confidently that's it. And if you dont know something
dont fake it, admit it honestly. Confidence, positivity and patience are the key. Placements are a
combination of hard work, preparation, and luck, but no matter how many rejections you face, don't forget
to show up every single day and keep working on yourself. You never know when it will finally be your
day, so don't stop believing in yourself. And always be happy and genuinely cheerful for others when they
succeed. Don't compare your journey with anyone else's. Everyone has their own journey, their own
timeline, and their own destiny.
END MEIN JO HOTA HAI ACHE KE LIYE HOTA HAI :))))
If you have any doubts, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn

Process Date:-

OA: 22nd August (Online from home on DoSelect platform)
Interview: 27th August (In-person in TPO)
Result: 31st August
Hello Guys, whoever reads this, this is the honest experience of my placement process. First of
all, dont be scared, dont panic, dont be anxious, actually be a little anxious it helps to stay
focused and keep improving yourself. My journey was like most of the students who got placed,
initially the resume was not being rejected, then I couldn't clear OAs. Before this interview I had
given only one interview that too just 2 days ago for a totally different role (consultant). So
leading to this interview I had zero hopes of clearing it. I was not good at DSA, I had completed
Striver's sheet till trees only, Graphs aur DP abhi karna baaki tha, Web Dev utna accha nahi aata,
bas ML aata tha woh bhi almost sabko basic aata tha (you will learn in 6th sem). Bas SQL aur
OOPs concepts acche se kiye the. I just answered their questions confidently, spilled out
everything I knew, and boom-I got selected. So, don't be disheartened, and most importantly,
don't compare your journey with anyone else's. Everyone has their own pace and journey.
[Resume Shortlisting]
Firstly we were shortlisted on the basis of our resumes. Till now what we had experienced is that
in the name of resume shortlisting mostly only our cgpa is considered. So please try to maintain a
high cgpa as possible. For this roughly everyone above 8 were selected. Koi kitna bhi bole
CGPA is very imp aur 8.5 ke upar rakhne ka try karo. Many of my friends and I were not
shortlisted in 2-3 companies because of this (aur mera cgpa 8.46 tha till sem 6).
OAL Around 120 students were shortlisted |
For OA we had:-

1) Aptitude - yaad nahi kitne questions the

2) 1 Coding question - a string was given, it contained alphabets and we were supposed to

compress the string, like 'aaaabbbcdeee' will become '4a3bcd3e' aisa.
--- PAGE 2 ---
We had 45 min to 1hr to complete.
Sources:-

1) OA ke liye Indiabix is the best to cover all the kinds of questions. Baaki try to solve them as

fast as possible. This helps us to recheck them later (if allowed) or gives us more time to do
coding questions (if applicable).

2) Coding ke liye ek hi sabko pata hai Striver's DSA sheet

Interviews Around 48 students were shortlisted
Interviews were after 1 week of the OA on 27th Aug. Pahele all of us settled in a room and we
were given pen and paper. And we were given 3 coding questions and were supposed to write its
solution on paper and submit it before the start of the interview.
Questions:-

1) Palindrome String

• Given a string containing alphanumeric characters, spaces, and punctuation,

determine whether it is a palindrome.

• Ignore spaces and punctuation; consider only alphanumeric characters.

2) Good String / Bad String

• Given a string containing lowercase alphabets and "?, determine whether it is

good or bad.

• More than 3 consecutive consonants or more than 5 consecutive vowels makes it

bad.
•i can be considered either a vowel or consonant.

3) Count Squares in an N × N Grid

• Given N, find the number of 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, ..., N×N squares contained in an N×N

square.
These questions were easy. I solved all three. The interview was conducted for all the students.
Tech Round 1:-
My turn came fairly early within the first 5 people. Firstly the interviewer introduced himself,
told about the company and what it does. He was from the data engineering team. He told some
more about what work he does and which tools he uses in his job. Then I introduced myself,
covered my interests, internships and projects. Then he picked one of my projects and asked me
what I did in it and some questions related to it like which database I used and why. He didn't
ask in too depth then he moved on to another project where I had used Devops tools such as
Docker, Jenkins and asked about it. I answered the questions and discussion moved on to SQL.
He gave me details of a table and asked me a few queries, a) Find avg salary of a department b)
Find departments with avg salary > 50000 c) Find department with 2nd highest avg salary.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Firstly I asked all the necessary details about the tables, like how many columns, what was the
primary key, etc and then I wrote and explained all 3 correctly. He was impressed how I
explained the 3rd one where I used the dense_rank window function and how it works and how
other rank functions work and I kept talking about whatever I knew about it. He then asked me a
DSA question, to find duplicates in an array. I wrote the solution on the paper explaining each
and every word I was writing. This not only helps you to show your thinking but also gives you
time to review your solution on the go. Also even if you make any mistake while writing then
don't panic. Explain to them the mistake, and correct your code. They appreciate this. Like in my
case, in my DSA question's solution, by mistake I looped into the vector again while pushing
duplicate elements in the answer vector, I was supposed to loop into the unordered map in which
I had stored the frequency of each unique element. In the middle of the solution I realised this
and corrected myself. The interviewer liked this thing. After he asked a few data related
questions such as what is batch processing vs batch streaming, database vs datawarehouse,
OLAP vs OLTP, I failed to answer OLAP vs OLTP as I didnt study it. I just told him I didn't
know about it. It is okay if you can't answer all the questions. Interviewers want to test your
approach and honesty along with your knowledge. I asked a lot of questions about the company,
about the role and what are the expectations. Companies love to talk about themselves (My
school friend who got placed in IDFC told me this
9). We even had a little conversation about
how Al developed and we as engineering students saw its growth, right from coding C and Java
in 1st year till Agentic AI. The round ended in about 30-40 minutes. He was very impressed and
he told me I did very well when I asked for my feedback. Do ask for it. I came out and was
called for the second round in 5 minutes.
Tech Round 2:-
In this round as well the interviewer introduced himself and told a little about his role. I started
with my introduction and project work like the first interview. He then picked a project and
asked about it in depth. It went for about 10 minutes and then he asked me a SQL question:-
SQL Question
Suppose you have a table called transactions with the following columns:
transaction_id
customer_name
transaction_amount
transaction_date
I want you to write a SQL query that returns:

• The top 10 customers having the highest total transaction amount.

• The result should contain customer_ name and their total_amount.

--- PAGE 4 ---

• After those 10 customers, there should be an 11th row with customer_name = 'Others'.

• The Others row should contain the combined transaction amount of all customers who

are not in the top 10.
For example:
customer_name
B
total_amount
95000
87000
J
42000
Others
315000
Initially I thought I couldn't do this but then I calmed myself and decided to start small. I first
told him about how I would write for top 10 customer_name using group by, order by and limit.
After this I thought for a minute and explained to him that to get the 'others' part I need to form
a query such as select customer_name NOT IN (those top 10). The interviewer told I thinking in
correctly direction and just hinted me to use the query which I had written for top 10. Then it
clicked to me, I could use CTE for it and I was correct. Now I was supposed to bring both these
parts together and after thinking for some time I remembered I can use UNION for it. The
interviewer just asked me what was the difference between UNION and UNION ALL not that it
affected my solution, just a side question. I told him that I didn't know and kept speaking loudly
about my approach for the solution. At the end he just helped me a bit and my solution was
correct.
Note:- See in any technical round it is very important that whenever the interviewer asks
you a solution to a question, you don't just think, you should also speak out what you think.
Keep speaking how you approach the problem and find a solution as it shows your problem
solving ability. I kept talking whatever I was writing and it helped me to explain my
approach in a better way.
After this he was happy with my ability to slowly build my solution rather than giving a direct
answer or giving up. I again asked a few questions to him regarding the expectations of a student
for this role. I also used up some points which I was told by the first interviewer and mixed all
those to keep the conversation going. This helps you to show the interviewer that you also paid
attention in the last interview and remembered the details. After this my second round was over
in about 30 minutes. Again within 2-3 minutes I was called for an HR round. Frankly for me it
was like in-n-out for those 2 hrs.
--- PAGE 5 ---

HR round:-

The HR round started with the senior HR manager introducing himself and asking me about my
family details, how many family members are there, where do I stay and am I comfortable in
travelling to the office. FYI, I live in Andheri East, so I was very close to the college, but the
office location was in Thane, Ghodbunder Road, which was quite far for me. Still, I said yes to
travelling. After this I just asked him how he traveled (Confidence dekho bhai ka
*). He started
talking about his professional journey for like 10-15 minutes. He asked me what my interests
were, why I wanted to become a Data Analyst. He asked me where do I see myself in the next 5
years and what is the impact of Al on Data Analytics and will Al take my job? For these
questions, I answered what came to me instantaneously. We can't decide these answers
beforehand and nor should we. We should give HR rounds like we are talking to a person whom
we know as it helps us to reduce stress and lets us give answers more openly. We should be true
to ourselves while answering these questions. At the end we shaked hands and he said good luck
for the future.

journey.prep:
1. Maintain a CGPA of 8.0+ - This is the eligibility cutoff for the initial shortlisting round for most

opportunities, with some having 8.5+

2. Know your basics well - Have good knowledge of OOP, Operating Systems, PnC, Probability,

SQL and the syntax of your preferred language (or the language the company focuses on) as the OA
and Interviews mostly focus on them. And try to look up interview puzzles online, i wish i had done
that, puzzles are really common in interviews. One more that comes to mind is 12 marbles riddle,
Ted-Ed has a series on logic puzzles, i think it might be helpful to do that.

3. Do DSA consistently - You don't need to go deep into competitive programming, but build a strong

foundation so that you can solve LeetCode Medium questions on your own.
I was able to pass all test cases in the first programming question and one in the second (where I used
a simple return due to time limits). I wasted too much time on the 20 MCQs before attempting
coding, so my advice is to attempt coding first since it carries more marks.
Resources: LeetCode 150, NeetCode 250

4. Match your resume to the job - Align your projects and skills with the role you're applying for.

Include moderately relevant or slightly unrelated projects if they're impressive or if you can
relate the skills learned to potential interview questions.
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Be ready to justify your choices - You should be able to explain your projects and answer questions

about the technical skills mentioned in your resume.

6. Write project titles like short summaries - Keep them clear and descriptive, since that's often

what interviewers notice first when scanning your resume.
Thank you and all the best for your placements.
~ Yateen Vaviya | Resume ]

1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Resume + Behavioural + Finance Knowledge Interview)

1.
Online Assessment [ 100+ candidates appeared for this round]
The online assessment consisted of a 1-hour MCQ and programming test conducted on the
HackerEarth platform. It comprised a total of 22 questions: 20 MCQS focused on mathematics and
logical reasoning, and 2 programming problems. Each MCQ carried 4 marks, while each
programming question carried 20 marks.
Eligibility to appear for the assessment required a minimum CGPA of 8.0.
The mathematics and logical section featured questions based on permutations and
combinations, probability, and ratios with a few questions on filling the blank line of code or
predicting output of a given program, with several problems involving colored balls and
wine-water mixing ratios. Not entirely sure but a few people, including me thought a few of the
options were wrong.
The programming section included two problems of different difficulty levels:

• The first was a LeetCode medium-easy (Codeforces 1100) level question involving sorting,

greedy algorithms, and two-pointer techniques.

• The second was a LeetCode medium-hard (Codeforces 1400) level problem focused on

number theory, prefix and suffix GCDs, and implementation.
Overall, the test was considered challenging, and only a few candidates managed to solve both
programming questions successfully.
Brushing up on PNC, probability and ratios will help you a lot, along with DSA, like doing the
NeetCode 250 or Leetcode 150
--- PAGE 2 ---
2.
Interview Round 1 [ 40+ candidates appeared for this round]
This round was conducted within 2 hours after the OA (approx 20 minutes after the OA results came
out). Since this was my second time giving interviews on campus, I didn't feel very nervous here.
The interviewers were very welcoming and helpful, they even gave gentle nudges when I got stuck,
which kept me calm throughout.
They began by asking why I chose this role over a purely technical one; I explained that my skills
and interests aligned more with this domain. They then asked about my finance knowledge, I
admitted it was limited (mostly from movies), but when they asked about terms like "investment"
and "IPO" I explained my understanding of IPOs.
The technical portion focused heavily on Python and core computer-science concepts. I was asked
Python syntax and semantics questions (what certain constructs can and can't do), time complexity
for operations, and methods for built-in data structures. They quizzed me on differences between list,
dictionary, set, and tuple (e.g., whether lists can hold mixed types), how to access keys and values in
a dict, and common list/dict operations like appending and joining,searching using operators and
methods. There were also NumPy/Pandas questions (what they're used for, the two primary pandas
structures, how to add a column, and how to access/perform on a cell) and SQL questions (types of
joins, the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and query examples involving WHERE,
HAVING, and aggregations).
Finally, they gave two puzzles. The first was the classic bird-and-two-trains problem: two trains
approaching at 50 km/h, 100 km apart, with a bird flying back and forth at 100 km/h until the trains
meet and the second was the probability of at least one head when tossing three coins. I attempted
the bird problem by summing incremental distances, but wasn't able to solve it (the intended solution
uses total time and s=vts-vts=vt), and I explained my thought process for both problems. The
interviewer emphasized explaining my reasoning as I worked, which I think mattered as much as
arriving at the correct answer. The interview lasted about 20-25 minutes.

3. Interview Round 2 [15+ candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted at varying times. For me, it took place around 3-4 hours after my first
interview, while some other candidates had it much sooner. Like others, mine was a one-on-one
discussion with the Director, and it felt more like a conversation than a formal interview. I was
interviewing for the Investment Research Intern role.
The Director began by asking a simple pandas coding question, to find the difference in closing
prices of stocks from the previous day. I couldn't recall the exact syntax, so I wrote a basic version
and explained my thought process, including how I'd handle edge cases like the first element.
He then asked me why I chose this role, to which I replied that I'm interested in building new
things, as reflected in my resume and that I enjoy experimenting with new ideas and
technologies like MCP, LLMS, and integrations into projects (I phrased this as such because
their CEO mentioned about LLM during the orientation round).
--- PAGE 3 ---
Next, he asked if I had any relevant projects in this field, and I described my project on portfolio
management using LLMS, ML, and NLP. He followed up by asking about my finance knowledge
, I admitted I didn't have much, and he didn't probe further.
At one point, he mentioned that my portfolio seemed to focus mainly on machine learning, and
asked what I would do if the role didn't involve ML. I explained that I've also worked in backend,
frontend, and data science, so I could contribute in those areas too. He didn't seem entirely
convinced but moved on politely.
Toward the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about the specific nature of the
work involved in this role. He explained that it focuses on developing and testing new investment
strategies using algorithms on historical data, but not necessarily using machine learning. I
connected this to data science and said that it still felt similar in spirit; exploring hypotheses, trying
multiple models or algorithms, and analyzing which performs best and why.
Finally, I asked a few broader questions about how the company collaborates with external
managers for areas without dedicated divisions, how profits and risks are managed, and what
happens if a manager underperforms. He responded very clearly, avoiding heavy financial jargon,
and came across as humble, approachable, and genuinely engaging.
In the end, I was offered the Investment Research Intern role at Russell Investments. Among the 7
shortlisted candidates, the remaining 6 were offered the Tech Intern role. (Note: candidates had to
choose their preferred role before the OA, and I had opted for Research, while the others had chosen
Tech.)

journey.prep:
The biggest thing that helped me get selected was understanding concepts rather than simply
memorising definitions. I made sure I knew my resume thoroughly and could explain every project and
skill mentioned on it. For the technical rounds, having strong fundamentals in risk management, corporate
finance, accounting, derivatives, fixed income, and macroeconomics was extremely useful. I also tried to
connect concepts to real-world banking examples and explain the logic behind my answers instead of giving
textbook definitions. For the GD, presence of mind and current affairs were extremely important. I
would recommend having a strong understanding of basic macroeconomics and keeping up with financial
news. You do not need to speak 10 times-3-4 meaningful entries are enough if each contribution adds
something new to the discussion. Listen carefully to what the panel is actually asking and focus on building
the discussion rather than simply naming schemes or facts. In my case, I focused on concepts such as the
trade deficit, dollar demand, FIl outflows, safe-haven assets, interest rates and geopolitical events. I
was also fortunate to have watched a video on the Indian Rupee just two days before the GD, which helped
me significantly. During the interviews, I tried to stay confident, maintain a positive attitude, ask clarifying
questions when necessary, and reason through questions instead of panicking if I did not immediately know
the answer. One mistake I made was not preparing questions to ask the interviewers beforehand; I would
strongly recommend preparing 2-3 thoughtful questions because it takes very little time and can leave a
strong final impression. Overall, know your resume, understand the fundamentals, stay updated with
markets, communicate clearly, and focus on quality rather than quantity of answers.
The following are the resources I used during my preparation. I will also attach my detailed list of the risk
topics I studied for this role separately.

• Derivatives

Financial Statements & Accounting: CFL - Accounting Fundamentals
Banking Risks: Banking Risk playlist
Banking Risk Topics
Lehman Brothers Case
Silicon Valley Bank Case

• Market Awareness / Current Affairs: Regular financial and market news

• Quantitative Aptitude: IndiaBix + 1-2 CAT previous-year papers

• Resume / ATS: Resume Worded

• Concept clarification: ChatGPT / Claude

• Indian Rupee / GD

• Resume (my resume is very basic, refer other resumes too)

Feel free to contact me anytime if you have any doubts regarding the preparation or interview
process.
