PPT - 31/7/2026

Round 1: Resume Shortlisting - 4/8/2026

Round 2: Online Assessment (Online) - 5/8/2026

Round 3: Group Discussion- 11/8/2026

Round 4: Technical Interview 1 - 11/8/2026

Round 5 : Technical Interview 2 - 11/8/2026

Round 6: HR Interview - 11/8/2026

1. Resume Shortlisting [250+ students applied]

More than 250 students applied, out of which 118 students were shortlisted for the next round. The basic
eligibility criterion was a CGPA of 7.0+. I would recommend maintaining a CGPA of 8.0+, as this makes
you eligible for almost every company during placements, while 8.5+ is a very strong position. For the
resume, I would recommend maintaining an ATS score of 70+ as a safe target and ensuring that the resume
is relevant to the job description. I used Resume Worded to check and improve my ATS score rather than
relying on random ATS-checking websites, and I would recommend using it as well. My resume was
average overall, but I had specifically tried to make it ATS-friendly and included relevant projects and skills
aligned with the role, which I believe helped me get shortlisted. There was no interview or test in this round;
the main focus was on meeting the eligibility criteria and getting through the resume screening. My main
advice is to maintain a good CGPA, keep the resume to one page, use relevant keywords from the job
description, and highlight projects that demonstrate skills related to the role.

2. Online Assessment (Online) |118 students shortlisted]

The Online Assessment was attempted by 118 shortlisted students and consisted of 45 questions in 45
minutes for a total of 45 marks, with four sections: Corporate Finance & Financial Accounting (10
questions), Market Awareness (10 questions), Quantitative Aptitude (15 questions), and English Usage
(10 questions). There was no negative marking, with 1 mark awarded for every correct answer. The
Corporate Finance and Accounting section was easy to moderate and required a good understanding of
--- PAGE 2 ---
fundamentals such as financial statements, cash flows, and basic corporate finance concepts. Market
Awareness was the most difficult section, ranging from medium to difficult, and required both general
market awareness and some niche financial knowledge; I would strongly recommend staying updated with
the latest finance and market news through regular current-affairs reading. Quantitative Aptitude was easy
to moderate, and preparation from IndiaBix is more than sufficient for the level of most questions; I also
solved 1-2 CAT previous-year papers, and a few questions in the test were directly similar to questions
from those sources. The English Usage section was very easy and did not require separate preparation.
Overall, the test was quite time-consuming, and I had only around 3-4 minutes remaining when I
submitted it, so time management is extremely important. For preparation, I would recommend
strengthening basic Corporate Finance and Accounting concepts, regularly following financial and market
news, practising Quant from IndiaBix along with a few CAT-level questions, and focusing on speed rather
than spending too much time on any individual question.

3. Group Discussion [ 29 students were shortlisted after OA ]

After the Online Assessment, 29 students were shortlisted for the Group Discussion, and the shortlist
was released just one day before the GD. Unlike investment banking roles where the topic may
sometimes be provided beforehand, the topic for this GD was given on the spot, so I had prepared
mainly with the interview rounds in mind. There were 8 candidates in my panel and 2 panelists
conducting the discussion. At the beginning, the panelists asked whether we were more comfortable
discussing the Indian economy or the US economy. I took the initiative and said that I was comfortable
with the Indian economy and asked the other candidates about their preference. Since no one objected,
we decided to go with the Indian economy, which worked in my favour because I had a strong
understanding of macroeconomics. The topic given was "How is the Indian Rupee performing currently,
what affects it, and discuss its impact." The panel was primarily testing whether candidates understood
the fundamental factors affecting the rupee, such as trade deficit, foreign investment, interest rates, dollar
demand, and global events, rather than simply naming government schemes. I made around 3-4 entries,
but focused on making each one meaningful and building on the discussion. My first entry focused on
the trade deficit and India's dependence on the US dollar. In my second entry, I discussed how during
periods of geopolitical uncertainty, investors tend to move towards safe-haven assets such as US
Treasury bonds, which can lead to foreign investors withdrawing investments from emerging markets
such as India, increasing demand for dollars. I then connected this to the rupee, explaining that when
dollar demand increases while dollar supply is relatively insufficient, the dollar strengthens against the
rupee; combined with India's trade deficit, this puts additional pressure on the rupee. A major lesson for
me was that understanding the underlying economic concepts is more important than simply memorising
schemes or current-affairs facts. Several candidates discussed government schemes, but that was not
really what the panel was testing. I also made one small mistake during my first entry by looking directly
at the panelist instead of addressing the group, but I noticed her reaction and immediately corrected
myself; interestingly, she later mentioned that she had noticed this and appreciated my presence of mind.
I was also told during my second technical interview that my GD contributions had helped build the
framework for the discussion. My biggest recommendation for a GD is do not speak just for the sake of
speaking around 3-4 strong entries are enough if each one adds a new perspective or builds on an
existing point. Be clear about what the panel is actually asking, understand basic macroeconomics, stay
updated with current events, listen to the other candidates, and most importantly, maintain your presence
of mind throughout the discussion.
--- PAGE 3 ---

4. Technical Interview 1 [14 students were shortlisted]

After the Group Discussion, 14 students were shortlisted for Technical Interview 1. There were two
interviewers, one from Liquidity Risk and the other from Credit Risk. I entered the room confidently,
greeted both interviewers with a smile, and tried to maintain a positive and conversational atmosphere from
the beginning. One of the interviewers asked me about my favourite risk domain. Since my resume included
a Credit Risk project, I answered that I found both Credit Risk and Liquidity Risk interesting, which
allowed me to connect with the areas of expertise of both interviewers. The Liquidity Risk interviewer then
asked what I found interesting about liquidity risk, so I explained the concept with a banking example and
connected it to the Lehman Brothers collapse. I also tried to use realistic figures and examples involving
large banks wherever possible rather than keeping my answers purely theoretical. She then realised that we
had not started with my resume and asked me to walk through it. I had a DCF valuation model of Apple on
my resume, and the Credit Risk interviewer asked me to explain it in detail. I explained the complete
valuation process, including Cost of Equity, Cost of Debt, WACC, and the significance of each
component. They were satisfied with my explanation and then asked whether I knew other valuation
techniques. I mentioned that I had heard about LBO valuation, after which they asked me about peer
comparison/comparable companies analysis. I clarified whether they meant peer comparison and then
explained it using examples, including Apple and companies from different industries. I explained that
companies should be compared with businesses having similar operating models and customer segments
rather than simply comparing companies because they sell similar products; for example, Apple would be
better compared with companies such as Samsung than with a company whose business model and
consumer segment are fundamentally different. They liked the answer and then asked me to explain the
basic balance sheet of a bank, including where loans and customer deposits appear. I was then asked a
macroeconomics question: what does the RBI do with interest rates during inflation, and why? I
explained that inflation essentially means rising prices or "mehngai", and walked through the mechanism in
simple terms: when inflation is high, the RBI can increase the repo rate, which makes borrowing more
expensive, reduces loan demand and overall spending, and eventually helps bring demand closer to the
available supply, thereby controlling inflation. I made sure to explain the entire chain rather than simply
saying "RBI increases rates during inflation." The interview then moved towards technology, where I was
asked whether I knew about LLMs. I mentioned that I had two LLM-related projects in my technical
portfolio and briefly explained my financial-literacy project using Agentic Al, although it was not
included on my resume. Another question was "When does the seller of a call option make money?" My
approach was to reason it out rather than immediately quote a formula. I explained that I had mostly
approached options from the buyer's perspective: a call-option buyer benefits when the underlying price
rises; therefore, the seller benefits when the buyer's position loses value, meaning the option expires out of
the money or its value falls sufficiently relative to the premium received. The interviewer was impressed by
the reasoning-based approach. At the end, I was asked whether I had any questions. One mistake I made
was not preparing questions beforehand. I eventually came up with a question on the spot about how a
global bank such as J.P. Morgan manages regulatory compliance across different countries, particularly
when regulations from authorities such as the RBI and the US Federal Reserve differ. However, I would
strongly recommend preparing at least 2-3 thoughtful questions beforehand, as it takes only a few
minutes and can leave a strong final impression. Overall, the biggest lesson from this interview was to
understand the fundamentals deeply rather than memorising definitions. If you can explain concepts
logically, connect them to real-world examples, and remain confident when you do not immediately know
an answer, the interview becomes much more conversational
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Technical Interview 2 [6 students shortlisted]

After Technical Interview 1, 6 students were shortlisted for Technical Interview 2. There were two
interviewers, and interestingly, they were the same panelists who had conducted my Group Discussion.
This helped because they already had some context about my performance in the GD, and the interview
gradually became quite conversational as I became more comfortable with them. The interview started with
the usual "Tell me about yourself', after which they cross-questioned me on my resume, particularly my
Credit Risk project, and asked me to explain what credit risk means. They then noticed that I had
mentioned Financial Derivatives in my skills and began questioning me on derivatives. I started with the
basic definition that derivatives are financial instruments whose value is derived from an underlying asset,
and then explained the four major types: forwards, futures, options, and swaps. I explained that forwards
are generally OTC contracts, then moved to futures and discussed their exchange-traded nature and
concepts such as margin calls. I then explained options, highlighting the key difference that the buyer has
the right but not the obligation to exercise the contract, and finally explained swaps using an interest-rate
swap as an example. They were satisfied with the explanation and then asked whether I knew about option
Greeks. I explained the major Greeks and, in particular, connected Delta and Gamma to the concepts of
speed and distance/time from physics. This was one of the answers that seemed to impress them the most
because I was not simply giving textbook definitions but connecting financial concepts with concepts I
already understood from another domain. They then asked me about the banking balance sheet, specifically
where loans appear. I first asked a clarifying question about whether they meant loans taken by the bank or
loans given by the bank, and after they clarified that they meant loans given by the bank, I explained their
treatment on the balance sheet. The interview then moved to the fixed-income market, where they asked
how bonds and interest rates are related. I explained the inverse relationship between bond prices and
interest rates with examples and discussed why changes in interest rates affect existing fixed-income
securities. Towards the end, the interview became much more casual, and the interviewers asked me to
loosen up and tell them how I would introduce myself if they met me in a social setting. I spoke about my
interests outside academics, including football, and this helped make the conversation more natural. Finally,
they asked me why I had chosen this role, which brought the interview to an end. My biggest takeaway
from this round was that interviewers can move from very technical questions to casual questions very
quickly, so candidates should be comfortable with both. More importantly, do not just memorise
definitions-try to connect concepts to real-world examples or ideas from other subjects, because
demonstrating how you think can make a much stronger impression than simply reproducing textbook
answers.
HR interview [3 students appeared]
After Technical Interview 2, 3 students appeared for the HR Interview. It was a short and relaxed round.
The interviewer went through my resume and asked why I wanted the role, to which I explained my interest
in both finance and technology and how this role lies at the intersection of both. She also asked where I
stay and one behavioural question: "Tell me about a decision you made that people did not like." I gave a
brief example from my experience as Head of Operations at E-Cell, where I sometimes had to ask
teammates to stay until work was completed, highlighting my sense of ownership and responsibility. The
interview then ended, and the results were announced around 45 minutes later, with 2 out of the 3 students
selected.
--- PAGE 5 ---
